en: I meditate in my mind upon that Lord Śaṅkara, the Lord of Ambikā, who is auspicious from beginning to end, whose nature is unborn and equal, the noble one, ageless and immortal, the divine Self, the five-faced one, whose character is the powerful play of the five, and the Lord of the Mother. Vyāsa said: In the field of Dharma, the great field, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī, at Prayāga, the supreme and meritorious place on the path to the world of Brahmā.
The sages, who had purified their souls and were devoted to the vow of truth, possessed of great luster and great fortune, performed a great sacrificial session.
Having heard of that sacrificial session there, the great sage Vyāsa’s disciple, Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas and lord of munis, arrived to behold it.
Seeing the charioteer approaching, the sages were then filled with joy; with very serene minds, they performed worship according to the prescribed rites.
Then those great-souled ones, devoted to the Vinaya, being well-pleased, spoke with palms joined in reverence after offering praise according to the prescribed rite.
O Romaharṣaṇa, O omniscient one, it was indeed through the weight of your good fortune that you acquired the entire science of the Purāṇas from Vyāsa at every point.
Therefore, you are indeed the vessel for these wondrous stories, just as the ocean is the repository for gems of great value.
Whatever has been, whatever is yet to be, and whatever other entity exists—there is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
You have come here for the sake of seeing him by the power of my desire; you ought not to depart in vain without performing some benefit for us.
We have heard all the truth regarding what is auspicious and inauspicious from you even before; yet we do not attain satiety, for our desire to hear it arises again and again.
Now, O Sūta of noble mind, there is but one thing remaining to be heard; please tell me that secret as well, if you would grant me your favor.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, men will be devoid of merit; they will all be devoted to wicked conduct and turn their backs on truthful discourse.
Devoted to slandering others, longing for the wealth of others, their minds attached to the wives of others, and intent on harming others.

Deluded by the view that the body is the self, these nihilists possess the intellect of cattle; harboring hatred toward their mother and father, they treat women as deities and are slaves to their desires.
Brahmins seized by the planet of greed, living by the sale of the Vedas, have practiced their learning solely for the sake of acquiring wealth and are deluded by intoxication.
Having abandoned the duties of their own caste, they are for the most part deceivers of others; devoid of the three daily twilight prayers, they are bereft of the awakening to Brahman.
Lacking compassion, considering themselves wise, they violate their own conduct and vows; devoted to the exertion of agriculture, they are cruel by nature and impure in intent.
And likewise all the Kṣatriyas were characterized by the abandonment of their own duty; they associated with the wicked, delighted in sin, and were devoted to sexual misconduct.
They are not heroes, delighting in strife, intent on flight; they are Śūdras who follow the conduct of thieves, their minds enslaved by desire.
Deprived of the knowledge of weapons and missiles, abandoned by cows, Brahmins, and protectors, and lacking both refuge and forest, they were always like deer seeking the protection of a woman.

Deprived of the duty of protecting their subjects and the true Dharma, they were intent only on worldly enjoyment; being wicked, they joyfully brought about the destruction of their subjects and committed violence against living beings.

Those Vaiśyas were devoid of purificatory rites, habitually abandoning their own duties; they followed evil paths, were intent on amassing wealth for themselves, and practiced dishonest dealings with the scales.
Those who lack devotion toward their gurus, gods, and the twice-born are of evil intellect; they generally fail to feed the twice-born, being miserly and tight-fisted.

Those whose intentions are defiled by sexual passion for the lovers of their beloveds, whose minds are robbed of discernment by greed and delusion, and who have abandoned the great virtues such as public works (pūrta) and so forth;
In the same way, those Śūdras who are devoted to the conduct of Brāhmaṇas—fools of radiant appearance who are habituated to abandoning their own dharma.
They are further performers of austerities, stealers of the splendor of the twice-born, bringers of early death to children, and devoted to the recitation of mantras.
Those who worship the Śāligrāma stone and other such objects, yet are intent on performing fire-sacrifices (homa), harbor hostile thoughts, are crooked, and revile the twice-born;
The wealthy are performers of evil deeds; the learned are quarrelsome; those who preach the law while teaching its worship are the destroyers of the law.
Hypocrites who assume the appearance of virtuous men, yet are great in pride despite being generous givers; they regard themselves as lords and consider the Brahmins and others to be their servants.
Devoid of their own dharma, deluded, causing the intermixture of castes, cruel-minded, and always possessed of great arrogance, they are destroyers of the fourfold social order.
Considering those of their own high lineage as their kin, these fools—though performing virtuous deeds—cause the four castes to deviate from their paths and bring about the ruin of all social orders.
And women for the most part are fallen, showing contempt for their husbands, harboring malice toward their fathers-in-law, fearless, and eaters of impure food.
They are devoted to false meditation, of immoral conduct, and overwhelmed by passion; they are constantly engaged in union with paramours and are likewise averse to their own husbands.
Their sons were devoid of devotion toward their mother and father, possessed of evil intentions, constantly reciting what is not true knowledge, and their bodies were perpetually consumed by disease.
O Sūta, for these whose intellects are lost and who are habituated to abandoning their own dharma, what will be their destiny in this world and in the next?
Thus our minds are constantly filled with anxiety; for indeed, there is truly no higher dharma than that which consists in benefiting others.

Out of compassion, please tell me now that easy means by which there may be the immediate destruction of their great afflictions, and through which one indeed attains mastery over all philosophical systems.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, Sūta, having mentally remembered Śaṅkara, spoke to those sages.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sage’s Inquiry," in the Vidyeshvara-samhita of the glorious Shiva Mahapurana.
Sūta said: You have asked well, O virtuous ones; it is beneficial for the three worlds. Having remembered my guru, I shall speak out of affection for you; listen to that with reverence.
This supreme Śaiva Purāṇa is the very essence of the Vedānta; it effects the removal of the entire flood of sins and bestows the supreme goal in the hereafter.
O Brahmins, in this [Purāṇa] the supreme fame of Śiva—which destroys the impurities of the Kali age and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life—shines forth eternally.
O best of the twice-born, by the mere study of that supreme Śaiva Purāṇa, they shall attain a very auspicious state.
Sin, headed by the slaughter of a Brahmin, continues to flourish as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not indeed risen in this world—oh, how strange!
The great calamities of the Kali age will roam about fearlessly for as long as this Śiva Purāṇa does not indeed arise in the world; oh, how strange!
Indeed, all the scriptures dispute with one another only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen in this world, alas!
The true nature of Śiva is difficult to comprehend even for the great, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa indeed does not descend into this world—oh, how amazing!
The cruel soldiers of Yama shall roam about fearlessly for as long as this Śiva Purāṇa has not yet risen in the world, alas!
All the Purāṇas indeed roar upon the surface of the earth only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen in this world, alas!
All the sacred fords on the surface of the earth continue to dispute with one another, alas, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not yet risen in this world.
All the other mantras on the surface of the earth remain in dispute only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not indeed risen upon the earth.
All sacred fields on the surface of the earth remain in dispute only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not yet dawned upon the world.
All the sacred seats (pīṭhas) on the surface of the earth will remain in dispute only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not indeed rise upon the earth.
All other gifts on the surface of the earth remain in dispute only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not yet risen upon the earth.
All those gods continued to dispute upon the surface of the earth for as long as the Śiva Purāṇa had not yet dawned upon the earth.
All philosophical systems indeed contend with one another upon the earth only so long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen upon the earth.
O twice-born ones, O best of sages, I am unable to describe the fruit of reciting or hearing this Śiva Purāṇa in its entirety.
Nevertheless, O sinless ones, I shall describe its majesty to you in brief; listen with focused minds as it was told to me by Vyāsa in the past.
Indeed, whoever recites even a single verse or half-verse of this Śiva Purāṇa with devotion is liberated from sin in an instant.
Indeed, he who reads this Śiva Purāṇa every day with devotion according to his ability and without lethargy is called liberated while living.
Whoever always honors this Śiva Purāṇa with devotion, undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice day after day.
Whoever hears this Śiva Purāṇa from another source even with the desire for common worldly status, he too shall be liberated from sin through me.
Whoever pays homage to this Śiva Purāṇa from even a short distance shall obtain the fruit of worshipping all the gods; of this there is no doubt.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who, having personally transcribed this Śiva Purāṇa into a book, bestows it upon the devotees of Śiva.
Whatever fruit is difficult to obtain in this world from the study of the Śāstras and the articulated Vedas, that fruit shall accrue to him.
Indeed, he who, having fasted on the fourteenth day, expounds this Śiva Purāṇa in an assembly of devotees of Śiva, is most excellent.
For every single syllable, one shall obtain the fruit of the *gāyatrī-puraścaryā*; having enjoyed all desires here in this world, one shall attain liberation (*nirvāṇa*) at the end.
I shall declare the merit of him who, having fasted on the fourteenth day, remains awake throughout the night, whether he recites or even merely listens [to this].
At Kurukṣetra and all other sacred pilgrimage sites, on numerous occasions, he gave away wealth equal to his own during a solar eclipse that was visible in every direction.
Whatever great fruit one enjoys after giving [this] to Brahmins headed by Vyāsa, that same fruit shall accrue to him; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt.
Indeed, even the gods, with Indra at their head, shall await the command of anyone who chants this Śiva Purāṇa day and night.
Whoever constantly reads or listens to this Śiva Purāṇa, whatever virtuous deed they perform shall become multiplied ten millionfold.
He who, being composed in meditation, recites the Śrī Rudra-saṃhitā therein—even if he be a slayer of a Brahmin—becomes a purified soul in just three days.
O Rudra, he who, observing silence, recites that Saṃhitā three times every day in the presence of an image of Bhairava shall obtain all his desires.
O Rudra, for one who recites that Saṃhitā while performing circumambulation of a banyan tree and a bilva tree, the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted.
Beyond that, the Kailāsasaṃhitā is remembered as even more supreme; it is the manifest embodiment of Brahman, directly illuminating the meaning of the Praṇava.
O twice-born ones, Śaṅkara knows the entire majesty of the Kailāsasaṃhitā; Vyāsa knows half of that, and I know half of that.
In this regard, I shall speak of a portion; it is not possible to explain it in its entirety. By knowing even that much, people may attain purity of mind at that very moment.
O twice-born ones, that Raudrī Saṃhitā does not destroy whatever sin exists; though I search for it constantly, I do not see such a thing anywhere in the world.
By joyfully drinking that nectar produced from the churning of the ocean of Upanishads by Śiva and offered to Kumāra, one indeed becomes immortal.
One who is intent on performing expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin is liberated from them after reciting that Saṃhitā for just one month.
That *Saṃhitā* shall destroy, by its mere recitation, the sin arising from improper acceptance of gifts, unfit food, and wicked speech.
Whoever recites that Saṃhitā in a temple of Śiva or in a grove of Bilva trees obtains that fruit which is beyond the reach of words.
If one recites that Saṃhitā with devotion while feeding the twice-born at a Śrāddha ceremony, all his ancestors go to the supreme abode of Śambhu.
He who, fasting on the fourteenth day, recites that Saṃhitā at the root of a Bilva tree, is Śiva himself in person and is worshipped by the gods.
Any other Saṃhitā there as well bestows the fruit of all desires; both are to be known as distinguished, filled with divine play and supreme knowledge.
This Śaiva Purāṇa, equal to the Vedas, has been proclaimed; it was composed by Śiva himself as the first [Purāṇa], in accordance with the Brahman.
Likewise, the Vidyeśa, the Raudra, the Vaināyaka, the Aumika, the Mātra, the eleven Rudras, the Kailāsa, and the Śatarudraka.
The Koṭirudra-sahasra, the Koṭirudra likewise, the Vāyavīya, and the one known as Dharma—thus are they distinguished according to their divisions.
The collection consists of twelve [parts] and is considered most meritorious; O Brahmins, listen with reverence as I declare their total number in its entirety.
The Vidyeśa Purāṇa consists of ten thousand verses; likewise, the Rudra, the Vaināyaka, the Auma, and the one called Mātṛpurāṇa each consist of eight thousand verses.
O twice-born ones, there are thirteen thousand Rudras, eleven thousand, six thousand on Kailāsa, and half of that for the Śatarudra.
The *Koṭirudra* is three times [the former], amounting to eleven thousand; that which is known as the *Sahasrakoṭirudra* is said to consist of ten million verses by way of its textual count.

The Vāyavīya [Tantra] consists of four hundred [verses], the Gharma [Tantra] one thousand, and the Ravi [Tantra] one thousand; thus, by the distinction of Śaiva numerical systems, they total one hundred thousand.
That was then condensed by Vyāsa into twenty-four thousand verses; therein, the fourth Purāṇa is indeed the Śaiva, consisting of seven Saṃhitās.
O Śiva, that ancient Purāṇa which was previously intended by you, measuring one hundred crore verses, was indeed forgotten at the time of the primordial creation.

In the past, during the Dvāpara and subsequent ages, the Purāṇa was divided eighteenfold; then, at the beginning of the Kṛta age, it was condensed to four hundred thousand verses by Dvaipāyana and others.
The Śiva Purāṇa has indeed been declared to consist of twenty-four thousand verses in number; it comprises seven Saṃhitās and is equal to the Veda.
There, the first is to be known as Vidyeshvara; the second is Raudri; the third is called Shatarudra; and the fourth is Kotirudra.
The fifth is indeed named Mauma, the sixth is known as Kailāsa, and the seventh is called Vāyavīya; thus, these seven are considered the Saṃhitās.
The divine Purāṇa named Śiva, consisting of seven books, exists as equal to Brahman; it stands supreme over all, bestowing the ultimate goal.
He who reads this Śiva Purāṇa, consisting of seven Saṃhitās, in its entirety with devotion, is said to be liberated while living.
Hundreds of Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Āgamas do not equal even a small fraction of this Śiva Purāṇa.

The stainless Śaiva Purāṇa, proclaimed by Śiva, was not compiled in its entirety by Vyāsa, who was inclined toward the Śaiva tradition; yet it is briefly presented here for the benefit of all living beings, as it is incomparable in destroying the threefold suffering and bestowing auspiciousness upon the virtuous.

In this world, the Dharma free from deceit has been proclaimed as preeminent, consisting of the realization of Vedānta; its subject matter is to be known by wise men within themselves who are free from envy, and it is here alone that the three aims of life are perfectly established.

Indeed, this *Śaiva Purāṇa-tilaka* is truly a noble Purāṇa, resplendent with Vedānta and the Vedas, and sung of the Supreme Reality; whoever reads or hears it with supreme devotion shall surely attain the highest state, for he is beloved by Śambhu.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of Sūta, the supreme sages said to him, "Recite this wonderful Purāṇa, which contains the entire essence of the Vedānta."
Having heard these words of the sages, Sūta was greatly delighted; remembering Śaṅkara, he spoke to the best of sages.
Sūta said: "O all you sages, listen, having remembered the flawless Śiva, to this Śaiva Purāṇa which is devoted to the Purāṇas and born from the essence of the Vedas."
Wherein the triad of devotion, knowledge, and dispassion is sung with love.
The existent reality, which is to be known through the Vedanta, has been described in particular detail.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to this Purāṇa born from the essence of the Vedas. Long ago, after a vast period of time had passed and kalpas had repeatedly elapsed...
When this aeon had arrived and the work of creation had begun, the sages belonging to the six lineages were conversing with one another.
A very great dispute arose as to "this is supreme" and "this is not"; they went to the imperishable Brahmā, the Creator, to question him.
With words imbued with humility, they all spoke with palms joined in reverence: "For you are the sustainer of the entire world, the cause of all causes."
"Who is that person who is more ancient than all principles and higher than the highest? Brahmā said: "From whom words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach him..."
Because all this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest—is first brought forth together with all the elements and the senses.
This is the God, the Great God, the omniscient Lord of the universe; he is perceived through supreme devotion, and never otherwise.
Rudra, Hari, Hara, and likewise other lords of the gods, constantly desire to behold him with supreme devotion.

What need is there for much speaking here? One is liberated through devotion to Śiva. Divine grace arises from devotion to the deity, and grace gives rise to devotion; just as here the seed comes from the sprout, or as the sprout comes from the seed.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, go to the earth for the sake of propitiating the Lord and perform a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) lasting for a thousand years.
Only by the grace of that very Lord Śiva, the Master of Sacrifice, is the essence of the knowledge declared in the Vedas—the means and the goal—truly understood.
The sages said: Now, what is the supreme goal to be attained, and what is its supreme means? What is the nature of the practitioner therein? Tell us this according to the truth.

Brahmā said: The goal to be accomplished is the attainment of the state of Śiva; the means for that is service [to Him]; and the practitioner is one who, by His grace, is free from desire for transient fruits and the like.
Having performed the action prescribed in the Vedas, which yields great fruit when offered [to the Lord], one attains the state of the Supreme Lord through the sequence beginning with *sālokya*.
The supreme fruit for all, according to their respective degrees of devotion, and its manifold means, have been directly taught by the Lord himself.
Summarizing for you the essence therein, I shall proclaim the means of accomplishment: hearing it with the ear and likewise reciting it with speech.
Mental reflection upon Him is called the great means of accomplishment; Maheśvara is to be heard, celebrated, and reflected upon.
Thus, according to the authority of the Vedas, that supreme goal is to be attained by this means; proceed, therefore, you who are solely devoted to the accomplishment of all aims.
Having perceived directly with the eye, people act therein; for when something is not perceptible, one acts everywhere after knowing it through the ear.
Therefore, first of all, the wise and discerning person should listen from the mouth of the guru; thereafter, they should accomplish the other two: chanting and reflection.
When this practice has been well-perfected through the sequence ending in reflection, Śiva-yoga arises; by means of that, one gradually attains the stages beginning with *sālokya*.
Afterwards, all diseases of the limbs and all worldly pleasures dissolve; through practice, this indeed becomes a hardship, but it is auspicious from beginning to end.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: O Brahman, what is the nature of reflection (manana), and what is the nature of hearing (śravaṇa)? Or how is its glorification (kīrtana) performed? Please explain this correctly as it is.

Brahmā said: That continuous reflection which consists of the purification of worship, recitation, qualities, form, playfulness, and names by means of a mind that delights in right reasoning—that reflection, attainable through the vision of the Lord, is the most preeminent among all excellent spiritual practices.

Whether through song, sacred scripture, spoken words, or even by means of the names, qualities, forms, pastimes, and glories of Śambhu, that which is a clear and flavorful hymn of praise to Him constitutes the middling means of accomplishment here.

O wise ones, when by whatever means and wherever a mass of sounds centered on Śiva is directed with great firmness toward the faculty of hearing—as one might focus intently upon the amorous play of a woman—that indeed is what is world-renowned here as "śravaṇa" (listening).

Through association with the virtuous, there first arises hearing [of the Lord]; then the chanting of the names of the Lord becomes firm; thereafter, that meditation becomes the most excellent; for indeed, everything comes to pass when the glance of Śaṅkara falls upon one.
Sūta said: O lords of sages, I shall relate to you an ancient account concerning the greatness of this means of accomplishment; listen with focused attention.
In ancient times, my preceptor Vyāsa, the son of the sage Parāśara, performed austerities with great devotion on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī.
While traveling there by chance in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, the venerable Sanatkumāra beheld my preceptor.
Having ascended into meditation and become awakened, that sage saw the son of Aja; bowing down in great agitation, he spoke with supreme curiosity.
Having offered him the arghya water, he presented a seat worthy of a deity; then the Lord, being pleased, spoke with a deep voice to him who stood bowed before him.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, you should contemplate the Reality which is the object of direct perception; that is Śiva, who is without companion here—for what purpose do you perform penance?
Thus addressed by the prince, the sage spoke his own intention: "Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are held in high regard within the path of the Vedas."
Thus, out of compassion for you, I have established [this teaching] in many ways in the world; such as I am, who have become a guru to all in every respect.
The most wonderful knowledge that is the means to liberation does not arise; I perform austerities for the sake of liberation, yet I do not know the cause thereof.
O best of Brahmins, having been thus requested by the sage Vyāsa, the Lord Kumāra, being fully capable, spoke the definitive conclusion regarding the cause of liberation.
Listening to Śambhu, chanting his names, and meditating upon him are the three most excellent means; these have been declared as the practice sanctioned by the Vedas.
Formerly, indeed, being agitated and distracted by other means of accomplishment, I performed penance on Mount Mandara, which is immovable.
Then, by the command of Śiva, the blessed Nandikeśvara arrived; he is my compassionate lord, the witness of all, and the sovereign of the Gaṇas.
He spoke to me with affection regarding the supreme means for liberation: the hearing and chanting of Śambhu’s names, and the contemplation thereof, which is sanctioned by the Vedas.
"O Brahman, Śiva has repeatedly told me that for liberation there is a triad of means; therefore, practice this triad beginning with hearing [the scriptures]."
Having spoken thus to Vyāsa, the son of Vidhi departed with his followers in his celestial chariot to that most magnificent realm.
Thus has the supreme ancient account been told in brief. The sages said: "O Sūta, you have described the triad beginning with Śravaṇa as the means to liberation."
If one is incapable of the triad beginning with hearing [the scriptures], what must a person do to be liberated? By what cause or action can liberation be attained without effort?
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the first Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sūta said: One who is unable to perform the triad beginning with hearing [the scriptures] should install a Śiva-liṅga or an image of Śaṅkara, and by worshipping it daily, he shall cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
One should indeed transport the materials according to one's capacity without deception; one should offer them for the sake of the *liṅga* and the image (*bera*), and should worship continuously.
With devotion, [one should offer] a pavilion, a gateway, a sacred ford, a monastery, and likewise a holy field, as well as a festival, clothing, fragrance, garlands, incense, and lamps.
Various kinds of food as an offering, together with cakes and side dishes, as well as an umbrella, a banner, a fan, and a chowrie, along with all their constituent parts.
One should maintain everything toward the *liṅga* and the image (*bera*) as if it were toward a king—circumambulation, prostration, and likewise recitation according to one's capacity.

One should daily perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the dismissal (visarga) with true devotion. Having thus worshipped the Lord Śaṅkara in either a linga or a ber image, [one should proceed].
One attains perfection through the grace of Śiva even by abandoning such practices as hearing the scriptures; by the mere worship of the Liṅga and the Bera, the great men of old were liberated.
The men said: "In every case, the hosts of deities are worshipped in their images alone; how then is Śiva worshipped everywhere both in his phallic emblem (liṅga) and in his image (bera)?"
Sūta said: O lords of sages, this question is meritorious and most wonderful; regarding this matter, Mahādeva alone is the speaker—no other person exists anywhere.
I shall proclaim that which was spoken by Śiva, as heard in due order from the mouth of my guru: because he is of the nature of Brahman, Śiva alone is proclaimed to be partless (niṣkala).
Because it possesses form, it is likewise whole; therefore, it is both whole and partless. Due to its partlessness, its sign (liṅga) has become formless.
Likewise, because it possesses all parts, his embodied form is endowed with attributes; yet, because he is both with and without parts, the Supreme is designated by the word "Brahman."
Furthermore, [the Lord] is constantly worshipped by people in both the *liṅga* and the *bera*; for since others are not Brahman, they never possess partlessness (*niṣkalatva*).
Therefore, those lords of the gods are not worshipped in that partless *liṅga*, nor are the other hosts of deities, because they are not Brahman and are merely individual souls (*jīva*).
Because they consist entirely of silence, they are worshipped in the form of mere icons; Śaṅkara is the life-force of these others, while Brahman is the life-force of Śaṅkara.
Because it illuminates the meaning of the Praṇava as established by the essence of the Vedānta, Nandikeśvara was questioned in this very manner long ago on Mount Mandara.
By the wise sage Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā. Sanatkumāra said: [This is] for all those who wish to bring under their control Śiva and all other deities in every respect.
The image alone has been heard of and seen many times for the purpose of worship; yet, in the worship of Śiva alone, both the Liṅga and the image are observed.
"Therefore, O auspicious one, tell me that truth which provides perfect awakening. Nandikeśvara said: "This question is unsurpassed, a secret concerning the characteristics of Brahman."
O sinless one, I shall relate to you, who are endowed with devotion, that which was spoken by Śiva; for because Śiva is of the nature of Brahman and is partless, he is himself partless.

The *liṅga* is universally accepted in all the Vedas for the worship of that very [Brahman]; and because it is the totality of that very [Brahman], it is likewise both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
Furthermore, in worship, the Sakala form is esteemed by the world; this is because Śiva and others possess life and are entirely complete in every respect.
In the determination of the Vedas, even a mere portion is accepted for the purpose of worship; however, in the manifestation of the gods, it is indeed the entire form that is required.

Indeed, the *liṅga* and the *bera* (image) of Śiva are seen when they are beheld. Sanatkumāra said: "O highly fortunate one, you have spoken regarding the dissemination of the *liṅga* and the *bera*."
Having distinguished that [nature] of Śiva and of others according to ultimate reality, therefore, that alone is the supreme [reality], arising as the *liṅga*, the *bera*, and so forth.

"O Lord of Yogins, I wish to hear the characteristics of the manifestation of the Liṅga. Nandikeśvara said: "Listen, my child; out of affection for you, I shall speak according to the ultimate truth."
Long ago, in a great and world-renowned eon that had arrived, the two high-souled ones, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, fought with one another.
To dispel their pride, the Supreme Lord manifested His own form between them in the shape of a formless pillar.
Then, from that pillar which was marked by his own characteristic signs, Śiva, desiring the welfare of the worlds, revealed his own formless (niṣkala) self as his own liṅga.
From that time onwards, among the worlds, the partless (niṣkala) emblem of the Lord and likewise the embodied (sakala) image of Śiva alone were established.

For other deities, however, only a *bera* (image) is prescribed; that respective *bera* of the deities bestows their respective auspicious enjoyments. But for Śiva, the nature of both the *liṅga* and the *bera* auspiciously bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said: O lord of yogis, in ancient times, Viṣṇu, whose seat is the serpent, once slept with supreme splendor, surrounded by his own attendants.
Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, having arrived there by chance, questioned the lotus-eyed one regarding his most beautiful bed.
Who are you that lie there like a man, even upon seeing me, acting so haughtily? Arise, my child; look upon me, your protector, who has come here.
If one should behave with arrogance upon seeing an arrived Guru worthy of veneration, a penance is prescribed for that deluded person who acts with hostility.
Having heard these words, though enraged, he behaved outwardly as if calm: "May it be well with you; welcome, my child! Stay; enter here upon this seat."
"Why does your face, with its uneven eyes, shine like that of a tiger? Brahmā said: "O child Viṣṇu, the Great Pride has arrived through the force of Time."
"And you, O child, are the grandfather and the protector of the world. Viṣṇu said: "O child, this entire world resides within me; yet you perceive it as if you were a thief."
"You are a son born from the navel-lotus of Manu; you speak in vain. Nandikeśvara said: "While the two deluded ones, Aja and Manu, were thus conversing there at that time..."
"I alone am the bridegroom, not you; I am the lord, I am the lord!"—desiring thus to slay one another, they both made preparations for battle.
The two heroic immortals, whose vehicles were the swan and the lord of birds, fought; likewise, the followers of Brahmā and the devotees of Viṣṇu then fought with one another.
Meanwhile, all the classes of gods, traveling in their celestial chariots, gathered together, desiring to witness that most wonderful battle.
Scattering showers of flowers while looking freely into the sky, he who has Suparṇa as his vehicle became enraged there at the chest of Brahmā.
He discharged irresistible arrows and many various weapons; then the enraged Brahmā released unbearable missiles at the chest of Viṣṇu.
Then, as they discharged arrows resembling tongues of fire and numerous other weapons, that spectacle in the field of battle between the two clearly appeared as a marvel.
Having observed this, the hosts of gods, deeply distressed, offered their praise; then Viṣṇu, exceedingly enraged and sighing, was emaciated by his own suffering.
The wise one aimed the Māheśvara weapon at Brahmā; thereupon Brahmā became violently enraged, causing the entire universe to tremble.
He discharged the terrible Pāśupata weapon at the chest of Viṣṇu; then it rose into the sky, resembling ten thousand suns.
With a thousand faces, exceedingly fierce, and terrifying with its violent winds—these two weapons there are formidable even to Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

Thus did the battle between Brahmā and Viṣṇu unfold against one another. Thereupon, O dear one, all the hosts of gods became deeply dejected and greatly distressed; like Brahmins during a royal upheaval, they spoke to one another.
Salutation to that Brahman who wields the triple trident, from whom proceed creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.

"Since it is impossible for others to do so without [Śiva's] grace, and since even a blade of grass here might by chance be consumed," having thus resolved upon seeking refuge with the Lord, they searched for Śiva’s abode and went to the peak of Kailāsa, where the Moon-crested One resides.
Having thus seen that supreme state of the Lord, which is the very form of the Praṇava, the gods were delighted and, having entered that abode, they prostrated themselves.
They too, in the midst of that assembly hall within the pavilion, beheld the bull among gods shining resplendently with Umā upon his jeweled throne.
With his right foot placed over the other, his lotus-like hands joined in the gesture of granting boons, attended on all sides by his own hosts, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
Being fanned by women of distinguished birth who were intensely devoted, being constantly praised by the Vedas, he was the Lord bestowing grace.
O child, having thus beheld the Lord, the hosts of great immortals, their eyes filled with the water of joy, prostrated themselves like a staff from afar.

Having observed those gods, the Lord summoned them along with their attendants. Then the God, the crest-jewel of the gods, gladdening the deities, spoke words that were profound in meaning and sweet with auspiciousness.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Īśvara said: "O calves, may it be well with you; does everything proceed according to my command? And as for the world and the lineage of the deities, do they not abide in their respective duties?"
O Asuras, the battle between Brahmā and Viṣṇu was already known to me; it has been recounted by you merely out of excessive fervor and redundancy.
Thus, with these honey-sweet words spoken by the youth, he, the husband of Ambā, fully satisfied that host of gods.
Then, the Lord of Hari and Dhātṛ issued an order to a hundred leaders of the Gaṇas right there in that assembly to proceed to the field of battle.
Then various kinds of musical instruments were played for the departure of the Supreme Lord, and the lords of the hosts, fully equipped and adorned with diverse vehicles and ornaments, set forth.

The Lord Īśvara, the husband of Ambikā, ascended his auspicious chariot, which was shaped like the syllable Om (praṇava), beginning and ending with that form, and adorned with five circles. All the gods, including Indra and his followers, followed him.

Honored by multitudes of dancing, by showers of flowers, and by groups of musical instruments, as well as by variegated banners, fans, and chowries, Paśupati, together with the supreme Goddess and his army, went to their field of battle.
Having observed their battle, he remained hidden, stationed upon a cloud; the sound of musical instruments had ceased, and the clamor of the great hosts was stilled.
Then the two heroes, Brahmā and Acyuta, desiring to slay one another, [attacked] with the Māheśvara weapon and likewise with the Pāśupata weapon.
Then the three worlds of Brahmā and Viṣṇu were scorched by the flames of the missiles; and Īśa, beholding that intense, untimely dissolution, was deeply moved.

In the midst of that, he became formless, his appearance terrifying like a great pillar of fire; and those two flaming missiles, capable of destroying the worlds, fell down in an instant once the great fire had manifested.
Having seen that wonderful, variegated, auspicious weapon which brought about peace, they said to one another, "What is this of such marvelous form?"
"What is this pillar that has arisen, appearing like fire and beyond the reach of the senses? Indeed, both its upper and lower parts are clearly visible to us."
Having thus resolved, the two heroes, who prided themselves on their valor, met together; intent upon that purpose and desiring to test it, they then set out with haste.
"Since we two are joined together there, a single task cannot be accomplished," having said this, Viṣṇu, who had assumed the form of a boar, departed from its presence.
Likewise, I, Brahmā, went with my body to behold its end; Hari, having pierced the abode of Pātāla, went to a very great distance.
He could not perceive the form of that pillar which possessed the brilliance of fire; exhausted, that Boar-Lord reached the front of the battlefield.
Then, O dear one, as Brahmā, your father, was traveling through the sky, he beheld a certain wonderful ketaki flower that had fallen away.

Observing that [the body] was exceedingly fragrant, unfading, and had remained so even after many years had passed, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, considered the task to be performed for those two.
Out of jest, his head moved due to a tremor; therefore, he sought to favor that fallen, excellent ketaka flower.
"O Lord of Flowers, King of Blossoms, why do you fall? By whom were you held? You have long since fallen from the midst of the pillar of the Primordial, the Immeasurable One."
"I do not perceive it; therefore, abandon your hope for seeing the end. I have come here in the form of a swan for the purpose of serving her and him."
"Friend, from now on you must do what I desire today: you must speak this with me in the presence of Viṣṇu."

"O Acyuta, I was seen by the Creator standing between the two pillars; I am the witness there. Having said this, he bowed again to the Ketaka flower. "Even untruth may be commendable in times of distress," such is the traditional teaching.

Seeing Acyuta there, exhausted by his long exertion and deprived of joy, he danced with delight and spoke to that Acyuta, who was the ultimate reality, while he himself followed the deceptive speech of a eunuch. Then Vidhi addressed Acyuta:
"O Hari, this very top of the pillar is being observed; surely this ketaka flower is the witness right there. Then, in his presence, the ketaka spoke falsely to his brother: "So it is."
Hari, reflecting as it were that this was indeed the truth, himself offered salutations to that Vidhi and worshipped him with the sixteen types of offerings.
To strike at the deceitful Brahmā, that Lord manifested there in embodied form; upon seeing his Master, he rose up again with trembling hands and took hold of His feet.

Since you possess a form devoid of beginning or end, let no reflection arising from desire prevail here through our deluded intellects. Therefore, O Compassionate One, be gracious; wipe away our impurity and forgive that which was performed by us as sport, even though it was ordained by you alone.

Īśvara said: "O child Hara, I am pleased with you because, even though you desire lordship, you have spoken words of truth; therefore, among people, there shall be equality between you and me, and you have also mentioned my honor."
Henceforth, you shall perform the installation and worship of the field (kṣetra) for yourself and for others.
Thus, in ancient times, the Lord, being pleased by his truthfulness, granted supreme equality with Himself to Hari while the assembly of gods looked on.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said: Then Mahādeva, desiring to destroy the pride of Brahmā, created from the middle of his eyebrows a certain wonderful being named Bhairava.
Then, having bowed to her husband Śiva there in the courtyard, she said: "O Lord, command me quickly; what task shall I perform here?"
O dear ones, this ritual is the manifest primordial deity of the worlds; you must surely worship him with a sharp sword with the utmost speed.

Seizing that fifth hair by its root with one hand—the hair of that arrogant liar—he raised his sword with his hands in a most distinct manner, shaking it as he prepared to strike off his heads in order to kill him.

Your father, his ornaments, garments, garlands, and upper cloth cast off, with his mass of hair disheveled, fell indeed at the lotus-feet of Bhairava, as unsteady as a creeper in a gale or a plantain tree in the wind.

O Father, desiring to see the ritual procedure, the compassionate Acyuta, having bathed the sprout-like feet of our Lord with his tears, spoke with palms joined in reverence, using words as indistinct as those of a child speaking to his own father.

Acyuta said: "Since you previously bestowed upon him this five-faced head, the emblem of the Lord, through your own effort, therefore forgive him now; he is worthy of favor, so grant your grace for the sake of this ritual."
Thus entreated by Acyuta, the Lord, being pleased in the assembly of the hosts of gods, then withdrew Bhairava from the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa).
Then the God said to the gambler Vidhi, who had his neck turned away: "O Brahmā, desiring honor, you have deceitfully assumed the status of the Lord."

"Therefore, you shall receive no honor in this world, such as a place of residence, festivals, and the like. Brahmā said: "O Lord, be gracious today, O possessor of great majesty! O granter of boons, I consider the release of my head to be the boon for me."
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the kinsman, the source of the universe; to the endurer of all defects, the source of auspiciousness, whose bow is the mountain.
Īśvara said: "Indeed, this entire world will not survive if it is free from the fear of a king; therefore, O child, slay those who deserve punishment and bear the burden of the world."
"I grant you a boon; accept this supreme and rare gift: in the Vaitanika, Grihya, and [Srauta] sacrifices, you shall be the preceptor."
"Without you, even a sacrifice that is complete in its parts and accompanied by sacrificial fees is fruitless. Then the Lord spoke to the rogue Ketaka, the false witness:
O Ketaka, you are wicked; you rogue, go far away from here! Let there be no love for you even in my flowers, and certainly none in my worship from now on.
When this was said by the Lord, all those born of the divine race then warded off the ketakī flower from his side and moved it elsewhere.
Ketaka said: "Salutations to you, O Lord! By your command, let my birth, which has been fruitless, be made fruitful, O Father; let my transgression be forgiven."
Your remembrance alone destroys the sin committed through ignorance as well as that committed knowingly; when such a person as you is seen by me, how could there be the fault of falsehood?
Thus praised by Ketaka in the assembly hall, the Blessed One said: "It is not fitting for me to wear you; I am the Lord whose word is truth."
My own people shall support you, and thereby your birth will become fruitful; indeed, you shall be over me under the guise of a canopy.
Having thus favored the Ketaka flower as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the Blessed One shone resplendent in the midst of the assembly, being praised by all the gods.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said: In the meantime, Vidhi and Mādhava, having bowed to the Lord, stood silently with their palms joined in reverence, positioned to his right and left respectively.
Having seated the god together with his family upon an excellent throne there, they two worshipped the worshipful one with meritorious articles fit for men.
The human form is to be known as a material object, lasting for either a long or a short duration; it is adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, crowns, jewels, and earrings.
With sacrificial threads, upper garments, garlands, linen, and finger-rings; with flowers, betel, camphor, sandalwood, and applications of aguru.
With incense, lamps, white umbrellas, fans, banners, and chowries, and with other divine offerings whose majesty transcends speech and mind.
They worshipped their husband with items suitable for him that were unobtainable by ordinary animals; whatever most excellent object was fit for the husband, they offered it upon his banner.
Desiring to bring that entire matter to a conclusion, the Lord, being delighted, presented it to the members of the assembly there individually and in due order.
A great clamor arose there from those seizing that object; it was there, in ancient times, that Śaṅkara was worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The Lord, who increases devotion, being pleased, spoke with a smile to the two who were bowing before him. The Lord said: "O children, I am today gratified by your worship on this great day."
Therefore, this day shall become even more meritorious; this lunar day is known as Śivarātri, and it is dear to me.
Furthermore, at this time, the man who performs worship of my linga and image shall perform the cosmic functions of the world, such as maintenance and creation.
On Śivarātri, one who has conquered the senses, fasting for a full day and night, should worship according to the prescribed rule and according to his capacity, without deceit.
Whatever fruit is obtained from my worship performed continuously for one year, that same fruit one obtains immediately by worshipping me on Śivarātri.
This is the time for the increase of my Dharma, like the moon for the ocean; herein lies my festival of consecration and other rites, which is a source of auspiciousness.
Furthermore, that time when I formerly manifested myself in the form of a pillar was during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under the asterism Ārdrā, O two children.
He who beholds me, the consort of Umā, or even my bull or my Liṅga, on the Ārdrā day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, is dearer to me than Guha himself.
Merely by seeing [it] on that auspicious day, the fruit is sufficient; if there is worship, the fruit is even greater, beyond the reach of words.
Since I have manifested upon this surface of the battlefield in the form of a *liṅga*, just like a *liṅga* itself, therefore let this place be known as Liṅgasthāna.
"This pillar, which is without beginning or end, shall exist as minute as an atom; indeed, it is for the sake of being seen by the worlds and for the sake of worship, O son."

This Liṅga brings about enjoyment; it is the sole means for both worldly experience and liberation. Through seeing, touching, and meditating upon it, it grants living beings release from the cycle of birth.
This linga that has arisen, resembling a mountain of fire, shall attain renown as Aruṇācala.
In this place, there will be many great sacred sites (tīrthas), and liberation for living beings shall come through both residing here and through death.
In this place—the abode of the people, which is auspicious with chariot festivals and other celebrations—whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted becomes ten millionfold in merit.
This field is even greater than all my other fields; by the mere recollection of it, embodied beings attain liberation.
Therefore, this field is most great and exceedingly beautiful; it is filled with every auspiciousness, bestows liberation upon all, and is auspicious.
Having worshipped me alone here in this linga as the Lord who possesses the linga, one attains sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, and indeed sārṣṭi.
These five—beginning with *sāyujya*—are considered the fruits of ritual action and the rest; all of you shall quickly attain every heart's desire in its entirety.
Nandikeśvara said: Having thus favored Vidhi and Mādhava, who were both humble, the Blessed One [spoke] regarding that army which they had previously struck down in battle against one another.
Raising them up with his own power by means of a stream of nectar, he spoke to the two of them in order to dispel their delusion and enmity.
I possess two forms: the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala). No one else possesses these; therefore, everyone other than me is not the Lord (anīśvara).

In front, the two children exist in the form of a pillar, and behind them in their own forms; the state of Brahmā is said to be partless (niṣkala), while the state of Īśvara is likewise with parts (sakala).
This twofold [power] is established for me alone, and not for anyone other than me; therefore, lordship over others does not belong even to you two at any time.
Out of ignorance of that most wonderful act of yours in which you have assumed the form of the Lord, I have arisen here upon this battlefield to refute it.
Abandon your pride and direct your mind toward me, the Lord; by my grace, every goal in all the worlds shall be revealed to you.
In this matter, the word of the Guru is the indicator or the repeated authority; out of affection for you, I shall speak of this hidden reality of Brahman.
I alone am the Supreme Brahman; my own nature consists of both parts and non-parts. Because of being Brahman, I am the Lord (Īśvara), and my function includes grace and so forth.
Because of my vastness and because of my nourishing power, I am Brahmā; O Keśava, I am Brahmā. Because of my equanimity and because of my pervasiveness, likewise, O children, I am the Self.
All other living beings are indeed without self, there is no doubt; and the lotus-born one performs the duties of the world, from grace at its beginning until the end of creation.

"Because of my very lordship, this [liṅga] is eternally mine and not that of anyone else; in the beginning, the partless liṅga arose for the purpose of establishing the realization of my nature as Brahman."
Therefore, in order to manifest clearly to you both that lordship which was previously unknown, I have become the "sakala" (the embodied one), and from that very moment, I am truly the manifest Lord.
Therefore, let my lordship as the possessor of all parts be quickly recognized in me; for this partless pillar is the indicator of my nature as Brahman.
Because it possesses the characteristics of a *liṅga*, this shall be my *liṅga*. Therefore, O two sons, you must worship it here perpetually.
This [liṅga] is eternally of my own nature and the cause of my presence; it is always to be greatly honored because of the non-difference between the liṅga and the possessor of the liṅga (the deity).
O dear sons, wherever such a linga of mine is established, there I am established, even though I am without foundation.
The fruit of establishing a single *liṅga* is said to be equality with me; indeed, when a second *liṅga* is established, the fruit is even oneness with me.

The *liṅga* should be installed as the primary element, while the *bera* (image) is secondary; yet, in the absence of a *liṅga*, that sacred field remains complete in every respect even with only the *bera*.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu said: "O Lord, tell us the characteristics of the fivefold duties beginning with creation. Śiva said: "I shall graciously explain to you this secret which makes known my duties."
Creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace—these five are my eternal, established cosmic functions, O Unborn and Undecaying One.
Creation is the intense activity of saṃsāra; its persistence is considered to be maintenance (sthiti). Destruction is its crushing, and its withdrawal is its transcendence.
Liberation from that is grace; thus, my fivefold duty is as follows: another carries out this duty silently, like a statue on a city gate.
The fourfold activity beginning with creation, which expands the cycle of worldly existence, and the fifth, which is the cause of liberation, is eternally and firmly established within me.
This very creation is seen among the five elements by my people: its manifestation in earth, its maintenance in water, and likewise its dissolution in fire.
Concealment occurs in the wind, and likewise, grace occurs here in space; everything is created by the earth, and everything grows by means of the waters.
Everything is moistened by fire and carried away by wind; everything is sustained by space—thus indeed is the knowable understood by the wise.
I possess five faces in order to bear these fivefold functions: four faces toward the four directions, and the fifth face in their midst.
"O sons, these two tasks known as creation and maintenance have been obtained by you through your ascetic penance; they are a most dear fortune granted to you by me, who am well-pleased."
Likewise, there is another supreme pair of duties belonging to Rudra and Maheśa; that which is called grace (anugraha) cannot indeed be attained by anyone else.
All that former karma has been forgotten by you two due to the passage of time; yet such karma was not forgotten by Rudra and Maheśa.
In appearance, dress, conduct, vehicle, as well as seat, and in weapons and so forth, we have made ourselves equal to him for his sake.
"O dear ones, this delusion has come about because of your lack of meditation; were my knowledge present, such pride would not exist, just as it does not exist in Maheśvara regarding his own form."
Therefore, for the sake of attaining my knowledge, recite from now on this mantra called Oṃkāra, which is mine and shatters pride.
I taught him my own mantra, the syllable Om, which is of great auspiciousness; the syllable Om was born from my mouth as the first awakening of my consciousness.
I am the designator and this mantra is the designated; for this mantra is indeed identical with my own self. Constant recollection of that [mantra] shall become recollection of me.
The letter A comes from the northern face, the letter U from the western face, the letter M from the southern face, and likewise the Bindu from the eastern face.
Thus, this Nāda unfolds in five ways from the central mouth; then, becoming unified once more, it becomes the single syllable "Om."
Everything consisting of name and form—the two lineages of the Vedas and the elements—is pervaded by this mantra, which reveals both Śiva and Śakti.
From this [monosyllable], the five-syllabled mantra was born, which awakens all beings; it follows the sequence beginning with the letter 'A' and proceeds in order starting from the letter 'Na'.
From this five-syllabled [mantra], the Mātṛkās are born in five divisions; therefore, from that head and four faces, the Gāyatrī indeed has three feet.
From that, the entire Veda was born, and from it, indeed, millions of mantras; through each respective mantra, its specific power is attained, and from this, all perfections arise.
By means of this root-mantra, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are accomplished; all these auspicious kings of mantras directly bestow enjoyment.

Nandikeśvara said: Again, having arranged a curtain there between the two of them, the Guru, together with Ambikā, slowly placed his lotus-hand upon their heads while they stood facing north, and imparted the supreme mantra.

Having recited the mantra three times according to the instructions of the *yantra* and *tantra*, he caused those two disciples to offer themselves as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) along with his own self.
With hands joined in reverence, they indeed approached that very God, the Teacher of the World, and spoke to him.
Brahmā and Acyuta said: Salutations to the one whose form is partless; salutations to the splendor that is without parts. Salutations to the Lord of all; salutations to you, the Self of all.
Salutations to the one expressed by the Praṇava; salutations to the one whose symbol is the Praṇava; salutations to the creator of the world and its origins; salutations to the five-faced one.
Salutations to you, whose nature is the five Brahmans, who performs the five cosmic acts; salutations to you, the Self, the Brahman, possessed of infinite qualities and powers.
"Salutation to the Guru Śambhu, whose form is both with parts and without parts. Having thus praised the Guru with these verses, Brahmā and Viṣṇu bowed down.
Īśvara said: "O two children, the entire truth has been told and demonstrated to you. Recite the Praṇava mantra, which was revealed by the Goddess and is my very self."
Knowledge becomes well-established, and all fortune becomes eternal; when recited on the day of Ārdrā, on the fourteenth lunar day, that recitation shall become inexhaustible.
By the movement of the sun, one great *drā* becomes ten millionfold; so too is the final portion of Mṛgaśīrṣa and the first portion of Punarvasu.

Ārdrā is always to be known as the [proper] time for worship, fire-oblations, and libations; however, the [actual] sight [of the deity] occurs at dawn, during the morning, and during the saṃgava period.
Likewise, the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) should be taken when it extends through the midnight hour; it is praised when it extends through the evening (pradoṣa) and is joined with the following day.
The Liṅga and the image (bera) are equal for those who worship; however, for those seeking liberation, the Liṅga is the supreme object of worship even more than the image.
The Linga should be installed with the mantra Omkara, and the image (bera) with the five-syllabled mantra; it may be installed by oneself or even by others, using pure materials.
"By worshipping with ritual offerings, my state shall become easily attainable. Having thus instructed the two disciples, Śiva vanished on the spot.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: How is the liṅga to be installed? What are its characteristics? And how indeed should it be worshipped—in what place, at what time, and by whom?
Sūta said: For your sake I shall speak; understand this with careful attention—at an auspicious and favorable time, at a holy place, and likewise on a riverbank.
Having installed a *liṅga* according to one's desire—whether it be made of earth or likewise of metal, as one pleases—in a place where there may be perpetual worship.
One obtains the fruit of worship through a *liṅga* endowed with the characteristics of the *kalpa*; one endowed with all characteristics bestows the fruit of worship immediately.
In this regard, the subtle [form] is distinguished from the gross; indeed, one should install that which is fashioned by Śiva, together with its characteristic marks and its pedestal.
The mandala may be square or likewise triangular; with a subtle central liṅga-pīṭha resembling a khaṭvāṅga, it yields great fruit.

First, a linga is fashioned from clay, stone, and so forth, using metals and other materials; for a stationary (sthāvara) linga, it is especially distinguished by having its pedestal (pīṭha) made of the same material as the linga itself.
One may wander with either a linga or its pedestal, except for a linga fashioned by Bāṇa; for the makers, the supreme measurement of the linga is twelve finger-breadths.
If it is deficient, the fruit will be small; if it is excessive, there is no fault. This applies when the maker's [measurement] is less by one finger-breadth, and likewise for the *cāra*.
First, a celestial palace (vimāna) should be constructed by artisans, filled with hosts of deities; therein, within a beautiful, firm inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) that resembles a mirror.
And the gates of the directions were adorned with the foremost of the nine gems: blue sapphire, ruby, lapis lazuli, and likewise emerald, which is dark green.
One should place pearls, coral, gomedaka, and diamonds—the nine gems—as well as a large substance, such as a linga, together with the Vedic texts in the center.

Having worshipped the Liṅga in its five locations with the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta in due order, and having offered oblations many times into the fire with sacrificial ghee, he should worship me, who am partless (niṣkala).
Having honored his guru and preceptor with wealth and desired objects, and his kinsmen as well, he should bestow sovereignty upon those who seek it, whether they be dull-witted or otherwise.
Having diligently gratified all living beings, both stationary and moving, [he placed them] in a pit filled with gold and filled with the nine precious gems.

Having first uttered "Sadyojāta" and other [mantras] along with "Brahman," and having meditated upon the supreme, auspicious Deity, one should then recite the Great Mantra, the syllable Om, resounding with the sound of *nāda*.
Having installed the *liṅga* there, one should join the *liṅga* with its pedestal (*pīṭha*). Having set down the *liṅga* together with its pedestal, one should bind it with a permanent coating.

In this manner, one should likewise install the supreme and most auspicious image (bera) in that very place; however, for the purpose of the festival, the image should be placed outside with the five-syllabled mantra.

One should receive [the initiation] from teachers who are honored by the virtuous, whether through a physical form (bera) or a linga; in this way, worship performed upon both the image and the linga bestows the state of Śiva.
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: the immobile and the mobile. They call the immobile "liṅga," as well as trees, shrubs, and so forth.
They say that even worms, insects, and the like are mobile lingas; thus, there is service to the immobile and the propitiation of the mobile.
The wise know that the worship of Śiva consists in attachment to each respective bliss; the entire sacred seat (pīṭha) is composed of Ambā, and the Śiva-liṅga is composed of consciousness (cinmaya).
Just as Śaṅkara remains holding Queen Umā upon his lap, so too does this Liṅga remain constantly holding the Pīṭha.

Having thus established the great liṅga, one should worship it with ritual offerings; the daily worship should be performed according to one's capacity, as well as the raising of the banner and other such rites.
Thus one should consecrate the liṅga, which directly bestows the state of Śiva; or else, one may worship the mobile liṅga with the sixteen types of ritual offerings (upacāras).

And one should worship according to the rule in due order—that which bestows the state of Śiva—performing the invocation, the seat, the water for honor (arghya), and likewise the water for the feet (pādya).
Then, indeed, there is sipping of water (ācamana), bathing preceded by anointing with oil (abhyaṅga), as well as clothing, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering (naivedya).

The waving of lights (nīrājana), betel-leaf offering, prostration, and the formal dismissal (visarjana); or else, having performed the offering of water for honor (arghya) and so forth, ending with the food offering (naivedya) according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should always perform, according to one's capacity, the consecration, the food offering, the prostration, and the libation, in their proper sequence, which bestow the state of Śiva.

Alternatively, whether it be a human-made linga, one made by a seer (ārṣa), one of divine origin, a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) one, an installed (sthāpita) one, or a unique (apūrvaka) linga—in any such case, one should perform worship with all the ritual offerings (upacāra) in whatever manner is appropriate.
Whatever fruit one enjoys when offering articles of worship, through circumambulations and prostrations, one attains the state of Śiva in due order.
The mere sight of the *liṅga* invariably bestows Śiva; it may be fashioned from clay, flour, cow dung, flowers, or *karavīra* blossoms and fruits.
Having carefully fashioned a liṅga from jaggery, fresh butter, ashes, or foodstuffs according to one's preference, one should worship it at the conclusion in accordance with that material.
Some desire worship in the same manner even on the thumb and other parts; however, in the rite concerning the *liṅga*, there is never any prohibition anywhere.
For Śiva indeed bestows fruit everywhere in accordance with one's exertion; alternatively, there is the gift of a linga, or even the value of a linga.
That which is given with faith to a devotee of Śiva bestows the state of Śiva; or else, one should constantly recite the Praṇava ten thousand times.

At the two twilights, one should know that reciting it a thousand times bestows the state of Śiva; at the time of recitation, one should practice it ending with the syllable *ma*, which purifies the mind.

The mental [recitation] is said to be for the sake of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is for all times; they know this [mantra] to be accompanied by the *praṇava* and joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*.

Then, one should constantly recite the five-syllabled mantra ten thousand times with devotion; or, at the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), it should be known that reciting it one thousand times bestows the state of Śiva.
For Brahmins, a mantra joined with the Praṇava at the beginning is distinguished; indeed, for the attainment of results, one should receive from a guru a mantra conjoined with initiation (dīkṣā).

The ritual bath with the water-pot (kuṃbhasnāna), initiation into the mantras, and the placement of the Mātṛkās—these are performed by a Brāhmaṇa whose soul is purified by truth; such a wise Guru is preeminent.
For the twice-born, [the mantra] begins with "namaḥ"; for others, it ends with "namaḥ"; and for women, they desire it to end with "namas" in some cases, according to the prescribed rule.
Some desire that for the wives of Brahmins, this [mantra] preceded by "namaḥ" be used; having performed five crores of recitations, one becomes equal to Sadāśiva.

One shall attain the state of Brahmā and the other gods through one, two, three, or four crores [of recitations]; or else, one may perform the recitation of each individual syllable one hundred thousand times.
Alternatively, one hundred thousand syllables should be known as bestowing the state of Śiva; indeed, ten million [syllables] are attained in a thousand days by means of a thousand [repetitions].
Through the daily feeding of Brahmins, one attains the desired success of mantras and other rites; indeed, one should recite the Gāyatrī one thousand and eight times every morning.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, should daily recite the Vedic mantras and hymns that bestow the state of Śiva in due order, remaining firm in his observances.
One mantra of Daśārṇa may consist of one hundred less than ten, or more than that; it may also be ten thousand, a thousand, or even one hundred minus one.
The complete study of the Vedas should also be known as bestowing the state of Śiva; one should recite many other mantras for a total of one hundred thousand syllables.
One should likewise recite monosyllabic mantras for ten million syllables; thereafter, one should indeed recite them a thousand times with devotion.

One should act in this manner according to one's capacity; thus, in due course, one shall attain the state of Śiva. One should maintain a single mantra that is pleasing to oneself constantly until the end of life.
One should recite "Om" a thousand times for all desired aims by the command of Śiva; likewise, one should perform tasks such as cleaning or tending flower gardens and the like.
Having performed [this] for the sake of Śiva and for the purpose of Śiva’s work, one shall attain the state of Śiva; likewise, one should always dwell in a sacred field of Śiva with devotion.
Since it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all beings, whether insentient or sentient, a wise person should therefore reside in a sacred field of Śiva until death.
They know that in a human sacred field (kṣetra), the area of merit extends one hundred cubits from the liṅga; likewise, in a sacred field of the ṛṣis, it extends for a thousand aratnis.
Likewise, it should be known that at Daivaliṅga, the sacred field extends for a thousand aratnis in measurement; on the earth itself, the holy area measures a thousand dhanus.
A pond, a well, and lotus ponds situated in a field of merit should be known as the "Ganges of Śiva," according to the word of Śiva.
Having bathed there, likewise having given gifts, and having performed recitation, one shall indeed go to Śiva; and having taken refuge in the sacred field of Śiva, one may dwell there until death.

Whether it be on the tenth day, after ten days, at the end of a month, or at the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite; or whether it be the annual Śrāddha (Ābdika) or even the offering of a Piṇḍa in a sacred field of Śiva—so it is said.
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall immediately attain the state of Śiva; or else, he may dwell there for seven nights or five nights.

By practicing for three nights or one night, in due order, one attains the state of Śiva; in this world, a person attains [their goal] through their own conduct in accordance with their respective caste.
By means of the extraction of the syllables and through devotion, a person shall immediately obtain the entire fruit of all that was performed with desire, yet with even greater excellence.
Everything performed without desire directly bestows the state of Śiva; [this applies] to the morning, midday, and evening—each one in turn throughout the three watches of the day.
The morning rite is to be known as [the time for] vidhi; likewise, midday is for kāmya rites. The evening is to be known as for śāntika rites, and it is exactly the same at night as well.
The time of midnight is indeed declared to be the two middle watches of the night; worship of Śiva performed specifically at that time grants the fulfillment of one's desires.
Knowing this, a person who acts accordingly shall partake of the fruit as described; however, in the Kali age, the attainment of results occurs specifically through ritual action.
Or even by some other means mentioned, through the distinction of qualification—if one possesses good conduct and fears sin—one shall obtain that fruit.
The sages said: Now, tell us in brief of the holy places (kṣetras), by resorting to which all women and men may attain the supreme state.

"O Sūta, best among the foremost of yogis, likewise [tell us] of the sacred sites of Śiva and their traditional accounts. Sūta said: "Listen with faith to all the sacred sites and their traditional accounts."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Listen, O wise sages, to the sacred field of Śiva which bestows liberation; I shall indeed describe its scriptures for the very purpose of protecting the world.
Indeed, by the command of Śiva, the earth—extending fifty crores [of yojanas] and including its mountains, forests, and groves—remains supporting the world.
In various places, the Lord, the Sovereign, out of compassion for the inhabitants of those regions, has fashioned sacred fields (kṣetra) for the sake of their liberation.
Some were acquired through the acceptance of the ṛṣis and others through the acceptance of the gods; yet others arose spontaneously, solely for the purpose of protecting the world.

In a sacred ford (tīrtha) or a holy field (kṣetra), one should always perform bathing, giving, recitation, and other such rites; otherwise, a person may incur disease, poverty, muteness, and other misfortunes.
Now, if a man meets his death in this land of Bhārata, he shall attain human birth again by virtue of having dwelt in the abode of Svayambhū.
O Brahmins, the commission of sin becomes firmly established in a [sinful] field; indeed, while residing in a field of merit, one should not commit even the slightest sin.
By whatever means possible, a person should dwell in a field of merit; there are numerous sacred fields on the shores of the ocean and along the banks of the hundred rivers.
The river Sarasvatī is declared to be meritorious and likewise possesses sixty mouths; a wise person who dwells on her various banks shall, in due course, attain the state of Brahman.
The Gaṅgā, born from the Himavat mountain, is a meritorious river with a hundred mouths; and upon its banks are many sacred fields, such as Kāśī and others.
In that regard, when Mṛga and Mṛgabṛhaspati are in conjunction, the Śoṇabhadra bank is indeed praiseworthy; it is auspicious and bestows desired fruits upon the ten-faced one.
There, by means of bathing and fasting, one shall attain the state of Vaināyaka; the twenty-four-faced Narmadā is a meritorious great river.
By bathing and residing there, one shall indeed attain the state of Viṣṇu; the Tamasā has twelve mouths, while the Revā is a river with ten mouths.
The Godāvarī is greatly meritorious, the destroyer of the sins of killing Brahmins and cows; she is said to have twenty-one mouths and bestows the world of Rudra.
The Kṛṣṇaveṇī is a holy river that brings about the destruction of all sins; it is said to have eighteen mouths and bestows the world of Viṣṇu.
The Tuṅgabhadrā has ten mouths and bestows the world of Brahmā; likewise, the meritorious Suvarṇamukharī is said to have nine mouths.
Right there, those who have descended from the world of Brahmā are born in great abundance; likewise, the Sarasvatī, the Pampā, and the auspicious maiden river Śvetanadī flow there.
By dwelling on the banks of these [rivers], one shall attain the world of Indra; the great river born from the Sahya mountain is known as the Kāverī, which is of great merit.
The twenty-seventh [river] is proclaimed as the bestower of all desired objects; its banks grant heaven and bestow the state of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The Śaiva rites bestow the world of Śiva and likewise grant one's desired fruits; one should bathe at Naimiṣa and Badara when Jupiter and the Sun are in Aries.
One should know that this bestows the world of Brahmā; likewise, one should perform worship and other rites, as well as bathing in the Indus River, when the sun is in Leo or Cancer.
They know that drinking the water of Kedāra and bathing there bestows knowledge; one should bathe in the Godāvarī during the month of Siṃha when Jupiter is in Leo.
"In the past, Śiva spoke thus: 'One should bathe in the Yamunā and the Śoṇa when the sun has entered Virgo, for that bestows the world of Śiva.'"
They know that at Dharmaloka and Daṇḍiloka, it bestows great enjoyment; likewise, one should bathe in the Kāverī when the Sun and Jupiter are in Libra.
They know that, through the greatness of Viṣṇu’s word, it bestows all desired objects when the month of Vṛścika has arrived and the Sun is likewise in Scorpio (Vṛścika) while Jupiter is also there.
By bathing in the Narmadā river, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu; likewise, by bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī on a Sunday when Jupiter is in the sign of Capricorn.
Just as a Brahmin’s word that "it bestows the world of Śiva" is true, so too should one bathe in the Jāhnavī during the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa when Jupiter is in that asterism.
Just as was the word of Brahmā that it bestows the world of Śiva, so too, having enjoyed the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, one shall attain knowledge at their conclusion.

In the month of Māgha, at the Gaṅgā, when the sun has entered Aquarius (Kumbha), one should perform a Śrāddha, or the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), or even the offering of water with sesame seeds.
They know this to be the deliverer of ten million ancestors of both lineages; they praise it at the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter and the Sun are in Pisces.
Bathing at each respective sacred ford during that month bestows the station of Indra; therefore, a wise person should dwell there, having resorted to either the Gaṅgā or the Sahyādrijā (Kāverī).
The destruction of sins committed at that time is certain; O Rudra, there are indeed many sacred fields (kṣetra) that bestow worldly realms.
The Tāmraparṇī is swift-flowing and bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā; indeed, on its banks there are sacred fields that grant the attainment of heaven.
Among them, there are many fields that bestow great merit; by dwelling in each of those places, a wise person obtains a corresponding fruit.
A wise and compassionate person should dwell [in this state] through right conduct, virtuous behavior, and constant meditation; otherwise, one shall not obtain that fruit.
Merit performed in a field of merit attains manifold prosperity; even a minute evil committed in a field of merit becomes great.
If it is for the sake of livelihood at that time, it will come to an end through merit; for they say that merit—whether physical or vocal—bestows sovereignty.
O twice-born ones, such mental sin as that would likewise be destroyed; yet mental sin is like adamantine cement, persisting through kalpa after kalpa.
For that [karma] perishes through meditation alone; it does not meet its destruction otherwise. Verbal [karma] is destroyed by a web of recitations, and bodily [karma] by the emaciation of the body.

Through giving, that which is produced by wealth perishes; it does not perish otherwise even in ten million kalpas. In some cases, merit perishes through sin, while [sin] perishes preceded by increase [of merit].
The seed-portion, the growth-portion, and the enjoyment-portion belong to merit and demerit; indeed, the seed-portion is destroyed by knowledge, while the growth is as previously described.

The portion [of karma] that is to be experienced can only be exhausted by experiencing it, and not otherwise even by millions of merits; for when the sprout of the seed is destroyed, only the remainder is capable of producing experience.
