Through the worship of the gods, through giving to Brahmins, and through the excellence of austerity, over time that suffering may become bearable for men. Therefore, one who desires happiness should dwell without having committed any sin.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: "Quickly proclaim the conduct of the virtuous by which a wise man may conquer the worlds; likewise, tell us of those things consisting of dharma and adharma, which bestow both heaven and hell."
Sūta said: A learned man endowed with good conduct is called a Brāhmaṇa by name; indeed, a Vipra is one endowed with both Vedic knowledge and conduct, while a Dvija possesses only one of these.
A Kṣatriya who serves as a king has little conduct and little Vedic knowledge; a Vaiśya, being engaged in agriculture and trade, possesses only a modicum of conduct.
A Śūdra who calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, or one who is himself a cultivator, envious, and malicious toward others, is called a Caṇḍāla-brāhmaṇa.

The king is considered the protector of the earth, while others are regarded as kṣatriyas; one who deals in the purchase and sale of grain and such is a vaiśya, while others are called merchants (vaṇij).
A Śūdra is said to be one who serves the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; a farmer is to be known as a Vṛṣala, and others are indeed Dasyus.
For everyone facing the east at dawn should contemplate, beginning with the gods, matters of dharma and artha, their associated afflictions, as well as income and expenditure.
Longevity, hatred, death, sin, as well as fortune, disease, nourishment, and power—these are the results of rising in the morning during each respective direction.
The final watch of the night is to be known as *uṣas*, and half a watch is called *saṃdhi*. Having risen at that time, the twice-born man should void his excrement and urine.
Having gone a long distance from the house, he likewise proceeded outside; facing north, he entered, and in the event of an obstruction, he faced another direction.
Facing away from water, fire, Brahmins, and other deities, one should cover the *liṅga* with the left hand and the mouth with the other hand.
Having discharged the waste and stood up, one should not look at that excrement; one should perform purification outside the water using only water drawn out [of a vessel].
Alternatively, without descending into a tirtha sacred to the gods, the ancestors, or the sages, one should cleanse the anus with earth seven times, five times, or three times.

Regarding the penis, [the amount of earth] should be the size of a karkoṭa fruit; for the anus, one handful (prasṛti) is prescribed. Then, having risen, one should perform the cleansing of the feet and hands, followed by eight mouthfuls of water (gaṇḍūṣa).
Using any vessel or piece of wood, one should discard the water outside and perform the brushing of the teeth with the index finger; this is what is prescribed.
Having paid homage to the water-deities with the mantra, one should perform the bath; if unable to do so fully, one may bathe up to the neck or even up to the waist.
Having entered the water up to the knees, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras; there, the wise person should offer libations to the gods and others with the water from the sacred site.
Having taken a washed cloth, one should wear it with five folds; and an upper garment (uttarīya) must likewise be worn in all ritual acts.
When bathing at sacred fords such as rivers, one should not wash the bathing garment; however, after bathing in a step-well, a well, a house, or similar locations, a wise person should wash it.
O twice-born ones, having thoroughly cleaned a cloth made of stone, wood, or similar materials, whether in water or on land, one should wring it out for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes using the mantra spoken by Jābāla; otherwise, if it falls into the water, one goes from here to hell.
One should sprinkle water on the head with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" for the pacification of sins; the sprinkling of the joints on the feet is said to be performed with the mantra "yasya".
Sprinkling [the water] on the feet, the head, and the heart; then on the head, the heart, and the feet; and finally on the heart, the feet, and the head—the wise know this to be the mantra-bath.
In the event of slight physical discomfort, ill health, fear for the king or the kingdom, or during times of extreme distress, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras.

In the morning, one should perform the sprinkling with the Sūryānuvāka; in the evening, with the Agnyanuvāka; and likewise in the middle of the day, after drinking water, one should perform the sprinkling again.

O twice-born ones, at the conclusion of the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cast water upwards three times; and with the mantra, one should indeed offer a single arghya oblation to the Sun in the center.
Then, when evening has arisen, one should offer [the oblation] on the ground facing the western direction; however, in the morning, one should offer it at midday with the fingers.
One should see the sun hanging through the space between one's fingers; having performed a circumambulation of oneself, one should perform the pure *ācamana* rite.

If the evening twilight (saṃdhyā) is performed even a moment before its time, it becomes fruitless; when the day has passed, the [proper] time is said to have become the wrong time according to the sequence.

If the daily [recitation] is missed during the day, one should regularly recite the Gāyatrī a hundred times in sequence; if more than ten days have passed, one should practice the Gāyatrī a hundred thousand times.
If, however, more than a month has passed since the obligatory rite, one should perform the initiation (upanayana) once again; [the deities are] Īśa, Gaurī, Guha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and Yama.

In this manner, one should indeed satisfy the gods for the accomplishment of one's purpose; then, having performed the offering to Brahman, one should perform the pure ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana).
The wise man [should perform this] at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a commendable monastery (maṭha), in a temple for mantras (mantrālaya), or there in a temple, or even in a house, in a fixed location.
Having paid homage to all the gods, with a steady intellect and a steady posture, one should first practice the Praṇava and thereafter practice the Gāyatrī.

Having understood the subject matter of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman, one should practice the Praṇava, [meditating upon] Acyuta, the creator of the three worlds and the sustainer [of them].
We worship Rudra, the self-luminous destroyer, as well as the functions of the organs of knowledge and action, the activities of the mind, and the intellects.

One should always urge others toward the Dharma that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as toward knowledge; meditating upon this goal with such an intellect, one certainly attains Brahman.
Or he may recite it alone daily for the fulfillment of his Brahminhood; the best of Brahmins should practice this one thousand times every morning.
And for others, one should recite according to one's capacity; at midday, one should recite a hundred times, and in the evening, it should be known as twenty times, accompanied by the eight *śikhās*.
Beginning from the mūlādhāra, one should likewise contemplate the Vidyeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Jīvātman, and Parameśvara, situated at the dvādaśānta.

With the thought that they are Brahman, one should recite the mantra "So'ham" while contemplating their unity; one should then visualize those very [deities] within the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and elsewhere, as well as outside the body.
Beginning from the principle of Mahat, one should gradually transcend each of the thousand bodies by means of a single recitation at a time.

One should join the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme; this is declared to be the principle of recitation (japa-tattva). The body consists of two hundred and ten [units], endowed with eight tufts of hair (śikhās).

Thus, the wise know that the recitation of mantras follows a specific sequence beginning with *japa*: one should know that a thousand recitations bestow the grace of Brahmā, while a hundred are known to bestow the grace of Indra.
Otherwise, for the sake of self-protection, he is born among the wombs of Brahmins; having thus attended upon the Sun, he should perform his duties daily in this manner.
One who has completed twelve hundred thousand [recitations] is declared a "full" Brāhmaṇa; however, one who lacks a hundred thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī should be employed in Vedic rites.
One should observe this rule until the age of seventy, after which one should practice renunciation; a renunciant should recite the Praṇava twelve thousand times each morning.
Day by day, as time passes, one should thus recite daily in sequence; indeed, when a month has gradually elapsed, [the goal is reached] through half a lakh of recitations.
Therefore, once this time has passed, one should perform the ritual summons again; by doing so, the evil is pacified, otherwise one shall go to the Raurava hell.

Therefore, one who desires [worldly] pleasure should exert effort toward dharma and artha, but not otherwise; a Brāhmaṇa should desire liberation and should constantly practice the knowledge of Brahman.
From dharma comes wealth; from wealth comes enjoyment; from enjoyment arises detachment. Through the enjoyment of wealth acquired by means of dharma, detachment is born.
Through the enjoyment of objects perceived erroneously, passion alone is produced; and Dharma is said to be twofold, consisting of both material wealth and the body.

Material wealth consists of sacrifices and the like, while physical wealth consists of bathing at sacred fords and so forth; through wealth one obtains more wealth, and through austerity one attains a divine form.

One who is free from desire attains purity; through purity, knowledge is attained—of this there is no doubt. Indeed, in the Kṛta age and others, austerity is praiseworthy, but in the Kali age, the dharma of material possessions prevails.

In the Kṛta age, the perfection of knowledge comes from meditation; likewise, in the Tretā age, it comes from austerity; in the Dvāpara age, knowledge comes from sacrifice; and in the Kali age, it comes from the worship of images.
Whatever the merit or the sin may be, its fruit is indeed of that same nature; through differences in substance, body, and limb, there occurs diminution, increase, decay, and so forth.
For unrighteousness is of the nature of harm, while righteousness is of the nature of happiness; from unrighteousness one obtains suffering, and from righteousness indeed happiness increases.

One should know that suffering arises from improper conduct regarding knowledge, while happiness arises from proper conduct; therefore, one should strive for the acquisition of dharma for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should provide a livelihood for a hundred years to a Brahmin together with his family consisting of four persons; that gift bestows the world of Brahmā.
They know that a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts bestows the world of Brahmā; a Kṣatriya should perform them for the sake of establishing a family of a thousand members.

One should know that ten thousand [repetitions] grant the world of Indra, while a hundred thousand grant the world of Brahmā; whatever deity a person places at the forefront when performing a gift [is the one to whom it accrues].
Those who know the Vedas understand that one attains those respective worlds; likewise, one who is destitute of wealth should always perform purification through austerity.
Having reached a sacred ford and through austerity, one enjoys imperishable happiness; now, with a well-composed mind, I shall explain the acquisition of wealth through righteous means.
A Brāhmaṇa should acquire wealth through the acceptance of gifts and by officiating at sacrifices with purity, and without resorting to wretchedness or excessive hardship.

The Kṣatriya attains success through the strength of his arms; the Vaiśya, through agriculture and the protection of cattle; and [the Śūdra] attains perfection through the giving of wealth acquired by righteous means.

Through the attainment of knowledge, the attainment of liberation occurs for all by the grace of the Guru; from liberation, the perfection of one's true nature arises, and one partakes in supreme bliss.
O twice-born ones, all of this indeed arises for men from association with the virtuous; a householder should certainly give away all things such as wealth and grain.
Whatever kind of object, fruit, or even grain is available at any given time, all of that should indeed be given to the Brāhmaṇas by one who desires his own welfare.
Water and food should always be given for the pacification of the affliction of hunger; likewise, the field, grain, raw food, and cooked food—thus food is of four kinds.
For as long as one thrives by hearing [the teaching] after having eaten a certain food, half of the merit earned during that time belongs to the giver; of this there is no doubt.
One should effect the purification of sin by giving away what has been seized or by means of austerity; otherwise, one shall go to the Raurava hell.

One should divide one's own wealth into three parts for the sake of dharma, for increase, and for one's own enjoyment; and one should perform daily, occasional, and optional rites according to dharma.

The practitioner should effect the increase of wealth by means of the portion for growth; he should enjoy his possessions through the portion for enjoyment, in a manner that is beneficial, moderate, and measured.

One-tenth of the wealth earned through agriculture must indeed be given for the purification of sin; with the remainder, one should perform dharma and other duties, otherwise one shall go to the Raurava hell.
Alternatively, if he should become evil-minded or truly suffer loss, a wise man should indeed take a sixth part from the profits of his trade.
In the case of a pure acceptance of a gift, the best of the twice-born should give a fourth part; however, when wealth arises unexpectedly, the best of the twice-born should indeed give half.
One should cast into the ocean all ill-bestowed gifts received from unworthy persons; a gift should be given only after being invited, for the sake of the prosperity of one's own enjoyment.
Everything asked for should always be given according to one's own capacity; for if the requested object is not given, one will indeed become a debtor in another birth.
A wise person should not praise the faults of others; especially so, O Brahmin, should one refrain from speaking of what has been heard or seen [of them].
A wise person should not speak anything that causes anger in the hearts of all living beings; and for the sake of attaining sovereign power, one should perform the fire-ritual at the two twilights.

But if one is unable [to perform both], then at a single time, according to the prescribed rule, one should offer rice, grain, clarified butter, fruit, a tuber, or likewise a sacrificial oblation, to both the Sun and the Fire.

One should prepare the *sthālīpāka* according to the rule and according to the prescribed ritual; or, in the absence of sacrificial offerings, one may perform merely the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*).
The wise know that constant application is called "perpetual" (ajasram); alternatively, it may consist of mere recitation or even the salutation of the Sun.
Thus those seeking their own welfare should act for the sake of their purpose according to the rules, being constantly devoted to the Brahma-sacrifice as well as to the worship of the gods.
Those who are constantly devoted to the worship of fire, as well as those intent on the worship of the guru, and who bring satisfaction to the brahmins—all such people are partakers of heaven.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: O Lord, please tell us in due order about the sacrifice to Agni, the sacrifice to the gods, and likewise the sacrifice to Brahman, as well as the worship of the guru and the satisfaction of the Veda.

Sūta said: Whatever substance one offers into the fire is called the Agni-sacrifice; indeed, for those residing in the stage of the religious student (brahmacarya), it consists solely of the placing of fuel-sticks.

O twice-born ones, for those in the first stage of life, there are likewise the ritual of kindling the fire with fuel, the observance of vows, and other specific sacrifices, continuing until the establishment of the domestic fire (aupāsana).
O twice-born ones, for forest-dwelling ascetics who have internalized the sacred fires within themselves, their offering consists of wholesome, moderate, and pure food eaten at the proper time.
Beginning with the kindling of the *aupāsana* fire, it is well-protected; whether in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or in a vessel (*bhāṇḍa*), that [fire] is declared to be perpetual (*ajasra*).
When the fire is certainly placed within oneself or in the kindling woods due to the power of a king or fate, out of fear of abandoning the sacred fire, it is said to be "deposited" (samāropita).
O twice-born ones, the evening oblation to Agni should be known as "wealth-bestowing," while the morning oblation to Sūrya is likewise to be understood as "life-prolonging."

For this is declared to be the fire-sacrifice (agniyajña), performed by day because of the sun's setting; it consists of that which one offers into the fire, dedicating it to all the gods beginning with Indra.

One should know that the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña) consists of rituals such as the sthālīpāka; likewise, rites beginning with the tonsure ceremony (caula) are to be understood as established in the common (laukika) fire.
A twice-born man should perform the Brahmayajña once for the satisfaction of the gods; that which is called Brahmayajña is the study of the Veda.
This month follows immediately after the Nitya; it is not prescribed thereafter. Listen with faith and respect to the sacrifice to the gods performed without fire.
In the beginning of creation, the Lord Mahādeva, the omniscient and compassionate one, fashioned the Vārāṇasīs for the benefit of all the worlds.
The omniscient physician of saṃsāra, the Lord who is the medicine for all medicines, first made his own day a turn that bestows health.
Then, after the birth of the Kumāra and once the difficult passage [of childbirth] was over, he made a vow for the attainment of his own supernatural power (māyā) and its excellence.
The Lord ordained a day for the removal of sloth and evil, and likewise for the protection of Viṣṇu, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
For the sake of nourishment and for the sake of protection, the Lord ordained a day; thereafter, he established a day that bestows long life, specifically for the one who creates long lives.
Indeed, for the sake of accomplishing the longevity of the world, the Lord ordained a day for Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the creator of the three worlds.
In the beginning, for the sake of the increase of the three worlds, merit and demerit were established; from those two [arose] the offices of Indra and Yama, the makers of those [results].
It is ordained as the bestower of enjoyments and the remover of death for the worlds; it reveals the sun and other luminaries in their true forms, which indicate pleasure and pain.
Having first conceived the lords of the days as established within the wheel of the luminaries, their worship on their respective days bestows their own specific fruits.
Health, prosperity, the pacification of diseases, nourishment, longevity, enjoyment, and the avoidance of death—in this sequence.
They declare that the fruit of the sequence of days is preceded by the propitiation of the deities; Śiva is the bestower of the fruit even for the worship of other gods.
For the pleasure of the gods, worship is ordained as fivefold: the recitation of their respective mantras, burnt offerings (homa), giving (dāna), and likewise austerity (tapas).
On the sacrificial ground, in an image, in the fire, and in the person of a Brāhmaṇa—this is indeed the propitiation performed with the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāras).
Due to the progressive superiority [of each subsequent one], in the absence of the preceding, the following [is used] for the pacification of diseases of the eyes, the head, and leprosy.
Having worshipped the Sun, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas for a day, a month, a year, or even for three years.

If the *prārabdha* karma is powerful, diseases, old age, and so forth may perish; the wise know that the fruit of reciting mantras and the like for one's chosen deity, as well as [the results of observing] days of the week and other such factors, [is likewise subject to this].
One should especially offer the pacification of evil on the first day of the lunar fortnight; for among the gods, it is particularly beneficial when offered to Āditya and to Brāhmaṇas.
On Mondays, a wise person should worship Lakṣmī and the other deities for the sake of prosperity; likewise, he should feed Brahmins together with their wives with offerings of ghee and rice.
On a Tuesday, one should worship Kāli and the other deities for the pacification of obstacles, and one should feed Brahmins with a meal consisting of black gram, mung beans, and cooked rice.
Likewise, on a Monday, a wise person should worship Viṣṇu with curd-rice; thereby, there is always prosperity in one's sons, friends, wife, and other kin.

Desiring long life on the day of Jupiter, or for the sake of the accomplishment of nourishment for the gods, the wise man should perform sacrifice with the sacred thread, a garment, milk, and clarified butter.
On a Saturday, for the sake of enjoyment, one should worship the gods with a concentrated mind and offer food endowed with the six flavors for the satisfaction of the Brahmins.

Likewise, for the satisfaction of women, auspicious items such as clothing should be given. O wise one, during the transit of Saturn (Manda), which removes untimely death, one should worship the Rudras and the goddesses.
One should worship the deities by means of an oblation of sesame seeds, by giving gifts, and by feeding them with sesame-rice; thus sacrificing, one shall obtain fruits such as good health.
In the constant sacrifice to the gods and in special sacrifices as well, in bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and in the satiation of the Brahmins;
In the conjunctions of lunar days and constellations, during the worship of their respective deities, and on the days of the week beginning with Sunday, the omniscient Lord of the World [is present].
In each respective form, he bestows fruits such as health upon all, according to the place and time, as well as according to the capacity of the recipient.
According to one's faith in the substance, as well as in accordance with worldly custom, the deity bestows health and other blessings in a graduated sequence.

At the beginning of an auspicious period, at the end of an inauspicious one, and on the days of one's birth-stars and house-entries, a householder should worship the planets, beginning with the Sun, for the sake of attaining health and other prosperities.
Therefore, indeed, a sacrificial ground for the gods bestows all desired fruits; for Brahmins it is accompanied by mantras, and for others it is according to the Tantras.
Men who desire auspicious results should always perform [this] on all seven days of the week, according to their ability and in accordance with their circumstances.
A poor man should worship the gods through austerity, while a wealthy man should do so with his riches; furthermore, he performs such dharma with faith.
Furthermore, after enjoying various pleasures, he is born upon the earth as a tree providing shade, a reservoir of water, an image of Brahmā, or a storehouse of righteousness.
One who possesses wealth should always perform [these acts] for the successful attainment of enjoyments; and through time and the ripening of merit, the perfection of knowledge arises.
O twice-born ones, the man who hears this chapter, or reads it, or even assists in its hearing, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice to the gods.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: "O Sūta, best among those who know all things, tell us in due order about the locations and other factors. Sūta said: "A pure house yields equal results in rites such as sacrifices to the gods."
Ten times more than that is a cow-pen; ten times more than that is a riverbank; ten times more than that is the root of a bilva, tulasī, or aśvattha tree.
One should know that [the merit of] a temple is ten times that of a general holy place; ten times that of a river; and ten times that of a river at a holy site.
The bank of the seven Gaṅgās would be ten times more meritorious than that; likewise the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Kāverī, and Tāmraparṇikā.
The Sindhu, Sarayū, and Revā are proclaimed as the seven Gaṅgās; from there, ten [yojanas] to the shore of the ocean, and ten more on the mountain peak.

That which is superior to all else should be known as that in which the mind finds delight; likewise, it should be understood that sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts yield their full fruit when performed therein.

In the Tretā Yuga it is remembered as three-quarters, and in the Dvāpara it is always known as half; in the Kali age it should be understood as one quarter, and in the period following that, it is less than a quarter.

The wise know that for one of pure soul, a day of purity yields merit equal to [the merit of] a sacred occasion; therefore, O wise ones, it should be understood that the merit tenfold greater occurs at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti).

At the equinox, it is ten times that; at the solstice, it is remembered as ten times that; at the transit of the sun into Capricorn, it is ten times that; and during a lunar eclipse, it is ten times that.
And therefore, they know that during a solar eclipse at the most excellent full time, it brings disease to the Sun, who is the form of the world, due to his conjunction with Rāhu.

Therefore, for the sake of pacifying that poison, one should perform ablutions, gifts, and recitations; because it is the time intended for the pacification of poison, that time is remembered as merit-bestowing.

They know that on one's birth-star and at the conclusion of a vow, [the time] is like an eclipse of the sun; and they know that the time of association with the great is like ten million solar eclipses.
Those established in austerity, those established in knowledge, as well as yogis and ascetics—these indeed are worthy recipients of worship, for they are the cause of the destruction of sin.
Or, by performing twenty-four hundred thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a worthy recipient who bestows the enjoyment of the full fruit [of his merit].
In the scriptures, the term *pātra* is employed because it protects (*trāyate*) from falling; and because it protects the donor from sin (*pātaka*), it is designated as a *pātra*.
Indeed, it is called Gāyatrī because it protects the singer from falling; for just as one who is destitute of wealth in this world does not bestow wealth upon another.
In this world, he who is possessed of wealth and bestows it upon another—being himself pure and of purified soul—is worthy to save men.
Indeed, one who is purified by the recitation of the Gāyatrī is called a pure Brāhmaṇa; therefore, in giving, in recitation, in fire-offerings, in worship, and in every ritual act—
A Brāhmaṇa is worthy to receive a gift and likewise to protect it; however, for food, the worthy recipient consists of both men and women who are hungry.

Having summoned an excellent Brahmin at the proper time with a well-composed mind, he spoke words concerning that matter which were meaningful, conducive to true awakening, and bestowing of desired fruits.
They know that a gift given by one who possesses desire yields the full fruit; however, they know that what is given immediately after a question yields only half the fruit.

O best of the twice-born, they know that what is given to a servant of such a person yields only a quarter of the fruit; however, this is not the case for a Brahmin who is merely by birth but is destitute of livelihood.
For wealth given for the sake of enjoyment in this world lasts for ten years; but for a Brahmin endowed with Vedic knowledge, it lasts for ten years in heaven.
For a Brahmin devoted to Viṣṇu who is engaged in the recitation of the Gāyatrī, that which is given for ten years is known to grant residence in Vaikuṇṭha, provided it is done with truthfulness.
They know that what is given to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva bestows Kailāsa; indeed, the giving of gifts by all is intended for the sake of enjoying those respective worlds.
A man who gives food consisting of ten ingredients to a Brahmin on a Sunday enjoys good health for ten years in his next birth.
Great respect, summoning, anointing, service at the feet, providing clothing, worship with perfumes and the like, and an abundance of ghee, cakes, and excellent rice.
The six flavors, side dishes, betel leaf with the right hand placed above the left, salutation, following behind [the guest], and the gift of excellent food—this constitutes the ten-fold offering.
A man who gives food consisting of ten ingredients to ten Brahmins on a Sunday likewise enjoys good health for a hundred years.
The fruit of the gift of food on days such as Monday and the rest should be understood to possess the specific quality of that particular weekday, both in this world and in the next birth.
By giving food consisting of ten ingredients to ten people on all seven days of the week for a hundred years, one enjoys health and other benefits.
Thus, by giving to a hundred Brahmins on a Sunday, a man enjoys good health for a thousand years throughout the entire world.

Likewise, by giving [gifts] for thousands [of years], one enjoys [the fruit] for ten thousand years; thus indeed should it be understood by the wise regarding the days of the week, beginning with Monday.
On Sunday, by giving food to thousands whose minds are purified by the Gāyatrī mantra, one indeed attains health and other blessings in the world of Satya.
Likewise, by giving ten thousand [loads], one enjoys [the fruits] in the world of Viṣṇu; but by giving food in the measure of a hundred thousand, one enjoys them in the world of Rudra.
Indeed, seekers of knowledge should give [gifts] to children with the thought that they are Brahmā; and men seeking sons should give to youths with the thought that they are Viṣṇu.

O Rudra, those men who seek knowledge should indeed offer gifts to the elders with the understanding that they are [the personified] Vedas; and the best of men who desire wisdom should offer them to children and women with the understanding that they are the [goddess] Bhāratī.

Those best of men who desire enjoyment should give to young women with the thought that they are Lakṣmī; those people who seek their own welfare should give to old women with the thought that they are Pārvatī.
That which is acquired through righteous conduct, by gleaning grains, or as a teacher’s fee, is called "pure substance"; the wise know it to be the bestower of full results.
Wealth acquired from receiving gifts from pure persons is called middling; wealth associated with agriculture and trade is called inferior.
They say that for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, wealth acquired through valor and trade is the most excellent; for Śūdras, it is that acquired as wages.

The wealth of women seeking religious merit—whether inherited from their fathers or received from their husbands—as well as cows and other such items, belongs to the twelve [deities] in the sequence beginning with Caitra.
Or, having gathered together at an auspicious time, one should give for the fulfillment of desired goals: cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, and molasses.
Silver, salt, and a pumpkin, as well as twelve virgins, [are offered] along with the gift of a cow, provided milk, and beneficial cow-dung.

The removal of misfortunes associated with wealth, grain, and the like is accomplished [by fire]; however, the removal of misfortunes associated with water, oil, and the like is accomplished by cow's urine.
Furthermore, the wise should understand that the nourishment of the three types of protection—bodily and so forth—is likewise achieved through milk, curd, and clarified butter.

O twice-born ones, the gift of land is for the sake of stability both in this world and the next; indeed, they know that the gift of sesame seeds is for the sake of strength and always leads to victory over death.
Gold increases the digestive fire and likewise bestows vigor; one should know that clarified butter brings nourishment, and they understand clothing to be a giver of long life.
Grain and cooked food for the sake of prosperity; molasses which provides sweet food; silver for the sake of increasing semen; and salt for the sake of the six flavors.
O twice-born ones, they know the Kūṣmāṇḍa [mantra] to be for the sake of the complete success of everything, bestowing nourishment and granting all enjoyments both in this world and in the next.
Indeed, the gift of a maiden bestows liberation for as long as one lives, while the fruit of trees such as the jackfruit, mango, and wood-apple bestows worldly enjoyment.

Likewise, the fruit of medicinal plants such as the plantain (kadali), as well as that produced from shrubs; and the fruit of black gram (māṣa) and mung beans (mudga), as well as leafy vegetables and the like.
Likewise, vegetables such as *marīca* and mustard seeds, as well as whatever fruit is prepared according to the season—that indeed should be given by a wise person.

The wise man should always grant satisfaction to the sense organs, such as the ear, for the sake of the ten enjoyments beginning with sound, and he should also grant contentment to the directions and other elements.
Having acquired the Vedic scriptures and understood them personally from the mouth of a guru, the conviction that "there is a fruit of actions" is called āstikya (theistic faith).

If one lacks the capacity due to fear of a relative or a king, then one's resolve and faith are diminished; in the absence of all these, even a poor person should worship through speech or through action.
One should know that verbal sacrifice consists of mantras, hymns of praise, recitation, and so forth; indeed, they understand physical sacrifice to consist of pilgrimages, vows, and the like.
By whatever means it may be—whether little or much—that which is performed with the thought of offering to the deity serves for one's enjoyment.
Both austerity and charity must always be practiced; one should also provide shelter for those adorned with the virtues of their own caste.

For the great satisfaction of the gods, this [rite] bestows all enjoyments; through it, the wise man shall obtain an excellent birth in this world and the next, along with eternal enjoyment. Indeed, by performing it with the intention of dedicating it to the Lord, one shall attain the fruit of liberation.
The man who constantly recites this chapter or listens to it shall develop a mind devoted to righteousness and attain the perfection of knowledge.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O best of beings, tell us the procedure for the worship of the earthen image, by which ritual of worship all desired goals are attained.
Sūta said: You have asked a most excellent question, which always bestows all desired objects and immediately pacifies suffering; listen, for I shall speak to you.
O twice-born ones, it wards off untimely death, destroys even death at its appointed time, and immediately bestows wife, sons, wealth, and grain.

Since from it everything arises—food and the like for consumption, as well as clothing and so forth—it is therefore the worship of images made of clay and other materials that grants one's desires on this earth.
The entitlement for both men and women in this matter is certain; one should take earth from within the water of a river, a pond, or a well.
Having purified it with fragrant powder and ground it well in a beautiful pavilion, one should fashion the image with one's own hands, thoroughly prepared with milk.
Having visualized her as endowed with all major and minor limbs, equipped with weapons, and seated upon the lotus posture, one should indeed worship her with great reverence.
A twice-born man should always worship Vighneśa, Āditya, Viṣṇu, Ambā, and Śiva, as well as the Śivaliṅga of Śiva.
One should perform [the worship] with the sixteen types of offerings for the sake of attaining that fruit; one should perform the sprinkling with flowers and the consecration accompanied by mantras.
The entire offering of cooked rice (śālyanna) should be measured by one kuḍava; however, in a human dwelling, one kuḍava is understood to be equivalent to one prastha.

For an offering to the gods, three *prasthas* are appropriate; for the Self-born (Brahmā), five *prasthas*. Know that in this way the fruit is complete, while two or three more would indeed be excessive.
By performing a thousandfold worship, a twice-born man truly attains the world of truth (Satyaloka). [The image should be] twelve finger-breadths in length, or twice that, or even more.
A single measure of the finger-breadth, and above that three sets of five; a vessel made of iron or wood is called "auspicious" (śiva) by the wise.
An eighth part of that is a *prastha*, which is considered to be four *kuḍavas*; likewise, there are ten *prasthas*, a hundred *prasthas*, and even a thousand *prasthas*.
The "Great Worship" (mahāpūjā) is said to consist of water, oil, and other fragrant substances used in appropriate measures for [the images of] humans, ṛṣis, and self-manifested deities.

From the consecration (abhiṣeka), there is purification of the self; from the fragrance, merit is obtained; from the food offering (naivedya), longevity and satisfaction are gained; and from the incense, wealth is attained.
One obtains knowledge from the lamp and enjoyment from the betel leaf; therefore, one should diligently perform the sixfold rite beginning with the bath.
Both prostration and the recitation of mantras bestow all desired objects; they should always be performed at the conclusion of worship by men seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having first honored them mentally, a person should always perform those respective acts; indeed, by the worship of the gods, one shall attain their respective worlds.
And in those intermediate worlds, whatever objects of enjoyment one desires are obtained; O twice-born ones, listen with faith as I shall explain their specific details.
By properly worshipping Vighneśa, one shall obtain all desired things in this world; especially on a Friday, or on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the months of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada.

In the month of Dhanus, during the Bhiṣag-Ṛkṣa (the constellation Aśleṣā), one should worship Vighneśa according to the prescribed rites; one may perform a hundred or a thousand worships, continuing for that same number of days.
Through constant faith in the gods and the sacred fire, it bestows sons and desired objects upon men; it pacifies all sins and destroys every kind of misfortune.

They know the worship of the days of the week (vārapūjā) to be that which bestows self-purification for Śiva and the others; it is the support for the lunar days, asterisms, and yogas, and it fulfills all desires.
Likewise, because it is devoid of increase and decrease, the wise know it to be the nature of the full Brahman; for all actions, beginning with the creation of Brahmā, arise from its arising.
Indeed, worship of the deities at the beginning of the lunar day (tithi) bestows full enjoyment upon men; however, for the ancestors, the first half of the night is recommended for their rites.
The latter part of the day is praised for the gods; if that lunar day (tithi) extends through midday, it should be accepted as occurring during the day.

Likewise, having properly examined the auspicious lunar mansions and other factors for the sake of the deity’s rites, one should perform worship, recitation, and so forth, taking into account the days of the week and other such details.
For "pūjā" is so called because one is honored by means of it; thus is the meaning applied to the Vedas, and through that ritual action, the accomplishment of the fruit of complete enjoyment arises.

Likewise, mental dispositions and knowledge arise from the application of desired objects of enjoyment; for in this way, the very meaning of the word "pūjā" (worship) is renowned in both worldly usage and the Vedas.

The daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites [are purified] by time; when the optional (kāmya) rite is properly performed, it purifies the daily rite, the month, the fortnight, and the year, respectively.
The attainment of the fruits of various respective actions and the gradual destruction of corresponding sins occur through the worship of Mahāgaṇapati on the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight.
The worship performed on the fourth lunar day of the month of Caitra destroys the sins of the fortnight, bestows the fruits of enjoying the fortnight, and grants the rewards for the entire month.

It should be known that this bestows the enjoyment of a rain of wealth when performed during the months of Siṃha or Bhādrapada, on a Sunday coinciding with the asterism Śravaṇā, on the seventh lunar day, and under the asterism Hasta.

On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform the worship of Āditya; and on the twelfth day of the bright fortnights of Jyeṣṭha, Bhādrapada, and Mārgaśīrṣa, under the asterism Śravaṇa.
They know that the worship of Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day brings about desired prosperity; the worship of Viṣṇu in the month of Śrāvaṇa bestows desired health.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving the twelve objects beginning with a cow, along with their ancillaries, that same fruit one attains by offering libations to Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship twelve Brahmins with the twelve names of Viṣṇu using the sixteen types of ritual offerings; thus, one shall attain His pleasure.
And thus, by means of the twelve names corresponding to each of all the gods, the twelvefold Brahma-sacrifice shall become a source of gratification for each respective deity.
On a Monday in the month of Karkaṭaka, on the ninth lunar day under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, one who desires prosperity should worship Ambā, the bestower of all enjoyments and fruits.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja bestows all desired fruits; it is especially so on a Sunday, and particularly on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Worship of Śiva is especially distinguished during Ārdrā and Mahārdrā; on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, it bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
It bestows long life, removes death, and grants all accomplishments to men; this occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the Mahārdrā nakṣatra, on the fourteenth day as well.
Or, on the day of Ārdrā in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped Śiva in His respective form with the sixteen services, one indeed beholds His feet.

The worship of Śiva should be known as that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; indeed, the worship of the deities presiding over the days of the week and so forth is especially distinguished during the month of Kārttika.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, the wise man should worship all the gods through gifts, austerity, burnt offerings, recitation, and observances.
By means of the sixteen services, the image, and the mantras of the Brahmins, as well as by feeding the Brahmins, one becomes a remover of suffering for those free from desire.
In the month of Kārttika, a sacrifice to the gods bestows all enjoyments; it shall indeed remove diseases and bring about the destruction of malevolent spirits and planetary influences.
By worshipping the Sun on Sundays during the month of Kārttika, and by the gift of oil and cotton, there shall be the destruction of leprosy and other ailments for men.
Through the gift of *harītakī* and black pepper, the giving of clothing, milk, and so forth, and through the consecration of a Brahmin, the wasting disease (*kṣayaroga*) shall be destroyed.
From the offering of lamps and mustard seeds, epilepsy shall be destroyed; for men, the worship of Śiva on the Kṛttikā constellation and on Mondays [yields great merit].
It shall pacify great poverty and bring about all forms of prosperity, through the gift of houses, fields, and so forth, as well as household utensils and the like.
By worshipping Skanda on Tuesdays falling under the Kṛttikā nakṣatra, and by the gift of lamps, bells, and other offerings, men shall indeed attain mastery over speech before long.
For men, worshiping Viṣṇu on the days of the Kṛttikās and on Mondays, as well as the gift of curd-rice, shall bring about a virtuous lineage.
During the asterism Kṛttikā on Thursdays, by performing sacrifices for Brahmā with wealth, and through the gift of honey, gold, and clarified butter, an increase in enjoyments shall come to men.
By performing the sacrifice with an elephant on a Friday coinciding with the Kṛttikā constellation, [one attains the desired result].
By the gift of perfumes, flowers, and food, there shall be an increase in the objects of enjoyment for men.

A barren woman obtains a virtuous son through the gift of gold, silver, and other such items; likewise, on Tuesdays coinciding with the Kṛttikā constellation, one should perform the salutation of the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas).
And the worship of the world-elephants, the serpents, and the guardians of the bridge, as well as of Tryambaka Rudra and Viṣṇu, the remover of sins.
It bestows knowledge upon Brahmā, as well as upon Dhanvantari and the Aśvins; it removes disease and untimely death, and grants peace from afflictions at any time.
Through the giving of salt, iron, oil, and black gram (māṣa) and other grains; and through the giving of the three pungents (trikaṭu), fruits, perfumes, water, and so forth.
By offering liquids and solids measured by a *prastha* and a *pala* respectively during the dawn hour in the month of Dhanus, one attains heaven; indeed, worship at that time is highly meritorious.
For the attainment of all perfections, it is declared that for Śiva and all others, an offering of śāli rice and sacrificial oblations (haviṣya) is prescribed in due order.
In the month of Dhanus, an offering of various kinds of food is especially recommended; in Mārgaśīrṣa, for one who gives food alone, every desired fruit shall come to pass.
The destruction of evil, the accomplishment of desired goals, health, and indeed righteousness; as well as the correct thorough understanding of the Vedas and their right practice.
One who gives food during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall obtain great enjoyments in this world and the next, eternal union [with the Divine], and the perfection of knowledge of the Vedānta.
One who desires worldly enjoyments should worship the gods at dawn during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for three days; however, he shall not be subject to the restrictions of the Dhanur-māsa vow.
The month of Dhanus is prescribed to last until the time of saṃgava; during this month of Dhanus, one should remain without food for a full month, having conquered the senses.
Until midday, the Brahmin should recite the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; thereafter, he should recite mantras such as the five-syllabled one up to seven times.
Having attained this knowledge, a Brahmin shall obtain liberation at the end of the body; for other men and women, it is achieved through bathing three times daily and the recitation of mantras.
By constantly reciting the five-syllable mantra alone, pure knowledge is attained; by always chanting one's chosen mantra, one obtains the destruction of great sins.
Especially during the month of Dhanus, one should perform a great offering of food (mahānaivedya) consisting of a bhāra of śāli rice and a prastha of black pepper.
The twelfth [offering] consists of all these counted together: a kuḍava each of honey and clarified butter, along with a droṇa of mung beans and twelve side dishes.
With cakes fried in ghee, sweetmeats, śālikā and other such foods, and with twelve portions of curd and milk, measured by twelve prasthas.
Likewise, together with coconuts and other fruits, it is accompanied by twelve betel nuts and provided with thirty-six leaves.
When it is combined with camphor, powdered sugar, and the five fragrant substances, along with betel leaf, it possesses the characteristics of a great food offering (mahānaivedya).
This great offering (mahānaivedya), having first been dedicated to the deity, should be distributed to His devotees according to the sequence of their castes.
Thus, by offering cooked rice as a sacrificial oblation, one becomes a ruler of the realm on earth; by the gift of a great sacrificial oblation, a man attains heaven.
O best of the twice-born, by the gift of a thousand great food-offerings (mahānaivedya), one shall attain a full lifespan in that world, Satyaloka.
And by the offering of thirty thousand great sacrificial foods (mahā-naivedya), having attained the world above that, one shall not be subject to rebirth again.
The offering of food (naivedya) is said to consist of thirty-six thousand [units]; when that much of the gift of food is offered, it is called "Great Fullness" (mahāpūrṇa).
The food offering for Mahāpūrṇa is considered the "birth-offering" (janmanaiivedya); by the giving of this birth-offering, rebirth no longer exists.

On an auspicious day in the month of Kārttika, one should perform the offering of food (naivedya) for the sake of one's birth; this should be done when the day is joined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti), one's birth asterism, the full moon, or other such occasions.

On the anniversary of one's birth, one should perform the excellent "birth-offering" (janmanaiivedya); likewise, during other months, on the day of the birth-asterism (janmarkṣa), and on the day of the full yoga.
Or even by mixing them slowly, one should perform it for a thousand [repetitions]; by the offering of one's very birth, one obtains the fruit of surrendering one's life.
Indeed, through the offering of one's birth, Śiva is pleased and grants His own union; therefore, one should cause this very offering of one's birth to be presented to Śiva alone.
In the form of the yoni and liṅga, Śiva is the determiner of birth; therefore, for the sake of ceasing rebirth, the worship of Śiva is indeed the [true] birth.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of Bindu and Nāda; Bindu is Śakti and Nāda is Śiva, and thus the world is composed of Śiva and Śakti.
This Bindu has Nāda as its support, and this world has Bindu as its support; for indeed, Bindu and Nāda are established as the foundation of the world.
Everything joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda* constitutes the process of *sakalīkaraṇa*; through this *sakalīkaraṇa*, one undoubtedly attains birth in the world.
The Liṅga, consisting of Bindu and Nāda, is said to be the cause of the universe; Bindu is the Goddess, Nāda is Śiva, and together they are called the Śivaliṅga.
Therefore, for the sake of ending rebirth, one should worship the Śivaliṅga; the Goddess is the Mother in the form of the Bindu, and Śiva is the Father in the form of Nāda.
When one's parents have been honored, there is indeed supreme bliss; for the sake of attaining that supreme bliss, one should worship the Śivaliṅga.
She is the Goddess, the mother of the worlds; he is Śiva, the father of the worlds. Indeed, compassion increases ever more for one who constantly serves his parents.
Indeed, through compassion, it bestows upon the worshiper the sovereignty that lies within; therefore, O best of sages, for the sake of attaining the bliss contained therein, [one should practice].
One should worship the Śivaliṅga in the form of one's father and mother; for Bharga is indeed the Puruṣa, while Bhargā is said to be Prakṛti.
The embryo whose internal substratum is unmanifest is called Puruṣa; the embryo whose internal substratum is manifest is called Prakṛti.
Since the progenitor possesses a womb containing the essence of manhood and so forth, his first birth is rightly described as being produced from a man.
The manifestation of primordial nature (prakṛti) is called the second birth; a living being undergoes birth and death through the Person (puruṣa).

It is necessarily cultivated from another source, and its birth is said to be through illusion (māyā); because it decays from the time of birth, it is therefore remembered as the "jīva" (the living one).
For it is indeed the referent of the term "jīva" that is bound and stretched by the fetters; therefore, for the sake of removing the fetters of birth, one should worship the Janmaliṅga.

Because it undergoes expansion (*bhaṃ vṛddhiṃ gacchati*), *bhaga* is said to be *prakṛti* (primordial nature) by implication; for she is the enjoyment of the primordial senses, such as sound and the rest, which consist of the primordial elements.

The primary etymological meaning of the word *bhoga* is "the enjoyment of this [world] belonging to Bhaga. However, Bhaga in its primary sense is *prakṛti*, while the Lord (*bhagavān*) is said to be Śiva.
The Blessed One is indeed the giver of fortune; no other is the bestower of fortune. The Blessed One is the Lord of Fortune (Bhaga), and is thus called Bharga by the wise.
The linga is accompanied by the yoni, and the yoni is joined with the linga; for the sake of enjoyment in this world and the next, and indeed for the sake of eternal enjoyment.
One should worship the Blessed Mahādeva, the Śiva-liṅga; the Sun is the progenitor of the world, and his emblem arises from that act of procreation.

A person should worship the possessor of the *liṅga* (the embodied soul) through the *liṅga* (the instrument of manifestation). That which serves as a sign to indicate the meaning of the *liṅga* is called a *liṅga*.
Indeed, that which leads the person (puruṣa) to the meaning, Śiva, is called a *liṅga*; furthermore, the union of the signs (*cihna*) of Śiva and Śakti is termed a *liṅga*.

Through the worship of one's own insignia, the Lord is pleased and the function of the insignia does not fail; indeed, by means of the function of the insignia, rebirth and its like are brought to an end.
One should worship the Śiva-liṅga with ordinary persons, both external and internal, and with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
Thus, worship on Sunday indeed brings about the cessation of rebirth; on Sunday, one should worship the Great Liṅga with the Praṇava alone.

On the first day of the lunar fortnight, an ablution with the five products of the cow is especially distinguished; these five products (pañcagavya) consist of cow dung, cow urine, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
One should offer milk and other substances individually, as well as honey and sugarcane juices; the food offering of cow’s milk and rice should be presented with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
The Praṇava is the Dhvaniliṅga, while the Nādaliṅga belongs to the Self-born (Svayaṃbhū). The Binduliṅga is the Yantra, and the letter Ma is the Pratiṣṭhita.
The letter *U* is the mobile liṅga, and the letter *A* is the form of the Guru; by constantly worshipping these six liṅgas, one is liberated while living—of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, worship with devotion to Śiva brings liberation from rebirth for human beings; by wearing rudrākṣa beads one gains a quarter [of the merit], and by wearing sacred ash, half.
By reciting the mantra three times over and worshipping with complete devotion, a man who honors both the Śivaliṅga and the devotee shall attain liberation.
O twice-born ones, for one who reads or listens to this chapter with a concentrated mind, their devotion to Śiva increases and becomes very firm.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O great sage, O Lord, please tell us in due order the majesty of the Praṇava, the six marks (ṣaḍliṅga), and the worship of a devotee of Śiva.
Sūta said: "O you whose wealth is asceticism, this question has been rightly asked by you. Mahādeva alone knows the answer to it, and no one else."
Nevertheless, I shall indeed speak of that through the grace of Śiva alone; may Śiva, who is ours and yours, grant us abundant protection.
For the wise know the *praṇava* to be indeed a new, inner boat for the great ocean of saṃsāra, which is born of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The expansion (prapañca) is not non-existent for you; they know it as *praṇava*. Because it leads you pre-eminently (*prakarsena*) to liberation, they know it as *praṇava*.
For those yogis who recite their own mantras and for the worshiper of their own mantra, having brought about the exhaustion of all karma, there arises indeed a new, divine knowledge.
They describe that very one as free from illusion, as ever-new, as preeminent, as the Great-Souled One, and as having a fresh, pure nature.
The wise know that as the *praṇava* because it indeed brings forth anew; the *praṇava* is said to be twofold, distinguished by its subtle and gross aspects.

One should know the subtle to be the single-syllable mantra, while the wise know the gross to be the five-syllable mantra; the subtle consists of five unmanifest phonemes, whereas the other consists of clearly manifest phonemes.
For one who is liberated while living, the subtle contemplation of the meaning of the mantra is indeed the essence of all things, continuing until the dissolution of his own body.
When it has dissolved into one's own body, one certainly attains the perfect Śiva; however, one who merely recites mantras certainly attains Yoga.
One who performs thirty-six million recitations will certainly attain yoga. Furthermore, the subtle [yoga] should be known as twofold, through the distinction between short and long.
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M, followed by that which is joined with Bindu and Nāda, and endowed with the divisions of sound and time.
Indeed, the long *praṇava* is thus situated within the hearts of yogis alone; that *makāra*, which is the essence of the three, is called the short *praṇava*.
Śiva, Śakti, and their unity constitute the syllable *ma*, which is the essence of the triad; thus, this short [syllable] should indeed be recited by those desiring the destruction of all sins.
The earth, wind, gold, water, fire, ether, sound, and so forth—these ten, along with the ten directions, are said to have proceeded from the lineage of Āśā.

For those engaged in worldly activity, it is indeed short; for those who have withdrawn from activity, it is long. At the beginning of the *vyāhṛtis* and at the beginning of mantras, it may optionally be joined with the subtle element of sound (*śabdakalā*).
It should be employed at the beginning of the Vedas, as well as during the salutations at the two twilights; by reciting it nine crores of times, a person becomes completely purified.
Furthermore, by another ninety million [recitations], one shall attain victory over the earth; and again, by another ninety million, one shall indeed attain victory over the waters.

Furthermore, by reciting it nine crores of times, one attains victory over fire; again, by nine crores, one attains victory over wind; indeed, by reciting it nine crores of times, one attains victory over space.
By reciting [the mantra] nine crores for each of the elements beginning with smell in their respective order, and again by reciting it nine crores for the ego (ahaṃkāra).
By reciting the mantra one thousand times, a person becomes eternally pure; thereafter, O twice-born ones, the recitation is indeed for the sake of one's own spiritual accomplishment.
Furthermore, by reciting the *praṇava* one hundred and eight crores of times in this manner, one who has been awakened shall attain the pure yoga.
Endowed with pure yoga, he is liberated while living, without a doubt; constantly chanting and constantly meditating upon Śiva in the form of the Praṇava.

Established in samādhi, the great lord of yogis is indeed Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages, meters, deities, and so forth upon his body, he should then perform the recitation (japa).

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Praṇava together with the Mātṛkā upon the body, one becomes a seer (ṛṣi); one obtains all the fruits of nyāsa, such as the ten mothers, the six paths (adhvan), and so forth.
For those who are active and mixed, the gross praṇava is prescribed; these Śiva-yogins are of three types, engaged in ritual action, austerity, and recitation.
One who is endowed with wealth and other possessions, as well as with the limbs beginning with the hands, and with acts such as prostration and worship, is called a Kriyā-yogin.
One who is engaged in worship, moderate in diet, endowed with mastery over the external senses, and free from malice toward others, is called a practitioner of austerity (*tapoyogin*).
One who is always endowed with these qualities, though ever-angry and devoid of all desires and the like, yet is perpetually devoted to japa and remains tranquil—him they know as a *japayogin*.
By worshipping the Śiva-yogins with the sixteen types of offerings, a pure man shall attain liberation through the successive stages beginning with *sālokya*.
Now I shall speak of the yoga of recitation; listen as I speak, O twice-born ones! Recitation is declared for the practitioner of austerity, for by reciting it, one purifies oneself.

O twice-born ones, the five principles beginning with "Namaḥ" followed by the name of Śiva in the dative case constitute the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva, which is indeed the form of the gross Praṇava.
By the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra alone, a person shall attain all perfections; one should always recite the five-syllabled mantra preceded by the Praṇava (Om).

O twice-born ones, having received the instruction of the guru in a pleasant dwelling on auspicious ground, one should begin on the first day of the waxing moon and continue until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.

The month of Māgha and the month of Bhādrapada are distinguished as the most excellent among all times; having eaten sparingly only once [a day], one should remain restrained in speech and with senses controlled.
By constantly serving oneself, one's king, and one's ancestors, one becomes pure through merely a thousand recitations; otherwise, one remains a debtor.

One should recite the five-syllable mantra five hundred thousand times while recollecting Śiva—Śiva who is seated in the lotus posture, the bestower of auspiciousness, and endowed with the Gaṅgā and the digit of the moon.
And with Śakti seated upon his left thigh, he beheld that radiant Lord, surrounded by great hosts of attendants, holding a deer and an axe, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Constantly recollecting Sadāśiva, the bestower of perpetual grace, one should first worship him mentally within the heart or within the solar orb.
Facing the east and performing pure rites, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra on the morning of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, after having completed the daily obligatory duties.
In a delightful and pure place, self-restrained and with a purified mind, one should recite the five-syllable mantra twelve thousand times.

One should invite excellent Brahmins who are followers of Śiva along with their wives; one should also invite a single preeminent teacher who is disciplined and possesses a form of Śiva accompanied by Ambā.
Then [he honored] the five devotees of Śiva, O best of the twice-born: Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta.

Having procured the materials for worship, one should commence the worship of Śiva; and having performed the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rules, one should commence the fire-oblation (homa).

Having performed the concluding rite at the end of the mouth [of the fire] according to its own sūtra, one should commence the homa sacrifice, offering either ten, or one hundred, or even one thousand oblations.
The wise man should himself perform the oblation with ghee from a tawny cow, or he may have it performed by devotees of Śiva one hundred and eight times.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the guru, as well as a pair of cattle; and one should meditate upon those [deities] in the forms of Īśāna and the others, and upon the guru together with Ambā.
One should perform the ritual bathing of one's own head with the water that has washed their feet; one will immediately obtain the fruit of bathing in thirty-six million sacred fords (tīrthas).

One should indeed offer them food consisting of ten ingredients with devotion; however, one should regard the teacher’s wife as the Supreme Goddess (Parā), following the sequence beginning with Īśāna.
Having worshipped with excellent food according to the extent of one's wealth, preceded by rudrākṣas and cloth, and accompanied by vaṭakas and apūpas;

Then, having performed the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna), one should provide an abundant feast. Thereafter, having offered prayers to the Lord of Gods, one should complete the recitation of the mantra.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), a person becomes a true master of mantra; furthermore, by repeating it five hundred thousand times, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
Starting from Atala and proceeding in order up to Satyaloka, one shall attain mastery over each respective world through five hundred thousand recitations.

If one dies in the middle [of the practice], then at the end of his enjoyments he shall be born on earth as a reciter of that mantra; and again, by five hundred thousand recitations, he shall attain proximity to Brahman.
Furthermore, by five hundred thousand [recitations], one shall attain sovereignty with a form identical [to the deity]; by striking one hundred million, one shall become directly equal to Brahmā.
Having thus attained union with the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman), one indeed enjoys desired pleasures until the dissolution of that Brahman.
When another kalpa has passed, he will be born as the son of Brahmā; then, radiant with ascetic fervor, he will gradually attain liberation.
The worlds were indeed fashioned in succession from the elemental effects such as earth; these fourteen worlds, beginning with Pātāla and ending with Satya, include the realms of Brahmā.
Above Satyaloka and ending with Kṣamāloka, there are fourteen worlds of Viṣṇu; in Kṣamāloka resides Kāryaviṣṇu, and in Vaikuṇṭha, the excellent city, [resides Mūrtiviṣṇu].
Having performed protection for the great serpent through the splendor of his activity, he presides over it; and above that, twenty-eight pure worlds are situated.
In the pure world of Kailāsa, Rudra indeed resides within the heart of all beings; fifty-six worlds above that lead upward, ending with Ahiṃsā.
Resorting to non-violence as his light in the city of Jñānakailāsa, Kāryeśvara remains presiding there, having caused all other things to disappear.
At the end of that is indeed Kālacakra, and beyond that is Kālātīta; there, presided over by Śiva, is the one called Kāleśvara.
Adopting the nature of a buffalo, he joins all beings with time; for he is indeed untruthful, impure, violent, and pitiless.

He has falsehood and the like as his four feet; he possesses all [evil] parts and assumes forms at will. He is the Fortune of Atheism, a wicked companion, and always possesses a voice outside the Veda.
Krodhasaṅga is dark-complexioned and wears the guise of a great buffalo; he is called Maheśvara for that duration, and indeed, Tirodhā remains for that same length of time.
For below that is the experience of karma, while above that is the experience of knowledge; for below that is the māyā of karma, while above that is the māyā of knowledge.
Indeed, when the enjoyment of the fruits of karma departs, it is called *māyā*; indeed, when the enjoyment of knowledge departs, it is called *māyā*.
Indeed, they know that above that is eternal enjoyment, while below that it is perishable; and below that there is concealment, whereas above that there is no concealment.
For below that there is indeed bondage by the noose, but above that there is no bondage; below that, those who follow actions performed for desire continue to revolve.
The enjoyment of the fruit of desireless action is proclaimed to be above that; below that, those devoted to the worship of the *bindu* undergo transmigration.
For those who worship the Liṅga without desire certainly ascend upwards from that point; whereas those who worship deities other than Śiva revolve below it.
Those who are solely devoted to Śiva proceed beyond that; below that is the limit of individual souls (jīva), while above that they possess the supreme limit.
Those who are worldly remain below that [level], while those who are liberated indeed go above it; those who worship material substances revolve below that level.
For those who worship the material substance of the Puruṣa proceed upwards from that point; below that is the Śakti-liṅga, while above that is the Śiva-liṅga.
Below that, the Liṅga is enveloped; above that, it is indeed without enclosure. Below that, the Liṅga is conceptualized; above that, it is truly not conceptualized.
Below that is the external liṅga, and above that is the internal one; below that indeed are the hundred and twelve worlds of Śakti.

Indeed, that which is below it is of the nature of the Bindu, while that which is above it is of the nature of Nāda; that which is below it belongs to the world of karma, whereas that which is above it belongs to the world of knowledge.
Indeed, the salutation (namaskāra) following that destroys pride and egoism; for it is said that the concealment born of birth cannot remain unabolished.
For in this way, the very meaning of the word "knowledge" consists in the removal of concealment; indeed, those who worship the material (ādhibhautika) remain turned away from that [reality].
Only the internal worshippers indeed proceed further than that, as far as the portion of the altar within the great Liṅga whose self is light.
Even the eightfold bondage beginning with *prakṛti* is established within the end of experience (*vedyanta*). In this same manner, all such things, whether worldly or Vedic, are to be understood.
Those who are endowed with the virtues of truth and the like, and those who are devoted to the worship of Śiva, cross over the wheel of time mounted upon the buffalo of unrighteousness.
Above that stands Dharma in the form of a bull, embodying the nature of celibacy (brahmacarya) and endowed with truth and other virtues, situated at the forefront of the world of Śiva.
He whose horns were forbearance, whose ears were tranquility, who was adorned by the sound of the Vedas, whose eyes were faith, and whose mind was heavy with wisdom through his breath—such was Vṛṣa.
The "bulls of activity" and so forth are always to be understood as existing within the causes and other factors; that bull of activity, which is Dharma, abides beyond time.
The lifespan of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa is said to constitute a single day for each respective deity; beyond that, there is neither day nor night, nor birth, death, and so forth.

Furthermore, those ending with the truth of cause (kāraṇasatya) belong likewise to the causal Brahman (kāraṇabrahman); they are always fashioned from the elements beginning with smell (gandha), and beyond that [is the unmanifest].
Indeed, the fourteen worlds abide as the very nature of subtle fragrance; furthermore, the fourteen worlds abide within Kāraṇaviṣṇu.
Furthermore, the worlds of Kāraṇarudra are considered to be twenty-eight; and again, those of Kāraṇeśa, situated above them, are fifty-six.
Beyond that is the realm known as Brahmacharyaloka, which is approved by Śiva; it is located right there in Jñānakailāsa, endowed with five enclosures.
Therein indeed is the primordial Liṅga, endowed with the five maṇḍalas, possessed of the five digits of Brahmā, and united with the primordial Śakti.
This is declared to be the abode of Śiva, the Supreme Self; there, the Supreme Lord is united with His supreme power (Paraśakti).
He is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is proficient in the fivefold acts: creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.
He whose nature is always meditation and who is ever intent on bestowing grace, shines resplendent, seated in the posture of samādhi, delighting in his own self.
Through the rites of twilight worship, meditation, and so forth, performed in succession, and through the constant performance of ritual sacrifices, his mind becomes intent upon the action of Śiva.
One should establish the knowledge of Śiva through the rites and actions of the Śiva-kaṇṭhas; all those who have entered that vision are indeed liberated, without a doubt.

Liberation indeed consists in delighting in one's own self through the very nature of the Self; it is attained by being well-established in the practices of ritual action, austerity, recitation, knowledge, meditation, and dharma.
Having obtained the vision of Śiva, one indeed attains the state of delighting in one's own self, just as the sun dispels impurity by means of its own rays.
Śambhu, who is expert in compassion, will dispel ignorance; once ignorance has ceased, the knowledge of Śiva arises.

Through the knowledge of Śiva, one shall attain the state of finding delight in the Self, which is one’s own true nature; upon the perfect realization of this self-delight, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Furthermore, by one hundred lakhs [of recitations], one shall attain the station of Brahmā; and again, by another hundred lakhs, one shall reach the station of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, by a hundred lakhs [of recitations], one shall attain the state of Rudra; and again, by another hundred lakhs, one shall attain the state of Īśvara.
Furthermore, by means of such recitation alone, being well-composed in meditation, one shall indeed attain the Kālacakra, which consists of the worlds of Śiva and the rest.
The Kālacakra consists of five wheels; in each successive stage, the Brahmā-wheel is characterized by creation and delusion, while the Vaiṣṇava-wheel is characterized by enjoyment and delusion.

The wise know anger and delusion to be the Raudra-cakra, and the rotation [of the senses] to be the Aiśvara-cakra; they know knowledge and delusion to be the Śiva-cakra—thus they understand the five cakras.
Furthermore, by ten crores [of recitations], one attains the station of Kāraṇabrahman; and again, by another ten crores, one shall obtain the sovereignty of that station.
Thus, having attained the station of Viṣṇu and others of great power in due order, and having likewise attained the sovereignty of those stations of the high-souled ones in succession;
Having recited the mantra one hundred and five crores of times without weariness, one attains the world of Śiva beyond the fifth enclosure.
There is a Rajasic pavilion there, the supreme abode of Nandin; and right there, the bull, whose form is asceticism, is seen.
That place of Sadyojāta is the supreme fifth enclosure; furthermore, the place of Vāmadeva is the fourth enclosure.
Afterwards, the supreme third enclosure is the abode of Aghora; the auspicious second enclosure belongs to Sāmba Puruṣa himself.
Then follows the first enclosure of the supreme Īśāna, then the station of Dhyānadharmā, and then the fifth pavilion.
There is the abode of Balinātha, which bestows full nectar; thereafter is the fourth pavilion, possessing the form of Candraśekhara.
The third pavilion is the supreme abode of Somaskanda; the second pavilion, the devotees say, is the dance pavilion.
First, the place of the primordial Māyā is most auspicious right there; beyond that is the inner sanctum, the supremely auspicious location of the Liṅga.
Because they were situated outside the Nandi-shrine, they did not know the glory of Śiva; Nandīśvara, remaining outside, was worshipping the five-syllabled mantra.
Thus, it was obtained by me again from Nandīśa through the lineage of gurus; beyond that, it is to be realized within oneself, O Śiva, and has not been experienced by anyone else.
"Only through the grace of Śiva can the majesty of the world of Śiva be directly known by all; it cannot be otherwise," so say the believers.
In this manner, indeed, the Brāhmaṇas who have conquered their senses shall be liberated. Now I shall describe the sequence for others; listen with respect as I speak.

According to the instruction of the guru, a Brāhmaṇa should indeed recite the five-syllabled mantra ending with "namaḥ" as his japa; following the prescribed rite, he should perform it five hundred thousand times for the sake of longevity.
To remove the state of womanhood, one should again recite five hundred thousand times; having become a man through the mantra, the wise one shall gradually attain liberation.
A Kṣatriya shall remove his status as a Kṣatriya by means of five hundred thousand [recitations]; and again, by another five hundred thousand, that Kṣatriya shall become a Brāhmaṇa.
Through the recitation of mantras, one attains success and shall gradually become liberated; a Vaiśya, moreover, by five hundred thousand [recitations], will cast off his Vaiśya status.
Furthermore, by five hundred thousand [recitations], he is called a mantra-kṣatriya; and again, by five hundred thousand, he will remove the state of being a kṣatriya.

Furthermore, the mantra for a Brāhmaṇa is said to consist of five hundred thousand recitations; and for a Śūdra, it consists of twenty-five hundred thousand recitations preceded by "Namaḥ" and ending with "Oṃ."
Having attained the status of a mantra-expert, one subsequently becomes a pure twice-born; this applies whether it be a woman, a man, a Brahmin, or anyone else.
One who is afflicted should always recite [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ* or preceded by *namaḥ*. Then, the Guru should likewise demonstrate the application for women in the proper sequence.

At the conclusion of five hundred thousand recitations, the practitioner, for the sake of pleasing Śiva alone, shall perform the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and the offering of food (naivedya), and worship the devotees.
Through the worship of a devotee of Śiva, Śiva becomes even more pleased; there is no difference between Śiva and the devotee of Śiva, for he is indeed Śiva himself.
Indeed, by the retention of the mantra whose nature is Śiva, one becomes Śiva himself; for in the body of a devotee of Śiva, one should become supremely devoted to Śiva.
