Devotees of Śiva know all ritual actions to be the performance of every Vedic rite; for as much as the mantra of Śiva is recited by anyone in due sequence, [so much merit is gained].
Until then, there is indeed the presence of Śiva in that body; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, for a woman devoted to Śiva, her very form becomes a linga of the Goddess.
As long as one recites the mantra of the Goddess, her presence indeed remains; the wise man should worship Śiva himself, for he is the very embodiment of sound.
Having himself become Śiva, he should worship the Supreme Śakti; for he should worship the Śakti, the image (bera), and the Liṅga, having depicted them through Māyā.
Considering the Śivaliṅga to be Śiva and one's own self to be of the nature of Śakti, and considering the Śaktiliṅga to be the Goddess and oneself to be of the nature of Śiva.

The Śiva-liṅga is of the nature of sound (nāda), while the Śakti is of the nature of the bindu; through their relationship as secondary and primary, they exist as a liṅga mutually attached to one another.

And one should worship Śiva and Śakti; through that fundamental contemplation, he becomes Śiva himself—[worshipping] the devotees of Śiva who are the very form of Śiva-mantras and the very form of Śiva.
One should worship with the sixteen services and thereby attain one's desired goal; likewise, through service and other acts toward a devotee of Śiva who bears the *liṅga*, [one attains the same].
The wise man should produce joy, for Śiva becomes most pleased; he should always [do this] together with his wife for those devotees of Śiva who are accompanied by their wives.
One should worship them with food and other offerings—five, ten, or even a hundred—being free from deceit regarding wealth, the body, the mantra, and meditative cultivation.
By means of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, one is not born again on earth. From the navel downwards is the portion of Brahmā; up to the throat is the portion of Viṣṇu.

The face is said to be the *liṅga*, the very body of a devotee of Śiva; [this applies] whether the deceased are those who have undergone cremation and other rites, or those who have died without such rites as cremation.
One should worship Śiva alone as the primordial father; having performed the worship of the primordial mother, one should also worship the devotees of Śiva.
Having reached the world of the ancestors, one who has died shall be liberated in due course; moreover, one endowed with austerity is superior to those ten who are merely engaged in ritual action.
One engaged in recitation (japa) is superior to hundreds endowed with austerity; one possessing the knowledge of Śiva is superior to thousands engaged in recitation.

Among hundreds of thousands of those possessing the knowledge of Śiva, one who is engaged in meditation is distinguished; among tens of millions of those engaged in meditation, one established in samādhi is distinguished.
Indeed, due to the progressive excellence of worship, there is a progressively superior fruit characterized by excellence, which is difficult even for the wise to discern.
Therefore, what man indeed knows the greatness of a devotee of Śiva? For the worship of Śiva and Śakti is the worship of the devotee of Śiva.
The man who performs this with devotion becomes Śiva himself and prospers through auspiciousness; he who reads this chapter, which is meaningful and in accord with the Vedas, [attains the same].
The Brahmin who possesses the knowledge of Śiva rejoices together with Śiva; O lords of sages, he who knows the distinctions should cause the devotees of Śiva to hear it.
O wise ones, through the grace of Śiva, there shall be the attainment of Śiva’s favor.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: "O best among those who know all things, please explain the true nature of bondage and liberation. Sūta said: "I shall speak of bondage, liberation, and likewise the means [to attain them]; listen with reverence."
The soul bound by the eightfold bondage beginning with *prakṛti* is called "bound"; the soul liberated from the eightfold bondage beginning with *prakṛti* is called "liberated."
The mastery over primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest is called liberation by its very nature; the bound soul, when released, is termed a liberated soul.

From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the intellect (buddhi), then the ego (ahaṃkāra) consisting of the qualities (guṇas), and the five subtle elements (tanmātras); these they know as the eightfold group beginning with primordial nature.
The body is said to arise from the eightfold nature (prakṛti) and so forth, and action arises from the body; again, the body arises from action, and thus birth and action occur repeatedly.
The body is to be known as threefold: gross, subtle, and causal. The gross is said to provide the capacity for activity; the subtle provides the enjoyment of the senses.
The cause, however, is for the sake of the self's enjoyment; according to the karma of the living being, one experiences pleasure and pain as the fruit of meritorious and sinful actions.
Therefore, bound indeed by the rope of karma, the individual soul (jīva) is constantly whirled around like a wheel by the actions pertaining to the three bodies, again and again.
To prevent the wheel from revolving, one should praise the maker of the wheel; the great wheel consists of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest, while Śiva is beyond primordial nature.
For Maheśa, the creator of the wheel, is indeed beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); he either drinks or vomits [it], just as a living child drinks water.

Śiva likewise presides over primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest, having brought them under his control; because everything has been brought under his control, he is remembered as Śiva. Indeed, Śiva alone is omniscient, perfectly complete, and free from desire.

Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, and eternally undiminished power, as well as infinite power—these constitute the mental sovereignty of Maheśvara which the Veda perceives.
Therefore, by the grace of Śiva, one shall come under the control of primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth; for the sake of obtaining the grace of Śiva, one should worship Śiva alone.
How can there be worship for him who is desireless and complete? An action performed for the sake of Śiva becomes a source of grace.
One should worship Śiva, directed toward the Liṅga, the image, or the devotee; one should worship with body, mind, speech, and even with wealth.
Indeed, through worship, Maheśa—Śiva, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—truly bestows his grace, especially upon the worshipper.

By the grace of Śiva, one's karma and other factors will gradually come under one's own control; when everything from karma up to primordial nature (prakṛti) has been brought under control, [then liberation is attained].
Then, declared to be "liberated," he shines, delighting in his own self; for when the body of action becomes subject to his will through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Then indeed, residence in the world of Śiva is called *sālokya*; one attains *sāmīpya* (proximity) to Śambhu when that [element] alone has come under control.
Then, through the attainment of union with Śiva by means of the weapons and other ritual acts, and upon obtaining great grace, the intellect shall also come under control.
But for a Buddhist, it is said that the effect arises from primordial nature (prakṛti), which is its creation; yet again, through great grace, primordial nature shall come under control.
Then the mental sovereignty of Śiva will become effortless; having attained the sovereignty of Śiva, such as omniscience and the rest, he shines within his own self.
Those devoted to the Vedas and Agamas declare that this is "union" (sāyujya). In this manner, liberation occurs gradually through the worship of the *liṅga* and other such forms by one's own effort.

Therefore, for the sake of Śiva’s grace, one should worship Śiva through ritual actions and the like; there should always be ritual action for Śiva, austerity for Śiva, and the recitation of mantras for Śiva.
One should practice the knowledge of Śiva and meditation on Śiva more and more; indeed, one should spend the time from sleep until death in the contemplation of Śiva.

"One shall worship Śiva with flowers such as *sadya* and others, and he will attain [him]. The sages said: "Tell us the complete procedure for the worship of Śiva in the form of the *liṅga* and other [forms]."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the sequence of the liṅgas exactly as it is; that very first liṅga is the Praṇava, which fulfills all desires.

Indeed, the subtle form is the nature of the *praṇava*, while the subtle form itself is fruitless; for the gross *liṅga* is indeed "with parts" (*sakala*), and it is called the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*).
Worship of these two is declared to be austerity; both directly bestow liberation. There are also many lingas that consist of the individual soul (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti).
Śiva alone knows how to describe those in detail, and no one else; I shall declare to you the recognized signs consisting of the movements of the eyebrows.

The first is the self-manifested *liṅga* (*svayambhū-liṅga*), the second is the *bindu-liṅga*, the third is the installed (*pratiṣṭhita*) one, the fourth is the mobile (*cara*) one, and the fifth is the *guru-liṅga*.
Pleased by the ascetic penance of the divine seers, Śarva indeed entered within the earth there for the sake of being present, as the seed in the form of sound.
Like the sprout of an immobile plant breaking through the earth, he was clearly manifest; because he was born of himself, they know him as Svayambhū (the Self-Existent).
Through the worship of the talliṅga, knowledge increases by itself, whether it be performed with gold, silver, and so forth, or upon the earth, or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having inscribed a Liṅga with one's own hand using the pure Praṇava mantra, and having likewise drawn a Yantra-Liṅga, one should perform the installation and invocation.
The linga, whether stationary or mobile, consists of bindu and nāda; this is indeed composed of contemplation (bhāvanā) as perceived by Śiva—of this there is no doubt.

Wherever Śambhu is present for the sake of the universe, there he bestows the fruit [of one's actions] upon that person; he is drawn with his own hand into a yantra, whether it be inanimate or non-artificial.
Having invoked Śambhu, one should worship him with the sixteen types of offerings; one attains sovereignty by oneself, and through practice, knowledge shall arise.
Indeed, by both the gods and the sages, for the sake of their own spiritual perfection, that which was performed with mantras by their own hands upon the pure maṇḍala—
The supreme *liṅga* established through pure contemplation alone is called the *pauruṣa-liṅga*, and it is said to be "installed" (*pratiṣṭhita*).
By the constant worship of the talliṅga, one shall attain human sovereignty, as well as [the status of] great Brāhmaṇas, kings, and those of great wealth.
A linga fashioned by an artisan and installed with mantras is indeed established as natural (prākṛta), and it bestows the enjoyment of worldly sovereignty.
That which is powerful and constant is indeed called *pauruṣa* (the human/spiritual); that which is weak and transient is indeed called *prākṛta* (the material/natural).
The linga, the navel, the tongue, the tip of the nose, and the crest-lock (śikhā) are, in sequence, the three worlds beginning with the waist; this is the final, spiritual (ādhyātmika) linga.

A mountain is declared to be *pauruṣa* (of human origin), while the surface of the earth is known as *prākṛta* (natural). Trees and the like are to be understood as *pauruṣa*, whereas shrubs and the like are known as *prākṛta*.

The sixty-day rice, common grain, and the human-like qualities of rice and wheat should be known; one should understand the "human" sovereignty as that which bestows the eight siddhis, beginning with *aṇimā*.
The orthodox proclaim that the first [category] concerns ordinary matters such as virtuous women, wealth, and so forth; among the mobile liṅgas, the rasa-liṅga is described first.
The Rasaliṅga shall grant all desired objects to Brāhmaṇas; the auspicious Bāṇaliṅga bestows great sovereignty upon Kṣatriyas.
A golden liṅga bestows the status of a great lord of wealth upon Vaiśyas, while a stone liṅga is auspicious for Śūdras, bringing about great purification.
A crystal *bāṇaliṅga* grants all desires to everyone; in the absence of one's own, another's [liṅga] is not prohibited for worship.
For women, however, the emblem of the Earth is especially prescribed when they have husbands; for widows who have remarried, it is proclaimed that it should be made of crystal.
For widows who have desisted from worldly ties, the *rasaliṅga* is especially recommended, O women of excellent vows, whether they be in childhood, youth, or even old age.
A liṅga made of pure crystal grants all enjoyments to women; for those engaged in worldly life, the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) bestows all desired objects on earth.
One should perform all acts of worship using only the vessel; at the conclusion of the consecration (abhiṣeka), one should offer the food offering (naivedya) consisting of śāli rice.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should place the liṅga in separate caskets within the house; then, for those who have completed the hand-worship, one should offer one's own food.
For those who have desisted from worldly activity, the supreme subtle liṅga alone is distinguished; one should perform the worship of the manifestation (vibhūti) and offer the manifestation itself.
Having performed worship, one should then always wear that liṅga upon the head. Vibhūti is said to be threefold, according to the world, the Veda, and the fire of Śiva.
One should bring ash produced from the fire of a funeral pyre for the purpose of purifying liquids, as well as for earthenware, wooden objects, metals, and likewise for grains.
For substances such as sesame seeds and likewise for items such as clothing, purification by means of ash is desired even when they have become stale.
For objects defiled by dogs and other such creatures, purification by means of ash is prescribed; one should apply the ash with water or without water as appropriate.

Likewise, one should wear the ash produced from the Vedic fire at the conclusion of those rituals; that which is generated by mantra and ritual action takes the form of ash within the sacrificial fire.
By wearing that ash, the karma projected upon one's own self becomes [neutralized]. One should burn *bilva* wood with the *aghora* mantra dedicated to the Self.
It is declared to be the Śivāgni; by it is burnt that which is born of the Śivāgni—either previously prepared cow-dung from a tawny cow, or simply any product of the cow alone.
One should burn śamī, aśvattha, palāśa, vaṭa, arka, amra, and bilva wood with the Śiva-fire; that ash born from the Śiva-fire is indeed pure.
Or one should burn a piece of wood in a fire of darbha grass while reciting the Śiva-mantra; having thoroughly purified it with a cloth, one should place it in a new water-pot.
That [ash] should be accepted for the sake of radiance, and it is also worshipped; for such indeed is the meaning of the word "bhasman" (ash), and Śiva acted accordingly in the past.
Just as a king takes the essence in the form of taxes from his own realm, and just as people indeed enjoy the essence after burning away the grain and other parts of the crop.

For just as the digestive fire, having consumed various and abundant foods such as those to be chewed, nourishes its own body with the most essential essence extracted from that essence; ||| so too does the supreme Self nourish the body by extracting the essence from all things. ||| Just as the fire within the stomach, having burnt many diverse kinds of food and the like, sustains its own body with the most excellent essence derived from that very essence; ||| even so does the supreme Self sustain the body by extracting the quintessential core from everything. ||| Just as the gastric fire, after consuming a great variety of foods and other substances, nourishes its own body with the most refined essence extracted from that essence; ||| in the same way, the supreme Self nourishes the body by taking the vital essence from all things. ||| For indeed, just as the internal fire, having consumed many diverse items such as solid foods, nourishes its own body with the most excellent essence drawn from that essence; Likewise, that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, though the creator of the phenomenal world, has grasped the essence of the world he presides over after having burnt it away.
Having burned away the phenomenal world, Śiva cast its ashes upon his own self; under the pretext of smearing himself with ash (uddhūlana), he took hold of the essence of the universe.
He established his own jewel within his own body; indeed, he formed his hair from the essence of space and his face from the essence of wind.
One should fashion the heart with the essence of fire, the waist with the essence of water, and the knees with the essence of earth; likewise, all other limbs should be formed accordingly.
The Tripuṇḍra is indeed the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Rudras; likewise, Maheśvara [is present] at the edge of the forehead in the form of a Tilaka.
Indeed, through the increase of his being, he himself considers all this to be "I"; by him alone has the entire essence of the world-process been brought under control.
Therefore, because there is no one who can subjugate him, he is remembered as Śiva; just as the "beast-killer" (mṛgahiṃsaka) is the slayer of all wild animals.
Since he has no fear of violence from wild beasts, he is therefore called "Siṃha" (Lion). "Śam" signifies eternal happiness and bliss; the letter "I" is remembered as the Puruṣa.
The letter *va* is power (*śakti*), nectar, and union; it is called Śiva. Therefore, having thus made one's own self Śiva, one should worship Śiva.

Therefore, one should first apply the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana) and thereafter wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Indeed, at the time of worship, it should be with water for the sake of purification, but without water [during other times].
Whether by day or by night, whether a woman or even a man, one should wear wet sacred ash with the Tripuṇḍra mark for the sake of worship.
Whoever performs worship after applying the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with water and sacred ash, the fruit of the complete worship of Śiva is indeed certain for that person alone.

By wearing the sacred ash with the Śiva-mantra, one indeed becomes a transcendent ascetic (atyāśramī); he is called a "Śiva-ascetic" (śivāśramī) because he is solely devoted to Śiva as his supreme goal.
For one who is solely devoted to the Śiva-vow, there is neither impurity due to death nor birth-impurity; he should wear a white mark of ash or clay on his forehead.

The characteristic of a devotee of Śiva is [transmitted] either from his own hand or from the hand of the Guru; the etymological analysis (vigraha) of the word "Guru" is said to be "one who obstructs [the disciple's] defects."
Having taken refuge in the form of the Guru, the Supreme Śiva, who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), restrains and dispels the qualities such as rajas along with their modifications.
Because he first dispels the three qualities (guṇas) and awakens one to Śiva, he is designated as the "Guru" for those disciples who have full trust.
Therefore, the wise one should understand that the body of the Guru is indeed the Guru-liṅga; the worship of the Guru-liṅga consists of service to the Guru.
One should practice learning through service by means of body, mind, and speech, regarding whatever has been previously spoken by the guru, whether it be possible or impossible to perform.
For one whose self is purified indeed acts [accordingly] even at the cost of life and wealth; therefore, such a person is called a disciple worthy of the teaching.
Having offered everything, including his body and possessions, to the guru, the good disciple should present the first-fruits of his cooking and eat only with the guru’s permission.
A disciple is called a "son" because of his constant union with the state of being a disciple; having indeed poured the semen of the mantra from the linga of the tongue into the womb of the ears.
A son born through the power of mantras should honor his father as a guru; for it is the biological father who immerses the son in the cycle of worldly existence.
The teacher, indeed the enlightener and father, delivers one from saṃsāra; having understood the difference between these two, one should worship the father as the teacher.

One should also serve the guru with personal attendance and with wealth acquired by oneself, attending to the limbs of the guru from the feet up to the hair, for these limbs are indeed the sacred symbols (liṅgas) of the guru.
One should worship with wealth in the form of sandals and other items for massaging the feet, as well as with ritual baths, consecrations, food offerings, and meals.
Worship of the Guru alone is the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Self; indeed, everything that remains after the Guru has received his portion serves to purify the self.
O twice-born ones, the remnants of the Guru, consisting of water, food, and so forth, which have been offered to Śiva, may be accepted and consumed by disciples who are devotees of Śiva.

Without the permission of the guru, everything becomes like that of a thief; therefore, one should diligently accept as a guru even one who is superior to one's own teacher, provided they possess specialized knowledge.

The goal to be accomplished is the liberation from ignorance, for it is the one who possesses specialized knowledge who is the liberator; and at the outset, the pacification of obstacles must be performed for the fulfillment of the ritual action.
A ritual performed without obstacles and with all its constituent parts truly becomes fruitful; therefore, a wise person should worship Vighneśa at the beginning of every rite.
For the sake of removing all afflictions, the wise person should worship all the deities; for fevers, knots, diseases, and the like are considered to be internal (ādhyātmika) afflictions.
Likewise, when piśācas, jackals, and the like appear in anthills and similar places, or when creatures such as lizards suddenly fall from the sky; |||
Also when there is the sight of a tortoise, a snake, a woman, or a wicked person in the house; and also regarding the subject of the birth of trees, women, cows, and so forth.
Future suffering arrives; therefore, they are considered material beings. Impurity, the fall of Saturn, and likewise great pestilence [arise from them].
Fever, pestilence, cholera, smallpox, and measles; the planetary transits at one's birth star, and the planetary conjunctions occurring in one's own zodiac sign.

Furthermore, the seeing of bad dreams and so forth are indeed considered *ādhidevika* (supernatural); likewise, [impurity] arises from touching a corpse, a *cāṇḍāla*, or an outcaste when one has gone inside the house.
When such an occurrence has arisen, which indicates future suffering, a wise person should perform a propitiatory sacrifice (śānti-yajña) for the pacification of that evil influence.
In a temple, or in a cow-pen, or at a sacred shrine, or even in the courtyard of a house—on a well-decorated platform two cubits in size and one span in height.
Having set aside a measure of rice or grain equal to a *bhāra*, and having circumambulated it, one should draw a lotus in the center and likewise draw them in the cardinal directions.
Having placed a large jar in the center, wrapped with thread and fumigated with fresh guggulu resin, one should likewise arrange jars in all the directions.
One should fill the pitchers, including those with sprouts, mango-branches, and brushes, in the eight directions with water purified by mantras and mixed with the five substances.
One should likewise cast the nine gems, beginning with sapphire, in their proper order; then the wise man should select a preceptor who is skilled in ritual action, together with his wife.
One should place an image of Viṣṇu made of gold, as well as those of Indra and the others, into the central pitcher along with their heads; having invoked Viṣṇu therein, one should worship him.

One should worship Indra and the others in due order in the east and the other directions according to their respective mantras, using each deity's name in the dative case followed by "namaḥ" at the end, in the proper sequence.
The preceptor alone should perform all the rites beginning with the invocation; together with the officiating priests, the preceptor should recite that mantra one hundred times.

At the western side of the pitcher, at the conclusion of the recitation (japa), the wise should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) ten million times, or one hundred thousand, or one thousand, or one hundred and eight times.
One should perform it for one day, or nine days, or even just the mandala itself, as is appropriate according to the time and place.

For the purpose of pacification, one should perform a *śamī* oblation, and for the purpose of livelihood, a *palāśa* oblation; one should offer these with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), rice, and clarified butter as the sacrificial materials, either by name or with a mantra.

Whatever material has been prepared at the commencement, one should carry that out until the completion of the rite; having caused the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) to be proclaimed, one should sprinkle [the materials] with water on the final day.
Thereafter, one should feed Brahmins according to the number of oblations; the preceptor and the wise officiating priests should likewise subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Having worshipped the planets beginning with Āditya at the very conclusion of all the oblations, one should indeed give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests and the nine gems in their proper order.
Then one should perform the tenfold gift, and thereafter the abundant gift; [this applies to] the wealth of children, the initiated, householders, and forest-dwellers.
Then, for the maidens who have husbands as well as for widows, one should offer all the ritual implements to the preceptor.
Yama is remembered as the lord of suffering for portents and plagues; therefore, for the sake of pleasing Yama, one should cause the gift of time (kāladāna) to be bestowed.
One should fashion [the image] with either a hundred niṣkas or ten niṣkas; one should depict Kāla in human form, holding a noose and a goad.
One should perform that gift of a golden image along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); thereafter, one should perform a gift of sesame seeds for the sake of attaining a full lifespan.
One should perform the offering of ghee while observing it in order to bring about the cessation of disease; one should feed a thousand Brahmins, or if poor, at least a hundred.
Even if one is poor due to a lack of wealth, one should perform the great worship of Bhairava according to one's ability, for the sake of pacifying spirits and other such obstacles.
One should perform the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and the offering of food (naivedya) in the presence of Śiva; afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas in the form of an abundant meal.
By performing the sacrifice in this manner, one shall attain the pacification of faults; one should perform this Śānti-yajña every year in the month of Phālguna.

In the event of an evil omen or similar occurrence, one should indeed perform [the rite] immediately or within a month; upon the commission of a great sin or the like, one should perform the worship of Bhairava.
When a great disease arises, one should again perform a ritual resolve; being poor in all possessions, one should then perform the offering of a lamp.
If one is unable even for that, having bathed, one should indeed perform some small gift; one should pay homage to the Sun-god one hundred and eight times with the mantra.
A wise person should perform [this] a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million times; by this sacrifice consisting of prostrations, all the deities shall be satisfied.
The intellect, when offered to your true nature, finds no pleasure in what is not you or in what is empty; and that which exists as our sense of "I" is cast off once you are seen.
I am indeed bowed down with my own body; O Great One, you are the Lord. My own nature is certainly not empty; I am now truly your servant.
One should perform the self-sacrifice and prostration as appropriate; then, having offered the food-offering (naivedya) to Śiva here, one should take up the betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
One should personally perform one hundred and eight circumambulations of Śiva; otherwise, one may have another perform a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million.
By circumambulating Śiva, every sin is destroyed in an instant; for disease is indeed the root of suffering, and sin is the root of disease.
For it is taught that the removal of sins occurs through dharma alone; dharma performed for the sake of Śiva is capable of dispelling evil.
In the Śivadharmas, it is declared that circumambulation is presided over by the Supreme; for the Praṇava, in the form of recitation, is indeed circumambulation through ritual action.
Birth and death are the pair known as the wheel of Māyā; indeed, that wheel of Śiva’s Māyā is called the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Starting from the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and proceeding in a clockwise direction, having moved from one step to the next, one should return to the sacrificial pedestal.
Then one should perform prostration; this is declared to be circumambulation. Departing [from the deity] constitutes rebirth, while "namas" is the surrender of oneself.
Birth and death are a pair bestowed by the Māyā of Śiva; one for whom this pair is bestowed by the Māyā of Śiva shall never again become a possessor of a self.
As long as the living being is dependent on action for the duration of the body, it is said to be bound; when the three bodies are brought under control, that is called liberation by the wise.
For Śiva, the supreme cause, is the director of the wheel of māyā; Śiva, however, wipes away the duality bestowed by the māyā of Śiva.
O wise ones, one should offer whatever pair of things has been prepared by Śiva back to Him alone; know that circumambulation and prostration are most dear to Śiva.
Circumambulations and prostrations before Śiva, the Supreme Self, as well as worship performed with the sixteen types of offerings, bestow their fruit.
Indeed, there is no sin on this earth that cannot be destroyed by circumambulation; therefore, one should destroy all evil solely through circumambulation.

Devoted to the worship of Śiva, observing silence, and endowed with virtues such as truthfulness, he should practice each one of these: ritual action, austerity, recitation, knowledge, and meditation.
Sovereignty, a divine body, knowledge free from ignorance and doubt, and proximity to Śiva—these shall be the fruits of ritual action and the other [means].
The fruit is attained through the instrument by means of the removal of darkness, and by the complete cleansing of birth through the intellect of the Knower.
A devotee of Śiva should perform rituals and other duties according to the place, the time, the body, the wealth, and what is appropriate.
A wise person should dwell in a place of auspiciousness with wealth acquired through righteous means—a place free from injury to living beings and devoid of excessive hardship.
They know that water and food consecrated with the five-syllable mantra bring happiness; or rather, they say that for a poor person, food obtained as alms becomes a bestower of knowledge.
The alms-food of a devotee of Śiva increases one's devotion to Śiva; they call the alms-food of a Śiva-yogin the "sacrifice of Śambhu."
By whatever means and wherever on earth one may be, one who always eats pure food and maintains silence should never reveal the secret.
One should indeed reveal the greatness of Śiva to the devotees; however, no one other than Śiva knows the secret of the Śiva-mantra.
A devotee of Śiva should dwell constantly taking refuge in the Śivaliṅga; by relying solely on the Sthāṇuliṅga, O brahmins, he becomes Sthāṇu himself.
Through the worship of the mobile liṅga, one will certainly be liberated in due course. Thus has been explained in brief everything regarding the supreme means and the goal to be attained.
That which was spoken by Vyāsa in the past and that which was indeed heard by me formerly—may there be welfare for you and for us, and may our devotion to Śiva be firm.
O wise ones, that man who always reads this chapter or hears it shall obtain the knowledge of Śiva through the grace of Śiva.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Śiva-liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, may you live long! You are blessed and possessed of devotion to Śiva. You have correctly described the greatness of the Liṅga, which bestows excellent fruits.
Now tell me again in detail about that place where the greatness of the earthen Liṅga of Maheśa has been declared as the most excellent of all.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, with true devotion and without exception; the greatness of the earthen liṅga of Śiva is being proclaimed by me.
Among these aforementioned types of lingas, the earthen linga is the most excellent; by worshipping it, O Brahmins, many have attained perfection.
O twice-born ones, Hari, Brahmā, the sages, and likewise the Prajāpatis, having worshipped the earthen liṅga, obtained everything they desired.
Gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as many others, having worshipped him, attained supreme perfection.
In the Kṛta age, the liṅga is made of jewels; in the Tretā, it is made of gold; in the Dvāpara, mercury is best; but in the Kali age, it is made of earth.
O Brahmins, among all the eight forms [of Śiva], the earthly form is indeed the most excellent; therefore, O sages, penance performed there yields great fruit, as it is not worshipped by others.
Just as Maheśvara is the eldest and most excellent among all the gods, so too is the earthen linga declared to be the most excellent among all lingas.
Just as among all rivers the celestial river (Ganges) is the eldest and most excellent, so among all lingas the earthen one is said to be the most excellent.
Just as the *praṇava* is remembered as the greatest among all mantras, so too is this earthen [liṅga] the most excellent, worthy of propitiation and indeed worship.
Just as among all castes the Brāhmaṇa is said to be the best, so among all Lingas the earthen one is said to be the best.
Just as among all cities Kāśī is remembered as the most excellent, so among all lingas the earthen one is declared to be the best.
Just as the Śivarātri vow is supreme among all vows, so too is the earthen linga (pārthiva) said to be the best among all lingas.
Just as among all goddesses the power of Śiva (Śaivī-śakti) is remembered as supreme, so too among all lingas the earthen one (pārthiva) is said to be the best.
If one worships a linga that is not made of stone, or a deity other than the one [prescribed], that worship becomes futile; likewise, bathing, giving gifts, and so forth become in vain.

The propitiation of the earthly deity (the king) is meritorious, auspicious, and increases longevity; it bestows contentment, nourishment, and prosperity, and should be performed by the most excellent practitioners.
Endowed with devotion and faith, one should worship the earthen linga—which grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims—using whatever offerings have been obtained.
He who, having fashioned an earthen linga with an auspicious pedestal, worships it, becomes wealthy and glorious in this very life and is born as Rudra at the end.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who worships an earthen liṅga with a bilva leaf at the three junctions of the day, from ten up to eleven times.
By this very body, one is glorified in the world of Rudra; it destroys the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch.
That wise one is indeed liberated while living; he is Śiva himself, without a doubt. Merely by the sight of him, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.
He who constantly worships Śiva by fashioning an earthen liṅga for as long as he lives goes to the abode of Śiva.
Having remained in the world of Śiva for immeasurable years with Mṛḍa, he returns with his desires fulfilled to become a lord of kings in Bhārata.
One who is free from desire should constantly worship the supreme earthen liṅga; he shall dwell forever in the world of Śiva and thereafter attain union with him.
If a Brahmin does not worship the earthen Śivaliṅga, he goes to a terrible hell, most dreadful, where one is impaled upon a trident.
One should fashion a beautiful liṅga according to some prescribed rite, and one should examine it with respect to the five-thread measurement (pañcasūtra) by means of the earthen [liṅga].
That [rite] must indeed be performed as a single unit; one should not perform it in fragments. For one who performs it in two parts shall never obtain the fruit of worship.
One should cause a linga to be fashioned from jewels, gold, mercury, crystal, earth, or ruby, provided it is unbroken.

The moving liṅga is known to be unfragmented, while the stationary is remembered as being in two parts; this distinction between fragmented and unfragmented is recorded for the moving and the stationary.
The railing is the Great Vidyā, and the Liṅga is the Lord Maheśvara; therefore, in a stationary Liṅga, the Śreṣṭhā and other [sections] are traditionally held to be complete.
A stationary linga should indeed be fashioned in two parts according to the prescribed rite; however, a mobile linga is declared to be unbroken by those who know the Shaiva Siddhanta.
Deluded by ignorance, some make the mobile linga into two parts; however, the sages who know the Siddhānta and are experts in the scriptures do not do so.
Those deluded men who fashion a stationary linga from a single piece or a mobile one from two pieces do not partake in the fruit of worship.

Therefore, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should joyfully fashion a linga with supreme delight—either an unbroken one known as "mobile" (cara) or a two-part one known as "immobile" (sthāvara).
Worship performed on an unbroken lunar day bestows the full fruit; however, worship performed on a divided lunar day is traditionally held to bring about great loss.
It has been stated by those who know the scriptures that worship performed on an unbroken, stationary [liṅga] does not bestow the fruits of one's desires and always results in adverse consequences.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Worshipping the Earthen Śiva Liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Now, the worship of the earthen image (pārthivārcā) for those devoted to the Vedas is described; according to the Vedic path alone, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having bathed according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras and having performed the Sandhyā rites according to rule, one should first perform the Brahma-yajña and then carry out the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having first performed the entire daily ritual according to his desire, a person should indeed wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads while preceded by the remembrance of Śiva.
For the sake of attaining the complete fruit of perfection according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas, one should worship the supreme earthen linga with supreme devotion.
The worship of the earthen image (pārthivārcā) is prescribed on a riverbank, by a pond, on a mountain, in a forest, in a temple of Śiva, or in any pure place.
O twice-born ones, having diligently brought clay produced from a pure location, one should fashion a Śiva-liṅga with great care.

For a Brahmin, a cow is remembered as fair-complexioned; for a Kshatriya, red; for a Vaishya, yellow-colored; and for one born of the feet (a Shudra), black—or indeed, whatever color she may have in each case.
Having diligently gathered earth for the purpose of fashioning the linga, one should place that auspicious clay in an exceedingly pure location.
Having purified it even with water and having gradually formed it into a lump, one should fashion an auspicious earthen linga according to the path of the Vedas.
Thereafter, one should worship with devotion for the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; I shall describe that method according to the prescribed ritual—listen!
One should sprinkle the articles of worship with the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," and one should effect the perfection of the site (kṣetrasiddhi) with the mantra "Bhūrasi."
One should perform the consecration of the water with the mantra "āpo asmān," and the binding of the crystal is said to be performed with the mantra "namaste rudra."
One should perform the purification of the site with the mantra "Śambhavāya," and one should also perform the sprinkling of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) with the mantra "Namaḥ" in the east.
With devotion, one should perform the excellent consecration of the Śaṅkara-liṅga using the mantra "To the blue-throated one" (Nīlagrīvāya), preceded by "Namaḥ."
Then, out of devotion, one who follows the Vedic path should indeed offer a beautiful seat with the mantra "rudrāya eta."
One should perform the invocation with the mantra "māno mahantam," and one should perform the seating with the mantra "yā te rudra."
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Śiva with the mantra "yāmiṣum," and one should carry out the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) with affection using the mantra "adhyavocat."
One should perform the deity-installation (*devatānyāsa*) with the mantra *asau jīvaḥ*; one should also perform the withdrawal (*apasarpaṇa*) with the mantra *asau yo 'pasarpati*.
One should offer water for the feet with the mantra "Namo'stu Nīlagrīvāya," the arghya with the Rudragāyatrī, and the water for sipping (ācamana) with the Tryambaka mantra.
With the mantra "payaḥ pṛthivyām," one should perform a bath with milk; and with the mantra "dadhikrāvṇo," one should cause a bath with curd to be performed.
Indeed, ghee is for the bath; with the mantra "ghṛtaṃ ghṛtam," and with the three verses beginning "madhu vātā," "madhu naktam," and "madhumān naḥ."

The bathing with honey and sugar is declared [to be part of this]; thus it is remembered as the "Five Nectars" (pañcāmṛta). Alternatively, the bathing may be performed with the five nectars while reciting the mantra for the water for the feet (pādya).
With the mantra "mānastoke" out of love, he should perform the binding of the waistband; or with the mantra "namo dhṛṣṇave," he should cause him to wear the upper garment.
With the four Vedic verses beginning with "yā te heti," a devotee, out of love, should perform the offering of a garment for Śiva according to the prescribed ritual.
With the verse "namaḥ śvabhyaḥ," the wise one should offer scented paste with affection; and with the mantra "namas takṣabhyaḥ," he should present unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
One should offer flowers with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ pāryāya," or offer bilva leaves with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ parṇyāya."
One should offer incense according to the prescribed rule with the mantra "namaḥ kapardine ca," and one should offer the lamp as stated with the ṛc verse beginning "nama āśave."
One should offer the supreme food offering with the mantra "namo jyeṣṭhāya"; furthermore, the sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed with the mantra "tryambakam".
One should perform the offering of the fruit with the verse beginning "imā rudrā ye," and one should offer everything to Śambhu with the verse beginning "namo vrajyāya."
Then, with the two mantras "mā no mahāntam" and "mā nastoke," one should worship the Rudras with eleven unbroken grains of rice (akṣatas).

With the three verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," one should indeed present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); then the wise man should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the mantra "devasya tvā."

Or one should perform the rite of lustration (nīrājana) for Śambhu with the Dīpa-mantra; and with devotion, one should offer a handful of flowers while reciting the three verses beginning with "imā rudrāya".
The wise man should perform circumambulation while reciting "māno mahāntam," and the person of refined intellect should prostrate with all eight limbs while reciting the mantra "mānas toke."
One should display the Śivamudrā with the mantra "eṣate," the Abhayāmudrā with "yatoyataḥ," and the Jñānamudrā with the "tryambaka" mantra.
One should display the Mahāmudrā with the mantra "namaḥ senāya," and one should display the Dhenumudrā with this verse: "namo gobhyaḥ."
Then, having displayed the five mudrās, one should perform the recitation of the Śiva-mantra; the expert in the Vedas should recite it with the Śatarudriya mantra.
Then, the expert in the Vedas should perform the five-limbed recitation; he should effect the dismissal of Śambhu with the mantra "devā gātuvidaḥ."
Thus has been described in detail the Vedic procedure for the worship of Śiva; now hear the excellent Vedic procedure in brief.
One should perform the fetching of clay with the verse beginning "sadyojātam," and one should perform the sprinkling of water with the verse beginning "vāmadevāya."
One should perform the fashioning of the *liṅga* with the *aghora* mantra, and one should perform the invocation according to the prescribed rule with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.
The wise practitioner should join Hara upon the altar with the Īśāna mantra; he should perform all other rites in brief.
The wise one should perform the worship according to the rules with the sixteen types of offerings, using either the five-syllabled mantra or that which has been imparted by the guru.
We meditate upon Mahādeva, the source of existence and the destroyer of existence; upon Ugra, the destroyer of the fierce; upon Śarva, who bears the moon upon his crest.
With this mantra, the wise person should worship Śaṅkara with great devotion, casting aside all delusion; for it is through devotion alone that Śiva bestows the fruit [of one's actions].
Having thus respectfully described the worship according to the Vedic sequence, O twice-born one, another method is now fully explained as being common to all.
The worship of the earthen liṅga has been proclaimed with the names of Śiva; listen to that, O best of sages, which bestows all desires.
Hara, Maheśvara, Śambhu, Śūlapāṇi, Pinākadhṛk, Śiva, Paśupati, and Mahādeva—these are the names in their respective order.
Bringing the clay, kneading it, consecrating it, and invoking [the deity]; likewise, bathing, worshiping, and the dismissal with the words "Forgive me."
All rites should be performed in sequence with names preceded by *oṃ*, ending in the dative case, and followed by *namaḥ*, with supreme devotion and joy.
Having properly performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the six limbs and the hands with the six-syllable mantra, one should then practice meditation.

One should meditate upon the immeasurable one, seated in the center of the Kailāsa throne, being worshipped by devotees such as Nanda and others; he who is the forest fire to the suffering of his devotees, embraced by Umā, and the ornament of the universe.

One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, adorned with a beautiful crescent moon, his limbs radiant with jeweled ornaments, holding an axe, a deer, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and gracious in appearance; seated upon a lotus, surrounded on all sides by hosts of immortals, clad in a tiger skin, the beginning of the universe, the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced, and three-eyed.
Having thus meditated and worshipped the supreme earthen liṅga, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra bestowed by the guru according to the prescribed rule.
O best of Brahmins, the wise man should praise the Lord of Gods with hymns while bowing down; he should indeed recite the Śatarudriya with its various names.
Then, having joyfully taken unbroken rice grains and flowers in his joined palms, he should pray to Śaṅkara with devotion and these mantras with great piety:
O Mṛḍa, O Lord of Beings, know that I am yours, that my life-breath is your virtue, and that my mind is always fixed on you; knowing this, O Treasure of Compassion, be gracious unto me.
Whether performed out of ignorance or with knowledge, may whatever recitation, worship, and so forth has been done by me become fruitful through your grace, O Śaṅkara.
"I am a great sinner, O Great River, and you are a purifier; having understood this, O Lord of Gaurī, do as you wish."
O Mahādeva, you are not known by the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Siddhāntas, nor even by the various ṛṣis; O Mahāśiva, how then could I know you?
In whatever way I am yours in all respects, O Maheśvara, I must indeed be protected by you; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
O Sage, having thus placed unbroken flowers upon Śiva, one should prostrate with devotion before Śambhu according to the rules, performing the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
Then the wise one should perform circumambulation according to the prescribed rite; furthermore, filled with faith, he should praise the Lord of Gods with hymns of praise.
Then, making a sound with the throat, one whose mind is pure and humble should prostrate; having respectfully made a formal request, one should then perform the dismissal.

Thus addressed, those tigers among sages [performed] the worship of the earthen image according to the prescribed rite; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and increases devotion to Śiva.
Whoever should read or even hear this chapter with a pure mind, being purified of all sins, shall attain all desires.
This supreme narrative bestows longevity, fitness, fame, and heaven; it grants the happiness of sons, grandsons, and progeny.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Earthen Śiva Liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, disciple of Vyāsa, salutations be unto you! O dear one, the procedure for the worship of the earthen image has been correctly explained by you.
O you who are compassionate toward the distressed, please graciously tell me, according to the prescribed rules, the number of earthen Śiva-liṅgas based on the different types of desires.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the ritual procedure for the worship of the earthen image, by the mere performance of which a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
If one worships another deity without having fashioned a clay linga, that worship becomes futile; self-restraint, charity, and other such acts likewise become in vain.
The number of earthen lingas is declared according to one's desire; O best of sages, this number immediately and certainly yields its fruit.
In that case, the initial invocation, the installation, and the worship are performed separately; all these, even when taking the form of a *liṅga*, should be understood as distinct from one another.
A man seeking knowledge should worship a Śivaliṅga made of a thousand measures of earth with devotion; for it certainly bestows that fruit.
A man seeking wealth should worship half that number of earthen liṅgas; one seeking a son, fifteen hundred; and one seeking clothing, five hundred.

One who desires liberation receives ten millionfold; one who desires land, a thousandfold; one who desires to show compassion, three thousandfold; and one who desires a sacred pilgrimage site, two thousandfold.
One who desires friends should perform it three thousand times; one who seeks subjugation, eight hundred; one who seeks to kill, seven hundred; and one who seeks to delude, eight hundred.

For one intent on eradication (*uccāṭana*), [one should recite] one thousand times as prescribed; for one seeking immobilization (*staṃbhana*), one thousand times; and for one seeking incitement to hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), half of that.

One who desires release from shackles should perform one thousand and five hundred [recitations] of the supreme [mantra]; in the case of fear of a great king, five hundred should be known by the wise.

In times of danger from thieves and the like, two hundred recitations of the *pārthiva* [mantra] are prescribed; in fear of *ḍākinīs* and other such beings, five hundred *japa-pārthivas* are said to be required.
O you who are afflicted by poverty, [this mantra] bestows all desires, whether five thousand or ten million times over. Now I shall declare the daily ritual; listen, O best of sages!
One Liṅga is declared to be the remover of sin; two Liṅgas grant the attainment of wealth; and three Liṅgas are said to be the supreme cause for the fulfillment of all desires.

Thus, according to the previously stated method of calculation, the sequence should proceed higher and higher; now, however, I shall state another opinion regarding the number, based on the differences among the sages.
Having fashioned ten thousand earthen lingas, the wise man shall certainly become fearless and shall remove the fear of great kings.

For the sake of liberation from imprisonment and similar misfortunes, a wise person should cause ten thousand [recitations] to be performed; likewise, in the event of fear of ḍākinīs and other such beings, one should cause seven thousand to be performed.
A sonless man should cause fifty-five thousand lingas to be fashioned; by means of ten thousand lingas, he shall obtain a lineage of daughters.
By means of ten thousand liṅgas, one shall attain the sovereignty of Viṣṇu and others; by means of a million liṅgas, one shall indeed attain incomparable prosperity.
Any man on earth who establishes even a single crore of lingas shall become Śiva himself; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
The worship of earthen liṅgas bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices; it eternally grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men who seek their desires.
For that person of evil conduct and wicked soul whose time passes constantly without the worship of the Liṅga, there shall be a great loss.
On one side are all gifts, various vows, sacred fords, observances, sacrifices, and the worship of the Liṅga; on the other side, they are so reckoned.
In the Kali age, the worship of the Liṅga is seen to be the most excellent in the world; yet, that it is not so is the firm conclusion of the scriptures.
By constantly worshipping this Liṅga, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation and wards off various calamities, a person shall attain union with Śiva.
The Liṅga consisting of the essence of Śiva’s names is eternally worshipped by the great sages; therefore, among all Liṅgas, it should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
O tigers among sages, the linga is said to be of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior—in terms of its measurement; listen as I describe it to you.
A beautiful linga four finger-breadths in height and endowed with a pedestal is declared by the sages learned in the scriptures to be the best.
Half of that is declared the middling, and half of that is remembered as the inferior; thus it is described as threefold, each succeeding one being superior to the preceding.
He who, endowed with devotion and faith, constantly worships the many-liṅga [form], shall obtain the desires cherished in his mind.
There exists no merit greater than the worship of the Liṅga within the four Vedas; this indeed is the settled conclusion of all the scriptures.
Having completely renounced this entire web of ritual actions without exception, the wise man should worship the single Liṅga with supreme devotion.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is worshipped through the worship of the Liṅga; for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, there is no other means of deliverance.
For those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and whose minds are attached to sense objects, there is no other raft in this world besides the worship of the Liṅga.
The gods headed by Hari and Brahmā, the sages, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, cāraṇas, siddhas, as well as the daityas and dānavas;
The Nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, the Garuḍas and other birds, as well as the other Manūs together with the Prajāpatis, the Kinnaras, and human beings.
Having worshipped with great devotion the Liṅga that grants the fulfillment of all aims, they obtained all their desired objects, whatever resided within their hearts.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or one born of the inverse order (pratiloma), one should constantly worship the Liṅga with devotion using its respective mantra.
O sages, what is the use of speaking at length? O twice-born ones, everyone—including women and others—possesses the right to worship the Śiva-liṅga.
For the twice-born, worship even by the Vedic path is excellent; however, for other living beings, the Vedic path is not approved.
"The worship of Vedic Brahmins must be performed according to the Vedic path and not by any other way; thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva."
For the twice-born whose minds have not been consumed by the curses of Dadhīci, Gautama, and others, faith in Vedic ritual never arises.
That mortal who, disregarding Vedic rites or even those prescribed by tradition (Smṛti), performs some other action, shall not obtain the fruit of his resolve.

Having thus performed the worship of Śambhu according to the prescribed rite up to the offering of food (naivedya), one should worship the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) who comprise the three worlds right there.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer—these are proclaimed as the eight forms.
One should worship these with their respective forms: Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Īśvara, Mahādeva, and Paśupati.
Then, with great devotion, one should worship the retinue of Śambhu there, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) in due order, using sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and leaves.
Īśāna, Nandin, Caṇḍa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vṛṣa, Skanda, Kapardīśa, Soma, and Śukra—in that order.
One should worship Vīrabhadra in front and likewise Kīrtimukha at the back; thereafter, one should worship the eleven Rudras according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having recited the five-syllabled mantra as well as the Śatarudriya, and having performed various kinds of hymns of praise, he likewise recited the Pañcāṅga.
Then, having performed circumambulation and bowed to the Liṅga, one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana). Thus has the entirety of the worship of Śiva been proclaimed with reverence.
One should always perform rites for the gods at night facing north; likewise, being pure, one should always perform the worship of Śiva facing north.
One should not take [the seat] in front of Śambhu, nor to the north of those joined with Śakti, nor to the west where the back is; therefore, one should resort to what is appropriate.
A wise person should never worship Śaṅkara without the triple mark of ashes, without a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, and without bilva leaves.
O best of sages, when ash is unavailable while the worship of Śiva is underway, therefore the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be made on the forehead even with clay.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Earth-Image Worship," in the Sādhya-sādhana-khaṇḍa of the first Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: "We have previously heard the statement that the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva is not to be consumed; O virtuous sage, tell us the definitive conclusion regarding that, as well as the greatness of the bilva fruit."
Sūta said: Listen now, all you sages, with full attention; I shall tell you everything out of affection. Blessed are you, who are devoted to the vows of Śiva.
A devotee of Śiva who is pure, clean, firm in his vows, and resolute in conviction should consume the *naivedya* (food offering) of Śiva and abandon the notion that it is unfit to be accepted.
Even upon seeing the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva, sins depart to a great distance; but when the food offering of Śiva is consumed as an act of devotion, millions of merits arrive.
Enough with even a thousand sacrifices, enough even with ten million sacrifices; when the food offering to Śiva has been consumed, one attains union with Śiva.
That house in which even the practice of offering food to Śiva arises becomes entirely purifying, being the cause of purification for others.
Having joyfully received the offering (naivedya) of Śiva that has arrived, one should eat it with effort while preceded by the remembrance of Śiva.
It is also said that the *naivedya* (offering) of Śiva which has arrived should be accepted at once; for if there is delay, a human being certainly incurs the connection with sin.
He in whom no desire arises to partake of the food offered to Śiva is the most sinful and the gravest of men; he certainly goes to hell.
It is declared that this may be consumed by a devotee who has received Śiva-initiation, whether it be in the heart, in a moonstone, or in an object fashioned from gold, silver, and so forth.
A devotee endowed with Śiva-initiation may consume the auspicious food offering (naivedya) from all liṅgas, which is known as "great grace" (mahāprasāda).

Listen with affection to the definitive conclusion regarding the consumption of the *naivedya* (food offerings) of Śiva for those men who are joined with other initiations (*dīkṣā*) and whose souls are devoted to the love of Śiva.
O twice-born ones, [the same applies] to a Liṅga produced from Śālagrāma, as well as to a Liṅga made of mercury, a stone, silver, or gold, and to one consecrated by gods or Siddhas.
In Kāśmīra, Sphāṭika, and Rātna, and among all the jyotirliṅgas, the consumption of Śambhu’s food offering is declared to be equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure if he wears the remains of an offering; by consuming it, all his sin is swiftly destroyed.
That which has the authority of Caṇḍa should not be consumed by human beings; that which does not have the authority of Caṇḍa should be consumed with devotion.
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a metal (lauha) liṅga, a perfected (siddha) liṅga, a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga, and in all images, Caṇḍa shall have no authority.
Whoever, having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, drinks the water used for bathing the Liṅga three times, their threefold sin is quickly destroyed in this world.
The leaf, flower, fruit, and water offered to Śiva are otherwise unfit to be taken; yet, through contact with the Śālagrāma stone, everything becomes sanctified.
O lords of sages, whatever substance is upon the liṅga is not to be taken; that which is outside the range of the liṅga’s touch should be known as supremely pure.
O best of sages, the determination regarding the food offering has thus been declared to you; now listen with attentiveness and reverence to the greatness of the bilva tree.
This bilva tree is the very embodiment of Mahādeva; it is praised even by the gods—how then can its greatness be fully known?
Whatever holy pilgrimage sites are renowned throughout the worlds, all those sacred places are truly present at the foot of the bilva tree.
The meritorious soul who worships Mahādeva, the imperishable one in the form of a liṅga, at the root of a bilva tree, shall certainly attain Śiva.
He who sprinkles his head with water at the root of a bilva tree shall be as one who has bathed in all sacred fords; he alone is a purifier upon this earth.
Upon seeing this unsurpassed basin at the root of this bilva tree, filled with water, Mahādeva becomes exceedingly pleased.
The man who worships the root of the bilva tree with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings attains the world of Śiva; his progeny increases and he dwells in happiness.
He who respectfully arranges a garland of lamps at the root of a Bilva tree shall become endowed with the knowledge of reality and enter within Maheśa.
Taking a branch of the bilva tree with its fresh sprouts in his hand, he who worships the bilva is liberated from all sins.
Whoever with devotion feeds one person devoted to Śiva at the root of a Bilva tree, his merit becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
He who gives milk-rice mixed with clarified butter at the root of a Bilva tree to a devotee of Śiva shall never be born poor.

O twice-born ones, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is said to be complete with all its limbs and sub-limbs; it is twofold according to the distinction between those who follow the path of worldly engagement (pravṛtta) and those who follow the path of renunciation (nivṛtta).

One should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) and all other rites for those engaged in the practice. At the conclusion of the consecration (abhiṣeka), one should offer an oblation of cooked rice (naivedya). At the end of the worship, one should place the liṅga in a pure casket within a separate room.
To those who have desisted from the worship with hands, one should offer one's own food; for those who have desisted, the supreme, subtle Liṅga itself is distinguished as superior.
One should perform worship with sacred ash and offer sacred ash as a gift; having performed the worship, one should likewise always carry the linga upon one's head.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Naivedya Offered to Śiva," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, disciple of Vyāsa, salutations to you! Tell us that very same supreme majesty of the sacred ash (bhasma) as it was told by Vyāsa.
Likewise, please speak with great affection regarding the supreme majesty named the *Rudrākṣa-māhātmya*; let this triad gladden my heart.
Sūta said: You have asked well, bringing benefit to the worlds. You indeed are most blessed, pure, and ornaments to your lineage.
And for those for whom Śiva himself is the supreme, auspicious deity, the discourse on Śiva shall always be dear to you in this world.
Blessed and fulfilled are those who worship Śiva; their very bearing of a body is fruitful, and their lineage is uplifted.
In whose mouth the name of Śiva—“Sadāśiva, Śiva”—resides, sins do not touch him at all, just as they cannot touch the charcoal of the khadira tree.
Salutations to you, O Śrī Śiva; whenever that mouth speaks, that mouth is a purifying sacred ford (tīrtha) that destroys all sins.
Furthermore, it is certain that whatever man beholds her face with a joyful heart shall obtain the fruit born of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
O twice-born ones, wherever these three always abide, that place is most auspicious; by the mere sight of it, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Veṇī.
The sacred ash bearing the name of Śiva, as well as the rudrākṣa bead—these three are considered to be of great merit, equal to the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī).
He in whose body these three always abide—his very sight in this world is difficult to obtain and removes all sins.

Just as there is not even the slightest difference between the two in the case of seeing a bamboo stalk, so too he who does not discern [the distinction] is the most sinful; of this there is no doubt.

One should abandon like a base person that man on whose forehead there is no sacred ash (vibhūti), on whose body there is no wearing of rudrākṣa beads, and from whose mouth does not issue speech consisting of Śiva.
That which is called Śaiva is like the Gaṅgā; Vibhūti is considered to be the Yamunā; and Rudrākṣa, as declared by Brahmā, is the destroyer of all sins.
The wise hold that the merit derived from three [acts] performed upon one's own body, when combined as one, is equal on the other side to the merit arising from bathing at Veṇikā.
Thus, it was weighed previously by Brahmā, the doer of good; and since it was found to be equal, it should therefore always be worn by the wise.
Indeed, from that day forward, that triad is maintained by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods; and its sight removes all sins.
The sages said: "Indeed, such a fruit has been proclaimed as arising from the triad beginning with the Name; you ought to describe its greatness in detail, O observer of noble vows."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, listen with devotion and respect to that greatness, for the sages are indeed of great wisdom, true devotees of Śiva, and the best among the knowers of truth.
O Brahmins, although it is deeply hidden even in the Śāstras, Purāṇas, and Vedas, I shall now reveal it out of affection for you.
O best of the twice-born, who besides Maheśvara can truly comprehend the greatness of that triad, which is the supreme reality and unreality within the entire cosmic egg?
O Brahmins, listen with pleasure to this supreme account, which removes all sins, as I speak of the majesty of the Name according to my devotion and in brief.
The mountains of great sins are reduced to ashes without effort by the forest fire of the name "Śiva"; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
O Śaunaka, various sufferings rooted in evil are destroyed solely by the name of Śiva; they cannot be destroyed by any other means whatsoever.
That man on earth who is constantly devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names is considered Vedic, meritorious, blessed, and wise.
O Sage, various kinds of dharmas become ready to yield their fruit immediately for those who have faith in the chanting of the name of Śiva.
O Sage, as many sins as there are on earth that perish through the name of Śiva, so many sins are not committed by men.
O Sage, the name of Śiva, when uttered even briefly by men, quickly destroys immeasurable heaps of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Those who, having obtained the boat of Śiva’s name, cross the ocean of saṃsāra, their root sins of saṃsāra perish without a doubt.
O Great Sage, the destruction of those sins that constitute the very root of saṃsāra is certainly brought about by the axe of Śiva’s name.
The nectar of Śiva’s name should be drunk by those afflicted by the forest fire of sin; for those scorched by the forest fire of sin, there is indeed no peace without it.
Those who are drenched by the continuous downpour of the nectar of the name "Śiva" never grieve, even in the midst of the forest fire of saṃsāra.
For those great-souled ones in whom great devotion to the name of Śiva has arisen, liberation occurs suddenly and in every respect.
O Lord of Sages, through penance performed over many lifetimes, devotion to the name of Śiva arises, which removes all sins.
It is my conviction that for one whose unbroken devotion is uniquely fixed upon the name of Śambhu, liberation is easily attained; it is not so for anyone else.
Even after committing many sins, one who is devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s name becomes completely liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Just as trees in the forest are reduced to ashes when consumed by a forest fire, so too are all those sins burnt away by the name of Śiva.
O Śaunaka, he whose limbs are constantly purified by ashes and who is devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names, indeed crosses over even this most terrible cycle of worldly existence.
Even after seizing the property of a Brahmin or killing many Brahmins, a man who is devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s name is not tainted by sins.
Having examined all the Vedas, it was determined by the ancients that the supreme repetition of Śiva’s name is the means for crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
O best of sages, what is the use of much speaking? I shall describe in a single verse the greatness of Śiva’s name, which removes all sins.
Indeed, the purifying power of Śambhu’s name lies in its capacity to remove sins; for a person is never able to commit a transgression that it cannot cleanse.
O Sage, in former times, King Indradyumna, though a great sinner, attained the highest state of existence through the power of Śiva’s name.
Likewise, O Sage, a certain twice-born woman who was a great sinner attained the supreme state of liberation through the power of Śiva’s name.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have told you the supreme majesty of the Name. Now listen to the majesty of the sacred ash (bhasma), which purifies even all that purifies.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Śiva’s Forest," in the section on the Means and the Goal within the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Bhasma is declared to be of two kinds, the supreme bestower of all auspiciousness. I shall describe its varieties; listen with attentiveness.
There is one to be known as Mahābhasma (the Great Ash) and a second called Svalpa (the Small); that which is called Mahābhasma is the supreme ash of various kinds.
That ash is said to be of three kinds: Śrauta, Smārta, and Laukika; indeed, ash itself is designated by various names according to its specific characteristics.
The sacred ash (bhasma) derived from the Śruti as well as that from the Smṛti is prescribed for the twice-born alone; for all others, there is another, worldly kind of ash.
The eminent sages have declared that for the twice-born, wearing [the marks] is performed with mantras; for others, it should be understood as mere wearing, devoid of mantras.
O great sage, the ash produced from burnt cow dung is said to be of the nature of Agni; even so, it is declared to be the substance for the *tripuṇḍra*.
The wise should collect the ashes arising from the Agnihotra sacrifice, or even those arising from other sacrifices, for the purpose of wearing the Tripuṇḍra.
One should perform the smearing with water-mixed ashes seven times using the mantras beginning with "Agnis" found in the Jābāla Upaniṣad.

The *Jābālas* have declared with great reverence that the application of the *tripuṇḍra* and the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) must be performed by those of all castes and stages of life, both through the sacred mantra and even beyond the mantra.
"One who seeks liberation should not abandon even through negligence the smearing with ashes and the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra); such is the traditional teaching."
Śiva and Viṣṇu likewise [wear] the horizontal tripuṇḍra; and Umādevī, Lakṣmī, and Vāc, along with other goddesses, do so constantly.

By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras, as well as by those of mixed castes, it is maintained through the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of ashes, even if performed in Apabhraṃśa languages.
Those who do not perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith possess no proper conduct consistent with their caste and stage of life.
For those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith, there is no liberation from saṃsāra even through ten million births.
Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith possess no knowledge of Śiva, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Those who do not perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith are possessed of great sins; such is the conclusion of the scriptures.
For those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark with faith, everything they perform indeed leads to contrary results.
O Sage, among those beings who are burdened with great sins and who hate Śiva, a very firm aversion toward the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of ashes arises.
Having performed the fire-ritual for Śiva, the knower of the Self who performs the *triyāyuṣa* rite is liberated from all sins by means of the ash that has been touched.
He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Śiva.
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with white ashes; for by doing so, one attains the worlds beginning with Bhuvana and, upon death, shall become liberated.

One should not recite the six-syllable mantra without having performed the bath with ashes; rather, having fashioned the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes according to the prescribed rule, one should then recite it.
Whether he be the highest or even the lowest, whether he be possessed of all sins, or even possessed of the sin of killing a cow, or whether he be a fool or even an outcast.
In whatever land he always resides, joined with prosperity and governance, there the presence of all sacred fords and sacrifices is perpetually established.
A living being endowed with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is worthy of worship by all gods and demons; even one burdened with sin becomes pure in soul, how much more so one who is possessed of faith?
In whatever land a knower of Śiva, endowed with the authority of his divine power, has gone even by chance, there all sacred fords (tīrthas) have gathered even until now.
What need is there for much speaking here? The wise should always wear sacred ash; they should always perform the worship of the Liṅga, and the six-syllabled mantra should be recited.
Neither by Brahmā nor by Viṣṇu, nor even by Rudra, the sages, or the gods, is it possible to fully describe the majesty of wearing the sacred ashes (bhasma).
Thus, even one who has fallen away from the conduct of his caste and stage of life, and whose caste-rites have been lost, is liberated from sin by wearing the *tripuṇḍra* even once.
Those men who perform rituals while abandoning one who wears the sacred ash have no liberation from the cycle of existence even after ten million births.
That Brahmin by whom the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has been made on his head with ashes has not studied everything from his teacher, nor has he performed everything [prescribed].
O Brahmin, a wise person should infer that those men who, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash, inflict physical violence upon him, will take birth as outcasts (caṇḍālas).
A devoted Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya should wear the ashes consecrated with the *Mānastoka* mantra on the aforementioned limbs.

A Vaiśya woman [is purified] by the same method as a Baka bird, while a Śūdra woman is purified by the five-syllable mantra; for other widowed women, the rule is declared to be the same as that for a Śūdra.
The rite for the householder is prescribed with the mantras beginning with the five Brahmans; the rite for the student is indeed performed with the Tryambaka mantra.
Now, the procedure for one residing in the forest is prescribed by means of the Aghora mantra; an ascetic, however, should apply the Tripuṇḍra and other marks using the Praṇava alone.

One who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī) should always contemplate, "I am Śiva," through the supreme [realization]; and the Śiva-yogin should likewise constantly maintain this through the Lord Īśāna.
