"The wearing of ashes, which is supreme, must never be abandoned by members of any caste, nor even by others who live according to their own means; such is the teaching of Śiva."
Indeed, for as many particles of ash as are established upon one's own body through the ash-bath, that wearer carries that many Śiva-liṅgas upon his person.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and even those of mixed castes; women, widows, children, and likewise heretics have all arrived.
Whether one is a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic, likewise a woman who is marked with the triple-tilaka of sacred ash is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Whether maintained with knowledge or without knowledge, it is like the burning power of fire; the ashes, whether maintained with knowledge or without knowledge, purify every person.

One should not eat even a small amount of water or food without wearing ashes and sacred beads (*akṣamālā*). Having eaten, whether as a householder, a forest-dweller, an ascetic, or a student, one becomes a defiler of the community (*saṃkara*). Such a person, a consumer of sin, goes to hell; however, that [sin] may be removed by the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* for the other castes, but for an ascetic, it is removed by the recitation of the primary *Praṇava*.
Those who revile the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself; and those who wear it with devotion wear Him Himself.
Fie on a forehead devoid of ashes! Fie on a village that is an abode of inauspiciousness! Fie on a birth that does not worship the Lord! Fie on knowledge that takes refuge in the inauspicious!

Those who revile Maheśvara, the support of the three worlds, and those who revile Hara, the wearer of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)—the very sight of them is a transgression. Indeed, they are born as equal to the saṃkara, the pig, the demon, the donkey, the dog, the jackal, and the worm; being supreme sinners, they become nothing but denizens of hell.

Having seen them [thus], let not even the moon and sun behold them by night or day, nor even in a dream; yet they might be liberated from that [sin] by the recitation of the Śruti and Rudra-sūktas, though they are disregarded [by others]. Indeed, hell results from conversing with those dull-witted people who censure a man established in the wearing of ashes and other such [sacred marks], for they are truly ignorant.

O Sage, one who does not follow the Tantras is not authorized here, nor is one who wears the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); one who lacks the mark of the heated discus is excluded from this sacrifice to Śiva.
In this regard, these many passages from the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad have been set forth; they should be investigated with diligence, and thereafter one should become devoted to the sacred ash (bhasma).

Even if one possesses sandalwood, it should indeed be worn mixed with the sacred ash for the *tripuṇḍra*; likewise, even a small amount of *vibhūti* (ash) should always be worn upon the forehead—if, that is, one still possesses intelligence.

Women, as well as the twice-born and others, including widows, should likewise wear the Tripuṇḍra mark with ashes up to the forehead. Similarly, those who abide in the stages of life (āśramas) should always wear this pure manifestation, which grants the fruit of liberation and destroys all sins.
He who applies the triple mark with ashes according to the prescribed rule is liberated from the multitude of great sins as well as the minor offenses.
Whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic; whether a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, as well as others who are fallen or base.
By properly applying the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rite for sacred ash, they become pure, having cast off the heap of their sins.
One who specifically wears the sacred ash is liberated from the sins of killing women or cows and from the killings of heroes and horses; of this there is no doubt.
The theft of another's property, the violation of another's wife, the censuring of others, the seizing of another's field, and the causing of pain to others.
The theft of crops, gardens, and so forth; acts such as setting fire to houses; and [the theft] of cattle, gold, buffaloes, sesame seeds, woolen blankets, and garments.
The acceptance of food, grain, water, and so forth from low-born persons, as well as from prostitutes, Matangīs, Śūdra women, and actresses;
Sexual intercourse with menstruating girls, widows, or women in their courses; and the sale of meat, hides, liquids, and salt.
Slander, false speech, and the giving of perjured testimony by witnesses—indeed, these and countless other various sins perish instantly through the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra.
The theft of Śiva’s property, the disparagement of Śiva anywhere, and the reviling of Śiva’s devotees cannot be purified by expiatory rites.
He who has Rudrākṣas on his limbs and the Tripuṇḍra mark on his forehead is to be honored even if he be a Cāṇḍāla; he is the most excellent among all the highest castes.
Whatever holy places exist in this world, and whatever rivers such as the Gaṅgā, one who wears the Tripuṇḍra on the forehead becomes as if bathed in them all.
There are seventy million great mantras preceded by the five-syllabled [mantra], as well as other mantras by the millions that are the causes for Śaiva liberation.
O Sage, all other mantras of the gods that bestow every happiness shall become subject to him who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka).
He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall uplift a thousand ancestors already born and a thousand yet to be born among his own kinsmen and relatives.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here on earth, long-lived and free from disease, one meets death with ease at the end of life.
Having attained a divine body, auspicious and endowed with the eight qualities of sovereignty, he ascended a celestial chariot served by the divine gods.
[He was honored] by all the Vidyādharas, by the Gandharvas of great splendor, and by Indra and the other world-protectors, in their respective worlds, in due order.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the positions of the lords of creatures, and having attained the station of Brahmā, he shall sport there with a hundred maidens.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures there for the duration of a Brahmā’s lifespan, one shall obtain enjoyment in the world of Viṣṇu until the passing of a hundred Brahmās.
Then, having reached the world of Śiva and obtained his desired and imperishable wish, he attains union with Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Having repeatedly examined the essence of all the Upaniṣads, it has indeed been determined that this very Tripuṇḍra is the supreme good.
That Brahmin who indeed censures the divine manifestation (vibhūti) is of a different birth; he goes to a terrible hell for as long as the four-faced Brahmā exists.

In ancestral rites, sacrifice, recitation, fire-offerings, the Vaiśvadeva ritual, and the worship of the gods, a person who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes a purified soul and conquers death.
A bath in water removes physical impurity; a bath with ashes ensures constant purity; a bath with mantras removes sin; and through the bath of knowledge, one attains the supreme state.
Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords, whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords—a man who performs the ash-bath attains that very fruit.
The ash-bath is the supreme sacred ford; it is equivalent to bathing in the Ganges day after day. Śiva is manifestly present in the form of ash, and ash is the purifier of the three worlds.
Neither that austerity, nor that meditation, nor that gift, nor that recitation is truly so, which has been performed by a Brahmin without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).

For forest-dwellers, virgins, those who have not undergone initiation, and likewise for those who are free from debt, [the rite] is accompanied by water before midday, but after that time it is devoid of water.
Thus, he who, with a disciplined mind, constantly applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is to be known as a devotee of Śiva; he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If even a single rudrākṣa on one's limb bestows great merit, then the birth of one who is devoid of the tripuṇḍra would be in vain.
Thus, the greatness of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has been briefly recounted by me; this secret of all living beings must be kept hidden by you.
O bull among sages, three lines indeed appear on all the aforementioned locations, such as the forehead and so forth, as described by the wise, O sage.
Starting from the middle of the eyebrows and extending as far as the ends of the eyebrows, one should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the forehead to that same measure.
A line made with the thumb in the middle of the ring and middle fingers, drawn in reverse order, is designated by the name *tripuṇḍra*.
Carefully taking the sacred ash with the three middle fingers, one should devoutly apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which is the supreme bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For each of the three lines, there are nine deities; I shall describe them for all the limbs—listen with attentiveness.
The letter *A* is the Gārhapatya fire, the earth, the quality of *rajas*, the *Ṛgveda*, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the morning extraction (*prātaḥ-savana*).
And Mahādeva is to be known as the deity of the first line by those foremost among sages who are devoted to the initiation of Śiva.

The letter *U* is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the principle of space (*nabhas-tattva*), and likewise the Yajurveda; it is the midday libation (*madhyandina-savana*) and consists of the inner self of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
And Maheśvara is to be known as the deity of the second line, O tiger among sages, by those who are devoted to the initiation of Śiva.
The letter *ma* and the Āhavanīya fire are the Supreme Self and the sky of darkness; the power of knowledge is the Sāmaveda, as well as the third extraction (*savana*).
And Śiva is indeed the deity of the third line; they should be known, O tiger among sages, as those devoted to the initiation of Śiva.

Having thus constantly paid homage with true devotion to the deities of the sacred sites, one who is pure should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); he shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Lord of Sages, having thus described the presiding deities in all the limbs, now listen with devotion to their associated sacred sites.
One should not place [the seed-syllables] in the thirty-two places, nor in the sixteen places, nor in the eight places, nor even in the five places.
On the head, the forehead, the two ears, and likewise the two eyes, the nose, the mouth, and the neck; and thus on the two hands thereafter.
At the elbows, at the wrists, at the heart, at both sides, at the navel, at the two testicles, as well as at the thighs, the ankles, and the knees.
In the two calves and the pair of feet, one should worship the thirty-two supreme locations: Fire, Water, Earth, Wind, Space, the Directions, the Guardians of the Quarters, together with the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Apa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
The wise should wear the Tripuṇḍra by means of these names alone, or, being composed, they should apply the Tripuṇḍra upon sixteen locations.
On the head, the forehead, the throat, both shoulders, the arms, the elbows, the wrists, the heart, and the sides of the navel.
Having thus established oneself on the back [of the seat], one should worship there the deities of the Aśvins, as well as Śiva-Śakti, Rudra, Īśa, and Nārada.
Vāmā and the other nine Śaktis—these are the sixteen deities; Nāsatya and Dasraka are proclaimed as the two Aśvins.
Alternatively, [one may perform it] on the head, the hair, and likewise on the two hands, the two arms, the heart, the navel, and the two thighs.
In the two knees, the two feet, and the back, there are sixteen [deities]: Śiva, Candra, Rudra, Ka, Vighneśa, and Viṣṇu.
Śrī herself is in the heart, and Śambhu is likewise in the navel; Prajāpati, the Nāgas, the Nāga maidens, and the daughters of the Ṛṣis are in both.
The oceans are in the two feet, and the sacred fords (tīrthas) are on the broad back; thus are the sixteen locations described, and now the eight locations are stated.
The secret place, the forehead, the two ears which are unsurpassed, the pair of shoulders, the heart, and the navel—this is the group of eight.
Brahmā, the seven sages (ṛṣis), and the deities are thus proclaimed; in this manner, O lords of sages, has it been declared by those who know the sacred ash (bhasma).
Alternatively, those who know the science of ashes say that these five locations—the head, the two arms, the heart, and the navel—are the places for the application of the ash.

One should perform [the rite] according to one's capacity, taking into account the place, time, and other factors; if there is an inability even to perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana), one should instead apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and so forth.

Remembering Śiva—the three-eyed, the support of the three qualities (guṇas), and the progenitor of the three Vedas—one should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead while reciting "Namaḥ Śivāya."
Having said "Obeisance to the two Īśas," one should apply the Tripuṇḍra on the two sides; and having said "Obeisance to the two Bījas," one should wear it on the two forearms.
One should perform [the offering] below for the two ancestors and likewise above for Umā and Īśa; then, one should offer behind the head, toward the west, saying "To Bhīma."
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, O highly wise one, O great lord whose form is Śiva, listen to the majesty of the Rudrākṣa; I shall describe it to you in brief.
The rudrākṣa, the supreme purifier, should be known as most dear to Śiva; it is remembered as the remover of all sins through sight, touch, and recitation.
O Sage, in former times, the greatness of the Rudrākṣa was described before the Goddess by Śiva, the Supreme Self, for the sake of benefiting the world.
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess Maheśānī, O Śivā; I shall describe the greatness of the rudrākṣa out of affection for you and with the desire for the welfare of my devotees.
O Maheśānī, in the past, for thousands of divine years, my mind became agitated while I was performing penance; therefore, I restrained it.
O Supreme Goddess, by the independent Supreme Lord who acts for the benefit of the world, my eye has been opened through his divine play.
From her two beautiful eyes, drops of water fell; there, those teardrops became trees known as Rudrākṣas.
Having attained a stationary state for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, they were given to the four castes who are devotees of Viṣṇu.
On the earth, Rudra created rudrākṣas born in Gauḍa, which are dear to Śiva; likewise in Mathurā, Ayodhyā, Laṅkā, and Malaya.
On Mount Sahya, as well as in Kāśī, in Daśārṇa, or likewise in other places, [one should act] because of the scriptural injunction that [these acts] shatter the mass of unbearable sins.
By my command, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were born; those Rudrākṣas on earth belong to those respective castes and possess auspicious eyes.
The wise should know the colors of the *rudrākṣa* beads in sequence as white, red, yellow, and black; men should wear *rudrākṣas* according to their own caste in that same order of colors.
Those who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and especially those devotees of Śiva, should always wear that fruit with its colors for the pleasure of the two Śivas.
That which is the size of an āmalaka fruit is declared to be the best; however, that which is the size of a jujube fruit is proclaimed as mediocre.
The lowest [level] shall be the measure of a *caṇa*; this procedure is now described. Listen with great affection, O Pārvatī, out of a desire for the welfare of devotees.
O Maheśvarī, even that which is merely the size of a jujube fruit is indeed fruit-bearing in this world, increasing happiness and good fortune.
That which is equal to the fruit of the *dhātrī* destroys all misfortunes; that which is similar to a *guñjā* berry accomplishes the fruit of all goals.
The lighter the [weight], the more abundant the fruit it bestows; for each successive unit, the wise have declared the fruit to be ten times greater.
The wearing of rudrākṣa beads is proclaimed for the purpose of destroying sins; therefore, whoever indeed wears them will certainly accomplish all their goals.
O Supreme Goddess, as the auspicious Rudrākṣa fruit is seen in the world, no other garland is seen to be like it.
O Goddess, Rudrākṣas that are even, smooth, firm, thick, and endowed with thorns are auspicious; they always grant all desires and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Rudra, one should avoid six types of rudrākṣas: those infested with worms, those that are split or cracked, those lacking thorns, those covered in sores, and those that are misshapen.
Rudrākṣa that has its own opening formed naturally is the best here; however, that which is produced through human effort would be mediocre.
The wearing of Rudrākṣa beads has been established as the destroyer of great sins; by wearing one hundred Rudrākṣas equal in number to the Rudras, a man becomes the very form of Rudra.
The fruit that is obtained here by maintaining eleven hundred [of these] cannot indeed be described even in hundreds of years.
A devoted and excellent man should properly fashion a crown from five hundred and fifty Rudrākṣas.
Devoted to worship, one should fashion a sacred thread from three hundred and sixty Rudrākṣas, arranged in three repetitions.
O Maheśvarī, three Rudrākṣas are prescribed for the crest-lock, and six each for the left and right ears.
One hundred and one [rosaries] are on the neck; on the two arms, O Rudra, according to the number [of fingers]; likewise at the two elbows and again at the wrists.
Those men devoted to the worship of Śiva should wear three sacred threads as the *upavīta*; the remaining five, which are equal in measure, they should wear around their waist.
O Supreme Goddess, whoever wears Rudrākṣas in this number indeed possesses that very form; he is to be saluted and praised by all like Maheśvara himself.
When one has established people in such a state through meditative postures and, upon seeing them, utters the word "Śiva," they are liberated from their sins.
This procedure for [the offering of] one hundred and so forth up to a thousand has been proclaimed; in its absence, another auspicious method is now described by me.
One should place one *rudrākṣa* on the topknot, carry thirty on the head, place fifty on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms.
One should wear twelve [strings] at the wrist and five hundred on the shoulders; one should fashion a sacred thread (upavīta) with one hundred and eight [strings].
Thus, all the gods bow down to that man of firm vows who maintains the Kṣānti-sahasrarudra; he is exactly like Rudra himself.
One Rudrākṣa on the topknot, forty on the head, thirty-two on the region of the neck, and one hundred and eight on the chest.
O Lord of Sages, there should be one [mark] on each of the ears, six on each of the arms, sixteen on each of the hands, and twice that number [thirty-two] by the measurement of the armpits.
He by whom even a mere count of [the syllables] is maintained with devotion is indeed a supreme devotee of Śiva; for he is to be worshipped like Śiva himself and should be constantly saluted by all.
It should be worn on the head with the Īśāna mantra, on the ear with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, on the throat with the Aghora mantra, and likewise on the heart with that same mantra.
The wise one should hold [the rosary] in his hands with the Aghora seed-mantra, and on his abdomen with the Vāmadeva mantra, strung with fifteen beads.
One should wear five, eleven, three, or fifteen rosaries; or else, one may wear all of them while reciting the root mantra.
Therefore, one should avoid consuming liquor, meat, garlic, onions, drumsticks (śigru), the śleṣmātaka fruit, and village pigs.
O Umā, the white rudrākṣa is prescribed here for those of brahminical body, the deep red for kṣatriyas, and the yellow one is repeatedly favored by the joyful.

It is cut, broken, shattered, and split asunder; therefore, O Elephant among Sages, this path declared in the Vedas must be maintained daily by Vaiśyas, and likewise by Śūdras, with devotion, O Kṛṣṇa.

A student, a forest-dweller, or a householder should wear these with strict discipline; for one who does not wear them shall never abide in the supreme state. This wearing of Rudrākṣas is attainable through meritorious deeds; by abandoning this, people go to all the hells.

First, those that are naturally lighter than the *āmalaka* fruit; then those bitten by thorns or infested by worms; likewise, those lacking the hollows for the thumb and fingers—these should not be worn by those desiring auspiciousness. Even the *rudrākṣas* as small as chickpeas are auspicious; O Umā, the subtle *rudrākṣa* is always most excellent and a source of blessings.

By the command of Śiva, Rudrākṣas must always be worn by those of all stages of life (āśramas) and all castes (varṇas), including women and Śūdras; indeed, for ascetics (yatīs), they are to be worn with the Praṇava.
Bearing [the burden] of deeds committed at night during the day, and bearing [the burden] of deeds committed during the day at night, one is liberated from all sins at dawn, midday, and sunset.
Those in this world who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), those who wear matted hair, and those who wear rudrākṣa beads—verily, they do not go to the realm of Yama.

Those who wear a single rudrākṣa on their head as well as the tripuṇḍra mark upon the middle of their forehead, and who indeed chant the five-syllabled mantra—they are holy men and must certainly be honored by you.
Bring to the abode of Yama that person on whose limbs there is no rudrākṣa, on whose forehead there is no tripuṇḍra, and in whose mouth there is no five-syllabled mantra.
Having repeatedly understood their power, those who wear the ashes and the Rudrākṣa beads are always to be honored by us; they must never be led away.
Thus Kāla commanded his own servants; thinking "So be it," they all remained silent, greatly astonished.
Therefore, O Great Goddess Pārvatī, the rudrākṣa is the destroyer of great sins; one who wears it is dear to me and becomes pure, even if he is a perpetrator of great sins.
He who wears Rudrākṣa on his hand, his arm, and likewise on his head, becomes invulnerable to all beings and wanders upon the earth in the form of Rudra.
He is indeed always to be saluted by all the gods and demons; for when seen, he is worthy of worship and destroys sin just like Śiva.
Even one who is devoid of meditation and knowledge, if he wears a rudrākṣa, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
Reciting a mantra with a rudrākṣa bead, the merit becomes ten millionfold; by wearing it, a person obtains merit ten billionfold.
O Goddess, for as long as that [power] remains within the body of the living being, for that long even a minor death does not afflict him.
Having seen one who is endowed with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), whose limbs are adorned with rudrākṣa beads, and who is muttering the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, one obtains the fruit of Rudra.
O beloved, a devotee who is dear to the five deities and likewise dear to all the gods should recite all mantras using a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
Devotees of Viṣṇu and other deities should also wear them, there is no doubt; but a devotee of Rudra, in particular, should always wear rudrākṣas.
Various types of rudrākṣas have been described; I shall now tell you their distinctions, O Pārvatī, listen with true devotion, for they bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śiva with one face is the manifest bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; by the mere sight of him, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is removed.
Wherever he is fully honored, there prosperity is indeed not far off; all calamities perish, and all desires are surely fulfilled.
The Lord of the gods of gods, who bestows the fruits of all desires, has two faces; that Rudrākṣa, in particular, swiftly destroys even the slaughter of a cow.
For Rudrākṣa is indeed three-faced and is the direct bestower of spiritual means at all times; by its power, all sciences (vidyās) truly become firmly established.
Brahmā himself, possessing four faces, removes even the sin of killing a human being; by mere sight and touch, he instantly bestows the fruits of the four aims of human existence.
The five-faced one is Rudra himself, the Lord known by the name Kālāgni; he is the bestower of liberation from everything and the granter of the fruits of all desires.
The five-faced one removes all such sins as approaching those who should not be approached and eating what should not be eaten.
By wearing the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, he who is known by the name Anaṅga has seven faces; O Queen of the Gods, by the mere retention of his name, even a pauper becomes a lord.
Rudrākṣa, Aṣṭavaktra, Vasumūrti, and Bhairava—by wearing these, one attains a full lifespan and, upon death, becomes a wielder of the trident.
Bhairava is nine-faced, and the sage is remembered as Kapila; Durgā, the great sovereign goddess, is the presiding deity of the wind and possesses nine forms.
One who is devoted to me should wear those Rudrākṣas on the left hand; he will surely become the Lord of All, equal to me—of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, Janārdana himself is the ten-faced one; by wearing [this image], O Queen of Devas, one shall attain all desires.
O Supreme Goddess, he who possesses eleven faces is Rudra; by wearing that rudrākṣa, one shall become victorious everywhere.
O Rudra, one should wear a twelve-faced rudrākṣa on the region of the hair; for all those twelve Ādityas are likewise situated there.
The Viśvedevas have thirteen faces; by meditating upon them, a person attains all desires and obtains good fortune and auspiciousness.
Whoever devoutly wears upon his head that Rudrākṣa, which is the supreme Śiva with fourteen faces, all his sins are destroyed.
Thus, O daughter of Śailēśvara, the varieties of rudrākṣa have indeed been declared according to their different faces; now listen with affection to their respective mantras in due order.

Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ 1 | Oṃ namaḥ 2 | Oṃ klīṃ namaḥ 3 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ 4 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ 5 | Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ 6 | Oṃ huṃ namaḥ 7 | Oṃ huṃ namaḥ 8 | Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ 9 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ namaḥ 10 | Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ 11 | Oṃ krauṃ kṣauṃ rauṃ namaḥ 12 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ 13 | Oṃ namaḥ ||
Endowed with devotion and faith for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, one should wear Rudrākṣas while reciting mantras, remaining free from laziness toward the deity.
O Rudra, that man on earth who wears a rudrākṣa without the mantra goes to a terrible hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Upon seeing one wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, as well as the ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and others who cause harm, [are struck with fear].
Whatever is artificial, as well as any malevolent sorcery (abhicāra) and the like—all that departs from afar upon seeing him whose form inspires awe.
O Pārvatī, upon seeing one who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, and other deities as well, become pleased.
O Maheśvarī, having thus understood the greatness of the rudrākṣa, they should be properly worn along with the mantras and with devotion for the increase of dharma.
Thus was the greatness of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, which bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, spoken by Śiva, the Supreme Self, in the presence of Girijā.

Those who wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads should be known as extremely dear to Śiva; indeed, through the power of wearing them, there is enjoyment of worldly prosperity and liberation, without a doubt.
He who wears the ashes and the rudrākṣa beads is called a devotee of Śiva; he who is intent on the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra is complete and stands face-to-face with the Truth.
Without the triple mark of ashes and without a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, even if Mahādeva is worshipped, he does not bestow the desired fruit.
O Lord of Sages, all that was asked has been fully explained—the greatness of sacred ash and rudrākṣa, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Whoever constantly hears this supreme and auspicious majesty regarding Rudrākṣa and sacred ash with devotion shall attain all desires.
Having enjoyed every happiness here in this world, accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, he shall obtain supreme liberation in the next world and become exceedingly dear to Śiva.
O lords of sages, this Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā has been narrated to you; by the command of Śiva, it eternally bestows all perfections and grants liberation.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the first Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

I bow to Śiva, the sole cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; he whose true nature is known by Gaurī’s husband, whose fame is infinite, who rests upon Māyā yet is free from Māyā, whose form is inconceivable, and who is pure, consisting of consciousness itself.
I bow to Śiva, the beginningless, the eternally tranquil, the one Supreme Person; for having created this entire universe by his own *māyā*, he abides within and without like the sky.

One should worship Śiva, who dwells within the other [the individual soul] while his own form remains hidden; he perceives this universe to create it, and the worlds eternally revolve around him like iron in the presence of a magnet.
Vyāsa said: Having bowed to Śambhu, the father of the world, to Śivā, the mother of the world, and to their son, the Lord of the Gaṇas, we shall now describe this.
Once, all the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, headed by Śaunaka, questioned Sūta with excellent devotion.
The sages said: We have heard that auspicious and excellent narrative from the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, known as the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa, which is delightful and compassionate toward its devotees.
O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, may you live long and be happy, since you cause us, dear father, to hear this supreme narrative concerning Śaṅkara.
O sinless one, though we are drinking the nectar of knowledge flowing from the lotus of your mouth, we remain unsatiated and desire to ask you something further.
Through the grace of Vyāsa, you have become omniscient and have achieved the fulfillment of all your duties; there is nothing unknown to you, whether it be past, future, or present.
Having obtained supreme grace through true devotion to my guru Vyāsa, everything has been understood in detail, and my entire life has been made meaningful.
Now speak, O wise one, of the unsurpassed form of Śiva, and indeed of all the divine deeds of both Śiva and Śivā without exception.
How can Maheśvara, who is devoid of qualities, attain the state of possessing qualities in this world? Through investigation, we all find that we do not know the true nature of Śiva.
How does Śambhu abide in his own essential nature prior to creation? And how does that Lord conduct himself while sporting during the course of creation?
And at the conclusion of that, how does the Lord Maheśvara remain? How does Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, attain a state of grace?
When he is pleased, what excellent fruit does that Great Lord bestow upon his own devotees and upon others? Tell us all of that.
We have heard that the Blessed One becomes gracious instantly; being supremely compassionate, that Great One does not take account of the devotee’s exertion.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—these three gods were born from the limbs of Śiva; among them, Maheśa was the full manifestation (pūrṇāṃśa), while the other was Śiva himself.
Tell me of his manifestation and his deeds in detail; O Lord, tell me of the manifestation of Umā and likewise of her marriage.
O sinless one, you must relate in detail that state of household life, as well as those other divine pastimes—indeed, all of this and whatever else remains to be told.
Vyāsa said: Thus questioned by them at that time, Sūta, filled with joy and remembering the lotus feet of Śambhu, replied to the lords of the sages.
Sūta said: You have asked well, O lords of sages; you are blessed, since your minds have become resolutely fixed upon the story of Sadāśiva.
Indeed, a discourse or inquiry concerning Sadāśiva purifies three types of people—the speaker, the questioner, and the listeners—just as the water of the Gaṅgā does.
O twice-born ones, what man could ever grow weary of reciting the virtues of Śambhu, who always brings joy to the three classes of beings, except for the slaughterer of animals?

For although it is the medicine for the disease of worldly existence, it is nevertheless sung by those free from craving; and because it is delightful to the mind and ear, it is indeed the bestower of all goals.
O twice-born ones, I shall relate the divine play of Śiva with diligence according to my understanding and in accordance with your questions; listen to it with respect.
Just as you have asked, so indeed was it asked by Nārada, who was impelled by Hari in the form of Śiva, to his father.
Having heard the words of his son, Brahmā, a devotee of Śiva, with a delighted mind, sang the glory of Śiva out of love, gladdening the best of sages.
O best of the twice-born, having heard those words spoken by Vyāsa and Sūta, they, filled with curiosity, questioned him regarding that excellent dialogue.
The sages said: "O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, best of Śiva’s devotees, O great-minded one! Having heard your delightful words, our hearts are filled with curiosity."

When did that great conversation between Vidhi and Nārada take place, which brought happiness and wherein the Lord of the Mountain’s playful sport, which liberates one from worldly existence, was revealed?
O dear one, out of affection for us, please recount the glory of Śiva preceded by the dialogue with Nārada, in accordance with each respective question.
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, Sūta, being well-pleased, spoke in accordance with their conversation.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sages' Inquiry," in the Section on Creation within the Second Book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: At that time, O Brahmins, Nārada, the best of sages and son of Brahmā, being humble in spirit, set his mind upon performing austerities.
There was a certain cave in the snowy mountains, exceedingly beautiful, near which the celestial river always flows with great velocity.
There, in that great and divine hermitage endowed with manifold splendors, Nārada of divine vision went to perform austerities.
Having seen her, that tiger among sages, pure in intellect, assumed a firm posture, observed silence, and performed breath-control before practicing penance for a very long time.
O twice-born ones, the sage entered that samādhi wherein the realization "I am Brahman" arises, which brings about the direct perception of Brahman.
While that best of sages, Nārada, was thus performing his penance, Śunāsīra trembled, overwhelmed by mental anguish.
Thinking thus in his mind, "This sage desires my kingdom; indeed, Hari has made an effort for the purpose of creating an obstacle to that," he [the king] acted.
Śakra, the leader of the gods, remembered Smara with his mind; Kāma, the son of the queen, arrived swiftly, his intellect focused on the task.
Then, seeing that Smara had arrived, the lordly king of the gods, his mind crooked regarding his own interest, addressed him: "Look closely at him quickly."
Indra said: "O best of friends, great hero, ever-doer of good, listen with affection to my words and assist me with your own self."
By your power, my pride in asceticism and that of many others has been destroyed; O friend, the stability of my kingdom shall always depend upon your grace.
For in a cave of the snowy mountains, the sage Nārada performs austerities, firm and possessed of great self-restraint, having fixed his mind upon Viśveśvara.
If he should not accept the kingdom according to the prescribed rule, fearing that it belongs to me, go there this very day and create an obstacle to his asceticism.
Thus commanded by Mahendra, that beloved Kāma, together with Madhu, went to that place and out of pride devised his own stratagem.
There he quickly displayed all his various arts; even while dwelling there, he manifested his power in many ways out of pride.
O best of sages, the mind of the sage did not undergo any change; indeed, his pride was cast away through the grace of Maheśa.
Listen with respect, O Śaunaka and others, to the reason for this: by the grace of the Lord, the power of Smara indeed has no effect here.
In this very place, Śambhu, the enemy of Smara, performed great austerities; it was here that he swiftly consumed Kāma, who had violated the penances of the sages.
Requested by the gods who had sought him out for the sake of pleasure and the sustenance of desire, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, spoke this.
"O gods, having attained a certain opportunity, Smara will live; however, no means for Smara shall prevail here."
O immortals, as long as this earth is visible here to people standing [there], it will undoubtedly never move from its place due to the power of the arrows of Kāma.
Thus, according to the words of Śambhu, Kāma, whose course was now rendered illusory, immediately went from Nārada to heaven, into the presence of Indra.
Smara related the entire account and the power of the sage; then, by his command, that lover of spring departed for his own abode.
The lord of the gods was struck with wonder and then praised Nārada, for he was ignorant of that event and deluded by the māyā of Śiva.
The Māyā of Śambhu is difficult to comprehend for all living beings here; the entire world is deluded by her, except for the devotee who has surrendered his self.
Nārada also remained there for a long time by the grace of the Lord; then, considering his own austerity to be complete, the sage desisted from it.
O Lord of Sages, Kāma, considering himself unconquerable, became arrogant; deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, he was rendered devoid of wisdom in vain.
Blessed, blessed is Mahāmāyā, the consort of Śambhu, O best of sages! Even Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others do not perceive her true nature.
Greatly deluded by her, Nārada, the best of sages, quickly went to Kailāsa to report his own conduct to me.
Having bowed to Rudra, the arrogant sage related his entire history, considering himself a great soul and remembering the victory of his own lord, Smara.
Having heard that, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke to Nārada, who was deluded by his own *māyā*, ignorant of the cause, and whose mind was distraught.
Rudra said: O dear Nārada, wise one, you are blessed; listen to my words. This must not be spoken anywhere, especially in the presence of Hari.
Even if questioned, you must not speak of my own conduct as you have told it; for it is to be hidden, hidden in every way, and must never be spoken of at any time.
I instruct you with particular care, for you are most dear to me; since you are a devotee of Viṣṇu, a devotee of Him is exceedingly devoted to me.
In this matter, the Lord Rudra, the progenitor, has been the teacher many times; yet Nārada, deluded by Śiva’s māyā, did not consider it beneficial.
The wise should understand that the course of future karma is powerful; it cannot be averted by anyone, for it is the very will of Śaṅkara.
Then that best of sages indeed went to the world of Brahmā; having bowed to Brahmā, he spoke of his own victory over desire through the power of his asceticism.
Having heard that, Brahmā then remembered the lotus feet of Śambhu; having understood the entire cause, he then forbade his son.
Nārada, the best among the wise, though instructed in what is beneficial, was deluded by Śiva’s māyā; the sprout of pride had taken root in his mind.
Whatever the will of Śiva may be in this world, that indeed comes to pass; for the entire universe is dependent upon him, since it remains within the thread of his word.
Then Nārada, his mind ruined and his thoughts fixed on the sprout of intoxication, went quickly to the world of Viṣṇu to recount his own conduct before Him.
Seeing the lord of sages, Nārada, approaching, Viṣṇu rose with reverence and went forward; knowing the reason, he quickly embraced him.
Having seated him upon his own seat and recollected the lotus feet of Śiva, Hari spoke these truthful words to Nārada, who had destroyed Madana.
Viṣṇu said: "From where have you come, dear one, and for what purpose have you arrived here? You are blessed, O tiger among sages; by your arrival, I myself am purified as a sacred ford."
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the sage Nārada became arrogant; deluded by pride, he recounted his entire conduct along with its attendant haughtiness.
Having heard the words of the sage, Viṣṇu then understood the entire cause of his agitation by remembering the lotus feet of Śiva in his heart.

Hari, whose soul was Śiva and who was the foremost of the devotees of Śiva, praised Giriśa with devotion; with palms joined in reverence, his mind purified and his head bowed, he lauded the Supreme Lord.
Viṣṇu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Blessed are you, O Śiva; blessed is your Māyā that deludes all.
Having thus offered praise to Śiva, the Supreme Self, he closed his eyes, meditated upon His lotus feet, and became silent.
Having understood what must be done for Śaṅkara, that protector of the universe, by the command of Śiva, spoke from his heart to the best of sages.
Viṣṇu said: "O tiger among sages, you are blessed—a treasure-house of austerity and noble intellect. O sage, you possess no triple-fold of worldly attachment, nor desire, delusion, and the like."
Indeed, transformations that bestow all manner of suffering arise for him immediately; you, however, are a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī), always possessed of knowledge and detachment.
"How could one who is wise by birth be subject to the transformations of desire? Having heard these and many other such words, that best of sages—
Having bowed in his heart, he laughed and replied these words to Hari. Nārada said: "O Lord, what is the power of Smara, if you have compassion for me?"
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, the sage departed as he pleased.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Austerities," in the first section (Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, disciple of Vyāsa, salutations be unto you! This wonderful tale, dear one, has indeed been narrated to us out of your compassion.
O father, after the sage had departed, what did Hari do thereafter? And where did Nārada go? You should explain that to me.
Vyāsa said: Having heard their words, the wise Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, remembered Śiva—the creator of various progeny—and replied.
Sūta said: When that sage Nārada had departed at his own will, Viṣṇu, who is skilled in the art of illusion, quickly employed his māyā by the will of Śiva.
In the middle of the Sage’s path, however, he established a great city, a hundred yojanas in extent, wonderful and most enchanting.
More delightful than his own world, adorned with various objects, rich in the pastimes of men and women, and filled with the four castes, it was supreme.
There, a king named Śīlanidhi, endowed with sovereign power, was engaged in a svayaṃvara for his daughter, accompanied by a great festival.
He was joined by the sons of kings who had arrived from the four quarters, all beautifully adorned in various costumes and eager to choose his daughter as their bride.
Having seen such a city, Nārada was then overcome with wonder; curious and inflamed by passion, he went to the gate of that king.
Seeing that best of sages arrive, King Śīlanidhi seated him upon an excellent jeweled lion-throne and paid him honor.
Then the king, having brought his excellent daughter named Śrīmatī, made her prostrate at the feet of Nārada.
Beholding that maiden, the sage Nārada, filled with wonder, said: "O King, who is this illustrious maiden, resembling the daughter of a god?"
Having heard those words of his, the king spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O Sage, this is my daughter, Śrīmatī by name."
Having reached the time for giving her away, she, endowed with all auspicious marks, arrived at her *svayaṃvara* seeking a noble and auspicious husband.
O Sage, tell me her entire fortune with respect according to her horoscope; tell me what kind of husband this daughter of mine will obtain.
Thus addressed, that tiger among sages, desiring her and overwhelmed by passion, spoke these words to the king after addressing him: Nārada said:
"O protector of the earth, this daughter of yours is endowed with all auspicious marks; she is highly fortunate, blessed, and an abode of virtues like Lakṣmī herself."
The Lord of All, the unconquered hero, the all-pervading one who resembles the Lord of Mountains—he, the conqueror of desire and the best of gods, will certainly become her husband.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, the sage departed according to his own will; yet, deluded by the illusory power of Śiva, he became helpless under the sway of desire.
Reflecting thus in his mind, that sage wondered: "How might I obtain her? How might she choose me alone from among the kings at the svayaṃvara?"
Beauty is always dear to all women; having seen that [beauty], she will undoubtedly become pleased and come under his control.
Having thus fashioned the form of Viṣṇu, Nārada, the best of sages, overwhelmed by passion, went swiftly to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having prostrated before Hṛṣīkeśa, he spoke these words: "In private, I shall relate my own story to you in its entirety."
When it was said, "So be it," and that had come to pass, Śiva’s will indeed became the agent of the action; and when the Lord of Śrī said, "Speak," the sage spoke to Keśava.
Nārada said: Your king is a treasure-house of virtuous conduct and is devoted to righteousness; he has a daughter with large eyes, Śrīmatī, who possesses an excellent complexion.
O Viṣṇu, she who is renowned as Jaganmohinī and is exceedingly beautiful even throughout the three worlds—I desire to marry her today; do not delay.
That king held a svayaṃvara at the desire of his daughter; thousands of princes arrived from the four quarters.
If you grant me your form, then I shall certainly obtain her; for without your form upon her neck, she will not wear the garland of victory.
"O Lord, grant me your own form; I am your servant and dear to you. May that illustrious daughter of the king indeed choose me."
The son said: Having heard these words of the sage, Madhusūdana, smiling and recognizing Śiva’s sovereign power, replied, being devoted to compassion.
Viṣṇu said: "O sage, go to your own desired place; I shall do what is for your benefit, for you are dearer to me than a preeminent physician is to the afflicted."
Having spoken thus to that sage, Viṣṇu granted him his own form as Hara’s face; having bestowed this grace upon him, he vanished from sight.

Thus addressed, the sage was delighted; having regained his own true form from that of Hari, he considered himself to have achieved his purpose, and he did not perceive the effort required for that transformation.
Then, having gone there quickly, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived at the place where the svayaṃvara was being held, crowded with princes.
O best of brahmins, that divine assembly hall for the svayaṃvara, filled with princes, shone exceedingly, like the supreme assembly of Śakra.
Nārada sat down in that royal assembly; having stood there, he reflected with a heart full of joy.
"She will certainly choose me and no other, for she does not know the ugliness of my face, O best of sages, as I am currently bearing the form of Viṣṇu."
All the people there beheld the sage in his former form; however, O twice-born ones, the princes and others did not perceive that difference.
There, two attendants of Rudra, having arrived for the purpose of guarding him, assumed the forms of Brahmins and remained hidden; there they perceived this supreme [event].
Thinking the sage to be a fool, those two attendants went near him and mocked him while conversing with one another.
Behold, Nārada, his form is indeed most excellent like that of Viṣṇu, yet his face is distorted and terrifying like that of a monkey.
"This princess desires [him] in vain, deluded by passion," they said, uttering these deceitful words and mocking him.
Overwhelmed by passion, the sage did not hear that speech as it truly was; deluded and desiring her, he gazed intently at that illustrious woman.
In the meantime, that daughter of the king, a woman of excellent complexion, arrived there from the inner apartments, surrounded by her female attendants.
Taking up a beautiful golden garland at that auspicious moment, she shone there in the midst of the svayaṃvara like Lakṣmī herself.
Taking the garland, that princess of virtuous vows wandered throughout the entire assembly, seeking therein the bridegroom who was her own heart's desire.
Seeing the sage with the face of a monkey and the body of Viṣṇu, she became enraged; but then, averting her gaze, she departed with a joyful mind.
Not seeing her own chosen husband there, whom she desired in her heart, which member of the assembly seated within did she not cast her garland upon?
In the meantime, Viṣṇu arrived in the form of a king; he was not seen by any others, but she alone beheld him.
Then, beholding him, that woman of excellent complexion, her lotus-like face radiant with joy, placed that garland upon his neck.
Taking her from there, the Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a king, immediately vanished and indeed departed for his own abode.
All the princes became despondent regarding Śrīmatī, while the sage, afflicted by passion, became exceedingly distraught.
Then those two attendants of Rudra, who were experts in knowledge and had assumed the form of brahmins, immediately spoke to Nārada, whose voice was faltering.
The two Gaṇas said: O Sage Nārada, you are indeed deluded by lust for no reason; desiring that [woman], look upon your own face as contemptible as that of a monkey.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the two of them, Nārada was struck with wonder; deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, he beheld his own face in a mirror.
Seeing his own face like that of a monkey, the sage became enraged and, being deluded, immediately pronounced a curse upon those two attendants there.
"Since you two indeed mocked me, a brahmin, may you both become rākṣasas born from the power of a brahmin, possessing his very form."
Having heard this curse from the attendants of Hara, those two best among the wise said nothing at all, for they recognized that the sage was deluded.
The two brahmins returned to their own abodes, remaining indifferent while offering praise to Śiva, always considering everything to be the will of Śiva.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Delusion," in the Section on Creation within the Second Book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, a truly wonderful story has been narrated. Blessed indeed is the Māyā of Śambhu; the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is subject to it.
When the two groups had departed by the will of the omnipresent Śambhu himself, what did the sage Nārada do—enraged and overwhelmed by passion?
Sūta said: Having bestowed upon them the appropriate curse, the sage, deluded, then beheld his own form reflected in the water by the will of Giriśa.
Not awakened by the will of Śiva, and remembering the deception practiced by Hari, he gave way to unbearable anger and departed for the world of Viṣṇu.
Enraged like a blazing fire, the maimed one, his wisdom lost by the will of Śiva, spoke words filled with insults.
Nārada said: O Hari, you are a great evildoer, a deceiver who deludes the universe; you cannot endure the success of others, being a master of illusion with a defiled heart.
In ancient times, assuming the form of Mohinī, you practiced a stratagem; you caused the Asuras to drink the wine of Varuṇa, but not the nectar.
O Hari, if Rudra, the Great Lord, had shown compassion and not drunk the poison, then all your illusory power (māyā) would have been destroyed; you speak thus only out of deceit.
O Viṣṇu, these deceptions are exceedingly dear to you; you do not possess a virtuous nature, for you have been made dependent by the Lord.
The Supreme Self, Śiva, who acts with independent agency, did not perform what was appropriate; rather, having meditated upon the power of that [other's] influence, he acted.
Having thoroughly understood your state, he fell into remorse; he, who had established the authority of the Vedas spoken by himself, declared the Brahmin to be supreme over all.
Knowing that, O Hari, I shall today discipline you by force, so that you may never again perform such an act anywhere.
Even now you remain fearless, for you have not yet abandoned association with the swift one; O Viṣṇu, you shall now reap the fruit of your own actions.
Having spoken thus to Hari, the sage, deluded by Māyā and despondent with anger, displayed his Brahmanic luster and uttered a curse.
O Viṣṇu, you, the deluder, have caused me to become agitated on account of a woman; you followed me in your own form, acting with deceitful intent.
O mountain, become a human being in that very form and experience that suffering; let those whom you have made my mouth become your companions.
"You, who inflict suffering upon others, shall experience the pain born of separation from your wife; for you are likely to be reborn in the human realm, deluded by ignorance."
Having thus cursed Hari out of delusion, Nārada, bewildered by ignorance, accepted that curse while praising the unborn Śāmbhavī.
Then Śambhu, the performer of great divine play, drew forth his own deluding Māyā, by which even the wise Nārada was enchanted.
When the illusion had vanished, the wise Nārada became as he was before—his mind filled with wonder, having attained awakening and being free from agitation.
Having fallen into remorse, he censured himself again and again; he then praised the illusory power of Śiva (Māyā-śāmbhavī), which deludes even the wise.
Then, having realized that all was the delusive play of his own self, Nārada, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, fell at the feet of Viṣṇu.
Addressed by Hari, the one of ruined intellect spoke these words: "Wicked words were uttered by me while I was deluded and possessed of evil intent."
"O Lord, although a curse was pronounced by him, render it now futile; for I have committed a great sin and shall surely go to hell."
O Hari, what means should I, your servant, employ? Instruct me in that by which the multitude of my sins may perish and hell shall not be mine.
Having spoken thus, that best of sages, Sumati, overcome with remorse, fell again with devotion at the feet of Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu, having raised him up, spoke these truthful words. Viṣṇu said: "Do not grieve, O my devotee; you are a worthy recipient of boons, of this there is no doubt."
Listen, dear one; I shall speak that which is for your benefit with certainty.
Hell shall not be yours; Śiva will grant you auspiciousness.
Since you, deluded by pride, rendered the word of Śiva false, that action, which yields its own fruit, has bestowed such a result upon you.
Everything has arisen by the will of Śiva; form this firm resolve. That Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Sovereign, is the remover of pride.

He is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the embodiment of existence, consciousness, bliss, and pure awareness; He is devoid of qualities, changeless, and beyond the modes of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
Having thus assumed his own *māyā*, he becomes threefold in form as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; though he is both devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and not devoid of qualities (*anirguṇa*).
Indeed, the Supreme Self, Maheśvara, who is called Śiva, being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman, the imperishable, the infinite, and Mahādeva.
Through service to Him, I am the creator of the ordinances and the protector of the worlds; I myself am always the destroyer of all in the form of Rudra.
The Witness, whose nature is Śiva, is distinct from Māyā and devoid of qualities; he acts according to his own will, sports at his pleasure, and bestows grace upon his devotees.
Listen, O sage Nārada, to this excellent means which bestows happiness, removes all sins, and always grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having said this, let all of Śaṅkara’s glory be without doubt; with a mind focused on no other, always recite the hymn of the hundred names of Śiva.
"By chanting which, all your sin will be swiftly destroyed. Having spoken thus to Nārada, Viṣṇu, filled with compassion, spoke again.
O Sage, do not grieve; nothing at all was done by you. Śambhu has performed all this of his own will; of this there is no doubt.
He took away your divine intellect through the intoxication of passion and affliction; that Maheśvara caused that curse to be pronounced against me by your mouth.
Thus the Conqueror of Death, the Destroyer of Time, who is solely intent on uplifting his devotees, personally manifested his own deeds in the world.
I have no master as dear to me as Śiva, the bestower of happiness; that Supreme Lord alone is the one who grants me all powers.
O sage, make Him alone your object of worship; constantly devote yourself to Him. Listen to His glory, sing it, and perform His worship perpetually.
O friend, he who approaches Śaṅkara through body, mind, or speech should be known as a wise man; he is called one liberated while living.
The mountains of great sins are reduced to ashes without effort by the forest fire of the name "Śiva"; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Therefore, these various sufferings rooted in evil are destroyed solely by the worship of Śiva; they cannot be destroyed in any other way whatsoever.
O Sage, he who always takes refuge in Śaṅkara with body, speech, and mind is a meritorious soul among Vaidikas, he is blessed, and he is wise.
Those for whom various spiritual practices are poised to yield immediate results develop confidence in the worship of Tripurāntaka.
O great sage, there are no sins whatsoever on earth that are not destroyed by the worship of Śiva.
O Sage, even immeasurable heaps of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish through the remembrance of Śiva; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Having obtained the boat that is the name of Śiva, they cross the ocean of saṃsāra; the root sins of saṃsāra are destroyed for them without a doubt.
O great sage, the destruction of those sins which constitute the very root of saṃsāra is certainly brought about by the axe that is the name of Śiva.
The nectar of Śiva’s name should be drunk by those afflicted by the forest fire of sin; for those scorched by the forest fire of sin, there is indeed no peace without it.
One who is completely drenched by the continuous downpour of the nectar of the name "Śiva" does not grieve even in the midst of the forest fire of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt.
Devotion to Śaṅkara does not arise in men whose minds are devoted to passion and hatred; for such as these, liberation can by no means occur suddenly.
Only for one who has performed austerity throughout infinite births does devotion arise toward Bhavānī, who is as dear as life itself.
Even if devotion to Śaṅkara has arisen, it is in vain if it is shared with others; rather, devotion to Śiva must be sought as something unswerving.
It is my firm conviction that for one who possesses unswerving and exclusive devotion to Śambhu, liberation is easily attained; it is not so for anyone else.
Even after committing infinite sins, if there is devotion to Maheśvara, one becomes completely liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Just as trees in the forest are reduced to ashes when consumed by fire, so too are the sins of the devotees of Śaṅkara burnt away.
He whose limbs are constantly purified by ashes and who remains intent upon the worship of Śiva, certainly crosses over this shoreless and most terrible cycle of existence.
Even after seizing the property of a Brahmin and killing many Brahmins, a man who is a servant of Virūpākṣa is not tainted by sins.
Having examined all the Vedas, the ancients determined that the supreme worship of Śiva alone is the means for destroying the cycle of worldly existence.
From this day forward, with diligence and heedfulness according to the prescribed rule, worship the Great Lord Sadāśiva together with Ambā with constant devotion.
Having thoroughly smeared yourself with ashes from head to foot with devotion, recite the six-syllabled Śaiva mantra, which is heard in all the Vedas.
With great effort and supreme devotion, wear Rudrākṣa beads, which are dear to Śiva, upon all your limbs according to the prescribed rite accompanied by mantras.
Listen constantly to the story of Śiva; always speak the story of Śiva; and worship the devotees of Śiva again and again with great effort.
Constantly take refuge in Śiva alone through heedfulness, since through the constant worship of Śiva, bliss is attained.
Placing the pure lotus-feet of Śiva upon your chest, O best of sages, first wander through the sacred sites of Śiva.
O sage, beholding the incomparable majesty of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, you should afterwards go to Ānandavana, which is most dear to Śambhu.
Having seen Viśveśvara there, perform worship with devotion; by bowing down and praising him especially, you will become free from conceptual constructions (nirvikalpa).
Therefore, O Sage, you must certainly proceed to the world of Brahmā for the sake of your own desire, out of devotion and in accordance with my command.
O Sage, having bowed to and especially praised his own father, Brahmā, with a delighted heart, he asked many times about the greatness of Śiva, which was worthy of inquiry.
That Brahmā, the foremost of the Śaivas, will with great affection cause you to hear the majesty of Śaṅkara and indeed the hymn of his hundred names.
O Sage, from this day forth, become a devotee of Śiva, dedicated to Śiva; you shall especially partake in liberation, for Śiva will bestow well-being upon you.
Having thus instructed the sage with affection, Viṣṇu, his mind serene, remembered Śiva, praised and lauded him, and then vanished from sight.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Instruction by Viṣṇu," in the first section (Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, when Hari had vanished, Nārada, the best of sages, wandered the earth beholding the Śiva-liṅgas with devotion.
O Brahmins, having wandered over the earth, he joyfully beheld numerous forms of Śiva that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, recognizing that Nārada of divine vision was wandering there, those two attendants of Śambhu approached him with well-disposed minds.
Having quickly bowed their heads in deep reverence and grasped his feet with the desire to be released from the curse, those two Gaṇas spoke with great respect.
The two attendants of Śiva said: "O son of Brahmā, O celestial sage, listen with affection to our words. We two are not truly Brahmins who have committed an offense against you."
O Brahmin, O Sage, we two, the attendants of Hara, have committed an offense against you, our minds deluded by illusion during the princess’s svayaṃvara.
The curse bestowed upon us by you was indeed prompted by the Supreme Lord; having recognized that time there to be inauspicious, silence alone was our life.
The fruit of one's own karma has been obtained; indeed, no one else is to be blamed. O Lord, be well-pleased and grant us your grace this day.
Sūta said: Having heard these words spoken with devotion and respect by the two attendants, the sage, feeling remorse, replied with affection.
Nārada said: Listen to my words, O Mahādeva, you who are most honored among the virtuous; they are pleasant, free from delusion, and true to their meaning.
Formerly, my mind was deluded by the power of Śiva’s will; having fallen into total confusion, I, whose intellect was impaired, cursed you both.
What has been spoken shall come to pass exactly so; nevertheless, O two attendants, listen as I declare the removal of the curse. Forgive my transgression today.
Having attained the sovereignty of the Rākṣasas through the prowess of that best of sages, may you both be endowed with great power, strong, and highly illustrious.
O sovereigns of all the Brahmāṇḍas, you two devotees of Śiva who have conquered your senses, having met death at the hands of one whose body is subordinate to Śiva, you shall attain your own station.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the high-souled sage Nārada, both attendants of Hara were pleased and returned to their own abodes with joy.
Nārada too, supremely delighted, meditating on Śiva with undistracted mind, wandered the earth, repeatedly beholding the sacred shrines of Śiva.
Then, having reached Kāśī, which shines above all, beloved by Śiva, bestowing the bliss of Śambhu, and identical in nature to Śambhu, that sage—
Having beheld Kāśī, he became one who had fulfilled his purpose; he gazed upon the Lord of Kāśī and, filled with supreme bliss, worshipped him with great affection.
Having achieved his purpose, that best of sages joyfully served Kāśī, bowing with devotion, praising it, and remembering it while overwhelmed with love.
Then, with his mind fixed on the remembrance of Śiva, Nārada, desiring to know the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva) in particular, went to the world of Brahmā.
Having bowed there with devotion according to the prescribed rite and having praised him with various hymns, he whose mind was fully devoted to Śiva questioned him regarding the true nature of Śiva.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, knower of the nature of Brahman, Grandfather, Lord of the universe! By your grace, I have [learned] all the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu.
I have heard of the path of devotion, the path of knowledge, the path of austerity so difficult to traverse, the path of charity, and the path of sacred pilgrimage sites.
The reality of Śiva and the procedure for his worship have not been understood by me according to their proper sequence; O Lord, please relate to me his various deeds.

O father, how is it that Śiva, though devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), is also Śaṅkara possessed of qualities (saguṇa)? Deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, I do not understand the true nature of Śiva (śivatattva).
How was Śambhu established in his own essential nature prior to creation? And how does that Lord conduct himself while sporting during the midst of creation?
And at the conclusion of that, how does the god Maheśvara remain? How does Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, attain a state of grace?
O Creator, tell me all this: what fruit does Maheśvara, being satisfied, bestow upon his own devotees and upon others?
It has been heard that the Blessed One becomes gracious instantly; that Great One, devoted to compassion, does not regard the effort of his devotee.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—these three gods are born from portions of Śiva; among them, Maheśa is the full portion, being Śiva himself, the Supreme.
Tell me of his manifestation and his deeds in detail; O Lord, tell me of the manifestation of Umā and likewise of her marriage.
O sinless one, you must relate in detail that state of household life, as well as those other divine pastimes—indeed, all of this and whatever else there may be.
O Lord of Creatures, tell me specifically of his birth, his marriage to Śivā, and likewise of Guha’s birth.
I have heard this from many before, yet I am not satiated, O Lord of the World; therefore, I have come to you for refuge—please show me your compassion.
Having heard these words of Nārada, his own son, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke these words there.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Inquiry," in the Section on Creation within the second book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Brāhmaṇa, best of the wise, you have questioned me well; you are one who constantly benefits the world, desiring the welfare of all beings.
Having heard which, the destruction of all sins of all worlds shall occur; that healthy reality of Śiva (śivatattva), I shall proclaim to you.
The Śiva-principle has not been truly known by me, nor even by Viṣṇu; its supreme form is wondrous and beyond the highest.
And at the time of the great dissolution, when all moving and stationary things had perished, everything was enveloped in darkness, devoid of sun, planets, and stars.
It is without moon, mind, day, or night; without fire, wind, earth, or water; devoid of primordial matter (pradhāna), empty space, and the void; and free from any other light.
Devoid of being unseen and so forth, abandoned by sound and touch, with unmanifested smell and form, and free from taste, it has no direction or face.
Thus, in the dense darkness of untruth that is impenetrable even by a needle, one who hears "That is the True Brahman" attains the One Reality.
When such a thing as this—which consists of both being and non-being—did not exist, yogis behold that continuously within the internalized space.
It is never an object of speech, nor is it within the range of the mind; it is devoid of name, form, and color, being neither gross nor subtle.
It is devoid of shortness, length, lightness, and heaviness; wherein there is no increase whatsoever, nor likewise any decrease.
The Śruti, however, declares with awe that He exists as Truth, Knowledge, Infinity, Supreme Bliss, and the Highest Light.
Immeasurable, without support, unchanging, and formless; devoid of qualities, accessible only to yogis, all-pervading, and the sole agent.

It is free from conceptual construction, free from undertaking, free from illusion, and free from affliction; it is non-dual, without beginning or end, without expansion, and consists of the nature of consciousness.
For him who thus conceptualized through the expression of names and the named, after some time, it is said that a second desire indeed arose.
And by His own sport, He who is formless fashioned for Himself a form, auspicious, consisting of all knowledge, and endowed with all sovereign qualities.

She who pervades all, who possesses all forms, who sees all, and who performs all actions; she who is to be venerated by all as the one, who is the primordial source of all, and who at all times is the refinement of everything.

He conceptualized that sovereign form, which is pure in nature, non-dual, without beginning or end, manifesting as all things, consisting of consciousness, and is the supreme Brahman—omnipresent and immutable—which then withdrew within itself.
Sadāśiva is indeed the embodied form of that which is formless and known as the Supreme; the wise have declared that Lord to be both immanent and transcendent.
At that time, even while wandering at will, his Śakti created from her own body a form that never departs from her own person.
They call that Pradhāna, the Supreme Prakṛti, Māyā, possessed of qualities (guṇavatī), the mother of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), and devoid of any modification.
That Śakti is called Ambikā, Prakṛti, and the sovereign of all; she is the eternal mother of the three gods and is indeed the primordial cause.
She had eight arms and beautiful faces of various forms; and in her face, there was always the splendor of a thousand full moons.
Adorned with various ornaments, endowed with various modes of movement, bearing various weapons, the goddess has eyes like full-blown lotuses.
Endowed with inconceivable splendor, Māyā is the source of all; when she is alone, she is one, but through conjunction, she becomes manifold.
He is the Supreme Person, the Lord, Śiva, Śambhu, and the Unconditioned; he bears the stream of the Mandākinī upon his head, possesses the crescent moon on his brow, and has three eyes.
Five-faced and serene in nature, with ten arms and holding a trident, he is as white as camphor, beautifully radiant, and his body is smeared with ashes.
And simultaneously with that power, by means of that which is the very nature of time, that Brahmā created the sacred field known as Śivaloka.
That very place is called Kāśikā, the most excellent field; it is the supreme reckoning of liberation, shining resplendent above all.
And while those two, who were embodiments of supreme bliss, were sporting in that delightful field, she too was an embodiment of supreme bliss.
O Sage, even at the time of universal dissolution, that sacred field is never abandoned by the two Śivas; therefore, they know it as Avimukta (the Unabandoned).
In ancient times, this place was named Ānandavana by the wielder of the Pināka bow; it was established immediately after Avimukta because it is the cause of bliss for the sacred field.
Then, O celestial sage, while Śiva and Śivā were sporting in that Ānandavana grove, a desire arose in them: "Indeed, another being must surely be created."
In whomsoever we, wandering at our own will, place our great burden, we achieve the state of liberation simply by lying down in Kāśī.
May he alone perform everything; may he alone protect you; and may he alone always conceal you for the sake of my grace.

Having contracted the ocean of the mind, which is tossed by the waves of thought, containing the jewel of sentient beings, seized by the crocodile of darkness, and entwined with the coral vines of passion;
By whose grace we two remain happily in the Ānandakānana forest, our mental fluctuations stilled, finding bliss even while the world outside is anxious with worry.
Having deliberated thus with that Śakti, the all-pervading Supreme Lord caused the nectar-essence to flow into his tenth limb on the left side.
Then a single Person appeared, the most beautiful in the three worlds, peaceful, overflowing with the quality of sattva, and an ocean of immeasurable profundity.
And thus, O Sage, endowed with patience, he became peerless; glorious, with the luster of a sapphire, his eyes like the finest lotuses.
O best of those who bear golden ornaments, clothed in a pair of fine silken garments, you are indeed unconquered, with your pair of powerful, blazing arms.
Then that man, having bowed down to Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, said, "O Master, tell me my names and my duties," and thus he spoke.
Having heard those words, the Lord Śaṅkara, the Great Ruler, smiling, spoke to that man with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Śiva said: Because of your all-pervasiveness, your name shall be celebrated as Viṣṇu; indeed, there will be many other names as well that bring happiness to devotees.
"Perform penance with firm resolve; it is the supreme means for accomplishing your purpose. Having said this, he then bestowed the sacred scripture (Nigama) through the path of his breath.
Then Acyuta, having bowed to Śiva, performed extensive penance; the Supreme Lord, along with His power (Śakti) and His world, vanished from sight.
Even after performing penance for twelve thousand divine years, Acyuta did not obtain his heart's desire: the vision of Śambhu, which bestows all things.
Having fallen into various doubts, Viṣṇu, remembering Śiva, respectfully reflected in his heart: "What should I do now?"
In the meantime, an auspicious voice issued forth from Śiva: "Penance must be performed once again for the removal of doubt."
Then, having heard that, he performed most severe penance for a long time, being entirely devoted to the path of meditation on Brahman.
Then that person, Viṣṇu, awakened from the path of meditation, was well-pleased and filled with wonder, thinking, "What is this great thing of yours?"
From the very limbs of that Viṣṇu, who was exerting himself, various streams of water indeed issued forth through the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva.
And that entire void which was pervaded, O Great Sage, became water in the form of Brahman, which destroys sins through its touch.
Then the weary Viṣṇu himself, being deeply delighted and utterly enchanted, slept for a long time within that water.
Even his name, Nārāyaṇa, was sanctioned by the Vedas; for at that time, there existed nothing else whatsoever except for that Primal Puruṣa.
In this interval of time, the principles (tattvas) of the Great-Souled One existed; listen, O wise one of great intellect, as I describe their manner to you.
From Prakṛti arose the Mahat, and from the Mahat the three qualities; from that, the ego (ahaṃkāra) was born, which is threefold according to the distinction of the qualities.

From that, the subtle elements (tanmātras) were born, and from them indeed the five gross elements (bhūtas); at that very time, the sense organs (indriyas), consisting of both knowledge and action, also arose.
O best of sages, you have described the enumeration of the principles; all of that is insentient by nature, except for the Puruṣa.
Having, by the will of Śiva, grasped those twenty-four principles unified as one, he slept within the form of Brahman.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Viṣṇu," in the first section (Sṛṣṭivyākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: While the divine Nārāyaṇa was asleep, an excellent lotus suddenly appeared from his navel by the will of the Creator.
It was endowed with infinite pillars, possessed a radiance equal to that of the karṇikāra flower, and was joined with an infinite extent and an infinite height measured in yojanas.
Resembling ten million suns, endowed with a beautiful voice, most wonderful, exceedingly delightful, lovely to behold, and unsurpassed.
Having exerted effort as before, that supreme lord Śaṃkara, the source of happiness, brought me forth from his own right limb as Kaiśāśīśa.
O Sage, having quickly deluded me with his illusory power (māyā), Maheśa sportively caused [the universe] to manifest from the lotus of his navel.
From that lotus, I was born as a son named Hemagarbhaka; I had four faces, a red complexion, and my forehead was marked with the triple-ash line (tripuṇḍra).
Deluded by that illusion and weak in knowledge, O lotus-born one, I did not recognize my own father, the progenitor of my body.
Whence has this anger come? What is my duty? Whose son was I born, and by whom have I been created now?
Thus, as I was fallen into doubt, my intellect occurred to me: "For what reason do I fall into delusion? That knowledge is indeed easy to attain."
Indeed, this place below is the site where the stalk of this lotus flower grows; he who made me shall surely be there, of this there is no doubt.
Having thus fixed his mind, O sage, he descended from the lotus and moved from stalk to stalk for a hundred years.
But I did not obtain that supreme lotus-abode there; instead, eager to go to Kamala, I fell once more into doubt.
