Then, O Sage, she ascended the lotus by way of its stalk; yet, being utterly deluded, she did not find the bud of the lotus.
As he wandered along the wrong path, another hundred years passed; yet there, remaining deluded, it seemed to him like only a single moment.
Then, O Sage, by the will of Śiva, a supreme and most auspicious voice arose from the sky, destroying delusion. It was the word "Tapa" (Austerity).
Having heard that voice from the sky, he then performed severe penance for twelve years with great effort in order to see his own father.
For at that time, the Lord Viṣṇu, four-armed and beautiful-eyed, quickly manifested himself before me alone in order to bestow his grace.
The Supreme One has the conch and discus as weapons in his hands and bears the mace and lotus; his entire body is dark like a rain cloud, and he wears yellow garments.
Adorned with great ornaments such as a crown, his lotus-like face serene, and resembling ten million gods of love, he was gazed upon by the deluded one.
Having seen that beautiful form—dark as time yet radiant as gold, the four-armed soul of all—he was filled with supreme wonder.
Having seen Nārāyaṇa of mighty arms in such a state, composed of both being and non-being, I was then filled with joy.
Then, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of the Lord Śambhu, whose nature is play, and failing to recognize him as my own father, I spoke to him with great joy.
Brahmā said: "Who are you? Speak! Having thus raised Sanātana with his hand, by that sharp and very firm blow of the hand, [he was shaken].
Having awakened and risen from his bed, the self-controlled one sat for a moment and beheld his eyes, which were as pure as lotuses moistened by sleep.
While I was seated there, the Blessed Lord Hari, having taken his seat upon the throne, rose up and, smiling, spoke sweetly once to Brahmā and to me.
Viṣṇu said: Welcome, welcome, O child, O Grandfather of great splendor! Be free from fear; I shall grant you all your desires, of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of his, O bull among gods, I, who had been bound by enmity through the quality of passion (rajas), spoke with a smile to that Janārdana.
Brahmā said: "O sinless one, having smiled here, you address me—the cause of the destruction of all—as 'child, child,' just as a teacher addresses a disciple."
The direct creator of the worlds and the instigator of primordial nature (prakṛti), the eternal, unborn Viṣṇu, who is Viriñci and born from Viṣṇu.
"Why do you speak out of delusion regarding the lotus-eyed Creator, the Ordainer, and the Soul of the Universe? You ought to explain this immediately."
The Veda declares me, by its own rule, to be self-born, unborn, and all-pervading; the grandfather, the self-ruling king, and the supreme Parameṣṭhin.
Having heard these words of mine, Hari, the Lord of Ramā, became enraged; he too said to me, "I know you from public report to be the creator."
Viṣṇu said: You have descended from my own imperishable body to create and sustain [the world]; yet you have forgotten Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, who is free from all ailment.
The Supreme Person, the Self of All, invoked by many and praised by many—Viṣṇu, the infallible Lord, the source and origin of the universe.
You were indeed born from the lotus of my navel from Nārāyaṇa, the mighty-armed, all-pervading Lord; of this there is no doubt.
"There is no fault of yours in this; it was an act of illusion performed by me upon you. Listen to the truth, O Four-faced One: I am indeed the Lord of all the gods."
The Lord who is the creator, the destroyer, and the sustainer has no equal to me; I alone am the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Reality, O Grandfather.
I alone am the supreme light; I am the all-pervading Supreme Self. Today, everything seen and heard in this world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is but me.
"Know all that, O Four-faced One, to be composed of me; it was created by me in the past as the manifest twenty-four principles."
Atoms are eternally bound within them, having produced anger, fear, and the like; and by their power, you manifest many limbs here through your divine play.

From that, I created the intellect (buddhi), and from that, the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra); from that, the subtle elements (tanmātra), the lotus-born [the mahat], and from that, the mind, the body, and the senses.
Knowing that the elements such as space and their derivatives exist by your divine play, O Lord of Creatures, O Creator, take refuge in me.

"I shall protect you from all sufferings; of this there is no doubt. Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Brahmā, filled with anger and deluded by Māyā, spoke with indignation: "Who are you?"
For what purpose do you speak so much speech that causes such great harm? You are not the Lord, nor are you the Supreme Brahman; there must be some other creator for you as well.
Deluded by Māyā, I engaged in a most terrible battle with that Hari, the great lord Śaṅkara.
Thus occurred that hair-raising battle between me and Hari in the midst of the ocean of dissolution, as we were bound by enmity through the quality of passion (rajas).
In the meantime, a Liṅga appeared before us both, indeed for the purpose of quelling our dispute and likewise for the sake of awakening us.
Abounding with thousands of garlands of flames, resembling hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction, it is free from decay and growth, and devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
Incomparable, indescribable, unmanifest, and the source of the universe—by its thousands of flames, the Blessed Lord Hari was deluded.
And he said to me, who was deluded there: "For what purpose do you now compete? A third has arrived here; let our battle take place."
How much less could anything produced here withstand the fire? I shall go down beneath this incomparable pillar of fire.
O Lord, for the sake of testing him, you ought to go upwards with great effort and speedily, as swift as the wind.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O sage, the Soul of the Universe immediately assumed his own form; having manifested as the Boar, he swiftly attained the state of a swan.
From that time forth, they have called me Haṃsa-haṃsa Virāj; whoever shall utter "Haṃsa-haṃsa," he too shall become a Haṃsa.
Indeed, having become like fire, endowed with wings on all sides, and possessing the speed of mind and wind, he formerly went upward and further upward.
Then Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe, became pure white; he was ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long.
He was as tall as Mount Meru, with white, sharp, and fierce fangs; he possessed a brilliance equal to the sun at the end of time, a long snout, and a great roar.
Having assumed the form of a boar—short-limbed, with variegated body, victorious, firm, and incomparable—he went into that ocean with speed.
Having wandered in this manner for a thousand years, Viṣṇu descended; from that time forth, he has been known in the worlds as Śvetavārāha.
O divine sage, there was a kalpa known as Nara; Viṣṇu, the powerful lord, wandered in many ways, having descended below.
The boar did not see even the slightest root of this sign; meanwhile, O destroyer of enemies, I too had ascended upwards for that length of time.
Desiring to know its end with all effort and great haste, I became exhausted; yet, not having seen its end, I have fallen downward through time.
In that very manner, the lotus-eyed Lord Viṣṇu, who resembles all the gods, rose up quickly with his great body.
Having come together with me and prostrated repeatedly before you, he stood there with a troubled mind, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śambhu.
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord from behind, from the sides, and indeed from the front, he wondered along with me, "What is this?"
That form is inexpressible, nameless, and devoid of karma; it is signless yet has attained the state of signs, and is beyond the scope even of the path of meditation.
Then, having made our minds composed and being devoted to salutation, both of us—myself and Hari—became truly steadfast.
We truly do not know your form, O Great Lord; who you are and what you are, we do not know. Salutations be unto you, O Maheśāna; show us your form quickly.
In this manner, O tiger among sages, as we remained there filled with pride, we offered salutations for nearly a hundred autumns.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispute between Viṣṇu and Brahmā," in the first section of the *Rudrasaṃhitā* within the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, while we two gods remained thus, constantly longing for a vision of you and free from pride, O sage.
Śambhu became compassionate, the protector of the distressed, the remover of the pride of the arrogant, and the imperishable Lord of all.
Then, O best of gods, there arose there a sound characterized by speech: "Om, Om," clearly manifest and protracted in its syllabic form.
Thinking, "What is this? I stood there with a contented mind before Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by all the gods and is free from enmity, as he uttered a great roar.
On the southern side of the Liṅga, he likewise beheld the eternal, primordial letter called A, and then the letter U to its north.
One should visualize the letter *ma* in the center and the *nāda* at its end as "oṃ"; then, having seen the first syllable like the solar disc on the right.
O best of sages, to the north is the syllable *U*, which resembles fire; and in its center is the syllable *Ma*, which resembles the orb of the moon.
Above that, he then beheld [the state] which possesses the luster of pure crystal, beyond the fourth (turiyatita), stainless, partless, and free from affliction.
Free from duality, absolute, empty, and devoid of both external and internal, it exists both externally and internally, and is established as the very essence of the external and internal.
Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, it is the cause even of bliss; it is the true, blissful, immortal, supreme Brahman, the ultimate refuge.
How much less could one born here possibly examine the origin of fire? I shall go down into that incomparable pillar of fire.
He meditated upon the Soul of the Universe, who is entered by both the Vedic word and its meaning; then, at that moment, there arose there a sage, remembered as the very essence of sages.
By that very sage, Viṣṇu came to know the Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate embodiment of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Devoid of thought, Rudra is that which words, together with the mind, cannot reach; failing to attain it, they turn back, yet he is expressible by means of the single syllable.
That sentence consisting of a single syllable is the immortal, the supreme cause; it is truth, bliss, the nectar of immortality, the supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
From the single syllable known as *A*, the Lord is born from the seed-syllable; from the single syllable known as *U*, Hari is the supreme cause.
From the single syllable known as *ma*, the Lord Nīlalohita is the creator; from the one known as *a* he is indeed the creator, while from the one known as *u* he is the deluder.

That which is called the letter *M* is eternally the bestower of grace; the pervasive Lord is indeed the possessor of the seed (*bījī*) called *M*, while the letter *A* is said to be the seed (*bīja*).

Hari, known by the syllable *ukāra*, is the source (*yoni*), the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa; he is the possessor of the seed (*bījī*) and that source is the seed itself, while Maheśvara is known as *nāda*.
The Seed-holder (Bījī), having divided himself and established himself according to his own will, produced from this Linga the seed of the Lord Bījī, which is the letter A.
Cast into the womb of the syllable *U*, it increased on all sides; it became a golden egg (*aṇḍa*), which was devoid of defining characteristics.
Likewise, for many years, the divine egg remained in the waters; then, at the end of a thousand years, it was divided into two by the Unborn One.
The egg was indeed situated within the waters by the Lord through his intervention; likewise, its beautiful golden shell remained positioned above.
From that [egg], Dyaus was born, and after that, Pṛthivī with her five characteristics; from that egg, Bhava was born, the four-faced one known by the syllable *ka*.
"He is the creator of all worlds; he alone is the threefold Lord. Thus, 'Om, Om' is uttered—so say the best of those versed in the Yajus."
Having heard the words of the Yajus, the Ṛks and Sāmans respectfully said to us at that time: "O Hari, O Brahman, it is exactly so."

In the meantime, the Blessed One, the protector of the universe, beheld another form, wonderfully beautiful, together with me.

Having seen that supreme form of Hari—most noble, of great heroism, and possessing the marks of a Great Man—I became one who has accomplished his purpose.

The letter *a* is indeed its head, while the long vowel *ā* is said to be the forehead; *i* is the right eye, and *ī* is the left eye.
The syllable *u* is said to be the right ear, and the syllable *ū* the left; the syllable *ṛ* is the right cheek of that Supreme Lord.
The letter *ū* is on the left cheek; *ḷ*, *ḹ*, and *ḹ* are in both nostrils; the letter *e* is on the upper lip, and the letter *ai* is on the lower lip of the Lord.
The letter *o* and likewise the letter *au* correspond respectively to the two rows of teeth; while the letter *am* belongs to the palate of that trident-bearing God of gods.
The five syllables beginning with *ka* are his five right hands, and likewise the five syllables beginning with *ca* are his five left hands.
The five syllables beginning with *ṭa* are his feet, and likewise the five syllables beginning with *ta*; the letter *pa* is his belly, and the letter *pha* is said to be his side.
The letter *ba* is on the left side, while the letter *bha* is said to be the shoulder; the letter *ma* is the heart of Śambhu, the great god and yogi.
The seven elements of the All-pervasive Lord indeed begin with the letter *ya* and end with the letter *sa*; the letter *ha* is the form of the navel, and the letter *kṣa* is said to be the nose.
Having thus beheld that form consisting of sound—which is both devoid of qualities and yet the essence of qualities—along with Umā, Hari attained his purpose through me.
Having thus beheld Maheśāna, Śiva, whose body is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), and having prostrated before him, Viṣṇu again looked upward.
The mantra originating from the syllable Oṃ, joined with the five groups (kalāpas), resembling pure crystal, and consisting of thirty-eight auspicious syllables.
Furthermore, there arose the mantra originating from the Gāyatrī, which bestows intelligence, accomplishes the purpose of all dharmas, and brings about subjugation.
The mantra consists of twenty-four syllables, is endowed with the four times, and is unsurpassed; then there is the five-fold white mantra, joined with the eight digits (kalās).
The *ābhicārika* [mantra] consists of approximately thirty auspicious syllables; that which is associated with the *Yajurveda* consists of twenty-five auspicious syllables.
The pacifying [mantra] is likewise joined with eight parts (kalās) and is very white; it is joined with thirteen parts and is red, together with Bāla and the others.
Furthermore, sixty-one syllables constitute the cause of the origin, growth, and dissolution of this supreme mantra.
Furthermore, [he taught] the Punarmṛtyujaya mantra, then the five-syllabled mantra, as well as the Cintāmaṇi mantra known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Then, having received from Hara the great Mahāvākya "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) as well as the five mantras, the Blessed Lord Hari chanted them.
Then, having seen him who possesses the form of the Kalās, the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas, the Lord whose crown is Īśāna, the ancient one known as Puruṣa;
The heart of Aghora, dear to the heart, the eternal Śiva who is the secret of all; the left foot of Mahādeva, adorned with the great lord of serpents.
Him who has feet on every side, who has eyes and hands on every side, the auspicious one, the sovereign lord of Brahman, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Accompanied by me, the blessed Viṣṇu, with a satisfied mind, praised the boon-granting Lord Śiva along with Ambā with pleasing words.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Body of Śabdabrahman," in the Section on Creation within the second book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, having heard the praise of himself performed by Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, that ocean of compassion, appeared with great joy and his consort.
He has five faces and three eyes, bears the crescent moon on his forehead, and wears matted locks; he is fair-complexioned, large-eyed, and his body is smeared with ashes.
Ten-armed and blue-throated, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful in every limb, his forehead marked with the triple line of sacred ash.
Having seen that god, the Supreme Lord, together with Vāmā, Viṣṇu, along with me, praised him again with pleasing words.
Then Hara, the Great Lord, the source of compassion, being pleased in spirit, granted a city to him [Śiva] and to Viṣṇu in the form of a dog.
Then he gave that knowledge to Hari, the Supreme Self; and the Supreme Self, O sage, gave it to me in turn out of compassion.
Having reached Nigama, Viṣṇu, having attained his purpose, bowed with joined palms along with me and questioned Maheśvara once again.
Viṣṇu said: O God, how are you pleased? O Lord, how am I to worship you? How should meditation be performed? And how do you come under one's control?
"O Mahādeva, what should be done by us two according to your command? O Śaṅkara, for our pleasure, always and everywhere give us your order."
O Great King, O Lord Śiva, having shown compassion toward us both, you should relate all of this as well as anything else, knowing us to be your own followers.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, the blessed Lord Hara, a treasure-house of compassion, became pleased; being well-pleased, he spoke these words with affection.
The illustrious Śiva said: "O best of gods, I am truly pleased with the devotion of you both; behold me, Mahādeva, and let all fear be cast away."
"My liṅga must always be worshipped and meditated upon as being just like this one which is seen here now; it must be treated with such effort."
Worshipped in the form of a *liṅga*, being pleased, I shall bestow manifold fruits upon all the worlds—many things desired by the mind.
O best of gods, whenever suffering should arise for you two there, the destruction of that suffering shall occur once my linga has been worshipped.
"You two, possessed of great strength, have been born from the two limbs—the right and the left—of my own Prakṛti, for I am the Lord of All."
From my right side, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, has arisen; and from my left side, you, Viṣṇu, have emerged from the Supreme Self.
"I am well-pleased with you both; I shall grant you whatever boon you desire. By my command, may your devotion to me become firm."
"O wise ones, fashion my image out of clay and, having performed various services to it, you shall attain happiness."
"O Brahman, you must indeed carry out the creation, for you are the observer of my command. O dear child, O Hari, you too must protect all that is moving and unmoving in this manner."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to us, the Lord bestowed upon those two an auspicious method of worship, by which Śambhu, when worshipped, bestows manifold fruits.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, Hari, together with me, prostrated before Maheśāna and replied with palms joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu said: "If affection has arisen [between us], and if a boon is to be granted to us both, let there be for us constant and unwavering devotion toward you."
Even though you are devoid of qualities, descend today through your divine play; O Father, grant us your assistance, for you are the Supreme Lord beyond all.
O Lord of the gods of gods, even our dispute was auspicious, since you have come here for the sake of pacifying our quarrel.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, Hara himself, bowing with his head and joining his palms in reverence, spoke again to Hari as he stood before him.

The illustrious Maheśa said: I am the author of dissolution, maintenance, and creation; I am both with attributes and without attributes. I am the Supreme Brahman, changeless, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
O Viṣṇu, O Hari, I am indeed divided into three by the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, according to the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution; yet I am eternally partless.
O Viṣṇu, since I have been praised by you and by Brahmā for my incarnation, I shall now make that prayer which you, who are affectionate toward your devotees, will surely fulfill.
O Brahman, my supreme form, such as this, shall manifest from your body in the world, renowned by the name Rudra.
Through my own portion, his power shall never be diminished; for there is no distinction between "I" and "he" in the performance of the ritual of worship.

Just as water and other substances do not truly possess the quality of touch due to contact with light, so too there is no bondage for me, who am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), despite [apparent] conjunction.
This form of mine is Śiva, and Rudra was likewise like Śiva at that time; O great sage, no distinction between them should indeed be made there.
For in reality, that which is of a single form is indeed divided into two within the world; therefore, one should never perceive any distinction between Śiva and Rudra.
Likewise, O Lord, the singularity of the substance gold does not change for the sake of its ornamentation; there is only a difference in name, not in the substance itself.
Likewise, the difference between various vessels made from a single piece of clay is not real; the presence of the cause itself within the effect is the illustration.
O gods, this must be understood by the best of the wise who possess stainless knowledge; having known this, no cause for differentiation should be perceived by you two.
And all that is visible, like every object, is considered by me to be the form of Śiva; I, you, the unborn Brahmā, and this Rudra who is yet to be—[all are Śiva].
It is of a single form and there is no division; indeed, in the case of division, there would be bondage. Nevertheless, my own nature is the eternal Śiva-form.
It is the root, eternally spoken, truth, knowledge, and infinite; having thus understood it, one should always meditate upon it with the mind according to its true nature.
Listen, O Brahmin, to that which I shall tell you, though it is a secret: you two have passed beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), for this [state] is indeed not of nature again.
In that regard, my command arises from the knitting of Brahmā’s brows; even among the qualities (guṇas), Hara is declared by me to be the primordial one characterized by tamas.
That which is declared as the *vaikārika* ego should be understood as such; it is not to be described as *tāmasa* either by name or in reality.
For this reason, O Brahmā, this must be done by you: become the creator of the universe, O Brahmā, and Hari shall be its protector.
And that portion of mine which shall be the agent of dissolution is this Goddess Prakṛti, the Supreme Sovereign known as Umā.
Her power, however, shall be the Goddess Śakti, and she will attend upon Brahmā; furthermore, another power of Prakṛti will arise there.
Then she will resort to Viṣṇu in the form of Lakṣmī; and again, by the name Kālī, she will certainly attain a portion of myself.
In the form of light, she will manifest there for the sake of her task; thus have the supreme and auspicious powers of the Goddess been described.
O best of gods, the functions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution belong eternally and sequentially to those [energies]; they are indeed portions of this Prakṛti, who is dear to me.
And you, O Brahmā, having resorted to Lakṣmī, ought to carry out the task here; and you, having obtained the goddess of speech, who is a portion of Prakṛti.
By my command, you ought to perform the work of creation here through the heart; I, for my part, shall resort to Kālī, who is a portion of my beloved and higher than the highest.
In the form of Rudra, I shall bring about the dissolution of this world consisting of the four castes and all its stages of life; this is my supreme task.
By performing various other duties besides those, you two shall attain happiness; endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom, you will be benefactors of the world.
"O Bhava, by my command, become today the bestower of liberation in this world; for the fruit that is obtained from seeing me is exactly the same as that from seeing you."
Thus, O Datta, you have granted me this boon today; it is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Viṣṇu resides within my very heart, and I indeed reside within the heart of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, my mind does not perceive any difference between the two; Hari is born from my left limb, and Brahmā is born from my right limb.
O Viṣṇu, I am the soul of the universe, born from the heart; I am indeed divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Bhava, who brings about the great dissolution.

Śiva is the creator, protector, and destroyer through the three qualities (guṇas) beginning with Aja (Brahmā), yet he is distinct from those qualities; he is the manifest witness, beyond both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Hari is the Supreme Brahman—non-dual, eternal, infinite, complete, and stainless; he is the protector of the three worlds, possessing internal darkness (tamas) and external purity (sattva).
With his inner essence consisting of sattva and his exterior enveloped in tamas, Hara is the one who effects the dissolution of the three worlds.

The Creator Brahmā is the author of the creation of the three worlds, both internal and external; thus, Śiva is remembered as the one who, though distinct from the qualities, exists within the three gods through those very qualities.
O Viṣṇu, out of affection protect this Grandfather who performs the work of creation; by my command, you shall become worthy of worship in the three worlds.
Even for Brahmā, Rudra alone shall be your object of worship; for he is the full incarnation of Śiva and the one who brings about the dissolution of the three worlds.
"In the Pādma Kalpa, your grandfather shall be born as my son; then you shall see me, and he too, the lotus-born one, shall see me."
Having spoken thus, Maheśāna Hara, the Lord and Sovereign of all, having shown incomparable compassion, spoke again with great affection to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śiva-Tattva," in the Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna (Account of Creation) of the first section of the Rudrasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The Supreme Lord said: "Listen to another command of mine, O Hari, O Viṣṇu of noble vows; you shall always be honored and worshiped in all the worlds."
When suffering arises in this world created by Brahmā, then you must be intent upon the destruction of all that suffering.
"I shall be your helper in every task, however difficult; I will slay your enemies, who are hard to overcome and exceedingly fierce."
O Hari, having assumed various incarnations, spread your supreme fame throughout the world; become the supreme savior.
For this Rudra, whose nature consists of qualities, shall always perform through this body that which is impossible for you to do for the worlds; of this there is no doubt.

You are indeed the one to be meditated upon by Rudra, and Hara is likewise the one to be meditated upon by you; there is no difference whatsoever between the two of you, nor anything that belongs to you apart from Rudra.
In reality, O Mahāviṣṇu, there is indeed oneness, and likewise even by virtue; even in sport, it is truly true, truly true—of this there is no doubt.
If any man who is a devotee of Rudra should revile you, all of his merit will quickly be reduced to ashes.
O Puruṣottama, O Viṣṇu, by my command, his fall into hell shall occur because of his hatred for you; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt.
In this world, you are the bestower of liberation to men and especially the bestower of worldly enjoyment; you are to be meditated upon and worshipped by devotees—perform acts of restraint and grace.
Having spoken thus, he took me by the hand and personally took hold of Hari, saying: "Be a helper at all times during times of distress."
Be the presiding lord over all, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon everyone; be in every way the most excellent, the fulfiller of all desires.
And by my command, O Hari, become the life-force for all beings; for that Rudra, who is my own body, is indeed to be worshipped in times of distress.
He who has truly taken refuge in you has indeed taken refuge in me; yet he who perceives a difference between us will certainly fall into hell.
Listen now to the lifespan and strength of the three gods, specifically those whose nature is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Four thousand yugas are said to be one day of Brahmā; his night is of equal duration—such is the measurement according to this sequence.
For them, thirty days constitute a month, and twelve of those months a year; the lifespan of Brahmā is proclaimed to be measured at one hundred such years.
A single day of Viṣṇu is said to consist of a full year of Brahmā; he too lives for a hundred such years according to his own measure.
A year of Vaiṣṇava time certainly becomes a single day of Raudra; when a hundred years have passed, Hara remains established in human form.
As long as the inhalation remains in the mouth, it originates from Sadāśiva; thereafter, it proceeds toward Śakti until the exhalation occurs.
And for all embodied beings, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, as well as Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, there is inhalation and exhalation.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred and sixty days and nights, O best of gods, have been declared as the measure [of the lifespan].
Six inhalations and exhalations constitute one *pala*; sixty *palas* are said to be one *ghaṭī*, and sixty of those make a day and night.
There is no counting the exhalations and inhalations; because it arises from Sadāśiva, it is remembered as imperishable.
"In this manner, you must protect this form at my command; meanwhile, the work of creation must indeed be carried out through your various qualities."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, the self-controlled Lord Hari prostrated before Viśveśa and spoke very softly.
Viṣṇu said: "O Śaṅkara, O ocean of compassion, O Lord of the universe, listen to this: following your command, I shall carry out all of this."
"You shall always be my object of meditation, and it shall not be otherwise; indeed, all your powers were obtained by me in the past."
O Lord, may Your supreme meditation never depart even for a single moment from my mind, nor ever go far away.
O Lord, whoever is my devotee yet shall utter censure against you, grant him a certain and permanent residence in hell.
O Lord, he who is devoted to you is indeed dearer to me; for one who understands this truly, liberation is not difficult to attain.
"Today my greatness has certainly been increased by you; however, if at any time I should prove devoid of virtue, may that be forgiven."
Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, having heard those excellent words of his, spoke to Viṣṇu with great affection: "Your lack of qualities has been forgiven by me."
Having spoken thus to Hari, that Supreme Lord, a treasure-house of compassion, touched him on all his limbs with both hands out of grace.
Having instructed us in various dharmas that remove all suffering, Hara, desiring our welfare, granted us numerous boons.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees, vanished instantly right there while he was still gazing at him with his vision.
Then, O Prakṛti, the ritual for the worship of the Liṅga was ordained in this world; Śambhu, when established in the Liṅga, is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The sacrificial altar is the Great Goddess, and the linga is Maheśvara himself; it is called a linga because the entire universe dissolves (layana) therein.
He who daily recites the *Laiṅga* narrative in the presence of a *liṅga* shall indeed become identical in form to Śiva within six months; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O great sage, I am unable to describe the fruit of the merit belonging to one who performs even a small act in the vicinity of the Liṅga.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Śiva-Tattva," in the Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna (Account of Creation) within the first section of the Rudrasaṃhitā, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate disciple of Vyāsa, salutations be unto you! Today we have been made to hear the most wonderful and supremely purifying narrative of Śiva.
Therein, the wonderful, great, divine, and auspicious origin of the Liṅga has been heard; by hearing its power, the destruction of suffering occurs in this world.
O ocean of compassion, following the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, please describe the procedure for the worship of Śiva, by which Śiva may become pleased.
Śiva is worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; tell me how that worship should be performed, just as it was heard from the mouth of Vyāsa.
Having heard those words of theirs—which were auspicious and in accordance with the Vedas—the sage spoke everything with affection, following the sequence of their questions.
Sūta said: O lords of sages, you have asked well regarding that secret; therefore, I shall today relate it to you according to my understanding and as I have heard it.
Just as that was asked by you, so indeed was it formerly asked by Vyāsa; it was heard from Sanatkumāra by Upamanyu.
Then, having heard about the worship of Śiva and other such matters from Vyāsa, he taught them to me out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
That was indeed heard by Kṛṣṇa from the high-souled Upamanyu; I shall now relate it just as Brahmā spoke it in the past.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the worship of the Liṅga in brief; it is not possible, O Sage, to describe it in detail even in a hundred years.
Thus, one should worship the pure and eternal face of Śiva’s form with supreme devotion for the attainment of the fruits of all desires.
Poverty, the suffering of disease, oppression arising from enemies, and sin—these four persist as long as one does not worship Śiva.
When the auspicious Lord Śiva is fully worshipped, all suffering dissolves; all happiness is attained, and thereafter liberation is reached.
Those who, having taken recourse to human birth, desire the primary happiness that comes from progeny—by them Mahādeva, the accomplisher of all purposes and goals, should be worshipped.
Let the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras perform the worship of Śaṅkara according to the rules and in due order, for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
Having risen at dawn during the hour known as Brahmamuhūrta, one should perform the remembrance of the Guru and likewise of Śambhu.
O sage, having performed the remembrance of the sacred fords (tīrthas) and also the meditation upon Hari, as well as upon me, the gods, and the sages and others;
Then one should recite an auspicious hymn of praise according to the prescribed ritual; thereafter, having risen, one should perform the evacuation of waste in the southern direction.
O Sage, listen with a focused mind; I shall now describe that very procedure for the evacuation of waste which you have heard should be performed in solitude.
For the sake of purification, a twice-born man should smear pure clay five times; a Kṣatriya four times, and a Vaiśya likewise three times.
A Śūdra should take earth twice for the sake of purification according to the rule; he should diligently apply it once to the anus and once to the penis.
O dear one, [one should perform this] ten times on the left hand, seven times on both hands, three times on each foot, and again three times on the two hands.
Women should perform the excellent practice of taking earth just like Śūdras; having washed their hands and feet, they should take the earth as previously described.
Then a man should use a tooth-stick according to the sequence of his own caste.
A Brahmin should use a tooth-stick measuring twelve finger-breadths; a Kshatriya, eleven finger-breadths; and a Vaishya should use one measuring ten finger-breadths.
A Śūdra should make it nine finger-breadths; this is the measurement prescribed by tradition. Having considered the defects of the times, one should avoid that which was seen [prescribed] by Manu.
O dear one, the sixth lunar day and others, the ninth, the day of a vow, the day of the sun's setting (the new moon), and likewise the day of a śrāddha ceremony are prohibited for brushing the teeth.

The ritual bath should indeed be performed according to the rules at sacred fords and other sites in their proper sequence; the bath should be performed with the appropriate mantras, taking into account the specific requirements of place and time.

Having first sipped water (ācamana) there with a washed cloth over the lower body, and standing in a secluded and auspicious place, one should then perform the ritual of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vidhi).
Having performed the appropriate preliminary rites and having steadied the mind, one should enter the hall of worship and then commence the ritual of worship.

Having undertaken the ritual procedure for worship and having indeed sat upon one’s own seat, one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other preliminaries, and then worship Hara in due order.
Having first thoroughly worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, as well as the gatekeepers and the guardians of the directions, one should thereafter prepare the pedestal.
Alternatively, having prepared an eight-petaled lotus and arranged the materials for worship nearby, one should sit there and then seat the Lord Śiva upon it.
Having performed the three sips of water (ācamana) and having washed his hands again, and having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), he should meditate upon Tryambaka in the center.
Five-faced and ten-armed, resembling pure crystal, adorned with all ornaments, and wearing a tiger skin as an upper garment.
Remembering his similarity [to Śiva], a man should always burn away his sin; then, having raised up Śiva, he should worship the Supreme Lord.

Then, having performed the purification of the body, one should place the root mantra in the proper sequence; everywhere, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the syllable Om alone.

Having performed the mental application in the heart, one should then commence the worship; one should also prepare the vessels for the water for the feet, the respectful offering, and the water for sipping.
The wise one should place nine various jars according to the ritual rule; having covered them with those very same *darbha* grasses, he should install them and sprinkle them with water.
In each and every one of those [vessels], the wise man should pour very cool water, casting the ritual substances into them while reciting the *praṇava*.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet with uśīra and sandalwood; likewise, one should include jasmine, kola, camphor, vaṭa root, and tamālaka.
Having ground it according to the rule, one should pour it into the water for sipping; this, mixed with sandalwood paste, one should cause to be offered into all the vessels.
One should worship Nandīśa at the sides of the God of gods; one should honor Śiva with perfumes, incense, and various lamps.

Then, having performed the purification of the *liṅga*, the man, filled with joy, should [worship] it with the appropriate multitudes of mantras beginning with *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should prepare a seat, such as the Svastika or Padma, with the syllable *praṇava*; from that [seat], one should contemplate the imperishable *aṇimā* facing the eastern direction.
Laghimā is indeed the southern [petal], Mahimā likewise the western; Prāpti is the northern petal, and Prākāmya belongs to the southeast.
Lordship is in the south-western petal, mastery is in the domain of the wind; omniscience is likewise in the north-east, while the pericarp is said to be the moon.
Below Soma is likewise Sūrya, and below him is this Pāvaka; one should arrange Dharma and the others below him in their proper order.

Having invoked the Supreme Lord with the mantra "I shall proclaim Sadyojāta," one should place the Unmanifest and so forth in the four directions, and the three qualities at the end of the Soma [quarter].
One should remain upon the seat with the Vāmadeva mantra; one should effect the presence [of the deity] with the Rudra-gāyatrī and perform the confinement with the Aghora mantra.
One should worship with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," having prepared water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīya), and then cause the offering of water (arghya) to be presented.

One should install Rudra according to the prescribed rite with water scented by sandalwood, and having consecrated it in a vessel for domestic rites (gṛhyapātra) through the procedure of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should bathe him with cow's milk accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava), as well as with curd, honey, and likewise with sugarcane juice.
Having worshipped Mahādeva with ghee, which brings about the fulfillment of all desires, one should consecrate him with meritorious substances while reciting the *praṇava*.
Then, having purified the vessels for the sacred water according to the prescribed rule with a white cloth, the practitioner should pour water into them while reciting the mantras.
One should not go so far as to throw away the sandalwood; instead, one should joyfully worship Śaṅkara there with beautiful grains of rice.
With kuśa grass, apāmārga, camphor, jasmine, campaka, and pāṭala flowers; with white karavīras, as well as mallikā, lotus, and blue water-lilies.
One should offer a stream of water to the Supreme Lord with various unprecedented flowers, as well as sandalwood and other such substances.
One should bathe the god Maheśvara with various vessels; worship preceded by mantras should be performed, which bestows all fruits.
O dear one, I shall proclaim to you those very mantras for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals; listen with attentiveness as I speak them in brief.
By means of the mantra being recited, as well as by the Vedic hymns—the Rudra, the Nīlarudra, the Suśukla, and the Subha—[he was purified].
Likewise with the Hotāra, the Śīrṣa, the auspicious Atharvaṇa, the Śānti, and again the Punassānti, as well as the Āruṇa and the Aruṇa.
And with words that were agreeable to his purpose, as well as with Devavrata himself.
With the Rathantara, with the Puṣpa hymn, with the [Puṣpa] Sūkta, with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, and likewise with the five-syllabled [mantra].
Streams of water should be poured out by the thousand, or by a hundred plus one, according to the Vedic path, or alternatively, by means of [specific] names.
Then, one should offer sandalwood, flowers, and so forth upon Śiva; likewise, one should cause mouth-fresheners and other such items to be offered with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) alone.
Then [he beheld] the God who resembles crystal, partless and imperishable, the cause of all worlds, consisting of all worlds, and supreme.
It is beyond the reach even of the gods such as Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Viṣṇu; for it is recorded by those who know the Vedas that in the Vedānta, it is indeed "unperceivable" (agocara).
Free from beginning, middle, and end, it is the medicine for all who suffer; known as the Śiva-principle, it is established as the Śivaliṅga.
One should worship upon the top of the liṅga using the mantra consisting of the syllable Om (praṇava) alone, with incenses, lamps, food offerings, and beautiful betel leaves.
Then, with a beautiful lustration rite performed according to the prescribed rules, [one should worship] with prostrations, hymns, and various other mantras as well.
Having offered the arghya and having scattered flowers at his feet, one should prostrate before the Lord of Gods and worship Śiva with one's own self.
Having taken flowers in his hand and risen with palms joined in reverence, he should again pray to Īśāna, to Śaṅkara, with this mantra:
Whether performed out of ignorance or knowledge, may whatever recitation, worship, and other rites have been done by me bear fruit through your grace, O Śaṅkara.
Having recited this, one should joyfully place flowers upon Śiva; then, having performed a rite for well-being, one should likewise offer various blessings.
Then, one should indeed perform the sprinkling (mārjana) over Śiva once more; thereafter, one should offer salutations, seek forgiveness, and again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having uttered the syllable *agha*, one should perform a salutation; then, endowed with all one's being, one should offer a prayer there once again.
Devotion to Śiva, devotion to Śiva, devotion to Śiva in birth after birth! Otherwise, there is no other refuge; you alone are my refuge.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, the bestower of all accomplishments, one should worship him with supreme devotion, especially with throat-sounds (galanāda).
Then, having performed a salutation together with his retinue and having attained incomparable joy, he should carry out his task as he pleases.
Thus, for one who worships daily, being solely devoted to devotion toward Śiva, every accomplishment indeed arises at every step.
He becomes eloquent, and his heart's desires certainly bear fruit; likewise, disease, suffering, grief, agitation, and artificiality [are dispelled].
Whether it be treachery, poison, or whatever suffering has arisen—that very suffering the supreme Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness, surely destroys.
For him, auspiciousness arises like the moon in the bright fortnight; his virtuous qualities certainly increase through the worship of Śaṅkara.
Thus, O best of sages, the ritual for the worship of Śambhu has been declared to you; what more do you wish to hear, or what will you ask next, O Nārada?
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Śiva," in the first section (Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Prajāpati, O dear one, you are blessed, for your mind is devoted to Śiva. O Creator (Vidhi), please explain this very same matter to me once again in full detail.
Brahmā said: O dear one, on one occasion, having summoned the sages and the gods from all sides, I, the lotus-born, spoke these excellent words with affection.
If you have faith in eternal bliss and if you desire the perfected ones, you must come with me to the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having heard these words, they indeed went along with me to where the Blessed Viṣṇu, the benefactor of all, resides.
Having gone there, O Sage, the gods approached Janārdana, the Lord of the World and God of Gods, after bowing down with their hands joined in reverence.
Then, seeing Brahmā and the other gods standing there, Viṣṇu, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, spoke these supreme words:
Viṣṇu said: "For what purpose have you come, Brahmā and the other gods and sages? Tell me everything out of affection; what task is there to be done now?"

Brahmā said: Thus questioned then by Viṣṇu and by me, the gods, having bowed again to him with affection, spoke these auspicious words to report what task remained to be done: "What is there now that must be performed?"
The gods said: "Whose service indeed should always be performed, which removes all suffering?"
Having heard these words, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke these words out of compassion and love for me, Sāmarasya.
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmā, listen; this has been correctly heard by the gods and by you previously. Nevertheless, it is being told to you and likewise again to the gods."
It has been seen and is being seen this very day; why then is it asked again now, O Brahman, by all the gods who are intent upon their various duties?
The god Śaṅkara, the destroyer of all suffering, who is to be served by those worthy of service, has always been worshipped; he has told this to me, and especially to Brahmā as well.
Everything presented here has been seen by you as a wonderful illustration; therefore, those who desire happiness must never abandon its worship.
Having abandoned Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods, who exists in the form of a *liṅga*, these sons of Tāra likewise perished along with their kinsmen.
Deluded by me, they were indeed driven far away by my māyā; deprived of Śiva, they have all been utterly destroyed and ruined.
Therefore, Hara, who bears the form of the *liṅga*, should always be worshipped; that best of gods should especially be served with faith.
O best of beings, it is solely through the worship of the universal liṅga that the gods, the Daityas, as well as I and you, O Brahmā, [attain our status]; how then has that been forgotten by you?
Therefore, O Brahmin, for the sake of desiring the fruit of all wishes, one should constantly worship that Liṅga of Śarva by whatever means possible.
That is a great void, that is blindness, and that is delusion—to not worship Śiva for even a muhūrta or a single moment.
Those who are devoted to Bhava, whose minds are bowed in reverence to Bhava, and those who constantly remember Bhava—they are not vessels for suffering.
Delightful mansions, women with charming ornaments, wealth that extends to complete satisfaction, and a lineage of sons, grandsons, and descendants.
Those fortunate ones who desire health and a physical body, as well as extraordinary status, or happiness in the abode of the gods—
And at the end, through the abundance of their prior merit, they worship Sadāśiva for the sake of the fruit of liberation or for devotion to the Supreme Lord.
Whoever, devoted to supreme faith, should worship the Śiva-liṅga daily, for him success is indeed fruitful, and he is not afflicted by sins.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus, the gods then prostrated themselves before Hari and requested [him to grant] his various forms (liṅgas) for the attainment of all desires by human beings.
Having heard that, O tiger among sages, Viṣṇu then spoke to Viśvakarman: "I, too, am devoted to the rescue of living beings."
O Viśvakarman, having fashioned auspicious lingas for Śambhu, they must be offered to all the gods at my command.
Brahmā said: Having thus fashioned the emblems according to their respective qualifications, Viśvakarman granted them the commissions of either me or Hari.
I shall relate that very thing today; listen, O best of sages: Śakra [gave] a ruby, and Viśravas’s son [gave] gold.
Dharma holds a yellow gem-studded [disc], Varuṇa a dark-blue auspicious one, Viṣṇu one made of sapphire, and Brahmā likewise one made of gold.
O Sage, the Viśvedevas are likewise [represented by] silver, as are the Vasus; the Aśvins, however, O Sage, are made of brass or of earth.
The goddess Lakṣmī [worships] a linga made of crystal, the Ādityas one fashioned from copper, Soma the King one made of pearl, and Vibhāvasu (Fire) a linga of diamond.
O best of Brahmins, the wives of the Brahmins likewise [offered] one made of clay; the Nāgas respectfully offered one made of sandalwood and one made of coral.
O Goddess, the yogi [worships] a linga made of fresh butter, likewise one made of ashes; the yakṣas [worship] a linga made of curd, and likewise the Chāyās [worship] one made of flour.
Brahmāṇī certainly worships a Śivaliṅga made of jewels; Bāṇa worships one made of mercury or earth, or even others.
Such were the lingas fashioned by Viśvakarman; indeed, all the gods as well as the hosts of sages worship them.
Having bestowed the lingas upon the gods out of a desire for their welfare, Viṣṇu explained the procedure for their worship to Brahmā, who wields the Pināka bow.
Having heard those words of his, I, Brahmā, together with the best of the gods, returned to my own abode with a mind overflowing with joy.
Having arrived there, O Sage, I duly explained to all the sages and the gods the ritual for the worship of Śiva, which grants all desired objects.

Brahmā said: "Listen, all you sages, together with the gods, being intent upon love; out of affection I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
O gods and lords of sages, having attained a human birth—which is difficult for all living beings to obtain—one must further attain a noble family, which is even more difficult to reach.
One should perform the prescribed rites for the sake of pleasing Śiva among Brahmins who are free from physical defects, well-behaved, and meritorious.
Whatever duty is prescribed for one's caste, that one must not transgress; as long as the means for giving are available, one should perform that duty.
The sacrifice of austerity is superior to thousands of sacrifices of ritual action; the sacrifice of recitation is superior to thousands of sacrifices of austerity.

There is nothing superior to the sacrifice of meditation; meditation is the means for attaining knowledge, because through meditation the sacrificer perceives his own desired object as being of equal flavor (samarasa).
For one who is constantly devoted to the sacrifice of meditation, Śiva is ever-present; for those possessing realized knowledge, there is no need for purification through expiatory rites or the like.
O Brahmin, for those people who know Brahman and are purified by knowledge, there is indeed no action; from the perspective of discernment, there is neither pleasure nor pain.
Dharma and adharma, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, and likewise the rules of meditation—these are always free from change for those immortals by virtue of that knowledge.
The Liṅga that brings supreme bliss, pure, auspicious, and imperishable—partless, all-pervading, and known to reside within the hearts of yogis.
O twice-born ones, the *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. The external is declared to be gross, while the internal is considered subtle.

Those who are devoted to the sacrifice of ritual action and those who delight in the worship of the gross Liṅga—possessing gross forms for the sake of the conceptualization of the unenlightened—they appear in subtle form.
He for whom the internal sign (liṅga) is not directly perceived should likewise conceive of it within the gross [external] sign, and not otherwise.

To the wise, it is subtle, stainless, directly perceived, and imperishable by virtue of its true nature; whereas to those who are unrefined, it is conceived as gross, such as in the case of the "Supreme" (utkṛṣṭa) and other [categories].

Aha! To one who speaks of the true nature of reality, there is indeed nothing else when examined through discernment: the world is entirely composed of Śiva, both partless and with parts, within the mind.
Thus, for those liberated through knowledge, there is no fault nor conceptual construction; likewise, there is no ritual procedure, nor anything prescribed or prohibited.
Just as a lotus in the water is not defiled by the water, so the man of knowledge, though dwelling in a household, is not bound by action.
As long as such knowledge has not indeed arisen in a man, for that long he should worship the god Śiva through ritual action.
And for the sake of the world's conditions, even though the sun is situated as one, it is seen as many in various receptacles such as bodies of water.
O gods, know that whatever is seen or heard in the world, whether it be of the nature of existence or non-existence, all that is the Supreme Brahman, whose essence is Śiva.
"In this world, when one examines the various reflections in water, there is a perceived difference; thus say others who have reached the true essence of the meaning of all the Vedas."
For one who possesses the realization that "the Supreme Lord in His entirety is directly present within the heart of every transmigrating being," what need is there for images and the like?
Thus, for one devoid of higher knowledge, the mental construction of an image is auspicious; for it is remembered as the support for a person to ascend to the highest state.
Without an object of focus, it is exceedingly difficult for people to attain the high state that is free from qualities; therefore, a physical image is prescribed as the object of focus.
O Goddess, the attainment of both the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) is certain; likewise, the image of all the gods brings about conviction.
This god is indeed most magnificent; for his sake, this worship with perfumes, sandalwood, flowers, and so forth—why would it be performed without an image?
One should worship the image only so long as the arising of gnosis occurs; if it is worshipped in the absence of gnosis, its downfall is certain.
For this reason, O Brahmins, listen to the ultimate truth: whatever action is prescribed for one's own caste must be performed with diligent effort.
Wherever and in whatever manner devotion is shown, worship and other such acts should be performed; for without worship, giving, and so forth, sin is not far off.
As long as sin remains in the body, so long does spiritual accomplishment not arise; but once that sin has departed, everything becomes fruitful for him.
Likewise, dye does not take well to a soiled garment; indeed, when it has been washed and purified, all the dye adheres perfectly.
And thus, through the perfect worship of the deities within the stainless body, the stage of knowledge arises; from that, the birth of higher realization occurs.
And the true root of consciousness is unwavering devotion; likewise, the true root of knowledge is said to be devotion alone.
The root of devotion is virtuous action, such as the worship of one’s chosen deity; its root is said to be the true guru, and the root of that is association with the virtuous.
Through association, a guru is obtained; from the guru comes the worship of mantras and so forth. From worship, devotion arises; through devotion, knowledge is born.
From knowledge arises higher consciousness (vijñāna) which illumines the Supreme Brahman; and when that higher consciousness has arisen, then duality ceases.
When all duality has ceased, there is freedom from the suffering of the pairs of opposites; indeed, one who is free from the suffering of the pairs of opposites becomes the very form of Śiva.
O celestial sages, for one who understands, pleasure and pain would not arise when encountering the pairs of opposites; and for him, there would be neither the prescribed nor the prohibited.
Such a person, having renounced the householder’s life, is rare in this world; if such a one exists in this world, he removes sins merely by being seen.
In this world, the sacred fords, the gods, and all the sages praise Śiva, who is identical with the Supreme Brahman and the most excellent possessor of knowledge.
Such sacred fords do not exist, nor do gods made of clay or stone; they purify only after a long time, but the man of realized knowledge purifies even by his mere sight.
As long as one remains in the householder stage of life, one should perform the worship of the image with affection for the five supreme deities.
Alternatively, Śiva alone is to be worshipped; the root is distinguished as supreme. When the root is watered, all the branches are likewise satisfied, and so too are all the gods.
When the branches are fully satisfied, the root is never satisfied; likewise, O best of sages, when all the gods are satisfied.
In every way, the satisfaction of Śiva should be understood by those of subtle intellect; for when Śiva is worshipped, all the gods are indeed worshipped.
Therefore, one who is devoted to the welfare of all beings should worship the god Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, for the attainment of the fruits of all desires.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Discernment between the Essential and the Non-Essential," in the section on the Description of the Ritual of Worship within the Narrative of Creation, in the first part of the Rudra-saṃhitā, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed procedure for worship; let it be heard, O sages and gods, for it brings about all desires and happiness.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should remember Śiva along with Ambikā; with palms joined and head bowed, one should offer prayers to Him with devotion.
Arise, arise, O Lord of Gods; arise, O You who dwell within the heart! Arise, O Consort of Umā, and bring auspiciousness to the universe.
I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion to it. O Mahādeva, abiding in my heart, I act exactly as I am directed by you.
Having spoken these words with devotion and having recollected the feet of the Guru, one should go outside toward the southern direction for the purpose of voiding excrement and urine.
Then, having performed the purification of the body through cleansing with earth and water, and having washed his hands and feet, he should perform the cleaning of the teeth.
When the lord of the day has not yet risen, having indeed performed the cleansing of the teeth, one should likewise rinse the mouth sixteen times with handfuls of water.
The first lunar days of each fortnight, as well as the ninth and the day of the Sun (Sunday), should be carefully avoided for brushing the teeth by a devotee, O celestial sages.

A person should bathe well according to the available opportunity, whether in rivers and such or at home; furthermore, bathing should be performed by a man in a manner that is not contrary to place and time.

On a Sunday, as well as during a śrāddha ceremony, at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), during an eclipse, at a great gift-giving (mahādāna), at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and likewise on a day of fasting (upavāsa).
Furthermore, even when a period of ritual impurity has arrived, a devoted man should not bathe with hot water; rather, he should bathe facing toward a sacred site (tīrtha) or similar place.
One should perform an oil massage according to the sequence of the lunar days (tithis) as they appear; however, for a daily massage, scented oil or even unscented oil may be used.
During a Śrāddha ceremony, during an eclipse, or on the first day of a lunar fortnight (pratipad) when fasting, mustard oil is not prohibited; otherwise, it is forbidden except during an eclipse.
Having thus considered the place and the time, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rule, facing either northward or eastward.
He should never bathe while still wearing the garment with which he ate; rather, he should bathe after changing into a clean garment, preceded by the remembrance of the deity.
One should perform the bath with that which was worn by another, provided it is not leftover food nor has it been worn at night; furthermore, one should discard what has been washed.

Then the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed, which grants satisfaction to the gods, sages, and ancestors; thereafter, one should wear clean clothes and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once again.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having gone to a pure place cleansed with cow dung and other materials, a beautiful seat should be prepared there.
One should likewise prepare a variegated seat made from pure wood, either filled or spread with a cloth; this bestows the fruits of all desires.
Furthermore, having sat upon whatever is appropriate, such as a deer skin and so forth, the wise man should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash.
Recitation, austerity, and likewise charity become fruitful through the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); in the absence of ash, water and so forth are prescribed for that purpose.
Having thus applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and worn rudrākṣa beads, a person, having accomplished his own duty, should again worship Śiva.
Having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) again three times preceded by the mantra, or alternatively, one may perform it once while saying, "A drop of the Gaṅgā."
Likewise, one should bring food and water there for the purpose of Śiva’s worship, as well as whatever other articles are available nearby according to one's capacity.

Having performed these, one should remain right there, maintaining fortitude; likewise, one should prepare a single vessel for the *arghya* offering, filled with water, scents, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Likewise, it should be placed on the right shoulder for the sake of preparing the ritual services; having performed the remembrance of the Guru and having obtained his permission.
Having performed the ritual resolve according to the rules and having indeed directed his desire [toward the goal], he should worship Śiva together with his retinue with supreme devotion.
Having displayed a single mudrā, one should worship the remover of obstacles (Vighnahāraka), who is endowed with accomplishment and wisdom, using substances such as vermilion and the like.
Having worshipped there with a hundred thousand offerings, one should bow again, using the names in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ," and preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
Then, having asked that god for forgiveness along with his brother, one should worship him with supreme devotion and prostrate before him again and again.
Having first worshipped the gatekeeper Mahodara, who always stands at the door, one should thereafter worship the virtuous Girijā.
Then, having worshipped Śiva with sandalwood, saffron, numerous incenses and lamps, and various kinds of food offerings;
Having paid obeisance, one should then go there into the presence of Śiva, whether there be an image made of earth, gold, or likewise silver in the house.
In the same manner, one should prepare another [liṅga] made of metal or even one made of mercury; having paid homage to it, one should worship it with devoted intent.
When she is indeed worshipped, then all [deities] become worshipped; one should establish a liṅga made of clay, having fashioned it according to the prescribed rite.

Those staying in their own homes must by all means observe the rules there; having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Having established them there in the temple of Śiva, one should worship the guardians of the directions; Śiva should always be worshipped at home through the application of the root mantra.
In that regard, however, there is no restriction whatsoever concerning the gatekeepers; for whatever linga is worshipped in the home, everything is established within it.
At the time of worship, having invoked the God together with his limbs and his retinue, one should perform the worship; there is no fixed rule in this matter.
Having established the presence of Śiva, one should prepare one's own seat; then, standing facing north, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once more.
Having washed his hands, he should thereafter perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); there, the man should perform ten repetitions with the root mantra.
The five mudrās should be formed; worship must certainly be performed with them at hand. Only after displaying these mudrās should a person carry out the ritual of worship.
Then, having offered a lamp there and performed obeisance to the guru, one should assume either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana).
Having assumed either the uttānāsanaka or the paryaṅkāsana posture, and remaining there as is comfortable, one should once again perform the practice.
Having performed the worship as previously described, one should cross over by means of the *vaṭṭaka* alone; or else, here in this house, one may do so by oneself—there is no fixed rule.
Thereafter, having become single-minded and having set out the materials for worship, one should wash the supreme liṅga with the arghya vessel.
Afterwards, a person should indeed invoke the deity with this mantra—the supreme Lord of Pārvatī, who resides upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Śambhu, who possesses the form described above, who is beyond qualities yet takes the form of the qualities, five-faced, ten-armed, three-eyed, and whose banner bears the bull.
White as camphor, with divine limbs, moon-crested, and wearing matted locks; clad in an upper garment of tiger skin and auspiciously dressed in elephant hide.
His body is encircled by Vāsuki and other serpents, and he is equipped with weapons such as the Pināka bow; before him, the eight Siddhis dance here incessantly.
The sound of "Victory! Victory! was offered by the devotees and worshippers; it was served by the gods and was difficult to behold due to its unbearable splendor.
The refuge of all beings, with a face like a lotus in full bloom, he who is ever praised by Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and extolled by the Vedas and the Śāstras.
"I invoke Śiva, who is compassionate toward his devotees and is bliss itself. Having thus meditated upon Śiva along with Ambā, one should provide him with a seat.

One should perform everything in the proper sequence using only words ending in the dative case; then one should indeed offer water for the feet (pādya) and then the water-offering (arghya) to Śaṅkara.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for Śambhu, the Supreme Self, one should thereafter joyfully bathe Śaṅkara with five substances.
Then, with devotion, one should offer the substances using Vedic mantras as appropriate, or by means of names accompanied by mantras, employing words ending in the dative case.
One should offer the desired substance upon Śaṅkara; thereafter, indeed, a water-based bath (vāruṇa-snāna) should be performed for Śiva.
One should diligently offer fragrant sandalwood and other unguents; one should likewise provide a stream of water using only scented water.

Having offered that [water] according to the available space with Vedic mantras, the six ancillary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), or by reciting the names eleven times (the number of Rudras), one should then wipe it clean with a cloth.
Afterwards, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and then present a garment; likewise, sesame seeds, barley, wheat, mung beans, and black gram.
They should be offered to Śiva alone with various kinds of mantras; thereafter, flowers should be given to the great-souled Pañcāsya (the Five-faced One).
To each face, according to the respective meditation and according to appropriate desire, [one should offer] lotuses, hundred-petaled lotuses, śaṅkhapuṣpa flowers, and other such [flowers].
With kusha grass flowers, dhattura, mandara, and those produced from the droṇa tree, as well as with tulasī leaves and especially bilva leaves.
One should worship Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, with supreme devotion; indeed, in the absence of everything else, even a single bilva leaf is to be offered to Śiva.
By the mere offering of bilva leaves, all worship is perfected; thereafter, fragrant powder and excellent scented oil [should be offered].
And various offerings should be presented to Śiva with supreme joy; thereafter, incense made of guggulu and aguru should be offered with delight.
Then a lamp soaked in ghee should be offered to that Śaṅkara; furthermore, one should devoutly offer him the *arghya* with this mantra.
One should perform the wiping of the face with a cloth with heartfelt devotion, saying: "O Śaṅkara, grant me beauty, grant me fame, and grant me enjoyment."
"Bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; having accepted this *arghya*, salutations to You! Then, various auspicious food offerings (*naivedya*) should be presented to Śiva alone.

Then, with affection, he should cause [the deity] to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), or do so without delay; thereafter, having offered betel leaf along with all its primary and secondary ingredients to Śiva.
One should perform the ārārtika offering with five wicks; four times at the feet and twice at the region of the navel.
One should indeed apply [the mantra] once to the mouth and seven times to the entire body; then, having performed the meditation as prescribed, one should recite the mantra.
A wise person should perform the mantra ritual according to the sequence and according to their knowledge; having performed the recitation of the mantra by the path instructed by the guru.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] according to the path taught by the guru, a person should recite the mantra; he should carry out the ritual procedure of the mantra according to the prescribed number and according to his knowledge.
One should joyfully praise the Bull-bannered Lord with various kinds of hymns; thereafter, one should perform circumambulation of Śiva very slowly.
Then a person should perform prostrations according to the rules with all eight limbs; thereafter, a handful of flowers should be offered with devotion using this mantra:

Whatever worship and other rites have been performed by me, whether out of ignorance or with knowledge, for the sake of Śiva, the Supreme Lord, and as a cause for the satisfaction of Śiva; [may all that be accepted].
O Śaṅkara, may that which has been done by me bear fruit through your grace; O Mṛḍa, I am yours, my life-breath is centered in you, and my mind is always fixed upon you.
Having understood this, O Lord of Gaurī, O Sovereign of Beings, be gracious to me; for those whose speech falters upon the ground, the ground alone is their support.
"O Lord, you alone are the refuge for those who have committed offenses against you. Having made such extensive petitions according to the proper ritual procedure, [he spoke].

Having offered a handful of flowers, one should again bow repeatedly, praying thus many times to Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees: "O Lord of Gods, O Master, go to your own abode along with your retinue; O Lord, you should come here again with respect at the time of worship."

One should dismiss [the deity] into one's own heart and place that water upon the crown of the head. Thus, O sages, the worship of Śiva has been explained in its entirety; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. What else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Śiva," in the first section (Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O illustrious disciple of Vyāsa, tell us according to authoritative evidence: with which flowers is Śambhu worshipped, and what specific fruit does he indeed bestow?
Sūta said: O Śaunaka and other sages, listen with respect to everything; today, with great pleasure, I shall relate the definitive account of the offering of flowers.
When questioned regarding this very procedure by the great seer Nārada, he spoke with supreme affection concerning the determination of the offering of flowers.
Brahmā said: One who desires prosperity should worship Lord Śiva with lotuses, bilva leaves, and likewise with śatapatra flowers, as well as with śaṅkhapuṣpa flowers.
If Śiva is worshipped with these [offerings] numbering one hundred thousand, O Brahmin, there will be the destruction of sins as well as the attainment of prosperity; of this there is no doubt.
Twenty lotuses are declared to constitute one *prastha*; half a *prastha* of *bilva* is defined as being with a thousand petals.
A thousand *śatapatra* seeds are defined as half a *prastha*; sixteen *palas* constitute one *prastha*, and ten *ṭaṅkas* are traditionally held to be one *pala*.
When one places [the object] on the scale using this very measure, one attains all desires; if, however, one is free from desire, one becomes Śiva.
O lords of sages, he who desires sovereignty and seeks to please the god Śaṅkara with the worship of kings should satisfy him with ten crores [of offerings].
The *liṅga* is Śiva; likewise, the flower, the unbroken grain of rice, that which is smeared with sandalwood paste, and furthermore, the stream of water.
Likewise, a suitable mantra and the unsurpassed bilva leaf, or else a hundred-petaled lotus or even a common lotus.
Likewise, it has been declared by the ancients that with *śaṅkhapuṣpa* flowers, one obtains divine fruit fulfilling all desires in every way, both here and in the hereafter.
Incense, lamp, food offering, water for honor, and likewise the waving of lights (ārārtika); circumambulation, prostration, the request for forgiveness, and the formal dismissal.
To him who has thus prepared the food along with its constituent parts, Śaṅkara indeed bestows sovereignty in every respect in this world.
A man who desires preeminence should indeed worship with half of that amount; one who is in prison should worship with a hundred thousand.
When one is indeed afflicted by disease, one should worship Śiva with half of that [amount]; and he who desires a daughter should likewise worship Śiva again with half of that.
Likewise, one who desires knowledge should worship Śiva with half of that [amount]; and he who desires eloquence should indeed worship Śiva with clarified butter.
For the purpose of driving away enemies, worship should be performed with that same measure; for killing, indeed, with one hundred thousand, and for bewildering, with half of that.
For the victory over neighboring kings, a worship involving ten million offerings is praised; for the act of subjugating kings, a number of ten thousand is recommended.

For the sake of fame, one should worship with a thousandfold [offerings] such as cattle and vehicles; however, one who desires liberation should worship Śambhu with five crores [of flowers] with great devotion.
One who desires knowledge should worship Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, with ten million [offerings]; one who desires the vision of Śiva should indeed worship him with half of that.
Likewise, the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra should be recited according to the nature of the desired fruit; when five hundred thousand recitations have been performed, Śiva indeed becomes manifest.

Someone attains [the goal] through a hundred thousand repetitions; in the second [birth], there is the attainment of the [divine] nature; in the third, the fulfillment of desires; and in the fourth, one beholds Him directly.
And when the fifth million has been offered, the fruit is granted without doubt; by this very mantra, however, the fruit shall arise at ten million recitations.
He who desires liberation should perform worship with *darbha* grass; O best of sages, it should be understood that the number [of recitations] is one hundred thousand in all cases.
One who desires long life should perform worship with dūrvā grass; one who desires a son should perform worship with dhattūra flowers.
The red-stalked thorn-apple (raktadaṇḍa-dhattūra) is traditionally held to bestow auspiciousness when used in worship; likewise, with flowers of the agasti plant, the worshipper attains great renown.
