If one worships Tulasi with Arka flowers, one obtains the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; likewise, with Kubjaka and Kalhāra flowers, one gains great splendor.
Worship with hibiscus flowers is known to bring death to enemies; likewise, oleanders (karavīra) are used here for the purpose of causing disease and eradication, respectively.

Through *baṃdhuka* flowers, one attains ornaments; through *jāti* flowers, there is no doubt that one brings [deities] to the assembly. By means of *atasī* flowers, one shall attain the state of being beloved by Lord Viṣṇu.
Likewise, liberation is attained by a man through *śamī* leaves; and by offering *mallikā* flowers, Śiva grants a most auspicious woman.
If one's house is not even freed from auspicious *yūthikā* flowers, then through *karṇikāra* flowers, men obtain an abundance of clothing.
In this world, by means of *nirguṇḍī* flowers, the mind attains purity; likewise, with a hundred thousand *bilva* leaves, one shall obtain all desires.
Through ornaments, necklaces, and flowers, one increases in the abundance of happiness; flowers produced in their proper seasons grant liberation—of this there is no doubt.
The flowers of the rājikā plant here bring about the death of enemies; one should offer a hundred thousand of these to Śivā, and she will grant abundant fruit.
There is no flower that does not please Śiva; therefore, setting aside the campaka and the ketakī, one should offer all other flowers.
Henceforth, O best of beings, listen with pleasure to the full measure and the fruit of the worship of Śaṅkara with grains.
O Brahmin, when rice is offered upon Śiva with perfect devotion according to the unbroken ritual procedure, an increase in prosperity arises for men.
The measure of the *prastha* is stated to be six [karṣas], and likewise half of that; furthermore, two *palas* are cited as being equal to one *lakṣa*.
Having performed the worship primarily with offerings to Rudra, one should place a very beautiful cloth upon Śiva; therein, the offering of rice grains is most excellent.
Having planted a single *śrīphala* fruit on top, likewise with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having offered incense and other offerings, one shall obtain the fruit of worship.

Two Prājāpatya offerings, silver, and an incalculable number [of coins] should be given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the instructor of that [rite]; indeed, the sacrificial fee is considered to be according to one's capacity.

Then, one should feed Brāhmaṇas there according to the number of the suns; thus, the worship of a hundred thousand [deities] is accomplished along with its ancillaries and preceded by the recitation of mantras.
In that case, the procedure for the mantra is declared to be one hundred and eight repetitions; and a hundred thousand palas of sesame seeds destroys even the most heinous sins.
The measurement of one hundred thousand is declared to be exactly eleven palas; there, worship should be performed as before with a desire for one's own welfare.
Therefore, Brahmins must indeed be fed here by a man; for the suffering born of great sins (mahāpātaka) certainly perishes at that very moment.
O Śivā, the barley-worship is likewise declared to be supreme when performed with one hundred thousand [grains]; furthermore, there are eight *prasthas* and also half a *prastha*.
The ancient measurement there consists of two *pala*s; and the worship of barley by sages increases the happiness of heaven.
The *prājāpatya* rite should be performed by Brāhmaṇas who desire its fruit; likewise, worship of Śaṅkara with wheat-based foods is indeed highly commended.
If his lineage is intended to increase up to a hundred thousand, it shall reach that number with half a *droṇa*, according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
O Lord, by worshipping with mung beans—either with seven *prasthas* or even with half a *prastha*—Śiva indeed bestows happiness.
The ancients have stated that one hundred thousand [repetitions] are completed by two palas; likewise, Brahmins should be fed in a number equal to that of Rudra (eleven).
Simply by worshipping Priyaṅgu, when the Supreme Self is the presiding lord of dharma, virtue, wealth, and desire increase; such worship brings all happiness.

The ancients have stated that one *lakṣa* [of coins] is equivalent to one *prastha* of that [grain]; likewise, a feeding of Brahmins (*brahmabhoja*) is said to be according to the measure of twelve thousand (*arka-saṃkhyā*).

The worship with black mustard seeds (rājikā) is remembered as causing the death of an enemy for Śambhu; likewise, one hundred thousand mustard seeds (sārṣapa) [weighing] twenty palas [is prescribed].
It is declared that by the worship of these alone, the death of an enemy is brought about; one should worship Śiva after adorning him with the leaves of *āḍhakī*.
A cow and likewise a bull, both well-adorned, should be given as gifts; worship originating from Marīci is remembered as that which brings about the destruction of enemies.
Having dyed [the image] with the petals of *āḍhakī* flowers, one should worship Śiva; for this worship bestows various pleasures and grants all fruits.
Thus, O best of sages, I have declared to you the measurement of grain; now, O lord of sages, listen with pleasure to the measurement of flowers.
And likewise, one *prastha* is said by Vyāsa—who demonstrates subtle measurement—to consist of *śaṅkhapuṣpa* flowers.
The measure of one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers is proclaimed to be eleven *prasthas*; likewise, the measure of *yūthikā* is the same, while that of *rājikā* is half of that.
The supreme measure for jasmine is twenty *prasthas*; likewise, the measure for sesame flowers is slightly less than that.
Furthermore, the measure for that which arises from the *karavīra* flower is remembered as being double; likewise, the wise have declared the measure for the *nirguṇḍī* flower to be the same.
Likewise, there is the measure for the *karṇikāra* flower, and again for the *śirīṣa* blossom; similarly, there is the measure for the *bandhujīva*, and the departure [measure] is by means of ten.
Having observed these and various other auspicious signs, one should perform the worship of Śiva for the sake of fulfilling all desires, or for the sake of liberation if free from desire.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the great fruit of the Dhārā-pūjā, by the mere hearing of which auspiciousness arises for men.
Having performed the worship of Śiva with devotion according to the prescribed rite, those intent on devotion should thereafter offer a stream of water.
For the purpose of pacifying fever and delirium, a stream of water brought by Śatarudriya, the eleventh hymn of Rudra, brings auspiciousness.
Or there, by the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, or by the Puruṣasūkta, or by the Ṣaḍaṅga-prayoga, or by the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya-mantra.
One should likewise perform the pouring of water-streams and other rites using the Gāyatrī, or with names ending in "namaḥ" preceded by the Praṇava, or with mantras declared in the Āgamas.

For the sake of increasing the continuity of happiness, the supreme worship of the stream [of offerings] should be performed with various auspicious and divine substances by one who wears sacred ashes with devotion.
A stream of ghee should be offered to Śivā for as long as it takes to recite a thousand mantras; then the expansion of one’s lineage occurs, of this there is no doubt.
In this manner, the worship of Śiva should indeed be performed with the mantra spoken by me; likewise, the feeding of Brahmins is declared by the lords of sages to be equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
At that time, a stream of milk alone should especially be offered; however, when the intellect becomes dull, it should be mixed with sugar.
In her arises an excellent intellect resembling that of Jīva; as long as ten thousand recitations of the mantra have not been completed, so long should there be worship with streams [of offerings].
And when an uprooting occurs within the body without any apparent cause, or wherever love and suffering have increased excessively;
Whenever quarreling constantly arises within one's own home, indeed, by performing this rite at that stream, all suffering dissolves.
Indeed, for the purpose of scorching one's enemies, a stream of oil should be offered over Śiva with great effort; the accomplishment of one's purpose will then certainly come to pass.
By that very oil in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, an increase in enjoyments arises; by mustard oil alone, the destruction of enemies will certainly occur.
Indeed, by worshipping Śiva with honey, one becomes the king of the Yakṣas; and a stream of sugarcane juice, O Śivā, brings joy to all.
The stream of Gaṅgā water alone bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; indeed, all these [streams] that have been described originate from Mṛtyuñjaya.
In that regard, ten thousand [offerings] should indeed be made according to the prescribed rule; and food should be served to Brāhmaṇas equal in number to Rudra (eleven).
O Lord of Sages, all that I was asked by you has been told; this indeed is fruitful in the world and brings about the fulfillment of all desires.
I shall describe, according to what I have heard, the fruit that one obtains through devotion by worshipping Śambhu together with Skanda and Umā according to the prescribed rite.
Having enjoyed every auspicious happiness here with sons, grandsons, and others, one thereafter goes to the world of Maheśa, which brings all forms of bliss.
With celestial chariots resembling ten million suns, capable of going anywhere at will, crowded with the daughters of Rudra, and provided with singing and instrumental music;
Having become Śiva, he sports until the dissolution of all beings; thereafter, having attained imperishable higher knowledge, he attains liberation.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Śiva," in the Section on Creation within the second book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, you are blessed, O best of the gods! Today, the most wonderful and supremely purifying story of Śiva has been made to resound.
Therein, the wondrous, great, divine, and auspicious origin of the Liṅga has been heard; by hearing its power, the destruction of suffering occurs here in this world.
And immediately thereafter, tell me specifically about the greatness and the deeds that occurred, as well as the manner of creation itself.
Brahmā said: Since you have asked so well, I shall relate to you in brief what occurred thereafter, exactly as it was heard by me in the past.
When that eternal deity in the form of Śiva had vanished, O best of Brahmins, both Viṣṇu and I attained supreme happiness.
And by me, as Viṣṇu, the forms of a swan and a boar were then assumed by those two out of a desire for the creation and protection of the worlds.
Nārada said: O Creator, O Brahmā, O one of great wisdom, there is a great doubt in my heart; having shown incomparable compassion, you ought to dispel it quickly.
How is it that you two have assumed the forms of a swan and a boar? Tell me the reason for this—why did you abandon your other forms?
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada and having remembered the lotus feet of Śiva, Brahmā spoke with reverence.
Brahmā said: When the swan ascends upward, its movement becomes steady; it possesses the discernment between reality and unreality, like the separation of water and milk.
The Haṃsaka distinguishes the true nature of ignorance and knowledge; for that reason, the Creator Brahmā assumed the form of a swan.
O Nārada, because discrimination was not attained, the *haṃsa* vanished—that which is the nature of Śiva, the reality, and the form of light.
How can knowledge arise for one who desires to engage in creation, since even discernment has not been attained by me, though I am in the form of a swan?
While moving, the gait of the Boar becomes motionless; indeed, the form of the Boar was assumed by Viṣṇu as he wandered in the forest.
Alternatively, that form was indeed fashioned by Viṣṇu, the protector of the worlds, for the purpose of creating the world-eon in the guise of a boar.
Indeed, from the day Hari assumed that form, every such day constitutes a kalpa; this kalpa is known by the name Vārāha.
When His will arose for those two to assume a form, that day was a Kalpa; that Kalpa was known by the name Vārāha.
Thus the question and answer have been given; now listen to the subject at hand, O Nārada. Remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, O Sage, I shall describe the process of creation.
When Mahādeva had vanished, I, the Grandfather of the worlds, intent upon meditation, began to contemplate how to carry out his word.
Having then paid homage to Śambhu and received that knowledge from Hari, he attained supreme bliss and set his mind upon performing creation.
And then Viṣṇu also, having prostrated there before Sadāśiva and having instructed me, O dear one, vanished from sight.
Having gone outside the cosmic egg and obtained the grace of Śambhu, Hari went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha and dwelt there forever.
Having remembered Śiva there, and indeed Viṣṇu with the desire for creation, I cast a handful of water into that very water which had been created previously.
From that, O Brahmin, an egg was produced, known as the twenty-fourfold; it became the form of Virāj for him who beheld the waters.
Then, having fallen into doubt, I performed most severe penance there for twelve years, devoted solely to the meditation upon Viṣṇu.
And at that time, dear one, Hari himself appeared; touching my body with joy, he spoke to me with great affection.
Viṣṇu said: "Choose a boon; I am pleased with you. O Brahman, by the grace of Śambhu, I am capable of granting everything; there is nothing that should not be given to you."
Brahmā said: "O highly fortunate one, this is fitting; I have been granted to you by Śambhu. Since he has now requested what was spoken [by him], give it to me, O Viṣṇu; salutations be unto you."
This cosmic egg, known as the Virāṭ form, consists of twenty-four principles; yet consciousness does not exist at the beginning, for it is seen to be initially insentient.
O Hari, you have appeared today through the grace of Śiva; indeed, by the manifestation of Śaṅkara, you have brought forth this cosmic egg endowed with consciousness.
When this was said, Mahāviṣṇu, devoted to the command of Śambhu, assumed an infinite form and entered that cosmic egg.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet; having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended the cosmic egg.
When Viṣṇu had entered that egg after being properly praised by me, the egg—known as the twenty-four principles—became endowed with consciousness.
Beginning from Pātāla and the other regions, Hari himself, the Lord of the seven worlds, shines there as the sovereign Vairāja Puruṣa.
The five-faced one indeed made the beautiful city of Kailāsa, which shines supreme above all, for his own residence.
O celestial sage, even when the universe and that Vaikuṇṭha are destroyed, there is never any destruction of those two here.
O best of sages, O dear one, relying upon the foundation of truth, I stand here; indeed, by the command of Mahādeva, I became desirous of creation.
Then, O dear one, as I desired to create, there appeared before me the creation of evil—the fivefold ignorance—which arose with deliberate intent and was like darkness.
Then, with a serene mind, by the command of Śambhu, I created the primary creation known as the "immobile" (sthāvara), which is free from attachment and characterized by meditative absorption.
Having seen that and knowing it to be a means for my own creation, I set forth a creation rich in suffering—the downward-flowing stream of animals—which is not conducive to spiritual perfection.
And knowing that [creation] to be ineffective, as I reflected further, there quickly arose the Sāttvika creation known as the Ūrdhvasrotas.
The creation of the gods is well-known as being truly and exceedingly conducive to happiness; yet, considering even that to be ineffective, I meditated upon my own Lord.
Then, by the command of Śaṅkara, the Rājasa creation appeared, known as the downward-streaming (avāksrotas), consisting of humans who are seekers of the supreme goal.
By the command of Mahādeva, the creation beginning with Bhūta then came into being; thus, this fivefold creation has indeed proceeded, brought forth by me.
Three types of creation are proclaimed as belonging to Brahmā by nature: among them, the first is the creation of the Mahat, and the second is the subtle elemental creation.
And the third is the Vaikārika; these are the three primary (prakṛta) creations. Thus, there are eight kinds of creations, including those derived from the primary ones.
The ninth is declared to be the Kaumāra [creation], which is both natural (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta); it is not possible for me to describe their further internal subdivisions.
Because its utility is limited, I shall describe the creation consisting of the twice-born, wherein occurred the great creation of Sanaka and the others known as the Kaumāra-sarga.
Indeed, my five mind-born sons, Sanaka and the others, who were equal to Brahmā, became endowed with great dispassion and firm in their vows.
And although commanded by me, those wise ones turned away from saṃsāra; with their minds one-pointedly fixed on the meditation of Śiva, they did not set their thoughts upon creation.
And having heard that reply, O best of sages, I became exceedingly fierce with anger and fell into delusion, O Nārada.
O Sage, as I was enraged, deluded, and overwhelmed, drops of tears indeed fell from my eyes due to my anger.
At that moment, Viṣṇu, having been remembered by me there with my mind, arrived swiftly and awakened me.
O best of sages, although I was instructed by Hari to perform penance for Śiva, I performed a most terrible and supreme penance.
And as I was performing penance for the sake of creation, from the region named Avimukta—specifically from between my own eyebrows and nose—[he emerged].
From Maheśa, the Lord of the three forms, there appeared the ocean of compassion; having become Ardhanārīśvara, he is the Lord of all, possessing complete auspiciousness.
To him who is unborn, Śaṅkara himself, the mass of splendor, the Lord of Umā, the omniscient creator of all, known by the name Nīlalohita.
Having seen him, bowed with great devotion, and offered praise, I, filled with joy, said to the Lord of the gods: "Create you various living beings."
Then, having heard my words, Maheśvara, the God of gods, created many hosts of Rudras who were equal to himself.
I spoke once again to this Great Rudra, Maheśvara: "O Lord, create progeny, for we are overcome by the fear of birth and death."
O best of sages, having heard these words of mine, Mahādeva, the ocean of compassion, laughed and immediately spoke to me with a smile.
Mahādeva said: "O Creator, overcome by the fear of birth and death, I shall not create progeny; they would be inauspicious, under the sway of karma, and submerged in the ocean of suffering."
"I am submerged in the ocean of suffering, and I shall uplift all beings by assuming the form of a teacher through the bestowal of perfect knowledge."
O Prajāpati, by my command you alone shall create all subjects who are rich in suffering; you shall not be bound by my power, for you will exist through Māyā.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to me, the illustrious Lord Nīlalohita, Hara, together with his attendants, suddenly vanished from my sight.
Brahmā said: Having quintuplicated the elements beginning with sound by means of my own self, from them I [created] the gross ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
O Nārada, I also created mountains, oceans, trees and the like, as well as other periods of time beginning with the *kalā* and ending with the *yuga*.
O sage, even after creating others up to the end of the cosmic cycle, I was not satisfied; therefore, O sage, having meditated upon Śiva with Ambā, I created practitioners (sādhakas).
From his two eyes he created Marīci, from his heart Bhr̥gu, from his head Agastya, and from his vital breath Vyāna, Pulaha, the best of sages.
From his *udāna* breath he produced Pulastya, and from his *samāna* breath Vasiṣṭha; from his *apāna* breath he produced Kratu, from his two ears Atri, and from his *prāṇa* breath Dakṣa.
Then I created you, the sage Kardama, from the lap of Chāyā; and from my will, I created Dharma, the means for accomplishing all means.
O tiger among sages, having thus created these supreme practitioners and accomplished my purpose, I became [liberated] through the grace of Mahādeva.
Then, O dear one, by my command, Dharma—born of resolve—assumed a human form and was set in motion by practitioners.
Then, O Sage, having assigned those various bodies to them, I created from my own diverse limbs immeasurable sons, beginning with the gods and the asuras.
Then, O sage, impelled by Śaṅkara who was within me, I divided my own body into two and became twofold in form.
O sage, half of himself he made into a woman and half into a man; from her he produced a pair, the supreme means for all accomplishments.
There, Svāyambhuva Manu was the Puruṣa, the supreme means; the woman named Śatarūpā was a yoginī, an ascetic.
Furthermore, O dear one, she was exceedingly beautiful when taken by that Manu; through the rite of marriage, he brought forth a creation accompanied by sexual union.
By him, upon her, were begotten a son named Priyavrata, as well as Uttānapāda, and furthermore, three daughters.
Ākūti, Devahūti, and Prasūti were thus renowned; he gave Ākūti to Ruci, but the middle one to Kardama.
He gave Prasūti, the younger sister of Uttānapāda, as a daughter to Dakṣa; by the offspring of those daughters, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was pervaded.
From Ākūti and Ruci was born a pair: Yajña and Dakṣiṇā. Twelve sons were born to Yajña from Dakṣiṇā.
O sage, from Kardama and Devahūti many sons were born; ten were born from Aja, as well as twenty daughters.
O Lord of Sages, thirteen daughters beginning with Śraddhā were given by Dakṣa to Dharma; hear now the names of those wives of Dharma.
Faith, Fortune, Fortitude, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, as well as Action, Wealth, Wisdom, Modesty, Peace, Success, and Fame—these are the thirteen.
From those two, eleven younger daughters with beautiful eyes were born: Khyāti, Satpathasambhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and likewise Kṣamā; |||
Sannati, Anurūpa, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā; as well as Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and the sage Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Atri, the best of sages; Vasiṣṭha, Agni, and the Pitṛs, in their proper order.
The eminent practitioners, Bhṛgu and others, took those renowned maidens as wives; thereafter, the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were completely filled.
Thus, O Lord of Ambikā, by Your command, many countless and preeminent twice-born ones were born according to their respective karma.
According to the division of the Kalpas, sixty daughters of Dakṣa are proclaimed; of these, ten were given to Dharma and twenty-seven to the Moon.
Dakṣa gave thirteen according to the prescribed rite to Kaśyapa; O Nārada, he gave four to Tārkṣya, who was of supreme form.
He gave two daughters each to the descendants of Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva; from them and by means of them, the manifold creation of moving and non-moving beings was produced.
O best of sages, thirteen daughters were given by Dakṣa to that high-souled Kaśyapa according to the prescribed rites.
The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, both stationary and living, are pervaded by their offspring; indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is empty.
The gods, the sages, and the Daityas were born; as were the trees, the birds, and all the mountains and creeping plants.

Thus, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, from the depths of Pātāla up to the limit of Satyaloka and reaching as far as the Pole Star (Dhruva), is indeed pervaded by those born of Dakṣa’s daughters.
The entire cosmic egg was pervaded [by Him], and it was never empty; thus was the creation perfectly brought about by Brahmā at the command of Śambhu.
She named Satī, who was always protected by Rudra at the tip of his trident, was formerly created by Śambhu, the Viṣṇu of all, for the sake of penance.
She herself, having arisen from Dakṣa for the very purpose of the world's work, performed many divine sports for the sake of uplifting her devotees.
He whose left limb is Vaikuṇṭha and whose right limb is I myself, and from whose heart Rudra was born—he is remembered as the threefold Śiva.
I, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas); yet Śiva himself is eternally beyond qualities (nirguṇa), the immutable Supreme Brahman.
Viṣṇu is declared to be Sattva, I (Brahmā) am Rajas, and Rudra is Tamas; this is according to worldly convention by name, but in reality it is otherwise.
O Sage, Viṣṇu is considered to have darkness within and goodness without, while Rudra has goodness within and darkness without; as for me, O sage, I consist entirely of passion.
The goddess Surā is of the nature of rajas, yet she is Satī because of her sattva-form; Lakṣmī should be known as consisting of tamas, while Śivā is the supreme one who is formless.
Thus Śivā, having become Satī, was married by Śaṅkara; then, casting off her body at her father’s sacrifice, she did not take that [body] back and went to her own abode.
Furthermore, by the prayer of the gods, Śivā was born as Pārvatī; having performed extensive penance, she once again united with Śiva.
O Lord of Sages, many names arose for her: Kālikā, Caṇḍikā, Bhadrā, Cāmuṇḍā, Vijayā, and Jayā.
Jayantī, Bhadrakālī, Durgā, and the Goddess Bhagavatī; Kāmākhyā, the Granter of Desires, Ambā, Mṛḍānī, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
In that place, Pārvatī generally possesses numerous names that accord with her qualities and actions, and which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, the goddesses consisting of the qualities (guṇas) and the three gods consisting of the qualities, having come together, performed the various and supreme task of creation.
Thus, O best of sages, the manner of creation has been described by me; at the command of Śiva, the entire Brahmāṇḍa has been composed by me.
The Supreme Brahman is declared to be Śiva; his forms are the three gods—myself, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—in accordance with the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas).
He sports at his own will with Śivā in the delightful world of Śiva; for the Supreme Self is indeed independent, both devoid of attributes and possessed of attributes.
Indeed, his full incarnation is known as Rudra, who is Śiva himself; he made his delightful abode on Kailāsa, and even upon the destruction of the cosmic egg, there is truly no destruction of him.
Sūta said: O lords of sages, having heard these words of Brahmā, Nārada bowed again with humility and questioned him once more.
Nārada said: When indeed did Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, come to Kailāsa? And where was his friendship with the high-souled Kubera?
What did Hara do there, he who is perfectly complete and auspicious in form? Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, how he went to Kailāsa and formed a friendship with the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
In the city of Kāmpilya, there lived a consecrated priest named Yajñadatta, born into a family of Soma-sacrificers and highly proficient in the science of sacrifice.

He was a wise scholar who knew the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), proficient in the Upanishads and other branches of knowledge; he was highly honored by kings, exceedingly generous, and a vessel of fame.
Devoted to the service of the sacred fire and intent upon the study of the Vedas, he was handsome, with beautiful limbs and a form resembling the orb of the moon.

This Dīkṣita had a son named Guṇanidhi; having been initiated with the sacred thread, he mastered the eight branches of knowledge extensively. Later, unknown to his father, he became addicted to gambling.
Having repeatedly taken much wealth from his mother, he gave it to the gamblers and established a friendship with them.
He had abandoned the conduct of a Brahmin, was averse to the twilight prayers and ritual bathing, and was a reviler of the Vedas and scriptures, as well as a censurer of the gods and Brahmins.
Devoid of mindfulness and proper conduct, he indulges in the diversions of song and instrumental music, maintaining a continuous succession of attachments for actors, heretics, and jesters.
Although urged by his mother, he did not go to his father's side; being occupied with other household duties, the initiated one [remained] with the wife of the initiated one.
Whenever he asks her, "O auspicious one, my son Guṇanidhi is not seen by me in the house; what is he doing? [she would reply].
She should say, "At such and such a time," [adding] "but now he has gone outside, having bathed and worshipped the gods for this much time."
Having completed his studies, he went with his friends, the twice-born, for the purpose of further study; meanwhile, his mother, thinking "he is my only son," entreated the initiated one [to stay].
That initiated boy did not know anything of that ritual action or that conduct; then, in his sixteenth year, [the preceptor] performed for him the entire ceremony ending with the tonsure (keśānta).
Then, that initiated Yajñadatta had the taking of the hand of his son performed according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
O Nārada, every day his mother, her heart softened with affection, would seat that son—a treasure-house of virtues—and gently instruct him.
"O son, that great-souled one is prone to anger; enough of this! If he learns of your conduct and knows both you and me, he will strike you."
I shall always conceal your misconduct before your father; for your father is honored by the world because of his virtuous conduct, and not indeed because of his wealth.
O dear one, true knowledge and the company of the virtuous are the wealth of Brahmins; why do you not, with a joyful heart, practice *suruci* (excellent conduct) toward them?
"Your ancestors of old attained renown here as true śrotriyas, learned in the Vedas, consecrated, and performers of soma sacrifices."
Abandoning association with those of evil conduct, be devoted to the company of the virtuous; fix your mind on true knowledge and practice the conduct of a Brahmin.
Since you are equal to your father in appearance, fame, lineage, and character, why are you not ashamed? Why do you not abandon your own wicked conduct?
"You are nineteen years old and she is sixteen; marry this woman of virtuous conduct and be devoted to your father."
Indeed, your father-in-law is worthy of respect from everyone on account of his virtues and character; why then do you not feel shame? Abandon this wicked conduct, my son!
O son, your maternal uncles are incomparable in learning, character, lineage, and other virtues; yet you do not fear even them, for you are pure in both lineages.
Behold these young sons of Brahmins living in the neighborhood; behold also these disciples of your father, who are worthy of discipline even within their own homes.
O son, when the king hears of your misconduct, he will lose faith in you and deprive you of your livelihood.
Even today, people say that this is merely the behavior of a child; hereafter, they will regard your state as being truly consecrated.
"Everyone will revile both your father and me, saying, 'The son upholds his mother's conduct through such foul speech.'"
Even your father was not more sinful, for he followed the path of the Śruti and Smṛti; Maheśvara is the witness to me, whose mind is fixed upon his feet.
"Even by one who has bathed after a funeral rite, the face of a wicked man is not to be looked upon here; oh, how powerful is that destiny by which you were born!"
Though instructed by his mother every moment, that man of extremely dull intellect did not abandon that practice, for he was difficult to enlighten and addicted to vice.
Who here has not been ruined by these vices: hunting, drinking, calumny, falsehood, theft, gambling, and adultery?
Whatever the foolish-minded man sees in the middle house, he shall take that and hand over to the gamblers, including base metals, clothing, and so forth.
Having once stolen the jeweled ring from her father’s hand that had been placed within his house, she took it and offered it into the hand of the gambler.
Having been recognized by the Dīkṣita, the gambler said to him as he was in his hand: "From where did you obtain this ring?"
Then, having been questioned repeatedly with persistence by him, he said to him: "O Brahmin, why do you so loudly accuse me? What theft have I committed?"
The seal has been obtained; it was indeed delivered by your own son. For yesterday, he won my mother's garment and took it away.
"This ring was not entrusted to me alone; much wealth was also delivered by him to other gamblers."
Jewels, base metals, fine silken garments, ornaments and the like, as well as various vessels made of bell-metal and copper.
Stripped naked and bound every day by gamblers, there is no dice-player on the face of the earth equal to him.
O Brahmin, until this very day, how was it that you did not recognize your son as the crest-jewel of gamblers, skilled in immodesty and misconduct?
Having heard this, his neck bowed low under the weight of shame, he covered his head with his garment and entered his own palace.
Then his wife, a woman of great devotion to her husband, spoke to that Yajñadatta, who was consecrated for sacrifice and devoted to the performance of Vedic rites.
Yajñadatta said: "Dīkṣitāyani, where is that son Guṇanidhi, you rogue? Or rather, let him be; what have I to do with him? Where is my auspicious ring?"
"O you who were taken by me from my finger at the time of massaging my limbs, you who are made of jewels—bring her back quickly and give her to me!"
Having heard those words, that Dīkṣitāyanī became afraid; she then spoke while completing her midday bathing rites.
I am occupied with the rites of offerings and the like for the worship of the gods; O you who are dear to guests, this time for our guests might pass by.
Just now, while I was preoccupied with preparing cooked food, I placed it in some vessel; I do not know where it has been forgotten.
The initiated one said: "O mother of a wicked son, O you who always speak the truth! Whenever I ask you, 'Where has my son gone?'"
"You should say, 'At that time, at that time,' if he has now departed; having finished his studies, he has gone outside with two or three friends for the purpose of further study."
"Where is that madder-dyed garment, my wife, which was given by me? He who receives it constantly in his abode—tell me the truth and cast away your fear."
Now that jeweled water-pot is no longer seen, nor is that triple-folded cloth made of silk thread which was offered by me.
Where is that southern bronze vessel, and where is that Bengal copper jar? And where is that ivory bedstead for pleasure and amusement?
Where is that wondrous statue from the mountain region, resembling the luster of the moon, her fingertips adorned by the busy holding of a lamp?
What is the use of much speaking? I am angry with you, though you are of noble birth, for no reason; I shall eat [only] when I marry.
"I am childless because of that wicked man who defiled our family; arise, bring water, and you must offer him a handful of sesame seeds."

It is better for men to be childless than to have a wicked son who brings disgrace upon the family; one should abandon a single individual for the sake of the lineage—this is the eternal rule of conduct.
Having bathed and performed his daily rites on that very day, the initiated one obtained the daughter of a certain Vedic scholar and took her hand in marriage.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Guṇanidhi," in the Sṛṣṭyupākhyāna (Account of Creation) within the first section of the Rudrasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard that account of his own past and having censured himself, the son of the initiated one (Dīkṣita) looked toward a certain direction and departed.
After traveling from there for some time, Guṇanidhi—the wicked son of Yajñadatta—stood there, his enthusiasm vanished and himself abandoned.
He fell into great anxiety: "Where shall I go? What shall I do? I am not one who has mastered the sciences, nor am I very wealthy."
He whose wealth is in another land prospers immediately with happiness; yet there is danger from thieves regarding that wealth, for such an obstacle arises from every direction.
How is it that I, born into a family of priests, have met with such great calamity? Alas, destiny is indeed powerful; it brings about the consequences of future actions.
I have nothing to beg for, nor do I have any acquaintances anywhere; nor is there any wealth by my side—what, then, could be my refuge in this situation?
Since my mother has always provided me with delicious food even before the sun had risen, whom should I ask for it here today? My mother is not present here.
Brahmā said: O Nārada, while he was thus reflecting there many times, the sun went to the mountain of setting, leaving him in great distress at the foot of the tree.
At that very moment, a certain devotee of Maheśvara, taking sacrificial offerings with him, went out from the city.
Surrounded by his kinsmen and having fasted on Śivarātri, he went forth to worship the Lord Īśāna with various kinds of great divine offerings.
Then, having entered the temple of Śiva, that devotee, whose mind was fixed on Śiva, worshipped Śaṅkara with a pure heart in a fitting manner.
Having smelled the fragrance of cooked food, that twice-born Yajñadatta’s son—abandoned by his father, deprived of his mother, and hungry—followed after it.
"This food, various and abundant, was prepared by me for Śiva during the night; yet, while all those devoted to Śiva were asleep, it has been taken by me by chance."
Having thus taken hold of hope, he sat down at the door of Śambhu and beheld the great worship performed by that devotee.
When the devotees had performed the dances, songs, and other rites and had fallen asleep for a moment, Bharga entered the temple to take away the food offering.
Seeing the lamp’s light fading, he took a wick from the fold of his own garment and, having made it into a lamp, illuminated it so that he might see the cooked food.
Then the son of Yajñadatta, with great devotion and joy, suddenly took many portions of cooked food from the offering made to Śiva.
Then, as he was going outside in haste taking cooked food, someone who was fast asleep woke up from the blow of his foot.
"Who is this? Who is this, rushing so fast? Seize him! Seize him! Thus that crowd cried out with voices raised high in fear.
As soon as he arrived out of fear, he was struck down by the city guards while fleeing; in an instant, he fell into blindness.
O Sage, the son of Yajñadatta consumed the food offering because of Śiva’s grace and indeed by the power of his future merit.
Then, having arrived bound by the fierce soldiers of Yama, who held nooses and mallets in their hands and desired to lead him to Saṃyamanī;
Meanwhile, the attendants, wearing garlands of networks of tinkling bells and bearing tridents in their hands, arrived bringing a divine celestial chariot to lead him away.

The attendants of Śiva said: "O attendants of Yama, release this brahmin, who is supremely righteous; this brāhmaṇa is not deserving of punishment, for he has burnt away the entire accumulation of his sins."
Having heard these words, the hosts of Yamarāja then spoke to the hosts of Mahādeva and became exceedingly terrified.
Then, beholding the attendants of Śambhu, those servants of Yama were terrified and, bowing down, spoke thus: "O Gaṇas, this brahmin is a man of evil conduct."
The Yamagaṇas said: "Transgressing the family tradition, he is averse to the words of his parents; he has fallen away from truth and purity, and is devoid of the twilight prayers and ritual bathing."
Let aside his other deeds; let alone one who has transgressed the sacred offerings of Śiva. Behold here before your very eyes: he is untouchable for those such as you.

Those who consume the remains of offerings made to Śiva, those who step over the remains of offerings made to Śiva, and those who give away the remains of offerings made to Śiva—their very touch brings demerit.
Having perceived the danger, one should either drink it or else touch it; the wealth of Śiva must be utilized, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
"You are the authority regarding these matters, not we; if there is even a trace of dharma in him, O members of the assembly, we shall hear it."
Having heard these words of the Yāmas, the attendants of Śiva, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, spoke to those followers.

The servants of Śiva said: "The duties of Śiva which are subtle are perceived by those like you; how could they be perceived by those with coarse vision, who are only perceivable by those with subtle insight?"
O Gaṇas, listen here with careful attention to that deed which was performed by this very Yajñadatta’s son.
As the shadow of a lamp fell upon the top of the linga, he warded it off at night by giving the wick of the lamp from the hem of his own garment.
Furthermore, another supreme dharma has arisen there for him: it belongs to those who, even incidentally, hear or utter the names of Śiva.
The worship being performed according to the prescribed rite was observed by him, who had fasted on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight with a steady mind.
Indeed, today he shall go with us to the world of Śiva, and as a follower of Śiva, he will enjoy great pleasures there for some time.
Then this king of Kaliṅga shall become cleansed of all impurity, for he is surely a most excellent twice-born man who is exceedingly dear to Śiva.
"Nothing else should be said; you must go back the way you came, O messengers of Yama, with hearts full of great serenity, to your own world."
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having heard those words of theirs, all the messengers of Yama turned their faces away and returned to the world of Yama by the same way they had come.
O Sage, the Gaṇas reported everything to Śamana, recounting that entire event from the beginning according to the facts as told by the messengers of Śambhu.
The King of Dharma said: "O hosts, listen all with attention to my words; out of affection, carry them out accordingly, preceded by my command."
Those attendants in the world who wear the triple mark with white sacred ash must all be avoided; they should never be brought near.
Those Gaṇas who smear themselves with white sacred ash must all be avoided; they should never be brought near.
For whatever reason, anyone in the world who assumes the guise of Śiva must be avoided by all; they should never be welcomed.
Those in this world who wear rudrākṣas and those who wear matted hair must all be avoided; they should never be brought near.
Indeed, those who wear the dress of Śiva for the sake of livelihood must all be avoided; they should never be brought [into the community].
Indeed, those who wear the dress of Śiva even through hypocrisy or deceit must all be avoided; they should never be brought near.
Thus Yama commanded his own servants; accepting his word with "So be it," they all remained silent with pure smiles.
Brahmā said: Having been liberated from the messengers of Yama by the attendants, that twice-born man of pure mind went swiftly to the world of Śiva along with those Gaṇas.
Having enjoyed all pleasures there and having served both Śiva and Aśiva, he became the son of Ariṃdama, the lord of Kaliṅga.
Named Dama, he was devoted to the service of Śiva; even as a child, he practiced devotion to Śiva along with other children.
Then, when his father had passed away, the youth gradually obtained the kingdom; out of affection, he caused the teachings of Śiva to be practiced everywhere.
O twice-born one, that king Durdama, who was himself self-controlled, knew no other dharma except for the offering of lamps in all the temples of Śiva.
Having summoned all the village headmen residing within his domain, he issued this command: "Lamps must be offered in the temple of Śiva."
Otherwise, this would indeed be true, and he shall be punished by me; for it is declared in the Śruti that Śiva becomes pleased by the offering of a lamp.
In every place surrounding a village, and wherever there are temples of Śiva, a lamp must always be lit there without hesitation.
"Out of fear that my head would undoubtedly be cut off for the offense of disobeying my command, lamps were lit at every Shiva temple."
By this very dharma, King Dama lived his entire life; having attained great prosperity through dharma, he eventually succumbed to the power of time.
Indeed, through the power of his latent impression from that lamp, he lit many lamps and became the lord of Alakā, taking refuge in the flames of jewel-lamps.
Thus, even that which is performed as little as it may be bears fruit in time when directed toward Śiva; knowing this, those who desire great happiness should practice devotion to Śiva.

Where is that heir of the initiated one, who always takes no delight in any worldly dharma? By the turn of fate, he has come to the temple of Śiva to steal its wealth—he who dispels the delusion of the world by the light of the wick of his own self-interest illuminating the crest of the Liṅga.
Having obtained the kingdom in the region of Kaliṅga, he always delighted in righteousness; and due to the awakening of his former latent impressions, he illuminated lamps in the temple of Śiva.
O Lord of Sages, behold this position of a world-guardian; it is now being enjoyed here by one who possesses the nature of a mere mortal.
Thus has been told the life story of Guṇanidhi, the son of Yajñadatta, which brings satisfaction to Śiva and grants all desires to those who hear it.
And how he came to form a friendship with Sarvadevaśiva—listen with one-pointed mind, my dear, as I tell you that as well.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Guṇanidhi’s Attainment of the True Goal," in the section on the Narrative of the Journey to Kailāsa within the Narrative of Creation, in the first part of the Rudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O gods, in the Pādma Kalpa, Viśravas was born from Pulastya, who was a mind-born son of mine, Brahmā; Vaiśravaṇa was his son.
Therefore, this city of Alakā was enjoyed by him; it was created by the Architect of the Universe after he had propitiated the three-eyed God in the past through most formidable asceticism.
When that kalpa had passed and the Meghavāhana kalpa had begun, this Yājñadatti, Śrīda, performed most difficult austerities.
Having realized the power of devotion to Śambhu through that mere lamp, [he] formerly reached Kāśikā, the illuminator of consciousness, belonging to the Enemy of Tripura.
Having awakened the eleven forms of Śiva by means of the jewel-lamps of the mind, one who is rich with the oil of exclusive devotion becomes absorbed in Him and immovable through meditation.
The great vessel of oneness with Śiva is nourished by the fire of austerity and is free from the blows of the moths that are the great obstacles of desire and anger.

Having established the Śāmbhava Liṅga—which is free from wind due to the restraint of the vital breaths, stainless because of the stainless gaze, and worshipped with the flower of true being—[one should meditate].
He performed that austerity until his body was reduced to skin and bone, for a period of ten million years.
Then the Lord himself, the Sovereign of the Universe, together with the large-eyed goddess, beheld the lord of Alakā with a serene inner soul.
Having fixed his mind upon the linga and remaining there in the form of a pillar, he said, "I am the giver of boons; therefore, speak, O Lord of Alakā."
As soon as that ascetic opened his eyes and looked, he beheld one whose splendor exceeded that of a thousand rising suns.
In front of him, he beheld Śrīkaṇṭha, the moon-crested Lord of Umā; his own visual power being overwhelmed by that splendor, he closed his eyes.
He spoke to the Lord of the gods of gods, who transcends the path of one's desires: "O Lord, grant me the capacity of sight to behold your own feet."
This alone is the boon, O Lord, that you are beheld directly before my eyes; what need is there for any other boon, O Master? Salutations to you, O Moon-crested One!
Having heard those words, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, touched him with the palm of his hand and granted him the power of vision.
First extending his eyes, he gazed only at Umā; and having attained that power, Yājñadattis became [transformed].
Who is this woman, beautiful in every limb, who stays near Śambhu? What austerity has she performed that it surpasses even my own penance?
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what love! What great good fortune and splendor!"—thus that son spoke again and again, indeed most excessively.
As he gazed with a cruel eye, speaking this again and again, his left eye burst open due to his looking toward the left.
Then the goddess said, "O Lord, why does that wicked ascetic, having looked at me repeatedly, say: 'You must create for me the splendor of my penance'?"
Again and again he gazes at me with his right eye, envying my beauty, my love, and the perfection of my good fortune.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, the Lord laughed and said to her: "O Umā, this is your son; he shall not look with a cruel eye."
"Beholding the splendor of your asceticism, how could one possibly describe it? Having thus addressed the Goddess, the Lord spoke to him again.
"I grant you boons, my child, for I am gratified by this asceticism. You shall be the lord of treasures and the sovereign of the Guhyakas."
O King of kings, you who are firm in your vows, be the lord of the Yakṣas and Kinnaras, and the giver of wealth to all the Puṇyajanas.
"I shall always maintain friendship with you and dwell in your presence, O friend, near Alakā for the sake of increasing your joy."
"Come, fall at her feet; she is indeed your mother, O Yājñadatta, who is devoted to you with a most gracious heart."
Brahmā said: Having thus granted the boons, Lord Śiva spoke again to Śivā: "O Queen of the Gods, show favor toward this ascetic daughter of yours."
Having heard these words of Śambhu, Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, spoke with a very gracious mind to Yājñadatta.
The Goddess said: "O child, may your stainless devotion to Bhava be eternal; indeed, let you become one-eyed through your left eye, which has burst open."
"O son, let the boons granted to you by the god remain exactly as they were; however, because of my jealousy regarding your beauty, you shall be known by the name Kubera."
Having thus granted these boons, the Lord Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, then entered the abode named Vaiśveśvara for the sake of Dhanada.
In this manner, this giver of wealth attained friendship with the illustrious Śambhu; and not far from the city of Alakā was Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kubera’s Friendship with Śiva," in the Kailāsagamanopākhyāna (The Narrative of the Journey to Kailāsa) within the first section of the Rudrasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Sage Nārada, listen to the excellent account of Śiva’s arrival at Kailāsa, the best of mountains, through the power of Kubera’s penance.
Having granted the boon of lordship over treasures and departed for his own supreme abode, the Lord of the Universe, the bestower of boons upon Kubera, reflected within his heart.
My true nature is born from the limbs of the Vidyā; complete and performing the work of dissolution, I shall go to Kailāsa, the abode of the Guhyakas, in that very form.
Rudra is indeed born from my heart; he is a full manifestation (pūrṇāṃśa), the fruitless Brahman, served by Hari, Brahmā, and the others—stainless and non-different from me.
In that very place, assuming his own form and becoming a friend, I shall sport and dwell with Kubera, and I shall perform great penance.
Having reflected thus, Rudra, eager to go to Śiva’s abode, sounded his own ḍhakkā drum there, which was his auspicious path in the form of sound.
The sound of her [chanting], which inspires enthusiasm, filled the three worlds; it was diverse, dense with sound, and joined with the movement of invocation.
Having heard that, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as the sages, the personified Āgamas and Nigamas, and the Siddhas, indeed went there.
All the gods, asuras, and others went there with great celebration; all the Pramathas also went, wherever they might have been stationed.
The Gaṇapas are highly fortunate and honored by all the worlds; I shall state their number—listen with careful attention.
And Śaṅkhakarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, advanced with ten crores of Gaṇas; likewise, Kekarākṣa with ten, and Vikṛta with eight.
Viśākha was with sixty-four, Pāriyātraka with nine, the illustrious Sarvāntaka with six, and Dundubhi with eight.
For Jālāṅka, the leader of the Gaṇas, was accompanied by twelve crores; likewise were the illustrious Samada and Vikṛtānana with seven crores each.
Indeed, Kapālī is with five, the auspicious Sandāraka with six, while Kaṇḍuka and Kuṇḍaka are here with ten million times ten million.
Viṣṭambha went with eight [attendants], and Candratāpana with eight.
Mahākeśa was surrounded by a host of a thousand times ten million attendants.
Kuṇḍī with twelve hundred, as well as the auspicious Parvataka; Kāla and Kālaka each with one hundred, and Mahākāla indeed with one hundred.
Agnika indeed with a hundred crores, Abhimukha with one crore, Ādityamūrdhā with one crore, and likewise Dhanāvaha with one crore.
Sannāha was with a hundred [crores], Kumuda likewise with ten million; Amogha and Kokila were each with ten billion, as was Sumantraka.
Another is Kākapāda with sixty [attendants], the lord Saṃtānaka with sixty, Mahābala with nine, and Piṅga and Piṅgala.
Nīla [ruled] over ninety [crores], as did Pūrṇabhadra; likewise, the mighty Caturvaktra [ruled] over seven crores of the lords of the gods.
Surrounded by twenty hundred thousand times ten million [attendants], the Lord of All arrived there indeed for the purpose of proceeding to Kailāsa.
Kāṣṭhāgūḍha with sixty-four crores, Sukeśa and Vṛṣabha likewise; Caitra with seven crores—this is the Lord Nakulīśa.
Lokāntaka, the radiant-souled one, and likewise the lord Daityāntaka; the god Bhṛṅgin, the illustrious Riṭi, and likewise the beloved of the God of gods.
Aśani and Bhānuka, along with Sanātana, were accompanied by sixty-four crores; and Nandīśvara, the lord of the Gaṇas, possessed great strength and was accompanied by a hundred crores.
These and other leaders of the hosts, innumerable and possessed of great strength, all have a thousand hands and wear crowns of matted hair.
And all of them had the moon as their crest-ornament, were blue-throated, and three-eyed; they were adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crowns, and other ornaments.
Resembling Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, and shining like ten million suns, the lords of the Gaṇas arrived there.
These leaders of the Gaṇas and others, who possessed great pride and stainless luster, went there with great joy, longing for the sight of Śiva.
Having gone there and beheld Śiva, they bowed and offered supreme praise; all of them, led by Viṣṇu, stood with palms joined in reverence and heads bowed low.
Thus, together with Viṣṇu and the others, Maheśa, the Supreme Lord, went with affection to the Kailāsa of the high-souled Kubera.
Kubera also, accompanied by his retinue, respectfully worshipped Śambhu upon his arrival with devotion and various offerings.
Then, for the sake of pleasing Śiva, he worshipped Viṣṇu and the other gods, as well as the Gaṇas and others who are surely followers of Śiva.
Then Śambhu, with a joyful mind, embraced Kubera, smelled his head, and stood near Alakā together with all [his attendants].
The Lord commanded Viśvakarman to construct on the mountain dwellings for himself and for others, according to their respective needs, using various materials.
Then, O Sage, having gone there with the permission of Śambhu, Viśvakarman quickly fashioned various kinds of structures.
Then Śambhu was delighted by the request of Hari at that time.
Having bestowed his grace upon Kubera, the Supreme Lord departed for Mount Kailāsa; at an auspicious moment, he entered his own abode.
The one who is affectionate toward his devotees, out of love, made them all have a protector; then all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, as well as the other sages and Siddhas, joyfully consecrated Śiva.
All of them, with various offerings in their hands, honored him in due order; they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) preceded by a great festival.
Then, O Sage, there was a rain of flowers that was a source of auspiciousness; the Apsarases, being well-pleased, danced there, intent upon singing.
There, cries of "Victory! and "Homage! arose, refined by all; at that time, there was great enthusiasm among everyone, which increased their happiness.
Then Śambhu, seated upon his lion-throne, shone with exceeding splendor, being constantly served by Viṣṇu and all the others as was appropriate.
Then all the gods and others praised him individually with meaningful and pleasing words—Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
Having heard their praise with a serene soul, Śiva, the Lord and Master of All, joyfully granted them the boons desired by their hearts.
Then, O sage, by the command of Śiva, they all went to their respective abodes, their desires fulfilled and filled with joy, as did I along with Viṣṇu.
Having seated Viṣṇu and me upon the throne, the Supreme Lord Śambhu, having addressed him with great affection and bestowed his grace, spoke.
Śiva said: O Hara, O Vidhi, you two fathers are most dear to me; you are the best of gods, eternally engaged in the protection and creation of the three worlds.
"Go always without fear and remain in your own abodes by my command; for I am indeed the bestower of happiness upon you both, and I shall always be your witness."
Having heard these words of Śambhu and having bowed deeply at his command, Hari and I returned to our own abodes with delighted minds.
At that very moment, Śaṅkara, being well-pleased, joyfully seated the Lord of Treasures (Nidhipa) and, taking him by the hand, spoke these auspicious words:
Śiva said: "O friend, I have been won over by your love; come to friendship with me. Go to your own place without fear, O sinless one; I am always your companion."
Having heard these words of Śambhu, Kubera, with a delighted mind and filled with joy, went to his own abode by His command.
On Mount Kailāsa, the best of mountains, Śambhu—accompanied by his attendants, devoted to yoga, acting according to his own will, and intent on meditation—spoke.
In some places he contemplated his own self, and in others he became absorbed in yoga; with a mind free from constraints, he spoke of various collections of ancient histories with delight.
In certain beautiful places on Mount Kailāsa, Maheśvara, the connoisseur of various pastimes, sported with joy along with his attendants.
Thus, this Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, who is the very nature of Rudra and the foremost among yogis, performed various divine sports upon his own mountain.
Having spent some time without a wife, that Supreme Lord later obtained his own consort, born from the wife of Dakṣa.
Maheśvara dwelt with that virtuous daughter of Dakṣa; devoted to worldly custom, O celestial sage, he became happy.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, this incarnation of Rudra has been described to you, as well as his journey to Kailāsa due to his friendship with the Lord of Treasures.
The divine play contained within that [reality] has also been described, for it increases knowledge and eternally bestows the fruit of all desires both in this world and the next.
Whoever should read this narrative or listen to it with a concentrated mind, having attained worldly enjoyment in this life, shall obtain liberation in the next.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Śiva’s Journey to Kailāsa," in the first section (Kailāsopākhyāna) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, you know everything by the grace of Śaṅkara; for you have narrated to me the wonderful and auspicious stories of Śiva and Śivā.
O Lord, having heard this supreme discourse on Śiva which has issued from the lotus of your mouth, I am indeed not yet satiated; I truly wish to hear it once more.
O Brahmā, that Maheśāna who was previously described by you as Rudra—the full portion of Śaṅkara himself, the self-controlled one whose abode is Kailāsa—[is he not here?].
That yogi, whose goal is the dissolution of all the gods beginning with Viṣṇu, sports eternally as a great lord, free from dualities and devoid of transformation.
He became a householder once again, having married the most excellent woman, Maṅgalā, his own ascetic wife, out of love and at the request of Hari.
First she was the daughter of Dakṣa, and later she was the daughter of the Mountain; how is it that she is considered the daughter of both by means of a single body?
How did that Pārvatī, while remaining [in her own form], again approach Śiva? O Brahman, you ought to tell me all this and whatever else [is related].
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the celestial sage Śaṅkara, Brahmā became delighted in mind and spoke these words.
Brahmā said: Listen, O dear one, best of sages; I shall tell you an auspicious story, by hearing which your birth will become fruitful—of this there is no doubt.
"O dear one, in the past, upon seeing my own daughter named Sandhyā together with her sons, I became agitated, tormented by the arrows of desire."
Then Rudra, the supreme lord and great yogi, was remembered as Dharma; having censured me, O dear one, he went to his own abode along with his sons.
Because I was deluded by Māyā and, though a proclaimer of the Vedas, possessed a foolish intellect, I committed an improper act together with the Supreme Lord Śambhu.
Out of envy for that, I, a fool deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, devised many schemes along with my sons to bewitch him.
Then, O Śambhu, supreme lord, all those means became fruitless for them as well as for me, O lord of sages.
Then, along with those who were distressed by the means [of their situation], I remembered the Lord of Ramā; that wise one, devoted to the worship of Śiva, arrived and enlightened us.
Awakened by Rameśa, who reveals the true nature of Śiva, I abandoned my envy for him; yet, being utterly deluded, I did not relinquish that stubbornness.
Having served Śakti, he then, out of affection for her, begot her upon Vīriṇī, the daughter of Dakṣa and sister of Aśiknī, through his own son, for the purpose of deluding Hara.
Having become Soma, the daughter of Dakṣa, and having performed unbearable austerity, she became the wife of Rudra through her devotion, acting for the welfare of her devotees.
The Lord Soma, having become a householder, performed a supreme pastime; there, with an unchanging mind, he deluded me during his own wedding.
Having married her and returned to his own mountain, he—being independent, possessing a self-dependent form, and being greatly deluded by the power of his creative will—enjoyed himself.
As that sage dwelt in that manner—tranquil, free from agitation, steadfast in his virtuous conduct—a great length of time passed, bringing him happiness.
Then, by his own will, a rivalry with Rudra arose in Dakṣa, who was utterly deluded, infatuated by his own māyā, and full of pride.
Due to its power, the highly arrogant and deluded Dakṣa, being utterly infatuated, reviled Hara, who is supremely peaceful and free from all transformations.
Then Dakṣa, the lord of all, being filled with pride, himself performed a sacrifice; having invited all the gods and others, as well as Viṣṇu and me.
Being thus affected and overwhelmed with rage, he did not invoke Rudra; likewise, deluded by fate, he did not call his own daughter there by the name of Satī.
When she was not given away by her father, whose mind was deluded by illusion, then the highly virtuous Śivā, possessed of excellent wisdom, performed her divine play.
Then, having arrived there and received the command of Śiva, she went to her father’s house, even though she had not been invited by the arrogant Dakṣa.
Having observed that he had not obtained his portion from Rudra and having received contempt from his father, he then reviled them all there and performed the abandonment of his body.
Having heard that, the God, the Lord of Gods, having manifested unbearable anger, tore out a large mass of matted hair and brought forth Vīrabhadra.
To him who asked, "What should I do after having produced him along with his attendants?", he commanded the destruction of the sacrifice, preceded by every form of insult.
Having received that command, the lord of the Gaṇas, endowed with great strength and possessing immense power and prowess, went there swiftly and suddenly.
At his command, the hosts there caused great affliction; he punished them all, leaving not a single one remaining.
Having conquered Viṣṇu along with the gods through great effort, that best of Gaṇas cut off Dakṣa’s head and offered that head as an oblation into the fire.
Causing great calamity, he swiftly brought about the destruction of the sacrifice; then he went to his own mountain and prostrated before the Lord Śiva.
Thus did the destruction of the sacrifice occur; for it was seen in the world of the gods that it had been carried out there by the attendants of Rudra, headed by Vīrabhadra.
O Sage, this principle should be known as that which is approved by the Śruti and Smṛti: O Lord of Splendor, when Rudra is enraged, how can there be happiness in the world?
Then Rudra, having heard that supreme hymn of praise, became gracious; he, who is compassionate toward the distressed, made the petition of them all fruitful.
And as before, that great-souled Śaṅkara, the Great Lord who delights in various divine sports, displayed his compassion.
For by him, Dakṣa was restored to life, and all there were honored; then the sacrifice was performed once again by the compassionate Śaṅkara.
And there in the forest, Rudra was especially worshipped with devotion by all the gods, beginning with Viśva, whose minds were perfectly serene during the sacrifice.
The flame born from the body of Satī, which brings happiness to the world, fell upon that mountain; there it was worshipped as the bestower of bliss.
Renowned as Jvālāmukhī, the supreme goddess who grants the fruit of all desires became the remover of sins through the mere sight of her.
Now he is worshipped in the world for the attainment of all desired fruits, through manifold arrangements and mutual great festivals.
Then that virtuous goddess became the daughter of Himālaya, and at that time the name Pārvatī became famous for her.
Furthermore, having propitiated that very Supreme Lord through rigorous austerity, she took refuge in him as her husband.
O Lord of Sages, all this that I was asked has been fully explained; by hearing this, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Concise Life Story of Satī," in the second section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the resident of the Naimiṣa forest, the best of sages asked for the story that destroys all sins.
Nārada said: O Creator, O Creator, O highly fortunate one! While listening to the auspicious story of Śambhu from your lotus-like mouth, O Great Lord, I am not yet satiated.
Therefore, O Creator of the Universe, tell me all that auspicious and divine life-story of Śiva, accompanied by the glory of Satī; I desire to hear it.
How indeed was the auspicious Satī born among the wives of Dakṣa, and how did Hara set his mind upon the act of seizing her as his wife?
Or how was Satī, who in former times abandoned her body due to Dakṣa’s wrath, born again as the daughter of Himavat and returned to the celestial realm?
And how did Pārvatī’s most severe penance and her marriage come to pass? And how did she become half the body of the Destroyer of Smara?
Explain all of this in detail, O Mahāmati; there shall be no one else like you who can sever our doubts.
Brahmā said: Listen, O sage, to all the auspicious glory of Satī and Śiva—purifying, supreme, divine, and the most secret of secrets.
O Sage, Śambhu previously spoke this to Viṣṇu, the best of devotees, when questioned by him with great devotion for the sake of helping others.
Then, O best of sages, that wise Viṣṇu, the foremost of Śiva’s devotees, being questioned by me, joyfully explained it to me in detail.
I shall relate this ancient narrative, which is endowed with the glory of Śiva and Śivā, and which bestows the fruits of all desires.

Formerly, when the divine Śiva was devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka), formless, devoid of power (śakti), pure consciousness alone (cinmātra), and beyond both being and non-being;
O Brahmin, that Lord, though endowed with qualities, became twofold in form and possessed of power; he was Soma, of divine appearance, changeless, and higher than the highest.
O best of sages, Viṣṇu was born from his left side, I, Brahmā, from his right side, and Rudra was born from his heart.
Brahmā became the creator of the universe, Viṣṇu the protector, and Rudra himself the agent of dissolution; thus Sadāśiva manifested in three forms.
Having propitiated that very one, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created all those progeny, beginning with the gods, asuras, and humans.
Having created the Prajāpatis, the best of gods headed by Dakṣa, I considered myself perfectly pleased and all-surpassingly exalted.
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Dakṣa, and Bhṛgu—these were the great-souled lords.
O sage, when I created my mind-born sons, then a woman of beautiful form was born from my mind.
By name she was Saṃdhyā; she ended the day and performed the evening twilight prayers. She was exceedingly beautiful, with lovely eyebrows, and she enchanted the minds of the sages.

Neither in the world of the gods, nor among mortals, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala), has there ever been, even throughout the three periods of time, a woman endowed with such perfect virtues.
Having seen her, I arose and reflected upon what was in my heart: "Dakṣa and the other creators, as well as Marīci and the others, are my sons."
O best of sages, while I, Brahmā, was reflecting in this manner, a charming and most wonderful person appeared from my mind.
With the luster of gold upon his body, broad-chested, with a well-formed nose, possessing well-rounded thighs, hips, and shanks, and with dark, curled manes;
With eyebrows arched like a bow, restless, and with a face resembling the full moon; his broad chest was as expansive as a door-panel, adorned with a beautiful line of body hair.
Having the form of a cloud, a rutting elephant, or a crow, he is stout and wears fine blue garments; his hands, eyes, face, feet, and palms are slightly reddish.

With a slender waist and beautiful teeth, he possessed the scent of a rutting elephant; his eyes were like the petals of a full-blown lotus, and his sense of smell was gratified by the fragrance of filaments.
He has a neck like a conch shell, the fish-bannered one, tall in stature, with the makara as his vehicle; he possesses five flower-arrows, is swift-moving, and is adorned with a bow of flowers.
O dear one, the beloved, casting side-glances that cause his two eyes to roll, is attended by the fragrant breeze, which is steeped in the sentiment of erotic love.
Beholding that man, all those sons of mine, Dakṣa and the others, were filled with supreme eagerness, their minds overcome by wonder.
O dear one, the minds of my sons quickly became agitated; their hearts overwhelmed by passion, they could not maintain their composure at all.
Seeing me, the creator, the ordainer, and the lord of the worlds, that man bowed with his neck humbly bent and spoke.
The Puruṣa said: "O Brahmā, assign me to some task there; for today, O Creator, no other man is as worthy, appropriate, or illustrious as I."
"Tell me, O Lord of the three worlds, what is my proper pride, what is my fitting station, and who shall be my wife; for you are the creator and the master of the worlds."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of that high-souled Puruṣa, the Creator, being greatly astonished, did not say anything for a moment.
Therefore, having restrained his mind and properly cast aside his astonishment, Brahmā spoke to the Puruṣa while bringing forth that desire.
Brahmā said: "In this form of yours, and with your five flower-arrows, deluding both men and women, carry out the eternal creation."
In this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, all these living beings—gods and others alike—will cease to exist; there will be no support left.
Whether it be I, or Vāsudeva, or Sthāṇu, the Supreme Person—we shall all come under your control; what need is there to mention other mere sustainers of life?
Always entering the hearts of living beings in a concealed form, and having yourself become the cause of their happiness, carry out the eternal creation.
The mind of every living being is a wonderful and ever-constant target for the ease of your flower-arrows; you are forever the one who brings intoxication to all creatures.
Thus, I have again described to you that activity which sets creation in motion; my sons shall speak of these names of yours according to their true nature.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O best of gods, I gazed upon the faces of my sons and sat down for a moment upon my own lotus-seat.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Kāma," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then all those sages, the sons beginning with Marīci, understanding his intention, gave him a name appropriate to that occasion.
Having learned the news from elsewhere simply by observing his face, Dakṣa and the other creators granted him a dwelling place and a wife.
Then, having deliberated upon names, the twice-born sages, headed by Marīci, spoke together to this man: "O my son!"

The sages said: "Since you have been born from us as a result of our agitation, just as [the fire was born] from the friction-stick (vidhi), therefore you shall become famous in the world by the name Manmatha."
In the worlds you can take any form at will, for indeed there is no one equal to you; therefore, O Mind-born One, become renowned by the name Kāma as well.
Because of your intoxication, you are born as Madana; because of your pride, you are Sadarpaka; therefore, you shall also become renowned in the world by the name Kandarpa.
Since there shall be no valor among all the gods equal to yours, therefore you shall possess all stations and be all-pervading.
This Dakṣa will himself give his beloved wife to you; for he is the primordial Lord of Creatures, a Supreme Person who acts according to his own will.
And this maiden of beautiful form, born from the mind of Brahmā, shall become renowned throughout all the worlds by the name Sandhyā.
Since this excellent woman was born perfectly while Brahmā was meditating, she is renowned as Sandhyā; her radiant luster is like that of a jasmine flower.
Brahmā said: Then Manobhava, taking up his five flower-arrows, remained there in disguise and reflected upon his resolve.
Gladdening, that which is called "delighting," deluding, drying up, and likewise killing—these are said to be the means of causing delusion even for a sage.
"O Creator, that eternal duty which has been prescribed for me by Brahmā, I shall perform it right here in the presence of the sages."
The sages dwell here, as does Prajāpati himself; they shall today serve as witnesses to my resolve.
Even though Sandhyā was created by Brahmā, she has now sent this message: "Having examined the ritual action here, I shall delude you through my application."
Brahmā said: Having thus reflected in his mind and reached a firm conclusion, the god born of the mind (Kāma) equipped the flower-born [god] with arrows made of flowers.
Then Kāma, the best of archers, assuming the ālīḍha stance and drawing his bow with great effort, formed it into a circle.
O best of sages, when he had fixed his bowstring, fragrant breezes blew there, perfectly providing great delight.
Then the Enchanter also deluded all those mind-born beings, beginning with Dhātṛ, individually with his sharp flower-arrows.
Then, O sage, all those sages as well as I were deluded; together with my mind, I experienced a certain transformation from the very beginning.
All of them gazed repeatedly at the twilight with amorous agitation, for their passion had increased, since a woman is the nourisher of love.
Then Madana, having deluded them all again and again, caused them to undergo transformations of their senses accordingly.
When the Creator, his senses aroused, beheld her as "I," at that very moment forty-nine states of being were born from his body.
Being gazed upon by them, she too, due to the falling of the arrows of Kandarpa, repeatedly manifested emotions such as side-long glances and bashful concealment.
The naturally beautiful twilight, creating those emotions born of the mind, shone intensely like the celestial river with its slender ripples.
Then, O Sage, seeing that the twilight was joined with existence, I, Prajāpati, whose body was filled with dharma, conceived a desire.
Then, O best of the twice-born, all those sages headed by Marīci and Atri, as well as Dakṣa and the others, reached the primordial creator, the Indriya.
Seeing me and Sandhyā thus engaged in her own ritual, Madana then inspired confidence in Dakṣa, Marīci, and the other sages.
"That which has been assigned as my duty by Brahmā can indeed be performed by me"—this was truly contemplated then by the Self-born One.
Having thus observed the sinful fate of his brothers as well as his father, Dharma then remembered Śambhu, the Lord who protects righteousness.
Recalling in his mind the Dharma and Śaṅkara, the protector of Dharma, the son of Aja, becoming distressed, praised him with various words.
Dharma said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Protector of Dharma, salutations be unto you! For you alone, O Śambhu, are the creator of creation, maintenance, and destruction.

O Lord, You are Brahmā in creation, Viṣṇu in maintenance, and the bearer of the form of Hara during dissolution; though devoid of attributes, You are characterized by the three qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas.

You are Śiva manifest, beyond the three qualities (guṇas), the fourth state (turya), and transcendent to primordial nature (prakṛti); you are devoid of attributes, changeless, and skilled in manifold divine plays.
Protect, protect me, O Mahādeva, from this evil that is so difficult to overcome; for this is my father, as well as these brothers of sinful intent.
