Brahmā said: Thus praised by Dharma himself, the supreme lord Maheśāna, who is self-born, quickly arrived there indeed to protect Dharma.
Having been born and ascended into the sky, Śambhu, seeing Brahmā in such a state, laughed at me, Dakṣa, and the others in his mind, and mocked them.
Having laughed repeatedly at all those words of praise, O best of sages, the bull-bannered god spoke these words, putting them to shame.
Śiva said: "O Brāhmaṇa, how has this state of desire arisen in you? To look upon one's own daughter is certainly not appropriate for those who follow the Vedas."
Just as one regards a mother, a sister, or a brother’s wife, so too should one regard a daughter; a wise person should never view these with a perverted vision.
This very certainty regarding the path of the Vedas resides in your mouth; O Creator, how is it that you have caused it to be forgotten by mere desire?
O Brahmā, O four-faced one, your mind was ever vigilant in steadfastness; how is it, O Creator, that it has been loosened to take pleasure in base desire?
Since he was a solitary yogi who beheld the sun at all times, how could Dakṣa, Marīci, and the others have their minds so lustful toward women?
How is it that even Kāma, dull-witted and ignorant of the proper time, has just now, out of sheer arrogance, afflicted me with his distorted arrows? He is truly small-minded.
Fie upon that learning which is always his whose charming wife, having drawn his mind away from fortitude, plunges it even into fickle desires!
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his regarding Śiva in this world, I was instantly doubled in shame and became drenched with sweat in an instant.
Then, O Sage, having restrained the agitation of my senses, I abandoned that desire even though I wished to seize her—that twilight who had assumed a form according to her will—out of fear of her.
O best of the twice-born, from my body sweat fell; from that sweat, the Agniṣvātta classes of ancestors were born. Thus arose the classes of ancestors.
All of them resembled crushed collyrium, with eyes like full-blown lotuses; they were supremely meritorious ascetics who had turned their backs on worldly existence.
O Sage, sixty-four thousand are proclaimed as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, and likewise eighty-six thousand are the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
Then, from the body of Dakṣa, sweat fell upon the ground, and from that was born an excellent woman endowed with every virtue.
She was slender-limbed with a symmetrical waist, renowned for her fine line of body hair; she possessed soft limbs and beautiful teeth, and shone with the luster of fresh gold.
Delightful in every limb, with a face like the full moon and a lotus, she was renowned by the name Rati, capable of enchanting even the sages.
Indeed, six [sages], headed by Marīci, had their sensory functions fully restrained, with the exception of Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, and Aṅgiras.
And the seed of the four beginning with Kratu fell upon the earth; from them, O best of sages, other groups of Pitṛs were born.
Those known by the names Somapās and Ājyapās, as well as others called Sukālins—all of them are proclaimed as the Haviṣmats and the Kavyavāhas.
The sons of Kratu were the Soma-pās; likewise, from Vasiṣṭha came the Kālins; those known as the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya, and the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras.
O best of Brahmins, when those classes of ancestors of the worlds, beginning with the Agniṣvātta, had been produced, Kavyavāha [appeared] on all sides.
Having become the mother of the ancestors (Pitṛs) as Sandhyā, she became intent upon that purpose; faultless, beheld by Śambhu, she was devoted to righteous deeds.
In the meantime, Śambhu, having bestowed his grace upon all the twice-born and having duly protected the Dharma, quickly vanished from sight.
Then, ashamed by the words of Śaṅkara, I, the Grandfather, became enraged at Kandarpa and knit my brows in a frown.
O Sage, having seen his face and understood his intention, Manmatha too, fearing the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), quickly withdrew his arrows.
Then, O sage, filled with anger, I, the lotus-born one, blazed forth with great power like a fire desiring to consume everything.
Having performed an exceedingly difficult deed against Mahādeva, Kandarpa, deluded by pride, shall be consumed by the fire from the eye of Bhava.
"Thus, O best of the twice-born, the Creator granted me this inexhaustible boon in the presence of the assembly of ancestors and the self-restrained sages."
Thus terrified upon hearing that most dreadful curse, the Lord of Rati abandoned his arrows at that moment and appeared visibly before her.
O Sage, with his pride humbled, he spoke these words to me, Brahmā, while the hosts of ancestors and Sandhyā were listening: "I am the son of Dakṣa and the others."
Kāma said: "O Brahmin, for what reason have I been cursed so harshly by you? I am innocent toward you, O Lord of the World, who follow the path of justice."
And you have said that my deed was done by me, O Brahmin; yet a curse is not appropriate for me in this matter, since nothing else was done by me.
"I am Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu; all of us are within the range of your vision"—this which was spoken by you has also been tested by me.
O Brahmin, there is no fault of mine here, for I am innocent; yet this curse, O Lord of the World, is a terrible decree of fate.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, I, Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds, replied to Madana, who was self-restrained, while repeatedly subduing him.
Brahmā said: "Since this Sandhyā is my own daughter, yet you have targeted me for this out of desire, I have therefore pronounced this curse."
Now, O Mind-born One, being both peaceful and wrathful, I speak to you: listen with your doubts dispelled, be at ease, and abandon fear.
O Madana, having been reduced to ashes by the fire from Bharga’s eye, you shall likewise quickly regain your body thereafter.
When Hara forcibly takes a wife, then he himself shall restore your body.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Madana, I, the Grandfather of the worlds, entered within while the lords of sages, my mind-born sons, were looking on.
Having heard these words of mine, all those sons of my mind, filled with passion, became joyful and quickly returned to their homes.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Curse and Grace of Kāma," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Viṣṇu’s disciple, O highly wise one, O Brahmā, O Lord, Creator of the world! This wonderful story you have told is filled with the nectar of Śiva’s divine play.
What happened after that, O dear one? Tell me that story now, for I am filled with faith to hear it, as it concerns the narrative of Śambhu.
Brahmā said: When Śambhu had gone to his own abode and I, the Creator, had vanished, Dakṣa then spoke to Kandarpa, recollecting those words of mine.
Dakṣa said: "O Kandarpa, this daughter of my body is endowed with excellent beauty and virtues; accept her as your wife, for she is equal to you in her qualities."
This woman of great splendor shall always be your companion; according to your desire, she will remain under your control in accordance with dharma.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, he placed her—who was born from the sweat of his body—before Kandarpa, and having given her the name "Rati," he bestowed her upon him.
O Nārada, having married that beautiful daughter of Dakṣa, who could enchant even the sages, Smara too rejoiced exceedingly.
Then, beholding his auspicious wife named Rati, Madana—his soul pierced by her excellence and enraptured by Rati—fell into a swoon.
The beloved Gaurī, with eyes like a deer's, became joyful at that moment; and his wife Lolāpāṅgī was likewise his equal in pleasure.
Beholding her pair of eyebrows, Madana conceived a doubt: "Has the Creator placed my bow here upon her for its destruction?"
O best of the twice-born, having observed the swift movement of her side-long glances, I no longer had faith in the swiftness or the beauty of my own weapons.
Having inhaled the scent of her naturally fragrant and steady breath, Madana abandoned his longing for the Malaya breeze.
Beholding her face, which resembled the full moon and was graced with auspicious marks, Madana could not discern the difference between it and the lunar orb.
Her two breasts, resembling golden lotus buds, shone with their pair of nipples as if encircled by bees.
Her breasts were firm, full, and elevated; between them hung a beautiful, slender garland reaching down to the surface of her navel, shining like the moon.
That bow of the Flower-Arrowed One, which was once crowded with swarms of bees, Kāma forgot upon seeing her; for, having cast that aside, he gazes only at her.
Within the depths of his deep navel-cavity, the skin on his four sides was well-knit; and upon his lotus-face, there were two eyes like a pair of slightly reddened fruits.
With her body of moderate proportions and a natural radiance like that of gold, she was indeed seen by Kāma as if she were a golden altar, so exceedingly beautiful was she.
Kāma gazed upon her lovely pair of thighs, which were as smooth and soft as pillars of plantain, enchanting and equal to his own power.
Her two feet, with their heels and the edges of the toes slightly reddened, seemed as if the God of Love had, through this, instilled passion into her friend.
Her pair of hands was red with nails resembling *kiṃśuka* flowers, and it was captivating with its rounded fingers that had slender tips.
That lovely pair of arms, as long as a pair of lotus stalks, was soft, smooth, and shone for a long time like lustrous gold and coral.
The captivating mass of hair, resembling a dark blue cloud, shone like the thick tail-fur of a yak-cow, O beloved of Smara.
With eyes wide open in wonder, he received that woman named Rati, born from the Snowy Mountain, just as Mahādeva received the Gaṅgā.
She has beautiful arms marked with wheels and lotuses and adorned with fragments of lotus stalks; she is graced by the rippling waves of the manifold playfulness of her two eyebrows.
She possesses a lofty torrent of side-glances, is endowed with the lotuses of her own eyes, has fine body-hairs like moss upon the water, and sports as a creeper upon the tree of the mind.
With a deep lake-like navel, slender, and beautiful in every limb, she was the abode of all loveliness, shining like the goddess Ramā herself.
Adorned with twelve ornaments and endowed with the sixteen amorous graces, she was the enchantress of all the worlds, illuminating the ten directions.
Having thus beheld Rati, Madana eagerly took her by the hand, just as Hṛṣīkeśa took the supreme Lakṣmī who had approached him out of passion.
Then Kāma, deluded by joy and forgetting the terrible curse bestowed by Brahmā, spoke to Dakṣa.
Then, O dear one, there was a great festival that increased happiness; Dakṣa was exceedingly pleased, and my daughter rejoiced.
Having attained supreme happiness and reached the end of all suffering, Kāma rejoiced; and Rati, the daughter of Dakṣa, having obtained Kāma, likewise exulted.
Smara, though divided, shone together with Cetayā through her charming speech, like a cloud at twilight accompanied by a beautiful flash of lightning.

Thus the Lord of Rati, overcome with passion, took that Rati upon his heart, just as one who perceives through yoga grasps a sacred lore; and Rati too, having obtained her supreme husband, shone like Kamalā beside Hari, her face resembling the full moon.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Kāma’s Marriage," in the second section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, that best of sages, with a delighted mind, remembered Śaṅkara and spoke joyfully.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, O disciple of Viṣṇu, O great-minded one! You have narrated the wonderful pastimes of the moon-crested Lord.
For when Madana had taken a wife and returned home delighted, and Dakṣa had likewise gone to his own home, so did you, O Creator.
And when the mind-born sons had departed for their respective abodes, where did that Sandhyā go—the daughter of Brahmā and the mother of the ancestors?
What did she do, and by which man was she married? Tell me all this, especially the life-story of Saṃdhyā.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of that wise one, Brahmā, the son of Brahmā and knower of reality, remembered Śaṅkara with devotion and spoke.
Brahmā said: Listen, O sage, to the entire auspicious life-story of Sandhyā; having heard it, O sage, all women shall always become virtuous wives.
Indeed, that Sandhyā was formerly my daughter, born of my mind; having performed austerities and cast off her body, she has been born as Arundhatī.
Having become the daughter of Medhātithi, that wise woman, the best of sages, observed her vows at the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna.
She chose the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, whose vows were praised, as her husband; she became the foremost of women devoted to their husbands, venerable, worshipful, and awe-inspiring.

Nārada said: How was penance performed by that Saṃdhyā, for what purpose, and where? How did she cast off her body and become the daughter of Medhātithi? And how was it ordained by the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—that she chose the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, whose vows are celebrated, as her husband?
O Grandfather, tell me in detail and according to the truth this account of Arundhatī’s life, for my curiosity is great as I listen to it.
Brahmā said: Having previously seen my own daughter Sandhyā, I quickly set my mind upon desire; she, however, abandoned me out of fear of Śiva.
The mind of Sandhyā wavered, agitated by the arrows of desire, even though it was restrained by the great-souled sages whose minds were fully controlled.
Having heard Bharga’s words, which were full of derision toward me and spoke of his own instability and lack of restraint toward the sages, [I was struck with wonder].
Seeing such a state of passion that repeatedly deluded the sage, Sandhyā herself became deeply distressed there at the thought of approaching him for marriage.
Then, O Sage, after Madana had been cursed by Brahmā and by me, and after I had vanished and Śiva had departed to his own abode;
O best of sages, having fallen under the sway of indignation and reflecting thus, my daughter Sandhyā then became absorbed in meditation.
Meditating for a moment upon her former history, the high-minded Sandhyā quickly reflected as was appropriate at that time.
Sandhyā said: "As soon as he saw me, a young woman, my father was stirred by passion and conceived a longing for me."
As the mental Munis of purified souls were watching, their minds became filled with desire the very moment they beheld me, who was beyond all restraint.
My mind, too, has been churned by the evil-souled Madana, by whom my heart was violently shaken upon seeing all these sages.
Madana himself has obtained the fruit of this sin, he whom the enraged Grandfather cursed in the presence of Śambhu.
May I, as one who has committed my own sin, obtain the fruit of this evil deed; I do not desire any swift means for its purification.
Since my father and brothers, having seen me directly and with desire, conceived a longing for me, therefore there is no doer of evil greater than I.
Even I felt a surge of passion upon seeing them all, though they were my own brothers, as if they were my husband at his own home, transgressing every limit of propriety.
I myself shall perform the expiation for this heinous sin; I will offer myself as an oblation into the fire in accordance with the path of the Vedas.
However, I shall establish a single boundary here on this earth, so that embodied beings do not become possessed of desire as soon as they are born.
For this purpose, having performed most severe austerity, I shall establish the bounds of conduct and thereafter renounce my life.
In this body for which my father himself conceived a longing, there is no longer any purpose for my brothers.
That body by which I manifested lustful desire toward my fathers and my siblings was not a means for accomplishing merit.
Having thus reflected in her mind, Sandhyā then went to the excellent mountain named Candrabhāga, from which the river Candrabhāgā flows.
Then, knowing that Sandhyā had gone to that excellent mountain to practice austerities with self-restraint, I, Brahmā, spoke to my son.
Vasiṣṭha, who was self-controlled, omniscient, a yogi of knowledge, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, was seated nearby.
Brahmā said: "O son Vasiṣṭha, go to the high-minded Sandhyā, who has conceived a desire for asceticism; initiate her according to the prescribed rite."
O best of sages, as soon as she saw you, me, and herself likewise filled with desire, shame came upon her in the past.
Having reflected upon her former death and that unprecedented deed, she now desires to sacrifice her own life as well as yours.
She will establish the bounds of propriety among those who have transgressed them through her ascetic power; that virtuous woman has gone to the mountain named Candrabhāga to perform penance.
O dear one, she does not acknowledge any fruit of her asceticism whatsoever; therefore, act in such a way that she attains her desired goal according to the instructions.
O Sage, having cast off this form and assumed another form of his own, he stood near her, demonstrating the practice of asceticism.
Having seen this true form of yours as it was before, she will not obtain anything at all here; therefore, assume another form.
Brahmā said: "O Nārada, thus was I commanded by the compassionate Vasiṣṭha; saying 'So be it' to me, the sage went to the presence of Sandhyā."
There Vasiṣṭha then beheld the lake of the gods, full of virtues and equal to Lake Mānasa, as well as the twilight prayer performed upon its shore.
Standing on the bank, she made that lotus-bright lake shine like the sky at twilight, with the rising moon and stars.
Then the sage, having seen her there in such a state of great distress, being full of curiosity, gazed upon that large lake known as Lohita.
From that rampart, the river Candrabhāgā was seen by him as it flows toward the southern ocean along the great mountain.
Having burst through the western bank of the Candrabhāgā river, that stream flows toward the ocean just as the Gaṅgā flows from the Himavat.
Then, on that mountain by the Candrabhāgā river, having seen the twilight upon the banks of the Bṛhatlohita, Vasiṣṭha questioned her with reverence.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O blessed lady, for what purpose have you come to this desolate mountain? Whose daughter are you, and what is it that you intend to do?"
I wish to hear this; tell me, provided it is not a secret. Or else, why is your face, which resembles the full moon, so motionless?
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and having beheld that great soul blazing like a fire, [he spoke].
Then, having respectfully prostrated before the ascetic who maintained his bodily vows, shone with the matted locks of a celibate, Sandhyā spoke to him.
Saṃdhyā said: O Lord, learn from me that purpose for which I have come to this mountain, or that which shall be accomplished for me merely by the sight of you.
"O Brahmin, I have come to this uninhabited mountain to practice austerities; I am the daughter of Brahmā, born and renowned by the name Sandhyā."
If it is appropriate for you to bear with me, please instruct me; this secret intention of mine is not known by anyone else.
Having resorted to this penance grove without understanding the true nature of asceticism, I am withered by anxiety; indeed, my mind trembles.
Brahmā said: Having heard her words, Vasiṣṭha, the best among the knowers of Brahman, who himself was acquainted with all that ought to be done, did not ask anything further.
Then, having mentally called to mind Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, he spoke to her, who was self-restrained and firm in her resolve through asceticism.
Vasiṣṭha said: "Śambhu, who is the supreme great splendor, who is the supreme great austerity, and who is the supreme one to be propitiated—he should be held in the mind."
Worship that one Supreme Person, the primordial source of the worlds, who alone is the primary cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
"Worship Śambhu, the Lord of Gods, with this mantra, O lady of auspicious countenance; by that, you shall attain everything—of this there is no doubt."
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkara"—with this ending in "Oṃ," he began his vow of silence and austerity; listen as I describe it to you.
Bathing should be performed in silence, and the worship of Hara should be performed in silence; during the first and sixth periods, one should subsist on full vessels of water for both.
In the third [period], at the sixth meal-time, one should be intent on fasting; or, upon the completion of the austerity, the ritual act may take place at the sixth meal-time.
Thus, O Goddess, this practice known as silence and austerity bestows the fruit of celibacy and grants all desired objects; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus, directing your mind toward this, meditate upon Śaṅkara at will; he, being pleased with you, will grant your desired object before long.
Brahmā said: Then Vasiṣṭha, having sat down for the twilight rite of austerity, addressed her according to the prescribed rule, and thereupon the sage vanished on the spot.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Sandhyā," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O best of sons, O one of great wisdom, listen to the great penance of the twilight (saṃdhyā-tapas), by hearing which the multitude of sins is certainly destroyed at that very moment.
When Vasiṣṭha had departed for his own home after sitting down in a state of ascetic fervor, Sandhyā too, perceiving that state of asceticism, attained great joy.
Then, having assumed such a dress as was appropriate for her joyful mind, she began to perform penance on the banks of the Bṛhallohita.
As it was said by Vasiṣṭha that mantra is the means for accomplishing austerity, he worshipped Śaṅkara with that mantra and with true devotion.
As she performed that very great penance with a one-pointed mind, her consciousness fixed upon Śambhu, one cycle of four yugas passed away.
Then Śambhu became pleased, gratified by that austerity; having manifested his own form both internally and externally, as well as in the sky.
Whatever form she was contemplating, he appeared before her in that very form.
Then, seeing the Lord Śaṅkara before her—tranquil and with a gracious countenance—she rejoiced exceedingly within her mind.
"Overcome with trepidation, I shall speak; what shall I say, or how shall I praise Hara?"—having become thus lost in thought, she closed her eyes.
Having entered the heart of her whose eyes were closed, Hara bestowed upon her divine knowledge, speech, and two divine eyes.
She attained divine knowledge, the divine eye, and divine speech; having beheld the Lord of Durgā directly before her eyes, she praised the Master of the worlds.

Saṃdhyā said: Salutations to You, the creator of the world, whose form is without shape, attainable through knowledge, supreme, neither gross nor subtle, nor high; whose form is contemplated within by yogis.

I bow to you, the gracious one, whose nature is all-pervading peace, stainless, changeless, accessible through wisdom, immutable in its self-luminosity, resembling the path of the sky, and beyond the path of darkness.

Salutations to You, whose form is the one, pure, and radiant; unborn, consisting of consciousness and bliss, innate, and immutable; eternally blissful, serene through the manifestation of truth, and the bestower of glory.

Salutations to You, whose form is thus: it is to be manifested through the mode of knowledge, it is the diverse inclination of sentient beings, it is the object of meditation as the nature of the self, the essence, the further shore, and the most purifying among all purifiers.

Salutations to You, who are united with Yoga, whose form is pure, beautiful, and pleasing, adorned with jewel ornaments and white as clear camphor, and who holds in Your hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident and a severed head.
Salutations to you, from whom the sky, the earth, the directions, as well as water and light, and furthermore time and all forms, have arisen.
Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, whose form is unmanifest, from whom both Pradhāna and Puruṣa have emerged as his body.
Salutations again and again to You, who as Brahmā performs creation, who as Viṣṇu performs preservation, and who as Rudra shall perform dissolution.

Salutations again and again to the cause of all causes, the bestower of divine nectar, knowledge, and sovereign power; to the giver of prosperity within all worlds, whose nature is light, who is higher than the highest.

To you, Śambhu, from whose foot the earth, the quarters, the sun, the moon, fire, and wind are said to have emerged, and from whose navel the heaven and the intermediate space arose—to you, may there be my salutation.
You are the supreme, you are the Supreme Self, you are various forms of knowledge, and O Hara, you are the existent Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, and one devoted to inquiry.
How shall I praise that Lord Hara, who has neither beginning, middle, nor end, from whom the universe arises, and who transcends the reach of speech and mind?
How can he be described by me, whose forms even the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is austerity do not fully comprehend?
O Lord, what can qualities be known of you who are devoid of qualities by me, a woman? Even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, do not know your true form.
Salutations to you, O Great Lord; salutations to you, O embodiment of darkness. Be gracious, O Śambhu, Lord of Gods; salutations be to you again and again.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of hers, the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, was highly pleased and offered her praise.
Then her body was covered with bark garments and deerskins, and she was veiled by masses of matted hair, while her head shone with sacred grass.
Then, beholding her face which resembled a lotus withered by a heavy frost, Hara, overcome with compassion, spoke this to her.
Maheśvara said: "I am truly pleased by your supreme austerity, O blessed lady, and by your hymn of praise, O woman of auspicious wisdom; choose now a boon."
Whatever purpose you have in mind regarding a boon in this matter, I shall fulfill it; may prosperity be yours, for I am pleased with your vows.
Brahmā said: Having heard this from Maheśa, whose mind was then pleased, Sandhyā, being herself very well-pleased, bowed down again and again and spoke.
Sandhyā said: "O Maheśvara, if a boon is to be granted out of affection, and if I am worthy of a boon, and if I have become purified from that sin."
"O Lord, if you are now pleased with my asceticism, then let this first boon chosen by me be granted."
O Lord of Gods, as soon as living beings are born in this realm of space, let them not be equal [in status]; rather, let them indeed arise with their respective desires fulfilled.
For as I am renowned throughout all the three worlds for my conduct, so shall I be none other; thus have I chosen this one boon.
My creation shall not fall anywhere except where my desire lies; O Lord, whoever becomes my husband shall indeed be my dearest friend.
The man who looks upon me with lustful desire will then have his virility destroyed, and he shall become impotent.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of hers, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke with a very gracious soul to her who had been declared sinless.
Maheśvara said: Listen, O Goddess Sandhyā; your sin has been reduced to ashes. I have cast away my anger toward you, and you have become pure through the performance of penance.
"O blessed lady, whatever has been chosen by you, all that has indeed been granted by me, O Sandhyā, through my great pleasure with your ascetic penance and by virtue of your boon."
The first is the state of infancy, the second is called childhood; the third is the state of youth, and likewise the fourth is old age.
But when the third stage of life has arrived for embodied beings, they shall possess desires; however, in some instances, it may end with the second stage.
By your ascetic power, I have established a boundary in the world, so that embodied beings do not become possessed by desire immediately upon birth.
And may you attain such a state of virtue in this world as shall not be found in any other woman throughout the three worlds.
Whoever looks upon you with lustful desire, except for your husband, shall immediately become impotent and fall into weakness.
Your husband, O highly fortunate lady, shall be endowed with the power of asceticism and, together with you, shall live until the end of seven kalpas.
Thus, those boons which were requested by you from me have been granted by me. Furthermore, I shall tell you something else that occurred in your previous birth.
The sacrifice of your body in the fire has already been promised by you; I shall tell you the means for that, so perform it without any doubt.
And that Medhātithi, O sage, was at a twelve-year sacrifice; while the fire blazed up completely, you should act without delay.
And here, at the foot of the mountain on the bank of the river Candrabhāgā, Medhātithi performs a great sacrifice in a hermitage of ascetics.
Having gone there yourself, you shall not be noticed by the sages; by my grace, born from fire, you will become his daughter.
Whatever husband you desire as your choice, keeping him within your own heart, cast your body into the fire.
When you performed severe penance on the mountain during the twilight period for the duration of four yugas, that Kṛta Yuga having passed away;
Born in the first part of the Tretā age as the daughters of Dakṣa, they were endowed with eloquence and virtuous conduct, and were married according to their suitability.

In their midst, he gave twenty-seven daughters as wives; yet the Moon, having abandoned the others, became enamored of Rohiṇī alone. For that reason, when the Moon was cursed by the enraged Dakṣa, all the gods assembled in your presence.
Those gods, together with Brahmā, were not seen by you during the twilight; however, with your mind fixed upon me, having beheld the sky, you shall obtain them again.
Then the Candranadi was born for the sake of liberating Candra from his curse; at that very moment, it was created by the Creator, and Medhatithi arrived there.
In ascetic power, there is no one equal to him—none has been before, nor shall there be in the future—by whom the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, a great ritual ordinance, was undertaken.
There, a blazing fire has been kindled; cast your own body into it. You are now most pure, and let your wager be fulfilled.

"O ascetic woman, this has been established by me for your sake; therefore, O illustrious one, go to the sacrifice of the great sage. And having delivered his message to the Lord of Gods, he vanished right there."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Sandhyā," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O sage, after Śambhu had vanished upon granting that boon, Sandhyā also went to that very place where the sage Medhātithi was.
There, by the grace of Śambhu, she was not noticed by anyone; she indeed remembered that ascetic student who had given her instruction for her penance.
O great sage, in former times, having assumed the form of a religious student (brahmacārī), she was instructed by Vasiṣṭha to perform penance at the command of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Then Sandhyā, having mentally appointed that very Brahmin student as her husband and as the instructor of her ascetic practice, [approached him].
While the great sacrifice was being performed with the fire kindled, she remained unobserved by the sages; yet, seen through the grace of Śambhu, that daughter of Vidhi entered [the fire].
At that moment, her body, composed of sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), was consumed; from it spread an imperceptible fragrance of the sacrificial cake.
But the Fire, having burned her body, once again caused her pure form to enter the solar orb by the command of Śambhu himself.
Then Sūrya, having divided that body into three parts upon his chariot, established his own hair there for the pleasure of the ancestors and the gods.
O Lord of Sages, the upper portion of that body became the morning twilight (prātassandhyā), which occurs at the beginning and middle of the day and night.
The remaining portion of that [day], situated between the end and the middle of the day and night, became the evening twilight (saṃdhyā), which always bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
When the dawn (aruṇodaya) occurs first before the rising of the sun, then the morning twilight (prātaḥsaṃdhyā) arises, which brings delight to the gods.
Then, when the sun, which is ever like a red lotus, has set, the evening twilight also arises, bringing joy to the ancestors.
O Śambhunātha, the compassionate one, by means of his own mind and divine body, he indeed endowed her vital breaths with embodied existence.
But when the conclusion of the sage’s sacrifice had arrived, that daughter was obtained by the sage from the midst of the fire, possessing the brilliant luster of molten gold.
Then the sage, filled with joy, took that daughter; O sage, having bathed her for the sake of the sacrifice, he placed her upon his own lap.
The great sage, surrounded by his disciples, gave her the name Arundhatī and experienced great joy there.
Since she obstructed the Dharma for some reason or other, she herself consequently acquired the name "Trilokaviditā" (Known Throughout the Three Worlds).

Having completed the sacrifice and attained a sense of fulfillment through the acquisition of his daughter, that sage, endowed with prosperity, remained constantly in his own hermitage together with his circle of disciples, O celestial seer, ever devoted to her alone as his beloved.
Then that goddess grew up in that excellent hermitage of the sage, on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river, in the place known as Tāpasāraṇya.
When her fifth year had arrived, that virtuous woman then purified even the forest of ascetics along the Candrabhāgā river by means of her virtues.
Indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara caused her marriage to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, with Arundhatī as the witness.
At that wedding, there was a great festival that increased their happiness; all the gods and sages attained supreme joy in their minds.
From the water emitted from the hands of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, seven rivers—beginning with the Śiprā—were produced, which are exceedingly purifying.
O sage, Arundhatī—the daughter of Medhātithi, a great virtuous woman and the most excellent among virtuous women—shone brightly after obtaining Vasiṣṭha as her husband.
O best of sages, having obtained that beloved Vasiṣṭha as her husband, she shone brightly, for from her were born excellent and auspicious sons such as Śakti and others.
Thus, O best of sages, the conduct of the twilight has been narrated to you; it is sacred, purifying, divine, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Whether it be a woman or a man of auspicious vows who hears this, they shall attain all their desires; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Dvisaptati-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, Nārada became delighted in mind and spoke to him.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, O disciple of Viṣṇu, O great-minded one! You are blessed, for you are a devotee of Śiva and a revealer of the supreme reality.
A divine and excellent discourse, which increases devotion to Śiva, was proclaimed concerning Arundhatī and her true nature in a future birth.
Now, O knower of dharma, tell us the supreme, purifying life-story of Śiva, which destroys the greatest of sins and bestows the highest auspiciousness.
When they had taken wives, when their desire was seen to have been satisfied, and when they had departed, what then happened as the twilight approached for her who had gone to perform penance?
Sūta said: Having heard these words of that sage of purified soul, Brahmā became exceedingly pleased and spoke these words.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Nārada, best of Brahmins, to that auspicious account endowed with the divine play (līlā) of Śiva; you are blessed, for you are a devotee of Śiva.
O dear one, as soon as I had previously vanished, I was utterly bewildered; afflicted by the poison of Śambhu’s words, I constantly brooded over them.
Having reflected for a long time in my mind, deluded by Śiva’s Māyā, I indeed felt envy toward Śiva; listen to that as I tell it to you.
Then I went to that place where Dakṣa and the others were staying; having seen Madana with his retinue, I was indeed somewhat overcome with passion.
O Nārada, having addressed Dakṣa with great affection, as well as my other sons, I—who was utterly deluded by Śiva’s māyā—spoke these words.
Brahmā said: O Dakṣa, O Marīci and other sons, listen to my words; having heard them, you must indeed devise a means for the removal of my suffering.
Seeing my mere longing for my beloved, Śambhu censured me, and that great yogi has repeatedly uttered words of reproach against you as well.
Tormented by that suffering, I find no peace anywhere; therefore, you must indeed exert effort so that he may take his beloved.
"May he accept my beloved so that I may be happy and free from suffering; yet, upon reflection, I consider my desire for that which is so difficult to attain to be supreme."
Seeing my mere longing for a beloved, Śambhu censured me; how then will he accept a wife in the presence of the sages?
What woman indeed in these three worlds could remain with her mind fixed on him, such that she would disregard the path of yoga and cause him delusion?
Even Manmatha will not be capable of deluding him; for he is an extreme yogi who cannot endure even the mention of women's names.
And how could there be a middle creation by Hara, the primordial one, if he had not grasped the arrow? For that [middle creation] was not prevented by his word.
On earth, there will be certain great asuras bound by Māyā; some will surely be bound by Hari, and others by the methods of Śambhu.
Since Śambhu is averse to saṃsāra and likewise possesses absolute dispassion, he will perform no other action besides this one; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus and having gazed intently at my sons, Dakṣa and the others, I then joyfully spoke there to Sarasvatī, Madana, and Anaṅga.

Brahmā said: O my son, O you who desire boons, you are the bestower of happiness in every way. O you who are affectionate toward your father, listen with great pleasure to my words along with your wife.
O Mind-born One, you shine with this companion; and she, united with you as her husband, shines exceedingly.
Just as Hṛṣīkeśa is with his wife, as she is with Hari, as the night is joined with the moon, and as the moon is joined with her; so too was he joined with her.
In that very way, the splendor and the marital union of you two have been placed before me; therefore, you shall become the banner of the world, the Banner of the Universe (Viśvaketu).
"O child, for the welfare of the world, you must delude the wielder of the Pināka bow, so that Śambhu, being well-disposed, may quickly take a wife."
In secluded and pleasant places, on mountains, and by lakes—wherever the Lord goes, there he is accompanied by her.
Delude Hara, who has restrained his self and turned away from women; for there exists no other deluder of him besides you.
O Mind-born One, when Hari becomes filled with passion, there will be an end to your curse; therefore, act for your own welfare.
If Maheśvara, filled with passion, desires that woman of noble form, then Bhava, being a worthy and noble one, will also deliver you.
Therefore, accompanied by your wife, strive to delude Hara; having deluded Maheśvara, become the banner of the universe.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, O Lord of the World, Manmatha then spoke the truth to me, the Lord of the worlds.
Manmatha said: "O Lord, at your command I shall effect the enchantment of Śambhu; however, the great weapon of women is mine—therefore, O Blessed One, create a beautiful woman for me."
O Śambhu, since she has been deluded by me, O Creator, you must now employ the supreme means to bring about her further delusion.
Brahmā said: While Kandarpa was speaking thus, I, the Creator, that Lord of Creatures, became filled with anxiety, wondering by what means he might be deluded.
From the sigh that issued forth from me as I was overcome with anxiety, Vasantasena was born, adorned with clusters of blossoms.
Resembling a red lotus, with eyes like blooming water-lilies, his face was like the full moon risen at twilight, and he possessed a beautiful nose.
With the whorls on his feet like the Śārṅga bow, with dark and curly hair, resembling the sun encircled by the rays of twilight, he was adorned with a pair of earrings.
He has the gait of an elephant in rut, with thick and long arms, elevated shoulders, a neck like a conch shell, a very broad chest, and a full, handsome face.
Beautiful in every limb, dark-complexioned, and complete with all auspicious marks, he was most handsome to behold, enchanting to all, and an increaser of desire.
When such a spring had arisen, the source of flowers, a most fragrant breeze blew and even the trees were in full bloom.
Cicadas with sweet voices sang the fifth note by the hundreds; the lakes became filled with blossoming lotuses and clear water-lilies.
Seeing him thus arisen in such a supreme state, Hiraṇyagarbha then spoke these sweet words, which were an antidote to Mada.
Brahmā said: Thus, he shall always be your companion, resembling Manmatha; O God, having acted for your favor, he will accomplish everything for you.
Just as the wind is the friend of fire and assists it everywhere, so shall this person be your friend and always follow you.
Because it is the cause of delighting the inhabitants [of the world], let this be called "Vasanta" (Spring); for its function is to follow after you and likewise to gladden the people.
May this springtime adornment, the Malaya breeze of spring, always be the disposition of your friend, remaining ever under your control.
May Viṣvoka and the others, as well as the hāvas and the sixty-four arts, bestow their affection upon Rati, so that they may become her friends just as they are yours.
O Kāma, together with these companions headed by Vasanta, exert yourself greatly along with Rati and delude Mahādeva.
"O father, having reflected well with my mind, I shall diligently cultivate that lovely woman who will enchant Hara."
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by me, the eldest of the gods, Kāma was filled with joy; together with his wife, he then bowed at my feet.
Having bowed to Dakṣa and saluted all those mind-born sons, Manmatha went to that place where Śambhu had gone.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Spring," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the Satī-caritra, within the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: When Manmatha had departed for the abode of Śiva along with his followers, a wondrous event occurred; listen to that, O Lord of Sages.
Having gone there, the great hero Manmatha, the cause of delusion, quickly extended his power and bewildered all living beings.
Even while under his control, Vasanta manifested his own power to enchant Hara; O Sage, all the trees blossomed simultaneously.
The mind-born god, together with Rati, made various efforts; all living beings fell under his sway, but Śiva, the Lord of the Gaṇas, did not.
O Sage, Madana’s efforts regarding my seat were fruitless; having turned back, he then departed from my presence, his pride subdued.
O Sage, having offered salutations to me with a faltering voice, Madana, free from intoxication and remaining composed, spoke to me.
Kāma said: "O Brahmin, Śambhu is not to be deluded, for he is devoted to yoga; neither I nor anyone else has the power to delude that Śambhu."
"O Brahman, O Śiva, various means were employed by me together with my friend Rati, yet they all proved fruitless."
Listen, O Brahman, as I, a sage, relate to you those various efforts we made, O dear one, to delude Hara.
When Śambhu remained restrained, established in meditative absorption (samādhi), then by a fragrant, cool, and exceedingly swift wind—
I constantly terrified Rudra, the great three-eyed deity established in meditative absorption, with my efforts using that which causes delusion.
Likewise, taking up my bow and five arrows, I wandered about him, bewildering his attendants.
By my mere entrance, all living beings became completely submissive; yet the Lord Śaṅkara, along with his attendants, did not become agitated at all.
When that lord of the Pramathas had gone to the slopes of the Himalayas, I too arrived there at that very moment, accompanied by Rati and Madhu, O Creator.
When Rudra went to Meru, or when he went to Nāgakeśara, or when he went to Kailāsa, I went there at that time.
Once, when Hara stood having abandoned his meditative absorption, I then fashioned a pair of wheels before him.
And that pair of eyebrows, O Brahmin, repeatedly displaying gestures of amorous allure, manifested various emotions in the most excellent manner of a married couple.
Standing before Mahādeva, the blue-throated one, along with his attendants, the deer and birds likewise assumed a state of infatuation.
There, a pair of peacocks assumed a state of longing for the aesthetic flavor (rasa), adopting various movements by his side as well as in front of him.
"My arrow never found an opening in him at any time; I speak the truth, O Lord of the World: I have no power to delude him."
O illustrious one, listen to that which Madhu performed to delude him—a deed worthy of his nature; I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.
Campakas, kesaras, bālas, kāraṇas, as well as pāṭalas, nāgakesaras, punnāgas, kiṃśukas, ketakās, and karas.
Wherever Hara indeed resides, there he causes the māgadhī, mallikā, parṇabharā, and kuravaka flowers to blossom.
Fanning the lakes filled with blossoming lotuses with the breezes from Mount Malaya, he diligently made them exceedingly fragrant within the hermitage of Giriśa.
All the *sumanas* creepers bore clusters of sprouts, and there they entwined themselves around the trees with a long-standing affection.
Seeing those trees with their abundance of beautiful flowers and those fragrant breezes, even the sages fell under the sway of desire; how much more so others?
Even though this was so, Śambhu did not perceive the cause of my delusion; Śaṅkara felt only a sense of affection toward me and did not become angry.
Having thus seen all this and understood his disposition, I have turned away from Śambhu out of delusion; I tell you this for certain.
Once he has abandoned his meditative absorption, we shall not be able to remain within the range of his vision for even a moment; who could possibly delude that Rudra?
O Brahmin, seeing him with eyes like blazing fire, his matted locks formidable as a mass of flames, and possessing horns—who would be able to stand before him?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Bhava in this manner, I, the four-faced one, though desiring to speak, did not say anything; instead, I became overcome with anxiety at that time.
O Sage, having heard the words, "Manobhava is not capable of deluding Hara," I sighed deeply out of great sorrow.
Indeed, from the winds of my breath were born various forms of great power; they moved with flickering tongues, restless and exceedingly terrifying.
They all played countless varieties of musical instruments—those various drums and other instruments that were formidable and produced great sounds.
Then those great hosts, born from my breath, stood before me, Brahmā, and cried out, "Kill! Cut!"
While they were saying there, "Kill him! Cut him! Kāma, hearing those words, began to speak to Vidhi.
Then, O Brahmin, having addressed the Sage and beheld those hosts, Smara, the god of love, spoke while restraining the Gaṇas in their presence.
Kāma said: "O Brahman, O Lord of Creatures, O Initiator of all creation, who are these heroes that have arisen—so formidable and terrifying?"
O Creator, what work will these perform, or where will they abide? What are their names? Tell me that, and appoint them accordingly.
Having appointed them to my own task and granted them their station and name, O Lord of Gods, show me your appropriate grace and command me.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard those words, I, the creator of the worlds, spoke to Madana, instructing him on their past deeds and so forth.
Brahmā said: "As soon as these were born, they spoke these words: 'Kill! Because they said this again and again, let their name be 'Mārī' (the slayer)."
O Kāma, these hosts will always create obstacles for those beings who are devoted to various sensual pleasures, unless they perform their own worship.
O Mind-born One, in following you, these [senses] will undoubtedly always be your primary instruments and your companions; of this there is no doubt.
Whenever and wherever you go for the sake of your own duty, they shall go there at those very times to assist you.
They will cause mental confusion even for those who abide under the power of your weapons, and they will obstruct the path of knowledge for the wise in every way.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having heard these words of mine, he who was accompanied by Rati and his great followers became somewhat cheerful of countenance.
Having heard this, all those hosts as well surrounded Madana and me on all sides and remained there in their own forms, according to their desire.
Then Brahmā, out of affection, said to Smara: "Carry out my command; go together with these very ones once again to delude Hara."
Therefore, O Yava, apply your mind and act together with the hosts of Māra so that delusion may arise in Śambhu for the purpose of taking a wife.
Having heard these words, Kāma spoke again: "O divine sage, out of respect for me, bow down with humility."
Kāma said: "I have performed my task of deluding him with great effort; yet, O dear one, that delusion did not occur, nor will it occur, nor does it exist now."
Honoring the weight of your words and having beheld even the hosts of Māra, I shall go back there once more with my wife at your command.
The mind has indeed reached this certainty: "That delusion shall no longer exist. O Creator, I have this apprehension: "He might reduce my body to ashes."
Having spoken thus, O lord of sages, Kāma, together with Rati and filled with fear, then departed for the abode of Śiva along with his hosts of Māra-demons.
Then the Mind-born God (Kāma) exerted his power as before; for Madana, employing many means, brought forth various schemes.
He employed such a stratagem there that even the hosts of Māra were deluded; yet not even a trace of delusion arose in Śambhu, the Supreme Self.
Having returned after turning back, you then remembered my place; at that time, the host of Māra was devoid of pride and joy, standing before me as well.
Then Kāma, devoid of pride and free from all festive joy, bowed down to me and spoke, O dear one, standing before me along with Māra and Madhu.
O Creator, although an act was performed to delude him that was even more powerful than before, not even the slightest delusion arose in him whose soul was devoted to meditation.
My body was not even consumed there by that compassionate one; the cause was my former merit, for that Lord is indeed free from all change.
O Lotus-born One, if Hara should choose you as his wife, then employ a stratagem so that he becomes free from pride; this is my opinion.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Kāma, together with his retinue, departed for his own hermitage, bowing to me while remembering Śambhu—the bestower of pride and the protector of the distressed.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arising of the Gaṇas and the Power of Kāma," in the Satī-section of the Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, you are blessed, for your mind is devoted to Śiva; you have related this excellent life-story of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Soul.
Now tell me his story: when Kāma had returned to his own hermitage along with his attendants and Rati, what happened then, and what did you do?
Brahmā said: Listen with great affection, O Nārada, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, by the mere hearing of which a man becomes free from all mental transformations.
When Kāma had returned to his own hermitage accompanied by his retinue, learn from me what then occurred and what transpired.
O Nārada, my pride was destroyed and wonder arose in my heart; for me, a sage devoid of joy, my own desire remained unfulfilled.
How could he, who was free from sorrow, who held his mind steady in many ways, who was changeless, self-conquered, and devoted to yoga—that Śaṅkara—ever take a woman?
Having reflected thus in many ways, O Sage, I was then freed from intoxication; with my mind fixed on Śiva, I remembered Hari, who bestows his own body [upon his devotees], with devotion.
And I offered praise with auspicious hymns accompanied by words of supplication; having heard that, the Blessed One quickly became manifest before me in the past.
Four-armed, with eyes like lotuses, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, clad in shimmering yellow garments, Hari has a dark-complexioned body and is dear to his devotees.
Having beheld him, such a worthy refuge, I praised him again and again with love, my voice faltering with tears.
Having heard that hymn, Hari, the remover of the suffering of his devotees, became well-pleased and spoke to me as I had sought refuge in Brahmā.
Hari said: "O Creator, O Brahmā, O highly wise one, you are blessed, O maker of the worlds! For what purpose have you remembered me today, and why is this hymn of praise being performed?"
"What great suffering has arisen for you? Tell me that now before me; I shall pacify it all—there is no need for hesitation here."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, his face slightly uplifted with breath, he bowed to Viṣṇu with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Lord of Ramā, O bestower of honor, hear my message; having heard it, show compassion and remove this sorrow, O Kamāvaha.
O Viṣṇu, for the purpose of deluding Rudra, I dispatched Kāma along with his retinue, together with Spring and his kinsman Madhu.
They employed various means, but they were all fruitless; that yogi, who perceives all things with equanimity, fell into a state of bewilderment.
Having heard these words of mine, Hari, who is the knower of all that is to be known and an expert in the true nature of Śiva, spoke to me in amazement.
Viṣṇu said: "O Grandfather, for what reason has this thought arisen in you? O Brahmā, having reflected upon everything with your wise intellect, tell me the truth."
Brahmā said: Listen, my son, to that account of your deluding Māyā; the entire world is subject to it, being intent upon pleasure, pain, and the like.
O Lord of Gods, listen as I speak at your command: by whomsoever I was sent forth, I became intent upon committing a sin; hear that from me.
At the time of the commencement of creation, ten sons were indeed born, Dakṣa and the others; and there was also one daughter, Vāk, who was exceedingly beautiful.
From my chest Dharma was born, from my mind Kāma, and from my body another; yet, O Hara, upon seeing that daughter there, delusion arose within me.
Deluded by your māyā, I beheld her through false vision; at that very moment, Hara arrived and censured me as well as my sons.
He uttered a cry of reproach toward all, considering his own master to be another's lord—a man who was wise, a yogi, a lordly enjoyer, and one who had conquered his senses.
"O Hari, having become my son, you have reviled me even in my presence; indeed, this is a great sorrow for me, which I have spoken in your presence."
If he were to take a wife, I would be happy, my mind freed from sorrow; for this purpose, O Keśava, I have come to you for refuge.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, O Brahmā, Madhusūdana laughed and quickly spoke to me, gladdening the creator of existence.
Viṣṇu said: O Creator, listen indeed to my words, which dispel all delusion and are in accordance with the ultimate truth as accepted by all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures.
O Creator, how is it that you have today become so utterly deluded in mind? For even you, the speaker of the Vedas and the maker of all the worlds, have indeed become evil-minded.
Abandon your dullness, O dull-witted one; do not harbor such a thought. What do all the Vedas proclaim? Remember that with a virtuous mind.
O evil-minded one, you recognize Rudra as your own son, the Supreme Lord; yet though you are a reciter of the Vedas, O Brahmā, all your realized knowledge has been forgotten.
Indeed, considering Śaṅkara to be like an ordinary god, you have committed an act of hostility; today your good intellect has vanished, and likewise, a wicked mind has arisen.
Listen to the declared conclusion of reality; bring forth right understanding. Having determined that which is truly proclaimed by the Vedas, it brings about liberation from worldly existence.
Śiva is indeed the creator of all, the sustainer, and the destroyer; he is higher than the highest, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, devoid of qualities, and eternally existent.
The Supreme Self is indefinable, changeless, non-dual, and infallible; it is the infinite Lord, the end-maker, all-pervading, and the Supreme Sovereign.

The all-pervading creator of creation, maintenance, and destruction, who partakes in the three qualities (guṇas) and is characterized by rajas, sattva, and tamas, is known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Distinct from illusion yet devoid of effort, he is both illusory and skilled in illusion; though possessed of attributes, he is independent, self-blissful, and free from conceptual construction.
For Ātmarāma is free from the pairs of opposites, dependent on his devotees, and possessed of an excellent form; he is a yogi ever devoted to yoga and the one who reveals the path of yoga.
He who removes pride, the Lord of the World, always compassionate toward the distressed—how can you consider such a Master as your own son?
Abandon such false knowledge and truly take refuge in Him; worship Śambhu with your whole being, for when He is satisfied, He will bestow well-being.
If you have such a deliberation in your heart, O Brahmin, Śaṅkara may accept a wife; therefore, perform severe penance directed toward Śivā while remembering Śiva.
Perform meditation for the sake of Śiva, keeping that desire in your heart; if the Goddess of gods is pleased, she will accomplish every task.
If the virtuous Śivā were to take an incarnation as a human woman in this world, she would certainly become the wife of someone's son.
O Brahman, command Dakṣa to perform austerities with great effort, so that he may, out of devotion to Śiva's purpose, produce her as a wife for him.

O dear one, those two—Śiva and Aśiva—are dependent upon their devotees and are easily discerned; by their own will, they have become possessed of attributes (saguṇa), though their true nature is that of the Supreme Brahman.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, at that very moment Maheśa remembered his own lord Śiva; and having attained knowledge through his grace, he then spoke to me.
Viṣṇu said: O Creator, remember the words previously spoken by Śaṅkara when he was entreated by us two as we were about to be born by his will.
All of that has been forgotten by you; blessed is she who is the supreme Śāmbhavī, by whom everything is deluded—she who is difficult to comprehend except for Śiva.
For when Śiva, who is by nature devoid of attributes, assumes attributes by his own will, he first brings me into being and then you, and thereby performs his divine sport through his own power.
O Brahmin, at that time the Lord Śambhu instructed you in the work of creation, and the imperishable Soma, the progenitor, entrusted me with its preservation.
Then, having arrived at your abode with palms joined in reverence and heads bowed low, we said: "May you also, O Lord of All, become an incarnation, assuming qualities and form."
Thus addressed, the Lord, who is skilled in various divine sports, looked toward the heavens with great affection and, filled with compassion, spoke while smiling.
O Viṣṇu, my supreme form, which is indeed like this, shall manifest in the world from the body of Brahmā, renowned by the name Rudra.

May he who is my perfect form, who is always worthy of worship, who fulfills all desires, who is the agent of dissolution, the presiding lord of the qualities, the undifferentiated, and the bestower of excellent yoga—[grant me your grace].
Even the three gods shall take on my form, especially Hara; and the forms of Umā shall likewise become threefold, O sons.
The wife of Hari shall be named Lakṣmī; Sarasvatī shall be the wife of Brahmā; and the virtuous Satī shall become the wife of Rudra in her perfect form.
Viṣṇu said: Having spoken thus, Maheśvara, having shown his grace, vanished; we both became happy, each intent upon our respective duties.
O Brahmin, when the time had arrived, Śaṅkara himself, who dwells on Kailāsa, descended under the name Rudra, accompanied by his consort.
O Lord of Creatures, she who has descended shall be auspicious and named Satī; indeed, an effort must certainly be made for the sake of her birth.
Having spoken thus and shown supreme compassion, Viṣṇu vanished; and he, his envy gone, then attained even greater joy.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Brahmā and Viṣṇu," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second part (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahman, dear father, O one of great wisdom, best among speakers, tell us: when Viṣṇu had departed, what happened? And what did you do, O Creator?
Brahmā said: O best among the delights of the Brahmins, listen attentively to what I indeed did when the Lord Viṣṇu had departed.
I ever praise the Goddess Durgā, the beloved of Śambhu, the sustainer of the world, who consists of both knowledge and ignorance, who is pure, and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
I bow to her who pervades all, who is eternal, supportless, and undisturbed; the mother of the three gods, who is coarser than the coarsest, yet formless.
You are consciousness, supreme bliss, and the very nature of the Supreme Self; be gracious, O Goddess of gods, accomplish my task; salutations to you.
Brahmā said: O sage, O celestial rishi, while she was being thus praised by me, that Yoganidrā, my Caṇḍikā, manifested herself visibly before me.
Possessing the luster of smooth collyrium, beautiful in form, divine and four-armed, she sits upon a lion, her hand in the gesture of granting boons, with hair adorned by pearls and gems.
Her face is like the autumnal moon, her forehead bears a radiant crescent moon, and she possesses three eyes; she is beautiful in every limb, with the luster of lotus-petal nails upon her feet.
O Sage, having beheld that Umā, the very power of Śiva, right before his eyes, he—whose lofty limbs were bowed with devotion—indeed offered praise after prostrating himself well.

Brahmā said: Salutations, salutations to you, who are the form of both worldly engagement and withdrawal, and the form of maintenance and creation; you are the eternal, supreme power of all moving and non-moving beings, the enchantress of all.

You are that Śrī who is always a garland upon the form of Keśava; you are the Earth who sustains the entire universe; you are she who was formerly the Great Goddess who creates, and you are the supreme one beyond the qualities (guṇas) who destroys the three worlds.

You are indeed that which is honored by yogins, delightful to the mind; you are not within the essence of atoms. You are that which is realized in the hearts of yogins purified by the restraints (yamas) and so forth, and that which is known on the path of meditation of yogins.

Endowed with luminosity, purity, and other qualities, free from passion, you are indeed that Vidyā who rests upon various supports; bearing within yourself the immutable, unmanifest, and infinite-formed Time, you sustain the worlds.
O Śivā, you surely sow the seed of transformation eternally among all people, endowed with the qualities; you are indeed the primary source of the three qualities, and therefore you are beyond them.

You are the primordial essence (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas); you are that which exists as the substratum, free from these modifications. As such, you create, consume, and protect the world—the sole cause of the universe—by initiating it within the Supreme Brahman.

O Consort of Śiva, salutations to you, who are the seed of all worlds without exception, whose nature consists of both the object of knowledge and the means of knowing, and who are ever intent on the welfare of the world.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, that Kālī, the illuminator of the worlds, spoke with affection to me, the creator of the worlds, as one would address a person.
The Goddess said: "O Brahmin, understand for what purpose I have been praised by you; if you dare, let it be told quickly before me."
Even though [the obstacle] has arisen, the accomplishment of the task is certain; therefore, state your desire, for I, being devoted, shall fulfill it.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Goddess Maheśānī, having bestowed your grace upon me; O Omniscient One, by your command I shall declare that which resides within my heart's desire.
O Goddess of gods, he who was formerly your husband, born from my forehead, is that yogi known as Śiva-Rudra, who has indeed taken up residence on Kailāsa.
The Lord of Beings practices austerity alone, free from conceptual construction; being without a wife and devoid of transformation, he does not desire a second.
Delude him so that he may look upon another woman as his second, for apart from you, no one else shall be pleasing to his mind.
Therefore, you yourself become the enchantress of Hara through your form; having become the daughter of Dakṣa, O Śivā, become the wife of Rudra.
Just as you, assuming a physical form in the likeness of Lakṣmī, gladden Keśava for the welfare of the world, so do you act now.
Having seen my mere longing for a beloved, the bull-bannered god censured me; how then will he take a wife for himself by his own will?
O Hari, while the beloved has been taken away, how can there be an auspicious creation when He—the cause of this world—is indifferent in its beginning, middle, and end?
Thus lost in thought, I have no other benefactor for refuge but you; therefore, for my sake and for the welfare of the world, perform this for me while I am in distress.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Lakṣmī, nor the god of love, nor even I, O Mother of the World, nor anyone else indeed, can delude him except for you.
Therefore, having become the daughter of Dakṣa, you, the Great Goddess of divine form, become his wife; through devotion to me, delude the Lord, the Yogi.
O Goddess of the gods, Dakṣa, firm in his vows, having fixed his mind upon you, performs penance on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, directed toward you.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, Śivā then fell into reflection; and the Mother of the Universe, filled with wonder, spoke thus within her own mind.
The Goddess said: "Aha! What a great marvel it is that even the Creator of the Universe, the expounder of the Vedas, having become intent upon supreme knowledge—what is this Vidhātṛ saying?"
A great delusion, bringing misery, has arisen in the mind of Vidhi, since he desires to delude Him who is changeless and supreme.
This is the way of fate: it desires the best for one who is intoxicated with passion. What gain is there in this? For He is the Sovereign, free from delusion and beyond conceptual construction.
I am forever the servant of that Śambhu, who is known as the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and free from transformation; I am always subject to his command.
That very Śiva, the independent Supreme Lord, became known by the name Rudra in his full form for the sake of uplifting his devotees.
He is the lord of both Hari and Vidhi, and he is never inferior to Śiva; for he is devoted to yoga, free from illusion, the master of Māyā, and higher than the highest.
Considering that son of his to be like an ordinary god, Brahmā—deluded by ignorance—desires to delude him.
"If I do not grant the boon, the path of the Vedas would be violated; what then could I do so that the omnipresent Maheśvara would not be angry with me?"
Brahmā spoke: Having reflected thus, Śivā remembered that Maheśa with her mind; she then obtained the permission of Śiva and said to me, "O Durgā, [come] to me then."
Durgā said: "O Brahman, everything that has been spoken by you is indeed entirely true; there exists no one here other than me who can delude Śaṅkara."
"O Hari, it has been truly established by you that this eternal creation will not continue if you do not take a wife."
O Great Lord, since no means for deluding me exists for this [being], my effort today has become intense and redoubled because of your words.
O Creator, I shall strive in such a way that Hara, utterly deluded, will himself take a wife.
"Assuming the form of Satī, I shall become subject to his very will, O highly fortunate one, just as Lakṣmī is the beloved of Viṣṇu."
O Creator, out of compassion for him alone, I shall make such an effort that he too may always remain under my control.
"O Grandfather, having been born from the wife of Dakṣa in the form of Satī, I shall honor Śaṅkara through my divine play."
Just as another creature on earth remains under the control of a woman, so shall Hara come under the control of a woman through devotion to me.
Brahmā said: Having thus addressed me, O dear one, that Śivā, the Mother of the World, vanished right there while I was looking on.
When she had vanished, I, the Grandfather of the worlds, went to where my daughters were and described everything to them.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Durgā’s Praise and the Attainment of Brahmā’s Boon," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Purāṇa.

Nārada said: O Brahmin, O wise one, O sinless one who has received the boon of Śambhu, you have spoken perfectly; the account of the conduct of Śiva and Śivā has purified my birth and is for my benefit.
Now tell me: what boon did Dakṣa, firm in his vows, obtain after performing penance for the sake of the Goddess? And how did she become the daughter of Dakṣa?
Brahmā said: Listen, O Nārada; you are blessed by all the sages for your devotion. Hear how Dakṣa, firm in his vows, performed penance and obtained a boon.
Having received my command, the wise and capable great lord, desiring that goddess, the Mother of the World, composed himself and set out to worship her.
Having placed her, who dwells upon the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, within his heart, he began to perform austerities in order to behold Ambikā directly before his eyes.
For three thousand divine years, Dakṣa, self-restrained, with a controlled mind and firm in his vows, performed austerities.
Subsisting on air, fasting entirely, consuming only water, and eating only leaves, she passed that time meditating upon her who consists of the universe.
Devoted to difficult meditation and intent on austerity for a long time, he of firm vows propitiates the Goddess with many observances.
Then, O best of sages, as Dakṣa, who was disciplined by the restraints of yoga, worshipped the Mother of the World, Śivā appeared before his very eyes.
Then, having seen the Mother of the World, who is identical with the universe, directly before his eyes, Dakṣa, the lord of creatures, considered himself to have accomplished all that was to be done.

One should meditate upon Kālikā, who is seated upon a lion, dark-complexioned, with a beautiful face and four arms; she is enchanting, with her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a blue lotus and a sword.
Having prostrated before her, he praised the world-mother Suprabhā—with her reddened eyes and beautiful loose locks of hair—using various wonderful words.
Dakṣa said: O Great Illusion, O Sovereign of the World, O Great Goddess! Having shown me Your own form out of compassion, salutations be unto You.
Be gracious, O Primordial Goddess; be gracious, O You who are the form of Śiva. Be gracious, O Bestower of boons upon devotees, O Illusion of the World; salutations be unto You!
Brahmā said: Thus praised by Dakṣa, whose soul was disciplined, the Great Goddess spoke to Dakṣa, O Sage, even though she herself already knew his desire.
The Goddess said: "O Dakṣa, I am indeed greatly pleased by this excellent devotion of yours. Choose a boon that you desire; there is nothing that cannot be granted to you."
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the Mother of the World, Dakṣa, the progenitor of creatures, became exceedingly joyful and spoke, repeatedly addressing that auspicious goddess by her name.
Dakṣa said: O Mother of the Universe, O Great Illusion, if you are a granter of boons to me, listen to my words with great affection and fulfill my desire.
My lord Śiva, who was indeed born from Brahmā after being praised by him, is named Rudra; he is a complete incarnation of the Supreme Self.
Your incarnation has occurred for us; therefore, O Śivā, having descended to the earth, delude that Maheśāna and tell us who his wife shall be.
Other than you, no one else has ever been able to delude him; therefore, having become my daughter, you have now become the wife of Hara.
"Acting thus, O Sulīlā, become a deluder of Hara; this is my boon alone, O Goddess, which I have spoken truthfully before you."
Thinking "this is for my own sake alone," I was indeed impelled by Brahmā, even though it concerns all the worlds, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Lord of Creatures, the Mother of the Universe smiled and replied, having remembered Śiva in her mind.
The Goddess said: "O dear Prajāpati Dakṣa, listen to my supreme word. Out of devotion to you, I speak the truth; I am well-pleased and the bestower of all things."
"O Dakṣa, I am your daughter; I shall become your wife, Maheśvarī, subject to your devotion—of this there is no doubt."
O sinless one, having performed most difficult austerities and obtained that boon, I shall make such an effort so that I will become the wife of Hara.
For the accomplishment of the task cannot be achieved otherwise, and that Lord is changeless; Sadāśiva alone is eternally perfect and worthy of being served by both Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
"I am always his beloved servant, birth after birth; he indeed is my lord, Śambhu, who assumes various forms."
By the power of his boon, I descended from the forehead of Brahmā; by his command, I too shall descend here through the force of that same boon.
"Go to your own abode, dear one; I have recognized the messenger. I shall become the wife of Hara, and soon I will be born as your daughter."
Having spoken these virtuous words to Dakṣa and having taken Śiva’s command to heart, that goddess spoke again, recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
But nevertheless, O Prajāpati, I shall tell you that substratum with my mind; know it to be the truth from me, not a falsehood.
O ascetic, when you become indifferent toward me once again, I shall truly cast off my own body; otherwise, I shall remain within my own self.
"O Prajāpati, this boon is granted to you: in every cycle of creation, having become your daughter, I shall become the beloved of Hara."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Dakṣa, the chief progenitor, the Great Goddess vanished instantly right there while Dakṣa was looking on.
When Durgā had vanished, Dakṣa also returned to his own hermitage and attained great joy, thinking, "She shall become my daughter."
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Dakṣa Receiving the Boon," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, Vidhi, O one of great wisdom, best among speakers, tell us: after Dakṣa had departed for his home with affection, what happened immediately thereafter?
Brahmā said: Having gone to his own hermitage with a joyful mind, Dakṣa Prajāpati, by my command, performed a manifold mental creation.
Beholding that unincreased creation of beings, the progenitor Dakṣa reported it to my father, Brahmā.
Dakṣa said: "O Brahmā, dear father, Lord of Creatures, the subjects do not increase, O Master; indeed, all those created by me remain exactly as they were."
"What shall I do, O Lord of Creatures, so that they may increase by themselves? Tell me the means for that; I shall create progeny, of this there is no doubt."
Brahmā said: O Dakṣa Prajāpati, my dear son, listen to my supreme word; act upon it, O best of gods, and Śiva will bring you well-being.
O Lord of Creatures, please accept as your wife Asiknī by name, the lovely daughter of Prajāpati Pañcajana.
Having the quality of alternating with the left, you shall again bring forth this creation of beings, and you shall produce them in great numbers through a beloved woman of that same nature.
Brahmā said: Then, in order to produce offspring through the law of sexual union, he married the daughter of Vīraṇa at my command.
Then, upon his own wife Vīriṇī, that Prajāpati Dakṣa begot ten thousand sons known as the Haryaśvas.
O Sage, all those sons were of uniform conduct and character; they were constantly devoted to their father and dedicated to the path of the Vedas.
O dear one, all the sons of Dakṣa, as instructed by their father, went toward the western direction for the purpose of performing austerities.
There lies the Nārāyaṇa lake, a most purifying holy site, where the confluence of the celestial river and the ocean occurs.
By the mere touch of that [water], they became possessed of awakened intellects regarding the Dharma and the state of the Paramahamsas, their inner dispositions cleansed of all impurities.
For the sake of increasing progeny, those best of beings, the sons of Dakṣa, firm in soul and strictly restrained by their father’s command, performed austerities there.
And you, O Nārada, having learned that they were performing austerities for the sake of creation, went there, perceiving the profound intention of the Lord of the Earth.
"Without seeing him, how can you be prepared to perform the creation of the earth? Thus you spoke with reverence to Haryaśva, the son of Dakṣa.
Brahmā said: Having heard that which was spoken by you, those Haryaśvas, all of them possessing innate intelligence, then reflected deeply upon it themselves with unwearied minds.
How could one who does not know the instruction of the Great Teacher (Śāstrajanaka), which brings about cessation, venture to undertake creation while placing his trust in the [three] qualities?
