Having thus resolved, those sons, wise and of one mind, bowed to him, circumambulated him, and set out upon the path from which there is no turning back.
O Sage Nārada, you wander through other worlds by the mind of Śambhu; at that time, being free from modification, you were the one who directed the mental activity of Maheśāna.
When a great deal of time had passed, my son Prajāpati, having heard from Nārada about the destruction of his sons, was consumed by grief.
Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, Dakṣa lamented many times, repeatedly saying, "O you who have given birth to such a son! This state of being a father is the very seat of sorrows."
Having arrived with great affection, I consoled my son Dakṣa, demonstrating a spirit of peace and declaring that the Lord is indeed all-powerful.
Then Dakṣa, having been consoled by me, begot through Pañcajanī a thousand sons named Balāśva.
Commanded by their father, those sons of firm vows also went there; having attained perfection in the work of creating progeny, they joined their elder brothers who were already present.
Merely by touching that [water], their sins were destroyed and their intentions became pure; observing excellent vows, they performed great penance there while chanting the Brahman.
Knowing that they were intent on the creation of progeny, Nārada went to them and, recollecting the divine course of action, spoke these words as he had done before.
O Sage, having pointed out the path of your brother, you have made your vision fruitless; yet even those sons of yours attained the upward state, following the path of their uncle.
At that very moment, that Prajāpati Dakṣa beheld many portents; he was struck with wonder and became sorrowful in his mind, thinking, "This is my son."
Dakṣa, having heard that it was done by Pūrvavat, was greatly alarmed; overwhelmed by grief for his son, he lamented excessively over the loss of his son.
That wicked Dakṣa became enraged at you and said, "This man is evil! At that moment, you arrived there by chance as one who bestows grace.
Overcome with grief, Dakṣa, his lips quivering with rage, recognized him, struck him, and reproached him, crying out, "Fie! Fie! in condemnation.
Dakṣa said: O lowest of men, what have you done, appearing in the guise of a saint among the virtuous? You have shown the path of mendicancy to children who act like saints.
By you, merciless and deceitful, the obstruction of their welfare has been wrought for those who are not yet freed from the three debts, in both worlds.
A man who departs from his home after having discharged the three debts, yet leaves behind his mother and father while seeking liberation, goes downward.
You are merciless, utterly shameless, and a destroyer of the fame of those with children; indeed, you wander in vain among the attendants of Hari, O fool!
O lowest of the low, you have repeatedly acted unpropitiously toward me; therefore, as you wander about, your station in the worlds shall become unstable.
Then Dakṣa, out of grief, cursed you who were esteemed as a saint; deluded by Śiva’s māyā, he did not recognize it as the will of the Lord.
And you, O sage, accepted the curse with an unchanging mind; for this very Brahman, O holy one, endures it himself as well.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Curse of Nārada upon the Creation of Dakṣa," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In the meantime, O divine sage, having learned of his conduct quickly, I went there with joy, O Grandfather of the worlds.
O wise one, being well-versed as before, I comforted Dakṣa and, bringing you great joy, I established a deep affection for him.
Having consoled you, my own son, the best of sages and beloved of the gods, with great affection and having taken you with me, I returned to my own abode.
Then Prajāpati Dakṣa, having been entreated by me, begot upon his own wife sixty fortunate daughters.
O Lord of Sages, listen with great pleasure as I describe how he, unwearied, performed their marriages according to the Dharma and other rites; I shall speak of that very matter.
O sage, Dakṣa gave ten daughters to Dharma according to the prescribed rites; thirteen to the sage Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven to the Moon.
Bhūta gave two daughters each to the Aṅgirasas and the Kṛśāśvas; and another daughter was given to Tārkṣya, from whose offspring and descendants [the lineage] arose.
The three worlds have been filled by them; we shall not describe this in detail for fear of prolixity.
Some say that Śivā is the eldest, others the middle one; some say she is born after all of them, and thus there are three according to the differences in the kalpas.
Immediately after the birth of his daughter, the patriarch Dakṣa, together with his wife, being well-pleased, mentally offered that Mother of the World as an oblation.
Therefore, with love and full of humility, he offered salutations again and again with joined palms and praised him with a voice faltering with emotion.
Then that goddess, being satisfied, reflected thus in her mind: "I shall take an incarnation in Vīriṇī in order to fulfill my promise."
Then, O best of sages, the Mother of the Universe dwelt within the mind of Dakṣa; at that time, Dakṣa rejoiced exceedingly.
Then, after a mere moment, Dakṣa joyfully placed [the seed] in his wife; at that time, the compassionate Śiva dwelt within the heart of Dakṣa’s wife.
Indeed, all the signs of pregnancy appeared.
O dear one, Vīriṇī shone forth with a joyful heart and increased in stature; by the power of Śiva’s abode, she took on a form of great auspiciousness.
The skillful man, out of affection, performed the auspicious rites beginning with the *puṃsavana*, for the sake of his family, its prosperity, sacred learning, and the exaltation of his mind.
Then, as those rites proceeded, a great festival arose; and Prajāpati bestowed wealth upon the twice-born according to their desire.
Then, at that moment, all the gods, headed by Hari, having learned that the goddess was within the womb of Vīriṇī, were filled with joy.
Having arrived there, they all praised the Mother of the World, bowing down again and again to her who brings benefit to the world.
Then, having offered much praise with delighted hearts, they returned to their own homes from the abode of Dakṣa Prajāpati and Vīriṇī.
When nine months had passed, O Nārada, having brought about a worldly state, she, being full [of term] in the tenth month, attained an auspicious state.
O Sage, he then suddenly appeared before his mother at that moment which was auspicious, with the moon being favorably grasped by the planets and the stars.
As soon as she was born, that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) was greatly pleased; seeing her so intense with splendor, he considered her to be the Goddess herself.
O Lord of Sages, when that [vision] had arisen, there occurred a beautiful rain of flowers, the clouds poured down water, and the quarters of the sky quickly became tranquil.
The gods, having ascended into the sky, sounded auspicious musical instruments; the fires blazed forth and were then pacified, and everything became most auspicious.
Seeing that Mother of the World born from the reed-plant, Dakṣa joined his palms in reverence and praised her profusely with devotion.
Dakṣa said: O Maheśānī, salutations to you, O Eternal Mother of the Universe! O Great Goddess, O Truth, whose very nature is truth, have mercy upon me.
I bow to you, the auspicious, peaceful, great illusion, the yogic sleep who pervades the universe, who are praised by those learned in the Vedas as the one who brings about our welfare.
I bow to you, that supreme Maheśvarī, the sustainer of the world, whom the Creator fashioned of old for the purpose of creating the universe.
I bow to you, that supreme Maheśvarī, the sustainer of the world, whom Viṣṇu always employed for the preservation of the universe.
I bow to you, that supreme Maheśvarī, the sustainer of the universe, by whom Rudra was appointed for the destruction of the world and whom she always performs.
I bow to you, that auspicious Goddess, the mother of the three gods, who always assumes the forms of rajas, sattva, and tamas, and who brings about all effects.

Whoever meditates upon you, O Goddess, the supreme one whose nature consists of both knowledge and ignorance, for him both worldly enjoyment and liberation are forever held within the palm of his hand.
O Goddess, for one who beholds you, Śivā, the purifier, directly before their eyes, there shall certainly be liberation, as you are the illuminator of both knowledge and ignorance.
Those who praise the Mother of the World as Bhavānī, Ambikā, Jaganmayī, Durgā, and so forth—for them, everything shall come to pass.
Brahmā said: Thus praised by the wise Dakṣa, Śivā, the Mother of the World, then spoke to Dakṣa in such a way that his mother did not hear.
Everything was deluded, yet Dakṣa heard that truth; no one else did, for the Supreme Goddess Śivā spoke thus through various manifestations.
The Goddess said: "O Prajāpati, I was propitiated by you previously for the sake of a son; your desired object has been accomplished, so now maintain your ascetic penance."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the Goddess then assumed a state of childhood through her own power and wept before her mother.
Then, hearing that crying and the words of the women, the female servants also arrived there with great haste and much affection.
Seeing the form of Asiknī’s son, all the women rejoiced, and all the citizens then raised a cry of victory.
There was a great festival accompanied by song and instrumental music; Dakṣa and Asiknī attained joy upon beholding the auspicious face of their son.
Then Dakṣa duly performed the rites according to the sacred scriptures and family tradition; he bestowed gifts upon the twice-born and likewise gave wealth to others.
Singing and dancing occurred everywhere as was appropriate; musical instruments resounded many times, preceded by most auspicious sounds.
Then all the gods, beginning with Hari, together with their followers and having assembled with throngs of sages, celebrated the festival according to the prescribed rites.
Having seen Ambā, the daughter of Dakṣa and the supreme sovereign of the universe, they all bowed with humility and praised her with auspicious hymns.
All, being greatly delighted, uttered words consisting of "Victory! Victory! and joyfully praised Dakṣa and Vīriṇī, especially the latter.
Then, at her command, Dakṣa, filled with joy because she was praiseworthy in every virtue and essence, gave her the name Tadoṃ.
Other names for her arose subsequently from worldly usage; they are indeed bestowers of great auspiciousness and especially destroyers of suffering.
Then Dakṣa, having bowed to Hari, to me, and to all the immortals, as well as to the sages, joined his palms and worshipped them with devotion after offering hymns of praise.
Then Viṣṇu and all the others, having highly praised the son of Aja, returned with affection to their own abodes, while constantly remembering Śiva along with Śivā.
Therefore, having properly performed the customary purificatory rites for her daughter, the mother gave her breast milk and other nourishment according to the prescribed ritual for infants.
Protected by Sātha, Vīriṇya, Dakṣa, and the high-souled one, she grew day by day like the digit of the moon during the bright fortnight.
O best of the twice-born, all excellent qualities entered her even in childhood, just as all enchanting digits enter the moon.
When she was in the midst of her friends, acting according to her own true nature, she then drew the image of Bharga day after day, again and again.
When she sang those well-composed songs appropriate for childhood, she then remembered Sthāṇu, Hara, Rudra, the subduer of Smara.
Day by day, the incomparable compassion for that devoted woman grew ever greater toward the couple, even during her childhood, as it manifested repeatedly and constantly.
Having transcended all childish qualities and always acting for her own well-being, she constantly and repeatedly gratified her parents.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Birth and Childhood Play," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O sage, on one occasion I beheld that Satī standing by her father’s side along with you—she who is the very essence of the three worlds.
Seeing you honored by her father and herself being treated with respect, the virtuous lady, following the ways of worldly conduct, bowed down with joy and devotion.
At the conclusion of my prostrations, O Nārada, seeing Satī seated upon the auspicious throne offered by Dakṣa, you and I both stood there, and I addressed Vinatā.
O virtuous lady, obtain as your husband that very God who desires you and whom you desire—the omniscient Lord of the universe.
O auspicious lady, may he who has not taken another wife, nor does take one, nor will ever take one—may that peerless husband be yours.
Having spoken thus and remained for a very long time in the abode of Dakṣa, O Nārada, they were both dismissed by him and returned to their own place.
Having heard that, Dakṣa became joyful and free from distress; considering her to be the Supreme Goddess, he took back his own daughter.
Thus, through her delightful childhood pastimes, she who is compassionate toward her devotees abandoned her childhood state, having assumed a human form by her own will.
Having passed beyond childhood, that virtuous woman attained a certain degree of youth.
She was exceedingly captivating in all her limbs due to her ascetic practices.
Seeing her, who had reached the bloom of youth, Dakṣa, the lord of the world, reflected: "How shall I give this daughter to Bharga?"
Then she too desired to attain Bharga for herself; daily, having understood her father's intention, she approached her mother.
Then that supreme goddess, the friend of her mother Śivā Vairiṇī, being humble-minded, requested permission from Śaṅkara for the sake of performing penance.
Then Satī, firm in her vow, in order to obtain Maheśāna as her husband, propitiated him in her mother’s house with his permission.
In the month of Āśvina, on the lunar day called Nandā, he bowed with devotion to Hara and, having offered rice mixed with jaggery and salt, led him away.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, having worshipped with cakes and milk-rice (pāyasa) strewn all around, he remembered the Supreme Lord.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped Hara with rice mixed with sesame and barley, Satī passed her days with [the practice of] kīla.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, having kept a vigil at night, that virtuous woman worshipped Śiva in the morning with kṛśara-rice.
On the full moon day of Māgha, having kept a vigil at night, he, wearing wet clothes, performed the worship of Śaṅkara on the bank of a river.
Having kept a vigil during the night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, he worshipped [the deity] especially throughout all the watches of the night with actors.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, she worshipped Śiva with palāśa and damana flowers, and passing that night while constantly remembering him, she spent it.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Rādha, having worshipped the virtuous Rudra with offerings of sesame seeds, rice, and barley, she passed that month.
On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having worshipped Śaṅkara at night with garments and bṛhatī flowers while remaining without food, she passed that time.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, she, dressed in black garments, performed the worship of Rudra with bṛhatī flowers.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, she worshipped Śiva with sacred threads, garments, and purifying offerings.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, having worshipped with various kinds of flowers and fruits, he partook of a water-meal on the fourteenth day.
Restricting her diet strictly, she performed the worship of Śiva for a month while reciting prayers, using various kinds of fruits, flowers, and crops produced in that season.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva every month and every day, the goddess, who had assumed a human form by her own will, remained firm in her vow.
Having thus completed the entire Nandā-vrata with a well-composed mind, Satī meditated upon Śiva with love; her intellect became unwavering and focused on no other.
In the meantime, O sage, all the gods and sages, placing both Viṣṇu and me at their head, went to behold the asceticism of Satī.
Having arrived, she was seen by the gods like another personified Siddhi; deeply immersed in meditation on Śiva, she then attained the state of a Siddha.

All the gods, with palms joined in reverence, joyfully offered their salutations to the Truth; and the sages, as well as Viṣṇu and the others, with bowed shoulders and delighted minds, likewise paid homage.
Then Viṣṇu and all the other gods and sages, being highly pleased and filled with wonder, praised the penance of Satī.
Then, having bowed again to that goddess, those sages and gods immediately went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains and the beloved abode of Śiva.
Accompanied by Sāvitrī and filled with joy along with Lakṣmī, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva also went then into the presence of Hara.
Having gone there and beheld the Lord, they bowed deeply with great agitation; with palms joined and bodies bent low, they praised him with various hymns.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, the Blessed One, from whom this world of moving and unmoving beings proceeds—to the Puruṣa, the Great Lord, the Supreme Lord, the Great Soul."
Salutation to the primordial seed of all, whose form is consciousness, the supreme, the changeless Brahman, and the source of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.

That which one should understand as this, that by which this indeed shines forth, from what this arises, wherein this is contained, and to whom this belongs—you too, through diligent effort—[should know all this].
We bow to that self-existent one, who is higher than the high and beyond the other, the changeless Great Lord, who beholds this universe within his own self.

They have gone for refuge to the Supreme Brahman, who is the unperforated eye, the transcendent witness, the self of all, the bearer of manifold forms, and the one who has become the Self, shining with splendor.
Since neither the gods, the seers, nor the perfected ones know his station, what other living being could possibly be capable of knowing or perceiving it?
Desiring to behold your state, virtuous men free from attachment follow your conduct; you are our auspicious goal, possessing a world-conforming vow that is free from blemish.
No transformations such as birth and so forth exist in you that cause suffering; nevertheless, through your power of illusion (māyā), you indeed assume them out of compassion.
Salutation to You, the Supreme Lord of wondrous deeds; salutation to the Brahman, the Supreme Self, who is beyond the reach of words.
Salutations to the one who is formless yet possesses vast forms, whose power is infinite, the lord of the three worlds, the witness of all, and the omnipresent.
Homage to the lamp of the self, the perfection of the bliss of nirvāṇa; homage be to you, the essence of gnosis, the all-pervading Lord.
Salutations to the Lord of Kaivalya, who is easily attained through the state of actionlessness; salutations to You, the Supreme Person, the Highest Lord, and the Giver of all.
Salutation to the Knower of the Field, whose nature is the Self, and who is the cause of all cognition.
Salutations to the Great One, the supreme overseer of all, the primordial nature; salutations to you, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all, and the giver of everything at all times.
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one with five faces, who is eternally luminous; salutations to you, the witness of all the qualities of the senses, who is without cause.
Salutations again and again to the cause of the three worlds and to liberation; salutations to the swift bestower of liberation and the savior of those who have come for refuge.
Salutations to You, the supreme source of all traditional scriptures and sacred teachings, the ultimate refuge for Your devotees, and the embodiment of all virtues.
Salutations to Maheśvara, whose heat of consciousness is concealed by the forest of qualities; whose form is difficult for the deluded to attain, yet who eternally dwells in the hearts of the wise.

To Him who grants liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa) and bestows supreme liberation upon His devotees; to Him who is self-luminous, eternal, immutable, and whose consciousness is incessant.

To the inward-looking witness, the changeless one who possesses supreme sovereignty, whom they worship for the sake of the four aims of life while desiring their cherished ultimate goal—may You, who were once merciless toward us, now become gracious; salutations to You!
Those single-minded devotees do not desire any object whatsoever from You; they sing only of Your supremely auspicious deeds.
We praise you, the imperishable, supreme Brahman, whose form is unmanifest, all-pervading, attainable through the yoga of the inner self, and perfectly complete.
We bow to you, the Lord of all, who transcends the senses, who is without support yet the support of all, who is causeless, infinite, primordial, and subtle.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, as well as the worlds of moving and non-moving beings, were created by means of a trifling portion through the differentiation of name and form.
Just as the rays of the fire or the sun go forth and return repeatedly, so indeed this stream is called secondary (gauṇa).

O Lord, you are not a god, nor an asura, nor a mortal; you are not an animal, nor a twice-born brahmin; you are not a woman, nor a eunuch, nor a man; you are neither being nor non-being, nor anything at all.

You are the remainder after all negations; you are the creator of the universe, the protector of the universe, the one who effects the dissolution of the universe, and the soul of the universe. We bow down to that Lord.
We bow to You, the Lord of Yoga, whom yogis perceive when their karma has been consumed by yoga and their minds are perfected through yoga.

Salutations to you, whose impetus is irresistible, who consist of the three powers and are composed of the triple Vedas; salutations to the protector of the serene, salutations to you of manifold power.
O Lord of the difficult-to-reach, who leads those with dull senses to the supreme path; O You who are devoted to the upliftment of devotees, salutations to You of hidden splendor!
Alas, I of deluded intellect do not know myself by my own power of mind; therefore, we bow down to You, the Great Lord, whose majesty is insurmountable.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Mahādeva, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, remained silent before the Lord with their necks bowed in true devotion.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Nandā Vow and the Hymn of Praise to Śiva," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard this hymn composed by Hari and the others, Śaṅkara, the creator of all beings, became exceedingly pleased and laughed.
But upon seeing Brahmā and Viṣṇu together with their wives, Hara addressed them appropriately and inquired about the reason for their arrival.
Rudra said: O gods and sages, you are now free from fear; tell me truly the reason for your arrival.
For what purpose have you come, and what business is there here? I wish to hear all of that, my mind being pleased by your praise.
Brahmā said: O sage, having been thus questioned by Hara, I, the grandfather of all the worlds, being urged by Viṣṇu, spoke to Mahādeva.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord, ocean of compassion! Hear from us, along with the celestial sages, the purpose for which we have come.
O Lord whose banner is the bull, we have come specifically for your sake; otherwise, this world would not be a fit place for those who seek their goals.
O Maheśvara, some future asuras will be slain by me; likewise, some will be slain by Hari, and others will be slain by you as well.
O Great Lord, some asuras will always be incapable of being slain by Māyā, while others will be capable of being slain by the son born of your own prowess.
By your very grace, O Śambhu, having destroyed the terrible asuras, you have brought about the supreme happiness of the gods and the eternal security and well-being of the world.
Since you are always engaged in yoga, free from attachment and aversion, and solely devoted to the object of compassion, you indeed should not be slain. Or rather, [you are] not to be killed by me.
O Lord, when they have been propitiated, how do creation and maintenance proceed? Therefore, O Bull-bannered One, it is fitting that this should be eternally so.
When the activities of creation, maintenance, and destruction are no longer to be performed, then neither the dissolution of our bodies nor that of Māyā is possible.
For we are of a single nature, though appearing distinct due to the diversity of our effects; if the diversity of effects is not established, then a difference in form is purposeless.
The Supreme Self, Maheśvara, is indeed one, yet divided threefold; by His own power alone, the independent Lord acts through His creative play by means of Māyā.
Hari was born from his left limb, while I am indeed born from his right limb; you, however, are Śiva himself, born from the heart of Śiva, possessing a complete body.
Thus we three have become, our essential natures distinguished by their respective splendors; O Eternal One, know in your heart that we are the reality consisting of Śiva, Aśiva, and their son.
O Lord, by your command and out of affection, Viṣṇu and I have been born together with our wives for the sake of a specific task, to perform the work of the world.
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world and for the happiness of the gods, accept this one most beautiful woman as your wife.
Listen to something else, O Maheśāna, a former event remembered by me, which was previously told to us by you yourself in the form of Śiva.
O Brahman, my supreme form, such as this, shall manifest from your body in the world, renowned by the name Rudra.
Brahmā became the creator, Hari the protector, and I, assuming the form of Rudra and manifesting through the qualities (guṇas), shall be the agent of dissolution.
"Having married a woman, I shall accomplish the highest purpose for the world"—recollecting this which you yourself spoke, fulfill your own promise.
O Lord, I am Hari, the creator acting according to your command; you are Śiva himself, manifested as the protector and the cause of dissolution.
Indeed, without you, we two are not capable of our respective duties; therefore, since we are devoted to the affairs of the world, choose one beloved woman for yourself.
Just as Lakṣmī is to Viṣṇu and Sāvitrī is to me, so now, O Śambhu, accept a beloved wife as your companion.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine in the presence of Hari, Hara, the lord of the worlds, spoke to me with a smiling face.
The Lord said: O Brahmā, O Hari, you two are indeed always most dear to me; upon seeing you, my joy truly becomes exceedingly great.
For you two are indeed distinguished among the gods, the lords of the three worlds; thus your discourse is most weighty, as you are devoted to the affairs of existence.
O best of gods, it is not fitting for me to perform a marriage, for I am one who is constantly devoted to austerity and penance, detached, and always known as a yogin.
He who stands on the excellent path of cessation, rejoicing in his own self, stainless, possessing the body of an avadhūta, a man of knowledge, a seer of his true nature, and free from desire.
For one who is changeless, devoid of enjoyment, eternally impure, and inauspicious—tell me now, what purpose could he have for a woman in this world?
For me, who am solely absorbed in yoga, there is indeed constant bliss; but a person devoid of knowledge considers himself a slave to many desires.
In this world, the act of marriage should be understood as a bond to another; therefore, I have no desire for it—this I tell you in truth, the absolute truth.
Indeed, my engagement here is not for my own sake, since I have correctly reflected upon my true self-interest; nevertheless, I shall do as you have said for the benefit of the world.
Whether considering these words as most weighty, or for the sake of fulfilling my command, I shall indeed perform the marriage; for I am always subject to the devotion [of my devotees].
But listen, O Brahmin Hari, to the kind of bridegroom I shall accept; my words are indeed appropriate.
"Command that yoginī who is capable of grasping my splendor in its various parts, so that she may become my wife, able to assume any form at will."
When I am engaged in yoga, she will likewise become a yoginī; when I am attached to desire, she will likewise become a passionate woman.
The wise who know the Vedas proclaim the syllable "Yam"; I shall meditate upon that eternal Śiva, whose form is light.
O Brahmin, when I am intent upon that future destiny which I am contemplating, may those obstacles that arise there be destroyed for me.
Whether you or I am Viṣṇu, we are both portions of Śiva, who is of the nature of Brahman; O highly fortunate one, it is fitting that you reflect upon this.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall remain without marriage due to anxiety over her; therefore, assign me a wife who will always follow my will.
In that regard, O Brahmin, choose one boon from me; however, if you have no faith in my words, she shall be abandoned by me.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of him and of Viṣṇu and Hara, I, with a delighted mind, spoke thus with a smile while bowing low.
Listen, O Lord Maheśāna, to the kind of woman you have sought; O Master, with great joy I shall describe to you such a woman as she is.
O Lord, that Umā was born in divided form to accomplish her purpose; likewise, Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī were formerly of two-fold form.
Pādmā became the beloved of Viṣṇu, and likewise Sarasvatī became mine; she did not exist as a third form, for she was intent on the welfare of the world's affairs.
O Lord, she who was the daughter of Dakṣa, known by the name Satī—she alone would be such a wife, for she would indeed be one who acts for your welfare.
O Lord of Gods, she is performing penance for your sake with firm vows; indeed, that virtuous woman of great splendor desires to obtain you as her husband.
O Maheśvara, go and grant her a boon; have compassion for her, and having given such a boon, marry her with great affection.
O Śaṅkara, this is the desire of Hari, of me, and of the gods: fulfill it with your gracious glance so that we may behold the festival with reverence.
May there be supreme auspiciousness, bringing happiness to the three worlds; indeed, all fevers shall be destroyed for everyone—of this there is no doubt.
Or rather, while we were still speaking these remaining words, Madhusūdana—the infallible Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees—assumed a playful form as a cowherd boy.
Viṣṇu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, compassionate Śaṅkara! Everything that was spoken by Brahmā is exactly as I have said; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Great Lord, show mercy toward me; make the three worlds well-provided for by bestowing your auspicious gaze upon them.
Brahmā said: O sage, having spoken thus, the wise Lord Viṣṇu became silent; then that Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, laughed and spoke these words of praise.
Then, having received permission from those sages and gods, we two, together with our wives, departed for our desired destination, filled with supreme joy.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prayer to Śiva by Viṣṇu and Brahmā," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, all the gods offered supreme praise to Śambhu, and from Śiva they obtained a boon; listen now with respect, O Sage.
Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina, she again observed a fast and worshipped the Lord of All with devotion.
Thus, when the Nandā-vrata was completed on the ninth day, Lord Hara appeared visibly before her as she remained absorbed in meditation.
Beautiful in every limb, fair-complexioned, five-faced, and three-eyed; with the moon upon his forehead, serene in soul, blue-throated, and four-armed.
Holding a trident, the Brahma-crown, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, radiant with ashes, his head adorned by the celestial river (Ganges), he is enchanting in every limb.
He is the abode of great loveliness, with a face equal to ten million moons; his splendor is like that of ten million Cupids, and in every way he possesses a form beloved by women.
Beholding Hara directly as her lord in such a form, Satī, with her face bowed down in great modesty, paid homage at his feet.
Then Mahādeva, the bestower of the fruits of ascetic practice, spoke to Satī, who was observant of virtuous vows, even though he desired her as his wife.
Mahādeva said: "O daughter of Dakṣa, O lady of excellent vows, I am pleased with this vow of yours; choose a boon, and I shall grant whatever is desired by you."
Brahmā said: Although Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, already knew her intention here, he spoke the words "Choose a boon," desiring to hear her response.
Though she was capable of speaking what resided in her heart, she was overcome by shame; thus, that which she desired remained once again concealed by modesty.
Upon hearing those beloved words of Śiva, she became immersed in love; and knowing this, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, became exceedingly pleased.
"Choose a boon, choose a boon," he said again quickly; for Śambhu, the inner controller and the refuge of the virtuous, was under the sway of Satī’s devotion.
Then, restraining her own modesty, when Satī spoke to Hara, saying, "O Giver of Boons, grant me a boon as you wish," he could not refuse her.
Then, without waiting for the conclusion of his speech, Śiva, whose banner is the bull and who is compassionate toward his devotees, said to her, "Become my wife."
Having heard these words of his, which brought about her desired fruit, she stood silent and delighted, having obtained the boon that was in her heart.
Standing before the lustful Hara, she of the lovely smile displayed her inner feelings and gestures that increase desire.

Then, having taken up the emotional states (bhāvas), the aesthetic flavor known as the erotic (śṛṅgāra-rasa) quickly entered the hearts of the two, along with the artistic skills, gestures, and expressions as they have been described.
O divine sage, upon their entry, those two who followed the ways of worldly play acquired a certain wondrous splendor, like that of the two moons.
Having obtained Hara, Satī, who possessed the luster of smooth, crushed collyrium, appeared like a streak of cloud near the moon, whose body was as brilliant as crystal.
Then that daughter of Dakṣa, being very pleased and bowing with her hands joined, spoke thus repeatedly to Hara, who is compassionate toward his devotees.
Satī said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the universe, having brought me within the sight of my father, accept me according to the rites of marriage, O Prabhū."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Satī, Maheśa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, looked at her with love and spoke these words: "So be it."
Dakṣāyaṇī also, having bowed to Śambhu and made her request with devotion, received his permission and went into her mother's presence, filled with joy and yet bewildered.
Hara, too, having entered his own hermitage on a plateau of the Himalayas, became intent on painful meditation due to his separation from the daughter of Dakṣa.
O celestial sage, having composed his mind and adopted a worldly course, Śambhu, whose banner is the bull, meditated upon me with his mind.
Then, being thus reflected upon by Maheśa, the wielder of the trident, I quickly entered before him, impelled by the success of Hara.
O dear one, on that plateau of the Himalayas where Hara dwells separated from her, Sarasvatī herself has arrived right there.
O celestial sage, seeing me accompanied by Sarasvatī, that Lord Śambhu, filled with longing and bound by love, spoke to Satī.

Śambhu said: O Brahman, because I was formerly intent on my own self-interest in the act of taking possession, that sense of ownership now appears to me as if it were truly mine even regarding my own self.
"Because I was propitiated with devotion by Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, a boon was granted to her by me through the power of the Nandā-vrata."
"O Brahmin, the boon was chosen by her from me, saying, 'Be my husband'; and I, being entirely pleased, said to her, 'Become my wife.'"
Then that virtuous daughter of Dakṣa said to me, "O Lord of the World, having brought me within the range of my father's sight, please accept me."
O Brahman, that too was accepted by me out of satisfaction with her devotion; she has gone to her mother's house, and I have come here, O Creator.
Therefore, go to the abode of Dakṣa at my command; speak in such a way that Dakṣa will quickly give that maiden to me.
Act in such a way that there may be no further separation from Satī for me; O Dakṣa, you who are proficient in all branches of knowledge, offer him consolation.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus in the presence of Prajāpati, Mahādeva, upon beholding Sarasvatī, immediately fell under the power of separation.
Thus commanded by him, I too, having fulfilled my duty and filled with joy, spoke thus to that Lord of the worlds, who is compassionate toward his devotees.
Brahmā said: O Blessed One, O Śambhu, having reflected upon what you have said, it is well-determined: for the chief interest of the gods is indeed my own as well, O Bull-bannered Lord.
Dakṣa himself will offer his own daughter to you; I too shall speak your words in his presence.
Brahmā said: Having thus addressed Mahādeva, the Lord and Sovereign of all, I departed for the abode of Dakṣa by means of an exceedingly swift chariot.
Nārada said: O Creator, O wise one, O highly fortunate one, O best among speakers, tell us what Dakṣa did thereafter to Satī when she had arrived at his home.
Brahmā said: Having performed penance and obtained the boon desired by her heart, Satī then went home and offered salutations to her father and mother.
Then she related all of that to her mother and father—how she had received the boons from Maheśvara through her friend Satyā, who was pleased by her devotion.
Having heard the entire account from the mouth of her friend, both the mother and father attained supreme joy and celebrated a great festival.
The noble-minded Vīriṇī gave wealth to the twice-born according to their desires, as did the high-souled [king] to others who were blind and distressed.
Vīriṇī, having embraced her daughter who increased her joy, smelled the crown of her head and, filled with delight, praised her again and again.
Then, after some time had passed, Dakṣa, the most excellent knower of dharma, reflected: "How can this daughter of mine be given to Śambhu?"
Even though Mahādeva had arrived, he departed pleased; how then will he come here again for the sake of his daughter?
Then I immediately dispatched someone to the presence of Śambhu, thinking: "This is not appropriate; if he were to restrain him in this way, my efforts would be in vain."
Or rather, I shall worship that very one whose banner is the bull, so that my daughter herself may become devoted to him.
In that very same way, even though he was worshipped with noble efforts, Śambhu desired [her] only because of the boon granted by him, saying, "May he become my husband."
While Dakṣa was reflecting thus, I suddenly appeared before him every day, accompanied by Sarasvatī.
Upon seeing me, his father, Dakṣa bowed down in salutation and stood before me; he then offered me a seat, as was appropriate for my own nature.
Then Dakṣa, though filled with anxiety, quickly became joyful and asked me, the Lord of all worlds, the reason for my arrival there.
Dakṣa said: "O Creator of the universe, what is the reason for your arrival here? Having bestowed your great favor upon me, please tell me, O Teacher of the World, why you have entered."
O Creator of the World, whether out of affection for your son or due to some purpose, you have come to my hermitage; I am filled with joy at the sight of you.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having been thus questioned by his son Dakṣa, I spoke these words with a smile, gladdening that Prajāpati.
Brahmā said: Listen, Dakṣa, to the purpose for which I have come to you; that which is for the benefit of your offspring is desired by me as well as by you.
The time has now arrived for that boon which your daughter, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, requested.
"I have certainly been dispatched by Śambhu to your presence for the sake of your daughter; therefore, consider what action would be most beneficial."
Having granted the boon, Rudra departed; from that time forth, Śaṅkara has not obtained peace by virtue of his separation from your daughter.
Madana, who had not yet found an opening, conquered Giriśa despite making repeated and great efforts with all his flower-made arrows.
Though pierced by the arrows of desire, he abandoned self-reflection and remained distracted, thinking only of Satī like an ordinary man.
Having forgotten the words he overheard in the presence of the Gaṇas due to his separation from her, he asks everywhere, "Where is Satī?", even though he has been deceived.
"O son, that which was previously desired by me, by you, and by Madana, as well as by the best of sages beginning with Marīci, has now been accomplished."
Śambhu, propitiated by your daughter, remains on the Himavat mountain, desiring to purify her because of her contemplation of him.
Just as Śambhu was propitiated by him through various states of being, through his very essence, and through that vow, so too is Satī propitiated.
Therefore, bestow upon him without delay the daughter of Dakṣa, who has been intended for Śambhu; by this, you will have fulfilled your duty.
I shall bring him to your abode with Nārada; you must bestow her upon him, for she was intended for his sake.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, my son Dakṣa, exceedingly delighted, spoke to me with great joy, "It is even so."
Then, O Sage, exceedingly joyful and eager, I went there, devoted to beholding the world, to where Giriśa was stationed.
O Nārada, when he had departed, Dakṣa too—along with his wife and sons—became one whose desires were fulfilled, as if filled with nectar.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Satī’s Boon," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: "O dear one, when you had gone to the side of Rudra, what happened there? What was the news, and what did Hara himself do?"
Brahmā said: Then, being well-disposed, I went to bring the Supreme Lord Śiva; indeed, I approached Mahādeva as he was residing on the Himavat mountain.
Beholding me, the creator of the worlds, approaching, the bull-bannered Lord repeatedly harbored doubts in his mind regarding the recovery of Satī.
Then Hara, out of affection and resorting to the ways of the world, playfully and with true devotion quickly spoke to me like an ordinary man.
Īśvara said: O eldest of the gods, what did that son of yours do for the sake of truth? Tell me so that my heart does not shatter from the god of love.
O eldest of the gods, while running toward me, a chaste woman, separation strikes me alone, having abandoned another who still bears life.
"O Brahmin, say 'She exists' so that I may constantly perform my duty; she is to be attained by me through non-duality—therefore, O wise one, act accordingly."
Brahmā said: O Sage Nārada, having heard these words spoken by Rudra, which were deeply imbued with worldly conduct, I spoke to Śiva while consoling him.
Brahmā said: O bull-bannered one, listen to that which my son has spoken for the sake of truth; understand it to be established as something impossible for you to achieve.
"I have resolved to give my daughter to him; furthermore, this task is even more dear to me than your own words."
"Since Śambhu, who was propitiated by my daughter for this very purpose, will himself seek me out again, she must be given to you, O Hari, at that time."
"O Creator, when an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable moment arrive, let him come into my presence; then I shall give my daughter as alms to Śambhu."
Thus Dakṣa spoke to me; therefore, O Bull-bannered One, go to his house at an auspicious moment and bring her back.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, O sage, Rudra—who is compassionate toward his devotees—adopted a worldly manner and spoke to me with a smile.
Rudra said: "I shall go with you and Nārada to that house; I alone am the creator of the world, therefore you, remember Nārada."
O Creator, remember your mental sons, Marīci and the others; together with them and my own attendants, I shall go to the abode of Dakṣa.
Brahmā said: Thus commanded by the Lord, who is devoted to the conduct of the world, I called to mind you, Nārada, as well as my sons Marīci and the others.
Then all those mind-born sons of yours gathered together; at the mere thought of me, they quickly and joyfully approached with respect.
Remembered by Rudra, Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the Śaivas, arrived swiftly with his own army and Lakṣmī, mounted upon Garuḍa.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation presided over by Bhaga, while the sun was in that position, Maheśvara departed.
Accompanied by all the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as those sages, Śaṅkara shone brightly as he proceeded along the path.
A great festival arose on the road for the gods and others who were traveling there, as well as for the hosts of Hara, their minds filled with joy.
The elephant, the cow, the tiger, and the serpent, as well as the matted locks and the crescent moon, all became ornaments according to their suitability by the will of Śiva.
Then, in an instant, Hara—accompanied by the powerful bull who was a yogi—reached the abode of Dakṣa with affection, led by Viṣṇu.
Then Dakṣa, self-controlled and with his hair standing on end from joy, went forward to meet him, accompanied by all his own followers.
There, all the hosts of gods were personally honored by Dakṣa; and the eminent sages sat down at his side in due order.
Surrounding all the gods and their hosts like the sages [surround Brahmā], Dakṣa brought Śiva from within his home.
Then Dakṣa, with a serene mind, personally honored Hara, the Lord of All, according to the prescribed rites after offering him an unsurpassed seat.
Then, with true devotion and according to the prescribed rites, he worshipped Viṣṇu, me, the brahmins, all the gods, and likewise the gaṇas.
Having performed the appropriate worship for them with offerings and other honors, the skillful Dakṣa again entered into a consultation with those mental sages.
Then my son Dakṣa, out of affection, said to me, his father: "O Lord, having prostrated yourself, you must perform the marriage rites."
Saying "So be it," with a heart full of joy, I rose up and then performed that entire task accordingly.
Then, at an auspicious moment and under a favorable rising sign endowed with the strength of the planets, Dakṣa joyfully gave his virtuous daughter to Śambhu.
Then, according to the marriage rite, the bull-bannered Lord, filled with joy, took the hand of that beautiful-bodied daughter of Dakṣa.
I, Hari, you and the others, the sages, the gods, and the hosts—all bowed down and praised the Lord with hymns of glorification.
There was a great festival preceded by dance and song; all the hosts of sages and gods attained supreme bliss.
Having given away his daughter, my son Dakṣa then felt his purpose was fulfilled; Śiva and Śivā were both pleased, and everything became an abode of auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of the Daughter," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having performed the rite of bestowing gifts upon Dakṣa, he, being well-pleased, gave various dowries to Hara and bestowed diverse wealth upon the twice-born.
Then Śambhu, having approached with joy and rising with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words along with Kamalā to the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Viṣṇu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord, ocean of compassion! You are the father of the worlds, dear one, and Satī is the mother of all.
"You two are playful incarnations, always for the welfare of the virtuous and for the sake of subduing the wicked; such is the eternal Vedic revelation."
O Hara, you shine with the luster of smooth, dark blue collyrium, just as I shine with Padmā, the daughter of Dakṣa, though we are joined in reverse order.
O Śambhu, by means of this truth of yours, grant protection to the gods, to men, and to the virtuous who wander through the cycle of existence; likewise, grant them auspiciousness at all times.
O Lord of all beings, O Master, whoever might become filled with desire upon seeing or hearing of her, you should slay him; this is my petition.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, the Omniscient One, smiled and said to Madhusūdana, "So be it."
O lord of sages, Hari returned to his own abode and remained there; he caused a festival to be celebrated and protected that deed.
Having approached the Goddess, I performed the entire fire-ritual in full detail, exactly as prescribed by the rules stated in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Then Śivā and Śiva, being greatly delighted, performed the circumambulation of the fire according to the prescribed rites, at the command of my preceptor and the twice-born.
Then, O best of the twice-born, a wonderful great festival took place there, providing joy to all, accompanied by instrumental music, song, and dance.
At that time, O dear one, a most wonderful and exceedingly marvelous event occurred there; listen as I tell it to you.
The Māyā of Śambhu is difficult to comprehend; by it the entire world—moving and unmoving, including gods, asuras, and humans—is utterly deluded.
O father, I who formerly desired to delude Śambhu through deceit, he, Śaṅkara, has in turn deluded me with ease by his divine play.
"He who desires to do harm to another will surely suffer that very harm himself. Thinking thus, a person should not inflict injury upon another.
O Sage, as Satyā was performing circumambulation of the fire, her two feet became visible from beneath her garment; that did I behold.
And with my mind possessed by passion, O best of the twice-born, I gazed upon Satī’s limbs, deluded by the illusory power of Śiva.
The more I gazed with curiosity at her beautiful limbs, the more Satyabhāmā became delighted, for she was indeed afflicted by love.
O sage, having seen Dakṣa’s daughter, that devoted wife, in such a state, my mind was possessed by desire, and I became longing to behold her face.
Out of shame, she did not look directly at the face of Śambhu, nor did she, overcome by bashfulness, reveal her own face openly.
Then, seeking a proper means to behold her, I, afflicted by desire, employed the "smoke-terrible" method; and after that, I did what followed.
Having cast many moist fuels into that fire, [the smoke] likewise arises from the moist substances due to the application of only a small offering of clarified butter.
Then smoke appeared there in great abundance on all sides, such that the sacrificial altar-ground was enveloped in darkness.
Then Maheśa, the Supreme Lord, the Master who performs manifold sports, covered his smoke-filled eyes with both hands.
Then, O Sage, having lifted up her garment, I, afflicted by lust, gazed indeed upon the face of Satī with a delighted inner soul.
O father, again and again I beheld the face of Satī; then, being helpless, I succumbed to a transformation of the senses.
Then, from the sight of that [form], my semen quickly fell upon the ground in four drops, resembling a mass of snow.
Then, O Sage, filled with apprehension and struck with wonder at that moment, I remained silent and covered that semen so that no one might perceive it.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, having perceived this with his divine eye, spoke these words out of anger because of that emission of semen.
Rudra said: "O sinner, what is this despicable deed committed by you? Out of passion, you did not look upon the face of my beloved during our marriage."
"You know this deed performed by Śaṅkara; has nothing been known? O Creator, there is nothing hidden from me even throughout the three worlds; how then [could you claim otherwise]?"
Whatever there is in the three worlds, whether moving or stationary—I am situated within that, O fool, just as oil is within sesame seeds.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to me, O dear one, Śaṅkara then, remembering the words of Viṣṇu, raised his trident and desired to slay Brahmā.
O best of the twice-born, when the trident was raised by Śambhu to strike me, Marīci and the others indeed raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
Then all the hosts of gods and likewise all the sages, overcome with fear, praised Śaṅkara as he blazed there.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge! O Lord of protection, protect Brahmā; O Maheśvara, show us mercy!"
O Maheśa, you are the father of the universe; Satī is considered the mother of the universe; and all beings, including Hari, Brahmā, and others, O Lord of the gods, are your servants.
O Lord, Your form and play are wondrous; Your Māyā is marvelous, O Master. By it all are utterly deluded, save for those who possess devotion to You, O Īśvara.
Brahmā said: Thus, the gods and those sages, being exceedingly distressed, praised Maheśvara, the Lord of the God of Gods, who was possessed by anger.
Dakṣa, alarmed, raised his hand and cried out, "Not so! Not so! and quickly approaching from in front, he sought to restrain the Lord of Beings.
Then, seeing Dakṣa present before him, Maheśvara, remembering the prayer of Hari, spoke these unpleasant words in reply.
Maheśvara said: O Prajāpati, that which has just been uttered by Viṣṇu, who is devoted to me, has also been accepted by me to be carried out right here.
"O Lord, may I slay that man who, having a desire for Satī, might even look upon her"—having said this, I shall now fulfill the word of Viṣṇu by killing Brahmā.
"How did Brahmā look upon Satī with longing? He became one whose seed was discharged; therefore, I shall slay the offender."
Brahmā said: When Maheśa, the Lord of Gods, had spoken thus while overwhelmed with anger, all people—including gods, sages, and humans—trembled.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and there was indifference on all sides; at that time, I became utterly overwhelmed, being completely deluded by that.
Then Viṣṇu, who is exceedingly dear to Maheśa and skilled in discerning what must be done, being wise, bowed down and offered praise to Rudra, who had spoken thus.
Having praised Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, with various hymns, he spoke this while standing before him, urging him to act quickly: "Restrain him!"
Viṣṇu said: O Lord of Beings, do not slay the Creator, the Master of the worlds; he has come today seeking refuge in you, who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge.
"I am your most beloved devotee, proclaimed as the king of devotees; considering my petition within your heart, show mercy toward me."
Furthermore, O Lord, hear my words which are pregnant with reason; reflect upon them, O Great Lord, having shown compassion toward me.
O Śambhu, this four-faced one has appeared to create progeny; now that he is slain, there is no other natural creator of beings remaining at present.
"O Lord, O you whose form is Śiva, we three gods shall repeatedly perform the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction by your command."
O Śambhu, if he were slain, who would perform your work? Therefore, O Lord, the creator and destroyer of the universe must not be killed by you.
O Lord, by this very means, the virtuous daughter of Dakṣa, Śivā, has indeed been arranged as a wife for your sake through a proper stratagem.
Brahmā said: Having heard this petition made by Viṣṇu, Maheśa, firm in his vows, replied to all of them while making his words heard.
Maheśa said: "O God of gods, O Lord of Ramā, O Viṣṇu, you who are as dear to me as my own life! Do not restrain me, dear father; this man is a wicked one and must be slain."
I shall fulfill the vow previously undertaken by me; I shall slay this wicked, four-faced one who has committed great sins.
I alone shall create all beings, both stationary and moving; or else, by my own power, I shall create another creator of the world.
Having slain him, I shall fulfill my own established vow; I will create another sole Creator—O Lord, do not restrain me!
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Lord of the Mountain, Acyuta, his heart breaking into a smile, spoke again, saying, "Do not say so."
Acyuta said: "The fulfillment of a vow is indeed appropriate for another person; O Lord of the slayable, consider this, for it does not apply to yourself, O Master."
O Śambhu, we three gods are your very self and nothing else; in reality, consider well that we are of one form and not distinct.
Then, having heard those words of Viṣṇu, who is so very dear to him, Śambhu spoke to him again, proclaiming his own state.
Śambhu said: "O Viṣṇu, Lord of all devotees, how is it that this Brahmā, who is my very self, appears before me right here in person as if he were entirely distinct?"
Brahmā said: Thus commanded by Maheśa in the presence of all, the one whose banner is Garuḍa then spoke this to Mahādeva, pleasing him.
Viṣṇu said: "O Sadāśiva, Brahmā is not distinct from you, nor are you distinct from him; O Supreme Lord, I am not distinct from you, nor are you distinct from me."
O Omniscient One, Supreme Lord Sadāśiva, you know everything; you wish to cause me to hear all things from your own mouth.
"By your command, O Lord, I shall speak; let all the gods, the sages, and others listen, holding their own minds fixed upon the Śaiva reality."
We three gods, O Lord, are the luminous portions of that which is both primary and secondary, possessed of parts and yet partless, and composed of light.
Who are you? Who am I? And who is Brahmā? These three distinct portions belong to You alone, the Supreme Self, as the causes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Contemplate yourself by means of your own self, you who have assumed a form for your own sport; you alone are Brahman with attributes, while we three are indeed your constituent parts.
O Hara, just as the head, neck, and so forth are the limbs of a single body, so too are those three *bhagas* the limbs of that one Lord.

That light which is cloudless, your own city, ancient, immovable, unmanifest, and of infinite forms; eternal, and devoid of attributes such as length and the like—you are Śiva, and therefore you are everything.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having heard those words of his, Mahādeva became well-pleased and did not kill me thereafter.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Marriage and the Līlā of Śiva," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, O Lord, foremost among the devotees of Śiva! You have narrated the wondrous life-story of Śambhu, which is the abode of all auspiciousness.
Therefore, O dear one, tell me what happened next regarding the Moon-crested Lord; relate the divine life-story of Satī, which destroys the entire multitude of sins.
Brahmā said: When Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, had desisted from our slaughter, everyone became fearless, happy, and joyful.
With shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, they all prostrated before him; with devotion, they praised Śaṅkara and joyfully raised shouts of victory.
At that very time, O sage, being pleased and free from fear, I praised Śaṅkara with devotion through various auspicious hymns.
Then, O sage, the Lord Śambhu, the performer of many divine sports, being pleased in mind, spoke these words to me while everyone was listening.
Rudra said: "O Brahmin, my dear son, I am pleased; now be free from fear. Touch your own head with your hand and carry out my command without hesitation."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Lord Śambhu, the performer of manifold sports, he touched his own head, assumed that same state, and prostrated before the bull-bannered god.
Just as I touched my own body with my own hand, immediately there stood before me that very form, mounted upon its bull-vehicle.
Then, my body overcome with shame, I stood with my face cast downward, while Indra and all the other immortals gazed upon me from every side as they stood around.
Then, overcome with shame, I prostrated before Maheśvara and, having offered praise, said: "Forgive me, forgive me!"
O Lord, tell me the expiation for the purification of this sin, as well as the restraint and the injustice, by which my sin may be removed.
Thus addressed by me, Śambhu—the Lord of All, who is affectionate toward his devotees—becoming exceedingly gracious, spoke to him as he bowed down.
Śambhu said: "With this very form, indeed presided over by me, perform penance with a tranquil mind, intent upon my propitiation."
You shall attain renown everywhere on earth by the name Rudraśiras, as the accomplisher of all rites for those twice-born who possess splendor.
Since this task of men has now been accomplished by you through your valor, therefore, having become a human being, you shall wander upon the surface of the earth.
But whoever shall see you in this form as you wander about the world, he will say, "What is this on the head of Brahmā?"—thus spoke the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva).
Furthermore, whoever hears all their actions out of curiosity shall immediately attain liberation from the sin of violating another's wife.
To the extent that people shall proclaim this deed of yours, to that same extent shall your purification from this sin come to pass.
O Brahmin, this indeed is the expiation I have declared for you; it will cause laughter among people in the world and bring about great reproach for you.
Indeed, this semen of yours, fallen into the middle of the sacrificial altar, was seen by me while you were afflicted by desire; it shall not remain here.
As many raindrops as of your semen fall upon the earth—measured at four drops—so many clouds shall arise in the sky to bring about the dissolution of all things.
In the meantime, right there in front of the celestial sages, from that semen were born clouds of corresponding size.
The Saṃvartaka, the Āvarta, the Puṣkara, and the Droṇa—these, O dear one, are the four kinds of great clouds that cause the dissolution of the world.
Then, O best of sages, by the will of Śiva, those clouds, thundering and releasing water with a gentle sound, fell from the sky with a deep roar.
When the sky was thus covered by those [clouds] roaring loudly, Lord Śaṅkara and the goddess, the daughter of Dakṣa, quickly became completely tranquil.
Then, O sage, being free from fear by the command of Śaṅkara, I brought the remaining wedding rites to completion.
And a rain of flowers, released by the hosts of gods with joy, fell everywhere upon the heads of both Śiva and Aśiva, O best of sages.
While musical instruments were being played, while they were singing, and while the best of Brahmins, filled with devotion, were reciting their disputations.
O Nārada, while Rambhā and other celestial women were dancing with great devotion, there was a magnificent festival among the wives of the gods.
Then the Supreme Lord, the master of the expansion of karma, being pleased and assuming a worldly form, spoke with affection to me as I stood with palms joined in reverence.
Īśvara said: "O Brahmin, all the meritorious deeds and the marriage rites have been performed. I am pleased; you are the officiating priest, so what sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) shall I give to you?"
"Ask for her, O eldest of the gods, even if she should be very difficult to obtain. Speak quickly, O illustrious one; there is nothing that I cannot give."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śaṅkara, O sage, I, with palms joined in reverence and a humble soul, bowed repeatedly to the Lord and spoke.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if I am worthy of a boon, then, O Maheśāna, out of great affection, grant me that which I shall speak."
O Maheśvara, you must always remain here upon this sacrificial altar in this very form for the purification of the sins of men.
O Moon-crested Śaṅkara, by means of which [power] one may establish one's own hermitage in his presence and perform penance for the destruction of this one's own sin.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the constellation presided over by Bhaga, on a Sunday, whatever man on earth gazes [upon it] with devotion;
At that very moment, O Hara, may his sins go to destruction; may his merit increase greatly, and may all diseases perish in every way.
Even a woman who is unfortunate, barren, one-eyed, or devoid of beauty will certainly become free from all defects simply by the sight of you.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, which bring all happiness to his own self, Śiva replied with a very gracious mind, "So be it."
Śiva said: "O Creator, for the welfare of all the worlds, I shall remain established upon that altar together with my wife Satī, in accordance with your word."

Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the Lord whose banner is the bull, together with his wife, remained there in the middle of the altar and, having assumed a form consisting of a portion of himself, spoke.
Then, having taken leave of Dakṣa, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord who is affectionate toward his own people, became intent on departing with his wife Satī.
In the meantime, the wise Dakṣa, bowing with humility and joining his palms in reverence, affectionately praised the bull-bannered Lord Śiva.
Then Viṣṇu and all the other gods, as well as the sages and their hosts, bowed down and praised him in various ways, joyfully raising shouts of victory.
Having joyfully placed Satī upon his bull by the command of Dakṣa, the Lord Śambhu himself, mounted on the bull, departed for the slopes of the Himalayas.
Then, near Śaṅkara, that woman of beautiful teeth and lovely smile shone while seated upon her bull, like Kālikā at the edge of the moon.
All the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as the sages beginning with Marīci, even Dakṣa was deluded, and likewise other people remained motionless.
Some played musical instruments, while others sang in melodious tones; they followed Śiva with joy, chanting the pure fame of Śiva.
Then, having been released from the Middle Path by Śambhu with affection, the skillful [Śiva] reached Vadhā along with his attendants; Śambhu was overwhelmed with love.
Although they had been dismissed by Śambhu, Viṣṇu and the other gods followed Śiva once again with supreme devotion and great joy.
Accompanied by all those hosts and joined by his own wife, Śambhu, the Truthful One, reached his own abode, which was graced by the Himavat mountain, filled with great joy.
Having gone there, he joyfully dismissed all the gods, as well as the supreme sages, after honoring them greatly and with great respect.
Having addressed Śambhu, all of them—Viṣṇu and the others, as well as the sages and the gods—with joyful faces, departed for their respective abodes after bowing to and praising him.
Śiva too, exceedingly delighted with his wife, the daughter of Dakṣa, sported while dwelling on a plateau of the Himavat, accompanied by Bhava.
Then, O Sage, Śaṅkara, the creator of the universe, together with his attendants and Satī, returned in great joy to his own abode, Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
O Svāyambhuva Manu, all this has been narrated to you, how in former times the marriage of Vṛṣāyana took place.
Whoever listens to this narrative with an undistracted mind at the time of a wedding, during a sacrifice, or at the commencement [of a rite], having first worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord;
All his marriage-related rites shall proceed without obstacle, and every other auspicious rite shall likewise always be free from impediment.

And a maiden, having heard this auspicious narrative with devotion, shall become virtuous, endowed with happiness, good fortune, character, conduct, and qualities; she shall be chaste and blessed with sons.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Marriage," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: "O dear one, O sinless one, your words are most excellent; for we have indeed heard the most wonderful and auspicious account of the two Śivas."
And this marriage has been heard of correctly as that which removes all delusion, is endowed with supreme knowledge, is the abode of auspiciousness, and is most excellent.
I have a further desire to know the auspicious conduct of Śiva and Śivā; therefore, O one of great wisdom, show incomparable compassion and describe it to me.
Brahmā said: O sage, your inquiry is truly that of one who is perfectly compassionate; for I have been urged by you, O gentle one, to describe the divine play of Śiva.
Having married the goddess Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and mother of the three worlds, he returned to his own abode with great joy; hear from me what he did there.
Then, O celestial sage, having reached his own abode and experiencing joy with his own host, Hara descended from his exceedingly beloved bull.
O celestial sage, having entered his own abode as was fitting, Śiva, accompanied by Satī and performing the duties of worldly life, rejoiced exceedingly.
Then Virūpākṣa, having obtained this daughter of Dakṣa, sent forth his own hosts, including the rivers and others, from the mountain cave.
And the Lord, an ocean of compassion, having adopted the worldly manner of speech, spoke these exceedingly kind words to all of them, Nandi and the others.
Maheśa said: "O my Gaṇas, whenever I remember you here with a mind full of respect for that remembrance, you shall then quickly come to my side."
When Vāmadeva had spoken thus, his own hosts—the rivers and others—greatly impetuous and heroic, flocked together from various places.
When they had departed, Īśvara too wandered about with her; together with the daughter of Dakṣa, he rejoiced intensely in secret.
Once, having gathered wild flowers and fashioned a beautiful garland, he placed it upon Satī in the position of a necklace.
Once, while she was looking at her own face in a mirror, Hara followed her and looked at his own face as well.
Sometimes, coming together, he repeatedly playfully twirls her earring, fastens it, releases it, and she herself even cleans it.
The bull-bannered god makes her feet, which are naturally reddish, fully crimson with his blazing fire.
Even when there was much that ought to be proclaimed loudly before others, he would whisper it into her ear, desiring to behold her face.
Even if he has gone far away, she will come with great effort and follow behind him, her mind fixed on his name and his eyes upon his back.
But the bull-bannered Lord, having vanished right there by means of his illusory power, embraced her; she, startled by fear, became agitated.
Upon her two breasts, which resembled golden lotus buds, he fashioned a decorative mark of musk in the shape of a bee.
Suddenly separating the necklace from her pair of breasts, Hara repeatedly applied his own touch of the hand to that very same spot.
Having repeatedly loosened his armlets, bracelets, and bangles, he then reattached them to their respective places.
"Your friend Savarṇā is coming at this very moment; let her go while she watches these high, swelling breasts of hers with boldness."
Once, his mind intoxicated by passion, the Lord of the Pramathas engaged in playful dalliance with his beloved, bringing them both great joy.
Having gathered lotus flowers and other beautiful blossoms, Śaṅkara respectfully fashioned floral ornaments for all his limbs.
In all the delightful mountain groves, Maheśvara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, sported together with Satī, his beloved.
Without her, Śaṅkara did not move; he did not stand still, nor did he exert himself. Without her, he found no comfort even in what was appropriate.
Having dwelt for a very long time on the mountain thicket of Kailāsa, he went by his own will to the plateau of Himavat, remembering that which is to be remembered.
When Kāma had entered there and was dwelling near Śaṅkara, he expanded his own innate disposition, having perceived the heart-felt intention of the Lord.
All the trees were in bloom, as were other flowering creepers; the waters were filled with blossoming lotuses, and likewise the lotuses were accompanied by bees.
When the proper season had arrived there, that Malaya breeze blew, fragrant with sweet-smelling flowers and delightful, endowed with a pleasing scent.
The Palāśa trees shone like the moon moist with the twilight; their blossoms, like the arrows of Kāma, glowed with joy from the foot of the mountain.
The lotus flowers in the lakes appeared like collyrium applied in streaks; the fair-faced goddess of the wind was intent on bewildering those men.
And *nāgakeśara* trees, beautiful in the presence of Śaṅkara, shone like the banners of the God of Love with their golden-colored blossoms.
In ancient times, having perfumed the breeze with the fragrant scent of clove creepers, he utterly deluded the minds of those filled with desire.
Beautiful, smeared with fire-like incense, and possessing sweet-sounding mango trees, they shone as if covered by the couch of the multitude of Cupid’s arrows.
The waters, free from impurity and filled with blossoming kuśa grass, shone like the minds of sages from which the emergence of pure light is clearly manifest.
Then the frost vanished upon contact with the sun's rays; and those who were previously perceived as having hearts of water were seen to be full of joy.
Then the nights, together with the moon, became serene; like beautiful women, the nights were charming when accompanied by their beloved.
At that time, Mahādeva, together with Satī, took delight for a very long duration in the excellent mountain groves and along the rivers according to his desire.
O Sage, the daughter of Dakṣa then shone so with him that Hara could not find peace for even a moment without her.
In the matter of enjoyment, the virtuous goddess, dear to his heart, seemed to enter the body of Hara, as if making him drink its essence.
Adorning her entire body with flower garlands fashioned by his own hands, he brought her fresh joy.
Through conversations, glances, smiles, and likewise through dialogues, Hara indicated to him that Girijā was his own wife.
Hara, his body sustained by drinking the nectar from that moon-like face, once assumed a slender and extraordinary form.
Bound by dwelling in her lotus-like mouth, by her beauty, and by her playful jests—as if bound by her virtues—this great elephant was no longer intent on any other activity.

Thus Maheśa took delight day after day with the daughter of Dakṣa in the caves upon the ridges and slopes of the Himalayan groves; O celestial sage, as he sported there, ten times ten and another five years passed away.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Playful Sport of Satī and Śiva," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Once, at the arrival of the rainy season, Dakṣa’s daughter spoke to the bull-bannered Lord who was staying on Mount Kailāsa.
Satī said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śambhu, you who are as dear to me as my own life! O Lord, giver of honor, hear my words and act accordingly upon hearing them."
This time of the arrival of the clouds has arrived, which is most difficult to endure; masses of clouds of many colors fill the sky and all the quarters with their symphony.
The swift winds blow, stealing away the heart, washed with the pollen of kadamba flowers and dragging along droplets of water.
Whose mind would not be violently agitated by the loud thundering of clouds that release torrents of rain and bear lightning as their banners?
Neither the sun is seen, nor is the lord of the night obscured by clouds; even by day, it shines like night, bringing about the calamity of separation for those who are parted.
O Śaṅkara, clouds driven by the wind, not remaining in one place and thundering, appear as if they were falling upon the heads of the worlds.
Struck by the wind, the great trees appear as if dancing in the sky; they strike terror into the hearts of the timid, yet are desired by lovers.
Behind the smooth, dark blue collyrium of the mass of clouds, a row of cranes appeared very high, like foam upon the surface of the Yamunā.
At the end of the night, a dark halo is seen surrounding the moon, like the blazing submarine fire within the ocean.
In this place, O Virūpākṣa, even the courtyards of the houses sprout crops; what more need I say regarding the growth of grain elsewhere?
This bright Himalaya mountain, with its dark, silver, and red [peaks], resembles the Ocean of Milk with its mass of clouds resting upon Mount Mandara.
And then, peerless Fortune resorted crookedly to the *kiṃśuka* trees; for in the Kali age, Fortune will abandon the virtuous and go to those who are high and low.
Thrilled repeatedly by the sound of the mandāra, stana, and pīlu trees, they constantly utter their cries in every forest, signaling their presence from behind.
Sweet and enchanting to the cātakas longing for the clouds, the showers fell like arrows of rain, striking the heat that had arisen on the path.
Behold the misconduct of the clouds toward my body with their showers of hailstones—those clouds which cover the peacocks and the cātaka birds when I am present!
Having witnessed the defeat even of their friend by Śikha and Sāraṅga, they feel joy toward Giriśa, though his mind is far away.
In this difficult time, the crows and the cakora birds have made their homes in the blue [sky]; how will you find peace without you?
We have a great fear today that the wielder of the Pināka bow might arise from the clouds; therefore, at my word, strive to find a dwelling place without delay.
Whether on Kailāsa, or on the Himālaya, or at Mahākāśī on this earth—O Bull-bannered One, establish your residence there in a manner suited to that place.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus repeatedly by that daughter of Dakṣa, Śambhu laughed, his abode of smiles illuminated by the rays of the moon resting upon his head.
Then the Great-Souled One, the Supreme Lord who knows all principles, spoke to the Goddess Satī with a smile parting his lips, gladdening her.
