Īśvara said: "O charming one, my beloved, wherever I must dwell for your pleasure, there the clouds shall never go."
Clouds move along the slopes of the mountain, even during the rains, O beautiful one, on that mountain which is ever crowned with snow.
Likewise, O Goddess, the clouds generally move along the foothills of Kailāsa; they never go beyond that point.
The clouds, such as the Puṣkarāvartakas and others, do not go above Mount Sumeru; having reached the base of Jambūdvīpa, they turn back.
When these lords of mountains have been described, tell me quickly which one among them would most appeal to your heart for a dwelling.
On the snow-born mountain, your curiosities during your free wanderings shall be joyfully sung by throngs of golden-winged birds with sweet-toned voices, whose sounds rise like waves.

Those perfected women (siddhāṅganās), having arranged their seats upon the earth, desire that which is offered with curiosity; they sport at will on the mountain with its jeweled terraces and serve them by offering fruits and other gifts.

The daughters of the serpent-lords, the daughters of the mountains, the daughters of the nāgas, and those with the faces of excellent horses—all of them shall constantly provide you assistance with expressions of joyful approval.

Having seen that incomparable form and his most beautiful face, women—whose own bodies are surpassed by his luster and whose lovely forms possess unblinking eyes—constantly treat their own bodies and their own sets of physical attributes with utter disdain.

Menakā, the wife of the King of Mountains, who is renowned throughout the three worlds for her beauty and virtues—she too will always bring delight to your mind there with her entreaties and other such means.

For this city, which possesses noble forms and is honored by the lords of mountains who seek your joy through their various divisions, must indeed always be governed by you with discipline; though it may occasionally be subject to grief, it should daily be filled with delight through virtues and other such qualities.
O beloved, do you wish to go to that place which is always filled with the splendor of spring, surrounded by groves and the delightful warbling of cuckoos?
The Himālaya, the king of mountains, which is surrounded by coolness and filled with many lakes abounding in water, and endowed with hundreds of lotus-pools.
Behold for a moment the flowers upon the grassy meadows, where trees known as "Kalpa" grant all desires, and where horses and elephants roam like cattle.
O Mahāmāyā, that temple was filled with various herds of deer, where the hosts of predatory beasts were pacified, and it was frequented by sages and ascetics.
It was resplendent with ramparts of crystal, gold, and silver, and was beautifully adorned on all sides by the expanses of lakes such as Mānasa.
It was filled with golden lotuses having jeweled stalks, both in bud and full bloom, as well as countless porpoises, tortoises, crocodiles, and dolphins.
O Goddess of the gods, it is likewise adorned with charming blue lotuses and the like, as well as with all kinds of fragrant substances and saffron.
It was adorned by young and lofty grassy banks, which were filled with pure, fragrant waters of brilliant clarity.
It was adorned with *śākhoṭa* trees that seemed to be dancing, avoiding their own origin, and beautified by *kāmadeva* cranes and intoxicated *cakrāṅga* birds.
Resounding with the joyful humming of bees and other insects that warble sweetly and cause delight, it serves as an inflamer of passion.
Of Vāsava, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa; of Agni, of the Lord of the West (Kauverya), of Māruta, and of the Supreme (Īśāna).
The lofty abode of the gods on Mount Meru, its peaks adorned by cities, was frequented by throngs of beautiful-limbed celestial nymphs such as Rambhā, Śacī, and Menakā.
But what do you desire—to sport upon this great mountain, the most delightful and essential among all the mountains that support the earth?
There, the goddess Śacī, accompanied by her friends and adorned by hosts of Apsarases, will constantly provide you with worthy assistance.
Or else, you desire a place on my Kailāsa, the king of mountains and eternal refuge, which is resplendent with the city of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).

In that place, which was as pure as the flood of the Ganges' waters, radiant as the full moon, and where the daughters of Brahmā were constantly heard chanting within the caves and upon the mountain peaks.
O beautiful one, you are endowed with various herds of deer, surrounded by hundreds of lotus-pools, and possess all excellent qualities even more than Mount Sumeru, the abode of true things.
In whichever of these places your heart desires to dwell, tell me that quickly; I shall make it your abode.
Brahmā said: When Śaṅkara had spoken thus, the daughter of Dakṣa then slowly addressed these words to Mahādeva regarding her own manifestation.
Satyuvāca said: "I desire to dwell with you on Himavat itself; establish your residence on that very great mountain without delay."
Brahmā said: Then, having heard those words, Hara, utterly bewildered, went together with the daughter of Dakṣa to the lofty peak of the Himālaya mountain.
Accompanied by hosts of perfected women and inaccessible even to birds, he went to the delightful peak, adorned with lakes and forests.
Accompanied by Satī, Śambhu reached the peak, which was variegated with jewels and adorned with lotuses of diverse forms, resembling the rising sun.
In that place, which was composed of crystal and clouds, adorned with rows of green trees, and endowed with various clusters of flowers and beautiful lakes.
The tips of the tree branches were in full bloom, frequented by humming bees, and likewise adorned with blossoming lotuses and clusters of blue water-lilies.
It was adorned with ruddy geese and other waterfowl, with kadamba ducks, swans, and herons, and resounded with the cries of intoxicated cranes, curlews, and blue-necked peacocks.
With the sweet warbling of male cuckoos attended by their flocks, and with horse-faced siddhas, apsarases, and guhyakas;
It was frequented by Vidyadhara goddesses and Kinnari women, and joined by matrons, mountain-dwelling women, and maidens.
It was adorned by the sounds of lutes, cymbals, and the intoxicating music of mṛdaṅgas and paṭaha drums, and by dancing apsarases who had arisen out of curiosity.
It was completely surrounded by divine ponds and large lakes, and was perpetually adorned with fragrant, blossoming flowers and groves of trees.
On the peak near the city of Śailarāja, the Bull-bannered Lord sported for a long time with Satī; such is the splendor of those who have become thus.
In that place equal to heaven, Śaṅkara sported joyfully with Satī for ten thousand divine years.
Sometimes Hara goes from that place to another region; sometimes the Goddess [goes] to the peak of Meru, which is always surrounded by gods.
Having gone again and again to various islands, as well as to gardens, forests, and the surface of the earth, he returned once more to that place and enjoyed the bliss of his virtuous wife.
He perceived no difference between day and night, nor did he distinguish between sacred knowledge and austerity; for Śambhu, with his mind fixed on the Truth, felt only pure joy.
In this way, they always beheld the face of Mahādeva as truth; and Mahādeva, too, everywhere and at all times beheld the face of Satī.
Thus, through their mutual union, Kālī and Śiva caused the tree of passion to grow by watering it with the waters of their affectionate sentiments.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Pastimes of Śiva and Śivā," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having thus sported with Śaṅkara, that Satī became exceedingly satisfied and yet became filled with great detachment.
One day, the goddess Satī, having met Śiva in private, bowed to him with true devotion and, placing her hands together in respectful salutation, spoke aloud.
Then, having bowed to the well-pleased Lord, that Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, spoke with devotion and palms joined in reverence, bowing low in humility.
Satyu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord, ocean of compassion! O Great Yogin, deliverer of the distressed, show mercy upon me.
You are the Supreme Person, the Lord, beyond the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas; you are devoid of attributes yet possessed of attributes, the witness, the changeless Great Master.
I am blessed, for I have become your beloved, a loving wife who delights in your company; you have become my husband and lord—O Hara, grant this through your devotion and affection!
O Lord, this supreme monastery has been completed by you after many years; I am satisfied, O Great Sovereign, and my mind is now at peace.
O Lord of Gods, O Hara, I desire to know the supreme reality that brings happiness, by which a living being may swiftly cross over the suffering of saṃsāra.
O Lord, please show mercy and tell me that reality by performing which a worldly soul may attain the supreme state and no longer remain subject to saṃsāra.
Brahmā said: O sage, thus did that virtuous Satī, the primordial Śakti and Great Goddess Maheśānī, who exists solely for the upliftment of living beings, inquire of Śaṅkara with true devotion.
Having heard that, Lord Śiva, who assumes a physical form by his own will, being supremely pleased and possessing a mind detached through yoga, spoke to Satī.
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, daughter of Dakṣa, O Maheśvarī; I shall proclaim that supreme reality by means of which one who possesses remorse becomes liberated.
O Supreme Goddess, know that supreme reality is consciousness; it is the second remembrance wherein one of pure intellect realizes, "I am Brahman."
O beloved, that [state] is rare in the three worlds, and one who knows it is scarce; such as I am, I am always the manifest Brahman, higher than the highest.
Therefore, devotion to Me, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is easily attained through My grace; it is indeed proclaimed to be ninefold.

Indeed, there is no difference between devotion and knowledge; the doer of the former always possesses happiness. However, true realization never arises for one who possesses that which is opposed to devotion.
O Goddess, due to the power of that [sin], being always devoid of devotion, I go even to the houses of the low-born and those of inferior caste; of this there is no doubt.

O Goddess, that devotion is considered to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā). That which is ritualistic (vaidhī) and that which is spontaneous (svābhāvikī)—the former is remembered as inferior, while the latter is superior.

The ultimate [attainment] is of two kinds due to the division of the ultimate; for those two are indeed each of two types. The ultimate is to be known as sixfold, while the second is recorded as being of one kind.

The wise know that [the path] to be manifold due to the distinction between what is prescribed and what is not prescribed; and because of the multiplicity of those two, the true nature of reality has been described elsewhere.
O beloved, those two [scriptures] with nine limbs each have been described by the sages; O daughter of Dakṣa, listen as I describe those nine limbs out of affection.
O Goddess, let there always be for me hearing, chanting, remembering, and likewise serving, as well as servitude, worship, and salutation.
The wise know that friendship and self-surrender are its nine limbs; indeed, many secondary limbs (upāṅgas) of that [worship] toward Śiva have been described.
Listen, O Goddess, to the characteristics of the nine limbs individually; for when the mind is fixed upon devotion to me, they indeed bestow both devotion and liberation.
Listening to that [teaching] while joyfully honoring the discourse with one's body and other faculties through a steady posture is what is called "listening."
Beholding my births and deeds with the space of the heart, their joyful recitation is called this "Kīrtana."
O Goddess, having seen me as all-pervading, eternally and everywhere at all times, one always attains fearlessness in the world; that is declared to be "recollection" (smaraṇa).
Beginning from dawn during the time of service, one should serve with a focused heart; constant fearlessness in the world is declared to be that [true] remembrance.

Service that is always performed with favorability toward the one to be served is indeed called "dear servitude" (priyadāsya), which is enjoyed by the hosts of gopīs through the savoring of the nectar of the heart.

Always acting in accordance with the wishes of my servants, the worship of the Supreme Self consists of the offering of the sixteen items, beginning with water for the feet, according to the prescribed rite.
When one touches the ground with all eight limbs through the sequential recitation of mantras and meditation by means of both mind and speech, that indeed is called *vaṃdana*.
"Whatever the Lord does for me, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the conviction that 'all of that is for my welfare' is the defining characteristic of friendship."
Having made everything, including the body and so forth, an offering to Him for His pleasure, that which is emptiness for the sake of sustenance is the surrender of the self.
The nine limbs [of my scripture] bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through devotion to me; they are exceedingly dear to me and are the generators of knowledge.
Indeed, many ancillary practices (upāṅgas) of devotion to me have been taught, such as the service of the bilva tree and others; these should be gathered together through careful reflection.

Thus, O beloved, this devotion of mine, complete with all its limbs and sub-limbs, shines forth as the most excellent of all; it is the mother of wisdom and dispassion, and the handmaid of liberation.
The arising of the fruits of all actions is always as dear to you as I am; he in whose mind she dwells eternally is always as dear to me as I am.
O Goddess of the gods, in the four yugas, and especially in the Kali age, there is no path in the three worlds that brings such happiness as devotion.
But in the Kali age, O Goddess, knowledge and dispassion, though appearing aged and devoid of festive joy, have become utterly worn out due to the absence of those who receive them.
Devotion yields its fruit perceptibly even in all ages; by its power, I am eternally under its sway—of this there is no doubt.
In this world, I am always the helper of that man who possesses devotion; I am the remover of his obstacles, and his enemy shall be punished—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, for the sake of my devotee, I, overwhelmed with wrath, burned my own protector with the fire born from my eye.
O Goddess, it is said that for the sake of my devotee, I once stood above the sun; filled with extreme wrath, I took up my trident and pursued him in the past.
O Goddess, for the sake of his devotee, I angrily abandoned Rāvaṇa along with his hosts; indeed, no partiality was ever shown toward him by me.
O Goddess, for the sake of my devotee, I indeed expelled Vyāsa, who was possessed by a wicked intellect, from Kāśī after having him punished by Nandin out of anger.
O Goddess of gods, what is the use of much speaking? For I am always dependent upon devotion; there is no doubt in this matter that I am entirely under the control of the person who performs it.
Brahmā said: Having thus heard the greatness of devotion, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, rejoiced exceedingly in her heart and bowed to Śiva with joy.
O Sage, with true devotion he again questioned him concerning that section of the scripture—a work that brings happiness to the world and is dedicated to the liberation of living beings.
The science of self-restraint and mantras, its greatness in particular, as well as other religious matters that truly effect the liberation of living beings.
Having heard that question from Satī, Śaṅkara, with a delighted mind, described it in its entirety with great affection for the sake of liberating all living beings.
There, Maheśvara indeed spoke the scripture together with its ritual manual, its five ancillaries, and the majesty of each respective supreme deity.
O Lord of Sages, [tell us] their stories based on history, as well as the greatness of devotion, the duties of the various castes and stages of life, and the duties of kings.

He heard the greatness of the duties of women, the eternal system of castes and stages of life, as well as the science of medicine and the science of astrology, which brings happiness to living beings.
Having shown compassion, Maheśāna has described in truth the supreme science of palmistry (sāmudrika) and many other scriptures in detail.
Thus, the omniscient Śiva and Satī, who bestow happiness upon the three worlds, have assumed forms endowed with excellent qualities for the sake of benefiting the world.
Then those two, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, sported in many ways on Kailāsa, on the Himavat mountain, and in other places.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Devotion," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Vidhi, O Lord of Creatures, O one of great wisdom, O compassionate one! You have caused us to hear the auspicious glory of Śiva and Satī, who bestows happiness.
Now, out of affection for the virtuous, tell me of that supreme and most excellent glory: what did that auspicious couple do, and how indeed did they conduct themselves?
Brahmā said: O sage, listen with love to the account of Satī and Śiva from me; having adopted a worldly course, they sported together every day.
Then, O Sage, the great goddess Satī did not obtain a separation from Śaṅkara while he was asleep; so say some of great intelligence.
O Sage, since these two powers are always joined together like speech and its meaning, how could their separation possibly occur in reality?
Or rather, because they delight in divine play (līlā), all that may come together; for whatever the Lord and Satī do, they remain within the ways of worldly existence.
Having been abandoned by her husband at Janaka’s sacrifice due to Śambhu’s disregard, that daughter of Dakṣa, seeing this, gave up her body there while united with him.
Furthermore, she herself appeared again in the Himalayas by the name of Satī; having performed extensive austerities, she obtained Śiva as her husband through marriage, becoming known as Pārvatī.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, Nārada then questioned the Creator regarding the great glory of Śiva and Aśiva.
Nārada said: O blessed Vidhi, disciple of Viṣṇu, tell me in detail that account of Śiva and Aśiva, which follows the conduct of their respective states of being.
For what reason did Śaṅkara abandon his wife, who was dearer to him than life? Therefore, O father, tell me this; we consider it to be truly wondrous.
O son born of the sacrifice, why did Śiva show you no regard? And how did she abandon her body after going there to the sacrifice of her father?
What happened there after that, and what did Maheśvara do? Tell me all of that; endowed with faith, I am eager to hear it.
Brahmā said: Listen, dear one, with supreme affection along with the sages, O Nārada, O most excellent son of great wisdom, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord.
Having paid homage to Maheśāna, who is served by Harya and the other gods, I shall proclaim the supreme Brahman and its most wonderful life-story.
Indeed, all this is the play of Śiva; for the Lord is the performer of manifold sports, independent and changeless, and Satī herself was likewise of that same nature.
Otherwise, O Sage, what purpose would there be in performing that ritual? He alone is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Lord.
He whom the Lord of Śrī, I myself, all the gods, the high-souled sages, and the Siddhas such as Sanaka and others always worship.
O dear one, that Lord Śaṅkara, who is Śiva, is he whose glory the Residue (Śeṣa) constantly and eternally sings with joy, yet never reaches the end.
This entire world is a delusion regarding reality, arising from His very sport; therein no one is at fault, for He is the all-pervading impeller.
Once, Rudra, the source of existence, skilled in divine play, wandered through the three worlds mounted upon his bull, accompanied by Satī.
Having arrived at the Daṇḍaka forest and wandering across the earth whose garment is the ocean, the Lord, for whom truth is his wager, showed the beauty of the land there to Satī.
There, Hara beheld Rāma accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, searching for his beloved Sītā, who had been carried off by Rāvaṇa through deceit.
Uttering "Alas, Sītā! with a mind possessed by the pain of separation, he looked here and there, weeping indeed again and again.

To one who desires the attainment of that [state], who asks in his heart about its course, whose intellect is lost, who is shameless, and who is overwhelmed by grief—[from Mars and the other planets].
The hero born of the solar dynasty, the son of King Daśaratha, the elder brother of Bharata, was now devoid of joy and shorn of his luster.
The noble-minded Hara, his desires fulfilled and dependent on the boon [he had granted], joyfully recognized Rāma as he wandered in the forest with Lakṣmaṇa.
Saying "Victory!", Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, moved elsewhere in that forest and did not grant his own sight to Rāma.
Having seen such a virtuous and enchanting play of Śiva, she, utterly amazed and deluded by Śiva’s māyā, spoke to Śiva.
Satī said: "O God of gods, Supreme Brahman, Lord of all, Supreme Sovereign! Hari, Brahmā, and all the other deities always serve you."
For you are indeed to be saluted by all, to be served, and to be meditated upon at all times; you are the supreme Lord, free from change, who is to be known with effort through the Vedānta.
"O Lord, who are these two men whose forms are distressed by separation? Wandering in the forest, they are afflicted and miserable, yet they are heroes and wielders of the bow."
Having seen the elder of those two, who is dark as a lotus, for what reason indeed have you now become so joyful and serene in soul, like a devotee?
"O Lord Śaṅkara, you ought to sever this doubt of mine; for a master, O Lord, deserves prostration from his very servant."
Brahmā said: The primordial power, the goddess Satī, that supreme sovereign Śivā, having come under the influence of Śiva’s Māyā, questioned the Lord Śiva in this manner.
Having heard those words of Satī, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord who is skilled in divine play, laughed and then spoke to Satī.
The Supreme Lord said: Listen, O Goddess Satī, with affection; I speak the truth and not deceitfully. By the power of the granting of this boon, you shall indeed offer obeisance with such reverence.
O Goddess, the two brothers named Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, born of the solar dynasty and sons of Daśaratha, are esteemed by heroes and endowed with wisdom.
The younger brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, was fair-complexioned and light; the elder, named Rāma, was Viṣṇu himself, a full incarnation free from all affliction.
"Having descended to the earth for the protection of the virtuous and for our welfare," having said this, that Lord, who brings about the remembrance of Śambhu, ceased speaking.
Even after hearing these words of Śambhu, his mind did not believe; for the Māyā of Śiva is powerful, she who deludes the three worlds.
Perceiving her mind to be distrustful, the eternal Śambhu, the Lord who is skilled in divine play, spoke these words:
Śiva said: Listen to my words, O Goddess; if your mind does not believe, then perform an examination of Rāma yourself with your own intellect.
O virtuous and beloved one, act in such a way that my delusion may perish; go there and remain for a while, staying beneath the banyan tree as an observer.
Brahmā said: By the command of Śiva, the goddess Satī went there and reflected: "How may I perform a test of Rāma, who wanders in the forest?"
Assuming the form of Sītā, I shall go into the presence of Rāma; if Rāma is Hari, he will understand everything, and not otherwise.
Having reflected thus, that virtuous Sītā, becoming devoted to delusion, approached Rāma’s presence for the purpose of testing him.
Seeing the virtuous lady in the form of Sītā and chanting the name "Śiva," the scion of Raghu laughed, recognized her, bowed, and spoke.
Rāma said: O Satī, tell me out of love: where has your Śambhu gone? For why have you come alone to the forest without your husband?
O virtuous lady, why have you abandoned your own true form and assumed this appearance? O Goddess, having shown compassion toward me, tell me the reason for that.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Rāma, the virtuous woman was then startled; remembering what Śiva had said and considering it to be infallible, she became deeply ashamed.
Recognizing Rāma as Viṣṇu and establishing his own true nature, and remembering the state of Śiva in his heart, Satī spoke with a serene mind.
The Lord Śiva, the independent Supreme Master, wandering over the earth with his attendants, came here into this forest.
For there he indeed saw you, intent on searching for Sītā, together with Lakṣmaṇa, separated from her and with your mind fixed upon Sītā.
Having bowed to you, he went to the foot of a banyan tree and stood right there, joyfully praising your supreme Vaiṣṇava majesty.
He became joyful merely upon seeing you, Hari, with four arms; yet he attained such bliss as he beheld this stainless form that it surpassed even that joy.
Having heard those words of Śambhu and having brought them to my mind, O Rāghava, I conducted that test for you by his command.
O Rāma, it is known to me that you are Viṣṇu; your entire sovereignty has been witnessed by me. Even then, O high-minded one, listen to this which remains beyond all doubt.
How are you to be saluted by him? Tell me the truth before me; make me free from doubt, lest you quickly incur sin.
Brahmā said: Having heard her words, Rāma’s eyes blossomed with joy; he remembered his lord Śambhu, and love increased even more within his heart.
O Sage, Satī did not go into the presence of Śambhu without his command; and after describing her own greatness, Rāghava spoke to Satī.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Test of Rāma," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Rāma said: O Goddess, once in the past, Śambhu, the supreme bestower of life, summoned Viśvakarman to his own world, which is beyond the highest.
By means of that [wealth], he had a beautiful and extensive mansion properly constructed within the cowshed of his own milch-cow, and therein a magnificent throne.
There, Śaṅkara had Viśvakarman fashion a great, divine, and most excellent parasol, ever wondrous, for the purpose of warding off obstacles.
He quickly offered oblations to Śakra and all the hosts of deities, as well as to the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and all the Upadeśas in their entirety.
All the gods and the Āgamas, the ritual procedures along with their sons, and even the sages; all the goddesses accompanied by Apsarases and endowed with various objects.
And from the gods, as well as from the rishis, the siddhas, and even the serpent-beings, he brought sixteen auspicious maidens each.
O Sage, having caused various musical instruments, headed by the lute and the drum, to be played by excellent singers, he celebrated a festival.
The materials suitable for the royal consecration, along with all medicinal herbs and waters from manifest sacred fords, were used to fill five ritual jars.
Likewise, Śaṅkara then had other divine arrangements brought by his own attendants; he caused the great sound of the chanting of the Vedas to be made.
Then, O Goddess, having summoned Hari from Vaikuṇṭha with a delighted mind, Maheśvara rejoiced because of his perfect devotion.
After seating Hari upon that excellent lion-throne for a short while, Mahādeva affectionately adorned him in every way.
Maheśa himself consecrated him, who was adorned with a beautiful crown and had performed the auspicious rites of kautuka, within the pavilion of the universe.
Since he had bestowed his own entire sovereignty—which was not to pass to anyone else—Śambhu, who is independent and affectionate toward his devotees, praised him.

He who is compassionate toward his devotees, independent, and the bestower of boons, spoke these words to Brahmā, the creator of the world, making known that [the power] was dependent upon his own choice.
Maheśa said: From this time forward, O Lord of the World, by my command, this Hari—Viṣṇu himself—has become worthy of my salutation; indeed, he hears everything.
O dear one, let all the gods and others bow down to this Hari; by my command, let these Vedas describe Hari just as they describe me.

Rāma said: Having spoken thus, Rudra himself, whose soul was gratified by devotion to Viṣṇu, who is the giver of boons and compassionate toward his devotees, bowed indeed to the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Then Hari was thus saluted by Brahmā and the other gods, as well as by all the demigods, sages, perfected beings (siddhas), and others.
Then Maheśa, being well-pleased and affectionate toward his devotees, granted great boons to Hari, the lord of the gods, in the assembly of the deities.

Maheśa said: "By my command, you are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of all worlds; you are the bestower of virtue, wealth, and desire, and the punisher of those who act with misconduct."
Lord of the world, worshiped by the world, possessed of great strength and prowess—you shall indeed be invincible in battle even for me in any place whatsoever.
Accept these three powers—will and the others—which have been bestowed upon you by me; they grant you the power for manifold divine plays and sovereignty over the three worlds.
O Hari, those who hate you must certainly be punished by me with great effort; O Viṣṇu, the supreme liberation must be granted by me to your devotees.
And take also this Māyā, which is difficult even for the gods and others to dispel; by her, the entire universe will become deluded and assume the nature of insentience.
O Hari, that right arm of mine is your own; indeed, you shall be both the creator and the protector of this very ordinance.
He who is Rudra is my heart; he is indeed myself, there is no doubt. He too is always to be worshipped by you, and certainly even by Brahmā and the other gods.
Abiding here, protect the entire world in particular, through various distinct incarnations and by means of diverse agents who act perpetually.
This place of yours, which possesses supreme supernatural power, shall become known as Goloka in my world, most brilliantly radiant.
"O Hari, those incarnations of yours who will appear on earth as its protectors—I shall certainly behold them with joy, by virtue of my own boon."
Rāma said: Having attained unbroken sovereignty through Hari, Hara himself, the Lord of Umā, sports at will on Kailāsa with his own attendants.
From that time forward, the Lord of Lakṣmī likewise assumed the guise of a cowherd; the master of the cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows went there with great affection.
That Viṣṇu as well, with a gracious soul, protected the entire world; by the command of Śiva, he assumed various incarnations as its sustainer and creator.
Now, by the command of Śaṅkara, he descended into four forms: "I am Rāma," and there [were] Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna.
Then, O Goddess, by my father’s command, I came today to the forest accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; yet, through the power of fate, I became sorrowful.
"My wife Sītā has been abducted by some night-stalker"; thus saying, I, separated from my beloved, shall search for her here in the forest with my kinsman.
If I have obtained the sight of you, O virtuous mother, it will by every means be well for me through your grace; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, by your grace, there will be no doubt that I shall obtain the boon of recovering Sītā after slaying that sinful Rākṣasa who causes you such sorrow.
What great fortune is mine this very day, since you both have shown me mercy; for he toward whom you feel compassion is a blessed and most excellent man.
Having spoken thus in many ways and having bowed deeply to the virtuous Śivā, the scion of the Raghus wandered in that forest by her command.
Then, having heard the words of the self-restrained Rāma, Satī became joyful, praising within her heart his devotion to Śiva.
Remembering her own deed with her mind, she felt profound grief; returning to the presence of Śiva, she stood there indifferent and pale.
As she walked along the path, that goddess reflected again and again: "I have not accepted what was spoken by Śiva; instead, I have harbored an evil thought toward Rāma."
"What answer shall I give upon going into the presence of Śaṅkara?"—thinking thus in many ways, he then experienced great remorse.
Having approached the presence of Śambhu, she bowed to Śiva with her heart, her face dejected, overwhelmed by grief, and bereft of luster.
Then, seeing her distressed, Hara asked after her welfare and spoke these words with affection: "How was that test conducted?"
Having heard Śiva’s words, Satī, her face bowed down, remained there in his presence, despondent with grief and saying nothing at all.
Then, having meditated, Maheśa, the great yogi who is skilled in manifold divine sports, understood within his heart the conduct of Dakṣa’s wife.
He then remembered his former vow made out of anger toward Hari; and being entreated by him, Rudra, the upholder of the bounds of morality, [acted].
Despondency arose in the mind of the Lord there, and he spoke thus: "He who is the speaker of Dharma, the performer of Dharma, and the eternal protector of Dharma."
Śiva said: "If I were to maintain as great an affection for the daughter of Dakṣa as I did before, my pure vow would be destroyed, even though I follow the ways of worldly play."
Brahmā said: Having reflected thus in many ways within his heart, he abandoned that Satī; yet, as the protector of the Vedic dharma, he did not cause the wager to be lost.
Then, having mentally abandoned that Satī, the Supreme Lord went to his own mountain; for that Lord indeed spoke the truth.
As Maheśvara was walking along the path, a voice from the sky spoke to him, making it heard by all there, and Dakṣa’s daughter in particular.
The Voice from the Sky said: "O Supreme Lord, you are blessed; today there is no other like you as a stake, nor any other great yogi or great lord in these three worlds."
Brahmā said: Having heard the voice from the sky, the goddess of radiant luster questioned Śiva: "O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, tell me, what wager has he made?"
Although questioned thus by Satī, the Lord Giriśa, who acts for the welfare of others, did not previously make his own wager before Kārttikeya regarding her marriage.
Then, O sage, Satī, meditating upon Śiva, her husband who was dearer to her than life itself, understood the entire reason for that abandonment by her beloved.
Then, having quickly realized her own abandonment by Śambhu, the daughter of Dakṣa grieved intensely; sighing repeatedly from him, she was overcome with sorrow.
Śiva, having understood her intention, concealed his mind-born passion; for the Lord, recounting many stories, indeed made his own vow true.
Relating various stories, he reached Kailāsa; remaining in that excellent state, the yogi, maintaining his meditative absorption, assumed his own true form.
There, O sage, Satī remained in her abode with a deeply despondent mind; yet no one perceived that conduct of Śiva and her.
In this manner, O great sage, a vast period of time passed for those two lords as they followed the worldly play while remaining in the bodies they had assumed.
Then Giriśa abandoned that meditation; thereafter, Satī, the Mother of the World who removes supreme suffering, knowing that [had happened], arrived there.
Then the Goddess addressed Śiva with a heart in anguish; the noble-minded Śambhu offered her a seat directly in front of him.
He spoke many delightful stories with great affection, and by performing such a divine play, he instantly rendered her free from sorrow.
As before, she obtained happiness and did not abandon her wager; O dear one, it should not be considered a wonder that this occurred with Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
"O Sage, thus do some sages speak regarding the discourse on Śiva and Aśiva; indeed, they are ignorant, for how could there be a separation between the two?"
Who can truly know the conduct of Śiva and Aśiva, for they always act out their deeds while sporting according to their own will?
Satī and Śiva are indeed always united, like speech and its meaning; their separation could only occur by the will of those two themselves.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Separation from Satī," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In ancient times, a great sacrifice was performed according to the prescribed rites for all the high-souled sages who had assembled at Prayāga.
There, the perfected ones—Sanaka and the other celestial sages, along with the Prajāpatis and the gods, who were wise and possessed the vision of Brahman—arrived.
I arrived there accompanied by my retinue, joined by the Nigamas and Āgamas, who were embodied and possessed of great splendor.
Indeed, their assembly became diverse and filled with festivities; there, a discourse on knowledge arose, originating from various scriptures.
At that moment, O Sage, the Lord Rudra, the master who brings welfare to the three worlds, arrived there accompanied by his consort and his attendants, uttering auspicious words.
Having seen Śiva, all the gods, as well as the Siddhas and the sages, bowed with devotion to that Lord and likewise offered hymns of praise, just as I have done.
All, filled with joy and satisfied by the sight of their Lord, stood in their respective places according to Śiva’s command, recounting their own experiences.
At that moment, the lord Dakṣa, the master of the Prajāpatis, arrived there by chance, highly pleased and radiant with splendor.
Having bowed to me, that Dakṣa, the lord of the universe, who is worthy of honor yet proud and averse to the ultimate reality, remained there by my command.
Honored with hymns and prostrations by all the divine sages, the one of supreme splendor, Dakṣa, joined his palms in reverence before those who were bowed low.
Then Maheśvara, seated upon his own throne, being independent and the supreme benefactor who creates various abodes, became skilled in assuming various forms.
Having seen Hara there with his head bowed, my son Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, being of an unpacified mind, suddenly became enraged at Rudra.
Beholding the great lord Rudra with a cruel gaze, Mahāgarva—devoid of wisdom—spoke aloud so that everyone might hear him.
For all these gods and asuras, as well as the best of brahmins and the sages, bow deeply before me; how then has he, who is surrounded by ghosts and goblins, become so high-minded like a wicked man?

Dwelling in cremation grounds and devoid of shame, why does he not now offer salutation to me? Having abandoned his duties, frequented by spirits and goblins, intoxicated, ignorant, and always a detractor of political wisdom.
Seeing heretics, wicked men of sinful character, and those who were arrogant revilers of the twice-born, as well as one constantly addicted to sexual pleasure with his wife, I proceeded to curse him.

Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, that great rogue, filled with rage, then addressed Rudra: "Let these best of Brahmins and likewise the gods listen; you ought indeed to make him worthy of being slain by me."

Dakṣa said: "This Rudra has indeed been excluded from my sacrifice; he transcends the [social] classes and possesses a form devoid of color. Let him receive no share along with the gods—he who dwells in cremation grounds and is of low birth."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words spoken by Dakṣa, many people, including Bhṛgu and others, censured Rudra—who was of wicked nature—considering him to be equal to the gods.
Having heard those words, the attendant Nandin, his eyes reddened with saliva and filled with intense rage, spoke quickly to Dakṣa, intent on pronouncing a curse.
Nandīśvara said: "O rogue, O great fool, O wicked-minded Dakṣa! How indeed have you excluded my Lord Maheśa from the sacrifice?"
How has this Hara been cursed—he by whose mere remembrance sacrifices become fruitful and sacred pilgrimage sites are purified?
"O evil-minded Dakṣa, this [sacrifice] of yours has been cursed in vain due to your brazen insolence; and the faultless, great lord Rudra has been mocked in vain."
By whom this universe was created, protected, and destroyed at the end—how could that Rudra, the Great Lord (Maheśa), be cursed by you, O lowest of Brahmins?
Thus rebuked by Nandin, Prajāpati Dakṣa, filled with rage, then cursed Nandin.
Dakṣa said: "May you all, O hosts of Rudra, indeed become outsiders to the Vedas; may you be abandoned by the path of the Vedas and likewise forsaken by the great ṛṣis."
Devoted to the doctrines of heretics, excluded from the conduct of the virtuous, they were addicted to drinking liquor and wore matted hair, ashes, and bones.
Brahmā said: Thus were the servants of Śiva cursed by Dakṣa; hearing that, Nandin, the beloved of Śiva, became possessed by extreme rage.
The radiant Nandin, son of Śilāda and beloved of Śiva, swiftly replied to that arrogant and great villain with these words.
Nandīśvara said: "O wicked and evil-minded Dakṣa! You have cursed the servants of Śiva in vain, due to your own impulsive rashness as a Brahmin, while remaining ignorant of the true nature of Śiva."
He was mocked by Bhṛgu and others who were evil-minded and deluded, for they, out of pride in their own Brahminhood, regarded the Great Lord Maheśāna as merely a brahmin.
Those wicked Brahmins here who have turned their faces away from Rudra, such as you, I shall cast my curse upon them by virtue of the power of Rudra’s splendor.
O Brahmins, may you remain constantly devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, turned away from the true essence of the Vedas, and proclaiming that there is nothing else.
O Brahmins, let those whose souls are devoted to sensual pleasures, who are intent on heaven, and who are possessed by anger, greed, and pride, always become shameless mendicants.
Placing the Vedic path before them, those Brahmins who perform sacrifices for Śūdras will indeed become impoverished and always devoted to accepting gifts.
O Dakṣa, all those who accept gifts from the unworthy shall go to hell; some among them will indeed always become Brahmarākṣasas.
He who, being of wicked mind, acts with malice toward Śiva—the Supreme Lord who is equal to the gods—shall truly turn away from the Unborn One.
Always dwelling in houses characterized by fraudulent practices out of a desire for vulgar pleasures, they expanded the system of ritual action and the eternal doctrine of the Vedas.
With his face devoid of joy, having forgotten the path of the Self, and being a beast fallen from his duties and always unrighteous, Dakṣa soon became goat-faced.
When those Brahmins were cursed there by the wrathful Nandin, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; and when Īśvara was cursed by Dakṣa, a great outcry ensued.
Having heard that, Śiva, the knower of reality and creator of the Vedas, repeatedly censured even the great sages Bhṛgu and others, as well as the brāhmaṇas.
Having heard the words of Nandin, Lord Sadāśiva, as if smiling, spoke these sweet words, enlightening him.
Sadāśiva said: Listen, O Nandin of great wisdom; you ought not to give way to anger. You have cursed the family of Brahmans in vain, having mistakenly thought that I too had been cursed.
The Veda consists directly of the syllables of mantras and is intensely composed of hymns; for the Self of all embodied beings is indeed established within the hymn.
Therefore, do not ever curse one who knows the Self while overcome by anger; for the Vedas must never be cursed by anyone, even by one of wicked intellect.
"I have been cursed; you ought not to understand this now according to the truth. Be at peace, O one of great intelligence, you who awaken Sanaka and the others."

I am the sacrifice, I am the sacrificial act, and I am all the limbs of the sacrifice in every respect; I am the one whose self is restrained and devoted to sacrifice, and indeed, I alone am that which lies beyond the sacrifice.
"Who is this? Who are you? And who indeed are these? In reality, I too am [unreal]. Reflect thus with such an understanding; for the twice-born have been cursed by you in vain."

Having cast off the fabrication of phenomenal proliferation through the knowledge of reality, O one of great intelligence, be wise, established in yourself, and free from anger and other such passions, O Nandin.
Brahmā said: Thus enlightened by Śambhu, Nandikeśvara became devoted to discernment; he grew calm and was freed from anger.
Śiva also, having quickly awakened him who was as dear to him as his own life, departed from that place with his attendants for his own abode, filled with great joy.
Dakṣa also, overcome with rage and surrounded by those brahmins, returned to his own abode, his mind entirely devoted to malice toward Śiva.
Then, remembering Rudra as he was being cursed, Dakṣa was filled with supreme rage; abandoning all faith, that man of deluded intellect became intent on reviling the worshippers of Śiva.
Thus addressed by Śambhu, the Supreme Self, Dakṣa’s evil-mindedness reached its peak; O dear one, listen as I describe that supreme wickedness of his.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Enmity with Dakṣa by Śiva," in the Satī-upākhyāna of the second section of the Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O sage, once a great sacrifice was commenced by him; then all the celestial sages were invited there by that initiated one.
All the great sages and the gods gathered there for the purpose of performing the sacrifice, having been deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva.
Agastya, Kaśyapa, Atri, Vāmadeva, as well as Bhṛgu, the venerable Dadhīci, Vyāsa, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama;
Paila, Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, Kakupa, Sita, Sumantu, Trika, Kaṅka, and Vaiśampāyana.
These and many other sages, filled with joy, went to the sacrifice of my son Dakṣa, together with their wives and sons.
Likewise, all the hosts of gods, the world-protectors of great prosperity, and all the subordinate deities were endowed with the power to cause sleep.
I, the creator of the universe, have been brought here from Satyaloka; I am praised along with my sons, my retinue, and the Vedas personified.
Likewise, having been entreated with various marks of respect from Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṇu was brought to the sacrifice together with his attendants and retinue.
Thus others also arrived at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, utterly deluded; they were all indeed honored by that wicked-souled Dakṣa.
Indeed, he gave to them divine palaces, highly precious, radiant, and vast, fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ.
In all those abodes, they were established according to their respective fitness; honored by me and by Viṣṇu, they all remained there without a king.
Then, while that great sacrifice was being performed at the holy site of Kanakhala, Bhrigu and other ascetics rich in penance were appointed by him as officiating priests.
Viṣṇu himself was the presiding deity there along with all the hosts of Maruts; I became Brahmā there, the one who demonstrates the ordinances of the three Vedas.
In the same way, all the guardians of the quarters, the gatekeepers, and the protectors, equipped with weapons and accompanied by their retinues, were always full of curiosity.
At his sacrifice, the personified Sacrifice itself appeared in beautiful form; and all the foremost of great sages became the bearers of the Vedas themselves.
In that great festival of sacrifice, Tanūnapāt also assumed his own form a thousandfold in order to quickly receive the oblation.
Eighty-eight thousand officiating priests offered oblations together with sixty-four thousand celestial sages who were chanters of the Udgītha.
The Adhvaryu priests, the Hotṛ priests, and as many as Nārada and others—the Seven Sages—all together composed various individual songs.

Indeed, at his own great sacrifice, Dakṣa chose all the hosts of Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas, along with the groups of Ādityas and their attendants, together with the sacrifices, the foremost of the Saṃkhyas, and all those who move among the Nāgas.

Multitudes of brahmin-sages, royal sages, and celestial sages, along with kings accompanied by their friends, ministers, and armies, as well as all the host-deities headed by Vasu, were chosen by him as the attendants of the sacrifice.
Then Dakṣa, joined with the initiation, having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony and having had rites for well-being performed, shone greatly together with his wife.
At that sacrifice, Śambhu was not invited by the evil-minded Dakṣa; for, having determined that he was a "skull-bearer," Dakṣa considered him unworthy of the sacrifice.
The virtuous Satī, though she was his beloved wife and even his own daughter, was not invited by Dakṣa to the sacrifice, for he perceived no merit in her.
While that great festival of Dakṣa’s sacrifice was thus proceeding, all those esteemed for their ritual expertise remained there, intent upon their own respective duties.
In the meantime, not seeing the Lord Śaṅkara there, Dadhīca, the devotee of Śiva, spoke these words with an agitated mind:
Dadhīca said: "O foremost of divine sages, listen with joy to my words: why has Śambhu not come to this sacrifice, this great festival?"
These lords of the gods, the great sages, and the world-protectors have indeed assembled; yet even so, this sacrifice does not shine brightly without that high-souled wielder of the Pināka bow.
That ancient Puruṣa, the bull-bannered, blue-throated Supreme Lord, by whom all auspicious things come to be and whom the great sages extol—He alone is not seen here.

Indeed, even inauspicious things become auspicious for the skillful person who has mastered them; furthermore, by means of the "three-fifths" [method], even cities immediately become auspicious thereafter.
Therefore, you yourself must swiftly issue the summons to the Supreme Lord, whether by means of Brahmā or Viṣṇu, the Lord of lords.
Now, by Indra, the world-protectors, the twice-born, and the Siddhas together, this Śaṅkara must be brought here in every way for the completion of the sacrifice.
"All of you must go to where the god Maheśvara is; bring Śambhu there together with Dākṣāyaṇī, acting with haste."
Therefore, everything shall become pure by Śambhu, the Supreme Self; for, O lords of gods, the Supreme Self has arrived here accompanied by Ambā.
Since by his remembrance and the utterance of his name all merit shall be attained, therefore the bull-bannered Lord should be brought with every effort.
If Śaṅkara arrives here, this sacrifice will indeed become purifying; otherwise, it will remain incomplete. I tell you this as the truth.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, Dakṣa, filled with rage, spoke quickly like a fool, laughing as it were, with a wicked mind.
Viṣṇu is the root of the deities, wherein eternal dharma resides; since he has been properly brought here by me, what is lacking in this sacrificial rite?
He in whom the Vedas, the sacrifices, and all various ritual acts are established—he, that very Viṣṇu, has come here.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived from Satyaloka together with the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, and various Āgamas.
Just as the king of the gods himself has come here along with the hosts of deities, so too have you, the sages free from all taint, arrived.
Whosoever among you have assembled here—worthy of sacrifice, tranquil, and fit recipients—you are all knowers of the essence of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, firm in your vows.
And in this very matter, what need have we for Rudra as well? O Brahmin, the maiden was indeed given by me at the instigation of Brahmā.
O Brahmin, this Hara is of no noble lineage; he is destitute of father and mother, the singular, insurmountable lord of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Self-conceited, foolish, stubborn, silent, and envious—he is unfit for this task; indeed, he was not brought by me at this time.
Therefore, such words must never again be spoken by any of you; let my great sacrifice be made fruitful by all of you.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Dadhīca spoke this speech, which was full of profound meaning, while all the gods and sages were listening.
Dadhīca said: "This great sacrifice is indeed incomplete without that Śiva; moreover, your destruction will surely come about specifically through him."
Having spoken thus, Dadhīci alone emerged from Dakṣa’s sacrificial enclosure and went quickly to his own hermitage.
Then other Śaivas who were followers of the doctrine of Śiva, as well as those who were preeminent, immediately departed from their own hermitages, having likewise uttered a curse.
When that sage had departed from the sacrifice, the evil-minded Dakṣa, a hater of Śiva, spoke these words while laughing at the other sages:
Dakṣa said: "The Brahmin named Dadhīca, who was dear to Śiva, has departed; and those others like him who have likewise left, they too have departed from my sacrifice."
"This has become most auspicious; indeed, it is approved by me in every respect. I speak the truth, O Lord of Gods, as do the deities and the sages."

Those whose minds are ruined, who are dull-witted, who delight in false speech, who are wicked, who stand outside the Vedas, and who are of evil conduct—such persons are to be excluded from sacrificial rites.
"O Brahmins and gods, all of you who are devoted to the recitation of the Vedas and led by Viṣṇu, make my sacrifice fruitful without delay."
Brahmā said: Having heard his words, all the celestial sages, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, performed a sacrifice to the gods in that sacrificial arena.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, the curse upon that sacrifice has been described by me; now listen with respect as the manner of its destruction is also proclaimed.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Sacrifice," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: When the celestial sages went to Dakṣa’s sacrifice with great festivity, at that very moment, the Lord was on Mount Gandhamādana.
In the fountain-house, surrounded by her female companions under a canopy, the virtuous daughter of Dakṣa engaged in various great sports.
Then the virtuous goddess, who was intent on her play, joyfully saw him proceeding quickly to Dakṣa’s sacrifice after having taken leave of Rohiṇī.
Seeing Vijayā accompanied by Sīmantā, that virtuous woman spoke to her excellent friend, who was dear to her as life and truly well-wishing.
Satyuvāca said: "O Vijayā, my best of friends and dear as life to me, where will this Moon go so quickly after taking leave of Rohiṇī?"
Brahmā said: Thus addressed, the truthful Vijayā went quickly into his presence and questioned that Moon as was appropriate, "Where are you going?"
Then, having heard what Vijaya had previously said with respect regarding his own expedition, he related all of that, including the festivities of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and so forth.
Having heard that, the goddess Vijayā, quickly filled with agitation, related everything that had been said by Śaśin to the virtuous lady.
Having heard that, the virtuous goddess Kālikā was then struck with wonder; reflecting upon the cause there and not understanding it, she pondered within her mind.
My father Dakṣa and my mother Vīriṇī—how is it that she, though virtuous, does not answer our call? Has she forgotten me, her dear daughter?
"I shall respectfully ask Śaṅkara about the cause of all this there. Having thought thus, she became firmly resolved to go there.
Then the goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, having stationed her excellent friend Vijayā there, quickly approached the presence of Śivā.
He saw him stationed in the midst of the assembly hall, surrounded by many hosts of great heroes, preeminent leaders of the troops, such as Nandin and others.
Then, having seen her lord, the master and her own husband, that daughter of Dakṣa quickly approached the presence of Śaṅkara to inquire about the cause of that matter.
Her beloved was placed upon his own lap by Śiva, who was filled with affection; she was gladdened by him with words preceded by great honor.
Then Śambhu, the great performer of divine play, the Lord of all who bestows happiness upon the virtuous, standing in the midst of his attendants, spoke quickly and with reverence to Satī.
Śambhu said: "O slender-waisted one, for what reason have you come here into the midst of the assembly so full of wonder? Tell me the cause of it quickly and with great affection."
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having been thus addressed by Maheśa at that time, Śivā quickly bowed down with joined palms and spoke to the Lord Satī.
Satyuvāca said: "I have heard that my father has a great sacrifice; there is a grand festival there, and the celestial rishis have assembled."
O Lord of the gods, O Master, why does your going to my father’s great sacrifice not please you? Tell me all of that, O Lord.
O Mahādeva, this indeed is the duty of friends: to associate with friends and perform that which increases their joy.
Therefore, O Lord, come with me today to my father’s sacrificial enclosure with every effort, at my request, O Master.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of hers, the Lord Maheśvara, pierced in his heart by the arrow of Dakṣa’s speech, spoke these truthful words.
Maheśvara said: O Goddess, Dakṣa, your father, is particularly hostile toward me.
All those others who were proud of him—headed by the gods and sages—were fools, devoid of knowledge, who came to perform the sacrifice for your father.
And those goddesses who go to another's house uninvited incur an insult that is even greater than death.
Even Indra, though he has gone to the supreme abode, becomes insignificant in such a state; what then to say of others? For such a journey is indeed a path of humiliation.
Therefore, neither you nor I should go to Dakṣa’s sacrifice; especially so, my dear, for I have spoken the truth.
For a person, even when struck by the arrows of enemies, is not as pained as he is considered to be when his vital organs are struck by the harsh words of his own kin.
O beloved, when the memory of the virtuous is destroyed by the six qualities such as learning and so forth—which are non-existent in others—the wicked do not see the abode of the many.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by that high-souled Maheśa, Satī, filled with wrath, spoke these words to Śiva, the best among those who know speech.
Satī said: "O Śambhu, Lord of all, that sacrifice would be fruitful through you; yet you have not been invited today by my father, who acts wickedly."
I wish to know all that—the disposition of that evil-minded one, as well as that of all the evil-minded celestial sages who have arrived here.
Therefore, O Lord, I shall go this very day to my father’s sacrifice; O Maheśvara, my protector, grant me permission to go there.
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by that goddess, the Lord Rudra himself—Śiva, the knower of all, the seer who perceives everything, and the creator of beings—spoke to Satī.
Śiva said: "O Goddess, if this is your desire, it is necessary for you to go there. O lady of excellent vows, at my word, go quickly to your father's sacrifice."
Having respectfully mounted this joyful bull, which was fully prepared, she performed the royal honors endowed with many virtues.
Having been told by Rudra, "Ascend the bull adorned [with ornaments]," Satī, being well-adorned and joined with him, went to her father’s abode.
The supreme Self bestowed the regalia of a great king, including an excellent parasol, chowries, and the like, as well as fine garments and ornaments.
Sixty thousand fierce Gaṇas went forth at the command of Śiva, filled with curiosity, joyful, and accompanied by great festivities.
Then, a great festival took place everywhere at that sacrifice, performed by the hosts of Vāmadeva for Satī, who is dear to Śiva.
The attendants felt great curiosity, they sang the praises of Śiva and Pārvatī, and the great heroes, beloved of Śiva, leaped with joy within the inner quarters.
In every way, O Mother of the World, there was great splendor during her departure; a joyful cry arose that filled the three worlds.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Pilgrimage," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Dakṣa’s daughter went there, where the sacrifice of great splendor was held, filled with the curiosity of the foremost gods, asuras, and sages.
There he beheld his father’s palace, endowed with various wonders, radiant and beautiful, and frequented by hosts of celestial sages.
Then the Goddess, descending from her own seat, went alone and quickly to the interior of Nandin’s sacrificial enclosure, standing at the gate.
Seeing that Asiknī had arrived, her illustrious mother and her sisters showed her due respect as was fitting.
Dakṣa paid no attention whatsoever even upon seeing her; nor did anyone else there, being deluded by Śiva’s māyā, out of fear of him.
Then, O Sage, that virtuous goddess, utterly amazed by the humiliation of all the worlds, bowed down to her mother and her father.
At that sacrifice, she saw the portions for the gods beginning with Indra; Satī did not assign a portion for Śambhu, and her anger became unbearable.
Satī said: Then Satī, filled with intense rage as if burning Dakṣa, looked upon everyone with a cruel gaze, having been utterly insulted.
Satī said: "Why was Śambhu, the most auspicious one by whom this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is purified, not invited by you?"
Śambhu is the sacrifice, the best among those who know sacrifice, the limb of sacrifice, the sacrificial fee, and the performer of sacrifice; without him, how can there be a ritual?
By the mere remembrance of whom everything becomes purified—alas! without him, everything performed will be impure.

Since all substances, mantras, and the like—whatever constitutes the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya)—are composed of him, how could the sacrifice have proceeded without Śambhu?
"Why did you show such disrespect toward Śiva, who is equal to the gods? O lowest of fathers, you have today become one whose intellect has fallen away."
O wretch, you do not even know that Hara, the Great Lord, by serving whom all the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu and Brahmā, have attained their respective stations.
"How have these gods, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, as well as the sages, come to your sacrifice without Śambhu, their own Lord?"
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Viṣṇu and all the others, she, the Supreme Sovereign whose nature is Bhava, addressed each of them individually while rebuking them.
Satyuvāca said: O Viṣṇu, do you not know Mahādeva in truth—that whom the Śrutis indeed describe as both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa)?
O Hari, although Maheśvara formerly taught you many times by placing his hand upon yours, using the forms of Śālva and others as examples.
Even that knowledge has not entered your mind, O evil-minded one; you seek a share in this sacrifice of Dakṣa without Śiva, your own master.
Formerly, having become five-faced, you were arrogant toward Sadāśiva; he made you four-faced, yet you have forgotten that wonder.
O Indra, do you not know the prowess of Mahādeva? Indeed, your thunderbolt was reduced to ashes by Hara, the performer of fierce deeds.
O gods, do you not know the prowess of Mahādeva? Here dwell the sages of Vasiṣṭha’s lineage; what have you done here to them?
In former times, the Lord went on a round for alms in the Dāruvana forest because he had been cursed by you sages as a mendicant, Rudra.
And how could you have forgotten what was done even by Rudra when he was cursed? By that very *liṅga*, the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, was consumed by fire.
All the gods, including Viṣṇu and Brahmā, as well as the other sages, became bewildered when they arrived here at the sacrifice without Śambhu.
All the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and the various scriptures, emerged from him who is restrained in speech; that Śambhu, the ultimate goal of the Vedas, cannot be known by anyone.
Brahmā said: Thus did the Mother of the World, the virtuous Satī, filled with anger and with a heart tormented by grief, utter these words of many kinds.
Viṣṇu and all the other gods, as well as the sages, having heard those words, became silent, their minds agitated by fear.
Then Dakṣa, having heard such words from his daughter and looking at Satī with a cruel gaze, spoke these words in anger.
Dakṣa said: What is the use of much speaking to you? There is no business here at present. Go or stay, O blessed lady; for what purpose have you come?
But this Śiva, who is understood by the wise to be inauspicious, is of no noble lineage, is outside the Vedic fold, and is the king of ghosts, spirits, and piśācas.
Therefore, O daughter, having understood this through my wisdom, I did not invite Rudra—who was wearing a peculiar disguise—to the assembly of gods and sages for the sake of the sacrifice.
Impelled by fate, you were given away by that dull-witted sinner to Rudra, who was ignorant of the truth, arrogant, and evil-minded.
Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, abandon your anger and be at peace; since you have come to this sacrifice, receive for yourself your rightful portion.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by Dakṣa, that daughter Satī, who was honored throughout the three worlds, became exceedingly enraged upon seeing her own father full of censure.
Then she reflected: "How shall I go to Śaṅkara? Desiring to see Śaṅkara, what answer shall I give when questioned?"
Then Satī, the mother of the three worlds, overcome with anger and sighing heavily, spoke to her father Dakṣa, whose mind was wicked.
Satyu said: He who reviles Mahādeva, or he who listens to another being reviled—both of them go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Therefore, O Lord, I shall abandon you and enter the fire; for what is the use of my life, dear father, while I hear such disrespect from my master?
If one is capable, one should forcibly cut out the tongue of Śambhu’s slanderer, especially so; then one will be purified, without a doubt.
If a person is unable [to do so], the wise one should indeed cover his ears while departing from that hell; by doing this, he becomes purified—so say the best of the learned.
Brahmā said: Having thus spoken these words on the principles of righteousness, she was overcome with remorse; with a tormented heart, she recalled the words of Śiva.
Then, becoming enraged, Satī spoke fearlessly to Dakṣa, and certainly to all those gods beginning with Viṣṇu as well as the sages.
Satyu said: "O father, you are a reviler of Śambhu; you shall come to repentance. Having experienced great suffering here, you will go to torment in the end."
In this world, for that Supreme Self who has no enemy and no friend, who is devoid of all enmity—except for you—who could possibly act as his adversary?
It is no wonder that the great are always censured by the wicked with envy; yet for those whose darkness has been dispelled by the dust of the Great One’s feet, that very censure is truly auspicious.
For those people whose name is uttered as "Śiva"—even if spoken only once by chance—that destroys all sin instantly.
Alas, this wicked man, being devoid of auspiciousness, hates Śambhu—the Lord of All, whose command is inviolable and whose stainless fame is sanctifying.
His lotus feet are well-served by the bees of the minds of the great, and are respectfully sought by all seekers of goals through the nectar of the Brahman.
Out of compassion for the welfare of the world, you rain down blessings swiftly upon those who seek them; yet, through your folly, you bear malice toward Him, the kinsman of all.

Or rather, what wise person other than you would consider that which is called Śiva to be inauspicious? Neither Brahmā and the others, nor the sages Sanaka and his brothers, nor any others perceive him as such.
Having scattered his matted locks in the cremation ground, that noble-minded one, wearing a skull and recognizing those garlands or ashes as [the Lord], dwelt there with joy.
That Śiva, the Supreme Lord, is he whose discarded floral offerings (nirmālya) the sages and gods reverently bear upon their heads.

Action is impelled as being twofold: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to its cessation; having distinguished these modes of conduct within the Veda, they should be investigated by the wise.
Likewise, both [contradiction and simultaneity] exist in that which has a single agent; however, O Śambhu, in the Supreme Brahman, no action whatsoever proceeds.
May the footprints of our ancestors, who have always resorted to us, never be yours; for in the sacrificial halls, they are consumed by the smoke-path and cast aside by you.
O dear one, you who possess a wicked intellect, do not harbor pride, for you have always been served by those with unmanifested marks (avyaktaliṅga) and by the avadhūtas.
What is the use of much speaking? You are wicked and evil-minded in every respect; I have no need whatsoever for this body produced from you.
Fie on that birth of a wicked person who commits offenses against the great in every way; a wise man must especially avoid association with him.
When the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, declared your lineage to be "Dākṣāyaṇī," I suddenly became deeply distressed in mind.
Therefore, having now truly cast off this body born of your limbs—a corpse that is ever contemptible—I shall surely become a bringer of happiness.
O sages, you who drink wine, listen all of you to my words: this action of yours is entirely improper, for you are evil-minded.
Indeed, you are all deluded, revilers of Śiva, and lovers of strife; you will certainly and entirely receive punishment from Hara, without fail.
Brahmā said: Having thus addressed Dakṣa and the others at the sacrifice, Satī then desisted; yet, following after Śambhu with her mind, she remembered her beloved of life.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Satī’s Words," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, when Satī, the beloved of Śaṅkara, became silent, what happened there? Tell me that with respect.
Brahmā said: Having become silent, the virtuous goddess, remembering her husband with reverence, suddenly sat down upon the ground in the north, her mind perfectly tranquil.
Having sipped water according to the rules and purified herself with her garment properly arranged, she closed her eyes, remembered her husband, and entered the path of yoga.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal, she of the white countenance then exerted effort to raise the udāna from the navel-center.
Having placed him in her heart and then established him upon her chest with her mind, Satī, the beloved of Śaṅkara’s very life, led him from her throat to between her eyebrows and down to her waist.
Thus, wishing to suddenly cast off her own body due to Dakṣa’s wrath, she performed the yoga of breath-control (*dhāraṇā*) through the path of yoga once her limbs were consumed by fire.
Then that virtuous woman, her mind fixed upon the path of yoga, saw nothing else there but the feet of her own husband.
With his sins destroyed and his body consumed by that fire, O best of sages, he was instantly reduced to ashes by His will.
And as they watched that in the sky and on the earth, a very great clamor then arose from the gods and others—exclamations of "Alas! Alas! filled with wonder, amazement, and fear.
Ha! Śambhu’s beloved is the supreme goddess, for she is indeed his deity. By what wicked person was Satī provoked that she gave up her life?
Oh, behold the truly great selflessness of this Dakṣa, whose offspring—both moving and unmoving—are the progeny of that Prajāpati who is his son!
Alas! Today that wise goddess Satī has become distracted in mind—she who is ever dear to the bull-bannered Lord, and who is always worthy of honor by the virtuous.
This Prajāpati, who has seized the Veda and possesses an intolerant heart, will indeed incur great infamy throughout the entire world.

He who, being an enemy of Śambhu, forcibly seized his own daughter when she was intent on marriage, shall experience the torments of the great hells and meet his death as a consequence of that transgression.
While the people were speaking thus, Satyā beheld that wonderful and terrible slaughter; immediately, her attendants rose up in fury with their weapons raised.
All those hosts of Śaṅkara, the Lord, numbering ninety-six million and possessed of immense strength, stood at the gate in a state of wrath and became enraged.
All the heroic leaders of Śaṅkara’s Gaṇas raised a great cry of "Hā! Hā! repeatedly, crying out, "Fie! Fie! Not so! in loud voices.
The quarters of the sky were pervaded by a great cry of "Alas! Alas! All the gods, the sages, and whoever else was present there were seized with fear.
Having consulted together, they all became enraged and raised their weapons; creating a universal dissolution with their cries and missiles, they filled the very quarters of the sky.
O divine sage, some there, overwhelmed with grief, struck their own limbs—heads and faces—with extremely sharp, life-ending weapons.
Thus, at that time, those two tens of thousands of Gaṇas met their destruction along with the daughter of Dakṣa; it was truly like a marvel.
The remaining hosts of the high-souled Śaṅkara stood joyfully with uplifted weapons, eager to slay the enraged Dakṣa.

O Sage, perceiving the force of those as they were rushing forward, the venerable Bhṛgu offered oblations into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with a Yajus mantra dedicated to the slayer of the sacrificial-destroyers.
And as the oblation was being offered by Bhṛgu, thousands of great Asuras named Ṛbhus, possessed of mighty prowess, sprang forth there.
O Lord of Sages, with those firebrands as their weapons, a most formidable battle took place there between the Pramathas, causing one's hair to stand on end for those who heard it.
Being struck on all sides by those great heroes, the R̥bhus, the Pramathas fled without effort, overcome by the power of their Brahmanic splendor.
Thus those hosts of Śiva were indeed slain and swiftly put to flight; by the will of Śiva and through his great power, that became like a marvel.
Seeing that, the sages, the gods headed by Śakra along with the hosts of Maruts, Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, and the world-protectors then became silent.
Some there, being greatly distressed, prayed to Lord Viṣṇu on all sides, while repeatedly deliberating upon the absence of the Brahmins.
Having thoroughly considered the future consequences, the highly intelligent gods, Viṣṇu and the others, became greatly distressed due to Rāvaṇa’s repeated destruction and flight.
O Sage, when the sacrifice had become thus, an obstacle arose for the evil-minded Dakṣa, that wretched Brahmin who was a hater of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Distress Arising from Satī’s Abandonment of Her Body," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, in the meantime, a voice from the sky spoke there in truth to Dakṣa, the gods, and the others as they were listening.
The voice from the sky said: "O Dakṣa, O you of wicked conduct, devoted to hypocrisy! What deed have you done, O great fool, that brings about such calamity?"
O fool, you have not honored the auspicious words of Dadhīci, the king of Śiva’s devotees, which bring joy to all; for those words are authoritative in this matter.
Having given you an unbearable curse, that Brahmin has departed from the sacrifice; even after that, nothing at all was understood by you, O fool, in your mind.
Then, how indeed was such great respect shown by us toward our own daughter Satī, who had come of her own accord to the house of Maṅgalā?
O you who are weak in knowledge, why have you not honored Satī and Bhava? You are deluded and vainly pride yourself on being the son of Brahmā.
She is truly to be worshipped by the virtuous; she bestows the fruits of all sins, the mother of the three worlds, the auspicious one who shares half the body of Śaṅkara.
She alone, when constantly worshipped, bestows all prosperity; she is Māheśvarī, the giver of all auspiciousness to her own devotees.
That divine power, when truly worshipped, constantly destroys the fear of saṃsāra; she grants the heart's desires and removes all calamities.
She alone, when constantly worshipped, bestows fame and prosperity; she is the supreme Parameśānī, the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She alone is the sustainer of the world, the one who performs its protection; she is the beginningless power who effects the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
She alone is remembered as the Mother of the World, the playful Mother of Viṣṇu, and the progenitor of Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Agni, Sūrya, and the other gods.
She is indeed Śambhu’s power, the Great Goddess, the giver of the fruits of austerity, dharma, and charity; she is the destroyer of the wicked, higher than the highest.
Such as this is the Goddess, whose wife she has always been and who is ever dear to him; yet no portion was given to her by you, a fool of perverse judgment.
For Śambhu is the Supreme Lord, the Master of all, higher than the highest; he is served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, and is the bringer of all auspiciousness.
For those perfected ones (siddhas) who long for the vision of this perform austerity; and those yogis who long for the vision of this engage in yoga.
The vision of Śaṅkara himself is declared to yield great fruit, even more so than sacrifices and other rites involving infinite wealth and grain.
Śiva alone is the creator of the universe, the lord of all sciences, the sovereign master, the supreme lord of primordial knowledge, and the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious.
"O wicked one, because you did not show proper respect today due to that power, for this very reason the destruction of this sacrifice shall indeed come to pass."
Indeed, there is misfortune for those worthy of worship when they are not worshipped; for she, Śivā, is not merely worshipped, but is the most worthy of all worship.
Even with a thousand heads, Śeṣa daily carries with affection the dust from His feet; such is the power of that auspicious Satī.
Having meditated incessantly upon whose lotus feet and having worshipped them with reverence, Viṣṇu attained the state of Viṣṇu; she is Satī, the beloved of that Śambhu.
Having meditated upon whose lotus feet incessantly and having worshipped them with reverence, Brahmā attained the status of Brahmā; she who is his beloved, Satī, [is likewise devoted].
