Having meditated incessantly upon his lotus feet and having worshipped them with reverence, Indra and the other guardians of the world attained each their own supreme station.
Śiva is the father of the world, and that virtuous Satī is the mother of the world; O fool, since you have not honored them, how will there be any welfare for you?
Misfortune has been transferred to you, and calamities have been transferred to you; for those two, Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, were not propitiated by you with devotion.
Thinking, "May I attain auspiciousness without having worshipped Śiva, the Source of Bliss," what is this irresistible pride? That pride shall perish today.
Having turned away from all the lords among these gods, who will provide you assistance? I do not see anyone at all who will do so for you.
If the gods now provide you with assistance, then they shall meet their destruction like moths in a fire.
"Let your mouth indeed blaze up this very day; let there be the destruction of the sacrifice! Let all those who are your allies also blaze up today with haste!"
And all the immortals shall take an oath for your misfortune; today they will provide assistance to this evil-minded one.
"Let the immortals depart from this sacrificial pavilion of their own accord; otherwise, your destruction will surely come to pass today in every way."
Let all others—the sages, the Nāgas, and the rest—depart from this sacrifice; otherwise, your destruction will surely come about today in every way.
Depart quickly from this sacrificial pavilion, O Hari; otherwise, your destruction will surely come today in every way.
Depart quickly from this sacrificial pavilion, O Creator; otherwise, your destruction will surely come today in every way.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, that voice from the sky, which brings about all auspiciousness, ceased while [the gods] were well-established throughout the entire sacrificial hall.
O dear one, having heard that voice from the sky, all the gods, beginning with Hari, as well as the sages and others, were filled with wonder.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Celestial Voice," in the Satī Section of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: Having heard the voice from the sky, what did the ignorant Dakṣa do then? And what did the others do? After that, what happened? Tell me.
The hosts of Śiva were indeed defeated by the power of Bhṛgu’s mantras; O high-minded one, tell me the truth: what did they do, and where did they go?
Brahmā said: Having heard the voice from the sky, all the gods and others were struck with wonder; they said nothing at all, remaining there utterly bewildered.
Those heroes who had fled, remaining by the power of the Bhrigu-mantras, those surviving attendants of Śiva sought refuge in Śiva.
Having bowed down with great reverence, they reported everything to Rudra of immeasurable splendor, as well as the events exactly as they had occurred.
The Gaṇas said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, protect us who have come to you for refuge! O Lord, please listen with respect to the news concerning Satī in full detail.
By the arrogant and most wicked Dakṣa, who was a devotee of Maheśāna, Satī was insulted and likewise disregarded by the gods.
He gave you no share, yet he bestowed portions upon the gods; the wicked and highly arrogant Dakṣa spoke harsh words aloud.
Then, O Lord, seeing that she had received no share in the sacrifice, Satī became enraged; having censured her father many times, she then consumed her own body by fire.
"Ten thousand hosts have died there out of shame; others among us, in our fury, have even cut off their own limbs with weapons."
Those terrifying beings were indeed prepared to destroy that sacrifice with speed, but they were repelled by their adversary Bhṛgu through his own power.
O Lord, Sustainer of the Universe, we have come to you for refuge; therefore, out of compassion, make us fearless from this worldly fear.
O Great Lord, at that sacrifice, all those wicked ones, led by Dakṣa, were exceedingly arrogant and treated you with particular contempt.
O Nārada, thus has the entire account of our own people and of Satyā been told; as for those of deluded intellect, do with them as you wish.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his own attendants, the Lord remembered Nārada in order to quickly learn everything regarding that conduct.
O divine-sighted celestial sage, you arrived there swiftly; having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, you stood there with palms joined in reverence.
Then that master praised you and asked for news of Satī, as well as her subsequent conduct regarding Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
O dear one, when questioned by Śambhu, you, whose very self is Śiva, immediately recounted all that had occurred and transpired at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having heard those words spoken from your mouth, O Sage, Rudra, whose prowess is exceedingly fierce, became instantly enraged.
Then Rudra, the agent of the world's destruction, having plucked out a single matted lock of hair, struck it with rage against the top of that mountain.
O Sage, O Lord, that matted hair of the Master split into two upon being struck, and a great roar arose, as terrifying as the final dissolution of the universe.
O celestial sage, from that matted hair was born the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, who is most terrifying in his eastern aspect.
Having encompassed the earth on all sides, he stood ten fingers' breadth beyond it; resembling the fire of universal dissolution, he was towering and possessed a thousand arms.
From the angry exhalation of the Lord Mahārudra there arose a hundred fevers and thirteen types of *saṃnipāta* disorders.
Mahākālī arose from the rear portion of his matted hair; O dear one, she is most terrifying and surrounded by millions of spirits.
All of them were embodied and cruel, terrifying to the worlds with their own voices; blazing with their own splendor, they seemed to burn everything on all sides.
Then the hero Vīrabhadra, skilled in speech, having prostrated before the Supreme Lord with his palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
Vīrabhadra said: O Mahārudra, O Great Fierce One, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire! O Lord, command me quickly as to what task must be performed by me.
O Lord, can the oceans be dried up in even half a moment? O Lord, can the mountains be ground to powder in even half a moment?
O Hara, in an instant I could reduce the entire universe to ashes; or in an instant, could I not likewise reduce the gods or the lords of sages to ashes?
O Śaṅkara, you are indeed the source of confidence for all the worlds; how much more so, O Īśāna, should you refrain from the harming of all living beings? What need is there even to mention it?
O Maheśvara, by your grace, there is nothing anywhere that is impossible for me; in prowess, no one equal to me has ever existed, nor will there ever be.
O Lord, whatever task you shall entrust me with for its accomplishment, I shall surely fulfill that task swiftly through your grace.
By the command of Śaṅkara, even the lowly cross the ocean of the world; am I not capable of crossing this great ocean of calamity by resorting to Hara?
O Śaṅkara, even with a blade of grass sent by you, a great task can be accomplished by me without effort in an instant; of this there is no doubt.
O Śambhu, although your purpose is accomplished by mere play, nevertheless I must be sent; for this is indeed your grace.
O Śambhu, such is my power as well, through your grace; O Śaṅkara, without your grace, no one possesses power at all.
Without your command, no one at all is actually capable of moving even a blade of grass; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it.
O Śambhu, O Maheśvara, just as all the gods and others are to be restrained by you, so too am I to be restrained by you, the restrainer of all embodied beings.
I bow to you, O Mahādeva; once again I bow to you. O Hara, send me away today with haste for the sake of accomplishing my own desired goal.
O Śambhu, a throbbing has arisen repeatedly in my limbs regarding my friend; victory will be mine today, so send me forth, O Lord.
A certain extraordinary joy and enthusiasm also arises within me; O Śambhu, my mind is firmly attached to your lotus feet.
At every step, there will be a continuous succession of a virtuous lineage.
Victory is always his, and prosperity is daily his, who possesses firm devotion to Śambhu and to you, the beautiful refuge.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words spoken thus, the Lord of Maṅgalā was satisfied; he spoke this blessing to him again: "O Vīrabhadra, victory to you!"
Maheśvara said: Listen with an attentive mind, my dear Vīrabhadra, to my words; that which must be performed with effort will quickly bring me satisfaction.
Now Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, a wicked man who is especially hostile toward me, arrogant and ignorant, has prepared himself to perform a sacrifice.
"O best of the Gaṇas, having reduced that sacrifice along with its officiants and attendants to ashes, return quickly to my abode."
Let there be Gandharvas, Yakṣas, or whoever else there may be; reduce even them instantly to ashes this very day with haste.
Let it be Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śacīpati, or even Yama; yet this very day, you must strive to cast them all down.
Let there be Gandharvas, Yakṣas, or whoever else there may be; reduce even them instantly to ashes this very day with haste.
Those who remain there, having transgressed the oath made by Dadhīci regarding me, must certainly be incinerated by you with great effort.

If even Viṣṇu and the other gods should come here by mistake along with their attendants, I shall quickly summon them with the various mantras of attraction and bring them forth with my fiery splendor.
Those who, being arrogant, have remained there having transgressed my oath—they are indeed my enemies; therefore, consume them with a garland of blazing fire.
Having set ablaze and reduced to ashes those present at the site of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, along with their wives and their wealth, return here again with all haste.
When you have gone there, O All-devouring One, even the gods will praise you with respect; at that time, quickly consume them with your very flame.

O you who are filled with garlands of flames, quickly consume even the gods who have committed offenses against you with your fires, while meditating upon me, the protector of the chapters of the Mādhyandinīya recension.
O hero, having set ablaze Dakṣa and all others there—along with their wives and kinsmen—drink the water sportively.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus, the protector of the boundaries of the Vedas, the enemy of Time and lord of all, his eyes copper-red with rage, ceased speaking to the great hero.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vīrabhadra and the Instruction of Śiva," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the illustrious Maheśa with reverence, Vīrabhadra was exceedingly gratified and prostrated before Maheśvara.
Having placed the command of the trident-bearing God of gods upon his head, Vīrabhadra then departed swiftly toward the sacrifice.
Then Śiva dispatched millions of Gaṇas for the sake of splendor, along with great heroes who resembled the fire of universal destruction.
Then those powerful hosts went before Vīrabhadra, and behind him also went the heroic hosts who were full of curiosity.
Accompanied by Vīrabhadra, hundreds of thousands of Gaṇas—attendants of the Destroyer of Time (Kāla)—all possessed the very form of Rudra.

Accompanied by those hosts, that great-souled Vīrabhadra—adorned with the dress and ornaments of Hara, possessing a thousand arms and girt with the lord of serpents—advanced seated upon his chariot, exceedingly powerful and terrifying.
The measurement of the chariot was indeed two thousand nalvas; and with great effort, ten thousand lions were employed as its mounts.
In the same way, there were many powerful lions as bodyguards, along with tigers, crocodiles, fish, and elephants by the thousands.
When Vīrabhadra set out swiftly for the destruction of Dakṣa, a rain of flowers was then released by the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
And the hosts praised, O hero, the deeds performed by Śipiviṣṭa; they all felt great curiosity regarding that festival of departure.
Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Īśānī, Cāmuṇḍā, Muṇḍamardinī, Bhadrakālī, as well as Bhadrā, Tvaritā, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Accompanied by these nine Durgās and joined by Mahākālī, she set forth with hosts of all the spirits for the destruction of Dakṣa.
Dākinīs and Śākinīs, Bhūtas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas; Kūṣmāṇḍas and Parpaṭas, Caṭakas and Brahmarākṣasas.
The Bhairavas and Kṣetrapālas, destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, those heroic guardians who carry out the command of Śiva, went forth with haste.
In that very manner, the circle of Yoginīs, accompanied by the sixty-four hosts, suddenly set forth in anger to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Listen, O Nārada, to the enumeration of all those hosts—the assembly of leaders who possess great strength and are endowed with fortitude.
And Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of hosts, advanced with ten crores; likewise, Kekarākṣa with ten, and Vikṛta with eight.
Viśākha was [protected] by sixty-four, Pāriyātrika by nine, and both Sarvāṅgaka and the heroic Vikṛtānana by six each.
Jvālakeśa, the bull among the Gaṇas, was intoxicated with pride along with twelve crores; Samada with seven, and Dudrabha with eight.
Kapālīśa is with five, and the Saṃdāraka Gaṇa is with six; likewise, Koṭikuṇḍa is here with ten million times ten million.
Viṣṭambha is the seventh in the group with eight vīra-koṭis; likewise, O dear one, Saṃnāda and Pippala each have a thousand koṭis.
Āveśana was likewise surrounded by eight [thousand], and Candratāpana by eight; Mahāveśa was surrounded by a thousand, and Gaṇapa by ten million.
O Sage, Kuṇḍī with twelve crores and likewise Parvataka, the best of the Gaṇas, set forth to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Kāla, Kālaka, and likewise Mahākāla, with a hundred crores [of followers], set out toward the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
And Agnikṛt with a hundred crores, Koṭyagnimukha with one crore, Ādityamūrdhā with one crore, and likewise Ghanāvaha.
Sannāha with a hundred koṭis, Kumuda with a koṭi, and Amogha and Kokila, the lord of hosts, each with ten million koṭis.
Kāṣṭhāgūḍha, Sukeśī, Vṛṣabha, and likewise Sumantraka, the lord of the Gaṇas, O dear one, set forth together with the sixty-four [Gaṇas].
Kākapādodara, the best of the Gaṇas, was accompanied by sixty crores; likewise, Santānaka, the bull among the Gaṇas, was with sixty crores.
And Mahābala, as well as Puṅgava, each with nine crores [of followers].
Likewise, O dear one, Madhupiṅga, the lord of the Gaṇas, set forth with ninety crores; and Nīla and Pūrṇabhadra did likewise.
The four-faced lord of the Gaṇas set forth with a hundred koṭis, as did Sukeśa and Vṛṣabha with sixty-four [koṭis] who were hidden within logs.
And Virūpākṣa, the lord of hosts with sixty-four crores; Tālaketu, Ṣaḍāsya, and Pañcāsya, the lords of the Gaṇas.
O Sage, he is Saṃvartaka, as well as Kulīśa, the self-effulgent Lord; he is Lokāntaka, the radiant-souled one, and likewise Daityāntaka.
The Gaṇas are Bhṛṅgī, the illustrious Riṭi, as well as Devadevapriya, Aśani, and Bhālaka, numbering sixty-four thousand.
Surrounded by twenty billion times a hundred thousand, the heroic Vīreśa, indeed Vīrabhadra, advanced at the command of Śiva.
Accompanied by thousands of millions and three additional millions of beings born from his pores, as well as by packs of dogs, the hero proceeded swiftly.
Then there was the great sound of kettledrums and conchs of various tones, as well as the sounds of ḍamarus, horns, and various types of trumpets.
During that great festival, they played those very same stretched-out bonds as if they were musical instruments, and various other instruments resounded with joy.
O great sage, during the expedition of Vīrabhadra together with his army, there occurred many auspicious omens that were conducive to happiness.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Vīrabhadra’s Departure," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: While Vīrabhadra was thus proceeding accompanied by his hosts, evil omens were seen by Dakṣa and by the gods as well.
O celestial sage, various portents of three kinds occurred when Vīrabhadra was accompanied by his hosts, all foreboding the destruction of the sacrifice.
O dear one, the throbbing of the right and left eyes, arms, and thighs occurred, portending various miseries and indicating evil in every respect.
Then, at that site of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, an earthquake occurred; and at midday, Dakṣa beheld the wondrous stars.
The quarters of the sky became deeply soiled, and the sun turned variegated; surrounded by a thousand halos, it appeared terrifying.
The stars fell, flashing with the brilliance of fire and lightning; at that time, the movement of the stars became crooked and turned downward.
Vultures, having touched the head of Dakṣa, emerged by the thousands; the sacrificial pavilion became shaded by the shadows of the vultures' wings.
Then, jackals howled on the sacrificial ground, and there occurred a shower of meteors accompanied by the appearance of white scorpions.
Harsh winds blew there, accompanied by showers of dust; and locusts arose, shaken by the swirling whirlwinds.
And by the winds, that sacrificial pavilion of Dakṣa—which had been newly and wonderfully constructed by Dakṣa himself through divine power—was blown upward.
Then Dakṣa and all the others vomited that wonderful blood, and they repeatedly spat out pieces of flesh still pierced by arrows.
And those lamps became trembling, like those struck by the wind; and they all became distressed, as if struck by a stream of weapons.
Then, at that very moment, showers of tears born from their cries fell like clusters of lotuses shedding frost in the forest at dawn.
For the eyes of Dakṣa and the others suddenly became clear, just as lotuses and water-lilies bloom at night and at the time of dawn respectively.
The god rained down blood, and the quarters were enveloped in darkness; a preternatural conflagration broke out, terrifying all people.
O Sage, when the gods and others beheld such portents of death, Viṣṇu and the rest then became exceedingly afraid.
Fainting on the ground, they fell, crying out, "Alas! We are slain!", like trees growing on a riverbank toppled by the force of the current.
Having fallen, those cruel ones stood upon the ground like slain serpents; then, like balls, they fell again and rose once more.
Then, tormented by grief, they wailed like female ospreys; their cries of lamentation seemed to provoke a dialogue of questions and answers.
Then all those inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, their powers rendered utterly blunted, rolled about on the ground up to their necks like tortoises.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice arose there, making itself heard to all the gods and especially to Dakṣa.
The voice from the sky said: "Fie on your birth from Dakṣa today! You are a great fool and evil-minded; there will come a great, unavoidable suffering arising from Hara."
Alas! Even those deluded ones, the gods and others, who remain here, will undoubtedly experience great suffering.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the sky and having seen those ill omens, Dakṣa was seized by extreme fear, as were the supreme gods and others.
Then Dakṣa, trembling and utterly distraught in mind, sought refuge with Viṣṇu, his own sovereign Lord and the husband of Indirā.
Prostrating deeply, overcome with fear and deprived of his senses, he praised and spoke to that Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who is affectionate toward his own people.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sight of Ill Omens," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Dakṣa said: O God of gods, Hari, Viṣṇu, friend of the distressed, ocean of mercy! Protection must be afforded by you to me and to this virtuous man.

You are the protector of the sacrifice itself, the performer of the sacrificial rite, and the very essence of the sacrifice; O Lord, let compassion be shown toward the sacrifice, and let there be no destruction of it.
Brahmā said: Having thus offered this various petition with great reverence, Dakṣa, his mind agitated by fear, fell at his feet.
Then Viṣṇu, having raised up Dakṣa whose mind was overwhelmed, and having heard those words of that evil-minded one, remembered Śiva.
Remembering Śiva, the Great Lord, his own Master and Supreme Sovereign, Hari, the knower of the reality of Śiva, spoke to Dakṣa while enlightening him.
Hari said: Listen, O Dakṣa, I shall speak to you according to the truth; listen to my words, which are beneficial to you in every way and bestow the happiness of the great mantra.
O Dakṣa, you have indeed shown contempt for Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self and Lord of all, because you did not know the truth.
Through disregard for the Lord, every action whatsoever becomes entirely fruitless and brings nothing but calamity at every step.
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped and he who is worthy of worship is not worshipped, three things will prevail there: poverty, death, and fear.
Therefore, with every effort, the Bull-bannered Lord should be honored; for from the Great Lord when not honored, a great danger arises.
Even now, we are all not able to prevail; I speak the truth: it is solely due to your misconduct that we have come to this.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Dakṣa became lost in thought; with his face turned pale, he remained silent, standing upon the ground.
In the meantime, Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, urged on by Rudra, arrived at the sacrifice accompanied by his army.
Some arrived from behind, some came through the sky, and others likewise came, surrounding all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
By the command of Śarva, the heroic Gaṇas—fearless, possessing the prowess of Rudra, and being the best among heroes—numbering in the infinite, let out lion-like roars.
By that great roar, the three worlds were made to resound; the sky was shrouded in dust, and the quarters of the horizon were enveloped in darkness.
The earth, together with its seven islands, mountains, and forests, trembled, overwhelmed by great fear; and all the oceans there were agitated.
And seeing that great army, which was thus constituted and capable of destroying the world, all the immortals and others were struck with wonder.
Then, beholding the military mobilization and distressed by the sight of blood on his face, Dakṣa prostrated himself like a staff before Viṣṇu and spoke along with his wife.
Dakṣa said: "O Viṣṇu, it was by your very power that this great sacrifice was commenced by me for the successful accomplishment of this virtuous act; O Great Lord, you are the ultimate authority."
O Viṣṇu, you are the witness of all actions and the protector of sacrifices; O Great Lord, you are the essence of Dharma and the womb of the Vedas, the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, O Lord, protection must be provided for this sacrifice of mine; for there is none other than you who is capable, since you are the sovereign lord of all.
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, who was then deeply distressed, spoke to him, seeking to enlighten him as he remained averse to the true nature of Śiva.
Viṣṇu said: "O Dakṣa, I must indeed provide protection for your sacrifice; for my vow is well-known as true: the preservation of dharma."
"What you have said is indeed true; however, what was the transgression against him? Listen, O Dakṣa, I shall speak; abandon your cruel intent now."
O Dakṣa, why is that wonderful event which occurred in Naimiṣa, the field of Nimiṣa, not remembered? Has it been forgotten by you, who possess such poor intellect?
Moreover, due to Rudra’s wrath, who indeed here is capable of protecting you? O Dakṣa, that foolish one who protects you does not have his own welfare at heart.
"O evil-minded one, do you perceive therein what is action and what is inaction? Merely capable action will not exist at all times."
Know that it arises through the efficacy of one's own karma; indeed, there is no other giver of the fruit of action than the Lord.
And to him who is peaceful through devotion to Īśvara, whose mind is fixed upon Him, Śiva then bestows the fruit of his action.
Relying solely on isolated knowledge, those men who are devoted to the doctrine of no-God go to hell for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Furthermore, bound by the nooses consisting of karma from birth to birth, those who are essentially nothing but karma are cooked in the hells.
This Vīrabhadra, the lord of Rudra’s hosts and the crusher of enemies, born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath, has arrived at the sacrificial arena.
"He has come for the purpose of our destruction; of this there is no doubt. There is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for him to achieve, regardless of what the actual reality may be."
Having set all of us ablaze, this great lord will certainly become one whose heart is pacified; of this there is no doubt.
Since I have transgressed the oath of the illustrious Mahādeva out of delusion, I shall obtain suffering from wherever I am situated, along with you.
I have no power at all to prevent this act of Dakṣa and the others, because by violating my oath, I have become an enemy of Śiva.
Since there is no happiness for those who offend the Great Lord even throughout the three periods of time, I have therefore inevitably obtained this suffering today along with you.
The discus named Sudarśana will not strike him, because this is a Śaiva discus, which causes the dissolution of non-Śaivas.
Even without Vīrabhadra, this Īśvara-cakra will now go swiftly to the presence of Hara after having slain him.
Having transgressed the Śaiva oath, I stood before such a discus; yet, without striking me, it suddenly became supremely steady out of mere compassion.
Henceforth, even this wheel will certainly not remain; it will now quickly depart, filled with garlands of flames.
Even though Vīrabhadra is worshipped by us with promptness and respect, being overcome by great wrath, he will not protect us.
Alas, alas! An untimely dissolution has indeed come upon us today; oh, oh! Now that you have perished, our own destruction has arrived.
Indeed, there is currently no one in the three worlds who can be our refuge; for in this world, who could be a refuge for one who has betrayed Śaṅkara?
Even if one’s body is destroyed, those torments of Yama must still be endured; they cannot be withstood, for they bestow manifold sufferings.
Upon seeing a betrayer of Śiva, Yama himself, his teeth gnashing, casts that person directly into cauldrons of boiling oil; it cannot be otherwise.
I was indeed intent on departing in every way after taking an oath; nevertheless, I did not go quickly due to the sin of association with the wicked.
If we flee from here today, then Śarva, the wielder of the plow, will drag us away with his weapons.
Whether in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, or wherever else it may be—for from whence could it be that the weapons of the illustrious Vīrabhadra cannot reach?
And as many hosts as there are of the trident-bearing Śrī Rudra, the power of all of them is certainly of this same nature.
In ancient times, Śrī Kālabhairava effortlessly severed the fifth head of Brahmā with the very tip of his fingernail at Kāśī.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu stood with his lotus-like face extremely terrified; at that very moment, Vīrabhadra also reached the sacrificial pavilion.
While Govinda was speaking thus, the gods and others beheld the ocean-like army arrive, accompanied by Vīrabhadra.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu’s Words," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Indra, laughing at Viṣṇu who was intent on his own boastful talk, became desirous of fighting with the gods while holding the thunderbolt in his hand.
Then Indra mounted his elephant, Anala likewise mounted a goat, Yama mounted a buffalo, and Nirṛti mounted a ghost.
Varuṇa, mounted upon his shark, and Vāyu, mounted upon his deer, as well as Kubera, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, stood ready and alert.
Likewise, other hosts of gods, as well as yakṣas, cāraṇas, and guhyakas, all majestic, mounted their respective vehicles.
Observing their exertion, Dakṣa, with blood on his face, approached them together with his wife and spoke.
Dakṣa said: "By your power alone has this great sacrifice been commenced by me; for the successful accomplishment of this virtuous deed, you, O beings of great luster, shall be my authority."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Dakṣa, all the gods, including Indra, quickly set out for that place, prepared to engage in battle.
Then all the hosts of gods, endowed with strength, fought; Śakra and the other world-protectors were deluded by the māyā of Śiva.
Then there was a great battle between the gods and the hosts; they fought one another with sharp lances and iron arrows.
In that great festival of battle, conchs and kettledrums resounded; great dundubhi drums, paṭahas, ḍiṇḍimas, and other instruments rang out.
At that great sound, the gods, together with the world-protectors, praised [Śiva] and struck down those servants of Śiva.
O tiger among sages, the hosts of Śambhu, including Indra and the other world-protectors, were turned away and cut down by the power of Bhṛgu’s mantra.
Then, for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods and for the satisfaction of the one initiated, Bhṛgu, the performer of sacrifices, performed their eradication.
Seeing his own men defeated, Vīrabhadra was filled with rage; he placed those very bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas behind him as his retinue.
Placing those mounted on bulls at the forefront, the immensely powerful one himself took up a great trident and struck down the gods.
The gods, yakṣas, hosts of sādhyas, guhyakas, and even the cāraṇas—all these groups struck with spears with great speed.
Some were cut in two by swords, others were crushed by mallets, and the gods were then pierced by other weapons as well by the hosts of attendants.
Thus defeated, all the gods, intent on flight and abandoning one another, departed for the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.
Only those world-protectors, Śakra and the others, being of great strength, stood there eager and maintaining their fortitude in that terrible battle.
Then all the gods, headed by Śakra, having assembled there on the field of battle, questioned Bṛhaspati with humility and bowed heads.
The World-Protectors said: "O Guru Bṛhaspati, dear father, possessor of great wisdom, ocean of compassion! Speak quickly to us who ask: by what means shall victory be ours?"
Brahmā said: Having heard their words and having called Śambhu to mind with great effort, Bṛhaspati spoke thus to Mahendra, who was weak in wisdom.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Indra, everything that was previously spoken by Viṣṇu has indeed come to pass today; I shall explain that very thing—listen with attentiveness."
There is a certain lord of yakṣas who bestows the fruits of all actions; yet even he serves the doer, for he is not the master over his own creator.
Neither all mantras nor medicinal herbs, neither malevolent rites nor worldly [practices], neither ritual acts nor the Vedas, and likewise not even the two systems of Mīmāṃsā [are effective].
Furthermore, other treatises as well, joined with various Vedas, are not capable of being fully understood; thus do the ancients say.
The Great Lord cannot be known by one's own intellect even through ten thousand Vedas; He is known only through devotion by those who have no other refuge—such is the great Vedic revelation.
Indeed, through supreme tranquility and a vision that is entirely free from modification, Sadāśiva is to be known by means of his grace.
However, O Lord of the Gods, I shall explain for your benefit what is to be done and what is not to be done when they are intended, as well as the portion of success; listen to that indeed.
O Indra, having become like a child today, you have indeed come to Dakṣa’s sacrifice along with the world-protectors; what valorous deed will you perform?
These hosts, the companions of Rudra, are exceedingly wrathful; they have arrived for the purpose of obstructing the sacrifice and will undoubtedly carry it out.
In every way, there is truly no means whatsoever for anyone here to destroy the obstacles to the sacrifice; I speak this as the truth, the absolute truth.
Brahmā said: Having thus heard the words of Bṛhaspati, all those inhabitants of heaven—the world-protectors together with Indra—fell into deep anxiety.
Then Vīrabhadra, surrounded by hosts of great heroes, spoke to those world-protectors, Indra and the others, while keeping Śaṅkara in his mind.
Vīrabhadra said: "All of you have come for the sake of a heroic deed because of your childishness. I shall grant you a heroic deed; come into my presence."
O Śakra, O Śuci, O Bhānu; O Śaśin, O Dhanādhipa; O Pāśapāṇi, O Vāyu, O Nirṛti, O Yama, O Śeṣa!
"O hosts of gods and asuras, come here, O wise ones! O best of beings, I shall relate edifying legends (avadānas) until you are satisfied."

Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, filled with rage, immediately struck all those gods with white arrows. By those arrows, all the lords of the gods, headed by Vāsava, were slain.

Intent on flight, they fled in the ten directions. When the world-protectors had departed and the gods had scattered, Vīrabhadra indeed approached the vicinity of the sacrificial enclosure with his hosts of attendants.
Then all those sages, being greatly terrified, desiring to make a representation to the Lord of Ramā, quickly and suddenly spoke while bowing low with great reverence.
The sages said: "O God of gods, Lord of Ramā, Sovereign of all, Great Lord! Protect the sacrifice of Dakṣa; for you are the sacrifice itself, there is no doubt."
You are the performer of sacrifice, the form of sacrifice, the limb of sacrifice, and the protector of sacrifice; therefore, protect the sacrifice, for there is no protector other than you.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of those sages, Viṣṇu Hari, out of fear, indeed desired to fight with that Vīrabhadra.
Four-armed, well-armored, and bearing the discus as a weapon in his hands, that immensely powerful one emerged from the sacrificial enclosure accompanied by hosts of gods.
Vīrabhadra, trident in hand and accompanied by various hosts, beheld the great lord Viṣṇu, fully armed and desirous of fighting.
Seeing him, Vīrabhadra’s face became contorted with a frown; he was like Death toward a sinner, or like a lion toward an elephant.
Seeing Hari in such a state, Vīrabhadra, the crusher of enemies, surrounded by his heroic Gaṇas, spoke swiftly and with anger.
Vīrabhadra said: "O Hara, O Mahādeva, how is it that you have today transgressed your own oath? What pride has arisen in your mind?"
Do you possess the power to transgress the oath of Śrī Rudra? Who indeed are you, and who is your protector within the three worlds?
Why have you come here? We do not know that at all. Tell us, how were you born from the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice?
Did you not see what was done by the daughter of Dakṣa? And did you not hear what was spoken by Dadhīci?
And you too have come to this sacrifice of Dakṣa for the sake of a sacrificial portion; O mighty-armed one, I shall grant a portion to you as well.
"I shall tear open your chest with my trident, O Hara! Who has come today as your protector to stand by my side?"
I shall cast you down upon the surface of the earth; I shall consume you with fire; now that you are burnt, I shall quickly grind you to pieces.
O Hare, O Durācāra, O lowest of those averse to Maheśa! Do you not know the purifying majesty of the Śrī Mahārudra?
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, you stand before me desiring to fight; I shall send you to the state from which there is no return, provided you remain in your own person.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Vīrabhadra, the wise Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, spoke with affection while smiling.
Viṣṇu said: Listen, O Vīrabhadra; today I shall speak before you. Do not call me one who is averse to Rudra, for I am a servant of Śaṅkara.
He was previously entreated by Dakṣa, who was devoted solely to ritual action and ignorant of the true purpose, again and again for the sake of a sacrifice, out of delusion.
I am dependent on my devotees, as is that Great Lord; for Dakṣa is indeed my devotee, dear one, and therefore he has come here to this sacrifice.
Listen to my vow, O hero born from the wrath of Rudra; for you, O Lord, are the very embodiment of Rudra’s splendor and the protector of supreme majesty.
I shall restrain you, and you shall restrain me; whatever is destined to happen will happen, yet I shall exert my prowess.
Brahmā said: When Govinda had spoken thus, that mighty-armed one laughed and said, "I am well-pleased, knowing you to be dear to our Lord."
Then, laughing with great joy, Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, bowed low with humility and spoke to the god Viṣṇu according to the truth.
Vīrabhadra said: "O Great Lord, it was said by me that this was for the purpose of testing your disposition; now I speak according to the truth—listen with careful attention."
"Just as Śiva is, so indeed are you; and as you are, so is Śiva"—thus do the Vedas describe it, O Hari, according to the teaching of Śiva.
"By the command of Śiva, we are all indeed servants of Śaṅkara; nevertheless, O Lord of Ramā, out of respect for what is appropriate for discourse, [we shall speak]."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Vīrabhadra, that Acyuta laughed and spoke these words to Vīrabhadra.
Viṣṇu said: "O great hero, engage in battle with me without hesitation; being overwhelmed by your weapons, I shall depart for my own hermitage."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, he ceased and prepared himself for battle; then the mighty Vīrabhadra also, along with his own hosts, was ready for the fray.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Viṣṇu and Vīrabhadra," in the Satī-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, in that battle, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra, remembering Śaṅkara—who wards off all calamities—in his heart, [fought] with Viṣṇu.
Having mounted his divine chariot, the crusher of all enemies took up supreme weapons and let out a lion’s roar.
And Viṣṇu also, the powerful one, blew his own great-sounding conch named Pāñcajanya, as if to gladden his own followers.
Hearing that blast of the conch, those gods who had previously fled, abandoning the battle, quickly returned once more.
Vīrabhadra, along with his attendants, and the world-protectors including Indra, endowed with great strength, waged war against them after letting out lion-like roars.
A tumultuous and terrifying duel took place there between the hosts of world-protectors, as they roared with lion-like cries.
Śakra fought with Nandin, as did Anala and the Vaiṣṇavas; even the powerful Kubera, the lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas, fought as well.
Then Nandin was struck by Indra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
And Śakra was struck in the middle of the chest by Nandin with his trident.
Both powerful ones fought each other with affection, inflicting various blows as Nandin and Śakra vied for victory.
The pure one, extremely enraged, struck the rock with his spear; he too [the rock] swiftly struck the Fire-god with a sharp-edged trident.
The heroic Mahāloka, the leader of the Gaṇas, joyfully remembered Mahādeva and waged a tumultuous battle against Yama.
Having encountered the son of Nirṛti, Caṇḍa, becoming even more powerful, fought with supreme weapons, binding the son of Nirṛti tightly.
The hero Muṇḍa, possessed of great strength, fought with Varuṇa to the best of his power, as if causing wonder throughout the three worlds.
And Bhṛṅgī was struck by Vāyu with his own weapon of supreme power; and Vāyu was struck by Bhṛṅgī with his blazing trident.
Having encountered Kubera himself, the powerful hero Kūṣmāṇḍapati, meditating on Maheśvara in his heart, fought with great respect.
The great leader of the Bhairavas, joined with the circle of Yoginīs, tore asunder all the gods and drank their wonderful blood.
Likewise, the field-protectors there, desiring to devour the foremost of the gods, and Kālī as well, tore them apart and drank much blood.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor and slayer of enemies, fought with them, hurling his discus with such force that it seemed to burn the ten directions.
Seeing the wheel approaching, the powerful Kṣetrapāla came there with speed; having arrived, the hero suddenly seized it.
Seeing his discus swallowed, Viṣṇu, the conqueror of enemy cities, wiped the enemy's mouth and vomited that foe out.

Taking up his own discus, the one of great majesty, the sole lord of existence, became exceedingly enraged; that mighty hero fought with those great warriors who brandished various weapons and missiles in their fury.
Viṣṇu waged a great battle and fought with them joyfully, brandishing various weapons in a tumultuous conflict of terrifying prowess.
Then Bhairava and the others fought with him repeatedly, discharging various weapons, highly enraged and possessing supreme vigor.
Having thus witnessed their battle with Hari, who possesses incomparable splendor, the powerful one turned back, approached them, and fought with his own hands.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, of great splendor, raising his discus though fainting with exhaustion, the blessed Mādhava fought with that Vīrabhadra.
O Sage, between those two great lords of heroes, both wielding various weapons, there occurred a most terrible battle that made one's hair stand on end.
O God of gods, by the power of Viṣṇu’s yoga, innumerable and most formidable beings were born, bearing conchs, discs, and maces in their hands.
And those hosts, powerful like Viṣṇu and bearing various weapons, also fought with that speaking Vīrabhadra.
Having remembered the Lord Śiva, that hero struck them all with his trident and reduced them to ashes, for they were all equal in splendor to Nārāyaṇa.
Then, on the field of battle, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra struck Viṣṇu on the chest with his trident as if in mere play.
O Sage, suddenly struck by that blow, Hari, the Supreme Person, fell to the ground and lost consciousness.
Then there arose from the sacrifice a fierce splendor, resembling the fire of universal destruction, capable of burning the three worlds, intense, and terrifying even to heroes.
With eyes red with rage, that illustrious lord, that bull among men, rose up again and stood ready to strike, raising his discus.
The noble-souled Lord Śiva, as Vīrabhadra, paralyzed that most terrible discus, which possessed a radiance equal to the sun at the end of time.
O Sage, by the power of Śambhu, the great lord and master of illusion, Hari’s discus remained fixed in his hand and did not move, being certainly paralyzed.
Then Viṣṇu, addressed by Gaṇeśa and Vīrabhadra, stood paralyzed by him, motionless like a mountain peak.
Then, O Nārada, Viṣṇu was indeed paralyzed by Vīrabhadra; intent on summoning the sacrificer, he performed the rite that causes paralysis.
Then, O Sage, released from that paralysis, the Lord of Ramā, wielder of the Śārṅga bow, became enraged and seized his own bow, the Śārṅga, along with an arrow.
O Sage, when Vīrabhadra assailed the Śārṅga bow of Hari with three arrows, it broke into three pieces at that very instant, my dear.
Then Viṣṇu, having been awakened by my speech and perceiving that great host of unbearable splendor, set his mind upon vanishing from sight.

Having understood all this future destiny ordained by Satī—which is difficult for others to endure—they departed for their own world accompanied by their respective hosts, remembering Śiva, the independent Lord of all.
O son, having gone to Satyaloka, I was tormented by grief; afflicted by great suffering, I reflected: "What indeed must be done by me now?"
And when I, Viṣṇu, had departed, all the gods together with the sages were utterly defeated by the Gaṇas—those who subsist upon sacrifices.
Perceiving the great sacrifice to be ruined and beset by calamity, Yajña, indeed in the form of a deer, fled even though he was greatly terrified.
Then Vīrabhadra, seizing him as he was running toward the sky in the form of a deer, deprived him of his head.
Then that hero, having seized Prajāpati Dharma, Kaśyapa, Ariṣṭanemi, and the lord of sages Bahupatra;
The great host struck the sage Āṅgirasa, as well as Kṛśāśva and the eminent sage Datta, on the head with their feet.
And likewise, the powerful Vīrabhadra severed the tip of Sarasvatī’s nose and that of Devamātṛ with the point of his fingernail.
Then, with eyes overcome by fury, he indeed tore asunder other gods and beings as well, casting them down upon the surface of the earth.
Even after tearing apart the principal gods and the sages as well, Vīrabhadra was not pacified; his anger remained swift, like a king of serpents adorned with its hood.
Having uprooted his enemies like a lion uproots forest elephants, Vīrabhadra surveyed the directions every moment, wondering, "Who is there? Where?"
While the powerful Maṇibhadra was crushing Bhṛgu, he then stepped upon his chest with his foot and tore out his beard.
And Caṇḍa, with great force, tore out the teeth of Pūṣan, who had previously laughed while showing them as Hara was being cursed.
Indeed, Nandin, with his own eye, plucked out the eyes of Bhaga who had been cast to the ground in anger; he was one who signaled his curse by threatening with his eye.
There, Svadhā was mocked, as were Svāhā and Dakṣiṇā; likewise, the mantras and other tantras present there were ridiculed by the leaders of the Gaṇas.
The hosts, filled with rage, showered masses of earth upon the sacrificial fire; then those heroic groups rendered that sacrifice unspeakable.
Recognizing that [the child] had been forcibly hidden within the *antarvedi* out of fear of him, Vīrabhadra brought forth the one born of his own nature.
Having seized his head by the cheek, he struck it with a sword; yet, due to the power of yoga, that head became impenetrable for him.
Considering that head to be impenetrable by all manner of weapons and missiles, he stepped upon it with his feet at the chest and tore it off with his hand.
Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, cast the head of that wicked Dakṣa, the enemy of Hara, into the sacrificial fire-pit.
Then Vīrabhadra, brandishing his trident in his hand, cast them aside; enraged, those mountain-like beings blazed like the fire of universal destruction at the end of the age.
Having slain them without effort, Vīrabhadra then, filled with rage, set them ablaze with fire like moths in a blazing flame.
Then Vīrabhadra, seeing Dakṣa and the others consumed by fire, let out a loud, boisterous laugh that filled the three worlds.
Then, surrounded there by the splendor of heroism, a divine shower of flowers born from the Nandana grove fell upon Vīrabhadra and his hosts.
Then, cool, fragrant, and pleasant-scented breezes blew gently; simultaneously, the celestial drums resounded.
Then that hero, having accomplished his task and destroyed the dense darkness, went quickly to Kailāsa like the sun.
Seeing that Vīrabhadra had accomplished his task, the Supreme Lord Śambhu, with a satisfied mind, appointed him as the commander of the heroic Gaṇas.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Sacrifice," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second part (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of that Brahmā of immeasurable intellect, Nārada, the best of the twice-born, was struck with wonder and asked him with affection.
Nārada said: "Tell me, for what reason did Hari go to Dakṣa’s sacrifice, leaving Śiva behind, whereupon such contempt arose from him?"
Does Hari not know Śambhu, nor his prowess at the time of dissolution? How could he have waged war against his attendants like one who is ignorant?
This is my great doubt; O treasure of compassion, cut it asunder! O Lord, tell me of the life of Śambhu, which inspires the heart with vigor.
Brahmā said: O best of the twice-born, listen with affection to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, which removes all doubts for both those who inquire about it and those who practice it.
In ancient times, due to the curse of the sage Dadhīca, Hari’s knowledge was lost; accompanied by the gods and aided by Kṣuva, he went indeed to Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Nārada said: For what reason did Dadhīca, the best of sages, curse Viṣṇu? And why was that form of anger displayed toward him by Hari, who had been his ally?
Brahmā said: A king of great splendor known as Kṣuva was born; he became the friend of Dadhīci, the lord of sages and possessor of great power.
Long ago, due to their prolonged engagement in asceticism, a dispute arose between Kṣupa and Adhīca; it became renowned throughout the three worlds as being fraught with great calamity.
"In this regard, the Brahmin alone is the most excellent among the three castes; of this there is no doubt. Thus indeed spoke Dadhīca, the devotee of Śiva and knower of the Vedas.
Having heard those words of the great sage Dadhīca, King Kṣuva, deluded by the intoxication of his own splendor, spoke as follows.
Kṣuva said: The king bears the body of the eight world-protectors; therefore, the king is indeed preeminent, the lord and master of the castes and stages of life.
"O Sage, the Veda, which is devoted to that, declares: 'The King consists of all the gods; that Great Deity who exists is indeed I myself.'"
Therefore, O son of Cyavana, let the king be considered superior to the Brahmin; he must not be disregarded from now on, for I am to be honored by you in every way.
Brahmā said: Having heard that opinion of Kṣuva, which was contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti, Bhārgava, the best of sages, became exceedingly enraged.
Then, O sage, the highly effulgent Dadhīca, enraged yet out of respect for himself, struck Kṣuva on the head with his left fist.
Struck by the thunderbolt, that Dadhīca sneezed; then the evil-minded Kṣuva, the lord of the cosmic egg, roared exceedingly in great fury.
Struck by that thunderbolt, the descendant of Bhṛgu fell to the ground; then the upholder of Bhārgava’s lineage remembered Śukra, the creator of the Kṣuva plant.
Then Śukra, the yogi, having arrived swiftly, joined together the body of Dadhīca which had been struck by Kṣuva.
Having restored Dadhīca’s body as before, Bhārgava—the foremost devotee of Śiva and the promoter of the science of victory—spoke to his servant.
Śukra said: O dear Dadhīca, having worshipped Śiva, the Lord and Sovereign of All, I shall declare to you the supreme Vedic mantra known as Mahāmṛtyuñjaya.
We worship Tryambaka, the father of the three worlds, the Lord, the father of the triple sphere, the Great Sovereign of the three qualities.
Of the three principles and the three fires, which have manifested in three ways everywhere; and of the triple heaven and the three-armed one, which have manifested in three ways everywhere.
Mahādeva, the god of the three [gods], is fragrant and the increaser of nourishment; he exists everywhere among all beings, throughout the three qualities (guṇas), according to his creative action.
Among the senses, as well as among other gods and divine hosts, the Sun, the lord of the immortals, is fragrant like a sweet-smelling flower.

O best of the twice-born, O observer of noble vows, since the nourishment of primordial nature (prakṛti) proceeds from the Puruṣa, as do the various manifestations beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa).
O great sage, because he nourishes Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, the sages, the senses, and the gods, he is indeed known as Puṣṭivardhana.
O Prajāpati, one may attain that immortal god Rudra through ritual action, or through austerity, or through the study of sacred texts, yoga, and meditation.

By means of another truth, Bhava himself, the Lord, releases one from the subtle-pointed noose of death; for he is the one who effects both bondage and liberation, just as one [extracts] a cucumber from its stalk.
The *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* mantra is considered by me to be the most excellent of all; thus, devoted to its recitation with love, one should remember Śiva according to the prescribed rules.
Having recited [the mantra], offered oblations, and consecrated it with mantras, drink water day and night; by meditating on Śiva in his presence, there is no fear of death anywhere.
Having performed all the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and duly worshipped Śiva, he composed this [work] with undistracted mind for Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
I shall now describe his meditation, by meditating upon which and reciting the mantra, the wise practitioner shall become a perfected master of the mantra through the power of Śambhu.

I worship the three-eyed Mṛtyuñjaya together with Girijā, who pours water from a pair of jars held in his lotus-like hands over his head, who holds two elephant-trunk-shaped vessels in his pair of arms upon his lap, who has a rosary and a deer in his hands, who holds a lotus, and whose body is moistened by the nectar flowing from the moon situated upon his crest.
Brahmā said: Having thus instructed Dadhīci, the best of sages, Śukra departed for his own abode, O dear one, while constantly remembering the Lord Śaṅkara.
Having heard those words of his, the great sage Dadhīca indeed went to the forest with great joy to practice austerities, while remembering Śiva.
Having gone there, he performed penance with devotion while reciting with love that mantra known as Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, remembering Śiva according to the prescribed rite.
Having recited that mantra for a very long time and propitiated Śaṅkara through austerity, he indeed gratified Śiva, the Great Conqueror of Death.
Then, O great sage, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased in soul by that recitation, appeared before him with love.
Seeing his own lord Śambhu, that lord of sages rejoiced; having prostrated according to the rules with devotion, he offered praise with his hands joined in reverence.
Then, O Sage, Śiva, being pleased with affection toward Cyāvani, spoke with a very gracious mind: "Choose a boon."
Having heard those words of Śambhu, Dadhīca, the best among devotees, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, spoke to Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Dadhīca said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, grant me three boons: invincibility against the thunderbolt, immortality, and freedom from distress in every respect."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words spoken by him, the Supreme Lord was pleased and granted three boons to Dadhīca, saying, "So be it."
Having received the three boons from Śiva, the great sage, established in the path of the Vedas, went joyfully and swiftly to Kṣurasthāna.

Brahmā said: Having obtained invincibility from the Fierce One (Ugra), as well as the state of being struck by the thunderbolt and freedom from dejection, he struck the king of kings on the head with the sole of his foot.
Then King Kṣuva, filled with exceptional anger and proud of his reverence for Viṣṇu, struck Dadhīca in the chest with his thunderbolt.
That vajra did not suffice for the destruction of the great-souled Dadhīca; by the power of the Supreme Lord, the son of the Creator was struck with wonder.

Having observed both the invincibility and the lack of dejection of Vajra, as well as his exceedingly supreme power, Kṣuva, the son of the Creator, was filled with wonder in his heart at the sight of the lord of sages, Dadhīca.

Having quickly gone to the forest, he propitiated Hari Mukunda, the younger brother of Indra; for even the Protector of those who seek refuge was defeated by the servant of the Conqueror of Death, Dadhīca.
Pleased by his worship, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana, whose banner bears Garuḍa, granted him a divine vision.
Having beheld the god Janārdana with his divine vision, he bowed before the one whose banner is Garuḍa and praised him with pleasing words.
Having thus worshipped the invincible Lord, who is praised by the lords of the thirty gods and others, he gazed upon him with devotion, prostrated with his head, and made this request to Janārdana.
The King said: "O Blessed One, there was once a certain Brāhmaṇa renowned as Dadhīca; he was a knower of dharma and a humble soul who was my friend in the past."
By the power of Śaṅkara, he was forever invulnerable to all; having propitiated that Mahādeva, the conqueror of death, who is free from ailment.
That great ascetic Dadhīca, with contempt, violently struck me on the head with his left foot even as I was present there.
And with pride he said to him, "I do not fear anything from any quarter," for Hari, having obtained the supreme boons from the Conqueror of Death, was indeed filled with incomparable arrogance.
Brahmā said: Then, having realized that the high-souled Dadhīca was indeed incapable of being slain, Hari recollected the incomparable power of Maheśvara.
Having remembered this, Hari quickly said to Kṣuva, the son of Brahmā: "O Indra among kings, there is not even the slightest fear for brāhmaṇas anywhere."
O King, there is no fear for those especially devoted to Rudra; yet he causes suffering to me, a brahmin, along with the gods, for the sake of his curse.
O King of kings, by the curse of the Lord of the Gods at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, my destruction and my subsequent restoration shall come to pass.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, since no universal sacrifice can be performed without him, I shall make an effort, O Indra among kings, for the sake of your victory over Dadhīca.
Having heard these words, King Kṣuva said to Hari, "So be it," and remained right there out of affection for him, his mind eager for that pleasure.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Kṣuva and Dadhīca," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: For the sake of doing what was beneficial for Kṣuva, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, assumed the form of a brāhmaṇa and went to the hermitage of Dadhīci.
Having paid homage to the brahmin-sage Dadhīca, the Teacher of the World spoke to him, being intent on the task of Kṣuva and resorting to a stratagem against the lord of the Śaivas.
Viṣṇu said: "O Dadhīca, O brahmin-sage, O imperishable one devoted to the worship of Śiva! I choose a single boon from you; you ought to grant it."
Brahmā said: Being entreated by the God of gods, who desired the fulfillment of his purpose, Dadhīca, the best of Śiva’s devotees, quickly spoke these words to Hari.
Dadhīca said: "O Brahmin, your desire is known; you have come for the sake of a trivial task. You are indeed the Lord Hari himself, a master of illusion appearing in the form of a brahmin."
O Lord of gods, O Janārdana, by the grace of Rudra, my knowledge of the past, the future, and the present is always possessed of the three periods of time.
I know you to be Hari Viṣṇu; abandon this state of being a twice-born, O observer of noble vows! You have been propitiated by King Kṣuva, who possesses a wicked mind.
O Lord Hari, I know your very affection for your devotees; abandon this disguise and assume your true form—remember Śaṅkara!
If anyone should have fear toward me, who am devoted to the worship of Bhava, you ought to speak with effort, preceded by an oath of truth.
I speak nowhere falsely; with my intellect intent on the remembrance of Śiva, I fear nothing in this world, not even the gods, the Daityas, or others.
Viṣṇu said: "O Dadhīca of noble vows, your fear has vanished everywhere, because you are devoted to the worship of Bhava and are indeed all-knowing."
"O King of kings, by my command, you ought to say 'I am afraid' even once; for this is for the sake of suppressing your sneeze. "Homage to you! [he replied].
Brahmā said: Even after hearing those words of Viṣṇu, that great sage Dadhīca, the best among the devotees of Śiva, laughed and spoke fearlessly.
Dadhīca said: "I am never afraid of anything, anywhere, or from anyone, due to the power of Śambhu, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow himself."
Brahmā said: Then, having heard the words of that sage, Hari became enraged; raising his discus, he stood there desiring to consume the best of sages.
There, even in the presence of that king, lord of the gods, the most terrible discus became blunted against the brahmin by his power.
Seeing that discus with its edge blunted, Dadhīca, the manifest cause of both the existent and the non-existent, spoke with a smile to Viṣṇu himself.

Dadhīca said: "O Blessed One, that exceedingly terrible discus of Viṣṇu known as Sudarśana, which you obtained with great effort in the past—that auspicious discus of Bhava does not seek to slay me here."
Then the Blessed One, Hari, became enraged at him; you ought to exert yourself with all weapons in succession, beginning with the Brahmāstra, and with arrows and other missiles.
Brahmā said: Having heard his words and seeing that the human was devoid of prowess, Hari then angrily discharged all his weapons against him in succession.
Then the wise gods respectfully rendered assistance to Viṣṇu as he set forth to fight with that single brahmin.
Śakra and the other supporters of Hari swiftly hurled their respective weapons and missiles from all sides with great force upon Dadhīca.
Then, taking a handful of kusha grass and remembering Shiva, the self-controlled Dadhichi emitted the adamantine bone from all parts for the sake of all the gods.
O Sage, by the power of Śaṅkara, that handful of kuśa grass belonging to the sage indeed became a divine trident resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
He set his mind on burning the gods, along with their weapons and their topknots; that Śaiva fire blazed on all sides, its radiance exceeding even the foremost flames at the end of an eon.
And all the weapons that had been hurled by the gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa and Indu, bowed down before that trident.
All the gods, the inhabitants of heaven, fled, their prowess destroyed; only Hari, the foremost of masters of illusion, remained there, though afraid.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, emitted from his own body millions upon millions of divine hosts who were like himself.
And then, O celestial sage, those heroic attendants of Viṣṇu fought there against the single sage Dadhīca, whose soul was devoted to Śiva.
Then, having repeatedly subdued those hosts of Viṣṇu in battle, Dadhīca, the best of Śiva’s devotees, suddenly consumed them all with fire.
Then, in order to cause wonder to that sage Dadhīci, Hari, who is an expert in great illusion, quickly assumed a universal form.
In the body of that Hari, the best of the twice-born directly beheld a thousand living beings, including the gods and others, as well as Dadhīca himself.
At that time, there were ten million beings, ten million hosts, and ten million cosmic eggs within the body of Viśvamūrti.
Having seen all this there, Cyavana then spoke constantly to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, the unborn and omnipresent one who is praised by the world.

Dadhīca said: "O mighty-armed one, abandon your illusory power; through inquiry, appearances are understood. Thousands of things have been discerned, O Mādhava, yet they remain difficult to fully comprehend."
Behold within me the entire universe joined with you, unwearied; likewise, behold Brahmā and Rudra—I grant you divine vision.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the sage, whose body was filled with the splendor of Śambhu, revealed the entire universe within his own person to Cyavana.
Dadhīca, the best of Śiva’s devotees, being wise, fearless, and laughing while remembering Śaṅkara in his heart, burned Viṣṇu, the lord of gods.
Dadhīca said: "O Hari, what use have you for this illusion or the power of mantras? Therefore, you ought to strive diligently to fight against her who is intent on her desire."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of that sage, Viṣṇu, who was fearless at that time, became exceedingly enraged with that sage on account of Śambhu’s splendor.
And the gods fled once more toward that Lord Nārāyaṇa, desiring to fight with the powerful sage Dadhīci.
In the meantime, Kṣuva, accompanied by me, arrived there; he restrained Hari, the lotus-born Brahmā, and the gods, who were motionless.
Having heard my words, the brahmin was indeed not defeated; Hari went near him and bowed to the sage.
Becoming even more dejected, Kṣuva went there to the lord of sages, and having saluted Dadhīca, he made his request in a state of agitation.
Kṣuva said: Be gracious, O tiger among sages, crest-jewel of the devotees of Śiva! Be gracious, O Supreme Lord, who are difficult to perceive for the wicked.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the king and the host of gods, the brahmin Dadhīca, a treasure-house of asceticism, showed him favor.
Then, seeing Rama, Isha, and the others, the sage, overwhelmed with anger, remembered Shiva and Vishnu in his heart and cursed the gods as well.
Dadhīca said: "O gods, including Indra, and O lords of sages, let all of you, together with Lord Viṣṇu and his attendants, be destroyed by the fire of Rudra’s wrath."
Brahmā said: Having thus cursed the gods and looked at Kṣuva, the sage then said: "O Indra among kings, this best of the twice-born is to be honored by the gods and by kings alike."
"O Indra among kings, only the Brahmins are powerful and sovereign. Having said this, that manifest Brahmin entered his own hermitage.
Having paid homage to Dadhīca, Kṣuva went to his own home; Viṣṇu, along with the gods, returned to his own world as he had come.
Thus, that very place became a sacred ford known as Sthāneśvara; having reached Sthāneśvara, one attains union with Śiva.

O dear one, I have related to you in brief the dispute between Kṣuva and Dadhīca, who had incurred the curse of the king, as well as that between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, both of whom were excluded from Śiva.
Whoever constantly recites this dialogue between Kṣuva and Dadhīci, having conquered untimely death, shall go to the world of Brahmā at the end of the body.
Whoever enters into battle after reciting this, for him there shall never be fear of death, and he shall be victorious.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Viṣṇu and Dadhīci," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Nārada said: O Creator, O Creator, O one of great wisdom, O revealer of the true nature of Śiva! You have caused us to hear the most wonderful pastimes of Śiva, which consist for the most part of his dalliances with the Goddess.
O dear one, after the heroic Vīrabhadra had indeed destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice and departed for Mount Kailāsa, what happened next? Tell me that now.
Brahmā said: Then all the hosts of gods and the sages, defeated and their limbs mangled by the armies of Rudra, fled to my world at that time.
Having paid homage to the Self-Existent One and praised me profusely, they reported their own suffering in detail and in its entirety.
Having heard that, I, indeed, afflicted by grief for my son, reflected with an extremely agitated and tormented mind.
"What task must be performed by me today with haste that brings happiness to the gods, so that this sacrifice of Dakṣa may live and the deity may be complete?"
Having reflected thus in many ways, O Sage, I did not attain peace; then, remembering Viṣṇu with devotion, I obtained the appropriate knowledge.
Then, together with the gods and sages, I went to the world of Viṣṇu; having bowed and praised him with various hymns, I reported my suffering.
Act in such a way that the sacrifice may be fully completed and he may become a performer of divine worship; act so that all the gods and the sages may be happy.
O God of gods, O Lord of Ramā, O Viṣṇu, O bringer of happiness to the gods! We, along with the gods and sages, have certainly come to you for refuge.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, Brahmā, the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose very self is Śiva, remembered Śiva and replied with a distressed mind.

Viṣṇu said: For those who desire prosperity, such a course is not appropriate when one has committed an offense against a more powerful being; for in that situation, those who have offended must employ various means to ensure their own security.
O Creator, since all the gods had committed offenses against Śiva, the Supreme Lord, they offered a sacrificial portion to that Śambhu.
"Indeed, you all must propitiate him with a pure mind; then, having grasped the two feet of that auspicious one, you shall obtain further grace."
When that god is provoked to anger, the entire world—including the world-protectors and sacrifices—is swiftly destroyed by his command.
Quickly appease that god, who is separated from his beloved and whose heart has been pierced by the harsh words of the evil-minded Dakṣa.
O Creator, this alone is the supreme means for its pacification; I consider it to be the truth that has been spoken by me for the sole purpose of pleasing Śambhu.
Neither I, nor you, nor other gods, nor even the sages who bear bodies, know the true nature or the measure of his strength and valor.
Who indeed could desire to devise a means for that supreme Self, the other who is independent, unless he were utterly deluded and hostile?
O Brahmin, I too shall go with everyone to the abode of Śiva; having committed an offense against Śivā, I shall certainly seek forgiveness from Giriśa.
Brahmā said: Having thus commanded me, Brahmā, along with the gods and others, Viṣṇu set his mind upon going to that mountain together with the deities.

Hari, who embodies the gods, the sages, the lords of creatures, and others, went to his own abode on Śiva’s auspicious and excellent mountain, Kailāsa, together with the oceans and the hosts of sages.
It was eternally most dear to the Lord, constantly frequented by Kinnaras and others, by Naretaras, Apsarases, and those perfected in yoga, and exceedingly exalted.
It was resplendent on all sides with peaks composed of various jewels, variegated with diverse minerals, and filled with many trees and creepers.
It was crowded with various herds of deer, filled with various birds, and possessed various flowing springs for the immortals and the wives of the siddhas.
It was resplendent with the luster of silver, beautified by various species of trees and other features such as diverse caves and mountain ridges that seemed to draw one in with their charm.
Proclaimed by great beings such as tigers and others, it was free from cruelty, endowed with every beauty, divine, and causing great wonder.
It was rendered utterly pure by the true Gaṅgā, who arises from the most meritorious place, who is the creator of all purifiers, and who is the footstep of Viṣṇu.
Having seen such a mountain named Kailāsa, beloved of Śiva, the gods led by Viṣṇu, along with the lords of sages, were filled with wonder.
In its vicinity, those immortals beheld the beautiful city named Alakā, the great and divine abode of Kubera, the friend of Rudra.
And nearby they beheld the divine Saugandhika forest, filled with all kinds of trees, where that sound was not heard.
Outside of that, there are two divine, exceedingly purifying rivers, Nanda and Alakanandā, which destroy sin merely by being seen.
The celestial women, having constantly descended from their own world and embraced [the men], plunge into the waters there and sport with them, exhausted by passion.
Having left the city of the Lord of Yakṣas and the Saugandhika forest, those gods, as they were proceeding, beheld from nearby the banyan tree of Śaṅkara.
It was spread out, casting an unshakable shadow, with its branches extending for three-quarters of its span; it rose a hundred yojanas in height, devoid of nests and free from heat.
Visible to those of great merit, exceedingly beautiful and most purifying, the divine site of Śambhu’s yoga is supreme and frequented by yogis.
In that banyan tree, which was the refuge of those seeking liberation and was filled with great yoga, Viṣṇu and all the other gods beheld Śiva seated there.
He was being joyfully worshipped by the sons of Vidhi, who were great Siddhas ever devoted to Śiva, peaceful and possessing tranquil forms.
Likewise, he was constantly attended by his friend Kubera, the lord of the Guhyakas and Rākṣasas, and especially served by his own hosts and kinsmen.
The Supreme Lord, the friend of the universe, who out of affection assumes the excellent form desired by ascetics and is beautifully adorned with ashes and other such marks.
O Sage, as you were seated comfortably upon a mat of kusha grass, you proclaimed this supreme knowledge to me who questioned you, while all the virtuous ones listened.
Having placed the left foot upon the right thigh at the knee, he stands with his arms and forearms holding a rosary, in the *sattarka-mudrā*.
Having thus beheld Śiva, Viṣṇu and all the other gods then quickly bowed down, joining their palms in reverence with heads humbly inclined.
When Rudra, the refuge of the virtuous, arrived as one who could be perceived, the Lord Viṣṇu rose and offered salutation with his head bowed.
Then Śiva, whose feet are worshipped by all the divine beings beginning with Viṣṇu, bowed to Viṣṇu and Kaśyapa, who are the true refuge of the worlds.
To Viṣṇu, who was being saluted with reverence by the gods and was himself honored by the hosts of Suras, Siddhas, and great sages, [Brahmā] spoke as he bowed down respectfully.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of Śiva," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Viṣṇu and the others said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord who establishes worldly conduct! By your grace, we know you as Brahmā, the Sovereign, and Śambhu."
Why do you delude us, O Father, with your supreme illusion that is ever difficult for men to discern and utterly enchanting, O Supreme Lord?

You are the primordial source of both the material nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), as well as of the womb and the seed of the universe; you are the Supreme Brahman, the Transcendent, and beyond the reach of mind and speech.
You alone create, protect, and consume the universe by Your own independent power, sporting with Your own essential Śiva-Śakti like a spider with its web.
O Lord, you alone, devoted to compassion, have created the sacrifice with the thread of Dakṣa, O All-pervading One, for the perpetual attainment of the three Vedas.
By you alone have the boundaries been established in the world, which the pure Brahmins—firm in their vows and expert in the path of the Vedas—revere.
O Lord, you are indeed the foremost among all auspicious things for the doer; yet, in the mouth of others, you are the source of inauspiciousness, or beneficial, or mixed, or even the opposite.
For you alone are indeed the eternal giver of the fruits of all actions; for all things have been declared as your glory, and you are their Lord, as heard in the Vedas.
Those of separate intellects, who perceive only action, who are piercing and evil-minded, being deluded and filled with envy, wound others with harsh words.
O Lord, let there also be the destruction of those slayers of the gods; O Blessed One, Supreme Ruler, O Sovereign Lord, show mercy!
Salutations to Rudra, the peaceful one, to Brahman, the Supreme Self; salutations to the one with matted hair, the Great Lord, the light, the Great One.

For you are the creator of the creators of the universe, the sustainer, and the great-grandfather; you are both composed of the three qualities and devoid of qualities, beyond both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
Salutations to you, O blue-throated one, the creator, the supreme self, the universe, the seed of the universe, and the cause of joy for the world.

You are the syllable *oṃ*, you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*, the initiator of all undertakings; you are the utterance *haṃta* and the formula *svadhā*, the eternal consumer of the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors.
O you who are devoted to dharma, how was the sacrifice destroyed by you? O Mahādeva, you are a friend to the Brahmins; O Lord, how have you become a destroyer of the sacrifice?
O Lord, you are the protector of the Brahmins, of cows, and of Dharma; you are the eternal refuge for all living beings.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord Rudra, whose splendor is like that of the sun and is immeasurable; salutations to the divine Bhava, who consists of the essence of water.
Salutations always to Śarva, who has the form of the earth and is eternally fragrant; salutations to Rudra, whose nature is fire and who possesses great splendor.
Salutations again and again to you, Īśa, to Vāyu, and to Saṃsparśa; salutations to you, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), the sacrificer, and the Ordainer (Vedhas).
Salutations to you, Bhīma, whose form is space and who consists of sound alone; salutations be to you, Mahādeva, Soma, and the one who has come forth.
Salutations to you, the fierce one, who has the form of the sun; salutations to you, the master of action; salutations to you, the death of Death; salutations to you, O Rudra, in your wrath.
Salutations to you, O Śiva, the Terrible, the Beneficent, and the Auspicious! You are the fierce one of all beings and their controller, because you are our Śiva (the Benevolent).
Salutations to you, the benefactor of all, the embodiment of the universal Brahman, the destroyer of suffering, the Lord of Ambikā, and the Consort of Umā.

Salutations to you, Śarva, who possesses all forms, the Supreme Person, the Highest Self, who is devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence, and the cause of the Great Principle (Mahat).
Homage again and again to the one born in many ways throughout the world, the abundant one; to the Blue One, to Nīlarudra, to Kadrudra, and to Pracetas.
Homage to you, the most bountiful god, Śipiviṣṭa; homage to you, the most exalted, the eternal slayer of the enemies of the gods.
Salutations again and again to Tārā, Sutārā, Taruṇa, Sutejas, the golden-haired god, and Maheśa.
Salutations to you, the source of bliss for the gods; salutations to you, the all-pervading Supreme Self; salutations to the Supreme One; salutations to you, the blue-throated Lord.
Salutation to the golden one, the supreme lord, whose body is of gold; salutation to the formidable one, who possesses a fearsome form and delights in formidable deeds.
Salutations to you whose body is smeared with ashes and who wears rudrākṣa ornaments; salutations be to you, the short, the long, and the dwarf.

Salutations again and again to you, O God, who wields the bow from afar and the sword at close range; salutations to you, the wielder of the bow, the trident-bearer, the mace-wielder, and the plow-holder.
Salutations indeed to the bearer of various weapons, the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, to Sadya, to him of sudden form, and to Sadyojāta.
Salutation to you who are the left, who possess a beautiful form, and who have a beautiful eye; salutations again and again to the non-terrible one, the supreme lord, the formidable one.
