Salutations to the Lord who is the Tatpuruṣa, to the Ancient Being (Purāṇapuruṣa), to the bestower of the goals of human existence, to the observer of vows, and to the Supreme Abider (Parameṣṭhin).
Salutations to you, the Ruler; salutations again and again to the Lord; salutations to Brahman, whose form is Brahman, the manifest Supreme Self.
You are fierce toward all the wicked, you are the restrainer, and you are auspicious to us; salutations to you, the consumer of the Kālakūṭa poison and the one who protects the gods and others.
Salutation to the Hero, to Vīrabhadra, to the protector of heroes, to the wielder of the trident, to Mahādeva, the Great One, the Lord of all creatures.
Salutations to the heroic-souled Śrīkaṇṭha, the possessor of excellent knowledge, the wielder of the Pināka bow; salutations to the infinite and subtle one; salutations to you, the wrath of Death.
Salutations to you, the Supreme, the Supreme Lord, who are higher than the highest; salutations to you, the all-pervading one, whose form is the universe, who are higher than the highest.
Homage to the consort of Viṣṇu, to the field of Viṣṇu, to the Sun; to Bhairava, the refuge, the three-eyed one, the playful wanderer.

To the conqueror of death, to sorrow, to that which consists of the three qualities, to the soul of all qualities, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and who is the bridge to the cause of all things.
For the entire world is pervaded by you with your own splendor; you are the Supreme Brahman, changeless, consisting of consciousness and bliss, and luminous.
O Maheśvara, all the gods, headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Candra, as well as the sages and others, have been produced from you.
Since you sustain the entire universe by dividing your body into eight parts, you are the Lord of Eight Forms (Aṣṭamūrti), the primordial one, and the embodiment of compassion.
Out of fear of you this wind blows; out of fear of you the fire burns; the sun shines out of fear of you; and death runs everywhere.
O Ocean of Compassion, Great Lord, be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign! Protect us, protect us always, for we are lost and deprived of our senses.
O Protector, O ocean of compassion, we have been constantly protected by you alone from various calamities; likewise, O Śambhu, protect us now as well.
O Lord, O Maker of Grace, quickly perform the restoration of the sacrifice of the Prajāpati Dakṣa, which remains unfinished, O Lord of Durgā.
May Bhaga and Anumati be propitiated, and may the sacrificer live; may the teeth of Pūṣan grow back, and the beard of Bhr̥gu as before.
O Śaṅkara, may there be health for all the gods and others who have been favored by you, even those whose limbs were shattered by your weapons and stones.
"O Lord, may you have a full share in the remaining sacrificial rites; your sacrifice has been ordained with a portion for Rudra, and never otherwise."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Prajāpatis and the Lord of Ramā, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, intent upon seeking forgiveness.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Devotion of the Devas," in the Satī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, having been entreated by the illustrious Brahmā, the Lord of Progeny, and indeed by the Sage, became forever gracious.
Having consoled the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, and having smiled, the Supreme Lord, a treasury of compassion, spoke while bestowing supreme grace.
Śrī Mahādeva said: Listen attentively to my words, O best of gods; I speak to you both according to the truth, dear ones, for I have always endured your anger.
I do not consider it a sin in the case of children; I have merely applied punishment there because they were overcome by my illusory power (māyā).
This destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice was not brought about by me at any time; rather, whatever one hates in others will happen to oneself.
One should never perform an action that causes distress to others; for whatever one hates in others will eventually happen to oneself.
Let the head of Dakṣa, whose sacrifice has been decapitated, indeed become the head of the goat-faced one; and let the god Bhaga behold his share of the sacrifice with the eye of Mitra.
The god named Pūṣan, who eats well-ground offerings at sacrifices with his teeth, had his teeth broken by those performing the sacrifice; this which I have spoken is the truth.
"Bhṛgu, who has acted in opposition to me, shall indeed have his beard gone; as for the gods, let them all have their natural limbs restored, since they granted me this destruction."
May the Aśvins [be the charioteers] with their two arms, and Pūṣan with his two hands; let the other Adhvaryus also become the drivers. This has been spoken by me out of affection for you.

Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord, the compassionate one, the God who is the sovereign of the moving and the unmoving, and the emperor who acts in accordance with the Vedas, became silent.
Then all those gods and others, including Viṣṇu and Brahmā, having heard what Śaṅkara had spoken, were thoroughly satisfied and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then, having taken leave of Śambhu, Viṣṇu, along with me and the celestial sages, went once more to that sacrificial ground of the gods with supreme joy.
Thus, at their request, Śambhu went to Kanakhala, the sacrificial enclosure of Prajāpati, accompanied by Viṣṇu and the other gods.
Then Rudra beheld that destruction which had been wrought by Vīrabhadra there, specifically the ruin of the sacrifice and of the celestial sages.
Svāhā, Svadhā, as well as Pūṣan, Tuṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Sarasvatī; likewise all the other Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and the Fires.
And many others there—yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas—were torn apart, mangled, or even killed on the field of battle.
Having seen such a sacrifice, the Lord summoned the great hero Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, and spoke to him with a smile.
O Vīrabhadra of mighty arms, what deed is this that you have done? O dear one, a great punishment has been swiftly inflicted by you upon the celestial sages and others.
"Bring Dakṣa here quickly, by whom this was done in such a manner; O dear one, the sacrifice has been rendered defective, for its fruit is such as this."
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, Vīrabhadra, filled with haste, brought the headless trunk before him and cast it down at Śambhu’s feet.
O best of sages, seeing him headless, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, spoke to Vīrabhadra in his presence with a smile.
When he asked, "Where is my head?", the lord Vīrabhadra replied, "O Śaṅkara, at that very moment, my head was offered as an oblation into the fire."
Having heard these words of Vīrabhadra, the Lord Śaṅkara affectionately commanded the gods to do exactly as had been previously stated by him.
Having performed in its entirety that which the Blessed Lord Bhava spoke, I [instructed] Viṣṇu and all the others, as well as Bhṛgu and the rest, with haste.
Then, by the command of Śambhu, they joined the head of Prajāpati’s sacrificial animal to the body of a goat for the sake of the rite.
As his head was being joined together, Prajāpati, gazed upon by the auspicious vision of Śambhu, immediately rose up like one who had just awakened, having regained his life-breath.
Having risen, Dakṣa beheld Śambhu, the ocean of compassion, standing before him with a joyful mind, full of affection, and with a perfectly serene intellect.
Formerly, O Hara, his soul was indeed turbid with great hatred; yet, by the mere sight of Śiva, he instantly became as stainless as the autumnal moon.
Then, though desirous of praising his lord, he was unable to do so due to his intense devotion; moreover, overcome by longing and remembering his deceased daughter, he was distraught.
Then Dakṣa, his mind serene yet filled with shame, bowed down and praised Śiva, the benefactor of the world, namely Śaṅkara.

Dakṣa said: I bow to the God, the giver of boons, the most excellent Maheśvara, the eternal treasury of knowledge; I bow to Hara, the Lord of the lords of gods, who is ever-abundant in bliss and the sole kinsman of the world.

I bow to the Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe, the ancient one, the Brahman that is the very nature of my own self. I bow to Śarva; I bow to Bhava, the source of all existence; I bow to Śaṅkara, who is higher than the highest.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, have mercy; salutations be unto you! O Śambhu, O ocean of compassion, forgive my transgression today.
O Śaṅkara, you have indeed bestowed a favor upon me under the guise of punishment; for I am a wicked man of deluded intellect, O Lord, and I did not know your true nature.
Today I have realized the truth: you are considered supreme above all; you are Maheśvara, served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others, and known through the Vedas.

You are the wish-fulfilling tree for the virtuous and the eternal wielder of the rod of punishment for the wicked; for you are the independent Supreme Self, the bestower of desired boons upon your devotees.
From his mouth, the Supreme Lord first created the twice-born, who uphold knowledge, austerity, and vows, in order for them to fully realize the reality of the Self.
Like a cowherd protecting his cattle from all calamities, he who has taken up the rod of punishment is the protector of the boundaries for those who are wicked.
Struck by me with arrows of ill-spoken words, the Supreme Lord—who bestows grace upon me—has rendered the hopes of the gods exceedingly wretched.

O Lord Śambhu, you are the Supreme beyond the supreme, the friend of the distressed; O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, may you be satisfied by this offering of your own making, which is most worthy of praise.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Maheśāna, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, the Lord of great power, the self-restrained Prajāpati fell silent.
Then Viṣṇu, with a serene soul, having bowed deeply with palms joined in reverence, praised the bull-bannered Lord with a voice faltering with tears.
Viṣṇu said: O Mahādeva, O Maheśāna, O bestower of grace upon the worlds, you are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the kinsman of the distressed, and a treasure-house of compassion.
The Lord is all-pervading, acting according to His own will, and His glory is known through the Vedas; by Him grace has been bestowed, and we have been made both virtuous and non-virtuous.
O Maheśa, this wicked Dakṣa, my devotee, censured you in the past; that must be forgiven today, since you are free from all change.
O Śaṅkara, although an offense was committed by me out of delusion, a battle was waged against you by your attendant Vīrabhadra on my behalf.
"You are my master, the Supreme Brahman; I am your servant, O Sadāśiva. Indeed, I am always to be nourished by you, since you are the father of all."
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord, ocean of compassion! You are the independent Supreme Self, the supreme ruler, the immutable beyond duality.
O Lord, you have bestowed this grace upon my son; disregarding his humiliation, please restore the sacrifice of Dakṣa.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; dispel all curses. You are my enlightened inspirer; you alone are thus my protector.
Having thus praised Maheśāna, the Supreme One, O great sage, he joined his palms in reverence and bowed his head in humility.
Then Śakra and the other gods, the world-protectors of virtuous mind, praised the god Śaṅkara, whose lotus-like face was serene.
Then all the gods, as well as others—the perfected seers and the lords of creatures—with delighted minds, joyfully praised Śaṅkara.
Likewise, the gods, nāgas, members of the assembly, and the brahmins, having bowed with supreme devotion, praised him individually.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispelling of Dakṣa's Sorrow," in the Satī-khaṇḍa, the second part of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Thus praised by the Lord of Ramā, by me, by the celestial sages, and by others as well, Mahādeva became truly gracious.
Then Śambhu, having fixed his gaze of compassion upon all the sages, gods, and others, as well as upon Brahmā and Viṣṇu, spoke thus to Dakṣa.
Mahādeva said: Listen, O Dakṣa, I shall speak; I am pleased, O Prajāpati. Though I am indeed independent and the Lord of all, I am always subject to my devotees.
O Dakṣa Prajāpati, virtuous people always worship me in four ways; among them, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.
The afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower as the fourth; the first three are common, while the fourth is indeed distinguished.
Among them, the man of knowledge is considered most dear to Me, and he is said to have My own form; there is no other more beloved than him—this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth.
I am the knower of the Self, attainable through knowledge by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedantic scriptures; yet those of small intellect strive to reach me without knowledge.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by austerity at any time, can deluded men, who are under the sway of karma, attain Me.
You wish to cross over saṃsāra by means of ritual action alone; for that very reason, I became enraged and acted as the destroyer of your sacrifice.
From this time forward, O Dakṣa, regarding me as the Supreme Lord, become intent on knowledge through your intellect and perform your duties with a concentrated mind.
Moreover, O Prajāpati, listen with a virtuous mind to my words; for the sake of dharma, I shall speak of a secret concerning you, even though you possess all qualities.
I, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are the supreme cause of the world; [He is] the Self, the Lord, the Witness, self-perceiving and devoid of all distinctions.
O Sage, having entered my own *māyā* composed of the *guṇas*, I—being "He"—assume the designations appropriate to the actions of creating, protecting, and destroying the universe.
In that non-dual, supreme, absolute Brahman which is the Self, the ignorant person perceives beings as distinct from Brahman and the Lord.

Just as a man never entertains the notion of "another's" regarding his own limbs such as the head or hands, even so does one devoted to Me never entertain the notion of "another's" regarding any living being.
O Dakṣa, he who perceives the single nature within all beings, and sees no distinction among the three gods, attains peace.
That lowest of men who conceives a sense of division among the three deities shall surely dwell in hell for as long as the moon and stars exist.
A wise person who worships all the gods while regarding Me as the Supreme attains that knowledge by which eternal liberation is achieved.
Without ritual devotion, Vaiṣṇava devotion indeed does not arise; and without devotion to Viṣṇu, devotion toward me is never produced anywhere.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Sovereign of all and the Compassionate One, addressed these words there while everyone was listening.
If a devotee of Hari should revile me, or likewise one who is a devotee of Śiva, their curses would take effect, and there would indeed be no attainment of the ultimate reality.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard these words of Maheśa which bring happiness, all those present there—the gods, sages, and others—rejoiced.
Then Dakṣa, devoted to the worship of Śiva, became filled with great joy along with his family; and the gods and others likewise, regarding Śiva as the Lord of all, rejoiced.
Just as the hymn of praise was composed for Śambhu, the Supreme Soul, so too was a boon granted to him by Śambhu, whose mind was filled with satisfaction.
O Sage, having been thus instructed by Śiva, the devoted follower of Śiva, Dakṣa, with a serene mind, quickly performed the sacrifice to completion through the grace of Śiva.
He indeed gave portions to the gods and a full share to Śiva; he bestowed gifts upon the twice-born, having obtained the grace of Śambhu.

Then, having duly completed that very great ritual for the god according to the prescribed rules, Dakṣa, the lord of creatures, together with the officiating priests, performed the rites according to the injunctions.
Thus, by the grace of Śaṅkara, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, the lord of sages, Dakṣa’s sacrifice there became complete.
Then all the celestial sages, praising the glory of Śaṅkara, went to their own abodes satisfied, and even the others were happy at that time.
Viṣṇu and I, being well-pleased, also sang with great joy each of our own supreme glories of Śambhu, which always bestow all auspiciousness.
Honored with affection by Dakṣa, Mahādeva, the one who grants the true goal, departed for his own mountain Kailāsa, well-pleased and accompanied by his attendants.
Having returned to his own mountain, Śambhu remembered his beloved Satī and recounted her story to his principal attendants.
The wise Lord spent much time recounting his deeds, adopting a worldly course to demonstrate his mastery over desire.

The Lord, the agent of all that is not governed by worldly laws, is the Supreme Brahman, the refuge of the virtuous; O Sage, where could there be delusion for him, or grief, or any further transformation?
Viṣṇu and I alone know that distinction; never anyone else—not other sages, gods, humans, or yogis.
The infinite majesty of Śaṅkara is difficult for even the wise to comprehend; yet it is known by the devotee through true devotion, effortlessly, by his grace alone.
For even a single transformation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, reveals such a state to the worlds by manifesting it in that manner.
O Sage, by reading and hearing this, every wise person in the world attains a divine, auspicious state and supreme happiness even in this life.
Thus Satī, having abandoned her own body, was born again as the daughter of Dakṣa from Menā, the wife of Himavat; so it is well known.
Having performed penance there once more, she chose Śiva as her husband; then, having become Gaurī with half of his body as her left side, the auspicious goddess performed wondrous divine sports.
Thus has been described your most wonderful life-story of Satī, which is divine, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants all desires.
This narrative is sinless, purifying, and the cleanser of others; it leads to heaven, bestows fame and long life, and yields the fruit of sons and grandsons.
O dear one, he who hears this with devotion or causes devoted men to hear it shall obtain the fruit of all actions and attain the supreme goal in the hereafter.
Whoever reads or causes others to read this auspicious narrative shall, after enjoying all worldly pleasures, attain liberation in the end.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Dakṣa’s Resolve," in the second section (Satī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī! This second section, the Satī-khaṇḍa, contained within the Rudra-saṃhitā, is completed.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, how did the goddess Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who abandoned her body at her father’s sacrifice, become the daughter of the Mountain and the Mother of the World?
How did she perform such extremely severe penance and obtain Śiva as her husband? Please explain this to me who asks you thoroughly and in detail.
Brahmā said: Listen, O tiger among sages, to the supreme account of Śiva’s deeds—purifying, most divine, auspicious, and the remover of all sins.
When the goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, the supreme sovereign, sported joyfully and playfully with Hara on the Himācala mountain.
Knowing, "She is my daughter," Menā, the beloved of Himācala, served her with the luster of a mother and an abundance of all prosperity.
When the Supreme Goddess, having been met at the sacrifice by her father Dakṣa, was not honored and became enraged, she abandoned her own body.
At that very time, O Sage, Menakā, the beloved of Himācala, desired to propitiate that Goddess who was residing in the world of Śiva.
Having resolved in her heart, "May I become his daughter," Satī cast off her body and set her mind on becoming the daughter of Himavat.
When the time had arrived, that goddess, praised by all the gods, being virtuous, cast off her body and out of love became the daughter of Menakā.
By name she was the goddess Pārvatī; having performed most difficult penance, she indeed obtained Śiva as her husband once again through the instruction of Nārada.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, Vidhi, O one of great wisdom, best among speakers, tell me of the birth, the marriage, and the life of Menakā.
Blessed indeed is the goddess Menakā, from whom was born this virtuous daughter; therefore, that devoted wife is honored and blessed by all.
Brahmā said: Listen, O sage Nārada, to the origin of Pārvatī’s mother, as well as her marriage and life story, which are purifying and increase devotion.
O best of sages, in the northern direction there exists the great mountain Himavat, the lord of mountains, which is possessed of great splendor and abundant prosperity.
Its dual nature is well known through the distinction between the mobile and the immobile; I shall describe its subtle form in brief.
Having plunged deeply into the eastern and western oceans, he stands there, a delightful mine of various jewels, like a measuring rod for the earth.
It was filled with various trees, beautifully adorned with diverse peaks, and constantly frequented by happy animals such as lions and tigers.
It was a formidable treasury of snow, variegated with various wonders, inhabited by celestial sages, perfected beings, and seers, and held dear by Śiva.
The abode of austerity, its soul exceedingly purified and purifying even for great-souled ones; it bestows the ultimate perfection of asceticism and is an auspicious mine of various minerals.
He indeed possesses a divine form, delightful and beautiful in every limb; he is an unchanging portion of Viṣṇu, the king of mountain kings, beloved by the virtuous.
For the stability of his lineage and for the sake of increasing righteousness, that mountain, desiring the welfare of his ancestors and the gods, wished to perform his own marriage.
At that moment, O Lord of Sages, the gods, disregarding their own interests in every way, approached the divine ancestors and spoke with affection.
The gods said: "O fathers, listen all of you with pleased minds to our words—if you desire to accomplish the work of the gods, that must be done quickly and exactly as we say."
Having married with great affection your eldest daughter named Menā, who is the very embodiment of auspiciousness, by the mountain king known as Himavat;
Thus, there will be a great gain for all, and for you immortals, there shall be the destruction of suffering at every step.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the other [son] and having reflected upon them, those ancestors remembered the curse upon their sons and said "Om" to his speech.
The father gave his daughter to the Himālaya according to the proper rites; there was a great festival at that most auspicious wedding.
Haryaśva and the other gods, as well as all those sages, arrived there, remembering Bhava and Vāmadeva with their minds.
Having given manifold gifts, they caused a festival to be celebrated; having highly praised the divine ancestors, they extolled the Himālaya.
Filled with great joy, all those gods along with the lords of sages returned to their respective abodes, remembering Śiva and Śivā.
Having performed many auspicious rites and having duly married his beloved wife, the Lord of Mountains returned to his own abode and attained great joy.
Brahmā said: O Lord of Sages, the excellent marriage of Himavat with Menā was described by me with affection as being conducive to happiness; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Himācala," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O wise Creator, now speak with due respect regarding the origin of Menā; likewise, relate her curse as well, and dispel my doubt.
Brahmā said: Listen with great affection, O Nārada, to the origin of Menā from the perspective of discernment; O most excellent son, O highly wise one, I shall speak of it along with the sages.
O Sage, my son named Dakṣa who was mentioned previously—sixty sons, the causes of creation, were born to him.
He performed their marriage with Kaśyapa and other suitors; all that is known to you, so now hear what is relevant, O Nārada.
Among them, he gave his daughter named Svadhā to the Pitṛs; she had three fortunate daughters who were embodiments of Dharma.
O Lord of Sages, hear from me their names, which are purifying, always dispelling obstacles, and bestowing great auspiciousness.
The eldest daughter was named Menā, the middle one was Dhanyā, and the youngest was Kalāvatī; all these daughters were born from the mind of the Pitṛs.

Those born of no womb and those born of their own nature are considered the sons of the world through their inherent power; by pronouncing the auspicious names of these [goddesses], a person shall obtain all desires.
Worthy of worship by the world, eternal mothers of the universe, bestowers of the supreme, those Yoginīs are the highest repositories of knowledge, pervading the three worlds.
O Lord of Sages, at one time three sisters went to Śvetadvīpa, the realm of Viṣṇu, for the purpose of beholding him.
Having offered salutations to Viṣṇu and performed his praise with devotion, they remained there by His command; thus a great and harmonious assembly was formed.
At that very moment, O Sage, the perfected ones (siddhas) Sanaka and the others, sons of Brahmā, went there, bowed to Hari, offered praise, and remained by his command.
Upon seeing the sages headed by Sanaka, all those present there quickly rose; having bowed to the gods and others who were seated there and honored by the world, they remained standing.
O Sage, those three sisters, deluded there by the illusory power of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Soul, and rendered helpless by fate, did not rise from their seats.
The deluding power (mohinī) of Śiva is most profound for all the worlds; the entire universe is dependent upon it, and she is proclaimed as the will of Śiva.
That very [karma] is called *prārabdha*; indeed, it has many names. It occurs solely by the will of Śiva; no deliberation should be made in this matter.
Having come under her control, they indeed did not even bow down to her; merely gazing at her in amazement, they remained standing right there.
Seeing such a course of action by him, even those lords of sages, Sanaka and the others, though possessed of knowledge, gave way to an unbearable and supreme anger.
Deluded there by the will of Śiva, the lord of yogis, Sanatkumāra, spoke to them with anger, inflicting a curse as a rod of punishment.

Sanatkumāra said: "You three sisters are indeed deluded and bereft of true wisdom; for even though you are the daughters of a father, you have certainly failed to understand the reality of the Vedas."
Since we rose from our seats and even offered salutations out of pride, being deluded by our human nature, may we indeed remain far removed from heaven.
"Let these three women, deluded by ignorance, come into being; by the power of their own karma, may they receive such a fruit."
Brahmā said: Having heard this, those three virtuous women were greatly startled; they fell at his feet with their heads bowed low.
The daughters of the Pitṛs said: "O best of sages, ocean of compassion, be gracious now! We fools did not offer our salutations to you with true devotion."
And that fruit has been obtained, O Brahmin; there is no fault on your part, O great sage. Grant us your favor here, so that we may attain heaven once again.
Brahmā said: O dear one, having heard those words, that sage—his soul tranquilized and impelled by the illusory power of Śiva—then spoke regarding the removal of the curse.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen with delighted minds to these three daughters of the Pitṛs; my words shall destroy your sorrow and grant you happiness at all times.
Let Jyeṣṭhā become the beloved wife of the mountain Himavat, who is a portion of Viṣṇu; her daughter shall indeed be Pārvatī.
His second beloved wife shall be a blessed Yoginī named Janakī; her daughter will be Mahālakṣmī, known by the name Sītā.
And Kalāvatī, the youngest daughter of the Vaiśya Vṛṣabhānu, will become Rādhā, his beloved; she shall be born at the end of the Dvāpara age.
Menakā, together with her husband and by the grace of Pārvatī, shall go to Kailāsa, the supreme state, in that very body.
Blessed is Sīradhvaja, born of Janaka’s lineage, who through Sītā shall become a great yogi liberated while living and will go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Out of affection for her daughter, Kalāvatī, together with Vṛṣabhānu, shall become liberated while living and go to Goloka; of this there is no doubt.
Without adversity, where and for whom will greatness arise? For those of virtuous deeds, once suffering has passed, happiness—which is so difficult to attain—will flourish.
"You are all the daughters of the Pitṛs, sporting in heaven; and the exhaustion of your karma has occurred through the sight of Viṣṇu."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Sages, his anger having subsided, spoke once more after mentally recollecting Śiva, the bestower of knowledge, enjoyment, and liberation.
Furthermore, listen with affection to my words which always bestow happiness: "Blessed are you, beloved of Śiva; indeed, you are worthy of honor and constant worship."
The goddess Pārvatī, the daughter of Menā and the Mother of the Universe, shall become the beloved of Śambhu after performing most difficult penance.
Fortunate is the daughter Sītā, who is remembered as the wife of Rāma; following worldly custom, she shall sport with Rāma.
Rādhā, the daughter of Kalāvatī, who dwells directly in Goloka, shall become the wife of Kṛṣṇa, bound by secret love.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and being praised by his brothers, the venerable Sanatkumāra vanished right there.
Those three sisters, O dear one, were the mind-born daughters of the Pitṛs; having been cleansed of their sins and attained happiness, they quickly departed for their own abode.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of Previous Events," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, O wise one, O highly intelligent one, speak to me, O best among speakers; what happened after that, O excellent teacher of Viṣṇu?
This wonderful and auspicious account of Menā’s former life has been told, and her marriage has been heard in full; now, relate the supreme narrative that follows.
After marrying Menā, what did that mountain do thereafter? And how was Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, born of her?
Having performed penance that was difficult to endure, how did she obtain Hara as her husband? Tell me all of this in detail—the glorious fame of Śaṅkara.
Brahmā said: O sage, listen with great affection to the auspicious and glorious account of Śaṅkara; by hearing which, even a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is purified and shall attain all desires.
O Nārada, when the Mountain King returned home after performing Menā’s marriage, a great festival broke out throughout the three worlds.
Himācala, being well-pleased, celebrated a supreme festival; with a virtuous mind, he honored the brahmins, his kinsmen, and others.
All the twice-born, being well-pleased, gave him their excellent blessings and departed for their respective abodes, as did his kinsmen and others.
Himācala, being well-pleased, sported with Menā in their comfortable home, and also in other excellent places such as the Nandana groves and other forests.
At that moment, O Sage, all the gods led by Viṣṇu and the high-souled sages went into the presence of the mountain.
Seeing those gods who had arrived, the great mountain bowed with joy; out of devotion, he honored them while praising his own good fortune.
With palms joined and head bowed, he indeed praised him with great devotion; a great thrill of horripilation arose in the Mountain, and tears of love fell.
Then, having bowed down with a joyful and serene mind, O Sage, Himālaya, the mountain of snow, spoke while remaining prostrate to Viṣṇu and the other gods.
Himācala said: Today my birth is fruitful; today my great penance is fruitful; today my knowledge is fruitful; today my ritual actions are fruitful.
I have become blessed today; blessed is my entire land; blessed is my lineage as well as my wife; everything is blessed, without a doubt.
Since you have all assembled together at once, command me with affection, regarding me as a servant worthy of your favor.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Mahīdhra, those gods, headed by Hari, were then pleased and spoke, perceiving that their own purpose would be accomplished.
The gods said: O Himācala, of great wisdom, listen to our beneficial words; we shall gladly tell you the purpose for which we have all come.
O Mountain, she who was formerly Umā, the mother of the world and daughter of Dakṣa, having indeed become the wife of Rudra, sported upon the earth for a very long time.
Having received disrespect from her father and remembering her own vow, Ambikā then abandoned that body and went to her own abode.
O Himavat, that story is well known in the world and to you as well; if this were so, there would indeed be a great benefit for the host of gods.
All those gods shall likewise be under your control.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu and the others, the Lord of the Mountains, with a gracious soul, respectfully replied, "So be it."
Then, having instructed them in that ritual with the utmost reverence, Śaṅkara himself went for refuge to Umā and his wives.
Establishing their minds upon that auspicious spot, the gods remembered the Mother of the World; having prostrated themselves there many times, they praised her with devotion.
The gods said: O Goddess, Mother of the worlds, dweller in the realm of Śiva, beloved of Sadāśiva, Durgā, O Maheśvarī, we bow to you!
With devotion, we praise the auspicious Śakti, the purifier, the peaceful, the nourishing, the supremely holy one, whose form is both great and unmanifest.
We bow to you, who are auspicious, the bestower of auspiciousness, pure, gross, subtle, and the supreme goal; you who are well-pleased by both inner knowledge and true knowledge.
You are faith, you are fortitude, you are prosperity; you alone are the range of all experience. You are the radiance residing in the sun, illuminating your own manifold expansion.
We bow to that [power] which, within the structure of the cosmic egg, nourishes the world and its living beings—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
You are Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; you are Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.
You are the livelihood of all the worlds; you are the triple Veda, the embodiment of Dharma.
You are sleep in all beings; you indeed are hunger and satisfaction; you are thirst, luster, and complexion, and you are always the giver of all bliss.
You are the prosperity of those who perform meritorious deeds; you are always the elder sister of the sinners. You are the peace of all the worlds; you are the nurse who nourishes all living beings.
You are the ultimate essential nature of all five elements and the creator of their essence; for you are the policy of those who uphold policy and the very embodiment of resolve.
You are the song of the Sāmaveda, the knot of the Yajurvedas, and the oblation; likewise, you are the measure of the Ṛgveda and the supreme goal of the Atharvaveda.

The power of the entire host of gods, consisting of darkness (tamas) and perceivable solely through the quality of the Creator (dhātṛ), which takes the form of Śiva from the manifestation of passion (rajas), and which is heard here as the bringer of welfare when praised—[to her be salutation].

We bow indeed to her who is a boat for crossing the terrible suffering of the body of existence in the ocean of saṃsāra, who is free from all bonds, and who is skilled in the play of maintaining the eightfold yoga while delighting in dwelling on the Vindhya mountains.

O Jantu, through your steadfastness, you always spread happiness for all beings in their noses, eyes, mouths, arms, chests, and minds; while the world passes away as if into sleep, may you, O Blessed One, be gracious to us for the sake of protecting the stability of existence.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Maheśānī, Umā, Satī, the Mother of the World, they all stood with hearts full of great love, desiring a vision of her.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Deity," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Thus praised by the gods, the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress, the Mother of the Universe, appeared before the gods.
She was seated upon a divine, most wonderful chariot made of jewels, equipped with a network of tiny bells, and provided with a choice, soft cushion.
Her radiant limbs shine with a brilliance exceeding ten million suns; standing in the midst of a mass of her own splendor, she possesses a supreme form and uniform luster.
The incomparable Mahāmāyā, the consort of Sadāśiva, possesses the three qualities yet is devoid of qualities; she is eternal and dwells in the realm of Śiva.
Caṇḍī is the mother of the three gods, Śivā, the destroyer of all suffering; she is the Mother of All, the Great Sleep, and the savior of all her own people.
But by the power of that mass of splendor, Śivā was seen by the gods; desiring to see her, those gods then praised her once again.
Then all the hosts of gods, headed by Viṣṇu, desiring a vision, beheld that Mother of the World there indeed, having obtained her grace.
A mass of joy arose among all the inhabitants of heaven; they bowed down to her again and again and praised her especially.
The gods said: O Śivā, O Śarvāṇī, O auspicious one, O Mother of the Universe, O Maheśvarī! We gods bow down to you in every way—you who destroy all afflictions.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, neither the Vedas nor the scriptures in their entirety know your greatness, which transcends both speech and mind; they can only contemplate it.
Even the Veda always expresses that [reality] with extreme caution by means of the exclusion of what it is not; what then can be said of the opinions of others?
Many devotees, having attained Your grace through devotion, know that for those devotees who have sought refuge, there is no fear or the like anywhere.
Listen with great pleasure to this petition, O Ambika, whose servants we always are; O Goddess, Great Goddess, we describe ourselves as being lowly.
Having formerly been the daughter of Dakṣa, she became the beloved of Hara; she destroyed the great sorrow of Brahmā and others.
Having received disrespect from your father, you abandoned your body at the dictate of a wager; you went to your own world, for even Hara experienced suffering.
O Maheśvarī, that task of the gods was not completed even after it had begun; the sages and gods were distressed, and we have come to you for refuge.
O Maheśānī, fulfill the desire of the gods; O Śivā, let the words of Sanatkumāra be made fruitful.
O Goddess, consort of Rudra, descend once more to the earth and perform your divine play as is fitting, so that the immortals may attain happiness.
O Goddess, may even Rudra, who dwells upon Mount Kailāsa, be happy; may all beings be happy, and may suffering perish entirely.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, all the immortals, headed by Viṣṇu, overwhelmed with love, remained silent, their forms bowed down in devotion.
Śivā too became highly pleased upon hearing the praise offered by the immortals; then, having reflected on its cause and remembered her lord Śiva, she was filled with joy.
Then the goddess Umā, compassionate and affectionate toward her devotees, smiled and spoke, addressing those gods headed by the Lord of Māyā.
Umā said: O Hara, O Vidhi, O gods, and O sages, be free from distress; all of you listen to my words, for I am pleased—of this there is no doubt.
My conduct everywhere brings happiness to the three worlds; all this, including the delusion of Dakṣa and so forth, was performed by me alone.
"I shall undoubtedly manifest my full incarnation upon the earth; there is no doubt. There are many reasons for this, which I shall relate to you with great reverence."
In the past, O dear one, Himācala and Menā served me with supreme devotion, just like parents serving their own son, while I was in the form of a cow.
"Now perform service to me constantly with great devotion; Menā especially shall do so there as my daughter—of this there is no doubt."
"Let Rudra go, and you all take birth in the house of Himavat; therefore I too shall descend, and there will be the destruction of suffering."
"Go all of you to your own abodes and may you find happiness for a long time. Having descended and become the daughters of Menā, you shall serve with zeal."
"I shall become the wife of Hara; this is my own well-guarded resolve. For the wondrous play of Śiva is indeed enchanting even to the wise."
O gods, from the moment my own body, born of Dakṣa, was abandoned by me after seeing the disrespect shown toward my father at that sacrifice of my lord, [I have remained here].
From that time forward, that lord Rudra, known as Kālāgni, became naked and swiftly devoted himself to meditation upon me.
Seeing my father's wrath during the sacrifice, the virtuous Satī went there and, out of love and reflecting that she was a knower of dharma, she cast off her own body.
Having abandoned his worthy abode and assumed an extraordinary appearance, Maheśvara could not endure separation from Satī, who was my very form.
On my account, he became greatly distressed and assumed a disreputable appearance; from that time forward, he abandoned the highest pleasure born of desire.
Listen further, O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O sages, and O gods, to the world-protecting pastimes of the Great Lord Maheśvara.
Distraught by separation, he lovingly fashioned a garland from my bones; though awakened to truth, he alone found no peace anywhere.
That lord wept loudly here and there like one who is helpless; wandering everywhere at all times, he could not distinguish between what was appropriate and what was inappropriate.
Thus Lord Hara performed this divine play, demonstrating himself to those filled with desire; he spoke words like a lover, as if agitated by separation.
In reality, the Supreme Lord is unchanging, undepressed, unconquered, perfectly full, auspicious, the Master, the sovereign of Māyā, and the Lord of all.
Otherwise, what purpose could there be for him in delusion or desire? Even through some transformation, that Lord is not tainted by illusion.
O gods, the omnipresent Rudra intensely desires to take my hand; he intends to manifest an incarnation on earth in the home of Menā and Himācala.
Therefore, for the sake of pleasing Rudra, I shall descend, assuming a worldly state within Menā, the wife of Himavat.
Having become a devotee dear to Rudra and having performed most difficult penance, I shall accomplish the work of the gods; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Go all of you to your own homes and worship Bhava constantly; by his grace, all suffering will perish, there is no doubt.
By the grace of the Compassionate One, may there always be auspiciousness; for that reason, I shall become worthy of salutation and worship in the three worlds as his mother.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus while the gods were looking on, O dear one, that auspicious Mother of the Universe vanished and quickly reached her own world.
Viṣṇu and all the other gods, as well as the sages, filled with joy, offered salutations in that direction and returned to their respective abodes.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, the conduct of Durgā has been described to you; it always bestows happiness upon men and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind, or read it, or cause it to be read, shall obtain all their desires.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Consolation of the Devas," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: When the goddess Durgā had vanished and the hosts of immortals had returned to their own abodes, what happened immediately thereafter?
How did Menā and the Lord of the Mountains perform supreme austerity? And how, O dear one, was a daughter born to that Menā? Tell me that.
Brahmā said: O best of Brahmins, O most excellent son, listen to that great narrative; having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, I shall relate it, which increases devotion.
O dear one, when the host of gods had departed after giving their instruction, the Lord of Mountains, as well as Haryā and Menakā, performed supreme austerity.
Day and night, the couple, contemplating Śivā and Śambhu, constantly performed their worship perfectly with minds imbued with devotion.
With great joy, the queen worshipped the Goddess who is dear to the Mountain-dweller along with Śiva; and for the sake of her constant satisfaction, she gave gifts to the twice-born.
Beginning from the month of Caitra, for twenty-seven years, she, devoted to her desire for offspring, worshipped Śivā every day.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform the rite on the ninth lunar day with sweetmeats (*modaka*), flour-offerings (*balipiṣṭa*), milk-rice (*pāyasa*), perfumes, and flowers.
At Oṣadhiprastha on the Gaṅgā, having fashioned an earthen image of Umā, he worshipped her with offerings of various articles.
At times she remained without food; at times she was firm in her vows; at times she subsisted on air; and at times she lived on water alone.
With her mind fixed on Śiva, Menakā, possessing supreme and radiant luster, spent twenty-seven years with great affection.
At the end of twenty-seven years, Umā, the mother of the world, who is identical with the world and the beloved of Śaṅkara, became exceedingly well-pleased.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon Menā, that Supreme Goddess, being well-pleased by her excellent devotion, manifested herself before her.
Endowed with divine limbs and situated in the midst of a circle of light, she appeared before Menā's eyes and spoke while smiling.
The Goddess said: "Choose a boon, O great virtuous lady, whatever resides in your heart; for I am well-pleased with your ascetic penance, O beloved of the mountain."
"Whatever you have requested through your asceticism, vows, and meditative concentration, I shall grant all of that to you whenever it is desired."
Then, seeing the goddess Kālikā standing visibly before her, Menakā bowed down and spoke these words.
Menā said: "O Goddess, your form has now been seen by me directly. I wish to praise you; be gracious, O Kālikā!"
Brahmā said: Then, having been addressed thus by Menakā, Kālikā, the enchantress of all, with a very gracious soul, embraced Menakā with both her arms.
Then Menakā, having attained great knowledge, praised Kālikā Śivā—who had become manifest before her eyes—with pleasing words and with devotion.
Menā said: I bow down to Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, Caṇḍikā, the upholder of the universe, the Great Goddess who bestows all desires and goals.
I perpetually bow to Māyā, the mother of the universe, who is eternal bliss, the yogic sleep, eternally perfected, and adorned with a garland of the essence of auspiciousness.

To the maternal grandmother Sadānandā, who destroys the sorrow of her devotees, who is the ideal for all women until the end of the kalpa, and who is the very embodiment of the intellect of all living beings.

You are the cause of the severing of bonds for ascetics; what power of yours could be sung by those like me? You are indeed the [personification] of violence or of the Atharvaveda; as such, eternally fulfill my desire.

The aggregate of elements is joined with those respective subtle principles (tanmātras), which are devoid of existence, eternal or non-eternal, and transcendent; you, however, are their power, eternally of a constant form, a woman united in yoga, capable throughout time.

You alone are the womb that sustains the worlds; you alone are the eternal primordial nature beyond all. O Mother, you who are the eternal one whose form is Brahman and who act according to your will—be gracious to me today.
O Jātavedas, you are the fierce power residing within; you are the burning power of the sun’s rays; you are the delighting power of the abundant moonlight—to you, that Caṇḍī, I offer praise and bow.

You are the beloved of virtuous women, you are the eternal consort of those whose vital energy is drawn upward; you are the desire of all the worlds, and you are the sustainer, just as you are for Hari.

O Goddess, you who, having assumed desired forms, are the agent of creation, maintenance, and destruction; you who are the cause of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—be gracious today, and once again, salutations to you!
Brahmā said: Then, having been thus praised, the goddess Durgā Kālikā spoke once again to the goddess Menakā, saying, "Choose a desired boon."
Umā said: "O you who sport upon the Himālaya, you are indeed as dear to me as my own life. Whatever you desire, I shall certainly grant it; there is nothing that I would not give."
Having heard these words of Maheśānī, which were like nectar, that delighted Menakā, the beloved of the mountain, spoke.
Menā said: "O Śivā, victory, victory! O wise one, O Maheśvarī, O Mother of Bhava! If I am worthy of a boon from you, I choose yet another excellent boon."
O Mother of the World, may I first have a hundred sons—long-lived, heroic, and endowed with prosperity and spiritual accomplishments.
Afterwards, there was likewise one daughter, endowed with beauty and virtue, who brought joy to both families and was worshipped by the three worlds.
O auspicious one, become my daughter indeed for the sake of the gods' mission; likewise, O Mother Bhavānī, become the wife of Rudra and perform your divine play.
Brahmā said: Having heard what Menakā had spoken, the Goddess, her mind serene, spoke these words with a smile, fulfilling her desire.
The Goddess said: "May you have one hundred sons endowed with prowess; among them, one shall first be born as the chief, the most powerful."
"I shall become your daughter, O Lord, satisfied by your devotion; served by all the gods, I shall carry out your divine purpose."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the Supreme Goddess Kālikā, the sustainer of the world, vanished on the spot even as Menakā was looking on.
Menakā too, having obtained the desired boon from Maheśānī, attained immeasurable joy, O dear one, and even the hardship of her asceticism vanished.
Having offered salutations in that direction with a deeply joyful mind, she entered her own abode while loudly uttering cries of "Victory! (Jaya).

Then he reported that matter to his own master, and he informed him of the excellent jewel as well, with eloquent words that were like a repetition of what was already understood by its own characteristic marks.
Having heard those words of Menā, the Lord of Mountains was delighted; with affection, he praised his beloved wife, who was devoted to Śivā.
O sage, when their sexual union had proceeded in due course of time, Menā became pregnant, and that fetus grew day by day.
She gave birth to an extraordinary and most excellent son, fit to be enjoyed by the wives of the Nāgas, named Maināka, who formed a true friendship with the ocean.
O divine sage, even when Vṛtra’s enemy was enraged, he felt a pain in his winged head, which had been wounded by the thunderbolt as its wings were being severed.
The preeminent among his hundred sons, possessed of great strength and prowess, he was established as the sole sovereign over the mountains born of himself, like the king of mountains.
A wonderful and great festival took place there in the city of Himācala; through the excessive joy of the couple, all their afflictions were brought to an end.
He bestowed gifts upon the twice-born and gave wealth to others; yet, between the two of them, their affection for the pair of Śiva’s auspicious feet was even greater.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Menā’s Attainment of the Boon," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, the third part of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then that couple, with devotion and respect, called to mind Bhava and Ambikā there for the sake of procreation, for the purpose of the gods' mission.
Then, having cast off her body through the yoga of Caṇḍikā in the presence of her father, she desired once more to become the wife of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva).
Then, in order to make her own word true, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who grants all desires when pleased, entered the mind of the mountain with her full manifestation.
Then that high-minded one, a mass of splendor and invincible like the fire, shone forth with a brilliance even more intense than before.
Then, due to his state of meditative absorption, the Mountain bestowed a full portion of Śiva’s essence upon his beloved at that auspicious moment.
By the grace of the Goddess who dwells in his heart, the compassionate one who bestows happiness upon the Mountain, the wife of the Mountain conceived a child.
Menā, the beloved of the mountains, who always dwells within a circle of splendor, shone forth most brilliantly as the supreme refuge for all beings in the world.
Menā bore the auspicious signs of pregnancy that portended the happiness of her husband and the desired, blissful cause of joy for the gods.
With her body withered and her ornaments incomplete, facing toward the *lodhra* tree, the night—like a woman at the waning of the moon—waits for the time, observing the constellations.
Then, O Sage, having smelled the fragrance of the clay on his face in private, the Lord of the Mountains attained such satisfaction that his love for him increased even further.
In what things did Menā not express her longing? The Mountain, out of modesty, repeatedly asked his friend about whatever she desired.
Having approached, she quickly saw that which she had desired as the thorn of her pregnancy-longing; it was brought to her, for indeed there is nothing unattainable even in the three worlds.
Having endured the distress of pregnancy, Menā, her limbs swelling with growth, shone like a young creeper adorned with abundant new leaves.
He regarded his queen as the very womb of the mountain, like the earth containing a treasure within its depths, or like a *śamī* tree with fire hidden inside.
The wise man performed the appropriate rites for his beloved wife, for his own mental satisfaction, for the wealth he had earned himself, and for the exalted study of the sacred scriptures.
In due time, he, full of confidence, beheld Menā on the verge of childbirth; and in the inner chamber presided over by physicians, he saw the sky overspread with clouds.
Upon seeing his beloved of auspicious limbs—who was then the Mother of the Universe residing within the womb and endowed with great splendor—the Lord of the Mountains rejoiced exceedingly.
At that moment, O Sage, the gods headed by Viṣṇu, as well as the sages, having assembled, offered praise to Śivā while she was still within the womb.
The gods said: "O Durgā, victory! Victory! O wise one, Mother of the Universe, Great Goddess! O you who are firm in truth, devoted to truth, the triple truth, and whose very form is truth!"
We have come to you for refuge—you who abide in truth, who are well-pleased with truth, who are born from truth, who are truth itself, who are the essence of truth, and whose eyes are truth.
O beloved of Śiva, O Great Sovereign, O destroyer of the suffering of the gods; O Mother of the three worlds, O Consort of Śarva, O all-pervading one, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
O Sovereign of the three worlds, manifest yourself and perform the work of the gods; for by your grace, O Great Goddess, we have all truly found our protector.
From you alone all beings obtain happiness and the supreme bliss; indeed, without you, nothing at all shines, even within the three worlds.
Brahmā said: Having thus offered many hymns of praise to Maheśānī while she was still within the womb, the gods, with their minds gratified, then departed each to his own abode.
When the ninth month had passed and the tenth month was complete, Kālikā, the Mother of the World, brought forth her movement from within the womb.
Then there was a most auspicious time, with the planets and stars stilled; the sky attained clarity, and indeed light shone in every direction.
The earth, abounding in auspiciousness and containing its sacrificial grounds, villages, and oceans, truly saw lotuses bloom in its lakes, rivers, and ponds.
O Lord of Sages, various winds of pleasant touch blew, all the virtuous rejoiced, and the wicked immediately fell into distress.
The gods, having arrived in the sky, sounded their drums; a rain of flowers fell there, and the best of the Gandharvas sang.
The Vidyadhara women and the Apsaras likewise danced in the sky; at that time, there was a great festival for the gods and others in the expanse of the heavens.
At that moment, the goddess Śivā Satī, who was her primordial power, manifested before Menā in her own form.
In the spring season, during the month of Madhu, on the ninth day under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, she was born at midnight like Gaṅgā from the orb of the moon.
At that moment, from the womb of Menakā, Śivā emerged in her true form, appearing like Lakṣmī arising from the ocean.
Then, when she had been born, Bhava became pleased; a favorable wind blew, deep, fragrant, and auspicious.
A rain of flowers fell preceded by a rain of water; the fires blazed and were then extinguished, and the clouds thundered at that time.
As she was being born, everything became complete; all suffering in that city of Himavat came to an end.
At that moment, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, arrived there happily and with affection beheld the Mother of the World.
They praised that auspicious Mother Kālikā, the beloved of Śiva, who possesses a divine form, who is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and who dwells in the realm of Śiva.
The gods said: O Mother of the World, Great Goddess, bestower of all perfections, you are indeed the performer of the work of the gods; therefore, we always bow down to you.
In every way, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, perform what is auspicious for the gods; the desire of Menā has been fulfilled, so now fulfill that of Hara as well.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised the goddess Śivā and having bowed deeply before her, Viṣṇu and the others departed for their respective abodes, delighted and extolling her supreme state.
O Nārada, seeing her thus born, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, the dark-complexioned goddess Menakā attained great joy.
Beholding that divine form, the beloved of the mountain attained realization; recognizing her as the Supreme Sovereign, she praised her with great joy.
Menā said: O Mother of the World, O Great Goddess, you have shown supreme compassion; for you, O Ambikā, have manifested before me, shining resplendently.
O Śivā, you are the primordial source of all powers, the mother of the three worlds; O Goddess, you are eternally beloved by Śiva, the supreme one praised by all the gods.
Have mercy, O Great Goddess; remain established in my meditation. Assume this very form visibly, like that of a daughter.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Menā, the wife of the mountain, Lord Brahmā replied to the goddess Śivā, who was dear to the enemy of Mura and possessed of auspicious offspring.
The Goddess said: "O Menā, in the past you served me well and were devoted to me; being highly pleased by your devotion, I have come before you to grant a boon."
Hearing my words, "Choose a boon," that boon was chosen by you: "Become my daughter, O Great Goddess; perform what is for the benefit of the gods."
Having thus granted you that boon, I respectfully departed for my own abode; and when the time arrived, O beloved of the mountain, you became my daughter.
I have assumed this divine form today so that you may remember me; otherwise, in your mortal state, there would be ignorance regarding me.
Thinking of me with the feeling of a daughter or with divine devotion, and having established affection for me even once, you two shall go to my supreme state.
I shall perform the work of the gods by enacting a wondrous sport upon the earth; I shall become the wife of Śambhu and I shall deliver the virtuous.

Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Ambikā, the auspicious one, became silent through her own power of illusion (māyā); while her mother was looking on with affection, she immediately assumed the form of a daughter.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Birth," in the third section (Pārvatī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Menā, having become that daughter of great splendor, wept there, adopting the worldly way.
O Sage, because of the spreading splendor of the infant’s brilliance all around his auspicious bed, the midnight lamps were instantly deprived of their luster.
Hearing that charming weeping, all the women of the household were filled with joy; they arrived there in a flurry of excitement, led by affection.
Then that attendant of the inner apartments quickly informed the king of the auspicious birth of Pārvatī, which bestows happiness and accomplishes the purpose of the gods.
The birth of a daughter was quickly announced by her attendant in the inner apartments; for that king, there was nothing, not even the white parasol, that was not to be granted.
The mountain king, accompanied by his priest and virtuous brahmins, went there with joy; he beheld his daughter, who was radiant with a beautiful luster.
Seeing such a maiden, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, radiant and most beautiful, the Lord of Mountains rejoiced exceedingly.
All the citizens there—both men and women—rejoiced; at that time, there was a great festival, and musical instruments resounded profusely.
Auspicious songs were sung and courtesans danced; having performed the birth-rite (jātakarma), he bestowed gifts upon the twice-born.
Then, having arrived at the gate, Himācala, with a joyful heart, celebrated a magnificent festival and bestowed wealth upon the mendicants.
Then, at that auspicious moment, Himavat, together with the sages, bestowed upon his daughter a name that brings happiness, beginning with "Kālī."
Then, with great joy and respect, he gave abundant gifts to the twice-born and caused various festivities to be held, preceded by songs.
Having thus celebrated a grand festival and gazing upon Kālī again and again, the mountain king, together with his wife and despite having many sons, attained great joy.
There, that auspicious goddess grew up in the home of the king of mountains, like the Gaṅgā during the rainy season or like moonlight in autumn.
Thus Queen Kālikā, lovely-limbed and beautiful to behold, grew day by day more charming, like a digit of the moon’s orb.
Her kinsmen called that beloved of her relatives—who was endowed with the quality of excellent character—by the family-appropriate name of Pārvatī.
O Sage, having been forbidden from practicing austerities by her mother, that beautiful-faced Kālikā thereafter became known as Umā throughout the world.
Even for one who has a son, the sight of him does not bring such satisfaction as that which was found by Pārvatī in her offspring named Skanda, who was endowed with every auspicious fortune.
O Lord of Sages, for the swarm of bees finds a special attachment to the mango tree among the countless flowers of spring.
Purified and adorned by her, that mountain Himālaya became like a wise man refined by eloquent speech.
As a lamp is [enhanced] by a flame of great radiance, and as the world is [illumined] by the three paths, so too was the Mountain [rendered glorious] by Girijā through the path of righteousness.
And she, having entered into the midst of her female companions, repeatedly took delight in her childhood with artificial balls, with sons [in play], and upon the sandy banks of the Gaṅgā.
Then, O Sage, at the time of instruction, that goddess Śivā, with a restrained mind and great devotion, recited the Vidyā from her true Guru.
The sciences of her previous births returned to her, just as a flock of swans reaches the celestial river in autumn, or as the light of great medicinal herbs reaches the night.
Thus, indeed, a certain pastime of Śivā has been well described; O Sage, listen with love as I shall now relate another pastime.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of Pārvatī’s Childhood Pastimes," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Once, impelled by Śiva, you—possessing knowledge of Śiva and being the foremost among those who know Śiva’s divine play—went with affection to the abode of Himācala.
O Sage Nārada, having seen you and bowed down, the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva) worshipped you; and having summoned his own daughter, he made her fall at your feet.
Having bowed again to you, O Lord of Sages, the Himālaya spoke with palms joined in reverence, his head deeply bowed, mindful of his own duty.
Himālaya said: O Sage Nārada, O wise one, O excellent son of Brahmā, O Lord! You are omniscient, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare of others.
Tell me the Matsutā-jātaka, arising from its merits and defects: whose beloved will my fortunate daughter become?
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having been addressed thus by Himavat, the lord of mountains, you gazed upon the hand of Kālikā and especially her entire body.
O dear one, the wise Nārada, skilled in speech, who knows all that has transpired and whose mind is joyful, spoke to the mountain out of curiosity.
Nārada said: "O Menā, O King of Mountains, this daughter of yours has grown like a digit of the moon—the primordial digit endowed with all auspicious marks."
She bestows ultimate happiness upon her husband, increases the fame of her parents, is a great virtuous woman among all women, and always brings about great joy.
O Mountain, all the auspicious marks are present on your daughter's hand; however, there is one mark that is inauspicious—listen now to its fruit according to the truth.
The yogi is naked, devoid of qualities, free from desire, abandoned by mother and father, without honor, and dressed in inauspicious garb; such indeed is her husband.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words and considering them to be true, the couple—Menā and Himācala—became deeply distressed.
O Sage, having heard those words of Śiva, the Mother of the World, perceiving him by his characteristics to be Śiva himself, rejoiced greatly in her heart.
Thinking, "The word of Nārada is not false," Śivā then felt great affection for the pair of Śiva’s feet within her heart.
Then, O Nārada, the mountain spoke piteously within his heart: "O sage, what remedy should I employ? For this extreme suffering has arisen."
Having heard that, O Sage, you, who are skilled in speech and a source of great wonder, spoke to Himācala with auspicious words, gladdening him.
Nārada said: Listen with affection, O Mountain, to my words; they are true and not false. The writing of Brahmā upon the lines of the hand is certainly never in vain.
O Mountain, her husband shall be such as that; of this there is no doubt. Listen with pleasure to the means for that, by performing which you will obtain happiness.
Such is the bridegroom: the Lord Śambhu, who assumes forms through his divine play; in him, all family defects are equalized by his excellent qualities.
A fault in a powerful person does not lead to suffering, for it is only in one who lacks power that it causes pain; the sun, fire, and the Ganges are to be known as illustrations of this.
Therefore, out of discernment, give your own auspicious daughter to Śiva; for Śiva is the Lord of all, the one to be served, the changeless, the sovereign, and the imperishable.
That Śiva, who is swift in granting grace, will undoubtedly accept her; for he is especially won over by asceticism, should Śivā indeed perform penance.

For that Śiva, the Lord of all, is indeed capable in every way; he is the destroyer even of the *kulipa* [the cosmic egg], yet he remains subject to Brahmā and is the bestower of the skin [of the world].
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O dear sage, you, being curious and a knower of Brahman, addressed the king of mountains once more, gladdening him with auspicious words.
She will be the beloved wife of Śambhu, ever devoted to Hara; she shall be a great virtuous woman of excellent vows, increasing the happiness of her parents.
This ascetic woman will bring Śambhu’s mind under her control, and he, for his part, will not marry any other woman except her.
A love such as theirs is like unto none else; it has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again, nor does it prevail at present.
O best of mountains, you must perform for these two whatever divine tasks are to be done, whether they have perished or are yet alive again and again.
O Mountain, by means of this daughter, Hara shall become Ardhanārīśvara; thus, he and Harṣadina shall be united once again.
This daughter of yours, having propitiated Maheśvara, the Lord of all, through the power of her asceticism, shall take half of Hara’s body.
Having propitiated that Hara through austerity, she who was golden-hued like a golden cow (Svarṇagaurī) shall become this daughter of yours, even more radiant than lightning.
This girl shall attain renown by the name Gaurī; she will be worshipped by all the hosts of gods, as well as by Hari, Brahmā, and the others.
"O best of mountains, you ought not to give this to anyone else here; and this secret of the gods must never be disclosed."
Brahmā said: O celestial sage Nārada, having heard these words of his, Himavat, who is eloquent in speech, addressed you with these words, O Muni.
Himālaya said: O wise sage Nārada, I have indeed a certain request to make; listen to it with affection and grant me joy.
It is heard that Mahādeva, having abandoned all attachments and possessing self-control, constantly performs austerities, remaining beyond even the perception of the gods.
O celestial sage, how could he, while established on the path of meditation, cause his mind—dedicated to the Supreme Brahman—to falter? In this regard, I have a great doubt.
The supreme imperishable Brahman, resembling the flame of a lamp, is one's own nature known as Sadāśiva—changeless, unborn, and unsurpassed.
That [Self] is both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities, without distinction and without activity; therefore, it perceives everything everywhere, yet it does not look outward.
Thus it is constantly heard from the mouths of the Kinnaras who have come here with great joy, O Sage; surely that speech cannot be false.
In particular, it is heard that he was directly named Hara; listen as I relate the covenant he made in former times.
"O beloved Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, I shall choose no other woman but you; I will not take another as my wife—I tell you this truth."
Thus, he had previously made a vow equal to truth; once she has died, how could he himself take another?
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, that mountain remained silent before him. O celestial sage, having heard that, you then spoke according to the true reality.
Nārada said: "O high-minded King of Mountains, you should indeed not entertain anxiety; this daughter of yours, Kālī, was formerly born as the daughter of Dakṣa."
Her name was Satī, which always bestows all auspiciousness; indeed, having become the daughter of Dakṣa, she became the beloved of Rudra.
Having likewise encountered such disrespect at her father’s sacrifice and from Śaṅkara as well, Satī, beholding that and becoming filled with wrath, cast off her body.
Furthermore, this very auspicious Ambikā has been born in your house; she will become Pārvatī, the wife of Hara—of this there is no doubt.
O Sage, you have related all of this in detail to the King—the former form and the life-story of Pārvatī, which increases one’s devotion.
Having heard all that previous history from the mouth of the sage at the time of Kālī, the Mountain, together with his sons and wife, then became free from doubt.
Then, having heard that story from the mouth of Nārada, Kālī lowered her face out of shame, her countenance broadened by a smile.
Having touched her with his hand and heard of her life story, the Mountain smelled her head repeatedly and seated her at the end of his own seat.
Then, O Sage, having seen her again as she stood there, you spoke to her, gladdening the King of Mountains along with the sons of Menakā.
"But O King of Mountains, what indeed shall be her throne? Therefore, her seat shall always be upon the thigh of Śambhu."
Having reached the seat upon Mount Hara, your daughter shall remain there perpetually, where the sight or even the thought of anyone else shall never reach.

Brahmā said: O Nārada, having spoken these noble words to the Lord of the Mountains with such affection, you departed for heaven at that very moment. The Lord of the Mountains, his heart filled with beautiful joy, likewise went to his own home, which was enriched with every kind of prosperity.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Nārada and Himālaya," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, my dear father, you have related this wise and wonderful story concerning Śiva out of compassion; my joy has increased exceedingly.
O dear one, when Vidhi had departed for his own abode and I too had indeed vanished from divine sight, what happened after that? Please tell me that now out of compassion.
Brahmā said: O sage, after you had departed for heaven and some time had passed, Menā once approached the presence of the Mountain and bowed down to him.
Standing there with humility, the virtuous Girikāminī, whose dear son was her very life, spoke to her own lord, the sovereign of the mountains.
Menā said: "Due to the nature of women, I have not fully understood the words of the sage. Perform the marriage of this maiden with a handsome bridegroom."

In every respect, the wedding there would surely bring unprecedented happiness; moreover, the bridegroom of the Daughter of the Mountain would be born of a noble lineage endowed with auspicious marks.
For this daughter of mine is dearer than life; act in such a way that she may be happy and well-pleased upon obtaining an excellent husband—salutations be unto you!
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus, Menā, her face bathed in tears, then fell at her husband’s feet; raising her up, the Mountain, the best among the wise, spoke to her as was fitting.
Himālaya said: Listen, O Goddess Menakā, for I speak the truth according to reality; cast aside this delusion, for the word of a sage is never false.
If you have affection for your daughter, then instruct her respectfully: "With a steady mind and devotion, she should perform penance for Śaṅkara."
O Menakā, if Śiva, being pleased, takes Kālī’s hand in marriage, everything shall become auspicious and the inauspiciousness foretold by Nārada shall perish.
All inauspicious things are auspicious in Sadāśiva; therefore, quickly instruct your daughter to perform penance for the sake of attaining Śiva.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Mountain, Menā became exceedingly pleased; she then approached her son to instruct him regarding his inclination.
Upon seeing her son’s delicate and tender body, Menakā was then deeply distressed; both of her eyes quickly became filled with tears.
The beloved of the Mountain was unable to instruct her daughter; Pārvatī quickly understood that gesture of her mother’s.
Then that goddess Kālikā, the omniscient Supreme Sovereign, immediately spoke to her mother, consoling her again and again.
Pārvatī said: O Mother, O highly wise one, listen; this very day, during the hour of the goat (ajamuhūrta), I saw a dream at night. I shall tell it to you; please show me your grace.
And that compassionate Brahmin, a practitioner of austerities, affectionately instructed me, O Mother, to perform intense penance dedicated to Śiva.
Brahmā said: Having heard that, Menakā quickly summoned her husband there and related the dream she had seen in its entirety.
Then, having heard from Menakā the dream concerning his daughter, the Lord of the Mountains, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to his beloved, addressing her with these words:
Girīśvara said: O beloved, at the end of the final watch of the night, a dream was indeed seen by me as well; listen to it with great affection, for I shall speak of it with due respect.
A supreme ascetic, bearing the excellent boon spoken by Nārada, arrived with great joy at the outskirts of the city to perform penance.
Taking my daughter with me, I went there even more joyful; I recognized that Lord Śambhu, who had been described as the supreme boon-granter by Nārada.
Having instructed his daughter to serve that ascetic, he indeed requested him [to accept her], but he did not then agree to it.
A great dispute arose, one esteemed by the Sāṃkhya and Vedānta schools; then, by his command, my daughter remained there.
"Keeping that desire in her heart, she served him with devotion; thus was this dream seen by me, O fair-faced one, which I have related to you."
Therefore, O beloved, consider for some time that its fruit must be tested; understand for certain that this alone is what is appropriate here for me.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having spoken thus, the king of mountains and Menakā, their hearts pure, remained there testing the fruit of that [action].
In this manner, after a few days had passed, the Supreme Lord, the refuge of the virtuous and the creator of all, wandered everywhere, deeply distressed by his separation from Satī.
There, the Lord, endowed with certain virtues and his mind distressed by separation from the love of Satī, arrived with great joy to perform penance.
Devoted to the service of Pārvatī, she performed her own penance there; accompanied by her two friends, she remained constantly engaged in it for the sake of obtaining his favor.
Although pierced by the arrows sent by Smara, who had been dispatched by the gods for the purpose of deluding him, the Lord Śambhu did not undergo any transformation.
Having burned Smara right there with the fire from his eye, and remembering my words, he became enraged and then vanished from my sight.
Then, after some time, having destroyed the pride of the Daughter of the Mountain through her excellent penance, Maheśvara became pleased and was propitiated.
Adopting worldly custom, Rudra, having been propitiated by Viṣṇu, married Kālī; thereafter, there was great auspiciousness.
Thus, O dear one, has this supreme and divine life-story of the all-pervading Śaṅkara been told to you in brief; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Concise Life of Śiva," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, preceded by the description of the dream.
