Nārada said: O blessed disciple of Viṣṇu, O Creator, O lord, foremost among the devotees of Śiva, you ought to recount this divine play of Śiva to me with affection from Vyāsa.
What did Śambhu do while separated from Satī? And how did he come to the excellent plateau of the Himavat to perform penance?
How did the dialogue between Śivā and Aśiva occur, and how was my desire extinguished? And how did Pārvatī, having performed penance, attain Śiva and Śambhu?
O Brahmin, you ought to tell me all of that and other supreme, auspicious accounts of Śiva’s holy deeds, which bestow great bliss.
Sūta said: Having heard this question of Nārada, Vidhi, the best among the lords of the worlds, spoke with great affection after remembering the lotus feet of Śiva.
Brahmā said: O divine sage, listen with reverence to that glory of the foremost devotee of Śiva; it is purifying, auspicious, and the most excellent increaser of devotion.
Having returned to his own mountain, Śambhu, distressed by separation from his beloved, remembered his dear goddess Satī within his heart, who was dearer to him than life itself.
Addressing the assembly and lamenting for her, he described her qualities—which increase one's love—with great affection, demonstrating the ways of worldly conduct.
Then, having abandoned the auspicious state of household life, he became a Digambara; skilled in divine play, he wandered again through all the worlds.
Having obtained a vision [of the Lord] somewhere, Śaṅkara, who brings happiness to his devotees, returned once more to the mountain, distressed by separation from his virtuous wife.
Having diligently composed his mind, he practiced the concentration that destroys suffering, and he beheld his own imperishable true nature.
Thus did Sthāṇu remain for a very long time, with the three guṇas destroyed; he is the changeless Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Māyā, the self-effulgent Master.
Then, after he had passed immeasurable years, he finally abandoned that meditative absorption; when that occurred, I shall quickly relate his conduct to you.
From the forehead of the Lord, a drop born of fatigue fell upon the earth, and there it quickly became a child.
O Sage, he had four arms and a reddish hue, with a beautiful form; he possessed extraordinary splendor, was glorious, radiant, and difficult for others to endure.
That infant wept before the Supreme Lord, who was devoted to the conduct of worldly life like an ordinary father.
Then, having reflected with a wise mind and assumed the form of a beautiful woman, the Earth appeared right there, instilling fear in Śaṅkara.
Quickly rising, she placed the excellent child upon her lap and affectionately suckled him with the milk produced from her own breast.
Out of affection, she kissed her son’s face and playfully smiled at him; for she was truly his mother, bringing about the welfare of the Supreme Lord.
Having witnessed that conduct, Śambhu—the curious one, the creator of the world, the virtuous one, the inner witness, and Hara—laughed and then spoke, knowing the essence of the matter.
Blessed are you, O Earth; out of affection, protect this son of mine, a boon of great splendor born from the sweat of your exertion.
O Earth, although this child is my servant, may he be known by your name and remain forever free from the three miseries, as he does what is pleasing to you.
This boy will indeed be a virtuous giver for you; he will also be a bestower of happiness upon me. Accept him according to your pleasure.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Rudra—the performer of worldly conventions, the changeless one, and the beloved of the virtuous—ceased, his mind now somewhat released from the pain of separation.
Having received the command of Śiva, that Earth departed quickly; she reached her own abode with her sons and indeed attained ultimate happiness.
Having received the name Bālabhauma and quickly becoming a youth, he served the Lord Śaṅkara for a long time in that city of Kāśī.
By the grace of Viśveśvara, the son of the Earth (Mangala), having attained the status of a planet, quickly went to a divine world, most excellent and beyond the realm of Śukra.
Thus has been told the life of Śambhu, joined with his separation from Satī; O Sage, listen now with reverence to the performance of Śambhu’s ascetic penance.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Bhauma and the Playful Sport of Śiva," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Mountain, that daughter of yours, Śakti, who is worshipped by the worlds, became eight years old while remaining in the home of Himālaya as a virtuous woman.
O Nārada, Giriśa, knowing that birth and being distressed by the separation from Satī, made her wonderful within himself and rejoiced exceedingly.
In that very interval, Śambhu, having adopted a worldly course, desired to perform penance properly in order to fully concentrate his mind.
Having taken leave of certain peaceful and eminent leaders of the Gaṇas, such as Nandin and others, he went to the excellent Himalayan plateau at the descent of the Gaṅgā.
O Sage, there the Gaṅgā, the supreme purifier that destroys the entire flood of sins, formerly descended, having flowed forth from the city of Brahmā.
Standing there, the self-controlled Hara commenced his penance; unwearied, he meditated one-pointedly upon his own Self.
The state of knowledge of the mind is eternal, of the nature of light, free from ailment, consisting of the universe, consciousness-bliss, devoid of duality, and without support.
While Hara was intent on meditation, the Pramathas became absorbed in meditation; some others, such as the Gaṇas Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and the rest, did likewise.
At that time, some of the attendants of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, performed service; however, others remained silent, for certain gatekeepers did not utter even a sound.
In the meantime, the Himālaya mountain came there out of respect, having heard that Śaṅkara was arriving at Auṣadhiprastha.
The lord of the mountains, together with his attendants, bowed down to the Lord Rudra; well-pleased, he honored him and praised him with palms joined in reverence.
Himālaya said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Kapardin, Śaṅkara, Lord! By you alone, the Lord of the worlds, the three realms have been protected.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who assumes the form of a yogi; salutations to you who are devoid of attributes, and to you who sport while possessing attributes.
Salutations to you, Śambhu, who dwells on Kailāsa, the wanderer through all worlds; salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, who assumes forms through divine play and wields the trident.
Salutations to the Supreme Self, who is free from change due to the fullness of his inherent qualities, who is effortless, who is beyond all movement, and who is steadfast.
Salutation to the one who creates external enjoyments, who is affectionate toward his people, the Lord of the three qualities, the Master of Māyā, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.

Salutations to you, who are served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others; to you whose very nature is Viṣṇu and Brahmā; to you, the bestower of Viṣṇu and Brahmā; O beloved of your devotees, salutations be to you!
Salutations to you, who delight in austerity, who bestow the fruit of supreme penance upon those established in ascetic practice, who are fond of tapas, who are peaceful, and whose form is Brahman.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord who possesses all qualities, who alone brings about worldly transactions and establishes the conduct of the world.

O Great Lord, Your divine play is inconceivable and bestows happiness upon the virtuous; for Your very nature is dependent on Your devotees, and as the performer of actions, You are indeed subject to Your devotees.
O Lord, you have come here through the rise of my good fortune; you have made me one who has a protector, for you are described as being compassionate toward those who offer gifts.
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my life is fruitful; today everything of mine has become fruitful, since you have arrived here.
"Knowing me to be your unwavering servant, O Maheśvara, grant me your command; with single-minded devotion, I shall perform service to you with great joy."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Lord of the Mountain, Maheśvara slightly opened his eyes and beheld the Mountain together with his attendants.
Having thus seen the king of mountains together with his retinue, the bull-bannered Lord of the World, established in the yoga of meditation, spoke as if smiling.
Maheśvara said: "I have come to perform secret penance upon your back; act in such a way that no one may approach nearby."
You are a great soul, an abode of asceticism, and the eternal refuge of sages, as well as of gods, rākṣasas, and other high-souled beings.
The eternal abode of the twice-born and others, ever purified by the Gaṅgā, the benefactor of all, and the sovereign lord of mountains.
O King of Mountains, self-restrained and well-pleased, I am performing penance here at the site where the Gaṅgā descends, having taken refuge in you.
"O Lord of Mountains, by what means may my asceticism here be free from obstacles? Therefore, O best of mountains, exert yourself now in every possible way."
O best of mountains, this alone is my supreme service: go to your own home with true affection and accomplish that with diligence.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds, the creator of all beings, became silent; then the King of Mountains, out of affection, addressed Śambhu in this way.
Himālaya said: "O Lord of the World, O Supreme Lord, you have been honored by me today. Since you are present here in my domain, what may I request of you?"
O Maheśāna, you who cannot be attained even by the gods through great austerity when they are intent on their efforts—you yourself have now appeared before us.
"There is no one else more meritorious than I, nor is there anyone else more meritorious than I; and yet you have come before me for the sake of penance."
O Supreme Lord, I consider myself superior even to the king of the gods; for you, together with your retinue, have come and made me a recipient of your grace.
"O Lord of Gods, you who are independent and supreme ascetic, grant that my work be free from obstacles; O Master, I shall perform service accordingly, for I am forever your servant."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, that king of mountains quickly returned to his own abode and related that account with great respect to his beloved wife.
O Nārada, having summoned all his attendants and his own followers who were being led away, the Lord of Mountains spoke to them according to the truth.
Himālaya said: "From this day forward, let no one else go for the descent of the Gaṅgā; by my command, let her descend upon my peak. I speak this truth."
If anyone goes there and encounters that great rogue, I shall punish him especially; this which I have spoken is the truth.
O Sage, having thus quickly restrained all his own attendants, the Mountain made a great effort; listen as I tell you of it.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Meeting between Śiva and the Mountain," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then the lord of mountains, being delighted, took a collection of excellent flowers and fruits and went into the presence of Hara together with his daughter.
Having gone there and bowed to the Lord of the Three Worlds, who was absorbed in meditation, he requested from him his daughter Kālī, who was a marvel to his heart.
Having placed all the fruits, flowers, and other offerings before him, and having brought his daughter forward, the King of Mountains spoke thus to Śambhu.
Himācala said: "O Blessed One, my daughter has been brought here, eager to serve you, the moon-crested one, out of a desire to worship you."
O Lord, if you have favor toward me, grant permission for her to serve Śaṅkara constantly along with her two friends.
Brahmā said: Then Śaṅkara beheld her, having just entered the prime of youth, with the luster of the petals of a blooming blue lotus and a face resembling the full moon.
She was the manifestation of all playful postures and auspicious attire; she had a neck like a conch shell, large eyes, and was radiant with a pair of beautiful ears.
She was enchanting with a pair of arms whose extremities were as long as lotus stalks; her breasts were thick, full, firm, and resembled the buds of lotuses.
She possessed a slender waist adorned with the three folds of skin, and she was graced by a pair of feet resembling land-lotuses.
She was the crest-jewel of the host of women, capable of causing even the mind of a sage—firmly bound within the cage of meditation—to fall away at the mere sight of her.
O dear one, having seen her in such a state—captivating to those in meditation, the enhancer of the body, the tantras, and the mantras, and capable of assuming any form at will—
The great yogi quickly closed his eyes and meditated upon his own supreme form—the ultimate reality, beyond the three qualities, eternal, and unsurpassed.

Then, he beheld the all-pervading Lord of all, engaged in austerity with eyes closed, wearing matted hair and adorned with the crescent moon, the one to be known through the Vedānta, seated upon the supreme throne.

Himācala bowed his head once more, yet that mountain king, whose courage was undaunted, fell into doubt; he, the best among those skilled in speech, addressed these words to the sole kinsman of the world.
Himācala said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion! O All-pervading Lord, open your eyes and look upon me who have come to you for refuge.
O Śiva, O Śarva, O Maheśāna, O Lord who brings joy to the world! I bow to you, O Mahādeva, the one who turns back all calamities.
O Lord of Gods, neither the Vedas nor the scriptures in their entirety know you; the path of your majesty always transcends both speech and mind.
Indeed, all the Vedas describe You with constant and repeated awe by means of the exclusion of what You are not; what then can be said of the opinions of others?
Many devotees, having obtained Your grace through devotion, know that for those devotees who have sought refuge, there is no longer any delusion or the like anywhere.
"Listen to this request from me out of affection for my servant; O Father, by Your Majesty’s command, I indeed describe it because of his wretchedness."
I am fortunate, O Mahādeva, by your grace, O Śaṅkara; considering me your own servant, O Lord, please show me mercy—salutations be unto you!
"O Lord, I shall come every day for the sake of seeing you; O Master, together with this daughter, you should grant me your command."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Maheśvara opened his eyes; abandoning his meditation and reflecting, the God of gods spoke these words.
Maheśvara said: "O Mountain, you must come to see me constantly; having established Kumārī in my abode, there shall be no other way for me to grant you a vision."
Brahmā said: Having heard such words from Maheśa, the father of Śiva, Acala, with his face bowed low, replied thus to Giriśa.
Himācala said: "Tell me why I should not come with her; is she unfit for service? I do not know the reason for this."
Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, whose banner is the bull, smilingly spoke to the mountain, specifically demonstrating the worldly conduct of false yogins.
Śambhu said: "This maiden, with beautiful hips, slender form, moon-like face, and auspicious appearance, must not be brought near me; I forbid it again and again."
Women are known to be of the nature of illusion by the wise who have mastered the Vedas; indeed, a young woman is especially a creator of obstacles for ascetics.
I am an ascetic and a yogi, eternally untainted by illusion; I have no need for a woman through any reasoning—what use is she to me, O Mountain?
Furthermore, O best of ascetics, you should not speak thus, for you are an expert in the Vedic dharma, a wise man, and a preeminent knower of truth.
O Acala, through association with that [worldly object], the arising of sense-objects occurs swiftly; dispassion perishes, and consequently, one's virtuous austerity falls away.
Therefore, O Mountain, an ascetic should not form an attachment to women; for she is the root of great worldly objects and the destroyer of knowledge and dispassion.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and much more, the great yogi Maheśvara, the Lord and best among great yogis, ceased speaking to that Lord of the Mountains.
O celestial sage, having heard these words of Śambhu—which were free from malice yet devoid of desire and harsh—the father of Kālī became startled; likewise, somewhat agitated, he remained silent.
Having heard the words spoken by the ascetic and perceiving that the Lord of the Mountains was thus startled, Bhavānī then bowed to Śiva and spoke these clear words.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Śiva and Himācala," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Bhavānī said: O Lord, O expert in wisdom, listen from me to that answer which was spoken by you, an ascetic yogi, to the King of Mountains.
O Śambhu, endowed with the power of austerity, you perform extensive penance; this resolve to practice penance has arisen in you, O Great-Souled One.
That power should be known as Prakṛti, the source of all actions; by her everything is fashioned, maintained, and destroyed.
"Who are you, O Blessed One, and what is your subtle primordial nature (prakṛti)? Let that be reflected upon; for how can Maheśvara exist in the form of a *liṅga* without a primordial nature?"
"You are worthy of worship, you are worthy of salutation, and you are always to be meditated upon by all living beings. Having reflected thus upon your nature, let all that be spoken from the heart.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Pārvatī, Maheśa, intent on performing a great act of grace, laughed heartily and, with a serene soul, spoke these words.
Maheśvara said: "By means of supreme austerity alone, I destroy primordial nature (prakṛti). Devoid of primordial nature, I, Śambhu, abide in accordance with reality."
Therefore, the wise should never engage in association with Prakṛti; they should remain free from modifications and devoid of worldly conduct.
Brahmā said: O dear one, having been addressed thus by Śambhu according to worldly convention, Kālī laughed heartily and spoke these sweet words.
Kālī said: O Lord Śaṅkara, O Yogin, as for the words spoken by you—that she might not be Prakṛti—how is it that you have transcended her?
Having reflected upon this, one should speak according to reality exactly as it is; for by its very nature, all this is perpetually bound.
Therefore, you must neither speak nor perform anything at all; know in your mind that every word and every composition is merely worldly.
Whatever you hear, whatever you eat, whatever you see, and whatever you do—all that is the work of Prakṛti; the claim [of agency] is false and meaningless.
O Lord Śambhu, if you are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), for what purpose do you perform penance now on this Himavat mountain?
By nature you have been swallowed; you do not know your own self, O Hara. If you did know your own self, O Lord, for what purpose would you perform penance?
What is the use of verbal debate between me and you, O yogin? For the wise know that inference is not a valid means of knowledge when direct perception is present.
As long as the objects of the senses remain within the range of embodied beings, all that must be understood by the wise through their intellect as being merely material (prākṛta).
O Lord of Yogis, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to my supreme word: she is I and you are the Puruṣa; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Indeed, it is through my grace that you are considered possessed of qualities and endowed with form; without me, you are devoid of desire and are incapable of performing any action whatsoever.
For you are always dependent on others, performing various actions and subject to their power; how then can you be changeless, and how indeed can you be unstained by me?
If your word is true that you are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), then you should have no fear while in my presence, O Śaṅkara.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of hers, which were set forth in the Sāṃkhya scriptures, Śiva—who is established in the doctrine of Vedānta—spoke these words to Śivā.
Śrī Śiva said: "O Girijā, if you speak thus as an upholder of Sāṃkhya, then perform for me daily service that is not forbidden, O sweet-spoken lady."
If I am the Supreme Lord, Brahman, untainted by Māyā, known through the Vedānta, and the master of Māyā, then what will you do?
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to Girijā, the Lord—who delights his devotees and bestows grace upon them—addressed these words to the Mountain.
Śiva said: O Mountain, right here upon your most beautiful and excellent peak, I dwell on this earth through supreme austerity, beholding the blissful nature of the ultimate reality.
O Lord of Mountains, you must grant me permission to perform penance; without such permission, it is impossible to perform any austerity whatsoever.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the trident-bearing God of gods, Himavat bowed to Śambhu and spoke these words.
Himavat said: "The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is indeed yours. O Mahādeva, having become insignificant, I say this to you."
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Himavat, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, laughed and spoke respectfully to that king of mountains, saying, "Go."
Permitted by Śaṅkara, Himavat went to his own home; together with Girijā, he remained there, visiting [Śiva] every day.
Even without her father, that Kālī, ever intent on devotion, went daily to the presence of Śaṅkara with her two friends for the sake of service.
O dear one, by the command of Maheśa, no group of attendants, such as Nandīśvara and others—even though they were pure and obedient to his orders—prevented her from entering.
The dialogue between Śiva and Śivā, who are non-different according to thorough inquiry, is declared to be a source of happiness, as it concerns the Sāṃkhya and Vedānta perspectives.
At the word of the King of Mountains, Śaṅkara, the protector of cows, out of respect took his daughter to his side and close to him.
The Lord of the Cows spoke these words to Kālī and her two companions: "Let her serve me constantly; let her go, for she may remain here free from fear."
Having spoken thus to the goddess, Hara—the changeless Great Yogi, the Lord who performs manifold divine sports—took her for his service.
This alone is the great fortitude of the steadfast and the truly ascetic: that even when encountering obstacles, they are not thwarted by those obstacles.
Then, having returned to his own city with his attendants, the lord of mountains, together with his beloved, rejoiced exceedingly in his heart, O lord of sages.
And Hara, with his own mind free from obstacles, remained intent on meditating with devotion upon the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation.
Accompanied by her two friends, Kālī remained constantly engaged in coming and going as she served Mahādeva, the moon-crested Lord, every day.
Having washed the feet of Śambhu, he drank that water from his feet; then, with a cloth purified by fire, he performed the wiping of his body.
Having worshipped Hara according to the rules with the sixteen-fold service, and having prostrated himself again and again, he went daily to his father's house.
O best of sages, as she thus served Śaṅkara while remaining intent on meditation, a great length of time passed for Śivā.
Once, Kālī, accompanied by her two friends in the hermitage of Śaṅkara, performed a beautiful song with excellent rhythm that increased the passion of love.
Sometimes she herself would fetch kuśa grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel; at other times, she dwelt there performing the consecration of the site together with her two friends.
Once, while staying fixedly at home, she who was intensely devoted to the Moon-bearer looked upon the Moon-crested Lord with longing and was filled with wonder.
Then, seeing her standing there free from attachment, the Lord of Beings reflected upon her, perceiving that she was established within the bodies of all beings.
Śiva did not accept Kālī as his wife, even though she stood near him, possessed of a mass of great beauty that could enchant even the sages.
But Mahādeva, seeing her again thus with her senses restrained and constantly devoted to his service, thought compassionately:
As soon as this Kālī undertakes her ascetic practice and vow, I shall seize her once she is divested of the seed of pride.
Brahmā said: Having reflected thus, the Lord of Beings quickly resorted to meditation; indeed, the Great Lord, the master of great yoga, became engaged in his great divine play.
O Sage, while that Śiva, the Supreme Soul, was thus absorbed in meditation, no other thought whatsoever remained established in his heart.
Kālī, however, served Śambhu every day with true devotion, constantly meditating upon the form of that Great Soul.
Hara, devoted to meditation, gazed constantly at Kālī as she remained steadfast; having forgotten his former thoughts, though he was looking at her, he did not see her.
In the meantime, by the command of Brahmā, the gods headed by Śakra and those sages respectfully dispatched Smara to that place.
Afflicted by the highly powerful asura Tāraka, they sought through desire to bring about a union between Kālī and Rudra.
Having gone there, Smara employed every means at his disposal; yet Hara was not disturbed in the least, and he reduced him to ashes.
O sage, by his command Pārvatī also became free from pride; then, having performed great penance, the virtuous lady obtained Śiva as her husband.
Pārvatī and Parameśvara became well-pleased; for, devoted to the service of others, they indeed accomplished the work of the gods.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord," in the third section (Pārvatī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Viṣṇu’s disciple, O great devotee of Śiva, O Vidhi, you have correctly related this supreme account of both Śivā and Śiva.
O Brahmin, by which son was the asura Kāstāraka—who oppressed the gods—slain? Tell me that story, which takes refuge in Śiva.
How did Śaṅkara, the self-controlled one, reduce Smara to ashes? O Lord, please tell me with great kindness that wonderful deed of the Master.
How did Śivā perform such exceedingly fierce penance for the sake of happiness? How did the primordial power, supreme over the world, obtain Śambhu as her husband?
O great wise one, tell all of this in its entirety and in detail to me, who am full of faith, your own son, and whose nature is auspiciousness.
Brahmā said: O best of sons, O highly wise celestial sage of celebrated vows, I shall speak after remembering Śaṅkara; listen to all of his deeds.
First, O Nārada, hear about the very birth of Tāraka, for whose sake a great effort was made by the gods who have taken refuge in Śiva.
My son is Marīci, and Kaśyapa is his offspring; he has thirteen wives who are the daughters of Dakṣa.
Diti was his eldest wife, and she gave birth to two sons: Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger.
Those two Daityas, who were the givers of great suffering, were slain by Viṣṇu in the forms of Nṛsiṃha and Kroḍa; thereafter, the gods attained happiness and became free from fear.
Diti was distressed and sought refuge with Kaśyapa; having again served him with devotion, that woman of virtuous vows conceived a child.
Having discerned this, the great Indra, seizing the opportunity and exerting great effort, entered there and repeatedly shattered that embryo with his thunderbolt.
By the power of that vow, her fetus did not perish; and by the turn of fate, as she slept, seven sons were born to her in seven [successive nights].
Those sons of his became gods, all of them known by the name Maruts; they went to heaven, having been made subject to Indra, the king of the gods.
Then Diti, repenting of her own deed, again approached her husband and, through supreme service, made that sage well-pleased.
Kaśyapa said: "Perform austerities, becoming pure, for ten thousand years of Brahmā; if that [merit] is attained, then a son shall be born to you as before."
O sage, that penance was thus completed by Diti with faith; then, having conceived a fetus from her husband, she gave birth to such a son.
He became the son of Diti named Vajāṅga, who was like an immortal; a hero whose body was true to his name, possessed of great prowess, and powerful from his very birth.
At his mother's command, that son immediately seized the lord of the gods by force and inflicted various punishments upon the immortals as well.

Having seen that even Śakra and the others, who are difficult for others to behold, have attained such extreme misery, even the immortals, including Śakra and his peers, experienced suffering due to their own karma.
Then, having quickly arrived there with Kaśyapa, I, who am always devoted to the welfare of the gods, caused the gods to abandon him through well-composed songs.
Then, having dismissed the gods, that Vajrāṅga spoke with reverence—he who was a devotee of Śiva, possessed of an exceedingly pure soul, free from agitation, and of serene intellect.

Vajrāṅga said: "Indra is wicked and a slayer of living beings; he pursued his own self-interest at my mother's expense. Today he has obtained the fruit [of his actions]; let him indeed rule his own kingdom."
"O Brahmin, all this has been done by me solely under the command of my mother; indeed, I have no desire for the enjoyments of any world whatsoever."
O Sūta, best among the knowers of the Vedas, O Creator, impart to me the essence of reality, by which I may be eternally happy, changeless, and of serene intellect.
Having heard that, O Sage, I said with affection: "The state called Sāttvika is known as the Essence of Reality; therefore, I shall create a single, excellent woman."
Having bestowed her, named Varāṅgī, upon that son of Diti, both Kaśyapa, her father, and he himself departed for their own abodes well-pleased.
Then Vajrāṅga, the Daitya, having resorted to a sāttvika disposition and cast off his āsura nature, attained happiness free from enmity.
Indeed, no sattvic emotion arose in the heart of that woman of excellent limbs; yet, being desirous, the virtuous lady approached her husband with various acts of devotion and faith.
Then, through her service, the Great Lord quickly became pleased; that husband of hers, Vajrāṅga, then spoke these words.
Vajrāṅga said: "Tell me, my beloved, what do you desire? What dwells in your heart? Having heard that, she bowed to her husband and spoke of her own heart's desire.
Varāṅgī said: "O Lord of the virtuous, if you are indeed pleased, grant me a son who is possessed of great strength, a conqueror of the three worlds, and a bringer of sorrow to Hara."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his beloved, he was struck with wonder and became agitated; yet that wise one, being of a pure nature and free from enmity, spoke thus within his heart.
He indeed desires hostility with the gods; this is not pleasing to me. What should I do? Where should I go? How might my wager not be lost?
The desires of the beloved shall indeed be fulfilled, even if the three worlds were to come into being; yet gods and sages alike would remain exceedingly burdened by affliction.
"If my beloved were not to be reunited with me, then hell would be mine; for I have heard that in either case, there is indeed a loss of dharma."
O Sage, thus did Vajrāṅga wander in that crisis of dharma; there, he reflected with his intellect upon the relative strength and weakness of the two sides.
O Sage, by the will of Śiva, that wise king of the Daityas accepted her words; he spoke the words "So be it" to his beloved.
For that purpose, however, he—having conquered his senses—performed another intense and difficult penance for many years with great devotion, directed toward me.
Having seen that great austerity of his, I went to grant him a boon; with a very gracious mind, I said to him, "Choose a boon."
Then Vajrāṅga, seeing me, the omnipresent Lord, standing there pleased, bowed deeply, offered many praises, and chose a boon for the benefit of his beloved.
Vajrāṅga said: "O Lord, grant me a son for my mother—one who will bring great benefit, who possesses great strength, great majesty, and great capability, and who is a treasure-house of asceticism."
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard those words, I replied, "So be it," and having given that [boon], I went to my own abode; then, dejected, I remembered Śiva.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vajrāṅga and His Austerities," in the Tārakotpatti section of the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, within the second Rudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then that lady of excellent limbs conceived a fetus out of devotion to him; indeed, it grew within her for many years with great luster.
Then, when the time was fulfilled, that woman of beautiful limbs gave birth to a son who possessed a massive body and great heroism, blazing forth toward the ten directions.
And at that very moment, great portents occurred as causes of sorrow, when that son was being born from Varāṅgī, bringing both joy and grief.
O dear one, I shall describe those three types of portents that indicate misfortune and cause fear to all the worlds—those occurring in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
Meteors and thunderbolts fell with a great roar, terrifying and fearsome; and prominent comets, portending misery, rose up.
The earth, along with its mountains, trembled; all the quarters blazed; and all the rivers, especially the oceans, were agitated.
A wind of harsh touch blew forth, emitting deep roars like "hūṃ" sounds; accompanied by a swarm of whirlwinds and bearing dust as its banner, it uprooted the great trees.
O best of Brahmins, halos repeatedly appeared around the moon and the sun; they were harbingers of great terror and portents of the destruction of happiness.
Then, at that moment, thunderclaps indicative of danger, resembling the rattling of chariots, issued forth from the crevices of the mountains.
With the hooting of jackals and owls, the inauspicious female jackals vomited fire from their mouths and howled hideously within the villages.
Then and there, those village lions, raising their necks, let out various cries like singing and like weeping.
O dear one, intoxicated by the fury of their "khār-khār" roars, those rutting elephants, crushing the earth with their trunks, then rushed here and there in vast herds.
The birds, their minds terrified by the donkey, flew up from their nests; crying out with agitated hearts, they found no place to settle.
Overcome with fear, they voided excrement and urine in the cow-pen and the forest; like cattle that have been beaten, they wandered about and found no rest.
The cows lay down there, yielding blood as their milk, with eyes full of tears and overwhelmed by fear; the clouds became givers of terror, raining down pus.
There, the statues of the gods wept as they were about to fly up; trees fell even without wind, and a battle of the planets occurred in the sky.
O best of sages, many such portents arose; the ignorant people there believed that the dissolution of the universe had occurred.
Then Prajāpati, having reflected, gave that Asura of great power the name Tāraka; for indeed, Kaśyapa [bestowed it] after due consideration.
His own prowess suddenly manifesting, the Great Hero grew with a body as solid as stone, like the Lord of Mountains.
Then that high-minded Daitya Tāraka, possessed of great strength and prowess, requested permission from his mother to perform ascetic penance.
Having obtained the boon, that master of great illusion, who could delude even the masters of illusion, set his mind upon performing austerities in order to achieve victory over all the gods.
Having gone to the Madhu forest, he who was a fulfiller of his guru’s command performed most severe penance according to the rules, directed toward the ritual procedure.
With his arms raised and standing on one foot, gazing at the sun with his eye, he performed penance for a hundred years with a firm mind and steadfast vows.
Touching the earth with his big toe, that firm-souled Tāraka, the lord and king of the asuras, performed such penance for a hundred years.

For a hundred years he subsisted on water, for a hundred years he lived on air alone; for a hundred years he remained standing in water, and for a hundred years he performed penance upon the bare ground.
Likewise, he remained in the fire for a hundred years; for a hundred years with his face turned downwards; and for a hundred years standing upon the earth on the palm of his hand.
O Sage, for a hundred years he indeed hung from the branch of a tree with his face turned downwards, drinking the pure smoke with both feet.

In this manner, the king of the Daityas performed even more arduous penance according to the prescribed rites, directed toward the fulfillment of his desire—an austerity difficult even for those who hear of it to endure.
O Sage, as he was performing penance in that very manner, a great splendor issued forth from his head, spreading everywhere and causing a great calamity.
O sage, by that very [fire], those worlds of the gods became almost entirely consumed; all the celestial rishis fell into misery on every side.
Then Indra, the lord of the gods, was seized by great fear, thinking: "Someone is surely performing penance today and will violate my position."
"This Lord will dissolve the universe even prematurely"—fallen into such doubt, they could find no certainty.
Then all those gods and sages, having consulted together among themselves, went to my world in fear; dejected, they approached me.
Having prostrated before me and praised me with great devotion, they all, with distressed hearts, joined their palms in reverence and reported everything that had occurred to me.
Having thoroughly determined the cause of that with my virtuous intellect, I went to the place where that asura was performing penance, in order to grant him a boon.
I spoke these words: "O Sage, choose a boon; you have performed such intense austerity that there is nothing that cannot be granted by you."
Having heard these words of mine, the great asura Tāraka bowed to me, praised me profusely, and chose a most dreadful boon.
Tāraka said: "When you, the granter of boons, are pleased, what could be unattainable for me? Therefore, O Grandfather, hear from me the boon I request of you."
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, having shown compassion toward me, two boons should be given to me.
O Great Lord, in this entire world created by you, surely there shall be no man whatsoever who is equal to me in strength.
When my son, born from the seed of Śiva, becomes a general and hurls a weapon at me, then shall my death come to pass.
O lord of sages, having been addressed thus by that Daitya at that time, and having granted him such a boon, I quickly departed for my own world.
Having obtained that supreme boon desired by his heart, the Daitya, becoming exceedingly delighted, went to the city named Śoṇita.
Then, by my command, that great asura was consecrated in the sovereignty of the three worlds along with the other asuras by Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas.
Thereupon, that great Daitya became the leader of the three worlds; he issued his own commands, afflicting all things mobile and immobile.
That Tāraka ruled the three worlds according to his own will and protected his subjects while afflicting the gods and others.
Then the Daitya Tāraka seized the jewels of those world-protectors, such as Indra and the others, which they had surrendered of their own accord out of fear of him.
Out of fear of him, Indra surrendered Airāvata to him; then Kubera gave him nine treasures (nidhis).
The bright horses were given by Varuṇa, and Kāmakṛt by the Ṛṣis; likewise, out of fear, the divine Uccaiḥśravas was surrendered to him by Sūrya.
Wherever any auspicious object was seen by that asura, he seized it with force; thus, the three worlds became devoid of essence.
O Sage, the oceans likewise yielded jewels to him out of fear; the earth bore crops without being ploughed, and all creatures were like wish-fulfilling cows.
The sun shines in such a way that its heat does not become unbearable; the moon is visible with its radiance, and the wind blows favorably for all.
Whatever wealth belonged to the gods, the ancestors, and others—all that was seized by the evil-minded asura.
Having brought the three worlds under his control, he himself became Indra; as a master of his senses, he was an unrivaled lord and ruled a marvelous kingdom.
Having expelled all the gods from there, he then established the Daityas; he himself appointed those born of divine origin to their respective duties.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, being thus defeated and rendered helpless and extremely distressed, sought refuge with me, O Sage.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Austerities and Kingdom of the Asura Tāraka," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then all those gods, being oppressed by Tāraka, bowed deeply to the Lord of Creatures and praised him with supreme devotion.
Having heard that truthful and heart-touching hymn of praise from the immortals, I became exceedingly well-pleased and replied to the denizens of heaven.
Welcome! Indeed, you have all been free from obstacles in your respective duties; tell me, for what purpose have you all come here?
Having heard these words of mine, all those inhabitants of heaven bowed down to me and, being oppressed by Tāraka, spoke to me with humility and distress.
The gods said: "O Lord of the World, the Daitya Tāraka, emboldened by your boon, has forcibly cast us out from our positions and seized them himself by might."
Is it not known to you what suffering has come upon us? Quickly destroy that suffering; we have come to you for refuge.
Day and night, he indeed tormented us wherever we stayed; even as we fled, we saw Tāraka everywhere.
O Lord of all, O Father, because of the suffering that arose from Tāraka’s food, we have all been tormented and rendered utterly distressed.
Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Vāyu, as well as all the other guardians of the quarters, are subject to his will.
All those possessing human attributes, accompanied by all their retinues, serve that great Daitya; they are never independent.
Thus afflicted by him, the gods were always under his control; intent on performing whatever he desired, they all became his dependents.
That exceedingly powerful Daitya, Tāraka, seized all those women and all the hosts of Apsarases.
Sacrifices do not proceed, ascetics do not practice austerities, and no acts such as charity or dharma are carried out in the worlds.
His commander-in-chief is the Dānava Krauñca, a great sinner; having gone to the depths of Pātāla, he oppresses the subjects incessantly.
"O Creator of the World, this entire triple universe has been forcibly seized by that sinful and merciless Tāraka."
And we shall go to that place which you shall designate; for we were kept at ease by being restrained there by that Lord of the World, the enemy of the gods.
You alone are our refuge, our teacher, our sustainer, and our protector; for we are all utterly overwhelmed, scorched by the fire known as Tāraka.
By him, through cruel means, all our powers have been destroyed; he is like potent medicines administered during a complication or a combined derangement of the humors.
In that very Sudarśana, the discus of Hari, where our hope for victory lay, it became blunted as if a flower had been placed upon his throat.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard these words of the gods, I replied to all the deities with speech appropriate for that occasion.
Brahmā said: "O dwellers of heaven, it was by my very word that the Daitya named Tāraka was brought to growth; therefore, his slaying by me is not fitting."
Therefore, his slaughter is by no means proper, since he has now attained growth; for even a poison tree, having been nurtured, is unfit to be cut down by one's own hand.
Indeed, Śaṅkara is capable of performing every one of your tasks; however, though urged, he is not himself able to act in return.
But he who is named Tāraka shall meet his own destruction through his own sin; I am merely the one who provides you with instruction as to how you should act.
"Tāraka is not to be slain by me, nor by Hari, nor by Hara, nor by anyone else, nor even by the gods; this is spoken as the truth by virtue of my boon."
O gods, if a son were born from the seed of Śiva, he alone—and no other—would be the slayer of the Daitya named Tāraka.
O best of gods, perform that means which I declare; by the grace of Mahādeva, he will certainly attain success.
She who was formerly Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, having abandoned her body, was reborn from the womb of Menakā; this story is indeed known to you.
Śiva will certainly take her hand in marriage; therefore, O dwellers of heaven, devise a means to that end.
Therefore, exert yourselves with the utmost effort to ensure that the semen does not fall upon Pārvatī, the daughter of Menakā.
No other woman whatsoever has the power to forcibly make that Śambhu, whose semen is drawn upward, one whose semen is discharged.
That daughter of the King of Mountains, now in the full bloom of youth, performs austerities on the Himālaya mountain and constantly serves Hara.
At the command of her father Himavat, the auspicious Kālī, together with her two friends, forcibly serves the Supreme Lord while he remains absorbed in meditation.
While that woman of excellent complexion was indeed being worshipped before him in the three worlds, Maheśa, absorbed in meditation, did not waver even in his mind.
O gods, strive with diligence so that before long you may bring about a wife for him just as Candraśekhara did for Kālī.
"Then, having gone to the place of that Daitya Tāraka, I shall restrain him from his obstinacy; O immortals, you may return to your own abodes."
Having spoken thus to the gods, I quickly approached the asura named Tāraka and, addressing him with great courtesy, spoke these words.
Brahmā said: You protect this kingdom of ours, this heaven which is the very essence of splendor; you desire even more than that for which you have performed great penance.
Neither a superior nor an inferior boon has been granted by me for the sake of sovereignty over heaven; therefore, renouncing heaven, exercise your rule upon the earth.
O best of gods, all activities worthy of the gods must be performed right there; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Having spoken thus and awakened that asura, I, the Lord of all, remembered Śiva along with Śivā and vanished on the spot.
Tāraka also, having abandoned heaven, came to the earth; staying in the city named Śoṇita, he ruled over the entire kingdom.
Having heard those words of mine, all the gods bowed deeply to me and, being well-composed by Śakra, went with joy to the abode of Śakra.
Having gone there, gathered together, and deliberated with one another, all those Maruts affectionately spoke these words to Maghavan:
The gods said: "O Maghavan, you must carry out everything exactly as spoken by Brahmā, so that desire may indeed arise in Śambhu for Śivā."
Brahmā said: Having thus reported the entire account to the Lord of the Gods, all those deities departed for their respective abodes, filled with joy.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Consolation of the Devas," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: When those gods had departed, Śakra, being greatly oppressed by the wicked Daitya Tāraka, indeed called Smara to mind.
At that very moment, Kāma, the lord who conquers the three worlds, arrived with his retinue; he was full of pride, accompanied by Rati, and beloved of delight.
Then, having offered his salutation and standing before him with a highly uplifted mind and palms joined in reverence, O dear one, Smara spoke to Śakra.
Kāma said: What task has arisen for you? For what reason have I been remembered? O Lord of Gods, tell me the truth; I have come here to perform it.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Kandarpa, the Lord of the Gods spoke with affection, praising them as "well-said" and "fitting."
Śakra said: "Your undertaking is excellent, for you are prepared to perform that task which has come before me; you are blessed, O Makaradhvaja!"
Listen to my words as they are presented; I shall speak them before you. Whatever is my task is indeed yours, and not otherwise.
I indeed have many very great friends; however, remember that there is no true friend equal to you anywhere.
"O Father, this supreme pair of thunderbolts was fashioned for my victory; yet the thunderbolt might indeed become fruitless, but you shall never [be so]."
Who indeed could be dearer than one from whom benefit arises? Therefore, as you are the best of friends, you ought to perform my task.
This suffering has arisen within me, incurable and born of time; it cannot be dispelled by anyone at all except for you.
The examination of a donor occurs during a famine; that of a hero, in battle; that of a friend, in times of calamity; and that of women, when the family is in distress.
O dear one, when a crisis in discipline has arisen, it is not otherwise than the truth that has been spoken regarding Avitatha, who is so deeply affectionate even in his absence.
"O best of friends, since my downfall has indeed been brought about by another and cannot be averted, today your own trial shall take place."
Not only is this task of mine conducive to happiness, but it is undoubtedly the task of all the gods and others as well.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Maghavan, those whose banner is the sea-monster (the gods) spoke words profound with love, preceded by a gentle smile.
Kāma said: "For what reason do you speak thus? I shall not give you an answer; for in this world, one who performs a service with ulterior motives is neither seen nor spoken of as such."
He who speaks much in times of distress—what work will he accomplish? Nevertheless, O Great King, I shall speak; listen, O Lord.
O friend, whoever performs severe austerities in order to draw you away from your path, I shall certainly cause that enemy of yours to fall in every way.
In an instant, with a mere sidelong glance from this excellent woman, I shall cause the downfall of gods, sages, and dānavas; as for men, they do not even enter my reckoning.
Let the vajra remain far away, indeed, along with the many other weapons; what business will they have with me, O friend, when I am present?
I could undoubtedly cause even Brahmā or Hari to fall; there is no counting others—I could even cast Hara down.

My five arrows are indeed soft, and they are made of flowers; my bow is threefold and made of flowers, and its string is composed of bees. My strength is indeed my beloved Spring, who is considered my minister.
I am the god Pañcabala; Sudhānidhi is my friend.
The commander-in-chief is Śṛṅgāra, the soldiers are the *hāvas* and *bhāvas*, and all of them are gentle, O Śakra; and I myself am likewise.
Whatever task is fulfilled by which means, a wise person should employ that very means; therefore, assign to me every task that is suitable for me.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Śakra was greatly delighted; bowing down, he spoke with a voice that brings the happiness of one’s beloved desires.
Śakra said: "O dear one, O Mind-born, you alone are capable of performing that task which has been intended by me in my mind; its accomplishment cannot come from anyone else."
Listen, O Kāma, best of friends; I shall explain to you the truth as it is, regarding that for which this desire has arisen in your mind today, O Manobhava.
The great Daitya named Tāraka, having obtained a wonderful boon from Brahmā, became invincible to all and a source of suffering for everyone.
By that, the world is oppressed, for many dharmas have been destroyed; all the gods and likewise all the sages are suffering.
A battle was fought by him against all the gods according to their strength; formerly, the weapons of them all became fruitless there.
The noose of the Lord of Waters was broken; the Sudarśana discus of Hari became blunted when it was hurled by Viṣṇu at his throat.
The death of this evil-minded one was proclaimed by Prajāpati from the child born of Śambhu’s seed, for he was indeed a great lord of yogins.
This task must be performed by you properly and with great effort; from that, O best of friends, there will be supreme happiness for us gods.
Therefore, remembering the duty of friendship in your heart, you ought now to perform for me as well that which brings happiness to all the world.
For Śambhu, having undertaken supreme austerity on the king of mountains, that Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, is independent and not subject to desire.
And I have heard it commanded by my father that the gods and Pārvatī, accompanied by her own companions, remain near him, serving him.
O Māra, you must certainly act in such a way that Śiva, whose self is disciplined, develops an intense longing for her.
By acting thus, you shall become successful; all suffering will perish, and your fame shall endure in the world—this shall not be otherwise.
Brahmā said: Thus addressed, Kāma, his lotus-face in full bloom with love, spoke to the Lord of Gods: "I shall do so, without a doubt."
Having spoken these words to him, Kāma—deluded by the Māyā of Śiva—quickly accepted his speech, saying, "So be it," and "Om."
Where the Lord of Yogins himself was performing supreme austerity, he went there with great joy, accompanied by his wife and his son.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Śakra and Kāma," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having gone there, the arrogant Smara, deluded by Śiva’s māyā, stood at first spreading the dharma that causes infatuation and pride.
And that dharma of spring spread everywhere, O lord of sages, in Auṣadhiprastha, the place of penance for Maheśa.
And the forests of trees were in full bloom there, O great sage; they were especially so in that place due to his power, O lord of sages.
Indeed, the fragrant blossoms of the mango trees in the Aśoka groves shone forth, acting as powerful inciters of longing.
And the kairava flowers, frequented by bees, became especially provocative of the onset of passion.
The sweet warbling of the cuckoo, which kindles desire, has indeed approached—most delightful, captivating, and exceedingly dear.
Likewise, O Sage, there arose various sounds of bees, all of which were enchanting to everyone and even kindling the fire of passion.
The bright luster of the moon, indeed scattered in every direction, became like a female messenger for lovers and beloved women.
At that time, O virtuous one, the lamp of the seasons served as an incentive for the proud, while a pleasant breeze blew—though it was disagreeable to those separated from their lovers.
Thus, the expansion of spring, which causes the onset of passion, became exceedingly difficult for the forest-dwelling sages there to endure at that time.
O Sage, even those devoid of consciousness were then possessed by lust; what need is there to describe the state of those living beings who possess awareness? ||1||
In this way, he displayed his own power, which was exceedingly difficult to endure, acting as an inflamer of desire for all living beings.
O dear one, seeing that untimely sign of spring, the Lord Hara, who had assumed a body for his own divine play, then considered it a supreme wonder.
Then Līlākara performed there a most difficult penance; for Hara, the Lord who removes suffering, is indeed the master of those who have conquered their senses.
When spring had fully arrived there, Kāma, filled with passion, stood at his left side, having drawn back his mango-blossom arrow.
He spread his own splendor, deluding all people; for who would not be infatuated upon seeing Kāma united with Rati?
While the divine couple were thus engaged in amorous play, Śṛṅgāra also, accompanied by his attendants and manifesting various gestures and emotions, entered into the presence of Hara.
Madana resided there openly, yet he remained outside the heart; at that time, he did not see any flaw in Śambhu through which he might enter.
And when Smara found no opening against that best of yogis, Mahādeva then became utterly bewildered by great fear.
Who indeed is capable of approaching Śaṅkara, who resembles a blazing flame of fire, is endowed with an eye in his forehead, and is established in meditative absorption?
In the meantime, Śivā, accompanied by her two friends and having brought many flowers, went there for the purpose of worshipping Śiva.
Whatever great beauty is described by the world upon the earth, all of that—and even more—is certainly present in that Pārvatī.
When her seasonal menses were accompanied by such beautiful blossoms, how could that beauty be described even in hundreds of years?
When that daughter of the mountain had approached Śiva, at that very moment Śaṅkara abandoned his meditation and remained still for a moment.
Having found that opening, Madana first gladdened the moon-crested Lord standing at his side with an arrow called Harṣaṇa.
O Sage, Pārvatī, accompanied by Śṛṅgāra and the other emotional states (bhāvas), as well as by Surabhi, then went to Hara to assist Kāma.
Drawing that very bow for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the trident, Smara, remaining well-composed, swiftly discharged that flower-arrow at him.
Having paid homage to Śiva, who comes constantly and eternally, and having performed worship before him, she stood in his presence.
There, Pārvatī was indeed seen by the Lord, the dweller of the mountain, as she, out of her feminine nature, was covering her limbs with great bashfulness.
O Sage, having well-remembered that boon formerly granted by Brahmā, the Lord Śiva also joyfully described her limbs.
Śiva said: What is his face, and what is the moon? What are his eyes, and what are the two blue lotuses? These two eyebrows are the bows of the great-souled Kandarpa.
Furthermore, is her lower lip the bimba fruit? Is her nose the beak of a parrot? Is her voice the warbling of a cuckoo? And is her waist a sacrificial altar?
Why indeed is her gait described? Why is her form repeatedly described? And why are the flowers and likewise the garments described again and again?
Whatever grace and beauty exists in creation has been fashioned together in one place; there is no doubt that all her limbs are beautiful in every respect.
"Oh, how exceedingly blessed is this Pārvatī of wondrous form! There is no woman of such beautiful form in the three worlds who is her equal."
She is a treasure-house of exquisite beauty, possessing wondrous limbs; she is the enchantress of even sages and the increaser of supreme bliss.
Brahmā said: Having thus described his limbs again and again, Hara indeed ceased, owing to the influence of the boon granted by Brahmā.
As Śaṅkara moved his hand within the fold of her garment, she, due to her feminine nature, became ashamed there and stepped away to a distance.
O Sage, repeatedly revealing her own limbs and gazing at them again and again with beautiful glances, Śivā was filled with great joy and broke into a lovely smile.
Seeing such an act at that time, Śambhu fell into a state of delusion; and Maheśvara, the great player, spoke these words.
By the mere sight of her, great bliss arises sufficiently; but what happiness would there be if I were to embrace her?
Having reflected thus for a mere moment and then worshipped Girijā, the great yogi, being fully awakened and profoundly dispassionate, spoke as follows.
What strange event has occurred? Have I fallen into delusion? For today, though I am the Lord and Sovereign, I have been transformed by passion.
If I, being the Lord, so desired, I could indeed touch another's body; then what other wretched and powerless person would not do this or that?
Having thus attained dispassion and assumed that cross-legged posture, the Supreme Lord, the Soul of All, restrained him; for how could He, the Supreme Ruler, fall here?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Transformations Caused by Kāma," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, within the third section of the Rudra-saṃhitā, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Vidhi, O highly fortunate one, what occurred immediately after that? Please tell me out of your grace that story which destroys all sins.
Brahmā said: Listen, my dear, to that story of what occurred thereafter; out of affection for you, I shall relate the joy-bestowing play of Śiva.
Seeing this calamity of his fortitude, the great yogi Maheśvara was struck with wonder and thereafter reflected thus within his mind.
Śiva said: "Have obstacles arisen while I am performing this supreme austerity? By what evil-doer has my mind been disturbed here?"
Out of affection, I have indeed composed a description concerning another's wife; herein a violation of dharma has occurred, and the boundaries of the Vedas have been transgressed.
Brahmā said: Having reflected thus, the great yogi, the Supreme Lord and refuge of the virtuous, then looked around in all directions, filled with apprehension.
On his left side, he saw Kāma standing with his arrow drawn, desiring to discharge his shaft, arrogant and deluded in mind.
O Nārada, upon seeing such passion in the Supreme Soul, the Lord of the Mountains, a surge of wrath arose in him at that very moment.
O Sage, Kāma, stationed in the intermediate space, took up his bow along with an arrow and discharged an irresistible and infallible weapon at Śaṅkara.
But that unfailing weapon became futile against the Supreme Self; it was completely neutralized when the Supreme Lord became enraged.
When his own brother Śiva had become powerless, Manmatha was quickly seized by fear; standing before him, he trembled upon seeing the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya.
Overwhelmed by fear, O tiger among sages, that Smara remembered all the thirty gods, beginning with Śakra, when his own efforts had proven fruitless.
O Lord of Sages, all those gods, Śakra and the others, being well-remembered by Kāma, arrived there; having bowed to Śambhu, they indeed offered hymns of praise.
While the gods were offering praise, from the third eye of Hara—who was indeed enraged—there issued forth a great [flame].
From that [point] in the middle of his forehead, a fire suddenly emerged; blazing with upward-pointing flames, it shone intensely with a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Having quickly flown up into the sky and then descended to the surface of the earth, he whirled around himself again and again and fell upon the ground.
O virtuous one, he indeed reduced Madana to ashes at that very moment, before the words of the gods—“Forgive him! Forgive him!”—could even reach his ears.
When that heroic Smara was slain, the gods were overcome with grief; distressed and crying out loudly, they wept, asking, "What has happened?"
Then the daughter of the King of Mountains, her limbs white and her form transformed, went to her own abode, taking her circle of female companions with her.
At that moment, her pleasure there turned into unconsciousness; overcome by the grief born of her husband's death, she fell down as if dead.
And when consciousness had returned, Rati, utterly overwhelmed, then lamented there, uttering various words.
Rati said: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? What has been done here by the gods? Having summoned my lord, they have destroyed that arrogant one."
"Alas, alas, O Lord! Remember me, O Master, O beloved of my life, O bestower of happiness! What indeed has happened here? Alas, alas, my dear one, my dear one!"
Brahmā said: Thus lamenting and speaking many words, she then struck her hands and feet and tore out her hair.
O Nārada, having heard that lamentation at that time, all the forest-dwellers there became sorrowful, even the immobile beings.
In the meantime, all the gods there, headed by Śakra, remembered Maheśvara and, having consoled Rati, spoke to her.
The gods said: "Take some of this ash and protect it with care; cast away your fear. That Lord will restore you to life, and you shall regain what is dear to you."
There is no one who bestows happiness, nor is there anyone who bestows suffering; everyone experiences the results of their own actions. O Deva, you grieve indeed in vain.
Brahmā said: Having thus consoled Rati, all the gods approached Śiva; having propitiated Śiva with devotion, they spoke these words.
The gods said: "O Blessed One, O Lord, please listen to these auspicious words of ours. Having shown compassion, O Maheśāna, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge."
O Śaṅkara, reflect well with great affection upon this work of Kāma; O Maheśvara, that which has been composed here by Kāma was not for his own sake.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, O Śaṅkara, know that this deed was caused to be done by Tāraka against all the gods who were oppressed by him; consider it not otherwise.
O Lord Giriśa, Rati, being alone and afflicted by grief, laments; you must always console her.
O Śaṅkara, if you desire to effect the dissolution of all beings through this anger, then remember that [destruction] which was brought about by the gods together with me.
Seeing the suffering of that Rati and that the deities are almost destroyed, you must therefore act to dispel Rati’s grief.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of theirs, the blessed Lord Śiva was pleased and spoke these words to all the gods.
Śiva said: O gods and all sages, listen to my words with reverence; that which has occurred through my anger shall be exactly so and not otherwise.
Kāma, the lord and master of Rati, remains bodiless only so long as Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rukmiṇī, has not descended upon the earth.
When, residing in Dvārakā, he shall procreate sons, then Kṛṣṇa will indeed give rise to desire for Rukmiṇī.
"He shall undoubtedly have the name Pradyumna; however, as soon as that son is born, Śambara will carry him away."
Having seized him and cast him into the ocean, Śambara, the best of the Dānavas, will think him dead and, being deluded, will return to his own city in vain.
And you must remain in that city at your ease for as long as it pleases; there, the recovery of your husband Pradyumna will take place.
There, O gods, Kāma, having joined forces and slain Śambara in battle, will become happy under the name Pradyumna, [reuniting] with his own beloved.
O gods, taking his very own wealth, he shall go back to the city together with her; my word is true.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, the gods, their hearts somewhat relieved, bowed with folded hands and prostrated bodies, and spoke to him.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Lord, ocean of compassion! Quickly restore Kāma to life; O Hara, protect the life-breaths of Rati!"
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the immortals, the Supreme Lord, the ocean of compassion and sovereign of all, spoke again with a gracious mind.
Śiva said: "O gods, I am well-pleased; I shall restore him to life within this interval. That Kāma, having become one of my attendants, shall sport there eternally."
"O gods, this narrative must not be told before anyone; go to your own abodes, and I shall destroy suffering in every respect."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Rudra vanished while the gods were offering praise; all the gods became exceedingly delighted and their astonishment departed.
Then, O Sage, having comforted her and remained steadfast in the word of Rudra, they spoke those words of his and departed for their respective abodes.
O lord of sages, Kāmapatnī then went to the city as commanded, awaiting that time ordained by Rudra.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Desire," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, tell me where that flame of fire born from the eye of Hara went; relate that deed of the moon-crested Lord.
Brahmā said: When the fire from Śambhu’s third eye quickly reduced him to ashes, Kāma then blazed forth everywhere, utterly frustrated.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; O dear one, all the gods and sages quickly sought refuge in me.
All of them, agitated, bowed deeply, offered praise, joined their palms, and with downcast faces reported that suffering to me.
Having heard that, I remembered Śiva and, after reflecting thoroughly on its cause, I went there with a humble mind for the sake of protecting the three worlds.
Desirous of burning [him], he was intensely illuminated by garlands of pure flames; yet, through the power of Śambhu’s grace, he was quickly paralyzed by me with my own acquired splendor.
Then, O Sage, desiring to burn the three worlds with a fire consisting of his wrath, he [assumed] the forms of Vāḍava, Antaka, Ārṣa, and Saumyajvālāmukha.
Taking that body of Vāḍava by the will of Śiva, I, the Lord of the worlds, went to the ocean for the welfare of the world.
O Sage, seeing that I had arrived, Sāgara assumed his human form and, with palms joined in reverence, came into my presence.
Then, having prostrated before me and praised me according to the prescribed rite, he spoke with great affection to me, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Sāgara said: O Brahman, sovereign of all, for what purpose have you come here? Command me with great favor, regarding me as your own servant.
Then, having heard Sāgara’s words, I remembered Śaṅkara and, bringing worldly welfare to pass, spoke with great joy.
Brahmā said: Listen, O dear one, O highly intelligent one, you who bring welfare to all the worlds; impelled in my heart by the will of Śiva, I shall speak to you with affection, O Ocean.
This wrath of Maheśa, the great lord in the form of Vāḍava fire, having quickly burnt Kāma, then became desirous of burning everything.
Requested by the gods who were quickly oppressed, and by the will of Śaṅkara, I arrived there swiftly, O dear one, and indeed paralyzed that pure being.
O Agastya, taking on the form of a Vāḍava fire and carrying him with you, I, the compassionate one, designate you as the reservoir for the waters.
This wrathful one of Maheśa has assumed the form of Vāḍava; he, Jvālāmukha, must be supported by you until the dissolution of all beings.
When I have arrived and dwell here, O lord of rivers, then you must relinquish this wondrous wrath of Śaṅkara.
"Food and water shall be yours for this [being] eternally; you must guard him with great effort so that he does not enter another [womb]."
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by me, the Ocean then certainly consented to take up the Vāḍava fire, which was otherwise impossible for anyone else to restrain.
Then, having entered the ocean in the form of the Vāḍava fire, he, being pure and illuminated by garlands of flames, fiercely consumed the masses of its waters.
Then, O Sage, when his mind was fully satisfied, I went to my own abode; the Ocean, having assumed a divine form, bowed to me and vanished.
The entire world attained well-being, being liberated from that fear of existence; O great sage, the gods and the sages became happy.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Account of Vaḍavānala," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, dear father, O one of great wisdom, disciple of Viṣṇu, creator of the three worlds, this wondrous story of the high-souled Śaṅkara has been told.
When Smara had been reduced to ashes by the fire from Śambhu’s third eye, and he had entered the ocean—tell me, what happened after that?
O ocean of compassion, tell me now: what did the goddess Pārvatī, the daughter of the mountain, do after that? And where did she go with her two companions?
Brahmā said: Listen with respect, O dear one of great wisdom, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, my master, who is the performer of great deeds.
When the pure one born from the eye of Śambhu indeed spoke to Madana, a great and wonderful sound arose by which the sky was completely filled.
And perceiving that Kāma was indeed consumed by that great sound, she, terrified and agitated, went to her own home along with her two friends.
At that sound, Himavat, accompanied by his retinue, became astonished and deeply distressed, remembering his daughter who had departed from there.
Seeing his daughter utterly overwhelmed and weeping due to her separation from Śambhu, the lord of mountains, the sovereign of the peaks, was overcome with grief.
Having approached her, he wiped her two eyes with his hand; saying, "Do not fear, O auspicious one, do not weep," he then took hold of her.
Taking his daughter quickly onto his lap, the Lord of the Himavat mountain then led her to his own abode, consoling her as she was deeply overwhelmed.
When Hari had vanished after burning Smara, Śivā became utterly distraught due to the separation from him; indeed, she found no peace anywhere.
Then, having gone to her father’s house and met with her mother, Śivā, that daughter of the Earth, considered herself to have been born again.
She censured her own form and cried out, "Alas, I am ruined! Even though she was consoled by her friends, the daughter of the Mountain King did not regain her composure.
Whether sleeping or drinking, bathing or walking, or even standing in the midst of her friends, that auspicious lady did not find even the slightest bit of happiness.
"Fie upon my own nature, as well as my birth and my actions!"—thus she spoke constantly, ever recollecting the deeds of Hara.
Thus Pārvatī, her mind distressed by the separation from Śambhu, found no happiness at all; she cried out, "Śiva! Śiva! again and again.
Dwelling in her father’s house, her mind fixed upon the wielder of the Pināka bow, Śivā then grieved, O dear one, and fainted again and again.
Then the king of mountains, Menakā, Maināka and the other principal sons, and all [the others], being of undaunted spirit, consoled her; nevertheless, she did not forget Hara.
Then, O wise divine sage, you were directed by the slayer of Bala to come to the slopes of the Himalayas at your own will.
Then, having been honored by that high-souled mountain and seated upon an excellent throne, you indeed inquired after his welfare.
Then the Lord of the Mountain related from the beginning the maiden’s conduct, her service to Hara, and the burning of Kama by Hara.
Having heard this, O Sage, you said, "Worship that auspicious Śaileśa"; then, having taken leave of him and remembering Śiva in your mind, you stood up.
Having abandoned him in private, they hurriedly approached that Kālī; "O sage, you are a knower of truth, a benefactor of the world, and a beloved of Śiva."
Having approached Kālī and awakened her, you—being the best among all the wise and remaining devoted to her welfare—spoke these truthful words with reverence.
Nārada said: Listen, O Kālī, to my words; I speak the truth, being devoted to compassion. It is beneficial for you in every way, free from defect, and the grantor of true desires.
And Mahādeva was served by you here through austerity alone; for he, who bestows grace upon the wretched, destroyed your pride.
And that lord of yours, the great yogi Maheśvara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, having burnt Smara, has become dispassionate toward you, O Śivā.
Therefore, endowed with great austerity, you must propitiate the Lord for a long time; refined by penance, Rudra will make you his second wife.
And you too, O Goddess, shall never forsake Śaṅkara, Śambhu; by no means will you take another husband by force, except for Śiva.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of yours, O sage, that Kālī, the daughter of the mountain, breathed a little and spoke to you joyfully with her hands joined in reverence.
Śiva said: O omniscient one, O Lord who brings benefit to the worlds, O sage, grant me indeed a mantra for the purpose of propitiating Rudra.
No spiritual practice whatsoever succeeds for anyone without a true guru; I have heard this truly in the past—this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Pārvatī, the best of sages instructed her in the five-syllabled mantra of Śambhu according to the prescribed rites.
And you, O Sage, spoke these words to her, generating faith: "O Sage, the power of that King of Mantras is supreme above all."
Nārada said: Listen, O Goddess, to the most wonderful power of this mantra, by the mere hearing of which Śaṅkara becomes propitious.
This mantra is the sovereign king of all mantras and the granter of desires; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation to an extreme degree, and is exceedingly dear to Śaṅkara.
O fortunate one, by reciting this according to the prescribed rite, Śiva will surely and swiftly become manifest to you once he has been propitiated.
Meditating on that form and remaining firm in her vow for five years, she chanted the mantra; for Śiva is quickly pleased with one who is devoted to Śivā.
"Act thus, O virtuous lady; Maheśvara is to be attained through austerity. Indeed, the fruit of all things is obtained through austerity alone, and never otherwise."
Brahmā said: O Nārada, having thus spoken to Kālī at that time, you, who are dear to Śiva, departed for heaven as you pleased, intent on the welfare of the gods.
And Pārvatī, O Nārada, having then heard those words of yours, became exceedingly pleased and then obtained the supreme five-syllabled mantra.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction of Nārada," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O divine sage, when you had departed, Pārvatī, with a joyful heart, considered Hara to be attainable through penance and set her mind upon performing austerities.
Then, taking her two friends Jayā and Vijayā with her, she questioned her mother and father through those two companions.
Having first gone to her father, Himavat, the lord of mountains, she bowed deeply and, filled with humility, questioned him.
The two friends said: "O Himavat, listen; now the words of your daughter are being told, concerning herself, her body, and likewise her beauty."
For he desires to bring fulfillment to this family of yours; he is to be won over by asceticism, for he will not come into view by any other means.
Therefore, O best of mountains, grant your command now with respect, that Girijā may go to the forest and perform penance.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having been thus questioned by his two friends and by Pārvatī, the King of Mountains reflected deeply and then spoke these words.
Himālaya said: "This is highly pleasing to me; let it be made pleasing to Menā as well. Since this is how it must be, what could be more excellent than this?"
