There is no doubt that my lineage will achieve its fulfillment; if it indeed pleases my mother, what could be more auspicious than that?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words spoken by their father, those two friends then went to their mother, and at her command, they departed together with her.
O Nārada, having gone to Pārvatī’s mother and bowed deeply with joined palms, they both spoke these words with reverence.
The two friends said: "O Mother, O Goddess, listen to the words of your daughter; salutations to you! Having heard them with great favor, it behoves you to act accordingly here."
Desirous of performing supreme penance for the sake of Śiva, your daughter has obtained her father's permission and now seeks your leave as well.
O devoted wife, if she who desires to bring her own nature to fulfillment should perform penance according to your command, she shall likewise undergo that austerity.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having spoken thus, the two friends then remained silent; Menā, her mind distressed, did not accept those words.
Then Pārvatī herself, with her hands joined in reverence and her mind humble, having remembered the lotus feet of Śiva, spoke to her mother.
Pārvatī said: "O Mother, tomorrow morning I shall go to perform penance in order to attain Maheśvara; grant me permission today to depart for the penance grove."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of her daughter, Menā was overcome with grief; then, having summoned her daughter, the virtuous woman spoke to her in distress.
Menā said: "O auspicious daughter, if you were distressed in the past because you wished to perform penance, then perform penance now within the house; O Pārvatī, do not go outside."
"Where are you going to perform penance? The gods are in my home, as are all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and various holy sites (kṣetras)."
"O daughter, you must not act with impetuosity, nor go anywhere outside; what have you accomplished before, and what will you accomplish again?"
"O child, your body is delicate, whereas asceticism is great and harsh; therefore, you must perform penance here, and do not go outside."
It has never been heard that women go to the forest of asceticism seeking the fulfillment of their desires; therefore, my daughter, do not set out for the sake of penance.
Brahmā said: Thus, though her daughter was repeatedly dissuaded by her mother, she found no happiness at all without having propitiated Maheśvara.
Because she was restrained from going to the forest for asceticism by Menā, Śivā then received the name "Somā" (the Moon-like one) for that reason.
Then, O Sage, knowing that Pārvatī was distressed, Menā, the beloved of the mountain king, gave her instructions for the sake of her ascetic penance.
O best of sages, having received her mother’s command, Pārvatī, firm in her vows and mindful of Śaṅkara, then found peace within her heart.
Then Śivā, having joyfully prostrated before her mother and father, and having remembered Śiva along with her two female companions, set forth to perform austerities.
Having discarded many opinions and various garments, he quickly donned bark-cloths and fastened the beautiful girdle made of muñja grass.
Having cast aside his necklace and likewise the supreme deer-skin he wore, he went there toward the descent of the Gaṅgā to practice asceticism.
And that plateau of the Himavat, named Gaṅgāvataraṇa, is where the mind-born god of love was consumed by Śambhu while he was engaged in meditation.
Then that ridge of the snowy mountain was seen to be empty of Śiva; for, O dear one, Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, had arrived there at that time.
Having stayed for a moment at that place where, in former times, Śambhu performed difficult penance, she became afflicted by the pain of separation.
"Alas, O Hari! there the daughter of the Mountain, Pārvatī, weeping and afflicted by extreme suffering, lamented, overcome with anxiety and grief.
Then, after a long time, Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, steadying her delusion through fortitude, became initiated there for the sake of religious observance.
She performed penance there at the most excellent Śṛṅgītīrtha; indeed, because of the performance of that penance, it came to be known as Gaurīśikhara.
And there, O Sage, beautiful and sacred trees were planted by Śivā for the purpose of testing those who partake in the fruits of their penance.
Then, having purified the ground and constructed a beautiful altar, she began a penance that was difficult even for sages to perform.
Having quickly restrained all her senses with her mind, she performed supreme austerity there at Samupasthānika.
And during the summer, having placed a blazing fire all around her day and night, she remained in its midst, constantly reciting the mantra.
And during the rainy seasons, she remained constantly on the bare ground with a very steady posture, having been sprinkled upon the surface of a stone slab by a stream of water.
Devoted to her practice, she remained constantly within the water during the cold; she fasted there even amidst the frost and throughout the nights.
Thus performing penance and devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, Pārvatī meditated there upon Śiva, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Watering with joy the auspicious trees she had planted herself along with her friends, she offered hospitality there every day whenever she found the opportunity.
She endured the wind as well as cold rain of various kinds, and likewise the unbearable heat, by means of her virtuous mind.
And although various sufferings occurred there, she did not take them into account; O Sage, having fixed her mind solely on Śiva, she remained steadfast.
The Goddess spent immeasurable years performing austerities in succession: first by subsisting on fruits, and second by feeding on leaves.
Then, having cast away even the leaves, the daughter of Himavat, the goddess, abstained from food and became intent upon the practice of asceticism.
Because the daughter of Himavat had abandoned leaves as her food, the auspicious goddess was called by the name Aparṇā by the gods.
Standing on one foot and recollecting Śiva while muttering the five-syllabled mantra, Pārvatī performed great penance.
Clad in rags and bark, wearing a mass of matted locks, and intent upon the meditation of Śiva, she surpassed the sages by means of her asceticism.
Thus, as Kālī was performing penance and meditating upon Maheśvara in the forest of asceticism, three thousand years passed by.
Having stayed there for a moment—at that place where Hara had performed austerities for sixty thousand years—that auspicious goddess Śivā then reflected.
O Mahādeva, do you not know me now as one established in religious observances, because of which I have not followed after you for so long, though I am devoted to you?
In both the world and the Veda, Giriśa is always praised by the sages; for Śaṅkara is omniscient, the soul of all, and the seer of all.
The God who bestows all prosperity, who experiences all states of being, who eternally grants the desires of his devotees, and who wards off all afflictions.
If I have indeed renounced all desires and am devoted to the bull-bannered Lord, then may Śaṅkara be well-pleased with me here.
O Nārada, if the mantra consisting of five syllables spoken therein has been recited daily with great devotion according to the prescribed rite, may Śaṅkara be well-pleased.
If I am truly devoted to Śiva, the Lord of All, as described without any change of heart, may Śaṅkara be exceedingly pleased with me.
Thinking thus constantly, she performed austerities for a very long time, with her face turned downward, free from all agitation, wearing matted hair and garments of bark.
Thus she performed such penance as is difficult even for sages; and remembering this, the men there were struck with supreme wonder.
Indeed, they all assembled for the purpose of beholding that splendor; considering themselves blessed, those esteemed ones spoke as follows.
For the great, approaching those who have increased in righteousness is said to be beneficial; there is no limit to the power of austerity, and dharma must always be honored by the wise.
Having heard and seen this, what other austerity could possibly be performed? There has never been, nor will there ever be in this world, an austerity greater than this.
Speaking thus, they all highly praised the penance of Śiva and, filled with joy, departed for their own abodes—even those whose limbs had become calloused.
O great sage, now hear another [account] of the supreme and wondrous power of Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, which arises from her ascetic penance.
And those who were by nature hostile, having come to that hermitage, became free from hostility at that time through his power.
Although lions and cows were constantly possessed by defects such as passion and the like, by his majesty they did not harm one another there.
Furthermore, O best of sages, even cats, mice, and others who are by nature enemies were never at any time provoked to hostility there.
O best of sages, there were trees laden with fruit, various kinds of grasses, and diverse flowers in that place.
Then that entire forest became comparable to Kailāsa, and her asceticism then took the form of spiritual perfection.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Pārvatī’s Penance," in the third section of the second book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, while Pārvatī was thus performing penance for the sake of attaining Śiva, a long period of time passed, yet Hara did not manifest himself.
Then the Himalaya, having arrived with his wife, sons, and ministers, spoke to Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess, who was firm in her resolve.
Himālaya said: "Do not grieve, O illustrious Pārvatī, because of this austerity. Rudra is not to be seen, O child; he is detached from worldly things, of this there is no doubt."
"You, though slender and of delicate limbs, shall become deluded by asceticism; of this there is no doubt. I tell you the truth, the absolute truth."
Therefore arise and come with me to your own home, O woman of excellent complexion; what use have you for that Rudra, by whom Smara was long ago consumed?
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, since Hara will not come to take you as his bride because you are changeless, how will he ask for you?
Just as the moon situated in the sky cannot be grasped, even so, O sinless one, know that Śambhu is difficult to attain in this world.
Brahmā said: Thus was the virtuous lady addressed by Menā, and likewise by Sahyādri, as well as by Meru, Mandara, and Maināka.
In this manner, the daughter of the mountain was addressed by others as well—by Kṣitibha, Krauñca, and the rest—who were free from affliction and who employed various modes of speech.
Brahmā said: When Tanvī had been thus addressed by all while remaining established in austerity, she, possessing a pure smile, spoke to Himavat while laughing.
Pārvatī said: "O Father, O Mother, was what I previously spoke forgotten by you? Now, O kinsmen, listen once more to my vow."
I shall satisfy with my ascetic penance that Śaṅkara, who is dispassionate and by whom Smara was consumed in his wrath, for he is compassionate toward his devotees.
"May all of you, filled with great joy, go each to your own abode; he will surely be satisfied—there is no need for further deliberation on this point."
For I shall bring here that very Madana by whom [Kāma] was burnt and by whom the forest of the mountain was burnt, through the power of my asceticism alone.
Sadāśiva is indeed always well-served by the great power of austerity; know this, O highly fortunate ones, for I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.
Having thus addressed Menakā, her father Himālaya—the kinsman of Maināka—and Mandara, the daughter of the king of mountains, the eloquent Śivā quickly became silent.
Thus addressed by Śivā, those wise lords of mountains, headed by the Lord of the Golden Mountain (Himavat), departed just as they had come, repeatedly praising Girijā and filled with great wonder.
When those suns had departed, she, surrounded by her companions and firmly resolved upon the supreme goal, performed even more intense ascetic penance.
O best of sages, by that great austerity, the three worlds—including all moving and stationary beings, as well as gods, asuras, and humans—were indeed scorched.
Then all the gods and asuras, the yakṣas, kinnaras, and cāraṇas, the siddhas, sādhyas, and sages, the vidyādharas and great serpents—
The Prajāpatis, the Guhyakas, and others likewise fell into a state more miserable than the most miserable, yet they did not know the cause of it.
All of them, including Śakra and the others, having consulted with their preceptor and being overwhelmed, went to me, Brahmā, on Mount Sumeru with all their limbs scorched by heat, seeking refuge.
Having gone there and quickly prostrated themselves, agitated and with their splendor vanished, they all praised me and spoke to me in unison.
The gods said: "O Lord, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, was created by you; why indeed has its cause not been understood by you, whose mind is so distressed?"
Therefore, O Brahman, tell us the cause; you ought to let us know it, O Lord, for there is no protector other than you for the gods whose bodies have been consumed by fire.
Brahmā said: Having heard their words, I remembered Śiva in my heart and reflected in my mind upon the entire fruit of Girijā’s penance.
Realizing that the entire universe had been consumed by them, I went swiftly to the Ocean of Milk with all of them here, out of reverence, to inform Hari of this.
Having gone there and seen Hari shining upon his comfortable throne, I bowed deeply, offered excellent hymns of praise, and spoke with joined palms along with the gods.
Save us, save us, O Great Viṣṇu, we who have come to you for refuge and are tormented by the supreme and fierce asceticism of the practicing Pārvatī.
Having heard these words of us gods, headed by me, the Lord of Ramā, seated upon the serpent-couch, spoke to us.
Viṣṇu said: "I have understood the entire cause of Pārvatī’s present asceticism. Accompanied by you all, I shall go today to the Supreme Lord."
"O immortals, let us now pray to Mahādeva for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, so that he may take her hand in marriage and bring Girijā to him."
O God of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow, we shall now act in such a way that Śiva will indeed grant a boon to Śivā right there.
Therefore, we shall go to where Rudra, the great lord, dwells today, endowed with fierce austerity and supremely auspicious.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, all the gods and others, greatly terrified by him who was suddenly enraged, desirous of burning them, and intent on destruction, spoke.
The gods said: "We shall all not go to the great and radiant Virūpākṣa, who is enraged, most terrifying, and possesses a splendor like the fire of cosmic destruction."
Just as Madana, who was difficult to overcome, was formerly burnt by him, so too will he, filled with wrath, burn us; of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard those words of Śakra and the others, Hari, the Lord of Ramā, spoke to all those gods while consoling them.
Hari said: "O gods, all of you listen to my words with affection and respect; that Lord, the destroyer of the fear of the gods, will not consume you."
Therefore, O wise ones, you should go with me, considering Śambhu, the bestower of auspiciousness, as our refuge, O illustrious ones.

We go for refuge to that Śiva, the ancient Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, whose form is most excellent, the primordial and supreme, the embodiment of the Supreme Self for those engaged in austerity, who is higher than the highest.
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by the powerful Viṣṇu, all the gods then went with him, desiring to see the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then Viṣṇu and all the others, filled with curiosity, went to that hermitage by the force of their path in order to first behold the asceticism of Śailaputrī.
Then, beholding the asceticism of Pārvatī, they were pervaded by her splendor; they bowed down to that sustainer of the world, who was the very embodiment of light and established in penance.
Praising her penance, which was the direct source of their own perfection, the gods then went to the place where the bull-bannered Lord resided.
Having gone there, O Sage, those gods then sent you forth; they stood at a distance while watching you from afar, as you were reduced to ashes by Hara through his power over desire.
O Nārada, having then gone to the abode of Śiva, you, who were always fearless and especially devoted to Śiva, beheld the Lord with a gracious countenance.
Having returned there, O sage, he then diligently summoned the gods, including Viṣṇu and the others, and led them to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Then Viṣṇu and all the others, having gone there, beheld the Lord Śiva seated at ease, gracious and affectionate toward his devotees.
Śambhu was seated upon his yogic belt, surrounded by his attendants; he bore the form of asceticism and possessed the nature of the Supreme Lord.
Then Viṣṇu, myself, and other gods, Siddhas, and lords of sages, having prostrated, praised him with hymns (sūktas) accompanied by the Vedas and Upaniṣads.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Consolation of Pārvatī and the Vision of Śiva and the Devas," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third [section], the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The gods said: "Salutations to the god Rudra, the ender of Madana; salutations again and again to the one worthy of praise, the one of manifold splendor, the three-eyed one."
Salutations again and again to Śipiviṣṭa, the terrible one with terrifying eyes; salutations to Mahādeva, the sovereign lord and master of the triple heaven.
You are the protector of all worlds, the father, the mother, and the Lord; you are Śambhu, the Sovereign, and Śaṅkara, and you are especially compassionate.
O Lord, you are the sustainer of the entire world; you ought to protect us. O Maheśvara, who else besides you is capable of destroying our suffering?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the gods, Nandikeśvara, filled with supreme compassion, began to petition Śambhu.

Nandikeśvara said: O best of gods, Viṣṇu and the other hosts of deities, along with the assemblies of sages and Siddhas, are especially eager to behold you. Having been threatened by the foremost of Asuras and seeking a remedy for their plight, they have fallen into a state of utter defeat.
Therefore, O Lord of All, you must indeed protect the sages and the gods; for you have been described as the kinsman of the distressed and especially as one who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Brahmā said: Thus earnestly entreated by the compassionate Nandin, Śambhu gradually ceased his meditation and opened his eyes.
Then the Lord Śambhu, the supreme knower and the Supreme Self, having ceased from his meditative absorption, spoke to all the gods.
Śambhu said: "O lords of the gods, why have you all—Hari, Brahmā, and the rest—come into my presence? Tell me that reason quickly."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, all the gods, filled with joy, looked toward the face of Viṣṇu for the purpose of making their request.
Then Viṣṇu, the great devotee who acts for the welfare of the gods, spoke these words concerning this most important task of the deities as prompted by me.
"O Śambhu, Tāraka has wrought a most extraordinary calamity for the gods; all the deities have come together to report a distress more grievous than any other."
O Śambhu, the Daitya Tāraka will indeed be slain by your own legitimate son; my word shall not be otherwise.
Having reflected thus, O Mahādeva, show mercy; salutations be unto you! O Lord, deliver the gods from the distress caused by Tāraka.

Therefore, O Lord Śambhu, you must take Girijā with your right hand; by that very act of taking her hand, accept her who has been given by the Lord of Mountains, she who is possessed of great majesty.
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Śiva, who is devoted to yoga, being pleased, spoke while showing the true goal to all of them.
Śiva said: When the goddess Girijā, the most beautiful of all, was accepted by me, at that time all the lords of the gods, as well as the sages and seers, [were present].
They shall have their desires fulfilled, yet they will not be able to endure the path of others; that Durgā shall bring Smara back to life from the moment of his grasping her hand.
"O Viṣṇu, Madana was indeed burnt by me for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all, according to the word of Brahmā; no hesitation should be felt in this matter."
Having thus reflected with the mind regarding the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, O Lord of the Gods, you, being wise, should not act with obstinacy against all of us.
"O Viṣṇu, since Kāma has been consumed by me, the great task of the gods has been accomplished. Let all remain free from desire with me; this is my firm resolve."
"Just as I and all the gods [have done], so shall you, without effort and fully engaged in supreme austerity, perform what is exceedingly difficult to do."
O gods, by means of that meditative absorption, may you indeed become free from passion, endowed with supreme bliss, and truly devoid of all change.
O Creator Hari, you have forgotten that past event wrought by Smara; let Mahendra, the sages, and the gods reflect upon all of that.
In ancient times, O Purā, the great archer Madana forcibly brought about the destruction of the meditative concentration of all the gods.
For desire leads indeed to hell, and from it anger is born; from anger arises delusion, and from delusion one falls away from austerity.
Lust and anger must be abandoned by you, O best of gods; and all of you must consider my words as such, never otherwise.
Brahmā said: Having thus proclaimed this, the Blessed Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, caused the gods, as well as Vidhi, Viṣṇu, and the sages, to recite it.
Śambhu became silent once again, resorting to meditation; he sat like the ancient Sthāṇu, surrounded by his attendants.
Śambhu, by means of his own self, meditated upon his very self within himself—stainless, without appearance, changeless, and free from affliction.
Higher than the highest, eternal, free from "mine-ness," unrestrained, beyond sound, devoid of qualities, attainable through knowledge, and supreme beyond the supreme.
Thus contemplating that supreme essential nature and established in meditation, the author of many births became immersed in supreme bliss.
And seeing the Lord of All established in meditation, all the inhabitants of heaven—Hari, Śakra, and all the others—bowed down and spoke to Nandin.

The gods said: "What shall we do now? Śambhu, the source of all happiness, has become detached and is established in meditation. You are his friend, O Śaṅkara, the omniscient one who serves him with purity."
O Lord of the Gaṇas, by what means may Giriśa become gracious? Explain that means to us; we have come to you for refuge.
Brahmā said: O Sage, having been thus petitioned by the gods headed by Hara and others, Nandin, the attendant dear to Śambhu, replied to those deities.
Nandīśvara said: O Hara, O Vidhi, O Śakra, O gods, and likewise O sages, listen indeed to my words which bring about the satisfaction of Śiva.
If you are indeed determined today to take Śiva as a husband, then all of you, out of extreme humility, offer him praise with devotion.
Mahādeva is subject to devotion, not to ordinary means; even that which ought not to be done, the Supreme Lord performs through the power of true devotion.
"O all you gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, act in this manner; depart without delay by the same path by which you came."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, O Sage, Viṣṇu and the other gods, thinking "So be it," praised Śaṅkara with great joy.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord who is an ocean of compassion! Lift us up from this great suffering; protect us, for we have come to you for refuge.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Śaṅkara with many words of entreaty, all the gods wept with melodious voices, their minds overwhelmed with love.
Remembering Śambhu in his mind and endowed with supreme devotion, Hari acted upon my very piteous petition.
Brahmā said: Thus praised intensely by the gods, by Hari, and by me, Śambhu, the Great Lord Maheśvara, ceased from his meditation out of affection for his devotees.
Beholding them with a compassionate gaze, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke with a deeply serene soul, gladdening Harya and the others.
Śaṅkara said: O Hara, O Vidhi, and you gods headed by Śakra, why have you all come together at once? Speak the truth before me.
Hari said: "O Maheśāna, you are omniscient; you are the inner controller and the Lord of all. Do you not know what resides in my heart? Nevertheless, I shall speak even at your command."
O Mṛḍa, manifold suffering has arisen for us all from the demon Tāraka; indeed, for that reason, the gods have propitiated you.
That auspicious lady was indeed born from Himālaya, the mountain, for your sake; because of a son born to her from you, his death shall come, and not otherwise.
Since this boon was granted by Brahmā to that Daitya, he, being subject to no death from anyone else, oppresses the entire world.
At Nārada’s instruction, she performed severe penance; by its splendor, the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were pervaded.
O Supreme Lord, go indeed to grant a boon to Śivā; O Master, dispel the suffering of the gods and bring us happiness.
"O Śaṅkara, there is a great enthusiasm in my heart to witness your marriage; therefore, do what is appropriate."
O Supreme among the supreme, the very moment has now arrived for that boon which was granted to Rati by you; quickly make your own wager fruitful.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and bowed to him, Viṣṇu, the gods, and all the great sages stood before him, praising him with various hymns.
Even Śaṅkara, who is dependent upon his devotees and the protector of the boundaries of the Vedas, having heard those words of the gods at that time, laughed and quickly replied.
Śaṅkara said: O Hari, O Vidhi, and all you gods, listen with respect; I shall speak as is appropriate, with distinction and discernment.
Indeed, it is not proper for men to perform marriage rites; for marriage is known as a great shackle, a firm bondage.

In this world, there are many harmful associations, and among them, association with women is the most excessive; one may be liberated from all other bonds, but one is not released from the bond of association with women.
Even one firmly bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released; but one who is tightly bound by the fetters of women and the like is never released.
Sense objects, which cause great bondage, increase incessantly; for one whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects, even liberation is difficult to attain, even in a dream.
If the wise man desires happiness, he should abandon sense objects according to the prescribed rule; for they declare that sense objects are like poison, by which one is destroyed.
A person falls from their state in an instant through conversation with a sensualist; the teachers describe "sensual object" (viṣaya) as white sugar-cane and indravāruṇī liquor.
Although I indeed know all this knowledge in its particular details, nevertheless, I shall make your prayer bear fruit.
I am indeed dependent upon my devotees; under their influence, I perform all actions. For it is well known throughout the three worlds that I act in ways that are not consistent with my own nature.
Indeed, the wager was made fruitful by the lord of Kāmarūpa for King Sudakṣiṇa, who had fallen into the power of Nala.
I am the creator of affliction for Gautama, yet I am the self of Tryambaka who brings happiness; I am especially the bestower of curses upon those wicked ones who inflict suffering.
O gods, out of my nature of being affectionate toward my devotees, I have always diligently removed the distress of the deities whenever poison was drunk for the sake of liquor.
For the sake of my devotee, having become a householder, I endured much hardship with great effort on many occasions and removed the suffering of the sage Viśvānara.
O Hari, O Brahmā, what is the use of speaking at length? I tell you the truth: you all know it truly that I have a wager.
Whenever and wherever misfortune befalls my devotees, at that very moment and in every way, I always remove it instantly.
I know the suffering arising from Tāraka that has arisen for all of you; I shall destroy it from the Asura. I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Although I have no desire whatsoever for building a residence, I shall marry the daughter of the Mountain for the sake of producing a son.
"Go to your own homes, O all you gods, free from fear; I shall accomplish your task—there is no need for hesitation in this matter."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Hara became silent and entered a state of meditative absorption (samādhi). O Sage, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, returned to their own abodes.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Acceptance of Pārvatī’s Marriage," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, the third section of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: After those gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as all the sages, had departed with affection, what happened thereafter?
O father, what has been done? Why has Śambhu come to grant a boon? Tell me how and after how much time; speak so as to bring me joy.
Brahmā said: When those gods, headed by Brahmā, had departed for their own hermitages, Bhava, remaining in meditative absorption, became intent upon testing their ascetic penances.
Having made his own self into the Self by means of the Self, he meditated within his very self upon that which is higher than the highest, established in itself, and free from all constraints.
The Blessed One, the Lord whose banner is the bull, is the reality that has become that very thing; he is the charioteer whose course is unknown, Hara, the Supreme Lord.
Brahmā said: O dear one, Girijā then performed supreme austerity; by that austerity, even Rudra was struck with great wonder.
Though dependent upon his devotees, he did not otherwise waver from his meditative absorption; rather, Hari, the creator, called to mind the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others.
All seven sages, their faces serene, arrived quickly by mere thought; they all praised the ritual procedure extensively.
Having prostrated before that Great Lord, they, filled with intense joy, praised him with faltering voices, their hands joined and their necks bowed low.
The Seven Sages said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord, ocean of compassion! We have indeed become most fortunate, since we have now been remembered by you."
For what purpose have we been remembered? Grant us that instruction, O Lord; show mercy to us who are like your own slaves; salutations be unto you!
Brahmā said: Having heard this petition of the gods, the ocean of compassion spoke with affection, smiling as his lotus-eyes blossomed wide.
Maheśvara said: O seven sages, my dear ones, listen to my words with attention; you are well-versed in all branches of knowledge and act for our benefit.
Now Pārvatī, the daughter of the mountain and mistress of the gods, performs austerities with a firm mind upon the mountain known as Gaurīśikhara.
O twice-born ones, desiring to obtain me as her husband, that woman, attended by her friends, abandoned all other desires and reached a firm resolve.
Go there, O best of sages, by my command; with hearts full of love, perform a test of his steadfastness.
O you of excellent vows, by my command there must be no doubt that your speech shall always be uttered with deceptive intent; this is what must be said by you.
Brahmā said: Thus commanded, those sages went swiftly to that place where the radiant daughter of the mountain, the Mother of the World, was shining.
There she saw Śivā herself, like another perfection of asceticism incarnate, possessing supreme splendor and shining with great luster.
Having bowed to her with their hearts, those seven sages of excellent vows, being especially honored, spoke these words while remaining humble.
The sages said: "Listen, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain! For what purpose do you perform this penance? Which god do you desire, and what is the fruit [you seek]? Tell us that now."
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by the twice-born, the goddess Śivā, daughter of the Lord of Mountains, replied with these truthful words, though they were profoundly secret, in their presence.
Pārvatī said: O lords of sages, listen with affectionate hearts to my words; I shall indeed express my own reflection, which has been pondered by my own intellect.
O Brahmins, you will surely laugh upon hearing my impossible words; there is indeed a contraction [of meaning] from description—what can I do?
For this mind is indeed very firm, yet it acts independently and performs tasks beyond its capacity; it desires to build a massive, towering wall upon the surface of the water.
"Having received the command of the celestial sage, I shall perform very firm penance, making it my heart's desire that Rudra indeed become my husband."
My mind, a bird without wings, flies forcefully into the sky; may Lord Śaṅkara, the ocean of compassion, fulfill that hope.
Brahmā said: Having heard her words, those sages laughed and, honoring Girijā with affection, spoke these deceptive and false words.
The sages said: "O daughter of the Earth, although we are wise, we did not know the conduct of that cruel-minded celestial sage who vainly prided himself on his learning."
Nārada is a speaker of falsehoods and a disturber of the minds of others; by listening to his news, ruin occurs in every way.
In this regard, listen with a virtuous mind to this most beautiful historical narrative; for as it gradually awakens you, grasp it with affection.
For Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, having begotten ten thousand beloved sons by his wife at his father’s command, engaged them in ascetic penance.
Those sons went to Lake Nārāyaṇa in the western direction; having made a vow for the sake of penance, Nārada indeed went there.
Having proclaimed that deceptive instruction there, the sage Nārada, by his command, caused them all not to go to their father's house.
Having heard that, Dakṣa became enraged; though his mind was consoled by his father, he then procreated sons numbering a thousand and dispatched them.
Those sons also went there for the sake of penance by their father’s command; Nārada too went there once more to give him further instruction.
He gave them that instruction, and they followed the path of their brothers; they did not return to their father’s house, being devoted to the life of mendicants.
Thus, O Daughter of the Mountain, the virtuous conduct of Nārada is renowned; now hear of another such conduct that produces dispassion in men.
The Vidyādhara Citraketu, who existed in former times, gave him instruction consisting of his own teachings and left that house empty for him.
Having given his own instructions to Prahlāda and having caused supreme suffering to Hiraṇyakaśipu, he, the shatterer of the intellects of others, departed.
Having heard that wisdom of the Sage which delights the ear, he generally abandons his own home and wanders for alms.
Indeed, Nārada, who was previously foul-souled, now possesses a body that shines at all times; we, his former companions, recognize him especially well.
They praise the crane as virtuous, yet he eats fish in every way; one who lives together with others should know the conduct of those with whom one dwells.
Having indeed received that instruction, you too, though esteemed by the wise, have become a fool in vain and are performing difficult penance.
O young girl, for whose sake you perform such extensive penance—he is undoubtedly the enemy of Madana, eternally indifferent and free from all change.
Bearing an inauspicious body, shameless, homeless, and of low birth, dressed poorly and associating with ghosts, spirits, and the like, the wielder of the trident is indeed naked.
That rogue, having destroyed your discernment through his own illusion, deluded you with a clever ruse and indeed caused you to perform penance.
O Goddess of gods, O daughter of the Mountain, reflect upon this yourself: having obtained such a boon, what happiness will there be?
Having first married the virtuous Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, that fool did not provide for her maintenance at all for several days, despite being possessed of intelligence.
Having thus assigned that very fault to her, the Lord himself abandoned her; meditating upon his own stainless nature, free from sorrow, he rejoiced in bliss.
For he is solitary, extinguished in the supreme state, unattached, and indeed non-dual; therefore, O Goddess, how can the sustenance of noble women be possible through him?
Even now, having received our instruction, come home and abandon your evil intent; O highly fortunate one, it will lead to your own welfare.
For Viṣṇu, the Lord who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, the husband of Lakṣmī, and the master of various divine sports, is indeed the bridegroom worthy of you, possessing all excellent qualities.
"Therefore, we shall arrange for you a marriage that bestows all happiness; abandon such obstinacy as this, O Pārvatī, and be happy."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, smiled and spoke again to the sages who were experts in knowledge.
Pārvatī said: "O lords of sages, O twice-born ones, what you have spoken according to your own knowledge is true; nevertheless, my stubbornness indeed cannot be relinquished."
"Since your own body is born of stone, hardness is its innate and inherent state. Having reflected thus with a discerning mind, you ought not to forbid me."
"I shall never abandon the beneficial words of the celestial sage; those who know the Vedas understand that the speech of gurus is indeed beneficial."
For those whose firm conviction is that the word of the gurus is truth, there is supreme happiness here and hereafter, and never anywhere any unhappiness.
If one does not hold in one's heart the conviction that "the word of the gurus is true," then for such a person there will be suffering, never happiness, both in this world and the next.
O twice-born ones, the word of the gurus must never be disregarded; whether one dwells at home or in a desolate place, my stubborn persistence always grants happiness.
O best of sages, that which has been well-spoken by you, I shall describe its distinction in another way, briefly.
Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the abode of qualities (guṇa) and a dweller [in the world], whereas Sadāśiva is said to be devoid of qualities (aguṇa); the reason for this is now stated.
Śiva is Brahman, the unchanging; he assumes a form for the sake of his devotees, yet he does not wish to display worldly sovereignty.
Therefore, this most beloved state was maintained by Śambhu, who is supreme bliss, in the form of an Avadhūta for the sake of the Paramahaṃsas.

The desire for ornaments and the like belongs to those smeared by illusion, but not to Brahman; that Lord is devoid of qualities, unborn, free from illusion, whose course is unperceivable, and all-pervading.
O twice-born ones, Śambhu does not bestow grace through the birth or other qualities of the Dharma; it is only through the grace of the Guru that I know Śiva in his true essence.
O Brahmins, if Śiva does not perform my marriage, I shall remain forever unmarried; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.

If the sun should rise in the western quarter, if Mount Meru should move, if fire should attain coldness, or if a lotus should bloom upon a rock on a mountain peak—nevertheless, my resolve shall not waver; I tell you this as the truth.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and quickly bowed to those sages, that daughter of the mountain ceased speaking, remembering Śiva with an unwavering mind.
The sages, having thus understood the firm resolve of the Daughter of the Mountain, uttered words of victory there and bestowed their most excellent blessings.
Then, O Sage, having bowed to that Goddess with delighted minds, those sages who had performed her test departed swiftly for the abode of Śiva.
Having gone there and bowed to Śiva, they reported that event to him; then, having obtained his permission, they returned to the heavenly world with respect.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Test Conducted by the Seven Sages," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: When those sages had departed for their own world, Śaṅkara himself, the Lord who brings forth progeny, desired to test the penance of the Goddess.
Śambhu, his mind delighted, went to Pārvatī’s grove in order to test her under a disguise, assuming the form of a matted-haired ascetic.
Extremely aged and bearing the body of a brahmin, blazing with his own splendor and joyful in mind, he appeared carrying a staff and an umbrella.
There he saw the goddess standing, surrounded by her female companions upon the altar, as pure as a digit of the moon.
Beholding that goddess, Śambhu, assuming the form of a celibate student, then approached her with affection, for he is ever-kind to his devotees.
Seeing that Brahmin, wonderful in his splendor, as he had arrived, the goddess Śivā honored him with all kinds of offerings for worship.
Having been well-honored with various offerings and worshipped with supreme joy, Pārvatī affectionately and respectfully inquired after the welfare of the brahmin.
Pārvatī said: "In the form of a celibate student (brahmacārī), who indeed are you and from where have you come? You illuminate this forest; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas."
The Brahmin said: "I am one who moves according to my will, an aged man with a wise Brahmin body; I am an ascetic who bestows happiness upon others and is a benefactor, without a doubt."
Who are you, whose daughter are you, and for what purpose do you perform this difficult penance in this lonely forest—a penance that is hard even for sages to attain?
"You are neither a child nor an old woman; you appear beautiful and young. Why, then, do you perform such severe penance in the forest without a husband?"
"O auspicious lady, why are you, an ascetic woman, the companion of someone? O goddess, that ascetic does not support you and has gone elsewhere."
Tell me, in whose family were you born? Who is your father, and what is your lineage? You possess great beauty and fortune; why then do you delight in asceticism in vain?
Are you Lakṣmī, born from the Vedas? Or are you the beautiful Sarasvatī? Among these [goddesses], who indeed are you? I do not venture to speculate.
Pārvatī said: "O Brahmin, I am not the source of the Vedas, nor am I Lakṣmī or Sarasvatī; I am the daughter of Himācala, currently known by the name Pārvatī."
Formerly, in another birth, I was born as the daughter of Dakṣa named Satī; because my husband was censured by my father, I abandoned my body through yoga.
In this very birth, even Śiva, by the power of fate, having reduced Manmatha to ashes, departed from me.

O Brahmin, when Śaṅkara had departed, I, terrified by the heat [of worldly existence], came from my father’s house and arrived with firm resolve at the bank of the celestial river to perform austerities.

Having performed severe austerities for a very long time, you were about to enter the fire when, failing to find your beloved who was dearer than life itself, you stood still for a moment upon seeing me.
"Go; I shall enter the fire, for I have not been accepted by Śiva. In whatever birth I may obtain a new life, I shall choose Śiva as my husband."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Pārvatī entered the fire in his presence, even though she was being repeatedly forbidden by the Brāhmaṇa standing before her.
As Pārvatī was about to enter the fire, by its power, the fire itself instantly became like sandalwood paste at that very moment.
Having stayed within her for a moment and then leaping up toward heaven, the twice-born Śiva suddenly laughed and questioned the slender-limbed woman once more.
The twice-born one said: "O blessed lady, alas for your penance! Indeed, nothing at all has been understood; your body was not consumed by fire, nor was your desire attained."
Therefore, O Goddess, speak truly and according to your desire regarding your heart's wish in my presence, before this most excellent of brahmins who bestows all joy.
O Goddess, you must relate everything according to the rules and with your whole being; therefore, friendship has arisen between us, and this matter must certainly not be concealed by you.
"O Goddess, what boon do you desire? Beyond this, I wish to ask you something; for it is in you alone, O Goddess, that the fruit of all this is seen."
If one indeed remains in austerity for the sake of another, that is merely austerity; it is like taking a jewel in one's hand and discarding it to collect glass.
How have you rendered such beauty of yours useless? Having discarded many garments, you have donned skins and the like.
Tell me truly the cause of all this austerity, so that upon hearing it, I, the best of brahmins, may attain joy.
Brahmā said: Thus questioned then by him who was urging his companion, Ambikā, firm in her vows, related all of that through her friend's mouth.
And impelled by her, Pārvatī’s beloved friend named Vijayā—a knower of vows who was dearer to her than life—spoke to Jaṭila.
The friend said: "Listen, O virtuous one, I shall relate the supreme life-story of Pārvatī and the entire reason for her penance, if you wish to hear it."
This daughter of the king of mountains, the snowy Himalaya, is my friend; she is renowned by the name Pārvatī, and is also known as Kālī and Menakā.
She has been married by no one, nor does she desire anyone other than Śiva; for three thousand years, she has been engaged in the practice of ascetic penance.
For that purpose, this friend of mine has undertaken such penance; O virtuous one, best of the twice-born, listen as I explain the reason for this.
Having slain the gods headed by Indra, as well as Hari and Brahmā, Pārvatī desires to obtain as her husband the wielder of the Pināka bow.
O twice-born one, this friend of mine indeed planted trees in the past; on all of them, fruits, flowers, and the like have grown.
For the sake of the caravan of forms, as an ornament for the family of progenitors, with Maheśāna in mind, and for the favoring of Kāma.
"O ascetic, my friend is performing severe penance at the instruction of Nārada; how could her heart's desire not bear fruit?"
O best of the twice-born, that which was asked by my friend—the desire in her heart—has been told by me out of affection; what else do you wish to hear?
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard these words of Vijayā exactly as they were, that matted-haired Rudra smiled and spoke these words.
The matted-hair ascetic said: "O friend, what has been told here is inferred to be a jest; if it be the truth, then let the Goddess speak for herself."
Brahmā said: When that twice-born man with matted hair had spoken thus, the goddess Pārvatī addressed that brahmin with her own mouth.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and the Matted-Haired One," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Pārvatī said: Listen, O best of the twice-born, O matted-haired one, to my entire account; that which was spoken by my friend today is indeed the truth, exactly so and not otherwise.
In thought, in word, and directly through action, with the devotion of a husband—I speak the truth and not untruth—that Śaṅkara has indeed been chosen by me.
I know that this rare object is difficult for me to obtain; nevertheless, my mind is so filled with longing that I am now performing penance.
Brahmā said: Having spoken these words to him, the Daughter of the Mountain then remained silent; hearing Pārvatī’s speech, the Brāhmaṇa there spoke.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "Until this time, I have indeed had a great desire: 'What object does the Goddess long for that she performs such immense penance?'"
Having understood all that, O Goddess, and having heard it from your lotus-like mouth, I shall depart from this place; do as you wish.
If you do not speak to me, our friendship would be fruitless; therefore, whatever must be done should be told to me easily and as it truly is.
Brahmā said: Having spoken these words to him, just as he desired to depart, the goddess Pārvatī bowed and addressed that twice-born man.
Pārvatī said: "O best of Brahmins, where will you go? Stay and speak what is for our benefit. When she had spoken thus, he who held the staff stood there and replied:
The twice-born said: "O Goddess, if you wish to hear and establish me with devotion, I shall tell you all that truth by which your wisdom may arise."
I know Mahādeva in every way according to the nature of the Guru; I shall speak the truth indeed, so listen with attentiveness.
The great god Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, is smeared with ashes, wears matted hair, is clothed in a tiger skin, and is wrapped in an elephant hide.
Bearing a skull, his entire body entwined by a multitude of serpents, smeared with poison, a consumer of forbidden food, he was three-eyed and terrifying.
His birth is unmanifest, he is eternally devoid of domestic enjoyments, naked, ten-armed, and always accompanied by spirits and ghosts.
For what reason do you desire that husband? O Goddess, where has your wisdom gone? Speak now, reflecting upon this.
Previously, I heard of the terrifying vow of that [being]; listen as I recount it to you today, if you have a desire to hear it.
In ancient times, the virtuous Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, chose the bull-vehicled Lord as her husband; however, due to destiny, their union was interrupted.
Satī was abandoned by Dakṣa at the sacrifice because she was the daughter of Kapālī; likewise, Śambhu was excluded from the distribution of sacrificial portions.
Thus, being intensely agitated by anger due to that very insult, she abandoned her dear lives there; and by her, Śaṅkara was likewise abandoned.
You are a jewel among women, and your father is the king of all monarchs; why then do you seek such a husband through such severe asceticism?
Having given away gold coins, you wish to take up glass; having abandoned pure sandalwood, you wish to smear yourself with mud.
Abandoning the splendor of the sun, you desire the light of a firefly; casting aside fine Chinese silk, you desire a garment of skin in this world.
Having abandoned living at home, you desire to dwell in the forest; O Lord of Gods, you wish for iron after having discarded a supreme treasure.
Having abandoned the world-protectors such as Indra and taken a vow following Śiva, this is indeed not seen now as something contradictory in the worlds.
Where are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, and where indeed is that three-eyed one? You have the face of the moon, while Śiva is remembered as five-faced.
This divine braid upon your head shines like a serpent; it is renowned as being like the famous mass of matted locks of Śiva.
Sandalwood paste upon your body and the ashes of Śiva’s funeral pyre—where is your silken garment, and where is Śiva’s elephant hide?
Where are the divine ornaments and where are the serpents of Śaṅkara? Where are all the mobile deities, and where is he who is fond of offerings to the spirits?
Where is the sounding of the mṛdaṅga drum, and where is the ḍamaru? Where is the ensemble of kettledrums, and where is this inauspicious sound of horns?
Where is the sound of a drum, and where is this inauspicious noise of gargling? This supreme form of yours is not at all fitting for Śiva.
If he were a substantial entity, how could he be naked? He has no vehicle, nor does he possess even the slightest equipment such as a bullock.
Among those qualities said to bring happiness to women when sought in a bridegroom, not even a single one is found in Virūpākṣa.
Your beloved Kāma was also burnt by that Hara; then, showing disregard for you, he abandoned you and went elsewhere.
Neither his birth nor his knowledge of the sciences is seen; his companions are indeed Piśācas, and poison is visible in his throat.
Since you are always alone and especially free from passion, O Hari, you ought not to engage your mind in this way.
Where is your necklace, and where is that garland of skulls? Where is your divine body-unguent, and where is the ashes of the funeral pyre upon her body?
"O Goddess, everything—form and the rest—is contrary to both you and Hara; indeed, this does not please me, so do as you wish."
Whatever non-existent thing there may be, you yourself strive for it all; therefore, withdraw your mind from that, or if you do not wish to, then do so.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of that brāhmaṇa, Pārvatī, with an enraged mind, spoke to the twice-born who was intent on censuring Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Deceptive Words of the Religious Student," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Pārvatī said: "I had understood only this much—that someone else had arrived; now everything is known, especially that you are incapable of being slain."
"O Lord, what has been spoken by you is known; it is not false, nor otherwise. For if that which was uttered by you were indeed contradictory, it would not have been spoken by you."
Sometimes Maheśvara is seen wearing such a disguise; by his own divine play, the Supreme Brahman assumes a physical form out of his own will.
Intent on deceiving me in the guise of a religious student (brahmacārin), you have come and spoken with deceitful words based on fallacious reasoning.
I know the true nature of Śaṅkara with great particularity; therefore, having reflected well, I shall speak of the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva) as it truly is.

In reality, Brahman is devoid of qualities; it becomes possessed of qualities through its causal state. How could there be a genus for that which is qualityless yet whose nature consists of qualities?
For Sadāśiva is the foundation of all sciences; what need has that perfect Supreme Self for any science?
In ancient times, the Vedas were given to Viṣṇu by Śambhu in the form of his breath; who is there a supreme lord equal to him at the beginning of the kalpa?
Since he is the primordial source of all things, how could there be a measurement of time for him? From him, however, Prakṛti was born; what then could be the cause of his power?
And to those who always worship that Śaktīśa Śaṅkara with devotion, Śambhu grants that eternal triad of powers.
By worshipping that very [deity], the living being conquers death and becomes fearless; therefore, it is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name "Mṛtyuñjaya" (Conqueror of Death).
By partiality toward him alone, Viṣṇu attains the state of Viṣṇu, Brahmā attains the state of Brahmā, and the gods likewise attain their status as gods.
Just as the king of the gods first goes for the purpose of beholding Śiva, so too do the bhūtas and others, who are devoted to him, serve as the gatekeepers of Śiva.
Even if his crown is pierced by staffs, it becomes polished on all sides; what need has he for many allies, for he is himself a great lord?
What could not be attained here by serving him who possesses such auspicious form? What is lacking for that god, since Sadāśiva desires me?
One would remain poor for seven births unless one serves Śaṅkara; by serving him, however, Fortune shall become an unfailing companion to that person.
Since the eight Siddhis always dance there to please Him with their faces turned downwards, how could that which is for His benefit ever be difficult to obtain?
Even if one does not practice auspicious rites here for Śaṅkara, nevertheless, auspiciousness arises for that person through mere remembrance of him.
Since all desires are fulfilled in every way through the power of his worship, how could there be any transformation in him who is eternally changeless?
Those whose mouth constantly utters the auspicious name "Śiva"—by the mere sight of such a person, others always become purified.
If, as you have stated, the ash from the funeral pyre were impure, how could it be constantly worn upon their bodies by the gods with their heads bowed?
How can that deity—who is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the worlds, endowed with qualities, yet also known as Śiva who is beyond qualities—be understood?
The nature of Brahman, the supreme self Śiva, is devoid of attributes; how indeed can those like you, who are turned away from that reality, understand it?
Those who are of evil conduct and sinful have emerged from among the gods; they do not know the true nature of Śiva, whose form is beyond all attributes.
That man who, in this world, reviles Śiva without knowing the truth, his merit accumulated since birth is reduced to ashes.
Because you have here uttered censure against Hara of immeasurable splendor, and because you have performed worship for me, I shall therefore partake of your sin.
Upon seeing one who hates Śiva, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on; upon seeing one who hates Śiva, one should perform an expiation.
"O wicked one, you have said, 'I know Śaṅkara'; yet in truth, the eternal Śiva himself has not been recognized by you."
In whatever way Rudra may exist, or however many forms he may possess, he is eternally my most beloved—changeless and dear to the virtuous.
Neither Viṣṇu nor even Brahmā is equal anywhere to that Great Soul; how much less others such as the gods, who are eternally subject to Time?
Having thus reflected with my own intellect according to the true reality of things, I have come to this forest for the sake of Śiva and am performing extensive penance.
He alone is the Supreme Lord, the Ruler of all, who is affectionate toward his devotees; indeed, my desire is to attain him, the one who bestows grace upon the wretched.
Brahmā said: O Sage, having spoken thus, that daughter of the Lord of Mountains, Girijā, ceased speaking and meditated upon Śiva with an unwavering mind.
Having heard those words of the goddess, that twice-born student of sacred knowledge was just beginning to utter a reply when—
Then Girijā, whose mental disposition was attached to Śiva and who was averse to any censure of Śiva, quickly spoke to her friend Vijayā.
Girijā said: "O friend, this lowest of the twice-born must be restrained with great effort; for he intends to speak again and will surely engage in the censure of Śiva."
Indeed, sin shall accrue not only to the one who utters the censure of Śiva, but whoever hears that censure shall also become a partaker of sin in this world.
One who reviles Śiva must be executed in every way by the servants of Śiva; if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he should indeed be abandoned, and one must depart from that place immediately.
"This wicked man will surely revile Śiva again; yet, because he is a Brāhmaṇa, he must not be killed—he should be abandoned and avoided in every way."
Leaving this place this very day, let us go elsewhere without delay, so that there may be no further conversation with this ignorant man.
Brahmā said: O sage, as soon as Umā had spoken thus and lifted her foot, Śiva himself was directly supported by his beloved.
Having assumed a beautiful form and meditated upon Śiva in whatever manner was appropriate, Śiva showed it to Pārvatī and spoke to her as she stood with her face cast down.
Śiva said: "Where will you go, leaving me? You must not be abandoned by me again. I am pleased; choose a boon, for there is nothing that should not be granted to you."
From this day forward, I am your slave, purchased by your ascetic penances; I have been bought by your beauty, for whom even a single moment is as a yuga.
"O Girijā, O Maheśvarī, let this shame be abandoned by you; for you are my eternal wife—consider this with your wise intellect."
O firm-minded one, you have been tested by me in many ways; therefore, forgive this offense of mine, who am merely following the ways of worldly play.
But I do not see anyone like you, my beloved, in the three worlds; I am entirely at your disposal, O Śivā—let your desire be fulfilled.
"Come, my beloved, to my side; you are my wife and I am your husband. Together with you, I shall go quickly to my own home, the best of mountains."
Brahmā said: When this was spoken by the God of gods, Pārvatī attained great joy and cast off that ancient suffering born of her ascetic penance.
O best of sages, let all that effort of yours be lost; once the fruit has arisen, the prior labor of a living being should come to naught.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Pārvatī’s Vision of Śiva’s Form," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmā, O Creator, O highly fortunate one, what occurred after that? I wish to hear all of that; tell me, you who possess the glory of Śiva.
Brahmā said: O divine sage, listen attentively; with joy I shall relate the story that destroys great sins and increases devotion to Śiva.
O twice-born one, having heard the words of Hara, the Supreme Soul, and beholding his form which brings joy, Pārvatī rejoiced exceedingly.
The great virtuous goddess Śivā, exceedingly happy and her face blossoming with affection, replied to the Lord who stood near her.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods, you are my protector; have you forgotten what occurred in the past, for whose sake you violently brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice?"
O God, for the sake of accomplishing the task of the gods who were distressed by the acquisition of Tāraka, you and I were born together from Menā. You, O Lord, commanded me.
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if you show me mercy, become my husband, O Īśāna; fulfill my word, O Lord.
"I shall go properly to my father’s house with your younger sister; let that pure and supreme fame indeed be made manifest."
O Lord, O Master, you must go to the slopes of the Himalayas; then, becoming a mendicant skilled in playful guile, you should ask for me from there.
You must act in such a way as to proclaim your fame throughout the world; make all of my father's efforts fruitful, and thus honor my home.
Enlightened by the sages and surrounded by his kinsmen, my father will undoubtedly carry out your word with joy.
Formerly, when I was indeed given to you by my father as the daughter of Dakṣa, you did not perform the marriage ceremony there according to the prescribed injunctions.
The planets were not worshipped by that skillful father of mine; because of that, this great flaw has arisen in the domain of the planets.
Therefore, O Lord Mahādeva, you ought to perform my marriage according to the prescribed rite for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Let Himavat know correctly that the manner in which the marriage is to be performed must certainly be such that he may recognize the auspicious penance accomplished by his daughter.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, Sadāśiva, being well-pleased, spoke these words with affection to Girijā, as if smiling.
Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess Maheśānī, to my supreme word; act accordingly so that it may be appropriate, highly auspicious, and immutable.
O fair-faced one, beings beginning with Brahmā are impermanent; O beautiful lady, know that all this which is seen is perishable.
Having attained both oneness and multiplicity, though devoid of qualities, he is indeed endowed with qualities; he who shines with moonlight has become possessed of supreme radiance.
O Goddess, I have indeed been made both independent and dependent by you; for you alone are the primordial nature (prakṛti), the creator of all, and the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā).

This entire world has been fashioned out of illusion, yet it is sustained in every way by your supreme intellect; it is sprinkled with the nature of the Supreme Self by those of virtuous conduct who follow the true path, and the host is encompassed within the Self.
Which are the planets, which are the groups of seasons, or what other planets are there according to you? And what has been said now, O Goddess of excellent complexion, for the sake of Śiva?

Through the distinction between our qualities and our activities, we have manifested ourselves in this world for the sake of devotees, out of our disposition as those who are affectionate toward their devotees.

For you are indeed the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti), composed of the qualities of passion, purity, and darkness; you are constantly skilled in activity, both possessed of attributes and yet devoid of them.
O slender-waisted one, I am the Self of all beings here; I am changeless and desireless, assuming a form according to the wishes of my devotees.
O daughter of the mountain, I would not go to the Himalayas to see your father; therefore, I would never beg of you by becoming a mendicant.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, even one who is most venerable due to great virtues and a high-souled person immediately incurs lightness of status by the mere utterance of the word "Give."
Having understood this, O auspicious lady, what do you say to us? Whatever task must be done by your command, O blessed one, do as you wish.
Brahmā said: Although thus addressed by him, that virtuous goddess, lotus-eyed, spoke to Śaṅkara with devotion, bowing down again and again.

Pārvatī said: You are the Self (Ātman) and I am Prakṛti; there is no need for deliberation on this point. We are both independent yet subject to our devotees, and though devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), we also possess qualities (saguṇa).
O Śambhu, O Lord, you must act upon my words with great effort: "Entreat me; O Śaṅkara, grant the good fortune of Himavat."
Have mercy, O Great Lord; I am your devotee eternally. For I am always your wife, O Protector, in birth after birth.
You are indeed Brahman, the Supreme Self, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), changeless, desireless, independent, and the Supreme Lord.

Nevertheless, even though He possesses attributes, He is here solely intent on the upliftment of His devotees; He wanders about, yet remains absorbed in His own Self, being an expert in manifold divine sports.
In every way, O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, I know you; what is the use of speaking much, O Omniscient One? Indeed, have mercy.
Spread your fame throughout the world after performing a most wonderful feat, so that people may sing of it well, O Lord, and thereby cross the ocean of existence without difficulty.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and bowing repeatedly to Maheśāna, Girijā, with shoulders bent and palms joined in reverence, became silent.

When he had been addressed thus by her, the Great-souled Maheśvara, for the sake of mimicking the ways of the world, thought "So be it," and became filled with joy, smiling as he intended to do exactly that.
Then Śambhu, having become invisible, departed for Kailāsa with a heart drawn by separation from Kālī, yet filled with great joy.
Having gone there, Maheśāna, overflowing with supreme bliss, related that entire account to Nandin and the others.
Having heard this, all those hosts, including Bhairava and the others from every side, became exceedingly joyful and celebrated a supreme festival.
O twice-born Nārada, there was great auspiciousness there; the suffering of all was destroyed, and even Rudra attained joy.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Śiva and Śivā," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Vidhi, dear father, O highly fortunate one, you are blessed and a seer of the supreme truth; by your grace, this wonderful narrative has been heard by me.
O high-minded one, tell me: when Pārvatī, the source of all auspiciousness, had gone to her own mountain with Hari, what did she do and where did she go?
Brahmā said: Listen with great pleasure, my dear son, to what occurred immediately thereafter; I shall relate it while remembering Śiva, now that Hari has departed for his own abode.
Pārvatī also, accompanied by her friends and assuming a meaningful form, went to the house of her own father, calling out, "O Mahādeva!"
Upon hearing that Pārvatī was arriving, Menā and Himācala, overwhelmed with joy, ascended a divine vehicle and set forth.
The family priest, the citizens, numerous friends, as well as other relatives and all others, arrived there together.
Then all the brothers, headed by Maināka, departed, filled with great joy and uttering shouts of victory.
Having established an auspicious water-pot upon the resplendent royal road, which was adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, fruits, and branches.
Accompanied by Brahmins together with their family priests, by sages who discourse on the Veda, by women, and by dancing girls, the scene was further graced by lordly elephants and mountains.
On all sides, it was surrounded by clusters of plantain trunks and by groups of women accompanied by their husbands and sons, holding lamps in their hands.
It was joined by throngs of twice-born men chanting auspicious sounds, accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments and the blaring of conch shells.
In the meantime, Durgā went near her own city; as the goddess was entering the town, she saw her parents once again.
Seeing the two of them running forward with minds overwhelmed by joy, Kālī was greatly delighted and, together with her companions, bowed down before them.
Having bestowed their full blessing, they both placed her upon their chests, crying out, "O child! as they wept, overwhelmed with love.
Then her own kinswomen, as well as other women and even her brothers' wives, joyfully and with great affection gave her firm embraces.
Truly, you have perfectly accomplished the noble task of rescuing your lineage; by your constant virtuous conduct, we all have been purified.
Thus, having praised her all together, they bowed down to her with great joy; and with delight, they worshipped Śivā with sandalwood paste and beautiful flowers.
At that moment, the gods stationed in their celestial chariots in the sky joyfully rained down a shower of auspicious flowers; having bowed to her, they praised her with hymns of praise.
Then, having placed her upon an excellent, splendid chariot, all the brahmins and others joyfully led her into the city.
Then the Brahmins, the family priests, her friends, and other women ushered Śivā into the house with great honor.
The women performed the cleansing rites, O Brahmins, and they offered their blessings; Himavat and Menakā, his mother, rejoiced exceedingly, O Lord of Sages.
A daughter is better than a bad son; thus she considered her own hermitage to have borne fruit. Himavat, meanwhile, was praising you and Nārada, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
The lord of mountains gave wealth to the Brahmins and the bards; during that great festival, he had the twice-born recite auspicious hymns.
O Sage, thus the parents, brothers, and sisters-in-law, delighted by their own daughter, lived together in the courtyard with great joy.
Then, O dear one, Himavat, being exceedingly joyful and clear-minded, honored them all with affection and went to the Gaṅgā to bathe.
In the meantime, Śambhu, who is fond of play and compassionate toward his devotees, assumed the form of an excellent dancer and went into the presence of Menakā.
Holding a horn in his left hand and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in his right, with a patched garment on his back and clad in red robes, he is an expert in dance and song.
Then, assuming the form of a dancer, he joyfully performed various beautiful dances and most enchanting songs before the assembly of Menakā.
There he sounded the horn and the hand-drum with a beautiful sound; there he produced various great and enchanting melodies.
To see her, all the citizens—both men and women, as well as children and the elderly—certainly arrived there in haste.
O Sage, having heard that beautiful song and seen that captivating, exquisite dance, everyone—including Menā—was suddenly struck with wonder.
Having fallen into a swoon, that Durgā beheld Śaṅkara within her heart, bearing the trident and other emblems, and exceedingly beautiful.
Adorned with supernatural powers, beautiful, and garlanded with bones; his face radiant with three eyes, and having a serpent as his sacred thread.
To Maheśvara, who was fair-complexioned, the friend of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, and in every way most enchanting, he said, "Choose a boon."
Seeing Hara thus situated within her heart, she bowed down to him and chose this mental boon: "May you become my husband."
Having affectionately granted such a boon to Śiva from his heart, that mendicant then vanished right there and began to dance beautifully once more.
Then Menā, her mind delighted by his prosperity, went with affection to give him excellent jewels placed in golden vessels.
He did not accept those offerings, but instead requested that auspicious alms; then, out of curiosity, he prepared to perform beautiful dancing and singing once again.
Having heard those words, Menā became exceedingly astonished and grew very angry; she rebuked the mendicant and desired to cast him out.
In the meantime, a mountain came there from the Gaṅgā; he saw before him a mendicant in human form standing in the courtyard.
Having heard all that had transpired from the mouth of Menā, he became greatly enraged and gave orders to his attendants to expel that actor.
Like a great fire, difficult to touch, blazing and full of intense splendor, no one was able to drive that best of sages outside.
Then, O dear one, that mendicant, who was skilled in various playful arts, displayed his infinite power to the mountain.
There Śaila beheld him, swiftly assuming the form of Viṣṇu—wearing a crown and earrings, clad in yellow garments, and possessing four arms.
Whatever flowers and other offerings were given to the wielder of the mace at the time of worship, he saw all of that upon the body and head of the mendicant.
Then the Lord of Mountains beheld the four-faced creator of the worlds, who was red in complexion and reciting the hymns of the Vedas.
Then the King of Mountains beheld for a moment the very form of the Sun, whose nature is the eye of the world—a sight that caused wonder.
Then, O dear one, he beheld that most wonderful form of Rudra, accompanied by Pārvatī, beautiful, smiling, and possessed of great splendor.
Then [he saw] that which is the nature of light, formless, stainless, free from limiting adjuncts, effortless, most wonderful, and without material shape.
Thus he beheld many forms there; he was instantly filled with great wonder and endowed with supreme bliss.
Then that excellent monk indeed requested alms from her, the woman who had given birth, reaching as far as Durgā; he accepted nothing else whatsoever.
Deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, the lord of mountains did not accept [the gift]; the mendicant took nothing at all and then vanished right there.
Then, this excellent realization arose in Menā and the Lord of Mountains: "The Lord Śiva, having deceived us both, has gone to his own abode."
Having reflected upon those two, supreme devotion toward Śiva alone arose within them—a divine devotion that grants great liberation and bestows all bliss.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival of Pārvatī's Return," in the third section (Pārvatī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Nārada, having perceived the supreme and unwavering devotion of those two toward Śiva, all the gods, headed by Śakra, reflected thus.
The gods said: "If Śaila bestows his daughter upon him with single-minded devotion, he will certainly attain liberation immediately in Bhārata."
If the earth, the repository of infinite jewels, were to depart having abandoned [this place], then the earth would certainly and truly become false to its name "Jewel-Womb" (Ratnagarbhā).
Having abandoned his state as an immobile being and assumed a divine form, he will give his daughter to the wielder of the trident and go to the world of Śiva.
He shall attain the same form as Mahādeva; of this there is no doubt. Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there, he will thereafter obtain liberation.
Brahmā said: Having reflected thus and consulted with one another, all the gods, greatly amazed, desired to dispatch their preceptor there.
Then, O Nārada, Śakra and all the other gods, seeking to accomplish their own purpose, went with affection and humility to the abode of their preceptor.
Having gone there and bowed to the Guru, all the gods, including Indra, respectfully reported the events that had occurred to that Guru.
The gods said: "O Preceptor, go to the home of Himālaya for the accomplishment of our purpose; having gone there, exert yourself to utter censure of the Wielder of the Trident."
Durgā will choose no other boon than Pinākin; by giving away his daughter against his will, he shall quickly obtain the fruit thereof.
O Mountain, now at this very time, remain upon the earth; establish yourself, the repository of many jewels, upon the ground of the Guru.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the god, he placed his hand upon [the boy's] ears; yet that preceptor did not accept it, remembering the name "Śiva."
Then, having called to mind Mahādeva, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati spoke to the foremost of the gods, reproaching them again and again.
Bṛhaspati said: "All the gods are intent on their own interests and are destroyers of the welfare of others; having indeed reviled Śaṅkara, I shall certainly go to hell."
O gods, let someone among you go to the presence of the mountain; having awakened the lord of mountains, he shall accomplish what is desired.
If he remains in Bhārata happily after giving his daughter against his will, he will certainly attain liberation by giving his daughter to him with devotion.
Afterwards, all the Seven Sages will awaken the mountain; Durgā will choose no other boon than one from the wielder of the Pināka bow.
"Or else, O gods, go with Vāsava to the world of Brahmā; relate what has happened to him, and he will accomplish your task."
Brahmā said: Having heard that, those gods deliberated and came to my assembly; bowing with great respect, they all reported what had occurred.
O Sage, having heard those words of the gods which were a censure of Śiva, I, the speaker of the Vedas, lamented and said to those deities:
Brahmā said: "O children, I am not able to commit the unbearable censure of Śiva, which takes the form of the destruction of prosperity and is the very seed of calamities."
O Suras, go to Kailāsa and gratify Śaṅkara; dispatch him quickly back to the home of Himālaya.
He should go to Upaśaileśa and indeed practice self-reproach; self-reproach is considered conducive to fame, whereas reproaching others leads to one's own destruction.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, those gods bowed to me with joy and quickly departed for Kailāsa, the mountain that is the lord of all mountains.
Having gone there and beheld Śiva, all the gods, with their heads bowed and palms joined in reverence, praised Hara.
The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion! We have come to you for refuge; show us mercy, salutations be unto you!
