O Lord, you are affectionate toward your devotees, always accomplishing the tasks of your devotees; you are the uplifter of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, and the liberator from the calamities of your devotees.
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Maheśāna, all the gods, together with Indra, respectfully reported that entire event to him.
Having heard those words of the gods, Maheśvara accepted them; having consoled and smiled at them, he sent the gods back to their own abodes.
All the gods rejoiced and, having quickly returned to their own abodes, considering their purpose accomplished, they constantly praised Sadāśiva.
Then the Blessed One, Śambhu, the Great Lord who is affectionate toward his devotees, the master of illusion and free from all change, departed for the king of mountains.
When Śaila sat in the midst of the assembly, filled with joy, surrounded by his circle of kinsmen and accompanied by Pārvatī herself.
In the meantime, Sadāśiva indeed arrived there, carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in divine garments, and wearing a brilliant tilaka.
Holding a crystal rosary in his hand and wearing a śālagrāma stone around his neck, the twice-born man, dressed in the garb of a holy man, chanted the name of Hari with devotion.
Upon seeing him, Himālaya, together with his retinue, rose up; out of devotion, he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before the unprecedented guest.
Pārvatī bowed with devotion to the lord of her life who was in the form of a brahmin; having recognized him in her mind, the goddess praised him with supreme joy.
O dear one, the wise Śiva affectionately offered a blessing to all, but in his heart he desired for Pārvatī something even greater than her own wish.
The Brāhmaṇa joyfully accepted everything, beginning with the madhuparka offering, which had been given with great reverence by Himāṅga, the sovereign of mountains.
O Sage, having honored that best of brahmins according to the prescribed rites with great affection, Himādri, the foremost of mountains, inquired after his welfare.
Then Śaileśa asked him again, "Who are you? Thereupon, the lord of brahmins quickly spoke these respectful words to the lord of mountains:

The lord of brahmins said: "O best of mountains, I am a brahmin, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and the most excellent among the wise; adopting the livelihood of a water-carrier, I wander upon the surface of the earth."
Moving by mind, all-pervading, and omniscient through the power of my guru, I am a benefactor of others, pure in soul, an ocean of compassion, and a destroyer of mental transformations.
I have learned that you wish to give your own daughter to Hara—this divine girl who is like a lotus, possessed of excellent form and auspicious marks.
To the one who is without support, unattached, of ugly form, and devoid of qualities; to the yogi who dwells in the cremation ground and has the form of a snake-catcher.
To him who is clothed in the directions, whose limbs are deformed, who wears serpents as ornaments, whose family and name are unknown, who is of evil conduct, and who wanders without a fixed abode.
To him whose body was smeared with ashes, who was highly enraged, devoid of discrimination, whose age was unknown, and who always wore a coarse matted lock of hair;

Salutations to the one who is the support of all, to the wanderer, to the one adorned with a serpent-necklace, to the mendicant, and to him who has forcibly abandoned the path of the Vedas and is devoted to the wrong way.
O Acala, this mind of yours is certainly not conducive to auspiciousness; awaken, O best among the wise, born as you are from the lineage of Nārāyaṇa!
In this act of giving Pārvatī, the great multitude will not be worthy recipients, yet their faces shall become smiling as soon as they hear of it.
Behold, O Lord of Mountains, you have not even a single kinsman; and though you are a great mine of jewels, you possess no wealth whatsoever belonging to him.
O Lord of Mountains, quickly and with great care inquire after your kinsmen, Menakā, and all your sons—with the sole exception of Pārvatī—and likewise consult with all the learned men.
O best of mountains, medicine never appeals to the sick; rather, unwholesome food, which always causes great harm, is constantly desired by them.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, that Brahmin, filled with joy, quickly ate and went to his own abode; while Śiva, the performer of various divine sports, remained there in peace.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Māyā," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the Brāhmaṇa, Menā, her eyes clouded by grief and her heart tormented, spoke to Himālaya.
Menā said: "Listen, O Lord of Mountains, to my words which will bring happiness in the end. Ask all the foremost devotees of Śiva what was said by the Brāhmaṇa."
O Lord of Mountains, having heard that censure of Śambhu uttered by that Vaiṣṇava twice-born man, my mind is indeed exceedingly despondent.
"O Lord of the Mountain, I will not give my daughter to that Rudra; for he is ill-favored in form and character, while she is endowed with auspicious marks."
If you do not heed my words, I shall die without a doubt; I will either leave my home immediately or consume poison.
"Having bound Ambikā by the neck with a rope, I shall go to the dense forest; I will drown her in the great ocean—I will not give my daughter to him."
Having spoken thus, Menā immediately went to her chamber of anger; abandoning her necklace and weeping in grief, she made her bed upon the ground.
In the meantime, dear one, those seven sages were suddenly remembered by Śambhu, whose soul was distressed by separation.
And when all those sages were called to mind by Śambhu, they immediately arrived in person like other celestial wish-fulfilling trees.
Arundhatī likewise arrived there like another personified Siddhi; seeing them, who were as radiant as the sun, Hara abandoned his own recitation.
O Sage, having stood before the most excellent Śiva, bowed, and praised him, those ascetics then considered themselves to have achieved their life's purpose.
Then, overcome with wonder, they stood there again after offering salutations; with palms joined in reverence, they spoke to Śiva, who is worshipped by the worlds.
The sages said: O Great King, Sovereign of the Earth, we describe our own good fortune as being superior to that of all the inhabitants of heaven; how much more so that which is the best of all?
In the past, he performed threefold austerity and the highest study of the Vedas; previously, he offered oblations into the sacred fires and visited various holy fords.
Whatever merit has arisen from speech, mind, or body, and whatever has been produced through remembrance—all that is gathered together today by virtue of your grace and your remembrance.
The man who indeed constantly worships you becomes one who has accomplished all his purposes; what merit can be described for those whose very remembrance is yours?
O Sadāśiva, we have become the most excellent of all beings through your remembrance; yet you do not enter the path of our desires in any way whatsoever.
Just as dwarfing is the fruit for one born blind, as sight is for the mute, as eloquence is for the dumb, and as the discovery of a treasure is for the pauper; so too is this [the fruit] for you.
O Lord, just as the crushing of a mountain by a cripple or the birth of a child from a barren woman is impossible, so too has this vision of you become difficult for us to attain.
From this day forward, O lords of sages, you have become worthy of honor and worship in the worlds; by the mere sight of you, they have attained their own exalted state.
What need is there for much speaking here? O Lord of Gods, indeed, by the mere sight of you, the sovereign of all gods, everyone has attained honor.
If there is anything further to be done for those who are fulfilled, O Supreme Compassion, then you should grant a favorable task suitable for your servants.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of theirs, Śambhu, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), following worldly custom, spoke these pleasing words.
Śiva said: "The sages are always worthy of worship, and you especially so; O brahmins, it was for your sake that I performed this remembrance."
Indeed, my condition is known by you as one that is beneficial; it must be specifically accomplished for the sake of the success of the worlds.
Suffering has arisen for the gods because of that evil-souled Tāraka; and Brahmā granted him two boons, saying, "What can I do, O unassailable one?"
The eight forms of mine that have been described by the supreme sages are all for the sake of benefiting others, and not for my own sake; this is clear.
And so, I desire to perform a marriage with Śivā; indeed, she has performed austerities that are difficult even for the great sages to accomplish.
To her, the supreme fruit should be given—whatever is desired and conducive to her welfare; for such is my wager, which clearly bestows bliss upon my devotees.
At the word of Pārvatī, I, skilled in divine play, assumed the form of a mendicant and went to the mountain's house, whereby I purified Kālī.
Having recognized me as the Supreme Brahman, that couple, through their supreme devotion, desired to give their daughter to me in accordance with the Vedic tradition.
Impelled by the gods, I indeed uttered that censure with a Vaiṣṇava soul, in order to destroy my own devotion to him at that time.
Having heard that, the two of them became utterly despondent and deprived of hope; for now, O sages, they do not wish to give their daughter to me.
Therefore, sirs, go certainly to the abode of Himācala; having gone there, awaken that best of mountains and his wife.
One should strive to speak words that are consistent with the Vedas; in every way, one must act so that this becomes the highest duty.
"O most excellent ones, I desire to perform a marriage with his daughter; that marriage has been accepted by me, and such a boon was granted."
In this matter, what need is there for much speaking? Himālaya must be enlightened, and Menā likewise must be made to understand, so that the welfare of the gods may be secured.
Whatever ordinance may have been devised by you that is superior to that [of the gods], it must indeed be carried out by you; for you are the ones who share in the responsibility for the task.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, all those sages of pure intent attained great joy, having been graced by the Lord.
We have become blessed and in every way have fulfilled our purpose; we have become worthy of salutation by all and especially deserving of worship.
He who is indeed worthy of worship by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the accomplisher of all goals, sends us as messengers for a task that brings happiness to the world.
He is indeed the lord of the worlds and is considered the father; she is regarded as the mother. This union is most fitting; may it increase forever like the moon.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the divine sages then paid homage to Śiva and departed by way of the sky to where the city of Himavat is located.
Having seen that divine city, those sages were greatly amazed; praising their own merit, they spoke thus to one another.
The sages said: "We are meritorious and blessed, having seen this city of Himavat, since we have been appointed by Śiva himself to such a task."
Moreover, this supreme city is seen to surpass Alakā, Svarga, Bhogavatī, and especially Amarāvatī.
There were well-constructed and most delightful houses, and courtyards fashioned from various excellent crystals or variegated gems.
There were sun-crystals and likewise moon-crystals, and in every house there were various trees originating from heaven.
And likewise, the splendor of archways was seen in every house, with various and wonderful parrots, swans, and celestial chariots.
There were various multicolored canopies together with cloth festoons and arches; there were many reservoirs and various kinds of oblong ponds situated there.
Then, the various gardens were honored by those who were serene; likewise, all the men were like gods, and the women were like apsarases.
In this land of action, those who perform sacrifices and the citizens, desiring heaven, act all in vain by abandoning the city of Himavat.
As long as this has not been seen, men are intent upon heaven; O Brahmins, once this has been seen, what need is there for heaven?
Brahmā said: Having thus described that city, all those best of sages went to their home on Mount Himālaya, which was endowed with every prosperity.
Seeing those seven highly effulgent sages standing from afar on the path of the sky, resembling the sun, Himavat was struck with wonder and spoke.
Himavān said: "These seven, resplendent like the sun, are approaching my presence; I must now diligently perform worship for these sages."
We householders are blessed, bestowing happiness upon all, since such great souls as these come to our home.
Brahmā said: In the meantime, Himavat, having arrived from the sky and seeing them standing on the earth before him, approached them with great respect.
With palms joined in reverence and shoulders bowed, he prostrated deeply before the Seven Sages and performed their worship with great respect.
Then those seven sages, for his welfare, took hold of Himavat, the lord of mountains, and with serene countenances, spoke these words that were the abode of auspiciousness.
Having placed them at the forefront, he said, "Blessed is my household life," and having spoken thus, he brought forth seats and offered them with great devotion.
When they had sat down upon their seats, Himavat himself stood there at their command and then spoke to the sages, who were like radiant light.
Himālaya said: "I am indeed blessed and have fulfilled my purpose; my life is fruitful. I am worthy of being seen in all the worlds and am considered equal to many sacred pilgrimage sites."
Since you have come to my home, you who are the very form of Viṣṇu, what business do you perfect beings have in the houses of the wretched?
Nevertheless, there is a certain matter that must be told by me, your servant; out of great compassion, please grant it, so that my birth may become fruitful.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Seven Sages," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "Śiva is declared the father of the world, and Śivā is considered the mother of the world. Therefore, you must give your daughter to the high-souled Śaṅkara."
By acting thus, O Himavat, your birth shall become meaningful; for you will undoubtedly become the teacher of the Teacher of the World.
Brahmā said: O Lord of Sages, having heard these words of the seven ṛṣis, the King of Mountains bowed to them with palms joined and spoke as follows.
Himālaya said: "O highly fortunate Seven Sages, that which has been spoken by you has indeed already been accepted as authoritative by me, in accordance with the will of Giriśa."
Now, a certain brahmin devoted to the Vaiṣṇava dharma arrived and, out of great affection for Śiva, spoke these contrary words.
From that time on, Śivāmātā became deprived of her knowledge; she no longer desired the marriage of her daughter with that yogi, Rudra.
O Brahmins, having made a great resolve, she went to the chamber of anger; though being exhorted, she, deeply distressed and clad in soiled garments, did not heed it.

"I have become deprived of my wisdom; this is truly being proclaimed. I do not wish to give my daughter to Maheśa, who appears in the form of a mendicant. Brahmā said: "O Sage, having spoken thus, the King of Mountains, deluded by Śiva’s Māyā, remained silent there in the midst of the sages."
Then all those seven sages, having indeed praised the illusory power of Śiva, dispatched Menakā as a substitute for Arundhatī.
Then, having received her husband’s command, Arundhatī—who is indeed the giver of wisdom—went quickly to where Menā and Pārvatī were.
Having gone there, he saw Menā lying unconscious with grief; the virtuous woman spoke these sweet, attentive, and beneficial words.
Arundhatī said: "Arise, O virtuous Menakā! I am Arundhatī, come to your house; and the seven compassionate sages have also arrived."
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Arundhatī, Menakā rose up quickly and, bowing her head, spoke to her who was like a lotus in splendor.
Menā said: "Oh! What is this merit of ours today, we whose births are so blessed, that the daughter-in-law of Vasiṣṭha, the wife of the Creator of the World, has indeed arrived here?"
O Goddess, tell me specifically for what purpose you have come; I am indeed like a maidservant to you along with my son, so please show us mercy.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and having extensively instructed the virtuous Menakā, she departed with great joy to that place where those sages were also residing.
Then, all those experts in speech, having remembered the pair of Śiva’s feet, respectfully awakened Śaileśvara.
The sages said: O Lord of Mountains, hear our words which are for the sake of auspiciousness; give Pārvatī to Śiva and become the father-in-law of the Destroyer.
He diligently entreated the Lord of All, who had not been asked for it, regarding the rite of Brahmā’s marriage for the sake of Tāraka’s destruction.
Śaṅkara, the best of yogis, has no haste regarding union with a wife; at the request of Brahmā, the god will accept your daughter.
Your daughter has performed austerities and made a vow: "The Lord of Yogins will perform my marriage for two reasons."
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the sages, Himālaya laughed and, though somewhat afraid, spoke with great humility.
Himālaya said: "I do not see any royal paraphernalia whatsoever belonging to Śiva; nor do I see any support, any sovereign power, or any kinsmen or relatives."
"I do not wish to give my daughter to a yogi who is utterly detached; you are the sons of the Creator of the Vedas, so speak with certainty."
If a father gives his daughter to an unworthy suitor out of desire, delusion, fear, or greed, he is ruined and shall go to hell.
"I will certainly not give my daughter to the wielder of the trident of my own accord; O sages, let that arrangement be made which is appropriate."
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having heard these words of Himāga, Vasiṣṭha, who was skilled in speech, replied to him.
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Lord of Mountains, to my words which are in every way conducive to your welfare—consistent with dharma, true, and bringing joy both in this world and the next.
O Śaila, there are three kinds of speech, both worldly and Vedic; one who knows the scriptures understands them all through the eye of stainless knowledge.
One of sound intellect speaks what is untrue, harmful, belated, yet pleasant to hear at present; for an enemy never speaks what is truly beneficial.
That which causes displeasure at first but brings happiness in the end—a compassionate kinsman of righteous character surely teaches this.
Merely by hearing it, this speech is equal to nectar, bringing happiness at all times; it is the most excellent and desired word, whose essence is truth and which is beneficial.
"O Śaila, since there are these three kinds of speech proclaimed in the treatises on ethics, tell me which one among the three you wish for me to speak."
And Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods, though devoid of the perfection of Brahman, has his mind entirely immersed in the oceans of the knowledge of reality.
What desire could the Lord, whose nature is knowledge and bliss, have for worldly objects? A householder gives his daughter to one who possesses a kingdom and great wealth.
By giving his daughter to one who is suffering, a father becomes a slayer of his own daughter; for who knows that Śaṅkara is suffering, he whose servant is Kubera?

Indeed, by the mere play of a frown of his eyebrows, he is capable of creating and destroying the universe; for he is the attributeless Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).

And he whose threefold form is manifested for the purpose of creation—namely, the forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, which bring about creation, preservation, and dissolution—is [the Supreme Lord].
Brahmā resides in the world of Brahmā; Viṣṇu makes his abode in the Ocean of Milk; Hara has his dwelling on Kailāsa; all these are the manifestations of Śiva.
And Prakṛti, originating from Śiva, assumes threefold forms through her portions for the sake of playful creation, and also in manifold ways through her creative power (kalā).
Speech herself, the presiding deity of speech, is born from the mouth; Lakṣmī, the embodiment of all prosperity, is born from the chest.
Śivā manifested her presence within the splendors of the gods; having slain all the Dānavas, she bestowed prosperity upon the deities.
In another kalpa, he took birth from the womb of Dakṣa’s daughter; known by the name Satī, she obtained Hara as her husband, and Dakṣa gave her to him.
Having heard the censure of her husband, she abandoned her body through yoga; today, however, that auspicious lady has been born from the womb of Menā through you.
This Śivā is the wife of Śiva in birth after birth; in kalpa after kalpa, she is the supreme mother of the wise, appearing in the form of intellect.

She was ever born as the perfected one, the bestower of perfection, and the very embodiment of perfection; she is the Truth, and Hara himself, out of devotion, wears her bones and the ashes of the funeral pyre.
Therefore, give your auspicious daughter to Hara of your own free will; otherwise, she will go to her beloved’s place herself if you do not give her.
Having made this vow and beholding the innumerable suffering of your daughter, the Lord of Gods, assuming the form of a brahmin, came to the place where she was performing her penance.
Having comforted her and granted her a boon, Śambhu went to his own abode; then, O Mountain, at her request, he sought you, Śivā.
"That which was accepted by you both with hearts devoted to the worship of Śiva—O Lord of the Mountains, tell me, why has a contrary mindset arisen?"
Therefore, O Lord, having gone there at the request of the Master, we—the sages as well as Arundhatī—have been sent quickly to your presence.
Indeed, we shall instruct you after giving Pārvatī to Rudra; when this is done, O Mountain, there will be great joy for you.
O Lord of Mountains, if you do not give Śivā to Śiva of your own free will, their marriage shall nevertheless take place here by the force of destiny.
O dear one, Śaṅkara granted a boon to Śivā as she was performing penance; for that which is promised by the Lord never turns out otherwise.
Ah! The promise of the virtuous who abide by the Lord is difficult to transgress; what then need be said of the promise of the Lord himself in the midst of all the worlds?
The great Indra alone effortlessly severed the wings of the mountains, and Pārvatī likewise playfully shattered the peaks of Mount Meru.
O Śaileśa, when a single purpose is at stake, all forms of prosperity must indeed be destroyed; one should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family—this is the eternal Vedic injunction.
O lord of kings, having given his own daughter to the brahmin, Anaraṇya—having incurred fear from the brahmin—protected his own wealth.
Those who were learned in the treatises on statecraft quickly awakened him, as did his preceptors and the best of his kinsmen, who were terrified by the curse of a Brahmin.
O King of Mountains, you too, having given your daughter to Śiva, protect all your kinsmen and bring even the gods under your control.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, he laughed and, with a heart tormented by grief, inquired after the news of the king.
Himālaya said: O Brahmin, from whose lineage was that King Anaraṇya born? And how did he, having given away his daughter, protect all his royal fortunes?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the mountain, Vasiṣṭha, with a serene mind, spoke to that mountain the pleasant news concerning the king.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Consolation of the Mountain," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said: O lord of kings, that King Anaraṇya was born in the lineage of Manu; indeed, he belonged to the fourteenth Manvantara known as Indrasāvarṇi.
Anaraṇya, the best of kings and lord of the earth with its seven continents, was a devotee of Śambhu, especially so, being powerful and born in Maṅgalāraṇya.
Having appointed Bhṛgu as his domestic priest, he performed a hundred sacrifices; yet, even though the gods offered it to him, he did not accept the status of Śakra.
O Himālaya, that king had one hundred sons and one beautiful daughter named Padmā, who was equal to the goddess Padmālayā (Lakṣmī).
O best of mountains, that king’s affection for her was indeed greater than his affection for his hundred sons and even more so than for his daughter.
The queens were more dear to the king than his own life; all five of the monarch’s wives were endowed with great good fortune.
That maiden reached the prime of youth while in her father’s house; she dispatched a letter so that excellent suitors might come to seek her hand.
Once, the sage Pippalāda, eager to go to his own hermitage, beheld a Gandharva in a secluded place where he was performing austerities.
His mind was immersed with his wife in the ocean of the erotic sentiment, sporting with great love as he was an expert in the science of erotics.
Upon seeing her, that tiger among sages became filled with desire; his mind no longer intent on asceticism, he thought about taking a wife.
In this manner, some time passed for that very sage Pippalāda, who lived such a life yet whose mind was agitated by desire.
Once, while going to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river, the lord of sages beheld the young woman Padmā, who was as enchanting as the goddess Padmā herself.
The sage asked the people standing nearby, "Who is this girl? Bowing down, restrained by his curse, the people made their report.
The people said: "This daughter of Anaraṇya is indeed named Padmā, another form of Ramā; she is a woman of excellent limbs, an abode of virtues, and is sought after by the best of kings."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the people who spoke the truth, that sage was greatly agitated in his mind and became desirous of obtaining it.
O Mountain, having bathed and duly worshipped his chosen deity Śiva, the sage, filled with desire, went to the assembly of Anaraṇya for the sake of alms.
Upon seeing the sage, the king quickly prostrated himself, overwhelmed with fear; having offered the honey-mixture and other honors, he worshipped him with devotion.
Having accepted everything out of desire, the sage requested the maiden; the king became silent, unable to say anything at all.
The sage requested the maiden from him, saying, "O lord of kings, give her to me; otherwise, I shall reduce everything to ashes in an instant."
O Sage, all the hosts were shrouded by his splendor; the king, along with his attendants, wept upon seeing the brahmin afflicted by old age.
All the queens wept, unable to comprehend what ought to be done; the chief queen, the mother of the maiden, overwhelmed with grief, fell into a swoon.
All the sons became overwhelmed with grief; O Lord of Mountains, everything connected to the king became filled with sorrow.
In the meantime, a wise and most excellent brahmin, who was both a preceptor and a learned domestic priest, arrived in the presence of the king.
The king, having prostrated and offered worship, wept before them; he reported everything and immediately asked what was appropriate.
Then the king’s preceptor, a learned brahmin, and the domestic priest—both of whom were experts in the scriptures and political ethics—instructed the monarch.
Adopting the highest policy that brings benefit to all, he [consoled] the queens who were overwhelmed with grief, as well as the princes and the maidens.

The preceptor and the family priest said: "Listen, O King of great wisdom, to our words which bring about true welfare. Do not grieve along with your retinue; apply your mind rightly to the sacred scriptures."
O King, today or at the end of the year, the maiden must be given away to a worthy Brahmin, or to someone else, especially one who is distinguished.
We see no worthy recipient other than a Brahmin in the three worlds; having given your daughter to the sage, preserve all your own prosperity.
O King, by a single cause all prosperity perishes; yet, having abandoned everything else, one protects that [cause] which is the one who has sought refuge.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard the words of the wise man and having lamented again and again, the king indeed adorned his daughter with ornaments and gave her to the lord of sages.
O Mountain, having taken that beloved Padmā—who was like a lotus—and having married her according to the prescribed rites, that sage went joyfully to his own abode.
The king, having renounced everything and given his daughter to the elder, took dejection to heart and went to the forest for asceticism.
When her husband had thus departed for the forest, O Mountain, that beautiful woman also gave up her life out of grief for her husband and her daughter.
The venerable sons and servants fell into a swoon without the king; all the other people, perceiving this, lamented with heavy sighs.
Having gone to the forest and performed intense austerities, Anaraṇya propitiated Śaṅkara with devotion and went to the stainless world of Śiva.
Then the king’s eldest son, named Kīrtimān, being righteous, protected the subjects like his own children and ruled the kingdom.
Thus, O Mountain, I have related to you the auspicious history of Araṇya, how he protected his lineage and all his wealth after giving away his daughter.
O King of Mountains, you too, having thus given your daughter to Śiva, protect your entire lineage and bring all the gods under your control.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Anaraṇya," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O dear one, having heard the life-story of Anaraṇya together with the giving away of his daughter, what did the lord of mountains do? Tell me that.
Brahmā said: Having heard the account of Anaraṇya, including the giving away of his daughters, the Lord of Mountains again questioned Vasiṣṭha with palms joined in reverence.
Śaileśa said: O Vasiṣṭha, tiger among sages, son of Brahmā, ocean of compassion! You have narrated to me the most wonderful account of Anaraṇya.
Since the daughter of Anaraṇya obtained the sage Pippalāda as her husband, what did she do? That delightful account of her conduct [shall now be told].
The eminent sage Pippalāda, exceedingly decrepit with age, went to his own hermitage accompanied by that woman, the daughter of Anaraṇya.
O best of mountains, that ascetic, who was not overly lustful, dwelt there with great joy in that forest, constantly performing his own religious duties.
Then that daughter of Anaraṇya served the sage with devotion through her actions, mind, and speech, just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa.
Once, on the path, Dharma, assuming the form of a bull through his illusory power, beheld Susmitā as she was going to bathe in the celestial river.
Seated upon a beautiful chariot of jewels, adorned with various ornaments, endowed with fresh youth and splendor, he possessed a radiance like that of the assembly of Kāmadeva.
Having seen that beautiful Padmā, the all-pervading Lord Vṛṣa spoke, in order to ascertain the inner disposition of that sage’s wife.
Dharma said: "O beautiful one, O Lakṣmī, you who are truly worthy of a king, enchanting, in the full bloom of youth, and possessing eternal youth, O passionate one!"
O slender-limbed one, I tell you the truth: in the presence of the sage Pippalāda, who is old and afflicted by age, you do not shine at all.
Abandon this brahmin who is devoted to asceticism, merciless, and on the verge of death; look instead at me, O Indra among kings, a hero in love and afflicted by passion.
The virtuous Sundarī attains the beauty of her previous birth through merit; all of that becomes fruitful through the embrace of a connoisseur of aesthetic delight.
O beloved, having completely abandoned that husband, make me—your servant, who is dear to a thousand beauties and is an expert in the science of love—yours.
Sport with me in secluded, delightful forests, upon every mountain, and on the banks of rivers; make this birth fruitful.
Vasiṣṭha said: When he had spoken thus, that devoted wife, descending from her own chariot, spoke to him as he was eager to seize her by the hand.
Padmā said: "Go far away! Go far away, O most wicked lord of men! If you look upon me with lust, you will perish instantly."
Having abandoned Pippalāda, the best of sages, whose body was purified by asceticism, how could I resort to you, who are conquered by women and addicted to pleasure?
By the mere touch of one conquered by women, all merit perishes; one conquered by women is a great sinner, and even the sight of him brings about sin.
For that man who is conquered by a woman is always impure despite his ritual observances; him the ancestors, the gods, and all human beings alike revile.
Of what use is his knowledge, asceticism, recitation, fire-offerings, or worship; or what is the use of learning or charity for one whose mind has been stolen by women?
"Because you speak to me, your mother, having assumed the state of a woman, by that [act] there shall come a destruction of you through my curse at that time."
Vasiṣṭha said: O King, having heard Satī’s curse, Dharma abandoned his form; assuming his own original form, that Lord of Gods spoke while trembling.
Dharma said: "O Mother, know me to be Dharma, the teacher of the wise and the teacher of teachers; O virtuous lady, I am he who always regards the wives of others as his own mother."
I have come into your presence to discern your inner intent; I know your mind, yet I am impelled by destiny.
O virtuous lady, my subduing of you was done properly and not contrary to what is right; for the punishment of those who stand on the wrong path has been ordained by the Lord himself.
Salutations indeed to that Śiva, who is himself the bestower of happiness, suffering, and boons to all, and who alone is capable of granting both prosperity and adversity.
Salutations indeed to that Śiva, who is capable of ordaining enemy and friend, of bringing about affection and strife, and who can create and destroy the entire creation.
Salutations indeed to that Śiva, by whom milk was formerly made white, coldness was produced in water, and the fire was made to burn.
Salutations indeed to that Śiva, by whom primordial nature (prakṛti) was fashioned after performing intense penance from the beginning, and by whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others were created.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Dharma, the teacher of the world, stood before her; struck with wonder and gratified by her devotion to her husband, he said nothing at all.
Then that princess Padmā, the beloved of Pippalāda, being virtuous and understanding that dharma, spoke in wonder, O Parvata.
Padmā said: "O Dharma, you alone are the witness of all the actions of everyone; O Lord, why do you mock me by attempting to discern my mind?"
O Brahmin, all that was done by me did not constitute an offense; yet you were cursed by me out of ignorance and the nature of women, O bull among men, to no purpose.
I am now reflecting upon what the proper course of action for him should be; may that wisdom flash forth in my mind by which I shall indeed attain well-being.
Even if this sky and all the directions were to perish, or even if the winds should cease to blow, nevertheless, the curse of a virtuous woman can never be nullified.
O King of the Gods, you shine at all times, day and night, with truth complete in its four quarters, like the moon on the full-moon day.
If you were to perish, then there would be the destruction of creation; thus, though bewildered as to what ought to be done, I speak even in vain.
And there will be a destruction by one quarter in the Tretā age, O best of gods; in the Dvāpara, it will be by another quarter, and in the Kali age, O Lord, even the third quarter will perish.
At the end of the Kali age, all your limbs will be severed; when the Satya Yuga returns, you shall become whole once again.
In the Satya Yuga you are all-pervading, and in the others you exist in certain places; according to the arrangement of the ages, you will manifest in such and such ways.
"May these words of mine be true and bring you happiness; I am going to serve my husband, so go to your own home, O Lord."
Brahmā said: Having heard her words, Vṛṣa indeed became well-pleased; O son of Brahmā, he spoke thus to that virtuous woman who had spoken in such a manner.
Dharma said: "Blessed are you; you are devoted to your husband. May it be well with you, O faithful wife! Choose a boon, for your husband shall grant it for the sake of protecting you."
May your husband be young, a hero in love, and righteous; may he be handsome, virtuous, eloquent, and possessed of perpetual, stable youth.
O auspicious lady, may he live longer than Mārkaṇḍeya; may he possess wealth like Kubera and sovereignty like Śakra.
He was a devotee of Śiva, equal to Hari, and a perfected master (siddha) superior even to Kapila; in intelligence he was equal to Bṛhaspati, and in equanimity he was equal to Brahmā.
May you remain endowed with the good fortune of your husband for as long as you live; and likewise, O blessed lady, may you possess perpetual youth.
"You shall become the mother of ten virtuous and long-lived sons who will surpass even your own husband; of this there is no doubt."
O virtuous lady, may your homes be endowed with every prosperity, always radiant within and surpassing even the palace of Kubera.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, Dharma remained there on that best of mountains; she, having circumambulated him and bowed down, went to her own home.
Having thus bestowed his blessings upon Dharma, he departed for his own abode; and in assembly after assembly, he praised that Padmā.
She constantly took delight with her young husband in private; subsequently, virtuous sons were born who surpassed their father in qualities.
Every kind of prosperity arose, increasing the happiness of the couple, bringing an increase of all bliss and leading to well-being both in this world and the next.
O Lord of Mountains, you have related this entire ancient history; out of affection for that couple, it has been heard by you with the utmost reverence.
Having understood the truth, give your daughter Pārvatī to Īśvara; O Lord of Mountains, abandon your pride along with your wife Menā.
When seven days have passed, at an auspicious moment that is difficult to find, when the lord of the ascendant is situated in the ascendant and the Moon is conjoined with its own son (Mercury).
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Monday when the moon was in conjunction with the Rohiṇī asterism—pure, with the moon and stars clearly visible, and free from all defects.
To Jupiter, who is free from all false attachments and views of grasping at the unreal, who bestows virtuous offspring, and who grants good fortune to one’s husband.
O Mountain, by giving away your daughter Girijā—the Mother of the World, the Sovereign Primordial Nature—to the Father of the World, may you become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of the wise, fell silent while remembering Śiva, the Lord who performs manifold divine sports.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Padmā and Pippalāda," in the third section (Pārvatī-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Himālaya, along with his attendants, was filled with wonder; that lord of mountains spoke to the other mountains through his wife.
Himālaya said: O Meru, king of mountains, Sahya, Gandhamādana, Mandara, Maināka, Vindhya, and all you lords of mountains, listen to my words!
Vasiṣṭha indeed speaks thus: "What task of mine is being deliberated? Having considered everything with your minds, declare it exactly as you have resolved."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, Sumeru and the other mountains, having reached a firm conclusion, spoke with affection to Himālaya.
The mountains said: "What is the use of further deliberation now? The task has indeed been accomplished. O illustrious one, she has appeared solely for the sake of the gods' mission."
"She must be given away, saying 'To Śiva,' for the sake of Śiva, as she has descended for his purpose. Rudra is propitiated by her, provided she has been spoken of by Rudra."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Meru and the others, Himācala became exceedingly pleased, and Girijā laughed within her heart.
And Arundhatī enlightened Menā regarding that matter by means of a collection of various statements and also through diverse historical narratives.
Then Menakā, the wife of the mountain, having understood this, became clear-minded; she fed the sages, Arundhatī, and the mountain, and then she herself ate.
Then the wise Śailavara, having served those sages well, spoke with affection and joined palms, his mind serene and his delusions dispelled.
Himācala said: "O highly fortunate Seven Sages, listen to my words; all my wonder has vanished, for I have heard the life-story of Śiva and Śivā."
My body, my wife Menā, my sons and daughters, as well as Ṛddhi and Siddhi, and everything else belongs to Śiva alone and not otherwise.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, he then looked upon his daughter with respect and, having adorned her limbs, placed her upon the lap of the sage.
And then the King of Mountains spoke again with affection to the sages: "It has been decided by me that this portion must be given to him."
The sages said: O Mountain, Śaṅkara himself is the beggar and you are the donor; and Pārvatī, the goddess, is the alms. What could be more excellent than this?
Because of you, Himavat, the course of the mountain peaks is rendered similar; blessed are you, the sovereign of all mountains, the most excellent in every respect.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to the maiden, the sages of pure intent bestowed their blessing upon her, saying, "May you be a bestower of happiness to Śiva."
Having touched her there with your hand, may prosperity be yours; may your virtues increase just as the moon waxes during the bright fortnight.
Having spoken thus and joyfully offered flowers along with fruits to the mountain, all the sages then established their conviction.
Then Arundhatī, the supreme and virtuous wife of Śiva, joyfully gladdened Menā there and captivated her with her excellent qualities.
He groomed his mountain-like beard with turmeric and saffron, adopting worldly custom as the most excellent means for auspiciousness.
Then, on the fourth day, having fixed an excellent auspicious moment and being mutually satisfied, they went into the presence of Śiva.
Having gone there, bowed to Śiva, and praised him with various eloquent hymns, all the sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, spoke to the Supreme Lord.
The sages said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Lord, Great Master! Listen with affection to our words regarding that which has been done by your servants.
O Maheśāna, through various eloquent words from Bodhita, Girirāja, and Menā, he has undoubtedly awakened along with the Itihāsas.
Pārvatī has indeed been given in word by the Lord of Mountains; it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, proceed to the wedding accompanied by your Gaṇas and the gods.
Go quickly, O Great God, O Lord, to the home of Himācala; marry Pārvatī according to the custom for the sake of procreating offspring.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of theirs, Maheśāna—who is devoted to worldly conduct—became joyful in spirit and, smiling, spoke this.

Maheśa said: O highly fortunate ones, indeed neither the marriage ceremony nor its specific ritual has been seen or heard by me as it was performed by you in the past; therefore, let that procedure be explained in detail.
Brahmā said: Having heard those auspicious, worldly words of Maheśa, they laughed and replied to Sadāśiva, the God of gods.
The sages said: "Having quickly summoned Viṣṇu, especially along with his assembly, as well as Brahmā together with his sons, and likewise the god Śatakratu with affection,"
Likewise, [he saw] all the hosts of ṛṣis, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, as well as the siddhas, vidyādharas, and the throngs of apsarases.
O Lord, bring all these and others here with respect; they will accomplish your entire task, of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and received his command, all seven sages joyfully departed for their own abodes, praising the path of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Words of the Seven Sages," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O dear father, O wise one, now that the seven sages have departed, please show me your grace, O Lord, and tell me what Himavat did after they had gone.
Brahmā said: O Lord of Sages, after those seven sages, along with Arundhatī, had departed, I shall tell you what Himavat did.
Then, having taken leave of his brothers, Meru, and the others, the high-minded Himavat, lord of mountains, rejoiced together with his sons and his beloved.
Then, having been thus commanded, Himavat, with great joy, had the marriage date letter written with affection by Garga, his own family priest.
Then, with his joyful kinsmen providing various kinds of provisions, he dispatched that letter for the sake of Śiva’s welfare.
Those people, having gone there to Kailāsa into the presence of Śiva, offered that letter to Śiva after applying the tilaka mark.
Having been especially honored by their lord in a fitting manner, they all arrived at the vicinity of the mountain with joyful hearts.
Seeing the people who had arrived, having been especially honored by Maheśa and filled with great joy, the Mountain rejoiced exceedingly in his heart.
Then, filled with joy, he issued an invitation to all his kinsmen who resided in various lands, providing a source of happiness for them all.
Then, with great care, he had a collection of gold prepared, as well as various materials suitable for the performance of the wedding ceremony.
Many mountains of rice, and likewise of flattened grains (pṛthuka), as well as of jaggery, sugar, and salt.
He constructed ponds of milk, clarified butter, and curds, as well as of wheat and other grain flours, and likewise of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
There he constructed ponds filled with śaṣkulīs, svastikas, and likewise with sugar-candies, as well as with nectar and sugarcane juice.
Indeed, there were many varieties of *hiyaṅgava* rice and likewise of fermented liquors (*āsava*), as well as various collections of cooked foods of great and delicious flavor.
Various kinds of seasoned foods beneficial for the assembly and the gods, as well as various priceless garments that are purified by fire.
Having collected these and other substances—varieties of precious gems, gold, and silver—in accordance with the prescribed ritual, [he should proceed].
On the auspicious day, the mountain began to perform the rites of blessing; the women of the mountains had Pārvatī undergo the purificatory sacraments.
Seeing him, the women of the city’s brahmins, adorned themselves with ornaments and joyfully performed auspicious rites; they observed the traditional customs of the world.
There, Himālaya too, with a joyful heart, performed various auspicious rites preceded by excellent blessings, amidst a festive celebration.
With his whole being, he was deeply pleased and longed for the arrival of his circle of kinsmen; in the meantime, his relatives were invited.
They arrived joyfully, accompanied by their wives, sons, and retinues; at that very time, O celestial sage, listen with attention to the arrival of Giri.
I shall describe in brief, for the sake of increasing the pleasure of Śiva, that great mountain which is a divine temple and possesses a celestial form.
The assembly, together with its retinue, was resplendent with various jewels; having diligently gathered the essence of diverse gems and great precious stones, they were present there.
Well-dressed, adorned, and glorious, that mountain Mandara, rich in every beauty and accompanied by his wives and sons, went to the Himalaya.
Having gathered various offerings, the divine-souled and noble-minded Astācala also departed with his gifts.
Endowed with great splendor and filled with joy, he arrived, bringing excellent jewels and gems from the mountain of sunrise.
Surrounded by an exceedingly excellent retinue, the Great Blissful One arrived; for Mount Malaya, the king of mountains, came with his own retinue in respectful attendance.
Adorned with excellent celestial ornaments and accompanied by a great army, the one named Dardura arrived immediately, joyful and together with his wife.
Accompanied by great splendor, O dear one, the father went to the home of the Himālaya mountain; Niṣadha also, with a joyful heart, arrived along with his retinue.
Accompanied by his sons and groups of women, he went with joy to the home of the Himavat mountain; the highly fortunate Gandhamādana, the lord of the earth, arrived there as well.
Likewise, Karavīra, endowed with great majesty, and Mahendra, the best of mountains, came to the Himalaya. ||3||
Accompanied by his retinue, sons, and wife, and endowed with great splendor, Pāriyātra was indeed joyful in spirit and possessed of a mine of jewels and gems.

Accompanied by his attendants and retinue, Krauñca, the king of mountains, possessing a vast and powerful entourage, came from the snowy mountain range; that best of peaks arrived, respectfully bringing offerings.
Puruṣottamaśaila also, together with his retinue and respectfully taking great gifts, came to the Himavat mountain.
Accompanied by his wife and endowed with wealth, Nīla, full of grace and filled with joy, arrived at the house of Himāga.
Trikūṭa, Citrakūṭa, Veṅkaṭa, Śrīgiri, Gokāmukha, and Nārada likewise approached the abode of Himavat.
And Vindhya, the best of mountains, endowed with various riches, arrived with a joyful heart, accompanied by his wife and son, auspicious in appearance.
The great mountain Kālañjara, filled with much joy and accompanied by many hosts of sages, came out of affection to the Himālaya mountain.
The great mountain Kailāsa, filled with immense joy, arrived, acting out of compassion as the radiant Lord who shines above all.
O twice-born one, all other mountain lords who reside in other continents, as well as all the mountains here on this earth, came to the Himalaya.
O Sage, having been previously invited by him with joy, all the mountains arrived there out of affection, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī."
Then Śoṇabhadra and all the others indeed arrived with great joy and much splendor, thinking, "The marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī is taking place."
All the rivers, adorned with various ornaments and assuming divine forms, arrived out of affection, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā."
The Godāvarī, the Yamunā, the Brahmastrī, and likewise the Veṇikā came to the Himālaya mountain for the marriage of Śiva and Śivā.
Ganga, endowed with various ornaments and possessing a divine form, went forth with great joy and affection, thinking, "The wedding of Shiva and [Parvati] has taken place."
Narmadā, the daughter of Rudra and best of rivers, filled with great joy, departed swiftly with great delight, for the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī had taken place.
Then, with all of them having arrived from every direction to the snowy mountain, that divine city, endowed with every splendor, became crowded.
The great festival was preeminent with shimmering banners, flags, and arches; the sun was obscured by canopies, and it was likewise filled with various radiant splendors.
The Himalaya also, with great affection and various marks of respect, accorded proper honor to them both, each according to their respective status.
He settled everyone in various excellent locations, one by one, and satisfied them entirely with manifold provisions.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispatch of the Marriage Proposal, the Gathering of Preparations, and the Arrival of Śilā," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Himavat, the lord of mountains, being pleased, O best of sages, constructed his own city, which was wonderful and filled with supreme festivity.
The road was sprinkled with water, well-prepared, and adorned with supreme splendors; and at every gate there were auspicious items such as plantain trees and other offerings.
He prepared the courtyard, furnished with plantain pillars and provided with mango sprouts tied together with silk threads.
It was adorned with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, radiant with shining archways, and beautified by auspicious objects placed on all four sides.

In that very manner, filled with supreme joy, the Lord of Mountains performed everything for the sake of his daughter alone—placing the highly powerful Garga at the forefront—and indeed arranged what was appropriate for the occasion and most auspicious.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he respectfully had him construct a very extensive pavilion, beautiful with its altar and other features.
O celestial sage, it is ten thousand yojanas in extent, endowed with many characteristics and filled with various wonders.
Everything, both stationary and moving, was similar to those [beings] and captivating to the mind; it possessed a universal wonderfulness on all sides, rendered marvelous by various objects.
In that place, the mobile was especially conquered by the immobile, and indeed, the immobile itself was conquered there by the mobile.
In that place, the dry land was conquered by water and not otherwise; for what indeed is water and what is dry land? Even the most learned do not know.
In some places there were artificial lions, in others rows of cranes; and here and there were charming artificial peacocks.
In some places, artificial women were dancing with men, deluding all the people, while they themselves watched other artificial [beings].
In that same manner and by that very rite, the charming gatekeepers, both stationary and resembling mobile beings, stood holding bows in their hands.
Mahālakṣmī stood at the gate, an artificial image fashioned with wonder, endowed with all auspicious marks; they went forth carrying water and unbroken grains of rice.
There were indeed elephants, adorned and artificial, beyond comparison with anything real; likewise there were horses without their riders, and elephants without their mahouts.
Chariots drawn by charioteers, endowed with great wonders, as well as other mounts and artificial infantry.
O sage, it was indeed for the purpose of deluding both the gods and the sages that Viśvakarman, with a joyful heart, performed this deed.
O Sage, Nandin and an artificial image were stationed at the great gate; that [image] was like pure crystal, appearing exactly as Nandin himself.
Above it was the great divine Puṣpaka chariot, adorned with jewels, radiant with sprouts, and beautifully graced with white chowries.
On the left side are two elephants, resembling pure saffron, possessing four tusks, sixty years of age, in rut, and of great splendor.
In that same manner, he made two horses of great luster resembling the sun; they were divine, adorned with chowries, and decorated with celestial ornaments.
Likewise, the world-protectors were armored and enriched with excellent jewels; indeed, all the gods were fashioned according to their true forms by Viśvakarman.
For thus it was that all the sages, such as Bhṛgu and others whose wealth is austerity, as well as other secondary deities (upāsuras) and likewise other perfected beings (siddhas), were created.
And Viṣṇu, accompanied by all his attendants known as Garuḍas, was likewise fashioned as an artificial image, possessing a most wondrous form.
In that very same way, O Nārada, surrounded by my sons, the Vidyādharas, and the Siddhas, I was likewise created as an artificial being, reciting the hymns.
Likewise, an artificial Śakra was fashioned, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, accompanied by his own host, and resembling the full moon.
O celestial sage, what need is there for much speaking? Indeed, the entire assembly of gods was swiftly fashioned by Viśvakarman at the command of Himavat.
Thus was that pavilion made by him, possessing a divine form, filled with many wonders, and great enough to enchant even the gods.
Then, commanded by the Lord of the Mountain, the high-minded Viśvakarman diligently [constructed] those respective worlds for the residence of the gods and others.
And right there, great couches—radiant, most wonderful, delightful, and divine—were fashioned for them by Viśvakarman.
In that manner, he instantly fashioned a marvelous abode for Svayambhū, reaching up to the seven worlds, endowed with supreme splendor.
In the same way, he instantly fashioned another divine realm for Viṣṇu called Vaikuṇṭha, exceedingly radiant and endowed with various wonders.
Viśvakarman constructed that divine, wonderful, and supreme abode of Amareśa, endowed with all sovereign splendors.
He constructed beautiful houses for the world-protectors; likewise, out of affection, he built divine, wonderful, and vast dwellings.
And likewise, he indeed constructed various wonderful abodes for all the other immortals in due order.
Viśvakarman, of great intellect and having obtained a supreme boon from Śambhu, fashioned everything in an instant solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva.

In that very manner, he constructed the most wonderful, supremely radiant, and immensely lustrous abode of Śambhu, which was highly honored by the best of gods, marked with the emblem of the Lord of the Mountain, and beautifully situated within the world of Śiva.
Thus was this composition fashioned by Viśvakarman for the sake of pleasing Śiva; it is variegated, supremely wondrous, and most brilliantly radiant.
Having thus performed all these worldly affairs, Himācala joyfully awaited the arrival of Śambhu.
Thus, O divine sage, the entire heart-gladdening account of Himālaya has been told in its entirety; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Construction of the Pavilion and Other Structures," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O Creator, dear father, O one of great wisdom, disciple of Viṣṇu, salutations be unto you! O treasure-house of compassion, this wonderful story has been heard by us from you.
Now I desire to hear the account of the marriage of the moon-crested Lord, which is most auspicious and the destroyer of the entire multitude of sins.
What did Mahādeva do upon receiving that auspicious letter? Recite that divine narrative concerning Śaṅkara and his supreme self.
Brahmā said: Listen, O child of great wisdom, to the supreme glory of Śaṅkara, which Mahādeva achieved upon receiving the auspicious letter.
Then Śambhu, having joyfully taken that auspicious letter, laughed with a delighted soul; the Lord then bestowed honor upon them.
Having caused it to be recited, he properly accepted it according to the prescribed rites; then, having honored her greatly, he respectfully sent her away with her mother.
He said to those groups of sages, "The auspicious task has been properly accomplished; you must come to my wedding, for the marriage has been accepted by me."
Having heard these words of Śambhu, they were filled with joy; having bowed to him and circumambulated him, they departed for their own abodes, praising their supreme destiny.
Then, O sage, Śambhu, the lord of gods, accompanied by Umā, the Lord who performs great divine sports, quickly approached you while conforming to worldly custom.
You have arrived out of supreme affection, praising the highest ordinance; bowing with shoulders bent, humble in spirit, and with palms joined in reverence.
Repeatedly uttering shouts of "Victory! and praising his command, you should act according to his instruction, O wise one.
Then Śambhu, his soul delighted, displaying his worldly form, spoke to you, O best of sages, pleasing you with auspicious words.

Śiva said: Listen with affection, O best of sages; indeed, I shall speak to you today from my own mouth. I tell you this truth because you are dear to me, being the crest-jewel among the kings of devotees.
A great penance was performed by the goddess Pārvatī at your command; being gratified, I indeed granted her a boon that she should become my wife.
"I shall perform the marriage, for I am devoted to her will; and that auspicious moment has been determined and purified by the Seven Sages."
O Nārada, on the seventh day from today that will come to pass; resorting to worldly custom, I shall perform a great festival.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Soul, O dear one, you, with a serene mind, bowed to the Lord and spoke these words.
Nārada said: This is indeed your vow; you are considered to be subject to the will of your devotees. And that which was desired in the mind of Pārvatī has been perfectly fulfilled by you.
O Lord, you must tell me something that is similar to my own situation; for consider me your servant and show me mercy—salutations be unto you!
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having been addressed thus by you, Śambhu Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, replied with a gracious soul and great respect to you.
Śiva said: O Sage, at my word, you must certainly invite Viṣṇu and the other gods, as well as the sages and Siddhas, and all others from every direction.
May they all come with enthusiasm, endowed with every splendor, accompanied by their wives and groups of sons, out of affection and out of respect for my command.
O Sage, those gods and others who do not come here to my wedding festival must certainly not be considered my own kin by me.
Brahmā said: O Sage, having then received this command from the Lord, you, the beloved of Śaṅkara, went quickly to each of them and invited them all.
O Nārada, having quickly approached the presence of Śambhu, that best of sages remained there as His messenger, having received His command.
Śiva also remained there full of longing, eager for his arrival, while all his attendants danced in every direction amidst a great celebration.
At that very time, however, Acyuta, having fashioned his own disguise, quickly arrived at Kailāsa accompanied by his retinue.
Having prostrated before Śiva with true devotion, together with his wife and followers, he joyfully received His command and remained in that excellent place with a delighted mind.
Thus, accompanied by my own attendants, I quickly went to Kailāsa with joy; having prostrated before the Lord, I remained there full of bliss together with my followers.
Indra and the other guardians of the world arrived with their retinues; likewise, all were adorned, full of festive joy, and accompanied by their wives.
In the same way, the sages, nāgas, siddhas, and secondary deities, as well as others who had been properly invited, arrived here joyfully for the festival.
Then Maheśvara joyfully offered individual honors to all those who had arrived there, beginning with the immortals.
Then a great and most wonderful festival took place on Kailāsa; at that time, the celestial women performed dances and other arts as was appropriate.
At that time, O Sage, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, who had assembled there, remained in that place to cause the procession of Śambhu to take place.
Then, commanded by Śiva and constrained by the thought "this is mine," they all performed this entire service to Śiva as a task for Śiva.
Then those seven mothers, filled with joy, performed the supreme rite of adorning Śiva there once again, each according to her own capacity.
O best of sages, the natural attire of that radiant Supreme Lord then became devoid of ornaments, according to His own will.
At that time, the moon took its place upon his crown; indeed, his beautiful eye became a third, auspicious tilaka.
O Sage, those two serpents who were celebrated as his ear-ornaments became his earrings, adorned with various jewels.
The serpents stationed upon his other limbs became his ornaments, exceedingly beautiful and composed of various jewels.
The body-unguent was the manifestation of splendor arising from sandalwood and other substances; his divine silk garment became as beautiful as the elephant hide and other such ornaments.
Such a beautiful form has arisen, its complexion exceedingly difficult to achieve; even Īśvara himself has directly obtained sovereignty by his own nature.

Then all the gods, the Dānavas, the Nāgas, the Pataṅgas, the Apsarases, and the great ṛṣis, having gathered together in the presence of Śiva, were filled with joy and, amidst great festivities, exclaimed, "Aho! (How wonderful!)
They all said: "Go, go, O Mahādeva, for the sake of the marriage with the great goddess Girijā; show us your grace, O Maheśvara."
Then Viṣṇu, his mind delighted by the knowledge [of Śiva], bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara and spoke these words appropriate to the occasion.
Viṣṇu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; O Lord, the fulfiller of the needs of your own devotees, hear my petition.
O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, you ought to perform the rite of your own marriage here with the goddess, the daughter of the Mountain Lord.
O Hara, when the rite of marriage is performed by you, indeed everyone in that world shall attain supreme happiness.
O Lord, establishing the pavilion and performing the *nāndīmukha* rite according to the family tradition, carry them out with joy, proclaiming your own glory throughout the world.
Brahmā said: Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, devoted to worldly custom, performed that according to the prescribed rite.
For I was appointed by him to perform everything appropriate for prosperity; thus, with affection and due respect, I carried out those rites there along with the sages.
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhāguri, Guru, Kaṇva, Bṛhaspati, Śakti, Jamadagni, and Parāśara.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Śilāpāka, Aruṇapāla, Akṛtaśrama, Agastya, Cyavana, Garga, and Śilāda, O great sage.
Dadhīci, Upamanyu, Bharadvāja, Akṛtavraṇa, Pippalāda, then Kuśika, Kautsa, and Vyāsa along with his disciples.
These and many others came into the presence of Śiva; urged by me, they performed the rites there according to the prescribed rules.

All those who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences performed the protective rites for Maheśa according to the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas, having first performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony.
Likewise, all the sages, out of affection, performed numerous auspicious rites with the hymns of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as various other supreme prayers.
Out of affection for Śambhu and myself, they joyfully performed the worship of the planets and of all the deities situated within the maṇḍala for the sake of pacifying obstacles.
Then Śiva, being well-pleased, performed all appropriate worldly and Vedic rites and bowed joyfully to the twice-born.
Then Sarveśvara, having placed the brahmins and the gods at his vanguard, departed joyfully from that Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
Outside the Kailāsa mountain, the Lord Śambhu stood filled with joy, accompanied by the gods and the twice-born, accepting various offerings.
Then a great festival was held there by the gods and others, consisting of song, instrumental music, and beautiful dance, for the sake of pleasing Maheśa.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Invitation of the Devas, the Arrival of the Devas, and the Procession of Śiva," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, having summoned Nandin and all the Gaṇas, joyfully commanded them to go there along with him.
Śiva said: "May you all, having left a certain number of attendants here, proceed with me to the city on the mountain, preceded by a great festival."
Brahmā said: Then, having been thus commanded, those lords of the hosts (Gaṇeśas) set forth with joy, taking their respective forces; I shall describe them to you as best as I can.
And Śaṅkhakarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, accompanied by ten million Gaṇas, arrived at the city of Himācala in order to join with Śiva.
Keekarākṣa, who presides over a great festival, leads ten koṭis of Gaṇas; and Vikṛta, the leader of the Gaṇas, leads eight koṭis.
And Viśākha, the leader of the hosts, with four crores; and Pārijāta, the bull among the hosts, with nine crores.
The glorious Sarvāntaka has sixty [attendants], and likewise Vikṛtānana; Dundubha, the leader of the Gaṇas, has eight times ten million times ten million Gaṇas.
O Sage, the Gaṇeśa named Kapāla was accompanied by five crores, and the heroic Sandāraka by six crores of Gaṇas.
In this world, Kanduka and Kuṇḍaka each have eight crores of crores [of followers], while the Gaṇapa Viṣṭambha likewise has eight crores of crores of Gaṇas.
O best of sages, the joyful Gaṇapa Pippala went forth with ten billion followers, as did the heroic Gaṇeśa Saṃnādaka.
Likewise, Āveśana, the leader of the Gaṇas, went with eight koṭis, while Mahākeśa, the lord of the Gaṇas, went with a thousand koṭis.
O Sage, Kuṇḍa indeed went with twelve crores, and likewise Parvataka with eight crores; Vīra went with [seven] crores, as did Candratāpana.
Kāla, Kālaka, Mahākāla, and indeed Śatakoṭigaṇanātha, as well as the one named Agnika.
The leader of the hosts arrived with ten million [attendants] at Agnimukha; likewise, Ādityamūrdhā and Ghanāvaha each arrived with ten million.
Sannāha is indeed the leader of a hundred koṭis, as is Kumuda; likewise, Amogha and Kokila are leaders of a hundred koṭis each.
Sumantra, the leader of hosts, with sixty million hosts; and Kākapādodara, likewise Santānaka, with sixty million.
Mahābala with nine [koṭis], Madhupiṅga and Kokila, Nīla with ninety koṭis, and likewise Pūrṇabhadra.
Caturvaktra went with seventy million, Karaṇa with two hundred million, Gaṇeśāna with nine hundred million, and Romaka indeed with [one hundred] million.
O Nārada, Yajvāśa, Śatamanyu, and Meghamanyu—all these leaders of the Gaṇas departed individually with ten million followers each.
Kāṣṭhāṅguṣṭha, the leader of sixty-four crores; Virūpākṣa, Sukeśa, Vṛṣābha, and Sanātana.
Tālaketu, Ṣaḍāsya, Cañcvāsya, Sanātana, Samvartaka, Caitra, Lakulīśa, and Svayamprabhu.
O Sage, [the attendants] are Lokāntaka, the radiant Dīptātman, likewise Daityāntaka, the glorious god Bhṛṅgiriṭi, and Devadevapriya.
Aśani and Bhānuka, along with sixty-four thousand others, went forth for the sake of Śiva’s wedding, accompanied by Śiva himself in great celebration.
The Pramathas were led by Bhūtakoṭi with a thousand [attendants], Vīrabhadra with thirty million, and [the attendants] born from his body-hair with sixty-four crores.
Surrounded by twenty hundred thousand times ten million [attendants], Nandin and the other leaders of the Gaṇas went there for the festival of Śaṅkara.
Kṣetrapāla and Bhairava, accompanied by hosts numbering in the millions upon millions, arrived with joy at the great festival for the marriage of Śaṅkara.
These and other countless leaders of the hosts, possessed of great strength, went there with great joy and enthusiasm for the festival of Śaṅkara.
All of them have a thousand arms, wear crowns of matted hair, are adorned with crescent moons, possess blue throats, and have three eyes.
All were adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads and likewise smeared with sacred ash; they were further embellished with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crowns, and other such finery.
Resembling Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, endowed with the powers of atomization (aṇimā) and other qualities, and radiant like ten million suns, the lords of the Gaṇas shone there.
O Sage, some move upon the earth, some move in the netherworld (Pātāla), some move in the sky, and some move in the seven heavens.
O celestial sage, what need is there for further words? Out of affection for Śambhu, all the inhabitants of the worlds and their respective hosts arrived at the festival of Śaṅkara.
Thus, accompanied by the gods, the Gaṇas, and others, the Lord Śaṅkara went to the city of the Himavat mountain for the sake of his own marriage.
O Lord of Sages, listen now to what occurred there when the Lord of All arrived for the sake of the marriage, accompanied by the gods and others.
Having become the sister of Rudra, Caṇḍī, accompanied by a great festival, arrived there with great joy, bringing fear to her enemies.
Seated upon a corpse-throne, adorned with ornaments of serpents, she holds a highly radiant golden pitcher full [of nectar] upon her head.
Accompanied by her own retinue, with blazing faces and blazing eyes, she displayed great curiosity, filled with joy, and possessed of great strength.
There, O Sage, many millions of divine hosts of spirits, both deformed and of various other kinds, shone forth in great abundance at that time.
Then Caṇḍī, with her distorted face, went before them—filled with curiosity, delighted, and intent on causing an obstacle to their joy.
Then all the hosts of Rudras, numbering eleven crores and beloved by the fierce Rudra, were placed behind Caṇḍī.
Then the three worlds were pervaded by the resounding blasts of the hand-drums (ḍamaru), by the booming sound of kettledrums (bherī), and by the blaring of conch shells (śaṅkha).
Likewise, from the sounds of the drums, a tumultuous roar arose; it brought auspiciousness to the world and destroyed all that was inauspicious.
O Sage, all the gods, along with all the Siddhas and the world-protectors (Lokapālas), followed behind the hosts, filled with eager anticipation.
Then, O sage, as he proceeded through the midst [of the assembly], Rameśa, seated upon Garuḍa, shone brilliantly while being honored by a great multitude of warriors.
Fanned with chowries, surrounded by his own attendants and radiant companions, he was adorned with the various ornaments of his own attire.
Likewise, I too, while traveling on the path, was indeed rendered resplendent and beautiful by the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and the Āgamas, all of which had assumed embodied forms.
Accompanied by the great Siddhas beginning with Sanaka, as well as his sons who were Prajāpatis and his retinue, he was indeed intent upon the service of Śiva.
Standing upon the elephant Airāvata in the midst of his own army, the lord of the gods, Śakra, shone brilliantly as he proceeded, adorned with his name.
Then, as they were proceeding, those many sages shone with great longing for the wedding of Śiva.
Śākinīs, Yātudhānas, Vetālas, Brahmarākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, as well as others such as the Pramathas and so forth.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, Hūhū, and other excellent Gandharvas and Kinnaras went forth, joyfully playing their musical instruments.
All the mothers of the world, all the daughters of the gods from every quarter, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, and other celestial women;
These and other wives of the gods, the mothers of Bhava, all went forth filled with joy at the wedding of Śaṅkara.
Resembling pure crystal, the bull is most beautiful; he who is called Dharma by the Vedas, the scriptures, and the perfected great seers.
Mounted upon that bull, Mahādeva, who is devoted to righteousness, shone exceedingly as he proceeded, attended by all the gods and sages.

Accompanied by these great sages who had attained their fruits, Maheśa shone brilliantly, adorned with many ornaments, as he proceeded to the home of the mountain named Himālaya for the sake of Pārvatī’s marriage.
Thus has been told the life of Śambhu, his supreme festival of departure, and the noble conduct arising from the city of Himālaya; listen to this, O Nārada.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, having consulted among themselves and obtained the command of Śiva, O sage, Hari sent you first to the abode of the mountain.
Then, having bowed to the Lord of All, you departed ahead of Nārada; urged with affection by Hari, you proceeded toward the abode of Himācala.
O Sage, having gone there, you saw yourself filled with shame; it was an artificial form created there by Viśvakarman, which left you astonished.
O great sage, you became weary of that artificial self and turned your gaze toward the conduct of Viśvakarman.
He entered the pavilion of that Himavat mountain, which was adorned with jewels, graced with golden pitchers, and beautifully decorated with plantain trees and other ornaments.
O Sage, having seen that most wonderful and marvelous structure endowed with a thousand pillars, as well as the altar, you were indeed filled with amazement.
Then, O Sage Nārada, you spoke to the Lord of Mountains, being greatly astonished in your mind, your knowledge lost, and your intellect bewildered.
"O gods, led by Viṣṇu, why have you now arrived? Likewise, all the great ṛṣis, the Siddhas, and the secondary deities [have come]."
Mahādeva has arrived, mounted upon his bull and surrounded by his attendants; tell me the truth, O Lord of Mountains—is it for the sake of marriage?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, O sage, that mountain Himavat, his mind filled with wonder, spoke these truthful words to you.
Himavat said: "O Nārada, O one of great wisdom, Śiva has not yet arrived now for the sake of Pārvatī’s marriage, accompanied by his attendants and his retinue."
O Nārada, know with a steady mind that this wonderful creation was made by Viśvakarman; abandon your amazement, O divine sage, remain composed, and remember Śiva.
Having eaten and rested, being well-pleased and having shown compassion toward me, go to the presence of Śaṅkara along with Maināka and the other mountains.

O Mahāmata, having been entreated by these mountains, bring here quickly that which is auspicious; [bring him] who is accompanied by the gods and the hosts of great sages, whose sprout-like feet are worshipped by both gods and asuras.

Brahmā said: Having replied, "So be it," you indeed came quickly along with the daughter of the mountain and the others; having performed the necessary rites there and partaken of food, O high-minded one, you went into the presence of Śiva.
There, Mahādeva was seen, surrounded by the gods and others; he, the radiant one, was indeed saluted with devotion by you and those mountain deities.
Then, O sage, all the gods including Indra, as well as all the attendants of Rudra, questioned you along with Viṣṇu and me.
Filled with wonder upon seeing the mountains—Maināka, Sahya, Meru, and others—adorned with various ornaments, their minds were overwhelmed with doubt.
