The gods said: "O Nārada, O one of great wisdom, you appear truly amazed. Have you been honored by the descendant of Himavat, or not? Tell us in detail."
"O most excellent beings, why have these mountains—Maināka, Sahya, Meru, and others—so majestic and well-adorned, come here?"
"O Nārada, will that mountain give his daughter away in this birth or not? O father, tell me what is happening today in the house of Himālaya."
Thus, for us and for these dwellers of heaven whose minds are filled with doubt, dispel the uncertainty as we question you, O observer of noble vows.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard these words of Viṣṇu and the other inhabitants of heaven, you were indeed struck with wonder by the illusory power of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, and so you spoke to them.

And having approached me, Viṣṇu, in a secluded place, you, O sage, spoke these words to Śacīpati, the lord of all the gods, the one who clipped the wings [of the mountains] and the ancient enemy of the mountains: “O Muni, you spoke these words to me, Viṣṇu, as I stood in solitude: ‘[Speak to] the Lord of Śacī, the sovereign of all the gods, the one who clipped the wings [of the mountains], the ancient enemy of the mountains.’”

Nārada said: That wonderful and bewildering form was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, which indeed deludes all the inhabitants of heaven; for it was by means of that very form, through skillful artifice, that he desired to enchant all the gods out of love.
O Lord of Śacī, all that delusion previously wrought by you has been utterly forgotten; therefore, this one desires to conquer you even within the home of that high-souled mountain Dhruva.
I was utterly deluded by that radiant semblance; likewise Viṣṇu was made such by him, as were Brahmā and Śakra.
O Lord of Gods, what need is there for much speaking? All the hosts of gods have been rendered artificial through various forms; nothing whatsoever has been left remaining.
For the purpose of deluding all the gods, and especially [the chief among them], a wondrous illusion was created, intended to provoke laughter and amusement.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, the lord of the gods, his body agitated with fear, then quickly spoke these words to Viṣṇu, to Hari.
The Lord of the Gods said: "O God of gods, O Lord of Ramā, Tvaṣṭṛ will slay me; tormented by grief for his son, he will do so under this pretext and no other."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, Janārdana, the God of gods, spoke these words with a smile, then consoling Śakra.
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of Śacī, you were previously deluded by the Nivātakavacas—the Dānavas who are your ancient enemies—solely through the power of their great vidyā."
O Vāsava, by my word, this Himavat mountain as well as all other mountains have been made wingless.
Indeed, having seen these mountains through the power of illusion by means of mindfulness, those fools who wish to conquer them need not fear even in the city of the gods.
For the Lord Śaṅkara is indeed the master of us all and is affectionate toward his devotees; O Śakra, he will undoubtedly bring about our welfare in every way.
Brahmā said: While Śakra was thus conversing with a distracted mind, Giriśa, having been addressed by Hari, resorted to worldly behavior.
Īśvara said: "O Hari, O Sureśāna, what are you two saying to each other today? Having spoken thus, O Sage, Maheśāna replied to you.
What indeed does the great mountain say? Speak the truth, O Nārada; tell me the entire account, for you ought not to keep anything hidden.
Does Śaila give his own daughter or not? Tell me that quickly. What did you see there, and what did you do upon going there? O father, tell me all of that today with affection.
Brahmā said: O Sage, having been thus addressed by Śambhu there, you, who have the vision of the gods, recounted everything that was seen by you in that pavilion, including all its secrets.
Nārada said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, listen to my auspicious words; O Lord, there is indeed no fear whatsoever of obstacles regarding this marriage."
Śaileśa will certainly give you his daughter; these mountains have come here to bring you—of this there is no doubt.
But today, O Omniscient One, this wonderful illusion has been fashioned for the purpose of deluding the immortals; it is for the sake of curiosity, and there shall be no obstacle whatsoever.
At his command, O Lord, the great master of illusion, Viśvakarman, constructed within the house a wonderful pavilion filled with various marvels.
And an assembly of all the gods was created there as a delusion; seeing that, I was struck with wonder, being deluded by his māyā.
Brahmā said: O dear one, having heard those words, the Lord Śambhu, who ordains the conduct of the worlds, laughed with joy and spoke to all the gods.
Īśvara said: "If Himācala Parvata will indeed give his daughter to me, then what need have I for your illusory power (māyā)? Tell me, Viṣṇu, the truth of the matter."
"O Brahmins, O sages, O gods, speak the truth: what need have I for Māyā if the Mountain will give me his daughter?"

"For the fruit must indeed be accomplished by some means or other," so it is said by the wise who know the principles of logic. Therefore, let all those seeking their goals proceed with haste, led by Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: While Śambhu was thus conversing with the gods, he was brought under the sway of Smara, just as an ordinary man is brought under control by passion.
Then, by the command of Śambhu, Viṣṇu and all the other gods, as well as the high-souled sages, went to that place which dispels the delusion and confusion of the mind.
Placing you at their head, O Sage, they then went with wonder toward the most wonderful abode of Himavat and those other mountains.
Then Hara, accompanied by Viṣṇu and others, joined by his joyful hosts, arrived at the city of Upahaimāga, filled with delight.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction of the Pavilion," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, having heard that the omnipresent Lord had arrived near his own city, Himālaya, the lord of mountains, rejoiced.
Then, having gathered the necessary provisions, he dispatched the mountains and all the brahmins, who were capable of engaging in conversation.
With true devotion, the Mountain, his mind impelled by love, went in person to see the Lord who desires his life; praising his own good fortune with joy, his heart was uplifted by devotion.
Then, seeing the army of the gods, Himavat was filled with wonder; he went forward to meet them, thinking, "I am blessed."
Indeed, seeing that power, the gods were struck with supreme wonder; both the gods and the mountains attained the highest joy.
O Sage, the great army of the mountains and likewise that of the gods, having assembled, shone forth like the eastern and western oceans joined together.
Having come together with one another, those gods and the mountains considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose with supreme joy.
Then, seeing the Lord before him, Himālaya prostrated; all the mountains and the brahmins likewise bowed down to Sadāśiva.
Seated upon a bull, with a serene countenance, adorned with various ornaments, and illuminating the horizons with the divine beauty of his limbs.
His body was adorned with very fine, unblemished, excellent silken garments; his crown shone with precious gems, and he smiled with a pure radiance.
His limbs were adorned with ornaments, his radiant body possessed wondrous features, he was endowed with divine splendor, and he was served by the lords of the gods with chowries in their hands.
[He saw] Acyuta situated on the left, the Lord Vibhu situated on the right side, Hari situated at the back, and the gods and others situated at the rear flanks.
He who is praised by various kinds of gods and others, the benefactor of the world, who assumed a body for his own purpose, the Lord of all, the bestower of boons—[to him, Brahmā said].

He is both with attributes and without attributes, dependent on His devotees, and the source of compassion; He is beyond both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and His nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
On the right side of the Lord, he beheld Hari, the infallible one, mounted upon the son of Vinatā and adorned with various ornaments.
And on the left side of the Lord, O Sage, he indeed beheld me, four-faced and most resplendent, accompanied by my own retinue.
Seeing these two lords of the gods, who are always extremely dear to Śiva, the Lord of the Mountains, together with his retinue, bowed down with reverence.
Likewise, seeing the gods and others shining upon the back and at the sides of Śiva, that lord of the great mountain prostrated before them.
By the command of Śiva, the Mountain went before him to his own city, quickly followed by Śeṣa, Hari, Brahmā, sages, gods, and others.
O Nārada, all the sages, gods, and others, proceeding together with the Lord toward the city of the mountain, spoke at great length.
Having constructed a beautiful peak and installed the deities and other [objects] thereon, Himavat went to that place where the sacrificial altar was prepared according to the rules.
Having specially caused it to be constructed with four corners and adorned with jewels, and having performed the rites of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, he then conducted an examination.
Likewise, Himavat, the king of mountains, sent his sons into the presence of Śiva, who was accompanied by a full assembly including Viṣṇu and others.
Filled with great joy, Himavat, the king of mountains, desired to perform the auspicious rites preceded by a grand festival together with all his kinsmen.
Then those mountain-dwellers, having gone there and bowed down to him, spoke these words of entreaty to the Lord of Mountains along with their own retinue.
Then, by his command, those sons of the mountain went to their own abode; filled with joy, they announced to the king of mountains that he was coming.
Then, having heard the mountain’s speech ending in prayer, all the gods, including Viṣṇu and others, together with their Lord, were exceedingly delighted, O Sage, and rejoiced greatly.
Having dressed themselves in fine attire, all the gods, sages, and hosts, as well as others, set out with the Lord for the abode of the King of Mountains.
At that moment, O sage, Menā became desirous of seeing Śiva; she summoned you, O best of sages, to the presence of the Lord.
O Sage, you then went there, impelled by the Lord who desired to fulfill that purpose for the sake of Śiva’s heart.
Having bowed down to you, O Sage, Menā, her mind filled with wonder, spoke while desiring to behold the form of Śaṅkara, which dispels all pride: "O Lord, [show me] the form of Śaṅkara."
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Meeting at Devagiri," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Menā said: "O sage, I shall first behold that Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain; for what kind indeed is the form of Śiva, for whose sake this supreme austerity is being performed?"
Brahmā said: Thus, devoted to ignorance and desiring a vision of Śiva, she immediately came to the moon-chamber together with you, O sage.
Then Śiva, perceiving his own ego within her, spoke to Viṣṇu, O dear one, the Lord having performed a wonderful sport.
Śiva said: "By my command, you two, O parents, along with the gods, go each separately to the mountain gate; we shall follow afterwards."
Brahmā said: Having heard this, Hari summoned all those who were devoted to him; and all the gods, likewise eager, immediately set out.
O Sage, O Lord of the Universe, you likewise showed Menā, who was staying in her inner chamber, in such a way that her heart would be utterly shattered.
At that time, O Sage, Menā, beholding that most auspicious army and seeing it to be ordinary, became filled with joy.
And first, at that time, the Gandharvas—handsome and fortunate, richly clad in auspicious garments and adorned with various ornaments—arrived.
Accompanied by various vehicles and intent upon various musical instruments, they were joined by hosts of Apsarases and adorned with variegated banners.
Then, seeing Vasu there, her husband and supreme lord, Menā was filled with great joy and said, "This is Śiva."
"These are the attendants of Śiva; this is not Śiva, the husband of Śivā"—thus you spoke to her then, O best of sages.
Having heard this, Menā then became intent on reflection: "Who indeed might be superior to him, and what will he be like?"
In the meantime, the Yakṣas, Maṇigrīva and the others, and their army were seen by her, their splendor doubled.
And seeing her husband Maṇigrīva endowed with such splendor, Menā, filled with joy, said: "This is Rudra, the lord of Śivā."
"This Rudra is not the lord of Śivā; he is indeed a servant of Śiva," you said to the wife of the mountain; meanwhile, that Fire arrived.
Seeing his splendor, which was even twice as great as that, she said, "This is Rudra, the lord of Girijā," but then you replied, "No."
Just then Yama arrived, possessing twice the radiance of him; seeing him, Menā, filled with joy, said, "This is Rudra."
"You said 'no' to her indeed; at that moment Nirṛti arrived, the auspicious lord of the Puṇyajanas, possessing twice the splendor."
Seeing him, Menā joyfully said, "This is Rudra," but you replied to her, "No. Just then, Varuṇa arrived.
Seeing even twice that much splendor there, she said to him: "Is this Rudra, the lord of Girijā, or is it not? To which he replied: "It is not."
Just then, Vāyu arrived, possessing twice the splendor of the former; seeing him, Menā, filled with joy, said, "This is Rudra."
"You said 'no' to her; meanwhile, Dhanada arrived, the lord of the Guhyakas, possessing twice the splendor even than that."
Seeing him, Menā joyfully said, "This is Rudra," but you replied to her, "No. Just then, Īśāna arrived.
Seeing his splendor, which was even twice as great as that, she said, "This is Rudra, the lord of Girijā," but then you replied, "No."
Then Indra arrived, possessing twice the splendor of even that [light], the foremost of all the immortals, the lord of the triple heaven, adorned with various divine ornaments.
Seeing him, Menakā said, "This is Śaṅkara," but you then replied, "No, this is Śakra, the lord of the gods."
Just then the Moon arrived, possessing twice that splendor; seeing him, she said, "This is Rudra," but you replied, "No."
Just then the sun arrived, possessing twice that splendor; seeing him, she said, "He is here," but you replied, "No."
At that time, Bhṛgu and other lords of sages, all of whom were masses of splendor accompanied by their respective groups of disciples, arrived there.
And seeing Vāgīśa right there in their midst, Menakā said, "This is Rudra, the lord of Girijā," to which you then replied, "No."
Just then, Brahmā arrived—the supreme leader of the hosts of splendors, the manifest son of the best of sages, praised as if he were a mass of dharma itself. ||3||
O Sage, seeing him then, Menā was filled with great joy; she said, "This is the husband of Śivā," but you replied to her, "No."
In the meantime, the divine Viṣṇu arrived there, endowed with every splendor, glorious, dark as a rain-cloud, and possessing four arms.
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, wearing yellow garments, the self-ruling Lord, lotus-eyed and peaceful, whose vehicle is the king of birds.

Endowed with the characteristics of the conch and other [emblems], adorned with a crown and other ornaments, bearing the Śrīvatsa on his chest, the Lord of Lakṣmī is indeed possessed of immeasurable splendor.
Seeing him, her eyes became startled with great joy, and she said: "This is indeed Śiva himself, the husband of Śivā; there is no doubt about this."
Then, having heard Menakā’s words, the protector spoke: "This is not the husband of Śivā; rather, this is Keśava, Hari."
Śiva, the lord of Pārvatī, is the one who is authorized for all tasks of Śaṅkara and is dear to him; therefore, he should be known as the boon superior even to this.
I truly believe that it is not possible for me to describe its splendor; for He alone is the Lord of all, the Sovereign of all, and the Self-Ruling Master of the entire universe.
Brahmā said: Having heard his words, Menā considered her to be auspicious, highly fortunate, and a bringer of happiness to three lineages.
And with a serene face and a heart full of joy, she spoke, repeatedly describing her own great good fortune.
Menā said: "I have become blessed in every way now by the birth of Pārvatī; even the Lord of the Mountains is blessed today, and everything belonging to me is most blessed."
"Whichever of these gods, endowed with great splendor, I see as the leader, he shall become her husband here."
How can her good fortune be described, even in hundreds of years? It cannot possibly be described, for it consists in the vision of attaining the Lord.
Brahmā said: Thus spoke Menā, her mind overflowing with love; at that moment, the Lord Rudra, the performer of wondrous deeds, arrived.
O dear one, those hosts of wondrous beings, who stripped away the pride of Menā, revealed themselves as being untainted by illusion and free from all change.
O Sage Nārada, perceiving that he had arrived, you then spoke to Menā with great affection, pointing out the Lord of Śivā.
Nārada said: "O beautiful one, behold this very Śaṅkara himself, for whose sake Śivā performed great penance in the forest."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Menā, filled with joy, gazed upon that Lord with delight—the wonderful Īśāna, who possesses wonderful followers and a wondrous form.
At that very moment, the most wonderful army of Rudra arrived, accompanied by bhūtas, pretas, and the like, and joined by various hosts.
Some assumed the form of whirlwinds, making rustling sounds with their banners; some there had curved snouts, while others were likewise deformed.
Some were formidable and bearded, some were lame and sightless; some carried staffs and nooses, while others held mallets in their hands.
Some played discordant musical instruments, some contended with the sounding of horns, some played the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and some played the gomukha.
Some hosts have no faces, some have faces turned away, and some have many faces; some hosts have no hands, some have deformed hands, and some have many hands.
Some were eyeless and some had many eyes; likewise, some were headless and some had deformed heads; some were earless and some had many ears—these hosts wore various kinds of attire.
O dear one, there were many such powerful hosts with deformed appearances, as well as countless great heroes who were terrifying.
O sage, pointing her out with your finger, you then said, "Behold those attendants of Rudra, the servants of Hara, and Hara himself as well, O lady of beautiful countenance."
O Sage, upon seeing those innumerable hosts of bhūtas, pretas, and others, Menakā was instantly overwhelmed with terror.
In the midst of that is Śaṅkara himself, who is beyond attributes yet possessed of the highest qualities, seated upon his bull, five-faced, three-eyed, and adorned with sacred ashes.

To the one with matted hair, who bears the moon upon his crest, who has ten arms and carries a skull-bowl, who is clothed in an upper garment of tiger skin, and who holds the Pināka bow and the boon-granting gesture in his hands.
Seeing Virūpākṣa, who was equipped with a trident, deformed in appearance, and agitated, wearing an elephant hide, the mother of Śivā trembled with fear.
To her who was startled, trembling, overwhelmed, and with a bewildered mind, you said, pointing her out with your finger: "This is Śiva."
Hearing those words of yours, the virtuous Menā, burdened with grief, fell quickly to the ground like a creeper struck by the wind.
"Seeing this deformity, I have been deceived by my own stubborn persistence," having said this, Menakā fell unconscious there in an instant.
Then, attended by her friends with various efforts, Menā, the beloved of the Lord of Mountains, slowly regained consciousness.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Wondrous Pastimes of Śiva," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having regained her consciousness, Menā, the virtuous beloved of the mountain, lamented in great agitation and then uttered words of reproach.
There, first she repeatedly reproached her own sons for their failings, and then she spoke harsh words to her daughter.
Menā said: "O sage, you previously declared that Śivā would choose Śiva; subsequently, the task for Himavat was assigned for the purpose of her worship."
Therefore, the visible fruit has proven true, while the contrary [promise] was useless; O Sage, I am base and dull-witted, for I have been utterly deceived by you.
Furthermore, she performed austerities that are difficult even for sages to practice; yet this fruit of her efforts has been obtained, which brings only sorrow to those who behold it.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Who can dispel my suffering? My family and lineage are ruined; my life has been brought to its end.
"Where have the divine sages gone? I shall pluck out my beard! And that ascetic wife who came here of her own accord is a rogue."
"By whose fault has everything of mine now been destroyed? Having said this, he looked at his daughter and spoke these harsh words.
What evil deed have you committed, O wicked daughter, that has caused me such suffering? Having been given gold, you yourself, being so corrupt, have brought back mere glass!
Having abandoned the sandalwood paste, you have instead smeared yourself with mud; like a swan that has flown away, a crow has indeed been caught in the cage of your hand.
Having cast far away the net of Brahma, you have drunk the water of a well; having abandoned the sun, you have diligently grasped a firefly.
Having likewise abandoned rice, he indeed made a meal of chaff; having cast away clarified butter and oil, he ate kāraṇḍa with devotion.
Just as you abandoned service to a lion and instead served a jackal, so too have you abandoned the knowledge of Brahman and listened to base songs.
O daughter, having cast aside the highly auspicious splendor of sacrifice from your home, you have instead taken up the inauspicious ashes of the funeral pyre.
"Abandoning all the foremost gods, Viṣṇu and the other supreme lords, you have indeed performed such penance for the sake of Śiva out of a wicked mind."
Fie on you, fie on your intellect, fie on your beauty and your conduct; fie on the one who gave you counsel, and likewise fie on your two friends as well!
Fie on us two, and fie on your daughter, who are the ones who set her birth in motion! Fie on you, Nārada, for your intellect, and fie on the Seven Sages who gave you that good counsel!
Shame on my lineage! Shame on my skill! Shame on everything you have done! Let them take this milked-out wealth; for death shall be mine alone.
"Let this king of the mountains not come near me; let the Seven Sages themselves not show their faces to me."
Moreover, although everything was accomplished by all of you acting together, the family has been destroyed; why have I not become barren, and why has my fetus not miscarried?
Moreover, I am not dead, nor is my daughter dead; how could that be? Or else, why was she not devoured by the rākṣasa here in the sky?
"I shall cut off your head today; what use have I for these bodies? Having abandoned you, where could I go? Alas, alas! My life is ruined!"
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Menā fell unconscious upon the ground; agitated by grief, anger, and other emotions, she did not go into the presence of her husband.
O Lord of Sages, at that time there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! as all the gods gradually assembled there in his presence.
O divine sage, I myself arrived there in the past; upon seeing me, you spoke these words to her, O best of sages.
Nārada said: "O King, you have indeed not understood Śiva’s true and beautiful form; this form was assumed by Śiva through his divine play (līlā), and it is not his actual form."
Therefore, O devoted wife, abandon your anger and remain composed; perform your duty, casting aside obstinacy, and bestow auspiciousness upon Śiva.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of yours, Menā spoke these words to you: "Arise from here and go far away; you are a wicked, most base fellow."
When she had spoken thus, O Lord, all the guardians of the quarters, beginning with Indra, arrived in due order and spoke these words.
The gods said: O Menā, daughter of the Pitṛs, listen with joy to our words! This is indeed the supreme Śiva in person, the bringer of ultimate bliss.
And out of compassion, having seen the extremely difficult penance of your daughter, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his true devotees, granted her a vision and a boon.
Brahmā said: Then Menā, lamenting again and again, spoke to the gods: "I must not give my daughter to Giriśa, who possesses such a fierce form."
For what purpose, then, have all you gods been brought here? You are prepared to render her supreme form and name utterly futile.
When she had spoken thus, O Lord of Sages, the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, approached and spoke these words.
The Seven Sages said: "O Daughter of the Pitṛs, beloved of the mountain, we have come to accomplish a task; how then can we consider the contrary meaning expressed here?"
Brahmā said: "This indeed is the supreme gain, that there has been the sight of Śaṅkara; having become a worthy recipient of your gifts, he has come to your very abode."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Menā then rendered the words of the sages false; weak in wisdom, she replied to those ṛṣis with anger.
Menā said: "I shall cause you to be slain here with weapons and other means; I will not grant you the state of being Śaṅkara’s wife. All of you, go far away! You must not come near me."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, she, extremely overwhelmed, ceased speaking after lamenting; O Sage, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there because of her conduct.
Then Himālaya arrived there, deeply distressed; out of affection, he spoke to awaken her, revealing the truth.
Himālaya said: Listen to my words today, O Menā; why are you distressed, my dear? Who has come to our home, and why do you reproach them?
You know Śaṅkara, yet you have become overwhelmed upon seeing the formidable form of that Śambhu, who indeed possesses manifold forms and names.
I have recognized that Śaṅkara is the protector of all; he alone is the one to be worshipped among those worthy of worship, the agent of both grace and restraint.
Do not act with obstinacy; abandon this sorrow, O sinless one dear as my life! Arise quickly, O lady of excellent vows; you ought to perform what must be done.
Indeed, I am mindful of that which Śambhu, assuming a hideous form in the past, did when he arrived at the gate, performing various divine sports.
O Goddess, having witnessed that supreme majesty, I and you both then agreed to give our daughter; O beloved, make that promise binding.
Brahmā said: O sage, having spoken thus, that lord of mountains indeed ceased; then, hearing that, Menā, the mother of Śivā, spoke to Himālaya.
Menā said: "O Lord, let my words be heard; you ought to act accordingly. Having taken this daughter of yours, Pārvatī, and having bound her by the neck—"
Cast her down below without hesitation, for I shall not give her to Hara; or else, O Lord, go yourself to the ocean and bring back his daughter.

"Abandoning compassion, submerge her; O Lord of Mountains, then you shall be at ease. If you give your daughter to Rudra, who is of a fierce nature, then, O Master, I shall certainly cast off my body."
Brahmā said: When these words had been spoken there by Menā with persistence, Pārvatī herself arrived and spoke these charming words.
Pārvatī said: O Mother, your intellect has indeed become perverted and brings about inauspiciousness; for how can you, who are a follower of dharma, truly abandon dharma?
This Rudra is another manifest Lord, the source of all; he is Śambhu, the one of beautiful form who bestows happiness, as described in all the Vedas.
O Mother, this Maheśa is Śaṅkara, the sovereign lord of all gods and self-ruler; he possesses various forms and names, and is served by Hari, Brahmā, and the others.
He is the presiding authority over all, the creator and the destroyer, the Lord; he is changeless, the sovereign of the three gods, indeed imperishable and eternal.
For whose sake all the deities have arrived and been made into servants, and who today stands at your door amidst such celebration—what happiness could be greater than this?
Arise from here with diligence and make your life fruitful; give me to this Śiva and make your own hermitage meaningful.
O Mother, give me to the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara; O Mother, accept this request of mine, for I speak it to you with humility.
If you do not give me to him, I shall not choose any other boon; how could a jackal, a deceiver of others, ever obtain the portion belonging to a lion?
O Mother, this Hara has been chosen by me in thought, word, and deed; he has indeed been chosen, so do as you wish.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śiva, Menā, the beloved of the lord of mountains, lamented greatly and, filled with intense rage, took hold of that body.
With her fists and elbows, and biting her teeth, she—distraught and filled with extreme rage—struck her daughter.
O dear one, those sages there—yourself and others, O sage—seized it from his hand and cast it far away from that place.
Having seen them in such a state and having rebuked them again and again, she spoke once more, making her harsh words heard by everyone.
Menā said: "What indeed shall I do with this wicked Śivā, who is possessed by a spirit? I will either give her a potent poison or certainly throw her into a well."
I shall cut Kālī into many pieces with weapons and missiles, or indeed I shall drown my own daughter Pārvatī in the ocean.
Or else, I shall certainly abandon my own body this very moment; otherwise, I will not give my daughter Durgā to Śambhu, who has such a hideous form.
"What kind of terrible boon has this wicked woman obtained? She has indeed caused me, as well as the mountain and my lineage, to be held in ridicule."
Neither mother, nor father, nor brother, nor kinsman, nor even one born of the same lineage; neither beauty, nor cleverness, nor any dwelling whatsoever belongs to him.
He has neither clothing nor ornaments; he has no companions whatsoever. Indeed, he has no auspicious vehicle, nor youth, nor likewise wealth.
There is neither purity nor learning; what kind of body is this that causes such distress? Having seen what [fault] in him might I give my most auspicious daughter to him?
Brahmā said: O sage, having thus lamented at great length, Menakā then wept aloud, for she was overwhelmed by misery and grief.
Then, having arrived quickly, I spoke to Menakā about that supreme Śiva-tattva, the most excellent which removes false knowledge.
Brahmā said: You have joyfully agreed to hear my auspicious words, by hearing which with devotion your evil intellect shall perish.
Śaṅkara is the creator, sustainer, and likewise the destroyer of the world; you do not know his true nature, so why do you seek out suffering?
The Lord possesses manifold forms and names, performing various divine sports; he is the master of all, independent, the sovereign of Māyā, and free from conceptual construction.
Having understood this, you indeed thought, "Grant auspiciousness for the sake of Śiva"; therefore, abandon obstinacy and false knowledge, which destroy all undertakings.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by me, O sage, Menā, lamenting again and again, gradually cast aside her shame somewhat and spoke these words to me.
Menā said: "O Brahmin, for what reason do you render this most excellent form of hers useless? Why should this auspicious goddess not herself be slain?"
And you must not say, "Let her be given to Śiva. I will not give this daughter of mine, who is as dear to me as my own life, to Śiva.
Brahmā said: O great sage, when this had been spoken, the perfected ones, Sanaka and the others, arrived with great joy and spoke these words.
The Siddhas said: "This indeed is the supreme Śiva himself, the bringer of ultimate bliss; out of compassion, the Lord has granted his vision to your daughter."
Brahmā said: Then Menā, lamenting again and again, spoke to them: "I must not properly give her to Giriśa, who is of such fierce form."
For what purpose, O Siddhas, have you all, so full of worldly display, prepared yourselves to render her supreme form and name meaningless?
When she had spoken thus, O Sage, I was struck with wonder there, and all—the gods, Siddhas, sages, and humans—were filled with amazement.
At that time, having heard her firm and great resolve, Viṣṇu, the beloved of Śiva, quickly arrived and spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said: "She is the beloved mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, endowed with all virtues; she is the wife of Himavat, and her lineage is the supreme family of Brahmā himself."
Such companions as these are indeed blessed in this world; what more can I say? You are the very foundation of Dharma—how then can you abandon Dharma?
Has anything contradictory been said by the gods, the sages, by Brahmā, or even by me? Let this be well-considered by you yourself.

You do not know the true nature of Śiva, for he is indeed beyond qualities (nirguṇa) yet possesses qualities (guṇa); though appearing deformed, he is truly beautiful, the one to be served by all, and the refuge of the virtuous.
By him alone was the Goddess, the Sovereign Root-Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), created; and at her side, he then created Puruṣottama.
From those two, Brahmā likewise arose, and from him, in turn, through the nature of the qualities (guṇas), Rudra himself descended as the benefactor of the worlds.
From him likewise arose the Vedas, the gods, and whatever is seen in the world—both the stationary and the moving; all that was born from Śakra.
By whom has that form been described, or by whom is it known? Indeed, neither by me nor by Brahmā has it ever been attained.
Whatever is seen in the universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, know all that to be Śiva; no deliberation should be made in this matter.
He, indeed, has descended in such a beautiful form through his own divine play; for, by the power of Śiva’s asceticism, he has arrived at your very door.
Therefore, O wife of Himavat, abandon your sorrow and take refuge in Śiva; great bliss shall arise, and your affliction will come to an end.
Brahmā said: O sage, when Menakā had been thus enlightened, her mind, which had been awakened by Viṣṇu, became somewhat softened.
Yet Menā, deluded by Śiva’s Māyā, did not abandon her obstinate insistence on giving the maiden to Hara, and she accepted him.
And Menā, the beloved of the mountain, having understood something after hearing the charming words of Viṣṇu, spoke to Hari, for she was indeed the mother of Girijā.
If he should possess a beautiful body, then my daughter shall be given by me; not otherwise, despite millions of efforts—I speak these firm words as the truth.
Brahmā said: Having spoken these words, Menā, firm in her vows, became silent; she was blessed, impelled by the will of Śiva, and likewise enchanting to all.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Menā’s Enlightenment," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: "In the meantime, O sage, you were indeed swiftly impelled by Viṣṇu to go near Śambhu in order to propitiate him."
Having gone there, he indeed awakened Rudra by praising him with various kinds of hymns, desiring to accomplish the purpose of the gods.
Having heard your words with joy, Śambhu assumed his wonderful, supreme, and divine form, and displayed his compassion.
O Sage, seeing that beautiful Śambhu, whose own form surpassed even the God of Love, you were exceedingly delighted, for he was the supreme abode of loveliness.
Having praised him with various kinds of hymns and filled with supreme bliss, O sage, you went to that place where Menā stood together with all [the others].
Having arrived there, O Sage, being exceedingly gracious and overwhelmed with great affection, you spoke these words to Menā, the wife of the Mountain, gladdening her.
Nārada said: Behold, O large-eyed one, the unsurpassed form of Śiva; great compassion was shown toward her by that very Śiva, whose nature is mercy.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words, Menā, the beloved of the mountain, was struck with wonder; she beheld that form of Śiva, which bestows supreme bliss.
Resembling ten million suns, beautiful in every limb, wearing variegated garments, and adorned with various ornaments.
Extremely serene, with a beautiful smile, full of exquisite loveliness and captivating; fair-complexioned, endowed with radiance, and adorned with the crescent moon.
It was served with affection by all the hosts of gods, beginning with Viṣṇu; it was shaded by the sun held over its head and graced by the moon.
In every way delightful and adorned with ornaments, the great splendor of the mount cannot indeed be described.
The Gaṅgā and Yamunā held two beautiful chowries, and the eight Siddhas performed a beautiful dance before him.
And at that time, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other immortals likewise, having each adorned themselves in their own respective attire, proceeded together with Giriśa.
Likewise, at that time, various hosts of beings, shouting "Victory!", moved before the Lord of the Mountain, beautifully adorned and filled with great joy.
All the Siddhas, the Upasuras, and the Munis of great bliss, as well as all others, departed with Śiva, being well-pleased.
Thus all the gods and others, filled with curiosity and adorned by their own wives, praised the Supreme Brahman.
There, led by Viśvāvasu and joined by hosts of Apsarases, they sang before him of the supreme glory of Śaṅkara.
In this manner, O best of sages, a great and diverse festival took place there as Maheśa proceeded toward the mountain gate.
And at that time, O Lord of Sages, who is able to describe specifically that supreme bliss which belongs to the Supreme Self?
O Sage, seeing him in such a state, Menā stood for a moment as if fixed in a painting; then, out of affection, she spoke these words.
Menā said: "Blessed is my daughter, by whom such great penance was performed; through the power of which, O Maheśāna, you have arrived here at my home."
O Lord of Śivā, forgive that irredeemable blasphemy of Śiva which was indeed committed by me in the past; be well-pleased with me now.
Brahmā said: Having thus addressed her and praised him whose forehead is marked by the moon, Menā, the beloved of the mountain, bowed with joined palms and became overcome with modesty.
Then many women from the city, longing for the sight of Śiva, arrived there in great numbers, having abandoned their various worldly desires.
While bathing, a certain woman, filled with curiosity, went along with that powder to see Śaṅkara, the bridegroom of the Mountain’s Daughter.
But one woman, accompanied by her female friend and leaving the service of her husband, went with joy to behold Śambhu, holding a beautiful chowrie in her hand.
But one woman, leaving her infant who was eagerly drinking milk and was not yet satiated, went forth, longing for a sight of Śaṅkara.
One woman, while fastening her girdle, departed together with it; another then went forth having put on her garment inside out.
Leaving her beloved husband who was standing there for the sake of a meal, a certain dear wife departed out of affection, eager and curious to see the boon granted by Śiva.
A certain beloved wife, holding a small stick in her hand and with collyrium in her palm, went to behold the bridegroom of the Mountain’s Daughter after having applied it to one eye.
But a certain passionate woman, while staining her feet with red lac, heard that sound; abandoning it, she approached for the sake of seeing him.
Abandoning their various duties and leaving their homes, the women went [to him]; upon seeing the form of Śaṅkara, they then fell into a state of infatuation.
Then, agitated by love and delighted at the sight of Śiva, they placed his form in their hearts and spoke these words:
The city-dwellers said: "The eyes of the inhabitants of the Himalayan city have become fruitful; whoever beheld this form, their birth has indeed become meaningful."
His birth alone is fruitful, and his actions alone are fruitful, by whom Śiva—the destroyer of all sins—is seen directly.
Everything that was performed as penance by Pārvatī for the sake of Śiva has been accomplished; blessed is she, and fulfilled is her purpose, this Śivā who has obtained Śiva as her husband.
If Brahmā were not to unite this pair with joy for the sake of Śiva and Śivā, then all his labor would likewise come to nothing.
Thus, the excellent pair has been correctly composed and applied here; the meaningfulness of all [verses] has arisen, giving rise to every purposeful task.
Without austerity, the vision of Śambhu is difficult for men to obtain; yet, through the mere sight of Śaṅkara, all have attained the fulfillment of their purpose.
Just as Lakṣmī obtained Nārāyaṇa as her husband in ancient times, so too did the goddess Pārvatī, beautifully adorned, obtain Hara.
Just as Sarasvatī obtained Brahmā as her husband, so too did the goddess Pārvatī, beautifully adorned, obtain Hara.
We are all blessed women, and all men are most excellent, who behold Śaṅkara, the Lord of All and the husband of the Mountain-born Goddess.
Brahmā said: Having spoken these words, they worshipped Śiva with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice, and respectfully showered parched grain upon him.
All the women there, along with Menā, stood full of longing, extolling Menā’s fortune as even greater than that of the mountain.
O Sage, hearing such auspicious stories described by them, the Lord, together with Viṣṇu and all the others, then became greatly delighted.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of the Beautiful Form of Śiva and the Inhabitants of the City," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, with a gracious soul, went with his messenger, his own attendants, and all the other gods, full of curiosity, to the abode of the mountain.
Menā, the beloved wife of Himācala, also rose up with those groups of women from her own house and went inside.
For the purpose of performing the lustration rite for Śambhu, Satī, with a lamp-vessel in her hand, went respectfully to the gateway together with all the hosts of ṛṣis and women.
There she joyfully beheld Maheśāna, Śaṅkara, the husband of Girijā, who had arrived and was being attended by Menā and all the gods.
Having the beautiful hue of a campaka flower, with one face and three eyes, his countenance slightly smiling and serene, he is adorned with jewels, gold, and other ornaments.
Adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers, radiant with a crown of excellent jewels, possessing beautiful neck-ornaments, and graced with lovely bracelets and armlets;
He was most resplendent with a pair of wonderful, priceless garments that were fire-purified, incomparable, exceedingly fine, and beautiful.
Adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and beautiful saffron, holding a jeweled mirror in his hand, and with eyes brightened by collyrium.
Completely shrouded by its own radiance, it was exceedingly beautiful, extremely youthful, charming, and adorned with ornaments upon its limbs.
The beloved of the passionate woman, unperturbed, with a lotus-face like ten million moons, possessing a bodily luster exceeding ten million Cupids, and beautiful in every limb.
Seeing her husband-in-law, the lord Sudeva, standing thus before her, Menā abandoned her grief and was filled with joy.
She praised her own good fortune, the Daughter of the Mountain, the Mountain King, and her lineage; she considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose and rejoiced again and again.
With a blossoming face, that virtuous woman performed the lustration rite (nīrājana); there, Menā gazed joyfully at her son-in-law with longing looks.
Recalling what Girijā had said, Menā was filled with wonder; her lotus-like face blossoming with joy, she spoke this very thought within her mind.
Indeed, whatever was previously described by Pārvatī to me regarding that matter, I perceive the beauty of the Supreme Lord to be even greater than that.
"The great lord's exquisite beauty is now truly beyond description. Having thus fallen into a state of wonder, Menā returned to her own home.
The young women praised her, saying, "Blessed, blessed is the daughter of the Mountain! and some maidens spoke thus: "Goddess Durgā!"
"A bridegroom worthy of us has not been seen in this field of giving," some maidens said to the blessed Goddess Girijā.
The foremost of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced; and upon seeing the form of Śaṅkara, all the deities were filled with joy.
Musicians respectfully played various kinds of musical instruments with sweet-sounding notes, employing diverse artistic techniques.
Himācala, too, being delighted, then performed the rites at the gate; Menā also did so, preceded by a great festival along with all the women.
Having asked her question, she went joyfully to her own home; Śiva, for his part, went to the place indicated by the Gaṇas and the gods.
In the meantime, the attendants of the inner apartments of the mountain took Durgā outside to worship the family deity.
There the gods, free from blinking, beheld her with joy—she who possessed the hue of deep blue collyrium and was adorned by her own limbs.
Her eyes were averted from the three-eyed Lord, her gaze restrained by another; her face was bright with a gentle smile, captivating and full of sidelong glances.
Her mass of hair was beautifully braided and adorned with lovely leaf-shaped ornaments; it was graced by dots of musk together with a dot of vermilion.
Her chest was beautifully adorned with a necklace of the finest essence of jewels; she was graced with jeweled armlets and bracelets, and decorated with jeweled bangles.
Her beautiful cheeks were made radiant by two earrings of excellent gems, and her row of teeth shone brilliantly, eclipsing the luster of precious jewels with its own brilliance.
Her lower lip is like a honeyed bimba fruit and is adorned with jeweled lac; she holds a jeweled mirror in her hand and is embellished by a play-lotus.
She was adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron, her feet jingling with anklets and her soles shining with red lac.
Having beheld the primordial source of the universe, the mother of the world, all the gods and others, filled with devotion, bowed their heads together before the Goddess Sumanā.
The three-eyed Śiva, filled with joy, beheld her with the corner of his eye; seeing Satī’s true form, he abandoned the fever of separation.
With his eyes fixed upon Gaurī, Śiva forgot everything; with all his limbs covered in horripilation, he gazed at Gaurī’s face out of sheer joy.
Then Kālī, having gone outside the city and worshipped Kulāmbikā, entered the beautiful palace of her father along with the virtuous brahmin woman.
Śaṅkara, along with the gods, Hari, and Brahmā, likewise went joyfully to his own abode as directed by Himavat.
There they all remained in happiness, worshipping Śaṅkara, having been honored by the Lord of the Mountains with various kinds of excellent riches.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Boons and Other Matters," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Thereupon, that best of mountains, with great joy and enthusiasm, had a sacred thread for Durgā fashioned according to the Vedic mantras of Śiva.
Then Viṣṇu and the other gods, along with the sages, out of curiosity and at the request of Himācala, entered the inner chamber of the mountain.
Having established the conduct prescribed by the Vedas and the conduct of the virtuous according to the truth, they adorned Śivā with ornaments bestowed by Śiva.
Having first bathed her and then adorned her in every way, she was honored with the *nīrājana* rite by her female friends and the wives of the brahmins.
Adorned with a pair of unwashed garments, the woman of excellent complexion, the daughter of the great mountain and beloved of Śaṅkara, shone resplendently.
O Sage, that most excellent, divine, and wonderful bodice, adorned with various jewels, was worn by the goddess as she shone with exceeding splendor.
She wore a necklace adorned with divine jewels, as well as highly precious bangles made of pure gold.
Remaining right there, the fortunate daughter of the great mountain, the mother of the three worlds, shone forth as she meditated upon Śiva with her mind.
Then there was a great festival, bringing joy to both places; various gifts were distributed to the Brahmins as described.
There was also various great distribution of wealth to others, along with the entertainment of song and instrumental music amidst that festival.
Then Viṣṇu, I [Brahmā], Dhātṛ, Śakra and the other immortals, as well as all the sages, were filled with great affection and joy, celebrating with festive delight.
Having prostrated before Śivā with devotion and having recollected the lotus feet of Śiva, they received the command of Himavat and returned to their respective abodes.
In the meantime, Garga, who was highly proficient in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), addressed these words to Himavat, the king of mountains.
Garga said: O Himācala, lord of the earth, O Master, O Lord, bring Śambhu, the husband of Kālī, to your own abode for the sake of taking his hand in marriage.
Brahmā said: Then, knowing that the time was appropriate for the giving away of his daughter, as had been indicated by Garga, the Mountain rejoiced exceedingly in his heart.
Then the Mountain, desiring to bring Śivā, sent forth mountain-dwellers, brahmins, and others as well with great affection.
Those mountains and the twice-born, all bearing auspicious objects in their hands, gathered with great joy and affection where the god Maheśvara was.
Then, with the sound of musical instruments, the abundant voice of the Vedas, and accompanied by song and dance, there was indeed great enthusiasm there.
Upon hearing the sound of the musical instruments, all the attendants of Śaṅkara, together with the hosts of gods and sages, rose up simultaneously with joy.
With their minds overflowing with joy, they said to one another: "The mountains are coming here, desiring to bring Śiva."
Surely the time for taking her hand has now arrived; indeed, we consider that great fortune has been attained by us all.
"We are especially blessed that we shall surely witness with supreme joy the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, the abode of auspiciousness for all the worlds."
Brahmā said: While they were thus engaged in conversation there with great respect, all the ministers of the lord of mountains arrived.
Having gone there, they also entreated Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the others, saying, "The time appropriate for the giving away of the maiden has arrived; please come."
O Sage, having heard that, all those gods, Viṣṇu and the rest, rejoiced exceedingly in their hearts and quickly said "Victory! to the Mountain.
Śiva too rejoiced exceedingly, longing for the attainment of Kālī; he of wondrous form kept that sign secret within his mind alone.
Then a bath was performed by that wielder of the trident, who was well-pleased and intent on bestowing grace upon the worlds, accompanied by auspicious substances.
Having bathed and dressed in fine garments, surrounded by all of them, he was mounted upon the shoulders of the bull and well-served by the guardians of the world.
Placing their lord at their head, they all went to the abode of the Himavat mountain, playing musical instruments and displaying great enthusiasm.
The brahmins sent by Himāga, as well as those excellent mountains, were indeed the foremost attendants of Śambhu, filled with curiosity.
With a great umbrella held over his head and being fanned with chowries, that Maheśvara shone like the sun itself.
I am Viṣṇu, as well as Indra and the guardians of the world; we stand at the forefront, resplendent and endowed with supreme glory.
Then, during that great festival, conchs, kettledrums, paṭahas, ānakas, and gomukhas—various musical instruments—were sounded again and again.
In that very manner, all the singers sang most auspicious songs, and all the female dancers danced, accompanied by various rhythmic beats.
Accompanied by these, the sole kinsman of the world then proceeded with the splendor of the Supreme Lord, being served by all the lords of the gods and showered with flowers by those filled with joy.
Then Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, having been worshipped and being praised with many hymns of praise, entered the sacrificial pavilion.
The excellent mountains rescued Maheśa from the bull and, with great joy and amidst a grand festival, led him into their homes.

The Himalaya, too, having approached the Lord who was accompanied by the hosts of gods, bowed down according to the prescribed rites with devotion and then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having prostrated before all the gods, the sages, and others, he celebrated with great festivity; praising his own ritual procedure with joy, he paid them due honor.
Accompanied by the foremost of gods, he led that horse—unfallen and sovereign—to the interior of his own abode, preceded by the offering of water for the feet and respectful oblations (arghya).
He seated them all upon jeweled thrones in the courtyard—Viṣṇu, me, the Lord, and especially those who were most distinguished.
With joy, his friends, Menā, the wives of brahmins, and other matrons performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for him with affection.
The family priest, an expert in ritual duties, joyfully performed for the high-souled Śaṅkara all the necessary rites, beginning with the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
O Sage, urged by me, that priest then performed there whatever auspicious rites were appropriate for the occasion.
Having entered the inner altar with great joy along with the Himālaya mountain, [he went] where that maiden Pārvatī was, adorned with all ornaments.
The slender-limbed lady stood resplendent upon the altar; there, Lord Mahādeva was led by Viṣṇu along with me.
As they gazed at the auspicious moment, with Vācaspati at their head, there arose supreme festivities appropriate for the giving away of the bride.
Garga sat down there where the water-clock was located, and recited the syllable Om for as long as the remaining time on the clock lasted.
Garga, proclaiming "An auspicious day!", joyfully joined his palms together and showered Pārvatī and Śiva with handfuls of consecrated rice.
There, Rudra was worshipped with curd, unbroken grains of rice, and water mixed with kuśa grass by Pārvatī, who was exceedingly gracious and possessed of a beautiful countenance.
Gazing upon that Śambhu for whose sake she had previously performed supreme austerities with great devotion, that auspicious lady shone intensely.
O Sage, having been told this by me as well as by Garga and other sages, Śambhu, adhering to worldly custom, worshipped Śivā.
Thus, at that time, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who are composed of the entire universe, shone brightly as they worshipped one another.
Enveloped by the splendor of the three worlds and gazing at one another, they were then especially honored with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by Lakṣmī and other women.
Likewise, the wives of the twice-born and the women of the city performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana); beholding Śivā and Śambhu, they all attained great joy during that grand festival.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of Śiva’s Entry into the Interior of Himālaya’s Abode," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In the meantime, impelled by Garga Ācārya, Himavat, together with Menā, proceeded to give away his daughter.
Taking a golden pitcher, the highly fortunate Menā, adorned with garments and ornaments, took her place by the side of Himādri.
Then the delighted Śaila, together with his family priest, honored him with water for the feet and other offerings, and chose him as a boon by presenting garments, sandalwood paste, and ornaments.
Then Himādri said to the twice-born ones regarding the proclamation of the lunar day and other details: "Let the ritual application be recited now that this moment has arrived."
Having said, "So be it," all those best of the twice-born, who were knowers of the proper time, joyfully proclaimed the lunar day and other details, being supremely satisfied.
Then Himācala, prompted in his heart by Śambhu with affection and consecrated by the Supreme Lord, spoke to Śambhu while smiling.
O Śambhu, let your own lineage be told, as well as your preeminent branch and family; likewise, your name, Veda, and Śākhā—do not cause a delay in this matter.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Himādri, Śaṅkara, who is ever-pleasant-faced, never-turned-away, and eternally beyond grief, immediately fell into a state of sorrow.

At that time, while the Lord Maheśa was being gazed upon by the foremost of gods, sages, as well as hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Siddhas, with his face turned upward, he then broke into laughter there, O Nārada.
O Nārada, you who are a knower of Brahman and whose mind is fixed on Śambhu, having been mentally impelled there by Śiva, you indeed played the lute.
Then the wise one was indeed forcibly restrained by the lord of mountains, as well as by Viṣṇu, by me, by all the gods, and likewise by the sages.
"When you were told by the Mountain, 'Indeed, you have not ceased from worldly existence because of Śaṅkara’s will,' then do not play the lute now."
O wise one, when you were forcibly forbidden by him, O celestial sage, you replied to that Lord of the Mountain after clearly remembering Maheśvara.
Nārada said: "Indeed, you have fallen into a state of delusion and do not know anything at all; regarding that which is to be spoken—the subject of Maheśa—you are utterly turned away."
When you questioned Hara directly regarding the declaration of his own lineage, he spoke words at that time which were utterly ridiculous.
O Parvata, even Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others do not know his lineage, family, or name; what then can be said of others?
O Mountain, he in whom ten million Brahmās have dissolved in a single day—that very Śaṅkara has been seen by you today through the power of Kālī’s penance.
This Supreme Brahman is formless, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature; He is without shape, changeless, the Lord of Māyā, and higher than the highest.
For He who is named Agotrakula is independent and compassionate toward His devotees; indeed, by His own will, He assumes qualities, a physical form, and bears many names.
Whether of noble lineage or devoid of lineage, whether of low birth or of high birth—by virtue of Pārvatī’s ascetic penance, he shall today become your son-in-law; of this there is no doubt.
O best of mountains, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been deluded by Him who sports in divine play; thus, no one—even a wise man—recognizes Śiva.
By whom has the head of Maheśa, who is in the form of a *liṅga*, not been seen? For even Viṣṇu, having gone to the netherworld (*pātāla*), was not astonished by it.
O best of mountains, what is the use of much speaking? The Māyā of Śiva is difficult to transcend; the three worlds, as well as Hari, Brahmā, and the others, are all subject to it.
Therefore, my dear father, having reflected well and with great effort upon Śivā, you must not entertain even the slightest hesitation regarding such a bridegroom.
Brahmā said: O sage, having spoken thus, you, a man of knowledge who carries out the will of Śiva, replied once more to the Lord of Mountains, gladdening him with your speech.
Nārada said: Listen, O dear one, O great mountain, O father of Śivā, to my words; having heard them, you must indeed give your daughter to Śaṅkara.
Know that the lineage and family of Maheśvara, who assumes forms through his divine play while possessing attributes, is indeed nothing other than the primordial sound (nāda) alone.
Śiva is truly composed of sound (nāda), and likewise, sound is composed of Śiva; there is no difference between the two, namely between sound and Śiva.
O Lord of Mountains, because he was born first in the creation from Śiva—who possesses a form of playful attributes—he is the consumer of nectar (nāda) and is therefore the most excellent of all.
Therefore, O Himālaya, this lute has indeed been played today by me, Śaṅkara, the Lord of All, with my mind directed toward you.
Brahmā said: O sage, having heard those words of yours, the Lord of the Mountains, Himavat, attained great satisfaction, his mind freed from all astonishment.
Then Viṣṇu and the other gods, as well as the sages, all of them, their astonishment having vanished, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Having recognized the profundity of Maheśvara, all those wise ones, filled with wonder and great joy, spoke to one another.

By whose command this vast universe was brought into being, he who is higher than the highest, whose nature is innate consciousness, Śarva, the master of his own course and attainable through supreme devotion—that Lord of the three worlds has been clearly beheld by us today.
Then those foremost of mountains, Meru and the others, filled with agitation, spoke in unison to Himavat, the lord of mountains:

The mountains said: "Stay for today regarding the giving of the maiden; let there be no destruction of your purpose at the word of the Lord of Mountains. We speak the truth; there should be no hesitation in this matter—therefore, let the maiden be given to the Lord."
Brahmā spoke: Having heard those words of his friends, Himālaya, urged by the prescribed rites, gave his daughter to Śiva.
O Supreme Lord, I give this maiden to you; accept her as your wife, O Gracious One, Sovereign of All.
With this mantra, Himācala gave his own daughter Pārvatī, the mother of the three worlds, to that great Rudra.
Having thus placed the mountain, which was the source of auspiciousness, upon the hand of Śiva, he rejoiced exceedingly in his heart, having crossed the great ocean of desire.
With a Vedic mantra, the delighted Supreme Lord Giriśa quickly took the lotus-hand of Girijā with his own hand.
O Sage, touching the earth, Śaṅkara affectionately recited the mantra "Who would give [the fulfillment] of desire? thereby demonstrating the worldly way of conduct.
A great festival occurred everywhere, bringing joy to all; there was a roar of victory in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
All, being exceedingly joyful, uttered words of "Excellent! and "Salutations!"; the Gandharvas sang beautifully with affection, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Indeed, the citizens of Himācala rejoiced greatly in their hearts; there was truly great auspiciousness accompanied by a grand festival.
I, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and all the immortals and sages became exceedingly joyful, their lotus-like faces in full bloom.
Then the excellent mountain Himācala, being well-pleased, offered the gift of his daughter to Śiva in a manner that was entirely appropriate and complete in every respect.
Then his kinsmen, having worshipped Śivā with devotion, offered excellent materials to Śiva according to various prescribed rites.
O lord of sages, the Himalaya, with a delighted mind, gave various kinds of substances there for the pleasure of Pārvatī and Śiva.
She gave him auspicious amulets and various jewels, as well as diverse vessels fashioned from beautiful gems.
A hundred thousand cows, a hundred equipped horses, and a hundred thousand devoted female slaves adorned with excellent ornaments.
O Sage, there were indeed a hundred thousand chariots for the nāgas, adorned with gold and fashioned from the finest jewels.
Thus, having given his daughter Girijā Śivā to Śiva, the Supreme Lord, according to the prescribed rites, Himālaya attained the fulfillment of his purpose.
Then Śailavara, having joyfully recited the midday hymns, praised the Supreme Lord with beautiful words, his hands joined in reverence.
Then, commanded by him who was learned in the Vedas, those hosts of sages, filled with supreme joy, performed the head-consecration ceremony for Śivā.
Having uttered the names of the gods, they performed the rite of circumambulation; O Sage, there was then a great festival that brought immense joy.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Giving Away of the Daughter," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, by my command, the Lord had the Brahmins establish the sacrificial fire; he performed the oblation right there, having placed Pārvatī upon his lap.
Śiva offered oblations into the fire with mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; Maināka, the brother of Kālī, offered a handful of parched grain.
Then, O dear one, both Kālī and Śiva joyfully performed the circumambulation of the fire according to the prescribed rites, following the custom of the world.
There, the Lord of Girijā performed a most wonderful deed; listen to that very account, O divine sage, for I shall tell it to you out of affection for you.
At that moment, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, I beheld the beautiful moon-like nail upon the foot of the Goddess.
O celestial sage, upon seeing him at that time, I was indeed possessed by passion, my mind becoming exceedingly agitated.
Deluded by passion, I gazed upon her limbs again and again; then, from that very sight, my semen was immediately discharged upon the ground.
O Sage, I, the Grandfather, was ashamed by that flowing semen; I crushed it with my two feet, concealing it as it fell.
Having learned of that, O Nārada, Mahādeva became exceedingly enraged; he then desired to swiftly slay both you and Brahmā, who was deluded by passion.
O Nārada, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere there; all people trembled, and Viśvabhṛt was seized with fear.
Then, O Sage, Viṣṇu and the other gods praised Śambhu, who was blazing with anger and intent on destroying them with his splendor.
The gods said: O God of gods, pervader of the universe, Supreme Lord Sadāśiva! O Lord of the world, Master of the world, who art identical with the universe, be gracious!
You are the self, the cause, and the Lord of all beings; changeless, undecaying, eternal, free from conceptual construction, imperishable, and supreme.

That which is its beginning, its end, and its middle; that which is other than this, and that which is "I" and "without"; from which, being immutable, these [all] proceed—that is the Truth, Brahman, the Consciousness that you are.
Desiring liberation and firm in their vows, sages abandon attachment to both [worlds] and worship your very lotus feet.
You are Brahman—complete, immortal, free from sorrow, devoid of qualities, supreme, consisting of pure bliss, undisturbed, changeless, and without a material self.

For He is indeed the cause of the origin, maintenance, and withdrawal of the universe; yet, because He is independent of that [universe], the Lord of the Self is eternally self-sufficient and all-pervading.

You alone are the one who is both existence and non-existence, as well as non-duality itself; for there is indeed no distinction between entities, just as gold remains the same whether it is fashioned into a form or left unformed.

Since conceptual construction has been perceived by people regarding you due to ignorance, therefore there can be no remedy for that delusion on your part, for one who is free from limiting conditions does not [require it] inherently.
O Maheśāna, we are blessed by the mere sight of you; O Śambhu, bestower of joy upon those of steadfast devotion, please show us mercy.

You are the beginning and you are without beginning; you are the Supreme Person beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). You are the Lord of the universe, the Master of the world, changeless, and higher than the highest.
O Lord, this Brahmā, the Grandfather who is the universal form through the quality of passion (rajas), and Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, exist through the quality of goodness (sattva) by Your grace.
Kālāgnirudra is the Supreme Self through the quality of darkness (tamas); he is the supreme attribute, Sadāśiva, Maheśāna, the all-pervading Maheśvara.
The manifest, the Great One, the principle of being, the subtle elements, and the sense organs—all these, O Maheśvara whose form is the universe, are presided over by you alone.
O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, O Compassionate One, O Śaṅkara! Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; be gracious, O Puruṣottama.
The seven oceans and the directions are the garments of you, O mighty-armed one; the sky is the head of the All-pervading Lord, the ether is his navel, and from that, the wind is his nose.
O Lord, fire, the sun, and the moon are Your eyes; the clouds are Your hair; and the constellations, stars, and planets are Your ornaments.
How shall I praise you, O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading Supreme Lord? You are beyond the reach of speech and even of the mind, O Śaṅkara.
Salutations to you, the five-faced Rudra, whose form consists of fifty crores; to the supreme sovereign of the three, the most excellent one, the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Salutations again and again to the god Śaṅkara, who is indefinable, eternal, whose form is like a flash of lightning, and who is the color of fire.
Salutations again and again to you who, having assumed a most beautiful eight-cornered form resembling ten million flashes of lightning, abide in this world.
Brahmā said: Having heard their words, the Supreme Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, was pleased and swiftly granted me, Brahmā, freedom from fear.
Then, O dear one, all the gods there, headed by Viṣṇu, as well as the sages, became radiant with smiles and celebrated a supreme festival.
O dear one, from that semen of mine being repeatedly massaged, many exceedingly brilliant drops were produced there.
Many thousands of Vālakhilya sages were born from those sparks of his seed, which blazed with their own brilliance.
Then, O Sage, all those sages approached me with great affection and addressed me as "Father, Father," my dear.
Indeed, they were addressed by Nārada, who was impelled by the will of the Lord; but the Vālakhilyas there were filled with anger in their hearts.
Nārada said: "Go together, all of you, to Mount Gandhamādana; you must not remain here, for you have no purpose here."
Having performed intense penance there, they shall become lords of sages and disciples of the Sun; this was told to me by the command of Śiva himself.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus, all those Bālakhilyas then bowed to Śaṅkara and quickly departed for Mount Gandhamādana.
Then, O Lord of Sages, I was encouraged by Viṣṇu and the others—those high-souled ones impelled by the Supreme Lord—and I became free from fear.
And having known Śaṅkara—the Lord of all, who is affectionate toward his devotees, the accomplisher of all tasks, and the remover of the pride of the wicked—to be their refuge, they praised him.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord, ocean of compassion! You alone are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of everything in every way.
For by your will alone does everything, including all that is moving and unmoving, remain so; this has been specifically understood by me, just as oxen are held together by a rope.
Having spoken thus, I indeed offered my salutation with palms joined; and all the others, Viṣṇu and the rest, likewise praised that Maheśvara.
Then, having heard my pure hymn of praise along with those of Viṣṇu and all the others, Maheśvara became pleased on account of my wretchedness.
With a joyful heart, he granted me the supreme boon of fearlessness; everyone attained extreme happiness, and I, O Sage, rejoiced exceedingly.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Infatuation," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Thereafter, O Nārada, by the command of Śiva and out of affection for the marriage of Śivā and Śiva, I performed the remaining rites along with the hosts of sages.
Then, O brahmins, the ceremonial head-anointing of those two took place with great reverence; thereafter, they respectfully caused Dhruva to be presented for an audience.
Immediately after that, O best of Brahmins, the ritual of touching the heart took place, followed by the recitation of auspicious hymns amidst a great festival.
At the command of the twice-born, Śambhu applied vermilion upon the head of Śivā; at that moment, she became known as Girijā, possessing a wondrous beauty beyond description.
Then, by the command of the Brahmin, those two, seated together upon a single seat, attained a supreme splendor that brought joy to the hearts of their devotees.
Then, O Sage, having returned to their own abode, those two performers of wondrous deeds joyfully partook of the remnants (saṃsrava) at my command.
When the sacrificial marriage rite had thus been duly completed, the Lord Śiva gave me the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) for Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Then Śambhu gave the gift of a cow to the preceptor according to the prescribed rites, as well as other great gifts that bestow auspiciousness, out of affection.
Then he gave a hundred gold pieces to each of many Brahmins, as well as crores of jewels and numerous kinds of various goods.
At that time, all the immortals, as well as other living beings, both moving and stationary, rejoiced exceedingly in their hearts with shouts of victory.
A great many auspicious sounds and songs arose everywhere; the delightful sound of musical instruments resounded, increasing the joy of all.
Then Hari, the gods, the sages, and all the others, having taken leave of the mountain with great affection, quickly departed for their own abodes.
At that time, the women in the city of Śaila, filled with joy, brought Śiva and Śivā and went to the excellent abode of Kuha.
Those women there observed the worldly customs with great respect; then, a great enthusiasm arose everywhere, bringing joy to all.
Then, having brought that couple together—those who bring joy to the people—they joyfully performed the rites of hospitality in a most divine dwelling.
Then, having approached, the women of the city of the Lord of Mountains performed auspicious rites and escorted the couple to their home.
Uttering cries of victory, they performed the untying of the knots and other rites; smiling with side-long glances, their bodies were covered in horripilation.
Having entered the bedchamber, the excellent women fainted, praising their own good fortune as they gazed upon the Supreme Lord.
Possessing a magnificent form and attire, endowed with every charm, he stands in the bloom of fresh youth, enchanting the hearts of amorous women.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile and adorned with side-long glances, he was exceedingly beautiful; he wore very fine garments and was decorated with various jewels.
Then the divine ladies and sixteen noble women arrived, with great reverence, to behold that couple.
Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī and Jāhnavī likewise, Aditi and Śacī, as well as Lopāmudrā and Arundhatī.
Ahalyā, Tulasī, Svāhā, Rohiṇī, Vasundharā, Śatarūpā, Saṃjñā, and Rati—these are the wives of the gods.
Who is capable of counting those celestial maidens, nāga maidens, and enchanting daughters of sages who were stationed there?
When they had offered him a jeweled throne, Śiva sat there with joy; then the goddesses spoke to him in turn with sweet words and gentle smiles.
Sarasvatī said: "O lustful one, now that she has arrived joyfully before Mahādeva—she who is dearer to him than his own life—abandon your torment upon seeing the moon-like face of your beloved."
O Lord of Time, pass your time in the company of Satī; you shall never be separated from me, for I am forever dependent upon you.
Lakṣmī said: O Lord of Gods, casting aside shame and placing Satī upon your chest, remain with her; what shame is there in that, since life itself departs without her?
Sāvitrī said: "O Śambhu, having fed her, you should eat quickly; do not be distressed. Then, having sipped water, respectfully give her betel-leaf with camphor."
Jāhnavī said: O women, cleanse your hair while holding it with hands that possess a golden luster; for a passionate woman, there can be no greater happiness than the good fortune of her husband.
Aditi said: "O Śambhu, at the conclusion of the meal, for the sake of purifying your mouth, please give water with great affection to Śiva; such love between husband and wife is rare indeed."
Śacī said: "Having lamented for her sake and having placed Śivā upon your chest, you wandered about incessantly out of delusion; what shame do you feel toward your beloved?"
Lopāmudrā said: "O Śiva, it is the custom for women that after having enjoyed the bedchamber, one should offer betel to Śivā; you ought to go to sleep after giving her the betel."
Arundhatī said: "This virtuous woman was given to you by me, though she was not desired as a gift; having instructed her in various ways, you ought to provide her with excellent pleasure."
Ahalyā said: "Abandoning your state of old age, become exceedingly youthful, so that Menā, her mind intent on bestowing her daughter, may give her consent to you."
Tulasī said: "O Lord, Satī was abandoned by you and Kāma was burnt in the past; why then has Vasiṣṭha been sent away now?"
Svāhā said: "O Mahādeva, be firm now regarding the words of women; there is a custom in marriage wherein matrons possess boldness."
Rohiṇī said: O expert in the science of love, fulfill the desire of Pārvatī; you yourself, being full of passion, cross to the further shore of the ocean of the beloved’s longing.
Vasundharā said: "O Knower of the Inner State, you understand the disposition of women afflicted by desire; yet, O Śambhu, she does not constantly protect her own husband, the Lord."
Śatarūpā said: "One afflicted by hunger cannot indeed find satisfaction without enjoying divine pleasure; O Śambhu, it is fitting for a woman to do that by which she may attain contentment."
Saṃjñā said: "Quickly dispatch Śaṅkara with affection along with Pārvatī, having prepared a bed, betel, and jeweled lamps in a secluded place."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the women, Śiva himself spoke to them—he who is changeless, the Blessed One, the teacher of the teachers of the lords of yogins.
Śaṅkara said: O goddesses, do not speak such words in my presence; you are the virtuous mothers of the worlds—how can there be fickleness toward a son?
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, the celestial women became ashamed and, out of agitation, remained silent like painted dolls.
Having eaten the sweet food and sipped water for purification, Maheśa, with a joyful mind, enjoyed betel-leaf with camphor together with his wife.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Jest," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
