Brahmā said: On that occasion, perceiving the favorable moment, Rati, being well-pleased, spoke to Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward the distressed.
Rati said: "Having obtained Pārvatī, you have attained a fortune that is exceedingly difficult to find; for what reason has my lord of life been reduced to ashes so selflessly?"
"Indeed, my husband is my very life; O Kāmavīpāramātman, remove the intense anguish caused by our separation."
In this wedding festival, all people are happy; I alone, O Great Lord, am miserable without my husband.
O Lord Śaṅkara, grant me a protector; be gracious, O Supreme Master, friend of the distressed! Make your own word come true.
Knowing this, please show compassion: "Who else in these three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, is capable of destroying my suffering without you?"
O Lord, you who show compassion to the wretched, at this festival of my own marriage which bestows all joy, please make me too a partaker of that celebration.
For as long as my lord lives together with his beloved Pārvatī, there will undoubtedly be perfect enjoyment and fulfillment for me.
Since you are the Supreme Lord, you are capable of doing everything; O Lord of All, what is the use of much speaking here? Restore my husband to life at once.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, he gave the ashes of Kāma along with their knotted cords; and before Śambhu, he wept, crying out, "O Lord! O Lord!"
Hearing the lamentation of Rati, Sarasvatī and all the other goddesses wept and spoke words of extreme distress.

The goddesses said: You are named Bhaktavatsala (the one who is affectionate toward devotees), the kinsman of the distressed, and a treasure-house of compassion. O Kāma, revive us; grant us passion! Salutations be unto you.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words, Maheśvara became pleased; the Lord, an ocean of compassion, immediately cast a glance of grace.
By the nectar-like glance of the wielder of the trident, Smara emerged from the ashes, possessing his own form, dress, and insignia, with a body of wondrous beauty.
Seeing her husband in that form, with a smile of that same aspect, holding his bow and arrow, Rati bowed down to that Great Lord.
Having achieved her purpose, she praised Lord Śiva with palms joined in reverence, repeatedly extolling him—the bestower of the life of her husband—as the one who had restored her lord to life.
Having heard the praise of Kāma together with his wife, Śaṅkara became exceedingly pleased; with a mind moistened by compassion, he spoke.
Śaṅkara said: "I am pleased with this hymn of yours, O mind-born one, along with your wife. O self-existent one, choose a boon; whatever you desire, I shall grant it to you."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, Smara then laughed loudly; bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he spoke in a voice faltering with emotion.
Kāma said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord who is an ocean of compassion! If you are pleased, O Lord of all, become the bringer of joy to me.
O Lord, please forgive my transgression committed in the past; grant supreme affection for Your own people and devotion to Your feet.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Smara, the Supreme Lord, the ocean of compassion, being pleased, replied "Oṃ" and spoke to him while smiling.
Īśvara said: O Kāma, I am pleased with you; cast off your fear, O high-minded one! Go to the presence of Viṣṇu and remain stationed outside his abode.
Brahmā said: Having heard that, bowing his head, circumambulating and praising the Lord, he went outside, prostrated before Hari and the gods, and waited upon them.
Having conversed with Kāma, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, remembered Śiva in their hearts and bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
The gods said: "Blessed are you, O Smara, who were consumed by fire and then favored by Śiva; the Lord of All restored you to life with a compassionate glance."
Since there is no other giver of pleasure and pain than one’s own past actions, by whom can protection, marriage, and conception be prevented at the proper time?
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and having honored him with kindness, those immortals—Viṣṇu and all the others—then remained there, their desires fulfilled.
He too, being delighted, dwelt there by the command of Śiva; indeed, shouts of "Victory!", "Salutations!", and "Well done! arose.
Then Śambhu, having seated Pārvatī on his left side in the bedchamber, joyfully fed both her and him with sweet food.
Then Śambhu, the performer of worldly rites, having performed his duty there, took leave of Menā and the Mountain and departed for the abode of people.
Then, O Sage, there was a great festival and the sound of the Vedas arose; the people played the four kinds of musical instruments.
Then Śambhu, having returned to his own abode, paid homage to the sages; and according to the custom of worldly conduct, he was saluted by me, Hari, and the gods.
Then there arose the sound of "Victory! as well as the sound of "Homage!", along with the auspicious resonance of the Vedas, which destroys all obstacles.
Then Viṣṇu, I [Brahmā], Śakra, all the gods, along with the sages, the Siddhas, the Upasuras, and the Nāgas, praised him individually.
The gods said: Victory to you, O Śambhu, support of all! Victory, O Maheśvara, whose name is supreme! Victory, O Rudra, Great God! Victory, O Lord, sustainer of the universe!
Victory to you, O Lord of Kālī, O Master! Victory to you, the increaser of bliss! Victory to you, O Tryambaka, Lord of all! Victory to you, O pervasive Lord, Master of Māyā!

Victory to You, who are beyond qualities, free from desire, and transcendent of all causes; victory to You, the support of all through Your divine play, who assume forms at will—salutations be unto You!
Victory to you, O granter of the desires of your devotees, O mine of compassion! Victory to you, whose true form is bliss; victory to you, who are unmanifested by the qualities of Māyā!
Victory to you, O Supreme One! Be gracious, O Soul of All, Friend of the Wretched, Treasure-Trove of Compassion! Victory to you, O Unchanging One, Lord of Māyā, whose form transcends speech and mind!
Brahmā said: Having thus praised Maheśāna, the Lord who is the consort of Girijā, Viṣṇu and the others served him with supreme devotion, each according to his propriety.
Then, O Nārada, Śambhu, the Great Lord, the Sovereign who had assumed a body for his divine play, bestowed human status upon all of them there.
O dear one, having received the command of the Supreme Lord, all those beginning with Viṣṇu, exceedingly joyful and with serene faces, returned to their own abodes with due respect.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Revival of Kāma," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa, the third part of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then, O dear one, the wise Himavat, the best of mountains and most fortunate, prepared the courtyard for the purpose of the meal.
He properly performed the sweeping and smearing of that [shrine], and with devotion, he adorned it with various fragrant substances.
Then Śaila invited all the gods, as well as others including the Lord (Īśvara), along with his sons and other mountain-dwellers, for a feast.
O Sage, having heard the invitation to Śaila, that Lord, accompanied by Viṣṇu and all the gods and others, went there joyfully for the meal.
And Giri, having honored the Lord and all of them according to the prescribed rites, joyfully seated them upon excellent seats within the house.
Having served various kinds of excellent foods, he then, with palms joined in reverence, requested permission for the meal through a formal petition of respect.
Then, having been duly honored there, all those gods, led by Viṣṇu and placing Sadāśiva at their head, partook of the meal.
Then indeed, all having gathered together in unison from every side, they sat in rows and ate, laughing individually.
Nandi, Bhṛṅgi, Vīrabhadra, and the Vīrabhadra hosts, those highly fortunate ones, each separately partook [of the feast], filled with curiosity.
The gods, including Indra and the world-protectors, endowed with various splendors, those highly fortunate ones, enjoyed themselves together with the flavors of various kinds of laughter.
Then all the sages, the brahmins, and the seers such as Bhṛgu and others, sat in separate rows and ate with great delight.
And likewise, all the hosts of Caṇḍīs, having taken up their vessels, ate with joy, displaying various jests and creating a sense of wonder.
Thus, having eaten and sipped water for purification, Viṣṇu and all the others, filled with joy, affectionately went to their respective hermitages to rest.
At the command of the King, virtuous women, having prayed with devotion for the welfare of Śiva, caused him to dwell in their home during the supreme festival known as Vāsa.
Having taken his seat upon a beautiful jeweled throne presented by Menā, Śambhu, filled with joy, beheld the inner apartments.
It was ablaze with the splendor of hundreds of burning jewel-lamps, strewn with jeweled vessels and jars, and resplendent with pearls and gems.
Richly adorned with the splendor of jeweled mirrors, decorated with white chowries, and encircled by beautiful garlands of pearls and gems, it possessed supreme magnificence.
It was incomparable, great, divine, variegated, and most enchanting; it gladdened the heart, its grounds fashioned with various artistic arrangements.
Manifesting the incomparable and supreme power of one who has indeed been granted a boon by Śiva, it brilliantly displays that which is named the world of Śiva.
It was perfumed with various fragrant and excellent substances, brilliantly illuminated, blended with sandalwood and agallochum, and provided with beds of flowers.
It was fashioned by Viśvakarman, enriched with various wonderful and diverse designs, and strewn with excellent necklaces crafted from the finest essence of precious gems.
In some places there was the most enchanting Vaikuṇṭha, the creation of the gods; in other places the world of Brahmā, and in some places the cities of the world-protectors.
In one place was the delightful Kailāsa, in another the palace of Śakra, and in another the world of Śiva, shining resplendent above all.
Beholding such a house, which was a marvel to all who saw it, Maheśvara praised the Lord of the Snowy Mountains and became truly satisfied.
There, upon that most delightful and supreme jeweled couch, the Supreme Lord lay down, filled with joy and playful grace.
Himācala fed all his brothers in their entirety, as well as all others with great affection, and performed the remaining rites.
While Śaileśa was thus performing [the final yoga] and his most beloved Lord was sleeping, the entire night passed away and morning arrived.
Then, at the time of dawn, people devoted to steadfastness and enthusiasm began playing various kinds of musical instruments.
All the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, rose up filled with great joy; remembering their beloved Lord of Gods, they became alert and full of eagerness.
Having readied their own vehicles, eager to go to Kailāsa, they sent Dharma to the presence of Śiva.
Then, having come to the bedchamber by the command of Nārāyaṇa, the yogi Dharma spoke to Śaṅkara, the lord of yogis, words appropriate for the occasion.
Dharma said: Arise, arise! May it be well with you; become the lord of our Pramathas. Come to the abode of men and make them successful in their purpose there.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Dharma, Maheśvara laughed; he looked upon him with a compassionate gaze and indeed abandoned his couch.
Laughing, he said, "O Dharma, you go there first; I too shall come very quickly, of this there is no doubt."
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by Śaṅkara, he then went to the abode of the people; the Lord Śambhu himself was also intent on going there.
Knowing that, that multitude of women arrived there with great festivity; beholding the two feet of Śambhu, they indeed sang auspicious songs.
Then Śambhu, following the conduct of Bhava, having performed his morning rites and taken leave of Menā and the Mountain, departed for the abode of the people.
O Sage, there was then a great festival and the sound of the Vedas arose; the people played four kinds of musical instruments.
Then Śambhu, having returned to his own abode, paid homage to the sages; and according to the custom of worldly conduct, he was also saluted by me and Hari, as well as by the gods and others.
Then there arose shouts of "Victory! and likewise cries of "Homage!", along with the auspicious sound of the Vedas; a great tumult ensued.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Feast for the Suitors and the Bed of Śiva," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then Viṣṇu and the other gods, as well as the sages whose wealth is their austerity, having performed their necessary duties, set out on a journey to the mountain.
Then the excellent mountain, having bathed and diligently worshipped his own deity, summoned his citizens and kinsmen and went joyfully to the human habitation.
There, having worshipped the Lord, he joyfully made this prayer: "Please remain in my house for some days, together with all [your retinue]."
O Śambhu, by your mere glance I have achieved my life’s purpose; of this there is no doubt. Blessed am I, for you have come to my home together with the gods.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus at length, the Lord of Mountains joined his palms, bowed down, and invited the Lord along with Viṣṇu, the gods, and the others.
Then, having approached Śiva with their minds full of devotion, the sages, together with Viṣṇu, the gods, and others, joyfully replied.
The gods said: "O tiger among mountain-dwellers, you are blessed; your fame is most exalted. There is no person more meritorious than you anywhere within the three worlds."
At whose gate Maheśāna—the Supreme Brahman, the refuge of the virtuous, and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees—has arrived out of compassion, accompanied by his constant attendants.
The people’s dwellings were exceedingly delightful, and various honors were bestowed; moreover, the foods were unprecedented and beyond description, O Lord of Mountains.
Indeed, there is nothing wonderful about that place where the goddess Śivāmbikā resides; it is entirely complete and perfect. Blessed are you who have come here.
Brahmā said: Thus, an excellent mutual praise arose there; a manifold festival took place, accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas and the cries of "Victory! from the virtuous.
Auspicious songs were sung, throngs of Apsarases danced, the bards and others offered hymns of praise, and there was a great distribution of wealth.
Then, having taken leave of the Lord of Gods, the Mountain returned to his own home and began a festival of feasting according to various rites and procedures.
Out of affection, he brought the Lord for the sake of a meal as was appropriate, along with his retinue and the Lord himself, who was filled with curiosity.
Having washed the feet of Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and myself with great reverence, as well as those of all the immortals and sages according to the truth.
And Giriśa, accompanied by his kinsmen, with great affection seated those others who had arrived within the pavilion.
The Mountain gratified them with divine nectar and various kinds of food; indeed, they all partook [of it] along with Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and myself.
At that time, the women of the city joyfully hurled insults at them, laughing and looking at them with great effort while speaking in gentle tones.
O Nārada, having eaten and sipped water according to the rules, they took leave of the mountain and all departed for their own abodes, joyful and fully satisfied.
O Sage, on this third day as well, they were honored by the Lord of Mountains according to the prescribed rites with gifts, respect, hospitality, and other marks of esteem.
When the fourth day arrived, the rite of the fourth day was performed according to the rules for the sake of purification; yet, because it was lacking that [rite], it remained indeed incomplete.
There was a diverse festival with shouts of "well done! and cries of "victory!", as well as abundant giving, beautiful singing, and various kinds of dancing.
When the fifth day arrived, all the gods, filled with joy, made a request to the Mountain out of great affection for the sake of the procession.
Having heard that, the Lord of the Mountains spoke to the gods with palms joined in reverence: "O gods, please show me mercy and remain for a few more days."
Having spoken thus with affection to them—to the Lord Viṣṇu, to me, and to the others—he caused us to dwell there for many days, always with great respect.
In this manner, many days passed for those dwelling there; then the gods dispatched the Seven Sages to the presence of the Lord of the Mountain.
They awakened him and addressed Menā with words appropriate for the occasion; they joyfully and according to tradition praised and declared the supreme Śiva-tattva.
O Sage, having accepted those various requests through his own understanding, Śambhu, accompanied by the gods and others, went to the Lord of Mountains for the sake of the journey.
While the Lord of Gods, Śiva, was departing for his own mountain accompanied by the gods, Menā wept aloud and spoke to that ocean of compassion.
Menā said: "O ocean of mercy, having shown compassion, you will protect Pārvatī; O you who are easily pleased, you will forgive the thousand faults of Pārvatī."
And may my daughter be devoted to your lotus feet in birth after birth; she shall have no memory, even in dreams or in waking knowledge, of any lord other than Mahādeva.
O Conqueror of Death, by the mere hearing of devotion to you, one becomes endowed with tears of joy and horripilation; yet by your censure, one becomes silent, as if dead.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and then entrusted her daughter to him, Menakā wailed most bitterly and fell into a swoon before them both.
Then, having awakened Menā and taken leave of her, the Mountain likewise set out on his journey accompanied by the gods and preceded by a great festival.
Then all those Nirjaras, together with their hosts, set out on a journey toward the mountain in silence, bestowing auspiciousness upon the Lord.
In the grove outside the city of Himācala, the gods, together with their lord, remained joyful and full of celebration, searching for the arrival of Śiva.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, the auspicious journey of Śiva together with the gods has been described; now listen to the account of Śiva’s journey, which is joined with the festival of separation.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Pilgrimage," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then those seven seers spoke to the Lord of the Snowy Mountain: "O Mountain, cause your daughter to perform today the festival appropriate for the Goddess."
O lord of sages, having heard this and realizing the supreme nature of that separation, Giriśa became despondent due to his great love for a certain period of time.
After some time, having regained consciousness, the king of mountains then said, "So be it," and spoke this message to Menā.
O Sage, having heard the message from Śaila, Menā, overcome by joy and grief, prepared herself and set out to perform [the rites].
O Sage, Menā, the beloved of the mountain king, performed various festivals there according to the rules, following the Vedic injunctions and the customs of her own family.
He adorned Girijā with excellent garments of various jewels and with twelve ornaments, as magnificent as those of a king.
Having understood Menā’s intention, a certain virtuous wife of a twice-born man instructed Girijā in the supreme vow of devotion to her husband.

The wife of the twice-born said: O Daughter of the Mountain, listen with great affection to my words, which increase righteousness, bestow joy in this world and the next, and grant happiness to those who hear them.
Blessed is the woman devoted to her husband; no other is more especially worthy of honor. She is the purifier of all worlds and the destroyer of the multitude of all sins.
O Śivā, she who serves her husband with love as if he were the Supreme Lord enjoys all pleasures here in this world, and at the end, attains the auspicious state together with her husband.
And [there were] Sāvitrī, Lopāmudrā, Arundhatī, Śāṇḍilyā, Śatarūpā, Anasūyā, Lakṣmī, Svadhā, and Satī—all devoted to their husbands.
Saṃjñā, Sumati, Śraddhā, Menā, and likewise Svāhā—many other virtuous women as well have not been mentioned here for fear of prolixity.
By means of that very bull of wifely devotion, they attained the state of being honored by all; they became worthy of reverence even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, as well as by the lords of sages.
Therefore, you must always serve your husband Śaṅkara, the Lord; he is the bestower of grace upon the distressed, worthy of service by all, and the refuge of the virtuous.
The dharma of devotion to one’s husband, as proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, is great; it is certain that no other dharma is as excellent as this when it is thus described.
A woman devoted to her husband should eat only after her beloved husband has eaten; she should remain by his side, O auspicious one, as long as he lives, in every way.
She should sleep when he sleeps, and the wise woman should always wake before him; she should always act for his benefit, being dear to him and free from deceitful intent.
O Śivā, one should never show oneself without ornaments; however, when he has gone abroad for the sake of some business, one may remain devoid of adornment.

A woman devoted to her husband should never utter his name; even when reviled, she should not revile him in return, and even when struck, she should remain gracious. She should say, "O Master, please show mercy," and "May you strike me."
When summoned, she should leave her household chores and go to his side; quickly, with palms joined in reverence and full of affection, she should bow deeply and speak thus.
"For what purpose have you been addressed, O Lord? Let that favor be granted; then, being thus instructed, she shall perform her duty with a very serene mind."
One should not stay for long at the door, nor go to another's house; having received any truth whatsoever, one should never surrender it to anyone anywhere.
She herself should prepare all the requisites for worship that have not been mentioned, awaiting the opportune moment as is appropriate and beneficial for the time.
She should never go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords without her husband's permission; indeed, she should avoid from afar the sight of public assemblies and festivals.
But that woman who, seeking the merit of sacred fords, drinks the water from her husband's feet—in him, all sacred fords and holy sites reside; of this there is no doubt.
The devoted wife should eat the remnants of her husband's meal and whatever other food he desires, saying "This is a great favor," after it has been given by her husband.
One should not eat without having first distributed [the food] among the gods, the ancestors, guests, the circle of attendants, the cows, and the families of mendicants.
With her household utensils kept in order, skillful, joyful, and averse to wasteful expenditure, that goddess should always be devoted to her husband.
Without her husband's permission, she should not perform fasts, vows, or similar observances; otherwise, there is no fruit from them, and she shall go to hell in the next world.
When her husband is comfortably seated, resting at ease and enjoying himself according to his own will, she should never rouse him even for matters concerning the household.
Whether her husband is impotent, in a difficult situation, diseased, or even aged; whether he is happy or suffering, she must not disregard her one and only husband.
A woman in her menses must not show her own face for three nights, nor should she let anyone hear her voice, until she becomes pure through bathing.
Having bathed well, she should look at the face of her husband and never that of another; or else, having meditated upon her husband in her mind, she may gaze at the sun.
Turmeric, saffron, vermilion, collyrium and the like, a bodice, betel-leaf, and auspicious ornaments and so forth.
Desiring long life for her husband, a devoted wife should not remove the ornaments of the hair, the braided tresses, or the decorations of the hands and ears.
One should never, under any circumstances, form a friendship with a washerwoman, a harlot, a female bard, or an unfortunate woman.
She should never converse with a woman who hates her husband; she should never stand alone anywhere, nor should she ever bathe naked.
A virtuous woman should never stay anywhere—neither on a mortar, nor on a pestle, nor on a water-pot, nor even on a grinding stone; neither on a mechanical device nor on the threshold.
She should never display boldness except at the time of sexual union; wherever the husband finds pleasure, there she should be full of affection.
When her beloved is joyful, she should be joyful; when he is dejected, she should be dejected. The devoted wife should always seek the welfare of her husband.
Virtuous and steadfast, she should remain uniform in both prosperity and adversity; possessing fortitude, she should never allow her own nature to undergo any transformation.
Even when ghee, salt, oil, and other provisions are exhausted, a devoted wife should not tell her husband "there is nothing," nor should she involve him in arduous labors.
O Goddess of the gods, for a devoted wife, her own husband alone is considered superior to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or even Śiva; indeed, for her, her husband is Śiva himself.
She who performs vows, fasts, and religious observances in transgression of her husband takes away his longevity; upon death, she goes to hell.
A woman who, intent on anger, gives a retort when she has been addressed, is born as a dog in a village or as a jackal in a desolate forest.
A woman should never occupy a high seat, nor should she go into the presence of the wicked; nor should she ever speak words of cowardice to her husband.
One should not utter slander, and one should abandon quarreling from afar; in the presence of gurus, one should never speak loudly nor laugh.
Seeing him returning from outside, they quickly honored him with food, water, and meals, as well as with betel leaves, garments, and the massaging of his feet.
In that very way, she who, being herself delighted, gladdens her beloved with flattering words and supreme inducements of perspiration, has thereby gladdened the three worlds.
A father gives in moderation, a brother gives in moderation, and a son gives in moderation; one should always honor the husband, for he is the giver of the unlimited.
The husband is a god, the husband is a guru, and he is dharma, sacred fords, and vows; therefore, setting all else aside, she should worship her husband alone.
That evil-minded woman who, having abandoned her husband, wanders about in secret, is born as a cruel female owl dwelling in the hollow of a tree.
If, having been struck, she desires to strike back, she is a tigress or a female cat; and she who casts a sidelong glance at another is one with squinting eyes.
She who abandons her husband and eats sweet food alone shall become either a sow in a village or a female jackal eating its own excrement.
She who speaks unpleasantly after having done a favor is indeed born mute; she who is envious toward a co-wife becomes unfortunate again and again.
She who, having disregarded her husband's gaze, looks toward another man, is born as one-eyed, averted-faced, or even misshapen.
Just as a body devoid of life becomes impure in an instant, so too a woman deprived of her husband is always impure, even if she has bathed well.
Blessed is that mother in the world, blessed is that father, and blessed is that husband, in whose house dwells a goddess-like wife devoted to her husband.
Three generations on the father’s side, three on the mother’s side, and three on the husband’s side—these nine enjoy happiness in heaven through the merit of the devoted wife.
Those of evil conduct who break their moral discipline cause the downfall of three families—of their father, mother, and husband—and they themselves suffer in both this world and the next.
Wherever the foot of a devoted wife touches the earth, there indeed shall it become a destroyer of sin and most purifying.
Even the all-pervading sun, the moon, and the wind touch the wife devoted to her husband for their own purification; it cannot be otherwise.
The waters always long for the touch of a devoted wife; today our dullness has been destroyed, and we have become purifiers of others through you.
The wife is the root of the householder's life; the wife is the root of happiness. The wife is for the attainment of the fruits of dharma; the wife is for the increase of progeny.
In every house, are there not women proud of their beauty and charm? Yet, it is only through devotion to the Lord of the Universe that a woman devoted to her husband is obtained.
O wife, he who possesses you conquers both this world and the next; for one without a wife is not fit to perform rites such as sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and guests.
Indeed, that householder in whose home there is a devoted wife should be known as one who daily devours others, just as a Rakshasi devours them with her old age.
Just as the body becomes purified by bathing in the Ganges, so too everything becomes purified by the sight of a devoted wife.
There is no difference between the Gaṅgā and that woman who regards her husband as a deity; she is Umā and Śiva in person. Therefore, a wise person should worship them both.
Tāra was the husband and Śrutī the wife; Kṣamā was she and Svayaṃtapa was he. He was the fruit and Satkriyā was she; O Śivā, those two husband and wife were truly blessed.
Thus has the dharma of the devoted wife been described to you, O Queen of the Mountain Kings; now listen with great affection and attentiveness as I explain its various divisions.
O Goddess, those women devoted to their husbands are said to be of four kinds, distinguished as superior and so forth; they remove the sins of those who remember them.
The superior, the middling, the inferior, and the most inferior—listen attentively as I describe their characteristics.
O blessed lady, she whose mind constantly and certainly sees only her own husband even in dreams, and no other as a husband, is proclaimed as the highest type of woman.
O Daughter of the Mountain, she who perceives her husband with a virtuous mind as if he were a father, brother, or son, is indeed called a Madhyamā devoted wife.
O Pārvatī, she who, having understood her own duty with her mind, does not commit transgression, is indeed called "lowly" [in name] but is actually one of excellent conduct.
She who commits adultery out of fear for her husband or his family is indeed called the lowest of chaste wives by the ancient sages.
All four of them were devoted wives who destroyed sins for Śiva; they were purifiers of all the worlds, bringing joy both here and in the hereafter.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, through the request made by the three gods, a certain Brahmin who had died due to the curse of Vārāha was restored to life by the woman Atri.
Knowing this, O Daughter of the Mountain, you must always serve your husband with affection; it is that which eternally grants all desires in the auspicious state.
You are the Mother of the World, the Great Goddess; Śiva himself is your husband. Indeed, by remembering you, women become devoted wives.
O Goddess, what purpose is served by this narration in your presence? Nevertheless, O Śivā, it has been told by me today according to the custom of the world.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and bowed deeply to her, that brahmin woman ceased speaking; Pārvatī, the beloved of Śaṅkara, attained great joy.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Devoted Wife," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then that Brahmin woman, having instructed the goddess in that vow, addressed Menā and said, "Arrange her departure."
Having replied, "So be it," she became overcome by love; holding fast to her fortitude, yet distressed by the pangs of separation, she called out to Kālī.
Embracing him again and again, she wept most loudly; Pārvatī also wept aloud, uttering words of compassion.
Śailapriyā and Śivā also fell into a swoon, afflicted by grief; and the wives of the gods likewise fainted at the sound of Pārvatī’s weeping.
All the women wept, and everything became senseless; the Lord of Yogis himself wept as he departed—who else could be more powerful than him?
In the meantime, Himālaya quickly arrived there with all his sons, as well as his ministers and other brahmins.
Overcome by delusion, she wept herself, placing her calf upon her breast; crying out "Where are you going? she repeatedly made the place seem empty.
Then the family priest, most eminent in wisdom, out of compassion used the knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) along with the brahmins to awaken them all happily.
Pārvatī bowed with devotion to her mother, father, and guru; then, as Mahāmāyā, she wept aloud again and again in accordance with worldly custom.
At the very sight of Pārvatī’s weeping, all the women wept as well—especially Menā, her mother, her sisters, and her brothers.
Again and again, Śivāmātā, the other female attendants, the brothers, and their father wept out of love, bound by deep affection.
Then the Brahmins, having assembled, respectfully enlightened him; they announced an auspicious moment that would bring supreme happiness to the journey.
Then Himālaya, having steadied Menā through fortitude and discernment, had a palanquin brought for the purpose of Śivā’s mounting.
The Brahmin women there caused Śivā to mount [the palanquin]; her father, mother, and the twice-born all bestowed their blessings upon her.
And Menā, the mountain-dweller, likewise gave the great queen various articles of service and a collection of diverse auspicious objects difficult for others to obtain.
O Sage, Śivā, having bowed to all her gurus, as well as her father and mother, the brahmins, the family priest, her sisters, and other women, departed.
The wise Himācala also, accompanied by his son and overcome by affection, went there to where the Lord, together with the gods, had arrived, bringing joy to all.
With joy and preceded by a great festival, they all bowed with devotion to the Lord and, offering praises, entered the city.
I cause you, who possess the memory of past births, to remember; if you remember constantly, then speak. O Goddess of gods, you are always dear to me as my own life, even through mere play.
Brahmā said: Having heard this from Maheśa, her own lord, the virtuous Pārvatī, the eternal beloved of Śaṅkara, spoke with a smile.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of my life, I remember everything; you have become silent so that I may speak. Now, quickly perform what is appropriate for this occasion. Salutations to you!"
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his beloved, which were like hundreds of streams of nectar, the Lord of the Universe, who conforms to worldly conduct, rejoiced exceedingly.
Śiva, having gathered the necessary provisions, fed the gods, headed by Nārāyaṇa, with food made enchanting by various ingredients.
Likewise, the Lord affectionately fed all the others who had gathered for his wedding with various kinds of delicious food.
Then, having eaten, all those gods—adorned with various jewels, together with their wives and their attendants—bowed down to the moon-crested Lord.
Having praised him with pleasing words and circumambulated him filled with joy, they then departed for their own abodes while extolling the marriage ceremony.
O Sage, Śiva himself bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and to me, following worldly custom, just as Viṣṇu bows to Kaśyapa.
Having embraced him and bestowed blessings, and having recognized him as the Supreme Brahman before Śiva once again, I offered an excellent hymn of praise.
Having taken leave of Viṣṇu with joined palms, I joyfully praised the marriage of Śiva and Śivā and departed for my own supreme abode.
Śiva also remained on his own mountain, sporting joyfully with Pārvatī; all the Gaṇas attained great happiness as they served the two Śivas.
Thus, dear one, has been described this most auspicious marriage of Śiva, which destroys sorrow, generates joy, bestows long life, and increases wealth.
Whoever should constantly hear this, pure and with a mind focused upon it, or should cause others to hear it according to the rules, shall attain the world of Śiva.
This wonderful narrative has been told, which is a source of auspiciousness, the pacifier of all obstacles, and the destroyer of all diseases.
It brings fame, leads to heaven, and bestows long life; it produces a succession of sons and grandsons, grants all desires in this world, and always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It pacifies untimely death, brings about great peace, and is auspicious; it pacifies all evil dreams and is a means for achieving intelligence, wisdom, and other virtues.
This, which causes the satisfaction of Śiva, should be recited with effort and affection during all festivals of Śiva by people desiring auspiciousness.
One should recite it with great joy at the time of the consecration of deities and others especially, and at the commencement of every undertaking for Śiva.
Or, having become pure, one who hears this auspicious life-story of Śiva and Śivā shall have all their undertakings accomplished; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Departure for Kailāsa," in the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus ends this third section, the Pārvatī-khaṇḍa.

|| Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. || Salutations to Śrī Gaurī and Śaṅkara. Now begins the fourth section, the Kumāra-khaṇḍa, within the Rudra-saṃhitā. I praise Śiva—Śaṅkara—who is pleased by Nandana (Kārtikeya), whose mind is equanimous, who is beloved of love, the bestower of love, the perfect one, the fulfiller of all, the sole abode of complete and absolute sovereignty; who is Truth, composed of Truth, the manifestation of the three truths, beloved of Truth, the giver of Truth, praised by Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and who assumes a form through his own grace.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, after marrying Girijā, what did Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, do upon returning to his own mountain? Please tell me that.
How indeed was a son born to Śiva, the Supreme Soul—for whose sake the Lord, though delighting in the Self alone, took up the hand of Śivā?
O Brahman, how did the death of Tāraka come about, O benefactor of the gods? Having shown compassion toward me, tell all of this in its entirety.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Nārada, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), with a very gracious mind, remembered Śaṅkara and replied.
Brahmā said: O Nārada, listen as I shall recount the life of the moon-crested Lord Śiva—the divine narrative of Guha’s birth and the righteous slaying of the demon Tāraka.
Listen, for today I shall tell a story that destroys sin; by hearing which, a human being is certainly liberated from all sins.
This narrative is sinless, a supreme secret, and most wonderful; it removes the torment of sin and destroys all obstacles.
It bestows all auspiciousness, it is the essence, it is captivating to all who hear it; it grants happiness, it is the seed of liberation, and it cuts away the very root of karma.
Having arrived at Kailāsa and married Śivā, Śiva also attained supreme splendor; he then reflected upon the duties of the gods and the suffering of the people caused by those divine affairs.
When the Blessed Lord Śiva went directly to Kailāsa, all the Gaṇas, being exceedingly joyful, provided him with various kinds of happiness.
A great festival took place when Śiva arrived at Kailāsa; the gods, their minds overflowing with joy, returned to their own realms.
Then Śambhu, the Great God, taking hold of the auspicious Girijā, went to a secluded place that was most divine and enchanting.
Having prepared a delightful bed, smeared with flowers and sandalwood paste—wonderful, supreme, auspicious, and provided with all objects of enjoyment.
There the Blessed Lord Śambhu, the bestower of honor, sported with the Daughter of the Mountain for a period of a thousand years according to the measurement of the gods.
By the mere touch of Durgā’s limbs, Śiva was playfully rendered unconscious; she too, having fainted from the touch of Śiva, did not regain consciousness day or night.
O sinless one, while they were thus engaged in enjoyment and following the ways of the world, a great length of time passed for them as if it were but a moment.
Then, O dear one, all the gods, led by Śakra, gathered together at once and, having come to Mount Meru, held a consultation.
The Suras said: "The Lord Śambhu, the master of yogis, free from transformation, delighting in his own self, and stainless, has performed this marriage for the sake of our purpose."
His son has not been born, and we do not know the reason for this; why, then, is such delay being made by that Lord of Gods?
In the meantime, the gods learned from Nārada, who possesses divine vision, of that limited duration of enjoyment while the two were sporting together.
Having long observed their enjoyment, those gods became anxious; placing me, Brahmā, at their head, they went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed to him, I related the entire desired account; all the gods stood motionless like figures in a painting.
Brahmā said: For a thousand years, according to the measurement of the gods, Śaṅkara remained intent on sexual union; motionless as a yogi, he did not desist at all.
The Blessed One said: "There is no cause for anxiety; all will be well for the Sustainer of the World. O Lord of Gods, seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the Great Lord."
For those people who have joyfully sought refuge in Maheśa with their minds, and who are devoted to Prajeśa, there is no fear from anywhere at any time.
O Creator, the destruction of this amorous passion will not occur now; for an action performed at the proper time attains success, and not otherwise.
Who here is capable of interrupting the desired enjoyment of Śambhu? Indeed, after a full thousand years, he will cease of his own accord.
He who, by some means, causes the interruption of sexual union between a woman and a man, shall suffer separation from his wife and children in birth after birth.
In this world, he shall be one whose knowledge has fallen away, whose fame is destroyed, and who is devoid of fortune; at the end, that sinner goes to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred thousand years.
The great lord of sages, Durvāsas, caused this Śakra, who was joined with Rambhā, to cease from sexual pleasure; indeed, that became the cause of the separation of his wife.
Furthermore, having obtained and served another woman of auspicious hands, he cast off the fever of separation for a thousand divine years.
The preceptor restrained Kāma as he was embracing Ghṛtācī; within six months, Candra indeed abducted his wife.
Having again propitiated Śiva and waged a battle consisting of stars, he obtained Tārā while she was pregnant and abandoned the fever of separation.
The great seer Gautama made Candra, who was with Mohinī, desist from sexual union; thus, his separation from his wife occurred.
Hariścandra caused a plowman to be driven about, joined with a Śūdra woman, rendered motionless; hear now the fruit of that.
Fallen from his wife, son, and kingdom, and struck by Viśvāmitra, he then propitiated Śiva and was indeed liberated from that affliction.
O best of the twice-born, neither out of fear nor for any other reason did the gods prevent Ajaamila, even though he was united with a low-caste woman, nor did any of them restrain her.
Everything is to be accomplished through the *niṣeka*, and the *niṣeka* is powerful, O Ordainer; since that *niṣeka* indeed bestows its fruit, by whom can it be obstructed?
And that act of Śambhu’s enjoyment lasted for a thousand divine years; when the thousand years were complete, the lords of the gods went there.
Whatever effort you shall certainly undertake that would cause one to fall to the ground, by that very effort, there shall arise a son of the Lord named Skanda.
Now go to your own abode, O Creator, together with the hosts of gods; let Śambhu enjoy himself with Pārvatī in a secluded place.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, the beloved of Kamalā went quickly to his inner apartments; O lord of sages, the gods also returned to their own abodes along with me.
Furthermore, due to the movement of Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti, the earth—though supported by Śeṣa and the Tortoise—was overcome by the weight and trembled violently.
Indeed, by the weight of the tortoise, the wind that supports all things was paralyzed, and the three worlds became overwhelmed with fear.
Then all the gods, with dejected minds, sought refuge with me and with Hari; they reported that entire event in its entirety.
The gods said: O God of gods, Lord of Ramā, Sovereign who provides protection to all! Protect us, who have sought refuge in you, our minds agitated by fear.
I do not know for what reason the vital breath of the three worlds has been paralyzed; the three realms, including all things mobile and immobile, are thrown into agitation by the sages and the gods.
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having spoken thus, all the gods, together with me, stood before Viṣṇu, distressed, silent, and deeply sorrowful.
Having heard that and taking all the divine food, Hari went quickly to Mount Kailāsa, the beloved abode of Śiva.
Having gone there with the gods and with me, Hari, the beloved of the deities, proceeded to the abode of Śiva, desiring to behold Śaṅkara.
Having seen Śiva there, Viṣṇu was filled with wonder along with the gods; full of humility, he questioned the attendants of Śiva who were stationed there.
Viṣṇu said: "O Śaṅkaras, O hosts of attendants, where has Śiva, the lord of all, gone? O merciful ones, please tell us out of affection, for we are indeed distressed."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the gods, the hosts of Śaṅkara, who are identical in essence with Hari, spoke with affection to the Lord of Ramā.
The attendants of Śiva said: O Hari, listen; out of devotion to Śiva, we shall tell you the truth regarding the entire account that took place together with Brahmā and the gods.
The Lord of All, Mahādeva, who is expert in the divine play of Rāsa, established us here with great affection and went to the abode of Girijā.
O Lord of Ramā, we do not know what Śambhu, the Great Lord, is doing within that cave; many years have passed by.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having heard those words from them along with me and the gods, Viṣṇu was greatly amazed and went to the gate of Śiva.
Having gone there, O Sage, I then addressed that Hari, the beloved of the gods, with piteous words in a loud voice before the deities.
O best of sages, while staying there with the gods, Hari, together with me, praised Hara, the lord of all worlds, with great devotion.
Viṣṇu said: O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, what are you doing within? Protect all the gods who are afflicted by Tāraka; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
O Lord of Sages, having thus praised Śambhu in many ways with words accompanied by the *soma* mantra, Hari wept there, afflicted by the pain of Tāraka.
O Lord of Sages, a tumultuous cry of distress arose there among the inhabitants of heaven, mingled with the chanting of auspicious hymns by those afflicted by the asuras.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Pastimes," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having heard that, Mahādeva, who is expert in the knowledge of yoga and has abandoned all desire, did not abandon his union out of fear of Pārvatī.
Śiva, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, arrived at the gateway of the gods' abode, near the deities who were being tormented by the Daitya.
Upon seeing the Lord Śiva—who is kind to his devotees—along with Hari and myself, all the gods then became exceedingly joyful.
Having heard these words of the gods, the Lord Bhava replied with a dejected soul and a heart filled with anguish.
Having bowed with great affection, O Sage, all those gods, with shoulders bent low, praised Śaṅkara together with me and Hari.
The gods said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord, ocean of compassion! You are indeed the inner witness of all; you know everything, O Śaṅkara."
O Lord, perform the work of the gods; protect the deities, O Maheśvara! Having shown compassion, slay the Daityas, the great lords such as Tāraka and the rest.
Śiva said: O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O all you gods, the course of your minds is as follows: whatever is destined to be will surely come to pass; there is no one who can prevent it.
O immortals, listen to what has been brought forth; whatever has arisen, that indeed has arisen. Who will now receive this semen fallen from my head?
Having said, "Let him take it," he caused it to fall upon the ground; for Agni, having become a pigeon, was indeed impelled by all the immortals.
Then, with its beak, it consumed the entire Śambhava virility; in that interval, O Sage, Girijā arrived there.
And upon the delay in the arrival of Śiva’s messenger, she beheld the foremost of the gods; having learned that entire account, Śivā was filled with great wrath.
Then he spoke to all the gods, beginning with Hari.
The Goddess said: "O you entire hosts of gods, you are especially wicked; you are always intent on achieving your own selfish ends, and for that purpose, you inflict suffering upon others."
"O gods, having propitiated Maheśāna, the supreme lord, for the sake of their own interests, they destroyed my monastery; thus I have become barren."
O gods, happiness can never belong to anyone who opposes me; therefore, suffering shall indeed befall you wicked inhabitants of heaven.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus to all the gods headed by Viṣṇu, the auspicious Śivā, daughter of the King of Mountains, blazing with fury, uttered a curse.
Pārvatī said: "From this day forward, let the wives of the gods be barren; and let all the gods who oppose me be filled with sorrow."
Brahmā said: Having thus cursed all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, the sovereign of all, being enraged, spoke to Pāvaka, the consumer of Śiva’s seed.

Pārvatī said: "O pure one, always remain one whose soul is afflicted, becoming a consumer of all things; you do not know the true nature of Śiva, for though you perform the work of the gods, you are a fool."
O you rogue, O great villain, you who possess the wicked intellect of the wicked! That you did not consume the seed of Śiva—which is indeed fit to be consumed—is truly proper.
Brahmā said: O Sage, having thus cursed Agni along with Īśa, the daughter of the mountain, Śivā, departed swiftly for her own abode, remaining dissatisfied.
Having gone there, O lord of sages, Śivā diligently and properly awakened Śiva, and gave birth to a supreme son named Gaṇeśa.
O Sage, I shall describe that entire account in your presence; now listen with great pleasure as I speak of the birth of Guha.
The gods indeed consumed food and other offerings offered by Pāvaka and others; according to the Vedic word, all those deities consequently became pregnant.
Then, unable to endure his prowess, all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were indeed tormented; their intellects were lost due to the supreme command of Śiva.
Then all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, being utterly bewildered and scorched by the flames, quickly went for refuge to the Lord of Pārvatī.
Having gone to the gateway of that abode of Śiva, all the gods, bowing low with palms joined in reverence, praised Śambhu along with Śivā with great affection.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord of Girijā, Great Master! O Protector, what has happened now? Your Māyā is difficult to overcome."
We have been born with embryos within us, being scorched by your seed; O Śambhu, show us mercy and ward off this condition.
Brahmā said: Having heard this praise from the immortals, O sage, the Supreme Lord, the husband of Śivā, quickly arrived at the gate where the gods were stationed.
When Śaṅkara arrived at the gate, all the gods, including Viṣṇu, bowed down and joyfully praised the dancer who is kind to his devotees.
The gods said: O Śambhu, O Śiva, O Maheśāna, we bow especially to you; protect us who have sought refuge in you and are being consumed by [your] seed.
"Take away this suffering, take it away! For we shall certainly die. Who else besides you is capable today of warding off the suffering sent by the gods?"
Brahmā said: Having heard these most piteous words, the Lord, the King of the Gods, who is affectionate toward his devotees, then laughed and replied to the deities.
Śiva said: O Hari, O Vidhi, and all you gods, listen to my words! Happiness shall be yours today; indeed, remain attentive.
O all you gods, vomit forth this my virility immediately; by my command, O illustrious ones, you shall thereby be especially happy.
Brahmā said: Having accepted this command upon their heads, Viṣṇu and all the other gods quickly performed vomiting while remembering the imperishable Śiva.
That [semen] of Śambhu, golden-hued, wondrous, and mountain-like in form, fell upon the earth; it was exceedingly radiant, as if touching the very heavens.
All the gods, including Indra and the other immortals, became joyful; they praised Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
O Lord of Sages, Pāvaka was not at all happy there; then Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, indeed gave him his supreme command.

Then that fire-god, free from doubt, bowing with palms joined in reverence before the sage, praised Śiva and, being at ease, spoke these words: The fire-god, his doubts dispelled, bowed with palms joined in reverence before the sage; having praised Śiva, he became happy and spoke these words.
Agni said: "O God of gods, O Great Lord, I am your servant and I am deluded; forgive my transgression and indeed ward off my burning."

"O Lord, you who are compassionate toward the distressed, you are Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord. Thus addressed, the Fire-god, his soul pleased, replied to the one who is compassionate toward the distressed.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śuci, that supreme lord Śambhu, whose soul was gracious and who is compassionate toward the distressed, replied to Pāvaka.
Śiva said: "An improper act has been committed by you, for my semen was indeed consumed. Therefore, due to the excess of your sin, this burning shall not cease even by my command."
Now you are indeed happy, O pure one, having come for refuge to me; therefore I have become pleased, and all suffering shall perish.
"Carefully deposit my semen into the womb of a certain virtuous woman; you will indeed become happy, especially with a mind free from burning anguish."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Śambhu, the pure one, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, spoke slowly and affectionately to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of his devotees.
O Lord, O Maheśvara, this splendor of yours is difficult to approach; there is no one in the three worlds capable of bearing it within their womb except for Śakti.
O best of sages, when the Fire-god spoke thus, you, acting for his benefit and impelled by Śaṅkara, addressed the Fire-god from within your heart.
Nārada said: Listen to my words, O Fire, which remove your burning pain; they are auspicious, bestowing supreme bliss, delightful, and warding off all hardships.
"O Fire, having employed this means, become one who consumes [only] with ease. O Father, this has been properly spoken by me out of respect, according to the will of Śiva."
O pure one, at dawn, place this great semen of Śiva within the bodies of those women who perform their ritual baths during the month of asceticism (Māgha).
Brahmā said: O Sage, at that time the wives of the seven sages arrived there in the morning, having undertaken their religious observances and desiring to bathe during the month of penance (Māgha).
O Sage, having bathed, those six women, afflicted by great cold, desiring to depart, went near the flames of fire.
Seeing them thus deluded, Arundhatī, who was well-conducted and wise, by the command of the Lord of the Mountain, forbade them with particular severity.
O Sage, those six wives of the sage went there out of delusion and by force, seeking to dispel their own cold, being utterly bewildered by the Māyā of Śiva.
O Sage, those drops of semen immediately entered all his bodies through the pores of his skin; the fire became devoid of burning.
Having vanished quickly, the Fire-god, in the form of a flame, departed for his own world in happiness, while mentally remembering you and that Śaṅkara.
O noble one, those women, who were pregnant and tormented by the burning heat, went to their own homes, O dear one, while Arundhatī remained distressed by the fire.
O dear one, having seen the fate of their own wives, the lords, agitated by anger, quickly consulted with one another and abandoned those women, O dear one.
Then, seeing all six women who had committed adultery, they were overcome with great sorrow, O dear one, and their minds became deeply agitated.
The wives of the sages then cast off that seed of Śiva, which had taken the form of an embryo; thereafter, they became free from burning on the slopes of the Himālaya mountains.
Unable to endure that semen of Śiva and trembling with fear, Himādri, afflicted by the unbearable heat, quickly cast it into the Gaṅgā.
O lord of sages, even Gaṅgā cast that unbearable power of the Supreme Self into a clump of reeds by means of her own waves.
That semen, having fallen there, quickly became a boy who was handsome, fortunate, glorious, radiant, and a source of increasing joy.
O Lord of Sages, on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the manifestation of that son of Śiva occurred upon the earth.
At that time, O Brahmana, why were the daughter of the snowy mountain and Giriśa not happy there on their own mountain?
From Śivā’s two breasts, milk born of bliss flowed forth; and having gone there, O Sage, everyone experienced exceeding happiness.
O dear one, there was auspiciousness that bestows happiness upon the virtuous throughout the three worlds; yet for the wicked, and especially for the Daityas, it became an obstacle.
Suddenly, O Nārada, a supreme sound of dundubhi drums arose in the sky, and a rain of flowers quickly fell upon the boy.
O best of sages, for all the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, there suddenly arose supreme bliss and a great festival.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śiva’s Sons," in the fourth section (Kumārakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O God of gods, Lord of creatures, Brahmā, Creator, Master! What happened there after that? Please tell me now; have mercy.
Brahmā said: At that moment, O dear one, the powerful Viśvāmitra, impelled by destiny, arrived there joyfully and by chance.
Having beheld that extraordinary splendor of his highly resplendent son, he became one whose desires were fulfilled; being well-pleased, he bowed down.
Viśvāmitra, who knew his own power, offered praise to him with a very serene mind and with words prompted by ritual injunctions.
Then, having become a son there, he was exceedingly delighted and, laughing with a wondrous joy, spoke to Viśvāmitra: "O Great One! he said.
Śivasuta said: O possessor of great knowledge, you have come here unexpectedly by the will of Śiva; O father, perform for me the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) exactly as prescribed in the Vedas.
"From this day forward, become my priest, bringing me joy; you shall always be worthy of worship by all, of this there is no doubt."
Brahmā said: Having heard his words, the son of Gādhi was indeed well-pleased; filled with great wonder, he spoke to him in a low tone of voice.
Viśvāmitra said: "Listen, my dear, I am not a Brahmin; I am the son of Gādhi, a Kṣatriya known as Viśvāmitra, a Kṣatriya who serves Brahmins."
"Thus has my own life-story been told by me to you, O excellent boy. Who are you? Tell me your own life-story in its entirety, for I am filled with wonder."
Brahmā said: Having heard his words, he related his own history; then the creator of great light spoke with great affection to that son of Gādhi.
Śivasuta said: "O Viśvāmitra, by my boon you shall be a Brahmarṣi; there is no doubt about this. And Vasiṣṭha and the others will always praise you with respect."
Therefore, by my command, you ought indeed to perform the consecration; all of this must be kept strictly secret by you and never disclosed to anyone.
Brahmā said: O celestial sage, he then performed for him, out of affection, the entire supreme consecration for the child Śiva according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
The Lord Śivabāla, the great benefactor, being well-pleased, bestowed supreme divine knowledge upon the sage Viśvāmitra.
The son of Śuci made Viśvāmitra his family priest; from that time on, that best of the twice-born became an expert in various divine sports.
O sage, thus have I related to you that pastime performed by Him; O dear one, listen with affection as I describe another of His pastimes.
At that moment, O dear one, he who was now named Śveta beheld there his own divine son, most supremely purifying.
Then Pāvaka went to him, and having seen him, embraced and kissed him; saying "O son," he gave him the weapon Śakti.
Guha took that spear and ascended that peak; he struck him with that spear, and Śṛṅga fell to the earth.
Ten padmas of heroic rākṣasas who had previously arrived quickly fled from his blows in order to kill him.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the earth with its mountains trembled; the three worlds were shaken, and the Lord of the Gods arrived there.
And on his right side, he struck him with a thunderbolt; from that, a single man named Śākha was born, possessed of great strength.
Then Śakra quickly struck him again on the left side with his thunderbolt; another man was born, a different powerful one named Viśākha.
Then Śakra struck that heart with his thunderbolt; however, another man of great strength emerged from it, known by the name Naigama.
Then the four great heroes of immense strength, Skanda and the others, rushed swiftly to slay Indra; thereupon, he (Indra) went for refuge to Soma.
O Sage, having become terrified, Śakra and his host of gods fled from that cave to their own world in great alarm; they did not discover the cause of the breach.
That boy remained right there, filled with bliss; O dear one, the Lord remained fearless as before, performing various divine sports.
At that moment, six women known as the Kṛttikās, having arrived there to bathe, beheld that boy of great splendor.
O Sage, all those Kṛttikā women set their minds on seizing him, and among them there arose a dispute centered on the desire to take hold of him.
To prevent that twelfth month from occurring, he indeed assumed six faces; he drank the milk of all [the cows], and they became satisfied, O Sage.
O Sage, having understood the intention of his mind, all those Kṛttikās then took him and went joyfully to their own world.
Having offered their breasts to that infant named Kumāra who desired them, they nourished the son of the Lord, whose radiance surpassed even that of the sun.
And those women who did not make the boy invisible to their eyes—he who was the object of their love even more than their own lives, O son, he is your foster-father.
And whatever garments were difficult to find even in the three worlds, they gave those to him out of love, as well as excellent ornaments.
Day after day, they nourished that boy, the Great Lord, especially by feeding him highly praised and delicious foods.
Then one day, dear father, that child, the son of the Kṛttikās, went to the divine assembly of the gods and performed a noble deed.
The boy, a performer of great wonders, indeed displayed his own most marvelous majesty to all the gods, including Viṣṇu, bringing them immense delight.
Upon seeing him, all those gods, along with Acyuta and the sages, were filled with extreme wonder and questioned that boy.
Having heard "Who are you?", he said nothing at all; he went quickly to his own abode and remained hidden just as before.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Kārtikeya’s Play," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: O God of gods, O Lord of creatures, O Creator, what happened after that? Please tell me now out of compassion, together with the divine play of Śiva.
Brahmā said: O Sage, while that son of Śambhu was being held by the Kṛttikās, some time passed without the daughter of the Himālaya being aware of it.
At that moment, Durgā, her lotus-like face smiling, spoke to her lord Śambhu, the sovereign of the gods and the supreme master.
Pārvatī said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, listen to my auspicious words; by the great weight of my past merit, you, O Lord, have been obtained by me.
Out of compassion, O Bhava, you became intent on ascetic practices among the foremost of yogis; there, O God, you brought about the destruction of my pleasure.
O Lord, that seed which fell upon the ground did not enter my womb; O God, where has it gone, and by what destiny was it concealed?
O Maheśvara, how is it that the prowess of my master has become fruitless for you? Why has it gone in vain, or why has he been born as a child somewhere?
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Pārvatī, the Lord of the Universe smiled and, having summoned the gods and the sages as well, spoke, O lord of sages.
Maheśvara said: "O gods, listen to my words; you have heard Pārvatī's speech. Where has my infallible seed gone, and by whom has it been concealed?"
If he does not deserve punishment, he shall not fall swiftly into fear; yet a king who is capable but fails to punish one who oppresses his subjects and devours them is himself a consumer of sin.
Having heard those words of Śambhu and deliberated among themselves, they all spoke in turn before the Lord, filled with fear.
Viṣṇu said: Let those who have concealed your prowess be liars in this world of Bhārata; let them be perpetual revilers of their gurus and those who take pleasure in censuring their elders.
Brahmā said: He by whom your virility was suppressed in the meritorious field of Bhārata shall not be entitled to your service or worship there.

The world-protectors said: "That sinner by whom your prowess was concealed through the delusion of [seeing you as] fallen—his vessel is utterly filled with the continuity of that very penance and karma."
The gods said: "That fool who, having made a promise, does not bring it to fulfillment, is a vessel for sin—he by whom your prowess was concealed."
The wives of the gods said: "She who reviles her own husband and goes to another man, she who is bereft of maternal kinsmen, and by whom your seed was concealed."
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the gods, Hara, the Lord of the gods of gods, spoke these fearful words to Dharma and the others, who are the witnesses of all actions.
Śrī Śiva said: "O Lord, why was that seed of mine, the Blessed Maheśvara, not consumed by the gods? Surely it must have been consumed, for the seed of my Lord is never in vain."
And you all are witnesses forever to every action; what is hidden from you, or what are you able to know or speak?
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the Lord, those in the assembly trembled; looking at one another, they spoke in turn before the Lord.
Brahmā said: "While Rati was standing there, his semen fell upon the surface of the earth; I knew that it was infallible due to the intense wrath of Śaṅkara."
The Earth said: "Incapable of enduring that seed, I cast it into the fire long ago. Therefore, O Brahmin, you ought to forgive me, a weak woman, for this which was difficult to bear."
Vahni said: "O Śaṅkara, being unable to endure your unbearable virility on Mount Kailāsa, I immediately cast it off in the form of a pigeon."
The Mountain said: "O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the World, O Supreme Lord, being unable to endure your power, I immediately cast that unbearable [seed] into the Gaṅgā."
Gangā said: "O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the worlds, I was unable to endure your virility; O Lord, O Master, being greatly distressed, I cast it into the forest of reeds."
Vāyu said: His seed fell upon the arrows, and immediately a boy was born, O Śambhu, exceedingly beautiful on the pure bank of the celestial river.
Sūrya said: O Lord, seeing the child weeping, I went to the western mountain; impelled by the wheel of time, I was unable to remain during the night.
Candra said: O Śambhu, having found the weeping infant and taken him, the group of Kṛttikās went to their own abode while traveling toward Badarikāśrama.
Jala said: "O Lord, having brought this crying child here, those [goddesses] nourished your son, who possesses the splendor of the sun, by giving him milk to drink."
Saṃdhyā said: "Now, having nourished that son in the forest of the Kṛttikās, they affectionately and with curiosity gave him the name Kārttikeya."
Rātri said: They did not allow the boy to pass beyond the range of their vision—he who was the object of their affection even more than their own lives, and who was the son of their protector.
Dinam said: "Whatever garments and excellent ornaments there were, and whatever praised delicacies, they indeed fed him."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of theirs, the Destroyer of Cities was satisfied; attaining joy, he affectionately bestowed abundant sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins.
Having received news of her son, Pārvatī, with a joyful heart, gave ten million jewels and vast wealth to the Brahmins.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Menā, Sāvitrī, and all women, as well as Viṣṇu and all the gods, gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then the Lord of the mountain, together with the gods and sages, dispatched messengers to those hosts where his son was.
Vīrabhadra, Viśālākṣa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Karākrama, Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Mahonmada.
He has the face of Gokarṇa and the countenance of Dadhimukha, resembling a blazing crest of fire; there are one hundred thousand Kṣetrapālas and three hundred thousand Bhūtas.
O Nārada, [he saw] the Rudras and the Bhairavas, whose prowess was equal to that of Śiva, as well as others of deformed appearance, beyond counting.
All those messengers of Śiva, with various weapons and missiles in their hands, being arrogant, surrounded the abode of the Kṛttikās.
Seeing all those Kṛttikās with their minds agitated by fear, they spoke to Kārttikeya, who was blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
The Kṛttikās said: "O child, countless armies have surrounded our abode; what should be done, where should we go? A great danger has arrived."
Kārttikeya said: "O auspicious ladies, cast away your fear; for what fear can there be while I am present? I am a child difficult to restrain—by whom, O mothers, can I be held back?"
Brahmā said: In the meantime, Nandikeśvara, the lord of the army, sat down before Kārttikeya and spoke.
Nandīśvara said: "O brother, listen to my auspicious account; so too, O mothers, listen. I have been impelled by Maheśa, the destroyer Śaṅkara."
O dear one, on Mount Kailāsa, all the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, were seated in the assembly hall during a great and auspicious festival.
Then Śivā, having addressed Śaṅkara, the benefactor of all, in the assembly, spoke for the purpose of searching for you.
Śiva questioned those gods in succession for the sake of attaining you; they, however, each gave a reply as was appropriate.
In this place, the Kṛttikās, they all—Dharma and the others, who are the witnesses to the actions of dharma and adharma—proclaimed you as the Lord.
In ancient times, the secret dalliance of Pārvatī and Śiva took place; and when Śambhu was beheld by the gods, his seed fell upon the earth.
He threw it onto the ground; the fire cast it into the ocean; that mountain was thrown by the fire into the Gaṅgā; and she, with great force, cast it into the forest of reeds by means of her waves.
In that regard, you were indeed a child who was not born, for you are the lord capable of accomplishing the work of the gods; having been received there by the Kṛttikās, go now to the earth.
Śambhu, together with the gods, will perform your consecration; you shall obtain all weapons and you will slay the one named Tāraka.
"You are the son of the Destroyer of the Universe, yet these [goddesses] are unable to reach you, just as a dry tree in its own hollow is not capable of protecting itself from fire."
Though you are radiant, you do not shine among all these houses, just as the king of birds does not look splendid when falling into a great pit.
And you act so as not to obscure us with your brilliance, just as the sun, even when partially obscured by a digit of the moon, does not become hidden from human beings.
O Śambhava, you are Viṣṇu, the pervader of the worlds; no other has been born. Just as space is the pervader of everything and there is nothing for it to pervade, so are you.
The lord of yogis is not smeared even while participating in nourishment, just as the Self of living beings is not smeared by the performance of actions.
You are the origin of all things and the Lord; no stability can exist within you, just as yogis perceive themselves as a mass of qualities and splendors.
O brother, those men who do not recognize you are of ruined intellect; they pay no heed to you, just as frogs disregard lotuses that share their same dwelling place.

Kārttikeya said: "O brother, you know everything, including that knowledge which pertains to the three periods of time. You are a man of wisdom; what praise can be sufficient for you, since you have taken refuge in the Conqueror of Death?"
O brother, whatever karmas lead to birth in whichever various wombs, those very ones now bring you peace in this world.
The Kṛttikās, who possess wisdom and are Yoginīs who are portions of Prakṛti—by their breast milk, I have been constantly nourished through their great kindness.
I am the foster-son of these women, who are portions of myself; and they are portions of that Prakṛti; therefore, I am born from the power of my mistress.

O Nandikeśvara, there shall be no breaking of my vow by the daughter of the Lord of Mountains; for she is my mother according to dharma, just as these [other wives] are universally acknowledged to be.
"Sent by Śambhu, you are great and equal to the son of Śambhu; I shall come with you and behold the assembly of the deities."
Having spoken thus and quickly awakened the host of Kṛttikās, Kārttikeya set forth together with the attendants of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Nandin and Kārttikeya’s Search," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In the meantime, he beheld there an excellent chariot, wonderful, ever resplendent, and fashioned by Viśvakarman.
It had a hundred wheels, was very spacious, moved at the speed of thought, and was captivating; it was dispatched by Pārvatī and surrounded by her excellent attendants.
Then the infinitely wise Kārttikeya, born from the seed-power of the Supreme Lord, ascended with a grieving heart.
At that very moment, having reached the Kṛttikās, their hair disheveled and afflicted by grief, they began to speak these words right there like those who have gone mad.

The Kṛttikās said: "O ocean of compassion, you are indeed heartless, for you depart leaving us behind! This is not the dharma, that a son should abandon his group of mothers after having protected them."
"This son has been raised by us with affection, and according to dharma he is our own; what shall we do, where shall we go, and what indeed shall we do?"
Having spoken thus, all the Kṛttikās placed Kārttikeya upon their breasts; then, due to the impending separation from their son, they quickly fell into a swoon.
O Sage, having awakened them with words concerning the inner self, the prince ascended the chariot together with them and his attendants.
Having seen and heard many auspicious things that indeed bestow happiness, the prince went to his father’s palace together with his attendants.
Accompanied by Dakṣa and Nandin, and traveling on a chariot that moves with the speed of thought, Kumāra reached Kailāsa at the root of the imperishable banyan tree.
There Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara, who is skilled in various divine sports, stayed with the Kṛttikās and his foremost attendants, full of joy.
Then all the hosts of gods, the sages, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas, together with Viṣṇu and Brahmā, announced his arrival.
Then, having seen the son of Gaṅgā, Śiva went forth filled with joy, accompanied by others—by Hari, Brahmā, and the celestial sages.
Many conchs resounded, and bherīs and tūryas were played manifold times; there was a great festival for the gods whose minds were filled with satisfaction.
At that very moment, all the Gaṇas, headed by Vīrabhadra, followed him while performing their play with various rhythmic beats and melodies.
The panegyrists, being themselves praised, sang the praises of his virtues; with delighted minds, they uttered cries of "Victory! and "Homage!"
They went to see that unsurpassed son of Śiva, who was born from the arrow.
Pārvatī made the royal road auspicious and enchanting, having adorned the city on all sides with rubies and other precious gems.
Accompanied by virtuous women who possessed sons, she arrived, placing the thirty goddesses, Lakṣmī and the others, at her front.
By the command of Śiva, the divine apsarases, Rambhā and others, adorned with smiles and elegant attire, became intent upon music and dance.
Those who beheld that son of Gaṅgā, who resembled Śaṅkara, saw a great splendor pervading the three worlds.
Enveloped by that splendor, all quickly paid homage to the youth Kumāra, who shone like molten gold and possessed the brilliance of the sun.
Then, with shoulders bowed and delighting in the sound of "namas," they stood surrounding him, having approached from both the left and the right.
I, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and all the gods and others likewise prostrated themselves on the ground like staffs, surrounding the Kumāraka.
In the meantime, Śambhu and Girijā, filled with joy, arrived at the great festival and beheld their son with delight.

Then, beholding his son, the sole kinsman of the world—the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of all, who is truly endowed with the coils of a serpent and surrounded by the Pramathas—was filled with supreme and transcendent joy along with Bhavānī and embraced him with affection.
Then Śaktidhara, seeing Skanda and those two, Pārvatī and Śiva, quickly descended from his chariot and bowed with his head.
Embracing the youth with affection, Śiva, the benevolent Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord who bestows love, joyfully and with tenderness kissed him upon the head.
