Embracing Guha there, Pārvatī, overcome with agitation and overflowing with affection, caused him to drink from her breast which had begun to flow.
Then, having been honored with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by the gods together with their wives, who were filled with joy, the vault of the sky was pervaded by a great cry of "Victory! (jaya).
The sages with the chanting of Vedic hymns, the singers with their songs, and many others with musical instruments attended upon the youth there.

Then Maheśa, placing that infant who was blazing with radiance upon his own lap, shone forth as the husband of Bhavānī himself, visibly endowed with splendor, the most excellent among those possessed of sons.
The Prince, together with his own attendants and accompanied by the gods with great enthusiasm, arrived at the abode of Śiva in great happiness by the command of Śiva.
Then that couple shone there, walking together along a single path, being saluted by the sages and surrounded by the best of the gods.
The boy, filled with joy, played upon Śiva’s lap; he squeezed Vāsuki, who was situated on Śiva’s neck, with both his hands.
Then the Lord Śambhu, the compassionate one, smiling and looking upon the daughter of the mountain with a merciful glance, spoke to her who was assuming a playful form.

Then the Blessed Maheśa, together with Girijā, attained supreme joy through her intoxicating smile; yet the Lord, the sole kinsman of the world and the unique sustainer of the universe, being choked with love, said nothing at all.
Then Śambhu, the Lord of the World, being delighted and adopting a worldly manner, seated Kārttika upon a beautiful jeweled throne.
With joy, he bathed him with hundreds of jars filled with excellent gems and water from all the holy fords, consecrated by Vedic mantras.
Hari gave him a crown and armlets fashioned from the essence of the seven precious gems, as well as his own Vaijayantī garland and his discus.
Śiva gave him the trident, the Pināka bow, the axe, the spear, the Pāśupata arrow, the weapon of destruction, and the supreme vidyā.
I gave him the sacrificial thread, the Vedas, and the Mother of the Vedas (Sāvitrī), as well as a water-pot, the Brahmāstra weapon, and the lore that crushes enemies.
The Lord of the Gods gave him a lordly elephant and a thunderbolt; the Lord of the Waters gave him a white umbrella and a garland of jewels as a gift.
The Sun [gave] a chariot that travels by mind and a great heap of armor; Yama [gave] the staff of Yama; and the Lord of Nectar [gave] a jar of nectar and a treasury of nectar.
Hutāśana affectionately gave a great spear to his own son; Nirṛti gave him his own weapon, and Samīraṇa gave him the Vāyavya missile.
Kubera gave him a mace, and Īśa joyfully gave him a trident; all the gods joyfully bestowed various weapons and strategic means upon him.
Then Kāmadeva, filled with joy, gave him the weapon of desire (kāmāstra); and with supreme delight, he also gave him a mace and his own secret sciences.
The Ocean of Milk gave priceless jewels and a distinguished jeweled anklet; Himālaya indeed gave divine ornaments and garments.
Garuḍa gave his own son, named Citrabarhaṇa; Aruṇa gave [his son] named Tāmracūḍa, who was powerful and had feet for weapons.
Smiling and delighted, Pārvatī, with great affection, granted him supreme and excellent sovereignty as well as long life.
And Lakṣmī joyfully bestowed upon him divine prosperity, a magnificent and captivating necklace, and Sāvitrī granted him the entirety of perfected knowledge.
O Sage, other goddesses who had also gathered there likewise gave him suckling infants who were like their own selves.
O best of sages, a great festival took place there; everyone attained a state of joy, Śiva and Śivā especially so.
In the meantime, at that time, the powerful Rudra Bharga, laughing with joy, spoke to the gods beginning with Brahmā, O Sage.
Śiva said: O Hara, O Vidhi, and all you gods, listen to my words! I am pleased with you in every way; choose whatever boons you desire.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of Śambhu, O Sage, Viṣṇu and all the other gods, with cheerful faces, spoke to the Lord Paśupati.
O Lord, this Tāraka shall indeed be slain by the Kumāra; it is for that very purpose that this supreme narrative has come into being.
Therefore, this very day we shall set out, prepared to slay Tāraka; grant permission to Kumāra so that he may slay him for our well-being.
Brahmā said: Thinking "So be it," the Lord, moved by compassion, then granted a son to the gods to slay Tāraka.
Then, by the command of Śiva, all the gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, immediately set forth from the mountain together, placing Guha at their front.
Having emerged from Kailāsa at the command of Hari, Tvaṣṭṛ constructed a beautiful and wonderful city near the mountain.
There, Tvaṣṭṛ constructed for Guha a divine, wonderful, and most radiant palace; therein he fashioned an excellent lion-throne.
Then the wise Hari, with devotion, caused the auspicious consecration in the month of Kārttika to be performed by the gods using the waters of all the sacred fords.
Having adorned everything in every way, he caused the collection [of scriptures] to be housed; out of devotion, he joyfully performed the rites and the festival of Kārttika.
Indeed, Hari joyfully bestowed upon him the sovereignty over the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa); he applied the tilaka upon his forehead and honored him along with the gods.
Having bowed with affection to Kārttikeya along with all the gods and sages, he praised the eternal one, whose form is Śiva, with various hymns of praise.
Seated upon his excellent lion-throne, Kārtika shone exceedingly; having attained the status of a sovereign, he became the protector of the universe.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Consecration of Kumāra," in the fourth section (Kumāra-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Now, O Nārada, listen with great affection to that very Sūtikā whom the son of Gaṅgā manifested there—she who bestows devotion upon her own devotees.
At that very moment, a certain illustrious twice-born man named Nārada arrived there as a performer of the sacrifice, seeking refuge indeed with Guha.
Having approached Kārttikeya with a serene mind, that brahmin, having bowed deeply with auspicious hymns of praise, fully declared his own intention.
The Brahmin said: Listen to my words today, O Lord, and ward off my suffering; you are the master of the entire universe, and therefore I have come to you for refuge.
I began to perform the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha), but that goat, having broken its own tether, went back to my house.
I do not know where he has gone, though much searching was conducted for him; since he has not been found, this powerful failure will befall my sacrifice.
O Lord, while you are my protector, how could there be an obstruction to the sacrifice? O Sovereign of all, having reflected upon this, fulfill my desire.
O Lord, son of Śiva, leaving you who are the refuge, whom else should I go to—you who are indeed the master of the entire universe and well-served by all the immortals?
The Supreme Lord is the kinsman of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, easily served, and affectionate toward His devotees; He is well-praised by the gods, beginning with Hari and Brahmā.
Skanda, the delight of Pārvatī, is the supreme one, the scorcher of enemies; he is the Supreme Self, the bestower of the self, and the Lord of the virtuous who seek refuge.

O Lord of the wretched and the helpless, O Great Lord, O Son of Śaṅkara, O Sovereign of the three worlds, O Master! O Lord of Māyā, I have come for refuge; protect me, O Beloved of the Brahmins! You are dear to all lords, you are praised by Brahmā and the other gods who know all things; you are the embodiment of Māyā, the bestower of happiness upon your devotees, intent on protection, and the wielder of Māyā.

O mine of devotion, life-force, and virtues; You who are distinct from the three *guṇas*; beloved of Śambhu; Śambhu himself; the son of Śambhu; the bestower of gracious happiness; whose nature is pure existence and consciousness; the Great One; the omniscient one; the son of Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura; always subdued by true love; the six-faced one; dear to the virtuous; beloved by those who bow; the Lord of all; Śaṅkara; the slayer of those who commit treachery against the saintly; O Teacher of Śaṅkara; Lord of the cosmic egg; Master of all; whose feet are served by the immortals and others—protect me, O lover of service!

O Śaṅkara, who strikes fear into enemies and brings happiness to those who take refuge in you, I bow at your lotus feet; O Skanda, place my petition in your ear and always instill devotion to yourself in the hearts of people.

What can even a powerful adversary do to him, though he be skillful and protected on both sides by his own faction? Is it not Takṣaka, or some other flesh-eater, that you protect with such persistent pride?

Even the preceptor of the gods would not be capable of praising you; tell me, how then could I, one of dull intellect, do so, O most worshipful one? Whether I am pure or impure, noble or base—whatever I may be—I pray for the pollen of your lotus feet, O Skanda.

O Lord of All, O lover of devotees, O ocean of mercy, I am yours; I am your servant. O True Lord, may a hundred blessings come upon me, your attendant and leader of the hosts! O All-pervading Lord, you who destroy the suffering of your servants, you know even the slightest devotion offered by me anywhere. There is no other protector besides you, and there is no man more wretched than I, O Blessed One.

O Guha, you who perform auspicious deeds, who destroy the impurities of the Kali age, who are the kinsman of Kubera, whose heart is moist with compassion, who possess eighteen eyes and shine with six faces—may you complete my sacrifice for me.
You are the protector of the three worlds, compassionate toward those who seek refuge; as the performer and sustainer of sacrifice, you seize those who create obstacles.
O dispeller of obstacles for the virtuous, O cause of creation in every respect, O Lord, fulfill my son’s sacrifice; salutations be unto you!
O Skanda, you are indeed the protector everywhere; you alone are the omniscient one. You are the Lord of all, the sovereign ruler, the one who provides shelter and protection for everyone.
You alone are the knower of music, the supreme lord who understands the Vedas; you are the sustainer of all, the creator, the god of gods, and the refuge of the virtuous.

The delighter of Bhavānī, the son of Śambhu, the wise one, the self-ruling lord; he is the meditator, the object of meditation, the father of the ancestors, and the source of those whose nature is eternal.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, the emperor of the gods, the son of Śiva, dispatched his own attendant named Vīrabāhu for that purpose.
At his command, the great hero Vīrabāhu, having bowed with devotion to his master, departed swiftly for the purpose of searching for him.
He conducted a search throughout the entire sphere of the universe; he did not find that Unborn One anywhere, yet he heard of his distress.
Then he went to Vaikuṇṭha, and there he beheld that Unborn One (Aja), the exceedingly powerful one who had a throat as his sacrificial post, causing great affliction.
Seizing him by the two horns and overpowering him with great speed, the hero brought him before his master while he let out many cries of distress.
Seeing him, that lord Guha, who bears the weight of the universe and is the great creator of progeny, joyfully ascended the chariot along with Kārttikeya.
O Sage, in merely a moment, that unborn one wandered through the entire universe; yet, becoming quickly fatigued, he returned once more to his original place.
Having emerged from there, that Lord sat upon his own seat; while Aja remained right there, Nārada spoke to him.
Nārada said: "Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods! Grant me [the boon of] the Unborn, O ocean of mercy. Out of joy, may I perform a sacrifice; indeed, make me your companion."
Kārttikeya said: "O Brahmin, this goat is not fit for slaughter; go to your own home, O Nārada. May your entire sacrifice be complete, accomplished through my very grace."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words, the lordly twice-born one, his mind filled with joy, went to his own abode after bestowing upon him the highest blessing.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wondrous Deeds of Kumāra," in the fourth section (Kumāra-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having witnessed that conduct of the Lord, those gods, headed by Hari, became truly delighted, their minds fixed in trustful devotion.
Leaping and raising a roar, imbued with the splendor of Śiva, they placed Kumāra at their head and advanced to slay Tāraka.
Having heard of the exertion of the gods, the exceedingly powerful Tāraka also immediately set out with a vast army to fight against the deities.
Seeing Tāraka’s great force approaching, the gods, exerting themselves with might, uttered lion-like roars and were filled with wonder.
Then, impelled by Śaṅkara, the celestial maiden immediately spoke these words from above to Viṣṇu and all the other gods with great haste.
The Voice from the Sky said: "O gods, placing Kumāra at your head, you shall exert yourselves; having conquered the Daityas in battle, you will then be victors."
Brahmā said: Having heard that speech of Khecarī, all the gods became eager; uttering heroic shouts, they then indeed became fearless.
Placing the prince at their head, all those gods, filled with trepidation yet desirous of battle, went to the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
He went quickly to that place where the gods and Tāraka were, accompanied by a vast army and surrounded by many deities.
At his arrival, battle-drums resounded with the roar of clouds at the dissolution of the world, and other harsh musical instruments were likewise played.
Then those Daityas, roaring with the asura Tāraka, made the earth tremble with the treading of their feet, making a beautiful sound.
Hearing that most terrible roar, all the gods, free from fear, rose up simultaneously, desiring to fight Tāraka.
Having mounted the elephant, the Lord of the Gods placed the Kumāra before him, surrounded by a vast army of deities and the world-protectors.
Then kettledrums resounded, along with numerous bherīs and tūryas, as well as vīṇās, flutes, mṛdaṅgas, and the melodies of the gandharvas.
Having given the elephant to Mahendra, the prince ascended a vehicle that was filled with many wonders and endowed with various jewels.

Then, having ascended the celestial chariot, the illustrious son of Śaṅkara, endowed with all virtues and possessed of supreme splendor, shone forth as a great being while being fanned by magnificent yak-tail whisks.

Then that exceedingly radiant parasol of Pracetas, endowed with jewels and resplendent with various ornaments, was indeed held over the head of the youth by rays of immense luster like those of infinite moons.
Then all those gods, led by Śakra, assembled together; surrounded by their respective forces, those beings of great strength were eager for battle.
Thus the gods and the Daityas stood upon the earth, desirous of battle, having each formed their own separate military array with that great army.
Those two armies of the gods and the daityas shone against one another as they sought to slay each other, while being praised by bards.
Then both those armies, resembling forests, roared; they were terrifying to those lacking in heroism, yet bringing joy to the others.
In the meantime, there the great heroes—the Daityas and the gods—mad with strength and overwhelmed by rage, fought with one another.
A tumultuous battle ensued, crowded with gods and daityas; in an instant, the entire field became strewn with headless trunks and severed heads.
There, by the hundreds and thousands, those esteemed as heroes fell upon the ground, their limbs severed by great weapons and themselves slain.
The arms of some were severed by most terrible sword-strokes, and the thighs of other proud heroes were cut off in the battle.
Some had all their limbs crushed by maces and clubs, while others had their hearts pierced and were felled by nooses and broad-headed arrows.
Some were torn in their backs by spears, double-edged swords, and goads; even their severed heads fell upon the ground.
And there were indeed many headless trunks dancing there, leaping by the hundreds with their hands raised, grasping weapons.
Then, hundreds of rivers carrying blood began to flow there, and hundreds of bhūtas, pretas, and other beings assembled at that place.
Jackals and jackal-like dogs were there devouring much flesh; likewise, vultures, herons, hawks, and crows that feed on meat, ate very great quantities of the flesh of those who had fallen.
In the meantime, the exceedingly powerful one named Tāraka immediately set out with a vast army to fight against the gods.
Seeing Tāraka approaching, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle and desiring to fight, Śakra and the other gods immediately departed; then, a great roar arose from both armies.
Then there occurred a duel, a clash between gods and asuras, seeing which the heroes were filled with joy while the cowards were struck with fear.
In the battle, the powerful son of Diti, Tāraka, fought with Śakra; Saṃhrāda fought with Agni, and Yama himself fought with Jambha.
The great lord Varuṇa was with Nairṛta and Bala; Suvīra was with Vāyu, and Guhyarāj was with Pavamāna.
Śambhu, the foremost among those skilled in battle, fought with Īśāna; the Dānava Śumbha fought with Śeṣa, and Kumbha fought with Candra.
The potter, possessed of great strength and prowess, skilled in various modes of combat, fought with Mihira in battle using supreme missiles.
Thus, in that great battle, all the gods and asuras, having resolved upon their strength, fought one another in pairs.
O Sage, competing with one another in that war between the gods and asuras, those immensely powerful immortals and demons became invincible.
And then there occurred a tumultuous battle between those gods and dānavas seeking victory—a source of joy to the heroic and high-minded, yet a cause of terror to their opponents.
The earth became exceedingly fierce with numerous gods and asuras who had perished and fallen; at that time, it became inaccessible and most terrifying, yet it brought great happiness to the wise.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Commencement of the Battle," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Thus, O dear one, I have described to you the exceedingly tumultuous battle between the armies of the gods and the dānavas; now hear, O Nārada, concerning their lords.
Thus, in that exceedingly tumultuous battle which brought about the destruction of gods and dānavas, the lord of the gods was struck by Tāraka with a śakti weapon along with Ramā.
Immediately the elephant fell to the earth and he became unconscious; the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of the gods, fell into a state of extreme dejection.
In the same way, O dear one, all the world-protectors were defeated in battle by the even more powerful asuras, who were highly skilled in great warfare.
Other Nirjaras also, while fighting with the Daityas, were defeated; unable indeed to endure his splendor, they became intent on flight.
There, the victorious asuras, whose efforts were well-directed, roared with lion-like cries, intent upon a tumultuous clamor.
In the meantime, Vīrabhadra, filled with wrath, approached Tāraka—who considered himself a hero—accompanied by his heroic attendants.
Leaving Nirjarā behind, the powerful leader of the Gaṇas, born from the wrath of Śiva, then stood facing him, desiring to fight.
Then all those Pramathas and Daityas, filled with supreme joy, fought one another in battle, intent upon the great conflict.
Skilled in combat, they struck one another in the battle with tridents, spears, nooses, swords, axes, and sharp-edged spears.
Struck violently by Vīrabhadra with his trident, Tāraka suddenly fell to the ground, overwhelmed for a moment by a swoon.
Rising quickly, that hero Tāraka, the best of the Daityas, having regained consciousness, struck Vīrabhadra with force using his spear.
Likewise, the heroic Vīrabhadra, possessed of great splendor, swiftly struck Tāraka with a fierce, sharp trident.
Then Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas, powerful and esteemed as a hero, struck Vīrabhadra in battle with his own power.
Thus contending, those two, both experts in the science of war, struck each other in battle with various missiles and weapons.
Then, while everyone was watching, a tumultuous and hair-raising duel took place there between those two great-souled ones.
Then kettledrums, clay drums, war-drums, cymbals, and horns resounded, struck by the heroes, producing a most terrifying sound for those who heard it.
Fully armored, they fought on, their bodies mangled by blows; enraged at one another, they were like the planets Mercury and Mars.
Having thus witnessed that battle between Vīrabhadra and him, you, the beloved of Śiva, went there and spoke to Vīrabhadra.
Nārada said: O Vīrabhadra, great hero, you are the leader of the Gaṇas; desist from this battle, for your slaying does not seem right.
Having thus heard your words, Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, overcome with rage, then spoke to you with his palms joined in reverence.
Vīrabhadra said: "O best of sages, O one of great wisdom, hear my supreme word: I shall slay Tāraka; behold today my prowess."
And those heroes who bring their master into the assembly of battle—those sinners, great cowards, perish once they have entered the fray.
They fall into an evil state, and for them hell is certain; indeed, Vīrabhadra must be recognized [as such], and you should never speak against him.
Those whose limbs are pierced by weapons and missiles yet engage in battle fearlessly are praiseworthy both in this world and the next; they obtain wonderful happiness.
"Listen to my words, O gods, led by Hari: today I shall make the earth free of Tāraka and devoid of its Lord."
Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra, the wielder of the trident, together with the Pramathas, meditated upon Śambhu in his mind and indeed fought with Tāraka.
Mounted upon many bulls and bearing excellent tridents, that great hero, possessing three eyes, shone resplendent as he engaged in battle.
Making a great clamor, hundreds of fearless hosts, placing Vīrabhadra at their head, fought with the Dānavas.
Those Asuras as well, who lived for the sake of the Asura Tāraka—mighty and great heroes—fought on, crushing the Gaṇas in their fury.
Again and again there occurred a most fierce battle between the hosts and the foremost of the Daityas; then those hosts, exulting and skilled in supreme weapons, became victorious.
Defeated by those powerful hosts, the asuras turned their backs in battle; overcome with pain and agitated in mind, they became intent on flight.
Seeing his own army thus routed, the asura Tāraka, its protector, overcome with rage, went forth to slay the hosts of gods.
Having assumed ten thousand arms and swiftly mounting a lion, he struck down those gods and their hosts at the forefront of the battle.
Seeing that deed of his, the mighty Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, became exceedingly enraged and resolved upon his slaughter.
Remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he seized his supreme trident; by its splendor, all the directions as well as the sky were set ablaze.
In the meantime, the Lord, desiring to witness the great spectacle, immediately brought that battle to a halt before Vīrabāhu and the others.
Then, by his command, Vīrabhadra withdrew from the battle; thereupon Tāraka, the leader of the asuras, became enraged.
Then the asura, skilled in the employment of various weapons, rained down a shower of arrows upon the gods and instantly scorched them.
Having thus performed this great deed, Tāraka, the protector of the asuras and the best among the strong, became invincible even to all the gods.
Seeing the gods thus being struck down and overwhelmed with fear, Acyuta became enraged and quickly prepared himself for battle.
Taking up his discus Sudarśana and the Śārṅga bow, the Lord Hari, equipped with his weapons, advanced for battle against the great Daitya.
Then, O sage, a great battle took place between Hari and Tāraka, hair-raising and exceedingly fierce, while all were looking on.
Raising his mace, that Hari struck the asura with great vigor; the exceedingly powerful Daitya split it in two with his trident.
Then the Blessed One, the granter of fearlessness to the gods, being enraged, struck the leader of the asuras with volleys of arrows discharged from his Śārṅga bow.
That great hero among the Daityas, Tāraka, the slayer of enemy heroes, swiftly cut down all those arrows with his own sharp shafts.
Then the demon Tāraka swiftly struck Murāri with a spear; Harī fell to the ground, unconscious from that blow.
In an instant, the unshakable Acyuta rose up in wrath, let out a great lion’s roar, and seized his discus, which was filled with blazing flames.
With that [weapon], Hari struck the lord of the Daityas; afflicted by that great blow, he fell to the earth.
Rising once more, Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas and leader of the Asuras, endowed with exceeding strength, swiftly shattered the discus with his own power.
Again, with that great spear, she struck the beloved of the immortals; but Acyuta, the great hero, struck him back with his sword Nandaka.
In this manner, O sage, both the powerful Asura and Viṣṇu fought extensively with one another in battle, their forces remaining unhurt.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the General Battle between the Devas and Daityas," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, O Lord Guha, O son of Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, this battle between Viṣṇu and the demon Tāraka is useless and does not shine with glory.
"This powerful Tāraka cannot indeed be slain by Viṣṇu; he has been granted a boon by me. I tell you this as the truth, the very truth."
"O son of Pārvatī, there is no other slayer of this evil one except for you; therefore, O Great Lord, you must indeed carry out my word."
"Arm yourself quickly for the slaying of the Daitya, O scorcher of foes; you were born from Śaṅkara for the purpose of his destruction, O son of Śivā."
Protect, protect, O Great Hero, the gods who are distressed in battle! You are neither a child nor merely a youth; rather, you are the Lord, the Sovereign of All.
Behold Śakra, as well as Viṣṇu and the hosts of gods, all distressed; thus slay the great Daitya and make the three worlds happy.
By him Indra was formerly conquered along with the world-protectors, and even the great hero Viṣṇu was threatened by the power of his asceticism.
The entire three worlds were conquered by that evil-minded asura; now, through your presence, they have engaged in battle once again.
Therefore, Tāraka, that sinful man, must be slain by you; yet he cannot be killed by anyone else, O son of Śaṅkara, due to my boon.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of mine, Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara, laughed with a serene soul and spoke the words, "So be it."
Having resolved upon the slaughter of the Asuras, that great lord, the son of Śaṅkara, then descended from his celestial chariot and became a foot-soldier.
Then that most heroic Kumāra, the son of Śiva, shone as he ran about on foot, holding in his hand that great, radiant spear which was blazing with light like a massive meteor.
Seeing that immeasurable, six-faced one approaching—extremely fierce yet unperturbed—the Daitya spoke to the best of the gods: "This is Kumāra, the slayer of his enemies."
Indeed, as a lone hero, I shall fight with him alone; I myself shall slay all the heroes, as well as all the hosts along with the world-protectors and the leaders of the Haris.
Having spoken thus, that one of great strength then set out to fight, directed toward the prince; he seized a most wonderful spear and addressed the best of gods, saying: "Tāraka."
Tāraka said: "How is it that you have placed my son before me today? You gods are devoid of shame, O Śakra and Īśvara especially!"
Listen as I speak and describe in detail that contrary action which was performed by these two in the past, in opposition to the path of the Vedas.
In this matter, Viṣṇu was indeed deceitful and faulty, especially lacking in discernment; for it was by resorting to trickery out of wickedness that he formerly bound Bali.
By that very same effort, he previously deprived the two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, of their heads; yet, out of deceit, he abandoned the path of the Vedas.
Indeed, by assuming the form of a female seducer, he caused a breach in the ranks; during the drinking of the nectar by the gods and asuras, the path of the Vedas was thus defiled.
Having become Rāma, a woman was killed; indeed, Vālī was destroyed. Again, Vaiśravaṇa and the two Brahmins were slain; thus, the policy of the Śruti has been violated.
Since that man devoted to evil abandoned his own wife through wickedness, he likewise destroyed the path of the Vedas for the sake of his own selfish ends.
In his incarnation known as Rāma, he cut off the head of his own mother; furthermore, this evil-minded one insulted the son of his guru.
Having become black and behaving like other ignoble men, they have been corrupted from their family dharma; having abandoned the path of the Vedas, they have likewise performed their own marriages.
Furthermore, in his ninth birth, the path of the Vedas was indeed censured, and the doctrine of nihilism, which opposes the Vedic path, was established.
Thus, how could he who has committed evil by abandoning the path of the Vedas be victorious in battle and become the foremost among those who possess dharma?
His eldest brother was Śakra, who was considered a great sinner; for his own sake, he committed numerous sinful deeds.
For the womb of Diti was indeed cut open for the sake of his own self-interest; Gautama’s wife was indeed violated, and Vṛtra, though born of a Brahmin, was slain.
The heads of his preceptor, who was of the Viśvarūpa lineage and his own sister’s son, were indeed severed; thus was the path of the Veda destroyed.
Although Hari and Śakra had repeatedly committed many sins, they were utterly deprived of their splendor and, in particular, had their vigor destroyed.
By their power, you shall achieve victory in battle; for what reason have you come here to abandon your lives, having fallen into such folly?
Knowing this Dharma, their minds were not greedy for their own self-interest; for without Dharma, all the activities of the immortals would be fruitless.
"These two have today acted with great audacity by placing a child before me; I shall kill the boy, and that [retribution] will also fall upon them."
"Would a fool go far from here out of a desire to save his life? Having said this, he addressed the monkeys and spoke to Vīrabhadra.
O sinless one, many brahmins were slain by you in the past at Dakṣa’s sacrifice; today I shall show you the fruit of that deed.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, Tāraka—the foremost among warriors—by means of that act of reviling him, shook off his own merit and seized a most wonderful spear.
As the demon Tāraka approached the presence of the boy with great vigor, Śakra, preceded by Guha, struck him with his thunderbolt.
By that blow of the thunderbolt, Tāraka was shattered; his strength struck down by the reproach, he suddenly fell to the ground for a moment.
Though fallen, he rose up and struck him with all his might in fury; indeed, he threw Purandara, who was mounted upon his elephant, down to the ground.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Purandara fell; indeed, upon seeing that, distress entered the army of the immortals.
Listen to me regarding that deed performed by Tāraka in that very place, which was painful, the cause of his own destruction, and contrary to dharma.
Having stepped upon the fallen one with his foot and seized the vajra from his hand, he struck Śakra violently once more with that very vajra.
Seeing him thus humiliated, the Blessed One, possessing the majesty of Śakra and Viṣṇu, raised his discus and struck Tāraka.
Struck by the blow of the discus, he indeed fell to the earth; rising again, the lord of the Daityas struck Viṣṇu with a spear.
By that blow from the spear, Acyuta fell to the earth; his arm became massive, and the gods cried out in great distress.
In the twinkling of an eye, just as Viṣṇu himself was about to rise up, Vīrabhadra arrived before the Asura at that very moment.
Raising his trident, the powerful and mighty Vīrabhadra violently struck Tāraka, the lord of the sons of Diti.
Then, by that blow from the trident, he fell upon the earth; yet even though fallen, the immensely powerful Tāraka rose up once more.
Then, having become enraged, the great hero, the leader of all the asuras, struck Vīrabhadra in the chest with his supreme spear.
Vīrabhadra also fell to the ground, unconscious for a moment; he had certainly been struck in the chest by her supreme power out of wrath.
Those gods, along with their hosts, as well as the gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, cried out again and again with a great sound of "Alas! (hāhākāra).
In an instant, that one of great power, Vīrabhadra—the slayer of enemies—suddenly raised his trident, which flashed like lightning and blazed with radiance, and shone forth brilliantly.

Illuminating the expanse of the quarters with its own radiance, its orb equal to the orbs of the sun, the moon, and fire; possessing great splendor, inspiring fear in heroes, supreme, known as Time (Kāla), causing the ultimate end, and exceedingly brilliant.
Just as the mighty Vīrabhadra, desiring to slay the asura with his trident, was restrained by Kumāra.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Tāraka, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Vīrabhadra, and the Others," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the fourth Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having restrained that Vīrabhadra, Kumāra, the slayer of enemy heroes, desired the destruction of Tāraka, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva.
Then the immensely powerful Kārttikeya, endowed with great splendor, roared; he became enraged and prepared for battle, surrounded by a vast army.
Then "Victory! Victory! was cried out by all the gods and the gaṇas, and at that very moment he was praised with pleasing words by the celestial sages.
Then a most unbearable battle took place between Tāraka and Kumāra; it was exceedingly terrible and struck fear into all living beings.
And those two heroes, with spears in hand, fought each other while all there looked on in great wonder, O Sage.
With their bodies pierced by spears yet joined in a great feat of valor, those two of immense strength deceived one another like two mighty lions.
Relying upon Vaitālika and likewise relying upon the one known as Khecaraka, they both struck Śakti with their power, having taken recourse to that evil one.
With these mantras, those two great heroes, possessing immense strength and prowess, engaged in a wondrous battle, each acting as the other's adversary.
Displaying great strength and desiring to slay one another, those two experts in battle struck each other with the edges of their spears in the fray.
They struck one another on the head, the throat, as well as the thighs, the knees, the hips, the chest, the breast, and the back.
Then those two of great strength, skilled in various modes of combat, fought while desiring to slay one another, leaping about and uttering heroic shouts.
All the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras became spectators; there they said to one another, "Who will be victorious in this battle?"
Then a voice from the sky spoke, consoling the gods and addressing the asura Tāraka: "This Kumāra shall slay you here."
"Let there be no grief among all the gods; remain in happiness. For Śaṅkara himself has manifested for your sake in the form of a son."
Then, having heard that auspicious voice uttered in the sky, the young Kumāra, surrounded by the Pramathas and desiring to slay the lord of the Daityas, Tāraka, quickly became joyful.
With that spear, the mighty-armed Kumāra, possessed by wrath, struck the Asura Tāraka in the middle of his chest with great force.
Disregarding that blow, Tāraka, the bull among the Daityas, being enraged, struck Kumāra in turn with his own spear.
By that blow from the spear, the son of Śaṅkara fell unconscious; after a moment, he regained consciousness while being praised by the great sages.
Just as a lion intoxicated with pride desires to kill an asura, so did the powerful Kumāra strike Tāraka with his spear.
Thus, both the prince and Tāraka, experts in combat with spears, fought one another with great fury.
Intent on reaching the highest level of mastery, those two swift-footed warriors, desiring to conquer one another, fought as foot soldiers in a manner that was wondrous to behold.
Displaying various maneuvers and roaring with great prowess, those two struck each other with diverse multitudes of blows.
All the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras, intent on gazing [at him], were struck with supreme wonder; they said nothing at all there.
The purifying wind did not blow, and the sun became lusterless; the entire earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
In the meantime, the mountains, headed by Himālaya, moved there, overcome with affection and desiring to take back Kumāra.
Then, seeing all those mountains terrified with fear, the son of Girijā, the follower of Śaṅkara, spoke to them, seeking to awaken their understanding.
The prince said: "O fortunate ones, do not grieve; O mountains, do not harbor anxiety. Today I shall slay this most wicked man; behold it all."
Having thus consoled the hosts of immortals on the mountain at that time, and having bowed to Girijā and Śambhu, he took up the brilliantly radiant spear.
Desirous of slaying that Tāraka, the great lord Kumāra, the son of Śambhu and a mighty hero, shone forth with his hand raised in power.
Then, endowed with the splendor of Śaṅkara, Kumāra struck that Tārakāsura, the tormentor of the worlds, with that very power.
The great hero named Tāraka, the lord of all the hosts of asuras, suddenly fell to the earth with his limbs shattered.
O Sage, while everyone was looking on, Tāraka, having been struck by the Kumāra, the exceedingly heroic one, indeed met his destruction right there.
Seeing Tāraka fallen in that manner, the hero did not strike him again; instead, having gone to him who was lifeless in battle, he departed.
When that mighty Daitya named Tāraka had been slain, many asuras were then brought to destruction by the hosts of gods.
In that battle, some became terrified with palms joined in reverence; thousands of Daityas there had their limbs severed and mangled, and they died.
Then some Daityas, seeking refuge, were born as the prince's protectors; with palms joined in reverence, they cried out, "Save us! Save us! at that time.
How many were slain there, and how many fled? As they fled, distressed and struck by the hosts of the gods, they were pursued.
Desiring to live, they entered Pātāla by the thousands; fleeing in all directions, they were broken in hope and fell into a state of wretchedness.
Thus, O lord of sages, the entire army of the Daityas was routed; at that time, none remained there out of fear of the Gaṇas and the gods.
When that evil-minded one was slain, everything became free from thorns; then all those gods, headed by Śakra, attained happiness.
When the prince had thus attained victory, all the gods and the three worlds simultaneously became joyful and filled with great happiness.
Then Śiva, having learned of that victory of Kārtika, arrived there joyfully along with his attendants and his beloved.
Placing her own son, the prince who possessed the splendor of the sun, upon her lap, Śivā, overflowing with affection, fondled him with great joy.
Then Himālaya, having arrived surrounded by his sons, along with his kinsmen and followers, offered praise to Śambhu, Śivā, and Guha.
Then all the hosts of gods, the sages, the Siddhas, and the Cāraṇas, being greatly delighted, praised Śambhu, the son of Śaṅkara, and the daughter of the mountain who was exceedingly pleased.
Then the secondary gods (Upasuras) showered a vast rain of flowers; the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
At that time, musical instruments resounded with particular intensity, and shouts of "Victory! and "Homage! arose repeatedly and loudly.
Then Acyuta was especially pleased with me; he respectfully offered praise to Śiva, Śivā, and Kumāra.
Placing the prince at their head, the gods led by Hari and Indra, as well as other sages, joyfully performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then there was a great festival with the sound of singing and instrumental music, with the abundant chanting of the Vedas, and especially with hymns of praise.
O Sage, being praised by all the gods and their hosts with songs, musical instruments, and very gracious gestures accompanied by joined palms, the Lord of the World became manifest.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, having been praised by all, departed for his own mountain accompanied by Bhavānī, the Mother of the World, and surrounded by his own attendants.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of the Gods Following the Slaying of the Asura Tāraka," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: In the meantime, O sage, a mountain named Krauñca, afflicted by the arrow, came there for refuge to Kumāra.
Fleeing from the battle because he could not endure his divine majesty and power, he, endowed with the strength of ten million times ten thousand, pierced Mount Krauñca excessively.
Having prostrated at the lotus-feet of the prince with devotion, he respectfully praised Guha with words overflowing with love.
Krauñca said: O Kumāra Skanda, Lord of Gods, destroyer of the demon Tāraka! Protect me, who have sought refuge in you and am oppressed by Bāṇāsura.
O Mahāsena, having been utterly defeated in battle, he fled; yet coming back, O Lord, O Compassionate One, he tormented me. Alas! O Protector!
Afflicted by that and deeply distressed, I have come to you for refuge; O Lord of Gods, O Kārttikeya, take pity on me as I flee!
O Lord, destroy that Daitya named Bāṇa and make me happy; for you are the slayer of Daityas, especially the protector of the gods and the self-sovereign ruler.
Brahmā said: Thus praised by Krauñca, Skanda, the protector of devotees, was pleased; taking up his incomparable spear, he, who is Śiva, remembered it with his mind.
The son of Śaṅkara discharged that arrow, aiming at her; then a great sound arose, and the quarters and the sky blazed forth.
O Sage, having reduced that powerful Asura to ashes in a mere moment, that supreme Śakti went to the vicinity of Guha.
Then the Lord Kumāra spoke to Krauñca, the best of mountains: "Go fearlessly to your own home; that asura has been destroyed along with his army."
Having heard those words of his master, the king of mountains was then delighted; after praising Guha, the enemy of his foes, he returned to his own abode.
Then, O Sage, Skanda joyfully installed three sin-destroying lingas of Maheśa at that very spot according to the prescribed rites.
First, one should worship Pratijñeśvara; then, with reverence, Kapāleśvara; and then Kumāreśvara—this triad bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Furthermore, there near the pillar of victory, Guha, the Lord of All, joyfully installed the Liṅga named Stambheśvara.
Then all the gods there, headed by Viṣṇu, joyfully installed the liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Then the majesty of all the Śiva-liṅgas became wonderful; it granted all desires and bestowed liberation upon those who practice devotion.
Then all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, with delighted minds, joyfully desired to go to the best of mountains, placing Guha at their forefront.
At that moment, the son of Śeṣa, named Kumuda, oppressed by the Daityas, came for refuge to the Kumāra.
Indeed, that powerful asura named Pralamba, who had fled from this battle, followed Tāraka and caused havoc there.
Then Kumuda, the great son of Śeṣa, the lord of serpents, having sought refuge with Kumāra, praised the son of the Mountain-Dweller.
Kumuda said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, dear father, Great Lord! I am oppressed by Pralamba; I have come to you for refuge.
Protect me, who have come for refuge, O Pralamba-slayer, who am oppressed by the gods; O Kumāra Skanda, Lord of Gods, Destroyer of Tāraka, Greatly Resplendent One!

You are the kinsman of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, and affectionate toward those who bow before you; indeed, you are the subduer of the wicked, the refuge for all, and the ultimate resort of the virtuous.
Having been praised and thus petitioned by Kumuda for the sake of his destruction, he took up his own spear, recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
The son of Girijā hurled it toward Pralamba; then a great sound arose, and the quarters and the sky blazed forth.
Having swiftly reduced him and his entire army to ashes with her spear, she, whose gait is effortless, suddenly approached the presence of Guha.
Then the prince said to the young elephant Kumuda: "Go home without fear; that asura has been destroyed along with his army."
Having heard those words of Guha, that son of the lord of serpents, Kumuda, praised and bowed to Kumāra, and departed for Pātāla filled with joy.
Thus, O Lord of Sages, you have described to me the account of Kumāra’s victory and the slaying of Tāraka, an event that causes supreme wonder.
This divine [work] removes all sins, grants all desires to men, bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and provides both worldly enjoyment and liberation to the virtuous.
Those men endowed with great fortune who proclaim the divine life-story of Kumāra, possessed of excellent renown, go to the world of Śiva.
And those people who, endowed with devotion and faith, shall hear his glory, will attain divine liberation after having enjoyed supreme happiness in this world.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory of Kumāra and the Slaying of Bāṇa and Pralamba," in the fourth section (Kumārakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having seen Tāraka slain, all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, with joyful faces, praised the son of Śaṅkara with devotion.

The gods said: Salutations to you whose form is auspicious; salutations to you, the blessing of the universe! O friend of the universe, let there be salutations to you; salutations to you, the creator of the universe!

Homage to you, O God, slayer of the foremost of the Dānavas and destroyer of the life of Bāṇāsura; homage again and again to you, the father of Śaṅkara, whose form is pure and who is the annihilator of Pralamba.

You alone are the creator and the sustainer of the worlds; you alone are the destroyer, O son of Śuci—be gracious! This reflection of the world, consisting of the phenomenal universe, is yours; be gracious, O son of Śambhu, friend of the distressed!
O Lord who provides protection for the gods, protect us always, O Master! O Creator of the life of the gods, be gracious, O Mine of Compassion!
O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, having slain the Daitya Tāraka along with his retinue, all the gods have been liberated from their calamities.
Brahmā said: O sage, thus praised by the gods headed by Viṣṇu, the Lord Kumāra granted fresh boons to all of them in due order.
Then, seeing the mountain praising him, the son of Giriśa became exceedingly pleased and spoke, bestowing boons upon him.
Skanda said: "O mountains, you shall all indeed be worthy of worship by ascetics, as well as by those engaged in ritual action and those possessed of knowledge; you shall be served by them."
"O mountains, by my word you shall indeed become the distinguished forms and the linga-forms of Śambhu; of this there is no doubt."
This Himavat, the best of mountains, who is my maternal grandfather, shall indeed become a highly fortunate bestower of fruits for ascetics today.
The gods said: "By thus granting boons and slaying Tāraka, the lord of the asuras, you have made us all, including the mobile and immobile beings, happy."
Now indeed, with great affection, you ought to go to Kailāsa, the abode of the Mountain-Dweller, in order to see your mother and father, Śivā and Śambhu.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, having received his command and celebrated a grand festival, went to the mountain together with Kumāra.
As the powerful Kumāra was departing for Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara, a great and auspicious sound of "Victory! arose.
That prince ascended a celestial chariot of supreme splendor, adorned on all sides, delightful, and shining resplendently above all others.
O sage, Viṣṇu and I both then became fans of the yak-tail, and with great affection, we tirelessly stood at the head of Guha.
Then all the immortals, headed by Indra, performing service to Guha as was appropriate, departed for the four directions with great joy.
Proclaiming the victory of Śambhu, they reached the mountain of Śambhu; filled with joy, they entered there as auspicious sounds resounded.
Having seen Śiva and Śivā, Viṣṇu and all the others quickly bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, joining their palms and remaining humble.
The prince, too, being humble of spirit, descended from the celestial chariot and joyfully prostrated before Śambhu and Śivā, who was seated upon her throne.
Then, O Nārada, having seen that prince, their son who was as dear to them as life itself, the divine couple Śiva and Pārvatī rejoiced exceedingly.
Having raised up the great lord, he placed him on his lap; out of affection and joy, he smelled his head and touched him with his hand.
Śambhu, the great lord and slayer of Tāraka, filled with the weight of great bliss and out of intense affection, performed a kiss upon the face of Kumāra.
Śivā also raised him up and placed him upon her own lap; out of great affection, she took his lotus-like face upon her head and kissed it.
O Nārada, O dear one, as the divine couple Śiva and Pārvatī performed their daily rites, their great joy then increased exceedingly.
Then there was a great festival of various kinds in the temple of Śiva; the sound of "Victory! and the sound of "Salutation! arose exceedingly on all sides.
Then, O Sage, all the hosts of gods headed by Viṣṇu, as well as the sages, having prostrated deeply before Śambhu with joy, praised him together with Śivā.
The gods said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees! Salutations, salutations to you manifold times, O Maheśvara, you who act out of compassion!"
O Mahādeva, your great play is wonderful and bestows happiness upon all virtuous beings, O Śaṅkara, friend of the distressed, Great Lord!
Thus, those of deluded intellect and ignorant, regarding your eternal worship, do not know the invocation nor the wondrous course of the Lord.
Salutations to you, the support for the stream of the Gaṅgā’s waters, whose essence is virtue; salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods.
Salutation to Maheśa, whose emblem is the bull, the lord of the Gaṇas; salutation to the God who is the Lord of all, the sovereign of the three worlds.
O Lord of all worlds, salutations again and again to you, the destroyer; O Lord of gods, eternal master of the three qualities, salutations to you, the sustainer and the creator.
To the one who is free from attachment, the Supreme Lord, the Auspicious One, the Supreme Self; to the one beyond phenomenal expansion, the Pure, the Ultimate, and the Imperishable.
Homage to you, Kāla, who holds a staff in hand and holds a noose in hand; homage to you, whose primary essence is the Vedic mantras and who possesses a hundred tongues.
O Supreme Lord, whatever has been, is, or will be—whether stationary or moving—all has arisen in every way from Your body.
Protect us always, O Master; be gracious, O Blessed One, O Lord! We have come to you for refuge in every way, O Supreme Lord.
Homage to you, the blue-throated Rudra, to you who are the utterance of Svāhā; homage to you who are formless, who possess form, and whose form is the universe.
Salutations again and again to Śiva, the blue-throated one, who wears the ashes of the funeral pyre upon his limbs; eternal salutations to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin and Śrīkaṇṭha.
To him whose body is bowed by all, who is himself bowed down by self-restraint, to Mahādeva, to Śarva, and to him whose feet are worshipped by all.
You are Brahmā among all the gods, the blue-and-red one (Nīlalohita) among the Rudras; you are the self of all beings, and by the followers of Sāṃkhya you are called Puruṣa.
Among mountains you are Sumeru; among the stars, the moon; among the sages, Vasiṣṭha; and likewise, among the gods, Vāsava.
O Maheśvara, you are the letter 'A' of all the Vedas; be our protector. And for the sake of the welfare of the world, you sprinkle all living beings with water.
O Maheśvara, O highly fortunate one, observer of the auspicious and inauspicious! O Lord of Gods, may you indeed strengthen us, the performers of your word.
O God of gods, homage be to you! We are unable to reach the end of even hundreds and thousands of millions of your forms.
Brahmā said: Having thus offered praise, all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu and others, stood before him, bowing repeatedly to Skanda and placing him at their lead.
Having heard the hymn of praise to the gods, Śiva, the Lord of All and Self-Ruler, became well-pleased and, being devoted to compassion, laughed.
With a highly serene soul, Śaṅkara—the Supreme Lord, the kinsman of the distressed, and the refuge of the virtuous—spoke to Viṣṇu and the other foremost of the gods.
Śiva said: O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O gods, listen to my words with respect; I am in every way the protector of the virtuous and a treasure-house of compassion for you, the gods.

The destroyer of the wicked, the Lord of the three worlds, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees; he is the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of all, remaining forever free from change.
O best of gods, whenever suffering may befall you, at those very times you should indeed worship me for the sake of happiness.
Brahmā said: Thus commanded, the gods headed by Viṣṇu, together with the great lords of sages, joyfully bowed down to Śiva, Umā, and Kumāra.
O Sage, recounting that beautiful glory of Śiva and Śivā, as well as that of Śāṅkara, they attained supreme bliss and departed for their own abodes.
The Supreme Lord Śiva also, together with Śivā, his attendants, and Kumāra, dwelt joyfully on that mountain out of affection.
Thus, O Sage, the entire divine and bliss-bestowing account of Kumāra’s life and the deeds of Śiva have been told; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Śiva and Śivā, Embellished by the Life of Svāmikārtika," in the fourth section (Kumāra-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard this most wonderful and excellent account concerning the enemy of Tāraka, Nārada, being well-pleased, then questioned Brahmā with affection.
Nārada said: O God of gods, Lord of creatures, treasury of the knowledge of Śiva, I have heard the virtuous account of Kārtika, which is superior even to nectar.
Now I wish to hear the supreme account concerning Gāṇeśa—his divine life-story, which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the great sage Nārada, Brahmā, with a serene mind, replied while remembering Śiva.

Brahmā said: O Creator, the birth of Gaṇeśa from the Supreme Being is declared to vary according to different kalpas; his head was severed when struck by Śani, and an elephant’s face was joined to him.
Now the origin of Gaṇeśa as described in the Śvetakalpa is told, wherein his head was severed by the compassionate Śiva.
No doubt should be entertained in this matter, O Sage; Śaṅkara is the creator of all. For that Śambhu is indeed the Lord of all, both devoid of attributes and possessed of attributes.
O best of sages, the entire universe is created, sustained, and likewise destroyed by His divine play; listen now with respect to what is being presented.
When Śiva had been wedded and had departed for Kailāsa, after some time had passed, the birth of Gaṇapati occurred.
And at that very same time, her friend Jayā, along with Vijayā, met with Pārvatī and became intent on deliberation.
All the hosts of Rudra are devoted to the command of Śiva; they are all ours as well, led by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin.
Those attendants are indeed innumerable; not one of them belongs to us. They all stand at the gate, devoted solely to the command of Śaṅkara.
"Even though all of them are ours, nevertheless our mind does not meet with them; therefore, O sinless one, you must create at least one who is truly ours."
Brahmā said: Having spoken these beautiful and beneficial words with her two friends, the goddess Pārvatī then considered them and resolved to carry them out.
Then, on one occasion, while Pārvatī was bathing, Sadāśiva, having rebuked Nandin, entered the interior of the house.
Seeing Śaṅkara approaching at an improper time, the Mother of the World rose up; that beautiful lady was indeed embarrassed as she was immersed in water.
At that moment, the Goddess, filled with great curiosity, considered his words to be beneficial and conducive to happiness.
Thus, at all times when she had given birth, the supreme goddess Pārvatī, the sovereign of the highest, would sometimes reflect thus in her mind.
"May there be some servant of mine who is most auspicious and accomplished; by my command, he shall not deviate here even by a single line from another."
Having reflected thus, that goddess fashioned from the impurities of her body a man endowed with all auspicious marks.
Free from defects in every limb, beautiful in every part, vast and enriched with all splendor, it possessed great strength and prowess.
Then, having given him various garments, as well as diverse ornaments and many unsurpassed blessings, she [departed].
"You are my son; you belong to me, for there is no one else here who is mine. When he had spoken thus, the man bowed to Śivā and spoke.
Gaṇeśa said: "What task do you have today? I shall perform what you have requested. When he had spoken thus, Śivā then replied to her son.
Śiva said: "O dear one, listen to my words: from this day forth, be my gatekeeper. You are my son; you belong to me, for there is no other who belongs to me."
"O my son, no one at all shall enter my house by force anywhere without my command; this which I have spoken is the truth, dear father."
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O sage, he gave him an exceedingly firm staff; and beholding his beautiful form, she was filled with joy.
Having kissed his son’s face with great affection and embraced him out of compassion, he placed the Lord of the Gaṇas, who held a staff in his hand, at his own doorway.
Then, O dear one, the son of the Goddess, a great hero with a staff in hand, stood at the door of the house, desiring the welfare of Pārvatī.
Having stationed her son Gaṇeśa at her own door, Śivā herself remained there with her companions while she bathed.
At that very time, O tiger among sages, Śiva arrived at the gate—full of curiosity and skilled in various divine sports.
And the lord of the Gaṇas, not recognizing him as Śiva, said: "O Lord, you must not go now without your mother's permission."
"Your mother is staying here for the purpose of bathing; where are you going? Go away now! Having said this, she then seized his staff in order to restrain him.
Seeing him, Śiva said: "O dull-witted one, whom do you forbid? O one of evil intellect, do you not know me? I am Śiva; it is not otherwise."
Struck by that staff by Gaṇeśa, Maheśvara, who is full of divine play, being provoked to anger, replied to his son.
Śiva said: "You are a fool; you do not know that I am Śiva, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain. I am going to my own home, O child; why indeed do you obstruct me?"
O Brahmin, having spoken thus as Maheśa was entering, the leader of the Gaṇas became enraged and struck him again with a staff.
Then Śiva, becoming enraged, commanded his own Gaṇas: "Who is this that remains here, and what is being done? Look, O Gaṇas!"
Having spoken thus, Śiva remained there outside the house, enraged; the Lord, who delights in the ways of worldly existence, performed many wonderful and beautiful sports.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Gaṇeśa," in the fourth section (Kumārakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Then those attendants, filled with wrath, went there by the command of Śiva and questioned that gatekeeper, the son of the Mountain-Dweller.
The attendants of Śiva said: "Who are you? From where have you come? Or what do you intend to do? Depart from here this very day to a great distance, if indeed you wish to live."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of his, the son of Girijā, fearless and with staff in hand, spoke thus to the gatekeepers.
Gaṇeśa said: "Who are you, and from where have you come, O handsome ones? Go far away! For what purpose indeed do you stand here as adversaries?"
Brahmā said: Having heard his words and laughing among themselves, all the Śiva-gaṇas, who were great heroes free from pride, spoke.
Having said "one another," all those attendants of Śiva, with minds filled with anger, spoke back to that gatekeeper Gaṇeśa.
The attendants of Śiva said: "Listen, for we are the excellent gatekeepers, the attendants of Śiva; we have arrived by the command of the Lord Śaṅkara to turn you back."
Thinking that you too are one of my attendants here, I would not kill you as you have been killed; stay at a distance, for why do you seek death of your own accord?
Brahmā said: Although addressed in this manner, Gaṇeśa, the fearless son of Girijā, rebuked the attendants of Śaṅkara and did not open the door at that time.
Then all those Śaiva groups there, having heard those words, went to Śiva and reported that entire account to him.
Then, O Sage, having heard those words, Maheśvara, whose pastimes are wondrous, rebuked his own Gaṇas and spoke, for he is the ultimate refuge of the worlds.
Maheśvara said: Who is this that stands here, and what does he say, so exalted as if toward an enemy? What will this one of wicked intellect do? He surely desires his own death.
Let this new gatekeeper be kept at a distance; how can you speak of his conduct, remaining as if you were eunuchs?
Addressed by their Lord Śambhu with his wondrous play, those Gaṇas returned to that very place and spoke to the gatekeeper.
The attendants of Śiva said: "Ho there, O gatekeeper! Who are you, and by whom were you stationed here? You do not even greet us; how do you wish to remain alive?"
"We are all gatekeepers standing here; why do you revile us? Even a jackal who has seized a lion's throne seeks after auspiciousness."
O fool, you roar only so long as the prowess of the Gaṇas has not been experienced by you right here; once it is experienced, you shall fall.
Thus addressed by them, he became greatly enraged; then, seizing a staff with both hands, he struck those mocking attendants.
Then the son of Śivā, the fearless lord of the Gaṇas, having rebuked those great heroes of Śaṅkara, spoke to the lords of the Gaṇas.
Śivāputra said: "Go, go far away from here! Otherwise, I shall indeed show you my own exceedingly fierce prowess, and you will become a great object of ridicule."
Having heard these words of the son of Girijā, the attendants of Śaṅkara then spoke thus to one another.
The attendants of Śiva said: "What should be done? Where should we go? Why is he not being dealt with? We must maintain our boundaries; otherwise, what would you say?"
Brahmā said: Then all the attendants of Śambhu, having gone about one krośa from Kailāsa to where Śiva was stationed at a distance, spoke to him thus.
Śiva, the supreme lord, with trident in hand and fierce resolve, laughed and spoke to all those attendants of his who were esteemed as heroes.

Śiva said: "O Gaṇas! You are of eunuch-like intellect, not heroes, though you imagine yourselves to be so. You are not fit even to speak in my presence; what could one who has been rebuked possibly say?"
"Let him go, let him be beaten—whosoever may prevail here! What is the use of saying more? He must simply be driven far away."
Brahmā said: O lord of sages, having been thus rebuked by that god Maheśa, all those excellent Gaṇas went there and spoke.
The attendants of Śiva said: "O child, listen indeed! Why do you speak so insolently? Go far away from here; otherwise, death shall be yours."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of those who were surely carrying out Śiva’s command, the son of Śivā then became distressed, wondering, "What shall I do?"
In the meantime, having heard their quarrel as well as his at the door, the queen said to her female companion, "Look!"
Having arrived there, her friend learned the news; having observed the situation for a mere moment, she then went joyfully into the presence of Śivā.
Having gone there, O Sage, that entire event which had occurred was related in its entirety by her friend in the presence of the Daughter of the Mountain.
The friend said: "O Maheśvarī, those heroic attendants of Śaṅkara will certainly rebuke whichever of our own group stands at the gate."
And how is it that Śiva and all his attendants enter your house by force without even waiting for an opportunity? This is not at all auspicious for you.
Indeed, he alone has acted rightly, for no one else was admitted; yet here he experiences suffering as well as contempt and the like.
But from this point on, a verbal dispute shall be carried out between us; and once that verbal dispute has been conducted, let them indeed depart in peace.
A verbal dispute has indeed been made here; having conquered him through victory, let everyone enter accordingly, O beloved, and never otherwise.
"In this very place of ours, we have all been utterly humiliated; therefore, O auspicious goddess, you must not abandon your supreme pride."
O virtuous lady, Śiva now behaves like a monkey at all times; what will he do with his ego, and how will it be favorable to me?
Brahmā said: Oh, Satī remained there for a moment, under the power of Śiva’s will.
Then Pārvatī, having become Manasī, spoke with pride.
Śiva said: "Aha! You have not remained still for even a moment; why was such force used? And how, moreover, should one act here—with humility or otherwise?"
"It shall come to pass; what has been done will surely happen and not otherwise. Having spoken thus, the friend was then sent away by her beloved.
Having arrived, she related everything that had been told by her beloved, and then described that Gaṇeśa, the son of Girijā.
The friend said: "Well done by you, O blessed one! Let them not enter by force; for these hosts are before you—how could they conquer one such as you?"
Whatever has been done and whatever remains undone must be performed by you; for one who has been conquered, there is no enmity again, nor is it certain.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of her and of his mother, Gaṇeśvara attained supreme bliss, abundant strength, and great exaltation.
Having girded his loins and likewise bound his turban, and touching his shanks and thighs, he joyfully spoke these fearless words to all those attendants.
Gaṇeśa said: "I am the son of Girijā, and you likewise are the attendants of Śiva; both of us have attained equality, so let what is to be done be performed once more."
"O gentlemen doorkeepers, how is it that I am not the doorkeeper? It is certain that you were stationed there and I was stationed here."
And when it has been firmly resolved by you that you shall remain here, then you must carry out the fulfillment of Śiva’s command.
But now, O heroes, I am fulfilling my duty here by obeying the command of Śiva; I am acting truthfully, as has been determined by me to be appropriate.
Therefore, all you attendants of Śiva, listen to my words with respect: whether by force or through humility, you must not enter the temple again.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by the Gaṇa, all those Gaṇas were filled with shame; they went into the presence of Śiva, and having prostrated before him, stood before him.
Having stood there, they all reported that wonderful event; with joined palms and bowed shoulders, they praised Śiva and stood before him.
Having heard all that account as it was told by his own attendants, Śaṅkara, adopting a worldly manner, spoke these words.
Śaṅkara said: "Listen, all you Gaṇas; this battle is not appropriate. You here are indeed our own, as is that host of Gaurī."
"If discipline is indeed imposed, Śambhu will always be subject to a woman; such a reputation would surely arise in the world, O Gaṇas, and it would be contemptuous of me."
In this matter, the maxim that "what ought to be done must be done" is of the highest importance; for how can that lone, childish host display any prowess?
And you, O lords of the Gaṇas, are exceedingly skilled in battle in this world; how then will you abandon the fight and incur the reproach of my people?
"How should a woman perform a rite of possession, especially in the presence of her husband? By performing it, that daughter of the mountain will surely obtain its fruit."
Therefore, all my heroes, listen with respect to these words: battle must be waged by all means, regardless of what may come to pass.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, Śaṅkara, who is skilled in various divine sports, ceased speaking, O best of sages, demonstrating the ways of the world.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispute among the Gaṇas," in the fourth section (Kumāra-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: Having been addressed thus by that Lord, they reached a firm resolve; then, fully prepared, they went there to the temple of Śiva.
Gaṇeśa, having likewise seen those best of Gaṇas arrived and standing there having assumed the arrogance of battle, spoke this to them.
Gaṇeśa said: "Let all the leaders of the Gaṇas, the protectors of Śiva’s command, come here; for I alone am a child who is a protector of Śiva’s command."
Nevertheless, let the goddess Pārvatī behold the strength of her son, and let Śiva likewise behold the strength of his own attendants once again.
O Bhavānī and Śiva, there was a battle between the powerful and the child, and previously you all, who were experts in warfare, engaged in combat.
"I have never done this before; I am but a child, yet it is being done now. Nevertheless, there is shame for you all here in the presence of Girijā and Śiva."
But for me it shall not be so; rather, the opposite will occur. Here, shame shall fall upon me alone, and upon you, as well as upon Girijā and Śiva.
O lords of the Gaṇas, having understood this, you must engage in battle after seeing your master, and I shall do so after seeing my mother.
"What kind of battle is being waged? Let it be as it must be!"—in the three worlds, indeed, no one at all is capable of restraining him.
Brahmā said: Thus rebuked, those whose arms were adorned with staffs arrived, bearing various kinds of weapons.
Grinding their teeth and uttering "huṃ" sounds again and again, while crying out, "Look! Look!", those hosts approached.
Nandī arrived first and, seizing one foot, dragged him away; Bhṛṅgī, running up, seized the second foot of the Gaṇa.
While they were still dragging him by his feet, the Gaṇa struck them with his hand; then, seizing their two hands, he himself lifted up their feet.
Then the heroic son of the Goddess, the Lord of the Gaṇas, seizing a massive iron club and standing at the gate, began to crush them all at that time.
The hands of some were severed, the backs of others, the heads of some, and the skulls of others.
Some had their knees struck there, and others likewise their shoulders; those who indeed came directly before him were all struck in the heart.
Some fell upon the ground, some fled in various directions; the feet of some were severed, while others went into the presence of Śarva.
Indeed, not one among them could stand face-to-face in battle; they fled in the ten directions like deer upon seeing a lion.
Likewise, all those hosts departed by the thousands; then he too, having turned back, stood at the main gate.
Just as Time is seen to be terrifying at the end of a kalpa, so too was he seen to be the bringer of dissolution for all.
And at that very time, all the gods, including Sarama, Īśa, and Sureśvara, being urged by Nārada, assembled here.
Then they all spoke thus, desiring the welfare of Śiva: standing before Śiva and bowing to him, they said, "O Lord, please grant us your command."
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of all, and all are Your servants; You are the creator, the eternal sustainer, and the destroyer of the universe, O Supreme Lord.

O Lord, though you are inherently devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), you manifest through play (līlā) in the forms of rajas, sattva, and tamas; what kind of play have you performed today? Tell me that now.
Brahmā said: O best of sages, having heard their words and seeing that the Gaṇas were divided, Maheśvara then informed them of everything.
Then, O best of sages, Śaṅkara, the Lord of All and Master of the Daughter of the Mountain, laughed and spoke to me, Brahmā.
Śiva said: "O Brahmā, listen; a certain boy stands at my door, possessed of great strength, staff in hand, warding off entry into the house."
This one, who dealt a great blow and struck down my attendants, has here forcibly brought about the defeat of my hosts.
"O Brahman, you yourself must go; this one of great power must be propitiated. O Creator, O Brahmā, you must act in such a way that there may indeed be peace."
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Lord, O dear one, being deluded by ignorance and unaware of the truth, we all went into his presence along with the best of sages.
And seeing me approaching, that mighty Gaṇeśa became enraged; coming forward, he tore out my beard.
"Forgive me, forgive me, O Lord! I have not come for the purpose of war; I am a Brahmin, one to be favored, a performer of peace, and free from malice."
O Brahman, while he was speaking thus, that great hero Gaṇeśa, a child of extraordinary prowess, seized a club.
Seeing that mighty Gaṇeśa grasping his iron club, I then fled away with great speed.
Crying out "Go! Go!", they were then struck by that iron club; some fell down of their own accord, while others were struck down by him.
And some, having attained proximity to Śiva, immediately informed Śiva of that entire event in its full detail.
Having seen them in such a state and having heard their account, Hara, who is skilled in divine play, conceived boundless wrath.
Then he commanded all the hosts of gods headed by Indra, the Gaṇas led by the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), and the Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas.
And they all departed in every direction as was appropriate, for they were intent on slaying that host, having received Śiva’s command and raising their weapons.
Whatever weapon each one possessed, all of those were specifically hurled with force upon Gaṇeśa.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; all the people dwelling in the three worlds fell into the utmost state of doubt.
Indeed, even the lifespan of Brahmā has not passed away, nor does the cosmic egg go to destruction prematurely; rather, it surely perishes by itself through the power of Śiva’s will.
All of them arrived there, including the six-faced one and the others; the gods found their weapons rendered useless and were struck with the utmost wonder.
In the meantime, the Goddess Jagadambā Vibodhanā, having learned of all that conduct, conceived boundless wrath.
Then, O Lord of Sages, that goddess created two powers there for her own retinue, for the sake of providing assistance in every way.
O great sage, one [of them] stood there assuming a fierce form, stretching out her cavernous mouth which resembled a dark mountain.
She is of the nature of a single lightning flash, endowed with many hands; she is the terrifying Great Goddess who inflicts punishment upon the wicked.
All the weapons were released by the gods and their hosts; seizing them with his own mouth, he quickly hurled them back at the two of them.
The divine weapon, the iron club (parigha), was not seen again on any side; thus was that most wonderful feat performed by the two of them there.
A single fool agitated the entire, insurmountable army, just as in ancient times the ocean was churned by the great mountain.
By him alone all were struck down—Śakra and the other gods as well as the Gaṇas of Śaṅkara—and they then became utterly distressed.
Then, having all gathered together and sighing again and again, they spoke to one another, distressed by those blows.
The hosts of gods said: "What should be done? Where should we go? The ten directions are no longer discernible; he brandishes his iron club, whirling it now to the left and now to the right."
Brahmā said: At this time, the foremost of Apsarases, with flowers and sandalwood in their hands, as well as the sages headed by you, were indeed intensely eager for the great battle.
O best of sages, they all gathered together indeed to witness the battle; at that time, O excellent sage, the sky and the path of the sun were filled by them.
Seeing that battle, they were indeed struck with great wonder; for such a supreme combat had never been seen by them even once before.
Then the earth, together with the oceans, trembled, and even the mountains fell, creating the conditions for the onset of battle.
The heavens were churned by the hosts of planets and stars; everyone fell into a state of agitation. At that time, all the gods and all the Gaṇas fled.
Only the valiant Ṣaṇmukha did not flee there; then the great hero, having checked them all, stood before him.
In that battle, by means of those two powers, all [the gods] were rendered fruitless; all the weapons were cut down and withdrawn by the immortals and the Gaṇas.
All those who remained there then approached the presence of Śiva; all the gods and all the Gaṇas had fled at that time.
Then all of them, having gathered together and bowed repeatedly to Śiva, quickly spoke these words: "O Lord, who is this foremost of the Gaṇas?"
This battle has indeed been heard of before, but now it is seen again in many ways; such a thing as this has never been seen nor heard of before.
O Lord, let this be considered for a moment; otherwise, victory will not be achieved. You alone, O Master, are the protector of the universe; of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā said: Having heard those words, Rudra became exceedingly enraged; and having manifested his wrath, he departed from that very place along with his attendants.
And that entire host of gods, together with Viṣṇu the wielder of the discus, having celebrated a great festival, followed after Śiva.
