In the meantime, O Nārada, having bowed with devotion to Maheśvara, you indeed spoke to the God of gods with palms joined in reverence.
Nārada said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, O All-pervading Lord, hear my words; you alone are the omnipresent Master, expert in manifold divine sports.
O Śaṅkara, by performing this great sport, you have stripped away the pride of the Gaṇas; and by bestowing abundant strength upon him, you have likewise removed the pride of the gods.
O Lord Śambhu, you who strike down all pride, by your own independent power, you have displayed your own wondrous strength throughout the world.
O Lord, lover of your devotees, do not perform that pastime now; instead, honor and exalt your own attendants and the immortals as well.
"Do not play now; abandon [it], O bestower of the state of Brahman! Having spoken thus, O Nārada, you indeed then vanished from sight.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle with Gaṇeśa," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the second Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Nārada, having heard this, Maheśāna, who bestows grace upon his devotees, became desirous of drinking water because of those words of yours, even though he was that child.
Having summoned Viṣṇu and consulted with him, the three-eyed god, accompanied by the gods and joined by a great army, stood face-to-face against him as well.
And the gods, endowed with great strength and great enthusiasm, gazed upon by the true vision of Śiva, fought against him while remembering the lotus feet of Śiva.
Then Hari, the hero of great strength and prowess, whose weapons were the Great Goddesses and who was devoted to the form of Śiva, fought with him.
Then the heroic leader of the Gaṇas, endowed with great strength by the gift of the Śakti weapon, suddenly struck the foremost of the immortals and Hari with his staff.
O sage, all the hosts of immortals there had their strength paralyzed by that Viṣṇu; struck by his staff, they turned their faces away in retreat.
O sage, Śiva too, having fought for a long time with his army and beholding that most formidable being, was struck with supreme wonder.
"He must be slain by means of deceit alone; otherwise, he cannot be killed again. Having resolved his mind thus, he stationed himself in the midst of the army.
When the auspicious God was seen—both formless and yet possessing the nature of the qualities—and when Viṣṇu had arrived for the battle, all the deities [assembled].
Then the hosts of Maheśa attained great joy; all of them, having gathered together with mutual affection, celebrated a festival.
Then the heroic son of Śakti, having performed his own worship with a heroic gait, first worshipped Viṣṇu, the bringer of all happiness.
"And I shall cause him to be deluded; then let him be slain by you, O Lord. He must not be killed without a stratagem, for he is of the nature of darkness and difficult to overcome."
Having formed this resolve there and consulted with Śambhu, Viṣṇu, having received his command, became intent on deluding [the world] through the Śaiva path.
O Sage, seeing Hari in such a state, the two powers likewise merged into him; having bestowed the power of their energy upon that Gaṇeśa, they became one with him.
Then, when the two Śaktis had merged together, Gaṇeśa, being exceedingly powerful, hurled his iron club at the very place where Viṣṇu himself was stationed.
Having made some effort in this matter, he deceived that destiny by remembering Śiva, the Great Lord, his own master who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Seeing his face turned toward one side, Śaṅkara also arrived, taking up his own trident and filled with great rage, desiring battle.
That heroic and mighty son of Śivā beheld the approaching Maheśvara, Śambhu, with trident in hand, desirous of slaying his own [son].
Remembering the lotus feet of his mother, that great hero, the leader of the Gaṇas, empowered by the energy of Śiva, struck him on the hand with his spear.
Seeing the trident fallen from the hand of Śiva, the Supreme Self, he, accompanied by his messenger, took up the Pināka bow.
The Lord of the Gaṇas struck him down to the ground with his iron club; likewise, five hands were destroyed, and he took up a trident with the remaining five.
"Alas! Surely a most grievous sorrow has now arisen for me. What did Bhavācārin say when asked by the Gaṇas whether he would return again?"
In the meantime, the heroic Lord of the Gaṇas, endowed with the strength granted by Śakti, struck the gods along with their hosts using his iron club.
The gods, along with their hosts, were afflicted by the iron club and fled to the ten directions; none remained in the battle against that one who struck with such wonder.
And seeing that Gaṇa, Viṣṇu said, "He is blessed; he is of great strength, a great hero, a great warrior, and one who delights in battle."
Furthermore, many deities were seen by me, as well as many Dānavas, Daityas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
No one at all in the entire three worlds can attain equality with this Lord of the Gaṇas in terms of splendor, beauty, valor, virtues, and other such qualities.
While speaking thus to him, that lord of the Gaṇas, the son of Śakti, whirled his iron club and hurled it at Viṣṇu.
Having grasped his discus and recollected the lotus feet of Śiva, Hari then swiftly shattered the iron club with that discus.
The Gaṇa hurled a fragment of the Parigha at Hari; however, having been seized by the bird Garuḍa, it was rendered fruitless.
As time passed in this manner, both great heroes—Viṣṇu and the Gaṇa—fought with one another.
Furthermore, the powerful Vīravara, the son of Śakti, who was known as Smṛtaśiva, seized an incomparable staff and struck Viṣṇu with it.
Unable to endure that blow, he fell to the ground; however, rising quickly, he indeed fought with that son of Śivā.
Having reached this interval, the trident-wielder likewise approached from the north and severed that head with his trident.
O Nārada, when the head of that very Lord of the Gaṇas was severed, the army of the Gaṇas and the army of the gods became perfectly still.
"Nārada has come and reported everything to the Goddess. O proud lady, listen: you must not abandon your pride now."
Having spoken thus, you, Nārada, who are fond of the Kali age, vanished from that place; Śambhu, the sage who is forever changeless and the one who moves within the mind, remained.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle with Gaṇeśa and the Severing of Gaṇeśa’s Head," in the Kumāra-khaṇḍa of the fourth Rudra-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Purāṇa.
Nārada said: O Brahmin, O one of great wisdom, now that the entire account has been heard, tell me what the Great Goddess did; I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Brahmā said: Listen, O tiger among sages; I shall now certainly relate that history of the Mother of the Universe which occurred immediately thereafter.
Then the Gaṇas played mṛdaṅgas and paṭahas, and they celebrated a great festival once that lord of the Gaṇas had been slain.
O Lord of Sages, even as Śiva cut off that head and experienced such agony, the goddess Girijā became exceedingly enraged.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Alas! Misery has come upon me. How might this suffering of mine, this extreme agony, now be destroyed?"
My son has been destroyed today by all the gods as well as the hosts; I shall destroy them all, or I shall bring about the dissolution of the world.
Thus distressed, she, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, being enraged, instantly created hundreds of thousands of Śaktis.
Having then paid homage to the auspicious Mother of the World, who had been manifested, they, blazing with splendor, said: "O Mother, let it be commanded."
O lord of sages, having heard that, that Mahāmāyā, the power of Śambhu who is Prakṛti, intent upon anger, replied to them all.
The Goddess said: "O goddesses who are my powers, you must now bring about the dissolution here at my command; no hesitation should be entertained in this matter."
O friends, devour by force the gods, the sages, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas—both those belonging to us and those who are strangers!
Brahmā said: Commanded by him, all those Śaktis, intent upon wrath, prepared to effect the destruction of all the gods and others.

And on the full moon day of Kārttika, the gods, the sages, those possessing sacred fords, and the lords of munis always go there for the purpose of beholding Kumāra.
Whoever should behold the Lord on the full moon day of Kārttika when it coincides with the Kṛttikā constellation, all his sins shall be consumed and he shall obtain the fruit desired by his heart.
Umā too, having fallen into sorrow at the separation from Skanda, spoke piteously to her husband: "O Lord, go there with me."
For the sake of that happiness, Śambhu himself went to the mountain with a portion of his own self; there he became the light-liṅga named Mallikārjuna, which bestows bliss.
Even today, Śiva is seen there together with Śivā, the fulfiller of the desires of all his own devotees and the refuge of the virtuous.
Perceiving that Śiva had arrived, the prince, becoming detached from him, was eager to go elsewhere.
Requested by both the gods and the sages, Kārttikeya also remained at a distance, staying in that place after leaving a space of three yojanas.
O Nārada, afflicted by affection for their son, Śiva and Umā indeed go on every lunar festival to behold that Kumāra.
On the day of the new moon, Śambhu himself goes there; on the day of the full moon, Pārvatī certainly goes there.
O Lord of Sages, whatever account of Kārtika Gaṇeśa you asked about has been fully related by me to you.
Having heard this, a wise man is liberated from all sins; he always obtains beautiful and desired objects of every kind.
Whoever recites it, causes it to be recited, hears it, or causes it to be heard, shall attain all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
A Brāhmaṇa shall possess the splendor of sacred knowledge, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious, a Vaiśya shall be abundant in wealth, and a Śūdra shall attain equality with the virtuous.
The sick person shall be liberated from disease; one possessed by fear shall be freed from fear; and a man afflicted by the disturbances of spirits, ghosts, and the like, shall no longer suffer.
This narrative is sinless, conducive to fame, and an increaser of happiness; it bestows long life, leads to heaven, is incomparable, and brings about sons, grandsons, and progeny.
It bestows liberation and the supreme knowledge of Śiva; it causes delight to both Śivā and Śiva, and increases devotion to Śiva.
This auspicious [text], which bestows the non-duality of Śiva and is permeated by Sadāśiva, should always be heard by devotees free from desire and by those seeking liberation.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Gaṇeśa’s Marriage," in the fourth section (Kumāra-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Kumāra-khaṇḍa, contained within the Rudra-saṃhitā.

Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Gaurī and Śaṅkara. Nārada said: We have heard this supreme, bliss-bestowing account of the life of Śambhu as a householder, along with the noble stories of his attendants, Skanda, and others.
Now, out of great affection, tell us the most excellent and supreme account of how Śaṅkara, as Rudra, sported while slaying the wicked.
How did the powerful Blessed One burn the cities of the enemies of the gods with three cities simultaneously by means of a single arrow?
Relate all this—the eternal life-story of the moon-crested Lord, who sports through his māyā, which bestows happiness upon the gods and sages.
Brahmā said: "O best of sages, in former times Vyāsa asked this very same thing, and Sanatkumāra spoke to him; that I shall now relate."
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great wisdom, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, how he, the heart-stealer of the universe, burnt Tripura with a single arrow.
O lord of sages, when the asura Tāraka had been slain by Skanda, the son of Śiva, his three sons, the Daityas, were filled with remorse.
The eldest among them was named Tāraka, Vidyunmālī was the middle one, and Kamalākṣa was the youngest; all were always equal in strength.
They were masters of their senses, armored, self-controlled, speakers of truth, firm-minded, great heroes, and indeed haters of the gods.
Having gone to a cave in Mount Meru, those three performed a most wonderful penance, renouncing all their exceedingly beautiful and delightful enjoyments.
In the springtime, having abandoned all their desires, the sounds of singing and musical instruments, and even their festive celebrations, those three sons of Tāraka practiced austerities.
In summer, having overcome the radiance of the sun and kindled fires in all directions, they stood in their midst and offered oblations with devotion for the sake of attaining perfection.
Felled by his great prowess, they all became utterly unconscious; like those who have lost their fear during the rainy season, they bore the rain upon their heads.
In the autumn season, those who are hungry partake of food that is produced then—delightful, unctuous, substantial, and pleasing, consisting of unsurpassed fruits and roots.
Having conquered hunger and thirst through self-restraint, and having given away various kinds of drinks, they remained like stones when it came to eating.
Those great-souled ones remained established in the four directions without support, having taken refuge on the mountain during the winter with supreme fortitude.
Enveloped in bodies of frost and clad in garments drenched with water, they remained in the midst of the waters during the cold season, having assumed bodies of fine linen.
Undaunted, they all gradually increased their asceticism; those three excellent sons performed penance, directed toward Brahmā.
Having undertaken fierce austerity and remaining fixed in supreme discipline, those foremost of Dānavas emaciated their own bodies through penance.
Placing even a single foot upon the ground for a hundred years, those exceedingly powerful ones remained there, performing supreme austerities.
For a thousand years, those evil-minded ones, subsisting only on air and appearing most formidable, performed austerities, having reached a state of supreme torment.
Indeed, for a thousand years they remained standing on their heads, and for a hundred years they remained with their arms raised upward.
Thus, having fallen into supreme suffering, these Daityas, devoted to their stubborn persistence, remain in such a state day and night without weariness.
O Sage, it is my conviction that in this manner a great length of time passed for those Tārakas, who were devoted to Brahman and practiced dharma with great austerity.
Then the great Brahmā, the preceptor of gods and asuras, appeared; highly illustrious and gratified by their asceticism, he came to grant them a boon.
Then the Grandfather of all beings spoke these words with conciliation to all of them, together with the sages, gods, and asuras.
Brahmā said: "O great Daityas, O sage, I am pleased with your austerity; I shall grant you everything—ask for whatever boon you desire."
"For what purpose has this great penance been performed? Tell me, O enemies of the gods; I am the giver of all penance and the creator of all things at all times."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, they all slowly reflected upon their own state; then, with palms joined in reverence, they prostrated before the Grandfather and spoke.
The Daityas said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted by you, [grant us] invincibility against all embodied beings among all creatures."
O Lord of the World, make us firm; protect us from our adversaries—may old age, disease, and all such things never reach us, nor may death ever come upon us.
"It is our intention that we all shall become ageless and immortal; we shall bring all others in the three worlds under the sway of death."
What is the use of vast fortune, what need indeed for the best of cities, or for other abundant enjoyments, or even for power and sovereignty?
O Brahmin, for one who is seized by death and certain to die within five days, everything is surely in vain; indeed, it is as if it were not so.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of those Daityas and ascetics, Brahmā, recollecting Śiva—the Lord of the Mountains and his own master—replied.
Brahmā said: "There is no such thing as immortality for all; therefore, O Asuras, desist from this. Choose another boon, whatever indeed pleases you."
O Asuras, some being who has been born, will surely be born, or may be born somewhere; yet there shall be no one on this earth who is free from old age and immortal.
Except for Khaṇḍaparaśu and Hari, the destroyer of Time, those two—dharma and adharma, which are supreme, unmanifest, yet possessing manifest forms—[could not exist].
If that asceticism is practiced for the sake of afflicting the world, it should be known as having gone to waste; therefore, asceticism must be well-performed.

O sinless ones, having reflected upon this with your own intellect—that which cannot be achieved even by gods or asuras, that which is difficult to attain or exceedingly hard to accomplish—deceive death.
Therefore, relying on your own strength, choose some cause for death such that Death himself is not chosen; guard against that [cause] individually.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the Ordainer (Brahmā), they remained in meditation for a moment; then, having reflected, they spoke to the Grandfather of all the worlds.
The Daityas said: "O Blessed One, although we are possessed of great prowess, we have no dwelling place; for we cannot live in comfort, being constantly assailed by our enemies."
"Grant us three cities that are indeed free from illusion and most wonderful, flourishing with every prosperity, and unassailable even by the dwellers of heaven."
"O Lord of the World, O Teacher of the Universe, by your grace we shall indeed traverse this earth, having established ourselves in three cities."
Then Tārakākṣa said: "Viśvakarman shall construct for me a golden city that is impenetrable even by the gods."
Kamalākṣa, however, requested a very great city made of silver, while the delighted Vidyunmālī requested a great one made of diamond and iron.
O Brahmin, when these [planets] are pure, situated in a single sign, at the time of midday conjunction, and the Moon is positioned in Puṣya;
Higher and higher in the sky, resting amidst playful clouds, the clouds named Puṣkarāvarta rained down during that time.
Likewise, at the end of a thousand years, we shall meet one another; these cities will attain a state of unification, and not otherwise.
The god who embodies all the gods, out of sport toward me, stood upon a chariot provided with every requisite, though such a thing was impossible.
"May he who is eternally our enemy, the one clad in animal skins (Śiva), destroy our cities with a single impossible arrow!"
"He is worthy of being saluted, worshipped, and honored; how could he burn us?"—having thus reflected in their minds, they realized that such a person is rare to find on this earth.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the creator of the universe, remembered Śiva and said to them, "So be it."
He gave an order even to Maya: "O Maya, where are your three cities—the golden one, the silver one, and the iron one?"
Having thus instructed Maya, Brahmā entered visibly into heaven, indeed into his own abode, while those sons of Tāraka looked on.
Then, through his ascetic power, the wise Maya constructed cities for Tārakākṣa made of gold and for Kamalākṣa made of silver.
The three types of excellent fortresses—Vidyunmālinī, Āyasī, and the third—are indeed to be known as being located respectively in heaven, in the sky, and on earth.
Having given three cities to those gods, Maya himself entered therein, being solely intent on their welfare.
Having thus obtained three sons, the offspring of Tāraka, possessing great strength and prowess, entered [the city] and enjoyed all manner of pleasures.
It was filled with wish-fulfilling trees, crowded with elephants and horses, interspersed with various palaces, and covered with networks of jewels.
It was adorned with celestial palaces resembling the solar disc, facing every direction, made of ruby and shining like the moon.
With divine palaces and gate-towers resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, crowded with celestial women, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas;
In every house there were shrines of Rudra, and established fire-sacrifices; there were the best of the twice-born, learned in the scriptures and ever devoted to the worship of Śiva.
It was beautifully adorned with ponds, wells, tanks, and oblong lakes, as well as with garden trees of the highest quality that had descended from heaven.
It was eternally adorned with the finest rivers, streams, and lakes, and was enchanting with many kinds of trees that bore fruits fulfilling all desires.
It was adorned with herds of intoxicated elephants, beautiful horses, chariots of various forms, and palanquins.
With various separate places for the practice of the *samayas* and other teachings, and with diverse, distinct schools for the study of the Vedas;
That which is unseen by mind or speech is always perceived by great-souled men of virtuous conduct and merit, who are accompanied by righteousness.
Everywhere, the most excellent ground was sanctified by devoted wives who were habituated to serving their husbands and turned away from evil practices.

It was filled with illustrious Daitya heroes, together with their wives, sons, and twice-born brahmins, who were knowers of the true meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti and were devoted to their own duties.
They had broad chests and bull-like shoulders, were always devoted to the practice of battle, and were both peaceful and enraged; likewise, there were hunchbacks and dwarfs.
With dark, curly hair resembling the petals of a blue lotus, all of them protected by Maya, well-trained, and eager for battle.

It is surrounded on all sides by those who delight in excellent battles, whose vigor is purified through the worship of Aja and Śiva, and who, resembling the Sun, Vāyu, and Mahendra, are very firm and well-honored by the destroyers of the gods.
Whatever dharmas are proclaimed in the Śāstras, Vedas, and Purāṇas, those dharmas are always dear to Śiva; they are present there in their entirety.
Thus, having obtained the boon, those sons of Tāraka, the Daityas, took refuge with Maya, the disciple of Śiva, and dwelt there.
Having driven out the entire triple world and entered the cities, they established a great kingdom, always devoted to the path of Śiva.
Then, O Sage, a great length of time passed for those of meritorious deeds as they dwelt happily and according to their pleasure, governing the excellent kingdom.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Tripura," in the Tripuravadhopākhyāna (The Narrative of the Destruction of Tripura) within the fifth section, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, of the Rudrasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O son of Brahmā, O one of great wisdom, O best among speakers, tell me what happened after that; how did the gods become happy?
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the infinitely wise Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra spoke, recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, scorched by that radiance, the gods, including Indra and the others, all consulted together in their distress and went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having bowed with affection to the Grandfather, all the gods, having observed the opportune moment, surrounded him and informed him of their suffering.
The gods said: "O Creator, all the inhabitants of heaven have surely been tormented by Maya, the lord of Tripura and the son of Tāraka."
Therefore, O Ordainer, we have come to you for refuge, for we are indeed suffering; devise a means for their destruction so that we may be happy once more.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus petitioned by the gods, the Creator Bhava, smiling, then replied to them all, whose minds were terrified of Maya.
Brahmā said: "O gods, you need not fear those Dānavas in particular; I shall tell you the means for their destruction, and Śarva will bring about your welfare."
The Daitya has grown arrogant from my favor and does not deserve death at my hands; nevertheless, let merit increase once more in the city of Tripura.
O all you gods, including Indra, pray indeed for the welfare of Śiva; if the Lord of All is pleased, he will accomplish your task.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, all the gods, including Indra, being distressed, went to that place where the bull-bannered Lord Śiva resides.
Then, having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods, they all, with palms joined in reverence and shoulders bent low, praised Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
The gods said: Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, the ordainer of all creation; salutations to you, Viṣṇu, the powerful one who effects the maintenance of the world.
Homage to you who have the form of Hara, the bringer of the destruction of all beings; homage to you, Śiva, who is beyond the guṇas and possesses immeasurable splendor.
Salutations to the Great Self, who is devoid of states, immutable, radiant, whose nature is that of the great elements, and who is untainted.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Beings, who can endure the great burden; who removes craving, whose form is free from enmity, and who possesses abundant splendor.
Salutations to you, the wielder of the trident, who is like a forest fire that destroys the great forest of the mighty Daityas, and who acts as an axe to the trees of the Daityas.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord, for the destruction of the great Danujas; salutations to you, the husband of Ambikā, the wielder of all weapons.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, Supreme Soul, Maheśvara! Salutations to you, the blue-throated Rudra, whose form is that of Rudra.

Salutation to You, who are known through the Vedanta; salutation to You who transcend all paths. Salutation to You whose nature consists of the qualities, yet who possesses the qualities and is simultaneously devoid of them.
O Mahādeva, salutations to you, the delighter of the three worlds; salutations to you as Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Vāsudeva.
Salutations to you, the divine Saṃkarṣaṇa, the destroyer of Kaṃsa; to you, O Dāmodara, the crusher of Cāṇūra and the dispeller of sorrow.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Acyuta, O All-pervading Lord, O Mṛḍa, O Śaṅkara, salutations to You! O Adhokṣaja, O Enemy of the Elephant, O Foe of Kāma, O Consumer of Poison!
To the god Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, whose very nature is Nārāyaṇa, and who is born from the body of Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to you who possess all forms, who destroy the great hells; salutations to you, the remover of sins, O Lord whose vehicle is the bull!
To Him whose form is time consisting of moments and so forth, who bestows strength upon His devotees, who possesses manifold forms yet is the Form itself, and who crushes the hosts of Daityas.
Salutations to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to Him who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins; salutations to You, who possess a thousand forms and a thousand limbs.

Salutations to the one whose form is Dharma, who is the essence of all beings; O Hara, salutations to the Self of all beings! Salutations to the one whose nature is the object of Vedic knowledge, and to the one who is fond of the Vedas.

Salutations, repeated salutations, to the one whose very nature is the Veda, to the speaker of the Veda; to the one who is reachable by the path of virtuous conduct, and who travels upon that path of virtuous conduct.
Salutations to you, Viṣṭaraśravas, and to the one whose nature is truth; salutations to you who are fond of truth, who are truth itself, and who are accessible through truth.
Salutations to you, the wielder of *māyā*; salutations indeed to you, the Lord of *māyā*. Salutations to you who are Brahman, to Brahman, and to the one born of Brahman.

Salutations to You, O Lord, for Your austerity; salutations to the bestower of the fruits of austerity; to the one worthy of praise, the praise itself, and whose mind is eternally delighted by hymns of praise.
To him who is pleased by sacred revelation and right conduct, who is fond of praise and virtuous behavior, whose nature is fourfold, and who takes the form of beings born in water and on land;
O Lord, all the gods and others are your manifestations by virtue of their excellence; you are Indra among the gods, and you are considered the Sun among the planets.
Among the worlds you are Satyaloka; among rivers you are the celestial river (Ganges); among colors you are white; and among lakes you are Lake Mānasa.
Among mountains you are the father born of the mountain; among cows, you are the fulfiller of desires; among oceans, you are the Ocean of Milk; and among metals, you are gold.
Among the castes, you are the Brāhmaṇa; among men, O Śaṅkara, you are the king. Among the fields of liberation, you are Kāśī; among sacred fords, you are the king of holy places.
Among all stones you are the crystal, O Maheśvara; among flowers you are the lotus, and likewise among mountains you are the Himavat.
In verbal discourse you are Bhārgava, and among poets you are Kavi; among birds you are indeed Śarabha, and among predators you are esteemed as the Lion.
O Bull-bannered Lord, among stones you are the Śālagrāma stone; indeed, among all forms worthy of worship, you are the Narmadā-liṅga.
O Supreme Lord, you are Nandīśvara among animals, the bull; in the Vedas, you are the form of the Upaniṣads; and for the sacrificers, you are the cool-rayed moon.
Among those who possess majesty, you are the fire; among the devotees of Śiva, you are Acyuta; among the Purāṇas, you are the Mahābhārata; and among letters, you are the syllable 'Ma'.

You are the *praṇava* among seed-mantras, you are the poison of formidable [serpents], you are indeed the pervasive space among all that pervades the sky, and you are the Supreme Self among all selves.
Among the senses you are the mind; among gifts you are the gift of fearlessness; among purifiers you are water; and likewise, among things that sustain life, you are the nectar of immortality.
Among all gains, you are the gain of a son; among those possessing speed, you are the wind; and among all daily rites, you are considered the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti).
Among sacrifices you are the Aśvamedha; among ages you are the first age; among all the lunar mansions you are Puṣya; and among lunar days you are the new moon.
You dwell in all seasons and you are the transition at all sacred junctures; among species of grass you are the kuśa, and among thick trees you are indeed the vaṭa.
Among yogas you are Vyatīpāta; among creepers you are the Somavallī vine; among intellects you are the intellect of dharma (dharmabuddhi); and you are the wife of friends.
O Maheśvara, you are the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) for pure practitioners; among all the jyotirliṅgas, you are considered the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara).
You are the Dharma for all kinsmen; you are the highest among the stages of life (āśramas); you are liberation among all castes; and among the Rudras, you are Nīlalohita.
Among the Ādityas you are Vāsudeva, and among the monkeys you are Hanumān; among sacrifices you are the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña), and among those who bear weapons, you are Rāma.
Among the Gandharvas you are Citraratha, among the Vasus you are Pāvaka, and you are certainly the intercalary month among months; you are the fourteenth day among sacred observances.
Airāvata is considered the foremost among the lordly elephants, Kapila among the Siddhas; you indeed are Ananta among the Nāgas, and you are Aryaman among the Pitṛs.
You are Time for those who measure time, and you are indeed Bali among the Daityas; what need is there for much speaking, O Lord of Gods, for you truly pervade the entire universe?
For you abide as a single part, yet you remain both outside and fully immanent.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Mahādeva, the bull-bannered one, with various kinds of divine hymns, all the gods lauded the trident-bearing Supreme Lord.

O Sage, Vāsava and the other gods, who were experts in pursuing their own interests, bowed with shoulders bent and palms joined in reverence; though dejected, they replied concerning the matter at hand for the sake of their own ends.
The gods said: "O Mahādeva, O Blessed One, all the gods, including Indra, have been defeated by the sons born of Tāraka, together with their two brothers."
O best of sages, the three worlds were brought under his control; all the perfected ones (siddhas) were destroyed, and the entire world was devastated.
That cruel one himself seized all the sacrificial portions; indeed, he promoted unrighteousness and obstructed the sages.
O Śaṅkara, the sons of Tāraka are certainly unslayable by all beings; by their will, they perform all actions.
Before it is destroyed by the terrible Daityas who dwell in Tripura, let such a policy be adopted by which the world may be protected.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Indra and the other inhabitants of heaven as they addressed him, Śiva spoke this reply to them.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Hymn to the God," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śiva said: "O Overseer of Tripura, this man is indeed meritorious at present; wherever merit prevails, he must never be slain by the wise."
I know the great and total distress of the gods; those Daityas are powerful and cannot be slain by either gods or asuras.
All those sons of Tāraka were indeed meritorious and bound by their vows; yet, the slaying of all those city-dwellers was difficult to accomplish.

Knowing full well the betrayal of a friend, how could I—though fierce in battle—commit such an act? For the Self-born One himself has previously declared that there is great sin in betraying a well-wisher.

For the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful person, there is no atonement.
"Those Daityas are my devotees; how can they be slain by me, O gods? Let this be considered by you, who are indeed knowers of dharma, according to the principles of righteousness."
They must not be killed as long as they have shown devotion to me; nevertheless, O gods, you must inform Viṣṇu of this reason.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having heard those words, all the gods, led by Śakra, immediately reported the matter first to Brahmā.
Then, having performed the prescribed rites, all the gods, together with Indra, quickly proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha, which was endowed with every splendor.
Having gone there and beheld Hari, the gods, overcome with awe, bowed down and praised him with great devotion, their palms joined in reverence.
Immediately thereafter, they quickly reported all the causes of their own suffering to that powerful Viṣṇu, as previously described.
Then, having heard of the suffering of the gods and what had been bestowed upon the abode of Tripura, and having understood their vow, Viṣṇu spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said: This is the truth: wherever there is eternal dharma, there suffering shall not arise, just as darkness does not remain when the sun is seen.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words, the gods were overcome with grief; with their lotus-like faces withered, they spoke again to Viṣṇu.
The gods said: "How indeed should it be performed? How is suffering dispelled? How may we become happy? How shall we remain [in that state]?"
How can the inhabitants of Tripura possibly remain righteous while living there? Indeed, all the residents of Tripura will surely bring about suffering for the gods.
Or rather, let the destruction of Tripura be ordained here; otherwise, let the assembly of the gods certainly be made timeless.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, those gods, having repeatedly lamented their grief, neither remained nor departed from this place, O best of gods.
Seeing them in such a state—deprived [of their splendor] yet endowed with humility—the glorious Nārāyaṇa likewise reflected in his mind as follows.
"What task remains for me to perform in the affairs of the gods, since I have you as my ally? For those sons of Tāraka, the Daityas, are devotees of Śiva."
Having reflected thus at that time, the powerful Viṣṇu then remembered the imperishable sacrifices for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Merely by the remembrance of Viṣṇu, those sacrifices quickly arrived at that very moment where Śrīpati, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), was staying.
Then, having bowed down to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Ancient One, the Puruṣa, Hari, they indeed praised him with their palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One, having seen those sacrifices, spoke to Sanātana; then the infallible Sanātana, looking toward the gods including Indra, replied.
Viṣṇu said: "By means of this very [sacrifice], O gods, always worship the Supreme Lord for the destruction of the three cities and for the prosperity of the three worlds."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the words of the wise Acyuta, the god of gods, those deities, having prostrated with love, praised the Lord of Sacrifice.
Having praised him thus, O Sage, the gods, their rites completed according to the injunctions prescribed for sacrifice, then worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice.
Then, from that sacrificial pit, thousands of hosts of spirits with massive bodies, armed with spears, javelins, and maces, sprang forth.
The gods beheld those hosts of beings by the thousands, with spears, javelins, and maces in their hands, and armed with staffs, bows, and stones.
Equipped with various weapons and wearing diverse garbs, they were then like Rudra at the fire of universal destruction and comparable to the sun at the end of time.
Seeing them standing before him after having prostrated, the glorious Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice and the observer of the ocean-like command, spoke to those beings.
Viṣṇu said: "O beings, listen to my words; you who are striving for the sake of the gods' purpose, all of you, being exceedingly powerful, go at once to Tripura."
Having gone, having burned, having pierced, and having shattered the three cities of the Daityas, you have returned as you came; O beings, you ought to come again for the welfare of all.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of the Blessed One, those hosts of beings then bowed to that God of gods and went to the three cities of the Daityas.
Having gone there and entering the splendor of the Lord of Tripura, they were instantly reduced to ashes like moths in a fire.
And those others who remained, intent on flight, emerged from the opening and approached Hari in a state of agitation.
Having seen them and having heard that entire account in its entirety, the Blessed One, Hari, the Supreme Person, reflected upon it with his mind.
With a mind tormented by the thought, "What must be done now? What task remains to be performed?", he perceived that all the gods, including Indra, were likewise consumed by distress.
"How shall I accomplish the work of the gods by forcibly destroying those three cities of the Daityas?"—thus he became overwhelmed with anxious thought.

"There is no destruction for those who are righteous through the practice of sorcery; of this there is no doubt. Thus the Lord himself has declared, he who establishes the authority of the Vedas and right conduct.
For those Daityas who dwell in Tripura are all most righteous; therefore, O best of gods, they have attained invincibility, and not otherwise.
But even after committing a very great sin, those who worship Rudra are liberated from all their transgressions, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
Indeed, through the worship of Rudra, all desires are fulfilled for the gods; moreover, an abundance of various enjoyments and the power of subjugation are surely attained upon the earth.
Therefore, those Daityas who enjoy that [fruit], being devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, shall attain manifold kinds of prosperity as well as liberation in the hereafter.
Then, having created an obstacle to their dharma through my own illusory power, I shall destroy Tripura in an instant for the sake of the gods' mission, even while those Daityas look on.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, then resolved to subsequently create an obstacle to the dharma of those enemies of the gods.
As long as the Vedic duties persist, as long as the worship of Śaṅkara continues, and as long as pure rites and the like endure, so long indeed shall there be no destruction.
Therefore, it must be done in this manner; from that, the Vedic dharma will proceed. Having abandoned the worship of the *liṅga*, the Daityas will come to be—of this there is no doubt.
Having thus resolved, Viṣṇu then devised a means to obstruct the dharma of those Daityas by means of the fragmentation of the Vedas.
At that very moment, Viṣṇu, who assists the gods, spoke to them; he had been commanded by Śiva himself, at Śiva’s command, for the protection of the three worlds.
Viṣṇu said: "O all you gods, go certainly to your own abodes; I shall perform the work of the gods according to my wisdom, of this there is no doubt."
I shall certainly turn them away from Rudra with great effort; once he knows them to be devoid of devotion to him, he will reduce them to ashes.

Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having placed his command upon their heads, those immortals were comforted; full of confidence, they departed for their respective abodes, and Brahmā too was filled with joy.
Then Viṣṇu performed that which was most beneficial for the sake of the gods; let that very [account], which completely destroys all sins, be heard properly.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Dharma of the Elemental Tripura," in the Tripuravadha episode of the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: And the imperishable one of great splendor created a single person born from his own self, composed of *māyā*, for the purpose of obstructing the dharma of those [gods].
Shaven-headed and wearing withered garments, he carried a basket and a vessel, holding a *puñjikā* flower in his hand and shaking it at every step.
The sage’s hand, along with his garment, was constantly disappearing into his mouth as he uttered the word "Dharma" with a faltering voice.
Having paid homage to Viṣṇu, he then stood before him; with palms joined in reverence, he then spoke these words to Hari.
O Arhan, I have worshipped Acyuta; now command me, what shall I do? O Lord, tell me my names and also my place, O Master.
Having heard these auspicious words of his, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, becoming pleased in mind, spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said: Listen, for I shall tell you the purpose for which you were created. O highly wise one born from my own body, you are my very form; of this there is no doubt.
"Born from my own body, you ought to perform my work; you shall always be worthy of worship by me—of this there is no doubt."
"Your name shall indeed be 'Arihan,' for no other names are auspicious for you. Later I will tell you of your place; listen with respect to what is at hand."
The scripture consisting of illusion, composed of illusion, contains sixteen thousand verses; it is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti, and it is devoid of the system of castes and stages of life.
"Compose a treatise consisting of Apabhraṃśa and likewise one consisting of the doctrine of karma; by such effort, its expansion will come to pass."
"I grant you the power of emanation; it shall come to pass that various illusions will quickly be under your control."
Having heard those words of Hari, the Supreme Soul, that master of illusion (Māyī) bowed down and replied to Janārdana.
Muṇḍī said: "O Lord, O Master, quickly command that which must be done by me; by your command, every action shall become fruitful."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, he taught him the scripture concerning illusion (māyāmaya); for in this very world there is the perception of heaven and hell, and not otherwise.
Viṣṇu spoke to him again, recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva: "All these Daityas, the inhabitants of Tripura, are to be deluded."
They must certainly be initiated and taught with diligence; by my command, O high-minded one, no fault shall be yours.
The Dharmas pertaining to the Śruti and the Smṛti are revealed therein; of this there is no doubt. O ascetic, by means of this knowledge, all [obstacles] are certainly to be burst asunder.
O Shaven-headed One, you ought to go for the purpose of destroying the inhabitants of Tripura; having fully revealed the dharma of darkness, destroy the three cities.
And then, O Lord, having gone back once more to the desert region, you must remain in accordance with your own dharma until the Kali age has passed away.
When that age has begun, let your own dharma be made manifest; furthermore, it must be practiced by you through your disciples and their disciples in turn.
By my command, your dharma will certainly attain expansion; by being ever intent on my permission, you shall attain my own state.
Thus was the command then given by the powerful Viṣṇu; at the instruction of the God of gods, Hari vanished from his heart.
Then that shaven-headed one, observing the command of Hari, likewise created disciples; at that time, he himself taught the four Māyāmaya scriptures according to their true nature.
Just as he himself was, so too were those four auspicious shaven-headed ones; having offered salutations, they stood there before Hari, the Supreme Self.
Then Hari himself, the protector of Śiva’s command, being exceedingly pleased, spoke those four words to the sage there.
Just as I am, so shall you become by my command; you are blessed, and you shall attain the supreme state in this world, of this there is no doubt.
Then those four shaven-headed ones, having resorted to the heretical dharma, held alms-bowls in their hands and wore garments made of rags.
Wearing only soiled garments and remaining silent, they spoke with great joy, saying: "Dharma is gain; it is the supreme reality."
Holding brooms made of strips of cloth, they moved very slowly indeed, out of fear of harming living beings.
O Sage, they all then, filled with joy, paid homage to the Blessed Lord and stood once more before him there.
Then Hari, taking them by the hand, presented them to his preceptor and spoke with great affection, specifically mentioning their names.
Just as you are, so too are these; they are indeed mine, without a doubt. That original form is called "Pūjya" (the Worshipful) because of its being worthy of worship.
"Let these names—Ṛṣi, Yati, Kīri, and Upādhyāya—be well-known as your own."
Furthermore, both my auspicious name and yours should be taken up; that name "Arihan" should be meditated upon, for it destroys all evil.
You yourselves must perform deeds that bring happiness to the world; for those who act in accordance with the welfare of the world, there will be the highest destination.

Sanatkumāra said: Then, having prostrated before him, that master of illusion (Māyī), accompanied by his disciples, immediately departed for Tripura, which was under the will of Śiva and protected by Umā.
Having quickly entered that city, urged by Viṣṇu, the self-controlled sage then employed his illusory power against that master of great illusion.
Having established himself in the city grove accompanied by his disciples, he then set in motion an illusion that deludes even the masters of illusion.
O Sage, by the power of the worship of Śiva, that Māyā suddenly did not move at all in Tripura; then the ascetic became despondent.
Then, with his enthusiasm lost and his mind bewildered, he remembered Viṣṇu and praised him greatly within his heart, while his heart burned with anguish.
Remembered thus, Viṣṇu quickly recalled Śaṅkara in his heart; having received his command mentally, he swiftly called Nārada to mind.
As soon as he was remembered by Viṣṇu, Nārada appeared; having bowed and offered praise, he then stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then Viṣṇu, the best among those who possess the wisdom of sages, who is ever devoted to the welfare of the world and always intent on accomplishing the work of the gods, spoke to that Nārada.
"O dear one, by the command of Śiva it is said: 'Go quickly to Tripura. There the sage went with his disciples for the purpose of deluding those well-settled inhabitants."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, Nārada, the best of sages, went quickly to that place where the sage, the foremost of magicians, was located.
Nārada too, being a master of illusion, at the command of his illusory Lord, entered that city and was initiated by that master of illusion.
Then Nārada, having gone into the presence of the lord of Tripura and inquired after his welfare and other matters, reported everything to the king.
Nārada said: A certain ascetic devoted to dharma arrived there; he was indeed preeminent in all branches of knowledge and endowed with the highest mastery of Vedic learning.
And having seen many dharmas, we have seen that none are equal to this again; we are well-initiated here, having beheld the eternal Dharma.
O best of Daityas, O great king, if you have the desire for that dharma, then you must once again receive initiation into that dharma.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, which were pregnant with great meaning, the lord of the Daityas was amazed in his heart; deluded, he spoke there.
"Since Nārada has been initiated, we too shall obtain initiation"; having understood this, he indeed departed of his own accord.
Having seen him in that form at that time, deluded by such an illusion, he paid homage to that Great-Souled One and spoke these words to him.
The Lord of Tripura said: "O Sage of pure intent, initiation must be granted by you to me; I shall become your disciple—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
Having heard these pure words of the king of the Daityas, that eternal sage replied with great care.
O best of Daityas, if my command is to be carried out by you, then the initiation must be granted by me; it cannot be otherwise, even with ten million efforts.
Having heard these words, King Māyāmaya became agitated; with palms joined in reverence, he quickly spoke these words to that ascetic.
The Daitya said: "Whatever command you shall give, it shall be exactly so and not otherwise; I will not transgress your command—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the Lord of Tripura at that time, the best of sages removed the cloth from his face and spoke.
"O Lord of Daityas, receive initiation, the most excellent among all dharmas; by means of the ritual of initiation, you shall attain the fulfillment of your purpose."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that master of illusion quickly bestowed upon the king of the Daityas the initiation prescribed by his own dharma, according to the rules of ritual procedure.
O Sage, when that king of the Daityas had been initiated along with his brothers, all the inhabitants of Tripura there also became initiated.
O Sage, at that moment, the entire city of Tripura belonging to that master of great illusion was swiftly pervaded by the disciples and grand-disciples of the Muni.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Initiation of Tripura," in the Yuddhakhaṇḍa (Fifth Section) of the Rudrasaṃhitā (Second Book) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Pārāśarya.
Vyāsa said: When the king of the Daityas had been initiated and deluded by that master of illusion, what did the illusorist say then, and what did that lord of the Daityas do?
Sanatkumāra said: Having bestowed initiation upon him, the Yati Aṛihan, whose lotus feet were served by disciples such as Nārada and others, spoke to the king of the Daityas.
Arihaṇ said: Listen, O Lord of Daityas, to my words, which are pregnant with true knowledge, the entire essence of Vedānta, and the most supreme secret.
Samsara, established from beginningless time and devoid of agent and action, manifests by itself and dissolves by itself alone.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as far as the body extends, the Self alone is the sole Lord therein; there is no second ruler over it.
Those names known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the names of these embodied beings; just as for people like us, names such as "Enemy-Slayer" (Arihan) and so forth are spoken.
Just as the body of those such as ourselves dissolves at its own time, so too do the bodies of all beings, from Brahmā down to a mosquito, dissolve at their own respective times.
When this body is examined, there is nothing superior anywhere; food, sexual intercourse, sleep, and fear are the same everywhere.
For every embodied being, upon reaching the limit of their lack of food, attains exactly the same degree of satisfaction, neither more nor less.
Just as we, having drunk the drink, would become joyful and free from thirst, so too it is for others who are thirsty; there is no distinction between the small and the great.
Let there be thousands of women who are the very ground of beauty and charm; yet, at the time of sexual union, only one is truly employed here.
Let there be more than a hundred horses, and let there be many of each kind; yet, for mounting, there shall be only one for myself, and never a second.
The very same happiness that arises from sleep for those reclining on a couch is also found by those who sleep upon the earth as their bed.
Just as there is fear of death for embodied beings such as ourselves, so too is there fear of death for all creatures from Brahmā down to the smallest insect.
If one reflects with the intellect, all embodied beings are equal; having ascertained this, no one should ever harm anyone anywhere.
There is no dharma on the surface of the earth equal to compassion for living beings; therefore, compassion for living beings should be practiced by men with every effort.
When one living being is protected, the three worlds are protected; likewise, when one is slain, they are slain. Therefore, one should protect and not kill.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; evil is that which causes suffering to oneself. Liberation is independence from others; heaven is the enjoyment of one's desires.
This has been stated by the ancient sages as being certainly established by valid means of knowledge; therefore, non-violence must be practiced by men who fear hell.
There is no sin equal to violence in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile; the violent person goes to hell, while the non-violent person goes to heaven.
There are many kinds of gifts; what is the use of those that yield only meager fruits? There is not even a single gift here in this world that is equal to the gift of fearlessness.
In this world, four kinds of gifts have been proclaimed by the supreme sages, after they had examined various scriptures, for the sake of happiness both here and in the hereafter.

Fearlessness should be granted to those who are afraid, and likewise medicine to those who are diseased; knowledge should be given to seekers of learning, and food should be given to those afflicted by hunger.
Whatever gifts have been proclaimed here as being of great merit, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of fearlessness to living beings.
Indeed, the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is inconceivable; one should diligently practice them for the sake of acquiring the wealth of their names.
Having acquired wealth in abundance, one should indeed thoroughly honor the twelve sense-bases; what is the use of honoring anything else in this world?
The group of five organs of action and the five organs of perception, along with the mind and the intellect—these are declared here to be the auspicious twelve sense bases (āyatanas).
For living beings, heaven and hell exist right here and nowhere else; happiness is declared to be heaven, and suffering is indeed hell.
When pleasures are being enjoyed, the relinquishing of the body that occurs—this alone should be understood as the supreme liberation by those who contemplate reality.

When the afflictions, together with their latent impressions, have been utterly severed, that which remains is certainly to be known by those who contemplate reality as the supreme liberation, which is pure non-cognition.
This authoritative scripture is proclaimed by the exponents of the Vedas: "One should not harm any living beings," for there is no other [scripture] that incites violence.
That which is called "pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma" and which causes delusion is false in this world; it is no authority for those who possess knowledge, as it prescribes the immolation of animals.

Having cut down trees, slaughtered animals, and created a mire of blood, and having offered sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other substances into the fire—strange indeed is it that heaven is thus sought after!
Having thus declared his own view and having made the Lord of Tripura hear it, the ascetic spoke again with reverence to all the citizens.

Then [he studied] the dharmas taught in the Vedas, which produce conviction through perceived results, which accomplish solely the happiness of the body, and which are superior even to the Buddhist scriptures.
That which is declared by the Śruti as "Bliss is the form of Brahman" must indeed be understood exactly so; the conceptualization of manifoldness is false.
As long as this body remains healthy, as long as there is no impairment of the senses, and as long as old age is still far off, one should strive for happiness.
In ill health, in the impairment of the senses, and in old age, how can there be happiness? Therefore, those who desire happiness should give even their own bodies to supplicants.
Since we have not been born for the purpose of gratifying the mental dispositions of those who beg, this earth is not burdened by us, even less so by oceans, mountains, and trees.
The body is transient and destined for swift decay; accumulations are subject to exhaustion. Having realized this, the wise man should strive for the true well-being of the self.
This body is food for dogs, crows, and worms in the morning; that this body ends in ashes is proclaimed as the truth in the Veda.
This distinction of caste is vainly imagined among people; since the human condition is common to all, who is unrighteous and who is superior?
This is called the creation of Brahmā and others by the ancient sages; in his birth, two sons were renowned as Dakṣa and Marīci.
It is said that thirteen beautiful-eyed daughters of Dakṣa were married by Mārīca Kaśyapa according to the path of righteousness.
Even by mortals of the present day, whose intellect and prowess are meager, this inquiry—which is both accessible and inaccessible—is being pursued in vain.
The fourfold caste system, said to have arisen together from the mouth, arms, and thighs [of Brahmā], is a mere conceptual construction made by those of old; it does not hold up under scrutiny.
If four sons are born from one body, whether from one [father] or from some other source, would they then attain different complexions?
Therefore, this distinction between the high-born and the low-born does not appear; hence, no one should ever conceive of any difference among human beings anywhere.
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, having thus addressed the lord of the Daityas and the citizens, that ascetic, together with his disciples, zealously caused the Vedic dharma to perish.
He violated the great dharma of women devoted to their husbands, as well as the self-control of all men.

One should especially [perform] the duties toward the gods, as well as the duties of the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the duties of sacrifice, vows and the like, and particularly the śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should perform the worship of Śiva specifically preceded by the propitiation of the Liṅga, as well as the worship of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and others according to the prescribed rites.
That ascetic, a master of illusion and the foremost among deceivers, violated all rules regarding bathing, giving gifts, and other rites, especially on festival days.
O best of Brahmins, what need is there for much speaking? By that master of illusion, all the Vedas and whatever dharmas exist were cast far away from Tripura.
All the women of Tripura, who had taken refuge in the duties of wives, were deluded and abandoned their supreme resolve to serve their husbands.
Having practiced the spell for attraction and even that which brings others under one's control, men, infatuated with the wives of others, rendered them fruitful [of their desires].
The women dwelling in the inner apartments, as well as the princes, the citizens, and the city women—all were utterly infatuated by them.
Thus, when all the citizens had become entirely averse to their own duties, that which is other than Dharma flourished.
And Māyā, as well as Alakṣmī herself, went to Tripura at the command and by the appointment of that Lord Viṣṇu, the God of gods.
That fortune which they had obtained through their ascetic penance from the Lord of the Gods has now departed, having been cast out by the command of the Lord Brahmā.
Having bestowed such a delusion of intellect, fashioned by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, upon them, Nārada became successful in his purpose in an instant.
Nārada was likewise of such a nature as that illusionist; nevertheless, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, he did not undergo any transformation.
O Sage, even the king of the Daityas, together with his two brothers and Maya, had his power rendered blunt there by the will of Śiva.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Bewildering of Tripura," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, when that lord of the Daityas, along with his kinsmen and brothers, was thus deluded, what happened then? Tell me all of it, O Lord.
Sanatkumāra said: When Tripura had become thus, when the Daityas had abandoned the worship of Śiva, when all the duties of women were destroyed, and when wicked conduct prevailed;
Like the Lord of Lakṣmī who has accomplished his purpose, Hari went to Kailāsa together with the gods to report that deed to the Lord of Umā.
Standing near him along with the gods, that Lord of Ramā, as well as Brahmā, then [remained] in supreme meditative absorption for a long time.
Then, having mentally attained the omniscient Brahman, that Hari, the Supreme Person, praised Śaṅkara with pleasing words after having worshipped him.
Viṣṇu said: Salutations to you, the Great Lord, the God, the Supreme Self; to Nārāyaṇa, to Rudra, to Brahmā, whose form is Brahman.
Having done this and prostrating before Mahādeva like a staff, he recited the Rudra-mantra originating from Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Standing in the water, with his mind fixed on that alone, the Lord, remembering Śambhu—the Supreme Lord and his own Master—within his mind, [performed] one and a half crores [of recitations].
Then all the gods, with their minds fixed on him, [approached] Maheśvara.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, the soul of all, to Śaṅkara, the remover of distress; to Rudra, the blue-throated one, whose form is consciousness, the wise perceiver."
For you are always our refuge, the warder-off of all calamities; O destroyer of the enemies of the gods, you alone are always to be saluted by us, your own selves.
You are the beginning and you are without beginning; you are self-blissful, imperishable, and the Lord. You are the direct creator of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the Sovereign of the universe.
You alone are indeed the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds; for having become Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, you are the sole agent.
You are the savior in this world, the imperishable sovereign of all; the bestower of boons, consisting of speech, that which is expressed, and yet devoid of both the expressible and the expression.
The Lord is to be entreated for the sake of liberation by yogis who are the foremost among those who know yoga; for you indeed abide within the cavity of the heart-lotus of yogis.
The Vedas and the virtuous proclaim you to be the very nature of the Supreme Brahman; today they declare you to be the Reality, the mass of splendor, higher than the highest.
O All-pervading One, O Śarva, O Soul of all, O Lord of the three worlds, they call you the Supreme Self; in this world, you alone are Bhava.
O Teacher of the World, everything seen, heard, praised, and all that is being known, they say is smaller than an atom and greater even than the great.
I bow to you everywhere—you whose hands and feet extend to the ends of all directions, whose eyes, heads, and faces are on every side, and who possess ears and a sense of smell in every direction.
I bow down to you from all sides—you who are omniscient, all-pervading, the Lord of all, unobstructed, whose form is the universe, and whose eyes are manifold.
I bow down to you from all sides—you who are the Lord of All, the presiding witness over existence, the Truth, the Auspicious, the Unsurpassed, and resplendent like ten million suns.
I bow down to you from all sides—you who are the universal deity, without beginning or end, the thirty-sixfold principles, the Lord, and the impeller of all.
I bow down to you from all sides—you who set the nature of everything in motion, the great-grandfather of all, the Lord who embodies everything.
Thus do the Vedas—and those who know the essence of the Vedas—speak of the Self-Existent One, the giver of boons, the abode of all, and the knower of the essence of the Vedas.
That which has been done by you in this world is manifold and invisible to us; indeed, the gods, asuras, brahmins, and all others—both the stationary and the moving—depend upon you alone.
O Śambhu, beloved of the gods, protect us, the deities who have no other refuge; O Lord of the Three Cities, having slain the Asuras in an instant, [save us] who are as good as destroyed.
O Supreme Lord, they have been deluded by Your māyā today; O Master, they have been cast out from righteousness according to the reasoning set forth by Viṣṇu.
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, by the power of our good fortune, those Daityas have been born having renounced all worldly dharmas and taken refuge in the scriptures of the Buddha.
You are indeed always the performer of deeds for the gods, O bestower of refuge; we have come to you for protection—do as you wish.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Maheśāna, the gods stood before him with their palms joined in reverence; they were distressed, their bodies bowed low.
Thus praised by the lords of the gods and others, the Lord Īśvara, the master of all, mounted his bull and went there joyfully, accompanied by the recitation of Viṣṇu’s name.
Having embraced Viṣṇu and descended from the back of Nandin, he, with a serene mind, beheld everyone there with a steady gaze, his hand supported by Nandin.
Then, beholding the gods with a compassionate glance, Hara, the lord of Pārvatī, being pleased, spoke to Hari in a deep voice.
Śiva said: O Lord of the Gods, I have now understood this task for the sake of the gods, as well as the power of Viṣṇu’s māyā and that of the wise Nārada.
O best of gods, I shall undoubtedly bring about the destruction of the three cities of those Daityas who are devoted to unrighteousness.
But those great Daityas, though firm-minded devotees of mine, must be slain by me alone once they have abandoned their excellent virtue under some pretext.
Whether it be Viṣṇu or another who shall slay them—all those Daityas residing in Tripura who have been deprived of their virility and are devoid of devotion to me.
O lord of sages, having heard these words of Śambhu, all the inhabitants of heaven became despondent, as did Hari.
Seeing the gods and Viṣṇu remaining indifferent, Brahmā, the creator of existence, spoke these words to Śambhu with his palms joined in reverence.
Brahmā said: No sin whatsoever exists in you, since you are the foremost knower of yoga, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, and the eternal protector of the celestial sages.
It is indeed by your teaching that they have been deluded; you are their instigator. Though they have abandoned their own dharma and worship you, they are nonetheless fit to be slain by others.
Therefore, O Mahādeva, protector of the lives of the gods and sages, you must destroy the Mleccha tribes for the sake of protecting the virtuous.
That sin does not exist for you according to dharma, O King; therefore, you should protect the virtuous twice-born and indeed purify [the land] of thorns.
If you desire here or elsewhere sovereignty over all the worlds rather than your own kingdom, then protect [it] without delay.

The lords of sages, the lords of gods, as well as sacrifices, the Vedas, and all the scriptures and so forth—these, O Lord of the gods of gods, are indeed your progeny; and this Viṣṇu as well is certainly so.
O Lord, you are the deity who is sovereign over all, the universal emperor, and the Lord of all; this entire world, beginning with Hari, is indeed your retinue.
You are the crown prince, Hari is your splendor, I am your priest, Śakra is the executor of royal affairs, and he is the observer of your commands.
All other gods as well, O Lord, are constantly restrained by your command; they perform their respective duties eternally—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara, whose soul was serene, replied to the Creator, the lord of the gods.
Śiva said: "O Brahman, if I am proclaimed as the king of the gods and the sovereign emperor, then there is no such manner [of rule] that a lord like me would not accept here."
There is no such great divine chariot, nor a charioteer like him, nor even a bow, arrows, and so forth, that can bring victory in battle.
Having mounted [the chariot], taken up my bow and arrows, and concentrated my mind, I shall slay even the most powerful Daityas in battle.
Sanatkumāra said: Today, the gods, together with Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra, were filled with great joy; having heard those words of the Lord, they bowed and spoke to Maheśvara.
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, let us become of that same nature as yours; O Master, let us indeed be equipped with chariots and the like for the sake of battle."
Having spoken thus and perceiving the will of Śiva, all those gods, being delighted, stood together with palms joined in reverence and spoke individually.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Śiva," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of all the gods and others, Hara—the protector and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees—accepted them with great pleasure.
In the meantime, O Sage, the auspicious Goddess Śivā, accompanied by her two sons, arrived at that place where Hara was joined by the gods.
Then, seeing Śivā arrive, Viṣṇu and all the others quickly bowed down with great humility; filled with wonder and their agitation gone, they prostrated themselves.
"Victory to you!"—these auspicious words were uttered by all the sages, who remained silent, not knowing the reason for his arrival.
Then the Goddess, filled with wonderful curiosity, being praised by all the gods, spoke with affection to her Lord, who is skilled in various divine sports.
The Goddess said: "O All-pervading Lord, behold your son Ṣaṇmukha, who shines like the sun; O best among those who possess sons, he is adorned with excellent ornaments."
Thus awakened by these words of mere worldly measure, Śiva, the Lord, found no satiety as he drank the nectar from Skanda’s mouth.
Maheśvara did not even remember the Daityas who had arrived, being overwhelmed by his own splendor; instead, he embraced Skanda, smelled the crown of his head, and spoke these words.
Then the Mother of the World, having consulted with her Lord right there, remained for a moment and then rose up, she who is expert in manifold divine sports.
Then Śambhu, full of playful grace and being saluted by all the gods, entered his abode together with Sanandī, the six-faced one, and the daughter of the mountain king.
O Sage, all those gods stood by the side of the door of the wise God of Gods; they were then greatly agitated and dejected in mind.
"What should be done? Where should we go? Who might be the giver of our happiness?"—thus they spoke, crying out, "Alas! We are ruined! as such thoughts arose within them.
Beholding one another, Śakra and the others became utterly overwhelmed; reproaching their own fate, they spoke these faltering words.
"We are sinful here," said some; "we are indeed unfortunate," said others; and other gods said, "Those lords of the Daityas are the fortunate ones."
In that very interval, having heard their various cries, the immensely powerful Kumbhodara struck the gods with his staff.
Overcome by fear, the gods fled while crying out "Alas! Alas!", and other sages fell down; indeed, a state of total agitation ensued.
Indra, however, became exceedingly distressed and fell to the ground on his knees; the other celestial sages likewise, being greatly distraught, fell upon the earth.
All the sages and gods, gathered together and equally agitated, approached Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who were of friendly mind toward one another.
"O sages, Kaśyapa and all the others, behold this power of destiny! At that time, they all spoke of the fear and calamity regarding Hari’s world."
"Others, O twice-born ones, said, 'The task was not completed due to ill fortune,' while still others were greatly astonished, asking, 'Why has this obstacle arisen?'"
O Sage, having heard these words spoken by Kaśyapa and the others, Hari took up speech, consoling the lords of the sages and the gods.
Viṣṇu said: O gods and all you sages, listen to my words with reverence. For what reason have you fallen into suffering? Abandon all this suffering.

O gods, consider that the propitiation of the Great One is not easily accomplished; it is heard in the scriptures that in the propitiation of the Great One, there will first be suffering. Once the gods recognize their steadfastness, He certainly becomes pleased.
"Śiva, the leader of all the Gaṇas and Yakṣas, is the Supreme Lord; let him be considered by everyone in their hearts as to how he might be brought under control."
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should then pronounce "namaḥ"; after that, "śivāya," and following that, the two auspicious syllables (Śrīṃ).
Then two *kurus* are proclaimed, and after that again for Śiva; likewise, *namaḥ* and the *praṇava*—thus, O wise ones, is the mantra always [recited].
"If you turn back again for the sake of Śambhu, then by chanting [the mantra] ten million times, Śiva will accomplish your purpose."
O sage, when this had been said by that powerful Hari, the gods once again performed the propitiation of Hara.
Hari, too, with his mind fixed on Śiva, performed japa along with Vidhi for the sake of accomplishing the task of the gods and especially that of the sages.
O best of sages, repeatedly uttering "Śiva," those gods, endowed with fortitude, stood there having formed themselves into a multitude numbering ten million.
In the meantime, Śiva himself appeared in person in his aforementioned form and spoke these words:
Śrī Śiva said: O Hara, O Vidhi, O gods, and O sages of auspicious vows, I am pleased; by virtue of this victory, choose whatever boon you desire.
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, Lord of the Universe, if you are pleased, then taking note of the distressed gods, let the three cities be destroyed."
Protect us, O Supreme Lord, Friend of the distressed, Compassionate One! By you alone have the gods been repeatedly protected from calamities at all times.
Sanatkumāra said: O Brahman, having heard these words spoken by those sages, including Hari and Vedhas, Maheśa then laughed inwardly and spoke again.
Maheśa said: O Hara, O Vidhi, O gods, and all you sages, listen to my words with heedfulness, considering the three cities to be destroyed.
And quickly provide the divine chariot, the charioteer, the celestial bow, and the supreme arrow—all that was previously promised.
O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, you are indeed certainly the sovereign lord of the three worlds; you ought to strive diligently to provide for me in every way as a universal emperor.
Considering the three cities to have been destroyed, you two, being appointed to the protection of creation, shall indeed provide assistance to the gods with diligent effort.
This mantra is of great merit, auspicious, and a source of joy to me; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grants all desires, and brings about the state of Śiva.

It brings wealth, fame, and long life to men who desire heaven and its objects; it grants liberation to those who are free from desire, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those already liberated.
The man who, having become pure, always recites this mantra, or hears it, or causes others to hear it, shall obtain all his desires.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Śiva, the Supreme Self, all the gods attained joy, and Hari and Brahmā did so even more.
At his command, Viśvakarman fashioned for the sake of the universe a divine chariot, supremely beautiful and composed of all the gods.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Devotion of the Devas," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, omniscient one, foremost among the devotees of Śiva, you of noble mind! This wondrous account of the Supreme Lord has been narrated by you, my dear.
Now, tell me of the supreme, divine chariot made of celestial materials, which was fashioned by the wise Viśvakarman for the sake of Śiva.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, that lord of sages, Sanatkumāra, spoke after remembering the lotus feet of Śiva.

Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great wisdom, O sage, to the construction of the chariot and other vehicles; I shall describe it according to my understanding, having called to mind the lotus feet of Śiva.
Then, by Viśvakarman, a divine chariot composed of all the worlds was constructed with great effort and reverence for the god Rudra.
Consisting of all beings, golden, and esteemed by all, the right wheel of the chariot is Sūrya and the left is indeed Soma.
The southern [wheel] indeed has twelve spokes, and likewise the northern has sixteen; upon those spokes, O best of Brahmins, are the twelve Ādityas.
O observer of noble vows, the sixteen digits of the moon are the spokes of his [the left-hand path's] wheel; likewise, the constellations are the ornaments of that very left-hand path.
O best of Brahmins, the six seasons are its felloes; the sky is its hub, and Mount Mandara is the seat of the chariot.
