Mount Asta and Mount Udaya are known as the two poles; Mahāmeru is the base, and the Keśara mountains are the supports.
Its two solstices were the two years of its speed; its yokes were the muhūrtas, and its pins were known as the kalās.
Its poles are said to be the ghoṇās; its axle-shafts are the kṣaṇas; its naves are the nimeṣas; and its shafts are known as the anulavas.
The sky is the protective covering of this chariot; heaven and liberation are its two banners. Its two poles at the end of the yoke are known as the source of worldly wandering and the cow of plenty.
The pole of the chariot is clearly the Manifest (vyakta), its growth is the Reed-forest (naḍvala), its corners are Ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), and the elements are known as its strength.
And his very sense-faculties are its ornaments on all sides; faith, O best of sages, is the path of this very chariot.
At that time, O observers of good vows, the ornaments themselves were the six limbs, and the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Dharmaśāstras were the secondary ornaments.
The mantras are known as the excellent mares (balāśaya-varā), endowed with all auspicious characteristics; their phonemes are the hooves, and their stages of life (āśramas) are the bells.
Furthermore, the serpent Ananta, adorned with a thousand hoods, is indeed its axle; the cardinal directions are the feet of this chariot, as are the intermediate directions.
The banners beginning with Puṣkara are made of gold and adorned with jewels; his four oceans are known as the leather straps for the chariot.
The foremost rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, were all adorned with every ornament; with the tips of their hands grasping chowries, they were all beautified in the form of women.
Taking their respective positions there, Āvaha and the other six winds graced the chariot, as did the seven [rivers] at the excellent golden staircase.
The Lokāloka mountain serves as a surrounding staircase for it on all sides; likewise, the external objects, such as the mind and so forth, are its beautiful ornaments.
All the Varṣaparvata mountains are known as the cords on all sides of that chariot; moreover, all the inhabitants of the netherworlds (Talātala) constitute its floor.
The Lord Brahmā is known as the charioteer, and the gods are remembered as the holders of the reins; the *praṇava* is the goad of that Brahmā, whose deity is Brahman.
The letter *A* is the great parasol, Mount Mandara serves as the handle for its side, the Lord of Mountains is his bow, and the King of Serpents himself is the bowstring.
The goddess Sarasvatī is the bell; the bow is Śruti in embodied form; Viṣṇu of great splendor is the arrow; and Agni is proclaimed to be the shaft.
O Sage, his four horses are said to be the four Vedas; the stars are their ornament, and beyond that, they are the remaining [constellations].
The army was produced from poison; the winds were known as the Vājakas, and the sages headed by Vyāsa became the draft-animals for the chariots.
O Lord of Sages, what is the use of speaking at length? I shall tell you in few words: whatever exists within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), all that is indeed remembered as being upon the chariot.
Thus, by that wise Viśvakarman, at the command of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, was this auspicious array of chariots and other vehicles duly fashioned.
Sanatkumāra said: Having harnessed the Vedas as horses to such a great, divine chariot filled with various wonders, Brahmā presented it to Śiva.
Having informed Śambhu and having repeatedly entreated the Lord of Gods with the consent of Viṣṇu and the other deities, he placed the wielder of the trident upon it.
Then, upon that divine chariot equipped with a chariot-fortress, the great lord Śambhu, who embodies all the gods, ascended.
He was indeed praised by the sages, as well as by the gods, gandharvas, and pannagas, and also by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the guardians of the worlds.
Surrounded by throngs of Apsarases skilled in song, Śambhu, the bestower of boons, shone forth upon seeing that charioteer.
Upon that [chariot] was yoked the chariot of Ārohaṇa, fashioned by the world and brought together from all quarters; the horses born of the Vedas fell to the ground with their heads bowed.
The earth trembled and all the mountains shook; Śeṣa suddenly quivered, distressed and unable to bear that burden.
Then, the Blessed One, the upholder of the earth, assuming the form of a lordly bull, rose up beneath this chariot and supported it for a moment.
In another moment, the lordly bull also knelt upon the ground, unable to endure the great splendor of Maheśa mounted upon his chariot.
Then the Blessed One, with reins in hand, raised the horses and brought that excellent chariot to a halt at the command of the God.
Then Brahmā, standing upon his excellent chariot, urged on the horses composed of the Vedas, which were harnessed and possessed the speed of the wind of the mind.
Indeed, with reference to those three ancient cities, they were situated in the sky while Maheśvara presided over them for the sake of the powerful Dānavas.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, the benefactor Śaṅkara, looking toward the gods, said: "Bestow upon me the lordship over the creatures (paśus); then I shall slay the asuras."
O best of gods, O most excellent of Daityas, those [beings] are to be slain only after you have designated them as distinct from the status of the gods and others; it cannot be otherwise.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of that wise God of gods, they all fell into despondency, apprehensive of their state as sacrificial animals.
Then, having understood their state of mind, Śambhu, the God of gods and Lord of Ambikā, smiled and out of compassion spoke thus to those deities:

Śambhu said: "O best of the wise, may there be no downfall for you even while in the state of a bound soul (paśu). Listen to the liberation from the state of a bound soul, and let it be accomplished."
"Whoever shall practice the divine Pāśupata [vow] will be liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśutva); this is the truth promised to you, so remain attentive."
And those others as well, O best of gods, who shall perform my Pāśupata vow—they shall be liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśu), of this there is no doubt.
He who causes [the disciple] to perform service for twelve years, or for three years as half of that, until he becomes lifelong (naiṣṭhika), is liberated from the state of being a beast.
Therefore, O best of gods, you shall perform this supreme, divine practice; then you will be liberated from the state of being sacrificial animals—of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Maheśa, the Supreme Soul, the gods, including Hari, Brahmā, and the others, replied, "So be it."
Therefore, indeed, all beings—both gods and the foremost of asuras—are the cattle of the Lord; and Rudra is Paśupati, the liberator from the bonds of the cattle.
Then, having taken up [the staff], that name "Pakṣupati" became well-known throughout all the worlds as a bestower of happiness for that Great Lord.
Then all the celestial sages, shouting "Victory! with joy, rejoiced exceedingly—Deveśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others as well.
And at that time, as for the form that was produced of that Great Being, it is truly impossible to describe it even in hundreds of years.
In this manner, Maheśāna, the Lord of all and the bestower of happiness upon everyone, went to destroy Tripura along with Maheśānī.
Then, in order to slay Tripura, all those foremost leaders of the immortals, possessing the brilliance of the sun, set forth upon elephants, horses, excellent lions, chariots, and bulls.
Then those lords of the gods, their arms equipped with various weapons—halas, śālas, musalas, and bhuśuṇḍis—and resembling great mountains themselves, set forth joyfully.
Richly adorned with various weapons and supremely radiant, Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other leaders went before that Great Lord, proclaiming the victory of Śambhu amidst a great festival.
All the sages, staff-bearing and wearing matted locks, rejoiced; and the sky-dwelling Siddhas and Cāraṇas showered rains of flowers.
O best of Brahmins, there are three sons, and all of them are lords of the Gaṇas; who is capable of counting their number? I shall mention only a few.

Surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas and the hosts of gods, Bhṛṅgī—the preeminent leader of all the Gaṇas—ascended his celestial chariot and went to the triple city of Tripura to destroy it, just as Mahendra ascends his.
Keśa, Vigatavāsa, Mahākeśa, Mahājvara, Somavallīsavarṇa, and likewise Somadarśanaka.
Somadhṛk, Sūryavarcas, Sūryapreṣaṇaka, Sūryākṣa, the one named Sūri, and Surasundara.
Praskanda, Kundara, Caṇḍa, Kampana, and Atikampana; Indra, Indrjava, Yantṛ, and likewise Himakara.
Śatākṣa, Pañcākṣa, Sahasrākṣa, Mahodara, Satījahus, Śatāsya, Raṅka, and Karpūrapūtana.
Dviśikha, Triśikha, and likewise Ahaṃkārakāraka; Ajavaktra, Aṣṭavaktra, Hayavaktra, and Ardhavaktraka.
Thus, these and many other immeasurable heroic leaders of the Gaṇas set forth, surrounding the Lord, who is devoid of both the perceived and the characteristics of perception.
Then, having surrounded Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, they became capable in an instant of mentally incinerating the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

They are capable of burning this entire world; yet here, the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva] is to burn Tripura. What need has Śambhu here for a chariot, or for his arrow, or for his attendants, or for the hosts of gods?
O Vyāsa, that very wielder of the Pināka bow, whose power is wondrous even to the gods, went there himself along with his own Gaṇas to burn those three cities of the enemies of the deities.
O best of sages, what other reason is there? I shall tell you: it is indeed for the sake of proclaiming [this] fame throughout the worlds, which removes the greatest of sins.
Moreover, this is indeed another reason for the conviction of the wicked: because among all the gods, none other is distinguished [as superior].

Sanatkumāra said: Then Śambhu, the Great God, mounted upon his chariot and accompanied by all his attendants, prepared to burn the entire Triple City of the enemies of the gods. Taking his stand at the head of the formation and fixing his supreme arrow, he made his bow ready and assumed the most wonderful *pratyālīḍha* posture.
Having fixed his gaze firmly upon his fist and having established his vision upon that fist, he remained there motionless for a hundred thousand years.
Then, on the thumb of that wielder of the trident, Gaṇādhyakṣa stood firm, destroying the Daityas; yet those cities did not enter within his range of vision.
Then, from the sky, Hara—bearer of the bow and arrow, with hair like *muñja* grass and three uneven eyes—heard a most beautiful voice.
"O sirs! As long as that Vināyaka has not been worshipped by the Blessed One, O Lord of the Lords of the World, he will not destroy the cities for now."
Having heard these words, the slayer of Andhaka summoned Bhadrakālī and then honored the elephant-faced one.
When Vināyaka had been worshipped with joy and was thoroughly satisfied as he went before him, the Blessed Lord Hara then beheld him in the sky.
Regarding the three cities of the high-souled Daityas, the Tārakas, some indeed speak thus, asserting that they were joined together exactly as they are described.
O Lord of Gods, in the case of the Supreme Brahman, the Great Lord who is the object of all worship, success in one's task cannot indeed be achieved through the grace of another.
He is independent, the Supreme Brahman, both possessing attributes and devoid of them; he is unperceivable by all, the Lord, the Supreme Self, and untainted.
Consisting of the nature of the five deities and worshipped by the five deities, he is the supreme Lord. There is no one to be worshipped by him; he alone is the object of worship and the abode.
Or rather, O Sage, everything regarding the conduct of that God of gods, the great Lord and giver of boons, is brought about by his divine play.
While that Great God remained there, having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, the cities quickly attained oneness with him in the course of time.
O Sage, when they had attained union there in Tripura, a tumultuous joy arose among the high-souled gods and others.
Then all the hosts of gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis uttered cries of "Victory! while praising the one of eight forms.
Then Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the lord of the worlds, said: "The time has also arrived for the act of slaying the Daityas."
O Maheśvara, O Lord, perform the work of the gods against those sons of Tāraka, the inhabitants of the three cities; for they have now attained unity.
O Lord of Gods, before these cities indeed reach separation [from their inhabitants], discharge your arrow and reduce Tripura to ashes.
Then, having strung his bow and fixed that arrow, Śarva worshipped the Pāśupata weapon and meditated upon Tripura.
Then the god Mahādeva, who is skilled in the play of granting boons, looked upon that with disdain for some reason or other.
The three cities, Virūpākṣa was capable of reducing to ashes in an instant; may that Supreme Lord, the refuge of the virtuous, protect us.
The Lord of Gods is capable of burning the three worlds with a mere glance; for the sake of increasing our fame, you ought to discharge your arrow here.
Thus praised then by all the immortals, headed by Viṣṇu and Brahmā, Maheśvara desired to burn those three cities with his arrow.
At the auspicious moment called Abhilāṣya, having drawn his wonderful bow and produced the sound of his palms against the bowstring—a roar that was utterly unbearable—[he spoke].
Having proclaimed his own name and addressed the great asuras, Ugra discharged the arrow that possessed the splendor of ten million suns.
That swift arrow, composed of Viṣṇu and having fire as its barb, blazed intensely; it, the remover of impurity, consumed those three Daityas residing in Tripura.
Then the three cities, having burned the earth girt by the four oceans, simultaneously reached the ground, reduced entirely to ashes.
Hundreds of Daityas were burnt by the fire residing in his arrow, crying out "Alas! Alas! due to their transgression against the worship of Śiva.
Tārakākṣa, having been consumed by fire, together with his two brothers, remembered his own lord, the god Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Endowed with supreme devotion, uttering various words as he gazed upon Mahādeva, he spoke to him in his mind.
Tārakākṣa said: "O Bhava, you are known; if you are pleased with us along with our kinsmen, by that truth, when will you consume us once again?"
We have obtained that which is difficult to find and unattainable even by gods and asuras; may our intellect, permeated by devotion to you, arise in birth after birth.
O Sage, while the Dānavas were speaking thus, they were wondrously consumed by that fire by the command of Śiva and reduced to ashes.
O Vyāsa, by the command of Śiva, other Dānavas as well—both young and old—were swiftly consumed and reduced to ashes by that fire.
Whether they were women or men, or whatever vehicles were there, all were consumed by that fire, just as the world is at the end of a kalpa.
Some excellent women were burnt after abandoning their husbands who had already reached their throats; others were women who were asleep, intoxicated, or exhausted from lovemaking.
Half-burnt and yet awakened, they wandered about, stupefied by delusion; not even the most minute thing remained by that terrible fire of Tripura.
One who is unrefined, whether liberated, stationary, or moving—except for the Daitya Maya, the imperishable Viśvakarman—[is subject to this].
But that which is not opposed to the gods, protected by the splendor of Śambhu, and has taken refuge in Maheśa—even in a time of calamity—remains steadfast for the true devotee.
For there exists no cause of destruction for the assembly of those Daityas and other beings, whether in their existence or non-existence, or in what has been done or left undone.
Therefore, the virtuous must indeed exert great effort; for the world is diminished by censure, so one should not perform such an action.
"Let there be no union for those inhabitants of Tripura; for this is the consensus of all, provided that it should come to pass through destiny."
Even there, those Daityas who worshipped Rudra along with their kinsmen all attained the status of Gaṇapatyas by the power of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Burning of Tripura," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O son of Brahmā, O highly wise one, you are blessed, O best among the devotees of Śiva! What did all the gods do after Tripura had been burnt?
Where has Maya gone, burnt up? Where have those husbands of yours gone? Tell me all of that, if it pertains to the story of Śambhu.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the blessed Sanatkumāra, son of Bhava, spoke while remembering the pair of Śiva’s feet.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, son of Parāśara, to the life-story of the Great Lord, which destroys all sins and follows the ways of worldly play.
When the entire Triple City, crowded with Daityas, had been burnt by Maheśvara, the gods there were especially struck with wonder.
At that time, all the gods, including Indra and Upendra, seeing the immensely radiant Rudra, were filled with agitation and said nothing at all.
Extremely terrifying and fierce, blazing in the ten directions, resembling ten million suns and like the fire of universal destruction.
Upon merely beholding the God and the Goddess, the daughter of Himavat, out of fear all the deities, led by Indra, trembled and stood bowed down.
Seeing the army of the gods then terrified, those bulls among sages said nothing; they remained still and bowed down on all sides.
Then Brahmā, too, being terrified upon seeing the form of Śaṅkara, praised him with a contented heart, together with the gods and composed in mind.
And Viṣṇu, filled with fear, [sought refuge] in Bhava Hara, the God of gods, the enemy of Tripura, who dwells with Girijā, the Great Lord who is subject to his devotees.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees, be gracious, O Supreme Lord, you who grant the welfare of all the gods!
Be gracious, O Lord of the worlds; be gracious, O bestower of bliss. Be gracious, O Śaṅkara, O Master; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
Oṃ! Homage to you, Oṃkāra, who delivers others by means of the syllable Ā; be gracious, O Lord of all gods, O Destroyer of Tripura, O Maheśvara!
O Śaṅkara, beloved of the boon-granting goddess, obeisance to You, the God who is expressible in manifold ways, yet devoid of qualities, and who transcends both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Salutations be to You, who are changeless, eternal, ever-satisfied, and luminous; who are stainless, divine, and yet possessed of the three qualities.
Salutations to you who possess all attributes; salutations to you, the Lord of Heaven; salutations to Sadāśiva, the peaceful, the Great Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Salutations to you, the omniscient, the refuge, the newly born; salutations to Vāmadeva, to Rudra, and likewise to the Puruṣa beyond that.
Salutations to you, the non-terrible (Aghora), who is easily served and dependent upon your devotees; salutations to Īśāna, the most excellent, who bestows bliss upon your devotees.
"Protect, protect us, O Mahādeva, all the gods who are terrified! Having burnt the three cities, all the immortals have been made successful."
Having thus praised all the deities, Brahmā and the others, being supremely delighted, offered their salutations individually to Sadāśiva.
Then Brahmā himself, having bowed down with shoulders bent and palms joined in reverence, praised the god Maheśvara, the enemy of Tripura.
Brahmā said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Śaṅkara, destroyer of Tripura! May I have supreme devotion toward you, O Mahādeva, that never departs.
O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, may I always be your charioteer; O All-pervading Supreme Lord, be ever favorable to me.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, the noble-minded Brahmā, bowing with shoulders bent and palms joined in reverence, ceased speaking.
The Blessed Lord Janārdana, having prostrated before Maheśvara and joined his palms in reverence, offered praise to Maheśvara.
Viṣṇu said: O Lord of the gods, O Maheśāna, O friend of the distressed, O compassionate one! Be gracious, O Supreme Lord; show mercy, O you who are dear to those who bow before you.

Salutations to you who are devoid of qualities, and again to you who possess qualities; salutations to you who are of the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti), and again to you who are the supreme spirit (puruṣa).

Salutations to the one whose nature consists of the qualities of the subsequent state, salutations to the soul of the universe; salutations to Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is peaceful and fond of devotion.
Salutations to Sadāśiva, to Rudra, the Lord of the worlds; may my firm devotion toward you increase today.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that most excellent among the foremost of Śiva’s devotees fell silent. Then all the gods, having prostrated, spoke to that Supreme Lord.
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion! Be gracious, O Lord of the worlds; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!"
Be gracious; you are the creator of all, and we bow to you with joy. May our devotion remain firm and eternal, never departing from us.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by Brahmā, Hari, and the immortals, Śaṅkara, the lord of gods and benefactor of the world, replied with a gracious soul.
Śaṅkara said: "O Vidhi, O Hari, and you gods, I am especially pleased. Speak your heart’s desire; choose all of you a boon with careful deliberation."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words spoken by Hara, O best of sages, all the gods replied with serene hearts.
All the gods said: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted by you, O Lord of the Gods of gods, then knowing us gods to be your servants, grant it to us."
O best of gods, whenever suffering should arise for the gods, you must always manifest yourself and destroy that suffering.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hari, and the immortals, the blessed Lord Ugra, with a gratified soul, replied simultaneously: "So be it, eternally."
O gods, I am pleased by these hymns; I shall certainly grant everything that is most desired in the world to those who recite or hear them at all times.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, who always removes the suffering of the gods, being pleased, bestowed everything that is indeed dear to all the deities.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Devastuti," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: In the meantime, seeing Śambhu pleased, the Dānava Maya—unburnt by virtue of the power of his compassion—approached him with great joy.
He bowed with affection to Hara and certainly to the other gods as well; with palms joined and shoulders bent in reverence, he bowed once more to Śiva.
Then, having risen and beheld Śiva, Maya—the best of the Dānavas—his soul filled with devotion, praised him with a voice faltering with love.
Maya said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, you are the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), free from all partiality.
O you whose form is light, salutations to you; O you whose form is the universe, salutations to you! Salutations to you, the pure self; repeated salutations to you, the purifier!
Salutation to You who possess manifold forms, who are eternal, and who transcend all form; salutation to You who possess divine form, who are divine, and whose appearance is most celestial.
Homage to the one whose nature is Śiva, the destroyer of all suffering for those who bow before him; repeated salutations to the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the three worlds.

Obeisance to you, who are accessible through devotion; to you, a mere atom of whose grace belongs to the devotees; to you, the bestower of the true fruit of austerity; O beloved of Śivā, O Lord of Śivā!
I do not know how to offer praise, O Supreme Lord who delights in praise; be gracious, O Lord of All, and protect me who has come to you for refuge.
Sanatkumāra said: O best of the twice-born, having heard this hymn of praise uttered by Maya, the Supreme Lord became pleased and spoke to Maya with respect.
Śiva said: "Choose a boon, O Maya, best of Dānavas; I am pleased. Whatever is desired by your mind, I shall grant it to you, without a doubt."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the auspicious words of Śambhu, Maya, the bull among the Dānavas, bowed to the Lord with bent shoulders and joined palms, and replied.
Maya said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, if you are pleased with me, and if I am indeed worthy of a boon, then grant me eternal devotion to yourself."
O Supreme Lord, may there always be friendship toward Your devotees, compassion for the distressed, and equanimity toward other living beings and the wicked.
O Maheśvara, may there never arise in me any demonic disposition; O Lord, may I always remain fearless, immersed in your auspicious worship.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus being entreated by Maya, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, compassionate toward his devotees, was pleased and replied, "O Lord."
Maheśvara said: "O bull among Dānavas, you are blessed; you are my devotee, free from all changeability. All the boons you have now desired have been granted to you."
Go to the world of Vitala, which is indeed more delightful than heaven itself, accompanied by your own retinue at my command.
Dwell there fearlessly, always joyful and devoted; by my command, no demonic disposition shall ever arise within you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having accepted this command of the high-souled Śaṅkara upon his head and having bowed to him as well as to the gods, he departed for Vitala.
In the meantime, those shaven-headed ones indeed assembled; having prostrated, they spoke to all those gods, beginning with Viṣṇu and Brahmā.
"O gods, where shall we go? What work shall we perform? Command us quickly; let us become those who carry out your instructions."
"O Hari, O Vidhi, O gods, we have committed an evil deed; the devotion to Śiva of the Daityas who were devotees of Śiva has been destroyed."
For those who oppose the devotees of Śiva, there shall be no dwelling in hell for even ten million kalpas, and certainly no liberation at all.
However, this evil deed was committed by us through your will; therefore, out of compassion, tell us how to pacify it, for we have come to you for refuge.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods spoke to those shaven-headed ones who stood before them with palms joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu and the others said: "O shaven-headed ones, you must never fear; by the command of Śiva, this entire and most excellent account has come to pass."
There shall be no miserable rebirth for you that brings suffering, because you dwell in auspiciousness and act for the benefit of the gods and sages.

Śambhu is the benefactor of the gods and sages, and he is dear to those who benefit the gods and sages; for those who act for the welfare of the gods, sages, and men, there is never any miserable rebirth.
From this day forward, for those men who have entered into this doctrine in the Kali age, we declare that a miserable destiny will befall them; this is the truth, there is no doubt in this matter.
By my command, you wise shaven-headed ones, must dwell in secret within the desert lands for as long as the Kali age shall endure.
When the Kali age has arrived, you shall establish your own doctrine; and in the Kali age, deluded and foolish people will embrace your teaching.
O lord of sages, having been thus commanded by the lords of the gods, those shaven-headed ones paid their respects and went to their respective hermitages as directed.
Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, the great yogi, having incinerated the inhabitants of Tripura and having accomplished his purpose, was worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods.
Accompanied by all his own attendants and by the goddess Śivā, the Lord, having accomplished this great task for the immortals, then vanished along with his sons.
Then, when the god Śiva had vanished along with his retinue, the wall, which was equipped with bows and arrows, also disappeared.
Then Brahmā, Hari, the gods, sages, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Nāgas, serpents, Apsarases, and likewise human beings were filled with joy.
They went joyfully to their respective abodes, praising the glory of Śaṅkara; having reached their own places, they attained supreme bliss.
Thus has been told to you in its entirety this great life-story of the moon-crested Lord, which indicates the destruction of Tripura and is endowed with supreme divine play.
It brings merit, fame, and long life; it increases wealth and grain; it bestows both heaven and liberation. What more do you wish to hear?
For whoever should always read or hear this supreme narrative, having enjoyed all desires in this world, shall attain liberation at the end.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gods' Departure for Their Own Abodes after the Praise Consisting of the Worship of the Gods Following the Slaying of Tripura," in the Sanatkumāra-Pārāśarya Dialogue of the fifth section, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, within the second book, the Rudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, O venerable son of Brahmā, I have previously heard that the Lord Śaṅkara slew the great Daitya Jalandhara.
O one of great wisdom, tell me the truth regarding the life of the Moon-crested Lord; who could ever be satiated by hearing His stainless glory recounted in detail?
Sūta said: Thus questioned by Vyāsa, the great sage, the son of Brahmā, who was skilled in speech, spoke these meaningful and composed words.
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, once Jīva and Śakra, with supreme devotion, went to Kailāsa in great haste to behold the Lord.
Then, having learned of the arrival of his preceptor and Indra, the Lord Śaṅkara, desiring to test the knowledge of those two who were intent on beholding him, [acted accordingly].
Then Sadgati, a Digambara, blocked that path; with his head adorned by matted locks, he stood there with a radiant countenance.
Then, as the Guru and Śakra were joyfully proceeding on their way, they beheld a terrifying man of wondrous form in the middle of the path.
He was possessed of great splendor, tranquil, with matted locks bound upon his head; he had mighty arms and a broad chest, was fair-complexioned, and his eyes were terrifying.
Then Purandara, intoxicated by his own authority and unaware that the man standing within his path was Śaṅkara, questioned him.
Purandara said: "Who are you, sir? From where have you come? Tell me truly your name. Is the Lord Śambhu established in his own abode, or has he gone elsewhere?"
Sanatkumāra said: Thus questioned by Śakra, the ascetic did not say anything at all; Śakra asked him again, but that naked mendicant spoke nothing.
Again Purandara, the lord of the rulers of the worlds, questioned him; yet the great yogi, the Lord who assumes forms by his divine play, remained silent.
Thus questioned again and again by Śakra, that venerable sky-clad ascetic said nothing at all, desiring to test Śakra’s knowledge.
Then the Lord of the Gods, proud of his sovereignty over the three worlds, became enraged; and having rebuked the matted-haired one, he spoke these words.
Indra said: "O you of wicked mind, although questioned by me, you have not given an answer; therefore, I shall strike you with my thunderbolt—who is there to protect you?"
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) then looked at him with wrath and raised his vajra to slay the naked one.
Seeing Purandara with the thunderbolt in his hand, the god Sadāśiva, Śaṅkara, brought about the immobilization of that falling thunderbolt.
Then Rudra, overcome with wrath, his eyes terrible and fearsome, suddenly blazed up as if burning everything with his splendor.
With his fury suppressed by the paralysis of his arms, the Lord of Śacī burned within like a serpent whose power has been restrained by a mantra.
Seeing that man blazing with his own splendor, Bṛhaspati quickly recognized him through his intellect and prostrated before the Lord Hara.
Then the noble-minded preceptor, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and began to praise the Lord.
The Guru said: Salutations to the God of gods, to Mahādeva, to the Self; to Maheśvara, the Sovereign, the Three-eyed One, and the one with matted hair.
Salutations to the Lord of the distressed, to Him who possesses all power, to the slayer of Andhaka, to the destroyer of Tripura, to Śarva, to Brahmā, and to the Supreme Being.
Salutations to you, Virūpākṣa, Rudra, the multiformed Śambhu; to you who are deformed, of exceeding beauty, and beyond all form.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of sacrifices yet the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices; salutations to you who take the form of the sacrifice and who set in motion the actions of others.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of time, to Time itself, and to the one who wears the serpent of time as an ornament; salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, who pervades everywhere.
Salutations to the slayer of Brahmā’s head, who is praised by Brahmā and Candra; let there be salutation to you, the friend of Brahman, and salutation to you, the Supreme Self.
You are fire, wind, and space; you alone are the waters and the earth. You are the sun and the moon; indeed, you are the entire circle of luminaries.
You alone are Viṣṇu, you are Brahmā; praised by them, you are the Supreme Lord. You are the sages beginning with Sanaka, you are Nārada, and you are the one whose wealth is austerity.
You alone are the Lord of all worlds; you alone are the very soul of the universe. You are the immanent essence of all, yet distinct from all; you alone are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).

Indeed, you create the worlds through the quality of passion (rajas) while assuming the name of Brahmā; through the quality of goodness (sattva), you take the form of Hari and pervade the entire universe.
You alone, O Mahādeva, assuming the form of Hara through the quality of darkness (tamas), sportively [withdraw] the entire universe composed of all five elements.
O Creator of the Universe, by the power of meditation upon you, the sun shines; nectar flows in the world, and the moon moves together with the stars.
O Śaṅkara, by the power of meditation upon you, the clouds pour down rain; by the power of meditation upon you, Śakra protects the three worlds like a son.
By the power of meditation upon you, all the gods and lords of sages perform their respective duties, remaining alert out of fear of you.
By serving your lotus feet alone, O Rudra, men on earth do not honor the gods and enjoy sovereignty over the worlds.
By serving your lotus feet alone, they have attained the supreme state, which is inaccessible even to those rich in yoga and difficult for all others to obtain.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, Bṛhaspati caused Purandara to fall at the feet of that Lord.
Having cast down Indra, the lord of the gods, with his neck bent low, Bṛhaspati, bowing with humility, spoke these words to Śiva.
Bṛhaspati said: O Great God, Lord of the distressed, I bow at your feet; lift me up and pacify your own anger born from your eyes.
Be pleased, O Mahādeva; protect me who has come to you for refuge! May this fire, born from the eye on your forehead, be extinguished.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his preceptor, Maheśvara, the God of gods and ocean of compassion, spoke with a voice deep as the rumbling of clouds.
Maheśvara said: "O Bṛhaspati, how indeed can a serpent put back its slough once it has been cast off? Likewise, I cannot restrain the wrath that has issued from my eye."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Śaṅkara, Bṛhaspati, his appearance distressed and his mind agitated by fear, spoke.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lord, O Blessed One, devotees are indeed always worthy of compassion. O Śaṅkara, make true your name 'the one who is affectionate toward his devotees'."
O Lord of Gods, you ought not to cast aside your own exceedingly fierce splendor elsewhere; O deliverer of all devotees, uplift Purandara.

Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by his preceptor, Rudra—the bearer of the name "Compassionate to Devotees," whose soul was serene, and who removes the suffering of those who bow before him—replied to the teacher of the gods.
Śiva said: "O dear one, pleased by this hymn of praise, I grant you an excellent boon: through the restoration of Indra's life, may you attain renown as 'Jīva' (the Living One)."
"This fire which has arisen from the eye on my forehead, the destroyer of the lord of the gods—I shall cast it far away so that it does not afflict Indra."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, he took him by the hand and cast that wondrous fire of his own splendor—which had arisen from the eye on his forehead—into the salt waters.
Then the Lord Rudra, the performer of great divine sports, vanished; and Guru and Śakra, liberated from fear, attained supreme happiness.
Having indeed obtained the sight of him for whose sake they had set out, the preceptor and Śakra, their purpose fulfilled, returned to their own abodes with joy.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Restoration of Śakra's Life," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, the fifth section of the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, omniscient son of Brahmā, salutations be unto you! Today I have heard this wondrous narrative concerning the high-souled Śambhu.
O Brahmin, when his own splendor, born from the eye on his forehead, was cast into the salt waters, what happened there, my dear? Tell me that quickly.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O dear one of great wisdom, to the most wonderful play of Śiva; by hearing it with faith, a devotee shall attain the goal of the yogins.
Then that splendor of Śiva, which had arisen from the eye on his forehead, was cast into the salt ocean and immediately attained the state of a child.
There, indeed, at the confluence of the Sindhu, the Gaṅgā, and the ocean, that boy, who was terrifying to all the worlds, wept loudly.
At the sound of his weeping, the earth trembled repeatedly; both heaven and Satyaloka were deafened by that cry.
By the mere crying of the child, all the worlds were terrified; the guardians of the quarters on every side had their minds thrown into utter agitation.
O best of Brahmins, what need is there for much speaking? O dear one, the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, trembled at the weeping of that powerful infant.
Then all those gods and sages, being greatly distressed, quickly went for refuge to Brahmā, the Grandfather and teacher of the world.
Having gone there, those gods and the sages, together with Vāsava, bowed down and, having praised him well, spoke to that Parameṣṭhin.
The gods said: "O Lord of the worlds, O Lord of the gods, danger has approached us; destroy it, O Great Yogi, for this extraordinary sound has arisen."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was struck with wonder, thinking, "What is this? and then desired to go there.
Then Brahmā, desiring to know that [matter], descended from Satyaloka with the gods; he then went to the ocean on the earth.
Just as Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, arrived there, he beheld that infant in the lap of the ocean.
Then Sāgara, beholding the arrival of the divine form according to the prescribed rite, bowed his head to the boy and placed him upon his lap.
Then Brahmā, filled with wonder, spoke these words to the ocean: "O mass of waters, tell me quickly, whose child is this marvelous infant?"
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the words of Brahmā, the Ocean was then delighted; bowing to and praising the Lord of Creatures, he replied with palms joined in reverence.
The Ocean said: "O Brahmin, O Lord of all the worlds, this boy was found by me, unaware, suddenly upon the confluence of the Sindhu and the Gaṅgā."
O Preceptor of the World, perform for him the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony; O Ordainer, you ought to declare all the fruits mentioned regarding his birth.
Sanatkumāra said: While the Ocean was speaking thus, that boy, the son of the Ocean, seized Brahmā by the throat, shaking him again and again.
And as that Creator, the maker of all worlds, was thus shaken and oppressed, O Kāleya, water issued from his two eyes.
With both hands placed upon the head of his son, who was born from the ocean and possessed of great splendor, Brahmā somehow managed to release his throat and spoke with reverence.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Ocean; for you, being truly intent on composure, I shall declare all the fruits of birth as stated for this son of yours.
"Since this water of mine was held back by him with his very eyes, let him therefore be known here by the name Jalandhara."
Right now he is a youth who has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, possessed of great prowess, steadfast, a warrior, and one who is indomitable in battle.
And you shall become profound like Guha in battle; a conqueror of all in combat, resplendent with every excellence.
The young boy shall become the sovereign of all the Daityas; he shall be the conqueror even of Viṣṇu, and there shall be no defeat for him from any quarter whatsoever.
"He shall be invulnerable to all beings except Rudra; he will now go back to that very place from which he originated."
His wife shall be devoted to her husband, increasing his good fortune; she will be beautiful in all her limbs, charming, sweet-spoken, and an ocean of virtuous character.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, he summoned Śukra and consecrated him in the kingdom; then, taking leave of the Lord of Rivers, Brahmā vanished.
Then, his eyes blossoming with joy at that sight, Sāgara took his son and went to his own home with delight.
With a joyful heart, he nurtured his young son through great means—the child who was beautiful in every limb, delightful, and possessed of most wonderful splendor.
Then the Ocean, having summoned the great asura Kālanemi, requested his daughter named Vṛndā for the sake of his own wife.
O Sage, the heroic Asura Kālanemi, the most eminent and wise among the asuras and skilled in his own duties, has rightly fulfilled the request of the Ocean.
According to the rites prescribed by Brahmā, she gave her own daughter, who was as dear to her as life itself, to the hero Jalandhara, who was born from the ocean.
Then, O Sage, there was a great festival at the wedding of those two; all the rivers and all the Asuras attained happiness.
Seeing his son together with his wife, Samudra attained great happiness; he bestowed gifts upon the twice-born and others according to the prescribed rites.
Those Daityas who were previously defeated by the gods and had taken refuge in Pātāla have now come to the earth's surface; having relied upon him, they dwell there free from fear.
Then those asuras, headed by Kālanemi, having given their daughter to that son of the Ocean, became exceedingly joyful; for, relying upon him, O Lord, they set out for victory.
And that heroic youth Jalandhara, the most valiant of asura heroes, having obtained an exceedingly beautiful wife and being self-controlled, ruled his kingdom through the power of Kavi.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth and Marriage of Jalandhara," in the section on the slaying of Jalandhara within the fifth book, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, of the second part, the Rudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Once, the noble-minded hero, the son of the ocean and husband of Vṛndā, was seated together with his wife and accompanied by all the asuras.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, Suvarcas, arrived there exceedingly pleased, appearing like a mass of splendor incarnate, illuminating all the quarters of the sky.
Seeing their preceptor approaching, all those asuras quickly bowed down with joyful hearts, and the son of the Ocean also paid him respectful homage.
Having bestowed his words of blessing upon them, Bhārgava, that treasury of splendors, sat down on a beautiful seat; they too remained as they were before.
Then the heroic Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, having beheld his own assembly hall with affection, became joyful, his excellent dominion unassailed.
Seeing Rāhu standing there with his head severed, that king of the Daityas, the son of the Ocean, quickly questioned Bhārgava as follows:
Jalandhara said: "O Lord, by whom was this severing of Rāhu’s head performed? O Guru, tell me that entire event exactly as it happened, according to the truth."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the son of the Ocean, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and replied in accordance with the truth.
Śukra said: O Jalandhara, great hero, helper of all the asuras, listen to the entire account; I shall relate it to you exactly as it happened.
In former times there was the heroic and mighty Bali, son of Virocana and great-grandson of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was the foremost among those who know the dharma.
Defeated by him, the gods went to Rama, the Lord of Lakshmi, for refuge; together with Indra, they recounted their situation, seeking to accomplish their own purpose.
Then, by his command, the gods, who were experts in the art of deception, made peace with the asuras for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose, O dear one.
Then, for the sake of the nectar of immortality, all those gods, together with the asuras, diligently undertook the churning of the ocean with Viṣṇu as their ally.
Then the enemies of the Daityas carried off the jewels; the gods seized them with effort, and even drank the nectar by means of a stratagem.
Then, through the assistance of Viṣṇu, those gods, possessing discuses and empowered by the drinking of the nectar, brought about the defeat of the asuras.
Hari severed the head of Rāhu as he was drinking the nectar; for Hari is always partial toward the assembly of the gods.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus the sage related to him the decapitation of Rāhu, as well as the churning of the ocean performed by the gods for the sake of the nectar.
The theft of the jewels, the defeat of the Daityas, and the drinking of the nectar by the gods—all this was related in detail.
Having heard that, the powerful Mahāvīra, the son of the Ocean, his eyes red with rage, then became incensed at the churning of his father.
Then, having summoned his excellent messenger named Ghasmara, he related in its entirety all the conduct that his self-possessed preceptor had described.
Then, having honored him repeatedly with affection and granted him assurance of safety, he dispatched his own skilled messenger into the presence of Śakra.
The wise messenger of that child of the ocean went to the stainless heaven, which was inhabited by all the gods.
Having gone there and quickly reached Sudharmā, that messenger, with his head unbowed out of pride, spoke these words to the Lord of the Gods.
Ghasmara said: "Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, is the lord of all the Daitya people; he is highly powerful, a great hero, and himself has Kavi as his companion."
"I am the messenger of that hero named Ghasmara, though I myself am not gluttonous; sent by that hero, I have come here into your presence."
O Jalandhara, listen to that which has been said by him whose command is unimpeded everywhere, who possesses exalted intellect, and who is the conqueror of all enemies of the Daityas.
Jalandhara said: "O lowest of gods! Why was my father, the ocean, churned by you with a mountain? And why were all the jewels of my father taken away?"
"What you have done today is not right; give those [items] back to me quickly! Come to me for refuge along with the gods, after having reflected thus."
"Otherwise, O lowest of gods, great fear will befall you, as well as the destruction of your kingdom; I tell you this truly."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the messenger, the lord of the gods was struck with amazement; remembering [the event], Indra, filled with both fear and wrath, spoke to him.
Since the mountains, who were formerly my enemies, were placed within his own belly out of fear of me, other sons of Diti who were my foes were likewise protected by him in the past.
Therefore, indeed, that entire collection of jewels was seized by me; my enemy shall not abide in happiness—this I tell you truly.
In former times, even the Daitya Śaṅkha, the son of the Ocean, was a hater of me; yet, with a deluded mind, he was eventually abandoned [by his evil ways] through association with the virtuous.
Indeed, that evil-minded one, a perpetrator of violence against the assembly of the virtuous, was slain by my younger brother Hari within the depths of the ocean—the most wicked of sinners.
Therefore, O messenger, go quickly and tell him in truth everything regarding the cause of the churning of the ocean, the son of the sea.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus dismissed by Indra, the highly intelligent messenger named Ghasmara quickly went to where the heroic Jalandhara was.
Indeed, that speech which had been spoken by Śakra was then related in its entirety by that wise messenger to the king of the Daityas.
Having heard that, the Daitya, his lips quivering with rage, swiftly made preparations with the desire to conquer all the gods.
Then, during the exertion of the lord of the asuras, the sons of Diti arrived from the cardinal directions and likewise from the netherworld by the tens of millions.
Then the great hero, the powerful son of the Ocean, went forth accompanied by ten million commanders of forces, headed by Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Surrounded by his entire army, he immediately reached heaven; he blew his conch born of the ocean, and the heroes everywhere raised a shout.
Having gone to the celestial realm, the Daitya took his place in the Nandana grove, surrounding his entire army and letting out a roar like that of a lion.
Seeing that great army of troops standing there surrounding the city, the gods, clad in armor, went forth from Amarāvatī for battle.
Then a battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas, fought with maces, iron clubs, arrows, bludgeons, axes, and spears.
They rushed at one another and struck each other; in an instant, both armies became drenched in a flood of blood.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and infantrymen fallen and being felled, the earth in battle shone as if with masses of clouds at twilight.
In that battle, Bhārgava restored to life those Daityas who had died by means of the *amṛtajīvinī* lore, using drops of water consecrated with mantras.
Likewise, Aṅgiras brought divine herbs from Mount Droṇa again and again and restored even the gods to life in that battle.
Seeing them thus risen once again in battle, Jalandhara, overcome by anger, spoke these words to Bhārgava:
Jalandhara said: "The gods have been slain by me in battle; how is it that they rise up again? For it has been heard that the Saṃjīvinī lore exists nowhere else."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the son of the Ocean, the preceptor Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu, with a serene soul, replied to Jalandhara.
Śukra said: "O dear one, having brought divine herbs from Mount Droṇa, this Aṅgiras is indeed reviving the gods; know my words to be true."
"O father, if you desire victory, listen to my auspicious words: then, quickly seize Droṇa with both your arms and cast him into the ocean."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by his preceptor Bhārgava, that lord of the Daityas went swiftly to where that king of mountains stood.
Then, having swiftly seized Droṇa with both arms, the Daitya quickly hurled him into the ocean; there was nothing strange in this regarding the power of Hari's splendor.
The great hero, the son of Sindhudvīpa, returned once more to the great battle; having mustered a vast army, he struck at the gods with various kinds of missiles.
Then, seeing the gods slain, the Preceptor went to Mount Droṇa; however, there the one honored by the gods did not find that lord of mountains.
Having learned that Droṇa had been seized by the Daityas, Dhiṣaṇa, overwhelmed with fear and agitated in mind, approached the gods and spoke.
The Guru said: "O all you gods, flee! There is no great mountain Droṇa; it has certainly been destroyed by the Daitya, the son of the Ocean."
This great Daitya Jalandhara cannot be conquered, for he is born from a portion of Rudra and is the crusher of all the immortals.
O gods, I have understood his power as it was manifested by himself, as I recalled in its entirety the conduct of Śakra when he insulted Śivā.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words proclaimed by the preceptor of the gods, the deities abandoned all hope for victory, being utterly overwhelmed by fear.
Being struck from all sides by that king of the Daityas, they abandoned their fortitude and fled in the ten directions, including Indra himself.
Seeing the gods routed, the Daitya, the son of the Ocean, entered Amarāvatī amidst the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and cries of victory.
When the Daitya had entered the city, the gods, led by Śakra and tormented by the Daitya, reached a cave in the Golden Mountain and dwelt there.

At that very moment, O Sage, having properly installed Śumbha and the other chief Daityas in all the offices formerly held by Indra and the others, he himself entered the golden cave and the other subterranean abodes.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Gods and Jalandhara," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, within the fifth section (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Seeing the Daitya approaching once more, all the gods, including Indra, trembled with fear and fled together in haste.
Having placed Prajāpati at their head, they all proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha; all the gods, together with Prajāpati, bowed down and offered hymns of praise.
The gods said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, O mighty-armed one, O Blessed One, O Madhusūdana! Salutations to you, O Lord of the lords of gods, O destroyer of all the Daityas!
Obeisance to you, Viṣṇu, who assumed the form of a fish and carried away the Vedas; obeisance to the one who sported in the ocean of dissolution with the virtuous king Satyavrata.
Salutations to You who, in the form of a tortoise, bore Mount Mandara for the gods as they exerted themselves intensely in the task of churning the ocean.

Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, the Protector; salutations to the one whose nature is the sacrifice and who exists as the Boar; salutations to him who bears upon his head the Earth, the support of all beings.
Salutations to you, Vāmana, Viṣṇu known as Upendra; O All-pervading Lord, you who deceived Bali, the lord of the Daityas, by means of the form of a brahmin.
Salutations to Paraśurāma, who rendered the world of Kṣatriyas devoid of Kṣatriyas; to you who acted for the benefit of your mother, yet were enraged and intent on harming the wicked.
Salutations to Rāma, the delight of the world, the personification of moral discipline, the swift destroyer of Rāvaṇa, and the husband of Sītā.
Salutations to You, O Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, whose wisdom is profound, who delights in the pastimes of Rādhā, and who performs manifold divine sports.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Māyā, who possess a hidden body, who cause the censure of the Vedas, and who appear in the forms of the Teacher of Yoga, the Jaina, and the Buddhist.
Salutations to you in the form of Kalki, the bringer of the end to the mlecchas, who possesses infinite power and establishes the true Dharma.
Salutations to you, O Lord, who have assumed the form of Kapila for the sake of Devahūti; salutations to the great soul who teaches Sāṃkhya-yoga and to the teacher of Sāṃkhya.
Salutations to the Supreme Swan, who converses with supreme knowledge; salutations to the Ordainer, whose nature is knowledge, by whom the Self becomes perfectly serene.
Salutations to Vedavyāsa, who divided the Vedas for the welfare of all the worlds and composed the Purāṇas.
Thus, salutations to you, O Lord Brahmā, who, through forms such as the Fish and others, are intent upon the work of your devotees and are the agent of creation, preservation, and destruction.

Salutations to You, the destroyer of the distress of Your servants, the bestower of happiness and auspiciousness; salutations to Hari, who is clad in yellow garments and whose vehicle is Tārkṣya; repeated salutations to the performer of all actions, the sole agent, and the refuge.
Othunderbolt that destroys the suffering and afflictions of the immortals tormented by the Daityas; salutations to You, who recline upon the couch of Śeṣa and whose eyes are the sun and the moon.
O Ocean of Mercy, O Lord of Ramā, protect us who have come to you for refuge; all the gods have been driven out of heaven by Jalandhara.
The sun was expelled from his place, as were the moon and the fire; the king of the nāgas was driven from Pātāla, and Dharmarāja was cast out.
Those gods do not shine at all as mortals wander about; we have come to you for refuge—let his slaughter be considered.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these piteous words of the gods, Madhusūdana, that ocean of compassion, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, cast away your fear; I shall go to the battlefield and display my prowess against the Daitya Jalandhara."
Having spoken thus, the enemy of the Daityas, whose mind was distressed, rose up suddenly; out of compassion for his devotees, he swiftly mounted Garuḍa.
Seeing her beloved departing together with the gods, Lakṣmī, born from the ocean, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence and eyes filled with tears.
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, if I am always your beloved and your devotee, then why, O ocean of compassion, is my brother to be slain by you in battle?"
Viṣṇu said: "I shall display my prowess against the Daitya Jalandhara; praised by them, I will go forth for battle with all haste."
Because he is born from a portion of Rudra, because of the word of Brahmā, and out of affection for you, this Jalandhara is not to be slain by me.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword, went with speed to fight with the gods headed by Śakra.
Making a lion’s roar, he quickly reached that very place where the Daitya Jalandhara was, while the gods blazed with the splendor of Viṣṇu.
Then, oppressed by the wind from the wings of Aruṇa’s younger brother as he flew with the speed of the wind, the Daityas whirled about in the sky like clouds tossed by a whirlwind.
Then Jalandhara, seeing the Daityas afflicted by the whirlwind, rose up and, out of anger, swiftly approached Viṣṇu with these words.
In the meantime, the gods, nourished by the splendor of Hari and endowed with great strength, fought with great joy.
Beholding the army of the gods arrived and prepared for battle, he commanded the exceedingly arrogant Daityas in the fray.
Jalandhara said: "O best of Daityas, wage today an insurmountable battle against Indra and the other gods, who are ever feeble despite their great strength."
The Mauryas numbered in the hundreds of thousands, the Dhaumras in the hundreds, and the Asuras and Kālakeyas likewise numbered in the crores.
By my command, let hundreds of thousands of Kālakas, Daurhṛdas, and Kaṅkas, as well as others endowed with their own forces, set forth.
All were ready and set forth, accompanied by a vast army; equipped with various weapons and missiles, they were fearless and free from doubt.
O Śumbha and Niśumbha, you two of great prowess, destroy in an instant these insignificant gods who are cowards in battle!
Sanatkumāra said: Thus commanded by Jalandhara, the Daityas, who were experts in warfare, fought against all the gods, who were accompanied by their fourfold armies.
With maces, sharp arrows, spears, pattisas, and tomara darts, and some with axes and spikes, they struck one another.
There, endowed with strength, they struck the enemies with various weapons; likewise, the great heroes among the gods, empowered by Hṛṣīkeśa, fought with sharp arrows, roaring like lions.
Some struck one another with sharp arrows, some with maces and lances, and others with axes and spears.
Thus a great battle took place between the gods and the demons, exceedingly fierce and causing terror even to the sages and the perfected ones (siddhas).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle of the Gods," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Daityas of great prowess struck all the gods, whose minds were agitated by fear, with spears, axes, and sharp-edged pikes.
Their bodies pierced by the weapons of the Daityas, all the gods, including Indra, fled from the battlefield with minds agitated by fear.
Then, seeing the gods intent on flight, Hṛṣīkeśa Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa, swiftly advanced to do battle.
With his lotus-like hand beautifully adorned by the Sudarśana discus, which radiated light in all directions, he shone as the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees.
Bearing a conch, a sword, a mace, and the Śārṅga bow, he was filled with wrath; a great hero possessing formidable weapons, he was skilled in all forms of warfare.
Having twanged his bow named Śārṅga, he let out a roar; by that great sound, O Sage, the three worlds were filled.
And with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow, the Lord Viṣṇu, filled with wrath, indeed severed the heads of the sons of Diti by the millions.
Then, oppressed by the wind from the wings of Aruṇa’s younger brother as he flew with the speed of the sun, and tossed about by the whirlwind, the Daityas wandered through the sky like clouds.
Then, seeing the Daityas tormented by the wind, Jalandhara—the great Daitya who strikes fear into the hosts of gods—became exceedingly enraged.
Seeing him crushing the Daityas, the hero, his lips quivering, rushed with speed toward Hari to fight.
He let out a great roar that struck fear into both gods and asuras; from hearing it, the ears of the Daityas were split asunder.
Then, filled by the terrifying and great roar of the Daitya Jalandhara, the entire world trembled.
Then a great battle took place between Viṣṇu and the lord of the Daityas, as they filled the sky with their arrows until it became devoid of any open space.
And by that battle between the two, O Sage, there arose among the gods, asuras, rishis, and siddhas a mutual and extreme astonishment at the terrifying spectacle.
Viṣṇu, with a flood of arrows, cut down the Daitya’s banner, parasol, bow, and shafts; then, striking him in the heart with a single arrow, he struck him down.
Then the Daitya, rising up with mace in hand and full of haste, struck Garuḍa on the head and felled him to the ground.
Filled with rage, his lower lip quivering, the Daitya struck Viṣṇu in the heart with a sharp trident of flashing luster.
Viṣṇu, as if laughing, cut the mace with his sword; then the slayer of Daityas, having strung his Śārṅga bow, pierced him with sharp arrows.
Overcome with rage, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, swiftly struck the Daitya Jalandhara with a terrifyingly sharp arrow.
Seeing that arrow approaching him, the exceedingly powerful Daitya cut it with his own arrow and swiftly struck Viṣṇu in the heart.
The heroic Keśava, too, having cut that great-armed arrow discharged by the asura into pieces the size of sesame seeds, let out a roar.
Then Bāṇa, trembling with rage, fixed an arrow upon his bow; but the one of great strength cut that shaft down with another arrow.
Vāsudeva, moreover, for the destruction of Bāṇa, the enemy of the gods, fixed [his arrow] upon his bow with fury and roared like a lion.
Then the powerful Jalandhara, lord of the Daityas, his lower lip bitten in rage, cut asunder with a white arrow the Vaiṣṇava bow named Śārṅga.
Furthermore, that one of fierce valor and great heroism, who causes fear even to the gods, struck Madhusūdana with exceedingly sharp arrows.
With his bow severed, the blessed Keśava, the protector of the world, hurled his supreme mace at Jalandhara for his destruction.
That mace, hurled by Hari, resembling a blazing fire and possessing an infallible course, swiftly struck his body.
Struck by her, the great Daitya Jalandhara, though intoxicated with pride, did not waver even slightly, like one struck by a garland of flowers.
Then Jalandhara, enraged and intoxicated by the pride of battle, hurled a trident shaped like fire at Hari, striking terror into the gods.
Then Viṣṇu, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, swiftly and forcefully severed that trident with his sword named Nandaka.
When his trident was severed, O Lord of Daityas, he suddenly leaped up and, approaching quickly, struck Viṣṇu firmly in the heart with a clenched fist.
That great hero Viṣṇu, disregarding that pain, struck Jalandhara firmly in the heart with his clenched fist.
Then those two of great strength fought with a wrestling match, making the earth resound with their arms, fists, and knees.
O best of sages, having fought for such a long time with that asura, he was indeed struck with wonder and felt exhaustion in his heart.
Then the blessed Lord, the master of illusion and the best among those who know illusion, being pleased, spoke to the king of the Daityas in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.

Viṣ�难以忍受地狂傲，你真是幸运，身为大主宰，面对这些最精良的巨神兵，你竟然丝毫不感到畏惧。 Viṣṇu said: "O best among the foremost Daityas, you are blessed; for you, a great lord intoxicated by battle, are truly not afraid of these excellent and mighty weapons."
Indeed, by these very fierce weapons, many Daityas have been slain; in the great battle, those intoxicated heroes, their bodies mangled, met their death.
"O great Daitya, I am pleased with you because of your battle; you are a great being. No hero equal to you has been seen in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile."
Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas; I am pleased with your valor. I shall grant you even that which is not to be given, whatever dwells in your mind.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the illusory Hara, the highly intelligent Jalandhara, king of the Daityas, replied.
Jalandhara said: "O Bhāvuka, if you are pleased, then grant me this boon: dwell with my sister, together with me and your retinue, in my own home."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of that great Daitya, the Lord Hari, the Master of the Gods, with a dejected mind, replied, "So be it."
Then Viṣṇu, together with all the hosts of gods and accompanied by Ramā, arrived at the city named Jalandhara and dwelt there.
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, having reached his own abode with his sister and Viṣṇu, dwelt there with a mind overwhelmed by joy.
Then Jalandhara, having installed the Dānavas in the offices of the gods, returned to the surface of the earth with great joy.
Having brought under his own control whatever collection of jewels existed among the gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, the son of the Ocean remained there.
Having stationed the exceedingly powerful Daitya Niśumbha in the subterranean realm of Pātāla, that mighty one brought Śeṣa and the others to the surface of the earth.
Having made the hosts of gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, as well as the serpents, rākṣasas, and humans, his own citizens, he ruled over the three worlds.
Having thus brought the gods under his own control, Jalandhara protected his subjects with righteousness, as if they were his own biological sons.
While he ruled the kingdom according to Dharma, no one was seen who was diseased, nor suffering, nor emaciated, nor dejected.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Viṣṇu and Jalandhara," in the Jalandhara Episode of the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O lord of sages, while that great asura was thus ruling the earth with righteousness, the gods became miserable because of their fraternal relationship with him.
All those gods, being distressed, went for refuge to Śiva—the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of all, the Supreme Master—in their minds.
They praised the Blessed Maheśvara with pleasing words, the giver of all things and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees, for the sake of ending their own suffering.
Having summoned him, Mahādeva, the granter of all desires to his devotees, dispatched Nārada with the intent of accomplishing the work of the gods.
Then the divine sage Nārada, a man of wisdom, a devotee of Śambhu, and the refuge of the virtuous, went to the city of the Daityas by the command of Śiva to inform the gods.
All those gods, led by Vāsava, became greatly agitated; seeing the sage Nārada approaching swiftly, they all rose up from their seats.
Having bowed with affection, the gods, led by Śakra, their faces filled with longing, offered a seat to the sage Nārada.
Having bowed deeply to that best of sages as he sat comfortably upon his seat, the deities, led by Vāsava, spoke again in distress to the lord of sages.
The gods said: "O best among the foremost sages, O compassionate one, hear our suffering! Having heard it, destroy it quickly; you are the Lord, the beloved of Śaṅkara."
The gods have been utterly routed by the Daitya Jalandhara; we are distressed and agitated, deprived of our own abodes and of our lord.
The sun was drawn from its own place, as was the moon; likewise were the fire-god, Dharmarāja, and the other world-protectors.
Indeed, by that exceedingly powerful one, all the gods have been oppressed; we have fallen into great misery and have come to you for refuge.
In battle, that powerful Jalandhara, the great Daitya who crushed all the immortals, brought Hṛṣīkeśa under his own control.
Under his control and dependent upon him, Hari dwelt in his abode; Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by Lakṣmī and is the accomplisher of all our goals.
O high-minded one, exert yourself for the destruction of Jalandhara; you have arrived among us by the power of destiny as the eternal accomplisher of all our goals.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of those immortals, that tiger among sages, Nārada, being compassionate, consoled them and spoke.
Nārada said: "O gods, I truly know that you have been defeated by the king of the Daityas; you have indeed fallen into misery, being afflicted and driven from your positions."
"I shall accomplish your own purpose through my own power; there is no doubt in this. For you have encountered suffering, O immortals, because I have become as favorable to you."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, O best of sages, and having consoled all the gods, he went to the assembly hall of Jalandhara to see the beloved of the Dānavas.
Then, seeing the best of sages arrive, the god Jalandhara rose with supreme devotion and offered him an excellent, superior seat.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites, the lord of the Dānavas, filled with great wonder, laughed heartily and then spoke these words to the best of sages.
Jalandhara said: "O Brahmin, from where have you come, and what have you seen anywhere? O Sage, command me as to the purpose for which you have arrived here."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, the great sage Nārada, with a serene soul, replied indeed to Jalandhara.
Nārada said: O Jalandhara, lord of all Dānavas and Daityas, O high-minded one! You are blessed, O lord of all the worlds; for you alone are the enjoyer of jewels.
O best of the lords of Daityas, hear indeed the reason for my arrival; I shall tell you everything regarding the purpose for which I have come here.
O Lord of Daityas, I went by chance to the peak of Kailāsa, where there is a great forest of wish-fulfilling trees extending for ten thousand yojanas.
It was filled with hundreds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus), brilliantly illuminated by wish-granting gems (cintāmaṇis), entirely made of gold, divine, and adorned with wonders everywhere.
There I beheld Śaṅkara seated with Umā—fair-complexioned, beautiful in every limb, three-eyed, and crowned by the moon.
Seeing that great marvel, a reflection then arose in me: "Could such growth exist anywhere else in the three worlds, or not?"
O Lord of Daityas, I have likewise recollected your prosperity; desiring to behold it, I have come here into your presence.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this from Nārada, that lord of the Daityas, Jalandhara, respectfully showed him his entire prosperity.
Having seen him, the wise Nārada, the excellent accomplisher of the gods' work, spoke to that lord of the Daityas, Jalandhara, at the instigation of his master.
Nārada said: "O excellent hero, you now possess complete and abundant prosperity; for you are indeed the lord of the three worlds—what wonder could possibly arise from this?"
Jewels, heaps of gems, elephants, and other such riches—whatever treasures there are, they all shine here today within this house.
The jewel among elephants, Airāvata, was brought by you from Śakra; likewise, O great hero, the jewel among horses, Ucchaiḥśravas, was brought from the Sun.
The wish-fulfilling tree has been brought by you, as well as the treasures of the Giver of Wealth; indeed, the swan-drawn celestial chariot of Brahmā has also been brought by you.
Thus, O Lord of Daityas, whatever excellent jewels shine in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, all of them are present in your house.
Beholding this manifold prosperity of yours, complete and beautifully adorned with elephants, horses, and other riches, I am well-pleased, O great hero.
O Jalandhara, that most excellent jewel of a wife is not in your house; therefore, you ought especially to bring back that jewel among women.
O Jalandhara, indeed, all the excellent jewels that may be in one's house certainly do not shine at all if the jewel of a wife is absent; they are surely in vain.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, the king of the Daityas, his mind agitated by passion, spoke.
Jalandhara said: "O Nārada, divine sage, salutations to you, O great lord! Where is that most excellent jewel of a wife? Tell me that now."
O Brahman, if that jewel exists anywhere within the cosmic egg, I shall bring it from there; this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt.
Nārada said: On the exceedingly beautiful Mount Kailāsa, which is densely crowded with prosperity, Śambhu dwells there, naked and assuming the form of a yogin.
His wife was indeed most beautiful, endowed with all auspicious marks; she was named Pārvatī, lovely and charming in every limb.
Such a form, never seen anywhere else and full of wonder, was beheld; it is most marvelous, enchanting even to great yogis, beautiful to behold, and a source of supreme supernatural power.
"O hero Jalandhara, today I imagine in my own mind that there is no one more prosperous than Śiva, nor anyone in the three worlds who possesses such a jewel of a wife."
Who can be compared to her, by whom the four-faced Brahmā was formerly submerged in the ocean of her beauty and abandoned his own self-composure?
For by her playful charm, even the enemy of Madana (Śiva), though free from passion and independent, was brought under his own control.
O Lord of Daityas, although you are the sovereign of all jewels, such prosperity as that which belonged to the enjoyer of the jewel among women did not belong to you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that divine sage Nārada, world-renowned and intent on performing a service for the gods, departed through the sky.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Celestial Sage and Jalandhara," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the fifth section (Yuddha-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, when Nārada had indeed departed for heaven, what did that king of the Daityas do? Tell me that in great detail.
Sanatkumāra said: When Nārada had departed for heaven after taking leave of that Daitya, the king of the Daityas became afflicted by the fever of love upon hearing of his form.
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, subject to Time and deprived of his intellect, being utterly deluded, summoned his messenger Rahu and sent him forth.
Beholding him arrived with a mind overcome by passion, Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, having fully awakened him, spoke thus.
Jalandhara said: "O best of excellent messengers, accomplisher of all tasks, O highly wise son of Siṃhikā, go to Mount Kailāsa!"
There dwells a yogi named Śambhu, an ascetic wearing matted locks, whose entire body is adorned with ashes, who is dispassionate and has conquered his senses.
"Having gone there, O messenger, you must speak with a fearless heart to that yogi Śaṅkara, who wears matted locks and is free from passion."
O ocean of compassion, what would become of you, a yogi, with that jewel of a wife—a forest-dweller frequented by spirits, ghosts, and piśācas?
O Yogin, such a course is fitting for you in this world where I am the lord of men; therefore, give to me, whose arm is adorned with jewels, your own jewel of a wife.
Whatever excellent jewels exist in the three worlds, they are all mine; know that the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, is under my control.
Indra’s jewel among elephants, the supreme jewel Uccaiḥśravas, and likewise the Pārijāta tree were seized by force and suddenly taken away.
A celestial chariot yoked with swans stands in my courtyard; it is composed of jewels, supremely divine, most excellent, and a marvel wrought by the Creator.
The divine treasure-jewel beginning with Mahāpadma belongs to me; and in my house stands the Varuṇa umbrella that drips gold.
The great garland Kiñjalkinī, with its ever-fresh lotuses, belongs to my father and to me alone; likewise, the noose belongs to the Lord of the Quivers (Kamapati).
I forcibly took from him that excellent power which grants the departure of death; in return, Śuci gave me two divine garments of pure white.
"O Lord of Yogins, thus all my jewels shine; therefore, O wearer of matted locks, you too must give me your jewel of a wife."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words, he was ushered in by Nandin; with eyes wide with wonder and amazement, Rāhu entered the formidable assembly hall.
Having gone there, [he beheld] Śiva himself, the God of gods, the Great Lord, whose darkness was dispelled by his own splendor and who shone with the smearing of ashes.
Hara, who was shining amidst the royal paraphernalia, most wonderful, beautiful in every limb, and adorned with divine ornaments.
And that messenger named Rāhu, his body overcome by the splendor of Śambhu, bowed to him out of pride and approached his presence.
Then, seated at the head of that [assembly], the son of Siṃhikā, desiring to speak and urged by the signal, addressed these words to Tryambaka.
