"I am the messenger sent by him, the eternal sovereign of the three worlds who is served by the Daityas and Pannagas; I have come here into your presence."
Rāhu said: Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, became the lord of all the Daitya hosts; he became the sovereign of the three worlds and the leader over all.
That powerful king of the Daityas, who is like the Destroyer to the gods, has addressed you, a yogin; listen to what he said.
O bull-bannered one, hear the command of that lord, the master of all jewels, the sovereign of the Daityas, who possesses great divine power.
How could the auspicious daughter of Himavat be the wife of one who dwells eternally in cremation grounds, who wears a garland of bones, and who is clothed only by the directions?
I am the supreme lord of jewels, and she is designated as the jewel among women; therefore, she is suitable for me alone, and certainly not for you who subsist on alms.
The three worlds are under my control; I enjoy the sacrificial portions, and whatever jewels exist in these three worlds are in my own abode.
"We are enjoyers of jewels, while you are indeed a naked ascetic; give me your jewel of a wife, for subjects bring happiness to their king."
Sanatkumāra said: While Rāhu was speaking thus, from the space between the eyebrows of the wielder of the trident (Śiva), there emerged a fierce being with a voice like a violent thunderbolt.
With a lion’s face and a flickering tongue, his great eyes ablaze with fire, with hair standing erect and a withered body, he was like another Narasimha.
That man, possessing a massive body and mighty arms, with shanks as long as palm trees and terrifying in appearance, rushed swiftly and impetuously toward Rāhu.
Seeing him approaching to devour him, Rāhu, overcome with fear, fled with great speed and seized him from the outside.
Rāhu said: O God of gods, O Great Lord, protect me who have come to you for refuge; you are the Lord, possessed of supreme sovereignty, always to be worshipped by both gods and asuras.
"O Mahādeva, this man, your servant who is most terrifying, has come here to devour me, a Brāhmaṇa, O Īśāna."
Protect me from this, O Lord of Gods, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge; act so that he may not devour me, salutations to you again and again!
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having heard those words of the brahmin, the Lord Mahādeva, who is dear to the distressed and the helpless, spoke to his own attendant.

Mahādeva said: "O best of the Gaṇas, a messenger who is a lord and a Brāhmaṇa, especially one named Rāhu who has come for refuge, must indeed be protected by those worthy of providing refuge; he is not to be punished."
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, whose soul is compassion, he who had heard the syllables "Brāhmaṇa" suddenly released Rāhu along with his attendants.
Then, having released Rāhu in the sky, that man approached the presence of Śiva with a piteous voice and made this petition to Mahādeva:
The man said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, mine of compassion, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, my food has been taken away by you.
"O Lord, hunger afflicts me, and I am utterly emaciated by hunger. What food should I eat, O Lord of Gods? Command me, O Master."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of that man, the great lord, whose splendor was wonderful, being curious and seeking his own welfare, replied.
Maheśvara said: "If your hunger is extreme, if this famishing distress afflicts you, then quickly devour the flesh of your own hands and feet."
Sanatkumāra said: Thus commanded by Śiva, the man ate his own flesh produced from his hands and feet until he was left with only his head remaining.
Seeing him reduced to nothing but his head, Sadāśiva, being well-pleased, spoke with wonder to that man of terrible deeds:
Śiva said: O great Gaṇa, you are blessed, for you are the observer of my command; O best of beings, I am exceedingly pleased with this deed of yours.
Indeed, you shall always be known by the name Kīrtimukha, acting through my agency; you are a great host, a great hero, and the terrifier of all the wicked.
"You are dear to me; therefore, you must always be worshipped by my devotees in my image. Those who do not perform your worship are certainly not doing what is pleasing to me."
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus obtained the boon from Śambhu, that man rejoiced; from that time forward, O Lord of Gods, he has remained at the gate as Kīrtimukha.
That assembly is especially worthy of worship during the adoration of Śiva; for those who do not first honor it here, their own worship shall be in vain.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Messengers," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, you have narrated to me this wonderful story concerning the purifying divine play of the great lord Śaṅkara.
Now, O great sage, out of compassion for me, please tell me with great affection: where has Rāhu gone after being released by the Puruṣa?
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, whose intellect is immeasurable, the great sage, the son of Brahmā, replied with a serene soul.
Sanatkumāra said: He who was liberated by Rāhu remained in that Varvara region; therefore, he became known on earth by the fame of being "Varvara" (the Varvara).
Then, considering himself to have been born again from that source, he became free from pride and slowly departed for the city of Jalandhara.
O Vyāsa, having approached Jalandhara, he related all those deeds of the Lord to the lord of the Daityas.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard that, Jalandhara—the son of the Ocean and the most excellent of the lords of Daityas—became powerful, his body agitated with rage.
Then, his mind overcome by anger, that best of Daityas issued orders for the mobilization of all the Daitya armies.
Jalandhara said: "Let all the Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, as well as the heroes beginning with Śumbha and Niśumbha, indeed march forth accompanied by their own forces."
The Koṭis, those born of the Vīra clan, the Kaṃbuvaṃśyas, the Daurhṛdas, the Kālakas, the Kālakeyas, the Mauryas, and likewise the Dhaumras.
Having thus commanded, the powerful son of the Ocean, the lord of the Asuras, quickly set forth, surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas.
Then, in front of him, Śukra’s head was severed by Rāhu; his crown, having slipped, then fell to the ground with great force.
The sky, filled [with them], shone like the heavens with clouds during the rainy season; many ill omens arose, portending a great sleep of death.
Having thus witnessed his exertion, those gods, together with Indra, went unobserved to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.
Having gone there and beheld Śiva, all the gods, together with Indra, bowed deeply; with shoulders bent and palms joined, they offered praise.
The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion! Salutations to you, O Maheśāna; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
O Lord, we, along with Indra and the other gods, are utterly distressed by the most terrible affliction caused by Jalandhara; having been dislodged from our positions, we now dwell upon the earth.
O Lord, O Master, you do not know how this transgression occurred; therefore, for our protection, slay the son of the Ocean.
O Lord, that Garuḍa-bannered one whom you previously appointed for our protection is no longer capable of protecting us today.
Dependent upon him, he stays today in his house along with me; and we gods remain there, subject to his command.
O Śambhu, we have come here into your presence unobserved; that powerful son of the Ocean is coming to engage you in battle.
Therefore, O Lord, O Omniscient One, you ought to slay that Jalandhara in battle without delay; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, all those gods, together with Indra, bowed to the Lord and stood humbly before Maheśa, gazing at his feet.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the god, the bull-bannered Lord laughed and, quickly summoning Viṣṇu, spoke these words.
Īśvara said: O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Mahāviṣṇu, the gods have assembled here; tormented by Jalandhara and utterly overwhelmed, they have come to me for refuge.
O Viṣṇu, why was Jalandhara not slain by you in battle? Furthermore, you abandoned your own Vaikuṇṭha and went to his house.
For you have been appointed by me for the protection of the virtuous and for the restraint of the wicked, as one who moves with complete independence.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Maheśa, Hari, whose banner is Garuḍa, being humble in spirit, bowed with palms joined in reverence and replied.
Viṣṇu said: "Because you were born from a portion of me, and because you are likewise the brother of Śrī, I did not slay him in battle; now, you must kill this Dānava."
O Lord of the Gods, I tell you this truth: he is of great strength and great heroism, the conqueror of all the inhabitants of heaven and of others as well.
A battle was waged by me for a long time against that one who was accompanied by the gods; yet my stratagem did not take effect against that bull among the Dānavas.
"Being pleased by that valor, I indeed said, 'Choose a boon. Having heard these words of mine, he chose an excellent boon."
"O Mahāviṣṇu, let my sister live with me in my house along with her father-in-law; she is dependent on me. Having said this, I went to that house.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, that Maheśvara Śaṅkara, compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees, laughed and spoke with great joy.
Maheśvara said: O Viṣṇu, best of gods, listen to my words with respect; I shall slay the great Daitya Jalandhara, of this there is no doubt.
Go to your own abode without fear; let the gods also surely depart, free from apprehension and devoid of doubt, considering the lord of the asuras to be slain.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Maheśa, the Lord of Ramā, together with the gods, departed quickly for his own abode, his doubts dispelled.
In the meantime, O Vyāsa, that powerful lord of the Daityas, possessed of great prowess, went to the mountain slope together with his armored asuras.
Then, having besieged Kailāsa with a vast army, he, resembling Time itself, stood there uttering a great lion’s roar.
Then, hearing the tumultuous clamor arising from the roar of the Daityas, the Great Lord of Lords, the performer of great divine sports and the destroyer of the wicked, became enraged.
The great lord Hara, the source of great light, the curious Mahādeva, having enumerated his own mighty hosts beginning with Nandin, gave them instructions.
At the command of Śiva, all the Gaṇas, headed by Nandī, Bhaṭamukha, and Senānī, equipped themselves for battle with great haste.
All the hosts descended from Kailāsa, intoxicated with rage; indeed, those great heroes leaped forth for battle, uttering war-cries.
Then, indeed, a terrible battle took place in the valleys of Kailāsa between the lords of the Pramathas and the Daityas, thick with weapons and missiles.
Resounding with the blasts of kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, and conchs that gladden heroes, and with the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots, the earth trembled.
Filled with showers of spears, javelins, arrows, clubs, nooses, and sharp-edged spears, the sky shone as if covered by scattered pearls.
The earth shone with slain elephants, horses, and foot soldiers, just as it had once been covered by the great mountains struck down by the thunderbolt.

At that time, the earth became impassable, thick with the mire of fat, blood, and flesh from the multitudes of Daityas struck down by the Pramathas, as well as from the Gaṇas struck down by the Daityas.
In battle, Bhārgava repeatedly restored by force the hosts of Daityas slain by the Pramathas through the power of the Mṛtasañjīvanī [life-restoring] mantra.
Seeing them all thus agitated and afflicted by fear, the entire host reported Śukra’s conduct to the God of gods.
Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Rudra gave vent to a fierce rage; he became terrifying and exceedingly fierce, blazing forth in all directions.
Then, from the mouth of Rudra, there emerged an exceedingly terrifying Kṛtyā, with shanks as tall as palm trees, a sunken belly, a gaping maw, and breasts that crushed the trees.
O best of sages, she swiftly reached the field of battle and roamed about, most terrifying, devouring the great asuras.
Then, free from fear, she quickly went into the midst of the battle to where that descendant of Bhṛgu resided, surrounded by the foremost lords of the Daityas.
O sage, having pervaded the sky with her own splendor and having made the earth her own portion, she took Bhārgava into her womb and vanished into the heavens.
Seeing the descendant of Bhṛgu fleeing, the hosts of Daitya troops, though intoxicated by battle, departed from the fight with their faces withered.
Then the army of the Daityas, afflicted by the fear of the Gaṇas, broke apart like a heap of straw scattered and struck down by the force of the wind.
Seeing the Daitya army broken out of fear of the Gaṇas, Niśumbha, Śumbha—the two generals—and Kālanemi became exceedingly enraged.
Those three of great strength chose the army of the Gaṇas, discharging showers of arrows like clouds during the rainy season.
Then those volleys of the Daityas' arrows, like swarms of locusts, obstructed the sky and all the directions, causing the army of the Gaṇas to tremble.
The hosts, pierced by hundreds of arrows and raining down streams of blood, resembled *kiṃśuka* trees in springtime and could not discern anything at all.
Then, seeing their own army broken, Nandi, Lambodara, Kārttikeya, and the others—those indignant ones—hurriedly and forcefully repelled the foremost of the Daityas.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the General Battle between the Gaṇas and the Asuras," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the fifth section (Yuddha-khaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudra-saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having seen those lords of the Gaṇas—Nandin, Gajavaktra, and Ṣaṇmukha—the Dānavas rushed forward in indignation for a duel.
Kālanemi rushed at Nandin, Śumbha at Lambodara, and Niśumbha, filled with apprehension, charged at the six-faced god.
Niśumbha forcefully pierced Kārttikeya’s peacock in the heart with five arrows; it fell down, rendered unconscious.
Then Śaktidhara, enraged, pierced his chariot, the horses, and the charioteer with five arrows.
With another sharp arrow, the hero, intoxicated by the battle, swiftly struck Niśumbha, the enemy of the gods, and let out a roar.
The great hero Asura, named Niśumbha, who possessed exceeding prowess, struck the roaring Kārtikeya with his arrow in battle.
Then, just as Kārttikeya was about to seize the spear in his wrath, Niśumbha with great speed struck him down with his own spear.
Thus, O Vyāsa, there occurred right then a great battle between Kārttikeya and Niśumbha, as they both roared with the shouts of heroes.
Then Nandīśvara pierced Kālanemi with arrows; with seven more, he cut down his horses, his banner, his chariot, and his charioteer.
And Kālanemi, becoming enraged, cut off Nandin’s bow with extremely sharp, feathered arrows discharged from his own bow.
Then the heroic Nandīśvara, having cast aside that great asura Kālanemi, struck him firmly in the chest with his trident.
With his heart pierced by the spear, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he uprooted a mountain peak and struck Nandin with it.
Then Śumbha and Gaṇeśa, mounted respectively upon a chariot and a mouse, pierced each other with volleys of arrows as they fought.
Then Gaṇeśa pierced Śumbha in the heart with a feathered shaft and, with three arrows, felled the charioteer to the ground.
Then Śumbha, becoming exceedingly enraged, pierced the lord of the Gaṇas with a shower of arrows and the mouse with three; he then roared with a voice like a thundercloud.
The mouse, its body pierced by arrows and suffering intense pain, began to tremble; and Lambodara fell down and became a mere foot-soldier.
Then Lambodara, having struck Śumbha in the heart with his axe, felled him to the ground; he then mounted his mouse.
The powerful Gajamukha again prepared for battle; laughing, the two [deities] struck the great elephant in anger with goads as if with a whip.
Both Kālanemi and Niśumbha swiftly pierced Lambodara with arrows resembling venomous serpents, striking him simultaneously out of rage.
Seeing him being thus tormented, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra rushed forward with speed, accompanied by ten million bhūtas.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, Vetālas, hosts of Yoginīs, Piśācas, throngs of Ḍākinīs, and the Gaṇas also went forth together.
Then, with shouts of "kila-kilā," lion-roars, and gurgling sounds from hand-drums (ḍamarukas), the earth resounded and trembled.
Then the spirits, rushing forward, devoured the Dānavas; leaping up, they cast them down and danced upon the field of battle.
In the meantime, Nandin and Guha, who had become Vyāsa, regained their senses and stood up, roaring loudly in the battle.

Nandī and Kārttikeya arrived with great haste and struck the Daityas in battle with continuous volleys of arrows. With the Daityas cut, pierced, slain, fallen, and likewise devoured, that army then became agitated and dejected of countenance.
Thus Nandi, Kartikeya, the powerful Vikata, Virabhadra, and the other hosts roared loudly in the battle.
Niśumbha and Śumbha, the two generals of the son of the Ocean, as well as the great Daitya Kālanemi and other Asuras, were thus defeated.
Then, seeing his army utterly shattered, the powerful son of the Ocean advanced against the hosts in a chariot adorned with many banners.
Then, O Vyāsa, even though they had been defeated, the Daityas became exceedingly jubilant; intent on battle, they roared loudly at that time.
O Sage, all the hosts of Rudras, including Nandin, Kārtika, Daṃtyāsya, Vīrabhadra, and others, roared triumphantly.
There arose the clamor of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the sound of conchs and kettledrums, and likewise the lion-roars of both armies.
The space between heaven and earth became completely covered by the multitudes of Jalandhara’s arrows, as if by masses of mist.
Having pierced Śailādi with five arrows and Gaṇeśa with five shafts, he struck Vīrabhadra with twenty and roared with the sound of a thundercloud.
Then the great hero Kārttikeya, the son of Rudra, swiftly pierced the Daitya Jalandhara with his spear and let out a roar.
With his eyes wide open, that Daitya, his body pierced by the spear, fell to the ground; yet, being of great strength, he quickly rose up again.
Then Jalandhara, the preeminent among the Daityas, his soul overcome with rage, struck Kartikeya in the heart with a mace.
O Vyāsa, demonstrating the effective power of the mace, the son of Śaṅkara quickly fell to the earth due to the boon granted by Brahmā.
In that very manner, Nandī fell to the ground, struck by the mace; even the great hero, the slayer of enemies, was somewhat agitated in mind.
Then the exceedingly powerful Gaṇeśvara, having remembered the lotus feet of Śiva, became enraged; having reached the Daitya, he cut his mace with his axe.
Vīrabhadra pierced the Dānava in the heart with three arrows, and with seven more, he cut down his horses, banner, bow, and parasol.
Then the lord of the Daityas, exceedingly enraged, raised a terrible spear and struck down Gaṇeśa; he then mounted another chariot.
Then that mighty lord of the Daityas, filled with rage, disregarded Vīrabhadra in his heart and rushed forward with great speed.
He quickly struck Vīrabhadra with a sharp venomous serpent, and the great hero Jalandhara, king of the Daityas, let out a roar.
Vīrabhadra, also enraged, cut that arrow with a sharp-edged shaft and pierced him in turn with a great arrow.
Then those two, the best among the foremost of heroes, resembling the sun, fought with one another for a long time using various weapons and missiles.
Then Vīrabhadra, with his arrows, struck down his horses; he also swiftly severed the bow and the banner of the chariot-warrior.
Then that king of the Daityas, armed with an iron club, leapt up; possessed of great strength, he quickly reached the vicinity of Vīrabhadra.
With a massive iron club, he struck Vīrabhadra; the heroic son of the Ocean, accompanied by his army, roared at the head of the host.
With his massive iron club, the leader of the host, Vīrabhadra, had his head split open; he fell to the earth and shed profuse blood.
Seeing Vīrabhadra fallen, the hosts of Rudra fled from the battlefield in fear, crying out to Maheśvara.
Then, hearing the clamor of the hosts, Candraśekhara questioned the heroic leaders of the Gaṇas standing by his side.
Śaṅkara said: "O great heroes, consider why such a great clamor has arisen among my attendants; I must certainly restore peace."
Just as that Lord of the Gods was respectfully questioning his attendants, those foremost of the Gaṇas arrived before their Master.
Seeing them distressed, the Lord Rudra asked after their welfare; and those attendants related the events exactly as they had occurred in full detail.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, the Lord who performs great divine sports, granted them fearlessness, increasing their great enthusiasm.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Special Battle," in the Jalandhara episode of the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the great lord Rudra, of fierce form, mounted upon his bull, approached the battlefield accompanied by hosts of heroes, as if laughing.
Beholding Rudra approaching, the fierce Gaṇas who had previously been defeated returned once more to the battle with lion-like roars.
Uttering heroic shouts, those other hosts of Śaṅkara, festive and armed with weapons, struck down the Daityas with showers of arrows.
Indeed, upon seeing the terrifying Rudra, all the Daityas fled; at the sight of that personage of Śiva, they ran away out of fear, just as sins flee.
Then Jalandhara, seeing the Daityas turned back in battle, rushed toward the Lord of Caṇḍī, discharging arrows by the thousands.
Thousands of lords of the Daityas, headed by Niśumbha and Śumbha, rushed impetuously toward Śiva in their fury, biting their lips.
The hero Kālanemi, Khaḍgaroman, Balāhaka, Ghasmara, Pracaṇḍa, and others as well, went to Śiva.
O Sage, all those heroes, Śumbha and the others, swiftly covered the hosts of Rudra with arrows and severed their limbs.
Seeing the host of Gaṇas shrouded in the darkness of arrows, Hara cut through that web of shafts and covered the sky with his own arrows.
Then he afflicted the Daityas with storms of arrows and struck them down to the earth with masses of fierce volleys of shafts.
Likewise, he severed Khaḍgaroman’s head from his body with a battle-axe; and with a khaṭvāṅga staff, he split Balāhaka’s head in two.
Having bound the gluttonous Daitya with a noose, he struck him down upon the earth; and with a sharp arrow, O great hero, he cut down Pracaṇḍa as well.
Some were struck down by the bull, and others were felled by arrows; the asuras were unable to remain standing, like elephants tormented by a lion.
Then, his soul overcome with rage, that great Daitya, remaining steadfast, laughed and spoke to Śumbha and the other Daityas, censuring them in battle.

Jalandhara said: "What is the use of uttering the mother's name while fleeing and being struck from behind? For those who consider themselves heroes, killing one who is terrified does not bring praise nor grant heaven."
O little ones, if you have faith or strength in this great enterprise within your hearts, stand before me for a moment, provided you have no longing for vulgar pleasures.
Death in battle is excellent; it bestows the fruits of all desires, especially bestows fame, and is even proclaimed to grant liberation.
Having pierced the orb of the sun, he shall indeed go to the supreme state—the wandering mendicant of supreme knowledge who is slain facing the enemy in battle.
The wise should never, at any time or place, fear death; for it cannot be warded off by any means whatsoever.
O heroes, death is born together with the body of those who are subject to birth; whether today or after a hundred years, death is indeed certain for all living beings.
Casting aside that fear of death, fight in battle with joy; in every way, there is supreme bliss both here and hereafter, without a doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, he indeed exhorted his own heroes many times; yet, filled with fear, they could not maintain their courage and fled swiftly from the battlefield.
Then, seeing his own army intent on flight, the great hero Jalandhara, son of the Ocean, became exceedingly enraged.
Then Jalandhara, his soul overcome with rage, challenged Rudra to battle with a voice as fierce as a thunderbolt.
Jalandhara said: "Fight with me today; what is the use of these [others] being slain by you? O wearer of matted locks, show whatever strength you possess!"
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the great Daitya Jalandhara struck Śambhu, the bull-bannered Lord who performs deeds without effort, with seventy arrows.
Before those arrows of Jalandhara could reach him, Mahādeva swiftly severed them with his own sharp shafts, as if laughing.
Then, O Sage, with seven arrows he cut down the horses, the banner, the umbrella, and the bow of the Daitya Jalandhara; this was not surprising for Hari.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that Asura, the son of Pāthodhi, rushed furiously toward Śiva, raising his mace with great speed.
The Lord Maheśvara, of great divine play, suddenly cut that mace hurled by him into two pieces with swift arrows, O son of Parāśara.
Nevertheless, raising his fist in great rage, the great asura rushed forward with immense speed, swiftly intent on slaying him.
At that very moment, Jalandhara was swiftly driven back a distance of one krośa by Īśvara, whose actions are performed without effort, with a torrent of arrows.
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, perceiving Rudra to be superior in strength, unleashed a wondrous Gandharva illusion intended to delude Rudra.
But by the power of his illusion, numerous hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases manifested for the purpose of deluding Rudra.
Then the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases sang and danced, while others played cymbals, flutes, and drums.
Seeing that great marvel, Rudra was utterly bewildered by the Gaṇas; he did not even perceive that the weapons had fallen from his hands.
Seeing Rudra become one-pointed in meditation, the Daitya Jalandhara, impelled by desire, quickly went to where Gaurī was staying.
Having stationed the two exceedingly powerful ones named Śumbha and Niśumbha in battle, he—possessing ten staff-like arms, five faces, three eyes, and wearing matted locks—[remained].
Mounted upon a great bull and resembling Rudra in every respect, O Vyāsa, that Jalandhara became manifest through his asuric māyā.
Then, beholding Rudra approaching, Bhavavallabhā emerged from the midst of her companions and came into his line of sight.
As soon as the lord of the Danavas beheld Pārvatī of beautiful limbs, he discharged his semen and his body became paralyzed.
Then, having realized he was a Dānava, Gaurī, overwhelmed with fear, vanished and went swiftly to Lake Uttaramānasa.
Then, having vanished like a flash of lightning in an instant, the Daitya went with speed to fight again where the god Maheśvara was.
Then Pārvatī also remembered Mahāviṣṇu in her mind; at that moment, she beheld that god seated nearby.
Seeing him bowing with palms joined in reverence, Pārvatī, the mother of the world and beloved of Śiva, spoke with a gracious mind to Viṣṇu.
Pārvatī said: O Viṣṇu, the Daitya Jalandhara has performed a most extraordinary feat; is that conduct of that evil-minded one not known to you?
Having heard those words of the Mother of the World, the one whose banner is Garuḍa bowed to Śivā with palms joined and neck bent low, and replied.
The Blessed Lord said: O Goddess, by your grace that event has been known to me. Whatever you command me, O Mother, I shall perform with your permission.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Pārvatī, the mother of the world, spoke again to Hṛṣīkeśa, providing excellent instruction on the principles of righteousness.
Pārvatī said: "The path has indeed been shown by him; you should understand it as such. By my command, cause that woman’s dharma of devotion to her husband to fall away."
O Lord of Ramā, that great Daitya could not have been slain otherwise; for there is no dharma on the surface of the earth equal to devotion to one’s husband.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this permission and having placed it upon his head, Hari went quickly back to the city of Jālandhara in order to employ a stratagem.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle with Jalandhara," within the "Episode of the Slaying of Jalandhara" in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, omniscient one, best among speakers, tell me: what did Hari do there, and how did she abandon dharma?
Sanatkumāra said: Viṣṇu, having gone to Jālandhara, the capital city of the Daitya, set his mind upon breaking the chastity of Vṛndā.
That best of illusionists, assuming a wondrous form, personally stationed himself in the garden of that city and showed Vṛndā a dream.
Then, at night, the goddess Vṛndā, his devoted wife of virtuous vows, beheld a terrible dream due to the power of Hari’s māyā.
Indeed, in the midst of her dream, she beheld her husband through the power of Viṣṇu’s Māyā, mounted upon a buffalo, smeared with oil, and naked.
Adorned with black flowers, frequented by hosts of flesh-eaters, having gone toward the southern direction, that shaven-headed one was then enveloped in darkness.
At the end of the night, she beheld many such evil dreams, including one in which her own city, along with herself, was suddenly submerged in the ocean.
Then, having awakened, that young woman, reflecting upon her dream, repeatedly beheld the risen sun as being pierced by a hole and devoid of luster.
Realizing this was undesirable, she wept, overwhelmed by fear; she found no peace anywhere, even in the city gates, watchtowers, or courtyards.
Then, accompanied by her two friends, she went to the city garden; yet even there, the young woman found no happiness anywhere.
Then that wife of Jalandhara, her mind despondent and agitated, wandered from forest to forest, yet she did not perceive herself at all.
Then that young woman wandered about and saw two extremely terrifying Rākṣasas with lion-like faces, their teeth gleaming as they stared at her.
Seeing them, she was then utterly overwhelmed and intent on flight; she beheld a peaceful ascetic accompanied by his disciple, who was observing a vow of silence.
Then, having reached his neck out of fear, she clasped her own creeper-like arms around it and said, "O Sage, protect me; I have come to you for refuge."
Then, seeing her distressed and pursued by the rākṣasa, the sage quickly turned those two fierce beings away with a mere *huṃ* sound.
Seeing those two turned away and fled, terrified by the sound of that "hum," O Sage, the wife of the lord of the Daityas was filled with great astonishment in her heart.
Then Vṛndā, freed from fear by that Lord of Sages, bowed down like a staff upon the ground with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
Vṛndā said: O Lord of Sages, ocean of compassion, dispeller of the suffering of others, I have been protected by you from this terrible fear arising from the wicked.
O ocean of compassion, you are indeed capable in every way, even though you are omniscient; I wish to make a certain request, so please listen to it out of grace.
"O Lord, Jalandhara, my husband, has gone to fight Rudra; tell me, O observer of noble vows, how he fares there in battle."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words, the sage, who knew the proper method, assumed a guise of silence; desiring to accomplish his own purpose, he gazed upward out of compassion.
Then the two monkey chiefs arrived, bowed before him, and stood at his side; subsequently, directed by the signal of his creeper-like eyebrows, they ascended into the sky.
Having gone for half a moment and returned, they stood again before him; O Lord of Sages, his very head and trunk, as well as his two hands, were there.
Seeing that headless trunk and those two hands of the Son of the Ocean, she fell to the ground in a swoon, distressed by the calamity that had befallen her husband.
Vṛndā said: O Lord, you who formerly used to delight me with pleasant conversations, why do you not speak today to me, your beloved, who am innocent?
By whom were the gods, along with the gandharvas, conquered together with Viṣṇu? How has he, the conqueror of the three worlds, been slain today by an ascetic?
O best of Daityas, my words were not accepted by you because you did not know the true nature of Rudra; for I declared that Śiva is the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, you have indeed been recognized by me through the power of your service; for you were not [recognized] while you were arrogant and under the sway of evil company.
Having spoken thus in many ways, his beloved wife, though established in her own duty, lamented piteously with a heart consumed by grief.
Then, summoning her fortitude while shedding tears born of sorrow, she bowed deeply with palms joined in reverence and spoke to that best of sages.
Vṛndā said: O ocean of mercy, best of sages, you who are devoted to helping others! O holy one, having shown compassion toward me, please restore my lord to life.
Since you are considered by me to be capable of restoring him to life, therefore, O Lord of Sages, bring back to life this lord of my life.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that wife of the Daitya, devoted to her husband, fell at his feet, emitting sighs of sorrow.
The sage said: "He cannot be brought back to life, for he was slain in battle by Rudra; those who are slain in battle by Rudra never live again."
Nevertheless, overcome with compassion and knowing the eternal dharma that those who have come for refuge must be protected, I shall restore him to life.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having spoken thus and having restored her husband to life, that sage Viṣṇu, the best among all masters of illusion, then vanished from sight.
Quickly restored to life by him, that son of the Ocean rose up; embracing Vṛndā with a joyful heart, he kissed her face.
Then Vṛndā, seeing her husband, became joyful in heart; she abandoned all sorrow and considered it as if it were a dream.
Then, with a heart full of devotion and love having arisen within her, she took delight for many days in the midst of that forest, united with him.
Once, at the conclusion of their amorous play, having seen Viṣṇu as that very same person, Vṛndā, filled with anger, rebuked him and spoke these words.
Vṛndā said: "Fie upon that character of yours, O Hari, you who approach the wives of others! You have been fully recognized by me as a deceiver, a hypocrite in the guise of an ascetic."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, O Vyāsa, she who was devoted to her husband’s fidelity became filled with wrath and, displaying her own splendor, cursed Keśava.
O great villain, enemy of the Daityas, defiler of the dharma of others! O rogue, accept this curse bestowed by me, as virulent as all poisons combined.
Those two who were manifested by you through your illusory power and shown to me as your own, they themselves, having become Rākṣasas, will carry off your wife.
And you too, afflicted by the grief of losing your wife, wander in the forest with the monkey as your companion; here is the lord of serpents who has entered into discipleship under you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Vṛndā then entered the sacrificial fire, even though she was being restrained by Viṣṇu, whose mind remained deeply attached to her.
At that moment, O sage, all the gods, headed by Brahmā, arrived together with their wives in the sky, desiring indeed to behold the true state [of the deceased].
Then, while all the gods were looking on, that supreme and great light belonging to the wife of the lord of the Daityas swiftly departed for the world of no-return.
That splendor of the multitude dissolved into the body of Śiva, while a cry of "Victory! Victory! arose among the rows of immortals stationed in the sky.
Thus, O sage, the great queen Vṛndā, the most excellent daughter of Kālanemi, attained supreme liberation through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Then Hari, repeatedly recollecting her and covered with the dust and ashes from Vṛndā’s funeral pyre, remained right there; though exhorted by hosts of gods and Siddhas, he found no peace.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Violation of Vṛndā’s Chastity and Her Abandonment of the Body," in the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O wise and excellent son of Vidhi, this wonderful account has been narrated; tell me, what happened next in the battle, and how was the Daitya slain?
Sanatkumāra said: When the lord of the Daityas had arrived there for battle and the Gandharva weapon had vanished, the bull-bannered god Śiva regained his consciousness.
Seeing that illusion vanish, Śaṃkara, the Buddha, who is the destroyer, became exceedingly enraged, having resorted to a worldly state.
Then Śiva, his mind filled with wonder, again went forth in fury to battle Jalandhara; and that Daitya, seeing Śiva returned, covered him in the fray with a torrent of arrows.

Hara, the destroyer of the three worlds, cut down that fierce net of arrows discharged by the exceedingly powerful Jalandhara with his own excellent shafts; there was nothing surprising in this for him.
Then Jalandhara, beholding Rudra’s wondrous prowess, created Gaurī through his illusory power, as if to delude the Three-eyed Lord.
Śiva beheld Pārvatī, bound upon the chariot and weeping, as she was being seized by the Daityas Niśumbha and Śumbha.
Seeing Gaurī in such a state and observing her worldly conduct, even Śiva became like an ordinary man, his mind filled with anxiety.
Standing with his face cast downwards in silence, skilled in various playful arts, his limbs relaxed and his spirit despondent, he had forgotten his own prowess.
Then Jalandhara swiftly pierced Rudra with three arrows, which sank up to their feathers into his head, his chest, and his belly.
Then the Lord Rudra, whose essence is knowledge and who delights in great play, assumed in an instant a fierce form, terrifying with garlands of flames.
Seeing his exceedingly great and terrible form, the great asuras were unable to stand before him; they fled in the ten directions.
O Lord of Sages, even Niśumbha and Śumbha, those two renowned and most excellent heroes, were utterly unable to stand in battle.
At that very moment, the illusion created by Jalandhara became concealed; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on all sides in the battle.
Then, seeing Śumbha and Niśumbha fleeing, Rudra, filled with wrath and uttering a reproach, pronounced a curse upon them both.
Rudra said: "You two are wicked, exceedingly cruel, and offenders against me; you have turned your backs from this battle, acting as punishers of Pārvatī."
"One who has turned his back should not be slain; therefore, you two are not to be killed by me. Having fled from my battle, you shall both become the victims of Gaurī."
While Gaurī’s lord was speaking thus, Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean, blazed like a flaming fire and became exceedingly enraged at Rudra.
In the battle against Rudra, he rained down sharp arrows with great velocity; indeed, the surface of the earth became completely shrouded by the darkness of those shafts.
As soon as Rudra swiftly cut down his multitude of arrows, the powerful one immediately struck the bull with his iron club.
By that blow, the bull turned away from the field of battle; though being dragged by Rudra, it did not remain upon the battlegrounds.
Then, O lord of sages, Mahārudra displayed his own exceedingly unbearable splendor to everyone in the world; this is the truth.
Thereupon, the Lord Rudra, assuming a fierce form, became suddenly and intensely enraged, as terrible as the fire of universal destruction.
Seeing the Daitya standing before him like a mass of clouds, and even having heard of his invincibility by others, he nevertheless prepared for battle.
Honoring the word of Brahmā, the Lord and protector of the worlds, extending his grace from his heart, set his mind upon slaying him.
Becoming intensely enraged, the wielder of the trident playfully used his big toe to swiftly create a great, fierce, and wonderful wheel in the vast waters.

Having whetted his discus in the waters of the ocean and remembering the three worlds, the Blessed One, the Foe of Tripura—the destroyer of Dakṣa, Andhaka, Antaka, the three cities, and the sacrifice—acting as the end-maker of the three worlds, spoke with a laugh: "The three worlds have been slain by this [discus]! Thus spoke the Lord who destroyed the three cities.
Mahārudra said: "O Jalandhara, this discus was fashioned from my foot in the great waters; if you are strong enough to lift it, stay and fight, but not otherwise."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, his eyes blazing with anger, as if burning him with his very gaze, he looked at Śaṅkara and spoke.
Jalandhara said: "O Śaṅkara, having drawn a line [of battle], you shall indeed kill me along with your hosts, and then kill the worlds together with the gods, just as Garuḍa takes his own portion."

I am capable of destroying everything moving and unmoving, including Indra himself. O Maheśvara, who in the three worlds is impenetrable to my arrows? By my very childhood, the Lord Brahmā—who is the strongest among sages and the foremost of the gods—has been utterly conquered by my ascetic power; this is indeed fitting for me.

In an instant, the entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, was consumed by you; O Rudra, what more could you have done than even to conquer the Blessed Lord through your ascetic power?
Indra, Agni, Yama, Kubera, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and the others could not endure him, just as serpents cannot bear the scent of the Lord of Birds.
O Śaṅkara, I have found no vehicle either in heaven or on earth; having reached all the mountains, the lords of the Gaṇas were even overcome by me.
The glorious Mandara, the lord of mountains, and the beautiful Nīla and Meru, were all overcome by my staff-like arms for the sake of scratching my itching back.
On the Himavat mountain, for the sake of sport, the Gaṅgā was held back by my arms; and victory over the dwellers of heaven was won by my servants, the Aroṇas.
Having seized the mare by the mouth with his hand, he bound it; at that very moment, everything then became a single ocean.
The nāgas, beginning with Airāvata, were cast upon the waters of the ocean; and the Blessed Lord Indra, together with his chariot, was hurled a hundred yojanas away.
Even Garuḍa was bound by me with the serpent-noose of Viṣṇu; and women such as Urvaśī and others were brought by me into the interior of my prison.
"O Rudra, you do not know me—Jalandhara, the great Daitya, the son of the Ocean, who possesses great strength and brings victory to the three worlds."
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus addressed Mahādeva, the son of the Ocean then neither moved nor remembered the Dānavas slain in battle.
Intoxicated and undisciplined, he slapped his arms with the strength of his forearms and insulted Mahādeva with words of bitter syllables.
Having heard those inauspicious words uttered by the Daitya, Mahādeva laughed and assumed a state of supreme wrath.
Rudra seized in his hand that discus named Sudarśana, which had been fashioned from his big toe, and prepared to strike with it.
The Lord Hara hurled that discus named Sudarśana, which resembled ten million suns and was like the fire of universal dissolution.
Scorching heaven and earth with its force, it reached Jalandhara and swiftly severed his great, wide-eyed head.
The body fell from the chariot onto the earth, making the surface of the ground resound; and as for the head of the son of the Ocean, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
His body fell in two parts like a mountain of collyrium; it was as if a great mountain had been split in two by a thunderbolt falling into the ocean.
The entire world became filled with his fierce blood, O lord of sages, and consequently the whole earth became transformed.
By the command of Rudra, all that blood and flesh reached Mahāraurava and became this pool of blood here.
That fire emerged from his body and merged into Rudra, just as that which arose from Vṛndā’s body dissolved into Gaurī.
Seeing Jalandhara slain, the gods, gandharvas, and pannagas became exceedingly joyful and exclaimed, "Well done, O God!"
All the gods, Siddhas, and lords of sages attained a state of great joy; showering flowers, they loudly sang his praises.
The celestial nymphs, overwhelmed with love, danced with great joy; with melodious voices, they sang sweetly in harmony with the Kinnaras.
O sage, when the Lord of Vṛndā was slain, all the quarters became serene, and the winds—of the three kinds—blew auspiciously with pleasant touch.
The moon became cold, the sun blazed with intense heat, the fires grew dim, and the sky became distorted.
Thus, O Sage, when that son of the Ocean had been slain by Hara of the curved form, the entire triple world attained a state of well-being beyond measure.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Jalandhara," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Brahmā and the other gods, as well as all the sages, bowed down and praised the Lord of the God of Gods with pleasing words.

The gods said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; you are indeed the bestower of happiness upon the virtuous and the constant destroyer of the suffering of your devotees."
O Lord, you are of most wonderful and beautiful pastimes, accessible through devotion yet difficult to approach; you are hard to propitiate by the wicked—be forever gracious.
Indeed, even the Veda does not know your greatness in its true essence; rather, all the great-souled ones sing of your sublime glory according to their own understanding.
Your greatness is exceedingly profound; those beginning with the Thousand-faced One (Sahasravadana) always sing of it with great affection, for they indeed purify their own voices.
"O Lord of Gods, by Your grace, even a knower of Brahman may become dull-witted; for the Vedas indeed declare that You are always accessible through devotion alone."
You are indeed compassionate toward the distressed and ever-pervasive everywhere; through true devotion, You manifest as the changeless refuge of the virtuous.
O Maheśāna, by devotion alone many have attained perfection; having enjoyed all happiness here, they become free from suffering through the state beyond change.
In ancient times, the Lord of the Yadus, a devotee of the Daśārhas, attained perfection; and his wife Kalāvatī, O Lord, attained the supreme state through devotion alone.
Likewise, King Mitrasaha and his beloved Madayantī, O Lord of Gods, attained supreme liberation through devotion alone to you.
Likewise, the daughter of the foremost of the Kaikeyas, named Sauminī, attained supreme happiness through devotion to you—a state difficult even for great yogis to obtain.
O Lord, that best of kings, Vimarṣaṇa, having enjoyed various pleasures for the duration of seven births through devotion to you, attained the supreme goal.
Candrasena, the best of kings, having enjoyed all pleasures through devotion to you, was freed from suffering and attained supreme happiness both in this world and the next.
The son of a cowherd woman, Śrīkara, having enjoyed a good state in this world through devotion, attained supreme happiness in the hereafter as a disciple of Mahāvīra.
You are the remover of suffering and the bestower of liberation for King Satyaratha; you have indeed caused Prince Dharmagupta to cross over and attain happiness in this world.
Likewise, O Great Lord, by Your grace You made that Brahmin, who observed pure vows, free from poverty, devoted to You, and endowed with knowledge through his mother.
Citravarmā, the best of kings, attained the supreme goal through devotion to you, having always enjoyed in this world pleasures difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Prince Candrāṅgada, together with Queen Sīmantinī, having abandoned all suffering, attained happiness and the supreme goal.
Even the base and wicked Brahmin named Mandara, who had gone to a prostitute, became your devotee, O Śiva; having worshipped you, he attained the supreme goal along with her.
O Lord, by Your grace toward Your devotee, the king’s son attained auspiciousness and happiness, free from suffering; and through his mother, he attained the supreme goal.
O Maheśvara, even that wicked man who was always devoted to the enjoyment of all women became liberated through service to you, becoming a consumer of pure food.
Śambara was a devotee of Śaṅkara and always wore the ashes of the funeral pyre; O Śambhu, due to his observance of the ash-rite, he went to your city with his wife.
O Lord, the son of Bhadrasena and the son of the minister were likewise Sudharma and Śubhakarmā, who always wore rudrākṣa beads.
And by your grace, those two—the monkey and the cock who were ornaments of Rudra in their previous birth—were liberated and enjoyed true happiness here.
O Lord, devoted to the upliftment of your devotees, Piṅgalā and Mahānandā, these two courtesans, attained the supreme state through their devotion to you.
Śāradā, the daughter of a brahmin, had fallen into widowhood while still a child; yet, through the power of your devotion, she became possessed of sons and good fortune.
Bindugu was indeed a mere Brahmin who enjoyed the company of courtesans, yet his beloved wife, Vancuka, having heard of his fame, attained the supreme goal.
"O Lord, O Maheśāna, O Friend of the Wretched, O Abode of Compassion, many living beings have attained perfection through the state of devotion unto you."

You are the Supreme Brahman beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the Supreme Lord beyond the individual soul (puruṣa); you are devoid of qualities yet the substratum of the three qualities, and you are the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
O Maheśvara, you are the performer of various deeds, eternally changeless, and the Lord of all; we, Brahmā and all others, are your servants.
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; protect us always, O Śiva! We are your subjects, O Protector, and have forever gone for refuge to you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus offered praise, those gods, headed by Brahmā, along with the lords of sages, then became silent, their minds fixed upon the pair of Śiva’s feet.
Then Śambhu, the Great Lord, having heard that auspicious hymn of praise from the gods, immediately granted excellent boons and vanished right there, the Lord.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were delighted; their enemies having been slain, they returned to their respective abodes, joyful and singing the glorious praises of Śiva.
This supreme narrative, the subduing of Jalandhara, is the meritorious life-story of Maheśa, which destroys the flood of great sins.
This meritorious hymn of praise to the God destroys all sins; it bestows constant happiness and grants joy to Maheśāna.
Whoever reads or causes this twofold narrative to be read, having enjoyed supreme happiness in this world, shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn to the God," within the Jalandhara-vadha episode of the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, the fifth section of the Rudra-saṃhitā, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O son of Brahmā, salutations to you; you are blessed, O best among the devotees of Śiva, since this great, divine, and auspicious narrative of Śaṅkara has been recited by you.
Now, O sage, please tell me with great affection of the Vaiṣṇava’s conduct: after he had enchanted Vṛndā, what did he do, and where did he go?
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great wisdom, O most excellent among the best of Śiva’s devotees, to this Vaiṣṇava narrative, which is exceedingly pure and enriched by the deeds of Śambhu.
When the gods, beginning with Brahmā, had become silent, Maheśvara, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, spoke with great favor.
Śambhu said: "O Brahmā, all you foremost of gods, Jalandhara—though he was a portion of myself—has been slain by me for your sake. I speak the truth, the absolute truth."
"O dear ones, tell me truly: have you not attained happiness? For it is for your sake that my divine play proceeds, though I am forever free from change."
Sanatkumāra said: Then Brahmā and the other gods, their eyes wide with joy, bowed their heads to Rudra and related the deeds of Viṣṇu.
The gods said: "O Mahādeva, the gods have been protected by you from the fear born of enemies; yet something else has arisen—what shall we do regarding that?"
O Lord, Vṛndā, having been thoroughly deluded by Viṣṇu through his efforts, was quickly reduced to ashes in the fire and attained the supreme goal.
Viṣṇu, bewildered by Vṛndā’s beauty, remains infatuated; he wears the ashes from her funeral pyre, deluded by your Māyā.
Though he was earnestly awakened by us and the assemblies of perfected sages, that Hari did not wake, being utterly deluded by your māyā.
Have mercy, O Great Lord; awaken Viṣṇu, awaken him! All this, including the material world with its moving and non-moving beings, is dependent upon you.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the inhabitants of heaven, Maheśa, who is of great divine play and acts according to his own will, replied to them as they stood with palms joined in reverence.
Maheśa said: "O Brahmā, O all you gods, listen to my words with reverence. My Māyā, known as Mohinī, is difficult for all the worlds to overcome."
The entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—is dependent upon her; by her alone was Viṣṇu deluded, so that Hari became subject to desire.
That great goddess named Umā is the supreme mother of the three gods; she is declared to be the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the divine woman, whose essence is the Daughter of the Mountain.
O gods, go for refuge to her who removes the delusion of Viṣṇu—the one worthy of refuge, the enchanting Māyā, known as Śivā, the granter of all desires.
Offer praise to her, which brings satisfaction to my power; if she is well-pleased, she will accomplish every task.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, having spoken thus to those gods, the five-faced Lord Śambhu, Hara, suddenly vanished along with all his own attendants.
And at the command of Śambhu, the gods, including Brahmā and others along with Indra, praised Mūlaprakṛti, who is affectionate toward her devotees, with their minds.

The gods said: We bow to that Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), from whose arising proceed the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which are the agents of the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction; and by whose will this universe expands through existence and non-existence.

Protect us; you who are established as the supreme power throughout the entire world, possessing twenty-three well-proclaimed qualities, whose form and actions even the three worlds do not know—that Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), we bow before her.

We perpetually bow to that Mūlaprakṛti, who is affectionate toward her devotees, for those men who are constantly endowed with devotion never encounter poverty, delusion, the loss of excellence, or other such misfortunes.
O Great Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign of us gods, perform your task! O Śivā, O Durgā, O Goddess, salutations be unto you!
When the battle between Jalandhara and Śambhu, the dweller of Kailāsa, had commenced for the sake of his slaughter at the command of Gaurī, O Śiva...
O Goddess, Vṛndā was indeed thoroughly deluded by Viṣṇu through his efforts; she was made to abandon her own husband and, having been reduced to ashes in the fire, she attained her destination.
Jalandhara has been slain in battle; we have been liberated from that fear by Giriśa, who, out of compassion, bestows grace upon his devotees.
By His command, we have all come to you for refuge; for you, O Goddess, are Śambhu and [Śivā], both devoted solely to the upliftment of your devotees.
Viṣṇu, bewildered by Vṛndā’s beauty, indeed remains there, wearing the ashes from her funeral pyre, fallen from knowledge, and utterly deluded.
O Maheśvarī, although he was awakened by the hosts of perfected deities, Hari did not then wake up, being utterly deluded by your māyā.
Have mercy, O Great Goddess; awaken Hari, awaken him, so that he, with a pure mind, may protect his own world and perform the work of the gods.
Praising him thus, those gods beheld there in the sky a sphere of splendor, with its flames pervading the quarters of space.
O Vyāsa, from the midst of that [assembly], all the immortals, beginning with Brahmā and including Indra, heard the celestial, wish-fulfilling voice of Sarasvatī moving through the sky.
The voice from the sky said: "I alone abide divided into three forms through the three qualities: Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Surā, corresponding to the qualities of Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas."
Go there indeed with respect to them; by my command, they will be pleased and shall fulfill their desire.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, as the gods listened to those words with eyes wide open in wonder, that great light then vanished from their sight.
Then all those gods, having heard those words with reverence and impelled by his speech, bowed down to Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Surā.
And all those gods, beginning with Brahmā, with their heads bowed in great devotion, praised all those goddesses with various kinds of words.
Then, O Vyāsa, those goddesses appeared before him instantly, illuminating the quarters of the sky with their most wonderful splendors.
Then, having seen them, those immortals, with minds full of serene joy, bowed down and praised them with devotion, and announced their own purpose.
Then, seeing those gods prostrate before him, he who is compassionate toward his devotees gave them seeds and spoke these words with affection:
The goddesses said: "Sow these seeds where Viṣṇu resides; from that, your purpose will attain fulfillment."
Sanatkumāra said: O sage, having spoken thus, those goddesses then vanished; for they were the powers (śaktis) of Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, composed of the three guṇas.
Then all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and including Indra, were satisfied; taking those seeds, they went to where Hari was stationed.
O Sage, those gods, remembering them, cast those [bones] upon the ground of the funeral pyre of Vṛndā; they remained there as portions of the power (śakti) of Śiva.
O Lord of Sages, from the seeds that were sown, three types of forest trees arose: the dhātrī, the mālatī, and the tulasī.
The Dhātrī is known as originating from Dhātrī; Mālatī is known as originating from Mā; and Tulasī originates from Gaurī; these possess the qualities of Tamas, Sattva, and Rajas respectively.
O Sage, having seen the trees in the form of women, Viṣṇu then rose up toward them due to the agitation of an excessive passion.
Having seen him, he entreated her out of delusion, his mind attached by desire; and Tulasī and Dhātrī also gazed upon him with passion.
And because that seed had been previously bestowed upon Lakṣmī by Māyā herself, the woman born from it became intent on jealousy toward him.
Therefore, she acquired the highly contemptible name "Barbarī"; yet, out of affection for her, the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants always grant him joy.

Then, his suffering forgotten, Viṣṇu, being satisfied and saluted by all the gods, went to Vaikuṇṭha along with those two. O best of Brahmins, in the month of Kārttika, the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants are always to be known as dear to all the gods, and especially so to Viṣṇu.
Even there, O great sage, the Tulasī plant is exceedingly blessed and most excellent; surpassing even Gaṇeśa, it bestows affection upon all and grants all desires.
Having beheld Hari residing in Vaikuṇṭha, Brahmā, Indra, and those other immortals bowed down and praised Mahāviṣṇu, and then indeed departed for their respective abodes.
O best of sages, even Vaikuṇṭha, remaining in his own world, became free from delusion and possessed of perfect understanding; he became happy, constantly remembering Śiva as he had done before.
Thus is this narrative, which destroys the flood of sins and grants all desires to men; it destroys all afflictions born of desire and increases all higher knowledge.
Whoever should recite this constantly, or cause it to be recited with devotion, or hear it, or cause it to be heard, shall go to the supreme goal.
Having recited this most excellent narrative, the wise hero who enters into battle will be victorious; of this there is no doubt.
This bestows the knowledge of Brahman upon the Brahmins, grants victory to the Kshatriyas, bestows all wealth upon the Vaishyas, and indeed grants happiness to the Shudras.
O Vyāsa, it bestows devotion to Śambhu, destroys the sins of all, and always grants the state of ultimate felicity both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess's Praise and the Destruction of Viṣṇu’s Infatuation Following the Slaying of Jalandhara," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, O sage, listen with love to another account of Śambhu’s deeds, by the mere hearing of which devotion to Śiva becomes firm.
How the heroic Dānava named Śaṅkhacūḍa, a thorn to the gods, was slain by Śiva with his trident at the forefront of battle.
Listen with great affection, O Vyāsa; out of my deep love for you, I shall relate that divine, purifying, and sin-destroying account of Śambhu’s deeds.
The son of Marīci and son of Dhātṛ was the sage Kaśyapa; he was a most righteous creator of beings, a lord of creatures (Prajāpati) commanded by Brahmā.
Dakṣa, out of affection, gave him his thirteen daughters; their extensive progeny cannot be fully described here.
Who in the three worlds is capable of describing in detail that universe wherein all things—gods and others, moving and unmoving—came into being?
Listen now to the narrative at hand, which is endowed with the divine play of Śambhu; I shall relate that very account today, which increases one's devotion. Listen!
Among those wives of Kaśyapa, Danu alone was an excellent woman; she was highly beautiful, virtuous, and increased in fortune through her husband's grace.
Danu had many very powerful sons; their names are not mentioned here, O Sage, for fear of prolixity.
Among them was one named Vipracitti, possessed of great strength and prowess; his son was Dambha, who was righteous, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and had conquered his senses.
That heroic son was not born; consequently, he became absorbed in anxiety, and having made Śukrācārya his preceptor, he received the Kṛṣṇa-mantra.
He performed supreme austerity at Puṣkara for a hundred thousand years; firmly bound in posture, he chanted the mantra of Kṛṣṇa steadfastly for a long time.
As he was performing that austerity, a blazing light issued forth from his head and spread everywhere; indeed, that splendor was difficult to endure.
Scorched by that [weapon], all the asuras, sages, and likewise the Manus, placing Sunāsīra at their head, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having bowed down to the Creator, the bestower of all prosperity, they praised him while distressed and spoke their own story in detail.
Having heard that, the Creator (Brahmā) also went with them to Vaikuṇṭha in order to inform Viṣṇu of everything exactly as it was.
Having gone there, they all bowed down to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds and the supreme protector, and with palms joined in reverence, they praised him with humility.
The gods said: "O God of gods, we do not know what the cause here has arisen; by whose splendor have all these become so tormented? Tell us that."

O Friend of the distressed, you are the protector of your dependents who have purified their souls; O Lord of Lakṣmī, you who are worthy of seeking refuge, protect, protect those who have come to you for shelter!
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Brahmā and the other inhabitants of heaven, Viṣṇu, who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge, laughed and spoke with affection.
Viṣṇu said: "O immortals, remain well-composed and undisturbed; do not fear. No calamities shall occur, for the time of dissolution has not arrived."
Indeed, a Dānava named Dambha, who is my devotee, is performing austerities seeking a son; I shall pacify him by means of granting a boon.

Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having been addressed thus, all those gods, beginning with Brahmā, maintained their composure and departed for their respective abodes in every direction, remaining well-settled.
Acyuta also went to Puṣkara to grant a boon, for there the Dānava named Dambha was performing penance.
Having gone there, Hari spoke to his devotee, who was chanting his own mantra, consoling him with truthful words: "Choose a boon."
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu and seeing him standing before her, she bowed down with great devotion and praised him again and again.
Dambha said: O God of gods, salutations be unto you, O lotus-eyed one! O Lord of Ramā, Sovereign of the three worlds, bestow your grace upon me.
"O you of great strength and prowess, grant me a devoted son, a hero who conquers the three worlds and is invincible to the dwellers of heaven."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by the lord of the Dānavas, Hari granted him that boon; and having turned him away from his fierce penance, O Sage, he then vanished.
When Hari had departed, the lord of the Dānavas, having offered salutations to that direction, went to his own home with his purpose accomplished and his desires fulfilled.
In a short time, his fortunate wife became pregnant; she shone with extreme splendor, illuminating the interior of the house.
O Sage, he who was the foremost of Kṛṣṇa’s attendants, the cowherd named Sudāmā, entered her womb because he had been cursed by Rādhā.
Then, at the proper time, that virtuous woman gave birth to a son named Suprabha; having summoned many sages, the father performed the birth-rites for him.
O best of the twice-born, there was a very great festival when he was born; on an auspicious day, his father gave him the name Śaṅkhacūḍa.
He grew up in his father’s house like the moon in the bright fortnight; having mastered the sciences during childhood, he became exceedingly radiant.
Through his constant childhood play, he spread joy for his parents; he became beloved by everyone, especially by those of his own clan.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, following the instruction of Jaigīṣavya, that Śaṅkhacūḍa performed [penance] at Puṣkara for a long time with great devotion to Brahmā.
With his senses restrained, he chanted the Brahma-vidyā imparted by his guru, having become one-pointed in mind and having withdrawn his faculties.
While that Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa was performing penance at Puṣkara, the omnipresent Lord Brahmā, the preceptor of the worlds, went quickly to grant him a boon.
Then Brahmā said to the lord of the Dānavas, "Choose a boon. Seeing him, he bowed down deeply and, being humble, praised him with truthful words.
He requested from Brahmā the boon of invincibility against the inhabitants of heaven; Brahmā, with a very gracious mind, said to him, "So be it."
He gave to Śaṅkhacūḍa the divine armor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most auspicious of all auspicious things in the world, which bestows victory everywhere.
Go to Badarī together with Tulasī; indeed, perform the marriage ceremony right there, for she is performing penance out of desire.
Fate commanded him, "She is the daughter of Dharmadhvaja," and at that very moment, while he was looking on, it vanished instantly.
Then Śaṅkhacūḍa, having perfected his austerities at the great Puṣkara, bound upon his neck that armor which is the most auspicious of all blessings for the world.
By his command, that brahmin, having achieved his heart's desire through ascetic penance, arrived swiftly at Badarikāśrama with a joyful countenance.
And the Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived there by chance, at the place where Tulasī, the daughter of Dharmadhvaja, was performing penance.
Beautiful, with a lovely smile, slender, and adorned with auspicious ornaments, she gazed with sidelong glances at that very same supreme person.
Having seen her—graceful, charming, well-behaved, beautiful, and virtuous—he dwelt near her and spoke sweetly to her.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: Who are you? Whose daughter are you? Why do you stand here, and what are you doing? Why have you become silent? You ought to acknowledge me, your servant, here.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words, she spoke to him who was full of desire.
Tulasī said: "I am the daughter of Dharmadhvaja, and as an ascetic I am performing penance. I dwell in this grove of austerity; who are you? Go as you please."
The female species is enchanting, yet like poison even to Brahmā and the other gods; she is censurable, a source of faults, an illusion, and indeed a shackle for those who follow her.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to Sarasa, Tulasī became silent; seeing her smiling, he too began to speak.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "O Goddess, that which has been spoken by you is not entirely false; some part is true and some part is false. Listen to this from me."
Among those women who are devoted to their husbands, you are the foremost; yet it is my conviction that I am neither a man of sinful vision nor one driven by lust, just as you are not.
"I come now to your side by the command of Brahmā; O beautiful one, I shall take you as my wife through the Gāndharva rite."
"I am indeed Śaṅkhacūḍa, the one who causes the gods to flee; do you not know me, O blessed lady? Have I never been heard of?"
I am a descendant of the Danu lineage, specifically the dull-witted son of Danu; formerly, I was a cowherd named Sudāman and an attendant of Hari.
Now, as the lord of the Dānavas, due to the curse of Rādhikā, I am a rememberer of my past lives; by the power of Kṛṣṇa, I know everything.

Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Śaṅkhacūḍa ceased speaking before him. When he had been addressed with such truthful words with great respect by the lord of the Dānavas, Tulasī, pleased and smiling, began to speak.
Tulasī said: "I have now been defeated by you through your discernment of the true nature of beings; that man alone is blessed in this world who is not defeated by a woman."
Even if he is honored, that man who is conquered by a woman is eternally impure; his ancestors, the gods, and all human beings alike despise him.
A Brahmin becomes pure after ten days in the case of a birth or a death; a Kṣatriya after twelve days, and a Vaiśya after fifteen days.
"A Śūdra shall be purified in one month; such is the instruction of the Vedas. A man conquered by women is never pure, except through cremation on the funeral pyre."

Therefore, the ancestors do not accept the offering of rice-balls and libations because of their lack of desire; likewise, the gods do not accept the flowers, fruits, and other such offerings given by him.
Of what use to him are knowledge, good sons, austerity, recitation, burnt offerings, or worship; or what is the use of learning or charity for one whose mind has been stolen away by women?
I have tested you for the sake of knowing the power of your knowledge; indeed, after testing her beloved, a woman seeking a lover should choose her husband.
Sanatkumāra said: While Tulasī was speaking thus, at that very moment Brahmā arrived there; having been greeted, he then spoke these words.
Brahmā said: "O Śaṅkhacūḍa, what are you doing conversing with her? Take her as your wife by the Gāndharva rite."
You are indeed a jewel among men, and she is a virtuous jewel among women; the union of the wise with the wise is full of merit.
O King, who would renounce happiness that is free from conflict and difficult to obtain? He who abandons the happiness of non-conflict is a beast; of this there is no doubt.
O virtuous lady, why do you examine such a beloved husband, who possesses such qualities and is the crusher of gods, asuras, and dānavas?
Dwell with him for a very long time at all times, O beautiful one, wherever you desire throughout all the worlds.
In the end, he will attain Śrī Kṛṣṇa once again in Goloka; and when he has passed away, you shall attain the four-armed Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus bestowed this blessing, Brahmā departed for his own abode; and the Dānava took her as his wife according to the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
Having thus married Tulasī, he went to his father’s abode; there, in a delightful bedchamber, he took delight with Ramā.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s Performance of Austerities and Marriage," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: When Śaṅkhacūḍa had returned to his own home and was married, the Dānavas and others rejoiced, having performed penance and obtained their boon.
Quickly departing from their own worlds and joined by their respective preceptors, all the gods assembled together and arrived in his presence.
Having bowed to him with humility and praised him with various marks of respect, they remained right there with great affection, perceiving the Lord to be full of splendor.
Seeing that the family preceptor had departed, the son of Dambha also prostrated with great devotion and supreme respect, performing a full-body obeisance (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
Then Śukra, the family preceptor, having seen that unsurpassed blessing, recounted the account of the gods and the Dānavas at that time.
That enmity of the asuras was innate, as was their defeat, the victory of the gods, and the assistance rendered by Jīva.
Then, after all the gods had celebrated a great festival, the Preceptor Brahmā formally installed him as the sovereign lord of the Dānavas and other Asuras.
Then a great festival arose among the Asuras, whose souls were filled with joy; and they all, with great affection, presented him with various offerings.
Then the heroic and powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa, the son of Dambha, having attained the consecration of kingship, shone like the king of the gods.
Leading a vast army of Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, he mounted his chariot and swiftly set out to conquer Indra’s city.
As that lord of the Dānavas proceeded while they performed service for him, he shone like the moon among the stars, or like the king of planets among the planets.
Hearing that Śaṅkhacūḍa was approaching, Indra, the self-ruling lord of heaven, prepared together with all the immortals to fight with him.
Then a tumultuous battle indeed took place between the Asuras and the Suras—a battle that brought joy to heroes, struck fear into cowards, and caused the hair to stand on end.
A great clamor arose from the heroes roaring in battle, and likewise there was the sound of musical instruments there, which increased their valor.
The gods, being more powerful, became enraged and fought with the asuras; the asuras suffered defeat and fled out of fear.
Seeing them fleeing, the lord Śaṅkhacūḍa himself roared a lion’s roar and fought together with the gods.
With speed and violence, he wrought slaughter among the inhabitants of heaven; all the gods fled, unable to endure his fierce splendor.
Remaining here and there in the caves of mountains, wretched and dependent upon him, they were not independent; they were lusterless like the oceans.
That heroic and powerful lord of the Dānavas, the son of Dambha, having conquered all the worlds, seized all the offices of the gods.
He brought the three worlds under his own control and took all the sacrificial portions for himself; he even became Indra himself, and the entire universe was thus governed.
He established his authority over the domains of Kubera, Indra, Sūrya, Agni, Yama, and Vāyu, according to his own power.
Of the gods, asuras, danavas, and rakshasas; of the gandharvas, nagas, kinnaras, and the inhabitants of the ocean.
That great hero, the immensely powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa, became the sovereign of the three worlds and of all others.
Thus did the great Śaṅkhacūḍa, the sovereign lord of the kings of kings, enjoy sovereignty over all the worlds for many years.
In his kingdom there was no famine, no pestilence, and no inauspicious planets; there were neither mental anxieties nor physical diseases, and the subjects were always happy.
The earth yielded crops of many kinds without being tilled, and various medicinal herbs were always fruitful and succulent.
The mines of jewels and the oceans, which are repositories of gems, as well as the trees that always bear flowers and fruit, and the rivers carrying their waters, [all flourished].
Without the gods, all living beings would be happy and free from affliction; all others—the four castes and stages of life—would remain steadfast in their respective duties.
While he existed, no one in the three worlds was miserable; only the gods were sorrowful, owing to their enmity toward their brother.
That powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa was the supreme friend of Kṛṣṇa; devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous soul was a constant resident of Goloka.
Due to the power of his previous curse, he had entered a Dānava womb; yet, O Sage, even while in that state of being a Dānava, he did not possess the mind of a Dānava.
Then, O dear one, all the hosts of gods, having been defeated and deprived of their kingdom, consulted together with the sages and proceeded to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Having seen the Creator there, and having bowed to and especially praised him, they, being deeply distressed, related the entire account to Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, having comforted all the gods and the sages, went together with them to Vaikuṇṭha, the world that bestows happiness upon the virtuous.
There Brahmā, together with the hosts of gods, beheld the Lord of Lakṣmī, adorned with a crown and earrings, and decorated with a forest garland.
The four-armed Lord, wearing yellow garments, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, and served by the Siddhas such as Sanandana and others.
Having seen Viṣṇu, all the gods, led by Brahmā, along with the lords of sages, bowed down and praised the omnipresent Lord with devotion, their hands joined in reverence.
The gods said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha, Master! O Śrī Hari, Teacher of the three worlds, protect us who have come to you for refuge.
You alone are the protector of the worlds, O Lord of the three realms, O Acyuta, O Master! Abode of Lakṣmī, Govinda, the very life-breath of your devotees—salutations be unto you!
