Having praised him thus, all the gods wept before Hari; hearing that, the Blessed Viṣṇu spoke this to Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said: For what purpose have you come to Vaikuṇṭha, which is difficult even for yogis to attain? What distress has arisen for you? Tell me the truth before me.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Hari, and having prostrated himself again and again, he stood with his palms joined in reverence, his neck bowed low in humility.
Then he related the account of what Śaṅkhacūḍa had done—the narration of the gods' distress—in the presence of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Soul.
Having heard those words, the Blessed Lord Hari, who knows all things in every way, laughed and spoke that secret concerning Brahmā.
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lotus-born One, I know the entire account of Śaṅkhacūḍa, as well as that of my devotee, the cowherd of great splendor, from long ago."
Listen to this entire account, an ancient history; no doubt should be entertained, for Śaṅkara will grant you welfare.
And above all is the world of Śiva, higher than the highest, where Śambhu—the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord—shines forth in splendor.

He who is the presiding lord of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the bearer of the three powers, who is both devoid of attributes and possessed of attributes, is the supreme light whose nature is self-manifest.

O Brahman, from her were born three sons who are the agents of creation and the other cosmic functions; endowed with the qualities of sattva and the rest, they are known by the names Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara.
For that very Supreme Self sports together with Umā, where, liberated from Māyā, He is the ordainer of the eternal and the non-eternal.
And near that is Goloka, the cow-pen of Śaṅkara; by his will, Kṛṣṇa, who possesses my own form, dwells there indeed.
Commanded by him for the sake of guarding those cows, he was always happy; having attained that happiness, he too, being skilled in recreation, sported there.
His consort is known as Rādhā, the Mother of the World; she is the supreme form of Prakṛti, the fifth, who sports with great delight.
There are many cowherds and cowherd girls there who are his offspring; they are constantly devoted to pleasant pastimes and follow in the footsteps of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
That very same being, now deluded by this [illusion] through the sport of Śambhu, has attained a demonic birth in vain due to a curse that brings him his own suffering.
In ancient times, his death was ordained by Kṛṣṇa with the trident of Rudra; thereafter, having cast off his own body, he shall become an attendant (pārṣada).
Knowing this, O Lord of Gods, you should not fear; O Śaṅkara, go for refuge, and he will immediately provide for your welfare.
Both you and all the immortals remain here free from fear.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, together with Vidhi, went to the world of Śiva, mentally remembering Śambhu, the Lord of all, who is affectionate toward his devotees.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Life and Deeds of Śaṅkhacūḍa, Preceded by the Description of His Rule as King," within the Śaṅkhacūḍavadhopākhyāna (The Narrative of the Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa), in the fifth section, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, of the second book, the Rudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, at that very moment, Brahmā went to the most divine world of Śiva, which is without support and non-material.
With a joyful countenance, Viṣṇu entered the interior of the palace, which was strewn with various jewels, radiant, and exceedingly brilliant.
Having reached the first gate, which was variegated and frequented by hosts of attendants, it was adorned with supreme splendor, exceedingly lofty, and most beautiful.
And he saw the gatekeepers seated upon jeweled lion-thrones, adorned with white garments and decorated with ornaments of precious gems.
[He saw] heroes with five faces and three eyes, possessing beautiful fair-complexioned bodies, bearing tridents and other weapons, and adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Both Brahmā and Rameśa, bowing down with humility, related the account concerning the purpose of their audience with the Lord.
They gave him permission, and by their command he entered the supreme gateway, which was exceedingly beautiful, variegated, and of supreme luster.
He reported the news to the gatekeeper for the purpose of reaching the Lord’s presence; commanded by him, he entered through another [gate].
Having thus entered through fifteen gates, the Lotus-born One reached the great gate and beheld Nandin there.
Having bowed down properly and praised him as before, Viṣṇu was commanded by Nandin and entered the inner chamber slowly with joy.
Having gone there, he beheld the lofty assembly hall of Śambhu, radiant with splendor, surrounded by attendants whose bodies were shining and well-adorned.
With forms like those of Maheśvara, possessing ten arms and auspicious luster, with five faces and three eyes, and as brilliant as the blue-throated Śitikaṇṭha.
Adorned with ornaments of Rudrākṣa beads set with excellent gems and smeared with sacred ash, it was square, heart-stealing, and shaped like the orb of the new moon.
It was beautifully adorned with the finest diamonds fashioned into necklaces of lordly gems, set with priceless jewels, and graced with lotus petals.
By the will of Śaṅkara, it was fashioned from the finest rubies, rendered wondrous and variegated with various patterns by means of garlands of nets of māṇikya gems.
It was provided with hundreds of staircases fashioned from syamantaka gems, and adorned with beautiful sandalwood sprouts tied with knots of golden thread.
It was most enchanting, encircled by pillars of sapphire, well-refined, and everywhere perfumed with fragrant breezes.
There, Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, beheld Śaṅkara accompanied by Ambā, extending for a thousand yojanas and well-filled with many attendants.
And he was dwelling in the Middle Country, surrounded by moons and stars, seated upon a variegated lion-throne fashioned from priceless jewels.
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a garland of jewels, his entire body smeared with ashes, he held a toy lotus.
And he saw him before him, smiling with joy at the singing and dancing.
He was peaceful, with a serene mind, the beloved of Umā, and greatly radiant; he had consumed the fragrant betel offered by the Goddess.
He was served with supreme devotion by the Gaṇas with white whisks, and praised by the Siddhas whose necks were bowed low in devotion.
The Supreme Lord, who transcends all qualities, the progenitor of the three gods, the all-pervading, the thought-free, the formless, yet who assumes form by His own will—Śiva.
[He who is] without guile, unborn, and without beginning; the Lord of Māyā, higher than the highest; always the supreme master, even beyond both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Having thus beheld him who was so distinguished, most perfect, and impartial, Viṣṇu and Brahmā bowed down with palms joined in reverence and offered praise.
Viṣṇu and Vidhi said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Brahman, Lord of all, O one beyond the three qualities, O undisturbed one, O Lord, progenitor of the three gods!"
We have come to you for refuge; O All-pervading Lord, protect us who are suffering, afflicted by Śaṅkhacūḍa, distressed, and though we have a protector, yet deprived of one, O Supreme Lord.
This world which is presided over is known as Goloka; its presiding lord is this all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, who is himself presided over by you.
Then Sudāmā, the foremost of his attendants, being impelled by fate and cursed by Rādhā, became the Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa.
O Śambhu, expelled by him and oppressed on all sides, the gods, deprived of their authority, wander upon the surface of the earth.
Without you, he cannot be slain by any of the inhabitants of the three heavens; therefore, O Great Lord, slay him and bring happiness to the worlds.

You alone are the truth, devoid of qualities, infinite, and possessed of infinite prowess; yet, while possessing qualities, you are the manifestation of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the Supreme Person (puruṣa).

O Lord, at the time of creation, you are Brahmā, the creator, through the quality of rajas; through the quality of sattva, you are Viṣṇu, the protector who effects the preservation of the three worlds.

In the dissolution, Rudra is the agent of the world’s destruction through the quality of *tamas*; in the state beyond the three qualities (*niṣtraiguṇya*), he is called Śiva, the fourth state (*turya*) whose nature is light.
Through your initiation, you are the protector of the cows in Goloka; and Kṛṣṇa, staying within your cow-pen, sports day and night.
You are the cause of all, the Lord, the supreme Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; you are changeless, the eternal witness, the Supreme Self, and the Sovereign Lord.
He is the helper of the poor and the helpless, the protector of the destitute, the kinsman of the lowly, the Lord of the three worlds, and one who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge.
Lift us up, O Lord of Gaurī; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! We are dependent on you, O Master; do as you wish.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, having spoken thus to those two gods, Hari and Brahmā then ceased, bowing to Śiva with joined palms in a humble manner.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the God of Gods," in the Śaṅkhacūḍavadha section of the fifth book (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard the words of Hari and Viṣṇu, who were deeply distressed, Śambhu laughed and spoke with a voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud.
Śiva said: O Hara, my child, O Brahmā, abandon all fear entirely; welfare shall undoubtedly come to pass regarding that which has arisen from Śaṅkhacūḍa.
O Lord, I know in truth the entire account of Śaṅkhacūḍa and formerly that of Sudāmā, the cowherd who was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa.
By my command, Hṛṣīkeśa, having assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa, resides in the beautiful cow-pen within Goloka, which is presided over by me.
Thinking "I am independent," he formerly considered that to be his own delusion; thus deluded, he acted as if acting according to his own will and engaged in many diversions.
Seeing that exceedingly fierce delusion, I myself, by means of my own illusory power, withdrew their right understanding and caused them to be cursed.
Having thus performed that divine play, I withdrew my illusory power (māyā); at that time, those wise ones, endowed with knowledge, were liberated from delusion.
Having approached me, they became humble and bowed down to me; with palms joined and heads bowed low, they offered praise with devotion.
With their minds overwhelmed by shame, they related the entire account; distressed, they spoke these words before me: "Save us! Save us!"
Then, being well-pleased with them, I, as Bhava, spoke these words: "O Kṛṣṇa, abandon all fear; you shall all do so by my command."
"I shall always protect you with affection; it will be well for you. All this has come to pass by my will; of this there is no doubt."
Go to your own abode together with Rādhā and your attendants; there is no doubt that he will become a Dānava here in Bhārata.
"I shall indeed lift the curse from you both at the appointed time"; having accepted my word thus with their heads bowed, together with Rādhā, they did so.
The wise Śrī Kṛṣṇa was exceedingly delighted and returned to his own abode; the two [others], intent on my worship, remained there filled with fear.
Realizing that everything was dependent on him and not independent, and considering himself truly his own, that Sudāmā became the lord of the Dānavas due to the curse of Rādhā.
The evil-minded Śaṅkhacūḍa, a hater of the gods who is skilled in the ways of dharma, constantly oppresses the entire host of deities with great force.
Deluded by my māyā, he has taken extremely wicked mantra-practitioners as his allies; let him quickly abandon that fear now that I am indeed the ruler.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, while Śiva was thus recounting this narrative in the presence of Hari and Brahmā, another event occurred; listen to that as well.
In that very interval, Kṛṣṇa, together with Rādhā, his attendants, and the virtuous cowherds, arrived to propitiate the Lord Śambhu.
Having bowed to the Lord with true devotion and having approached Hari with respect, he stood there by the command of Śiva, being honored by Brahmā with affection.
Then, having bowed again to Śambhu and having realized the true nature of Śiva, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, freed from delusion, praised him with palms joined in reverence.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Brahman, refuge of the virtuous! Forgive my transgression and be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
From you, O Śarva, everything arises; in you, O Maheśvara, everything resides. You are everything, O Lord of all; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
You are the supreme light, manifest, all-pervading, and eternal; with you as our protector, O Lord of Gaurī, we are all truly protected.
Considering myself superior to all, I lived relying on delusion; as a result, I have obtained this curse and become a left-handed one.
O Lord, that cowherd named Sudāmā, who was my foremost attendant, has entered a demonic womb due to the curse of Rādhā.
Lift us up, O Lord of the Fort; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Grant us release from this curse today; protect us who have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, together with Rādhā, ceased speaking; and there, Śiva, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, became pleased.
Śrī Śiva said: O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Gopīs, cast off your fear and be happy; O dear one, all this has been performed by me as I have bestowed my grace upon you.
May prosperity be yours; go to your own supreme abode, and always remain vigilant in your own office.
Dwell as you please, having recognized me as the Supreme beyond the supreme; perform your own task without distraction, together with Rādhā and your attendants.
In the excellent Vārāha-kalpa, having experienced the power of the curse together with the youthful Rādhā, he will indeed return once more to his own [abode].
O Kṛṣṇa, that Sudāmā who was indeed your attendant and most dear friend has now taken birth in a Dānava womb and is truly afflicting the world.
Due to the power of Rādhā’s curse, that Dānava, an enemy of the gods, known by the name Śaṅkhacūḍa, was a follower of the Daityas who oppressed the deities.
Driven out by him, the gods including Indra were constantly tormented; deprived of their offices and disfigured, they all fled in the ten directions.
Brahmā and Acyuta have indeed come for that purpose as my refuge; I shall effect their liberation from suffering, of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to Kṛṣṇa, Śaṅkara addressed Hari and Vidhi with respect and spoke these words that destroy all suffering.
Śiva said: O Hara, O Vidhi, listen to these words of mine with affection. Go quickly, O fathers, fearlessly for the sake of the gods' joy.
To Rudra, the dweller of Kailāsa, who is my own form, perfect and supreme, who has manifested for the sake of the gods' mission while assuming a distinct form.
For this very purpose, the Lord, who is my own form and most perfect, dwells on Mount Kailāsa by the power of his devotees, O Hari.
There is no difference between me and you; he alone is to be served by both of you, as well as by all beings, moving and unmoving, including the gods and others, at all times.
The man who creates a division between us two shall go to hell; even in this world, he shall suffer great misery, deprived of sons and grandsons.
Having bowed down again and again to the Lord of Durgā who had spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rādhā and his attendants, departed for his own abode.
O Vyāsa, Hari and Brahmā, filled with joy and freed from fear, bowed repeatedly to the Lord and quickly departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Having arrived there and reported the entire account to the gods, Brahmā and Viṣṇu took them with them and went to Mount Kailāsa.
There he beheld the Lord Maheśāna, the beloved of Pārvatī, whose body was dedicated to the protection of the distressed, and who is the leader of the gods endowed with all attributes.
With hands joined and shoulders bowed, all of them, endowed with humility, praised him with devotion as before, their voices faltering.
The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord of Girijā, Śaṅkara! We have come to you for refuge; protect the gods who are overwhelmed by fear.
Slay Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Dānavas and the destroyer of the gods; by him the gods have been distressed and defeated in battle.
Deprived of their authority, they wander about like men on earth; for the world of the gods became difficult for them to behold out of fear of that.
O Savior of the Wretched, Ocean of Compassion, deliver the gods from this peril! O Great Lord, slay that lord of the Dānavas and [thus save] Śakra from fear.
Having heard these words of the gods, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke with a smile in a voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud.
Śrī Śaṅkara said: "O Hara, O Vidhi, O gods, go certainly to your own abodes; I shall slay Śaṅkhacūḍa along with his hosts—of this there is no doubt."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Maheśa, which were like nectar, they all became exceedingly joyful, considering the Dānava already as good as slain.
Then Hari went to Vaikuṇṭha and Vidhi to Satyaloka; having prostrated before Maheśa, the gods and others likewise departed for their own abodes.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction of Śiva," in the section on the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, within the fifth book (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord Mahārudra, the refuge of the virtuous and the destroyer of wicked time, resolved in his mind to slay Śaṅkhacūḍa according to the will of the gods.
Having made Citraratha, the desired lord of the Gandharvas, his messenger, he joyfully dispatched him quickly to the presence of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
By the command of the Lord of All, that messenger went to that city, which was superior to the city of Mahendra and more magnificent than the abode of Kubera.
Having gone there, he beheld in its midst the excellent abode of Śaṅkhacūḍa, resplendent with twelve doors and provided with gatekeepers.
Having seen that excellent gateway, Puṣpadanta beheld it and, free from fear, related the entire account to the gatekeeper.
Having passed through that gate, he entered joyfully into the interior, which was exceedingly beautiful, delightful, spacious, and well-adorned.
Having gone there, he beheld that Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Danujas, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the midst of a circle of heroes.
He was surrounded by lords of the Dānavas and served by thirty million others, as well as hundreds of millions more who wandered about with weapons in their hands.
Seeing him in such a state, Puṣpadanta was filled with wonder and recounted the events of the battle as they had been told by Śaṅkara.
Puṣpadanta said: "O Lord of Kings, O Master, I am a messenger of Śiva named Puṣpadanta. Listen to what has been spoken by Śaṅkara himself; I shall tell it to you."
Śiva said: "Give up the kingdom and the authority over the gods now; otherwise, engage in battle with me, the supreme one, for the sake of the virtuous."
"The gods have sought refuge with me, the Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, who is the refuge of the virtuous. Enraged, I shall slay you as Mahārudra, without a doubt."
I am Hara; indeed, I have granted fearlessness to all the gods. I am the wielder of the rod of punishment for the wicked and am truly affectionate toward those who seek refuge.
"Will you give up the kingdom, or will you engage in battle? O Lord of Dānavas, reflect well upon these two options and tell me the truth."
Puṣpadanta said: "O lord of the Danujas, that which was spoken by Maheśa has been reported to you by me; the word of Śambhu is never false."
"I wish to go quickly to my master Hara; having gone there, I shall tell Śambhu what you have said here to me—please tell me that."
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus heard the words of the virtuous lord Puṣpadanta, the messenger of Śiva, the king laughed and spoke to him.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "I shall not give the kingdom to the gods; the earth is to be enjoyed by heroes. O Rudra, I shall grant you battle for your partiality toward the gods."
That hero upon whom one might advance would be the lowest on earth; therefore, O Rudra, I shall undoubtedly go to you first.
"I shall come at dawn after considering a heroic expedition; you go and speak these words of mine to Rudra."
Having heard these words of Śaṅkhacūḍa, that messenger of Śambhu laughed heartily and spoke haughtily to the lord of the Dānavas.
O Indra among kings, even other hosts are not fit to stand before Śaṅkara; how much less so can he [stand] before him?
Therefore, you must restore the offices of the gods in their entirety; otherwise, O enemy, go to the netherworld if you wish to live.
Know him, O best of Dānavas, to be our common immortal; for Śaṅkara is indeed the Supreme Self, the Lord of all lords.
All the gods, headed by Indra, along with the Prajāpatis, the Siddhas, the Munis, and the lords of the serpents, always abide by his command.
He is indeed the Lord of both Hari and Brahmā; for He is both devoid of attributes and possessed of attributes, by the mere contraction of whose eyebrows the dissolution of all occurs.
He is the perfect form of Śiva, the cause of the destruction of the worlds, the refuge of the virtuous, the slayer of the wicked, changeless, and higher than the highest.
O bull among Dānavas, even he who is the sovereign of Brahmā and the Great Lord of Hari does not disregard his command.
O Indra among kings, what is the use of much speaking? Having reflected with your mind, know Rudra to be Maheśāna, the Supreme Brahman whose nature is consciousness.
"Give back the kingdom and all the offices of the gods; in this way, my dear, it will be well for you, otherwise there will be danger."
Santkumāra said: Having heard this, the powerful lord of the Dānavas, Śaṅkhacūḍa, deluded by destiny, spoke to that messenger of Śiva.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "I shall not of my own accord give up my kingdom nor my authority; this is my firm resolve. Without a battle with Maheśa, I tell you this truth."
The entire world, including all that is mobile and immobile, should be understood as dependent upon time; for everything arises from time and perishes through time.
Go to Śaṅkara Rudra and tell him exactly what I have said; let him do what is appropriate, and do not engage us in further talk.
Sanatkumāra said: O excellent sage, having spoken thus, that messenger of Śiva went to his own master and related the matter exactly as it was, O Puṣpadanta.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, the king of the gods, Giriśa, then spoke with anger to Vīrabhadra and the other Gaṇas.
Rudra said: "O Vīrabhadra, O Nandin, O Kṣetrapālas and the eight Bhairavas! All you Gaṇas are equipped with armor, armed with weapons, and full of strength."

By my command, let them both depart today along with the two princes; let Bhadrakālī also set out for battle with her own army. For the sake of slaying Śaṅkhacūḍa, I myself shall depart this very day with all haste.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus issued his command, Maheśāna set forth accompanied by his army; all the hosts of heroes followed him, filled with great joy.
In the meantime, Skanda and Gaṇeśa, the commanders of all the armies, equipped with weapons, armored, and joyful, exerted themselves in the presence of Śiva.
Vīrabhadra, Nandin, Mahākāla, Subhadraka, Viśālākṣa, Bāṇa, Piṅgalākṣa, and Vikampana.
Virūpa, Vikṛti, Maṇibhadra, Bāṣkala, the one named Kapila, Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, Vikara, and Tāmralocana.
Kālankara, Balībhadra, Kālajihva, Kuṭīcara, Balonmatta, Raṇaślāghya, Durjaya, and likewise Durgama.
These and others are the excellent lords of the armies of the Gaṇeśas; I shall now describe their number—listen with careful attention.
Śaṅkhakarṇa, the crusher of enemies, was joined by ten crores; and Kekarākṣa, the deformed one, was accompanied by eight crores.
Viśākha was with sixty-four, Pāriyātrika with nine, and the glorious Sarvāntaka as well as Vikṛtānana were each with six.
For Jālaka was the leader of a host with twelve crores; the illustrious Samada was the leader of seven, and Dundubha was the leader of eight.
Karālākṣa is accompanied by five, while the excellent Saṃdāraka is with six; likewise, Kaṇḍuka and Kuṇḍaka are here with ten million times ten million.
Viṣṭambha, the most excellent of all beings, is a leader of a host of eight here; Pippala is with a thousand, and Saṃnāda is likewise.
Āveśana was surrounded by eight [crores], as was Candratāpana; Mahākeśa was surrounded by a thousand crores of Gaṇapas.
The hero Kuṇḍī was with twelve [attendants], as was the auspicious Parvataka; Kāla and Kālaka were each with a hundred, as was Mahākāla.
Agnika with a hundred crores, Agnimukha with one crore, Āditya with half a crore, and likewise Ghanāvaha.
Sanāha was with a hundred, as was Kumuda with ten million; Amogha and Kokila were each with a hundred million, and so was Sumantraka.
Kākapāda [ruled] with sixty crores, and likewise Saṃtānaka with sixty; Mahābala with nine, and Madhupiṅgala with five.
Nīla, the lord of gods, with ninety [crores], and likewise Pūrṇabhadra; and Caturvaktra of great strength, with seven crores.
Then, twenty thousand times a hundred crores of those heroes likewise arrived there for the festival of battle.
Vīrabhadra was accompanied by a thousand koṭis of Bhūtas, three koṭis of Pramathas, sixty-four [koṭis] of Lomajas, and three koṭis more.
Kāṣṭhārūḍha, Sukeśa, Vṛṣabha, and the blessed Virūpākṣa, as well as Sanātana, [are each accompanied] by sixty-four [goddesses].
Tālaketu, the six-faced one, and the powerful five-faced one; likewise Saṃvartaka, Caitra, and Laṅkulīśa, the Lord himself.
Lokāntaka, the radiant-souled one, and likewise the lord Daityāntaka; the glorious god Bhṛṅgīriṭi, who is dear to the God of gods.
Aśani and Bhānuka likewise with sixty-four thousand; Kaṅkāla, Kālaka, Kāla, Nandin, and Sarvāntaka as well.
These and other innumerable leaders of hosts, possessed of great strength, set out joyfully for the sake of battle with Śaṅkhacūḍa, free from fear.
All of them had a thousand arms, wore crowns of matted hair, were adorned with crescent moons, possessed blue throats, and had three eyes.
All were adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads and likewise smeared with sacred ash; they were further embellished with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crowns, and other finery.
Resembling Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, they were endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and possessed the brilliance of ten million suns; they were highly skilled in the art of warfare.
O Sage, some move upon the earth, some move in the netherworld (pātāla), some move through the sky, and some move in the seven heavens.
O divine sage, what is the use of speaking at length? All the attendants of Śiva who dwell in all the worlds went forth for battle against the Dānavas.
The eight fierce Bhairavas, the eleven Rudras who are swift, the eight Vasus, Vāsava, and those twelve Ādityas—[all these] quickly [attained their state].
Agni and Candra, Viśvakarman and the two Aśvins, Kubera and Yama, as well as Nirṛti and Nalakūbara.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, Budha and Maṅgala, as well as the other planets, the powerful Kāmadeva, and Maheśa [were present].
Ugradaṃṣṭra, Ugradaṇḍa, Koraṭa, and Koṭabha; and the goddess Bhadrakālī herself, the great sovereign Maheśvarī with her hundred arms.
Seated upon a celestial chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels, she was clothed in red garments and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Dancing, laughing, and singing with joy in a melodious voice, she granted fearlessness to her own people and struck fear into her enemies.
She bore a formidable, highly flickering tongue extending for a yojana, as well as a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a sword, a shield, a bow, and arrows.
A skull-bowl, circular in shape and deep, extending for a yojana; a trident touching the sky, and a spear extending for a yojana.
A mallet, a pestle, a spear, a sword, a formidable shield, the Vaiṣṇava weapon, the Vāruṇa weapon, the Vāyavya weapon, and the serpent-noose.
The Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Gāndharva, the Brahmāstra, the Gāruḍa, as well as the Pārjanya, the Pāśupata, the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon, and the Pārvata.
The Mahāvīra, the Saura, the Kālakāla, the Mahānala, the Maheśvara weapon, the Yāmya, the Daṇḍa, and likewise the Saṃmohana.
Then she held in all her hands the powerful divine weapon *astra*, the supreme hundredfold divine weapons, and various other [missiles] as well.
Having arrived, she stood there together with thirty million yoginīs and thirty million formidable ḍākinīs.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and kinnaras;
Surrounded by them, Skanda bowed to the moon-crested Lord and, at his command, remained by his father’s side as an attendant.
Then Śambhu, having assembled his entire army, set out for battle with Śaṅkhacūḍa, O Rudra, being entirely fearless.
At the foot of a beautiful banyan tree on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river, Mahādeva remained there for the sake of delivering the gods.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Mahādeva’s March for Battle," in the Śaṅkhacūḍavadha section of the fifth book (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O son of Vidhi, O sage of great intelligence, may you live for many years! You have related this most magnificent and wonderful life-story of the moon-crested Lord.
When Śivadūta had departed from there, what did the powerful Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa do? Tell me that truth in great detail.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, after the messenger had departed from there, the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa went inside and spoke this news to Tulasī.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: O Goddess, having heard from the mouth of Śambhu’s messenger that I am prepared for battle, I am going to fight; grant me your firm command.
Having spoken thus, that wise man, through various means of awakening his beloved, sported with joy, disregarding Śaṅkara.
Immersed in an ocean of bliss, that couple sported throughout the night with various arts of love and hundreds of endearing caresses.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed his morning duties, and having first completed his daily rites, he bestowed infinite gifts.
Having made his son the lord of kings over all gifts and charities, and having entrusted his wife, the kingdom, and all prosperity to his son, he departed.
The king consoled his beloved wife as she wept again, and having engaged her in various conversations, he dissuaded her from following him on her journey.
Having respectfully summoned his own heroic general, he, being prepared and intent on waging war, gave him his command.
Śaṅkhacūḍa said: "O General, today let all these heroes, who delight in battle and have prepared themselves for every task, go forth to the fray."
Let the sixty-eight heroic Daityas and Dānavas, skilled in battle, quickly set forth with their armies, powerful Kaṅkas, and free from fear.
Indeed, let fifty families of asuras, each possessing the prowess of ten million, go forth for battle against Śambhu, the partisan of the gods.
And let a hundred families of the Dhaumras, fully armored, quickly go forth for the sake of battle at my command, by the grace of Śambhu.
Let the Kālakeyas, the Mauryas, the Daurhṛdas, and the Kālakas set out fully prepared for battle at my command, along with Rudra.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus issued his command, the lord of the Asuras, the mighty Indra of the Dānavas, set forth with a vast army, surrounded by many thousands.
And his commander-in-chief was an expert in the science of war, a great chariot-warrior, a mighty hero, and the foremost among car-fighters in battle.
Accompanied by three hundred thousand akṣauhiṇīs, he indeed established his camp; then, inspiring terror in the brave, he emerged from the camp for battle.

Having ascended a celestial chariot fashioned from the finest jewels, he set forth for battle, placing his circle of elders at the forefront. He went to the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā river, where the auspicious Akṣayavaṭa tree stands, and to Siddhāśrama, the field of perfection for the Siddhas that bestows complete success.
Then there is the abode of Kapila in the sacred field of Bhārata, situated to the east of the western ocean and to the west of Malaya.
To the north of Śrīśaila and to the south of Gandhamādana, it is five yojanas in width and a hundred times that in length.
In Bhārata, there is the delightful river Puṣpabhadrā, which resembles pure crystal and bestows great merit; it is full of water and is the Sarasvatī.
The beloved wife of the Salt Ocean, ever endowed with good fortune and residing in Sarasvatī, she emerged from the Himalayas.
Keeping Gomanta to her left, she entered the western ocean; having gone there, Śaṅkhacūḍa beheld the army of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s Departure," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having remained there, the lord of the Dānavas made a highly wise messenger his envoy and dispatched him to Śaṅkara, the great lord of the Dānavas.
Having gone there, the messenger beheld Candrabhāla seated at the foot of a banyan tree, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Having assumed a yogic posture, with a smiling gaze joined by the mudrā, [he saw him] resembling pure crystal, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
Holding a trident and a battle-axe, clothed in a tiger-skin garment, the peaceful lover of Gaurī with three eyes, who removes death from his devotees.
To the bestower of the fruits of austerities, the creator of all prosperity, the one easily pleased with a gracious countenance, and the granter of grace to his devotees.

To Viśvanātha, the seed of the universe, the universal form, and that which is born from the universe; the sustainer of the universe, the creator of the universe, and the cause of the dissolution of the universe.
He is the cause of causes, the one who enables crossing the ocean of hell; he is the bestower of knowledge, the seed of knowledge, and the eternal bliss of knowledge.
Having descended from his chariot and beheld him, that messenger of the lord of the Dānavas bowed his head in salutation to Śaṅkara and Kumāra.
To his left was Bhadrakālī, and Skanda stood before him; Kālī, Skanda, and Śaṅkara bestowed blessings upon him for the welfare of the world.
Then that messenger of Śaṅkhacūḍa, an expert in the supreme scriptures, bowed to Śaṅkara, joined his palms, and spoke these auspicious words.
The messenger said: "I am the messenger of Śaṅkhacūḍa, come here into your presence. O Maheśvara, tell me the truth: what do you desire now?"
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the blessed Lord Mahādeva, with a gracious soul, spoke to him.
Mahādeva said: Listen, O messenger of great wisdom, to my words which bring happiness; having reflected upon it without dispute, this must be told to him.
Brahmā, the ordainer of the worlds and father of Dharma, is the knower of righteousness; Marīci is his son, and Kaśyapa is known as his offspring.
With affection, Dakṣa gave him thirteen of his own daughters; among them was the virtuous Danu, who increased his good fortune.
Danu had four sons who were Dānavas of intense splendor; among them, one was Vipracitti, possessed of great strength and prowess.
His son was the righteous and highly intelligent Dambha, a lord of the Dānavas; you are his eldest son, a virtuous soul and a sovereign of the Dānavas.
Formerly you were a cowherd boy, a protector of cows and righteous among cowherds; now, by the curse of Rādhikā, you have become a lord of the Dānavas.
Although you have entered the womb of a Dānava, in reality you are not a Dānava; knowing your own past vow, abandon now your enmity toward the gods.
Do not harbor malice toward them; enjoy your own station with respect. Having reflected upon it, do not rule the kingdom excessively or with agitation.
Give back the kingdom to the gods and preserve my favor, O Dānava; dwell happily in your own kingdom, and let the gods remain in their own stations.
Enough with hostility toward living beings; what need is there to speak of treachery against the gods? All those born of Kaśyapa’s lineage are of noble birth and pure in their deeds.
Whatever sins there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sin incurred by betraying one's kinsmen.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus, Śaṅkara spoke many auspicious discourses based on the Śruti and Smṛti to him, awakening him to the supreme knowledge.
Instructed by Śaṅkhacūḍa, that messenger, the best among those who know logic, spoke these words with humility, deluded by destiny.
The messenger said: "O Lord, that which has been spoken by you is not otherwise; those words are exactly so. However, let my report, which is true and according to the facts, be heard."
"O Lord, you have just now stated that there is great sin in betraying one's kinsmen; tell me, is this not also the case for the Īśas, Asuras, and the gods?"
If you say "of all," then I shall speak of that after due reflection; state the final conclusion therein today and dispel my doubt.
O Maheśvara, why did that wielder of the discus sever the heads of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the two foremost Daityas, in the ocean of dissolution?
O Giriśa, why did you, renowned as one who sides with the gods, engage in battle with Tripuras and reduce them to ashes?
Having seized all his possessions, Bali was sent away; and at the entrance to Sutala and the other regions, Gadādhara stands to rescue him.
How was Hiraṇyākṣa, along with his brothers, slain by the gods? And how were the asuras, such as Śumbha and others, struck down by the gods?
Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, the nectar was consumed by the gods; we were the ones who bore the hardship therein, while they all enjoyed the fruit.
This universe is a plaything of Time, the Supreme Self; whenever He bestows it upon anyone, that person then attains sovereignty over it.
The enmity between the gods and the dānavas is constant and perpetual; their defeat and victory are subject to time and occur in succession.
And in the event of a conflict between these two, your departure would be fruitless; for that [conflict] does not please you, the Lord, who are impartial toward all who are related to you.
This shamelessness of yours, who are the high-souled lord of all gods and asuras, is now to contend with us.
Since fame increases through victory and loss occurs through defeat, you should reflect upon this with your mind, as it is the opposite for you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words, the three-eyed Lord laughed and spoke to the lord of the Dānavas in a manner that was both appropriate and sweet.
Maheśa said: We are indeed dependent upon our devotees and are never independent; by His will we perform our actions, nor do we belong to the faction of anyone else.
In the past, at the request of Brahmā, even Hari first engaged in battle with the two foremost demons, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, in the ocean of universal dissolution.
In former times, at the request of the gods, he—acting for the welfare of his devotees—brought about the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu for the sake of Prahlāda.
Furthermore, I have previously heard that the battle with Tripuras, which resulted in their being reduced to ashes, was carried out by me at the request of the gods.
In ancient times, at the request of the gods, there was a battle between Sarveśvarī, the mother of all, and Śumbha and his followers; their slaughter was carried out by her.
Even now, all the thirty gods went to Brahmā for refuge; that Lord Hari, along with the gods, has come to me for refuge.
O messenger, it was indeed due to the power of the prayers of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others that I, the lord of the gods, went forth for the sake of battle.
For you are indeed the foremost of the attendants of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa; and among all those Daityas who have been slain, there are none at all who are equal to you.
O King, what great shame is there for me in fighting with you? I am the lord sent here with humility for the sake of the gods' mission.
Go, O Śaṅkhacūḍa, and convey these words of mine to him; let him do what is appropriate here, for I shall accomplish the task of the gods.
Having spoken thus, Maheśvara Śaṅkara ceased there; the messenger of Śaṅkhacūḍa rose up and went into his presence.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with Śiva’s Messenger" in the Śaṅkhacūḍavadha section of the fifth book, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, within the second part, the Rudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having gone there, that messenger delivered the words of Śiva in full detail, according to the facts, and with the certainty of their true essence.
Having heard that, the powerful Dānava lord Śaṅkhacūḍa, with great joy, accepted the very prospect of battle.
He quickly mounted his vehicle along with his ministers and commanded his own army for battle against Śaṅkara.
Śiva swiftly dispatched his own army and the gods; though he is the Lord of all, he himself also prepared for battle as if in sport.
The commencement of battle occurred swiftly; musical instruments resounded profusely, and a great clamor as well as the shouts of heroes arose.
O sage, a great battle took place between the gods and the dānavas; there, the hosts of both gods and dānavas fought according to the rules of righteousness.
Mahendra himself fought together with Vṛṣaparvan, and Bhāskara fought with Vipracitti according to the law.
Viṣṇu engaged in a supreme battle with Dambha, Kāla with Kālāsura, and Hutāśana with Gokarṇa.
Kubera was [faced] by Kālakeya, Viśvakarman by Maya, Mṛtyu by Bhayaṅkara, and likewise Yama by Saṃhāra.
Varuṇa was mounted upon Kālambika, Samīraṇa upon Cañcala, Budha upon Ghaṭapṛṣṭha, and Śanaiścara upon Raktākṣa.
Jayanta was born with Ratnasāra, the Vasus with hosts of splendors, the two Aśvins with radiant forms, and Nalakūbara with Dhūmra.
Dharma was [mounted] by Dhuraṃdhara, Maṅgala by Gaṇakākṣa, Vaiśvānara by Śobhākara, and Manmatha by Pipiṭa.
By Gokāmukha, by the Asura named Khaḍga, by Dhūmra, by Saṃhala, and by the powerful Viśva;
With the assistance of Śiva, the twelve Ādityas, led by Palāśa, fought righteously against the other Asuras.
The eleven Mahārudras fought with the eleven terrifying Asuras, who were heroes of great strength and prowess.
Mahāmaṇi fought with Ugracaṇḍa and the others; Candra fought with Rāhu, and Jīva fought with Śukra according to the rules of dharma.
Nandīśvara and all the others, together with the foremost of the Dānavas, fought in a great battle; they have not been mentioned separately in detail.
Then, O Sage, Śambhu stood at the foot of the banyan tree with Kālī’s son, while all the hosts of troops fought incessantly.
Adorned with jewel ornaments and accompanied by ten million givers, Śaṅkhacūḍa dwelt upon a beautiful jeweled throne.
Then a great battle occurred, a crushing conflict between the gods and the asuras; various divine weapons moved about in that great slaughter.
Javelins, spears, and battle-axes; discuses, slings, and lances; mallets, swords, and barbed arrows; iron clubs, pikes, and battle-axes were [arrayed].
Arrows, javelins, swords, and *śataghnīs* by the thousands, as well as *bhiṇḍipālas* and other weapons, shone resplendent in the hands of the heroes.
In that great festival of battle, the heroes there severed each other's heads as both armies roared at one another in the fray.
There were many elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers; various mounts and riders there were completely shattered.
With their arms, thighs, hands, hips, ears, and feet severed; with their banners, arrows, armor, and excellent ornaments cut to pieces.

The earth shone, strewn with the heads of those whose thighs were like the trunks of elephants—heads from which the crowns had been torn away along with the earrings, and which were deprived of all animation by their fury.
With great arms, with ornaments, with severed weapons, and likewise with other limbs, or suddenly with heaps of pearls;
In that battle, warriors running about saw headless trunks with their own eyes, and they leaped up there with their excellent arms raised, holding weapons.
Leaping exceedingly, those heroes of great strength and prowess fought one another there with various weapons and missiles.
Having struck down warriors in battle with gold-tipped arrows, some let out heroic roars like rain-bearing clouds.
With a mass of arrows from all sides, the hero completely covered the heroic warrior along with his chariot and charioteer, just as a cloud covers the sun during the rainy season.
Charging at one another, those who fought in single combat engaged in battle; challenging each other, they advanced forward, piercing one another in their vital organs.
And from all sides, hosts of heroes with various arms, banners, and weapons were seen in that great battle, uttering lion-like roars.
Each one blew his own great-sounding conch shell; there, the great heroes, filled with joy, performed their leaping maneuvers.
Thus, for a very long time, there occurred a great battle between the gods and the dānavas—fierce, formidable, and a source of joy to the heroes.
This is the divine play of the Great Lord Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, by which everything—gods, asuras, and humans—is brought about according to his will.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mutual Combat," in the Śaṅkhacūḍavadha section of the fifth book (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all the hosts of gods, defeated by the Dānavas, fled in fear, their bodies wounded by weapons and missiles.
Turning back, they went for refuge to Śaṅkara, the Lord of All; with voices faltering, they cried out, "Save us! Save us, O Lord of All!"
Seeing the defeat of those gods and others, and hearing their fearful words, that Śaṅkara indeed gave vent to a great rage.
Beholding them with a compassionate gaze, he granted fearlessness to the gods and increased the strength of his own hosts through his splendor.
Then, commanded by Śiva, Skanda, the great hero and son of Hara, fought fearlessly in battle against the hosts of Dānavas.
Having manifested his wrath and uttered a heroic roar, that god who is the slayer of Tāraka slaughtered a hundred akṣauhiṇīs in battle.
The lotus-eyed Kālī caused their blood to flow; having severed their heads, she devoured them instantly.
He then drank the blood of those Dānavas simultaneously and engaged in various kinds of battle, terrifying to both gods and Dānavas.
Taking up a hundred lakhs of lordly elephants and likewise a hundred lakhs of men with a single hand, he playfully cast them into his mouth.
Thousands of headless trunks danced profusely in the battle, and a great tumult arose, terrifying even the cowards.
Again, Skanda, becoming highly enraged, unleashed a rain of arrows and struck down crores of the leaders of the asuras from their positions.
Then the Dānavas, their bodies wounded by the net of Skanda’s arrows, all fled in terror, fearing death.
Vṛṣaparvan, Vipracitti, Daṇḍa, and Vikaṃpana—all of them fought with Skanda one after another in succession.
And Mahāmārī fought on and did not turn her back; yet they became wounded in limb, tormented by the spear of Skanda.
O Sage, victory then belonged to Mahāmārī and Skanda; the kettledrums resounded in heaven and a rain of flowers fell.
Having seen that most terrible and wonderful battle of Skanda, which brought about the destruction of the Dānavas like the dissolution at the end of an aeon according to its very nature.
Seeing that calamity caused by the great pestilence and rooted in destruction, he suddenly became exceedingly enraged and then personally prepared for battle.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, equipped with various weapons and missiles, providing fearlessness to all heroes, and adorned with diverse precious gems.
Amidst the great heroes, Śaṅkhacūḍa proceeded in the midst of the chariot; drawing his bow to his ear, he unleashed a shower of arrows.
That shower of arrows of his, difficult to ward off and terrifying, as well as a most dreadful darkness, arose at the place of slaughter.
All the gods, including Nandīśvara and others, fled; Kārttikeya alone remained at the forefront of the battle.
And for the mountains, serpents, nāgas, and likewise for the trees, the king brought about a rain that was irresistible and terrifying.
Struck by that vision, Skanda, the son of Śiva, became like two suns enveloped by a dense mist.
And he displayed various kinds of his own illusory power as shown by Maya; O best of sages, none of the gods or the Gaṇas perceived it.
At that very moment, the immensely powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa, a master of great illusion, severed his bow with a single divine arrow.
He shattered that divine chariot, cut through the chariot-fenders, and rendered the peacock mangled with a divine weapon.
He hurled a sun-bright, lethal spear at his chest; by that blow, he suddenly fell into a swoon for a moment.
And having regained his composure, Kārtika, the slayer of enemy heroes, mounted his own vehicle, which was fashioned from the finest essence of the best jewels.
Having remembered the feet of Maheśa together with Ambikā, the six-faced one took up his weapons and missiles and waged a fierce battle.
The son of Śiva, with his divine weapon, furiously cut down all the serpents, mountains, trees, and rocks.
He warded off Vahni with a Pārjanya arrow and effortlessly severed both the chariot and the bow of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
He donned his armor, all his weapons, and his crown resplendent with a tiara; he uttered the cry of a hero and roared again and again.
He hurled a spear, radiant as the sun, at the chest of the lord of the Dānavas; by that blow, he fell into a most profound swoon.
Having dispelled that affliction for a mere moment, that one of great strength regained his composure, rose up, and roared like a lion.
With his spear, he struck the mighty Kārttikeya as well; making the unfailing weapon bestowed by the Creator effective, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Kālī took him up in her lap and brought him into the presence of Śiva; and Śiva, too, by means of his knowledge, restored him to life as a matter of sport.
The powerful son of Śiva gave infinite strength and rose up; he then set his mind once more upon departing from that place.
In the meantime, the heroic and mighty Vīrabhadra fought in battle with the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Whatever weapons the Dānava rained down in battle, the hero effortlessly cut them all apart with his own arrows.
The lord of the Dānavas discharged divine weapons by the hundreds, but the powerful Vīrabhadra cut them down with his arrows.
Then the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa became exceedingly enraged; he struck him on the chest with his spear, and he trembled and fell to the ground.
In an instant, having regained consciousness, Gaṇeśvara rose up; and Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, once again took up his bow.
In the meantime, Kālī went once more to the battlefield, desiring to devour the Dānavas and protect her own people, according to the wish of Kārttikeya.
The heroes followed him, as did Nandīśvara and the others, along with all the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
There were many musical instruments by the hundreds, as well as honey-carriers; furthermore, all the heroes on both sides stood ready once again.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Śaṅkhacūḍa and his Army," within the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second part (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having gone to the battlefield, she indeed let out a lion’s roar; and by that roar of the goddess, the Dānavas fell into a swoon.
He repeatedly let out a most inauspicious, loud, boisterous laugh; then he drank the honey-wine and danced upon the front lines of battle.
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugradaṇḍā, and Koṭavī drank the honey-wine; and other goddesses there danced in the battle and drank the honey-wine.
Then a great clamor arose among the hosts of gods; all the celestial multitudes and others rejoiced, roaring loudly.
Seeing Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa quickly arrived at the battlefield; the Dānavas were seized with fear, and the king granted them freedom from fear.
Kālī hurled a fire resembling the crest of the fire of universal dissolution; the king swiftly struck it down with ease by means of the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
That goddess immediately hurled the Nārāyaṇa weapon at him; seeing the Dānava to be hostile, that weapon increased in size.
Seeing him, who resembled the crest of the fire of universal dissolution, Śaṅkhacūḍa fell prostrate on the ground like a staff and bowed again and again.
Seeing that weapon withdrawn and the Dānava bowing down, the goddess then discharged the Brahmāstra, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Seeing it blazing forth, he prostrated himself upon the ground; then the lord of the Dānavas warded it off with the Brahmāstra.
Then the enraged lord of the Dānavas, drawing his bow with great force, hurled divine weapons at the Goddess, accompanied by sacred mantras.
He made his meal in battle, opening his mouth wide; he roared with a loud laugh, and the Dānavas were struck with fear.
He hurled a spear a hundred yojanas long at Kālī; she, with a net of divine weapons, shattered it into a hundred pieces.
And he indeed hurled the Vaiṣṇava weapon at Caṇḍikā, but Kālī warded it off with the Māheśvara weapon.
Thus a battle continued for a very long time between them; indeed, all the gods and even the Dānavas became mere spectators.
Then the great goddess Kālī, enraged and resembling Death itself in battle, wrathfully seized a Pāśupata arrow consecrated with mantras.
Just before he was about to hurl it, an incorporeal voice arose to forbid him: "O Goddess, do not indeed cast this weapon at Śaṅkhacūḍa out of anger."
O Caṇḍikā, there is no death even from the unfailing Pāśupata weapon for the hero Śaṅkhacūḍa; therefore, consider another means.
Having heard this, Bhadrakālī did not hurl that weapon; instead, she devoured a hundred lakhs of Dānavas with ease, as if driven by hunger.
The terrifying one rushed with speed toward Śaṅkhacūḍa, but the Dānava warded her off with a fierce divine weapon.
Then the enraged lord of the Dānavas swiftly hurled a sword that was as fierce as the summer sun, with a sharp edge and extremely terrifying.
Seeing him approaching, blazing with rage, Kālī opened her mouth and devoured him as he watched.
The lord of the Dānavas cut down other divine weapons as well; those that had been obtained from before were reduced by him to a hundred fragments.
The great queen went toward him with speed to eat again, but that glorious lord of all siddhas vanished from sight.
With impetuous force, Kālī struck him with her fist; not seeing the Dānava, she shattered his chariot and indeed slew his charioteer.
Then the illusory Śaṅkhacūḍa, arriving swiftly, hurled with great force a discus at Bhadrakālī that resembled the cresting fire of universal destruction.
Then that goddess playfully seized that discus with her left hand and quickly made it into food for her own mouth out of rage.
With great fury and speed, the Goddess struck him with her fist; the lord of the Dānavas reeled and fell into a swoon for a moment.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, that powerful one rose up; out of regard for her as his mother, he did not engage in hand-to-hand combat with her.
Having seized the Dānava and whirled him around again and again, the Goddess, with great fury and speed, hurled him upward.
The powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa leapt up with speed; having descended and bowed to Bhadrakālī, he rose once more.

With a joyful heart, he ascended the celestial chariot fashioned from the finest essence of jewels, which was beautiful and captivating; though not bewildered even in the great battle, he nevertheless boarded it.
Indeed, that Kālikā, driven by hunger, drank the blood of the Dānavas; in the meantime, an unembodied voice arose there.
And now, O Goddess, a hundred thousand of the lords of the Dānavas remain in battle; they are arrogant and roaring together—therefore, enjoy them, O Sovereign.
Do not set your mind on slaying the lord of the Dānavas in battle; O Goddess, it is certain that this Śaṅkhacūḍa is invulnerable to you.
Having heard those words issued from the expanse of the sky, the goddess [beheld] the flesh and likewise the blood of many dānavas.
Having eaten and drunk, Bhadrakālī went into the presence of Śaṅkara and related the account of the battle in its entirety, from beginning to end and in proper sequence.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Kālī’s Battle" in the Śaṅkhacūḍa-vadha section of the Yuddha-khaṇḍa, within the second Rudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O highly wise one, tell me the truth—what did Īśāna do after hearing what Kālī had said, and what did he say? I have a great curiosity.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the words spoken by Kālī, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, Śambhu, the performer of great divine sports, laughed and comforted her.
Having heard the voice from the sky, Śaṅkara, who is proficient in the knowledge of reality, himself went to the battlefield along with his own attendants.
Mounted upon a great bull, accompanied by Vīrabhadra and others, and attended by Bhairavas and Kṣetrapālas who are equal to himself.
Having reached the battlefield and assumed a heroic form, Maheśa shone forth there even more brilliantly; Rudra appeared like Death personified.
Having seen Śiva, Śaṅkhacūḍa descended from his celestial chariot and prostrated himself on the ground with his head in supreme devotion, like a staff.
Having bowed to him, he ascended the celestial chariot by means of yoga; he quickly donned his armor and took up his bow along with its arrows.
A battle between Śiva and the Dānava lasted for a hundred years; it was as fierce as a torrential downpour of arrows from two clouds raining simultaneously.
The great hero Śaṅkhacūḍa discharged dreadful arrows, which Śaṅkara indeed cut down with ease by means of his own volleys of shafts.
Then Mahārudra, the three-eyed one, the punisher of the wicked and the refuge of the virtuous, struck his limbs with showers of weapons out of anger.
The swift Dānava, seizing a sharp sword and a shield, struck Vṛṣa, the excellent vehicle of Śiva, upon the head.
When his mount was struck, Rudra effortlessly severed his sword and his brilliantly shining shield with a razor-sharp arrow.
When his shield was severed, that asura then hurled a spear; Hara split it in two with his own arrow as it came toward him.
Inflamed with anger, the Dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa hurled his discus; but Hara suddenly pulverized it with a blow from his fist.
Whirling his mace with force, he hurled it at Hara; but it was suddenly shattered by Śambhu and reduced to ashes.
Then, taking up an axe in his hand, Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Dānavas, agitated by rage, rushed toward Hara with great speed.
Having drawn back his flood of arrows, Śaṅkara effortlessly felled that asura, who held an axe in his hand, swiftly to the surface of the earth.
Then, regaining consciousness in an instant and mounting his excellent chariot, he shone, pervading the entire sky while grasping divine weapons and arrows.
Upon seeing him approaching, Hara respectfully sounded his hand-drum and also made the unbearable twang of his bowstring.
The Lord Giriśa filled the quarters with the sound of his horn and roared himself, terrifying the asuras at that time.
Having caused the great elephants to be stripped of their pride by his mighty roars, the Lord of Bulls suddenly filled the sky, the earth, and all the directions.
Leaping up with great force, he struck the earth and the sky with his two hands; by that sound, the previous roars were cast away.
The field-protector let out a most inauspicious, loud, and piercing laugh, and Bhairava too raised a great roar in that great battle.
A great and terrifying clamor arose in the midst of the battle; then, the cry of "hero! resounded everywhere throughout the ranks of the hosts.
All the Dānavas were terrified by those harsh and fearsome sounds; hearing them, the mighty lord of the Dānavas became exceedingly enraged.
When Hara cried out, "Stay, stay, O evil-minded one!", the gods and those Gaṇas quickly exclaimed, "Victory! Victory! to him.
Then, having arrived, that son of Dambha, possessed of great prowess, hurled at Rudra a spear that was exceedingly terrifying with its garlands of flames.
As she was proceeding with the radiance of a mass of fire, she was quickly repelled by Kṣetrapāla, who arrived at the battle with a great meteor produced from his mouth.
Once again, a great battle commenced between Śiva and the Dānava; the earth and the heavens, along with the mountains and the waters of the oceans and lakes, trembled.
Then Śambhu cut down the arrows released by Dambhi, and he [Dambhi] in turn cut down the thousands of fierce arrows discharged by him by the hundreds with his own shafts.
Then Śambhu, enraged, struck him with his trident; unable to endure that blow, he immediately fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then, in an instant, that asura regained consciousness and, having taken up his bow, struck Rudra and all those others with arrows.
Having fashioned ten thousand arms, the powerful Śaṅkhacūḍa suddenly covered Śaṅkara with ten thousand discuses.
Then the enraged Rudra, lord of Durgā and destroyer of Durgā’s afflictions, swiftly cut those discuses to pieces with his own supreme arrows.
Then, suddenly and with great speed, that Dānava, surrounded by a vast army, seized his mace and rushed toward Hara to slay him.
As he charged forward, Hara, the enraged destroyer of the pride of the wicked, cut off his mace with a sharp-edged sword.
When his own mace was severed, the Danava became exceedingly enraged; the radiant one seized a flaming trident that was unbearable for his enemies.
As Sudarśana approached the lord of the Dānavas with a trident in hand, Hara swiftly pierced him in the heart with his own trident.
A supreme being emerged from the heart of Śaṅkhacūḍa, which had been pierced by the trident; the powerful one cried out, "Stay! Stay! to him.
As he was quickly departing, Bhīma laughed aloud and then severed his head with a sword; it fell to the earth.
Then, opening her mouth wide in fury, Kālī devoured those many asuras, violently crushing their necks with her fierce fangs.
Kṣetrapāla, agitated with rage, devoured many other Daityas; some perished, severed by his terrible weapons, while others were mangled.
The wise Vīrabhadra destroyed many others out of wrath, and Nandīśvara slew many other harassers of the immortals.
Thus, having donned their armor in great anger, those many heroic hosts then destroyed numerous Daityas and Asuras who were the oppressors of the gods.

In this manner, a great portion of his army perished there; many other heroes, overwhelmed by fear, fled in all directions. Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaughter of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s Army," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having seen his own army—its foremost and most numerous divisions—as well as those heroes equal to his own life, slain, the Dānava became exceedingly enraged.
He spoke these words to Śambhu: "I shall remain; stand firm in battle! What is the use of slaying these today? Engage in combat face-to-face."
Having spoken thus, O Sage, that lord of the Dānavas, having donned his armor and made a firm resolve, went forth into battle toward Śaṅkara.
The Dānava hurled divine weapons at Mahārudra and unleashed a rain of arrows, just as a cloud pours down a rain of water.
He created various illusions that were invisible yet terrifying to behold, and which were inconceivable even to all the most excellent hosts of gods.
Seeing them there, Śaṅkara effortlessly discharged his divine Māheśvara weapon, which destroys all illusions.
By his splendor, her illusions were then swiftly destroyed; even those very divine weapons became devoid of luster.
Then, in the battle, the mighty Maheśāna, for the sake of slaying him, suddenly seized a trident that was irresistible even to those of great splendor.
At that very moment, an incorporeal voice arose to prevent him: "O Śaṅkara, cast aside the trident; otherwise, listen now to my prayer."
Indeed, you are capable in every way of destroying the universe in an instant; O Lord, what need is there now for a single demon, Śaṅkhacūḍa?
Nevertheless, O Lord, the boundary of the Vedas must not be destroyed by you; listen to it, O Mahādeva, and make it truly bear fruit.
As long as this supreme and most formidable armor of Hari remains in his hand, and as long as the virtue of Satī persists in his wife Satyā, [so long shall he remain invincible].
O Śaṅkara, O Lord, make the word of Brahmā true: that for this Śaṅkhacūḍa there shall be neither old age nor death.
Having heard this voice from the sky, Hari then replied, "So be it"; and by the will of Hari, Viṣṇu, the refuge of the virtuous, arrived and gave him his command.
Then Viṣṇu, the best among the wielders of illusion, assuming the guise of an aged brāhmaṇa, approached Śaṅkhacūḍa and spoke to him.
The old brahmin said: "O Lord of Danavas, give alms to me who have now arrived."
I shall not speak now openly, O you who are compassionate toward the distressed; I will speak to you later, and you will again make it true.
The king of kings, with a serene face and eyes, said, "Om"; and the man, seeking armor, said deceitfully, "I am here."
Having heard that, the lord of the Dānavas—who was devoted to Brahmanas, truthful in speech, and powerful—gave that divine armor, which was as dear to him as his own life, to the Brahmin.
Having thus assumed this armor through his illusory power, Hari indeed took on the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa and went toward Tulasī.
Having gone there, Hari, the Lord who is skilled in illusion, quickly performed the infusion of his seed into her womb for the sake of the gods' purpose.
In the meantime, the Lord, urging Śambhu with his own words, seized a blazing trident for the sake of slaying Śaṅkhacūḍa.
That spear, named Vijaya, belonging to Śaṅkara, the Supreme Soul, shone forth, illuminating all directions as well as heaven and earth.
Resembling the sun at midday or the cresting flames of the fire of universal destruction, it is impossible to ward off, invincible, unfailing, and a slayer of enemies.
A most fierce wheel of splendors, consisting of all weapons, missiles, and arrows, it was unbearable and terrifying to all the gods and asuras alike.
Having effortlessly assumed the form of the entire Brahmāṇḍa for the sake of its withdrawal, the Supreme Being remained there, blazing intensely as one unified mass.
A thousand *dhanus* in length and a hundred *hasta*s in breadth, it is the very nature of Jīva and Brahman, eternal in form and uncreated.
By the command of Śiva, that trident, having fallen in an instant upon the crown of Śaṅkhacūḍa as it was whirling in the sky, quickly reduced him to ashes.
Then the trident, having swiftly encircled Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, departed through the sky with the speed of a Brahmin’s thought, having accomplished its purpose.
Kettledrums resounded in heaven; Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang; sages and gods offered praise, and throngs of Apsarases danced.
A continuous rain of flowers fell upon Śiva; Hari, Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, as well as the sages, offered their praises.
Then, by the grace of Śiva, Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Dānavas, was liberated from the curse and regained his former form.
From the bones of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the genus of conch shells indeed came into being; and the water from a conch shell is highly praised by everyone, with the exception of Śaṅkara.
O great sage, the water from the conch is especially dear to Hari and Lakṣmī, as well as to their kinsmen, but not to Hara.
Having thus slain him, Śaṅkara, mounted upon his bull and surrounded by Soma, Skanda, and the Gaṇas, departed for the world of Śiva, exceedingly joyful.
Hari went to Vaikuṇṭha, and Kṛṣṇa remained in his own state; the gods, filled with supreme bliss, returned to their own realms.
The world attained supreme well-being, bringing about the removal of all obstacles; the sky became stainless, and the entire earth was most auspicious.
Thus has been told the life-story of Maheśa, which brings great joy, removes all suffering, bestows prosperity, and fulfills all desires.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and the dispeller of all obstacles; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, granting the fruit of all desires.
The wise person who would constantly hear this life-story of the Moon-crested Lord, or cause it to be heard, or read it, or cause it to be read;
One shall obtain wealth, grain, sons, and happiness here; of this there is no doubt. One attains all desires, and especially devotion to Śiva.
This incomparable narrative destroys all calamities, generates supreme knowledge, and increases devotion to Śiva.

A Brāhmaṇa shall become endowed with spiritual luster, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious, a Vaiśya born of the third caste shall be rich in wealth, and a Śūdra, by hearing this, shall attain the state of the most excellent.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa indeed performed the act of impregnation; you should tell me by what effort he did so within the womb of Tulasī.
Sanatkumāra said: Nārāyaṇa, indeed the performer of the tasks of the gods and the refuge of the virtuous, sported with that Ramā in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Listen now to that very account of Viṣṇu, which brings great joy—the account of Hari, the fulfiller of Śiva’s command and the mother of the worlds.
Having heard a voice from the sky in the midst of the battle, Lord Śambhu dispatched [the messenger], who took the supreme armor of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Then, by means of his own illusory power, Hari quickly assumed the form of a brahmin and, taking on the appearance of Śaṅkhacūḍa, went to Tulasī’s house.
He sounded the drum near the door of Tulasī and, right there, awakened Sundarī with shouts of victory.
Having heard that, the virtuous woman, filled with supreme bliss, gazed upon the royal highway through the window with great reverence.
Having given wealth to the Brahmins, she performed auspicious rites; and knowing that her own husband had arrived, she quickly adorned herself.
Having descended from his chariot, Viṣṇu, the master of illusion who performs the work of the gods, went to the palace of that goddess while assuming the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Seeing her beloved arrived before her, she was filled with joy; she washed his feet, bowed down to him, and wept.
He seated the auspicious one upon a beautiful jeweled throne and offered him betel leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other fragrances.
Today my birth has truly become fruitful, and my life has indeed attained its purpose, as I behold the Lord of my life, who had gone to the battlefield, returned once more to my home.
Having spoken thus, she gazed at her beloved with a sidelong glance and a joyful smile, and inquired about the events of the battle with a sweet voice.
Tulasī said: That Lord, the foremost among gods, is the destroyer of countless universes; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other deities always abide by his command.

In this world, he is the progenitor of the three gods; he is both composed of the three qualities (triguṇātmā) and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). By the will of his devotees, he manifests with qualities (saguṇa) as the impeller of Hari and Brahmā.
At the request of Kubera, Hara—assuming qualities and form, residing on Kailāsa, lord of the Gaṇas, the Supreme Brahman, and the refuge of the virtuous—[appeared].
By the mere measure of a single *pala* of which, ten million cosmic eggs are destroyed; and by whom many Viṣṇus, Brahmās, and others have passed away in a mere instant.
O Lord, you went forth to wage war together with him; how did that battle proceed with him who was aided by the gods?
"Are you well, having returned here after defeating that Supreme Lord? Tell me exactly how your victory came about."
Having heard these words of Tulasī, the Lord of Ramā, assuming the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, smiled and spoke these nectar-like words to her.
The Blessed One said: "When I, who am fond of battle, went to the field of war, a great clamor arose and a great conflict commenced."
A battle took place between the gods and the dānavas, both seeking victory; there, the daityas were defeated by the immortals who were proud of their strength.
Then I waged war there against the gods who were fierce in their strength; those gods were defeated and went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
Rudra also came to the battle for the sake of assisting him; by him indeed was I held at bay for a long time, O you who are arrogant with strength.
O beloved, our battle lasted for a full year; O lovely one, there was the destruction of all the asuras.
Brahmā himself caused joy for us both, and by the command of Brahmā, the offices of the gods were bestowed upon us.
Śiva went to his own abode, the world of Śiva; he attained supreme well-being, for all affliction had indeed been removed.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds lay down to rest; there, the Lord of Ramā rejoiced with her, his consort, in great joy.
That virtuous woman, due to the transgression of one who brings about the destruction of happiness, reflected upon everything and said to him, "Who are you?"
Tulasī said: "Who are you? Tell me quickly; I have been enjoyed by you through your magic power. Since my status as a virtuous wife has been cast aside, I shall indeed curse you!"
Sanatkumāra said: O Brahmin, having heard the words of Tulasī and out of fear of the curse, Hari playfully assumed his own most enchanting form.
Seeing that form of Tulasī and recognizing Viṣṇu by his characteristic marks, she became enraged at the abandonment of her devotion to her husband and spoke to him.
Tulasī said: "O Viṣṇu, you have no compassion; your mind is like stone. By the violation of my duty as a wife, my husband has indeed been slain."
Since you are a wicked person devoid of compassion and are like a stone, therefore, by my curse, become a stone yourself this very moment.
Those who call you an ocean of compassion are undoubtedly deluded; for how could a devotee be slain without cause, even for the sake of another?
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, that virtuous Tulasī, the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa, wept bitterly, afflicted by grief, and lamented repeatedly and intensely.
Then, seeing her weeping, that supreme lord Viṣṇu called to mind the god Śaṅkara, by whom the entire world is deluded.
Then Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared; he was bowed to and praised with humility by Hari.
Seeing Hari overwhelmed with grief and his beloved wife lamenting, he enlightened them both through reasoned discourse—he who is compassionate toward the distressed.
Śaṅkara said: "Do not weep, O Tulasī; for a person experiences the fruit of their own actions. In this ocean of karma that is worldly existence, there is no one at all who bestows pleasure or pain."
Listen to what is presented here, which is free from suffering; Hari, being well-disposed, listens to it. I shall speak that which brings happiness to both, for the sake of your own happiness.
Austerity was performed by you, O blessed lady; this is indeed the fruit of that very austerity. How else could it be, since it has manifested in you in such a way?
Having cast off this body and assumed a divine form, sport eternally with Hari and become equal to Ramā.
"May this body of yours, once cast off here, become a river; in Bhārata, it shall take the form of merit and be renowned as the Gaṇḍakī."
O Great Goddess, for how long will Tulasī remain the foremost form in the practice of worshiping the gods by virtue of my boon?
Dwell in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld in the presence of Hari; become the Tulasī tree, the most excellent and beautiful among all flowers.
O Goddess presiding over the tree, you shall possess a divine form in Vaikuṇṭha and eternally engage in play with Hari in private.
"You, who are the goddess presiding over rivers and who bestows great merit in Bhārata, shall become the wife of Haryaṃśa, the lord of the salt ocean."
And Hari, indeed in the form of a mountain, will establish his abode on the banks of the Gaṇḍakī in Bhārata due to your curse.
There, scorpions and insects with sharp fangs and terrifying forms will tear it apart and fashion a wheel out of its hollows.
For that Śālagrāma stone is indeed a bestower of great merit according to its specific varieties; it shall be known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and so forth, based on the particular marks of the discus.
O Viṣṇu, the Śālagrāma stone is your union with Tulasī; it is eternally identical in form to you and increases manifold merit.
O auspicious lady, he who breaks a Tulasi leaf upon a Śālagrāma stone will suffer separation from his wife in a future birth.
He who performs [the worship] while cutting the *tulasī* leaves or setting aside the conch shell shall be deprived of his wife and shall remain diseased for seven births.
Indeed, he who keeps a Śālagrāma stone, Tulasī, and a conch together in one place is a man of great wisdom; he shall become beloved by Lord Hari.
You shall be dear to Śaṅkhacūḍa for the duration of one Manvantara; any separation from Śaṅkha will bring you nothing but sorrow.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara then described there the greatness of the Śālagrāma stone and of Tulasī, which bestows great merit.
Then, having become invisible and having gladdened both Hari and her, Śambhu, who is indeed the ever-bestower of happiness upon the virtuous, went to his own abode.
Having heard these words of Śambhu, Tulasī became delighted; casting off that body, she indeed assumed a divine form.
The Lord of Kamalā went with her to Vaikuṇṭha, and immediately the river Gaṇḍakī was born from her body.
That mountain, Acyuta, which bestows merit upon men, also exists on its shore; there, O Sage, even insects make many kinds of holes.
Those pebbles that fall there into the water bestow great merit; however, those remaining on dry land are known as *piṅgalās* and indeed lead to affliction.
Thus, everything has been told to you in accordance with your questions—the meritorious life-story of Śambhu, which bestows all desires upon men.
This narrative has been told, interwoven with the majesty of Viṣṇu; it is meritorious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Tulasī’s Curse," in the Śaṅkhacūḍavadhopākhyāna (The Episode of the Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa) within the fifth section, the Yuddhakhaṇḍa, of the second book, the Rudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
