Nārada said: Having heard the account of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa and the deeds of the moon-crested Lord, I am as satisfied by you as a person who has drunk nectar.
Such was the conduct of that high-souled Maheśa as he performed his divine sports by resorting to Māyā, bestowing joy upon his devotees.
Brahmā said: Having heard of the slaying of Jalandhara, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, questioned this very matter with the lord of sages, the son of Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra spoke to Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, after highly praising the auspicious life-story of Maheśa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the auspicious life-story of Maheśa, concerning how Andhaka attained the status of a Gaṇapati of Śambhu, the Supreme Self.
O Lord of Sages, having previously engaged in a supreme battle with him, he repeatedly propitiated that Great Lord through his virtuous nature.
The wondrous majesty of Śambhu, the protector of those who seek refuge, who is truly affectionate toward his devotees, and who sports in manifold divine pastimes.
Having heard this majesty of the bull-bannered Lord, the sage who was the son of Gandhavatī, bowing with devotion, spoke these words of great significance to that lord of sages, the son of Brahmā.

Vyāsa said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of Sages, who indeed was this Andhaka? In whose lineage on earth was he born—of what powerful man? Of what nature was that great-souled and mighty preeminent one, and whose son was Andhaka?"
Tell me today all of this, together with its secret, through the grace of the son of Brahmā; for I have indeed learned it correctly from Skanda, the son of Maheśa, whose realization is immeasurable.
How did that Andhaka, who became the lord of the Gaṇas, attain the status of a Gaṇapati from Śambhu, the possessor of supreme splendor? He is indeed most blessed.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the son of Brahmā then spoke to Janaka, the father of Śuka, who was desirous of hearing the supreme and most authoritative glories of Maheśvara.

Sanatkumāra said: In ancient times, that Lord who bestows grace upon his devotees came from Kailāsa, accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain and his hosts of attendants; indeed, the sovereign of the gods descended from his own mountain to Kāśī, desiring to sport there.

Having established that capital city, and having made the hero named Bhairava its protector, turn the wheel—which brings happiness to the people—therein; go forth together with Śailajā and conquer many [realms].
Once, having gone to the mountain named Mandara by virtue of his excellent power, he sported there extensively, accompanied by Śivā and the foremost heroes of the hosts of Mānāgas.
Then, as he stood on Mount Mandara facing the eastern direction, Pārvatī playfully and sportively closed the eyes of the matted-haired Lord of fierce valor.
With her lotus-like hands, which possessed the luster of coral, gold, and a lotus, she closed her eyes; as Hara’s eyes were closed, in an instant, a great darkness arose.

And from the contact of that touch, the water of intoxication flowed from Maheśvara’s hands onto her; heated for a moment by the fire on Śambhu’s forehead, a great drop of water emerged upon his brow.
Then he became a fetus with a terrifying mouth, fearsome, devoted to anger, and ungrateful; blind, deformed, with matted hair, black, non-human, monstrous, and covered in thick hair.
Singing, laughing, weeping, dancing, and licking his lips with a most terrible roar, Bhava spoke with a smile to Gaurī regarding that newborn of wondrous appearance.
The illustrious Maheśa said: "O beloved, you have closed your eyes and performed this deed; why then do you fear me? Hearing those words from Hara, Gaurī, smiling, opened her eyes.
When the light had arisen, a being of terrible form appeared, even more blind than the darkness itself; seeing such a creature, Gaurī questioned Maheśa, that Supreme Person.
Gaurī said: "O Blessed One, who is this deformed being born right before us, so terrible and fearsome? Tell me the truth: for what reason was he created, by whom, and whose son is he?"
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his beloved, the Lord Hara—the creator of the universe who makes sport—smiled slightly and spoke to Līlākara, the mother of the three worlds.
Maheśa said: Listen, O Ambikā, you who perform wondrous deeds; this one of marvelous and fierce valor has been born while my eyes were closed by you—he is my sweat-born son, named Andhaka.

And you shall be his benefactor, acting appropriately toward the Gaṇas through your friendship and compassion; he must be protected by you, for, O Noble Lady, having deliberated upon this alone with your intellect, it is what must be done.

Sanatkumāra said: Then Gaurī, having heard the words of her servant, out of a disposition of compassion and accompanied by her friends, protected [the child] with many various means, just as one would protect one's own son.
Then, during that very season of winter, Hiraṇyanetra, desiring a son, set out; having observed the extensive lineage of his elder brother’s offspring, he was impelled by his beloved wife.
Then the Asura, born of Kaśyapa, resorted to the forest and performed austerities for the sake of a son; like a piece of wood, he had conquered the faults of anger, desiring a vision of Maheśvara.

O best of the twice-born, the wielder of the Pināka bow, being fully pleased by his penance, went to that place in order to grant him a boon; having arrived there, Maheśa, whose banner is the bull, spoke to that foremost of Daityas.

Maheśa said: "O Lord of the Daityas, do not let the host of your senses fall away; for what purpose have you undertaken this vow? Speak your desire, for I am Bhava, the giver of boons; whatever you wish, I shall grant it all."

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard the words of Maheśa, the Daitya Kanakākṣa was exceedingly pleased; with palms joined in reverence and head bowed, he spoke after bowing down to the Lord of the Mountain with various hymns of praise.

Hiraṇyākṣa said: "O Moon-forehead, I have no son who is possessed of great heroism and worthy of the Daitya lineage. For that purpose, I have undertaken this vow; O Lord of Gods, grant me such a son of great heroism."

And since even the five sons of my brother, beginning with Prahlāda, who possessed infinite prowess, have gone to their end here saying "this is not mine," and I too am now one whose lineage has ceased, who would desire this kingdom as his own?

Having seized the kingdom of another by his own power, he enjoys it, or else he enjoys his own as seen from his father’s perspective; yet here he is called "son," while there he is called "father," and by that [reversal], even he becomes the son.

An upward path is ordained for those with sons by the wise, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma; all beings exist for that purpose, and therefore one should employ animals through one's own power.

Furthermore, if there were no worlds for one who has no karmic continuity, then people would not desire them from the gods; yet, constantly worshipping the lotus-face of the Lord of the Gods, they thus petition for nothing less than a single son.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the Daitya king, Bhava, who is compassionate, was pleased and said to him: "O scorcher of the Daityas, there is no son born of your own virility; however, I shall grant you a son."
"Choose my own son, named Andhaka, whose valor is equal to yours and who is unconquered; setting aside all sorrow, accept him as your very own son."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the high-souled Hara—the lord of the origin of beings, the fierce enemy of Tripura—being pleased, together with Gaurī, gave his son to that Hiraṇyanetra.
Having obtained a son from Hara, that high-souled Daitya circumambulated Rudra in due order, honored him with numerous hymns of praise, and, being satisfied, returned to his own kingdom.
Then, having obtained a son from Giriśa, the Daitya Caṇḍaparākrama, having conquered all the gods without exception, brought this earth to his own land after descending to Rasātala.
Then Viṣṇu, of infinite prowess, having assumed the preeminent and formidable body of a Boar—the embodiment of all things and consisting of sacrifice—was propitiated by the gods, sages, and Siddhas.
Having split the earth with various blows from his snout and entered the depths of Pātāla, he pulverized hundreds of Daityas with his trunk and with his foremost, unbroken tusks.

Having crushed the armies of the night-stalkers with kicks that flashed like thunderbolts, he was thereafter endowed with wondrously fierce splendor by means of the Sudarśana, which resembled ten million suns.
He severed the blazing head of Hiraṇyanetra and consumed the wicked Daityas; then, being greatly delighted, he consecrated his own Andhaka there as the king of the lords of the sons of Diti.

Then, having returned to his own abode and seeing the earth being raised by the sprout, the high-souled one was delighted; he nourished the earth from the depths of Pātāla and likewise restored its former portion.
Consecrated by all the gods, by the delighted sages, and by that lotus-born Brahmā, Hari—assuming the form of a boar with a formidable body and accomplishing a great task—departed for his own realm.
When the lord of the asuras, Hiraṇyākṣa, had been slain by the divine one in the form of a boar, all the gods, all the sages, and all other living beings became happy.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, when that enemy of the gods had been slain, what did his elder brother, the great asura, do next?
O Lord of Sages, I have a great curiosity to hear this; therefore, O son of Brahmā, having shown compassion, please narrate it to me. Salutations to you!
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, that lord of sages, Sanatkumāra, spoke while recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, when his brother had thus been slain by Hari in the form of a boar, Hiraṇyakaśipu burned with rage and grief.
Then, in order to bring about the destruction of the subjects, he commanded those heroic Asuras who delight in slaughter; for he is indeed one who takes pleasure in enmity toward Hari.
Then those Asuras, who delight in slaughter, took their master’s command upon their heads and began the destruction of the gods and living beings.
Then, when the world was thus oppressed by the evil-minded asuras, the gods abandoned heaven and wandered upon the earth unobserved.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, grieving for his deceased brother, performed the water-libations and other rites, and then consoled his wife and the others.
Then that lord of the Daitya kings indeed desired for himself a state of invincibility, freedom from old age and death, being without rival, and sole sovereignty.
He performed most rigorous penance in a valley of Mount Mandara, with his arms raised, his gaze fixed on the sky, and his big toe resting upon the earth.
While he was performing those austerities, all the gods, endowed with strength, conquered all the Daityas and regained their own abodes.
From his head arose a smokeless fire consisting of ascetic power; fanned on all sides, it scorched the worlds above, below, and across.
Scorched by that [heat], the gods abandoned heaven and went to the world of Brahmā; with their faces distorted by the power of his asceticism, they made a representation to the Creator.
Then, O Vyāsa, having been thus petitioned by the gods, the self-born Creator, surrounded by Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, and others, went to the hermitage of the lord of the Daityas.

Having scorched all the worlds, he then beheld the Lotus-born Brahmā who had arrived there; and the Creator, the Grandfather, spoke to him in order to grant a boon, saying, "Choose a boon. Hearing the sweet words of the Ordainer, he, whose intellect was undeluded, spoke these words.

Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of Creatures, O Grandfather, O God, I have never at any time experienced fear of death from weapons, missiles, nooses, thunderbolts, dry trees, great mountains, water, fire, or the blows of enemies."

O Lord of Creatures, what is the use of many words from the gods, the Daityas, the sages, and the Siddhas—all living beings created by You? [They do not exist] in heaven or on earth, by day or by night, neither above nor below.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, the lotus-born Brahmā, filled with compassion, spoke thus to the lord of the Daityas: "I am pleased; receive everything you desire. Then, having mentally bowed to Viṣṇu, he addressed him.
"Enough with your asceticism; your desire is fulfilled after ninety-six thousand years. Arise and rule the kingdom of the Dānavas! Upon hearing these words, he became well-disposed.

Having been consecrated to the kingdom by his great-grandfather, he set his mind upon the destruction of the three worlds; intoxicated with power, he subverted all righteous duties and even conquered all the gods in battle.

Then, out of fear, all the gods headed by Indra, having received the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), became oppressed by the foremost of the Daityas and went to the Ocean of Milk where Hari lies.
Thinking him to be the bestower of happiness, they indeed propitiated Viṣṇu intensely by means of hymns; then, he being pleased, they reported all their own suffering to him.
Having heard all of his suffering, the Lord of Ramā was pleased and granted boons; rising from that bed, Upendra spoke with various words suited to him.
Having consoled all the gods and sages, he whose splendor was equal to that of Vaiśvānara said: "O lords of the gods, I shall slay the Daitya by force; go now, satisfied, to your own abodes."

O lord of sages, having heard the words of Rāmeśvara, all those lords of the asuras, headed by Śakra, were thoroughly satisfied; considering the younger brother of Hiraṇyākṣa to have been slain, they departed for their own abodes.
Assuming a form that was matted-haired, formidable, with fangs as weapons, sharp claws, and a well-formed nose; leonine yet human, with a wide-gaping mouth, as terrifying as ten million suns.
Equal in power to the fire at the end of an eon, pervading the entire universe—what need is there for many words? Even as the sun was setting, the Great-Souled Lord entered the city of the Asuras.
Having waged war with those powerful Daityas and having slain them, the Man-lion seized the hosts of Daityas; moving there with impetuous valor, he shattered various asuras.

Seeing him of incomparable power, all those Daityas indeed roared in that very manner. And beholding that lion who consists of everything, the son of the lord of the Daityas named Prahlāda said to the king: "Why has this king of beasts, who embodies the universe, arrived here?"
Prahlāda said: "This Lord Ananta has entered the city within you in the form of a man-lion (Nṛsiṃha). Desist from battle and seek refuge; I shall behold the formidable form of the Lion."

"Since there is no warrior even in the three worlds who can subdue the king of beasts, rule the kingdom! Having heard these words of his son, the evil-minded one said to him: "Why are you afraid of this, my son?"

Having spoken thus to his son, that king, the lord of the sons of Diti, addressed the foremost heroes among the bulls of the Daityas: "O heroes, seize this lion, whose brow and eyes are distorted with rage."
By his command, those foremost of Daityas then entered the lion, desiring to seize him; in an instant they were consumed like moths entering a fire out of a longing for its form.

Even though the Daityas had been consumed by fire, the king of the Daityas waged war against the lord of beasts with all his weapons and every kind of missile, such as spears, double-edged swords, nooses, goads, firebrands, and the like.

O Vyāsa, as those two preeminent heroes, weapons in hand, fought on with their minds fully possessed by mutual rage, a full day of Brahmā passed while they roared at one another with the sound of warriors.
Then that Daitya, suddenly assuming many arms equipped with weapons and beholding him, rushed from all sides toward the lion-like Nṛsiṃha as he was engaged in combat.

Then, having engaged in a most unbearable and fierce battle with all manner of weapons and every kind of missile, that preeminent great Daitya, bearing his trident, approached Narasiṃha as his own forces were being destroyed.

Then, having been seized by the lord of beasts with his many arms as strong as the essence of mountains, he was pinned between those limbs with his knees, while the king’s sprout-like claws—capable of piercing the vital organs of a dānava—were driven into him.

Having instantly produced a heart-lotus mixed with blood using his claws as weapons, he departed from the living being; at that moment, the victim became like a log of wood, with all his limbs repeatedly crushed to powder.

When that enemy of the gods had been slain, Viṣṇu, of wondrous prowess, being pleased, addressed Prahlāda—who had offered his salutations—and having consecrated him in the kingdom, departed thereafter for an inconceivable destination.

Then, O Brahmin, all the lords of the gods, exceedingly delighted, bowed to Viṣṇu in that direction and departed for their own abodes—Brahmā and the others—together with the worshipful Lord, whose task was accomplished.

The birth of Andhaka from Rudra has been described; the death of Hiraṇyākṣa by Varāha; the destruction of his brother by Nṛsiṃha; and, as a related incident, the attainment of the kingdom by Prahlāda.

Now listen, O best of the twice-born, to the power of Andhaka as obtained through his service to Śiva; indeed, [I shall tell] of his battle with Hara and subsequently his lordship over the Gaṇas of that Lord of the Mountain.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Andhaka, the Attainment of the Lordship of the Gaṇas, and the Slaying of Hiraṇyanetra and Hiraṇyakaśipu," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: Then, once while engaged in recreation with his brothers—who were intoxicated with pride and filled him with jesting words—the son of Hiraṇyākṣa was addressed thus: "O blind one, what use have you for a kingdom today?"
Hiraṇyanetra, however, became deluded and fond of strife; for though he had propitiated Giriśa with terrible austerities, he obtained you—deformed, misshapen, and indeed deprived of eyes.

Therefore, you indeed have no share in the kingdom; how could one born of another lineage obtain the kingdom? Let this be considered by you yourself; for it is true that we alone are the rightful heirs to it.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs and having reflected upon them with his own intellect, he, feeling dejected, pacified them with various words and departed at night for a solitary forest.

There he performed austerities for ten thousand years, reciting his prayers with one foot raised; deprived of food, his arms held upward by his vows, he practiced that which cannot indeed be accomplished even by the gods and asuras.

Having kindled the fire, he indeed offered his own flesh from his body along with blood for a full year; having cut it from his body daily with a sharp blade, he offered it into the fire accompanied by mantras.
Then that corpse, consisting only of sinews and bones, had all its blood gone to decay; when there was no more flesh in his body, he desired to cast the frame into the fire.

Then he was beheld by all the inhabitants of the abode of the thirty gods, who were filled with great wonder and fear; thereupon, being praised with hymns, the Creator, the Sustainer, was quickly propitiated by the immortals.
Then the Grandfather, having restrained him, said to him: "Choose now this boon; O Dānava, take that which you desire to obtain, even if it is very difficult to attain in all the worlds."
Having heard the words of the Lotus-born One, the Daitya bowed down in distress and said: "May those who struck my kingdom with such cruelty—those headed by Prahlāda—be my servants."
"May divine sight indeed come to me who am blind; may Indra and the other gods become my tributaries; and may there be no death for me from gods, daityas, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, or humans."

Having heard those most terrible words from Nārāyaṇa—the enemy of the lords of the Daityas—who is all beings, who consists of all things, and who is Śarva, the lotus-born Brahmā became greatly apprehensive and spoke to him.

Brahmā said: "O Lord of Daityas, all this shall come to pass; therefore, take some means for its destruction. For there is no one who has not been born, nor will there ever be, who has not entered the mouth of Death."
"Indeed, let even those like you, O virtuous beings, abandon life that is exceedingly long. Having heard these conciliatory words from the Grandfather (Brahmā), the Daitya spoke to him once more.

Andhaka said: "Among all women who exist throughout the three periods of time—whether superior, middling, or inferior—there is indeed one who is like a jewel among them, who is always like a mother even to me."

"She is unapproachable by body, speech, or even mind, and is difficult for the world of men to obtain; may my destruction come to pass as I desire her, O Blessed Self-Existent One, lest I lose my status as the lord of the Daityas."
Having heard those words, the lotus-born Brahmā was greatly amazed; having quickly received the command from Śambhu, he remembered the lotus-feet of Śaṅkara and then spoke to Andhaka.
Brahmā said: "O best of Daityas, whatever you desire shall indeed all come true according to your wish. Arise, O lord of Daityas, obtain your desire; always engage in battle with heroes."

O Lord of Munis, having heard these words of the Creator, the son of Hāṭakanetra—now reduced to nothing but sinews and bones—quickly prostrated with devotion before the Lord of the World and spoke thus to that God.

Andhaka said: "O Lord, having entered the enemy's army, how indeed shall I fight with this body? Render me, who am but skin, sinews, and bones, nourished with flesh; and do not touch me today with your meritorious hand."

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard his words and having touched his body with his hand, that lotus-born one departed for his own abode together with the lords of the gods, being honored by hosts of sages and perfected beings.
As soon as he was touched, the king of the Daityas became whole-bodied and strong; his eyes were restored, he became handsome, and filled with joy, he entered his own city.

Then, having renounced their entire kingdom to him, the lords of the Dānavas, headed by Prahlāda, perceived that he had returned having obtained his boon and became his subjects, submitting to his will.

Then Andhaka, accompanied by his host of servants and joined by his army, went to conquer heaven; having defeated all the gods in battle, he made the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) a payer of tribute.

In battles, he conquered the Nāgas, Suparṇas, excellent Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and even humans; as well as the lords of mountains, trees, all four-footed creatures, and those with lion-like faces.

Having brought this triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, under his own control, he indeed subjected it to himself; then, having gone to many thousands of women with beautiful banks, he [enjoyed them].
Accompanied by those beautiful women who dwell in the netherworld, on earth, and in heaven, he took delight upon other lovely mountain ranges and along the banks of rivers.
While sporting with them, the lord of the Dānavas, standing in their midst, drank for his pleasure the divine and excellent human beverages that remained after they had drunk.
Furthermore, having obtained other divine juices, fruits, and fragrant roots, as well as excellent vehicles and superior dwellings fashioned by Maya;
Thus, for Andhaka, as he sported here, tens of thousands of years passed away amidst flowers, water-offerings, incense, food, and ointments, all most beautifully adorned and wonderful to behold.

That foolish and best of Daityas, whose intellect was blinded by intoxication and who had formed evil associations, did not know anything auspicious that would truly bring happiness to himself in the hereafter; he was perpetually blind.
Then, having overcome all his principal sons with fallacious arguments, that great-souled one, becoming intoxicated, wandered together with the Daityas, destroying all Vedic dharmas.

Overcome by the intoxication of wealth, he did not respect the Vedas, the twice-born, the gods, or his teachers; thus, driven by fate and with his life-span exhausted, he passed away while wasting his youth in idle days.
Then, at one time, having traveled for many millions of years upon this earth with his army, he went joyfully to Mount Mandara.

Beholding there that splendor resembling gold, he, intoxicated with pride, wandered about with his armies; and having reached that king of mountains for the sake of sport, he out of delusion made up his mind to dwell there.
Having joyfully established a beautiful and firm city there by his power, the lord of the Daityas then proceeded to settle that most wonderful city in due order upon the peak of Mount Mandara.
Duryodhana, Vaidhasa, and Hasti—the two ministers of that most excellent of Dānavas—once beheld a woman of beautiful form upon a fine mountain plateau; indeed, all three of them saw her there.
Those swift-moving and excellent Daityas, having quickly approached the lord of the great Daityas with joy, all spoke with extreme affection to Andhaka, the best of heroes, exactly as they had seen.

The ministers said: "O Lord of Daityas, a certain sage was seen here inside the cave, his eyes closed in meditation; he was adorned with a garland of Rudrākṣas, bore the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, and had the skin of a lordly elephant girt around his waist."

His entire body was enveloped by the coils of the lord of serpents; he was adorned with a garland of skulls and possessed matted locks. Holding a trident in his hand, he carried a quiver of arrows and a great bow, and his rosary of beads was laid open.

Bearing a sword, a trident, and a staff, with matted hair and four arms, his form was indeed fair; smeared with ashes, possessing radiant splendor, he was the foremost of ascetics, wondrous in every aspect of his appearance.
Not far from him, he saw a man who was a monkey with a terrifying and formidable face; he was armed with every weapon, his hands were rough, and he stood guarding a white, aged bull.
As that ascetic sat there, a certain woman of beautiful form, youthful, charming, auspicious, and like a jewel upon the earth, was seen by him standing at his side.

She who is draped in coral, pearls, gems, gold, jewels, and fine garments, and embraced by auspicious garlands—he who has seen her shall be truly possessed of vision; what need is there for anything else to be seen here?
She is a divine woman worthy of honor by Maheśa, the beloved wife of the meritorious sage; indeed, she is fit to be properly brought before you, O Lord of Daityas, enjoyer of excellent jewels.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of theirs, that Daitya, overcome by lust and with all his limbs trembling, suddenly dismissed Duryodhana and the others into the presence of the sages.

Having approached that immeasurable sage of great vows, those excellent ministers of his, who were well-versed in the royal policy of the gods, O Lord of Munis, bowed to him and delivered the command of the Daityas.
The ministers said: "The high-souled son of Hiraṇyākṣa, the sovereign of the Daityas named Andhaka, the lord of the three worlds, sits here today, sporting at the command of Śiva."
We are indeed his ministers, O hero of the Angas, and have come into your presence; listen with an attentive mind, O ascetic, to that which he has sent you to say.

Whose son are you, O wise and best of sages, and for what purpose do you sit here so comfortably? To whom does this beautiful, auspicious young woman belong, O lord of sages, that she is to be given to the lord of the Daityas?

Where is this body of yours—smeared with ashes, adorned with a garland of skulls, and misshapen? And where are the quiver, the excellent bow, arrows, sword, bhushundi, trident, thunderbolt, and tomara?

Where is the most holy Jāhnavī at the tip of [Śiva’s] matted locks, and where is this moon or a fragment of a corpse-bone? Where is the long-faced serpent, a fire of poison, and where is the union with her of full breasts?
Mounting an old ox is inauspicious, yet he does not even look at one; bowing at twilight is a religious duty for him, yet where is his meal? This is contrary to the ways of the world.
"Give back the woman with conciliatory words; O fool, why do you practice penance for the sake of a woman? This is improper and unworthy of you, since I am the lord of jewels in the three worlds."
Lay down your weapons now as I have commanded; later you shall attain your own purity. If you transgress my inviolable command, you will lose this entire body.
Having considered Andhaka to be evil-minded, the preeminent Maheśvara, whose nature conforms to worldly ways, spoke thus to the Daitya with a smile after hearing all those words of the messenger.
Śiva said: "If I am Rudra to you, what would be gained by me, and why do you speak such a falsehood? Listen, O Lord of Daityas, to my power; it is not right for you to speak words in this manner."

I do not remember my father anywhere, even within the depths of a cave, for he was a terrible man whose conduct was never practiced by others; I perform this vow of animal sacrifice, yet I, the most ignorant and deformed, do not remember my mother.

This [attachment] is rootless, yet it is firmly established in me; all this is mine and is very difficult to abandon. This wife of mine is young and beautiful; she is the all-enduring success for one who has gone everywhere.
"O Rākṣasa, take now whatever is pleasing to you! Having said this much, Śambhu, disguised as an ascetic, fell silent before them.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these profound words, those Dānavas bowed their heads to him and then went to the son of the best of Daityas, who had made a vow for the destruction of the three worlds.

Having bowed down to the king, the lord of the Daityas, those of undaunted spirit spoke to him while he was intoxicated; they all first uttered cries of victory and then related that which had been said by Rudra with a smile.

The ministers said: "Where is the night-stalker, whose valor and fortitude are fickle; where is that wretched Dānava, devoid of strength? Where is that cruel, ungrateful, and eternally sinful Dānava who fears the son of the Sun?"

The lord of all the Daityas was addressed as "King" by that ascetic sage with a smile; for Vīravara, possessed of great splendor, had surely considered the three worlds as mere straw through his own intellect.

Where am I and where are these dreadful weapons, and where is this battle that strikes such terror into Death itself? And where is this "hero," a night-stalker with a face like a monkey, his limbs worn out by old age?

Where is this true nature of yours, and where is this unfortunate one? Where is your strength, and where are these mere creepers? If you are indeed capable, then strive to do battle; come then and accomplish something!
In this world, there is no weapon as terrible as the thunderbolt that can destroy one such as you; yet where is your body, so soft as a lotus? Having reflected thus, do whatever pleases you.

The ministers said: "O Lord of the Dānavas, these and other such words were spoken by the ascetic for your welfare. O King, he spoke to you with a smile, saying that a battle with him here is not appropriate for you."

If you understand through these many empty and senseless ravings uttered by us, then, once you have been joined with austerities as an ascetic, you will indeed remember these words of the sage later on.

Sanatkumāra said: Then, having heard their words, that dull-witted one blazed with rage, like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter; for those words were true and beneficial, yet they were crooked and very sharp.
Grasping his sword and intoxicated by the granting of the boon, Viparītadeva, pierced by the arrows of Love, began to imitate a fierce wind as he prepared to go there.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Messenger," in the narrative of Andhaka’s attainment of the status of Gaṇapati, within the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: Then he who moves with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut, his eyes rolling from drinking the liquor, the one of great majesty accompanied by a vast army, a fierce hero who marches like a preeminent warrior, departed.
Then the Daitya, pierced by the arrows of Love, beheld the cave whose path was blocked by Vīraka; just as a moth, approaching a lamp, gazes longingly at it.

Thus having been shown [the way] repeatedly and quickly, even though he was being tormented again and again by Vīraka, that foolish Andhaka, the lord of the great Daityas, remained with his body utterly consumed by the fire of lust.

Though he was tormented by terrifying displays of stones, trees, thunderbolts, water, fire, serpents, weapons, and missiles, he was not to be further oppressed; rather, he was asked: "Who are you that have come here?"

Having heard that speech, he expressed his own view to him; then that Daitya engaged in battle with Vīraka for a moment in a wonderful and immeasurable manner, but was defeated in the conflict by the more heroic one.
Then, leaving the front of the battle, his throat parched with hunger and thirst, he fled; and when his excellent sword was shattered, exhausted and devoid of pride, he ran away.

Then the foremost sons of Diti, led by Prahlāda, engaged in battle with Vīraka; though they were exceedingly fierce, their minds were restrained by the goad of shame as they fought with hundreds of various weapons.
There Virocana waged war, as did Bali, Bāṇa, Sahasrabāhu, Bhaji, Kujambha, Śambara, and other heroic ones such as Vṛtra.
While fighting, they were defeated on all sides and split in two by Gaṇavīraka; indeed, as many Dānavas lay slain, the hosts of Siddhas proclaimed, "Victory! alone.

In that terrifying place, thick with blood and mire, crowded with throngs of flesh-eating beasts, and filled with the midst of fat, marrow, meat, and putrid pus, where jackals were engaged in their predatory play.
When the Daityas had been defeated, the Lord Pinākin, having consoled his beloved Dākṣāyaṇī, spoke to her concerning the most formidable Mahāpāśupata vow which he had previously performed with me.

Śiva said: "Therefore, that strength which was mine has perished, since I, an immortal, have fallen among mortals. O Goddess, due to your company, I have become like a planet whose merit is exhausted, [wandering] day and night."

Having produced that divine and most wonderful [state], and having again attained an even more formidable excellence, I therefore practice a most terrible vow, O beautiful one, truly fearless and free from sorrow.

Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken these words, the Great-souled One took up his drum and struck it softly. Having gone there, blazing with fierce asceticism, he entered a most sacred and very formidable forest.
For even by the gods and asuras, it might be possible to traverse such a distance in merely a thousand years; yet Pārvatī, staying on Mount Mandara, awaited the arrival of Bhava.
Devoted to her husband and endowed with the virtues of moral conduct, she remained perpetually alone and fearful; protected by her son Vīraka, she dwelt within the cave, overcome by sorrow.
Then that Daitya, intoxicated by the boon and his fortitude shattered, returned to that cave accompanied by those chief warriors and by arrows produced from Māra.
Abandoning food, drink, and sleep, he waged a most wonderful battle there for five hundred and five days and nights with his army against Vīraka, filled with rage.
With swords, spears, along with slings, maces, and bhushundis, as well as excellent shafts, fierce crescent-headed arrows, vitastis, and flaming tortoise-faced arrows;
With foremost iron arrows, sharpened spears, battle-axes, javelins, mallets, swords, clubs, mountains, trees, and even divine weapons, the hosts of Daityas [assailed him].

The radiant weapon, its body split asunder, did not fall; rather, having struck the entire closed door of the cave with those weapons hurled by the arms of the Daityas, it subsequently fainted right at the entrance of the cave.
For a mere moment, the hero’s weapon-nets were completely covered by all the Daityas; yet, beholding those most terrible sons of Diti, it became impossible for them to uncover [the weapons] again.

Out of fear, the goddess, together with her companions, remembered the Grandfather (Brahmā) and Viṣṇu; staying within the cave, she caused the entire army of my preeminent hero to be recalled to mind.
As soon as she had thought of them, Brahmā appeared assuming a female form, and the Lord Viṣṇu likewise; and Indra, together with all his armies, arrived having assumed female forms.

Then those hosts of great-souled lords of sages, as well as the Siddhas, Nāgas, and Guhyakas, having transformed themselves into women, entered the interior of the cave of the daughter of the mountain king.

Because it was improper for them to enter the inner apartments while residing in a well-governed kingdom, they then displayed thousands of women of shapely hips, even though their number was infinite.

Divine and most wonderful sights were seen within the cave of Gaurī by those engaged in the rites for Śiva; the women were overjoyed, as was the daughter of the mountain king within the interior of the cave.

Accompanied by many hundreds and thousands of women, kettledrums resounded with a voice like the clouds at the end of an eon; and conch shells, which grant victory in battle, were blown by those women of beautiful hips.

Recovering from his swoon, that hero Vīraka, possessed of wonderful and fierce valor, stood before him; seizing the weapons of the great chariot-warriors, he struck the son of Diti with those very weapons.

Then Brāhmī raised her staff in opposition; Gaurī, her mind overwhelmed with wrath, likewise stood ready; and Nārāyaṇī, holding a conch, mace, excellent discus, and bow, filled the space with her staff-like arms.

Then, with a plow-staff in her hand, adorned with the sky as her garland, and possessing a complexion like gold, she who was born of Vaidarbha and held a thunderbolt in her hand emerged, possessing fierce speed and agitated by thousands of torrents.

She has a thousand eyes, is steadfast in battle, and is difficult for even hundreds of Daityas to conquer; she is invincible. She is the Vaiśvānarī Śakti with a fierce countenance, and she is the Yāmyā Śakti, formidable with a staff raised in her hand.
With a very sharp sword raised in her hand and a formidable bow, Nairṛti arrived; holding a water-vessel and a noose for elephants, she emerged, desiring battle.

The goddess born of fierce winds, whose body was emaciated by hunger and who held a goad in her hand, and the one born of Kubera, who grasped in her hand a mace resembling the fire at the end of an aeon.
Yākṣeśvarī, Tīkṣṇamukhā, Virūpā, Nakhāyudhā, and Nāgabhayaṃkarī—these and hundreds of other goddesses indeed emerged and crowded the field of battle.
Having seen that army, which was boundless and shoreless, the goddesses became pale of complexion and utterly amazed; agitated and trembling with fear, their inner spirits were indeed dejected.

Having fixed their minds upon him, all those wives of the gods, headed by Vidhiśakti, [honored] Senāpati, who possessed most terrible valor, because of his being highly esteemed by the daughter of the Mountain Lord.

The principal sons of Diti waged a great battle such as had never occurred before, having resolved in their minds that retreat was death; yet others, by virtue of the granting of boons, [fought] with women.
Then Gaurī, accompanied by her companions, waged a most wonderful battle there, having appointed as her general in that conflict Vīraka, who was fierce in valor and preeminent in marvelous intellect.

The king, the son of Hiraṇyanetra, being of virtuous deeds, formed a great array; and having honored Viṣṇu and observed him toward the southern quarter, he created that most formidable formation named Gilana.

When his mouth had been made formidable through the performance of that rite, the Lord arrived there, clothed in a hide and filled with the radiance of a thousand suns as terrible as those at the end of an aeon, truly enraged.
Then, after a thousand years had passed, seeing that Maheśvara had arrived, the women, together with Vīraka, waged a most intense great battle, filled with joy.
Having bowed her head to Gaurī and Giriśa, and displaying her husband’s extraordinary valor, Gaurī joyfully engaged in combat with Hara, the son of the Mountain King.
Taking him by the neck, he entered the cave and dismissed thousands of Rāmās; having honored Gaurī with hundreds of marks of respect, he stationed Vīraka at the mouth of the cave.
Then, having seen Gaurī and Giriśa, the lord of the asuras, who was indeed skilled in statecraft, quickly dispatched his own messenger named Vidhāsa to the presence of Śiva.
Though his limbs were shattered by those various blows sent by the hosts of gods in that battle, he spoke these fierce words with pride, having entered and prostrated with his head before Śambhu.

The messenger said: "I was sent here and entered the cave; indeed, this Andhaka spoke these words to you: 'There is no need for you to have anything to do with this woman; release the young and beautiful lady.'"

"O ascetic, you are one who mostly dwells in penance; therefore, enjoy that which was desired within me and has now been forgiven by me. Thinking 'the sage must be opposed,' you are not a sage, O ascetic, but rather an enemy."

O ascetic rogue, you who are a great adversary among the Daityas, fight with speed against me after being struck down; I shall indeed lead you to the abode of Yama, which is as fitting for you as the depths of Pātāla.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words from the mouth of the messenger, the great three-eyed Lord—the refuge of the virtuous and the destroyer of the pride of the wicked—blazing with indignation, spoke to him with anger while wearing a garland of skulls.
Śiva said: Your speech is indeed manifest and exceedingly fierce; you have spoken the truth, so depart quickly. Engage in battle with me by force, if indeed you are capable by your own strength.

What purpose would there be for one who is powerless on this earth through wives, wealth, or even most enchanting things? Let the Daityas come, intoxicated by their strength; I have indeed acted after such reflection.
How can even the maintenance of my body be possible, given my lack of power? Let them do whatever is ordained for them; as for me, I shall do whatever is to be done by me—of this there is no doubt.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words from Hara, even though he was of such a nature, he departed from him with joy; then, uttering roars and shouts of defiance, he went toward the presence of the lord of the Daityas.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Commencement of Battle and the Dialogue between Messengers," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: Understanding his intention, that king of the Daityas took up a mace and, accompanied by his army, quickly set out; he then placed before him a most terrible weapon named Gila, which could not be pierced even by the best of the gods.

Having reached the mouth of Maheśvara’s cave, he pierced it with weapons as brilliant as thunderbolts; others then showered Vīraka with weapons, while still others likewise assailed the daughter of the mountain.
For some would break the beautiful gateways, destroy the flowers and leaves, and ruin the fruits, roots, pleasant water, and even the pathways of the garden.
Some, filled with joy, even began to shake the sun-bright peaks of the mountain; then Hara, the wielder of the trident, grew enraged and summoned his own army.

And other most dreadful beings, with their hosts and armies, along with the gods headed by Viṣṇu, followed as soon as they were summoned, accompanied by chariots, elephants, horses, bulls, and cattle.

All those gods, together with hosts of spirits, were present upon camels, donkeys, excellent birds, and lions; as well as upon tigers, deer, boars, cranes, and along with fish, aquatic creatures, and the foremost of porpoises.
And by various other hosts of living beings, with scattered gadflies and cracked cremation grounds; with serpents, hundreds of pretas, piśācas, divine celestial chariots, and lotus-pools.

Accompanied by rivers, streams, and mountain-dwellers, they approached with palms joined in reverence; bowing down to the one with matted hair (Kapardin), those of undaunted spirit stood there, having appointed Vīraka as their commander-in-chief.
Then the wielder of the Pināka bow dispatched the gods, whose mounts were rested, to the battle; sent by Maheśvara, those foremost warriors set out for the fight, firm and destined for victory.

All of them waged a battle with Śuṅgila, resembling the end of a Yuga, devoid of all restraint and utterly terrible against the army of the lord of the Daityas; indeed, in that conflict, the gods were swallowed up by him out of rage.

At that moment, all those fighting—the foremost among them being Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Sun, and the Moon—were swallowed up by that Vidhasa; yet, when the army was thus devoured, Vīraka indeed remained.

Then Suvīraka, the best of eloquent speakers, having abandoned that cave at the head of the battlefield and entered [the presence of] Śarva, prostrated with his head before the enemy of Smara and, overcome by grief, related what had occurred.

O Blessed One, today this army is being devoured by the son of an Asura; that Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the three worlds and the crusher of Daityas, has been swallowed. The moon and the sun, as well as the boon-granting Brahmā and Indra, have been swallowed; and all of them—Yama, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Kubera—have been swallowed.
I stand here alone and humble; what should be done by me now, while the lord of the Daityas, together with his hosts, remains invincible and joyful in heart?

Having encountered you, who are invincible, the god Viṣṇu himself—possessing the speed of the wind and free from fear—approached Kaśyapa’s son, Kanakakaśipu, with sharp claws out of devotion; yet, O Blessed One, being subject to the power of your remnants, he opened his mouth wide to devour him, intending to destroy the impurity of the three worlds.
Thus cursed by Vasiṣṭha and the other seven sages, the lords of the worlds, he remained in that state for a very long time together with the Daityas.

Then he spoke to them with affectionate words for their own benefit: "O best of sages, when will my liberation from this terrible state come about? For at the time of battle, I was addressed by those enraged ones with words such as 'seize! and so forth; therefore, [I am now] thoroughly shattered in the face by terrible arrows and blows from fists."

"Indeed, in the forest named Badarī, that sacred abode of Hari, you shall reach the Supreme by steadying yourself and becoming free from all impurity. Then, at their word, that swallower of demons, though afflicted by hunger, wandered daily from battle, yet again filled with joy and fragrance.

This world is filled with a terrible darkness, just as it is when the sun and moon have risen; Śukra is your supreme enemy, causing extreme distress. He restores the Daityas, slain by the gods, to life through the power of the science of immortality, making them vigorous again, visible once more, and free from hundreds of wounds.
It would be better for me to give up my life than for you to be chosen as a witness for even a moment during the time of battle while I am performing my duty.

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this from his virtuous son, the Lord of the Pramathas became enraged; after meditating for a long time, the Lord of the three worlds first created an incomparable being known as Sāman, whose body had the form of the sun’s rays. Then, by means of that [being] and through its name, the darkness was destroyed by him with a laugh.

In this world, the sage Vīraka once again waged a great battle against the demons with their distorted faces; he who was produced by the preeminent sage after consuming powdered stone, and who, having fought a conflict, formerly conquered even the city.

That very Mahārudra was indeed instantly swallowed by the son of Diti; thereafter, Nandin—foremost among warriors, a great abode even for hundreds of the best of sages, and endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and great fortitude—was equipped with sharp arrows, spears, and swords.

Having observed this, the blessed Kapardin, desiring battle, mounted his excellent bull and stood facing the Danava with his mouth open; muttering a divine mantra that causes the swallowing and disgorging of what is swallowed, he made himself ready, having prepared his bow and arrows that were like thunderbolts.

Then, having taken all that [army] along with his own incomparable strength and accompanied by Viṣṇu, the sage Vīraka emerged from the mouth of Vidhvasa. All the enemies of the Lord of Kamala (Viṣṇu), including the Moon, the Day-maker (the Sun), and the Lord of the Wind, were cast forth; and that joyful army once again engaged in a great battle.

When Śukra subsequently restored to life with the power of his knowledge those sons of Diti who had been slain in battle, he was then bound like a sacrificial animal by the Gaṇas and brought before the Lord of Beings; thus was that preceptor of the Dānavas swallowed by the enemy of Tripura.

When [the city] was destroyed, that entire abode of the enemy of the gods—known as Śukra—was conquered, shattered, utterly broken, and even crushed by the gods; while the numerous throngs of spirits, delighting in devouring the corpses of the Daityas, danced with their hands raised, brandishing sharp arrows and spears.

In that battle strewn with various kinds of vultures, tigers, and intoxicated vetālas with extremely firm claws and beaks, their mouths gaping wide to swallow corpses and carcasses, the progenitor of the lineage of Kanakakaśipu fought for a long time and was finally defeated by Hari, Hara, and Mahendra.

When the army had entered the netherworld, as well as the mountain clefts, the waters, and the oceans, and when the host was thus diminished, Andhaka—the best of the Daityas, the foremost of those who cause destruction like a forest fire in the wrath of the gods, and the shatterer of the universe—had his pride crushed by Hari with terrible blows of his mace.

Indeed, he who had been granted a boon did not abandon the village; for his body was then tormented by the lord of the gods with terrible blows. Thereupon, roaring loudly and summoning the Lord of the Pramathas, he swiftly conquered the gods with floods of weapons and missiles, as well as trees, mountains, and waters, while calling out softly.

Standing there and fighting with various kinds of weapons fallen on the battlefield, all of which were completely exhausted, Girijā then tormented Rudra with trees, serpents, masses of thunderbolts, collections of misshapen weapons, illusions, deceptive contrivances, and hundreds of *śambara* spells.

There, the wise and heroic Mahāsattva, equal to the enemy of Tripura, employed another deceptive trick against Śaileśa. Though rendered powerless by the infatuation of hundreds of celestial maidens, that son of Diti was not slain by the gods; instead, his body was instantly shattered by a multitude of weapons and missiles.

The ground, utterly pervaded by the hosts of Andhakas who had fallen upon it from the flow of that [blood], bore a most terrible and hideous countenance resembling their own selves; yet, with his body like the fire at the end of an aeon, the Lord of Beings, the enemy of Tripura, pierced through that most dreadful form with his trident.

When the army became entirely other than an army due to the excessively hot drops of flesh issuing from wounds caused by the strike of Paśupati’s weapon, then the wise Viṣṇu, through his yogic power, summoned the Lord of the Pramathas and assumed a fierce form with a deformed face, yet unconquered even by women.
Terrifying, withered, and overcome by many creeper-like arms, the enraged and venerable Lord emerged from the ear onto the battlefield-head of Śambhu.

Standing on the battlefield, that Goddess, who adorned the earth with the pair of her feet and was praised by all the gods, had her mind impelled by me; afflicted by hunger, she drank that army born of the sons of Diti and that very warm blood at the head of the battle, which was soiled by the mud of her flowing saliva.

Then one Daitya, though his blood was dried up, continued to fight with terrible blows from his palms resembling thunderbolts, with his knees and feet, and with his nails shaped like diamonds, as well as with his mouth, arms, and head; he did so while remembering the eternal, unborn Kṣatriya duty ordained for his own lineage, O Lord of the Mountain.

Having been pacified in battle, his heart was later pierced by the Lord of the Pramathas; impaled upon a trident, he remained suspended in the sky like a pillar. His lower body withered under the rays of the sun, his frame decayed, while his body was moistened by the showers from clouds accompanied by wind.

Though his body was shattered into fragments resembling pieces of ice from the sun, that bull among the Daityas did not even then give up his life; then Śambhu, the ocean of supreme compassion, being pleased and praised by him, affectionately granted him the status of Gaṇapati.

Then, at the conclusion of the battle, the lords of the worlds, along with their consorts, duly worshipped the Lord of the Pramathas with various kinds of hymns; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, bowing with shoulders bent, praised him profusely with supreme eulogies, and being delighted and comforted, they uttered cries of "Victory! Victory!"

Together with those delighted ones, he sported joyfully in a cave of the best of mountains; having honored the beautiful-eyed goddess with various offerings, he issued his command for play, having obtained the joyful daughter of the mountain king as well as his sinless son, who had been released from the terrible mouth of Vidhvasa.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle with Andhaka," within the "Episode of the Slaying of Andhaka" in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: In that great, terrible, and hair-raising battle, the wise Śukra, lord of the Daityas, was devoured by the enemy of Tripura.
Thus I have heard this in brief; tell it again in detail. What did the great yogin do while staying within the belly of the wielder of the Pināka bow?
How was it that Śambhu’s digestive fire did not burn that semen—[a fire] which is like the time of destruction at the end of an eon, and which possesses the blazing splendor of Bhārgava?
How did the wise one emerge from the cage-like belly of Śambhu? And for how long did that descendant of Bhṛgu worship him?
And yet he obtained that supreme knowledge which pacifies death. What, O dear one, is that supreme knowledge by which death is indeed warded off?
How did Lebhendhaka attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas after emerging from the trident of Śambhu, the God of gods, who sports in the divine play of a sage?
O one of great intelligence, have mercy and tell me all of this in its entirety; O father, relate to me the nectar of Śiva’s divine play as I listen.
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa, who possesses immeasurable splendor, Sanatkumāra spoke while recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, to the supreme nectar of Śiva’s divine play. You are blessed, you are a foremost devotee of Śiva, and you naturally bring me joy.
As the battle between Śaṅkara and Andhaka proceeded, those two were the lords of the impenetrable array of spears and the mountain-like array [respectively].
O Sage, although victory formerly belonged to the powerful Daityas, through the power of Śiva, victory came to the Pramathas.
Upon hearing that, the great Daitya Andhakāsura became despondent; he became intent on reflection, wondering, "How might victory be mine?"
Then, withdrawing from that battle, the highly intelligent hero Andhaka went quickly and alone into the presence of Śukra.
Having prostrated before his own guru and descended from the chariot, he—the best among those who know the principles of conduct—spoke this after reflecting, with palms joined in reverence.
Andhaka said: "O Blessed One, having taken refuge in you, we maintain the status of your disciples; yet we are defeated and never victorious."
By your power, we always consider all the gods, together with their followers—even those headed by Hara, Uṣā, and Indra—to be as insignificant as blades of grass.
Then, by your grace, the gods will fear us just as elephants fear lions or serpents fear Garuḍas.
By your grace, the Daityas and Dānavas entered the impenetrable array of spears after having utterly routed the entire army of the Pramathas.
Having taken refuge in you, O Bhārgava, we always remain as steady as cows and move about without fear, even in the midst of a battle.
O Brahmin, protect, protect those who have come for refuge after renouncing the world, even the Asuras who were terrified and, though struck down by heroic enemies, are now dead!
Behold my excellent hosts, Huṇḍa and the others, who have been trampled by those foremost ones of terrifying prowess, who crush death itself; they have been slaughtered and cast down.
The time has now come for that excellent knowledge which you obtained in the past after drinking the smoke of chaff for a thousand autumns.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, let everyone today behold that fruit of your knowledge as you compassionately restore all the Asuras and Pramathas to life.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus heard the words of Andhaka, the wise Bhārgava then reflected with an agonized mind.
"What must I do even now? How might there be safety for me? The life-principle (jīva) that follows the process of the humors' combination is entirely unsuitable for me."
I shall employ against his qualities that weapon obtained from Śaṅkara; by it, the hero will crush those followers of Śaṅkara who were previously crushed in battle by the Pramathas.
Then, having reflected in his heart with wisdom upon the preeminent doctrine of those who have come for refuge, Śukra accepted her speech.
Then, having smiled slightly, Bhārgava, with a mind at ease, spoke to the lord of the Dānavas while remembering the lotus feet of Śiva.
Śukra said: "O dear one, everything that you have spoken is indeed true; for this acquisition of knowledge was undertaken by me for the sake of the Dānavas."
Having indeed drunk unbearable grain-smoke for a thousand years, this knowledge was obtained from the Lord, which always brings happiness to one's kinsmen.
By means of this knowledge, I shall raise up the Daityas who have been crushed by the Pramathas in battle, just as one who drinks water revives withered crops.
In this very moment, you shall see those Daityas of your own kin risen again, free from wounds, free from pain, healthy, as if having merely woken from sleep.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to Adhoka, the sage Śukra caused the vidyā to revolve, recollecting the Lord of Vidyās with reverence for each individual Daitya.
By the mere turning of the Vidyā-mantra, all those heroic Daityas and Dānavas rose up simultaneously, like those who had been sleeping, bearing their weapons.
Just as the Vedas are constantly practiced, or as clouds are [gathered] in battle, so too are objects given with faith to Brahmins in times of need.
Seeing those great asuras, Huṇḍa and the others, restored to life, all the asuras roared like clouds filled with water.
Furthermore, those of great strength and prowess, fearless and intent on battle, roared with terrible cries along with the Pramathas.
Seeing the Daityas and Dānavas restored to life by Śukra, all the Pramathas, led by Nandin and fierce in battle, were filled with amazement.
"O Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, this entire matter must be represented to him. Having reflected thus, those wise ones spoke to one another as follows.
While that sacrifice of battle, so wondrous in form, was thus proceeding among the lords of the Pramathas, the son of Śilāda, provoked to anger upon seeing the deeds of Bhārgava, approached Maheśa.

Having exclaimed "Victory!", Nandin spoke to the fierce Jayayoni, who was as bright as gold: "O Lord, the martial deeds of the lords of the Gaṇas are truly difficult to perform, even for the gods led by Indra."

O Lord, that which has been done today by the descendant of Bhṛgu is in vain; for he has playfully cast back toward us, one by one, those very enemies who were dead, using this science that grants life to the deceased.
The great lords of the asuras, such as Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Kumbha, Jambha, Vipāka, Pāka, and others, having returned today from the abode of Yama, roam about putting the Pramathas to flight.

For if he were to revive those foremost Daityas here again and again after they have been cast down, O Maheśa, how could there be victory for us, and how indeed could there be peace for the lords of the Gaṇas?

Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed in this manner by Nandin, the lord of the Pramathas, the God, the Lord of the lords of the Pramathas, then spoke with a smile to that Nandin, the king of all the lords of the Gaṇas.
Śiva said: "Nandin, go with extreme haste; having snatched that best of eminent brahmins from the midst of the sons of Diti, bring him here quickly, just as a hawk seizes a young quail."

Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by the bull-bannered Lord, Nandin let out a roar like that of a bull or a lion; and plunging swiftly into the army, he went to where the lamp of the Bhārgava lineage was located.

While he was being guarded by all the sons of Diti, who held nooses, swords, trees, stones, and rocks in their hands, the powerful Nandin agitated the Daityas and carried off Kāvya, just as a śarabha seizes an elephant.

With their garments slipping, their ornaments fallen, and their hair disheveled as they were seized by the powerful one, the enemies of the gods followed after him, letting out lion-like roars as if intending to liberate him.
Like fierce clouds, the lords of the Dānavas rained down upon Nandīśvara a torrent of thunderbolts, spears, swords, axes, towering discuses, and stones.

Having encountered that descendant of Bhṛgu and having burnt hundreds of weapons with the fire from his mouth, the Lord of the Gaṇas returned to the side of Bhava, with the host of his enemies distressed, as the war between the Asuras and the gods intensified.
"This is that Śukra, O Blessed One," he quickly announced to Bhava; and the God of gods took up the semen, like an offering presented by one who is pure.

Without saying a word, that protector of beings indeed cast the lord of poets into his mouth like a fruit; then all the asuras, uttering cries of "Hā! Hā! and "Ha! Ha!", let out a great, loud lamentation.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Śukra Being Swallowed," in the Andhaka-yuddha section of the fifth book, the Rudra-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O great sage, tell me the truth: when Śukra was swallowed by Rudra, what did the Dānavas do—the great heroes led by Andhaka?

Sanatkumāra said: When Kāvya had been swallowed by the Lord of Girijā, the Daityas became devoid of hope for victory, like lordly elephants deprived of their trunks or like bulls bereft of their horns.
They were like hosts of gods deprived of their heads, or like Brahmins devoid of Vedic study; like groups of beings lacking effort, or like those possessing effort yet bereft of fortune.
They are like women deprived of their husbands, like flights of arrows devoid of feathers, like lifespans lacking merit, and like sacred learnings bereft of vows.

Just as masses of ritual actions become devoid of their own fruits without the single power of magnificence, and just as Kṣatriyas are indeed without valor, and likewise the multitude of virtues without truth.
When Śukra had been carried off by Nandin and swallowed by Viṣādin, the Daityas, who had been striving for the festival of battle, fell into despair.
Seeing them devoid of enthusiasm, Andhaka, possessed of great wisdom and prowess, addressed the Daityas headed by Tuhuṇḍa and Huṇḍa.
Andhaka said: "By Nandin, who overpowered the sage, we have been deceived; indeed, today the very lives of us all have been stripped of their bodies."
Fortitude, heroism, conduct, fame, courage, splendor, and prowess—all these were simultaneously lost when that single descendant of Bhṛgu was taken away.
Fie upon us, by whom not even a single one—worthy of family worship, the best of the lineage, a guru, and all-capable—has been saved as a protector in times of calamity!
Therefore, O heroes, remembering the lotus feet of your preceptor, fight here without delay against those heroic Pramathas as your enemies.
Having remembered the lotus feet of my preceptor Kāvya, which bestow happiness, I shall destroy all the Pramathas along with Nandin.
Having slain these helpless ones today along with Sahadeva and Indra, I shall release Bhārgava, just as a yogi releases the soul from karma.
And even if that yogi, by means of yoga, were himself the master and were to depart from his body, our sovereignty would remain protected.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Andhaka, the Dānavas, whose voices resounded like thunderclouds and who were resolved upon death, spoke mercilessly to the Pramathas.
If our life-span remains, the Pramathas shall never be able to overcome us by force; but if our life-span has ended, what is the point of fleeing and abandoning our master in battle?
Those people who, possessing the wealth of great honor, depart from here having abandoned their master, they certainly go to the abode of Andhatāmisra.
Having repeatedly defiled their reputation with the darkness of infamy, those who are broken on the field of battle shall find no happiness, neither in this world nor in the next.
What is the use of gifts, what use are austerities, and what use are ablutions at sacred fords, if one bathes at the Dhārā-tīrtha, which removes the impurity of rebirth?
Having deliberated upon those words, those Daityas and Danujas sounded the war-drums and crushed the Pramathas in battle.
There, with floods of arrows, swords, and thunderbolts, and with hard stone weapons, as well as *bhuśuṇḍis*, *bhindipālas*, spears, javelins, and battle-axes—
Striking one another with skull-topped staffs, sharp-edged spears, tridents, clubs, and maces, they wrought a great carnage.
There arose the sound of drawn bows, of falling arrows, of *bhiṇḍipāla* and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, and of war-cries.
With the sounds of war-drums, the loud trumpeting of elephants, and the neighing of horses, a great clamor arose.
The space between heaven and earth was filled with the sounds of their shouting; and among both the brave and the timid, there arose a great bristling of the hair on their bodies.
And those [armies] whose perception of sound was shattered by the great roar of elephants and horses, whose banners and flags were broken, and whose weapons were exhausted.
Covered in the splendor of gushing blood, and deprived of horses, elephants, and chariots, the thirsty troops on both sides indeed fainted away.
Then, O sage, those heroic Pramathas, headed by Nandin, struck all the asuras with their might and achieved victory.
Seeing his army being shattered here and there by the Pramathas, Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed toward the Gaṇas.
Like mountains struck by falling thunderbolts, or like waterless clouds, the Pramathas perished by those weapons discharged from the rims of the bowls.
Seeing him as he went away and as he approached, whether at a distance or standing nearby, Andhaka pierced him with as many arrows as there were hairs on his body.
Seeing the army being shattered by the powerful Andhaka, Skanda, Vināyaka, Nandin, Somanandin, and the others [fled].
The powerful and heroic Pramathas, Śaṅkara’s own attendants, became enraged; those of great strength engaged in a wonderful battle.
By Vināyaka, Skanda, Nandin, Somanandin, Vīra, Naigameya, and the mighty Vaiśākha.
By these and other fierce hosts, Andhaka was likewise overwhelmed, as they rained down a torrential downpour from the falling streams of tridents, spears, and volleys of arrows.
Then a great clamor arose between the armies of the Pramathas and the Asuras; by that immense noise, Śukra, who was situated within the womb of Śambhu, [was disturbed].
Then, wandering like the wind which is homeless and seeks out openings, he beheld the seven worlds together with the nether regions within the body of Rudra.
The various worlds of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Indra, as well as those of the Ādityas and Apsarases, and the battle between the Pramathas and the Asuras.
Wandering all around within Bhava’s belly for a hundred years, he did not find an opening there, just as a wicked man finds no vulnerability in a pure person.
Then, by means of the Śāmbhava yoga in the form of semen, Bhārgava, having recited this supreme mantra, [emerged] from the cage-like belly of Śambhu.
Having emerged through the path of the *liṅga*, he then prostrated before Śiva; he was taken by Gaurī for the sake of a son and thus made her son, Vighneśvara.
Then, seeing Kāvya Bhārgava emerging through the path of semen, Maheśāna, the ocean of compassion, spoke while smiling.
Maheśvara said: "O descendant of Bhṛgu, since you have issued from my liṅga like semen (śukra), by that deed you shall possess whiteness (śuklatva); you are my son—depart!"
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by the Lord, Śukra, whose splendor was like that of the sun, bowed again to Śiva and praised him with palms joined in reverence.

Śukra said: You have infinite feet, infinite forms, and infinite heads; you are the auspicious one who brings an end to all things. With infinite arms—how shall I praise you, the one worthy of hymns, having prostrated with my head?

You are the eight-formed one; you are the infinite-formed one; you are the bestower of desires upon all gods and demons, yet you are also the unseen and the crusher. How can I praise you, who are such as this?
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Śiva and bowing again at Śiva’s command, Śukra entered the army of the Dānavas like the moon entering a mass of clouds.
Śaṅkara has declared this to be "swallowing" (nigīrṇana) in the battle with Kavi; hear that mantra which, when recited, [causes] Kavi to enter the belly of Śambhu.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Swallowing of Śukra," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: *Oṃ, obeisance to you, the Lord of Gods, who are saluted by gods and demons; to the Great God of the past and the future; to the one with green and tawny eyes; to the Powerful One whose form is intellect; to the one clad in tiger-skin; to the Son of the Forest (Araṇeya); to the Source of the three worlds; to the Sovereign; to Hara; to the Green-eyed One; to the Maker of the end of the ages; to the Fire; to the Lord of the Gaṇas; to the Protector of the World; to the One of Great Arms; to the One of Great Hands; to the Trident-bearer; to the One with Great Fangs; to Time; to Maheśvara; to the Imperishable; to the One whose form is Time; to the Blue-necked One; to the Large-bellied One; to the Chief of the Gaṇas; to the Self of All; to the Creator of All; to the All-pervading; to the Slayer of Death; to the One of Excellent Vows on Mount Pāriyātra; to the Celibate Student; to the One who has reached the end of the Vedānta; to the One who has reached the end of austerity; to Paśupati; to the Limbless One; to the Trident-handed One; to the One whose banner is the Bull; to Hari; to the Matted-haired One; to the Tufted One; to the Club-bearer; to the One of Great Renown; to the Lord of Beings; to the Dweller in the Cave; to the One who holds the lute, the *paṇava* drum, and the cymbals; to the Immortal; to the Beautiful One; to the One resembling the rising sun; to the Dweller in the cremation ground; to the Blessed One; to the Lord of Umā; to the Tamer of Enemies; to the One who struck out the eyes of Bhaga; to the Destroyer of the teeth of Pūṣan; to the Maker of the Kūraka weapon; to the Noose-handed One; to the Time of Dissolution; to the One with the Face of a Meteor; to the One whose Banner is Fire; to the Sage; to the Radiant One; to the Lord of People; to the Elevator; to the Progenitor; to the Fourth; to the Best of the World; to Vāmadeva; to the One whose speech is courteous; to the Mendicant from the left; to the One in the form of a mendicant; to the Matted-haired One; to the One who is himself matted; to the Stayer of Indra’s hand; to the Support of the Vasus; to the Sacrifice; to the Performer of Sacrifice; to Time; to the Wise One; to the Honey-maker; to the Moving One; to the Lord of Trees; to the One honored by the *Vājasaneyins*; to the Sustainer of the World; to the Creator of the World; to the Primeval Person; to the Eternal; to the Fixed One; to the Overseer of Dharma; to the Three-pathed One; to the Creator of Beings; to the Three-eyed One; to the Multi-formed One; to the Sun of ten-thousand-fold splendor; to the Divine One; to the Resounder of all musical instruments; to the Liberator from all afflictions; to the Binder; to the Sustainer of All; to the Supreme Dharma; to Puṣpadanta; to the Portion; to the Mouth; to the All-destroyer; to the One of Golden Fame; to the Guardian of the Door; to the Terrible One; to the One of Terrible Prowess; *Oṃ, obeisance, obeisance!* Sanatkumāra said: Having recited this supreme mantra, Śukra emerged from the cage of the belly through the path of the *liṅga*, like the intense semen of Śambhu.
Then, for the sake of a son, he was taken by Gaurī and made immortal and ageless by Viśveśa; glorious, he became like a second Śaṅkara.
When three thousand years had passed upon the surface of the earth, the sage Śukra, a treasure-house of the Vedas, was born again from Maheśvara.
He beheld Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, emaciated on the stake, meditating upon the Supreme Lord, a true ascetic endowed with fortitude.
To Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, the immortal, the eternal, Sthāṇu, the blue-throated one, and the wielder of the Pināka bow.
The bull-eyed one, the great object of knowledge, the Puruṣa who grants all desires; the enemy of Kāma, the burner of Kāma, the one whose form is desire, the one with matted hair.
Virūpa, Giriśa, Bhīma, adorned with garlands and clad in red garments; the Yogi, the burner of Time, the destroyer of Tripura, and the bearer of the skull-bowl.

It is one whose vows are secret, whose mantras are guarded, profound, and within the sphere of pure realization; it is the substratum of qualities such as *aṇimā* and the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds.
The hero, the slayer of heroes, the terrible, the deformed, the fleshy, the clever, the eater of great flesh, the insane, the fearsome, indeed Maheśvara.
He who causes the three worlds to tremble, the greedy one, the hunter, the destroyer of sacrifices, joined by the sons of the Kṛttikās, the mad one clothed in a tiger skin.
Clad in an elephant hide, agitated, adorned with serpents, he should grant [the boon]; he is the one who bestows the long-hanging Vetāla, the terrible one worshipped by Śākinīs.

He is non-terrible, the slayer of terrible daityas, possessing a terrible roar, the lord of the forest; his limbs are smeared with ashes, he wears matted hair, he is pure, and he is served by hundreds of bheruṇḍas.
The Lord of Beings, the Master of Spirits, who rests upon the five elements and moves through the sky; the enraged, the harsh, the fierce one, the Lord of Caṇḍī, the beloved of Caṇḍikā.
Fierce, lofty, and winged, constantly feeding on raw flesh, licking his lips, most terrible—he is Death, who is beyond the reach of death itself.
To Mṛtyumṛtyu, Mahāsena, who dwells in cremation grounds and forests; to Rāga, Virāga, and Rāgāndha, who is honored by hundreds of those free from passion.

O younger brother of Indra, he is the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; he is both dharma and adharma; he is truth and untruth; he is the form of existence and the form of non-existence; and he is without cause.
The Sun-god who is half-female, possessing the radiance of hundreds of millions of suns; the sacrifice, the Lord of Sacrifice, Rudra, Īśāna, the granter of boons, Śiva.
Indeed, by meditating upon these one hundred and eight forms of Śiva, the Supreme Self, the Dānava was liberated from that great fear.
He was consecrated by Kapardin with a divine shower of nectar; being satisfied, [Kapardin] released him from that point and lowered him down from the tip of the trident.
Then the great Daitya Andhaka was addressed by Maheśāna; the high-souled Lord spoke to the Asura with words of consolation regarding everything that had been done.
Īśvara said: "O, O Lord of Daityas, I am pleased with your self-restraint and your observance of vows; by your heroism and your fortitude, choose a boon, O you of noble conduct."

I, the granter of boons who am worthy of being honored, have been constantly propitiated by you, O best of the great lords of the Daityas, whose every impurity has been shaken off; you are indeed worthy of a boon.
Whatever merit you possess from sustaining your life, may that result in your liberation after three thousand years.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this, Andhaka, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, placed both knees upon the ground and spoke to the Lord, the consort of Umā.
Andhaka said: "O Blessed One, you who are higher than the highest, whom I previously addressed on the field of battle with words faltering from joy, though I was most wretched and distressed."
Whatever deed has been committed by me in the worlds out of delusion and censured by others—O Lord, since I did it unknowingly of you, do not take all of that to heart.
O Mahādeva, whatever evil I have committed even toward Pārvatī out of the fault of desire, may it be forgiven by me; I am wretched and exceedingly distressed.
Compassion must always be shown by you toward those who suffer, especially toward the wretched, the destitute, and those endowed with devotion.
Thus, wretched and filled with devotion, I have come to you for refuge; protection must be granted to me—this salutation with joined palms is offered by me.
