This Goddess, the Mother of the World, is well-pleased with me; having abandoned all anger, may she look upon me with a gracious countenance.
O Moon-crested One, where is her anger, and where am I—a wretched Daitya? Therefore, O Śambhu, Maheśvara, whose crest is the crescent moon, I am not one to endure that [wrath].
Where are you, the most noble one, and where am I, rendered helpless by the defects of desire, anger, and the like, as well as by old age and death?
This is your son Vīraka, mighty and skilled in battle; seeing me in such distress, do not yield to the power of wrath.
Possessing a complexion like snow, a pearl necklace, the moon, a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon itself, may I behold Pārvatī constantly as my mother with profound reverence.
"May I dwell forever with you both, devoted, free from enmity toward the gods, accompanied by my attendants, peaceful in soul, and intent upon yoga."
May I not remember again a hostile birth arising from the state of a Dānava; O Maheśāna, by your grace, grant me this supreme boon.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken these words, the lord of the Daityas observed silence; meditating upon the three-eyed God and looking toward his mother Pārvatī.
Then, having been beheld by Rudra with a truly gracious eye, he remembered his own previous history and his wondrous birth.
When that account was remembered, his desires were then fulfilled; having bowed to his mother and father, he thereafter became one who had accomplished his purpose.
Having been smelled on the head by Pārvatī and by the wise Śaṅkara, he obtained his desired object from the gratified Lord who bears the crescent moon upon His crest.
All this ancient history of Andhaka has been told to you, concerning his attainment of the status of a Gaṇapati through the grace of Mahādeva, which bestows supreme bliss.
The mantra known as Mṛtyuñjaya, which destroys death, has been declared; it should be recited with diligence, for it bestows the fruits of all desires.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Restoration of Life to the Andhaka Host," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, how the supreme knowledge that pacifies death was obtained by the sage Kāvya from Śiva, who is named Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death).
In former times, that descendant of Bhṛgu went to the city of Vārāṇasī and performed austerities for a long duration, meditating upon the Lord Viśveśvara.
O Vedavyāsa, he installed there itself a liṅga of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, and constructed a beautiful well in front of it.
With great effort, he bathed the Lord of Gods one hundred thousand times with five kinds of nectars (pañcāmṛta) measured in droṇas, using many fragrant bathing substances.
A thousand times, with great affection, he anointed the Lord of Gods with sandalwood and yakṣakardama pastes, following these with fragrant unguents.
With *rājacaṃpaka*, *dhatura*, *karavīra*, and *kuśeśaya* flowers; with *mālatī*, *karṇikāra*, *kadaṃba*, *bakula*, and *utpala*.
With *mallikā* and *śatapatrī*, with *siṃdhuvāra* and *kiṃśuka*, with *bandhūka* flowers, *punnāga*, and *nāgakeśara* blossoms;
With fresh mallī and cibilika flowers, with kunda and mucukunda, with mandāra, bilva leaves, droṇa, maruvaka, and vṛka, with granthiparṇa, damanaka, and the most beautiful mango sprouts.
With *tulasī*, *devagandhārī*, *bṛhatpatrī*, and sprouts of *kuśa* grass; with *nadyāvarta*, *agastya*, *śāla*, and *devadāru* trees.
With *kāñcanāra*, *kurabaka*, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and *kuruṇṭaka* flowers—each of these blossoms and even with other tender shoots.
With great care and much affection, he worshipped Śaṅkara with beautiful and auspicious leaves of various kinds, including thousand-petaled lotuses.
Honored with offerings of song and dance, he praised Śaṅkara profusely with hymns, with the thousand names, and with other songs of praise.
In this manner, Śukra worshipped Maheśvara for a thousand years of five-autumns (five-thousand years) by means of various kinds of rites.
When the god did not look upon her even slightly with a favorable countenance, she then undertook another vow that was terrible and exceedingly difficult to endure.
Having thoroughly washed away the great impurity called mental restlessness with the waters of meditative cultivation, along with the senses, repeatedly;
Having purified that jewel of his mind and offered it to the wielder of the Pināka bow, the sage spent a thousand autumns amidst a mass of smoke from parched grain.
Seeing Kāvya thus performing severe penance with a firm mind, Maheśvara became pleased with him and appeared before Bhārgava.
Then, emerging from that linga with a splendor exceeding a thousand suns, Virūpākṣa himself, the lord of Dākṣāyaṇī, spoke to him.
Maheśvara said: O treasure of asceticism, O highly fortunate one, O great sage, son of Bhṛgu! By this penance of yours, I am constantly and especially pleased.
O Bhārgava, choose every boon desired by your mind; out of affection, I shall grant you all your wishes, for there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these excellent words of Śambhu, which bestow great bliss, that poet became satisfied and immersed himself in an ocean of happiness.
With his body covered in horripilation from the mass of rising bliss, the twice-born Aṃbhojanayana joyfully prostrated before Śambhu.
Satisfied, with his mountain-like eyes blossoming, he praised the Eight-bodied One (Aṣṭatanu), placing his joined palms upon his head and saying, "Victory! Victory!"

Bhārgava said: O Lord of the Universe, O Jewel of the Sky, you who, surpassing all darkness with these rays of yours, bring to an end the desires of the night-stalkers, shine resplendently in the heavens for the welfare of the three worlds; therefore, salutations unto you.

O Moon, who shines excessively and beyond measure in the world and in the sky with great splendors, the eye of all the worlds; you who have dispelled all darkness and are filled with a flood of nectar—salutations to you!

O Purifier, you are the ever-moving wind-path itself, yet you are worthy of worship; O Life of the World, who here could live without you? For all beings are nourished by the wind that increases when stilled by you; O All-pervading One, salutations to you who bring satisfaction to the virtuous.

O sole Purifier of all, without the singular power of Your purifying fire, this world—though dead, yet possessing the divine activity of immortality—would not have lived; O Inner Soul of the universe, You are the Purifier who bestows peace at every step; salutations to You!

O Supreme Lord in the form of water, purifier of the world, you are surely the creator of diverse and wondrous virtuous deeds; O Lord of the Universe, since this entire world indeed becomes pure and stainless through immersion in your water, I bow down to you.

O Lord, this entire universe expands here because You provide space within and without the form of the ether; it always breathes through You out of its own nature, O Compassionate One, and thus undergoes contraction. Therefore, I am Your devotee and bow down to You.

O All-sustainer, you support this entire universe; O Lord of the Universe, who else but you is the enemy of darkness? Therefore, destroy that darkness, O you who are adorned with serpents! You are beyond the praiseworthy, higher than the highest; therefore, I bow down to you.

O Hara, this world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by these successions of forms belonging to your essential nature; O Lord whose form is the reflection residing within the inner self of all, O Eight-formed One, Supreme Soul, I, a servant of the Supreme Self, bow eternally to you.

O You whose form is for the benefit of the entire world, bound by these eight forms as if by an unbreakable bond, You indeed act for the welfare of all; O You who are the ultimate reality of the multitude of all goals, praised by those who bow down, I am prostrate before You, who are thus pervasive and most expansive.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus praised Bharga with these eight verses on his eightfold forms, the descendant of Bhrigu, with his head touching the ground, bowed down to him again and again.
Thus praised by the exceedingly radiant Bhārgava, Mahādeva rose from the earth, took hold of that prostrate twice-born man with his two arms.
With great affection, his face illuminated by the moonlight of his teeth, he spoke in gentle words as deep as the roar of a thundercloud.
Mahādeva said: "O best of brahmins, O dear Kavi, you are my devotee and a purifier, both by this most intense austerity and by the conduct practiced toward your own kin."
By the merit of installing the *liṅga*, by the worship of the *liṅga*, and by offering mental oblations that are pure and unwavering;
And because you have purified the great field of Avimukta through your conduct, I behold you with my two daughters; there is nothing whatsoever that you should not give.
With this very body, having entered the cave of my womb, you shall attain the status of a son through the path of my excellent organ.
Today I grant you a boon that is difficult even for my attendants to obtain—a boon which I have generally guarded from both Hari and Hiraṇyagarbha.
This stainless lore named Mṛtasaṃjīvanī was created by me alone through the great power of my asceticism. ||4||
O greatly pure one, O storehouse of pure austerity, I shall bestow upon you today that very Vidyā in the form of a mantra; for you possess the fitness for that knowledge.
O best of the Lords of Knowledge, for whomever you shall certainly cause this knowledge to revolve, that living being will surely attain truth.
Your splendor shall surpass the sun and the fire, and you shall be a star in the sky; blazing intensely, become the foremost among the planets.
Moreover, whether women or men shall undertake a journey while you are present, all their undertakings will perish by the mere cast of your glance.
O observer of noble vows, upon your rising, all religious rites for men in this world, such as marriages and others, shall become fruitful.
And all lunar days (tithis) associated with you shall be auspicious Nandās; those who are devoted to you will possess abundant virility and many offspring.
"This Liṅga established by you shall be known by the name Śukreśa; those mortals who worship it will attain perfection."
Those who throughout the year are devoted to the vow of eating only at night, and those who, on your day, have performed all the water-libation rites at Śukrakūpa;
Listen to the fruit that belongs to those who shall worship Śukreśa: those mortals shall have unbarren semen, they shall possess sons, and they shall have abundant virility.
They will undoubtedly be endowed with manliness and good fortune; all those people shall possess learning and partake in happiness.
Having thus granted the boons, the Lord dissolved into that Liṅga; Bhārgava too, with a satisfied mind, returned to his own abode.
Thus, O Vyāsa, I have told you how the lore named Mṛtyuñjayā was obtained through the power of austerity; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Mṛtasaṃjīvinī Vidyā," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, by your grace and out of affection, this wonderful and auspicious narrative, filled with the favor of Śambhu, has been heard by me.
Now I wish to hear the life-story of the Moon-crested Lord, how he indeed affectionately bestowed the status of a leader of the Gaṇas upon Bāṇāsura.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen with respect, O Vyāsa, to that story of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, concerning how he indeed affectionately granted the status of a Gaṇapati to the Asura Bāṇa.
In this very place is the virtuous conduct of the great lord Śaṅkara, and here also is the battle between Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu as he was favoring Bāṇa.
In this regard, listen to me as I relate a supreme and highly meritorious historical narrative (itihāsa) concerning the divine sports of Śiva, which brings delight to the mind and the ears.
The son of Brahmā was Marīci, who was a sage of great intelligence; among all the mind-born sons, he was the eldest, the most excellent, and a lord of progeny.
His son was the high-souled Kaśyapa, the best of sages, who greatly increased creation and was devoted even to Brahmā, his father.
O Vyāsa, his thirteen daughters, who were virtuous and devoted to their husbands, became the wives of the sage Kaśyapa.
Among them, Diti was the eldest; she is remembered as the mother of the Daityas, while the other daughters gave birth to the gods and all beings, both moving and stationary.
The two eldest sons of Diti were both possessed of great strength; Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger brother after him.
The sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu were four of the best among the Daityas: Hrāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, and Prahrāda, in that order.
For there was the great Prahlāda, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses; indeed, not even any of those Daityas were able to destroy him.
His son was Virocana, who became a supreme and great donor; he gave his own head to Śakra when the latter begged for it under the pretext of being a brahmin.
His son was Bali, a great donor and a beloved of Śiva, by whom the earth was given to Hari in the form of Vāmana.
His legitimate son was Bāṇa, a devotee of Śiva, who was indeed honorable, generous, wise, true to his word, and a giver of hundreds.
In former times, residing in the city called Śoṇita, that lord of the asuras ruled his kingdom after having conquered the three worlds by force, along with their protectors.
By the grace of Śaṅkara, those very attendants of Bāṇāsura, who was himself a devotee of Śiva, became like his own servants.
In his kingdom, the subjects were not distressed even after losing their immortality; for they had been suffering from the rivalry of co-wives and were practitioners of alien religious duties.
On one occasion, that great asura pleased Maheśvara with the Tāṇḍava dance accompanied by the music of his thousand arms.
Highly pleased and well-satisfied by that dance, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, looked upon him with a compassionate gaze.
The Blessed One, the Lord of all worlds, the refuge, who grants the desires of his devotees, invited that great asura Bāli to choose a boon.
Śaṅkara said: That great Daitya Bāṇa, the son of Bali, a wise and most excellent devotee, having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, praised the Supreme Lord.
Bāṇāsura said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who have sought refuge; O Maheśāna, O All-pervading Lord, if you are indeed pleased with me.
O Lord, always be my protector, stationed near me as the ruler of the city; for you, along with your sons and your hosts, are indeed the source of my complete delight.
Sanatkumāra said: Bāṇa, the son of Bali, was indeed deluded by the Māyā of Śiva; for although Maheśāna is certainly difficult to propitiate, he is the granter of liberation.
That Lord Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, having granted those boons to him, dwelt there with great love along with his attendants and his sons.
Once, on the bank of the river called Śoṇita, Hara engaged in sport with the gods and asuras in the beautiful city of Bāṇapura.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases likewise danced and laughed; the sages bowed, paid homage, and praised him.
All the foremost sages leaped for joy and likewise offered oblations; the hosts of Siddhas arrived and beheld the divine union of Śiva.
The fallacious logicians perished, as did the barbarians and their adversaries; the mother-goddesses stood facing him, and the terrifying apparitions were destroyed.
The faults of worldly existence were dispelled for those devoted to the true nature of Rudra; when he was seen, all the subjects attained supreme joy.
Seeing the behavior of the women, the sages and the perfected ones (siddhas) leaped for joy, and the seasons there also flourished with their own inherent power.
Gentle winds blew, grey with the pollen of flower filaments, and flocks of birds, greedy for honey, warbled from the branches of the trees.
And in the forests and groves, cuckoos, weighed down by the burden of flowers, should warble sweetly, producing passion.
Then, while sporting in the pleasure garden, the moon-crested Lord, intoxicated by the unconquered Kāma, looked at them and spoke to Nandin.
Candraśekhara said: "Go quickly from this forest to Kailāsa and, having adorned Gaurī, bring that dark-complexioned lady here, bringing Vāmā along with her."
Sanatkumāra said: Having agreed, saying "So be it," that messenger of Śaṅkara went there and, having bowed deeply with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Pārvatī in private.
Nandīśvara said: "O Goddess, Maheśvara, the God of gods, desires to see you, his own beloved, fashioned by me in this form; this was told to me by his command."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O best of sages, at those words, Gaurī—who was devoted to her husband—prepared with reverence to perform her adornment.
"I am coming to the Lord; go and speak to him on my behalf. Then Nandin, moving with the speed of thought, approached the presence of Rudra.
Then Rudra, who is beyond all delusion, spoke again to Nandin: "Go back once more, my son, and quickly bring Pārvatī here."
Having said "So be it," he went to her and spoke to the beautiful-eyed Gaurī: "Your husband wishes to see you, adorned in your charming attire."
O Goddess, Śaṅkara awaits you in many ways to sport with you; O Daughter of the Mountain, since your husband is thus afflicted by intense desire, please go to him.
Having been consecrated with all the alkaline substances and with one another, he immediately attained a state of being eager for a vision of Pārvatī.
Whichever woman with shapely hips this wielder of the Pināka bow, the enemy of Kāma, should choose, she shall certainly become the queen of all divine women.
Beholding her in the form of Gaurī, they played with the hosts of Manmathas; "This Kāma slays the enemy of Kāma," they said to one another, full of joy.
Whosoever among women, other than the daughter of Dakṣa, is able to touch it, let her go there without hesitation; she shall delude the Lord of Pārvatī.
There, Citralekhā, the daughter of Kūṣmāṇḍa, spoke these words: "I am Gaurī; in this beautiful form, I venture to touch Śaṅkara."
Citralekhā said: "In the past, Keśava, having resorted to the Vaiṣṇava yoga in its ultimate sense, assumed the form of Mohinī out of a desire to delude."
Then, having seen the transformation of Urvaśī’s form—Ghṛtācī into a dark form and Viśvācī into a body like that of Caṇḍikā—[the others did likewise].
Rambhā was the form of Sāvitrī, Menakā likewise that of Gāyatrī; Sahajanyā was the form of Jayā, and Puñjikasthalī that of Vaijayantī.
And for those Mothers who were not mentioned, other unnamed excellent Apsarases, endowed with their own respective sciences, subsequently assumed forms made of jewels.
Then, having seen their forms, Kumbhāṇḍanandinī, having understood the matter through her Vaiṣṇava power and her own yogic insight, mocked them.
Ūṣā, the daughter of the Asura Bāṇa and an expert in divine yoga, assumed the form of Pārvatī—a form that was divine, most wonderful, and auspicious.
The foot is said to be of incomparable luster, resembling a great red lotus, endowed with divine marks, and bestowing the desired objects of the mind.
Then, having perceived her intention for dalliance, Śivā—the daughter of the mountain, the knower of all things, and the inner controller of all—spoke.
Girijā said: "O friend, since you have indeed assumed my own form while wearing ornaments, O proud one, because of your desire when the proper time had arrived."
In this month of Kārttika, however, the seasonal rites are performed in Mādhava; specifically on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, at the onset of the terrible night.
A man shall eat you while you are sleeping in the inner apartments after having observed a fast; he has been made your husband by the gods, and with him you shall sport.
"Since from childhood you have been a devotee of Viṣṇu, being ever unwearied," she said, "So be it," while her face was lowered in her mind with shame.
Then the goddess Pārvatī, having adorned herself with festive ornaments, approached the presence of Rudra and sported with that Śambhu.
Then, at the end of their dalliance, O Sage, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished from sight, together with his wife, his attendants, and the deities.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of Ūṣā and the Description of the Marriage of Śiva and Śivā," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen to another account of Śiva, the Supreme Self, which is filled with affection for his devotees and bestows supreme bliss.
Formerly, an asura named Bāṇa, arrogant due to the fault of fate, pleased Śaṅkara by performing the Tāṇḍava dance.
Having perceived that Śiva, the beloved of Pārvatī, was satisfied in mind, the asura Bāṇa, with shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Bāṇa said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, crest-jewel of all the gods! By your grace I am powerful; hear my supreme words.
"A thousand hosts have been given by you, yet they have become a supreme burden to me; for in the three worlds, I find no equal opponent to face in battle other than you."
"O God, O bull-bannered one, what shall I do with even this thousand of arms, which are like mountains, without a battle?"
Scratching with my arms held close to my body, I desired to fight the elephants of the quarters; as I pulverized their cities and mountains, they too fled in fear.
By me, Yama was made my warrior, and the great Vahni was made my cook; likewise, Varuṇa was made a cowherd and the protector of my cattle.
Kubera became the superintendent of his elephants, and Nirṛti became his female attendant; even Indra was conquered in the world and made to pay tribute forever.
Tell me of the coming of battle, wherein these arms of mine shall be shattered by weapons and missiles discharged from the hands of the enemy.
Let them fall from the hands of the enemy, or let them be struck down in a thousand ways; O Maheśvara, fulfill this very desire of mine.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard that, Rudra became enraged; letting out a most wonderful loud laugh, he, the remover of afflictions for his devotees, spoke with great indignation.
Rudra said: "Fie, fie upon you, O you who are arrogant in every way, lowest of all the Daitya clans! Such words are not fitting for one devoted to the son of Bali."
And you shall soon experience a terrible quelling of this pride, through a great battle that arises unexpectedly with one who is powerful and equal to me.
There, those arms of yours, resembling mountains, shall fall to the ground like logs of firewood, severed by weapons and missiles and reduced to the state of plantain trunks.
O evil-minded one, when this banner of yours, which bears a human head joined with a peacock, falls, [then you shall perish].
While the weapons were kept in the armory, and without any danger caused by wind, the thought arose in his mind: "Then a most terrible battle has arrived."
"Having left behind this terrible battle, you should depart with all your troops; go now to that dwelling where Śiva resides."
"O evil-minded one, you shall likewise see those great portents there yourself. Having spoken thus, the Lord, who destroys pride and is affectionate toward his devotees, then became silent.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard that, Bāṇa worshipped Rudra with divine lotus-like hands joined in añjali, and having prostrated before Mahādeva, he returned to his own home.
Being questioned by Kumbhāṇḍa regarding what had occurred, he spoke joyfully; for the asura Bāṇa, ever eager, had been constantly scrutinizing that yogic power.
Then, by chance, once he saw that his own banner had been broken, the asura Bāṇa went forth joyfully for battle.
Having summoned his own army and joined by the eight Gaṇas, he performed a sacrificial rite for battle and beheld the honey of war.
Having observed every auspicious sign of the quarters, the son of Bali—the great hero, the mighty chariot-warrior—set forth with immense enthusiasm.
Having thus placed [the enemy] within the lotus of the heart, who will come from where—be he a warrior fond of battle, one who has mastered various weapons and missiles?
But whoever should cut my thousand arms like pieces of dry wood, I shall likewise cut him here into hundreds of pieces with extremely sharp weapons.
In the meantime, the time ordained by Śaṅkara indeed arrived, when that daughter of Bāṇa, Sujātā, had performed the auspicious rites.
Having worshipped Mādhava in the month of Mādhava at the dead of night, she fell asleep in the guarded inner apartments and attained the state of a woman.
Then, though sent by Gaurī, she was drawn away by divine illusion by the son of Kṛṣṇa’s son; weeping like one who is helpless, she was indeed led away.
And having been forced to eat that by Pārvatī’s friends, he was then brought to Dvārakā in the twinkling of an eye through divine yoga.
Having been thus crushed, she then rose up and, weeping with various cries, told her friends that she was resolved upon abandoning her body.
O Vyāsa, she was again reminded of her friend’s transgression against her self-realized soul; having seen that entire previous account, she then became [as she was before].
Then, O Sage, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, spoke to Citralekhā, the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, in a sweet voice.
Ūṣā said: "Friend, if this man was ordained by Pārvatī as my husband in the past, by what means may he be obtained by me according to the prescribed rite while remaining hidden from you?"
"In what family was he born, by whom my heart has been stolen? Having heard these words of Uṣā, her friend then spoke to her.
Citralekhā said: "O Goddess, how shall I honor that man whom you saw in a dream, since he is unknown to me?"
When he had spoken thus, the daughter of the Daitya, blinded by passion and longing for death, was then protected by her friend on that first day.
O best of sages, that highly intelligent Citralekhā, the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa and granddaughter of Bāṇa, spoke once more.
Citralekhā said: "I shall remove your distress, even if it be spoken of throughout the three worlds; I will bring you the man who has stolen your heart—point him out."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, he drew the gods, daityas, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others upon a cloth-scroll.
Likewise, he depicted those men among them—the Vṛṣṇis, Śūra, Ānakadundubhi, as well as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and Pradyumna, the best of men.
Seeing Aniruddha, the son of Pradyumna, depicted there, Uṣā was filled with shame; her face cast downward, her heart was overflowing with joy.
Ūṣā said: "O friend, that man whom I encountered at night is a thief—he who has swiftly stolen the jewel of my heart."
O beautiful lady, tell me everything: I wish to know him by whose mere touch I was so utterly deluded.
"In whose lineage was he born, and what is his name? When she was thus addressed, Yoginī spoke of his name and his lineage.
Having heard all that concerning his lineage and other matters, O best of sages, that passionate daughter of Bāṇa became eager and spoke.
Ūṣā said: "O friend, devise a means out of affection so that at this very moment I may obtain that beloved, the one dearer than life, by whatever means I might gain that husband."
"O friend, without whom I cannot bear to live for even a single moment, bring him here with diligent effort; O friend, make me happy."
Sanatkumāra said: O best of sages, having been addressed in this manner by the daughter of Bāṇa, that minister’s daughter was filled with wonder and became intent on deep reflection.
Then Citralekhā, swift as thought, addressed her friend; having learned that he was the grandson of Kṛṣṇa, she prepared to go to Dvārakā.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when the third day had passed, they reached the city of Dvārakā at the hour of Muhūrta just before dawn.
In a single moment, the divine Yoginī traveled through the sky; then, in the palace garden, she beheld the son of Pradyumna.
Sporting together with women, drinking the honey-wine of spring, he was dark-complexioned, beautiful in every limb, smiling, and in the prime of youth.
Then, having placed Mādhava upon the couch, she covered him with a veil of darkness through her yogic power of tamas.
Then, taking that bedstead upon her head, she reached Śoṇitapura within the blink of an eye, where the daughter of Bāṇa resided.
Afflicted by desire, her mind deranged, she assumed various forms; then, seeing him brought before her, she became terrified.
In that well-guarded inner apartment, during that new union, as soon as they began to sport, it was discovered at that very moment.
Standing at the gate of the inner apartments with cane-staffs in their hands, they observed the misconduct of the maiden through gestures and inference.
And there they also saw that man, possessing a divine form—youthful, handsome, courageous, and fond of battle.
Having seen him, those great heroes—the guards of the maiden’s inner apartments—reported everything to Bāṇa, the son of Bali.
The gatekeepers said: "O Lord, no one knew that someone had forcibly entered the inner apartments while hidden; who was it that thus violated your daughter by seizing her himself?"
"O mighty-armed lord of the Dānavas, look, look at him here! Do whatever is appropriate; we are not wicked."
Sanatkumāra said: O best of sages, having heard those words of theirs, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas was struck with wonder upon hearing of the daughter’s blemish.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Ūṣā," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the enraged Bāṇāsura went there and beheld him, whose body was graced with divine playfulness and who stood in the prime of youth.
Seeing him thus amazed, Bāṇa, his soul overcome with anger and exultant in battle, spoke these words as if laughing: "What is the reason for this?"
"Aha! This man is rich in beauty, audacious, and steadfast; yet who is this one who has arrived at the wrong time, cursed by ill fortune and deluded in intellect?"
"Kill with swift and most terrible weapons that man by whom my family conduct has been defiled and my dear daughter harmed; you must do so in anger."
O heroes, having bound that man of evil conduct, you must especially guard him for a long time in a formidable and terrible prison.
"I do not know who this Abhaya is, or who this one of terrible prowess may be"; having reflected thus, the highly intelligent Śarāsura became filled with doubt.
Then, by that evil-minded Daitya, an army of ten thousand was gradually commanded for the sake of slaying that hero.
Then, commanded by him, those fierce heroes quickly surrounded the entire inner apartment on all sides, shouting, "Cut! Pierce!"
Then, seeing the enemy army roaring, that Yādava took up an incomparable iron bar at the gate of the inner apartments.
Having departed from that palace like Yama with the thunderbolt in his hand, he slew those servants and returned once more to the inner apartments.
Thus, O best of sages, with eyes reddened by rage and empowered by the splendor of Śiva, he slaughtered ten thousand troops.
When a hundred thousand warriors had been slain, the Asura Bāṇa, filled with rage, seized Kubhāṇḍa and challenged him, who was intoxicated by battle, to combat.
Aniruddha, of great intelligence, was protected by the splendor of Śiva during the great duel in the great battle, his body blazing with light as the son of Pradyumna.
Then, with a sword obtained in battle, he slew ten thousand excellent chariot-horses belonging to the lord of the Daityas.
Then, for the sake of slaying him, Aniruddha took up a spear resembling the fire of time (Kālavaiśvānara) and struck him with it.
Then Bāṇa, having been struck firmly by him with a spear upon the seat of his chariot, that hero instantly vanished right there along with his horses.
Upon seeing that invincible son of Pradyumna, who had attained the sight of you, he stood gazing at all the directions, as immovable as a mountain.
Remaining invisible at that time, that Dānava, a deceitful warrior, struck him again and again with thousands of various weapons.
With serpent-nooses, that mighty one bound him—the great hero Śarāsura, son of Bali, a devotee of Śiva.
Having bound him and placed him within a cage, he ceased from the battle; then Bāṇa, filled with rage, spoke to the mighty son of the Sūta.
Bāṇāsura said: "O son of a Sūta, quickly cut off the head of this man, by whom my pure and noble lineage has been defiled through force by that wicked one."
"O sir, having cut all his limbs, give them to the Rākṣasas; then let even the flesh-eaters consume his blood and flesh."
Kill the sinner in the bottomless well overgrown with grass! O son of a charioteer, what is the use of much talk? He must certainly be slain by all means.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, the night-stalker Kumbhāṇḍa, whose mind was fixed on righteousness, spoke these words to Bāṇa, the best of excellent ministers.
Kumbhāṇḍa said: "O Lord, it is not proper to perform this deed; please reflect upon it. For my thought is that if he is slain, one's very self would be destroyed."
But this one, O King, is seen to be equal to Viṣṇu in prowess; he has been nurtured by the splendor of your wicked son, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Now, through the audacity of Candralalāṭa, you have yourself reached this state while remaining established in your manliness.
"By the grace of Śiva, this mighty grandson of Kṛṣṇa regards us as mere blades of grass, even though he has been forcibly bitten by serpents."
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken these words to Bāṇa, that Dānava, the most excellent knower of royal policy, spoke this to Aniruddha.
Kumbhāṇḍa said: "Who are you, and whose son are you, O hero? Speak the truth before me. By whom have you been brought here, you of evil conduct, lowest of men?"
"Praise the heroic lord of the Daityas; bow down to him with palms joined in reverence, repeatedly uttering these piteous words: 'I am conquered!'"
"If this is done, there shall be liberation; otherwise, there will be bondage and the like. Having heard those words of his, he spoke this reply:
Aniruddha said: O friend of the lowest of Daityas, O you who subsist on the pain of others' hands, O night-walker of wicked conduct! Alas, you do not understand the duty of an enemy!
It is my conviction that for a hero, both dejection and flight are worse than death; they are contrary to his nature and lead to his downfall.
For a Kṣatriya, death at all times facing the enemy in battle is better than lying on the ground like a wretched man with palms joined in supplication, even if he considers himself a hero.
Sanatkumāra said: He spoke many such words of the hero to him; having heard them, he, along with his arrows, was both amazed and enraged.
Then a voice from the sky spoke for the sake of consoling Bāṇa, while all the heroes and Aniruddha’s minister were listening.
The voice from the sky said: "O Bāṇa, O great hero, you ought not to give way to anger. You are the son of Bali, O wise one; you are a devotee of Śiva—let this be reflected upon."
Śiva is the Lord of all, the witness of actions, and the Supreme Sovereign; indeed, this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is dependent upon him.
He alone is always the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds; he assumes the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, and manifests as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
He is the Lord dwelling within all, the impeller who transcends everything; changeless, imperishable, eternal, the sovereign of Māyā, yet devoid of qualities.
"O son of Bali, by his will the weak should be known as strong and the strong as weak; having understood this in your mind, O high-minded one, remain established in yourself."
The Blessed One, who removes pride, who is expert in his divine sports, and who is affectionate toward his devotees, will now destroy your arrogance.
Sanatkumāra said: O great sage, having spoken thus, the voice from the sky ceased; and Bāṇāsura, following those words, did not slay Aniruddha.
But having gone to his inner apartments, he drank unsurpassed wine; with his mind perverted, he forgot my words and indulged in pleasure.
Then Niruddha was bound by the coils of serpents with virulent poison; yet, his mind still unsated for his beloved, he immediately called Durgā to mind.
Aniruddha said: O Goddess, refuge of all, I am bound and being consumed by serpents; come to me and grant me protection, O Yaśodā, you of fierce wrath!
O Great Goddess, you who bring about creation, preservation, and destruction for the devotee of Śiva—there is no protector other than you; therefore, O Śivā, protect me indeed!
Sanatkumāra said: Thus propitiated there by him, Kālī, who has the luster of crushed collyrium, arrived during the dead of night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
With blows from his fists, he shattered the cage, having reduced those terrifying arrows in the form of serpents to ashes.
Having released Niruddha, Durgā then led him into the inner apartments and vanished right there from sight.
Thus, O lord of sages, by the grace of the Goddess, the power of Śiva, Nirodha was liberated from his hardship; he became happy and free from all suffering.
Then, having achieved victory through the power of Śiva, Aniruddha, the son of Pradyumna, obtained his beloved daughter of Bāṇa and rejoiced.
Then, having drunk wine, his eyes intensely red with passion, he sported happily with his beloved daughter of Bāṇa just as before.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Amorous Pastimes of Aniruddha and Ūṣā," in the Ūṣā-caritra section of the fifth book (Yuddha-khaṇḍa) within the Rudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O best of sages, when Kṛṣṇa’s grandson Aniruddha had been abducted by the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, what did Kṛṣṇa do? Tell me that.
Sanatkumāra said: O best of sages, when Aniruddha had departed, Kṛṣṇa became deeply distressed upon hearing the sound of the weeping of those women.
As they grieved, not seeing Aniruddha nor Hari, four months of the rainy season passed away for those kinsmen.
Having heard from Nārada that news and the account of the bound man's deed, all the Vṛṣṇis, who had Kṛṣṇa as their deity, became deeply distressed.
Having heard that entire account, Kṛṣṇa, out of respect for the battle, summoned Tārkṣya and departed for Śoṇitapura at that very moment.
Pradyumna, Yuyudhāna, Sāmba, and Sāraṇa departed, as did Nanda, Upananda, Bhadra, and others who followed Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by twelve akṣauhiṇīs, those bulls among the Sātvatas besieged Bāṇapura from every direction on all sides.
Beholding the city gardens, walls, watchtowers, and gateways being shattered, he, filled with rage and accompanied by an equal force, marched out.
For the sake of Bāṇa, the Lord Rudra, accompanied by his son and surrounded by the Pramathas, mounted his bull Nandin and arrived to wage war.
A tumultuous, wonderful, and hair-raising battle took place there between Kṛṣṇa and his companions on one side, and Bāṇa’s protectors led by Rudra on the other.
There was a battle between Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, as well as between Pradyumna and Guha, and between Kūṣmāṇḍa and Kūpakarṇa, along with Bala.
Sātyaki fought with Bāṇa, the son of Bāṇa, against Sāmba; Garuḍa fought with Nandin, and others likewise with their respective adversaries.
Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, the sages, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the Gandharvas and Apsarases, arrived in their celestial chariots and aerial palaces to behold him.
O best of Brahmins, a most terrible battle took place between those scions of the Yadu lineage and the Pramathas of various forms, ending with Revatī.
Accompanied by his brother Rāma and the wise Pradyumna, Kṛṣṇa waged an incomparable battle against the Pramathas.
There, a battle took place with Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Vimukha, Tripāda, Jvara, and Guha.
Then, with those Pramathas of various forms, another fierce and hair-raising battle took place between them and the Vṛṣṇis.
At every step, there were many terrifying hollows, and nearby, powerful women devoid of shame.
Śauri caused the followers of Śaṃkara—the bhūtas, pramathas, and guhyakas—to flee with sharp-pointed arrows discharged from his Śārṅga bow.
Thus the heroes, headed by Pradyumna, who delighted in the great festival of battle, waged a most terrible war, destroying the enemy army.
Seeing his own army being shattered, the highly intolerant Rudra became filled with great wrath and let out a most formidable roar.
Having heard that, the hosts of Śaṅkara roared and fought; strengthened by the splendor of Śambhu, they crushed their adversaries.
And the wielder of the trident, remaining unperturbed, neutralized with his own manifest weapons the various and improper arrows discharged by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The Brahmāstra against the Brahmāstra, the Pārvata against the Vāyavya, the Pārjanya against the Āgneya, and his own [weapon] against the Nārāyaṇa.
The army of Kṛṣṇa, defeated by the opposing hero, fled; it did not stand firm in battle, O Vyāsa, before the full splendor of Rudra’s son.
O Sage, when his own army had been put to flight, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the scorcher of foes, indeed unleashed his own terrible fever named Śītala.
O Sage, when Kṛṣṇa’s army had been put to flight, a fever of coldness came upon Kṛṣṇa; he then approached Rudra, who was burning the ten directions.
Then Maheśvara, seeing him approaching, released his own fever; and the two fevers, that of Maheśvara and that of Viṣṇu, fought with one another.
Then the Vaiṣṇava, afflicted by the power of the Māheśvara, cried out; finding no refuge elsewhere, he praised the one whose banner is the bull.
Then the blessed Lord Hara, who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge, being pleased and freed from the fever caused by Viṣṇu, spoke to Viṣṇu’s cold fever.
Maheśvara said: "O Śītajvara, I am pleased; let your fear of my fever depart. Whoever remembers this dialogue between us shall have no fear of fever."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, the fever of Nārāyaṇa bowed to Rudra and departed. Seeing that deed, Kṛṣṇa was filled with fear and was greatly amazed.
Then, being tormented by the floods of arrows from Skanda and Pradyumna, the enraged Daitya, unable to endure their assault, struck Pradyumna with a spear.
Struck there by Skanda, even the powerful Pradyumna, shedding blood from his limbs, fled from the battle by force.
Struck by Kumbhāṇḍa and Karṇa with various weapons, even the mighty Balabhadra fled; though powerful, he did not remain in the battle.
Having assumed a thousand bodies and drunk water from the great ocean, Garuḍa destroys the clouds and the waters of the ocean with his whirlpools of wealth.
Then the powerful bull, the vehicle of Maheśa, becoming enraged, struck him with great force indeed with his two horns.
With his limbs shattered by the blow of the horn, Garuḍa was utterly amazed; he fled swiftly from the battlefield, abandoning Janārdana.
When this had happened, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, being greatly amazed by the splendor of Rudra, spoke thus to his charioteer: "Drive quickly!"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Sūta, listen to my words; drive my chariot quickly so that I may be near Mahādeva to speak these words.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Hari, the charioteer Dāruka, the foremost among those endowed with virtues, quickly drove that chariot toward the presence of Rudra.
Then, having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who had taken refuge in devotion to Śaṅkara, the protector of devotees, made this request with devotion.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge; I bow to you, the infinite power, the soul of all, the supreme Lord.
The supreme, peaceful, absolute, and sovereign Lord—the Brahman-liṅga which is mere pure consciousness and the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the universe.
Time, destiny, action, the individual soul, inherent nature, and indeed substance; the field, the vital breath, and the self—their collection constitutes modification.
O Lord of the universe, this stream of the sprouting of seeds is Your own māyā; therefore, I take refuge here in You, the Supreme Lord, who are bound by that [māyā].
By assuming various states through mere play, you truly sustain the gods and others; as the Lord of the World, you naturally destroy those who follow the wrong path.
For you are the supreme Brahman, the hidden light within the Vedic word; the stainless-souled perceive you as the absolute, like the infinite sky.
You alone are the primordial, non-dual Person, the Fourth (turya), the seer of the Self; you appear as the Lord, both with and without cause, and as possessing transformation.
O Blessed Lord, O Master, for the manifestation of all qualities through your own māyā, you, the Great Lord, are endowed with everything and yet distinct from everything in every respect.
Just as the sun, though obscured, illuminates forms and shadows with its own radiance, O Lord, so do you, the supreme seer, shine forth.
O Lord, O Bhūman, O Giriśa, O Śaṅkara, although you are concealed by your own qualities, you illuminate those very qualities within yourself; you are your own lamp.
Those whose intellects are deluded by your māyā, being deeply attached to children, wives, homes, and the like, rise and sink within the ocean of suffering.
Having obtained this human world bestowed by fate, he who, with his senses unsubdued, does not honor your feet is indeed to be pitied as a self-deceiver.
"O Blessed One, by your command I have come to sever Bāṇa’s arms; this arrogant Bāṇa was himself cursed by you, the destroyer of pride."
"Turn back from the battle, O Lord; let your curse not be in vain. O Master, give me your command regarding the severing of Bāṇa's arms."
Sanatkumāra said: O lord of sages, having heard these words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Great Lord Maheśvara, with a gracious soul, replied in praise of Kṛṣṇa.
Maheśvara said: "O dear one, you have spoken the truth; indeed, the king of the Daityas was cursed by me. By my command, you have arrived here for the purpose of severing Bāṇa’s formidable arm."
"What shall I do, O Lord of Ramā? O Hari, you are always dependent upon your devotees; yet, O Hero, how can the severing of Bāṇa’s arms occur while I am looking on?"
Therefore, by my command, paralyze me with the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon; thereafter, accomplish your own purpose as you desire and be happy.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by Śaṅkara, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was then amazed; having returned to his own abode, that lord of sages rejoiced.
Then, O Vyāsa, Hari, who is skilled in various weapons, quickly fixed the Jṛmbhaṇa missile upon his bow and discharged it at the wielder of the Pināka.
Having bewildered Giriśa with the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon so that he yawned, Śauri struck Bāṇa’s army with swords, clubs, and spears.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Asura Bāṇa, Rudra, Kṛṣṇa, and Others," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, omniscient son of Brahmā, salutations to you! O Sage, this wonderful story has been narrated to me by you, my dear father.
When Hari yawned in the battle by means of the yawning-weapon (jṛmbhaṇāstra) and Bāṇa’s army was destroyed, tell me, what did Bāṇa do then?
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, the lord of sages, the son of Brahmā, replied with a serene mind.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great wisdom, to this most wonderful tale concerning Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, O dear one, who follow the ways of worldly play.
While Rudra, along with his sons and his hosts, was resting in a playful manner, Bāṇa, the king of the Daityas, went forth to do battle with Kṛṣṇa.
Then the immensely powerful son of Bali, mounted on a horse controlled by Kumbhāṇḍa and wielding various weapons and missiles, engaged in an incomparable battle.
Seeing his own army destroyed, that lord of the Daityas became exceedingly incensed; the mighty son of Bali waged an incomparable battle.
The great hero Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who had obtained immense strength from Giriśa, roared loudly in that battle, regarding Bāṇa as being like a blade of grass.
O Lord of Sages, he made his own wonderful bow named Śārṅga twang, terrifying the remaining army of arrows.
Indeed, by that great sound produced from the twanging of the bow, the entire space between heaven and earth was completely pervaded.
Enraged, Hari drew his bow back to his ear and discharged various sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents at Bāṇa.
Then, beholding them as they approached, Bāṇa, the son of Bali, cut them down with arrows discharged from his own bow before they had even reached him.
Again that powerful Bāṇa, the crusher of enemy hosts, roared; all the Vṛṣṇis, whose very souls were Kṛṣṇa, became terrified and lost their senses.
Remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, that son of Bali, possessed of great pride, discharged his arrows at the exceedingly heroic Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa too, possessing great strength and remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, swiftly cut down those arrows with his own shafts before they could reach him, O enemy of the gods.
Rāma and the other Vṛṣṇis, all of them powerful and filled with agitation, provoked their respective warriors to anger and struck them down in battle.
Thus, for a very long time, there occurred between those two powerful ones a tumultuous battle that filled the listeners with wonder.
At that moment, the king of birds, filled with rage, crushed the entire army of Bāṇāsura with blows from his wings.
Seeing his own army being crushed and seeing that powerful one crushing it, Bali’s son—the king of the Daityas and supreme devotee of Śiva—became exceedingly enraged.
Having quickly remembered the lotus feet of Śiva, he, possessing a thousand arms, indeed displayed great valor that was unbearable for his enemies.
There, the slayer of heroes simultaneously discharged immeasurable arrows at all the Yadus, beginning with Kṛṣṇa, and at Garuḍa, each individually.
O Sage, that powerful one struck Garuḍa with one feathered shaft, Kṛṣṇa with another, and Bala with yet another; he likewise struck his other enemies as well.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the one of great heroism, who is the form of Viṣṇu and the slayer of the enemies of the gods, became enraged in that great battle and roared like Maheśvara.
Having simultaneously called upon Śaṅkara, he struck down that exceedingly fierce and powerful arrow with excellent shafts discharged from his Śārṅga bow.
Without agitation, Hari swiftly cut that bow and the parasol and other items; having slain the horses with his own arrows, he caused them to fall.
The great hero Bāṇa also, becoming enraged, roared aloud; he struck Kṛṣṇa with his mace, and he fell to the surface of the earth.
Then, O celestial sage, Kṛṣṇa rose up quickly and fought with that enemy, a devotee of Śiva, in accordance with his worldly pastimes.
Thus, for a long time, there occurred a very great battle between the two: Hari in the form of Śiva, and that powerful Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of Śiva’s devotees.
Then the powerful Kṛṣṇa, having engaged in battle with Bāṇa for a long time and having obtained strength by the command of Śiva, became exceedingly enraged, O lord of sages.
Then, by the command of Lord Śambhu, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, swiftly cut down many of Bāṇa’s arms with his Sudarśana discus.
His four remaining arms were exceedingly beautiful; by the grace of Śaṅkara, he quickly became free from all pain.
O Bāṇa, when Kṛṣṇa, having lost his mindfulness, was intent on cutting off [Bāṇa's] head, Rudra then arose, having attained the state of a hero.
Rudra said: "O Blessed One, son of Devakī, that which was previously commanded by me has been performed by you, O Brahmin, who are ever obedient to my command."
"Do not sever Bāṇa's head; withdraw the Sudarśana! By my command, let this discus always be ineffective against mortals."
"O Govinda, I previously gave you this discus, which is irresistible in battle and brings victory; therefore, withdraw from the fight."
O Lord of Lakṣmī, in the past, even when facing Dadhīci, Rāvaṇa, Vīra, Tāraka, and others, you did not abandon your discus without my command.
But you, O Janārdana, are the Lord of Yogins, the Supreme Self in person; devoted to the welfare of all beings, reflect upon this with your own mind.
I have granted him this boon: indeed, there shall be no fear of death for him. Those words of mine are always true; I am well-pleased with you.
O Hari, in the past this one was arrogant and intoxicated; scratching his arms, he said to me, "Give me battle," having forgotten his own true nature.
Then I cursed him, saying: "The one who shall cut off your arm will come before long; in no great time, you shall be stripped of your pride."
"By my command, Hari has arrived as the severer of your arms; therefore, turn back from the battle and go to your own home together with your bridegroom."
Having been addressed thus, Maheśvara established friendship with them; then, taking leave of him, he departed for his own abode along with his attendants and his sons.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Śambhu and having withdrawn the Sudarśana discus, Kṛṣṇa, victorious and with his limbs uninjured, entered the inner apartments.
Having consoled Aniruddha, who was reunited with his wife, he again took possession of the many heaps of jewels bestowed by Bāṇa.
Having taken her friend Citralekhā, a supreme yoginī, Kṛṣṇa then became pleased, his purpose accomplished by the command of Śiva.
Having bowed to Giriśa with his heart and taken leave of him who is praised by Bala, Hari, accompanied by his retinue, departed for his own city.
Having defeated Varuṇa, who opposed him in many ways, on the way, he reached the city of Dvārakā accompanied by great festivities.
Having dismissed Garuḍa and looked upon his friends with a smile, he then wandered at will through Dvārakā.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Severing of Bāṇa’s Arms and the Removal of His Pride," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nārada said: "When Kṛṣṇa had gone to Dvārakā with Aniruddha and his wife, what did Bāṇa do after that? Tell me the truth, O great sage."
Sanatkumāra said: When Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā with Aniruddha and his wife, Bāṇa became sorrowful, remembering his own ignorance within his heart.
Then Nandīśiva’s attendant spoke to the distressed Daitya Bāṇa, whose limbs were smeared with blood and who was filled with remorse.

Nandīśvara said: O Bāṇa, you who are a true devotee of Śaṅkara, do not feel remorse; for Śambhu is indeed compassionate toward his devotees and bears the name "Bhaktavatsala" (the one who is kind to his devotees).
O tiger among devotees, with the thought that "whatever has arisen by His will has arisen," consider it so; remember Śiva again and again.
Fixing your mind on the Primordial One, perform a great festival constantly; and show compassion toward His devotees again and again, O Śaṅkara.
Then, upon hearing Nandin’s words, the high-minded Bāṇa, though reduced by his enemy to nothing but his head, summoned his courage and quickly went to the abode of Śiva.
Having gone there and bowed to the Lord, Bāṇa—his mass of pride vanished and his mind overwhelmed with love—wept most piteously, utterly distraught.
Praising him with various hymns, bowing down and likewise offering salutations, he struck his feet as was appropriate and brandished his hands.
He performed the preeminent Tāṇḍava dance, beautified by the pratyālīḍha and other postures, as well as various forms of standing positions beginning with ālīḍha.
He received thousands of words of comfort accompanied by the raising of eyebrows, and thousands of nods of the head were bestowed upon him in great numbers.
And having gradually displayed waters of various forms, he likewise drenched the surface of the earth with streams of blood.
The great devotee Bāṇāsura, having forgotten his own true state, bowed down and propitiated Rudra, the wielder of the trident and the moon-crested one.
Then, having performed a great dance, the Blessed One Hara, who is compassionate toward his devotees and fond of dance and song, spoke joyfully to Bāṇa.
Rudra said: "O Bāṇa, dear son of Bali, I am well-pleased with your dancing. Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas, whatever dwells in your mind."
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, having heard these words of Śambhu, the boon regarding the healing of wounds was then accepted by Bāṇa, the lord of the Daityas.
Furthermore, there was the origin of arm-to-arm wrestling and the imperishable status of the Gaṇas; and the kingdom of Uṣā’s son in that place called Śoṇita.
The gods, and especially Viṣṇu, have become free from enmity; however, the wicked state of being a Daitya, characterized by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), has not [ceased].
O sage, there is especially constant and unwavering devotion to Śambhu; affection for the devotees of Śiva and compassion toward all living beings.
Having obtained boons from Śambhu, the great Asura Bali’s son, with eyes brimming with tears of love and palms joined in reverence, praised Rudra.
Bāṇa said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; I bow to you, O Maheśāna, friend of the distressed, ocean of compassion!
O Śaṅkara, ocean of compassion, you have shown me exceeding grace; O Lord, everything that had been taken away by my pride has been restored to me by you who are well-pleased.
You are indeed Brahman, the Supreme Self, all-pervading and the Lord of all; you are the Virāṭ, the fierce Lord whose body is the cosmic egg, the Supreme who is present in everything.
The navel is the sky, the mouth is fire, the water is the semen, the directions are the ears; heaven is your head, the earth your feet, and the moon is your mind, O Lord.
The sun is your eye, the ocean your belly, Indra your arm, wisdom your intellect, Prajāpati your organ of generation, and Dharma indeed is your heart.
O Lord, your body hairs are medicinal herbs and your hair is the clouds; you are the three qualities, the three-eyed one, and the Supreme Person who is the soul of all.
They say that the Brāhmaṇa was born from your mouth, and the Kṣatriya from your arms; they say the Vaiśya was born from your thighs, and the Śūdra from your feet.
O Maheśvara, you alone are to be worshipped at all times by all living beings; by worshipping you, a person certainly attains supreme liberation.
That mortal who abandons you—the beloved Self, the Lord—for the sake of sense-objects which lead to perverted ends, is like one who rejects nectar and consumes poison.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the gods, and the sages of pure intent have surrendered with their whole being to you, Śaṅkara, the beloved Lord.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus, the son of Bali, the demon Śara, ceased speaking; with his limbs blossoming with love, he bowed down to Maheśvara.
Having heard this from his devotee Bāṇa, the Blessed Lord Bhava said, "You shall obtain everything," and vanished right there.
Then, by the grace of Śambhu, Bāṇa attained the state of Mahākāla and became an attendant of Rudra, filled with great joy.

Thus, indeed, has been narrated here in words pleasing to the ear the most excellent life-story of Śaṅkara, who bears the name Śarva, the preceptor of all teachers, the wielder of the trident, who eternally sports within the midst of all the worlds.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Bāṇāsura’s Attainment of the Status of Gaṇapati," in the Yuddhakhaṇḍa of the second Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen with great affection, O Vyāsa, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, concerning how he slew the lord of the Dānavas, Gajāsura, with his trident.
When the Dānava Mahiṣāsura had been slain by the Goddess in battle, the gods attained happiness in former times for the sake of the welfare of the gods.
His son was the great hero Gajāsura, O Lord of Sages; remembering the slaughter of his father, which had been carried out by the Goddess at the request of the gods.
Recalling that enmity, he went to the forest for the sake of asceticism; aiming at the prescribed rule, he performed supreme penance with devotion.
"Conquered by desire, I shall become incapable of being slain by men or women. Having reflected thus in his mind, he became one whose heart was devoted to ascetic penance.
He performed most rigorous penance in a valley of the Himalayas, with his arms raised, his gaze fixed on the sky, and his body supported by the earth on his big toes.
With his mass of matted hair, that noble-minded Gajāsura, the son of Mahiṣāsura, shone like the sun at the time of universal dissolution with its rays.
From his head arose a smokeless fire consisting of ascetic power, which, being blown in all directions, heated the worlds—above, below, and across.
The rivers and oceans were agitated by the emergence from the head of Agni; the stars fell along with the planets, and the ten directions blazed.
Scorched by that [heat], all the gods, including Indra, abandoned heaven and went to the world of Brahmā; they made their petition as the earth trembled.
The gods said: "O Creator, we have been tormented by the penance of Gajāsura and are now distressed; we are unable to remain in heaven, and therefore we have come to you for refuge."
"Bring about his pacification and show compassion to restore the others to life; otherwise, the worlds will perish—truly, truly we speak this truth."
Thus petitioned by the gods, headed by Vāsava, Brahmā, the self-born, went to the hermitage of the foremost Daityas along with Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, and others.
Beholding him heating the worlds with his ascetic power, like the sun in the sky veiled by clouds, the Creator, struck with wonder, spoke while smiling.
Brahmā said: Arise, arise, O lord of Daityas! You have attained perfection through your penance, O son of Mahiṣa. I, the giver of boons, have arrived; choose a boon as you desire, my dear.
Sanatkumāra said: Rising up again and again, O Lord of Daityas, the son of Māhiṣa, gazing at the All-pervading Lord with his eyes, joyfully praised the God with a faltering voice.
Gajāsura said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods! If you will grant me a boon, may I indeed become invulnerable to men and women who are overcome by desire."
O Lord, you possess great strength and great heroism, and are forever unconquerable by the gods and others; O All-pervading One, you enjoy all the supernatural powers of every guardian of the world.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus requested by that Dānava, Śatadhṛti, pleased by his ascetic penance, granted him a boon that is indeed very difficult to obtain.
Having thus obtained the boons, the Daitya Māhiṣi and Gajāsura, with highly gratified minds, then returned to their own abodes.
Having conquered all directions and the three worlds, that great asura [subjugated] the lords of gods, asuras, and humans, as well as the gandharvas, garuḍas, and uragas.
Having conquered all these and brought them under his control, Viśvajit seized the abodes of the world-protectors along with their splendor.
He dwelt in heaven, which was endowed with the splendor of the celestial gardens, the very palace of Mahendra, built by Viśvakarman himself.

In that palace of Mahendra, the mighty and high-minded sole sovereign, who had conquered the worlds and whose fierce commands were formidable, took his delight; his pair of feet were worshipped by the gods and others who were humbled by his majesty.
Thus, having conquered the quarters as a sole sovereign and enjoying his beloved sense-objects according to his pleasure, he, whose senses were unsubdued, found no satisfaction.
Thus, for one intoxicated by power, arrogant, and acting contrary to the scriptures, after a long time had passed, a sinful intent subsequently arose.
This son of the demon Mahiṣāsura, a Dānava who delights in crushing others, excessively tormented the excellent twice-born and the ascetics on earth.
The evil-minded one tormented Suras, humans, and all the Pramathas—especially those endowed with righteousness—recollecting his former enmity.
Once upon a time, dear father, that mighty Dānava Gajāsura went to the capital city of Śaṅkara.
O Sage, when the lord of the asuras had arrived, a great clamor arose there among the inhabitants of Ānandana, crying out, "Save us! Save us!"
When this son of the demon Mahiṣa arrived in the city, he, arrogant with the intoxication of his own prowess, began crushing all the Pramathas.
At that moment, the gods, headed by Śakra and others who had been defeated by him, sought refuge in Śiva; having bowed down, they praised him with great reverence.
They reported the arrival of that Dānava in Kāśī, as well as the extreme suffering of the people there, and especially of their lords.
The gods said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, an asura has gone to your city and inflicts suffering upon your people; O ocean of compassion, slay him!
Wherever he indeed sets his foot upon the earth, there he makes the unstable stable by means of his own weight.
By the force of his thighs, trees fall along with their peaks; by the blow of his staff-like arms, even mountains are reduced to powder.
Even though the clouds leave the sky due to friction with his crown, they still do not abandon the blackness born from contact with his hair even today.
By the abundance of whose trust the great oceans become surging with high waves, and even the rivers, along with their timingilas, possess unceasing billows.
The height of this illusory being is nine thousand yojanas, and his body’s width is indeed exactly that much.
"That tawny hue and flickering movement of his eyes which was once compared to lightning is not perceived even today; yet here he comes in great haste."
Whichever direction this Dānava of unbearable power approaches, he thinks, "I am invincible to men and women who are conquered by desire."
Thus has the conduct of that Dānava been reported; O Lord of Devas, devoted to the protection of Kāśī, protect your devotees!
Sanatkumāra said: Thus entreated by the gods, Hara, who is ever intent on protecting his devotees, arrived there swiftly with the desire to slay him.
Beholding Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, arrived with trident in hand and roaring, Gajāsura roared in response.
Then there occurred between those two a great, fierce, and wonderful battle, as they produced heroic roars amidst the clashing of various missiles and weapons.
The exceedingly radiant Gajāsura, possessed of great strength and prowess, pierced Giriśa, the slayer of Dānavas, with sharp arrows.
Then Rudra, of fierce form, quickly cut those arrows into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his own exceedingly terrible shafts before they had even reached him, O Sage.
Then Gajāsura, enraged, rushed toward Maheśvara with a sword in hand, roaring loudly: "Today you are indeed slain by me!"
Then, recognizing that bull among the Daityas—who was approaching with a trident as his weapon—was incapable of being slain by any other means, he struck him with his own trident.
Pierced by that trident, the Daitya Gajāsura, considering himself as if turned into an umbrella, addressed Hara.
Gajāsura said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, I am your devotee in every way; I know you as the Lord of the three heavens, the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Smara.
O Maheśāna, O Destroyer of Tripura, O All-pervading One, your taking my life in this darkness is considered by me to be for my greatest welfare.
I wish to say something; listen to it, O Compassionate One! I speak the truth, not falsehood; O Conqueror of Death, please consider this.
You alone are worthy of veneration by the worlds, established above the universe; all must die in the course of time, yet such a death as this leads to the highest good.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, Śaṅkara, the ocean of compassion, the Lord, laughed and replied to Gajāsura, the son of Mahiṣī.
Īśvara said: O storehouse of great prowess, O best of Dānavas, O one of noble mind, Gajāsura, I am pleased with you; choose a boon that is agreeable to yourself.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Maheśa, the bestower of boons, Gajāsura, the lord of the Dānavas, replied with a tranquil mind.
Gajāsura said: "O sky-clad one, if you are pleased with me, then clothe me in this hide, O Maheśāna, which has been purified by the fire of your trident."
Of her own size, pleasant to the touch, offered as a prize upon the field of battle, beautiful to behold, most divine, and always bringing happiness.
May she always possess a pleasing fragrance; may she always be exceedingly tender; may she always be stainless; and may she always be most beautifully adorned.
O Lord, although this skin of mine has been exposed for a very long time to the blazing flames of great ascetic heat, it has not been consumed, because I am a treasury of the fragrance of merit.
O naked one, if this skin of mine were not meritorious, how then could its contact with your body have occurred on the field of battle?
And grant me another boon, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased: let your name be Kṛttivāsas (Clothed-in-Skin) starting from this very day.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being well-pleased, replied "So be it" to that son of Mahiṣāsura.
Then Maheśāna, who is fond of his devotees, spoke again with a joyful heart to that Dānava, Gajāsura, whose mind was purified by devotion.
The Lord said: "In this sacred field that is a means for attaining liberation, let this meritorious body of yours become my linga here, bestowing liberation upon all."
Known as Kṛttivāseśvara, it destroys great sins; it is the head of all liṅgas and bestows liberation.
Having spoken thus and taking up that great deed of Gajāsura, the Lord of Gods, clad in the directions as his garment, donned it.
O Lord of Sages, on that day a great festival arose; all the people residing in Kāśī as well as the Pramathas attained great joy.
Then Hari, Brahmā, and the other gods, their minds overflowing with joy, bowed with palms joined in reverence and praised that Great Lord.
When that Dānava, the buffalo-like Gajāsura, was slain, the gods returned to their own abodes, and the world attained well-being.
Thus has been told the life-story of Śambhu, which demonstrates his affection for his devotees; it leads to heaven, bestows fame and long life, and increases wealth and grain.
Whoever should hear this with devotion, or cause it to be heard while observing pure vows, shall enjoy great happiness and, in the end, attain supreme bliss.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Gajāsura," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, I shall recount the life-story of the moon-crested Lord, how Hara slew the son of Diti who roared like a kettledrum.
When the mighty Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, was slain by the god Viṣṇu in the form of Time (Kāla), Diti experienced great sorrow.
The wicked Daitya Dundubhinirhrāda, the maternal uncle of Prahlāda and a bringer of sorrow to the gods, consoled that distressed woman with his words.
Then the king of the Daityas, a master of illusion, having consoled Diti, reflected upon a means by which the gods might be easily conquered.
The heroic great asura Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by the gods along with Viṣṇu and his brother, by those enemies of the Daityas using deceitful means.
He reflected upon the means by which he might easily conquer the immortals: "Of what strength are they, what is their sustenance, and what is their support?"
Having deliberated many times and having ascertained the truth with certainty, the Daitya concluded: "Upon reflection, the Brahmins must certainly be the cause here."
Then the Daitya Dundubhinirhrāda, the enemy of the gods and a great villain, repeatedly pursued the Brahmins with the intent to kill them.

Since the gods are the consumers of sacrifices and sacrifices originate from the Vedas, and those Vedas have the Brahmins as their support, therefore, O twice-born ones, the Brahmins are the strength of the gods.
It is certain that all the Vedas, together with Indra, have the Brahmins as their support; the gods are sustained by the power of the Brahmins—there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
If the Brahmins are lost, the Vedas are lost; and because they are lost, the gods are perpetually destroyed.
When the sacrifices were destroyed, the gods, deprived of their food, became weak and easily conquerable; and once the gods were thus defeated, [the asuras would prevail].
I alone shall become the venerable lord of the three worlds; I shall seize the imperishable names and all the riches of the gods.
"I shall enjoy only pleasures in a kingdom where all thorns have been removed"—having thus resolved, the evil-minded villain thought again:
Where are there many twice-born ones, greatly augmented by Brahmanic luster, perfected in the study of the Vedas, and endowed with the power of austerity?
Vārāṇasī is indeed the abode of the majority of Brahmins; having first visited that city, I shall then proceed to other sacred sites.
For wherever there are holy fords (tīrthas) and wherever there are hermitages (āśramas), all those twice-born ones (agrajanmans) are present there by me today on every side.
Thus, having formed a resolve appropriate to his lineage, the deceitful Durvṛtta, known as Dundubhinirhrāda, even after reaching Kāśī, began to slaughter the twice-born.
Wherever those best of the twice-born go to gather sacrificial grass and kuśa, there that evil-minded one devours them all in the forest.
Just so that no one would know him, he again became concealed; having become a forest-dweller in the forest, he took the form of water in the reservoir.
Having an invisible form, a master of illusion, and beyond the reach even of the gods, he should remain during the day intent on meditation, like a sage in the midst of sages.
Observing the entry into and exit from the huts, he took the form of a tiger during the night and devoured many Brahmins.
Thus, free from hesitation, he devoured [the flesh] and did not even leave behind a skeleton; in this manner, many Brahmins were struck down by that wicked one.
Once, on the night of Śivarātri, a certain devotee, having performed the worship of the God of gods within his own hut, remained absorbed in meditation.
And that lord of the Daityas, Dundubhinirhrāda, arrogant in his strength, assumed the form of a tiger and set his mind upon seizing him.
Seeing Bhakta absorbed in meditation, his mind fixed on the vision of Śiva, and having performed the ritual placement of the weapon-mantras, he was unable to overcome him.
Then Śambhu, having gone everywhere and understood the intention of that evil-natured Daitya, set his mind upon slaying him.
Just as the tiger was about to seize him, Hara appeared—three-eyed, the jewel that protects the world, his intellect skilled in the protection of his devotees.
Beholding Rudra approaching, the Daitya, from the liṅga worshipped by his devotee, grew in that very same form until he was like a mountain.
Then, as soon as the Dānava beheld the Omniscient One with contempt, he seized him as he approached and crushed him in a vice-like armpit.
Then the five-faced one struck the five-faced one on the head with his fist—a fist harder than even a thunderbolt—though he was known as "Compassionate toward Devotees."
From that blow of the fist and the crushing pressure of the armpit, the tiger died, crying out in extreme agony and filling both heaven and earth with its roar.
With their minds trembling from that great sound, those whose wealth is asceticism gathered together at night, following the direction of the noise.
Beholding Īśvara, who had taken the lord of beasts as his mount, they all prostrated themselves and praised Śarva with cries of "Victory! Victory! (jaya-jaya).
The Brahmins said: We have been saved, we have been saved from this terrible obstacle! O Lord, show us favor; remain right here, O Teacher of the World.
In this very form, O Mahādeva, by the name Vyāghreśa, always provide protection for the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna.
O Lord of Gaurī, protect us who dwell at this sacred ford from all other calamities; destroy the wicked and grant fearlessness to Your devotees.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of those devotees, Candraśekhara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, replied "So be it" and spoke again to them.
Maheśvara said: "Whoever shall behold me here in this form with faith, I will undoubtedly cause the accumulation of their afflictions to fall away."
Having heard this account of my conduct and having remembered this Liṅga in his heart, a mortal entering into battle undoubtedly attains victory.
In the meantime, the gods, together with Indra, arrived, uttering cries of "Victory! amidst a great celebration.
Having bowed with love to Śaṅkara, all the gods, with palms joined in reverence and shoulders bent, praised him who is affectionate toward his devotees with eloquent words.
The gods said: "Victory to you, O Śaṅkara, Lord of gods, O Lord who removes the suffering of those who bow before you! We gods have been saved by the destruction of this roar of the drum."
O lover of devotees, you must always provide protection for your devotees; O Lord of gods, O Sovereign of all, O Master, you must slay the wicked.
Having heard these words of the gods, the Supreme Lord, saying "So be it," with a gracious soul, entered into dissolution within that linga.
Then the gods, filled with wonder, returned to their respective abodes with joy; those brahmins as well, out of great delight, departed just as they had come.
One who hears this supreme narrative concerning the origin of Vyāghreśvara, or causes it to be heard, or reads it, or likewise causes it to be read;
A man attains all desires wished for in his own mind; in the hereafter, he obtains liberation, freed from all suffering.
This incomparable narrative, consisting of the immortal syllables of Śiva’s divine play, leads to heaven, bestows fame and long life, and increases one’s sons and grandsons.
Supreme, bestowing devotion, auspicious, pleasing to Śiva, and itself auspicious; granting supreme knowledge, delightful, and the ultimate remover of all transformations.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of the Daitya Dundubhinirhrāda," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second Rudrasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen with great affection, O Vyāsa, to the life-story of the Supreme Lord, how he slew the Daitya by means of a sign directed toward his beloved.
