In former times, there were two great Daityas named Vidala and Utpala; they were invincible by men, great heroes, and exceedingly arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā.
O Brahmin, by those two men, who treated the three worlds as mere straw through the strength of their own arms, all the gods were utterly defeated in battle by the two Daityas.
Defeated by those two, the gods sought refuge with you, O Creator; having bowed to him according to the prescribed rites, they all spoke with great respect.
Thus Brahmā indeed spoke to them: "Those two are certainly to be slain by the Goddess; therefore, maintain your fortitude by respectfully recollecting Śiva along with Śivā."
This Supreme Lord Śiva, known as Bhaktavatsala, along with Śivā, shall bring about welfare in no long time.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to them, Brahmā then remained silent, remembering Śiva; and those gods, having attained joy, then departed each to his own abode.
Then, at the prompting of Śiva, the divine sage Nārada went to his abode and sang of the beauty of Śivā.
Having heard those words, the two Daityas, deluded by illusion and afflicted by the god of love, desired to seize the Goddess.
They both reflected constantly: "When and where will that Śivā, having attained her rise through the Creator's favor, become ours?"
At one time, Śambhu was sporting with great grace; out of sheer curiosity, Śivā played the game of ball.
Together with her friends, out of great affection and curiosity, she [remained] in the presence of Śiva.
Displaying the lightness of her limbs as she raised and lowered them, her eyes were agitated by bees delighted by the fragrance of her sighs.
The ground was made into a sacrificial altar by the falling flowers from her loosened braids, while she shone with drops of water trickling from the decorative leaf-designs on her perspiring cheeks.
Her body was covered by the radiance of her limbs as she moved across the path of her shimmering *colā* garment; with her lotus-like hands resting upon her broad hips, she struck the gleaming ball.
With the tips of her creeper-like eyebrows dancing as her eyes followed the sound of the ball, the Mother of the World, Mṛḍānī, was indeed seen playing.
And by two sons of Diti who move through the intermediate space, he was glared at as if they had already embraced him, while death itself stood near.
By those two men named Vidala and Utpala, who were arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā and who, by the strength of their own arms, treated the three worlds as mere straw;
Desiring to seize that goddess and being tormented by their misfortunes, they quickly ascended from heaven, employing the illusory power of Śambara.
Having assumed the illusory forms of attendants, they approached Ambikā; meanwhile, those two were exceedingly wicked in conduct and possessed extremely fickle minds.
Then, by Hara—the destroyer of the wicked—those two were recognized in an instant through his disdainful glance, arising from the flickering of his eyes.
Then Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, was glanced at by the God, who possesses all forms, with the words: "These two are demons; [drive them away], O Gaṇas! or "No! [as the case may be].
Then, O dear one, she understood that sign from the eyes of her own master, Śaṅkara, the supreme lord, who was filled with great curiosity.
Then, recognizing that sign, she who was half the body of the Omniscient One struck them both simultaneously with that very ball.
Struck by the ball of the Great Goddess, those two of great strength, being wicked, whirled around and around and then fell down.
Like a ripe fruit falling from its stalk when shaken by the wind, or like the peak of a great mountain struck down by the thunderbolt.
Having struck down those two great Daityas who were intent on committing an evil deed, the ball then underwent a transformation into the form of a *liṅga*.
Then that liṅga became known by the name Kaṇḍukeśvara; situated near Jyeṣṭheśvara, it wards off all evils.
At that very moment, the gods led by Hari and Brahmā, as well as the sages, having perceived the manifestation of Śiva, arrived there.
Then all the gods, having received boons from Śambhu by his command, went joyfully to their own abodes, as did the residents of Kāśī.
Having beheld Śaṅkara accompanied by Ambikā, they, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and praised him with devotion through pleasing words with great respect.
O Vyāsa, Śiva, the protector of Sāmbī, who is well-versed in sporting and recreation, also went to his own abode, joyful and accompanied by his attendants, for he is affectionate toward his devotees.
And the Kaṇḍukeśvara Liṅga in Kāśī is the destroyer of the wicked; it bestows enjoyment and liberation, and always grants all desires to the virtuous.
Whoever listens with joy to this incomparable narrative, or causes it to be heard, or reads it—for such a person, whence can there be fear of suffering?
Having enjoyed all kinds of unsurpassed happiness here, one indeed attains in the next world a divine state that is difficult even for the gods to reach.
Thus, O dear one, has that most wonderful life-story been described, which indicates the affection of Śiva and Śivā for their devotees and bestows auspiciousness upon the virtuous.
Brahmā said: Having spoken thus and taken leave of Vyāsa, my excellent son, praised by him, went through the air to Kāśī to witness the deeds of the moon-crested Lord.
O best of sages, this *Yuddhakhaṇḍa* has been proclaimed by me to you from within the *Raudrīya Saṃhitā*, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
This Raudrī Saṃhitā has indeed been described by me in its entirety; it is most dear to Sadāśiva and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever should recite daily this [hymn] which wards off the affliction of enemies, shall obtain all desires and thereafter attain liberation.
Sūta said: Having thus heard from his father the supreme glory of Śiva and having obtained the hundred names of Śambhu, the son of Brahmā became fulfilled and a follower of Śiva.
The dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada has been fully related by me; Śiva is indeed the foremost of all. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of the Daityas Vidala and Utpala," in the fifth section (Yuddhakhaṇḍa) of the second book (Rudrasaṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
This Yuddhakhaṇḍa is completed. This second Rudrasaṃhitā is completed.

I bow to the Great Lord Maheśvara, who is supreme bliss, whose divine play is infinite, who is the all-pervading Great One; to Śaṅkara, the primordial God, beloved of Gaurī, from whom Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśa were born.
Śaunaka said: O fortunate Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, ocean of knowledge and compassion, tell us of the incarnations of Śambhu by which he brought about the welfare of the virtuous.
Sūta said: O Sage Śaunaka, with your mind focused through true devotion and your senses subdued, I shall describe the incarnations of Śiva to you; listen, O sage.
O sage, having been asked this in the past by Sanatkumāra, Nandin—who is an embodiment of Śiva and the refuge of the virtuous—spoke to him while remembering Śiva.
Nandīśvara said: "Indeed, the incarnations of the Lord, the Sovereign of All, are innumerable throughout the kalpas; nevertheless, I shall describe them here according to my understanding."
The nineteenth kalpa should be known as Śvetalohita; the first incarnation is proclaimed to be Sadyojāta.
While Brahmā was thus meditating upon that supreme Brahman, a youth with a topknot, white and red in hue, was born from him.
Having seen that person, Brahmā recognized him as the Lord in the form of Brahman; having meditated upon him within his heart, he paid homage with palms joined in reverence.
Having recognized Śiva as the newly born, the Lord of the World rejoiced; and with a pure intellect, he meditated upon that Supreme Being again and again.
Then, as he was meditating, illustrious white youths appeared, who were the very embodiment of supreme knowledge and the supreme Brahman.
Sunanda, Nandana, Viśvananda, and Upanandana were his high-souled disciples, by whom that Brahman was encompassed.
And Sadyojāta Śambhu indeed bestowed knowledge upon the Creator; the Supreme Lord, being pleased and gracious, also granted him the power of creation.
Then the twentieth eon is proclaimed by the name Rakta; therein the Brahmā of great splendor assumed a red color.
As he was meditating with a desire for a son, the son of Vidhi appeared—wearing red garlands and garments, with red eyes and red ornaments.
Seeing that great-souled youth absorbed in meditation, he recognized him as Śiva Vāmadeva and bowed with palms joined in reverence.
From him were born four sons, clad in red garments: Viraja, Vivāha, Viśoka, and Viśvabhāvana.
That Vāmadeva is indeed Śambhu; the gratified Supreme Lord, being pleased, affectionately bestowed both knowledge and the power of creation upon the Creator.
The twenty-first kalpa is known as Pītavāsas, wherein the illustrious Brahmā became Pītavāsas (the Yellow-robed).
To Vidhi, who was meditating and desiring a son, a young boy was born—clad in yellow garments and the like, mature, possessed of great splendor and mighty arms.
Having seen him engaged in meditation and knowing that person to be Śiva, Brahmā then mentally prostrated before Gāyatrī, the consort of Śiva.
Having recited the mantra of the Great Goddess, who is honored by all the worlds, Mahādeva became gracious with a mind absorbed in meditation.
Then, divine youths appeared at his side, all dressed in yellow garments and established in the path of yoga.
Then, when that Pītavarṇa Kalpa of the Self-born One had passed, another Kalpa commenced, known by the name Śiva.
When the single ocean had passed away after a thousand divine years, Brahmā, desiring to create living beings, reflected in distress.
Then the one of great splendor beheld a boy who had appeared, dark-complexioned, possessed of great heroism, and blazing with his own radiance.
Wearing black garments and a black turban, with a black sacred thread, endowed with a black crest-lock, and having black bathing-powder and unguents;
Having seen that high-souled one, who was not terrible yet possessed of terrible prowess, he paid homage to the Lord of the gods of gods, the wonderful one, dark and tawny-hued.
Then Brahmā, assuming the form of Brahmā, meditated upon Aghora; he praised the imperishable one, who is affectionate toward his devotees, with pleasing words.
Then, by his side, there appeared four high-souled young boys, all dark-complexioned and adorned with dark bathing powders and unguents.
Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇaśikha, Kṛṣṇāsya, and Kṛṣṇakaṇṭhadhṛk—these are their unmanifest names; they are forms of Śiva, possessed of great splendor.
Such great-souled ones, for the purpose of Brahmā’s creation, set forth the yoga known as Ghorākhya, which is most wonderful and great.
Then, O lords of sages, another kalpa of Brahmā began, known by the name Viśvarūpa, which was most wonderful.
As Brahmā, desiring a son, meditated upon Śiva in his mind, Sarasvatī appeared in her universal form with a great resonance.
Such was that Blessed One, the Ruler, the Supreme Lord; resembling pure crystal and adorned with all ornaments.
Having seen him, he prostrated before that Brahmā, Īśāna, the unborn, the all-pervading Lord—the omnipresent, the giver of all, the all, who possesses beautiful form yet is devoid of form.
Having thus instructed Brahmā regarding the true path, the omnipresent Lord Īśāna, together with Śakti, fashioned four auspicious boys.
The Jaṭī, Muṇḍī, Śikhaṇḍī, and Arddhamuṇḍa were born; having instructed [others] in the true Dharma through yoga and performed their duties, they attained the state of yoga.
Thus, O omniscient Sanatkumāra, the origin of Sadyojāta and the others has been briefly proclaimed out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Then, O one of great wisdom, their respective activities—which bring benefit to the three worlds and are established throughout the entire universe—[were described].
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Ghora, the one known as Vāma, and the one known as Brahmā—these are the five renowned forms of Maheśvara.
Īśāna, who is of the nature of Śiva, is remembered as the most venerable and the first; he directly presides over the Kṣetrajña, the enjoyer of Prakṛti.
The second form is indeed called Tatpuruṣa, who is Śiva; he presides over the object of enjoyment, which consists of the substratum of the qualities (guṇas) and is omniscient.

For the sake of Dharma, the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) associated with its own limbs belongs to the wielder of the Pināka bow; that which exists within as the third [form] is the one known as Aghora.
Indeed, the fourth form of Śaṅkara is named Vāmadeva; he is the presiding deity of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra) and is always the performer of manifold tasks.
For the Lord of Śaṅkara is eternally of the nature of Īśāna; he is likewise the master of the ear, of speech, and of the all-pervading ether.
The wise, skilled in investigation, declare that the divine form of the Lord—which is called the Puruṣa—is the sovereign nature of the skin, the hand, touch, and the wind.
The wise declare that the form known as Aghora is the presiding principle of the body, as well as of taste, form, and fire.
The form of Śaṅkara known as Vāmadeva is traditionally held to be the lord of the girdle, the anus, taste, and likewise of water.
They know the form called Sadyojāta to be the Lord Śaṅkara, consisting of breath, the generative organ, smell, and the earth.
These forms of Śambhu are indeed to be worshipped with great effort by men seeking the highest good, for they are the sole cause of all auspicious things.
Whoever reads or even hears of the origin of Sadyojāta and the others, having enjoyed all desires, attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Five Brahma Incarnations of Śiva," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O dear one, O Sage, to the supreme incarnations of Maheśa, the Lord, which accomplish all tasks in the world and bestow happiness upon everyone.
This world consists of the eightfold forms of that Śambhu, the Supreme Lord; the entire universe exists pervading him, like clusters of gems upon a thread.
Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Īśāna, and Mahādeva—these are renowned as the eight forms.
Indeed, earth, water, fire, wind, space, the individual soul, the sun, and the moon are presided over by the eight forms of Śiva, beginning with Śarva.

It maintains the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, whose nature is that of the All-Sustainer; this is the certain conclusion regarding the form of Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, and the Scripture itself.
The form of Bhava, the Supreme Self, which consists of water and brings life to the entire world, is called Bhava.
O Lord of the virtuous, that form by which You sustain and cause the vibration of the entire universe, both internal and external, is called "Ugra" (the Fierce) by the wise.
The form of Bhīma, known as Bhīma, which provides space for all, pervades all, is of the nature of the sky, and shatters the multitude of kings.
The form of Paśupati should be known as the substratum of all souls, the dweller in all fields, and the severer of the bonds of the bound.
Illuminating the entire world, that form of Maheśvara known as Īśāna, which bears the name Divākara (the Sun), spreads through the heavens.
That which nourishes the entire universe, the immortal-rayed maker of night, is the form of Mahādeva and the name of Mahādeva.
The Self is the eighth form of Śiva, the Supreme Soul; because he pervades all other forms, the universe is therefore of the nature of Śiva.
Just as the branches of a tree flourish by watering its root, so too does this entire universe flourish through the worship of Śiva.
Just as a father becomes delighted here by the affection of his sons, grandsons, and others, so does Śaṅkara become delighted by the universal affection of the world.
If any embodied being whatsoever is subjected to restraint, it is undoubtedly an act of harm committed against the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva).
Worship with your whole being Rudra, the supreme cause, Śiva, who remains presiding over the universe through his eightfold form.
Thus have been declared those eight renowned sons of Vidhi in their true forms; devoted to the welfare of all, they are to be served by men seeking spiritual prosperity.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Eight Forms of Śiva," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O dear one of great wisdom, to that which fulfills all desires and rites—the unsurpassed form of Śiva known as Ardhanārīnara.
When all the creatures created by the Ordainer did not multiply, he became overwhelmed with anxiety and was pained by that sorrow.
Then a voice from the sky indeed spoke: "Perform creation born of the couple. Having heard that, Brahmā resolved to carry out creation through sexual union.
Since the lineage of women had not previously emerged from Īśāna, the Lotus-born Lord was therefore unable to effect creation through sexual union.
"Without the power of Śambhu, these creatures could not have been born. Reflecting thus, Brahmā proceeded to perform penance.
Having meditated with love in his heart upon the Supreme Lord united with His supreme consort Śivā, he performed that highest austerity.
As that self-existent one was engaged in intense austerity, Śiva quickly became pleased with him in a very short time.
Then, having entered the form of the Lord of Full Consciousness which grants all desires, Hara became half-man and half-woman and proceeded to the presence of Brahmā.
Having beheld that god Śaṅkara accompanied by his most excellent Śakti, Brahmā prostrated himself like a staff and, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise.
Then the god Mahādeva, the creator of the universe, the Great Lord Maheśvara, being well-pleased, addressed Saṃbhava with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Īśvara said: O child, child, illustrious one, my son, Grandfather! I have understood all that desire of yours in its true essence.
You have now performed penance solely for the sake of the prosperity of all creatures; pleased by that penance, I grant you your heart's desire.
Having spoken these most noble words, sweet by their very nature, Śiva separated the goddess Śivā from a portion of his own body.
Having seen that supreme Śakti, who had become separate and was present within Śiva, Brahmā, with a humble soul, prostrated himself and made a request to her.
Brahmā said: O Śivā, at the beginning I was created by the God of gods, your husband; and all creatures were assigned to me by Śambhu, the Supreme Soul.
O Śivā, all the gods and others were created by me through my mind; though they are created again and again, they do not undergo increase.
Having thus established creation as originating from sexual union, I now desire to cause all my offspring to flourish.
"The imperishable race of women did not originate from you in the past; therefore, the race of women is superior, and no power of mine exists against them."
Indeed, the origin of all powers is from you alone; therefore, I pray to you, the supreme power, the sovereign of all.

O Śivā, grant me the power to create the race of women; salutations be unto you! O Mother, O beloved of Śiva, know that the entire world, including all that moves and is immobile, exists for this purpose.
O Goddess who bestows boons, I pray for another boon from you; O Mother of the World, show me mercy and grant it. Salutations be unto you!
O omnipresent Ambika, for the sake of the increase of all things moving and unmoving, become the daughter of my son Dakṣa through the one Lord.
Thus entreated by Brahmā, the Supreme Goddess, saying the words "So be it," bestowed her power upon him for the sake of creation.
Therefore, that auspicious goddess Śivaśakti, who consists of the universe, created from the middle of her eyebrows a single Śakti whose splendor was equal to her own.
Beholding Śakti, Hara, the best of gods, the ocean of compassion, Maheśāna, the performer of divine play, smilingly spoke to Bhavāmbikā.
Śiva said: O Goddess, you have been propitiated by Brahmā, the supreme creator, through his ascetic penance; be gracious and, out of great affection, fulfill all his desires.
Having accepted that command of the Supreme Lord with her head, the Goddess, by the word of Brahmā, became the daughter of Dakṣa.
O sage, having thus bestowed that incomparable power upon Brahmā, that auspicious goddess entered the body of Śambhu, and the Lord Śambhu himself vanished from sight.
From that time forward, a portion for women was established in this world; that Creator attained bliss, and procreative creation came into being.
O dear one, this most excellent form of Śiva has been described to you; indeed, this form, half-female and half-male, bestows great auspiciousness upon the virtuous.
Whoever reads or even hears this sinless narrative shall enjoy all pleasures and attain the supreme goal.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Incarnation as Half-Female and Half-Male," in the Rudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, the life-story of Śaṅkara, which was joyfully and affectionately narrated by Rudra to Brahmā, always bestows happiness.
Śiva said: In the seventh Vārāha Kalpa, known as a Manvantara, the Lord Kalpeśvara, the illuminator of all the worlds, [appeared].
O Creator, at that time, during that Manvantara, he shall be the great-grandson of Mānava Vaivasvata, and there shall indeed be four Yugas.
O Brahmā, O Creator, for the sake of favoring the worlds and for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas, I foresee [this] at the end of the Yuga known as Dvāpara.
And through the simultaneous commencement of that first age, O Brahmin, at the beginning of the first Dvāpara, the self-effulgent Lord himself became Vyāsa.
Then, for the sake of the brahmins at the end of that age, in the Kali Yuga, I shall become the great sage named Śveta, joined with Śiva.
O Creator, at that time my disciples shall possess topknots on the delightful peak of Himavat, on Chāgala, the best of mountains.
Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāśva, and Śvetalohita—these four, through the yoga of meditation, shall go to my city.
Then, having known me truly as the imperishable, they will become my devotees, free from birth, death, and old age, and absorbed in meditative concentration upon the Supreme Brahman.
O Grandfather, I cannot be seen by men except through meditation, nor, my child, by means of practices such as charity and religious duty, which are causes for [worldly] action.
In the second Dvāpara age, Vyāsa will be the Prajāpati named Satya; at that time, I shall appear in the Kali age by the name Sutāra.
There too, I shall have brahmin disciples who are knowers of the Vedas: Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Hṛṣīka, and likewise Ketumān.
Through the practice of the four meditations, they shall go to my city; then, having known me truly as the imperishable, they will become liberated.
And in the third Dvāpara age, when Vyāsa is indeed Bhārgava, even then I shall exist as Damana in the vicinity of the city.
And there too, four sons shall be mine: Viśoka, Viśeṣa, Vipāpa, and Pāpanāśana.
O Four-faced One, I shall provide assistance to Vyāsa through my disciples; I shall firmly establish the path of renunciation here in this Kali age.
And when, in the fourth Dvāpara age, Vyāsa is remembered as Aṅgiras, even then I shall exist, known by the name Suhotra.
Even there, O Creator, those four sons of mine shall become great-souled practitioners of yoga; I shall tell you their names.
"O Creator, at that time I, along with my disciples—Sumukha, Durmukha, Durdarsha, and Duratikrama—will provide assistance to Vyāsa."
In the fifth Dvāpara age, Savitṛ will be remembered as Vyāsa; at that time, I shall become a yogi named Kaṅka, possessed of great ascetic power.
There too, those four sons of mine will become great-souled practitioners of yoga; hear their names from me.
Sanaka, Sanātana, the lord Sanandana, the pervasive Sanatkumāra, who is stainless and free from egoism.
Even there, O Creator, I, named Kaṅka, shall provide assistance to the Sun; indeed, I shall act as Vyāsa’s helper, increasing the path of renunciation.
Furthermore, in the sixth Dvāpara cycle, Mṛtyu will become Vyāsa, the author of the division of the Vedas and the creator of the world.
Even then, I shall exist by the name Lokākṣi, for the purpose of providing great assistance to Vyāsa and for the promotion of the path of renunciation.
There too, there will be four disciples of firm vows: Sudhāman, Virajas, Sañjaya, and likewise Vijaya.
But when Vyāsa is Śatakratu in the seventh cycle, O Brahmā, I too shall then become the powerful Jaigīṣavya.
I, an expert in the great yoga, shall firmly consolidate my practice while staying within a cave in Kāśī, a divine place, seated upon a mat of kuśa grass.
O Creator, I shall indeed provide assistance to Vyāsa and Śatakratu, and I shall deliver my devotees from the fear of saṃsāra.
In that age as well, I shall have four sons: Sārasvata, Yogīśa, Meghavāha, and Suvāhana.
For in the eighth eon, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, will become Vedavyāsa, the divider of the Vedas.
There too, O best among the knowers of yoga, I shall exist by the name Dadhivāhana and shall indeed provide assistance to Vyāsa.
Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and Śālvala—these four sons shall be born as yogins equal to me.
In that very same age, during the ninth cycle of time, there will arise an eminent sage named Vyāsa Sārasvata.
While Vyāsa is meditating for the sake of increasing the path of renunciation, even then I shall become known by the name Ṛṣabha.
Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, and Giriśa—these four shall be my disciples there, all of them excellent yogis.
Together with them, O Lord of Creatures, I shall strengthen the path of yoga; indeed, I shall provide assistance to the noble sage Vedavyāsa.
O Ordainer, assuming that form, I, the compassionate one, shall indeed effect the deliverance of you and many other suffering devotees.
O Creator, that incarnation of mine known as Ṛṣabha is indeed a performer of excellent yoga; he is the author of the Sārasvata and the mind of Vyāsa, and the accomplisher of various goals.
By this incarnation of mine, the prince Bhadrāyus—who had been abandoned by his father and was dead from the effects of poison—has indeed been restored to life.
Then, when that royal child had reached his sixteenth year, Ṛṣabha, who was possessed by Mada, suddenly went to his palace once again.
Honored by him, that sage—who was of noble form and a treasure-house of compassion—instructed him, O Lord of Creatures, in those dharmas conducive to the governance of a kingdom.
Then, with a gracious mind, he gave him a divine armor, a conch, and a radiant sword that destroys all enemies.
Then, out of compassion for those who are humble, he touched their limbs with his ash and granted them the strength of twelve thousand elephants.
Having thus properly consoled Bhadrāyuṣa along with his mother, the Lord Ṛṣabha, having been honored by her, departed at his own will.
O Vidhi, the royal sage Bhadrāyu, having conquered the hosts of his enemies, ruled the kingdom according to dharma after marrying Kīrtimālinī.
Thus has the ninth incarnation of Śaṅkara, Ṛṣabha, been described to you—He who is the refuge of the virtuous and the kinsman of the distressed, possessing such power.
Indeed, the supreme, great, and purifying life-story of Ṛṣabha—which leads to heaven, brings fame, and bestows long life—should be heard with diligent effort.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Ṛṣabha," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śiva said: In the tenth Dvāpara age, there was a sage named Vyāsa Tridhāman on the delightful peak of Himavat, Bhṛgutuṅga, the best of mountains.
There too, my sons—Bhṛgu and the others, who are equal to the Vedas—were Balabandhu, Narāmitra, and Ketuśṛṅga, whose wealth was their asceticism.
In the eleventh Dvāpara age, when Vyāsa Trivṛta appears, I shall then become an ascetic named Kali at Gaṅgādvāra.
Lambodara, Lambākṣa, Keśalamba, and Pralambaka—there too, four sons of firm vows will be born.
In the twelfth [age], Śatatejas will be the author of the Vedas; there too, I shall exist at the end of the Dvāpara age in this Kali age.
Having assumed a golden tunic and known by the name Atri, he indeed returned for the sake of assisting Vyāsa, his anger directed toward the path of renunciation.
O great sage, there he will have four sons who are omniscient, possessed of equanimous intellect, accomplished, and excellent yogis.
In that thirteenth yuga, Dharma will always be Nārāyaṇa; at that time, I shall become the great sage Vyāsa, known by the name Bali.
In the hermitage of the Bālakhilyas on Gandhamādana, the best of mountains, there were Sudhāman, Kāśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and the auspicious Virajas.
When Vyāsa is known as Rakṣa in the fourteenth cycle, I shall be Gautama in that lineage of Aṅgiras.
Even then, in that Kali age, those shall be my sons: Atri, Dvaśada, Śravaṇa, and Śraviṣkaṭa.
Vyāsa said: "In the fifteenth Dvāpara age, when Trayyāruṇi appears, then I shall become Vedaśiras, and likewise Vedaśiras."
That weapon of great power and the Vedaśīrṣa mountain, reaching the ridge of the Himavat on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī, [were established].
There too, I shall have four steadfast sons: Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, and Kunetraka.
When Vyāsa becomes a deity in the sixteenth yuga, then I shall indeed become Gokarṇa for the purpose of bestowing yoga.
And in that very place is that most meritorious forest named Gokarṇa; there too, my son, yogins equal to Ambu will come to be.
Kāśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, and Bṛhaspati—they too shall go to the abode of Śiva by that very same path.
In the seventeenth chapter, Vyāsa Devakṛtañjaya says: "I am known by the name Guhāvāsī (Cave-dweller) on a beautiful peak of the Himavat."
In the great and most lofty Mahālaya, the Himalaya is the sacred field of Śiva; there dwell Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahāyoga, and Mahābala.
In the eighteenth cycle, when Vyāsa was Ṛtañjaya, I was here on the auspicious peak of the Himavat under the name Śikhaṇḍin.
In that most meritorious field of accomplishment is the mountain named Śikhaṇḍin, as well as the forest of Śikhaṇḍin, which is frequented by the Siddhas.
Vācaḥśravas, Rucīka, Syāvāsya, and Yatīśvara—these sons, rich in asceticism, will also be born there.
In the nineteenth [incarnation], the great sage Vyāsa will indeed be Bharadvāja; even then, I shall exist by the names Jaṭī and Mālī.
There, on a peak of the Himavat, my sons were born together with Ambudhi: Hiraṇyanāman, Kauśalya, Lokākṣin, and likewise Pradhimin.
In the twentieth cycle, Gautama shall be the Vyāsa; there I shall be named Aṭṭahāsa, and men will be fond of loud laughter.
Right there on the ridge of the Himalayas is the great mountain Aṭṭahāsa, frequented by gods, humans, lords of yakṣas, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
There too, those sons of mine shall be excellent yogis: Sumantu, the learned Bābari, Kabandha, and Kuśikaṇdhara.
In that twenty-first age, when Vācas-śravas was the Vyāsa, I was then named Dāruka; from that [name], the auspicious Dāruvana forest [derived its name].
There too, those sons of mine shall be excellent yogis: Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, Ketumān, and Gautama.
But in the twenty-second [age], when Vyāsa is Śuṣmāyaṇa, then too I shall become a great sage in Vārāṇasī.
In that Kali age, the gods together with Indra shall behold me there by the name of Bhīma Lāṅgalin, as well as Śiva and Halāyudha.
There too, those sons of mine shall be very righteous: Bhallavī, Madhupiṅga, and likewise Śvetaketu.
In the twenty-third cycle, when the sage was Tṛṇabindu, I was indeed Śveta on the auspicious Kālañjara mountain.
There too, those ascetics shall be my sons: Uśika, Bṛhadaśva, Devala, and Kavi.
In the twenty-fourth cycle, when the powerful Yakṣa Vyāsa was the great yogi named Śūlin, he [resided] then in Naimiṣa during that Yuga.
There too, those ascetics shall become my disciples: Śālihotra, Agniveśa, Yuvanāśva, and Śaradvasu.
When Vyāsa shall be known by the name Śakti in the twenty-fifth [cycle], then I too, the great yogin, shall be the Lord Daṇḍī Muṇḍīśvara.
There too, those ascetics shall become my disciples: Chagala, Kuṇḍakarṇa, Kumbhāṇḍa, and Pravāhaka.
When Vyāsa Parāśara comes into being in the twenty-sixth [cycle], I too shall come to the city of Bhadravaṭa, known by the name Sahiṣṇu.
There too, those ascetics shall become my disciples: Ulūka, Vidyuta, Śambūka, and Āśvalāyana.
When Jātūkarṇya becomes Vyāsa in the twenty-seventh [cycle], I too shall then resort to the holy site of Prabhāsa as Somaśarman.
There too, those ascetics shall become my disciples: Akṣapāda, Kumāra, Ulūka, and likewise Vatsa.
In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, however, when Hari, the son of Parāśara, shall become the Vyāsa known by the name Dvaipāyana, the Great Sage.
Then, with a sixth portion, Kṛṣṇa, the best of men, the excellent son of Vasudeva, will become Vāsudeva.
Even then, through my yogic power (yogamāyā), I shall become one whose self is yoga, possessing the body of a celibate student (brahmacārin) for the purpose of causing wonder in the world.
Having seen a corpse abandoned in the cremation ground and observed that the body is subject to decay, he entered into the power of yogic illusion for the sake of the welfare of the brahmins.
"O Brahmā, I shall then dwell together with you and Viṣṇu in the divine and meritorious cave of Meru, known by the name Lakulī."
Then, that supreme field of accomplishment, known as Kāyāvatāra, will become widely renowned for as long as the earth endures.
There too, those ascetics shall become my disciples: Kuśika, Garga, Mitra, and Kauruṣya.
The yogis who are Brahmins, masters of the Vedas, and whose vital energy is drawn upward, having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, shall go to the city of Śiva.
Indeed, during the Vaivasvata interval, these incarnations of the Lord of Yoga were correctly proclaimed by the Supreme Self; they are of virtuous conduct in all cosmic cycles.
O Lord, there are twenty-eight Vyāsas in every Dvāpara age, and the incarnation of Yogeśvara occurs at the beginning of every Kali age.
The four disciples of the incarnations of the Lords of Yoga, who furthered the path of yoga, were each great Śaivas and imperishable.
These disciples of Pāśupata have their bodies smeared with ashes, wear ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, and have their foreheads marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra).

All the disciples were devoted to the Dharma and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; they were constantly engaged in the worship of the Liṅga, established both externally and internally.
Through devotion to me and through yoga, those who are established in meditation and have conquered their senses are counted by the wise as one hundred and twelve in number.
Thus, indeed, this characteristic of the incarnations has been proclaimed by me, from Manu onwards to Kṛṣṇa, according to the sequence of the twenty-eight yugas.
In that Kalpa, when Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana appears, the compilation of the collections of Śruti will constitute the definition of Brahman.
Having spoken thus and bestowed his grace upon Brahmā, Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, looked at him once more and vanished right there.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nineteen Śiva-Avatāras," in the Narrative of the Incarnations of Śiva within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus are the forty-two incarnations.
Now he speaks of the incarnation of Nandīśvara. Sanatkumāra said: "O Lord, how did you, born from a portion of Mahādeva, attain Śiva? I wish to hear all of that; you should tell it to me, O Master."
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen with attention, O sage, how I—who am born from a portion of Mahādeva—attained Śiva.
Desiring offspring, Śilāda was addressed with reverence by his ancestors, who, out of devotion and desiring his own elevation, urged him to rescue them.
There was a powerful man named Śilāda, who looked downward, was of virtuous nature, and lived according to the conduct of sages; he went to the world of Śiva.
With a steady mind and firm in his vows, that sage named Śilāda performed most difficult austerities for a long time, directed toward Śakra.
As he was performing penance, Śatakratu became pleased by his austerity; then the Lord of all the gods went to grant him a boon.
Śakra, with great affection, said to Śilāda: "O sinless one, I am pleased with you; therefore, O tiger among sages, choose boons."
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods and having praised him with hymns of devotion, Śilāda, that tiger among sages, spoke to him with his hands joined in reverence.
Śilāda said: "O Śatakratu, O Lord of the gods, O Master, if you are pleased with me, I desire a son of noble vows who is not born from a womb and is free from death."
Śakra said: "I shall grant you a son born of a womb, yet subject to death, for you who desire a son; otherwise, I will not grant one, for indeed there are none who are exempt from death."
"I will not give you my son, who is free from death and not born of a womb; for even Hari and the Lord Brahmā [cannot take him], much less anyone else, O great sage."
Those two as well, born from the limbs of Tripurāri, were accompanied by death; the measure of their lifespan has also been stated separately in the Nigama.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, abandon all hope for a son born without a womb and free from death; instead, accept a son who is suitable for yourself.
But Rudra, the Lord of Gods, Maheśvara, is pleased; indeed, he will grant you a son who is very difficult to obtain, free from death, and not born from a womb.
O great sage, neither I, nor the Lord Viṣṇu, nor Druhiṇa (Brahmā) are able to grant you a son who is not born from a womb and is free from death.
Propitiate Mahādeva with the desire for a son; he, the Lord of All and the Greatly Powerful One, will grant you a son.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, having spoken thus and having bestowed his grace upon that best of Brahmins, the compassionate Lord of the Gods, surrounded by the deities, departed for his own world.
When that boon-granting thousand-eyed one had departed, Śilāśana propitiated Mahādeva and satisfied Bhava through his ascetic penance.
Then, as he remained thus incessantly intent, a thousand divine years passed for that twice-born man like a single, wondrous moment.
The sage’s limbs were covered by an anthill, and he was surrounded on all sides by hosts of insects numbering in the lakhs and crores, including others with needle-like mouths that feed upon blood.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, that best of sages, Śilāda, remained in that cave until he subsequently became nothing but a skeleton.
Then the gratified Lord revealed his own divine form to him—a form endowed with celestial qualities, unattainable by those of perverse intellect.
To him who was performing austerities for a thousand divine years, the wielder of the trident, the lord of all gods, said: "I am the giver of boons."
The great sage Śilāda, who was absorbed in a profound meditative absorption and whose delight was entirely dependent on devotion to Śambhu, did not hear those words of Śambhu.
O tiger among sages, as soon as the muni was touched by that hand of Tripurāri, he immediately abandoned his course of asceticism.
Then, opening his eyes and beholding Soma, the embodiment of Śambhu, the sage quickly bowed with joy and fell at his feet, O Muni.
With his shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, Śilāda—his soul serene and his voice faltering with joy—praised the Supreme Lord.
Then the blessed Lord, the three-eyed God of gods, being pleased, said to that bull among sages, Śilāda, "I am the giver of boons."
"O high-minded one, what need have you for this austerity? I shall grant you a son who is omniscient and has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures."
Then, having bowed to the Lord of Gods and having heard that, the eater of stones (Śiva) spoke with words faltering with joy to the one adorned by the moon (Śiva).
Śilāda said: "O Maheśa, if you are pleased with me, or if you are a granter of boons to me, I desire a son equal to yourself—one who is free from death and not born of a womb."
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by him, the three-eyed god Śaṅkara, with a gracious soul, then replied to Śilāda, the best of sages.
Śiva said: O Brahmin, rich in asceticism, I was previously propitiated by Brahmā through penance, as well as by the sages and the best of the gods for the sake of an incarnation.
"I shall become your son, named Nandin, born not from a womb; O Sage of the worlds, you shall indeed be the father of my father."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, the compassionate Hara, looking at the sage who stood there having prostrated, quickly gave him his instructions and vanished on the spot.
When that Great God had departed, the great sage Śilāda returned to his own abode and then related [the event] to the sages.
And after some time, that father of mine, the best among those who know sacrifice, quickly cleared the sacrificial ground for the sake of a sacrifice.
Then, in an instant, by the command of Śambhu, I was born as his son; even before that birth, I had already come into being with a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.

Then the Puṣkarāvartaka and other clouds ceased their rain; the sky-dwellers, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Sādhyas sang [in praise]; and when I had become the son of Śilāda, those lords of ṛṣis showered a rain of flowers from all sides.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, as well as all the celestial consorts, arrived there with great joy; and Hari, Śiva, and Ambikā also came.
Then there was a great festival, and throngs of Apsaras danced; honoring me as well as the Liṅga, they praised them with joyful hearts.
Having praised Śilāda, who was highly worthy of praise, with excellent hymns, the two Śivas, the lords of all, departed for their own abodes along with everyone else.
And Śilāda, too, seeing me—a child with three eyes and four arms, wearing a crown of matted hair, and possessing the brilliance of the fire of the sun at the end of time—was struck with wonder.
Bearing the form of Rudra in every way, with blazing weapons such as the trident, he was bowed to with love by Mahānandabharas, who prostrated himself before him.
Śilāda said: "O Lord of the gods, since I have been gladdened by you, I shall be Nandin by name; therefore, I bow to you, the god Ānanda, the Lord of the universe."
Nandīśvara said: Delighted, my father, having prostrated deeply before Maheśvara, quickly went to his own hermitage like a poor man who has found a treasure.
When I went to the hermitage of the great sage Śilāda, I then abandoned that form and assumed a human one.
Seeing him established in human form, my father, honored by the world, was overcome with extreme grief and lamented, surrounded by his kinsmen.
Śilāda, the son of Śālaṅkāyana, who was truly devoted to his son, performed for me all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
And my father taught me the Vedas, along with all their limbs and sub-limbs in their entirety, as well as other scriptures, when I was five years old.
When the seventh year was complete, two sages named Mitra and Varuṇa arrived at his hermitage to see me, by the command of the Lord.
Having been honored by that sage and being well-seated, those two great-souled maharṣis looked at me again and again and spoke.
Mitra and Varuṇa said: "O dear one, Nandin, though he has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, his life is short; indeed, we did not see him live for more than ten years."
When the two [sages] had spoken thus, Śilāda, who was devoted to his son, embraced him and, afflicted by grief, wept most piteously and discordantly.
Seeing his father and grandfather fallen like corpses, he, with a serene mind, spoke in response while recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva.
"By what sorrow, dear one, are you trembling and weeping? From where has this suffering arisen? I wish to know it according to its true nature."
The father said: "O son, I am exceedingly distressed by the suffering of your premature death. Who indeed can take away my grief? To whom shall I go for refuge?"
The son said: "Whether it be a god, a dānava, Yama, or even Time (Kāla)—even if these, or indeed other people as well, should overcome me."
Moreover, my untimely death shall not come to pass; I do not deceive you. I speak the truth to my father, and I swear this oath to you.
The father said: "What is your austerity, what is your thorough knowledge, and what is your yoga and power, by which you shall overcome this terrible suffering, my son?"
The son said: "O father, I shall not evade death through asceticism nor through knowledge; by the worship of Mahādeva alone shall I conquer death, and not otherwise."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, O sage, I bowed my head at my father’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed for that supreme forest.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Nandikeśa," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said: O sage, having gone there and staying in a secluded place, I, being wise, performed a fierce penance that is difficult even for the holy sages to accomplish.
Having meditated upon the god Tryambaka within the cavity of the heart-lotus—the three-eyed, ten-armed, peaceful, five-faced, and eternally auspicious Śiva—
Established in supreme meditation, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind, I indeed performed the recitation of the Rudra-mantra on the holy northern bank of the river.
Then, while I was engaged in that recitation, the Supreme Lord Mahādeva, Soma, who is adorned with the crescent moon, being pleased and satisfied, spoke to me as I stood there.
Śiva said: "O Śailāda, I am the granter of boons to you, gratified by this penance. Well done, O wise one, you have performed excellent austerity; tell me what is in your heart."
Thus addressed by the god, he bowed his head at the god's feet and praised the Supreme Lord, the destroyer of old age and sorrow.
Then Śambhu [beheld] me, Nandin, endowed with supreme devotion, my eyes filled with tears, and properly bowed with my head at his feet.
Rising up, the Supreme Lord, the bull-bannered one who removes the greatest suffering, took hold of him with his two hands facing each other and touched him.
Having observed the leaders of the Gaṇas and the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, the Lord of the worlds looked at me with a compassionate gaze and spoke.
"O child Nandin, of great wisdom, whence comes this fear of death for you? These two brahmins were sent by me alone; you are equal to me, of this there is no doubt."
Immaculate, abandoned by old age, forever free from suffering, the Lord of the Gaṇas is imperishable and undecaying; he is the desired one, he is the father, and he is the kinsman.
Madbala shall always be by my side and remain my beloved forever; furthermore, by my grace, there shall be neither old age, nor birth, nor death for him.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, that ocean of compassion quickly untied his own garland of lotuses from his head and fastened it around my neck.
O Brahmin, with that auspicious garland fastened around my neck, I became three-eyed and ten-armed, like a second Śaṅkara.
Then, taking [him] by the hand, the Supreme Lord said: "Speak; what supreme boon shall I grant you today?"
Then, having taken the pure water resting in his matted locks and saying, "Nandi shall be here," the bull-bannered Lord released it.
Then five auspicious rivers began to flow, possessing excellent waters, great velocity, divine forms, and beauty.
Jaṭodakā, Trisrotas, Vṛṣadhvani, Svarṇodakā, and Jambunadī—these are proclaimed as the five rivers.
O Sage, this auspicious place named Pañcanada, situated on the back of Śiva, is supremely pure and located near Japeśvara.
He who, having reached Pañcanada, bathes and recites prayers, and worships Īśvareśvara, attains union with Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Then Śambhu said to Umā: "I shall consecrate Nandin as the lord of the Gaṇas; I will proclaim him—what do you think, O imperishable one?"
Umā said: "O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, you ought to grant [this] to Nandin; O Master, Śailādi is my most beloved son."
Nandīśvara said: Then Śaṅkara—the independent Supreme Lord, the giver of all, and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees—remembered his excellent Gaṇapa leaders.
Merely by the remembrance of Rudra, the lords of the Gaṇas arrived—all of them innumerable, full of great joy, and possessing the very form of Śaṅkara.
Those Gaṇeśas, having prostrated before Śiva and the Goddess, spoke auspicious words; those mighty ones, with shoulders bowed, joined their palms in reverence and paid homage.
The Gaṇeśas said: For what purpose have we been remembered, O God? Command us, O Great Lord! We, your servants, have arrived, O Destroyer of Tripura, O Granter of Desires.
"Shall we dry up the oceans, or Yama along with his servants? Shall we slay Death, Great Death, and especially the aged Lotus-born?"
"Let us bind Indra together with the gods, or Viṣṇu along with his attendants; or let us bring back the Daityas, highly enraged, together with the Dānavas."
"Whose terrible calamity shall we bring about today by your command? Or whose festival shall we hold today, O Lord, for the fulfillment of all desires?"
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of those hosts who spoke like heroes, the Supreme Lord praised those lords of the Gaṇas and spoke to them.
Śiva said: "This Nandīśvara is my son, the lord of all lords; he is beloved and the leader of the Gaṇas. Let my word be carried out by all."
"Everyone, with joy, consecrate him as the lord and protector of my hosts; from this day forward, this Nandīśvara shall be your master."
Nandīśvara said: Having been thus addressed by Śaṅkara, all those leaders of the Gaṇas replied, "So be it," and then brought together the necessary materials.
Then the gods, including Indra, as well as those headed by Nārāyaṇa, and the sages from all the worlds, arrived with joyful countenances.
O Blessed One, by the command of Śaṅkara, the Grandfather (Brahmā) also, with a concentrated mind, performed the entire consecration of Nandin.
Then Viṣṇu, Śakra, and likewise the guardians of the world, as well as the sages led by Pitāmaha, offered praises.
While they were thus offering praises, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the entire universe, placed his joined palms upon his head and, with a concentrated mind, offered hymns of praise.
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he uttered the cry of "Victory! Then all the leaders of the Gaṇas, followed by the gods and then the asuras, did likewise.
Thus praised and consecrated by the gods and the Brahmakas at that time, O best of Brahmins, I became Nandīśvara by the command of the Supreme Lord.
And there, by the command of the Supreme Lord, my marriage was performed with great joy and accompanied by a magnificent festival, in the presence of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods.
The daughter of the Maruts, the goddess Suyaśas, was captivating and divine; she became my wife, bringing delight to both my mind and my eyes.
There she obtained a moon-bright parasol, adorned with chowries held in the outstretched hands of a multitude of women.
And that supreme lion-throne was presided over by her and by me; it was adorned with great fortune and with fine ornaments such as a crown and the like.
And thus the supreme necklace was obtained and placed upon the neck of the Goddess, as well as the lordly bull, the white serpent, the lion, and the lion-banner.
A chariot and a golden necklace, auspicious and like the orb of the moon, as well as other objects, were indeed obtained by me, O Sage.
O great sage, having thus performed my marriage with that wife, I prostrated at the feet of Śambhu and Śivā, as well as those of Brahmā and Hari.
To me, who was in such a state along with my wife, the Lord Śiva, the master of the three worlds and compassionate toward his devotees, spoke with supreme affection.
Īśvara said: Listen, O virtuous son; you are my father and Suyaśā is dear to you. Out of affection, I grant you the boon that is desired in your heart.
O Nandīśa, O Lord of the Gaṇas, I am always pleased with you; together with the Goddess, my child, listen to my supreme word.
He is beloved, distinguished, and endowed with supreme sovereignty; he is a great yogi, a mighty archer, our father, and our grandfather.
Invincible and the conqueror of all, always worthy of worship and possessed of great strength; where I am, there you are, and where you are, there I am as well.
And this father of yours, my son, endowed with supreme sovereignty, shall become a leader of my Gaṇas, a devotee of great strength.
"O child, let it be so; these observances of yours shall likewise be fulfilled. Having been granted boons by me, they shall come into my presence."
Nandīśvara said: Then the illustrious Goddess, the giver of boons, spoke to Nandin: "Choose a boon from me, my son—whatever desires you wish for."
Having heard those words of the goddess, she then spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O Goddess, may I always possess supreme devotion at your feet."
Having heard my words, the goddess spoke thus: "So be it," to Suyaśā, who was most dear to Nandin and beloved by Śiva, with great affection.

The Goddess said: "O child, you shall indeed have your desired boon: you shall be three-eyed and free from rebirth; furthermore, may my devotion belong to your sons and grandsons, as well as to your husband."
Nandi said: Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the hosts of gods, being well-pleased by the command of Śiva, affectionately granted boons to those two.
Then the Lord Īśāna, taking me along with my lineage, ascended his bull together with his kinsmen and relatives and went to his own abode with the Goddess.
Then all the gods, Viṣṇu and the others, praising him, returned to their own abodes with joy, extolling Śiva as auspiciousness itself.
Thus, O child, O great sage, I have narrated to you my own incarnation, which bestows eternal bliss upon men and increases devotion to Śiva.
Whoever hears or causes others to hear this account of my birth as Nandin, as well as the granting of the boon, the consecration, and the marriage;
Whether one recites it oneself or causes others to recite it, being endowed with faith and devotion, one shall enjoy all happiness in this world and attain the supreme goal in the next.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation, Coronation, and Marriage of Nandikeśvara," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Thus ends the forty-third incarnation.
Now he speaks of the descent of Bhairava. Nandīśvara said: "O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen to the story of Bhairava, by the mere hearing of which devotion to Śiva shall become firm."
Bhairava is indeed the full form of Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self; the deluded, however, do not know him, being enchanted by the Māyā of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra does not know the majesty of the Great Lord; neither indeed does Viṣṇu, though he has four arms, nor even Brahmā, though he has four faces.
There is indeed nothing wonderful here; rather, the power of Śambhu is truly difficult to comprehend. Deluded by her, everyone fails to worship even that Supreme One.
If he knows himself as the Supreme Lord, then all those [powers] are destroyed by his own will; indeed, no one can ever overcome him.
Although the Great Lord is omnipresent, he is not perceived by those of deluded intellect; in this world, he who transcends the reach of mind and speech is understood only as a god.
In this regard, O great sage, I shall relate an ancient history; listen to it with faith, my dear, for it is the supreme cause of knowledge.
All the celestial sages went to the Lord Brahmā, who was staying on the wonderful and beautiful peak of Meru, desiring to know the true reality.
Having arrived there and performed the prescribed rites, all those lords of sages, with shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, questioned him with great respect.
The celestial sages said: O God of gods, Lord of creatures, Creator of the universe, Leader of the worlds! Tell us truly: what is that one imperishable reality?
Nandīśvara said: Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Maheśa, the Lotus-born One, failing to recognize his supreme nature, replied with conceit:
Brahmā said: O gods and all you sages, listen with devotion and a focused mind; I shall declare the supreme, immutable reality exactly as it is.
I am the source of the universe, the Sustainer, the Self-born, the Unborn, and the Lord; I am indeed Brahman, the beginningless portion, the one, stainless Self.
For I alone am the initiator of the worlds, and I alone am their withdrawer; there is no one else superior to me as the destroyer, O best of gods.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, while the Creator was speaking thus, Viṣṇu, who was present there, being deluded by Ajā and provoked to anger, spoke these words with a laugh.
O Brahmin, such foolishness is not fitting for one disciplined in yoga; since you have not realized the supreme reality, this is being spoken by you in vain.
The creator indeed of all worlds, the Supreme Self, the Highest Person, the sacrifice, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Māyā, and the ultimate refuge.
O Brahmā, this creation is being brought forth by you at my command; it cannot exist as the sustenance of the worlds without disregarding me, the Lord.

Thus, out of delusion regarding the three constituent qualities (guṇas), the two, each desiring victory over the other, spoke here to the Vedas as the authority in every respect concerning their respective bodies.

"They should be questioned specifically, for they are present there in embodied forms. Having said this, the two [sages] questioned all four of them, who were knowers of the authoritative means of knowledge.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu said: "The Vedas are the authority everywhere; they are the supreme, immeasurable foundation. Speak with confidence: what is the one imperishable reality?"
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of theirs, all those [Vedas], beginning with the Ṛgveda, spoke again according to the truth, while remembering the Supreme Lord.
If we two, O venerable gods, are the all-pervading creators and sustainers of the universe, then we shall declare the authoritative means of knowledge that will shatter your doubt.

Nandīśvara said: Having heard the injunctions declared in the Vedas, those two gods addressed the Śrutis: "What you have spoken is authoritative for us; however, let the truth be explained correctly."
The Ṛgveda said: He in whom all beings reside, from whom everything proceeds, and whom they call the supreme reality—he is indeed Rudra alone.
The Yajurveda said: He who is worshipped by all sacrifices and through yoga, he by whom we are indeed measured—he is the one, all-seeing Śiva.
The Sāmaveda said: He by whom this universe is set in motion, he who is meditated upon by yogis, and by whose light the universe shines—he alone is the supreme Tryambaka.
The Atharvaveda said: Those people who, through their devotion, behold the Lord of Gods—he is called the one, Kaivalya, Śaṅkara, who is beyond all suffering.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard this which was spoken by Śruti, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, utterly deluded by Māyā and devoid of discernment, smiled and spoke to those Vedas.
Vidhi and Hari said: "O Vedas, what is this that you speak, devoid of consciousness? What has happened to you today, for all your supreme wisdom has indeed perished?"
How does this Lord of Destruction, naked, yellow-hued, and grey with dust, sport incessantly with Śivā?
With a hideous appearance, matted hair, riding upon a bull, and adorned with serpents, he has attained the state of the Supreme Brahman; yet how can that state be devoid of attachment?
Having heard what was thus uttered by them, the all-pervading Praṇava, though formless, assumed a form out of affection and, expanding himself, spoke to the two of them:
Praṇava said: Indeed, the Lord Rudra, Hara, who assumes forms for his divine play, never sports with a power that is separate from his own self.
For he is the Supreme Lord, self-luminous and eternal; this auspicious Śakti is his very nature, consisting of bliss, and not adventitious.
Nandīśvara said: Although he was addressed in this manner by Brahmā and Viṣṇu at that time, his ignorance did not perish, due to the very *māyā* of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Then a great light appeared between the two of them, filling the space between heaven and earth with its own radiance.
O Sage, situated in the midst of a circle of light, he was seen there in human form with a most wonderful body by Vidhi and Kratu.
Then the fifth head of Brahmā blazed up with anger: "Who is this that assumes a human form between us two?"
While Vidhi was still contemplating this, in an instant, that three-eyed Great Being, Nīlalohita, was beheld.
Seeing him with the trident in hand, the eye on his forehead, and adorned with serpents and the crescent moon, Hiraṇyagarbha, being deluded, laughed and spoke.
Brahmā said: "O Nīlalohita, I know you; do not fear, O Moon-crested One! In ancient times, you, Rudra, manifested from the surface of my forehead."
Because of your weeping, you were given the name Rudra by me in the past; come to me alone for refuge, my son, and I shall grant you protection.
Nandīśvara said: Then, O Sage, having heard the arrogant speech of the lotus-born Brahmā, the Lord became exceedingly enraged, as if bringing about the dissolution of the universe.
Out of anger, the Supreme Lord produced from somewhere a terrifying man blazing with great luster, yet [he did so] out of affection.
Īśvara said: "O Kālabhairava, previously that lotus-born one was to be governed by you; since you shine like Time itself, you are therefore the manifest King of Time."
You are capable of sustaining the universe; because you are terrifying, you are remembered as Bhairava. Even Time itself will fear you; therefore, you are Kālabhairava.
Since you, when enraged, will crush those of wicked soul, you shall therefore attain the renown of "Āmardaka" everywhere.
"Since you shall devour the sins of your devotees at that very moment, your name shall indeed be 'Pāpabhakṣaṇa' (the Devourer of Sins)."
This city of liberation, Kāśī, is indeed more venerable than all others; and over it, O Kālarāja, you always hold sovereign authority.
Among those people who have committed sins, you alone are indeed their teacher; and Citragupta shall record their actions, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Nandīśvara said: Having accepted these boons, Kālabhairava then, at that very moment, severed the head of Brahmā with the tip of the nail of his left forefinger.
When a specific limb causes the failure of an undertaking, that very limb must be punished; therefore, since it was he who uttered the insult, his fifth head has been severed.
Then, seeing the head of Vidhi severed, Hari became even more terrified and devoutly praised Śaṅkara with the Śatarudriya mantras.
Even Hiraṇyagarbha, being afraid, chanted the Śatarudriya; thus, O Sage, they both became divested of their pride at that very moment.
They attained the knowledge that Śiva is the supreme Brahman manifest, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; he is the Supreme Self, transcending all qualities.
O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen to my supreme and auspicious teaching: as long as pride persists, so long must the protection of knowledge be maintained with particular care.
Having abandoned pride, a person knows the Supreme Lord; the Lord of the Universe, who is born as the destroyer of pride, slays the arrogant man.
Then, knowing that Viṣṇu and Vidhi were devoid of pride, the Supreme Lord Mahādeva became pleased; the Master granted them both freedom from fear.
Having comforted them, Mahādeva, pleased and affectionate toward those who bow before him, spoke to his own other form, Bhairava, the one with matted hair.
Mahādeva said: "This Viṣṇu is to be honored by you, as is Śatadhṛti himself; O Nīlalohita, wear even this skull of Brahmā."
To remove the sin of killing a Brahmin, show this vow to the world; resorting to the vow of the skull-bowl, wander constantly for alms.
Having spoken thus while he was looking on, Śiva, in the form of radiant energy, created a maiden renowned as Brahmahatyā and said:
Until they reach the divine city of Vārāṇasī, you, O Bhīṣaṇā, must follow after them in your fierce form.
You have access everywhere except for the city of Vārāṇasī; when you go to Vārāṇasī, be liberated from it at that very moment.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus commanded that Brahmahatyā at that time, the Lord Śiva, who is most wonderful, then vanished from sight.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Bhairava," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen with affection to another discourse concerning Bhairavī, which destroys great evils and increases devotion.
In his presence, even Bhairava became Time, the devourer of Time; by the word of the God of Gods, he bore the vow of the Kāpālikas.
With a skull in his hand, the Soul of the Universe wandered through the three worlds; yet even the terrible sin of Brahman-slaughter did not abandon that God.
Even by wandering from one sacred ford to another, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; therefore, let the entire majesty of the Enemy of Kama (Śiva) be understood.
Once, while wandering about even though being attended by his attendants (Pramathas), Hara, acting as a free-willed Kāpālika, went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Then [he saw] Mahākāla approaching—three-eyed, with serpents for earrings, born from a portion of Mahādeva, possessing a full form, and terrifying.
Seeing him, he whose banner bears Garuḍa fell to the ground like a staff; so too did the gods, the sages, and the celestial women from all sides.
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of Kamalā, having bowed to him and placed his joined palms upon his head, departed while praising him with various hymns of praise.
Then, O great sage, Hari, joyful and with a serene soul, spoke with delight to Padmā, the lotus-dweller, who had emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Viṣṇu said: "O beloved, O lotus-eyed one, you are blessed, O fortunate and sinless one! I too am blessed, O goddess of beautiful hips, that we both behold the Lord of the Universe."
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, the Lord and Sovereign of the worlds; he is without beginning, the refuge, the peaceful one, the primordial, and is reckoned as the twenty-sixth.
He is the omniscient one, the lord of all yogis, the sole leader of all beings; he is the inner self within all beings and the eternal giver of everything to all.
Those who are sleepless, free from sighing, tranquil, and devoted to meditation—let them behold with their intellect that which is seen within the heart-lotus.
He whom the knowers of the essence of the Vedas and the yogis of restrained mind recognize—he, the omnipresent one, having assumed form though being formless, approaches here.
Oh, how wonderful is the activity of the Supreme Lord! Even he whose name is constantly being uttered is a possessor of a body, though he is himself bodiless.
Upon seeing him, men on earth shall not undergo rebirth; here comes the Blessed Lord Tryambaka, adorned with the moon.
O Lakṣmī, today my two eyes, as broad as lotus petals and so blessed, have truly seen Mahādeva, the Great Lord, through them.
Fie, fie upon that station of the gods, having seen which one does not behold Śaṅkara—that place where liberation is attained, which brings an end to all suffering!
There is nothing inauspicious whatsoever in the world of the gods; yet, even having beheld the Lord of the Gods, we do not attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, his hair standing on end with joy, prostrated before Mahādeva, the bull-bannered one, and said this:
Viṣṇu said: "O All-pervading Lord, O Imperishable One who removes all sins, what is this being done by you, the omniscient God of gods and Sustainer of the worlds?"
O Lord of Gods, O three-eyed one of great intelligence, why do you play? O Virūpākṣa, destroyer of Smara, what is the cause of this activity of yours?
"For what purpose, O Blessed One, O Śambhu, do you wander for alms, O Lord of Power? This is my doubt, O Lord of the World, you who bestow sovereignty over the three realms."
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by Viṣṇu, the Lord Śambhu, the formidable Hara, being filled with wonder, replied to Viṣṇu while smiling.
Bhairava said: "The head of Brahmā was indeed severed by the tip of my fingernail; to destroy that sin, I am performing this auspicious vow."
Nandīśvara said: Thus addressed by Maheśa Bhairava, the Lord of Ramā, having reflected for a moment with his head bowed, again made this request.
Viṣṇu said: "Play as you wish, O dispeller of all obstacles; O Mahādeva, you ought not to conceal me with your māyā."
O Lord, in truth, in every kalpa, millions of lotus-seated ones have previously emerged from the calyx of your navel-lotus through the power of yoga.
O Lord, abandon this illusion which is difficult for those of unrefined self to cross; O Mahādeva, even Brahmā and the others have been deluded by your illusion.
O Lord of Śivā, I follow your activities exactly as they are; O Śambhu, Lord of all, refuge of the virtuous, this is solely through your grace.
O Hara, when the time for dissolution has arrived, you shall withdraw all the worlds, including the gods and all the sages, along with those belonging to the various castes and stages of life.
O Mahādeva, when sins such as the killing of a Brahmin have been committed, you have no dependence on others, O Śambhu; therefore, you sport according to your own will.
O Śambhu, O sinless one, just as a garland of bones shines upon the neck of Brahmā, so too does the slaughter of a Brahmin now cling to you.
Even after committing a very great sin, that man who remembers you, O Lord, the support of the worlds, his sin is dissolved.
Just as darkness cannot remain in the presence of the sun, even so, the sin of one who is devoted to you goes to destruction.
Whatever meritorious soul contemplates your two lotus feet, even the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin shall go to destruction for them.
O Lord of the World, that man whose speech is devoted to your name is not afflicted by evil, even if it be as massive as a mountain peak.
O Supreme Self, O Supreme Abode, You who assume a form by Your own will—O Lord, this curiosity of Yours is directed toward those who are wretched and dependent.
Today I am blessed, O Lord of Gods, for I behold that imperishable Supreme Lord, the embodiment of the universe, whom even yogis perceive.
Today is my supreme gain; today is my greatest auspiciousness. Having seen him, one who is satiated by the nectar of immortality regards even heaven and liberation as mere straw.
While Govinda was speaking thus, a pure lotus was offered by her, and alms-food named Manorathavatī was placed into his bowl.
Even the Lord went forth with supreme joy to wander for alms; elsewhere as well, Mahādeva and Bhairava assumed physical forms.
Seeing her following him, Janārdana called out to Brahman-slaughter and entreated her: "Release the wielder of the trident."
Brahmahatyā said: "Under this very pretext, I shall serve that bull-bannered Lord and purify myself, so as never again to behold rebirth."
Nandīśvara said: Even though she was addressed by Murāri, she did not leave his side; then Śambhu, with a smiling face, spoke these words to Hari as Bhairava.
Bhairava said: O bestower of great honor, I am satiated by drinking the nectar of your words. For this is indeed the nature of the virtuous, O Lord of Men, as you have stated.
"Choose a boon, O Govinda; I am the giver of boons to you, O sinless one. You, O Hari, are the foremost among my devotees and are free from all change."
Even monks do not rejoice so much in highly refined alms as they do in drinking the nectar of the mind, for indeed, they suffer from the fever of wandering for alms.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Bhairava, the Supreme Soul, Śambhu became exceedingly pleased and addressed Maheśvara.
Viṣṇu said: This alone is the praiseworthy boon, that I behold you, O God of gods, who transcend the path of mind and speech, as the sovereign of all beings.
This abundant vision of nectar is a great festival for me; O Hara, grant us the sight of you, which is like the effortless attainment of a treasure for the virtuous.
"O Lord, may there never be separation for me from Your pair of feet; this alone is my boon, O Śambhu—I choose no other boon whatsoever."
The illustrious Bhairavī said: "O Father, O great-minded one, let it be as you have spoken; you shall become the bestower of boons even upon all the gods."
Nandīśvara said: Having thus favored the enemy of the Daityas, who was wandering through the worlds of Mount Kailāsa and Indra’s realm, he went to the city named Vārāṇasī, the city of liberation.
Then, as soon as Bhairava of terrifying form had entered the field, Brahmahatyā cried out "Alas! Alas! and entered the netherworld.
The skull [of the Brahmin] immediately fell from the lotus-hand of Bhairava onto the earth; that became the sacred site known as Kāpālamocana.
Seeing the skull of Brahmā falling from his hand while everyone was looking on, Rudra danced with supreme joy.
The skull of Vidhi did not leave his hand, which was extremely difficult to bear; yet, as he wandered elsewhere, it fell from him in an instant at Kāśī.
The sin of killing Brahmā Śūlin, which never departs elsewhere, is destroyed in an instant at Kāśī; therefore, Kāśikā must indeed be resorted to.
Whoever remembers Kapālamocana, the supreme sacred site in Kāśī, their sins—whether committed here or elsewhere—are swiftly destroyed.

Having arrived at this most excellent of holy places and performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite, and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Placing the holy site of Kapālamocana before him, Bhairava remained right there, devouring the succession of sins of his devotees.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Supreme Lord, the beloved of the virtuous, manifested in the form of Bhairava, full of divine play.
By fasting on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and keeping a vigil in the presence of Kālabhairava, one is liberated from great sins.
Furthermore, any person who performs that vow with devotion shall be liberated from great sins through the night vigil and attain a favorable rebirth.
Whatever sin has been committed by living beings throughout many millions of births—all that goes to dissolution at the sight of Kālabhairava.
He who commits sins against the devotees of Kālabhairava shall become a fool and miserable, and will again attain a state of wretchedness.
Those who are devotees of Viśveśvara but not devotees of Kālabhairava shall experience great suffering, especially in Kāśī.
If a man, having dwelt in Vārāṇasī, does not resort to Bhairava, his sins increase like the moon during the bright fortnight.
If one does not worship Kālarāja in Kāśī on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight falling on a Tuesday, their merit will wane like the moon in the dark fortnight.
Having heard this meritorious narrative known as "The Origin of Bhairava," which removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin, one is liberated from all sins.
Even while remaining in a prison or having encountered the utmost calamity, one shall be released from distress upon hearing of the manifestation of Bhairava.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Playful Descent of Bhairava," in the Rudra-saṃhitā of the third section of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O Lord, he who is known by the name Vīrabhadra and who destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice should be understood as an incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The entire life story of Satī has been told; you have heard it many times before, so it has not been recounted here in great detail.
Henceforth, O best of sages, out of affection for you I shall speak of that; listen to the incarnation of the Lord Śaṅkara known as Śārdūla.
For the benefit of the gods, Sadāśiva assumed a divine and wonderful form as a Śarabha, possessing a radiance equal to blazing flames.
O best of sages, the incarnations of Śiva are infinite; they bring benefit to true devotees, and it is impossible to calculate their number.
Indeed, by one who has grown old over many eons, there might perhaps be a counting of the sky, of the stars, of the particles of dust upon the earth, and of the showers of rain.
The number of Śiva’s incarnations cannot be calculated even by the most wise over many lifetimes; know my words to be the truth.
Nevertheless, according to my understanding, I shall relate the divine account as I have heard it—the heroic exploit that indicates supreme sovereignty.
O Sage, when Jaya and Vijaya were cursed by you, they then became the two sons of Diti born from Kaśyapa.
The first was Hiraṇyakaśipu, and his younger brother was the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa; both of them were sons of Diti, born as attendants to the celestial sages.
Indeed, in former times, when requested by the Creator for the sake of uplifting the earth, that Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a boar, slew Hiraṇyākṣa.
O Sage, having heard that his heroic brother, who was like his own life, had been slain, Hiraṇyakaśipu became exceedingly enraged at Hari.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years, he obtained a boon from Brahmā; being pleased, [Brahmā granted] that no one within your creation should ever be able to kill him.
Having gone to the city called Śoṇita and summoned the gods from all sides, he brought the three worlds under his own control and ruled a kingdom free of all thorns.
O Sage, the sinful Hiraṇyakaśipu, who caused suffering to the twice-born and was the destroyer of all dharma, performed a sacrifice to the celestial sages.
When the king of the Daityas bore hatred toward his own son Prahlāda—a devotee of Hari—and especially toward Hari himself, enmity arose.
O sage, at that time during the twilight, Viṣṇu, having become filled with wrath, suddenly manifested from a pillar of the assembly hall in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
In every respect, O tiger among sages, the formidable body of Nṛhari blazed forth, most terrifying and striking fear into the foremost of the Daityas.
Then, at that very moment, the Daityas were slain by Nṛsiṃha; thereafter, Hiraṇyakaśipu waged a most terrible battle.
O best of sages, a great battle took place between them for a moment—a battle that was formidable, terrifying to all, and hair-raising.
In the evening, Nṛsiṃha, the Lord of Ramā and Sovereign of the Gods, dragged that preeminent Daitya across the threshold while the gods looked on from the sky.
Then, taking him onto his lap, he quickly tore open his belly with his claws and killed him while the inhabitants of the triple heaven looked on.
