When Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nṛsiṃha, who is indeed Viṣṇu, the world attained peace; however, the gods did not particularly feel secure at that time.
The celestial drums resounded, Prahlāda was filled with wonder, and Lakṣmī too was struck with amazement upon beholding the extraordinary form of Hari.
Although the lord of the Daityas was slain, the gods did not yet attain peace in their city; that flame of the Man-Lion had not yet been extinguished.
And by her, the entire world once again became agitated; even the gods fell into distress, wondering, "What will happen next?"
Speaking thus, they stood at a great distance out of fear, their faces like lotuses, agitated by the flames born of Nṛsiṃha’s wrath.
Having all assembled together, they sent Prahlāda to the presence of Hari for the sake of his pacification; thus entreated, Prahlāda then departed.
The Lord Nṛsiṃha, the ocean of compassion, embraced him with his chest; his heart became cool, yet the flame of Rudra did not cease.
Nevertheless, when the blazing flame of Narahari did not subside, the gods, having obtained what they desired, went for refuge to Śaṅkara.
Having gone there, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the sages, praised Śaṅkara for the sake of the happiness of the worlds.
The gods said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge! Protect us—all the gods and the worlds—who have sought your protection.
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, O Sadāśiva! When suffering arose in the past, we were your protectors then.
O Śambhu, when the ocean was churned by the gods and the jewels were distributed accordingly, you then took up the poison.
"O Lord, we were then protected by the one known as Nīlakaṇṭha; had you not drunk the poison, we would all have been reduced to ashes."
And it is well known, O Lord, that whenever suffering arises for anyone, then by the mere mention of your name, all suffering dissolves.
O Sadāśiva, it is now certain that you alone, O Lord, are capable of quelling this flame of the Man-Lion which afflicts us.
Nandīśvara said: Thus praised by the gods at that time, Śaṅkara, the supreme lord who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased in spirit, granted them fearlessness and replied.
Śaṅkara said: "O all you gods, Brahmā and the rest, go to your own abodes free from fear; I shall pacify whatever suffering there is, for this is indeed my vow in every respect."
For one who has gone for refuge to me, suffering has come to an end; he who has taken refuge in me is dearer to me than even his own life—of this there is no doubt.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard this, the gods then attained supreme bliss; remembering Śaṅkara with joy, they departed just as they had come.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deeds of Nṛsiṃha," in the Śārdūla Incarnation within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Thus entreated by the gods, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is compassion, set his mind upon destroying that being of great splendor known as Nṛsiṃha.
Thereafter, Rudra remembered the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra and spoke to his own Bhairava form, the cause of universal dissolution.
Then, laughing, the leader of the hosts arrived instantly, accompanied by the best of the hosts who were leaping here and there with loud bursts of laughter.
Surrounded by tens of millions of extremely fierce forms of Nṛsiṃha, he was encircled on all sides by heroic beings who were intoxicated and dancing with joy.
Surrounded by great heroes such as Brahmā and others who were playing with him as if with balls, and by others never seen before, he was honored by the brave.
With the radiance of the flames at the end of an eon, his three eyes gleaming; though weaponless, he wears a mass of matted locks adorned by the blazing orb of the crescent moon.
He possesses two sharp sprouts of fangs shaped like the crescent of the young moon, and is endowed with creeper-like eyebrows resembling fragments of Indra’s bow.
The quarters of the sky were deafened by his great and fierce *huṃ* sounds; dark as a blue cloud or collyrium, he was terrifying, with a formidable beard.
Brandishing his trident repeatedly with both the broken and unbroken sections of the musical instrument, the blessed Vīrabhadra also manifested the power of his supreme energy.
He himself made this request: "What is the cause for remembering [this] here? Command me, O Lord of the World; let grace be bestowed upon me."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words spoken by Vīrabhadra with respect, Maheśāna, the wielder of the rod for the wicked, looked upon him with affection and spoke these words.
Śaṅkara said: A terrifying danger has arisen at an improper time, even for the gods; extinguish this unassailable fire of Nṛsiṃha that is blazing forth.
Conciliate and awaken him first; why would he not be pacified by that? Then, manifest to him the state of Bhairava, which is supreme even beyond me.
"O Vīrabhadra, by my command, having withdrawn the subtle with the subtle and the gross with the gross energy, bring back his face and his hide."
Nandīśvara said: Thus commanded, the leader of the Gaṇas assumed a tranquil form and went with great speed to the place where Narasiṃha was staying.
Then Vīrabhadra, the destroyer, awakened Hari; the Lord spoke these words to him, as a father would speak to his own biological son.

Vīrabhadra said: O Blessed One, O Mādhava, you have descended for the sake of the world’s happiness; you have been appointed by the Supreme Lord Parameṣṭhin for the purpose of maintaining the universe.
In the past, while wandering in the single ocean, the Blessed One, in the form of a fish, cut through the wheel of living beings by binding it together with his very tail.
In the form of the boar, you bore up the earth; by this form of Hari, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain.
Bali was bound by Vāmana; now he has been bound again by you through your strides. You alone are the source, the imperishable Lord, of all beings.
Whenever any suffering whatsoever arises for the world, at each such time you descend and shall make it free from affliction.
O Hari, devoted to Śiva, there is no one superior to you, nor even equal to you; by you the Vedas and the Dharmas have been established upon the auspicious path.
For this purpose indeed was this incarnation undertaken: the Dānava has been slain, Hiraṇyakaśipu likewise, and Prahlāda has been well protected.
O Blessed One, your form as Narasimha is exceedingly terrible; O Soul of the Universe, withdraw it yourself right here in my presence.
Nandīśvara said: Thus addressed by Vīrabhadra with peaceful words, the Greatly Intoxicated Nṛsiṃha then gave way to a most terrible rage even greater than before.
And then, O sage, terrifying Vīrabhadra—the great hero—with his fangs, he spoke these most terrible and harsh words.
Nṛsiṃha said: "Go back to where you came from; do not speak what is not for my benefit. Now I shall destroy this entire world, both moving and unmoving."
For the destroyer, there is no destruction either by itself or by another; my teaching is everywhere established, and no teacher exists apart from it.
By my grace, indeed, everything proceeds free from fear; for I am the one who sets all powers in motion and withdraws them.
Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or power, know that, O Lord of the Gaṇas, to be a manifestation of my splendor.
They know me alone as the supreme one who knows the ultimate truth of the deities; the gods, such as Brahmā and Śakra, are my portions endowed with power.
In ancient times, Brahmā, the creator of the world, was born from the navel-lotus; he is supreme over all, independent, the agent of creation and destruction, and the Lord of all.
But this splendor of mine is supreme; what more do you wish to hear? Therefore, having come to me for refuge, go forth with your fever dispelled.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, understand this supreme state: that this entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is my own being.
"I am Time, the cause of the world's destruction; I have set out to withdraw the worlds. Know me, O Vīrabhadra, to be the death of Death itself; these gods live by my grace."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words full of pride from Hari, he of immeasurable prowess laughed and then spoke with contempt, his lips quivering.
Vīrabhadra said: Do you not know the Lord of the Universe, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is the destroyer? This false speech and this dispute will result only in your own destruction.
Which of your mutual incarnations remain at present? By which one has it been brought about that only a remnant of the story will remain?
Tell me that fault by which you have come to such a state; through it, you shall go to the southern region, which is expert in destruction.
You are Prakṛti, you are Puruṣa, you are Rudra; in you is all potency concentrated. From the lotus of your navel was born the five-faced Grandfather (Brahmā).
Established in fierce austerity, he meditated upon the blue-and-red Śaṅkara for the sake of creating the three worlds, [visualizing him] upon his forehead.
From his high forehead Śambhu was born for the sake of creation; therefore, I am the ornament of that God of gods who possesses the form of Bhairava.
"O Hari, I have been appointed by Rudra, the god of gods and lord of all, along with Vinaya and Bala, for your destruction."
Having merely torn apart a single demon, you, possessed by a fraction of that power, roar without weariness out of the arrogance of your ego.
For assistance rendered to the virtuous is indeed considered to lead to happiness, whereas assistance rendered to the wicked leads only to harm.
O Nṛsiṃha, if you consider Maheśāna to be a reborn being, then you are ignorant, excessively arrogant, and in every respect subject to transformation.
O Man-Lion, you are neither the creator nor the destroyer, nor even the sustainer; dependent and deluded in nature, you are indeed never independent anywhere.
O Hari, impelled by the power of the wielder of the Pināka bow like a potter’s wheel, you are the performer of various incarnations, yet you are always dependent upon him.
Even today, the skull of you who were in the form of a tortoise remains placed within the necklace of Hara; for one who has been consumed by fire is not bound.

Is it through forgetfulness that [the Lord], who caused the destruction of the demon Tāraka, now cries out as he holds the Boar-form Gaṇeśa—who was once tormented by the uprooting of his tusks—in his hand?

"You are burnt; behold, you have been pierced on the tip of the trident by me in the guise of Viṣvaksena. At the sacrifice of Dakṣa, your head was severed by me, who am the embodiment of radiant energy."
Even now, O Hari, the fifth head of your son Brahmā has not yet been rejoined after it was severed; have you forgotten that?
"You were defeated by Dadhīca in battle along with the hosts of Maruts; how have you forgotten that while scratching your head?"
O Cakrapāṇi, from where did you obtain this wheel that is dear to you as you stride forth, and by whom was it made? You have even forgotten that.
Since all the worlds were taken up by me while you lay under the power of sleep in the ocean, how can you be considered a person of sattva?
From you down to a blade of grass, everything is the manifestation of Rudra’s power; you yourself are the possessor of that power, yet you have been utterly deluded by fire.
For no man is indeed capable of beholding the majesty of that splendor; only those who perceive it as non-material behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having been born from Dyāvāpṛthivī, Indra-Agni, Yama, and Varuṇa, as well as from the moon within the belly of darkness, the Supreme Lord [manifested].
"You are Kāla, you are Mahākāla, the Great Lord who is the end-maker of Time itself; therefore, by means of your fierce power (ugrakalā), you shall become the death of Death."
Today you are the steadfast, the imperishable, the hero, the hero who protects all, the Lord; you are the dispeller of fever, the formidable one, the deer, the bird, and the golden one.
The four-faced Brahmā is not the teacher of the truth for the rest of the world, nor are others; Śambhu alone is the teacher of all—of this there is no doubt.
Having thus observed all this with your own mind as the very nature of dissolution, do not, O unwise Nṛhari, allow yourself to perish.
If you do not [submit] now, death will fall upon you like a thunderbolt of adamant upon a tree stump—upon you who possess the form of the Great Terrifier (Mahābhairava).
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra, who was fearless from any quarter, ceased speaking; for he had perceived the intention of Nṛsiṃha, who was the very embodiment of Śiva’s wrath.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Śarabha Incarnation," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O Nandīśvara, O one of great wisdom, that has now been understood. Having shown compassion toward me, please speak of it further out of affection.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by Vīrabhadra, Nṛsiṃha, overwhelmed with rage, roared and proceeded with great speed to seize him.
In the meantime, there arose a most terrible phenomenon, a cause for manifest fear, pervading the sky, invincible, and born from the splendor of Śiva.
Then, in an instant, that form of Vīrabhadra became visible; it was indeed golden and serene, neither produced by the sun nor born of fire.
Then all splendors were absorbed into that Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, who is like lightning and the moon, incomparable.
That great splendor was no longer manifest within the ether; it became marked with the common characteristics of Rudra and possessed a distorted form.
Then, while all the gods were beholding him with auspicious sounds such as shouts of "Victory!", the Supreme Lord became clearly manifest in the form of withdrawal.
The twice-born one had a thousand arms, matted hair, and the crescent moon as his crest; he was formidable with his well-developed body and his two wings and beak.
Exceedingly fierce with great fangs, his weapons being claws like thunderbolts; black-necked with mighty arms, he was four-legged and resembled fire.
His roar was as terrifying and deep as the thundering clouds at the end of an eon; his three eyes were turned toward the great, enraged fire of the Kṛtyā.
With prominent fangs and a protruding lower lip, Hara, joined with the utterance of "huṃ," manifested in such a form as Ugra.
At the mere sight of the noble one, his strength and prowess were destroyed; bearing the luster of the thousand-rayed sun, he now appeared like the flickering glow of a firefly below.
Then, wheeling about with his two wings and tearing at the navel and feet, he bound the feet with his tail and the circle of arms with his two forelimbs.
Tearing at his chest with his two arms, Hara seized Hari; then he went to the sky along with the gods and the great seers.
Out of fear, he suddenly seized Viṣṇu again and again, like a hawk seizing a serpent, lifting him up repeatedly and throwing him down repeatedly.
Flying up again and again, the Lord Hara, the infinite Ishvara, entered that bull of Hari, who was bewildered by the blows of his wings.
As he proceeded, all the gods praised him with words of salutation; Brahmā and the other lords of sages bowed down with reverence and affection.
Being led away against his will, with a dejected face and palms joined in reverence, Hari praised the Supreme Lord with graceful words.
Having praised him with those very one hundred and eight names, and having entreated that compassionate one, Nṛsiṃha once again made his petition to Śarabheśvara.
Whenever this thought of mine, corrupted by pride, should arise, O Supreme Lord, it must be removed by you alone.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus petitioned Śaṅkara with affection, Narakesarin bowed down and became powerless, defeated by the end of his life at the hands of Viṣṇu.
Then, in an instant, Vīrabhadra made that face extend to the end of his remaining limbs, forming the embodiment of his entire being, and endowed that body with power.
Nandīśvara said: Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, praised the god Śaṅkara, the sole benefactor of all the worlds, who had assumed the form of a Śarabha.
The gods said: "O Maheśvara, all the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Candra, as well as the great sages and the sons of Diti and others—all have been born from you."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra, as well as the sun and other deities and asuras—you indeed create them, you protect them, and you consume them; you alone are the Lord of all.
Because you take away saṃsāra, you are called Hara by the wise; because Hari has been subdued by you, you are called Hara by the wise.
Since you sustain the entire universe by dividing your body into eight parts, therefore protect us, O Blessed One, with the desired gifts of the gods.
You are the Great Being, Śambhu, the Lord of all, the leader of the gods; you are the selfless one, the changeless self, the Supreme Brahman, and the refuge of the virtuous.

The kinsman of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, of wondrous power, the seer of the Supreme Self; the wise one, the Virāṭ, the all-pervading, the Truth, whose characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of the gods, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, spoke to those deities and the ancient celestial sages.
Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes one and the same, so too Viṣṇu is merged into Śiva and not otherwise.
Viṣṇu alone, in the form of Nṛsiṃha, possessed of pride and great strength, the Man-Lion, set about the task of destroying the world.
He should be prayed to and saluted by my devotees who seek spiritual perfection; he is the foremost among my devotees and the bestower of boons upon my devotees.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, the Lord, the mighty king of birds, vanished right there while all the gods were looking on.
The blessed Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas and possessed of great strength, having stripped off the skin of the Man-lion and taken it with him, went to the mountain.
From that time forth, Śaṅkara has worn the skin of a man-lion; its face was designated as the central figure in his garland of severed heads.
Then the gods, free from fear and their eyes wide with wonder, departed as they had come, recounting this story.
Whoever reads or hears this supreme narrative, which is meritorious and imbued with the essence of the Vedas, shall attain all desires.
It brings fortune, fame, long life, health, and increases nourishment; it pacifies all obstacles and destroys all diseases.
It pacifies suffering, grants the fulfillment of desires, and is an abode of auspiciousness; it wards off untimely death, bestows intelligence, and destroys enemies.
This supreme form of the wielder of the Pināka bow, having the appearance of a Śarabha, must indeed be revealed to the devotees who act as servants of Śaṅkara.
This very [text] should be recited and heard by those whose nature is auspicious; it bestows divine ninefold devotion and grants clarity to the inner organ and the intellect.
On all festivals of Śiva, on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, and at the time of consecration, one should recite this, for it is the cause of the presence of Śiva.
And in times of fear caused by thieves, tigers, lions, oneself, or kings; and in other calamities such as portents, earthquakes, bandits, and rains of dust.
During the fall of meteors, during great winds, and during droughts or excessive rains, the wise man who is self-restrained, devoted to Śiva, and firm in his vows should recite this.
Whoever, free from desire, should read or even hear this vow of Īśvara, shall reach the world of Rudra and become an attendant of Rudra.
Having reached the world of Rudra, he rejoices together with Rudra; thereafter, O Sage, through the grace of Śiva, he attains union (sāyujya) with him.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śarabha Incarnation," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen with affection, O son of Brahmā, to the life-story of the moon-crested Lord; how Śiva descended out of love into the house of Viśvānara.
O Sage, he became a householder by name known as Agnilokapati; he was the supreme lord, the soul of all, possessing the form of fire and full of splendor.
In ancient times, on the delightful bank of the Narmadā, in the city of Narmapura, there lived a meritorious sage named Viśvānara, who was a devotee of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).

Established in the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), always devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman, he belonged to the Śāṇḍilya lineage; he was pure, a treasury of Brahmanic luster, and self-controlled.
He had mastered the meaning of all the scriptures, was ever devoted to righteous conduct, was highly proficient in Śaiva practice, and was an excellent knower of worldly customs.
Having reflected in his mind upon all the auspicious qualities of a housewife, Viśvānara married Kālakanyā, who was worthy of him, according to the prescribed rites.
Devoted to the service of the sacred fire and intent upon the five great sacrifices, he was constantly engaged in the six duties and cherished the gods, the ancestors, and guests.
When a great deal of time had passed in this manner, his wife named Śuciṣmatī, who was devoted to her vows, spoke to her husband, that foremost of the twice-born.
"O Lord, by your grace, I have indeed enjoyed all those pleasures appropriate for women that bring joy upon meeting with you."
O Lord, this which I have thus requested has long resided within my heart; you ought to grant it, for it is appropriate for householders.

Viśvānara said: "O lady of beautiful hips, what indeed is there that cannot be given by me, since you desire my pleasure and welfare? Therefore, O highly fortunate one, ask for it; I shall grant it without delay."
By the grace of Maheśī, nothing is difficult for me to attain, both in this world and the next, O auspicious one, she who brings about every blessing.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of her husband, she, who held her husband as a deity, spoke with a joyful face, joining her palms in humility.
Śuciṣmatī said: "O Lord, if I am worthy of a boon, and if a boon is to be granted to me, grant me a son equal to Maheśa; I choose no other boon."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of hers, that Brahmin of pure vows entered into meditative absorption for a moment and reflected thus within his heart.
Aha! What was sought by that slender maiden from me is indeed exceedingly difficult to obtain; let it remain far beyond the path of my desires, for He alone is the creator of all.
Having stood at her very mouth in the form of speech, Śambhu uttered this; who else would dare to alter it? Let it be so.
Nandīśvara said: Having reflected thus, that noble-minded sage Viśvānara, remaining steadfast in his vow of devotion to a single wife, then spoke to his consort.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus consoled his wife, the sage departed for penance to the place where Viśveśvara, the Lord of Kāśī himself, resides.
Having quickly reached Vārāṇasī and beheld that Maṇikarṇikā, he abandoned even the threefold suffering accumulated over hundreds of births.
Having seen all the lingas, headed by Viśveśa, and having bathed in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), tanks, wells, and lakes;
Having bowed to all the Vināyakas and having prostrated before Gaurī and Śarvā, and having fully worshipped Kālarāja Bhairava, the devourer of sins.
Having diligently praised the leaders of the Daṇḍanāyaka hosts and the Gaṇas, and having propitiated Keśava, foremost among whom is Ādikeśava;
Having bowed down again and again to Lokārka, Mukha, and Sūryāṃśu, he tirelessly performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having gratified the sages and brahmins with a thousand meals and other offerings, he worshipped the lingas with devotion through the services of the great ritual worship.
He reflected repeatedly: "What is the emblem that grants swift success, wherein penance may attain stability through the desire for a son?"
Having reflected for a moment, that wise sage Viśvānara quickly praised the Vīreśa Liṅga, which bestows sons.
From that place, thousands of incalculable Siddhas attained perfection; therefore, Vīreśvara is known as the supreme Siddhaliṅga.
Having worshipped the great liṅga Vīreśvara with devotion for one year, [one obtains] all life-span and desires, as well as many sons and other blessings.
I too, having propitiated Vīreśa here three times a day, shall quickly obtain a son as desired by my wife.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus resolved, the wise and accomplished brahmin Viśvānara, observing his vows, bathed in the waters of the Moon-well and undertook a religious observance.
For one month he took food only once a day; for one month he ate only at night; for one month he subsisted on unsolicited food; and then, for another month, he abstained from food altogether.
For one month he observed a vow of milk; for one month he subsisted on vegetables and fruits; for one month his food was a handful of sesame seeds; and for one month he lived on water alone.

For one month he subsists on the five products of the cow, for another month he observes the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, for one month he eats only water from the tips of Kuśa grass, and for one month he subsists on air alone.
In this manner, he performed that wonderful penance for a period of a year, worshipping with devotion the supreme Vīreśa Liṅga three times a day.
Then, in the thirteenth month, having bathed in the waters of the triple-pathed river at the very break of dawn, that twice-born man arrived before Vīreśa.
Then the ascetic gazed into the midst [of the fire] and beheld a child, a young boy of eight years of age, adorned with sacred ash and bearing the form of a *liṅga*.
With eyes reaching to his ears and deeply red lips, he has beautiful tawny matted locks upon his head and a face laughing with a smile while naked.
Wearing the attire appropriate for childhood, bearing the funeral pyre, he was reciting Vedic hymns while laughing with his own playful charm.
Beholding him and attaining great joy, the sage, his hair standing on end with thrill, uttered from the depths of his heart the words "Namo'stu" again and again.
The virtuous Viśvānara praised Śambhu, who is supreme bliss and appears in the form of a child, with eight verses that grant all desires.

Viśvānara said: Brahman alone is one, without a second; it is the entirety, the truth, the absolute truth. There is no diversity whatsoever here. Rudra is one; he does not abide as a second. Therefore, I take refuge in You alone, the Great Lord.

O Śambhu, you alone are the creator and the destroyer of all; though formless, you possess a single form within manifold forms. Just as the innermost reality (pratyagdharma), though one, appears as many, therefore I seek refuge in no other than You, the Lord.

I take refuge in that Great Lord, by whose knowledge this manifold world—which appears as real in the rope, the serpent, the mother-of-pearl, the mirage, the city of the Gandharvas, the water in the desert, and the rays of light—is seen to be non-existent.

Coldness in water, burning power in fire, heat in the sun, clarity in the moon, fragrance in a flower, and even ghee within milk—that which exists [in all these] is You, O Śambhu; therefore, I take refuge in You.

You perceive sound though you are without ears; you smell though you are without a nose; you come from afar with three feet; you see though you have three eyes; and you know tastes though you are without a tongue—who can truly know you? Therefore, I take refuge in you.

Neither the Veda knows You directly, O Lord, nor does Viṣṇu, nor the Creator of all, nor the lords of yogis headed by Indra, nor the gods; yet the Veda is Your devotee—therefore, I take refuge in You.
You have no lineage, nor even birth; there is no destruction, nor form, nor conduct, nor location. Even though you are such as this, you fulfill all desires for the three worlds; I worship you.

From you everything comes; indeed, you are everything, O enemy of Smara! You are the Lord of Gaurī, and you are the naked one, exceedingly peaceful. You are the old man, you are the youth, and you are the child; whatever reality exists, there is nothing other than you—to you I bow.

Nandīśvara said: Having thus offered praise, the brahmin fell upon the ground with his palms joined together; at that moment, the boy—who had surpassed both enemies and elders in strength—spoke to the god on earth (the brahmin) with great joy.
The boy said: "O Viśvānara, best of sages, O Earth-god, I have indeed been satisfied by you today; with a well-pleased soul, choose an excellent boon."
Then, rising up with a joyful heart, the virtuous and most excellent of sages, Sunirviśvānara, replied to Śaṅkara who was in the form of a child.
Viśvānara said: O Maheśvara, what is unknown to you, the omniscient Lord? You, the Blessed One, are the inner self of all; you, O Śarva, are the bestower of everything.
"O Great Lord, knowing that I am directed toward begging—a practice that causes wretchedness—what do you say to me? Do as you wish."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Viśvānara, the pure deity, possessing pure vows, then smiled with a pure smile and spoke to the child.
O pure one, that desire which you have formed in your heart for Śuciṣmatī will undoubtedly be fulfilled in a very short time.
O high-minded one, you shall become the son of Śuciṣmatī, renowned by the name Gṛhapati, pure and beloved by all the immortals.
This meritorious hymn of eight verses on longing has been recited by you; by reciting it three times a day for a year in the presence of Śiva, it shall grant all desires.
The recitation of this hymn bestows sons, grandsons, and wealth; it brings about all peace and destroys all calamities.
There is no doubt that this brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation; for it is equal to all hymns of praise and always grants all desires.
Rising early in the morning, having bathed well, and having worshipped the Liṅga of Śambhu, one who is childless shall obtain a son by reciting this hymn for a year.
This "Eightfold Prayer of Desire" must not be given to just anyone; it should be guarded with great effort, for it brings about the birth of even the most barren women.
Whether by a woman or even by a man, if this hymn is recited for one year according to the prescribed rule in the presence of a linga, it bestows sons; of this there is no doubt.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Śambhu, the refuge of the virtuous, vanished while in the form of a child; and that Brahmin Viśvānara, with a joyful heart, went to his own home.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation as Gṛhapati," in the third section, the Rudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Having returned home filled with great joy, that brahmin related the entire account to his beloved wife.
Having heard that, the Brahmin’s wife Śuciṣmatī attained great joy; filled with intense love, she praised her own destiny.
Then, in due course of time, that woman became pregnant after he had duly performed the rite known as *garbhādhāna*.

Thereafter, prior to the descent [of the fetus], the wise man properly performed the *puṃsavana* rite for the sake of increasing masculinity, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.

Then, in the eighth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) was performed by that compassionate one for the sake of the full development of the fetus and for the successful attainment of an easy delivery.

Now, therefore, regarding auspicious stars, [the Buddha], whose face is like that of the Lord of Stars, [spoke] when Jupiter was in a quadrant, the ascendant was auspicious, and the benefic planets were in their pairs.
To her, Śuciṣmatī, was born a son named Ariṣṭanemi, who extinguished all misfortunes and brought about the destruction of every calamity.

Śarva is the bestower of all happiness upon the inhabitants of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar; and the winds, borne by their vehicles, serve as the facial perfumes for the maidens that are the quarters of the sky.
Those rain-clouds showered down masses of flowers with pleasing fragrances; celestial drums resounded, and all directions became serene.
The minds of all beings became clear and free from agitation; the darkness was utterly dispelled, and even passion (rajas) became stainless.
Beings were endowed with goodness, and indeed a rain of nectar fell; auspicious speech arose in every way, becoming dear to all living creatures.
The Apsarases, headed by Rambhā, with auspicious objects in their hands, as well as thousands of Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, and mortal women [were there].
Gandharvas, uragas, and yakṣas, possessing beautiful forms and auspicious voices, arrived there in great numbers, singing auspicious songs.
Mārīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Agastya, Vibhāṇḍa, and the son of Māṇḍavī.
Lomaśa, Romacaraṇa, Bharadvāja, and Gautama; Bhṛgu, Gālava, Garga, Jātūkarṇya, and Parāśara.
Āpastamba, Yājñavalkya, Dakṣa, Vālmīki, Mudgala, Śātātapa, Likhita, Śilāda, Śaṅkha, and Uñchabhuk.
Jamadagni, Saṃvarta, Mataṅga, Bharata, Aṃśumān, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Kutsa, Śaunaka, Śruta, and Śuka.
Then Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Durvāsas, Śuci, Nārada, Tumburu, Uttaṅka, Vāmadeva, Pavana, Asita, and Devala.
Sālaṅkāyana, Hārīta, Viśvāmitra, and Bhārgava; Mṛkaṇḍu with his son, as well as Parvata and Dāruka.
Dhaumya, Upamanyu, Vatsa, and other sages, along with the daughters of sages, gathered at the auspicious hermitage of Viśvānara for the purpose of performing a rite of pacification.
Brahmā accompanied by Bṛhaspati, the god whose vehicle is Garuḍa, and the bull-bannered Śiva together with Gaurī and joined by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin.
The gods, headed by Mahendra, and the nāgas dwelling in the netherworld, as well as the great oceans together with the rivers, brought many jewels.
Assuming mobile forms, stationary beings went forth by the thousands; during that great festival, there was an untimely moonlight.
Having personally performed his birth-rite with devotion according to the prescribed rules, and having reflected upon the Veda, he gave him the name Gṛhapati because of his appearance.
Thus, on the eleventh day, he gave him a name according to the prescribed rite of naming, reciting the Vedic verses that signify its meaning.
And having greeted them with blessings spoken from the mantras of the four Vedas, the Grandfather (Brahmā), mounting his swan according to the convention, departed from the presence of all.
Having performed the protection appropriate for a child and followed the worldly custom, even Hara, having mounted his vehicle, went to his own abode along with Hari.
Oh, what beauty! Oh, what splendor! Oh, what auspicious marks upon every limb! Oh, the good fortune of Śuciṣmatī! Hara has appeared in person.
Or rather, what is so wonderful about this among the devotees of Śarva? Rudra himself manifested before them, for they were those by whom Rudra had been worshipped.
Thus praising one another, their hair standing on end with joy, they took leave of Viśvānara and all departed as they had come.
Therefore, those dwelling in the householder stage of life desire a son; for this is the eternal Vedic revelation: "Through a son, one conquers the worlds."
The house of one without a son is empty; the earnings of one without a son are in vain; the austerity of one without a son is severed; there is no purity for one who lacks a son.
There is no gain superior to a son; there is no happiness superior to a son; there is no friend superior to a son, neither in this world nor in the next.

Then, in his fourth month, the father performed the rite of departure from the house; at half a year, the first feeding of solid food was performed, and at half a year [of the third year], the tonsure ceremony was meaningfully carried out.
Then, having performed the piercing of the ears under the asterism of Śravaṇa, that knower of ritual procedures administered the vow in the fifth year for the sake of increasing spiritual luster.

Then, having performed the *upākarma* rite, the wise one taught the Vedas; for a year, he studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules, including the *pada* and *krama* recitations along with their auxiliary branches (*aṅgas*).
The powerful one, manifesting virtues such as humility, received from the mouth of his guru the entire collection of sciences as mere witnesses.
Then, in the ninth year, while he was devoted to the service of his parents, Nārada came to see Vaiśvānara Gṛhapati.
Having reached Viśvānara’s hermitage, the curious celestial sage took his place on half of the seat and in due course inquired after his welfare.
Then, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he spoke all that fortune and the duty of a son directly to Vaiśvānara.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by the sage, that illustrious boy, having obtained his parents' permission, bowed to Nārada and sat down humbly with devotion.
"O Vaiśvānara, come hither; sit upon my lap, sir! I shall examine your marks; show me your right hand."
Then, having observed everything—the palate, the tongue, and so forth—the wise Nārada, impelled by Śiva, spoke to Viśvānara.
Nārada said: O sage Viśvānara, listen with respect as I describe the marks upon my son; this son possesses auspicious marks on every limb and is endowed with great characteristics.
But the Creator should protect him who is endowed with all virtues, marked by all auspicious characteristics, and possessed of full, stainless digits, like the moon.
Therefore, this child must be protected with every effort; for even a virtue turns into a fault when the Creator becomes adverse.
"I suspect there will be an obstacle for him from lightning-fire in the twelfth month," having said this, Nārada departed for the world of the gods just as he had come.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Gṛhapati," in the narrative of the incarnation of Gṛhapati within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words spoken by Nārada, Viśvānara, together with his wife, considered them to be like a most terrible thunderbolt strike.
Crying out, "Alas, I am destroyed!", he struck his heart with his hand; overwhelmed by grief for his son, he fell into a deep swoon.
Śuciṣmatī too, afflicted by grief, wept most unbearably with loud cries and lamentations, her senses utterly overwhelmed.

Hearing this cry of distress, Viśvanara too cast off his delusion and rose up, crying out loudly, "What is this? What indeed? What is this? he said: "Where is that master of my house, who is my external life-breath, who dwells within my inner self, and who is the lord of all the senses?"
Then, seeing his parents overwhelmed with great sorrow, that young householder, born from a portion of Śaṅkara, smiled and spoke.
The householder said: "O mother, O father, what has happened? Tell me the reason for it now. Why are you weeping so excessively, and from where does such terror come to you both?"
Time is not able to seize me, who have taken refuge in the dust of your feet; for I am but a wretched, flickering, and insignificant creature.
Listen to my vow, O Antaka, for I am indeed Antanaya; I shall act in such a way that even Death himself will become terrified.
Having propitiated Mṛtyuñjaya, who knows all pride and bestows everything upon the virtuous, I shall recite the Mahākāla mantra; O father, I speak the truth to you.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of his, the brahmin couple, who had been scorched by the floods of untimely death, were now freed from their distress and spoke as follows.
The brahmin couple said: "Speak again! Speak again! Tell us once more, what is it like? What is it like? Time is not able to seize us; who is this wretched, flickering thing?"
For the destruction of our torment, you have described a great remedy characterized by the propitiation of the deity known as Mṛtyuñjaya.
And likewise, there is no refuge superior to that of Śambhu, for he removes sins and brings about that which transcends the path of one's desires.
Have you not heard, dear one, how in former times the Destroyer of Tripura protected Śvetaketu when he was bound by the noose of Time?
Śiva made the son of Śilāda, who was seized by death at only eight years of age, his own attendant Nandin, the delighter of the universe.
Having drunk the terrible Halāhala poison, which arose from the churning of the Ocean of Milk and resembled the fire of universal destruction, he protected the three worlds.
He who slew the exceedingly arrogant Jalandhara, who had seized the prosperity of the three worlds, with the discus produced from the lines on his beautiful thumb.
He who, in ancient times, with the fires arising from the falling of his single [arrow], dried up Tripura—which was infatuated by the sovereignty over the three worlds—with his solar radiance.
Granted, by the casting of his glance, Kāma brought even Brahmā and the other gods—who were being watched—to the state of bodilessness, despite their prowess in conquering the three worlds.
O son, go for refuge to Śiva, the sole creator of Brahmā and others, whose vehicle is the cloud, the infallible one, the jewel that protects the universe.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus obtained the permission of his parents, he prostrated at their feet, performed a circumambulation, comforted them greatly, and departed.
Having reached Kāśī, which is difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others, and which destroys the torment of the great dissolution while being protected by Viśveśvara;
It was resplendent with the necks of its mountains, which shone as if adorned by the necklace-like celestial river Ganges, and were graced by the consort of Hara, who possesses manifold virtues.
Having arrived there, that lord of brahmins first went to Maṇikarṇikā; having bathed there according to the prescribed rite, he beheld the Lord Viśveśvara.
With palms joined and head bowed, that wise one, filled with great bliss, prostrated before the protector who saves the life-breath of the three worlds.
Beholding that liṅga again and again, he rejoiced repeatedly in his heart; this is clearly the root of supreme bliss, of this there is no doubt.
Oh! There is no one more blessed than I in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, since today I have beheld the glorious and all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara.
It was solely for the rise of my fortune that the great sage Nārada came here in the past and spoke thus; consequently, I have achieved all my life's purpose.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus performed the breaking of the fast with the nectar-like juices of bliss, he then, on an auspicious day, installed the Liṅga that bestows all benefits.
He undertook formidable vows difficult for those of unrefined self to perform, [using] one hundred and eight jars filled with the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed and purified himself with a cloth, being thus cleansed in soul, he offers a garland made of blue lotuses to Śiva every single day.
Having fashioned [an image] out of one thousand and eight *sumanas* flowers, he subsists for either a fortnight or a month on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
For six months that steadfast one subsisted on withered leaves; for six months he lived on air alone; and for six months he consumed only drops of water.
In this manner, O Brahmins, the years of that great-souled one passed by as he practiced austerities with his mind fixed solely on Śiva, O Nārada.
In the twelfth year from his birth, as if to make true those words spoken by Nārada, the wielder of the thunderbolt approached him.
And he said: "Choose a boon; I shall grant whatever resides in your mind. O Brahmin, I am Śatakratu, and I am pleased with your auspicious vows."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Mahendra, the son of the sage spoke sweetly and with composure, uttering melodious syllables.
The householder said: "O Maghavan, O enemy of Vṛtra, I know you as the wielder of the thunderbolt; yet I do not choose a boon from you, for Śaṅkara is the granter of boons to me."
Indra said: "O child, Śaṅkara is not other than me; I am the God of gods. Abandoning your childishness, ask for a boon without delay."
The householder said: "Go away, O husband of Ahalyā, you wicked one, enemy of the lineage, chastiser of Pāka! I clearly do not seek any other god besides Paśupati."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of his, his eyes bloodshot with anger, he raised his terrible thunderbolt and terrified the boy.
Seeing the thunderbolt, which was filled with flashes of lightning, and remembering the words of Nārada, the boy fainted, overwhelmed by fear.
Then Śambhu, the lord of Gaurī and dispeller of ascetic toil, appeared; saying, "Arise, arise! May it be well with you," he seemed to restore her to life with his touches.
Having opened his lotus-eyes as if from sleep at the end of the day, he arose and beheld before him Śambhu, who surpassed a hundred suns in brilliance.
Beholding the eye upon his forehead, Kāla (the dark one) upon his neck, the bull-bannered Lord with the daughter of the mountain resting on his left side, and the moon-crested One;
Shining with matted locks, bearing the trident and the Ājagava bow as weapons, his limbs white as shimmering camphor, and clad in an elephant hide.
Having fully understood Mahādeva through the words of his guru and the sacred scriptures, he was choked with tears of joy, his throat constricted, and his body covered in horripilation.
And for a moment, Citrakūṭa-triputraka stood like a mountain; thus perfectly composed, he even forgot his own self.
When he was unable to offer praise, prostration, or even a single request, Śaṅkara smiled and spoke at that time.
Īśvara said: "O child, O householder, you have become afraid of Śakra with his thunderbolt raised in hand; alas! Do not fear, for I merely wished to test you."
Neither Śakra, nor the thunderbolt, nor even Antaka can prevail over my devotee; it was by me alone, in the form of Indra, that you were terrified.
I grant you a boon, O blessed one: may you become the recipient of the station of Agni; you shall be the bestower of boons upon all the gods.
O Agni, become the one who moves within all living beings; as the lord of the quarters, obtain sovereignty between Dharmarāja and Indra.
This Liṅga established by you shall be known by your name as Agnīśvara, the enhancer of all splendor.
For the devotees of Agnīśvara, there is no fear from lightning or fire; there is never any fear of impaired digestion, nor is there ever any untimely death.
Having duly worshipped Agnīśvara in Kāśī, which bestows all prosperity, even one who dies elsewhere by fate is honored in the world of Fire.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus and brought his kinsmen there while his parents looked on, Śiva consecrated Agni as the lord of the quarters and entered that very liṅga.
Thus, O dear one, I have described to you the descent of Agni as Janārdana, known by the name Gṛhapati, who is the supreme self of Śaṅkara.
The beautiful city of Citrahotr is delightful, bliss-bestowing, radiant, and excellent; those who are devoted to Jātavedas indeed dwell there.
Those of firm resolve who enter the fire, having conquered their senses, or women endowed with great courage—all of them possess the splendor of fire.
Brahmins devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, as well as those established in celibacy (brahmacārins) who never turn back from their vows, likewise possess the luster of fire in the world of Agni.
He who provides loads of fuel for the removal of cold during the winter, or constructs a fire-pit, shall dwell in the proximity of the sacred fires.
He who, endowed with faith, performs the cremation rites for a destitute person, or if unable himself, urges another to do so, is glorified in the world of Agni.
Fire alone is the supreme bringer of ultimate bliss for the twice-born; fire is certainly determined to be the teacher, the deity, the vow, and the sacred ford for all.
All impure things become pure in an instant through contact with fire; therefore, he is remembered as Pāvaka (the Purifier).
For this inner self is directly the fire that consumes; it may indeed cook morsels of meat in the belly, but not the flesh of a woman.
The fiery form of Śambhu is directly perceptible and consists of fire; it is the creator, the destroyer, and the protector—apart from this, what else can be seen?
This Citrabhānu is truly the eye of the Lord of the Three Worlds; in this world shrouded in blinding darkness, who else could be its illuminator?
All the inhabitants of heaven in the celestial realm partake of this which has been consumed: incense, lamps, food offerings, milk, curd, ghee, and sugarcane juice.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation as Gṛhapati," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O lord of sages, hear now of the incarnation of Śambhu as Yakṣeśvara—the destroyer of pride, who increases the devotion of the virtuous.

In ancient times, the gods and the Daityas, possessed of great strength and having formed an alliance for their own respective interests, churned the Ocean of Milk for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Formerly, while the nectar was being churned from the ocean of milk by the gods and the dānavas, there arose from it a poison possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Seeing him, O dear one, all the gods and Daityas, overwhelmed with fear, fled swiftly and sought refuge with Śambhu.
Having beheld Śaṅkara, the crest-jewel of all the gods, they all bowed down with their heads inclined and, accompanied by Acyuta, praised him with devotion.
Then the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased, drank the most terrible poison that afflicts the hosts of gods and demons.
He placed that fierce poison in his husband's throat; by vomiting it out, the Lord became blue-throated.
Then all the gods, freed from the burning pain of the poison by the grace of Śiva, churned that [ocean] once again.
From that, O Sage, many jewels issued forth; and from it, O Sage, indeed came the substance of immortality for both the gods and the dānavas.
The gods alone drank that [amṛta], and not the asuras, by the grace of Hari; thereupon, a very great jewel arose among them through mutual conflict.
Then, O Sage, a duel took place between the gods and the Dānavas; there, the moon, afflicted by him, fled out of fear of Rāhu.
Overwhelmed by fear, he went to the abode of Śambhu for refuge; having prostrated deeply, he praised him, crying out, "Protect me! Protect me!"
Then Śaṅkara, the bestower of fearlessness upon the virtuous and affectionate toward his devotees, that omnipresent Lord, placed the moon—who had come to him for refuge—upon his head.
Then, having arrived, Rāhu bowed deeply to Śaṅkara, the sovereign lord of all, and praised him with devotion using pleasing words.
Śambhu, having understood that intention, placed those heads—which had previously been severed by Acyuta and were known as "banners"—around his neck.
Then, in that battle, all the asuras were defeated by the gods; having drunk the nectar, all the gods, possessing great strength, achieved victory.
Viṣṇu and all the others became exceedingly arrogant; deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, they conceived pride within their hearts regarding their own strengths.
Then, O Sage, Lord Śaṅkara, the sovereign of all and the destroyer of pride, assumed the form of a Yakṣa and went quickly to where the gods were stationed.
Having seen all the gods headed by Acyuta, that lord of the Yakṣas, whose mind was filled with great pride, spoke to those great lords who were destroyers of pride.
The Lord of Yakṣas said: "O gods, for what purpose have you all gathered here together? Tell me the entire reason; I ask you."
The gods said: "O Great God, a most terrible battle took place here; all the asuras have been destroyed, and those who remain have fled in dispersal."
We are all great heroes, slayers of Daityas, and exceedingly powerful; compared to us, how insignificant are those Daityas, who always possess but meager strength?
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of the gods, which were filled with pride, Mahādeva, who was in the form of a Yakṣa, spoke these words while laughing at their arrogance.
The Lord of Yakṣas said: "O all you gods, listen with reverence to my words; I speak what is true and not false, which shall strip away all pride."
Do not harbor this pride; there is another Lord who is the creator and the destroyer. You have forgotten Maheśāna; you speak in vain, O you of futile strength!
O gods, if that pride of yours—which knows your own great strength—is indeed real, then cut down this blade of grass placed by me with your respective weapons.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, the Lord, the refuge of the virtuous, who had assumed the form of a Yakṣa, cast a single blade of grass before them and stripped away all their pride.
Then all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu and considering themselves heroes, displayed their prowess there and hurled their own weapons.
There, those weapons of the gods quickly became fruitless due to the power of Śiva, who removes the pride of the deluded.
Then a voice from the sky arose, dispelling the wonder of the gods: "O gods, this Yakṣa is Śaṅkara, the remover of all pride."
He alone is the supreme Lord—the creator, the destroyer, and likewise the sustainer; by His power alone all living beings possess strength, for otherwise they would have none at all.
Indeed, deluded by the power of his illusion, they have not even today awakened to their own Lord Śiva—the Lord whose very body is consciousness—due to their intoxication.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard this voice from the sky, they became free from pride; they bowed down to the Lord of the Yakṣas and praised that Supreme Lord.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who strip away all pride! O Lord of Yakṣas, whose great play is wondrous, your power of illusion (māyā) is truly marvelous, O Lord!"
Deluded even now by the illusion of you who have assumed the form of a Yakṣa, they speak with pride before you, each following his own separate path.
Now, O Lord Śaṅkara, by your grace alone, you are the creator, the destroyer, and the sustainer; there is no other. You alone are the thread of the illusion of knowledge.
You alone are indeed the instigator of all powers and of all beings; you are the restrainer as well, the Lord of All, the Supreme Self, imperishable and non-dual.
"By appearing in the form of the Lord of Yakṣas, our pride has been taken away by all of us; therefore we consider this to be a favor bestowed by the Compassionate One."
Then that lord of the yakṣas, having indeed favored all the gods and awakened them with various words, vanished right there.
Thus has been described this incarnation of Śambhu, which brings happiness; known as Yakṣeśvara, he bestows joy, is satisfied by the virtuous, and grants fearlessness.
This stainless narrative removes all pride; it constantly bestows perfect peace upon the virtuous and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men.
The wise person who hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard, attains all desires and thereafter obtains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation as Yakṣeśvara," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Now listen to the ten incarnations of Giriśa, beginning with Mahākāla, who are served through devotion in the section on worship.
Among them, the first is indeed Mahākāla, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the virtuous; there, his Śakti is Mahākālī, who grants the fruits desired by her devotees.
The second is named Tāra, and Tārā is likewise his Śakti; both bestow enjoyment and liberation, and grant happiness to their own servants.
Bhuvaneśa is indeed proclaimed as the third, called Bālā; Bhuvaneśī, called Bālā, is Śivā there, bestowing happiness upon the virtuous.
The Lord of Śrīvidyā is named Ṣoḍaśa; Śrīvidyā is the auspicious Ṣoḍaśī. The fourth [deity] bestows happiness upon devotees and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The fifth is known as Bhairava, who always grants the desires of his devotees; there, Bhairavī, the daughter of the Mountain, bestows the desires of her true worshippers.
This Śiva, named Chinnamastaka, is proclaimed as the sixth; and Girijā, who grants the desires of her devotees, is indeed Chinnamastakā.
The seventh is Dhūmavān Śambhu, the bestower of the fruits of all desires; there is also Dhūmavatī Śivā, who grants the wishes of her true devotees.
The eighth incarnation of Śiva is indeed the bestower of happiness, Bagalāmukha; there, the power (śakti) is the renowned Mahānandā, Bagalāmukhī.
The ninth incarnation of Śiva is proclaimed to be Mātaṅga; there, Śarvāṇī is Mātaṅgī, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
The tenth is Kamala Śambhu, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; there, Kamalā and Girijā protect their own devotees.
These ten measured incarnations of Śiva are bestowers of happiness; they always grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation to virtuous devotees.
These are indeed the ten incarnations of the great-souled Śaṅkara; they eternally bestow various kinds of happiness upon those who serve them with unwavering devotion.
O Sage, this majesty of the ten incarnations has been described; it should be known as bestowing all desires and as being imbued with the essence of the Tantras and Śāstras.
O Sage, the wondrous majesty of these primordial powers (ādi-śaktis) should be known as the bestower of all desires, for it contains within it the essence of the Tantras and other scriptures.
In rites such as the slaying of enemies, her power is considered supreme; she constantly inflicts punishment upon the wicked and increases the splendor of Brahman.
Thus, O Brahmin, have I described to you the ten auspicious incarnations of the Great Lord, together with their Śaktis, beginning with Mahākāla.
He who, devoted to faith, studies this stainless narrative on all the festival days of Śiva, shall become exceedingly dear to Śambhu.
A Brāhmaṇa shall possess Vedic splendor, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious, a Vaiśya shall indeed become a lord of wealth, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness.
May the followers of Śaṅkara, established in their own dharma and listening to this account, become especially happy and may they be devoted to Śiva.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ten Incarnations of Śiva," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Now listen to the eleven excellent incarnations of Śaṅkara; having heard of them, one shall indeed not be afflicted by the suffering arising from untruth and other such evils.
In former times, all the gods, led by Śakra, being defeated by the Daityas, abandoned Amarāvatī, their own city, and fled out of fear.
Afflicted by the Daityas, the gods went into the presence of Kaśyapa; with hands joined and shoulders bowed, they prostrated before him in great distress.
Having heard that, all the gods respectfully made their representation and reported everything—their own suffering and that defeat.
Then, O dear one, his father Kaśyapa, whose mind was devoted to Śiva, heard that report from Amaraka and became exceedingly distressed.
O Sage, having consoled them and regained his composure with a tranquil mind, the lordly sage then proceeded with great joy toward Kāśī, the city of Viśveśvara.
Then, having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and performed that rite with devotion, she worshipped Viśveśvara, the Lord of all, together with Ambā.
Having firmly installed a Śiva-liṅga, he performed extensive penance with great devotion, directed toward Śambhu, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
A great length of time passed while that sage was performing austerities, his mind fixed upon the lotus feet of Śiva and endowed with steadfastness.
Then Śambhu appeared to grant a boon to that sage, he who is the kinsman of the distressed and the refuge of the virtuous, for the sake of one whose mind was intent upon his own state.
And Maheśvara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being well-pleased, said to Kaśyapa, that tiger among sages and his own devotee, "Choose a boon."
Then, having beheld that Great Lord, Kaśyapa—delighted, with a serene mind, and with palms joined in reverence—bowed down and praised the Father of the Gods.

Kaśyapa said: O God of gods, O Maheśāna, you who are compassionate toward those who have sought refuge; you are the Lord of all, the Supreme Self, attainable through meditation, non-dual, and immutable.
O Maheśvara, you are the restrainer of the wicked, the refuge of the virtuous, the kinsman of the distressed, an ocean of compassion, and one whose intellect is expert in protecting your devotees.
"These gods are indeed yours and are especially devoted to you; now that they have been defeated by the Daityas, O Lord, protect them who are suffering."
Even Rāmeśa was powerless, and he too was repeatedly tormented by that misery; therefore, the gods, experiencing that suffering, sought refuge in me.
For that purpose, O Lord of the gods, O destroyer of the suffering of the gods, I have come before you to be pleased, so that you may fulfill my steadfastness in austerity.
O Maheśvara, I have sought refuge in you in every way; O Lord, fulfill my desire and destroy the suffering of the gods.
O Lord of Gods, I am especially distressed by the sorrows concerning my sons; O Lord, you who are the ally of the dwellers of heaven, make me happy.
O Lord Śambhu, having become my son, the gods and yakṣas were defeated by the exceedingly powerful daityas; now, grant joy to the gods.
O Maheśāna, may you always be the helper of all scribes, so that the affliction caused by the Daityas does not oppress the gods, O Lord.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus, Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, replied "So be it," and while he was looking on, the Blessed Hara vanished right there.
Kaśyapa also, greatly delighted, quickly returned to his own abode; and the Lord of Gods related the entire account with great care.
Then Śaṅkara, in order to make his own word true, was born from Kaśyapa through Surabhī, assuming eleven forms.
Then there was a great festival, and everything became permeated with auspiciousness; the gods, as well as the sage Kaśyapa, were filled with joy.
Kapālī, Piṅgala, Bhīma, Virūpākṣa, and Vilohita.
Śāstṛ (6), Ajapād (7), Hirbudhnya (8), Śambhu (9), Caṇḍa (10), and likewise Bhava (11).
These eleven Rudras are remembered as the sons of Surabhati; born for the sake of the gods' work, they are the very form of Śiva and the abode of happiness.
Those heroic Rudras, descendants of Kaśyapa, possessed of great strength and prowess, slew the Daityas in battle while providing assistance to the gods.
By the grace of that Rudra, all those gods, beginning with Śakra, having conquered the Daityas and become fearless, established their own kingdom with tranquil minds.
Even today, all those great Rudras, who are the very embodiment of Śiva, continue to shine eternally in heaven for the protection of the gods.
Those who are compassionate toward their devotees made their dwelling in the city of Ishana; there, those experts in various divine sports always cease from their activities.
Their followers, the Rudras, are proclaimed to be by the millions; they are stationed everywhere throughout the three worlds according to their respective divisions.
Thus, O dear one, these eleven incarnations of Śaṅkara have been described to you—the Rudras who bring happiness to all the worlds.
This narrative is stainless, a destroyer of all sins; it bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and grants the fulfillment of all desires.
O dear one, he who hears this or causes it to be heard with a concentrated mind shall enjoy every happiness in this world and thereafter attain liberation.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eleven Incarnations," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Now, O great sage, listen with affection to another account of Śambhu—how Durvāsas became Śaṅkara for the sake of dharma.
The son of Brahmā was an exceedingly ascetic master who knew Brahman; he was the wise husband of Anasūyā and a protector of the commands of Brahmā.
Because Brahmā had given him clear instructions, he, accompanied by his wife and desiring a son, went to the mountain named after the Three-eyed One (Tryakṣakula) to perform austerities.
Having performed breath control according to the rules on the bank of the Nirvindhyā river, the sage, free from dualities, practiced very great austerity for a hundred years.
With a resolute mind, he thought: "May that certain one Lord, who is immutable and the Great Master, grant me an excellent son."
A long time passed while he was performing that supreme austerity; then, from that place, a great and pure flame manifested.
By her, O lords of sages, all the worlds were nearly consumed; likewise, all the celestial rishis, including Indra and the others, were tormented.
Then, O sage, all the gods led by Vāsava and the sages, being greatly tormented by that flame, went quickly to the abode of Brahmā.
Having bowed and praised Him according to the prescribed rites, the gods reported their own sufferings; O dear one, Brahmā, together with the deities, then went to the supreme realm of Viṣṇu.
Having gone there, O Sage, and having bowed to and praised Ramānātha along with the gods, Brahmā recounted his own endless suffering to Viṣṇu.
And Viṣṇu, together with Brahmā and the gods, went quickly to the abode of Rudra; having arrived there and bowed to Hara, he praised the Supreme Lord.
Having praised Viṣṇu extensively, he reported his own suffering, as well as the supreme power of Śiva’s penance, which had produced a mass of flames here.
Then, O sage, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, having assembled there, consulted with one another for the welfare of the worlds.
Then Brahmā and the other gods—those three foremost among the givers of boons—went quickly to that hermitage to grant a boon to that sage.
Seeing them marked with their own respective signs, Atri, the best of sages, bowed down and praised them with affectionate words out of reverence.
Then, filled with wonder, that humble-souled Brahmin, the son of Brahmā, spoke to them with palms joined in reverence: "O you who are named Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara!"
Atri said: O Brahmā, O Hari, O Rudra! You are considered the worshipful ones of the three worlds; you are the sources and lords who perform the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction.
For the sake of a son, I meditated upon only one Lord—whosoever is renowned as a lord of the worlds—together with his own consort.
"O you three, foremost among the bestowers of boons, from where have you come? Having severed this doubt of mine, then grant me the desired boon."
Having heard his words, those three gods replied: "O Lord of Sages, exactly as you formed your resolve, so it has come to pass."
"We three are equal lords of existence, O bull among the bestowers of boons; therefore, three sons shall be born from our respective portions."
"Known throughout the world as the increasers of their parents' fame"—having been addressed thus, those three gods joyfully departed for their own abodes.
Having received the boon, O sage, that bestower of Brahman-bliss departed for his own hermitage with joy, accompanied by Anasūyā and filled with delight.
Then Brahmā, Hari, and Śambhu descended into that woman; with pleased minds, they manifested their various divine sports through the forms of sons.
From a portion of Vidhi, the Moon was born of Anasūyā from the lord of sages; indeed, that very same god appeared from the ocean when he had been cast in.
From a portion of Viṣṇu, Datta was born to Atri by that woman; it was he, O sage, by whom the supreme manual of renunciation (saṃnyāsapaddhati) was expanded.
Durvāsas, the tiger among sages and best of munis, born from a portion of Śiva, was begotten upon that woman by Atri as one who would propagate the excellent dharma.
Having become Rudra Durvāsas, who increases the splendor of Brahman, he, being devoted to compassion, conducted an examination of the dharma of many people.
O Lord of Sages, listen as I relate how that king Ambarīṣa, who was born in the solar dynasty, performed his test.
That Ambarīṣa, the best of kings and sovereign lord of the seven islands, indeed made a firm resolve regarding the vow of Ekādaśī.
"Having observed the vow on the eleventh day, I shall perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day"—thus was the king's resolve firmly established.
Having understood that restriction of his, Durvāsas, the best of sages and an incarnation of a portion of Śaṅkara, went into his presence accompanied by many disciples.
On the day of breaking the fast, perceiving that the twelfth lunar day was very short, he invited him as soon as he had resolved to take his meal.
Then Durvāsas, accompanied by his disciples, went for the purpose of bathing; there the sage delayed for a long time in order to test him.
Then, perceiving that obstacle to the Dharma, the king, in accordance with the injunctions of the scriptures, sipped water and remained there, awaiting his arrival.
In the meantime, the sage Durvāsas arrived there; knowing that the king had finished his meal, he assumed a physical form for the sake of testing him.
When that king became enraged, the sage born of a portion of Śaṅkara spoke these fierce words for the purpose of testing the bull.
Durvāsas said: "O lowest of men, having invited me and failed to feed me, you have drunk water; I shall show you the fruit of that, for I am indeed the wielder of punishment for the wicked."
Having spoken thus, his eyes copper-red with rage, he prepared to burn the king; at that moment, the divine discus situated there for the sake of protection rose up swiftly.
The Sudarśana discus blazed up intensely to burn that sage, for it did not recognize him as Śiva, being deluded by the māyā of Śiva.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice from the sky spoke to the high-souled Ambarīṣa, who was a devotee of Brahmā and a Vaiṣṇava.
The celestial voice said: "O King, this Sudarśana discus was bestowed upon Hari by Śambhu; today, O King, pacify it as it blazes against Durvāsas."
This Durvāsas is Śiva himself; he has offered the discus to Hari. O best of kings, do not consider him to be an ordinary sage.
This lord of sages has come for the purpose of examining your righteousness; seek refuge with him quickly, otherwise there will be destruction.
Nandīśvara said: O lord of sages, having spoken thus, the voice from the sky ceased; then Ambarīṣa also respectfully praised that partial incarnation of Hara.

Ambarīṣa said: "If there has been charity given or sacrifice performed, or if my own duty has been well-fulfilled, and if our lineage and the Brahmins are indeed our deities, then let Hari’s weapon be pacified."
If the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, is pleased with me as my devotee, then let this Sudarśana weapon, in particular, be pacified.

Nandīśvara said: While he was thus praising [Śiva] in the presence of Rudra, the Sudarśana discus of Śiva became completely pacified; for [Viṣṇu], having recognized him as a portion of Śiva, attained a perfectly enlightened mind.
Then King Ambarīṣa bowed down to that sage, recognizing him as an incarnation of Śiva who had come for the purpose of testing him.
Then that sage, born from a portion of Śaṅkara, became exceedingly pleased; having eaten and granted him his desired boon, he went to his own abode.
O Sage, O Lord of Sages, you have narrated the conduct of Durvāsas during the testing of Ambarīṣa; now hear another account of his life.

Furthermore, he indeed conducted a test of the son of Dasharatha according to the rule; for the sage had previously established a condition that, in the form of a sage, he would appear after a certain time.
At that very moment, O Sage, Saumitri was sent away by force by that sage; Rāma immediately abandoned his kinsman due to the power of the wager.
That discourse has been established in the world and expounded in many ways by the sages; therefore, it has not been told by me in detail, since it is known in every respect by the wise.
Seeing his firm commitment, the sage Durvāsas became well-pleased; with a highly gratified soul, he granted him a boon.
He indeed performed a test of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s vow as well; listen to that, O best of sages, for I shall relate that story.
At the prayer of Brahmā, Viṣṇu became the son of Vasudeva for the purpose of removing the earth's burden and for the protection of the virtuous.
Having slain the wicked, the great sinners, and the defilers who commit treachery against Brahman, he who bears the name Kṛṣṇa protected all the virtuous Brāhmaṇas.
That Kṛṣṇa, born of Vasudeva, practiced supreme devotion to Brahman; indeed, he constantly fed many Brahmins with delicious foods.
It became widely known that Kṛṣṇa was especially devoted to Brahmā; O sage, desiring to see him, the sage went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Having himself yoked Kṛṣṇa, who was accompanied by Rukmiṇī, to the chariot and made him steady, the well-pleased steed drew him along.
The Sage, having descended from his chariot and seeing her supreme steadfastness, became well-pleased with him and granted him the boon of having a body as hard as a diamond.
O sage, once while performing his ablutions in the Dyunadī river, the excellent sage Durvāsas, who was full of curiosity, became naked and felt ashamed.
Knowing this, Draupadī, while performing her bath there with devotion, covered his shame by giving him a portion of her own garment.
Taking that which had come near him by the current, the sage covered his private parts with it, and he became pleased with her.
And he granted a boon to Draupadī that increased the length of her garment; furthermore, by virtue of that boon, Draupadī made the Pāṇḍavas happy.
There were two wicked kings, Haṃsa and Ḍimbha, who treated him with contempt; that Lord, having issued a command to Hari, caused them to be destroyed.
By means of his extraordinary Brahmanic splendor, he established upon the earth the manual of renunciation (*saṃnyāsapaddhati*) according to the sequence of procedures prescribed in the scriptures.
Having awakened them through excellent instruction, he rescued many; by imparting knowledge especially, he brought many to liberation.
In this manner, Durvāsas performed many wonderful deeds that are auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and which grant all desires to those who hear them.
Whoever hears this life-story of Durvāsas with devotion and joy, or causes it to be heard by others, shall be happy both in this world and in the next.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of Durvāsas," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, listen now with affection to the life of Hanumān; hear how Hara quickly performed divine sports in that form, which were most excellent.
The supreme lords, out of affection, brought about the well-being of Rāma; O Brahmin, hear that entire account which brings all happiness.
At one time, the Lord Śambhu, the performer of wonders and possessor of all excellent qualities, beheld the form of Viṣṇu as Mohinī.
Śambhu, like one struck by the arrows of Kāma, agitated his own seed; the Lord caused his own virility to fall for the sake of Rāma’s mission.
And those seven sages, impelled by his mind and out of reverence for the sake of Rāma’s task, placed that semen upon a leaf.
For the sake of Rāma’s mission, that seed of Śambhu was deposited by those great sages into the daughter of Gautama through the ear, and likewise into Añjanā.
Then, in due course, from him was born Śambhu, who bore the name Hanumān; he possessed the body of a monkey and was endowed with great strength and prowess.
Hanumān, that lord of monkeys, though but a child yet possessed of great strength, quickly devoured the orb of the sun at dawn, perceiving it to be a small fruit.
Having recognized him as one of great strength and as an incarnation of Śiva, he released him at the request of the gods; and [the demon] obtained boons granted by the celestial sages.
Then Hanumān, exceedingly joyful, approached his own mother and respectfully related that entire account to her.
Then, by his command, that wise monkey went daily to the presence of the Sun and, without effort, recited all branches of knowledge from him.
By the command of the Sun, that portion of him, the best of monkeys and an emanation of Rudra, went into the presence of Sugrīva after receiving his mother’s command.
Indeed, having been insulted by his elder brother Vālin—who was a violator of his own sister—he dwelt on Mount Ṛṣyamūka together with Hanumān.
Then that wise and eminent monkey, the minister of Sukaṇṭha, who was born from a portion of Hara, acted entirely for the welfare of Sugrīva.
Having arrived there, the sorrowful Rāma, whose brother was present and whose wife had been abducted, formed a friendship with him that brought them happiness.
And Rāma caused Vālin, that elephant among monkeys—who was a sinner, a devourer of his brother’s wife, and one who considered himself a hero—to be slain.
Then, O dear one, by the command of Rāma, the wise Hanumān, lord of the monkeys, conducted a search for Sītā together with many monkeys.
Having learned that Sītā had gone to Laṅkā, the lord of monkeys went there, having swiftly leaped across the ocean which is impossible for others to cross.
There he performed deeds of marvelous character, endowed with valor; out of affection, he joyfully gave Sītā the excellent token of her husband.
Having caused her to hear the news concerning Rāma—which brought relief to her life—that heroic leader of the monkeys quickly dispelled Sītā’s grief.
Taking that magical knowledge, he returned to Rāma's presence; having struck down Rāvaṇa’s grove, he slew many rākṣasas.
Having slain that very son of Rāvaṇa along with many Rākṣasas, he, possessing great splendor and free from fear, caused a great upheaval there.
O Sage, when he was bound by Rāvaṇa, who possessed great strength, his garments were thoroughly smeared with oil and wrapped around him so tightly that they were set ablaze.
Leaping again and again, the monkey, born from a portion of Mahādeva, then set all of Laṅkā ablaze, having made that very [destruction] his pretext.
Having burned Laṅkā and avoided the house of Vibhīṣaṇa, that heroic elephant among monkeys then leapt into the ocean.
Having extinguished his own tail there, he reached the opposite shore; undaunted, the son of Śiva went into the presence of Rāma.
Without delay, the swift Hanumān, the best of monkeys, arrived at Rāma’s presence and presented him with Sītā’s crest-jewel.
Then, by his command, the heroic and powerful monkey constructed a bridge across the ocean, having brought together many great mountains.
