Having gone there from that place, Rāma, desiring to cross over as he had intended, installed and worshipped a Śiva-liṅga out of a desire for victory.
Having obtained victory through that boon and then crossed the ocean, he surrounded Laṅkā with his monkeys and waged war against the Rākṣasas.
Then that hero slew the asuras and protected Rāma’s army; he restored the wounded Lakṣmaṇa to life by means of the Saṃjīvinī herb.
Indeed, that Lord, the son of Mahādeva, made Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa happy in every way and protected the entire army.
That monkey, a great and powerful planet, destroyed Rāvaṇa along with his wealthy retinue and brought peace to the gods.
Having slain the one known as Mahīrāvaṇa along with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, he brought them from that place to his own abode after having protected them.
The bull among monkeys swiftly performed Rāma’s task in every way; he subdued the asuras and displayed various divine sports.
The Lord of Monkeys, himself having become the foremost of devotees and the bestower of happiness upon Sītā and Rāma, established devotion to Rāma in the world of mortals.
He is the giver of life to Lakṣmaṇa, the remover of the pride of all the gods, the Lord who is an incarnation of Rudra, and truly the one who delivers his devotees.
Hanumān is that great hero who always performs the work of Rāma; known in the world as the messenger of Rāma, he is the slayer of demons and is affectionate toward his devotees.
Thus, O dear one, I have related to you the excellent life-story of Hanumān, which is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and bestows the fruit of all desires.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard with a concentrated mind, shall enjoy all desires here in this world and, at the end, attain supreme liberation.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Hanumān’s Incarnation," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Now, O Sage, son of the Self-born, listen with affection to the supreme incarnation of the Lord Śaṅkara, which grants all desires to those who hear it.
Once, O tiger among sages, both Girijā and Śaṅkara, the supreme lords, desired to sport together according to their own will.
Having made Bhairava the gatekeeper, they entered the interior; there, those two who move like men were affectionately attended by various groups of female companions.
O Sage, after dwelling there for a long time, those two independent Supreme Lords, who perform manifold divine sports, became pleased.
Then the goddess Śivā, independent and appearing like one intoxicated, arrived at the door in that form through her divine play and received the Lord’s command.
Then Bhairava, beholding that goddess with the gaze of a man for a woman, was so infatuated by her form that he forbade her from going outside.
O Sage, when she was gazed upon by Bhairava with the look of a woman, the goddess Śivā became enraged; then Ambikā cursed him.
Śiva said: "O Bhairava, lowest of men, because you look upon me with the eyes of a woman, therefore you shall indeed become a human being upon the earth."
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, when Bhairava had been thus cursed by Śivā, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and he experienced suffering through that divine play.
Then, O lord of sages, Śaṅkara, who is skilled in various forms of conciliation, quickly approached him and comforted Bhairava.
O Sage, due to that curse, Bhairava then descended to the earth in a human womb, known by the name Vaitāla, by the will of Śaṅkara.
Out of affection for him, the omnipresent Lord Śiva also descended to the earth; accompanied by Śivā, he engaged in divine play, assuming a worldly course of conduct.
O Sage, the one called Maheśa was Śiva and Śāradā was Girijā; skilled in various pastimes, they sported with affection.
Thus, O dear one, I have related to you this excellent account of Maheśa, which bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and grants the fruit of all desires.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind, shall enjoy all pleasures here in this world and attain liberation in the end.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnations of Maheśa," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O wise son of Brahmā, O lord of sages, to the excellent incarnation of Śiva known as Vṛṣeśa, which is full of divine play and which removes the pride of Hari.
In ancient times, all the gods and asuras, afflicted by the fear of old age and death, formed an alliance with one another, desiring to seize the jewels [of the world].
Then, O delighter of sages, all the gods and asuras prepared to churn that Kṣīroda, the best of oceans.
"O Brahman, by what means shall this churning be accomplished for the sake of achieving our own purpose?"—thus all the gods and demons spoke with pure smiles.
Then, by the command of the Lord, a voice from the sky, deep-sounding like a thundercloud, spoke to the gods and the Daityas, heartening them.
The voice from the sky said: "O gods and asuras, churn the Ocean of Milk; for the wisdom of strength shall surely arise among you, without a doubt."
Make Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope; all of you, having gathered together, perform the churning with diligence.
Nandīśvara said: O best of sages, having then heard that voice from the sky, all the gods and asuras made preparations to carry it out.
Having well-secured Mount Mandara, the best of mountains—which shone like gold, was straight, and was adorned with various beauties—they all indeed departed.
Having propitiated that Lord of the Mountains, the gods and demons, commanded by him, forcibly uprooted [the mountain], desiring to carry it to the ocean of milk.
Having uprooted them all with their arms, they went to the city of the Ocean of Milk; yet, their vigor destroyed, they became powerless to bring him there.
Slipped from their arms, that exceedingly heavy Mount Mandara suddenly and immediately fell directly upon the gods and the demons.
Thus, with their efforts shattered, the gods and asuras were broken; yet, regaining their composure, they then praised the Lord of the Universe.
Impelled by his will, they all rose up again and, having carried that mountain to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, cast it into the water.
Then the hosts of gods and asuras, having made Vāsuki their churning rope and desiring to obtain the jewels, churned the ocean of milk.
While the Ocean of Milk was being churned, Śrī—the sovereign lady of the heavenly realm, daughter of Bhṛgu, and beloved of Hari—emerged from the ocean.
Dhanvantari, the moon, the great tree Pārijāta, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, and likewise the elephant Airāvata.
Then there was the liquor, the golden bow, the conch, and the cows that yield all desires; likewise, the jewel named Kaustubha and the nectar itself.
And as it was being churned again, the great poison Kālakūṭa arose, resembling the fire at the end of an eon and bringing fear to both gods and demons.
At the time of the birth of nectar, those drops which fell outside—from them were born many beautiful women of truly wondrous appearance.
With faces like the full autumn moon, possessing the radiance of lightning, the sun, and fire, they were adorned with divine jewels—necklaces, armlets, and bracelets.
Sprinkling the ten directions with the nectar-water of their loveliness, they truly madden the world with their long glances and the knitting of their brows.
They arose by the millions from the nectar that issued forth from Kāma; from that, the nectar was produced which wards off old age and death.
Keśava took hold of Lakṣmī, the conch, the Kaustubha gem, and the sword; Arka respectfully took the divine horse Uccaiḥśravas.
And Śacīpati, the lord of the immortals, took the Pārijāta, the best of trees, and Airāvata, the king of elephants, with great reverence.
For the protection of the gods, Śaṅkara, the benevolent Śambhu who is affectionate toward his devotees, voluntarily placed the Kālakūṭa poison and the moon upon his own neck.
O Vyāsa, all the Daityas, deluded by the command of the Lord, seized the woman named Surā; likewise, all the people seized Dhanvantari.
All those lords of sages seized the wish-fulfilling cow; meanwhile, the women remained there, generally deluded.
For the sake of the nectar of immortality, a great battle took place between the gods and the asuras, who were mutually agitated in mind and desirous of victory.
O Vyāsa, having defeated the gods by force, Bali and the other Daityas, who possessed the brilliant splendor of the fire and sun at the end of a yuga, seized the Soma.
O dear one, all the gods, including Śakra and the others, having been oppressed by force by the Daityas, fell into a state of fear and became agitated by the illusory power of Śiva.
Then, O sage, by the command of Śiva, that nectar was diligently seized from the Daityas by the Lord of Ramā through his illusory power in the form of a woman.
Assuming the form of a woman, Mohinī made those gods drink the liquor; having deluded all the gods, Hari, the best among the masters of illusion, acted thus.
Approaching her, the foremost of the Daityas said: "Let us drink this nectar; let there be no division here among the rows."
Having said this, all those Daityas and Dānavas, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, gave it to Viṣṇu, who was in a deceptive form.
In the meantime, having seen the women, the foremost of the Dānavas led them, who had arisen from the nectar, to their respective places as they pleased.
Their divine cities were even superior to heaven; they were well-guarded by formidable machines and constructed through the illusory power of Maya.
Having ensured that all were well-protected, the Daityas set out for battle, having indeed made a solemn pact that they would not touch one another's chests.
"We shall not touch these women, even if we are defeated by the gods. Having spoken thus, all those great heroic Daityas became eager for battle.
Finally, they let out lion-roars and blew their conchs individually, as if filling the sky and satiating the clouds.
A terrifying battle took place between the gods and the asuras, known as the Devāsura war, which was incomparable and famous throughout the three worlds.
All the gods, protected by Viṣṇu, attained victory; the Daityas fled from there, having been struck down by Viṣṇu along with the immortals.
The Daityas, deluded by the gods and by the high-souled Viṣṇu, entered Pātāla and its various chasms as the remnants of those who had been slain.
The mighty Viṣṇu, wielder of the discus, followed them as they had gone to the supreme netherworld (Pātāla) and stood there like those struck with great fear.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu beheld those women born of nectar—lovely, with faces like the full moon, and proud of their divine beauty.
Deluded by the arrows of desire, he found his fulfillment right there; indeed, he became engaged in dalliance with those excellent women.
From them, Viṣṇu begot sons of excellent prowess, who made the entire earth tremble and were experts in various modes of warfare.
Then indeed those sons of Hari, possessed of great strength and prowess, caused a great calamity that brought suffering both in heaven and on earth.
Then, perceiving the affliction of the world, the ageless sages prostrated before Brahmā and made a formal representation to him.
Having heard that, Brahmā took them and went to Mount Kailāsa; having seen Śiva there, he prostrated himself before him again and again along with the gods.
With shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, he praised him with various hymns, saying, "Victory to you, O God, Great God, Lord of All!"
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Lord, protect all the worlds which are being harassed by the sons of Viṣṇu, who dwell in Pātāla and are full of malice.
O Lord, Hari, his soul deeply attached to women who are like nectar, now dwells in Pātāla and indeed takes delight there, possessed as he is by worldly transformations.
Nandīśvara said: Thus was Śambhu praised extensively by Brahmā, along with the sages and the gods, for the sake of protecting the worlds and for the purpose of bringing Viṣṇu back.
Then the Blessed One, Śambhu, Maheśvara, the ocean of compassion, having perceived that affliction, assumed the form of a bull.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Vṛṣa to Counter the Oppression of Viṣṇu," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Then the wielder of the Pināka bow, bellowing in the form of a bull and uttering terrible roars, entered the opening there.
Due to the sounds of his trampling, the cities and towns were shaken, and a trembling indeed came over all the inhabitants of those cities.
Then Vṛṣa [beheld] the sons of Hari, with bows raised for battle, their great strength and prowess rendered bewildered by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva.
Then, O best of sages, those sons of Hari became enraged; roaring loudly, the heroes rushed toward Śaṅkara.
As those sons of Hari approached, Rudra, assuming the form of a bull, became enraged and tore at the sons of Viṣṇu with his hooves and horns.
With their limbs torn apart by Rudra, all those sons of Hari perished; they quickly became breathless and unconscious.
When those sons had become hostile, Viṣṇu, the best among the powerful, then emerged, bowed deeply, and went swiftly to the presence of Hara.
Seeing Rudra departing after having slain the son of Viṣṇu, Keśava struck him with arrows and divine missiles.
Then Mahādeva, in the form of a bull, powerful with pride and dwelling upon the mountain, became enraged and swallowed those weapons of Viṣṇu.
Then, O sage, having become greatly enraged, that Maheśvara, whose nature is like a bull, let out a most terrible roar, making the three worlds tremble.
Then, with speed, he tore at Viṣṇu with his hooves and horns—Viṣṇu who was overwhelmed by anger, deluded, and unaware that he was his own Hari.
Then, indeed, his body became distressed and his limbs grew limp; for Hari, deluded by Māyā, could not endure that unbearable blow.
His pride gone, Hari himself became bewildered and deprived of his senses; he then recognized the Supreme Lord sporting in the form of the bull.
Then, having recognized that the Lord of Gaurī had arrived in the form of a bull, he, with shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, spoke in a deep voice.
Hari said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord, ocean of compassion! O Maheśāna, I have been deluded by your māyā, my intellect being utterly bewildered.
O Lord, the battle has been fought by you, my master and lord; O Master, having shown compassion toward me, let that offense indeed be forgiven.
Nandīśvara said: O sage, having heard those words of Hari out of his distress, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, spoke to the Lord of Ramā.
"O Viṣṇu, O you of great intellect, how is it that you did not recognize me? You have fought with me today, yet all your knowledge has been forgotten."
Do you not know yourself, whose prowess is dependent upon me? You should not take pleasure in this; desist from such evil conduct.

How can knowledge be dependent on desire for one who dwells attached to women? O Lord of Gods, it is not fitting for you to remember [them], for your remembrance is the deliverance of the entire universe.
Having heard those words of Śambhu which bestow wisdom, Viṣṇu, feeling ashamed in his mind, spoke these words with reverence to Maheśvara:
Viṣṇu said: "I have my discus here; taking it with due respect, I shall go to my own world, obeying your command."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Hara, the Great Lord, whose nature is righteousness and who protects righteousness, replied again to Hari.
"You must not delay; you must depart from here quickly. By my command, O Hari, let the discus remain right here in this world."
Because of its arrangement like the sun within the continuum, and because it is spoken of as being Śiva himself, I shall give you another wheel that is even more terrible than that.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Hara drew a supreme, blazing discus, radiant as the fire of cosmic destruction, which indeed destroys all that is evil.
He gave the discus, which possessed the brilliance of ten thousand fierce suns, to Viṣṇu, the high-souled protector of all the gods and the lords of sages.
Having obtained another discus, the Sudarśana, which was supremely radiant, Viṣṇu, the best among the wise, spoke there to the gods.
O you best of all gods, listen to my words with respect; that which must be done should be performed swiftly, and thereafter there will be welfare for you.
In Pātāla there are divine, excellent women endowed with youth; let whoever wishes do so—let him engage in great dalliance with them.
Having heard those words from Keśava, the heroic sons of the gods, desiring to enter the netherworld, became intent on entering Pātāla together with Viṣṇu.
Then, perceiving that deliberation, the Blessed Lord Hara, out of anger, pronounced a terrible curse upon the eight classes of divine beings.
Hara said: "Excepting a peaceful sage or a Dānava born from my own portion, whoever enters this place shall meet his death in an instant."
Having heard these terrible words that increase the welfare of mankind, the gods, having been rejected by Rudra, returned to their own abodes.
Thus instructed by Śiva, Viṣṇu, the supreme lord of women, went to his own world, O Vyāsa; and that universe attained its natural state.
The Lord Śaṅkara, the master of the bull and compassionate toward his devotees, having thus accomplished the work of the gods, departed for his own mountain lord.
The incarnation of Śiva as Vṛṣeśvara has been described; it was Śarva who removed Viṣṇu’s delusion and brought happiness to the three worlds.
This sacred narrative is the supreme remover of the affliction of enemies; it bestows heaven, fame, and long life, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to the virtuous.

Whoever hears this with devotion, or indeed causes it to be heard while composed in mind, shall enjoy all desires and attain liberation at the end. Likewise, he who recites this or causes wise men to recite it [shall obtain the same].
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Śiva as Vṛṣeśvara," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O wise one, listen with great affection to the supreme incarnation of Maheśvara known as Pippalāda, which is the most excellent increaser of devotion.
The brahmin Dadhīci, the best of sages, who was previously mentioned—he was a great devotee of Śiva, possessed of great majesty, a descendant of Cyavana born in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
In battle with Kṣuva, Viṣṇu was defeated, along with the gods, and then cursed by him who had Maheshvara as his ally.
His wife was the highly fortunate Suvarcā by name; she was a virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, by whom the dwellers of heaven were cursed.
Therefore, the radiant Mahādeva, who is skilled in manifold divine sports, manifested within her under the name of Pippalāda.
Sūta said: Having heard these wonderful words of Nandīśvara, Sanatkumāra, the best of sages, spoke with his shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence.

Sanatkumāra said: O Nandīśvara, O one of great wisdom, you who bear the very form of Rudra himself; blessed are you, O dear one, for you are a true guru, and this wonderful story has been narrated by you.
O dear son, O son of Śilāda, it was heard by me long ago from Brahmā that Viṣṇu’s victory over Kṣuva in battle took place in the city of Viṣṇu, and that there was also a curse [upon him].
Now I wish to hear, O Suvarcā, about the divine curse that was given, and afterwards the life-story of Pippalāda, which is a source of auspiciousness.
Sūta said: Having thus heard the auspicious words of the son of Brahmā, Śailādi, with a delighted soul, remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and replied.
Nandīśvara said: O lord of sages, once all the gods, headed by Vāsava, were defeated by the Daityas who had Vṛtrāsura as their ally.
Having suddenly and immediately deposited all their respective excellent weapons in the hermitage of Dadhīca, the gods were instantly defeated.
Then all the gods, including Indra, as well as the sages, being thus slaughtered, quickly went to the world of Brahmā and reported their own calamity.
Having heard those words of the god, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, related everything in its true nature, including exactly what Tvaṣṭṛ intended to do.
O gods, this great and highly effulgent lord of all the Daityas, named Vṛtra, was produced by Tvaṣṭṛ through his ascetic penance for the purpose of slaying you.
Now, let an effort be made so that his death may come; listen to the means for this, O wise one, as I tell it to you for the sake of dharma.
In ancient times, the great sage Dadhīci, an ascetic who had conquered his senses, propitiated Śiva and obtained the boon of possessing adamantine bones.
"Entreat him for his very bones; he will give them to you, without a doubt. Having fashioned a thunderbolt from them like a staff, slay Vṛtra—of this there is no doubt."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of Brahmā, Śakra, accompanied by his preceptor and the gods, immediately went to the excellent hermitage of Dadhīci.
Seeing the sage there, Śakra, together with his preceptor and the gods, bowed down with palms joined in reverence, humble and filled with devotion toward him who was endowed with great splendor.
Having understood his intention, that sage, the best among the wise, sent his wife Suvarcā to another part of the hermitage.
Then the king of the gods, together with the immortals, intent on accomplishing his own purpose and devoted to the science of statecraft, spoke these words to the lord of sages.
Śakra said: "O Great Śaiva, all of us gods as well as the sages have been oppressed by Tvaṣṭṛ; we have come to you for refuge—you who are the protector and the giver."
"O Brahmin, give us your bones, for they shall indeed consist of great adamant; having fashioned my own thunderbolt from your bone, I shall slay the enemy of the gods."
Thus addressed by him, that sage, who was devoted to the service of others, meditated upon Śiva, his own Lord, and indeed cast off his body.
Having destroyed his bonds, the sage immediately went to the Brahma-world; a rain of flowers fell there, and everyone was filled with wonder.
Then Śakra, having quickly summoned the cow Surabhi, caused her to be licked; he then commanded the son of Tvaṣṭṛ to fashion a weapon from her bones.
Commanded by him, Viśvakarman fashioned all the weapons in their entirety from those bones—which were as firm as adamant and possessed the splendor of Śiva—using the power of Śiva himself.
He fashioned the *vajra* from bamboo, as well as the *brahmaśiras* arrow; with the bones of others, he created many weapons for both himself and others.
O Sage, Indra, having raised that thunderbolt and being strengthened by the splendor of Śiva, rushed furiously toward Vṛtra like Rudra attacking Antaka.
Then Śakra, well-equipped for battle, swiftly severed Vṛtra’s head with that thunderbolt, as if by his might he were cleaving a mountain peak.
Then, O dear one, a great festival arose among the inhabitants of heaven; the immortals praised Śakra, and showers of flowers fell.
Thus, O dear one, this account has been told to you incidentally; now listen with great devotion to the beginning of the incarnation of Śambhu as Pippalāda.
Commanded by him, that devoted wife Suvarcā, the consort of the high-souled sage Dadhīca, entered her own hermitage.
Having arrived there, that ascetic woman did not see her husband; yet, she performed all the household duties according to her husband's command.
O best of sages, Suvarcā returned there once more, beholding many inauspicious sights; seeing those gods, she was filled with wonder.
Having understood all this conduct of the gods at that time, the virtuous Suvarcā, the wife of the eminent rishi, became enraged; then, exceedingly furious, she pronounced a curse upon them.

Suvarcā said: "Aha! All these gods are most wicked; for they are clever only at their own interests, yet ignorant and greedy. Therefore, from this day forward, let all of them, including Indra, become animals," she declared.
Thus did that ascetic woman, Suvarcā, the beloved of the sage, pronounce a curse upon all those gods, including Śakra.
Then that high-minded woman of devoted virtue, wishing to follow her husband to the world of the Lord, prepared a funeral pyre with very pure sacrificial fuel.
Then, impelled by Giriśa, the bliss-bestowing Suvarcā spoke with a voice from the sky to the beloved of the sage, consoling her.
The voice from the sky said: "O wise one, do not act rashly; listen to my supreme words. The splendor of the sage is within your womb; bring it forth with diligent effort."
Therefore, O Goddess, you ought to perform your desired task; for it is the command of Brahmā that one who is pregnant must not burn her body.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, O lord of sages, that voice from the sky ceased; upon hearing it, the sage’s wife was struck with wonder for a moment.
Suvarcā, that great virtuous woman, desiring the world of her husband, sat down and once again tore open her belly with a stone.
That embryo of the eminent sage emerged from her womb, possessing a great and divine body, radiant and illuminating the ten directions.
O dear one, this Dadhīca is a direct incarnation of Rudra; having manifested himself by his own power, he is capable of performing divine sports.
Seeing her own divine son in his true form, Suvarcā, the wife of the sage, recognized in her mind that he was indeed an incarnation of Rudra.
The great virtuous woman became overjoyed; having bowed down quickly, she offered praise and established his true form within her own heart, O Lord of Sages.
Smiling at her son, Suvarcā, the mother with pure eyes, spoke with great affection, desiring the world of her husband.
Suvarcā said: "O dear one, O Supreme Lord, remain for a long time in the presence of this Aśvattha tree; O highly fortunate one, may you be the bestower of happiness upon all."
Command me now with great affection for the sake of the world of my husband; staying there with my husband, I shall meditate upon you in the form of Rudra.
Nandīśvara said: Thus did Suvarcā speak then to her son; that virtuous woman followed her husband with supreme concentration.
O Sage, having thus been reunited with her husband, the wife of Dadhīca reached the world of Śiva and joyfully served Śaṅkara.
In the meantime, O dear one, the gods along with Indra and the sages arrived there in haste, as if summoned, filled with joy.
Hari and Brahmā, together with their own attendants, went with great affection to Śaṅkara, who had descended upon the earth from Dadhīca through Suvarcā.
There, seeing Rudra who had descended and assumed the form of the sage’s son, they all bowed down and offered praise with palms joined together.
Then, O best of sages, there was a great festival for the gods; kettledrums resounded there and dancers danced with joy.
The sons of the Gandharvas and the Kinnaras sang, while the celestial musicians played their instruments; the immortals caused a rain of flowers to fall.
Having performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules for that son of Pippala, the father of Śarva—who was shining with splendor—all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, praised him once again.
Brahmā, with a serene mind, bestowed upon him the name Pippalāda; and he was addressed by Hari and the gods, saying, "Be gracious, O Lord of Devas."
Having spoken thus and granted him permission, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods all departed for their respective abodes after having celebrated a great festival.
Then the great lord Rudra Pippalāda performed austerities for a very long time at the foot of an Aśvattha tree, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
In this manner, as Pippalāda lived his life according to the ways of the world, a great length of time passed in his presence while he was engaged in ascetic penance.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Pippalāda," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Now, O excellent sage, listen to that great divine play which the Lord performed after establishing himself in the world with the desire to establish dharma.
Once, while going to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river, the lord of sages beheld the youthful Padmā, a beautiful and most enchanting portion of Śivā.
Desirous of reaching the abode of his father, King Anaraṇya, he who wanders through the worlds and is skilled in discerning the true nature of things departed.
Seeing him, the king of men, overwhelmed with fear, bowed down and, having offered the madhuparka and other honors, worshipped him with devotion.
Out of affection, the sage accepted everything and requested the maiden; the king became silent, unable to say anything at all.
The sage said to the king: "Give me your daughter with devotion; otherwise, I shall reduce everything, including you, to ashes."
Then all those royal people became shrouded by the splendor of the great sage Pippalāda, the son of Dadhīca.
Then the king, greatly terrified and lamenting again and again, gave the maiden Padmā, adorned with ornaments, to the aged sage.
Having married Padmā, the daughter of King Śivaṃśa, the sage Pippalāda took her and, filled with joy, returned to his own hermitage.
Having gone there, that excellent sage, though advanced in years and worn by age, spoke with that woman; for the ascetic was not at all lustful.
Then that daughter of Aṇaraṇya served the sage with devotion through her actions, mind, and speech, just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa.
Thus that Pippalāda, the best of sages and a portion of Śiva, having become a youth, sported with that young woman through his own divine play.
Ten high-souled sons were born to the sage, who was devoted to great asceticism; they were all equal to their father and increased the happiness of Padmā.
Thus indeed is the playful descent of the great Lord Śaṅkara; the eminent sage Pippalāda is a lord who performs manifold divine sports.
For it was by him, the compassionate one, that out of affection for the worlds—and having seen the unavoidable suffering of everyone in the world caused by Saturn—that boon was granted.
Until the sixteenth year from birth, that [state] shall not occur for men; likewise for the devotees of Śiva—this is indeed my truthful word.
If Śani should ever cause suffering by disregarding my word, then those men shall be reduced to ashes; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O dear one, out of fear of him, even when transformed, Śanaiścara, the best of planets, never inflicts suffering upon them.
Thus has been told to you the virtuous life of the great sage Pippalāda, who appeared as a man by divine play; it bestows the fruit of all desires.
Gādhi, Kauśika, and the great sage Pippalāda—these three, when remembered, destroy the affliction caused by Śanaiścara.
That man on earth who, with great devotion, either reads or even hears this account of Pippalāda, joined with the account of Padmā, [shall attain his desires].
For the purpose of destroying the affliction caused by Saturn, whoever should read or even hear this supreme narrative shall obtain all their desires.
Blessed is the eminent sage, the wise one, the great devotee of Śiva, beloved by the virtuous; his son is Maheśāna, known by the name Pippalāda, who has attained self-mastery.
O dear one, this sinless narrative bestows heaven, removes the nourishment of evil planets, grants all desires, and increases devotion to Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Pippalāda Incarnation," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O dear one, O sage; I shall describe the incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, known as Vaiśyanātha, which is supreme bliss.
Long ago in Nandigrāma, there was a certain courtesan, renowned as Mahānandā, who was a beautiful devotee of Śiva.
Endowed with great wealth, possessing abundant riches, and most resplendent; adorned with various jewels and overflowing with the sentiment of the erotic.
Skilled in all the arts of music and exceedingly captivating, both the queens and the kings were delighted by her singing.
Devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names and adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, that prostitute always joyfully worshipped Śambhu, the benefactor.
Having worshipped Śiva daily and serving the Lord of the Universe, she danced with supreme devotion while singing the glorious praises of Śiva.
Having adorned a monkey and a cock with rudrākṣa beads, she would constantly make them dance to the beat of her palms and to songs.
Seeing those two dancing, that prostitute, who was devoted to the worship of Śiva, laughed aloud with love along with all her companions.
Adorned with armlets and ear-ornaments made of rudrākṣa beads, the monkey dances like a child before her at her instruction.
With rudrākṣa beads fastened to his crest, the cock, an expert in dance, danced constantly together with the monkey, bringing benefit to all who watched.
Acting thus with great devotion and curiosity, that prostitute, who was constantly devoted to Śiva, became filled with supreme bliss.
O best of sages, as that courtesan practiced devotion to Śiva, a great deal of time passed for her in supreme happiness.
And once, having become a Vaiśya in her house, Śiva himself, auspicious and observant of vows, came there to test her disposition.

With his forehead adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), wearing ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, skilled in practice, devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names, matted-haired, and bearing the attire of a devotee of Śiva.
Wearing a mass of ashes and an excellent bracelet studded with great jewels upon his forearm, he shone, full of curiosity for others.
Having honored him who had arrived with supreme joy, that beautiful courtesan respectfully seated the merchant in her own place.
Seeing that most beautiful and excellent bracelet on his wrist, she felt a longing for it and, filled with wonder, spoke to him.
Mahānandā said: "This bracelet made of great jewels, resting upon your hand, immediately captivates my mind; it is worthy of the ornaments of a celestial woman."
Nandīśvara said: Having observed her thus longing for the hand-ornament rich with nine gems, the Vaiśya of noble mind spoke to her with a smile.
Vaiśyanātha said: "If your mind is filled with longing for this divine and excellent jewel, then take it yourself with great joy; what price will you give for it?"
The prostitute said: "We are indeed prostitutes who act according to our own will; we are not devoted wives. Adultery is the dharma appropriate for our family, without a doubt."
If you take this entire necklace as an ornament for your hand, I shall become your wife for three days and nights.
The Vaiśya said: "So be it, O beloved of heroes, if your word is true; I give you this jewel bracelet—be my bride for three nights."
In this legal proceeding, the moon and the sun are my witnesses; having said "Truth" three times, touch my heart, O beloved.
The courtesan said: "O Lord, having been your wife for three days and nights, I shall practice dharma together with you; this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Mahānandā, with great affection, took the moon and the sun as witnesses three times and touched their hearts.
Then that Vaiśya, having given her a jeweled bracelet and placed a linga made of gems into her hand, spoke as follows.
Vaiśyanātha said: "O beloved, this Śaiva Liṅga made of jewels, which is as dear to me as my own life-breath, must be protected by you and guarded with great effort."
Nandīśvara said: Having replied, "So be it," she took the jewel-born liṅga, placed it in the middle of the dance pavilion, and entered her home.
Having united with that Vaiśya, who acted like a libertine, she slept happily upon a couch adorned with a soft bedspread.
Then, at the hour of midnight, by the will of the Vaiśya lord, a voice suddenly arose within the dancing pavilion of the Sage.
O dear one, the great fire, intensely blazing and aided by a favorable wind, suddenly enveloped that very dance pavilion.
While the pavilion was burning, that courtesan rose up suddenly in agitation and released the monkey from its bonds there.
Once released from his bonds, that monkey, shaking off many sparks of fire, fled far away in fear along with that cock.
Seeing that linga, together with the pillar, completely consumed by fire and shattered into fragments, both the prostitute and the merchant fell into unbearable misery.
Having seen his own likeness, the linga, thus consumed by fire, the lord of the Vaiśyas then resolved upon death, desiring to understand that internal state.
The Great Lord, who delights in manifold sports, assumed a human body out of curiosity; seeing her thus distressed, he spoke to that sorrowful woman as she was sinking deeper into exhaustion.
The Lord of the Vaiśyas said: "When the Śiva-liṅga, which is as dear to me as my own life, has been shattered and burnt, I tell you the truth—there is no doubt—I have no desire to live."
"O auspicious lady, have a funeral pyre prepared for me quickly by your excellent servants; fixing my mind on Śiva, I shall enter the fire."
Even if Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the others were to come together and restrain me, nevertheless, O blessed lady, at this very moment I shall enter [the fire] and abandon my life-breaths.
Nandīśvara said: Perceiving him to be so persistent in his resolve, she, deeply distressed, had a funeral pyre prepared by her own servants outside her palace.
Then that wise Vaiśya Śiva, full of curiosity and desiring union, circumambulated the kindled fire alone and entered it while the men looked on.
O best of sages, having witnessed that conduct of his, the courtesan Mahānandā was greatly astonished, and the young woman fell into deep remorse.
Then that distressed courtesan, remembering the perfectly pure Dharma and looking upon all her kinsmen, spoke these piteous words:
Mahānandā said: "Taking the jeweled bracelet, I spoke the truth: 'For three days, I am truly the wife of that merchant, as he has agreed.'"
"By this deed committed by me, this Vaiśya, who was devoted to the vow of Śiva, has died; therefore, I shall enter the fire along with him."
"Abandoned by my preceptors who walk their own dharma and speak the truth—if you act thus out of love for me, may my truthfulness not perish."
Truth is the foundation of the supreme Dharma; through truth comes the highest goal. Through truth come both heaven and liberation; everything is established upon truth.
Nandīśvara said: Thus, though restrained by her kinsmen, that woman, being firm in her resolve and intent upon Satyaloka, set her mind on casting off her life.
Having given away all her possessions to the foremost of the twice-born and meditated upon Sadāśiva, she circumambulated that fire three times and indeed turned toward entering it.
As she was falling into the kindled fire with her mind fixed upon his own feet, Śiva himself—the soul of the universe—manifested and restrained her.
Beholding him—the three-eyed god of all gods, adorned with the crescent moon, and possessing the brilliance of ten million moons, suns, and fires—she stood there as if paralyzed, as if terrified.
Having comforted her—who was overwhelmed, terrified, trembling, and paralyzed—while holding her hands as tears flowed from her eyes, he spoke these words.
Śiva said: "In order to test your truthfulness, righteousness, fortitude, and unwavering devotion to me, I came to your presence having assumed the form of a Vaiśya."
Do not, having kindled the fire, burn down the dance pavilion; having burnt the jewel-liṅga, I have entered the fire.
Since you have entered the fire with me, recollecting the truth, I shall therefore bestow upon you enjoyments difficult even for the gods to obtain.
"Whatever you desire, O fair-hipped one, that very thing I shall give to you; for I am pleased by your devotion, and there is nothing that cannot be given to you."
Nandīśvara said: While Śaṅkara, the lord of Gaurī and lover of his devotees, was speaking thus, that prostitute Mahānandā addressed Śaṅkara.
The courtesan said: "I have no desire for enjoyments on earth, in heaven, or in the netherworld; I do not long for anything other than the touch of your lotus-feet."
My servants and maidservants, and all my other kinsmen, are intent upon beholding you; they have surrendered their livelihoods to you.
Having led all these along with me to my own supreme state, release them from the terrible fear of rebirth; salutations be to you!
Nandīśvara said: Then Maheśvara, having welcomed her words, led all of them together with her to his own supreme abode.
I have thus described to you the supreme incarnation of Vaiśyanātha, which bestows great bliss, removes suffering, and eternally grants joy to his devotees.

This supreme, most purifying, divine, and wondrous life-story of the Lord of Men, who is an incarnation of Śiva, bestows everything upon the virtuous and swiftly grants great bliss and supreme happiness.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind, shall not fall away from their own duty and shall attain a supreme destination in the next world.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, my dear, I shall describe the incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, as Dvijeśvara, which bestows happiness upon the virtuous.
O dear one, that best of kings named Bhadrāyu who was previously described is the one upon whom Śiva bestowed his grace in the form of a bull.
In order to examine that dharma, he appeared once more in the form of a lordly brahmin; I shall relate that very account.
O dear one, by the power of Ṛṣabha, that lord, having conquered his enemies in battle, ascended the throne and became known as Bhadrāyus.
O Brahmin, Kīrtimālinī, the daughter of Candrāṅgada and the auspiciously born daughter of Sīmantinī, became his wife; she was a most virtuous woman.
O Sage, once during the spring season, that Bhadrāyu entered a dense forest with his beloved for the sake of recreation.
Then that king sported in that delightful forest together with his beloved wife, who was the protector of those who sought refuge.
Then, awaiting the firm establishment of that Dharma, the Supreme Lord Śaṅkara performed a divine play right there together with Śivā.
Having both become Śivā and Śiva, that brahmin couple appeared in that forest through their own divine play, having created a tiger made of illusion.
Then, not far from that very spot, the two of them were running, overwhelmed by fear; pursued by the tiger, they continued to run while weeping.
Then, O dear one, when those two had been pierced, that lord of the earth, Bhadrāyus—the refuge of all and a bull among kṣatriyas—beheld them indeed crying out for protection.
Then those two tigers among sages, appearing as a brahmin couple through their own power of illusion, spoke to the great king Bhadrāyu, who was overwhelmed with fear.
The brahmin couple said: "Save us, save us, O Great King, you who are most knowledgeable in dharma! O Great Lord, this tiger is coming here to devour us both."
For this beast is violent, equal to Time itself, and a source of terror to all living beings; before it reaches and devours us, protect us, O knower of dharma!
Nandīśvara said: Having heard their lamentation in this manner, O lord of kings, that great hero very quickly took up his bow.
Just then, a highly deceptive tiger approached in great haste and seized that bride in the midst of that best of brahmins.
"O Lord of lords! O Beloved! Alas, Śambhu! O Teacher of the World!"—while she was thus wailing piteously, a terrifying tiger seized her.
Then the king struck the tiger with sharp, broad-headed arrows; yet it was not pained by them in the least, like the king of mountains by showers of rain.
That great being, Śārdūla, causing pain to the king at his own will, forcibly dragged that woman away and departed with haste.
Seeing the woman carried off by a tiger, the brahmin was greatly astonished; resorting to worldly ways, he wept excessively again and again.
Having wept for a long time, that Brahmin, the Lord who removes pride through his illusory power, spoke to King Bhadrāyuṣa.
The Lord of the Twice-born said: "O King, where are your great weapons? Where is your great protection, your mighty bow? Where is your strength, equal to twelve thousand great elephants?"
What use have you for your sword, or what use for your conch? What use for your knowledge of mantras and missiles, or what use for the power of your great weapons, or even for your vast majesty?
All of that has become fruitless, as well as whatever else resides within you—you who are not capable of preventing the slaughter of the forest-dwellers.
This is the supreme duty of a Kshatriya: the protection of the oppressed. Now that this duty, which is appropriate for your lineage, has perished, what is the use of your life?
Kings who know the Dharma provide protection for those who are distressed and have sought their refuge, even at the cost of their own lives and wealth; without doing so, they are like the dead.
For those deprived of protection from distress, death is better than life; for the wealthy who lack the means to drink, the state of a mendicant is better than the life of a householder.
It is better for the wise to consume poison or enter the fire than to fail to protect those who are miserable, helpless, and wretched.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard his lamentation and his self-reproach regarding his own prowess, the king, out of grief, reflected thus within himself.
Alas! My manliness has been destroyed today due to this reversal of fortune from the gods; today my fame has perished, and a terrible sin has been incurred.
The family tradition of dharma has been lost by me, unfortunate and evil-minded; surely my wealth, kingdom, and life itself shall come to an end.
And today, by giving up my own life which is so dear to me, I shall free this twice-born man from his grief, for he is afflicted by sorrow because his wife has been killed.
Having thus resolved in his mind, that best of kings, Bhadrāyu, fell at his feet and spoke, consoling him.
Bhadrāyu said: "O Brahmin, having shown compassion toward me, a mere kṣatriya of diminished luster, cast off your grief, O man of great wisdom; today I shall grant you whatever you desire."
"This kingdom, this queen, and even this body of mine—all this is at your disposal; what boon do you desire?"

The Brahmin said: What is the use of a mirror to a blind man? What is the use of a house to one who lives on alms? What is the use of a book to a fool? And what is the use of wealth to one who has no wife?
Therefore, having lost my wife and having already enjoyed all pleasures, I never again desire this chief queen of yours; let her be given to me.
He was a giver of wealth ending in the essence of mercury, of kingdoms, of elephants and horses, and even of his own body and wife—at no time was there anything he would not give.
The sin that has been accumulated through the enjoyment of another's wife cannot be washed away even by hundreds of expiatory rites.
The Brahmin said: "Let alone the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin or even the consumption of liquor; I shall dispel them by means of austerity—how much more so the sin of adultery?"
Therefore, give me your own wife; I have no other desire. By failing to protect those afflicted by fear, you will certainly go to hell.
Nandīśvara said: Thus, terrified by the words of the brahmin, the king reflected: "The great sin incurred by failing to protect [the sage] is better than giving away my wife."
Therefore, having given my wife to the foremost of the twice-born and being thus freed from sin, I shall immediately enter the fire, and my fame shall become known.
Having thus resolved in his mind and kindled the sacrificial fire, he summoned that twice-born man and performed the gift of his wife along with the libation of water.
Having bathed himself and become pure, he bowed to the lords of the gods; having circumambulated that fire three times, he meditated on Śiva with a concentrated mind.
Then, as he was about to leap into the fire with his mind fixed upon his own feet, the Lord of All, the Sovereign of the Twice-born, appeared and restrained him.

To that Lord—five-faced, three-eyed, wielder of the Pināka bow, adorned with the crescent moon, possessing a mass of long, tawny matted locks, and possessing the brilliance of ten million midday suns.

White as a lotus stalk, clad in an elephant hide, with the region of his head sprinkled by the waves of the Gaṅgā, adorned with a necklace of great serpents around his neck, and resplendent with a crown, a waistband, armlets, and bracelets.

The king beheld before him the Lord who had emerged, holding in his eight hands a trident, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga staff, an axe, a shield, a deer, the gesture of fearlessness, and the Pināka bow; he was seated upon a bull and adorned with a dark-blue throat.
Then, divine showers of flowers fell swiftly from the sky; celestial instruments resounded, and goddesses danced and sang.
There they arrived while being praised: Hari, Brahmā, as well as the Asuras, Indra and the others, Nārada and the other sages, and yet others as well.
Then there was a great festival that increased devotion, while the king looked on with his hands joined in reverence, bowed down by faith.

His heart expanding with the joy of that vision, his body drenched by a flood of rising tears, his hair standing on end, he praised [the Lord] with words in a faltering voice, his hands joined in the *añjali* gesture like a bud.
Then the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, praised by the king, being pleased along with Pārvatī, that treasure-house of compassion, spoke to him.
"O King, I am thoroughly pleased with your devotion, which exceeds even your religious merit. Choose a boon, along with your wife; I shall grant it to you, there is no doubt."
I have come here having become a brahmin for the purpose of testing your disposition; she who was seized by the tiger is indeed the goddess Śivā herself.
That tiger made of illusion, whose body remained unhurt by your arrows, desired to test your fortitude; it was for him that I requested your wife.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of the Lord, King Bhadrāyu bowed again, offered praise to his master, and with a prostrate body spoke.
Bhadrāyu said: "O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, this alone is my one boon: that you have become manifest before me, who am scorched by the heat of worldly existence."
Furthermore, O Lord, O Master, whatever boon you grant out of your own compassion, I choose this supreme boon from you, the best among the givers of boons: that I be abandoned by you.
O Maheśvara, my father Vajrabāhu was indeed accompanied by his wife; O Lord, I too am accompanied by my wife, yet I am always a servant at your feet.
O Maheśāna, there is a Vaiśya named Padmākara, and his son is called Sanaya; always keep all of them by your side.
Nandīśvara said: Then the queen, his wife Kīrtimālinī, being heedless, propitiated Giriśa with devotion and requested an excellent boon.
Satyu said: "Candrāṅgada is my father and Sīmantinī is my mother; O Mahādeva, I joyfully beg for their presence by your side."
Nandīśvara said: "So be it," said the Lord of Gaurī, who is gracious and affectionate toward his devotees; having granted them their desired boons, he vanished in an instant.
Bhadrāyu, having attained the grace of the wielder of the trident with great joy, enjoyed many worldly pleasures together with Kīrtimālinī.
Having ruled for a kingdom of ten thousand years with unimpeded prowess, he entrusted the kingdom to his son and went into the presence of Śiva.
Candrāṅgada, that lord of kings, and his queen Sīmantinī, having worshipped Giriśa with devotion, went to the abode of Śambhu.
O Lord, you have described to me this supreme incarnation of Maheśvara as Dvijeśvara, which bestows the highest bliss upon Bhadrāyu.

This supreme and most purifying life-story of the incarnation of Śiva, whose fame is pure—the story of the one known as Dvijeśa—is truly most wonderful; by hearing or reciting it, one attains the state of Śambhu.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind, does not deviate from their own duty and attains a favorable rebirth in the next world.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O wise one, O sage; I shall describe the ancient incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, known by the name Yātinātha, which brings supreme bliss.
O lord of sages, on the mountain named Arbuda, there lived a descendant of the Bhilla clan named Āhuka in its vicinity.
His wife was indeed named Āhukā, who was devoted to her vows; both of them were great Śaivas and worshippers of Śiva.
O Sage, at one time, a Bhilla who was always devoted to Śiva went very far away for the sake of food for his wife.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara, having assumed the form of an ascetic, arrived at that house in the evening for the sake of testing the Bhilla.
At that moment, the wise master of the house arrived there and, out of love, performed the worship of the Lord of Ascetics.
To examine that state of being, Śaṅkara, in the form of an ascetic and intent on his great divine play, spoke with affection to the frightened one whose voice was wretched.
Yatinātha said: "O Bhilla, give me this place for my residence this very day; I shall depart at dawn. May it always be well with you."
The Bhilla said: "O Lord, what you have spoken is true; now hear my words as well. My dwelling place is indeed very small; how could it be for you?"
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by him, the ascetic set his mind on departing; meanwhile, the Bhilla woman spoke these words, having indeed reflected upon her husband.
The Bhilla said: "O Master, give a place to this ascetic; do not turn away a guest. Reflect upon the duty of a householder; otherwise, there will be a destruction of dharma."
"Please remain comfortably inside the house with the ascetic; I shall stay outside, even though my weapons are large."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of the Bhilla woman, which were endowed with righteousness and auspiciousness, that Bhilla reflected upon them in his mind along with his wife.
Having sent the woman outside, how could I remain here? For a mendicant, going elsewhere would be unrighteous for oneself.
Neither of these two courses is at all appropriate for a householder; whatever is destined to happen will surely happen, so I must remain outside the home.
Having thus made his request, the Bhilla joyfully stayed those two inside the house, and after depositing their weapons there, he remained outside the dwelling.
At night, cruel and predatory beasts tormented him; yet he, too, then exerted a great effort according to his power.
Even though he was strong, that Bhilla, despite making such an effort, was forcibly devoured by predatory beasts impelled by his past karma (*prārabdha*).
Having risen in the morning and seeing the Bhilla who had been wandering in the forest devoured by predatory beasts, that ascetic indeed became exceedingly distressed.
Seeing that ascetic in such distress, the Bhilla woman, though she herself was suffering, restrained her own grief through fortitude and spoke these words.
The Bhilla said: "O ascetic, why do you grieve? What has happened now is auspicious. Blessed and fulfilled is he for whom such a death as this has come to pass."
O ascetic, I too shall follow him, becoming ashes in the fire; prepare the funeral pyre with great joy, for this is the eternal dharma of women.
Having heard those words and considering them beneficial, the ascetic himself prepared a funeral pyre; she then entered it in accordance with her own dharma.
In the meantime, Śiva himself appeared before her; praising her with affection, Hara said, "O blessed one! O blessed one! and spoke to her.
Hara said: "Choose a boon, O sinless one; I am pleased with your conduct. There is indeed nothing that cannot be given to you; I am especially subject to your will."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of Śambhu, which bestow supreme bliss, he attained extraordinary happiness and did not remember anything else at all.
Observing her state of mind, Hara became exceedingly pleased; and the Lord Śambhu spoke again to her, saying, "Choose a boon."
Śiva said: "This ascetic, who is my own form, shall take the form of a swan; out of affection, he will bring about your union with him in a future birth."
And the Bhillas will have a great son named Nala in the excellent city of Niṣadha; of this there is no doubt. He will be the son of Vīrasena.
O sinless one, you shall be the daughter of King Bhīma in the city of Vidarbha, and you will become renowned as Damayantī, endowed with all virtues.
And both of you, having united and enjoyed the most extensive royal pleasures, will certainly attain liberation, which is difficult even for the lords of yogis to obtain.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Śambhu himself then assumed the form of a liṅga; because he did not waver from his dharma, he is remembered as Acaleśa (the Immovable Lord).
That Bhilla and Āhuka became the sons of Vīrasena; O dear one, in the city of Niṣadha there was a great king named Nala.
That great Bhilla woman, Āhukā, became the daughter of Bhīma; in the city of Vidarbha, she was renowned as Damayantī, the wife of the king.
Śiva, known by the name Yatīnātha, also assumed the form of a swan and indeed caused the marriage of Damayantī with Nala to take place.
By means of that great merit resulting from his previous act of hospitality, the Lord Śaṅkara assumed the form of a swan and bestowed happiness upon the two of them.
Śiva, indeed, is the incarnation as Haṃsa, skilled in various narratives, and the bestower of supreme bliss upon both Damayantī and Nala.
This supreme and most sacred life-story of the incarnation of Śiva, whose fame is pure—the story of him known as Yatīśa and also called Haṃsa—is indeed most wonderful and bestows liberation.
Whoever hears or causes others to hear this auspicious account of the incarnations known as Yatīśa and Brahmahamsa shall indeed attain the supreme goal.
This narrative is sinless, bestowing the fruits of all desires; it leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, and is the supreme enhancer of devotion.
Having heard this account of Śambhu’s deeds while in the forms of the ascetic and the swan, one shall enjoy every happiness in this world and, at the end, go to the city of Śiva.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deeds of the Incarnation of Śiva Known as Yatinātha Brahmahaṃsa," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third section of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O Sanatkumāra, listen to the supreme incarnation of Śambhu, which bestows knowledge upon the world and is known as Kṛṣṇadarśana, the most excellent.
Those who were the sons of Śrāddhadeva had Ikṣvāku as their chief; among them, Nabha was the ninth, and Nābhaga is recorded as his son.
His son was Ambarīṣa, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu; Durvāsas became pleased with him because of his devotion to Brahman.
O Sage, listen to the life-story of Ambarīṣa’s grandfather, who is celebrated as Nabhaga, to whom Śiva imparted spiritual knowledge.
Nabhaga, the son of Manu, being highly intelligent and having conquered his senses, lived for a long time in the house of a preceptor for the purpose of study.
At that time, those sons, headed by Ikṣvāku, did not allot any portion to him, but instead took their own respective portions in due order.
Having each taken their respective shares, those highly fortunate and wise ones enjoyed the excellent kingdom without despondency, in accordance with the command of their father.
Later, that student returned there from the teacher’s abode, having studied all the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs in due order, as well as the Nabhaga [treatise].
O Sage, seeing all his own brothers divided, Nabhaḥ, desiring his inheritance, spoke out of affection to those led by Ikṣvāku.
Nabhaga said: "O brothers, having divided my share of the inheritance exactly as it was, you have all been well-pleased and have given to me who has come for the sake of my own portion."
"At that time we forgot about it, but now we shall divide your father's portion; take it, there is no doubt."
Having heard those words of his brother, Nabhaga was overcome with astonishment; he then approached his father and spoke to him.
Nabhaga said: "O father, all my brothers abandoned me and divided [the inheritance] among themselves; I, however, went to the family of my preceptor as a celibate student for the purpose of study."
Then, having come here, they respectfully asked me for the purpose of an inheritance; they said to me, "Divide [the property] for us," and for that reason I have come.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, having heard those words of his, Śrāddhadeva, the father, being amazed, consoled him who was devoted to truth and righteousness and spoke to him.
Manu said: "Do not speak thus, my dear; for that is indeed deceptive. For I am by no means the supreme inheritance, which is the means for all enjoyments."
Nevertheless, I have been given by those deceivers as their inheritance; listen now to the truth as I tell you the means for your livelihood.
Today the wise sages of the Aṅgirasa lineage are performing a sacrificial session; therein they become bewildered regarding the ritual procedure on every sixth day.
Go there, O Nabhaga; praise them well, O great poet, for then the sacrificial session will indeed consist of two hymns to the Viśvedevas and it shall be perfectly pure.
For when that ritual is completed, those Brāhmaṇas who have reached the end of their own [studies] will, being satisfied, give you the wealth remaining from their sacrifice.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of his father, Nabhaga, whose essence was truth, went with great joy to the place where that supreme sacrifice was being held.
Then, O Sage, during that sacrificial session, that wise descendant of Manu clearly recited two hymns dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
When the ritual was completed, those Brahmins and the descendants of Aṅgiras gave him what remained from their sacrificial session and departed for their respective heavens.
Knowing that he was about to accept those very things remaining from the excellent sacrifice, Giriśa immediately manifested himself along with his messenger.
The glorious person whose form is Kṛṣṇa, beautiful in every limb, has come to observe their disposition and to bestow that supreme knowledge and its portion.
Then Śaṅkara, Śambhu, the Lord who performs the test, approached from the north and spoke to that man, Nabhaga.
Īśvara said: "Who are you, O man, that seizes this property of mine? By whom have you been sent? Tell me everything truthfully before me."
Nandīśvara said: O dear one, having heard those words, the wise Mānava Nabhaga, with a humble soul, replied to the Puruṣa who appeared as Kṛṣṇa.
Nabhaga said: "This wealth, belonging to a sacrifice, was indeed given to me by the sages. Why do you prevent me, O Kṛṣṇadarśana, as I am taking it?"
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Nābhaga, which were spoken with truth, the person who had the appearance of Kṛṣṇa, being pleased in spirit, replied.
Kṛṣṇadarśana said: "O dear one, in this dispute between us, your father is indeed the authority. Go and ask him; he will speak that which is the truth as the authoritative standard."
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, having heard those words of his, the wise Nabhaga Mānava approached his father with affection and asked him about what had been said.
Having heard what was spoken by his son, Manu, the god of the Śrāddha rites, remembered the lotus feet of Śiva; his memory restored, he spoke to him.
Manu said: "O dear one, listen to my words: that god is Śiva, the Supreme Person; everything belongs to him alone, especially that which is obtained through sacrifice."
"The substance remaining from the sacrifice is proclaimed as the portion of Rudra"—this wise saying indeed arose in some instances by His will.
That divine Lord deserves everything without a doubt; how much more so the remnants of the sacrifice? For he is the omnipresent one, acting according to his own will.
The Lord has come here in that form for the sake of bestowing grace upon you; therefore, O Nabhaga, go there and truly propitiate him.
Seek forgiveness for your own offense, bow deeply, and offer praise; he alone is the Lord of all, the Master of sacrifice, and the Sovereign of the universe.
O dear one, even the gods such as Viṣṇu and Brahmā, as well as the Siddhas and all the ṛṣis, are indeed capable in every action only through his grace.
O best of sons, what is the use of much speaking? Go there quickly without delay and propitiate Mahādeva, the Lord of all, in every way.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Manu, the god of funeral rites (Śrāddhadeva), quickly dispatched his son to the presence of Śambhu; and he, having approached him, [did so].
And Nabhaga, bowing quickly with joined palms and head inclined, spoke with humility, his great intellect possessed by a most serene mind.
Nabhaga said: "O Lord, all this indeed belongs to you, whatever exists within the three worlds"—thus my father surely said; how much more so that which remains from the sacrifice?
O Protector, whatever words were spoken by me through ignorance and delusion, please forgive that offense; I propitiate you with my head bowed low.
Having spoken thus, Nabhaḥ, his mind exceedingly dejected, with palms joined in reverence, praised Maheśāna, bowing down before him who has Kṛṣṇa as his vision.
The wise Śrāddhadeva, pure in soul and bowing with palms joined in reverence, prostrated before the Lord, praised him, and asked for forgiveness for his transgression.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the omniscient and wise one, Vāsava and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas and the sages, arrived there.
Performing a great festival, all those who were abodes of merit praised him with devotion after bowing down individually and prostrating themselves.
Then Rudra, his soul serene and beholding them with a compassionate gaze, spoke with affection and a smile to Nabhaga, having seen Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇadarśana said: "That righteous speech which your father spoke is indeed exactly so; you too have spoken the truth, and you are a virtuous man—of this there is no doubt."
Therefore, I am well-pleased with your excellent vow in every respect; out of compassion for you, I grant you the eternal Brahman-knowledge.
Become indeed a possessor of great wisdom along with your priest; quickly accept all these goods now given by me out of compassion.
O Mahāmati, enjoy all happiness here without change; for through my compassion, you and the brahmins shall attain a happy rebirth.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, O dear one, the blessed Lord Rudra, who is affectionate toward the truth, vanished right there while everyone was looking on.
O best of sages, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and all the gods and others, having bowed with joy to that direction, returned to their respective abodes with delight.
Śrāddhadeva, together with his son, also returned to his own abode with joy; having enjoyed vast pleasures, he went at last to the city of Śiva.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this incarnation of Śiva been described to you; it is indeed named Kṛṣṇadarśana, which bestows bliss upon Nabhaga.
This sinless narrative bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the virtuous; for those who read or even hear it, it grants the fruit of all desires.
The wise person who remembers this account in the morning and in the evening becomes a poet and a knower of mantras; in the end, he shall attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of Kṛṣṇa and the Incarnation of Śiva," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Nandīśvara and Sanatkumāra.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O son of Brahmā, to this incarnation of the Supreme Lord known as Avadhūteśvara, which indeed removes the pride of Śakra.
O Sage, in ancient times, Śakra, accompanied by his preceptor and all the gods, went to Kailāsa in order to have a vision of the Lord.
Then, having learned of the arrival of his Guru and Indra, Śaṅkara, wishing to test the disposition of those two whose souls were devoted to beholding him, [acted].
The Lord, whose nature is that of an Avadhūta, performed various divine sports; he was naked, most formidable, and possessed a splendor like a blazing fire.
Indeed, that Śambhu, whose true nature is the Avadhūta and who is the goal of the virtuous, stood blocking the path with his form resplendent, wearing a hanging cloth.
Then, as Guru and Śakra were proceeding toward the presence of Śiva, they beheld a terrifying man of wondrous form in the middle of the path.
Then Śakra, intoxicated by his own authority, questioned the Sage, not realizing that Śaṅkara was standing within his own path as that very Person.
Śakra said: Who are you, appearing like a naked ascetic (digambara), and from where have you come? What is your renowned name? Tell me the truth without delay.
Is Śambhu established in his own abode, or has he gone elsewhere now? For I shall go with my guru and the gods for the sake of beholding him.
Nandīśvara said: Thus questioned by Śakra, that Puruṣa, the Lord Śaṅkara, who had assumed a body through his divine play and who destroys pride, did not say anything at all.
Śakra questioned him again, but that naked one did not speak; Śambhu, whose ways are inscrutable, creates great wonder.
Again Purandara, the sovereign lord of the three worlds, questioned him; yet that great yogi, the performer of great divine sports, remained silent.
Thus questioned again and again by Śakra, the Blessed One, who was naked, said nothing, desiring to destroy Śakra’s pride.
Then the Lord of the Gods, arrogant with the sovereignty over the three worlds, became enraged; rebuking the matted-haired one, he spoke these words in anger.
Indra said: "O fool, although you were questioned, you did not give an answer; therefore, I shall strike you with my thunderbolt. O evil-minded one, who is there to protect you?"
Having spoken thus, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrī) then looked at him with wrath and raised his thunderbolt to strike the naked one.
Seeing Śakra with the thunderbolt in his hand, Sadāśiva, the benefactor Śaṅkara, quickly paralyzed the fall of that thunderbolt.
Then that man, enraged, with terrifying eyes and fearsome in appearance, suddenly blazed up as if burning with his fiery splendor.
With an inner fury born from the obstruction of his arms, the Lord of Śacī burned like a serpent whose power has been restrained by a mantra.
Seeing that man blazing with his own splendor, Vṛhaspati reflected upon him with his intellect and quickly bowed down to Hara.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the noble-minded Guru bowed again like a staff before the Lord and praised him with devotion.
The Guru said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge; be gracious, O Lord of Gaurī, Sovereign of all; salutations unto you!
Deluded by your māyā, even all those beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu do not know you in truth; they know you only through your grace.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus praised Lord Śaṅkara, Bṛhaspati then caused Purandara to fall at the feet of that Lord.
Then, O dear one, the preceptor of the gods, the noble-minded and wise Bṛhaspati, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low with humility, spoke this.
Bṛhaspati said: O Mahādeva, Lord of the distressed, I bow at your feet; lift me up and grant me the truth—do not show anger, but show favor.
Be pleased, O Mahādeva; protect Indra who has come to you for refuge. This fire, born from the eye on your forehead, is approaching.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of his guru, the Lord, who had assumed the form of an avadhūta, spoke while smiling; he was an ocean of compassion and acted as a messenger for the virtuous.
Avadhūta said: "I shall restrain this splendor that has issued forth from my eyes due to anger; for how indeed can a serpent take back its slough once it has been cast off?"
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Śaṅkara, Bṛhaspati, his mind agitated by fear, spoke again with palms joined in reverence.
Bṛhaspati said: O Lord, O Blessed One, devotees are indeed always worthy of compassion; O Śaṅkara, make true your own name, "the one who is affectionate toward his devotees."
O Lord of Gods, you ought not to cast your own exceedingly fierce splendor elsewhere; as the uplifter of all devotees, please uplift Purandara.

Nandīśvara said: Thus addressed by his preceptor, Rudra—the one who bears the name "Bhaktavatsala" (the one who is affectionate toward devotees), whose soul is serene, and who removes the distress of those who bow before him—replied to Surejya (Bṛhaspati).
Rudra said: "O Preceptor of the Gods, I am pleased with you; I grant you an excellent boon. By restoring life to Indra, you shall attain the renown of being 'Jīva' (the Reviver)."
"This fire which has arisen from the eye on my forehead, capable of consuming the gods—I shall cast it far away so that it does not afflict Indra."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, he took hold of his own wondrous fiery splendor, which had arisen from the eye on his forehead, and cast it into the salt waters.
Then that splendor of Śiva, which had arisen from the eye on his forehead, was cast into the salt ocean and immediately became a child.
He became the lord of the asuras named Jalandhara, the son of the Ocean; the Lord Maheśāna slew him at the request of the gods.
Having thus performed his virtuous conduct, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, then vanished while in the form of an Avadhūta.
All the gods became happy and entirely free from fear; Guru and Śakra, released from danger, attained supreme bliss.
Having obtained a vision of him for whose sake they had set out, the preceptor and Śakra, their purpose fulfilled, returned to their own abodes with joy.
I have described to you that incarnation of the Supreme Lord known as Avadhūteśvara, who bestows supreme bliss and inflicts punishment upon the wicked.
This narrative is sinless, conducive to fame, and leads to heaven; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is divine, and grants the fruit of all desires.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind, shall enjoy every happiness in this world and, at the end, attain the state of Śiva.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Incarnation of Śiva as Avadhūteśvara," in the dialogue between Nandīśvara and Sanatkumāra, within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Now, O best of sages, I shall describe to you, O Brahmin, the incarnation of Śambhu, which, out of compassion for his devotees, destroys the doubt regarding womanhood.
In the land of Vidarbha, there was a king named Satyaratha; he was righteous-souled, devoted to truth, and beloved by the great devotees of Śiva.
O Sage, as that king protected the earth with righteousness, a great length of time passed in happiness through his adherence to the auspicious dharma.
Once, a great battle took place between that king and the Śālvas, who were besieging his city with vast armies arrogant in their strength.
Having waged a fierce battle with them, that king of Vidarbha, his vast army destroyed, was slain by the Śālvas through the turn of fate.
When that king had been slain in battle by the Śālvas, the remaining soldiers, overwhelmed with fear, fled together with the ministers.
Then, O Sage, his great queen, who was pregnant, went out at night from her own city while being diligently besieged by enemies.
Tormented by grief, that queen emerged and slowly departed; she went far toward the eastern direction, remembering the lotus feet of the Lord.
Then at dawn, that queen beheld a clear lake, for she had traveled a long distance through the grace of Śaṅkara.
Having arrived there, the king’s beloved wife, distressed and delicate, took refuge at the edge of the lake under a shady tree for the sake of dwelling.
There, by the power of destiny, at an auspicious moment endowed with all excellent qualities, the queen gave birth to a divine son, marked by every auspicious characteristic.
Then, by chance, the king’s wife, her mother, being exceedingly thirsty, descended into a lake for the purpose of drinking and was seized by a crocodile in the water.
As soon as he was born, that son—bereft of father and mother—cried out intensely on the shore of the lake, afflicted by hunger and thirst.
O Sage, as soon as that son was born and began crying in that forest, Maheśa, the inner witness and protector, became filled with compassion.
Impelled by the mind of the Lord who removes all fear, a certain woman, wandering for her livelihood as a mendicant, arrived there unexpectedly.
While carrying her own one-year-old child, that widow saw there a single, helpless infant who was crying out.
O sage, having seen that young man there in the uninhabited forest, that brahmin woman was struck with wonder and reflected deeply within her heart.
"Aha! A truly great marvel has now been seen by me—one that is inconceivable and beyond description, in every way, by either mind or speech."
The infant, the best among the radiant, lay alone upon the earth with his umbilical cord uncut, crying out though deprived of his mother.
He has no father or others here to assist him; what could have been the cause? Ah, how great indeed is the power of destiny!
I do not know whose son he is, nor is there anyone here who knows him; therefore, O mother, I ask you, for compassion has arisen within me.
"I wish indeed to nourish him like my own biological son; yet, without knowing his lineage, birth, and other such details, I do not venture to question him."
Nandīśvara said: While that excellent brahmin woman was thus reflecting, Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, bestowed great grace upon her.

Indeed, Maheśvara, the Great Performer of Divine Play, who is eternally free from all limiting conditions and always personally bestowing happiness upon his devotees in every way, assumed the form of a mendicant.
Thereupon, that supreme lord, the monk, suddenly arrived at the place where the brahmin woman, filled with doubt, was desiring to know.
The Lord, whose true nature is that of an eminent monk and whose movements are unknown, being a treasury of compassion, smiled and spoke to that Brahmin woman.
The eminent monk said: "O beautiful Brahmin lady, do not harbor doubt in your mind; do not grieve. Protect this boy with affection, for he is as pure as your own son."
"Through this child you shall attain the supreme good before long; therefore, nourish in every way this infant of great splendor."
Nandīśvara said: To him who had spoken thus—the storehouse of compassion in the form of a mendicant—that Brahmin woman respectfully and affectionately questioned Śambhu.
