The Brahmin’s wife said: "By your command, I shall indeed protect this boy like my own son; I shall nourish him, of this there is no doubt. It is by my good fortune that you have come here."
Nevertheless, I wish to know this specifically and in accordance with reality: who is he, whose son is he, and who are you that have come here?
O Lord, best of monks, knowledge repeatedly comes to me: "You are Śiva, the ocean of compassion; this child was formerly your devotee."
"Due to some fault of past karma, he has reached this state; having experienced its fruit, he shall attain the highest good through your grace."
Indeed, by your very māyā, I have become deluded and lost my way; sent by you, I have come for the purpose of protecting this [child].
Nandīśvara said: Thus, Śiva, in the form of a mendicant, spoke to that Brahmin woman who had attained wisdom through that vision and who especially desired to know more.

The excellent monk said: "Listen with affection, O wife of the brahmin, to the past deeds of this boy. O sinless one, everything concerning another shall be told to you with great pleasure and in accordance with the truth."
He is the son of the wise Satyaratha, king of Vidarbha, who was devoted to Śiva and dedicated to his own duty.
Listen: King Satyaratha was slain by his enemies in battle at Śālva; his wife, greatly distressed, departed quickly from her home in the night.
Having arrived here at dawn, she indeed gave birth to this son; then, descending into the lake while overcome by thirst, she was seized by a crocodile through the power of fate.
Nandīśvara said: Thus he related to him everything—the origin of his birth, the death of his father in battle, and the death of his mother by a crocodile.
Then, O Lord of Sages, that Brahmāṇī, being truly amazed, questioned again that wise mendicant who possessed the form of a perfected one (siddha).

The Brāhmaṇī said: O mendicant, why indeed was his father, that king, struck down by the Śālvas—his enemies—who possessed only meager wealth, while he himself was in the midst of excellent enjoyments?
Why was the mother of this infant quickly devoured by a crocodile? Because he was born without a protector and indeed without kinsmen from birth.
"Why is it that my son here has become such a very poor beggar? O Bhikṣu, tell me how there might be happiness for these two sons."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of hers, that mendicant, the Supreme Lord, with a gracious soul, spoke to the Brahmin’s wife while smiling.
The excellent monk said: "O wife of the brahmin, I shall answer all your questions in detail; listen with careful attention to this supreme narrative."
The father of this boy is that lord of Vidarbha; in a previous birth, he was that most excellent of kings, Pāṇḍya.
That Śaiva king, protecting the entire earth according to dharma and destroying all calamities, delighted his own subjects.
Once, on the thirteenth lunar day at dusk, he worshipped Śiva, the Lord of All, remaining without food and observing the vow of eating only during the day and night.
While he was worshipping Śambhu, the Mountain-Dweller, at nightfall with devotion, a great and most formidable sound then arose everywhere in the city.
Having heard that sound, the king, abandoning his worship of Śiva, went out from his palace out of fear that an enemy had arrived.
At that very time, however, his powerful minister, a vassal who had taken up arms, approached the presence of the king.
Seeing that enemy feudatory, he was overwhelmed by great rage and, without reflection, ordered the decapitation of Vṛṣanta.
While the worship of Śiva remained incomplete, the king—impure, his intellect lost, and devoid of auspiciousness—joyfully took his meal at night.
In Vidarbha, there was a king who, in this life, had observed the vow of Śiva; however, due to an interruption in his worship of Śiva caused by others, he was deprived of his enjoyments midway.
He who was my son in a previous birth became my son in this life; it is I alone who have been deprived of my sovereignty due to the neglect of Śiva’s worship.
In a previous birth, his mother deceitfully took the life of her co-wife; indeed, because of that sin, she was devoured by this crocodile in this present birth.
This conduct of theirs has been described to you: if Śivā is not honored with devotion, they fall into poverty.
This son of yours was, in a previous birth, an excellent Brahmin who spent his life accepting gifts rather than through virtuous deeds such as sacrifices.
Therefore, O lady of the twice-born, your son has fallen into poverty; for the sake of removing that fault, go for refuge to Śaṅkara.
"Indeed, let the worship of Śiva be performed by these two boys; for after the sacred thread has been put on, Śiva will bring about their welfare."
Nandīśvara said: Having thus instructed her, Śiva, who is most affectionate toward his devotees, revealed his supreme true form, having assumed the body of an excellent mendicant.
Then that Brahmin woman, recognizing him as the Lord Śaṅkara, bowed deeply and praised him with love, her voice faltering with emotion.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, having quickly assumed the body of a mendicant, vanished right there while she was looking on and trying to seize him.
Then, after that monk had departed, the brahmin woman, feeling confident, took that infant along with her own son and went home.
Having established her residence in the delightful village called Ekacakrā, she nourished her own son and the prince with excellent foods.
Having had the purificatory rites performed for them by Brahmins and having undergone the initiation ceremony, the two grew up in their own home, devoted to the worship of Śiva.
O dear one, by the command of the sage Śāṇḍilya, those two, established in their observances, performed the auspicious vow and offered worship to Śambhu at the time of dusk.
Once, that prince went to bathe in the river without his brahmin son and found an excellent jar containing a treasure.
As the king and the young brahmin thus worshipped Śambhu, the four months passed for them in perfect ease.
As they continued to worship Śambhu with even greater joy, a full year passed away in that very house of theirs.
O Sage, when a year had passed, that prince went to the edge of the forest with a brahmin, by the grace of the omnipresent Lord Śiva.
Having married the daughter of Gandharva—who had arrived there unexpectedly and been given by her father—he ruled a kingdom free from all thorns.
The Brahmin woman who had previously nourished him like her own son became his mother, and that son of the twice-born became his brother.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, he who was indeed named Dharmagupta enjoyed pleasures with that queen in the territory of Vidarbha.
I have now described to you the entry of the excellent monk, which brings happiness to Prince Dharmagupta of Śiva.
This narrative is faultless, sacred, purifying, and great; it is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, and it grants all desires.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind, having enjoyed all desires here in this world, shall at the end go to the city of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Life of the Incarnation of Śiva Known as Bhikṣuvarya," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Listen, dear one, I shall describe to you the incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, as Sureśvara, which brings about your welfare, O elder brother of Dhaumya.
The wise Upamanyu, son of Vyāghrapāda and beloved of the virtuous, was perfected through another birth and attained the state of a young sage.
Like a mere child with his mother, Upamanyu lived in the house of his maternal uncle; he was known as Vyāghrapādi, and by fate he was poor.
Once, having drunk very little milk at his maternal uncle's hermitage, he, longing for milk, affectionately begged his mother many times.
Having heard those words of her son, his ascetic mother then entered within and devised an auspicious plan.
Having ground seeds earned through the practice of gleaning and stirred them with water, she gave that artificial milk to her son after coaxing him.
Having drunk the artificial milk given by his mother, that boy, with beautiful teeth, spoke again to his mother, saying, "This is not milk."
Hearing her son’s weeping, she, distressed and possessing lotus-like hands, spoke to her son after wiping his eyes with both her hands.
The mother said: "Where can there be milk for us who dwell constantly in the forest? Without the grace of Śambhu, the attainment of milk is impossible."

"O son, whatever meritorious deed was performed by you in a previous birth dedicated to Śiva, that alone will surely be obtained; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. Hearing these words of his mother, that boy Vyāghrapādi—
He, whose soul was free from sorrow and who was devoted to his mother, replied to his mother.
"Enough of this grief, O Mother! If Śambhu exists as the benefactor, abandon your sorrow, O illustrious lady; all will be well."
Listen to my words, O Mother: if this Mahādeva exists anywhere, whether it takes a long time or not, I shall surely reach the Ocean of Milk.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus with affection and uttered, "May there be Śiva for me," that boy, having dismissed her and bowed deeply, proceeded to perform penance.
Residing on the Himavat mountain, subsisting on air alone and remaining composed, he constructed a temple with eight bricks and fashioned a linga made of clay.
Having invoked Śiva along with Ambā there with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra, that child indeed worshipped him with wild leaves, flowers, and other offerings.
Having meditated upon that Śiva accompanied by Ambā and reciting the five-syllabled mantra, and having worshipped him for a long time, he performed supreme austerity.
O Sage, by the ascetic power of that high-souled boy Upamanyu, the entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, was set ablaze.
In the meantime, the Lord Śambhu, having been entreated by Viṣṇu and the others, assumed the form of Indra in order to test his devotion.
Śivā became identical in nature to Śacī, all the Gaṇas became gods, Nandin became the elephant Airāvata, and everything indeed became composed of that essence.

Then Sāmba Śiva, accompanied by his attendants and assuming the form of Indra, went quickly to Upamanyu’s hermitage to bestow his grace. O lord of sages, Hara, having assumed the form of Indra to test the boy's devotion, spoke to that child in a deep voice.
Sureśvara said: "I am pleased with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows, by virtue of this penance. I shall grant all your desired wishes; there is no doubt in this."
Thus addressed by Śambhu in the form of Śakra, he replied with palms joined in reverence: "I choose devotion to Śiva."
Having heard that, Hari said: "You do not know me, the lord of the gods, Śakra, the sovereign of the three worlds, who is saluted by all the deities."
"O brahmin-sage, become my devotee; worship me alone at all times. I shall grant you everything—may it be well with you—so abandon Rudra, who is devoid of qualities."
Enough with this Rudra who is devoid of qualities; what purpose will he serve for you—he who, being excluded from the divine race, has fallen into the state of a Piśāca?
Nandīśvara said: Having heard that, the son of the sage, reciting the five-syllabled mantra, considered it an obstacle to his dharma and spoke to him who had come to perform it.

Upamanyu said: "Everything has indeed been told by you thus, regarding those who delight in censuring the Lord; and in this context, the god of gods' state of being devoid of qualities and his nature as a Piśāca [have been explained]."
Indeed, you do not know Rudra, the Lord of the lords of all gods, the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
That which the exponents of Brahman call both existent and non-existent, manifest and unmanifest, eternal, one, and yet many—that supreme boon I choose from him.
Indeed, those who know reality desire that supreme [state] which is free from the doctrine of causality and bestows the goal of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; therefore, I choose it.
There is no higher reality than Śambhu, the cause of all causes, the pervasive Lord who is superior to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, and who transcends even the Gaṇas.
I do not choose a boon from you, nor from Viṣṇu, nor even from Brahmā, nor from any other immortal; let Śaṅkara alone be the granter of my boon.
What is the use of saying more here? I shall state my own view of the truth: I do not clearly seek any other deity, such as Paśupati, or the like.
Listen to my state of being, O enemy of the mountains; this has been inferred by me today: that in another birth you committed a sin when you heard the censure of Śiva.
Upon hearing the censure of worldly existence, one should immediately renounce one's own body; having swiftly destroyed it, he goes to the world of Śiva.
"Let this desire of mine regarding the milk be set aside for now, O lowest of gods! Having slain you with the Śiva-weapon, I shall cast off this body."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Upamanyu resolved to die himself; having abandoned even his desire for milk, he prepared to kill Śakra.
Then, taking the ashes from their receptacle and consecrating them with the Astra-mantra, that sage released them while aiming at Śakra and let out a roar.
Having remembered the pair of feet of his chosen deity, Upamanyu remained intent on burning his own body, maintaining the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) of fire.
When the brahmin had thus resolved, the Blessed One, assuming the form of Śakra, gently restrained that yogin at the conclusion of his concentration.
At the command of Nandīśvara, Nandin, the beloved of Śaṅkara, seized with his mind that Aghora-weapon which had been discharged and cast forth.
Assuming his own true form, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One, revealed himself to the brahmin, with the young moon serving as his crest-ornament.
That Lord showed him a thousand oceans of milk, as well as oceans of curds and other products, and oceans of various kinds of foods and edibles.
Thus he beheld Śambhu upon his bull, accompanied by the Goddess and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, as well as by tridents and other divine weapons.
In the heavens the drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell; the ten directions were covered by gods headed by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra.
Then Upamanyu, overwhelmed by the waves of an ocean of bliss, fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, his mind bowed with devotion.
At that time, the Lord Bhava, smiling there, called out, "Come, come! and having smelled [the head] of [him], granted him boons.
Śiva said: "O child Upamanyu, I am pleased with your conduct regarding the boon; you are a firm devotee, O brahmin-sage, and have now been tested by me."
Always enjoy various foods and pleasures with your kinsmen as you desire; remain forever happy, liberated from suffering, and full of devotion to me.
O illustrious Upamanyu, this Pārvatī is indeed your mother; for today I have made you my son, and [bestowed upon you] eternal youth.
There were thousands of oceans of milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey, as well as entire oceans of all kinds of foods, both solid and soft.
"I have given these to you out of affection; accept them, O great sage! Likewise, O Dakṣa, [accept] immortality and eternal leadership over the Gaṇas."
Mahādeva is your father and Jagadambikā is your mother; choose with great joy the supreme boons that your heart desires.
May you be undecaying and immortal, free from suffering, illustrious, possessed of excellent splendor, wise, and a great lord.
Then Śambhu, with a gracious soul, remembering his great asceticism, again granted ten divine boons to the sage Upamanyu.
He bestowed upon him the Pāśupata vow, knowledge, the yoga of the vow, and the capacity for exposition according to reality, as well as his own station.
Having given him thus, Mahādeva took him by both hands, smelled his head, and presented him to the Goddess, saying, "This is your son."
And the Goddess, listening with affection, placed her lotus-hand upon the crown of his head and bestowed upon him the imperishable rank of Kumāra.
The Ocean of Milk, having approached him in embodied form, gave to him that which was sweet as milk, solidified, and imperishable.
With a satisfied mind, he granted him mastery over yoga, eternal contentment, the imperishable knowledge of Brahman, and supreme prosperity.
Having obtained divine boons and eternal youth from both that Śiva and from Śivā, he became filled with joy.
Then, with a serene mind, having bowed deeply with palms joined in reverence, he affectionately requested a boon from Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Upamanyu said: "Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Grant me your supreme, divine, and unfailing devotion."
O Mahādeva, grant me always faith toward my own kinsmen, as well as supreme devotion to Your service and Your constant presence [with them].
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Upamanyu, that best of the twice-born, with a tranquil soul and a voice faltering with joy, praised Mahādeva.
When he had spoken thus, the Lord Śiva, the master of all and sovereign of everything, with a gracious soul, replied to Upamanyu while everyone was listening.
Śiva said: "O child Upamanyu, you are blessed; you are especially my devotee. O sinless one, everything that was requested by you has indeed been granted by me."
May you be ageless and immortal, forever free from suffering; may you be worshiped by all, changeless, and the most excellent among devotees.
O best of the twice-born, your kinsmen, family, and lineage shall always be inexhaustible, and your devotion to me shall be eternal.
"O Sage, I shall always maintain my presence within your very being; stay here, my child, as you desire, and you shall feel no longing."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus and having granted him excellent boons, the Lord Sāmba, together with his attendants, immediately vanished on that very spot.
Upamanyu, his soul serene, having obtained the most excellent boons from Śambhu, went to his mother’s abode and described everything to her.
Having heard that, his mother attained great joy; he too became worthy of all worship and always experienced exceeding happiness.
Thus, O dear one, has been described to you the incarnation of Śiva, the Supreme Self, as Sureśvara, which indeed bestows happiness upon the virtuous at all times.
This sinless narrative bestows the fruit of all desires; it leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to the virtuous.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard while composed in mind, shall enjoy every happiness in this world and, at the end, attain the state of Śiva.
Nandīśvara said: O Sanatkumāra, with great affection, listen to the most purifying incarnation of the all-pervading Supreme Soul Śiva, known by the name Jaṭila.
In former times, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, having abandoned her body at her father’s sacrifice because she was disregarded by her own father, was born from Himavat through Menā.

Having gone to the dense forest, the auspicious Śivā, desiring Śaṅkara as her husband, performed very pure penance accompanied by her two friends. Then Śiva, who is skilled in various divine sports, dispatched the Seven Sages to that place of Pārvatī’s penance in order to thoroughly test her austerity.
Having gone there, those sages conducted an examination with great care; yet, despite their diligent efforts, they were not at all able to succeed.
Having arrived there, bowed to Śiva, and reported that event, they received his command and returned respectfully to the heavenly world.
When the sages had departed for their own abodes, the Lord Śaṅkara himself, the creator of all, desired to test the conduct of Śivā.
Then this Lord, the master who fulfills the desires of ascetics and is exceedingly serene, became the very embodiment of celibacy; the Sovereign was truly most wonderful.
Extremely aged, bearing the body of a brahmin, blazing with his own splendor and a joyful mind, he was radiant, carrying a staff and an umbrella.
Having thus assumed the form of a matted-haired ascetic, Śambhu, the benevolent Śaṅkara who is affectionate toward his devotees, went to the forest of Girijā, filled with great joy.
There he saw the queen standing upon the altar, surrounded by her female companions, like the pure crescent of the moon amidst the inner sanctum.
Śambhu, beholding them and the Goddess, assumed the form of a celibate student (brahmacārī) and, being affectionate toward his devotees, approached them with joy and longing.
Then, seeing that brahmin who had arrived—wondrous in his splendor, with hair upon his limbs, peaceful, and equipped with a staff and an antelope skin—she [perceived him].
With supreme affection, he worshipped the aged ascetic, who observed the vow of celibacy, wore matted hair, and carried a water-pot, with all kinds of offerings for worship.
Then the goddess Pārvatī, having worshipped him with supreme joy, respectfully inquired after the welfare of that celibate student.
"Who are you, appearing in the form of a celibate student (brahmacārin), and from where have you come? You illuminate this forest; tell me, O best among the knowers of the Vedas."
Nandīśvara said: Thus questioned by Pārvatī, that twice-born celibate student replied quickly and with affection, desiring to test Śivā’s disposition.
The religious student said: "I am indeed a twice-born religious student who approaches women out of desire; I am an ascetic who bestows happiness upon others and is helpful to them, without a doubt."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, that celibate Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, remained nearby, concealing his own form.
The Brahmachārī said: "What shall I say, O Great Goddess? There is nothing to be told; a great, perverse, and highly calamitous event is being witnessed."
While you are still in the prime of youth—a time conducive to excellent enjoyments and a cause of happiness—you are practicing asceticism in vain, despite possessing great comforts and fine luxuries.
Who are you, whose daughter are you, and for what purpose do you perform this difficult penance in the lonely forest—a practice undertaken by sages of self-restrained mind?
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words, the Supreme Goddess laughed and spoke with affection to that excellent celibate student.
Pārvatī said: Listen, O Brahmin, O celibate sage, to my entire account of past conduct; my birth now takes place in the land of Bhārata, in the home of Himavat.
Formerly, I was born in the house of Dakṣa as Satī, the beloved of Śaṅkara; I abandoned my body through yoga because my father censured my husband.
O twice-born one, having attained Śiva through great merit in this very birth, he abandoned me, reduced Manmatha to ashes, and departed.
When Śaṅkara had departed, I, ashamed because of the heat, came here from my father’s house to perform penance, self-restrained by the command of my guru.
In thought, in word, and directly in deed, I have remained devoted to my husband; I speak the truth and not a falsehood, for Śaṅkara has been won over by me.
I know that this object is difficult to attain; how might it be obtained by me? Nevertheless, out of mental longing, my asceticism now burns with fervor.
Having slain the gods headed by Indra, as well as Viṣṇu and Brahmā, I truly desire to obtain Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, as my husband.
Nandīśvara said: O sage, having heard these very firm words of Pārvatī, that matted-haired Rudra spoke these words with a smile.
The matted-hair ascetic said: "O Goddess, daughter of Himācala, what thought has been adopted by you? Having set aside the gods, for the sake of Rudra you perform such extensive penance?"
I know that Rudra; listen, for I shall tell you of him: that Rudra indeed has the bull as his emblem, possesses a transformed nature, and wears matted hair.
He is always solitary and especially free from passion; therefore, you ought not to unite your mind with that Rudra.
"O Goddess, everything—form and the rest—is contrary to both you and Hara; indeed, this does not please me. Do as you wish."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, Rudra, assuming the form of a celibate student (brahmacārī), censured himself in many ways before her in order to test her.
Having heard those invincible words of the brahmin, the goddess Pārvatī, becoming greatly enraged, replied to him who was intent on reviling Śiva.
For this much was known by me: that someone would be fortunate; however, now it appears that everything has been understood, yet he remains invulnerable.
"O fool, some rogue has come to you in the guise of a celibate student; you have committed an insult against Śiva, and because of that, I am filled with wrath."
"You do not know Śiva, for you are indeed turned away from Śiva; because my worship was performed by you, I have become filled with distress."
That man who, in this world, reviles Śiva without knowing the truth, his merit accumulated since birth is indeed reduced to ashes.
Having touched one who hates Śiva, one should perform an expiation.
"O wicked one, you say, 'I know Śaṅkara'; yet in truth, you have not recognized Śiva as the supreme Lord."
In whatever manner Rudra may exist through his illusory power (māyā), assuming many forms, he is the ultimate granter of my desires, changeless, and beloved by the virtuous.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus to him, the goddess Śivā declared the Śiva-tattva, wherein Rudra—the attributeless and imperishable—is described as Brahman.
Having heard those words of the goddess, that twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) was just about to begin speaking again when—
At that moment, Girijā, whose mental faculties were entirely absorbed in Śiva and who was averse to any disparagement of Śiva, quickly spoke to her friend Vijayā.
Girijā said: "O friend, this lowest of the twice-born must be restrained with effort; for he intends to speak again and will once more commit the blasphemy of Śiva."
Indeed, sin shall accrue not only to the one who reviles Śiva, but whoever hears that censure shall also become a partaker of sin in this world.
One who reviles Śiva must be executed in every way by the servants of Śiva; if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he should indeed be abandoned, and one must depart from that place immediately.
"This wicked man will surely revile Śiva again; yet, because he is a Brāhmaṇa, he must not be killed—he should be avoided and never looked upon."
"Let us leave this place quickly and go elsewhere without delay, so that there may be no further conversation with this ignorant man."
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, as soon as Umā had spoken thus and lifted her foot, Śiva himself directly caught hold of the cloth.
Having assumed his divine form and meditated upon Śiva in the prescribed manner, Śiva showed it to Śivā and spoke to her as she stood with her face cast down.
Śiva said: "Where are you going, leaving me? O Śivā, you must not be abandoned by me. You have been tested by me; O sinless one, you are firm in your devotion to me."
Desiring to manifest your own nature in the form of a celibate student (brahmacārin), I approached your presence and spoke various words to you.
I am deeply pleased by your devotion, especially toward Śiva; speak the boon desired by your heart, for there is nothing that cannot be granted to you.
From this day forward, I have been made your servant by your ascetic penances and your overflowing love; because of your beauty, even a single moment seems like an eon.
"Cast aside your shame; you are my eternal wife. Come, my beloved, let us go quickly with you to my own mountain."
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, she attained great joy; indeed, she instantly cast off all the suffering caused by her ascetic penance.
Then, seeing that divine form of Śiva, Śivā was overjoyed; yet, with her face cast down in modesty, she replied to the Lord with affection.
Śiva said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased and if you show me favor, then become my husband, O Lord of Gods. Thus was Śiva addressed by Śivā.
Having taken his hand according to the prescribed rites, he went with her to Kailāsa; having obtained him as her husband, Girijā accomplished the purpose of the gods.
Thus, O dear one, has the true nature of the celibate student been described to you by me; for he is indeed an incarnation of Śiva, a tester of the devotion of Śivā.
This sinless and supreme narrative has been recounted by me; whoever hears it with devotion shall attain happiness and the ultimate goal.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, hear of the incarnation of the all-pervading Śiva, the Supreme Soul, known by the name Sunartakanata.
For when the goddess Kālikā, Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, having gone to the forest, performed most pure penance for the sake of attaining Śiva.
Then, O sage, Śiva became pleased with her for her excellent penance; having thoroughly tested her conduct, he went joyfully to grant her a boon.
O Sage, with a highly pleased mind, Śaṅkara revealed his true form to her and said to that Śivā, "Choose a boon."
Having heard those words of Śambhu and beholding that supreme form, she rejoiced exceedingly in Śiva and, bowing deeply to him, spoke to him.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then become my husband, O Īśāna; show mercy upon me."
"With your permission, O Lord, I shall go properly to my father's house; you, O Master, must also go to my father's side."
O monk, beg from me at last, proclaiming your auspicious fame; out of affection, make my father’s entire household life fruitful.
Therefore, O Lord, O Great Ruler, you ought to perform the marriage according to the prescribed rite for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
O Lord, fulfill my desire; you are forever changeless. For your name is "Loving toward Devotees," and I am always your devotee.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by her, Śambhu, the Great Lord who is affectionate toward his devotees, replied with the words, "So be it," and vanished, returning to his own mountain.
Then Pārvatī also, accompanied by her two friends of her own age, went with affection to the house of her father, having assumed a form that was truly meaningful.
Having heard of Pārvatī’s arrival, Himācala, together with Menā and his retinue, went joyfully to see his daughter.
Seeing her with a most serene countenance, they brought her to their home; out of affection, Mahānandī and his wife caused a great festival to be celebrated.
Menā and the king likewise gave wealth to the twice-born and others, and they reverently performed auspicious rites accompanied by the sound of the Vedas.
Then Menā and Himavat, the mountain king, dwelt joyfully in the courtyard together with their daughter; he, however, went to the Gaṅgā to bathe.
In the meantime, Śambhu, who is fond of divine play and compassionate toward his devotees, assumed the form of an excellent dancer-actor and went into the presence of Menakā.
Holding a horn in his left hand and likewise a ḍamaru drum in his right, with a patched garment on his back and clad in red robes, he is an expert in dance and song.
Then, assuming the form of a dancer, he joyfully performed various dances and most enchanting songs in the courtyard of Menakā.
There he sounded his horn and the hand-drum with a beautiful sound; out of affection, he performed various magnificent and heart-stealing acts.
To see him, all the citizens—both men and women, as well as children and the elderly—certainly arrived there suddenly.
O Sage, having heard that music and seen that captivating, beautiful dance, everyone—including Menā—then suddenly fainted again and again.
Then Menā, her mind delighted by his messenger, quickly went with affection to give him jewels placed in golden vessels.
He did not accept those offerings, nor did he accept that auspicious alms-food; yet, out of curiosity, he again prepared to perform dance and song.
Hearing those words, Menā became exceedingly astonished and grew very angry; she rebuked the mendicant and desired to cast him out.
In the meantime, the king of mountains arrived there from the Gaṅgā; he saw before him a mendicant in human form standing in the courtyard.
Having heard all that account from the mouth of Menā, he became greatly incensed and commanded his attendants to cast the mendicant outside.
No one was able to lead that best of sages outside, for he was like a great fire—difficult to touch, blazing, and full of intense splendor.
Then, O dear one, that mendicant, who was skilled in various playful arts, displayed his infinite power to the Mountain.
There Śaila quickly beheld him assuming the form of Viṣṇu, and then, in an instant, the form of Brahmā and the form of the Sun.
Then, O dear one, he beheld that most wonderful form of Rudra, accompanied by Pārvatī, beautiful, smiling, and endowed with great splendor.
Thus he beheld there many forms of his; he became instantly filled with great wonder, overflowing with supreme bliss.
Then that excellent monk indeed begged for alms from her as she was performing the birth-rites; he accepted nothing other than food fit for the distressed.
Then the Supreme Lord, who had assumed the form of a mendicant, vanished; impelled by the words of Durgā, he quickly returned to his own abode.
Then, even Menā and the Lord of Mountains attained true knowledge: "The omnipresent Śiva has deceived us both and departed for his own abode."
"This daughter of mine, Pārvatī, who has performed great austerities, should be given to him"; having reflected thus, both of them developed supreme devotion to Śiva.
Therefore, Rudra, having brought great joy to his devotees, performed the marriage with Pārvatī with affection according to the prescribed rites.
Thus, O dear one, has he who is called Sunartakanata been described to you by me as an incarnation of Śiva who fulfills the word of Śivā.
This sinless and supreme narrative has been recounted by me; whoever hears it with devotion shall attain happiness and reach the highest goal.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Śiva as the Dancer named Sunartaka," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen to the incarnation of the all-pervading Lord Śiva, the Supreme Soul, which is known as the Brahmin in the guise of a virtuous man.
Perceiving Menā and Himālaya’s supreme devotion toward Śiva, all the gods became anxious and consulted one another with earnestness.
If Śaila gives his daughter to Śambhu with exclusive devotion, he will certainly and immediately attain the state of Nirvāṇa through Śiva.
If this repository of infinite jewels should attain liberation, then the earth named Ratnagarbhā (Jewel-Wombed) will certainly and surely become a falsehood.
Abandoning his instability and assuming a divine form, he shall give his daughter to the wielder of the trident and go to the world of Śiva.
Having attained a form identical to that of Mahādeva through the grace of Śambhu, and having enjoyed great pleasures there, he shall thereafter attain liberation.
Having reflected thus, O Sage, all the gods went to the house of their preceptor; having arrived, they informed the preceptor of their purpose, intent on accomplishing their own ends.
The gods said: "O Preceptor, go to the home of Himālaya for the accomplishment of our purpose; having disparaged Maheśa, cause his devotion to the mountain to cease."
O Guru, by giving his daughter to Śiva out of his own faith, that mountain shall attain liberation right here; let him indeed remain upon this earth.
Having heard these words of the gods and having reflected upon them, he spoke to them.
The Guru said: "O gods, let someone among you go to the vicinity of the mountain; I am unable to accomplish that which he desires."
Alternatively, O gods, go with Vāsava to the world of Brahmā and tell him your own story; he will accomplish your task for you.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard that and deliberated upon it, the gods went to the assembly of Brahmā; they reported all those events in the presence of the Creator.
Having heard those words and reflected upon them well, the Creator indeed said to them: "I shall never engage in that censure which always bestows suffering and causes distress."
O Suras, go to Kailāsa and propitiate Śaṅkara; dispatch that god back toward the abode of Himālaya.
Then he should go to Śaileśa and indeed practice self-reproach; reproaching others leads to destruction, while reproaching oneself is considered conducive to fame.
Nandīśvara said: Then all those gods departed quickly for Kailāsa; having prostrated before Śiva with devotion, they all sang of him immediately.
Having heard those words of the gods, Maheśvara accepted them; having consoled the gods, he sent them away with a smile.
Then the Blessed One, Śambhu, the Great Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees, the master of Māyā and free from all transformation, desired to go to the foot of the mountain.
Carrying a staff and an umbrella, dressed in celestial garments, and wearing a brilliant tilaka, he holds a crystal rosary in his hand and wears a śālagrāma stone around his neck.
Chanting the name of Hari with devotion, the twice-born man, wearing the garb of a holy mendicant, quickly went to the Himālaya mountains accompanied by his circle of kinsmen.
Upon seeing him, Himālaya, together with his retinue, rose up and prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, performing the eight-limbed salutation according to the prescribed rite.
Then Śaileśa asked that twice-born man, "Who are you? Thereupon, that best of brahmins quickly replied with great devotion to the worthy mountain:

The virtuous twice-born said: "O virtuous one, I am a mountain named Dvijāhva, a Vaiṣṇava who perceives the supreme truth; through the power of my guru, I am a benefactor of others, all-knowing, and omnipresent."
O best of mountains, I have known this through my own wisdom while in my own abode; therefore, casting aside all hypocrisy, listen with pleasure as I speak it before you.
You desire to give your own daughter, who is as beautiful as Padmā, to Śaṅkara, whose lineage and character are unknown.
O Lord of Mountains, this thought of yours is not appropriate for one who bestows auspiciousness; understand this, O best among the wise, born as you are from the lineage of Nārāyaṇa.
Behold his lordship over the mountains; yet he has not a single kinsman. Inquire with diligence regarding his own relatives and his beloved Menā.
O Mountain, inquire with diligence from all of them, beginning with Menā, excluding Pārvatī; for to one who is ill, even medicine seems like unwholesome food.
In this act of giving Pārvatī, the great multitude will not be worthy of you as a recipient; they will have smiling faces merely upon hearing of it.
Without support, always free from attachment, deformed, devoid of qualities, and imperishable; dwelling in cremation grounds, hideous, a seizer of serpents, and naked.
Adorned with supernatural powers as his ornaments, with his head encircled by the most excellent of serpents, you have transcended all stages of life and your movement is forever unknown.
Brahmā said: Having spoken such truthful words intent upon censuring Śiva, he indeed departed quickly for his own abode; for Śiva performs manifold divine sports.
Having heard those words of the brahmin, their bodies became emaciated; being intent upon contrary misfortunes, what shall we certainly do?
Then Rudra, having performed a great sacrifice that brought joy to his devotees, married Girijā and carried out the work of the gods.
Thus, O dear one, has been described to you that one called a twice-born in the guise of a virtuous man; for he is an incarnation of Śiva, O Lord, acting for the sake of the gods' mission.
This narrative is sinless, conducive to heaven, life-prolonging, and supreme; whoever reads or even hears it shall become happy and attain the highest goal.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, hear of the supreme incarnation of the all-pervading Śiva, the Supreme Self, known by the name Aśvatthāman.
O Sage, from a portion of the great-minded celestial seer Bṛhaspati, Droṇa was born of Bharadvāja; he was self-possessed and not born from a womb.
The best among archers, a hero, a brahmin-sage, and a knower of all scriptures; one of vast fame and great splendor, who was the most excellent of those skilled in all weapons.
The wise know him to be proficient in both the science of archery and the Vedas—the most excellent Drona, a performer of wondrous deeds who causes his own lineage to flourish.
O twice-born one, he was the preceptor of the Kauravas by virtue of his own strength; he was renowned among the six great chariot-warriors in the midst of the Kauravas.
For the sake of assisting the Kauravas, that best of the twice-born, Dronacharya, performed extensive austerities directed toward Shiva for the purpose of obtaining a son.
Then, O best of sages, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, appeared before Droṇa in a state of grace.
Having seen him, that twice-born Drona, with a heart greatly delighted, bowed down to him quickly, prostrating himself with his hands joined in reverence.
Pleased by his praise and ascetic penance, the Lord Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, said to Droṇa, "Choose a boon."
Having heard those words of Śambhu, Droṇa then spoke with humility: "Grant me a son born of your own portion, one who is invincible to all and possessed of great strength."
Having heard those words of Droṇa, Śambhu said, "So be it," and then vanished, O dear sage; he is ever curious and the bestower of happiness.
Droṇa, greatly delighted and free from all confusion, returned to his own abode and joyfully related that entire event to his wife.
Then, having found the opportune moment, the Lord Rudra, the destroyer of all, was born as a son to Droṇa through his own portion, he who possessed great strength.
O Sage, he became renowned on earth as Aśvatthāman; he was a preeminent hero with eyes like lotus petals, the destroyer of the enemy host.
He who was renowned in the battle at Bhārata, having received his father’s command, became a helper of the Kauravas, being possessed of great strength.
Relying upon that great hero, the Kauravas—Bhīṣma and the others of immense strength—became invincible even to the dwellers of heaven.
Out of fear of whom all the Pāṇḍavas were unable to defeat the Kauravas, even though they possessed eight great heroes and were all highly skilled.
Following the instruction of Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna performed an exceedingly severe penance; then, having obtained the weapons by the grace of Śambhu, he conquered them.
O Sage, the great hero Aśvatthāman, born from a portion of Mahādeva, even then, under the influence of his devotion to him, displayed his own prowess.
Having destroyed the sons of Pāṇḍu, though they were trained with great effort by Kṛṣṇa and other great heroes whose strength was otherwise irresistible to enemies.
Seeing Arjuna, accompanied by Acyuta, rushing toward him while overwhelmed by grief for his son, he fled away in his chariot.
He then discharged the weapon named Brahmaśiras over him; thereupon, a fierce radiance appeared in every direction.
Beholding that peril to his life, Arjuna, overcome by distress, dejected, his luster vanished, and seized by great fear, spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
Arjuna said: "O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, what is this, and from where does it come? I do not know. This unbearable radiance is approaching from every direction."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, the best of Śiva’s devotees, meditated upon Śiva along with his consort and respectfully replied to Arjuna.
Kṛṣṇa said: "Know that the son of Droṇa possesses the exceedingly fierce Brahma-weapon; for there is no other weapon whatsoever capable of countering it."
Quickly remember Śiva, Śambhu, your own lord and the protector of his devotees, by whom indeed was given to you your own supreme weapon that accomplishes all tasks.
"Let the power of his weapon be suppressed by the power of Śiva’s weapon. Having said this, Kṛṣṇa himself, intent on that purpose, meditated upon Śiva.
O Sage, having heard those words of Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha remembered Śiva in his heart, touched water, bowed to him, and then swiftly discharged the weapon.
O great sage, although the Brahmāśiras weapon was unerring and irresistible, it was immediately extinguished by the splendor of Śiva’s weapon.
Do not consider this a wonder in Śivā, who consists of all marvels; for she is the Unborn One who, by her own power, creates, sustains, and destroys the entire universe.
Then Aśvatthāman, born from a portion of Śiva, having understood this occurrence, O Sage, did not suffer at all as a devotee of Śiva, for his mind was satisfied by the will of Śiva.
Then the son of Droṇa set his mind upon destroying the child within Uttarā’s womb, so that this entire universe might be rendered devoid of Pāṇḍavas.
That great lord discharged the Brahmāstra, which possessed immense radiance and was irresistible to other weapons, aiming it at the womb of Uttara.
Then Jisnu’s wife, Uttara, her mind distressed and burning from that weapon, praised Krishna, the Lord of Lakshmi.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having meditated upon Śiva in his heart, praised him, and bowed down, understood that this was the weapon of the son of Droṇa intended to rid the earth of the Pāṇḍavas.
By the command of Śiva, he protected her with that radiant Sudarśana weapon, which had been given to him by Indra for his own protection.
Having learned that Kṛṣṇa had assumed his true form as an excellent devotee of Śiva by the command of Śaṅkara, he became dejected and gradually grew despondent.
Then Kṛṣṇa, his soul delighted, made all the Pāṇḍavas fall at his feet for the satisfaction of that king of Śiva's devotees.
Then the son of Droṇa, with a serene soul, having shown favor to Aśvatthāman, affectionately bestowed various boons upon the Pāṇḍavas and Kṛṣṇa as well.
In this manner, O dear one, the Lord Maheśvara performed a supreme sport by descending to the earth in the form of the son of Droṇa, O best of sages.
Aśvatthāman, an incarnation of Śiva endowed with great strength and prowess, who bestows happiness upon the three worlds, remains even today on the banks of the Jāhnavī.
O Lord Śaṅkara, this incarnation of yours as Aśvatthāman has been described; it bestows all perfections and grants the desired fruits to your devotees.
Whoever hears this with devotion or recites it with a concentrated mind shall attain their desired perfection and, in the end, go to the city of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Śiva as Aśvatthāman," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: Listen, O wise one, to the incarnation of the wielder of the Pināka bow known as Kirāta, who, being pleased, slew Mūka and granted a boon to Arjuna.
Defeated by Suyodhana, those Pāṇḍavas, who were indeed the most excellent of men, went to the forest named Dvaita together with that virtuous Draupadī.
At that very place, relying indeed upon the cooking pot given by Sūryadatta, the Pāṇḍavas then spent their time happily, it is said.
O best of Brahmins, Durvāsas, that preeminent sage, was sent by Suyodhana with great respect to the presence of the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of a challenge.
Accompanied by his own ten thousand students, he joyfully requested from them whatever food they desired in their hearts, and he received it from them.
Then, having been accepted by those various Pāṇḍavas, the ascetic sages, headed by Durvāsas, were sent forth for the purpose of bathing.
Then, O Lord of Sages, all those Pāṇḍavas, distressed due to the lack of food, resolved in their minds to give up their lives.
And when Draupadī called upon Kṛṣṇa, he arrived at that very moment; having eaten the vegetables, he brought them complete satisfaction.
Then Durvāsas, perceiving that his disciples were satisfied, departed once more; meanwhile, the Pāṇḍavas were liberated from their distress through the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Then those Pāṇḍavas asked Kṛṣṇa: "What will happen? A powerful enemy has arisen; O Lord, tell us what must be done."
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, having been thus questioned by those Pāṇḍavas, Śrī Kṛṣṇa then remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and spoke this to the Pāṇḍavas.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Listen, O best of the Pāṇḍavas; having heard it, you must certainly act accordingly—especially my own account, which is endowed with the service of Śiva."
And having gone to Dvārakā with the desire to conquer my enemies, I reflected upon the instructions of the high-souled Upamanyu.
Indeed, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, was propitiated by me; having been well-served for seven months on Baṭuka, the best of mountains, he became pleased.
The Lord of the Universe himself remained present and granted me my desired objects; through his power, I have obtained supreme and complete capability.
Now the God, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, is being served; you too should serve that Śambhu, who brings all happiness.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus and having comforted the Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa vanished; remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he quickly went to Dvārakā.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, by their might, dispatched the Bhilla for the purpose of testing the virtues of both him and Duryodhana.
He too, having understood all that excellence arising from Duryodhana’s qualities there to be authentic, returned once more to his masters.
O Lord of Sages, having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Pāṇḍavas became exceedingly distressed; they spoke to one another as follows.
"What should be done? Where should we go now in battle? For although we are all indeed capable, we are bound by the noose of truth."
Nandīśvara said: At that moment, Vyāsa arrived, his head adorned with ashes, wearing ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, and graced by a mass of matted hair.
Chanting the five-syllabled mantra, he was completely filled with love for Śiva; he was himself a mass of splendor, like another Dharma incarnate.
Seeing him, they were then delighted; rising up, they stood before him and offered him a seat beautifully adorned with kusha grass and deerskin.
There, they joyfully honored Vyāsa as he sat down; having offered various praises, they exclaimed, "We are blessed!"
Austerity well-performed and various kinds of gifts—all that has become fruitful; O Lord, they are satisfied by the sight of you.
O Grandfather, by the sight of you, suffering has been driven far away; yet, great misery was inflicted upon us by those wicked ones of cruel deeds.
When the vision of the Illustrious Ones arises, suffering will surely pass away; it has never failed to do so—this is the certainty that has been deliberated.
When one has reached the stage of life of the great ones and is capable in all duties, if suffering still occurs, destiny alone is the cause in this matter.
One should certainly depart from poverty, which is the cause of suffering; for this is the nature of the great, regarded as being like the wish-fulfilling tree.
One should count only the virtues of that great being according to its essential substance; O Lord, it is indeed by the power of the substratum that a person comes into being.
One should not entertain doubt here regarding their lightness or their greatness; for it is the very nature of the noble to protect the lowly.
In this world, the characteristic of a pauper is considered to lead to the highest welfare: namely, making every effort to serve virtuous people.
Henceforth, let neither fortune nor fault be given; for this reason, O Master, when you were seen, that was auspicious at that time.
Our minds are satisfied merely by your arrival; grant us instruction so that our suffering may quickly perish.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of the Pāṇḍavas, the great sage Vyāsa, becoming pleased in mind, spoke this.
O Pāṇḍavas, you indeed ought not to cause any hardship; you are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and truth has not been violated by you at all.
This is the nature of the virtuous, which remains most beautiful even unto the end of life: they never abandon righteousness here; truth is indeed the vessel that bears fruit.
Both you and they have attained equality with us; nevertheless, partiality toward those who are most righteous is indeed approved by the wise.
Indeed, first by the wicked and sightless Dhṛtarāṣṭra, dharma was abandoned out of greed, and thus your kingdom was seized.
Both you and they are undoubtedly his sons; when their father has passed away, these children are to be pitied by that high-souled one.
Afterwards, the son was likewise prevented by him from ever doing so; thus, no misfortune whatsoever arose because of that which was done then.
Furthermore, that which has occurred hereafter shall remain as it is and not otherwise; he is wicked, while you are most righteous and speakers of truth.
Therefore, at the end, that very same unwholesome result will certainly come to pass; for whatever seed has been sown, its sprout shall manifest right here.
Therefore, you must certainly not give way to sorrow under any circumstances; for what is auspicious will surely come to pass for you—there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, all those Pāṇḍavas, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, being gratified by Vyāsa, spoke these words once again.
The Pāṇḍavas said: "O Lord, what you have spoken is true; for by the wicked and evil-minded ones, suffering is indeed inflicted upon us incessantly, even in the forest, again and again."
"Therefore, O Lord, destroy my inauspiciousness; some auspicious gift should be given. It was previously stated by Kṛṣṇa that Śaṅkara is always to be propitiated."
We have been negligent and have rendered those words ineffective; therefore, let that path of the gods be taught to us once again now.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words, Vyāsa, filled with joy and recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva, spoke to the Pāṇḍavas with affection.
Vyāsa said: O Pāṇḍavas of righteous intellect, listen now to my words. What Kṛṣṇa has spoken is indeed true; I myself serve Śiva.
"May you serve [Śiva] with love; thus there shall always be incomparable happiness. For indeed, it is solely from the failure to serve Śiva that all suffering arises."
Nandīśvara said: Then, having deliberated upon those very five regarding the worship of Śiva, the eminent sage Vyāsa likewise declared Arjuna to be the fit candidate.
Having thus reflected upon a place for asceticism, that best of sages then spoke these words once more to the Pāṇḍavas, who were firmly established in righteousness.
Vyāsa said: Listen, all you Pāṇḍavas; I shall always speak for your benefit, having beheld the supreme Śiva, the ultimate Brahman, the goal of the virtuous.
Whatever is seen in the universe, from Brahmā up to the end of the three parārdhas, all that is the form of Śiva; it is to be worshipped and meditated upon again and again.
And he, Śaṅkara, the remover of all suffering, is to be served by everyone; Śiva becomes well-pleased through devotion in a very short time.
For Maheśa, being well-pleased, bestows everything upon his devotees; it is certain that he grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, both in this world and the next.

Therefore, Śambhu—the Supreme Person, Śaṅkara himself, the destroyer of the wicked, and the refuge of the virtuous—should always be served by those who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
However, first one should recite the Śakravidyā with a firm mind; this alone is prescribed for a Kṣatriya of superior renown who is composed in meditation.
And Arjuna, being firm, shall first recite the Śakra-vidyā; he will perform a preliminary test, and upon that, [the deity] will become satisfied.
Being well-pleased, he will always remove all obstacles; furthermore, he will likewise bestow upon Śiva a boon and a mantra.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, he summoned Arjuna and instructed him in the science of Upendra; then, having bathed and facing the east, the resolute Arjuna received it.
The best of sages bestowed the ritual for the king upon him; and Vyāsa, the noble-minded one, replied to that Dhanañjaya.
Vyāsa said: "Go from here now, O Pārtha, to the beautiful Indrakīla; staying indeed near the Jāhnavī, perform your penance properly."
"May this invisible lore always be a benefactor to you. Having thus bestowed this blessing upon him, the sage then spoke to them.
"Abiding by righteousness, let all these best of kings remain; success shall be preeminent in every way—no doubt should be entertained in this matter."
Nandīśvara said: Having thus bestowed his blessings upon those Pāṇḍavas, Vyāsa, the lord of sages, remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and vanished in an instant.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Instruction to Arjuna," in the context of the description of the Kirāta incarnation, within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: At that time, Arjuna was also seen there shining brightly; by means of the mantra in the form of Śiva, he bore an incomparable splendor.
Having seen Arjuna, all those Pāṇḍavas reached a firm conclusion: "Victory is certainly ours, since our splendor has become so vast."
"This task must be accomplished by you alone and never by anyone else; by the word of Vyāsa, it shines forth—make your life fruitful."
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, they, distressed by the longing for his absence, respectfully sent him back to that very place, even though he was unwilling.
Draupadī, overcome with grief and restraining her tears, that devoted wife then spoke these auspicious words.
Draupadī said: "O King, may the path you must diligently follow as instructed by Vyāsa be auspicious for you; may Śaṅkara indeed be the bestower of well-being."
Having respectfully bid farewell to Arjuna, all five of them, overcome by extreme sorrow, remained there together.
Standing there, they said: "Listen, O best of sages! Even in times of suffering, union with a beloved does not indeed result in further misery."
In separation, his suffering becomes twofold at all times; how, then, can there be fortitude here even for one who possesses fortitude?
Nandīśvara said: At that time, while the Pāṇḍavas were indeed experiencing suffering, Vyāsa—the lord of sages, an ocean of compassion, and the best of ṛṣis—arrived.
Then those Pāṇḍavas, bowing down and honoring him with respect, offered him a seat; yet, overwhelmed by grief, they joined their palms and spoke these words.
The Pāṇḍavas said: "Listen, O best of sages, O Lord; we are consumed by grief, yet having obtained the sight of you today, O sage, we have attained great joy."
"O Lord, dwell right here for some time for the sake of destroying our suffering; by the sight of you, O brahmin-sage, all suffering dissolves."
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus, that best of sages remained there for his pleasure; and by means of various stories, he did not arouse that [Nahuṣa’s] sorrow at that time.
While that discourse was being conducted by Vyāsa, O excellent sage, Dharmarāja, with a humble mind, bowed deeply and spoke this.
The King of Dharma said: "Listen, O best of sages, for the cessation of my sorrow is what I have in mind. I ask you, O highly wise one; it must be told by you, O Lord."
"Has anyone else ever experienced such suffering in the past? We alone have indeed encountered supreme misery; no one else at all."
Vyāsa said: In former times, a sorrow even greater than yours arose for that high-souled king named Nala, the lord of Niṣadha.
A most grievous sorrow arose for King Hariścandra; it was especially unspeakable and brought great grief to others as well.
O Pāṇḍava, the suffering of Rāma should likewise be understood as such, hearing which there would arise a great delusion even among women and men.
Therefore, it cannot indeed be described by me again; considering the body to be a heap of suffering, you should now renounce it.
That by which this [body] is sustained has undoubtedly pervaded it; indeed, birth within the mother's womb is the primary cause of suffering.
Even in childhood there is great suffering following the play of a child; even more so in youth, while enjoying desires that are themselves of the nature of suffering.
Indeed, through the coming and going of days and the manifold burdens of duty, one's lifespan is constantly diminished, yet one does not realize this.
Before death and after it as well, there is great suffering; various torments of hell are constantly experienced by ignorant men.
Therefore, this is false, but you must practice what is true; a person should act in such a way that Śambhu is pleased.
Nandīśvara said: Thus, all those brothers then spent their time with various conversations, once again following the paths of their desires.
Arjuna too, firm in his vows, went himself into the difficult mountains; having encountered a Yakṣa, he slew numerous bandits with that very [weapon].
Filled with joy in his mind, he went to that most excellent mountain; having arrived there, he reached a beautiful spot near the Gaṅgā.
Where the Aśoka grove stands, that is the supreme heaven; there he himself remained after bathing and bowing to his most excellent guru.
He himself performed exactly as instructed regarding his dress and other matters; first withdrawing his senses, he became established in the mind alone.
Having again fashioned a beautiful earthen linga with perfectly aligned proportions, he fixed his mind upon that unsurpassed mass of splendor before it.
Having bathed well at the three times of day, he then performed various forms of worship and repeatedly offered adoration to Hara there.
Then, seeing that splendor issuing from his very head, those moving beings were seized with fear, wondering, "When indeed did he enter?"
Then, having deliberated thus, they said, "This should be told to Indra"; and having spoken, they went quickly indeed into the presence of Śakra.
The spies said: "O Lord of Gods, we do not know whether he is a god, or a rishi, or the sun, or the radiant Vibhāvasu; we do not know him as he performs penance in the forest."
Burnt by his very splendor, they have come into your presence; we have reported that conduct of his, so let whatever is appropriate be done.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by those spies and having learned everything his son intended to do, he dismissed the guardians of his lineage and set his mind on going there.
O best of Brahmins, having become an aged Brahmin and a celibate student, Śacīpati went there indeed for the purpose of testing him.
Seeing him arrived then, the Pāṇḍava performed acts of worship; standing before him and having offered praise, he said, "Tell me now, from where have you come?"
Thus addressed by him, the Lord of the Gods, out of affection for him and for the sake of testing his fortitude, spoke these words to Pāṇḍu, who was filled with pride:

The Brāhmaṇa said: "O dear one, at this youthful age, what are you performing as penance now? Is it for the sake of liberation or for the sake of victory? In every respect, what is the purpose of this penance of yours?"
Nandīśvara said: Thus questioned by him at that time, everything was related once more; having heard that, the brahmin then spoke these words again.

The Brāhmaṇa said: "O hero, O best of the Kurus, that austerity which is performed for the sake of attaining happiness is not appropriate; rather, it is performed according to the duty of a Kṣatriya for the sake of liberation."

"Indra is indeed the giver of happiness, but he cannot be the giver of liberation. Therefore, you ought to perform supreme penance in every way. Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words, Arjuna then became enraged; yet, disregarding them, that self-restrained one of noble vows replied with humility.
Arjuna said: "Neither for the sake of a kingdom nor for the sake of liberation—why do you speak thus? It is solely at the word of Vyāsa that such penance is being performed."
Go from here, O practitioner of the holy life; do not wish to cause me to fall. What purpose indeed do you have here, O practitioner of the holy life?
Nandīśvara said: Thus addressed, he became pleased and showed his own wonderful and beautiful form, complete with its natural ornaments.
Then, seeing that form of Śakra, Arjuna was ashamed; Indra, having consoled him, spoke these words once again.
Indra said: "Choose a boon, O dear Dhanañjaya of great intellect! Whatever you desire in your heart, there is nothing that cannot be granted to you."
Having heard those words of Śakra, Arjuna then replied: "O Father, grant me victory in every way against one who is afflicted by his enemies."
Śakra said: "Those enemies of yours, led by Duryodhana, are powerful; Droṇa, Bhīma, and Karṇa—all of them are certainly invincible."

Aśvatthāman, the son of Droṇa, is a fierce portion [of Rudra] and exceedingly difficult to conquer; you shall be able to subdue him by my means. Listen to what is for your own benefit in every respect.
O hero, no one at present is able to perform this recitation; for Śiva is currently preeminent, and therefore victory now belongs to Śambhu.

Śaṅkara is the lord of all worlds, the master of the moving and the unmoving, and the self-ruling sovereign; he is capable of accomplishing everything and is the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I believe that Brahmā and the others, as well as Viṣṇu, the bestower of all boons, and all those others who are seekers of victory, are all worshippers of Śiva.
From this day forward, having abandoned that mantra, worship Śiva with devotion through the ritual of the earthen linga and through meditation upon Śiva alone.
O Bhārata, through manifold services and with your whole being, your success shall today be unshakable; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, he summoned all his attendants and said this: "You must always remain vigilant in the protection of this."
Having awakened his own followers and arranged for the protection of Arjuna and others, Indra, his heart overflowing with affection, spoke again to the one who bears the monkey-banner.
Indra said: "O Bhadra, O scorcher of foes, you must never again rule a kingdom through negligence; may this knowledge lead to your ultimate welfare."
The practitioner must maintain fortitude; Śiva is the protector in every way. He will bestow all prosperities and fruits equally—of this there is no doubt.
Nandīśvara said: Having thus granted the boon to Bhārata, the Lord of the Gods, remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, departed for his own abode.
The great hero Arjuna, having bowed deeply to the Lord of the Gods, performed such ascetic penance with a self-restrained mind, directed toward Śiva.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Arjuna’s Austerities," in the context of the description of the Kirāta incarnation, within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Nandīśvara said: Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rules, and likewise having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) and other rites according to the rules, he meditated upon Śiva with true devotion, just as it was described by Vyāsa.
Standing on the sole of one foot like the preeminent sage, he remained fixing his gaze upon the sun while reciting the mantra.
Performing penance with great devotion while recollecting Śiva in his mind, he muttered the five-syllabled mantra of Śambhu, which is the most excellent of all.
Your ascetic power was indeed such that the gods were struck with wonder; having returned to Śiva, they spoke again with composed minds.
The gods said: "O Lord of All, this man alone has performed austerities for your sake; O Master, why does he not grant whatever this man desires?"
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, the gods then performed various hymns of praise; fixing their gaze upon his feet, they stood there with steady minds.
Having heard those words, the great lord Śiva, possessed of noble intellect and a serene soul, laughed heartily and spoke these words to the gods.
Śiva said: "O gods, all of you go to your own abodes; this is the truth, there is no doubt. I shall accomplish your purpose in every way; there is no doubt in this."
Nandīśvara said: Having heard those words of Śambhu, all those immortals attained supreme certainty; they then turned back and returned each to his own abode.
In the meantime, a Daitya named Mūka arrived, having assumed the form of a boar and being sent by that evil-minded one.
O best of brahmins, Duryodhana, employing his powers of illusion, then followed the very path by which Arjuna was situated at that time.
Cutting down numerous trees like the peaks of a mountain and making various sounds, he moved along with extreme speed.
And Arjuna, having seen that asura named Mūka at that time, remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and became intent on reflection.
Arjuna said: Who is this that comes from where? He appears to be a man of cruel deeds; he is undoubtedly approaching to surely bring about my misfortune.
Such a thought occurs to my mind: he is indeed an enemy, there is no doubt; for many Daityas and Dānavas have already been slain by me.
Someone belonging to him may come again to settle an old enmity, or perhaps some friend who acts for the benefit of Duryodhana.
He upon seeing whom one's own mind becomes serene is certainly a benefactor; he upon seeing whom that very same mind becomes agitated is indeed an enemy.
Conduct reveals one's lineage; the body reveals one's food; speech reveals one's learning; and the eyes reveal one's affection.
By one's appearance, as well as by one's gait, gestures, and speech, and also by the movements of the eyes and face, the hidden mind is known.
The wise have declared that the eye is of four kinds—brilliant, impassioned, curved, and reddish—and they have described its respective emotional states individually.
It is brilliant upon meeting a friend, full of luster upon seeing a son, crooked in the company of a lover, and slightly reddish upon seeing an enemy.
But in this case, all my faculties and senses are turbid; he must surely be my enemy and must be slain, without a doubt.
O King, the word of my guru is now being fulfilled by you; he who causes me suffering must be slain by you in every way—no hesitation should be made in this matter.
"For this purpose, my weapons [are at your disposal], of this there is no doubt"; having reflected thus, he remained right there, fixing his arrow in place.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, indeed remained there for the purpose of protecting Arjuna and for the sake of testing his devotion.
Indeed, having quickly assumed a most wonderful form as a clever Bhilla along with his attendants for the sake of destroying that Daitya, he arrived.
Then, with his waistband fastened by women, the banner of the Lord of the North was raised; white lines appeared upon his body, and he himself was equipped with a bow and arrows.
Placing a quiver of arrows upon his back, he indeed departed; thus he became a member of the Gaṇas, and Śiva became the king of the Bhillas.
Making various sounds, the commander of the army marched forth; then the roar of the boar resounded throughout the ten directions.
Then Arjuna was agitated by that sound of the forest-dweller, and all those others, including the mountain-dwellers, were likewise agitated by those sounds.
"Aha! Could this be Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness here? For I have heard it before, and it was told to me again by Kṛṣṇa."
Vyāsa spoke thus, and having remembered it again, the gods likewise declared that Śiva is the doer of good and Śiva is the bestower of happiness.
He is himself declared to be the giver of liberation, for there is no doubt that he bestows liberation; by remembering his name, welfare certainly arises for men.
For those who worship with their whole being, suffering shall not occur even in a dream; if it should ever arise, it would then be produced solely from [past] karma.
This object of knowledge, though vast, is indeed small; of this there is no doubt. Or rather, it must specifically be understood as the fault of that which has already begun.
Alternatively, having exhausted much or little of what is to be experienced, Śaṅkara may at times, by his own will, remove it; of this there is no doubt.
He can turn poison into nectar, or indeed turn nectar into poison; if he so desires, he does exactly that—being so powerful, what can be forbidden?
Even when investigated in this manner, the minds of other ancient devotees and those of future devotees should always be brought here and made firm.
Whether fortune departs or remains, whether death stands near at hand, whether they utter censure or praise, may there be the destruction of suffering.
Śaṅkara, the ever-bestower of happiness, is born from both merit and demerit; yet at times, Śiva indeed inflicts suffering for the sake of testing one's character.
And it is declared that he bestows happiness at the end because of his compassion; of this there is no doubt. Just as gold, when purified, attains a state of purity.
Thus have I previously heard from the mouth of the Sage; therefore, by worshipping him alone, I shall attain supreme happiness.
While he was indeed reflecting in this manner, a boar arrived, right up until the moment of discharging his arrow.
Śiva also followed closely behind the boar; then, between the two of them, that wonderful horn was seen.
Having been told of his greatness, Śiva, who is affectionate toward his devotees, quickly went there for the sake of protecting Arjuna. Śaṅkara departed with great haste.
At that moment, they both released their arrows; Śiva’s arrow struck the tail, while Arjuna’s struck his mouth.
Having gone from Śiva’s tail and swiftly issued forth from his mouth, he dissolved into the earth; indeed, having gone from his tail, he departed.
The arrow fell at the side of Arjuna, and at that very moment, the boar-like Daitya fell dead upon the earth.
The gods attained supreme joy and showered flowers; uttering cries of victory and offering praises, they bowed down again and again.
Śiva was pleased in mind, and Arjuna arrived happily; then, having seen that cruel form of the Daitya, they both [remained there].
But Arjuna, with a mind full of particular joy, said: "Aho! This is indeed the best of Daityas, and his form is most wonderful."
Having come here for the purpose of killing me, I have been well protected by Śiva; undoubtedly, the Lord has bestowed wisdom upon me this very day.
Having reflected upon this, Arjuna there cried out "Śiva, Śiva! He bowed again to Śiva and praised him repeatedly.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Mūka," in the description of the Kirāta incarnation within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, listen to the divine play (līlā) of the Supreme Self, which is imbued with affection for His devotees and intensified by their steadfastness.
Then Śiva also swiftly dispatched his own servant for the sake of Bāṇa; at that time, Arjuna also arrived there.
Once, when Arjuna and his brother had both arrived for the sake of arrows, Arjuna then rebuked him and took the arrows for himself.
There, Gaṇa said to him, "O best of sages, for what purpose is this arrow being held? Let this arrow of ours indeed be released."
Thus addressed by that host of Bhillas, that best of sages, Arjuna, remembered Śaṅkara and spoke these words to them.
Arjuna said: "Why do you speak thus without knowing? You are a fool, O forest-dweller! My arrow has been discharged today; how could yours possibly be released again?"
The peacock feathers are in the form of lines and marked with my name; how did they become yours? Your very nature is difficult for you to abandon.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words, that lord of the Gaṇas laughed and addressed these words to Arjuna, who was in the form of a sage: "The hunter replied."
"O ascetic, listen! No penance is being performed by you; though you are an ascetic in appearance, you do not act according to the truth, but rather out of deceit."
How could an ascetic man speak falsely or act deceitfully? And you should know me not as one who is alone, but as a commander of an army.
Accompanied by many forest-dwellers, that lord remained there, fully capable in every way of performing both acts of punishment and favor.
This speech belongs to him who has now been led away by you; and this Bāṇa shall never remain by your side.
O ascetic, why do you wish to abandon the fruit of your penance by means of theft, deceitful injury, arrogance, and the breaking of truth?
"Truth is diminished by asceticism; this very thing has been heard by me. Therefore, from that asceticism, where will there be any fruit today?"
And you shall be released from that arrow, yet you will become ungrateful; for this arrow of my very master has certainly been discharged for your sake.
By him the enemy was slain, yet Bāṇa was protected; you are exceedingly ungrateful and likewise a performer of inauspicious penance.
"You do not speak the truth; what success do you desire from this? If there is a purpose, let my master be entreated by you with an arrow."
The king himself is capable of giving many such arrows as these today; why then do you beg of me in this manner?
Having abandoned kindness, you indeed seek to do harm; this is not proper for you to do now—abandon your fickleness!
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of his, Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā, then became enraged; yet, remembering Śiva, he spoke these measured words.
Arjuna said: Listen, Bhillas! I shall speak; your speech is not true. For I know you, O forest-dweller, to be exactly as your birth would suggest.
I am a king and you are a thief; how can there be an engagement in battle? I must wage war against those who possess armies, never indeed against the lowly.
Therefore, you shall likewise become masters like yourself, while we are declared to be the givers, and you forest-dwellers are thieves.
"How can the Bhilla king be entreated by me now in this manner? You yourself are the one who should entreat Bāṇa; why do you, a forest-dweller, not entreat me?"
"I shall give you arrows in that manner; indeed, I have many of them. However, the king will not grant permission for their delivery, so it must happen in this way."
Moreover, O forest-dweller, why do you provide such arrows? If I have some purpose to accomplish, why is it that you do not come now?
"Let your husband come; why do you speak thus now? Let him come and, having fought with me, defeat me in battle once again."
"O Bhilla, having taken this arrow, let your lord, the commander of the army, go happily to his own home; why is delay being made?"
Nandīśvara said: Having heard these words of Arjuna, who had indeed obtained true strength through the grace of Maheśvara, the Bhilla then spoke this speech.
