The Bhilla said: "You are ignorant; you are not a sage. Why do you desire death? Give me the arrow and remain at ease; otherwise, you shall become a partaker of suffering."
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by that Bhilla, a Gaṇa adorned with the true power of Śiva, the Pāṇḍava remembered Śaṅkara and spoke to him.
Arjuna said: "O Bhilla, O forest-dweller, listen to my words according to their true meaning. Your master will arrive; at that time, I shall show you the fruit [of your actions]."
It does not befit you to fight with me, your master; a battle between a lion and a jackal should be known as nothing but a mockery.
You have heard my words today; you shall see that one of great strength. Go, O Bhilla, to your own master and do as you wish.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, having been addressed thus by Pārtha, the Bhilla went to that place where the leader of the army, the Kirāta who was an incarnation of Śiva, was staying.
Then he related Arjuna’s words in full detail to the lord of the Bhillas, to that supreme soul of the Bhillas.
Having heard those words, that lord of the Kirātas was filled with joy; Śaṅkara, assuming the form of a Bhilla, arrived together with his own army.
And then Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, having seen the army of the Kirāta, took up his bow along with arrows and advanced toward him.
Then the Kirāta again dispatched that messenger, who spoke these words to the high-souled descendant of Bharata through his mouth.
The Kirāta said: "Look, O ascetic, at this army; release your arrow and depart now. Why do you desire death at this moment for the sake of such a trivial matter?"
Your brothers are afflicted with grief, as is your wife; beyond that, it is my conviction that the earth itself will now pass from your hands.
Nandīśvara said: Thus was it spoken by the Supreme Lord Śambhu, who had assumed a physical form for the sake of protecting Arjuna in every way, in order to test the steadfastness of Pārtha.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara then returned with his attendants and reported the entire event in detail to Arjuna.
Having heard that, the king spoke again to the messenger who had arrived: "It must be told to the commander of the army that everything will turn out contrary."
If I were to give you my own arrow, O Bāṇa, I would undoubtedly become a defiler of my lineage.
May my brothers also certainly be afflicted by suffering, and may those very sciences become fruitless; therefore, come indeed with certainty.
I have never heard of a lion being afraid of a jackal, nor does a king ever fear one who roams the forest.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus, he went back to his master, the Pāṇḍava, and reported everything that had been said, especially in detail.
Then that great god named Kirāta, accompanied by his army, having heard that, arrived at once with his troops to meet Arjuna.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between the Bhilla and Arjuna," in the description of the Kirāta incarnation within the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Seeing him arrive from there, Arjuna performed meditation upon Śiva, went to that place, and engaged in a most terrible battle with him.
And with various sharp weapons, the hosts tormented him; thus afflicted by them at that time, Pārtha remembered his lord Śiva.
Then Arjuna shattered their volley of arrows; when they discharged their weapons in battle, he then struck down all of Śarva's [missiles].
Afflicted by him, those hosts fled in the ten directions; though restrained by Gaṇeśa, they did not return to their master.
Both Śiva and Arjuna, possessed of great strength and prowess, fought with one another using various kinds of weapons.
Śiva too, having surely felt compassion in his mind, approached Arjuna; and then Arjuna struck him there with a firm blow.
Then Śiva indeed severed all the weapons and all the armor of Arjuna, so that only his bare body remained.
Then Arjuna, remembering Śiva, engaged in hand-to-hand combat with that commander of the army; though distressed by fear, he remained steadfast in his courage.
By that battle, the entire earth, together with its oceans, trembled; the gods fell into distress, wondering, "What will happen next?"
In the meantime, Lord Śiva, stationed in the sky, engaged in battle; Arjuna, remaining there, did likewise.
Flying up again and again, those two—the god and the king—engaged in combat; and the gods were filled with wonder upon seeing that marvelous battle.
Then, having recognized Arjuna’s superior state and remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he indeed held him by the feet, having obtained true strength through that meditation.
Then Arjuna, seizing his feet, whirled him around; Mahādeva, who is affectionate toward his devotees and the performer of protection, laughed aloud.
O Sage, it was Śiva alone who, out of subjection to his devotees, made himself a slave to him; for this deed could not have been otherwise.
Thereafter, Śaṅkara, smiling right there, suddenly revealed his auspicious and wonderful form out of his subjection to the devotion of his devotees.
As it is stated in the Vedic scriptures and the Purāṇas, that which was taught by Vyāsa for the purpose of meditation upon Puruṣottama bestows all perfections.
Having seen that beautiful form of Śiva absorbed in meditation, Arjuna himself became exceedingly astonished and ashamed.
Oh, what auspiciousness! What supreme fortune that he, the Lord of the three worlds himself in person, has been chosen by me as my master! Alas, what have I done now?
The Lord’s power of illusion is mighty, deluding even the masters of illusion; for by concealing His true form, the Lord has indeed deceived me.
Having reflected thus with his intellect, he, with palms joined and head bowed, prostrated before the Lord with affection; then, with a distressed mind, he spoke.
Arjuna said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, compassionate Śaṅkara, O Lord of all, my transgression must once again be forgiven by you.
"What have you done? Having concealed your true form, you have now deceived me! Fie on me, your servant, who engaged in battle with you, my lord!"
Nandīśvara said: Thus, that Pāṇḍava then experienced remorse and quickly prostrated at the feet of the great lord Śaṅkara.
Then the Lord Maheśa, whose soul was pleased and who is affectionate toward his devotees, having consoled Arjuna in many ways, replied to him.
Śaṅkara said: "Do not grieve, O Pārtha; for you are especially my devotee. This was done by me today merely for the sake of testing you; therefore, cast away your sorrow."
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus, the Lord raised Arjuna with his own two hands and caused him to feel ashamed before the hosts of his own attendants.
Then Śiva, the benefactor who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke again to Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu esteemed as a hero, gladdening him in every way with great love.
Śiva said: "O Pārtha, best of the Pāṇḍavas, I am pleased; choose a boon. By these blows and strikes, you have today honored me with worship."
This was done by me today out of my own desire; there is no fault of yours now. There is nothing that cannot be given to you; choose whatever you wish.
They have performed a virtuous deed for the sake of establishing fame and sovereignty over their enemies; you should not feel this sorrow, and you must abandon all despondency.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by that Lord Śaṅkara, Arjuna, remaining attentive, spoke to Śaṅkara with devotion.
Arjuna said: O Lord of auspicious light, what is the desired purpose of you, Śambhu, who are so dear to your devotees? O God, it must be described by me; you are ever-compassionate, O Sadāśiva.
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava then performed a hymn of praise for that great lord Śaṅkara, characterized by true devotion and in accordance with the Vedas.
Arjuna said: Salutations to you, the God of gods; salutations to the dweller of Kailāsa. O Sadāśiva, salutations to you; salutations to you who possess five faces.
Salutations to you, O Kapardin; salutations be to you, the three-eyed one; and salutations to him of tranquil form and a thousand faces.
O Blue-throated One, salutations to you; indeed, salutations to Sadyojāta. O Bull-bannered One, salutations to you, and to the Daughter of the Mountain who is your left limb.
O you who possess ten defects, salutations to you; salutations to you, the Supreme Self. Salutations to you who hold a hand-drum and a skull-cup, and who wear a garland of severed heads.
To you who resemble pure crystal, whose body is like pure camphor, who hold the Pināka bow in hand, and who bear the excellent trident.
Salutations to you who have a tiger skin as an upper garment and who wear elephant hide; salutations to you whose limbs are like serpents; O bearer of the Gaṅgā, homage be to you.
Salutations to you who possess beautiful feet, and salutations to you whose feet are slightly reddened; salutations to you, Gaṇeśa, who is served by the hosts of Nandin and the other attendants.
Salutations to the one who has the form of Gaṇeśa and who follows Kārttikeya; salutations again and again to the giver of devotion to devotees and the giver of liberation.

Salutations to you who are devoid of qualities; salutations again and again to you who possess qualities. Salutations to the formless and to the one with form, to the one who is whole and to the one who is partless.
Homage to him who took the form of a Kirāta to bestow grace upon me, who delights in battle, who is the hero of heroes, and who enacts various divine sports.
Whatever form is seen, all that is known as your radiance; you are the embodiment of consciousness within the three worlds, delighting through the distinctions of your own nature.
There is no end to the number of your virtues, just as there is none here for the particles of dust on the earth, nor for the stars in the sky, nor for the drops of rainwater.
Indeed, even the Vedas are not capable of enumerating your virtues; how then, O Lord, can I, who am of dull intellect, describe them?
Whether it be day or night, salutations be unto you; you ought to show mercy here. I am your servant, O Maheśāna; you are my master, O Maheśvara.
Nandīśvara said: Having heard his words, the Lord Śaṅkara, becoming exceedingly gracious and smiling, spoke again to Arjuna.
Śaṅkara said: What is the use of speaking at length? Listen to my words. Choose quickly a boon, my son; I shall grant it all to you.
Nandīśvara said: Having been addressed thus by him, Arjuna prostrated before Sadāśiva and, with palms joined in reverence and body bowed, spoke with words faltering with love.
Arjuna said: What could I say, since you abide as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all? Nevertheless, O Lord, what has been described by me today shall be heard by you.
Whatever distress from enemies has befallen me, may it vanish upon seeing you; act in such a way that I may indeed attain both worldly and supreme perfection.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus and paid homage to Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, Arjuna stood there with shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence.
And Śiva, the Lord, having likewise recognized Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava, as his most excellent devotee, became exceedingly pleased.
Maheśāna gave him his own Pāśupata weapon, which is invincible by all at all times, and spoke these words:
Śiva said: "I have given you my own great weapon; you shall become invincible. By means of this, achieve the task of victory over all enemies."
And I shall speak of Kṛṣṇa; he will provide you with assistance. He is indeed my very own self, my devotee, and the one who carries out my work.
O Bhārata, by my power, make your kingdom free from thorns; and always cause various righteous deeds to be performed by your brothers.
Nandīśvara said: Having spoken thus and placing his own hand upon the head of Arjuna, Śaṅkara, being honored by Arjuna, quickly vanished.
Then Arjuna, his soul serene, having obtained the weapon and the boon from the Lord, went to his own preeminent hermitage, remembering his guru Śiva with devotion.
All those brothers, filled with joy, met him as if he were their own life-breath returned; they attained happiness together, as did the most virtuous Draupadī.
All the Pāṇḍavas indeed found supreme auspiciousness and contentment; having heard the entire account, they were filled with joy and could not be satiated.
And a rain of flowers, mixed with sandalwood paste, fell upon the hermitage for the sake of that boar and for those high-souled ones.
Having joyfully paid homage to Śiva, who is both Dhanya and Śaṅkara, and knowing that the appointed time has arrived, victory shall indeed be yours.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa, having heard that Arjuna had arrived and learned that he had come for a meeting, went forth and met him with joy.
Therefore, I have declared that Śaṅkara is the destroyer of all suffering; he is constantly served by me, and he should be served by you as well.
Thus has been told to you the incarnation of Śaṅkara known as Kirāta; by hearing this or causing others to hear it, one shall attain all desires.

Thus end the eighty-eight incarnations. Thus concludes the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Kirāteśvara Incarnation," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā of the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Nandīśvara said: O Sage, hear of the supreme twelve incarnations of the Lord, which indeed take the form of jyotirliṅgas and perform various functions.
Somanātha is in Saurāṣṭra, Mallikārjuna on Śrīśaila, Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, and Amareśvara at Oṃkāra.
Kedāra is on the slopes of the Himavat; Bhīmaśaṅkara is with the Ḍākinīs; Viśveśa is in Vārāṇasī; and Tryambaka is on the bank of the Gautamī.
Vaidyanātha is on the cremation ground, Nāgeśa in the Dāruka forest, Rāmeśa at Setubandha, and Ghuśmeśa in the abode of Śiva.
O Sage, these twelve incarnations of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, bestow all bliss upon men through being seen or touched.
Among them, O Sage, the first is Somanātha, who brings about the destruction of the suffering caused by the moon; through worship, he is the destroyer of diseases such as consumption and leprosy.
The incarnation of Śiva known as Someśa is established in the form of a Liṅga; in the auspicious land of Saurāṣṭra, he was worshipped by the Moon in ancient times.
And right there is Candrakuṇḍa, which destroys all sins; by bathing there, a wise man is liberated from all diseases.
Having beheld Someśvara, the great liṅga which is the supreme self of Śiva, one is liberated from sin and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O dear one, the second incarnation of Śaṅkara is indeed known as Mallikārjuna on Śrīgiri, the bestower of the fruits of the devotees' desires.
O Sage, having been praised in the form of a *liṅga* for the sake of seeing his son, that Śiva went there from his own mountain with great joy.
O Sage, that second Jyotirliṅga bestows great happiness through its sight and worship, and grants liberation at the end; of this there is no doubt.
The incarnation of Śaṅkara known as Mahākāla indeed appeared in the city of Ujjayinī for the protection of his own people.
He who [slew] the asura named Dūṣaṇa, the crusher of the Vedic dharma, who had gone to Ujjayinī, the hater of brahmins and the destroyer of all.
Meditated upon by the Brahmins learned in the Vedas, he swiftly reduced him, who was dwelling in Ratnamālā, to ashes with a mere *huṃ* sound.
Having slain him, that Mahākāla remained there in the form of a *jyotirliṅga*, requested by the gods, as the protector of his own devotees.
Having beheld and diligently worshipped the Liṅga named Mahākāla, one attains all desires and obtains the supreme state hereafter.
Oṃkāra is the Supreme Lord; upheld by Śambhu, the Supreme Self, he is indeed the fourth incarnation, the bestower of the fruits desired by his devotees.
O Sage, Mahādeva, the fulfiller of the desires of Vindhya, manifested from his own earthen *liṅga* through the ritual installation performed with devotion.

Requested by the gods there, he remained established in a twofold form; in the form of a *liṅga*, he is indeed the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, being ever affectionate toward his devotees.
O Lord of Sages, the syllable Om is indeed the supreme liṅga named Praṇava, and the earthen liṅga is named Parameśvara.
O Sage, it should be known that even when merely seen or worshipped, this most divine Jyotirlinga grants the desires of devotees; thus has it been described to you, O great sage.
The fifth incarnation of Paramaśiva is Kedāreśa, who is established in Kedāra in the form of a Jyotirliṅga.
O Sage, when those two incarnations of Hari known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa were present there, Śiva was entreated by them at Kedāra on the Himālaya mountain.
And Śambhu, known as Kedāreśvara, who grants the desires of his devotees even through mere sight or worship, was constantly honored by those two.
He is the lord of this region, especially the lord of all; O dear one, he is the bestower of all desires and is indeed an incarnation of Śiva.
The sixth incarnation of the great lord Śambhu is known as Bhīmaśaṅkara; he is a performer of great divine play who brought about the destruction of the demon Bhīma.
He protected the king named Sudakṣiṇa, the lord of Kāmarūpa and a devoted worshipper, by slaying the wondrous demon who caused suffering to his devotees.
He himself, known by the name Bhīmaśaṅkara, was established within a ḍākinī; Śaṅkara was then entreated by him in the form of a jyotirliṅga.
O Sage, the seventh incarnation of Viśveśvara was indeed born in Kāśī; he is the embodiment of the entire universe and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He is always worshipped with devotion by all the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as by the Lord of Kailāsa and by Bhairava eternally.
Established there in the form of a Jyotirlinga, that Lord is the bestower of liberation; indeed, in his own city, he exists as the very embodiment of perfection.
Those who, through devotion to Kāśī and Viśveśa, constantly perform the chanting of their names, remain eternally untainted by karma and partake in the state of absolute liberation.
The eighth incarnation, known as Tryambaka, who appeared on the bank of the Gautamī at the request of Gautama, was the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
At the request of Gautama, he remained there in the form of a Jyotirliṅga, immovable out of affection and with the desire to please that sage.
Through beholding, touching, and seeing that Great Lord, all desires are fulfilled; from that, oh, liberation shall arise!
By the grace of Śiva, the purifying Gaṅgā, beloved of Śaṅkara, remained there under the name Gautamī out of affection for Gautama.
Indeed, the ninth incarnation therein is celebrated as Vaidyanātha; the Lord, the performer of many divine sports, manifested for the sake of Rāvaṇa.
Indeed, having employed the pretext of bringing that [body], Maheśvara established himself upon the cremation ground in the form of a Jyotirliṅga.
He became renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Vaidyanātheśvara; indeed, through seeing him, worshipping him, and through devotion, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Sage, this instruction on the majesty of Vaidyanātheśvara Śiva bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who read it or even hear it.
The tenth incarnation is proclaimed to be that of Nāgeśvara; he has manifested for the sake of his devotees, always bestowing punishment upon the wicked.
Having slain the Rākṣasa named Dāruka, the destroyer of righteousness, he protected his own devotee, the lord of the Vaiśyas, known by the name Supriya.
For the benefit of the worlds, Śambhu—the supreme being who performs manifold divine sports—remained there assuming the form of a Jyotirliṅga together with Ambikā.
O Sage, having seen that Śiva-liṅga named Nāgeśvara and having worshipped it, multitudes of great sins perish instantly.
O Sage, the incarnation as Rāmeśvara is remembered as the eleventh of Śiva; it was established by Rāma and brings delight to Rāmacandra.
Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being well-pleased, manifested as a Liṅga and out of love granted the boon of victory to Rāma.
O Sage, requested earnestly by Rāma to remain in the form of a jyotirliṅga, he remained at Setubandha, served by Rāma.
The majesty of Rāmeśvara became marvelous and incomparable upon the earth; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and always grants the desires of its devotees.
And that man who bathes Rāmeśvara with the very waters of the Gaṅgā with true devotion is indeed liberated while living.
Having enjoyed here all pleasures, even those difficult for the gods to obtain, and having thereafter attained supreme knowledge, one shall reach the liberation of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
The incarnation as Ghuśmeśvara is indeed the twelfth of Śaṅkara; he performs various divine sports, bestows bliss upon Ghuśmā, and is affectionate toward his devotees.
O Sage, in the southern direction, near Mount Devaśaila, the Lord, who brings delight to Ghuśmā, appeared in a lake.
O Sage, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, was pleased by that devotion and protected Ghuśmā’s son, Sudehya, who had been killed, restoring him in his entirety.
Requested by her, Śambhu indeed remained there in that lake in the form of a Jyotirliṅga, bestowing all desires, under the name Ghuśmeśvara.
Having seen that Śiva-liṅga and having worshipped it with devotion, one enjoys all happiness in this world and thereafter attains liberation.
Thus, this divine series of twelve Jyotirliṅgas, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been fully described by me to you.
Whoever reads or even hears this narrative of the Jyotirlingas is liberated from all sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This Saṃhitā, known as the Śatarudrīya, has been described by me; it contains the glorious fame of the hundred incarnations and bestows the fruit of all desires.
Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with a concentrated mind attains all desires and thereafter certainly obtains liberation.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of the Twelve Jyotirliṅgas," in the Śatarudra-saṃhitā, the third part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nandīśvara.

Salutations eternally to that Effulgence, whose body is half-conquered by the Daughter of the Mountain; who, though free from all transformation, assumes the form of the universe through his own Māyā alone; whose compassionate side-glances are said to possess the power known as heaven and liberation; and whom yogis always behold within their hearts as the non-dual bliss of inward consciousness.

May that indescribable splendor bring auspiciousness—a splendor whose gaze is playful with compassion, whose lotus-face is charming with a smile, which shines with a digit of the moon, which pacifies the three terrible afflictions, and which possesses a body of pure existence and consciousness vibrating with supreme bliss, encircled by the arms of the Daughter of the Mountain.
The sages said: "O Sūta, you have spoken perfectly out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, concerning the majesty of Śiva’s incarnations, accompanied by various narratives."
Speak again, O dear one, with great affection regarding the supreme majesty of Śiva connected to the Liṅga; you are blessed, O best among the devotees of Śiva.
O Lord, we are not yet satiated by hearing the delightful nectar of Śiva’s glory from your lotus-like mouth; let that very same account be told once more.
Whatever auspicious lingas exist upon the earth at various sacred fords (tīrthas), or whatever others are renowned and established in other locations;
O disciple of Vyāsa, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, describe those various divine lingas of the Supreme Lord.
Sūta said: O best of sages, you have asked well out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; O twice-born ones, out of affection for you, I shall relate those matters in brief.
O Sage, there is no end to the number of all Śiva-liṅgas; the entire earth consists of liṅgas, and the whole world is composed of liṅgas.
The sacred fords consist of the Liṅga; everything is established in the Liṅga. There is no numbering them, yet I shall say something of them.
Whatever object of sight is seen, whatever is described, and whatever is remembered—all that is indeed the form of Śiva; there is nothing else whatsoever.
Nevertheless, listen with pleasure; I shall relate according to what I have heard those very lingas which exist upon the earth, O best of sages.
Śambhu dwells in the netherworld, in heaven, and likewise upon the earth; everywhere he is worshipped by gods, asuras, and humans alike.
O best of beings, the three worlds—including gods, asuras, and humans—are pervaded by Śambhu in the form of a *liṅga* for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
For the sake of favoring the worlds, Maheśvara assumes various forms here at this sacred site as well as in other places.
Wherever and whenever Śambhu was remembered with devotion by his devotees, he would descend to that very place, perform the necessary task, and then remain there.
For the benefit of the worlds, he fashioned his own *liṅga*; by worshipping that *liṅga*, one attains perfection (*siddhi*).
O twice-born ones, there is no end to the number of lingas upon the earth; nevertheless, I shall describe the principal ones to you.
And among the principal ones here, I shall proclaim those which are the most important; by hearing which, a human being is liberated from all sins in an instant.
O best of beings, I shall now describe those Jyotirliṅgas which are the most preeminent here; by hearing of them, one's sin is dispelled.
Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra, Mallikārjuna on Śrīśaila, Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, and Parameśvara at Oṃkāra.
Kedāra on the ridge of the Himalayas, Bhīmaśaṅkara in Ḍākinī, Viśveśa in Vārāṇasī, and Tryambaka on the bank of the Gautamī.
Vaidyanātha on the cremation ground, Nāgeśa in the Dāruka forest, Rāmeśa at Setubandha, and Ghuśmeśa in the abode of Śiva.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites these twelve names shall be completely liberated from all sins and obtain the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments.
Whatever desire those best of men may have in view when they recite this, they shall indeed attain that very desire, just as the lords of sages do in the next world.
Those of virtuous intention who shall recite these [verses] with a mind free from desire—for them there will be no dwelling again within a mother’s womb.
By the worship of these alone, the suffering of the social classes is destroyed; liberation is certain both in this world and in the next.
Their offerings of food and eatables should be accepted with great care; indeed, all the sins of the one who performs that act are reduced to ashes in an instant.
O twice-born ones, even by Brahmā and the other gods it is not possible to fully describe the specific fruits of the luminaries and the *liṅgas*, nor can they be described by anyone else.
And for one who has worshipped it continuously for six months, the suffering arising from the mother’s womb shall not occur.
When one born of a low womb beholds a jyotirliṅga, his birth shall thereafter be in a pure and noble family.
Having obtained birth in a noble family, being wealthy and a master of the Vedas, one who then performs auspicious deeds attains imperishable liberation.

O lords of sages, whether one is a barbarian, an outcaste, or even a eunuch, by becoming a twice-born [through this rite], one becomes liberated; therefore, one should perform the vision of that [deity].
And I have described some of the fruits of the luminaries and the lingas.
O best of sages, let the secondary signs of the luminaries also be heard.
The Liṅga of Someśvara which is proclaimed as Antakeśa, that Liṅga, at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, is an Upaliṅga.
The secondary linga (upaliṅga) originating from Mallikārjuna is proclaimed as Rudreśvara, renowned in Bhṛgukakṣa as a bringer of happiness.
The Liṅga known as Mahākālabhava is renowned as Dugdhīśa; it is famous on the Narmadā and is remembered as the remover of all sins.
And that Liṅga born of the syllable Oṃ, known as Kardameśa, is famous at Bindusaras and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Born from Kedāreśvara, Bhūteśa on the bank of the Yamunā is declared to be the destroyer of great sins for those who behold it and likewise for those who worship it.
Born from Bhīma and Śaṅkara, it is remembered as Bhīmeśvara; renowned on the Sahya mountain, it increases great strength.
Born from Nāgeśvara, it is proclaimed as Bhūteśvara; situated on the bank of the Mallikāsarasvatī, it removes sins through its mere sight.
That which arose from Rāmeśvara is remembered as Gupteśvara; and that which arose from Ghuśmeśa is remembered as Vyāghreśvara.
O twice-born ones, I have here described the Jyotirliṅgas and Upaliṅgas, which remove sins through their mere sight and bestow all desired objects.
These are indeed the most preeminent and have attained the status of being primary; hear now, O best of sages, of other principal ones as well.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Jyotirlinga and its Subsidiary Lingas," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Kāśī on the banks of the Gaṅgā is indeed renowned as the bestower of liberation; it should be known as consisting of liṅgas and is remembered as the dwelling place of Śiva.
The Liṅga known as Avimukta is declared to be the primary one right there; Kṛttivāseśvara is manifest, and Vṛddhabālaka is equal to him.
Tilabhāṇḍeśvara, Daśāśvamedha, and Saṅgameśa, which is remembered as being at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
He who is proclaimed as Bhūteśvara, the eternal bestower of all goals upon his devotees, is renowned as Nārīśvara; he is situated near the Kauśikī river.
He himself exists on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī as Baṭukeśvara; he is renowned as Pūreśvara on the bank of the Phalgu, bestowing happiness.
Siddhanātheśvara likewise bestows success upon men through his mere sight; he is likewise renowned as Dūreśvara in the northern city.
There is indeed Śṛṅgeśvara by name, and likewise Vaidyanātha; and he who is renowned as Japyeśvara in the region of Dadhīciraṇa.
Gopeśvara is well-known, and Raṅgeśvara is remembered; likewise Vāmeśvara, Nāgeśa, Kājeśa, and Vimaleśvara.
Vyāseśvara is renowned, and likewise Sukeśa; Bhāṇḍeśvara is famous, and similarly Huṃkāreśa.
And he is renowned as Surocana, and himself as Bhūteśvara; likewise, he is called Saṅgameśa, the destroyer of great sins.

And then, on the bank of the Taptakā, there is Kumāreśvara; Siddheśvara is renowned, and Seneśa is likewise remembered. Rāmeśvara is proclaimed, and Kuṃbheśa is considered supreme. Nandīśvara, Puṃjeśa, and likewise Pūrṇaka are located at Pūrṇā.
In ancient times, Brahmeśvara was established by Brahmā during his ritual performance; indeed, at the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha, he bestows the fruits of the four aims of human existence.
Likewise, Someśvara is there, the warder-off of all calamities; and Bhāradvājeśvara, who increases spiritual luster.
Śūlaṭaṅkeśvara is said to be the manifest bestower of desires; and Mādhaveśa is located in that very place, the protector of his devotees.
Indeed, there was a well-known brahmin named Nāgeśa in the city of Sāketa, who especially brought happiness to those born of the Solar dynasty.
In the city of Puruṣottama, Bhuvaneśa bestows spiritual perfection; and Lokeśa, the great Liṅga, is the bestower of all bliss.
Kāmeśvara is the Śambhu-liṅga, and Gaṅgeśa is the purifier supreme; Śakreśvara is the perfected Śukra, acting out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Likewise, Vaṭeśvara is renowned as the bestower of the fruits of all desires; Kapāleśa is on the shore of the ocean, and Vaktreśa is the destroyer of all sins.
Dhautapāpeśvara is the Supreme Lord himself, present through his partial incarnation.
He is proclaimed as Bhīmeśvara and remembered as Sūryeśvara.
Nandeśvara should be known as the giver of knowledge, worshipped by the world; likewise, Nākeśvara is of great merit, and Rāmeśvara is remembered [as such].
Indeed, there is the one named Vimaleśvara and Kaṇṭakeśvara as well; likewise, Dhārtekeśa is at the confluence of the Pūrṇa and the Sāgara.
Candreśvara is to be known as the bestower of the fruits of lunar splendor; he is remembered as Siddheśvara, the bestower of all desires.
And Bilveśvara is renowned, as is Andhakeśa, where in ancient times the Daitya Andhaka was slain by Śaṅkara.
Having assumed his own form in part, Śambhu remains once more, renowned as Śaraṇeśvara, the eternal bestower of happiness upon the worlds.
Kardameśa is declared to be supreme, and Koṭīśa resides on Mount Arbuda; Acaleśa is also renowned, always bestowing happiness upon the worlds.
Nāgeśvara, however, dwells eternally on the bank of the Kauśikī; he is known as Ananteśvara and is a vessel of auspiciousness and welfare.
Yogeśvara is renowned, as is Vaidyanātheśvara; Koṭīśvara should be known, and he is remembered as Sapteśvara.
Bhadreśvara is renowned, as is Hara himself under the name Bhadra; likewise, Caṇḍīśvara and Saṃgameśvara have been proclaimed.
Whatever Śiva-liṅgas have arisen in the eastern direction, whether they be common or otherwise, those have been described here to you.
O best of sages, I shall now describe to you those Śiva-liṅgas that have appeared in the southern direction.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Śiva-liṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: In Brahmapurī is the Citrakūṭa Liṅga known as Mattagajendra; it was formerly installed by Brahmā and bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
To the east of that is the Koṭīśa Liṅga, which bestows all boons; to the west of the Godāvarī is that Liṅga named Paśupati.
In the southern direction, there is one known as Atrīśvara himself, for the sake of benefiting the worlds and for the happiness of Anasūyā.
The Lord himself appeared and, during a drought, brought life back to the people; he is indeed Śaṅkara himself, manifest through his own portion.
The sages said: "O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, how was the supreme and divine Lord Hara, who is without a mother, born? Tell us this truth, O you of excellent vows."
Sūta said: Well asked, O best of sages! I shall relate the auspicious narrative, by constantly hearing which one is surely liberated from sins.
In the southern direction, near Citrakūṭa, there is a great forest named Kāmada, which bestows benefit upon the asceticism of the virtuous.
And there, the sage named Atri, the son of Brahmā himself, performed extremely rigorous penance, endowed with freedom from malice.
O Sage, once in the past, right there, a hundred-year drought occurred by fate—a terrible and painful calamity for all living beings.
O lords of sages, at that time all the trees were withered, lacking both foliage and fruit; not even a drop of water was to be seen anywhere for daily use.
Moisture could not be found, and harsh winds blew from the ten directions; indeed, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose upon the earth, causing extreme suffering.
Seeing the dissolution of all beings, Atri’s beloved wife, who was virtuous, said to Atri: "I cannot endure this suffering."
Then that best of sages, remaining seated on his own seat, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times and became absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi).
The wise Atri, the best of sages, meditated by himself upon the supreme light situated within the self—the changeless Śaṅkara.
And while the Master was absorbed in meditation, those disciples went far away; then, being without food, they abandoned that sage, their own guru.
Then that devoted Anasūyā was left all alone.
And she constantly served that best of sages with joy, having made the king beautiful through a mantra according to the prescribed rites.
He worshipped Śaṅkara with mental offerings and, having served him again and again, praised Śaṅkara with devotion.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, having departed from the auspicious Lord, he performed a return-prostration by falling like a staff.
That Anasūyā, the beloved wife of the sage, maintained her excellent conduct; meanwhile, all the Daityas and Dānavas beheld that beautiful woman.
They became overwhelmed there and remained at a distance from his splendor; indeed, they stood far off just as one stands at a distance upon seeing fire.
Seeing her thus not coming near at that time, Anasūyā reflected upon the power of Atri’s asceticism and her own service to Śiva.
O best of Brahmins, she was distinguished by her refinement of mind, speech, and body; for that entire duration, the goddess indeed performed service.
For as long as the best of sages remained devoted to breath control, the couple there continued to be intent upon their respective duties.
O tiger among sages, when those two were thus established, no other being remained superior; at that time, Atri, the best of rishis, was likewise present.
Absorbed in supreme meditation, he did not perceive anything at all; and the virtuous Anasūyā likewise [perceived] her husband as Śiva himself.
And that virtuous woman knew nothing else whatsoever as supreme; for by his asceticism alone and by her devotion to him, all things were accomplished.
The gods, the sages, and all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, being filled with supreme affection, arrived together to behold the two of them.
And having witnessed that very penance, they were filled with supreme wonder; seeing that miracle of theirs, they declared their devotion to be excellent.
What is the distinction between the two—asceticism and devotion? Here, asceticism is said to be the service rendered to Anasūyā by Īśvara himself.
Having seen all that, they both declared that devotion is superior; indeed, even by the ancient sages, such difficult penance was performed.
"No one has ever done such a thing anywhere," they said; "Blessed is this sage, and likewise blessed is this Anasūyā."
When this supreme austerity is performed again out of love for others, such auspicious austerity is difficult to practice and most excellent.
"By whom is this being done in the three worlds? Indeed, it is not known. Having offered praise to those two alone, they [the others] departed as they had come."
Then they went there, yet Gaṅgā did not go without Giriśa; for Gaṅgā is devoted to my worship, she is virtuous, and she is deluded by dharma.
"Having rendered this service to her, I shall depart," she said; meanwhile, O lords of sages, Śiva remained absorbed in meditation, bound by his contemplation, while the sage Atri was present there.
Remaining there for a full portion of time, he went to that Kailāsa; and likewise, O best of sages, fifty-four [years] passed there.
Years passed by, yet there was no rain at all during that time, even as Atri remained thus absorbed in meditation through his ascetic penance.

At that time, Anasūyā made this resolve: "I shall not accept anything. Listen now to what happened while the sage remained thus engaged in his ascetic penance and while Anasūyā was devotedly serving him.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Anasūyā’s Triple Penance," in the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, the fourth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Once, that best of sages, Atri, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, being awake, spoke thus to his beloved: "Give me water."
That virtuous woman, having taken up her water-pot, went to that forest, thinking, "From where shall my water be brought?"
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? From where indeed is this water being brought?"—filled with such wonder, she beheld that Gaṅgā.
As she was following her, the goddess Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, who always assumes a beautiful form, spoke to her.
Gaṅgā said: "O Goddess, I am pleased with you; tell me now, where are you going? You are blessed, O fortunate one; I shall truly carry out your command."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having heard those words at that time, the ascetic wife of the sage, herself greatly startled, replied with affection.
Anasūyā said: "Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, and from where have you come? Speak the truth out of compassion; you are a virtuous and noble lady."
Sūta said: O lords of sages, when that wife of the sage had spoken thus, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, assuming a divine form, then addressed these words.
Gaṅgā said: "O virtuous lady, having witnessed your service to your husband and that of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, and having observed your righteousness, I have remained in your presence."
"O lady of pure smiles, I have come to you from the Gaṅgā because of your devotion; indeed, I have become subject to your will, so choose whatever you desire."
Sūta said: When this had been spoken by Gaṅgā, the virtuous woman bowed and stood before her, saying: "If you are pleased with me now, please grant me water."
Having heard these words, she said, "Dig a pit! and having quickly done so, she stood there for just a moment.
Having entered there, she then became the form of water; having attained a state of supreme wonder, she took up that water.
And Anasūyā, the wife of the sage, spoke these words for the sake of the happiness of the worlds to the most excellent river of divine form.
Anasūyā said: "O compassionate one, if you are well-pleased with me and remain so, you must stay here until my husband returns."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Anasūyā, which grant happiness to the virtuous, Gaṅgā spoke with a gracious mind: "O sinless one, you shall indeed grant this to me from Atri."
When she had spoken thus, that which was to be done was performed there unfailingly; having offered that divine water to her husband, she stood before him.
And that sage, having sipped water according to the prescribed rite with great joy, drank that divine water and attained happiness.
"Aha! That which is constantly drunk is not water at all. Having reflected thus, he quickly looked all around.
Beholding the trees withered and the quarters of the sky likewise parched, that best of sages said to her, "No rain has fallen again."
Having heard what she said, he then spoke again to his beloved, who replied "not this, not this" (*neti neti*): "From where have you brought this water?"
When he had spoken thus, O lords of sages, Anasūyā was filled with the utmost wonder and became deeply reflective within her mind.
If it is indeed announced by me, then there will be excellence for me; if it is not announced at all, then there will be no violation of my vow.
"Nor indeed would it be both; such is what must be reported to me. While this was being deliberated, she was questioned again and again.
Then, having attained spiritual awakening through the grace of Śambhu, that devoted wife said: "Listen, my lord; I shall tell you what has occurred."
Anasūyā said: "By the power of Śaṅkara and by your own meritorious deeds, the Gaṅgā has arrived right here; this water is indeed her own."
Sūta said: Having heard those words, the sage, his mind filled with wonder, spoke to his beloved with great affection while remembering Śaṅkara in his heart.
Atri said: "O dear, beautiful one, you speak words that are either true or false; yet I do not believe what you say to be according to the facts, for this is indeed difficult to obtain."
O auspicious one, how has that which is always impossible even for yogis and gods now come to pass? This causes me the greatest wonder.
"If it is indeed seen thus, then I shall become that very thing and not otherwise. Having heard those words, the wife who was dear to her husband replied.
Anasūyā said: "O Lord, O great sage, please come with me if you have a desire to see Gaṅgā, the best of rivers."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that devoted wife took her husband and went swiftly, remembering Śiva, to where the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, flows.
There, the devoted wife showed her husband the Gaṅgā, who was present in that pit in her own divine form.
Having gone there, the best of sages saw a beautiful pit filled with water up to its neck, and he exclaimed, "Blessed indeed is this!"
"What is my ascetic merit, and what indeed is that of others?"—having been addressed thus, the tiger among sages then praised her with devotion.
Then, having bathed well there in that auspicious water, that sage performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and again offered praise there repeatedly.
Then Anasūyā also, having bathed in those beautiful waters, performed her daily rites; and that virtuous woman of excellent vows likewise performed her duties.
Then he said to Gaṅgā, "I am going to my own place. When this was said, the virtuous woman spoke again to that best of rivers.
Anasūyā said: "O Goddess of gods, if you are pleased, and if there is compassion for me, O Goddess, you should remain steadfastly in this forest of asceticism."
"And one should not abandon the nature of the great even if it is not accepted. Having been told this, she joined her palms and praised her again and again.
And the Ṛṣi spoke thus: "O best of rivers, you must remain here; be favorable, O Goddess, and grant us our protection."
Having heard those charming words of hers, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, with a gracious mind, spoke these words to Anasūyā.
Gaṅgā said: "O Lord, if you grant me the fruit of one year's worship of Śaṅkara, then I shall remain for the sake of assisting the gods."
Likewise, I find no such satisfaction through gifts, nor indeed through bathing at sacred fords, nor through sacrifices, nor even through yogic practices, as I do through devotion to my husband.
O virtuous lady, it is the truth I have spoken: there is no other means by which the mind can find such delight as it does upon seeing a devoted wife.
Upon seeing a devoted wife, may my sins be destroyed; this chaste woman has become especially pure, equal to Gaurī herself.
Therefore, if you bestow it for the benefit of the world, then I shall attain stability, provided you desire my welfare.
Sūta said: Having heard these words, that devoted wife Anasūyā gave all the merit accumulated during that year to Gaṅgā.
For it is indeed the nature of the great to bring about the welfare of others; gold, sandalwood, and sugarcane juice serve as illustrations of this.
Having seen that act of Anasūyā and her great devotion to her husband, Mahādeva became pleased and quickly manifested himself before the king.
Śambhu said: "O virtuous woman, having seen this deed of yours, O devoted wife, I am pleased. Choose a boon from me, my dear, for you are most beloved to me."
Then that couple, beholding Śambhu—who had assumed a beautiful form and was endowed with five faces and other attributes—were filled with great wonder.
Having bowed and offered praise, with palms joined and filled with great devotion, they worshipped Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, and spoke.
The couple said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased and if the Mother of the Universe is pleased, then remain in this penance grove and become the bestower of happiness upon the worlds."
At that time, Gaṅgā was serene and Śiva was serene; both of them remained there where the best of sages was seated.
And there was a lord named Atrīśvara, the remover of others' suffering; and Gaṅgā herself was then stationed there in that pit by means of her illusory power.
Indeed, from that day forward, there has always been inexhaustible water there; for in that pit, which is a cubit deep, the Gaṅgā became the Mandākinī.
Right there, divine sages arrived together with their wives; all those twice-born ones had previously emerged from various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Devoted to sacrifices and offerings, those people, joined by those excellent sages, performed the fire-oblation (homa) using barley and rice.
Satisfied by those deeds, the clouds then sent down rain; O great lords of sages, supreme joy arose in the world.
Thus has the majesty of Atrīśvara been told to you, which brings happiness, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grants all desires, and increases devotion.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Atrīśvara," in the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, the fourth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: On the divine mountain Kālañjara, Maheśvara, who is Nīlakaṇṭha, always exists in the form of a liṅga, eternally bestowing bliss upon his devotees.
His divine majesty is proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis; there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) by that name, which destroys all sins through bathing therein.
O you of excellent vows, as for those Śiva-liṅgas that exist on the banks of the Revā, they bring all happiness here; their number is not known.
She is indeed of the nature of Rudra, removing sins through the mere sight of her; and whatever stones are situated within her, they are of the form of Śiva.
Nevertheless, I shall describe those other principal Śiva-liṅgas, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as they were taught by the lords of sages.
For there exists one named Ārteśvara, the remover of sins; he is renowned as Parameśvara and remembered as Siṃheśvara.
Śarmeśa and likewise Kumāreśvara here, as well as the renowned Puṇḍarīkeśvara and Maṇḍapeśvara.
There was one named Tīkṣṇeśa, who removed sins by his mere sight; and there was one named Dhundhureśvara on the bank of the Narmadā, who destroyed sins.
The one renowned as Śūleśvara is likewise remembered as Kumbheśvara; the one named Kubereśvara is similarly remembered as Someśvara.
The blue-throated Lord Maṅgaleśa, the great abode of auspiciousness, the divine Great Lord of Monkeys, was indeed installed by Hanūmat.
And thereafter, the god Nandika is proclaimed as the warder-off of ten million killings, the bestower of all desired objects and purposes, and indeed the giver of liberation.
Whoever worships Nandikeśa with supreme joy, for him there will be all-encompassing success constantly; of this there is no doubt.
O best of sages, for one who bathes there on the bank of the Revā, their desires are fulfilled and all their sin is destroyed.
The sages said: O high-minded one, how did his greatness come to be there? Please tell us now, out of your compassion, concerning Nandikeśa.
Sūta said: You have asked well; I shall relate it to you exactly as I have heard it. O Śaunaka and all you sages, listen indeed with reverence.
In former times, the best of sages was questioned by Yudhiṣṭhira himself; out of affection for you, I shall speak exactly as he spoke.
On the western bank of the Revā, there is indeed a city named Karṇikī; it shines, rich in great beauty and filled with people of the four castes.
There, a certain excellent brahmin born of Uttāna’s lineage went to Kāśī, having entrusted his wife to his two sons.
The brahmin died right there, and his two sons then heard of it; both sons performed that funeral rite for him.
And the wife, desiring the welfare of her sons, protected them; and she indeed divided the wealth, setting aside a portion for the two sons.
And she preserved some of her own wealth for the sake of death; consequently, that brahmin’s wife died after some time.
O brahmins, while performing various meritorious deeds, that brahmin’s wife did not die by the turn of fate.
When their mother did not release her life-breaths due to fate, the two sons, seeing that distress of their mother, then spoke.
The two sons said: "O mother, what deficiency exists? Whatever great suffering there may be, choose it truly with pleasure; we two shall perform it."
Sūta said: Having heard what was spoken by her, [he realized] that there was much deficiency therein; if that very thing were done, death would indeed occur with ease.
And to her eldest son, he said, "Tell me what you will do; indeed, I shall do that," and she then spoke it.
The wife of the twice-born said: "Listen with affection to my words, my son: formerly my mind had a longing to go to Kāśī, but now that is no longer possible, as I am dying."
"O son, my bones must be cast by you into the waters of the Gaṅgā without delay; today an auspicious merit will accrue to you, of this there is no doubt."
Sūta said: When his mother had spoken thus, that eldest son, devoted to his mother, addressed his mother—who was firm in her vows and on the verge of death.
The son said: "O mother, you should give up your life with ease, there is no doubt; having first accomplished your purpose, you may afterwards attend to my own."
Having thus placed water in his hand, as soon as the son had gone home, she died there, wholly intent on the remembrance of Hara.
Having performed all her funeral rites and completed the monthly ceremonies, he set out on his journey.
He who was indeed the most excellent of the two, renowned by the name Suvāda, took his bones and departed with the desire to visit sacred fords.
Then, having taken a certain servant and accompanied by him, he comforted his wife and sons out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his mother.

Having performed the śrāddha, the giving of gifts, and other rites of feeding according to the supreme injunctions, and having performed the recollection of auspicious deities, the twice-born man departed from his home.
Having traveled a yojana on that day, he stayed in a beautiful village of twenty hamlets; when the sun had set, he dwelt in the house of a certain brahmin.

That twice-born man performed the six daily rites, beginning with the twilight prayers, according to the prescribed rules; there he offered hymns and other praises to Śambhu, whose deeds are marvelous.
Then that Brāhmaṇa remained there accompanied by his servant, and two muhūrtas of the night passed away.
In the meantime, a certain marvel occurred there; listen with respect, O sages, for I shall tell it to you.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Death of the Brahmin Woman," in the *Nandikeśvara-māhātmya* of the fourth book, the *Koṭirudra-saṃhitā*, within the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: A single auspicious cow was also tied there in the courtyard; at that very time, a Brāhmaṇa who had gone outside returned during the night.
O lords of sages, seeing his own beloved cow standing in the courtyard yet unmilked, he spoke to her, desiring to milk her and overcome with distress.
"O beloved, that cow of yours has not been milked," she said; having spoken thus, she quickly summoned a woman and brought the calf for the purpose of milking.
O sages, the Brahmin, the master of the house, who was longing for milk, then made an effort to tie the calf himself to the stake.
O you of excellent vows, even as he was pulling him, the calf caused great pain to his foot; thus the Brahmin indeed fell into a state of suffering.
Stupefied with anger by that kick of the foot, the twice-born man then struck the calf very firmly with his hooves.
The calf, too, was oppressed by him and became exhausted; yet the cow was milked and the calf released by the twice-born man without anger.
Then, out of great affection, the cow began to weep while being milked; and seeing her weeping, the calf spoke these words.
Vatsa said: "O mother, why do you weep? What sorrow has come upon you? Tell it to me with affection. Having heard that, Gaurī spoke.
Listen, my son; I am truly unable to speak of my sorrow. Because you were beaten by that wicked man, I too have come to suffer.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of his mother, that calf, established in the certainty of his destiny, enlightened her and replied to his own mother.
What should be done? Where should one go? For we are bound by our past actions; indeed, as was done previously, so is it experienced now.
Action is performed while laughing, but it is experienced while weeping; there is no one who bestows suffering, nor is there anyone who bestows happiness.
The notion that pleasure and pain are bestowed by another is considered a false intellect; furthermore, when one thinks "I am the one who acts" in this regard, that is called false knowledge.
Suffering arises from one's own action, and happiness likewise arises from that very same action; therefore, action is honored, for everything is established upon action.
Both you and I, this mother, and these living beings and others—all of us are bound by our own karma; therefore, you should never grieve for them.
Sūta said: Having thus heard the words of her son, which were filled with wisdom, that cow, distressed and overcome with grief for her son, spoke this.
Gaurī said: "O child, I know all this—that living beings are subject to their karma; nevertheless, seized by Māyā, I experience suffering once again."
"Much weeping has been done, yet there is no pacification of this suffering. Having heard these words, the son spoke thus to his mother:
Vatsa said: "If I understand it to be thus, then why this weeping again? Since something is accomplished by acting, therefore abandon your grief now."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of her son, his mother, the cow, overcome with grief, sighed deeply and then spoke these words to her calf.
Gaurī said: "My sorrow would depart only if such sorrow were to befall even a Brāhmaṇa; I speak this as the truth."
And tomorrow morning, my son, he shall indeed be struck by me with my two horns; once struck, his life will depart instantly—of this there is no doubt.
Vatsa said: "The fruit of whatever action was performed first is now being experienced; O Mother, what fruit will you obtain from this killing of a Brahmin?"
Birth in Bhārata occurs through an equal balance of merit and demerit; upon the exhaustion of those two through experience, O Mother, liberation is attained.
Sometimes the destruction of karma occurs, and sometimes its fruition arises; therefore, you must not again exert yourself in performing such actions.
"Whence am I your son today, and whence are you my mother? Reflect upon this vanity of being a son and being a mother."
Know where is the mother, where is the father, where is the master, and where is the wife? No one here belongs to anyone; everyone experiences the results of their own actions.
Knowing this, O Mother, you should abandon suffering with great effort; you should practice auspicious conduct out of a desire for happiness in the next world.
Gaurī said: "I know this well, my son; yet this Māyā does not leave me. Because of your suffering, my own suffering is great; therefore, I shall indeed give that very thing back to her."
Furthermore, I have seen that place where the destruction of even the murder of a Brahmin occurs; indeed, my own sin of killing shall depart from there.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard these words of his own mother, the cow, the calf remained silent there and did not say anything at all.
O lords of sages, having heard that wonderful account of the two, the twice-born traveler was struck with wonder and reflected upon it within his heart.
Having seen this most wonderful event this morning, I must certainly go back from here; I must go to that place once again.
Sūta said: O brahmins, having reflected thus in his heart along with his servant, that twice-born man, devoted to his mother and filled with supreme wonder, fell asleep there.
Then, when morning had arrived, the master of the house arose; he awakened that traveler and spoke these words:
The twice-born said: "Why indeed do you sleep? It is already fully morning. Set out on your journey to that place where you desire to go."
He said: "Listen, O Brahmin; there is indeed pain in my body as a servant. Having stayed for a moment, I shall depart from here."
Sūta said: Having thus made this pretext, the man then fell asleep, in order to learn that entire wonderful and astonishing account.
At that time, during the milking, the Brahmin, desiring to go somewhere for a certain purpose, spoke to his own son.
The father said: "My son, I must go somewhere again for the sake of some business; however, my dear child, you must milk this cow of yours with great care."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that best of brahmins departed for some place; then the son arose there and released the calf.
Then his mother herself came there for the sake of milk; at that time, the son of the twice-born saw the calf, distressed and struck by a stake.
For, eager for milk, he led the cow to its side for the purpose of binding it; then the cow, becoming enraged, struck him with her horn.
Struck in his vital organ, he too fell down, having lost consciousness; and the people gathered there, crying out, "The boy has been harmed!"
While his father and others, crying out "Water! Water!", were still making every effort for as long as they could, by then the boy had already died.
When the boy died there, a great cry of lamentation arose; his mother was indeed distressed and wept again and again.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Who will dispel my suffering? Having lamented thus, he then struck the cow and set her free.
Then that cow, which was white in color, suddenly appeared dark; "Aha! Look! the people cried out to one another.
Then the Brahmin, seeing the two travelers, was struck with wonder and departed; he went to where the cow had gone and followed after her.
Then, raising its tail high, the cow quickly went toward the Narmadā; having arrived at the waters of the Narmadā near this Nandika, she stood there.
Having submerged herself three times, she indeed attained whiteness; having returned as she had come, the Brahmin was filled with wonder.
Oh, what a most blessed holy site, which wards off even the sin of killing a Brahmin! There, both he and his Brahmin servant submerged themselves.
Having bathed and departed while praising that river, they met on the way a certain beautiful woman adorned with ornaments.
She said to him, "O traveler, where are you going, so greatly amazed? O best of brahmins, speak the truth before me, casting aside all deceit."
Sūta said: Having thus heard those words spoken by the twice-born exactly as they were, that brahmin was addressed again there by the woman: "Please remain here."
Having heard what she said, the brahmin who was standing there replied with a humble mind, "What is it that you wish to say?"
And she said again: "Since you have seen that very spot here, cast your mother's bones there now; why go elsewhere?"
O best of travelers, your mother, having assumed a truly divine and excellent body, will swiftly attain the supreme state of Śambhu himself.
O best of the twice-born, whenever the auspicious seventh day of the bright fortnight arrives during the month of Vaiśākha, Gaṅgā always comes there.
"Today itself is that seventh day which exists there in the form of Gaṅgā. Having said this, O best of sages, the goddess Gaṅgā vanished.
And that twice-born man, having returned, cast half of his mother’s bones from his own garment into that sacred bathing place; at that moment, a marvel occurred.
And his own mother was seen to have attained a divine body: "You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and your lineage has been purified by you."
"May your wealth, grain, lifespan, and lineage indeed increase! Having repeatedly bestowed this blessing upon her son, she departed for heaven.
Having enjoyed there abundant and most excellent happiness for a long time, she indeed attained the supreme goal through the grace of Śaṅkara.
And the Brāhmaṇa son, having cast away the bones from there once more, became serene in mind; that pure-souled one returned to his own home.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Brahmin Woman’s Attainment of Heaven," in the *Nandikeśvara-liṅga-māhātmya-varṇana* within the fourth book, the *Koṭirudra-saṃhitā*, of the *Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Lord, describe this in detail: how did Gaṅgā arrive at the Narmadā specifically on the seventh day of the month of Vaiśākha?
And how was Īśvara born by the name Nandikeśa? O high-minded one, please relate that account as well with great pleasure.
Sūta said: O best of sages, you have asked well regarding the words concerning Nandikeśa; I shall now relate that discourse, which increases merit through the mere hearing of it.
A Brahmin woman named Ṛṣikā was the daughter of a certain twice-born man; she was married according to the prescribed rites to a certain twice-born man.
O best of brahmins, by the power of her past karma, that wife of the twice-born, though she was of virtuous conduct, indeed entered into widowhood from childhood.
Then that wife of the twice-born, devoted to the vow of celibacy, performed most severe penance preceded by the worship of the earthen linga.
At that moment, a powerful and wicked asura named Mūḍha, a master of great illusion, arrived there, struck by the arrows of desire.
Beholding that Sundarī, who was intensely passionate and glowing with beauty, he entreated her for sexual union, displaying various forms of greed.
Then that woman of virtuous vows, devoted to the meditation on Śiva, O lords of sages, cast her gaze upon him not at all with a lustful eye.
And that Brahmin woman, devoted to asceticism, did not honor him; for she was exceedingly intent on austerity, having taken refuge in meditation upon Śiva.
Then that foolish lord of the Daityas, having been spurned by that slender woman, became violently incensed and subsequently revealed his true form to her.
Then that evil-minded one spoke harsh words that caused fear; he terrified the wife of the twice-born man in many ways.
Then, terrified with fear, that slender wife of the twice-born, who had taken refuge in Śiva, repeatedly cried out "Śiva! out of affection.
Extremely distressed, that woman, uttering the name of Śiva, sought refuge in Śambhu for the sake of protecting her own dharma.
In order to protect those who had come for refuge and to establish virtuous conduct, Śiva indeed manifested himself for her joy.
Then Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, instantly reduced to ashes that lord of the Daityas named Mūḍha, who was overwhelmed by lust.
Then the Supreme Lord, his mind skilled in protecting devotees, looked upon her with a compassionate glance and said, "Choose a boon."
Having heard the words of Maheśa, that virtuous wife of the twice-born beheld the auspicious form of Śaṅkara, which generates bliss.
Then, having bowed down to that Śambhu, the bestower of supreme bliss, the virtuous woman, with palms joined in reverence, shoulders bent low, and pure intentions, offered praise.

The Ṛṣikā said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; you are the kinsman of the wretched, the Sovereign, and the eternal protector of your devotees.
By you, O Asura named Mūḍha, my dharma has been protected here; since this wicked one has been slain by you, the protection of the world has been accomplished.
Grant me supreme and unfailing devotion to Your feet; O Lord, this alone is my boon—what else could be greater than this?
O Lord Maheśvara, hear another prayer of mine: for the sake of benefiting the worlds, please remain established here.
Sūta said: Having thus praised Mahādeva, that Ṛṣikā of auspicious vows became silent; then Giriśa, the mine of compassion, spoke.
Giriśa said: "O Ṛṣikā, you are of virtuous conduct and especially my devotee; all the boons that were requested have indeed been granted to you."
In the meantime, the gods there, led by Hari and Brahmā, having perceived the manifestation of Śiva, went forth filled with joy.
Having prostrated before Śiva with great devotion, all those brahmins, being well-disposed, honored him; bowing down with folded hands, they praised him with focused minds.
At that time, the virtuous Gaṅgā, the celestial river, with a highly pleased soul, spoke to Ṛṣikā while praising her for that method.
Gaṅgā said: "For my sake, you must grant this word in the month of Vaiśākha; indeed, for the sake of my stability, you must certainly grant me proximity for even a single day."
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Gaṅgā, that virtuous woman of excellent vows spoke with affection, saying "So be it," for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
For the sake of her bliss, Śiva became well-pleased with her upon that earthen liṅga; Hara entered into dissolution within that liṅga by means of his full manifestation through her.
All the gods were highly pleased and praised Śiva and her; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, as well as the celestial river, returned each to their own abode.
From that day forward, this most excellent holy place became purifying; Śiva became renowned there as Nandikeśa, the destroyer of all sins.
O twice-born ones, on that day every year, even the Gaṅgā goes there with a desire for auspiciousness, for the purpose of washing away her own sin which was incurred from accepting [gifts] from men.
Having bathed there and properly worshipped Nandikeśa, a person is indeed liberated from all sins, including the slaughter of a Brahmin.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Nandikeśvara Śiva-liṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, listen with true devotion to those Śiva-liṅgas which are indeed renowned upon the earth in the western direction.
In the city of Kapilā, there is a most divine Śiva-liṅga named Kālarāmeśvara, which removes sins through its mere sight.
In the western ocean, he is remembered as Mahāsiddheśvara; he indeed bestows dharma, artha, and kāma, and likewise grants liberation.
Gokarṇa, situated on the shore of the western ocean, is a most excellent sacred field; it destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and bestows the fruits of all desires.
In Gokarṇa, there exist tens of millions upon tens of millions of Śiva-liṅgas; and countless sacred fords (tīrthas) stand at every step.
What is the use of saying more here? All the sacred sites and waters located at Gokarṇa, in their entirety, are liṅgas that have become manifest before Śiva.
O dear one, the greatness of the Śiva-liṅgas and of all the sacred fords at Gokarṇa is described in its entirety by the great seers in the Purāṇas.
For in the Kṛta age he is indeed white; in the Tretā age he is very red; in the Dvāpara age he is yellow-colored; and in the Kali age he will be dark-complexioned.
Though he possesses great strength and has traversed the depths of the seven netherworlds, he will become mild when the terrible Kali age arrives.
And having worshipped Mahābala and the Śivaliṅga here at Gokarṇa, even those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) proceed to the state of Śaṅkara.
O Gokarṇa, those sages who go there on an auspicious day under a favorable constellation and worship him with devotion shall become Rudras; of this there is no doubt.
Whenever any man whatsoever worships the Śiva-liṅga at Gokarṇa, he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the Lord Śaṅkara is always present there under the name Mahābala.
The leader of the Gaṇas installed that Liṅga, which had been obtained by the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa through terrible penance, at Gokarṇa.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Mahendra; the Viśvedevas and the hosts of Maruts; the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, and the Moon together with the stars.
These gods, traveling in celestial chariots along with their retinues, attend upon its eastern gate for the sake of his pleasure.
Yama, Death himself in person, Citragupta, and Pāvaka, together with the Pitṛs and the Rudras, took their place at the southern gate.
Varuṇa, the lord of rivers, along with hosts of rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, and those of great strength, resort to and serve the western gate.
Likewise, Vāyu, Kubera, and the goddess of the gods, Bhadrakālikā, together with the Mothers beginning with Caṇḍikā, have taken their place at the northern gate.
All the gods, along with the gandharvas, the ancestors, the siddhas, the cāraṇas, the vidyādharas, the kimpuruṣas, the kinnaras, the guhyakas, and the birds;
Various piśācas, vetālas, and the mighty daityas; all the nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, as well as all the siddhas and sages.
They praise that god and bow down to him of great power; they obtain their desired wishes and rejoice according to their pleasure.
Having worshipped that omnipresent Lord, many have performed great austerities there and attained supreme perfection, which bestows happiness both in this world and the next.
O twice-born ones, the Śiva-liṅga at Gokarṇa is declared to be the gateway to liberation; it is named Mahābala, and when worshipped and praised, it grants [liberation].
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, the worship of Mahābala grants liberation especially even to all sinners.
On this auspicious lunar day, people of all four castes and great multitudes from all regions arrive, desiring to witness the grand festival.
Women, the elderly, and children, as well as those dwelling in the four stages of life, having come there and beheld the Lord of Gods, attained the fulfillment of their purpose.
Then, by the power of her great strength, that outcaste woman worshipped the linga of Śiva and quickly went to the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Mahābala," in the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, the fourth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, you are blessed and the best among the devotees of Śiva. Who is this woman known as Cāṇḍālī? O Lord, tell us her story.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, listen with true devotion to that most wonderful tale, which is interwoven with the majesty of Śiva and increases the devotion of those who hear it.
In her previous birth, she was a Brahmin girl named Saumini, moon-faced and endowed with all auspicious marks; she later became a Cāṇḍālī.
Then, O twice-born ones, at the proper time, that maiden Saumini reached her youth and was given by her father to a certain son of a brahmin according to the prescribed rites.
Having obtained her husband, O best of the twice-born, she, endowed with auspicious vows and radiant with fresh youth, took delight with him for some time.
Then, O twice-born ones, her husband, a young brahmin afflicted by a severe illness, passed away due to the power of time.
When her husband had died, that woman, sorrowful and deeply despondent in mind, lived for some time in her home with virtuous conduct and excellent character.
Then, her heart possessed by the god of love and being a widow yet at a particular stage of youth, she became unchaste.
Knowing that she was of his lineage and that her evil deed had brought disgrace upon the family, they gathered together, seized her by the hair, and abandoned her after leading her far away.
A certain excellent Śūdra, seeing that woman wandering at her own will in the forest, took her as his wife and led her to his home.
Then she, a consumer of flesh who constantly drank wine and was fond of sexual pleasure, gave birth to sons by that Śūdra.
Once, when her husband had gone somewhere, that unfaithful Saumini, having drunk wine, desired a meal of flesh.
Then, when the rams had been tied up with the cows in the outer pen, she went forth at the onset of night, in the blinding darkness, taking her sword.
Without reflecting, that most wretched woman, out of a fit of intoxication and mistaking it for a ram, killed a single lowing calf because she was fond of meat.
Having brought that slain one into the house and recognizing him as a calf, the woman was terrified; by some meritorious deed, she cried out, "Śiva! Śiva!"
Having meditated on Śiva for a moment, she, longing for a meal of meat, slaughtered that very calf and made it her desired food.
O brahmins, when much time had passed in this manner, that Saumini fell under the power of Time and went to the abode of Yama.
Yama, too, having examined her dharma and her past actions, turned her back from dwelling in hell and made her a member of the Cāṇḍāla caste.
Then, fallen from the city of Yama, she entered the womb of a Caṇḍālī; thereupon she was born blind, her limbs as dark as extinguished embers.
Born blind and having lost both her father and mother in her childhood, she was not married by anyone; moreover, she was wicked and afflicted by the disease of leprosy.
Then, afflicted by hunger and miserable, with a staff in hand and deprived of sight, she sought to appease the fire of her stomach with a morsel of food left over from a Caṇḍāla.
Thus, having spent his vast life with great hardship, his entire body seized by old age, he experienced suffering that is difficult to overcome.
Once, on a day sacred to Śiva, as that Cāṇḍālī was about to go toward Gokarṇa, she noticed him approaching and followed after him.
Then that Caṇḍālī also, out of a desire for clothing and a place to stay, wandered slowly from place to place to beg from the great multitude of people.
Having gone there, that Caṇḍālī then wandered here and there, entreating the great multitude with humble words and outstretched palms.
As the Caṇḍāla woman was thus entreating with her palms outstretched, a single most meritorious traveler cast a cluster of bilva blossoms into them.
Having fallen into her hands, she reflected upon it again and again; then, concluding that it was unfit for consumption, she cast it away at a distance in her distress.
Released from her hand at night, that cluster of bilva blossoms fortunately fell upon the top of a certain Śiva-liṅga.
Thus, on the night of the fourteenth day of Śiva, although she repeatedly begged from the travelers for something, by the turn of fate she obtained nothing at all.
Thus, the vow of Śivacaturdaśī has become pure; even if performed through ignorance, the keeping of the vigil bestows supreme bliss.
Then at dawn, that woman, overwhelmed by great grief and miserable, slowly turned back toward her own country alone.
Exhausted by her long fast, falling at every step, she passed over that much ground and collapsed unconscious.
Then, by the grace of Śambhu, she went to the supreme state; having ascended a magnificent celestial chariot, she was swiftly led away by the attendants of Śiva.

O Brahmins, because this woman once uttered the name of Śiva, even if out of negligence or due to her unchastity, she has attained through that great merit a divine station of great power in this world.

Having fasted at Śrīgokarṇa on the auspicious lunar day dedicated to Śiva and having kept a vigil upon the head of the Lord Śiva, she indeed performed the worship with *bilva* leaves during the night.
And even today, she continues to enjoy the fruit of that very merit performed unintentionally, solely by the grace of Mahābala.
Such is the great Liṅga of Śaṅkara, possessed of great power, which instantly removes all sins and bestows supreme bliss.
Thus, O Brahmins, I have related to you this supreme majesty of the excellent Śiva-liṅga known as Mahābala.
Now I shall speak further of another wondrous majesty of his, by the mere hearing of which devotion to Śiva is swiftly produced.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of a Good State by the Cāṇḍālī Woman," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Indeed, in the illustrious lineage of Ikṣvāku, there was a most righteous king named Mitrāsaha, who was the foremost among all archers.
That king had a beloved and auspicious queen named Sudharmiṣṭhā, who was known for her virtue, just as Damayantī was to Nala.
Once, that king, fond of the hunt, accompanied by his friends and joined by a great army, went into the dense forest.
