While dwelling there, that king slew the night-stalker named Kamaṭha, a wicked and extremely evil man who caused suffering to the virtuous.
Then his younger brother, a wicked man who practiced deceit, thinking "I shall conquer him by means of trickery," went into the presence of the king as a deceiver.
Seeing him with a humble appearance, having come to offer his service, that lord of the earth, out of ignorance, appointed him as the superintendent of the kitchen.
Then, after sporting for some time in that forest, the king desisted from the hunt and returned joyfully to his own city.
When the anniversary of his father’s death arrived, the king invited his own preceptor, Vasiṣṭha, brought him to his home, and fed him with devotion.
Seeing that the vegetable and meat had been mixed with human flesh by the Rākṣasa disguised as a cook and placed before him, the Guru then spoke.
The Guru said: "Fie on you, O King, you who are but human flesh! Since this has been offered to me by you, a wicked man acting with deceit, you shall therefore become a Rākṣasa."
And having realized that it was caused by a Rākṣasa, the preceptor then reflected further and at that time pronounced a twelve-year curse upon him.
Recognizing that the curse was improper, the king, overwhelmed with rage, took a handful of water and prepared to curse his preceptor.
And then his beloved, virtuous, and righteous wife Madayantī, falling at his feet, indeed restrained him from that curse.
Then, his curse having been withdrawn due to the weight of her words, he released the water from his feet, which had become stained with impurity.
From that time forward, O lords of sages, that king became renowned in this world as Kalmaṣāṅghri (the one with defiled feet) because of the power of that water.
Indeed, due to the curse of his preceptor, the eminent sage, King Mitrasaha became a terrible, murderous rākṣasa who roamed the forests.
Assuming the form of a Rākṣasa, resembling Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time, that forest-dweller devoured various creatures, including humans and others.
Once, in a certain part of the forest, he, appearing like Death himself, beheld a young sage couple sporting together, having recently married.
Afflicted by the curse, that man-eating Rākṣasa seized the young son of the sage to devour him, just as a tiger seizes a fawn.
Seeing her husband held within her womb, his beloved wife became terrified; she made a supplication to him, speaking piteous words.
Although entreated many times, that pitiless and evil-minded man-eater cut off the head of the brahmin youth and devoured it.
Then that virtuous woman, distressed and lamenting intensely in her great sorrow, gathered her husband’s bones and prepared a formidable funeral pyre.
Following her husband as he entered the fire, that wife of a twice-born man cursed the king who had assumed the form of a Rākṣasa.
"From this day forward, whenever you come into contact with women, your death shall occur," she said, and the virtuous lady entered the blazing fire.
That king, having experienced the guru’s curse for its fixed duration and having resumed his own form once more, went to his own home filled with joy.
Having learned of the curse from the virtuous Brahmin woman, Madayantī, fearing greatly the state of widowhood, restrained her husband who was so fond of pleasure.
Childless and disenchanted with the enjoyments of sovereignty, the king abandoned all his royal splendor and departed for the forest.
He beheld the personified sin of Brahmin-slaughter, of most painful form and hideous appearance, approaching from behind him and threatening him again and again.
Seeking a way to break her [silence], the king, with a despondent mind, employed various means such as recitation, vows, and sacrifices.
When the twice-born could not turn back the king's sin of killing a Brahmin through various means such as bathing at sacred fords, he then went to Mithilā.
While she was in the outer garden, afflicted by intense longing, that king saw the sage Gautama approaching.

Approaching Gautama, whose intentions were pure, that lord of kings bowed repeatedly, having felt some measure of joy at the sight of him. Then, having been asked about his welfare, sighing long and hot breaths, and having obtained happiness through the touch of his compassionate gaze, the king spoke to him.
The king said: "O Sage, this Brahman-murder, so difficult to overcome, afflicts me, O dear one; though unobserved by others, it threatens me at every step."
Since I, consumed by a curse, have devoured the son of a brahmin, there can be no pacification of that sin even through thousands of expiatory rites.
"O Sage, while wandering about, I indeed employed various means for its pacification; yet the slaughter of a Brahmin has not ceased from me, a sinner—how could it?"
Today I perceive, as it were, that the fruitfulness of my birth has been attained, since by the mere sight of you, a weight of bliss has arisen within me.
Today, O illustrious one, grant peace to me, a sinner who has taken refuge at your lotus feet, so that I may attain happiness.
Sūta said: Thus commanded by the king, Gautama, his mind moistened with compassion, duly prescribed an expiation for those terrible sins.
Gautama said: "Excellent, O Indra among kings! You are blessed; abandon fear of great sins. For those who seek refuge, where is there fear when Śiva is their teacher?"
Listen, O highly fortunate King, to another established sacred field called Gokarṇa, an abode of Śiva that destroys even the greatest of sins.
In that place, there is no dwelling for the wicked, even for those who are great among the great; for Śiva himself is present there under the name Mahābala.
Among all Śiva-liṅgas, he is the sovereign emperor, possessed of great power; throughout the four ages, he assumes the four castes and removes all sins.
Gokarṇa, the supreme sacred site situated on the shore of the western ocean, is there; it contains a Śiva-liṅga that destroys even the greatest of sins.
Having gone there, those great sinners bathed repeatedly at the sacred fords, and after worshipping Mahābala, they departed for the abode of Śaṅkara.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, you too, having gone to Gokarṇa, the abode of Giriśa, and having fully worshipped that Liṅga, shall attain the fulfillment of all your purposes.
Having bathed in all those sacred fords and worshipped Mahābala, you shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Śiva.
Sūta said: Thus instructed by the high-souled sage Gautama, the king, with a heart full of great joy, proceeded toward Gokarṇa.
Having bathed well in those sacred fords and having worshipped Mahābala, he, with the entire flood of his sins washed away, attained the supreme state of Śambhu.
Whoever should constantly hear this beloved narrative of Mahābala, he goes to the world of Śiva together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Thus has been fully narrated the most wonderful majesty of the Mahābala-giriśa-liṅga, which removes all sins.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Mahābāhu-Śiva Liṅga," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, you are blessed, for your mind is devoted to Śiva; this wonderful narrative of the Liṅga of Mahābala has been recounted by you.
O sinless one, please describe the sin-destroying majesty of those Śiva-liṅgas that are located in the northern direction.
Sūta said: Listen with reverence, O Brahmins, especially those from the North; I shall proclaim in brief the majesty of the Śiva-liṅgas.
There is another sacred field called Gokarṇa, which destroys even the greatest sins; and there also exists the Mahāvana forest, which is pure and exceedingly vast.
Therein is an unsurpassed Śiva-liṅga named Candrabhāla, brought there by Rāvaṇa with true devotion, which bestows all spiritual perfections.
O lords of sages, his residence there, like that of Vaidyanātha, was for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds and because he is an ocean of compassion.
Having bathed at Gokarṇa and worshipped Candrabhāla, one attains the world of Śiva; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The supreme and most wonderful majesty of the Candrabhāla Liṅga cannot be fully described even by Vyāsa, for he is exceedingly fond of his devotees.
O Mahādeva with the moon upon your brow, the greatness of this supreme Liṅga has been described in some manner; now listen indeed to that of the other Liṅga.
The Śiva-liṅga known as Dādhīca is located at the excellent Miśra-ṛṣi-tīrtha; it was installed with great devotion by the lordly sage Dadhīci.
Having gone there and bathed at that sacred ford according to the prescribed rites, one should indeed worship the Śivaliṅga known as Dādhīceśvara with devotion.
Those who desire the fruits of pilgrimage should quickly worship the form of Dadhīca at that very place according to the prescribed rites, solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva.
When this has been done, O best of sages, a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; having enjoyed all happiness in this world, he shall attain the supreme goal in the hereafter.
In the sacred ford of the Naimiṣa forest stands a Śiva-liṅga established by all the sages, renowned as Ṛṣīśvara, which bestows happiness.
O lords of sages, by seeing and worshipping it, even sinful people attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, both in this world and in the hereafter.
At the Hatyāharaṇa Tīrtha, there is a Śiva-liṅga that removes sin; it should be worshipped especially, as it destroys ten million acts of killing.
At the Devaprayāga tīrtha, the Śiva-liṅga named Laliteśvara is always to be worshipped by men; it destroys all sins.
In the city known as Nayapāla, which is famous throughout the earth, there is a Liṅga named Paśupatīśa that bestows the fruits of all desires.
Indeed, that Śivaliṅga exists in the form of the region of the head; I shall describe its story in the description of Kedāreśvara.
There, the most wonderful Śiva-liṅga known as Muktinātha is located; by seeing and worshipping it, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained.
Thus, O best of sages, the excellent description of the Liṅga has been fully recounted; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Candrabhāla-Paśupatinātha Liṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O Sūta, by the grace of Vyāsa you know every subject; there is nothing unknown to you, therefore we question you."
And as for the fact that the *liṅga* is worshipped in the world—that which has been told by you is exactly so; there is no other cause for it here.
O Sūta, it is heard in the world that Pārvatī, the beloved of Śiva, is Bāṇarūpā; tell us the reason for this, exactly as you have heard it.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, I have heard from Vyāsa the various accounts concerning the different kalpas; I shall now relate that very account—let it be heard, O best of sages.
Listen attentively as I relate exactly that which occurred long ago among the twice-born in the Dāruvana forest, as it was heard in the course of my own narration.
In that place was the excellent Dārunāma forest, where the best of sages resided; they were constant devotees of Śiva, eternally and perpetually devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
Those lords of sages performed the worship of Śiva incessantly at the three times of day, praising him with various kinds of divine hymns.
Once, all those bulls among the twice-born, who were devotees of Śiva and solely intent on meditation upon Śiva, went into the forest to gather sacrificial fuel.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara himself, blue and red in hue, assuming a deformed appearance, arrived for the sake of testing him.
Naked, possessing great splendor, and adorned with ornaments of sacred ash, he performed wicked actions while holding a linga in his hand.
And with his mind intent on doing what was pleasing to those forest-dwellers, Hara himself, delighted by his devotees, went to that forest out of affection.
Upon seeing him, those wives of the sages were seized with great terror; others, agitated and filled with wonder, likewise gathered there once again.
Likewise, others embraced one another, while still others held onto each other’s hands; thus, due to their mutual friction, those women were then completely drenched with sweat.
At that very moment, the best of sages arrived; seeing him acting in opposition, they were distressed and overcome with anger.
Then, having fallen into distress, all those sages, deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, spoke thus: "Who is this? Who is this?"
And when that Avadhūta, naked as the sky, did not say anything at all, those supreme sages then spoke to that formidable man.
"Since you act in opposition [to us] and destroy the path of the Vedas, therefore let that linga of yours fall to the surface of the earth!"
Sūta said: When they had spoken thus, the linga of that Śiva of wondrous form, who was then an Avadhūta, instantly fell down in a moment.
That Liṅga is like fire; it burned everything that stood there in the past, and wherever it goes, it burns again.
It has gone to the netherworld and likewise to heaven; it has traveled everywhere on earth, for indeed it is not stable anywhere.
The worlds became agitated and the sages were deeply distressed; neither the gods nor the sages found any peace whatsoever.
But those gods and sages by whom Śiva was not known were all distressed; they gathered together and quickly went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having gone there, O twice-born ones, they all bowed and offered praise according to the prescribed rite, and related everything that had occurred to Brahmā, the creator of the universe.
Having heard those words and perceiving that they were deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, Brahmā bowed to Śaṅkara and spoke to those best of sages.
Brahmā said: "O twice-born ones, even you, who are knowers [of dharma], perform what is censurable; if those who are ignorant were to do so, what more need be said?"
Having thus offended the divine Śiva, who seeks what is auspicious? For he indeed does not attend to a guest at the time of midday.
Taking his very merit and placing his own demerit in its stead, the guest departs; how much more so, then, if it be Śiva himself?
As long as the auspicious Liṅga does not become stable within the three worlds, nothing good will ever arise anywhere; I tell you this truth.
O sages, you must act in such a way that well-being may be restored here for the Śivaliṅga; reflect upon this with your minds.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, those sages bowed down and spoke to Brahmā: "O Creator, what task must be performed by us? Please command that which is to be done."
Thus addressed by those lords of sages, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, then spoke himself to those lords of sages.
Brahmā said: "O gods, having propitiated the goddess Girijā, you should pray to Śiva: 'If she indeed becomes the form of the womb, then let that [union] become stable.'"
I shall now proclaim the method for that; listen all of you, O most excellent ones! Perform it with love, and she will become well-disposed toward you.
Having established a single water-pot and fashioned an excellent eight-petaled lotus, one should then fill it with water from sacred fords along with sprouts of dūrvā grass and barley.
Then, one should indeed consecrate that water-pot with Vedic mantras; having performed its worship according to the procedure prescribed in the Śrutis while remembering Śiva.
The supreme sages should consecrate that great liṅga with its water; sprinkled with the Śatarudriya mantras, it shall attain peace.
Having again established the auspicious Bāṇa, who is Girijā in the form of the Yoni, one should then install the Liṅga there and consecrate it with mantras once more.
One should gratify the Supreme Lord with fragrant sandalwood, as well as flowers, incense, and the like, and with offerings such as food oblations.
Furthermore, with prostrations, hymns of praise, meritorious acts, musical instruments, and songs, one should then perform a rite for well-being and likewise proclaim, "Victory!"
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, you who bring delight to the world; you are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer, yet you are beyond all syllables.
The beginning of the world, the source of the world, and yet contained within the world—be peaceful, O Great Lord, and protect all the worlds.
When this rite has been performed, well-being will surely come to pass; there is no doubt. No affliction shall exist in these three worlds, and there will be constant happiness.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, those twice-born ones and the gods, desiring the happiness of all the worlds, prostrated before the Grandfather and sought refuge in that Śiva.
Then Śaṅkara, having been worshipped with supreme devotion and entreated, became exceedingly gracious and spoke to them, O Maheśvara.
Maheśvara said: O gods and all you sages, listen with reverence to my words: if my liṅga were held in the form of a womb, then there would be happiness.
No one other than Pārvatī is capable of bearing my liṅga; once it is borne by her, my liṅga will quickly attain peace.
Sūta said: Having heard that, O lords of sages, the goddess Girijā, accompanied by the highly pleased ṛṣis and gods, then took hold of Brahmā and made her request.
Having propitiated Girijā and the bull-bannered Lord Śiva, and having performed the previously mentioned rite, the supreme Liṅga was installed.
According to the ritual procedure prescribed in the mantras, the gods and the sages likewise propitiated Girijā and Śiva for the sake of righteousness.
All the celestial sages, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, along with the three worlds consisting of the mobile and immobile, worshipped Śiva with particular distinction.
Śiva became exceedingly gracious, as did Śivā, the Mother of the World; and she indeed held that Liṅga in that very form at that time.
When the Liṅga was established for the worlds, prosperity then ensued; and that Liṅga, O twice-born ones, became renowned throughout the three worlds.
It is renowned as Hāṭakeśa and is also called Śivāśiva; by worshipping it, happiness comes to people in every way.
In this world, there shall be every prosperity, bringing manifold pleasures in abundance; in the next world, there is supreme liberation—of this there is no need for doubt.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Cause and Nature of the Liṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, I have affectionately related how Śiva became the form of the Liṅga, worthy of worship in the three worlds; what else do you wish to hear?
The sages said: "O Lord, please tell us the majesty of the Andhakeśvara Liṅga; likewise, out of affection, you ought to speak here of other Śiva-liṅgas as well."
Sūta said: Long ago, the Daitya Andhakāsura, the destroyer of the gods, dwelt taking refuge in a pit within the ocean and brought the three worlds under his own control.
Then, having emerged from that pit and oppressed the subjects once more, the Daitya of great prowess entered that same pit again.
O lords of sages, all the gods, being distressed, repeatedly prayed to Śiva and reported their entire suffering to him.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the gods, the Supreme Lord—the slayer of the wicked and the refuge of the virtuous—replied with a gracious soul.
Śiva said: "I shall slay that Daitya Andhaka, the destroyer of the gods; let the army be led forth, O deities, for I am coming along with my Gaṇas."
When that terrifying one, the enemy of gods and sages, had emerged from that pit, the gods then took refuge within the pit.
The Daityas and the deities engaged in a most dreadful battle; then, by the grace of Śiva, the gods became powerful.
Though he was also afflicted by the gods, as soon as he reached the pit, he was pierced with a trident by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Then, while there, he meditated upon Śambhu and prayed: "By beholding you at the time of death, one becomes such [as you are] in an instant."
Thus praised, Śaṅkara was then pleased and spoke these words there: "Choose a boon; I shall grant it to you."
Having heard these words, that Daitya, having bowed deeply to Śiva and praised him, spoke again, having adopted a state of pure goodness.
Andhaka said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, grant me auspicious devotion to yourself; having shown special compassion, please remain here indeed."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by him, Hara cast that Daitya into his pit; he himself remained there in the form of a Liṅga out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
And that man who constantly worships that Liṅga, Andhakeśa, will have his desires fulfilled within six months; of this there is no doubt.
A twice-born man who worships a Liṅga for the sake of his livelihood—that Liṅga which brings benefit to the world—for six months is indeed known as a Devalaka.
In that case, he would indeed become a *devalaka* here; for one who is called a *devalaka* has no entitlement to the status of a twice-born.
The sages said: "Who is declared to be a *devalaka*, and what is his duty? O one of great wisdom, tell us the truth for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
Sūta said: There was a brahmin named Dadhīci, most righteous and a master of the Vedas, who was constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to the scriptures of Śiva.
His son was indeed known by the name Sudarśana; his wife was Dukūlā, born of a wicked family.
And that husband was under her control; he had four sons, and he too used to perform the worship of Śiva constantly.
At that time, Dadhīci was indeed residing in another village; because of his connection with his kinsmen, he was not released by them.
Having spoken thus to his son, "Be devoted to the worship of Śiva," Dādhīci, the best of Śiva's devotees, departed, liberated.
His son, Sudarśana, also performed the worship of Śiva; in this manner, O lords of sages, a very long time passed away.
And so, once upon a time, Śivarātri arrived; on that day, they all fasted together by their own accord.
Having performed the worship, he departed and became known as Sudarśana; however, having engaged in sexual intercourse on Śivarātri, he returned here once again.
He did not bathe, nor was there any worship of Śiva performed by him that night; due to the ripening of that karma, the enraged Śaṅkara spoke.
Maheśvara said: "O wicked one, on Śivarātri you engaged in sexual union with a woman; and without having bathed, you, lacking discernment, performed my worship."
"Since you have acted thus after knowing this, therefore you shall fall into a state of insentience; become untouchable to me, and let your sight be seen only from afar."
Sūta said: Thus cursed by Maheśa, that Sudarśana, the son of Dadhīci, immediately became inert, deluded by the māyā of Śiva.
At that time, O brahmins, Dadhīci, the most excellent of Śiva’s devotees, arrived from another village and heard the news.
Rebuked by Śiva, he became exceedingly distressed; he wept, crying out, "Alas! I am ruined! in grief over his son's deed.
Dadhīca, who was esteemed by the virtuous, spoke again and again: "By this wicked son, my excellent lineage has been destroyed."
That son, though himself slain, quickly made his wife unchaste; having fallen into remorse, he was rebuked by his father.
Her father worshipped Girijā there with excellent rites and great effort, out of profound devotion, for the sake of his son's happiness.
Sudarśana himself also worshipped Girijā with great devotion, following the method of Caṇḍī-pūjā and with auspicious hymns of praise.
Thus, through various means and with great devotion, that father and son pleased the goddess Girijā, who is compassionate toward her devotees.
O Sage, by the power of their service, Caṇḍikā was then pleased, and Girijā adopted Sudarśana as her son.
Caṇḍikā herself propitiated Śiva for the sake of a son; though she was both angry and not angry, Caṇḍī’s mind became gracious toward her son.
Then, perceiving that Maheśa, whose banner is the bull, was pleased, he himself bowed down and placed him upon his lap.
Then, having herself performed the bath with ghee for her son, Girijā [bestowed] a sacred thread that was wound three times and joined with a single knot.
Then Ambikā, with affection, bestowed upon her son Sudarśana the Śivagāyatrī consisting of sixteen syllables.
Then this young student (baṭu) should perform the ritual worship accompanied by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) sixteen times, preceded by the word "Śrī" and the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
Worshipping the Bull-bannered Lord from the ritual bath until the prostration, with mantras, musical instruments, and offerings, likewise in the presence of the sages.
Then Caṇḍikā and Śiva, their souls well-pleased, indeed caused him to recite many name-mantras and spoke thus.
And whatever wealth, grain, or other property has been offered by me, all of that should be accepted by you; it shall not be a cause for fault.
"You are the primary agent in my affairs, especially in those of the Goddess; you must accept all the ghee, oil, and other offerings presented by me."
When there is a Prājāpatya yoga, then you alone shall be present; at that time, the worship is complete, otherwise it is entirely fruitless.
You must always apply a circular *tilaka* and perform your ablutions; you must also observe the *sandhyā* rite for Śiva and recite his *gāyatrī*.
Having first performed service to me, you may attend to other duties appropriate for your family. When all this has been done, O auspicious one, I have forgiven your faults.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, his four sons, who were then young brahmin students (baṭukas), were consecrated in the four directions by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
And Caṇḍī, having placed her son Sudarśana near herself, sent forth his sons after granting them many boons.
The Goddess said: "Between you two, whichever one becomes my *vaṭuka*, he shall always be victorious; there is no need for deliberation on this matter."
By him by whom you have been honored, I too have been fully honored; for you, O son, must always perform your own duty.
Sūta said: Thus were boons granted out of compassion by Śiva and Śivā for the sake of the worlds to that high-souled Sudarśana and his son.
Because they were established by the two Śivas, they are known as Vaṭukas; and because they became fallen from their asceticism, they are known as Tapodhamas.
By the grace of Śiva and Śivā, all have expanded in many ways; and the first worship of those great souls is the Mahāpūjā.
Therefore, as long as worship has not been performed for Śaṅkara, no other worship should be performed; even if it were performed, it would not be auspicious.
One should not abandon a *baṭuka*, whether he be auspicious or inauspicious; indeed, in the *prājāpatya* rite and at a feast, a single *baṭuka* is especially distinguished.
Furthermore, a distinction is observed here regarding the duties of Śiva and Śivā; listen to that, O wise one, just as I shall tell you, O sinless one.
In that very city, at the daily meal of King Bhadra, while he was observing the Prājāpatya vow in the presence of Andhakeśa.
Listen with great pleasure to that wonderful event which occurred due to Śiva’s grace; I shall relate it exactly as I have heard it.
A single banner was given to that king by Śambhu, who was pleased; and out of compassion, the king was addressed by that god of gods:
"O King, let the banner be raised in the morning; it shall fall during the night. And when my Prājāpatya vow is likewise completed, it shall happen again."
"Otherwise, this banner of mine would indeed remain steady even at night. Having spoken thus, Śambhu, the ocean of compassion, being pleased with the king, vanished from sight.
O great sage, such was the constant resolve of that king: he daily performed the Prājāpatya vow according to the prescribed rites for the worship of Śiva.
If the task is to be completed here, the banner should rise by itself in the morning and fall in the evening.
Once in the past, there was indeed a task for a young student here; that banner fell even without a Brahman feast being held.
Having seen that, the king then questioned the learned men there, who replied: "The Brahmins are indeed eating here, for the banner has not yet been raised."
"And how did he fall here? O Brāhmaṇas, tell me truly. Thus questioned, those Brāhmaṇas, the best among the learned, then spoke.
O Great King, in the past, during a feast for Brahmins, Vaṭuka was fed; Śiva, the son of Caṇḍī, was pleased by that, and therefore the banner fell.
Having heard that, the king, as well as all the other people there, were struck with wonder and then offered their praise.
Thus indeed was their greatness increased by Śaṅkara; therefore, they have been proclaimed as the most excellent Vaṭukas by the ancient knowers.
The worship of Śiva must first be concluded by them, and not otherwise; for according to the word of Śiva here, others have no entitlement [to perform it].
"Indeed, their deliverance must be accomplished so that the worship may be complete; listen to this much alone from them, and nothing else."
O lords of sages, all this that was asked has been fully explained; by hearing which, a man indeed attains the fruit of the worship of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Vaṭuka," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: Now, please relate the majesty of the luminous lingas, as well as their origin; tell us everything exactly as you have heard it.
Sūta said: Listen, O Brahmins; I shall describe its greatness as well as its origin, in brief and according to my understanding, just as I heard it from the true guru.
O best of sages, it is not possible to describe the majesty of these very [deities] even in hundreds of years; nevertheless, I shall tell it to you.
And Somanātha is indeed proclaimed as the first among them; O Sage, listen first to its greatness with careful attention.
O lords of sages, twenty-seven maidens, beginning with Aśvinī, were given by the high-souled Dakṣa to Candra.
Having obtained the moon as their lord, they shone with particular splendor; and the moon, too, having obtained them, shone incessantly.
Indeed, gold shines because of the gem, and the gem indeed shines because of the gold; hear now what happened during that time of theirs.
And among all his wives, she who was known by the name Rohiṇī was the one beloved; no other was ever so dear to him as she.
And others, having fallen into distress, went to their father for refuge; having approached him, they reported their suffering to him exactly as it was.
Having heard that from Dakṣa, we both then experienced great sorrow; so the twice-born ones assembled and spoke these words to Candra with a spirit of conciliation.
Dakṣa said: O treasury of arts, you were indeed born into a stainless lineage; how could there be any deficiency or excess in you toward all those who have sought your protection?
If it has been done, that which was done must not be done by you again; conduct characterized by unevenness is said to lead to hell.
Sūta said: Having personally entreated his son-in-law Candra, Dakṣa, having reached a firm resolve, indeed returned to his own abode.
Even Candra, deluded by the power of Śiva’s Māyā—by which the entire world is enchanted—did not act upon his words.
When auspiciousness is destined for someone, indeed, auspiciousness comes to pass for them; but when inauspiciousness is destined, how could auspiciousness come to pass for them?
Candra, too, under the influence of his powerful nature, did not heed those words; and being attached to Rohiṇī, he never regarded any other woman.
Having heard that, Dakṣa himself returned, filled with sorrow, and being skillful in right conduct, he made a request to Candra.
Dakṣa said: "Listen, O Candra, to that which was previously requested by me in many ways; since it was not honored by you, therefore you shall become subject to waning."
Sūta said: When he had spoken thus, Candra indeed became subject to waning in that very instant; a great cry of lamentation arose when the Moon had fallen into a state of depletion.
Then all the celestial sages, O sage, were overcome with grief and became distraught, exclaiming, "Alas! What must be done? How can this be?"
And having been informed by Candra, all the gods headed by Śakra, as well as the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, went to Brahmā for refuge.
O Sage, having gone there, the sages and gods, bowing and praising Brahmā while being greatly overwhelmed, related that entire event to him.
Having heard those words, Brahmā too was filled with supreme wonder; praising the illusory power of Śiva and making it known to them, he spoke to them.
Brahmā said: Alas! A great calamity has arisen, bringing suffering to all the worlds; for Candra is ever wicked, and Dakṣa has cursed him.
All these many deeds were performed by the wicked Candra; listen, O sages and gods, to the ancient account of Candra’s actions.
Having gone to the house of Bṛhaspati, Tārā was indeed abducted by that wicked one; she was his wife, and he then approached the Daityas once again.
Then, having taken refuge [with them], the Daityas waged war against the gods; and though forbidden by me and Atri, the Moon-god gave Tārā back to him.
Seeing that she was pregnant, he said, "I will not take her. Although we tried to dissuade him, he then accepted her with great difficulty.
"If she should lose the fetus here, I shall take it up again," he said; and so, O best of sages, when the fetus was again caused to be lost by me there, [he spoke thus].
"Whose embryo is this? she asked, "Is it Soma's? Thereafter, she was taken by him, even though I had tried to restrain him.
Such misdeeds of Candra are described in many ways; how much more so, then, since he continues to commit them even today?
Whatever has come into being is well-born; it certainly does not become otherwise. Therefore, I shall tell you the further means; listen with reverence.
One should go to the auspicious field of Prabhāsa with the deities of the Vraja; there, one should worship Śiva according to the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya.
Having placed the Lord there in front, may the Moon shine there eternally; and Śiva, being well-pleased, shall thereafter render that [place] imperishable.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Brahmā, all those divine sages returned and went to where Dakṣa Vidhū was.
Then, having taken hold of Candra and having consoled Dakṣa, all those immortals and sages went to Prabhāsa and performed [the rites] there.
Having invoked the excellent sacred fords, such as the Sarasvatī and others, he then performed worship with the earthen linga according to the ritual of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Then all those gods and the sages of pure intent, having installed Candra at Prabhāsa, returned joyfully to their respective abodes.
Candra performed penance continuously for six months, worshipping the Bull-bannered Lord with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.
Having completed ten crores of that mantra, the Moon, meditating upon the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, remained with a steady mind.
Upon seeing him, the Lord Śaṅkara became pleased; then the Master, who is affectionate toward his devotees, manifested himself and spoke to Vidhu, his own devotee.
Śaṅkara said: "Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever is desired by your mind. I am pleased, O Moon; I shall grant every unsurpassed boon."
Candra said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, what could be impossible for me? Nevertheless, O Śaṅkara, ward off the wasting away of my body."
"May my offense be forgiven, and may you always grant me prosperity. When he had spoken thus, Śiva then addressed these words:
Śiva said: "O Moon, let your digit wane day by day during one fortnight, and let that same digit increase continuously during the other fortnight."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, this being so, all the gods and likewise all the sages, their minds overflowing with joy, then arrived there swiftly.
Having arrived, they all then spoke words of blessing to Candra; bowing to Śiva and joining their palms, they prayed with great reverence.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Lord, salutations be unto you! O Śambhu, O Master, together with Umā, remain steadfast here."
Sūta said: Then, having been praised with true devotion by Candra in the past, Śaṅkara, the Lord, who was formless, again became possessed of form.
And being pleased with the gods for the sake of the greatness of that sacred field, Śaṅkara was established there under the name of Candra, for the glory of Candra.
And there was one named Someśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds, O twice-born ones, who destroys diseases such as consumption and leprosy through worship.
Blessed is he, fulfilled is his purpose, since by his name Śaṅkara himself—the Lord of the worlds—remains, purifying the surface of the earth.
That *kuṇḍa* was installed right there by all those gods; for it was indeed not divided between Śiva and Brahmā.
The Candra-kuṇḍa is renowned on earth as the destroyer of sins; the man who bathes there is liberated from all his transgressions.
Indeed, all diseases, including consumption and others that are truly incurable, all of them go to their destruction merely by bathing for six months.
Having circumambulated Prabhāsa, which arose from the treading of the earth, the pure-souled one obtains its fruit and, upon death, is glorified in heaven.
Having beheld the Somalinga, a person is liberated from all sins; having obtained the fruit desired by the mind, upon death, he aspires for heaven.
Whatever fruit one aims for when visiting this supreme sacred site, one attains that very fruit in every respect; there is no doubt about this.
Thus those sages and gods, having seen such a fruit, joyfully bowed to Śiva and took hold of the imperishable moon.
Having circumambulated that sacred ford and praising it, they departed; and Candra also performed his own ancient duty.
Thus has the entire origin of Someśa been fully described; in this manner, O lords of sages, the Someśvara Liṅga came into being.
The person who hears its origin or causes others to hear it attains all desires and is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Somanātha Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the origin of Mallikārjuna, hearing which a wise and devoted person is liberated from all sins.
That which was previously told, I shall now tell again: the divine life-story of Kumāra, which destroys all sins.
When Kumāra, the son of Śivā, the mighty slayer of Tāraka, had traversed the earth and returned once more to Kailāsa;
Then the celestial sage arrived and recounted everything that had occurred, including the marriage of Gaṇeśvara and so forth, while deluding him with his own cleverness.
Having heard that, the prince indeed bowed to his parents and went to Mount Krauñca, even though he was restrained by them.
When Girijā, the mother of the Kumāra, was distressed by his separation, Śambhu, who provides excellent enlightenment, then spoke to her.
"Why are you distressed, my beloved? Do not grieve, Pārvatī! A son shall come, O fair-browed one; let this intense sorrow be abandoned."
When Pārvatī, being deeply distressed, did not accept that proposal, Śaṅkara then dispatched divine sages there.
The gods and all the sages, together with their hosts, filled with joy and possessing great wisdom, went there indeed for the purpose of bringing back Kumāra.
Having gone there, they all bowed deeply to the prince and, after informing him in many ways, made their request with great reverence.
The Guru did not heed that prayer of the gods and others, which was filled with the command of Śiva, for Kumāra was overwhelmed by great egoism.
Then, having returned once more to the presence of Śiva and having received the command of Śaṅkara, they all bowed and departed for their respective abodes.
And at that time, when he had not yet arrived, Goddess Girijā experienced the sorrow born of separation from her son, and Śambhu likewise underwent supreme grief.
Then, deeply distressed and dejected, yet acting in accordance with worldly custom, they went out of great affection to the place where their son was staying.
And that son named Kumāra, having learned of his parents' arrival at the mountain, went three yojanas away out of a lack of affection.
When that son of theirs had gone far away to Mount Krauñca, the two of them remained seated there, having taken on the form of light.
Afflicted by love for their son, Śiva and Pārvatī indeed go on every auspicious occasion to behold their own son, Kumāra.
On the day of the new moon, Śambhu himself goes there; on the day of the full moon, Pārvatī certainly goes there.
Indeed, from that day forward, the single Linga of Śiva known as Mallikārjuna became renowned throughout the three worlds.
Whoever beholds that great Liṅga is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter, and he shall attain all his desires.
Suffering departs far away and one attains ultimate happiness; indeed, one shall never again experience the misery born from a mother's womb.
Abundance of wealth and grain, as well as stability and health, and the attainment of desired fruits arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
The second Jyotirliṅga is declared to be named Mallika; it bestows all happiness upon sight and was described for the sake of the world.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Second Jyotirliṅga, Mallikārjuna," in the fourth Koṭirudra-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Purāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, through the grace of Vyāsa you know every subject; yet, having heard the discourse on the luminaries, no satisfaction at all arises.
Therefore, O Lord, having shown incomparable compassion especially toward us, please tell us now about the third jyotirliṅga.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, I am blessed and I have fulfilled my purpose if I have attained the company of you venerable ones; indeed, the association with the virtuous is truly blessed.
Therefore, recognizing my own good fortune, I shall indeed relate this purifying, divine narrative that destroys all sins; listen to it with reverence.
The city of Avantī is delightful, bestowing liberation upon all embodied beings; it is dear to Śiva, exceedingly meritorious, and a purifier of the world.
There lived an excellent brahmin, devoted to auspicious deeds, who was a student of the Vedas and always engaged in Vedic rituals.
Having established the sacred fires and being constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, that twice-born man indeed worshipped the earthen image every single day.
Having experienced the fruits of all his actions, the twice-born man, who was always fond of the Vedas and devoted to perfect knowledge, attained the state of the virtuous.
Their four sons were likewise such excellent sages, always devoted to the worship of Śiva and never inferior to their parents.
Devapriya was the eldest among them, and after him came Priyamedha; the third was named Kṛta, who was a follower of dharma and firm in his vows.
And through the power of their merit, happiness increased upon the earth, growing continuously like the moon during the bright fortnight.
Likewise, their virtues, which brought happiness, flourished there; indeed, that city then became composed of the splendor of Brahman.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I relate exactly what was heard—the supreme event that occurred there in the meantime.
On the mountain Ratnamāla lived a great asura named Dūṣaṇa, a powerful king of the Daityas who was constantly hostile toward righteousness.
And by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he indeed held the world in contempt; the gods were defeated by him and likewise driven out from their positions.
On this earth, the Vedic laws and the laws of the Smṛtis have been utterly shattered by that wicked one, just as hares are by a lion.
As many Vedic duties as there were, all those have been cast far away; likewise, in every sacred ford and sacred field, Dharma has been driven to a distance.
"A beautiful city of Avanti is seen there once again. Having reflected thus, listen indeed to what was done by him.
Accompanied by a vast army, the great asura Dūṣaṇa approached, directing his aim toward all the brahmins stationed there.
Having arrived there, O Brahmin, that lord of the Daityas—a great villain and a hater of brahmins—summoned four of the best of the Daityas and spoke these words.
The Daitya said: "Why do these wicked Brāhmaṇas not obey my word? Devoted as they all are to the Vedic dharma, in my opinion, they are all deserving of punishment."
"O best of Daityas, all the gods and kings in this world have been defeated by me; why then should the Brahmins not be brought under my control?"
If there should be a desire to live, then [one must] abandon the Dharma of Śiva and the supreme Dharma of the Vedas, and become partakers of happiness.
"Otherwise, there will be doubt regarding their very survival; this is the truth spoken by me, so act upon it with vigilance."
Sūta said: Having thus resolved, those four Daityas became like fires in the four directions, just as they had appeared in the past at the time of universal dissolution.
Having thus heard of that exertion of the Daityas at that time, those Brahmins, being solely devoted to the meditation on Śiva, felt no distress there.
Resorting to fortitude, those brahmins did not waver even by a hair’s breadth from their supreme meditation; for who, being wretched, would move before Śiva?
In the meantime, that auspicious city was pervaded by them, and the people, being oppressed by them, approached the Brāhmaṇas.
The people said: "O Master, what must be done? Wicked ones have arrived; many people have been harmed, and they have come close by."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of theirs, those sons of Vedapriya—the brāhmaṇas who were always full of faith in Śaṅkara—spoke to them.
The Brāhmaṇas said: Listen; there exists no force that brings fear to the wicked, nor are there weapons such as those by which they have turned their faces away from you once more.
Indeed, in this world, there can be no insult to the Universal [Śiva] that would not also affect his substratum; furthermore, what could possibly happen here to Śiva, who is all-powerful?
May Śiva, the Lord, provide protection today from the fear of the asuras; for there is no other refuge in the world than Śiva, who is affectionate toward his devotees.

Sūta said: Having thus established their fortitude and performed the worship of the earthen image, those twice-born ones remained perfectly composed, intent on meditation; and then they were seen by the Daitya together with his army.

Dūṣaṇa spoke the words, "Let him be struck! Let him be killed! But that speech uttered by the Daitya was not heard at all by those brahmins, the sons of Vedapriya, who were solely devoted to the path of meditation on Śambhu.
Then, just as that evil-minded one desired to kill those brahmins, a loud sound arose from a pit in the place where the king was standing.
Then Śiva, assuming a formidable form, emerged from that pit; he is renowned as Mahākāla, the destroyer of the wicked and the refuge of the virtuous.
I have arisen as Mahākāla for the sake of those wicked ones such as yourself; you rogue, depart from the vicinity of the brahmins to a great distance!
Having spoken thus, Mahākāla Śaṅkara then swiftly reduced Dūṣaṇa and his army to ashes by means of a mere "huṃ" sound.
How much of his army was slain by him, and how much fled? And Dūṣaṇa too was killed by that Śiva, the Supreme Self, right here.
Just as all darkness goes to its destruction upon seeing the sun, even so that army perished upon seeing Śiva.
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell; all the gods, including Hari, Brahmā, and the others, likewise arrived.
Having bowed with devotion to that god Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, the twice-born ones praised him with various hymns, their hands joined in reverent salutation.
Having consoled the brahmins, Śiva himself, the Great Time (Mahākāla) and Maheśvara, being well-pleased, said, "Choose a boon."
Having heard that, all those twice-born ones then, with palms joined in reverence, bowed deeply to Śiva with devotion and spoke with their heads bowed low.
The twice-born said: O Mahākāla, O Mahādeva, O Lord who inflicts punishment upon the wicked! O Śambhu, O Śiva, grant us liberation from the ocean of worldly existence.
O Śiva, you must indeed remain right here for the sake of protecting the world; O Lord Śambhu, always deliver those men who behold you.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Śiva remained there in that beautiful pit for the sake of protecting his devotees, having granted them the supreme goal.
Those twice-born ones attained liberation, and at that time, the abode of Śiva in the form of a Liṅga extended for one Krośa in the four directions.
O twice-born ones, Śiva is renowned on earth by the name Mahākāleśvara; having seen him, not even the slightest suffering shall remain in one's dreams.
Whatever desire one has in view when one resorts to that particular emblem, one attains that very desire and shall obtain liberation in the hereafter as well.
All this, O you of excellent vows, has been fully narrated regarding the origin and majesty of Mahākāla; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Mahākāla Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O high-minded one, tell us once more of the greatness of the protectors of the Jyotirliṅga known as Mahākāla and of their devotees.
Sūta said: O Brahmin, listen with reverence to the greatness of the Mahākāla Liṅga, which increases devotion and provides protection to its devotees.
In Ujjayinī there was a great king named Candrasena, who knew the true meaning of all the scriptures, was a devotee of Śiva, and had conquered his senses.
O twice-born ones, that king had as his friend the Gaṇa Maṇibhadra, who was a chief among the attendants of Giriśa and was honored by all the worlds.
Once, that lord of the Gaṇas, Maṇibhadra, being of noble intellect and with a gracious countenance, gave him a great jewel, a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
That jewel indeed shines like the Kaustubha and resembles the sun; whether meditated upon, seen, or even heard, it certainly bestows auspiciousness.
Any bell-metal, copper, tin, stone, or anything else that touches the surface of its rays quickly turns into gold.
Wearing that wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) around his neck, King Candrasena, who took refuge in Śiva, shone exceedingly like the sun in the midst of the gods.
Upon hearing that Candrasena, the best of kings, possessed a wish-fulfilling gem around his neck, all the rulers of the earth became agitated in their hearts by desire.
All those foolish kings, being envious, sought that jewel from Candrasena by various means, for it had been obtained through divine grace.
O brahmins, that Candrasena, who was a firm devotee of Mahākāla, rendered the entreaties of all those kings truly futile.
All those kings of all the lands, having been humiliated by King Candrasena, then displayed great indignation.
Then all those kings, accompanied by their fourfold armies, became indeed intent on conquering Candrasena in battle.
All of them, having come together and established a mutual agreement and understanding, surrounded the four gates of Ujjayinī with their vast armies.
Seeing his own city being besieged by all the kings, the monarch went for refuge to that very Mahākāleśvara.
Free from conceptual construction, abstaining from food, and firm in his resolve, the king, with single-minded devotion, worshipped Mahākāla day and night.
Then the Blessed One, Śambhu Mahākāla, with a gracious mind, devised a means to protect him; listen to that with reverence.
At that very time, O Brahmins, a certain cowherd woman, wandering there with her child in that excellent city, went to the vicinity of Mahākāla.
Carrying a five-year-old child, that woman whose husband had departed observed with devotion the worship of Mahākāla performed by the king.
Having seen that most wonderful worship of Śiva performed by him, she prostrated herself and returned once more to her own camp.
Having seen all of that in its entirety, the son of the cowherd woman set his mind, out of curiosity, upon performing that worship of Śiva.
Having brought a pleasing stone into the empty interior of his camp, he [installed] a Śiva-liṅga with devotion not far from his own camp.
Having prepared offerings of perfumes, ornaments, garments, incense, lamps, unbroken grains, and so forth—using even artificial substances—he likewise presented the food offering.
Having worshipped him again and again with delightful leaves and flowers, and having performed various kinds of dance, he prostrated himself repeatedly.
At that time, out of affection, that cowherd woman called her son—who was of pure mind and deeply attached to Śiva—to take his meal.
When, despite being called many times, the boy—his mind intent on the worship of Śiva—did not desire food, then his mother went there.
Seeing him seated before Śiva with his eyes closed, he seized his hand, pulled it away, and struck him in anger.
When his own son did not come even though he was summoned and beaten, he destroyed that worship by casting the linga far away.
Rebuking her son who was crying out "Alas! Alas! in distress, that cowherd woman, filled with anger, entered her own home once more.
Seeing the worship of the trident-bearing God destroyed by his mother, the boy cried out, "O God of gods! and fell down.
Suddenly he lost consciousness, overwhelmed by grief; regaining his senses after a moment, he opened his eyes.
At that very moment, by the grace of Śiva, that infant immediately beheld there the beautiful abode of Mahākāla.
It has great golden gates with excellent panels and archways, and it is resplendent with a costly, stainless blue vajra-altar.
It was endowed with many variegated golden jars that were heated, and it shone with pillars of radiant jewels and floors of bound crystal.
In the midst of that, the son of the cowherd maiden beheld the jewel-liṅga of Śaṅkara, the ocean of mercy, accompanied by his own performed worship.
Upon seeing him, the child rose up suddenly with a mind full of wonder; he was as if submerged in an ocean of supreme bliss.
Then, having praised Giriśa and bowed down again and again, the boy went out from the temple of Śiva when the sun had set.
Then he beheld his own camp, resembling the city of Indra, suddenly turned into gold, variegated, and supremely radiant.
At the onset of night, he entered his palace, which was endowed with every splendor and strewn with clusters of jewels and gold, feeling great delight.
There he beheld his own mother sleeping, endowed with divine marks, her limbs radiant with jeweled ornaments, like a celestial nymph in person.
Then, O brahmins, that son, overwhelmed with joy, quickly raised up his mother, who was a recipient of Śiva’s grace.
Beholding that unprecedented wonder of her safety, as if everything had become new, she, deeply immersed in great bliss, embraced her son.
Having heard from the mouth of her son everything regarding the grace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, she petitioned the Master who constantly worships Śiva.
Having arrived suddenly at night, the king, his observances completed, beheld the power of the son of Gopikā, which had gratified Śiva.
Having seen all this, the lord of the earth, together with his ministers and domestic priest, was immersed in a state of steadfastness within an ocean of supreme bliss.
Shedding tears of love, King Candrasena, uttering the name of Śiva with affection, embraced that boy.
O twice-born ones, a great and wondrous festival took place there; everyone, overwhelmed with joy, performed the glorification of Maheśa.
Thus, due to those most wonderful deeds, the manifestation of Śiva’s greatness, and the excitement of the citizens, that night passed away as if it were a mere moment.
Then at dawn, having besieged the city, they stood ready for battle; and the kings heard of that event from the mouths of their spies.
And all those kings who had assembled together, having heard that, spoke thus to one another in great astonishment.
The kings said: "This King Candrasena is a devotee of Śiva and is difficult to conquer; he is the undisturbed lord of Ujjayinī, the city of Mahākāla."
In whose city there are such children devoted to the vows of Śiva—that King Candrasena is indeed a great servant of Śaṅkara.
Surely Śiva will become enraged because of this opposition; for through his anger, we shall all be utterly destroyed.
Therefore, this king must indeed perform propitiation; for when this is done, Maheśāna will show supreme compassion.
Sūta said: Having thus resolved, those kings, having abandoned their enmity and possessing pure intentions, all became well-pleased, laying down the weapons and missiles from their hands.
They entered the beautiful city of the mountain Mahākāla and, with the approval of Candrasena, paid their respects to Mahākāla.
Then those cowherd women went to the palace of the king, all praising his divine and great fortune.
There, having been met and honored by Candrasena, they sat upon costly seats and rejoiced, filled with great wonder.
Having beheld that abode of Śiva and the Śivaliṅga manifested through the grace of Gopasūnu, they fixed their supreme devotion upon Śiva.
Then all those kings, being pleased with the cowherd boy and seeking the grace of Śiva, gave many things to him.
In all countries, wherever cowherds dwell in great numbers, all the kings made him alone their sovereign.
Then, in the meantime, the radiant Hanumān, lord of the monkeys, appeared, honored by all the gods of the three worlds.
Upon his mere arrival, those kings, overcome with awe, rose to greet him and paid their respects, their bodies bowed low in devotion.
Seated in their midst and honored by them, the Lord of the Monkeys embraced the son of the Cowherd, looked at the king, and spoke as follows.
Hanumān said: "May it be well with you; let all the kings and all embodied beings listen. Aside from Śiva, there is no other refuge for those who possess bodies."
Thus, by good fortune, having observed the worship of Śiva, the cowherd’s son attained auspiciousness after worshipping Śiva even without the use of mantras.
This excellent devotee of Śambhu, who increases the fame of the cowherds, shall enjoy all pleasures here and attain liberation in the end.
In his lineage, an eighth descendant named Nanda, of great renown, shall arise; Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa himself, will become his son.
From this day forward, this cowherd boy shall attain great renown in this world by the name Śrīkara.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the son of Añjanī, the lord of monkeys who is Śiva himself, looked upon all the kings and Candrasena with a compassionate gaze.
Then, with great affection, he taught the wise Śrīkara, the son of a cowherd, the conduct of Śiva, which is dear to Śiva.
Then, while everyone was looking on, O twice-born one, Hanumān, being well-pleased, vanished right there along with Candrasena and Śrīkara.
All those rulers of the earth, greatly delighted and duly honored, took leave of Candrasena and returned as they had come.
Śrīkara too, possessed of great splendor, being thus instructed by Hanūmat, performed the worship of Śambhu together with Brahmins who were knowers of dharma.
The great king Candrasena and the cowherd boy Śrīkara both worshipped Mahākāla with supreme devotion.
In due time, both Śrīkara and King Candrasena, having propitiated Mahākāla, attained the supreme state.
Such is Mahākāla, the refuge of the virtuous and the destroyer of all that is evil; he is Śaṅkara, who is ever affectionate toward his devotees.
This supreme purifier, a secret that bestows all happiness, this celestial narrative has been told, which increases devotion to Śiva.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Mahākāla Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O illustrious Sūta, you have indeed narrated this wonderful account of the Liṅga named Mahākāla, which is the protector of its own devotees."
O best of knowers, please graciously describe the fourth Jyotirlinga, Oṃkāra, which belongs to the Supreme Lord and removes all sins.

Sūta said: O twice-born ones, I shall relate with affection how the Liṅga known as Parameśa came to be at Oṃkāra; listen, O supreme ṛṣis. Once upon a time, the venerable sage Nārada, possessed of supreme devotion, went to the Lord Śiva named Gokarṇa and served him.
Then that best of sages arrived at Vindhya, the lord of mountains; there he was honored by him with great respect.
"Everything exists within me and is never lacking"; having established this state of being, he stood before Nārada.
Having heard that measure of his pride at that time, Nārada, the destroyer of pride, remained there sighing; then, having heard this, Vindhya spoke as follows.
Vindhya said: "What deficiency have you perceived in me that is the cause of your sighing? Having heard those words, the great sage Nārada spoke this speech.
Nārada said: "Indeed, everything exists within you; furthermore, Meru is even higher than you. Even among the gods, there is never any equal division [of greatness] for you."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Nārada departed from there just as he had come; and Vindhya, being deeply distressed, thought, "Fie upon my life and all else!"
"Having propitiated Viśveśvara and likewise Śambhu, I shall perform my penance"; having thus resolved in his mind, he went for refuge to Śaṅkara.
He went there with great joy to where Oṃkāra himself was; and there, moreover, Śiva assumed an earthen form.
Having propitiated Śambhu for six months without interruption at that time, he, devoted solely to meditation on Śiva, did not waver from his place of austerity.
Having thus observed Vindhya’s asceticism, the Lord of Pārvatī was pleased and revealed his own form, which is difficult even for yogis to behold.
To him who was thus pleased, he said: "Speak what you desire in your mind; I am gratified by your austerity, for I am the bestower of the desires of my devotees."
Vindhya said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, grant me the desired intellect that accomplishes my own purpose, O Śambhu; for you are always affectionate toward your devotees."
Sūta said: Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Śambhu reflected for a long time in his heart: "The foolish-minded Vindhya desires a boon that causes distress to others."
What shall I do so that this granting of a boon may be auspicious for him? For a boon granted by me should not result in the suffering of another.
Sūta said: Nevertheless, Śambhu granted him that supreme boon: "O King of Mountains, Vindhya, do as you desire."
And at that time, the gods and the sages of pure intent, having worshipped Śaṅkara there, said, "You must remain here."
Having heard those words of the god, the Supreme Lord was pleased and, out of affection, acted accordingly for the sake of the happiness of the worlds.
The single liṅga that is the syllable Oṃ has become twofold; in the Praṇava, he who is named Oṃkāra is indeed Sadāśiva.
O twice-born ones, that which was born from Pārthiva was indeed the Supreme Lord; both of them bestow the desires of their devotees and grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then the gods and the sages likewise performed worship to him; having gratified the bull-bannered Lord, they obtained many boons.
The gods went to their respective abodes, and Vindhya too, being exceedingly delighted, O twice-born ones, accomplished his own purpose and abandoned his distress.
Whoever worships Śambhu in this manner shall indeed not dwell within a mother’s womb; and whatever desired fruit they seek, that too they shall obtain—of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: Thus has all this been told to you regarding the fruit arising from the syllable Om; hereafter I shall describe the supreme Liṅga, Kedāra.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Oṃkāreśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, those two incarnations of Hari known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa indeed performed austerities at Badarikāśrama in the land of Bhārata.
Requested by those two for worship in the earthen image, Śambhu, being subject to his devotees' will, comes daily to that liṅga, O Śiva.
As those two incarnations of Viṣṇu, the sons of Dharma and devotees of Śiva, were thus worshipping Śambhu, a long period of time passed away.
At one time, the Supreme Lord, being pleased there, replied: "I am gratified; let a boon be chosen from me."
When this was said, Nara and Nārāyaṇa themselves then spoke these words there, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted by you, may Śaṅkara himself remain here in his own form for the sake of receiving worship."
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the two of them at that time, Maheśvara Śaṅkara himself remained in Kedāra, which is sheltered by snow, in the form of light.
And having been worshipped by those two, he who removes all suffering and fear appeared for the benefit of the worlds and indeed for the sake of granting vision to his devotees.
Then Śambhu himself remained there, known by the name Kedāreśvara, eternally bestowing the desired objects of his devotees through both his sight and his worship.
In this world, both the gods and the ancient sages worship [him], for from the well-pleased Maheśvara they obtain the fruits desired by their minds.
Because the residents of Badarikāśrama constantly obtain [their desires] through the worship of Bhava, he is always the bestower of the desired objects of his devotees.
Indeed, from that day forward, even in a dream, suffering is very difficult to find for one by whom Kedāreśvara has been worshipped with devotion.
Indeed, whoever saw the Pāṇḍavas there, assuming the form of a buffalo and employing his illusory power, became intent on flight.
And he was held there by the Pāṇḍavas, standing with his face turned downwards; they even held his tail and entreated him again and again.
Abiding there in that form, he bore the name Bhaktavatsala; in Nayapāla, the upper portion [of his body] was present, remaining in that very form.
Indeed, having been worshipped, Śambhu himself remained there, constantly bestowing honors as well as commands, and granted boons.
Having performed the worship, those Pāṇḍavas then departed joyful, having obtained everything desired by their hearts and being liberated from all suffering.
There, in that field known as Kedāra, which is eternally manifest, he is likewise worshipped by the people of Bhārata.
Whoever, being dear to Hara, offers a bracelet there, that [gift] reaches the presence of Hara’s form, endowed with the very nature of Hara.
Likewise, by seeing that form, one is liberated from all sins; even he who has gone to the Badarī forest becomes liberated while living.
Indeed, having seen the form of Nara, as well as that of Nārāyaṇa, and of Śambhu Kedāreśvara, one becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are devotees of Kedāreśa and die while on his path become liberated even after they have departed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Having gone there with joy and worshipped Kedāreśa, and having drunk the water found there, one does not undergo rebirth again.
In this land of Bhārata, O brāhmaṇas, Naranārāyaṇeśvara and Kedāreśa are to be worshipped with great devotion by all living beings.
Śambhu, known as Kedāra, is the lord of this region; he is the Lord of all, especially so, and the granter of all desires—of this there is no doubt.
O best of sages, this which was asked has been fully explained; having heard it, one removes all sin—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Kedāreśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the majesty of Bhaimaśaṅkara, by the mere hearing of which a person obtains all their desires.
In the region known as Kāmarūpa, Śaṅkara himself descended in person out of a desire for the welfare of the world, becoming the vessel of auspicious bliss.
O lords of sages, listen with respect as I relate that purpose for which Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, has descended; I shall tell it to you.
O twice-born ones, in former times there was a Rākṣasa named Bhīma of great heroism, who was a source of suffering for all beings and a constant destroyer of dharma.
Born from Kumbhakarṇa by a female crab, he was possessed of great strength; he also took up residence on the Sahya mountain with his mother.
When Kumbhakarṇa, the terror of the worlds, had been slain by Rāma, the Rākṣasī herself then remained on Mount Sahya together with her sons.
O twice-born ones, once that wicked boy of terrible prowess, who brought suffering to the world, asked his mother Karkaṭī about Bhīma.
Bhīma said: "O mother, who is my father, where is he, and how have you remained all alone? I wish to know all of that; tell me now according to the truth."
Sūta said: Thus questioned then by that son, that wicked Rākṣasī spoke to her son: "Listen, I shall tell you."
Karkaṭī said: "Your father Kumbhakarṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, has been killed by Rāma along with his brother, despite being possessed of great strength."
O dear one, in the past, a powerful Rākṣasa belonging to Kumbhakarṇa once arrived here and forcibly took possession of my body.
That mighty one has gone to Laṅkā, leaving me right here; I have not seen him, for I am dwelling right here in Laṅkā.
My father was named Karkaṭa; my mother is considered to have been a Puṣkasī; and my husband was indeed Virādha, who was slain by Rāma in the past.
And I remained by the side of my parents when my beloved husband was slain; my parents died there, reduced to ashes by the rishi.
When they had gone there for the purpose of eating, they were then encountered by the highly exalted Sutīkṣṇa, a disciple of Agastya who was possessed of great ascetic power and filled with wrath.
In former times, I was born alone upon that mountain; afflicted by suffering, I lived there in misery, without support and without refuge.
At that very moment, indeed, the Rākṣasa who was the younger brother of Rāvaṇa arrived here; having formed an alliance with me, he departed.
Then you were born, endowed with great strength and prowess; and relying upon you once more, I shall bide my time.
Sūta said: Having heard her words, Bhīma of terrible prowess became enraged and reflected, "What shall I do against Hari?"
For by him my father was slain, as indeed was my maternal grandfather; and Virādha too was killed by him, causing me exceeding grief.
Thinking, "If I am to become his son, I shall afflict that Hari," Bhīma resolved thus and went forth to perform great penance.
Then, for a thousand years dedicated to the Brahmas, he performed great penance, relying solely on mental meditation.
With arms raised and standing on one foot, fixing his gaze upon the sun, that son of a Rākṣasa, Bhīma, remained standing there as he had done in the past.
A most terrible radiance issued from his head; scorched by it, the gods then went to Brahmā for refuge.
Having bowed with devotion to the Creator, they praised him with various hymns; together with Indra, they reported their suffering to Brahmā.
The gods said: "O Brahmā, the energy of that Rākṣasa is indeed intent on afflicting the worlds; O Creator, grant him that very boon which is being requested by the wicked one."
Otherwise, we shall all be consumed today by the intensity of your splendor and go to our destruction; therefore, grant us what we have requested.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, went to grant the boon and spoke these words.
Brahmā said: "I am pleased; choose a boon, whatever dwells in your mind. Having heard these words of the Creator, that Rākṣasa spoke.
Bhīma said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted by you, then grant me incomparable strength today, O Lotus-seated One."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that Rākṣasa indeed paid homage to Brahmā; and Brahmā, having granted him a boon at that time, departed for his own abode.
Then that Rākṣasa, having arrived at the house with great strength obtained from Brahmā, quickly prostrated before his mother and spoke haughtily: "O Bhīma! he said.
Bhīma said: "Behold my strength today, O Mother; I shall bring about a great dissolution of the gods, headed by Śakra, and of Hari along with his allies."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Bhīma of terrible prowess first conquered the gods together with Indra and drove them from their respective positions.
Then he conquered Hari in battle, even though he was sought after by the gods; thereafter, the Daitya joyfully began an expedition to conquer the earth.
Formerly, having gone there to conquer the lord Sudakṣiṇa, the sovereign of Kāmarūpa, a terrifying battle took place with him.
Then, O King, by the power of Brahmā and through the influence of his boon, the asura Bhīma conquered that great hero who had taken refuge in Śiva.
Having conquered that lord, the ruler of Kāmarūpa, Bhīma of terrible prowess indeed bound him and struck him.
O twice-born ones, the entire property and kingdom, along with all its appurtenances, were seized by that wicked Bhīma from King Śivadāsa.
And the king, who was most righteous, devoted to dharma, and dear to Śiva, was seized by him with fetters and placed in a secluded spot.
There, having then assumed an excellent earthly form, he began the worship of Śiva alone out of a desire to do what was pleasing [to him].
He then offered many praises to the Gaṅgā; having performed the mental bath and other rites, he worshipped Śaṅkara.
That best of kings performed that meditation according to the prescribed rite for earthly beings, having first executed it according to the injunctions.
Having performed all those acts preceded by prostrations, hymns of praise, and ritual gestures (*mudrā*) and postures (*āsana*), he joyfully worshipped Śaṅkara.
He chanted the five-syllabled mantra accompanied by the Praṇava; indeed, he found no opportunity at that time to perform any other task.
And his virtuous wife, renowned by the name Dakṣiṇā, the beloved of the king, out of affection made a royal gift at that time.
The couple, with single-minded devotion, constantly worshipped Śaṅkara, the benefactor of his devotees, remaining ever intent on the propitiation of Śiva.
The Rākṣasa, deluded by the pride of receiving boons, obstructed all my sacrificial rites and other activities, saying, "Let this indeed be given to me!"
Accompanied by a vast army of evil-minded rākṣasas, O best of sages, he brought the entire earth under his own control.

Having set aside the dharma of the Vedas, the dharma of the Śāstras, the dharma of the Smṛtis, and that born of the Purāṇas—having abolished all of that—he, being powerful himself, enjoyed [the kingdom].
O twice-born ones, the gods, including Śakra, as well as the sages, were oppressed by him; having fallen into extreme misery, they were driven out from the worlds.
Then all of them, including the gods, the asuras, and the sages, being thus distressed, went for refuge to Śaṅkara, placing Brahmā and Viṣṇu at their head.
Having praised Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, with numerous hymns of praise, they caused him to become gracious on the auspicious bank of the Mahākośī.
Having fashioned an image of the Earth and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, they praised her in succession with various hymns, prostrations, and other offerings.
Thus praised at that time by the gods with hymns and other offerings, Śambhu became exceedingly well-pleased and spoke these words to those deities.
Śiva said: O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O gods, and all you sages, I am pleased; ask for a boon—what service may I perform for you?
Sūta said: O brahmins, when these words had been spoken by Śiva at that time, the gods, having bowed deeply and joined their palms, then spoke to Śiva.
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, you know everything that resides in the minds of all; as the inner controller of all, nothing remains unknown to you."
Nevertheless, O Lord, please listen as we speak of our own suffering; by your command, O Mahādeva, look upon us with a compassionate gaze.
The powerful Rākṣasa Karkaṭīputra, born of Kumbhakarṇa and emboldened by a boon granted by Brahmā, torments the gods incessantly.
Slay this Rākṣasa named Bhīma, who causes such suffering; have mercy, O Great Lord, and do not delay, O Master!
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by all the gods, Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, said to the deities, "I shall effect his slaughter," and then spoke to them.
Śambhu said: "The King of Kāmarūpa is my supreme devotee; tell him this, O gods, and the task shall soon be accomplished."
O Sudakṣiṇa, O great king, O lord and master of Kāmarūpa! You are especially my devotee; therefore, perform my worship with devotion.
I shall slay the wicked Daitya named Bhīma, who has been empowered by a boon obtained from Brahmā and who has insulted you; of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: Then all those gods, filled with joy, went there and told that great king what had been spoken by Śambhu.
Having spoken thus to him, the gods attained supreme bliss, and all those great sages quickly departed for their own hermitages.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disturbance Caused by the Asura Bhīma," in the *Bhīmeśvara Jyotirliṅga-māhātmya* of the fourth book, the *Koṭirudra-saṃhitā*, of the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Śiva also went together with his attendants out of a desire for their welfare; he remained hidden near his devotee, staying there out of respect for the purpose of protection.
In the meantime, the Lord of Kāmarūpa then began an intense meditation in the presence of the king.
Someone went there and informed the Rākṣasa: "The king is performing such a malevolent rite for your sake."
Sūta said: Having heard that, the Rākṣasa became enraged and, desiring to slay him, took up his sword and went toward the king.
Having seen that which was situated there, beginning with the king, and having observed its purpose and its true nature, that Rākṣasa does something [in response].
"Therefore, I shall today forcibly kill this king along with his retinue. Having reflected thus, the Rākṣasa, filled with great rage, spoke to that king.
Bhīma said: "O wicked-souled king, what are you doing now? Speak the truth; I will not kill you, but otherwise I shall certainly slay you."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, the Lord of Kāmarūpa, filled with faith in Śiva, quickly reflected thus in his mind.
