That which is destined to happen will certainly occur; there is no one who can turn it back. In this matter, everything is dependent solely on *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions), and that *prārabdha* is remembered as Śiva.
The compassionate Śaṅkara certainly dwells here upon this earth; why does he not act for my sake here, and who is this Rākṣasa?
He will surely fulfill his promise in accordance with his own nature; for it is heard in the Śruti that the Blessed Lord Śiva is one whose vow is truth.
Whenever someone extremely cruel torments my devotee, then I shall undoubtedly slay that wicked one for the sake of his protection.
Having thus maintained fortitude and meditated upon the god Śaṅkara, Raseśvara prayed with true devotion through his mind alone.
"I am yours, O Great King; do as you wish. Indeed, I speak these words of truth here: do what is for my benefit."
Having reflected thus in his mind, the king, consecrated by the bond of truth, spoke these words of truth while disregarding the rākṣasa.
The king said: I worship the god Śaṅkara, the protector of his own devotees, the lord of all moving and unmoving beings, who is free from change.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the Lord of Kāmarūpa, Bhīma, his limbs trembling with rage, spoke these words.
Bhīma said: "I have come to know your true nature, O Śaṅkara; what indeed can you do to me? You were established as a servant by my paternal uncle himself."
For by relying upon that power, you seek to conquer; therefore, everything has already been conquered by you—there is no need for further deliberation in this matter.
"As long as Śaṅkara, your protector, has not been seen by me, so long you shall serve him regarding him as your master; it can never be otherwise."
O King, once I have seen it, all of that will become entirely clear; therefore, you must indeed keep this form of Śiva at a great distance.
Otherwise, you will undoubtedly experience fear today; I, of terrible prowess, shall deliver a sharp blow to your master.
Sūta said: Having heard those words, the king, the lord of Kāmarūpa, who possessed firm faith in Śaṅkara, quickly spoke these words to him.
The king said: "I am a base and wicked man, yet I shall not release Śaṅkara; moreover, my lord is the most excellent of all, and he will never let me go."
Sūta said: Having thus heard those words of that king whose soul was devoted to Śiva, the Rākṣasa Bhīma laughed and quickly spoke to the monarch.
Bhīma said: "He who constantly begs from me—what does he know of his own true nature? And what indeed is the steadfastness of yogis in the protection of their devotees?"
Having formed this resolve, you must stay far away by all means; I am indeed your master, and we two shall surely engage in battle.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, O best of kings, that devotee of Śambhu, firm in his vows and fearless, replied to Bhīma, who was always a source of misery for the worlds.
The king said: "Listen, O evil-minded Rākṣasa, this cannot be done by me; if it is being transformed by you, then from where do you derive such power?"
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, and having taken the army and rebuked that king, he then hurled his formidable sword at the monarch.
"Behold this very day the power of your master, which brings happiness to his devotees! Thus spoke that one of great strength, laughing, along with the rākṣasas.
O twice-born ones, as long as the sword did not touch the king, and as long as Hara himself had not yet manifested from that king; [so long did the king remain in his mortal state].
Behold, O Bhīmeśvara, I have manifested myself for the sake of protection; for this is my ancient vow: a devotee must always be protected by me.
"Behold my power, which swiftly brings happiness to my devotees! Having said this, he split the sword in two with his Pināka bow.
Furthermore, that Rākṣasa hurled his own trident once more; yet even that spear was shattered into a hundred pieces by Śambhu against the wicked one.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, Śakti was hurled by him at Śambhu; that too was quickly shattered into a hundred thousand pieces by Śambhu with his own arrows.
Then he hurled a spear at Śiva, but Śiva, with his trident, reduced it to pieces as small as sesame seeds in an instant.
Then a terrible battle took place between the hosts of Śiva’s attendants and the Rākṣasas, bringing sorrow to those who witnessed it.
And then, in an instant, the entire earth became agitated; all the oceans, along with the mountains, were thrown into turmoil.
All the gods and sages became greatly distressed and said to one another, "Indeed, our prayer to Śiva has been in vain."
And Nārada, having arrived there, with palms joined in reverence and head bowed, made a supplication to Śaṅkara, the destroyer of suffering.
Nārada said: "Forgive me, forgive me, O Lord, you who cause delusion! Let even a blade of grass or an axe indeed strike [him] very swiftly."
Thus entreated, the Lord Śambhu then reduced all the hosts of Rākṣasas to ashes by means of the weapon consisting of the syllable "Huṃ" alone.
O Sage, in an instant all those Rākṣasas were consumed by Śaṅkara; it was a marvel witnessed there by all the gods.
Just as a fire that has reached a forest conflagration would burn it down, so too did the army of the Rākṣasas perish in an instant by the wrath of Śiva.
And was it not known by anyone at that time that Bhīma himself, along with his retinue, had been burnt? Indeed, it is nowhere heard that he was not consumed by fire.
Then, by the grace of Śiva, the lords of sages attained peace; all the gods, headed by Indra, regained their composure, and the entire world was restored to health.
The flame of Maheśa’s wrath issued forth from forest to forest; its ashes pervaded the entire forest, covering all the rākṣasas.
Thereupon, medicinal herbs were produced that perform various functions; likewise, there arose changes in the physical forms of men as well as differences in their dress.
O twice-born ones, beings such as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas should depart from there to a great distance; furthermore, one should not perform any action that would cause them to remain there.
Then Śambhu was specifically entreated by the sages: "O Lord, you must indeed remain here for the sake of the happiness of the worlds."
This land of Ayodhyā is indeed a wretched place that brings suffering to its people; yet, upon seeing you there, prosperity will surely come to pass.
"You shall be known by the name Bhīmaśaṅkara, the accomplisher of all goals; this Liṅga is to be worshipped always as the warder-off of all calamities."
Sūta said: Thus entreated, Śambhu, the benefactor of the worlds, independent and affectionate toward his devotees, remained right there with joy.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Origin of the Bhīmeśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Hereafter, O best of sages, listen as I proclaim the majesty of Viśveśvara, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Whatever mere object is seen here in the world is, in its true nature, consciousness-bliss, changeless and eternal.
From that very state of delight in absolute liberation (kaivalya), there arose a desire for a second; he himself became possessed of attributes (saguṇa) and is designated as Śiva.
For that very [reality] is born in two ways through the distinction of male and female forms: he who is the male is known as Śiva, and she who is the female is called Śakti.
Two persons were also created from the two forms of Consciousness and Bliss.
O best of sages, O twice-born ones, at that time those two were not seen by him because of their own nature; meanwhile, they too saw their own mother and father.

When both Prakṛti and Puruṣa had fallen into great doubt, a voice then emerged from the Supreme Self beyond the qualities (Nirguṇa): "Austerity must indeed be performed; thereafter, the unsurpassed creation shall come forth."
Prakṛti and Puruṣa said: "O Lord Śiva, there is no place for penance anywhere at present; by your command, where must we stay to perform our austerities?"
And from that, he likewise created an auspicious and beautiful city, five krośas in extent, which was the essence of splendor and equipped with all necessary provisions.
Having manifested it, that [weapon] was sent by the quality-less Śiva; and it remained in the intermediate space near the Puruṣa.
Then, presiding over that [place] with the desire for creation, Hari performed penance for a long time, relying upon meditation on that [same object].
Then there arose streams of water and various other things; that void was pervaded by them, and nothing else could be seen.
Then Viṣṇu saw it and thought, "What is this wonder that is being seen? Having beheld that marvel, he shook his head in astonishment.
Then, O Lord, the jewel fell from Karna's ear in front of him; that became a great holy site (tīrtha) known by the name Maṇikarṇikā.
When that [land] five *krośas* in extent was being submerged by the flood of water, it was then swiftly held up by the attribute-less Śiva with his trident.
Viṣṇu slept right there with his own wife, Prakṛti; from the lotus of his navel was born Brahmā by the command of Śaṅkara.
Having received the command of Śiva, she then performed a wondrous act of creation within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), wherein the fourteen worlds were fashioned.
The sages have proclaimed that the extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) itself measures fifty crores of yojanas.
Reflecting, "How shall living beings bound by their actions within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) attain me again?", this Pañcakrośī was liberated.
This Kāśī is considered the bestower of auspiciousness in the world and the destroyer of karma; it is the illuminator of liberation, the giver of knowledge, and is very dear to me.
The self-manifested Liṅga of Avimukta was established by the Supreme Self; O portion of My own being, you must never abandon this sacred field.
Having spoken thus, Hara himself brought Kāśikā down from his trident and released her into the mortal world on earth.
Indeed, she certainly does not perish during the day of Brahmā; at that time, Śiva holds her with his trident, and the sages do as well.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, when creation was again performed by Brahmā, it was established; and because of its cultivation through ritual action, it is recited as "Kāśī."
The Avimukteśvara Liṅga resides eternally in Kāśī; it bestows liberation upon all people, even those who have committed great sins.
O lords of sages, liberation such as *sārūpya* and the like is obtained elsewhere; however, here alone is the supreme liberation of *sāyujya* attained by living beings.
For those who have no other refuge anywhere, there is the city of Vārāṇasī; its five-krośa expanse is greatly meritorious and destroys ten million acts of killing.
All the immortals desire death here, as do others; she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is forever beloved by Śaṅkara.
Brahmā praises her, as do Viṣṇu, the Siddhas, and the Yogins; likewise, the sages and all other beings dwelling in the three worlds always praise her.
Indeed, I am not able to describe the full majesty of Kāśī even in hundreds of years; therefore, I shall speak of it according to my capacity.

He who is indeed the lord of Kailāsa, possessing inner goodness yet appearing dark on the outside, known by the name Kālāgni—the unborn Bhava, who is both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities—spoke these words after many prostrations.
Rudra said: O Lord of the Universe, O Great Sovereign, I am yours, there is no doubt; O Mahādeva, together with your son Sāmba, show mercy toward me.
"And you should always remain right here out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. Deliver the world, O Lord of the World; this is my prayer, O Master of the Universe."
Sūta said: Even in Avimukta, that self-controlled soul, having entreated him again and again and shedding tears from his eyes, spoke joyfully to Śaṅkara.
Avimukta said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, the excellent medicine for the disease of Time! You are truly the Lord of the three worlds, to be served by Brahmā, Acyuta, and the others.
"O Lord, let the capital city be taken up by you in the city of Kāśī; I shall remain in a state of meditative absorption for the sake of inconceivable happiness."
You alone are the bestower of liberation and the granter of desires, and no other; therefore, remain forever together with Umā for the sake of bestowing grace.
O Sadāśiva, ferry all living beings across the ocean of existence; O Hara, accomplish the work of your devotees—I pray to you again and again.
Sūta said: Thus entreated by Viśvanātha, Śaṅkara, the sovereign of all, remained there for the benefit of the worlds.
Indeed, from the very day that Hara arrived at Kāśī, from that time onward, that Kāśī became the most excellent of all.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Rudra’s Arrival in Kāśī," within the "Glorification of Viśveśvara" in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O Sūta, if the great city of Vārāṇasī is thus meritorious, then tell us, O Lord, about its power and that of Avimukta."
Sūta said: O lords of sages, I shall describe succinctly and correctly the most beautiful majesty of Viśveśvara at Vārāṇasī; let it be heard.
Once, the goddess Pārvatī, out of supreme joy and a desire for the welfare of the world, questioned Śaṅkara regarding the greatness of Avimukta.
Pārvatī said: "Out of compassion for me and with a desire for the welfare of the worlds, you ought to recount the greatness of this sacred field in its entirety."
Sūta said: Having heard those words of the Goddess, the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, replied to Bhavānī for the sake of the welfare of living beings.
The Supreme Lord said: "Well asked by you, O blessed lady, this auspicious question that brings happiness to the worlds. I shall indeed tell you the true majesty of Avimukta."
This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine; it is in every way the cause of liberation for all living beings.
In this sacred field, the perfected ones (siddhas) always abide, having taken refuge in my vow; they constantly bear various emblems and ever long for my world.
Those who have conquered their self and subdued their senses practice the supreme Pāśupata yoga, which is revealed in the Vedas and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Maheśvarī, my dwelling in Vārāṇasī is always pleasing to me; hear now the certain reason why I have abandoned everything else.

He who is devoted to me and he who possesses realized knowledge—both of these partake in liberation; for them, no expectation of sacred pilgrimage sites is prescribed, as they are equal regarding what has been ordained.
Those two should be known as liberated while living; wherever they may die, they attain liberation immediately. This is the certain word spoken by me.
O Goddess, Supreme Power, listen with a focused mind to the special distinction that exists here at this most excellent sacred site known as Avimukta.
All castes and stages of life, whether children, youths, or the elderly—if they should die in this city, they will undoubtedly be liberated.
Whether she be impure or pure, a maiden or one who has reached maturity, a widow or even barren, or even one afflicted by the defect of menstruation;
O twice-born ones, whoever—whatever their state or refinement—may be born and dies in this sacred field, they shall attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Whether born from sweat, or from an egg, or from a sprout, or from a womb—one who dies here attains liberation in a manner that is not found anywhere else.
In this very matter, there is no dependence on knowledge, nor indeed any dependence on devotion; there is no dependence on ritual action here, O Goddess, nor is there any dependence on charity.

In this regard, there is no dependence on ritual refinement, nor is there ever any dependence on meditative absorption; likewise, for those of noble birth, there is here no dependence on names or dependence on worship.
Indeed, whatever person dwells in my field which bestows liberation, if they should die there in any manner whatsoever, they will certainly attain liberation.
This divine city of mine, O beloved, is more secret than the most secret; even Brahmā and the other gods do not know its majesty, O Pārvatī.
Therefore, this great field is remembered as Avimukta; it is superior to all [sacred sites] such as Naimiṣa, bestowing liberation upon one who dies there.
Truth is the secret essence of Dharma; equanimity is the secret essence of liberation; the wise know that Avimukta is the secret essence of all sacred fields and pilgrimage sites.
Whether eating, sleeping, playing, or performing various activities, a living being who gives up their life-breaths at Avimukta becomes fit for liberation.
Even after committing thousands of sins, it is better for men to attain the state of a *piśāca* than to possess the merit of a thousand sacrifices in heaven without the city of Kāśī.
Therefore, with every effort, the city of Kāśī should be resorted to; there, Sadāśiva is meditated upon by sages in an unmanifest form.
O beloved, whatever fruit men here perform penance aiming for, I certainly bestow that very fruit upon them in its entirety.
For those who cast off their bodies here, there is no bondage of karma from any source whatsoever; they shall thereafter attain union with the Self and their desired state.
Brahmā together with the celestial sages, Viṣṇu, or even the Sun-god—all these great-souled ones, as well as others, worship me here.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma, if he dies in this sacred field, shall certainly not enter saṃsāra again.

How much more so those who are free from the sense of "mine," steadfast, not established in the state of being a sentient being, devoid of hypocrisy, skillful, and free from worldly undertakings—all of them are absorbed in me.
A yogi may undergo birth through thousands of other lives; yet here, upon death, he attains supreme liberation in this very life.
Indeed, O Pārvatī, many liṅgas have been installed here by devotees; they grant all desires and bestow liberation in this world.
This field is proclaimed to extend five krośas in the four directions; it bestows immortality upon any living being who dies there on all sides at the time of death.
He who is free from sin, upon dying, attains immediate liberation; whereas he who dies with sin attains a multitude of bodies.
He who commits a sin in this sacred field known as Avimukta will certainly experience torment and only thereafter attain liberation.
Having endured the terrible torment for ten thousand years, O beautiful one, he then attains liberation after having exhausted his sin.
Thus have those destinies been fully described which belong to one of evil conduct; knowing this, a man should properly serve Avimuktaka.
There is no destruction of performed karma even in hundreds of millions of eons; whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced.
In this world, exclusively impure karma leads to hell; pure karma results in heaven; and by a combination of both, human birth is said to occur.
In this world, birth may be correct or incorrect, deficient or excessive; however, O Pārvatī, when both are extinguished, liberation occurs—this is indeed the truth.

O Maheśvarī, action is declared to be threefold in the Karma-kāṇḍa: that which is accumulated (saṃcita), that which is being performed (kriyamāṇa), and that which has begun (prārabdha); these are the causes of bondage.
That which arises from previous births and has been accumulated is called *saṃcita*; that which is experienced by the present body is proclaimed as *prārabdha*.
O Goddess of the gods, the wise know that action performed at present through one's birth—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is what is called "being done."
The exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma* occurs through experience, and otherwise [through death]; the destruction of both types of karma is achieved by means such as worship.
There is no destruction of any karmas except in the city of Kāśī; while every other sacred site is easily accessible, the city of Kāśī is difficult to attain.
If indeed the sight of Kāśī was performed with devotion in a previous birth, then having reached Kāśī, one shall meet death; and not otherwise.
When a person reaches Kāśī and performs a bath in the Gaṅgā, there occurs the destruction of both present and accumulated [karma].
It is certain that prārabdha-karma does not perish without being experienced; therefore, its exhaustion occurs only when death has taken place.
Even if one has previously performed meritorious deeds at Kāśī and later commits sin, one is led back again to Kāśī by the power of that former seed.
Then indeed all sins are reduced to ashes; therefore, a person should certainly resort to Kāśī, which utterly eradicates karma.
O beloved, even a single Brāhmaṇa who has resided in Kāśī—even by merely attaining residence in Kāśī—he thereafter finds liberation.
For one who dies in Kāśī, there is indeed no further birth; and for one who dies at Prayāga with a specific intention, there is the fruit of that desire.
If there were a union between those two, the fruit born of Kāśī would be in vain; if there were no union between those two, the fruit of the King of Tīrthas would be in vain.
Therefore, by my command, Viṣṇu shall indeed directly bring about a new creation as intended by his mind, and he will surely grant its fulfillment.
Sūta said: O best of sages, such is the great majesty of Kāśī, as well as that of Viśveśvara, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the virtuous.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the majesty of Tryambaka, by hearing which a human being is instantly liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Jyotirliṅga Viśveśvara of Kāśī," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Listen, O best of sages, to this story that destroys all sins, which I shall relate just as it was heard by me from Vyāsa, my true guru.
In former times, there was a renowned and excellent sage named Gautama; he had a most virtuous wife named Ahalyā.
For on the mountain named Brahma in the southern direction, he performed austerities for ten thousand years.
And once, O observers of excellent vows, there occurred a terrible drought lasting for a hundred years, and the worlds fell into suffering.
Not even a single moist sprout was to be seen upon the surface of the earth; how then could water, the sustainer of the life-breath of living beings, be found?
Then those sages, as well as humans, animals, birds, and wild beasts, fled from there in all ten directions.
Seeing her, the sages and brahmins, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), spent that most dreadful time in meditation.
Gautama himself also performed auspicious penance there for the sake of Varuṇa for six months, being entirely devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then Varuṇa arrived to grant him a boon; "I am pleased, choose a boon and I shall give it," he said, and [the other] spoke these words.
Then Gautama indeed requested rain from him at that time; thereupon, O twice-born ones, Varuṇa replied to that sage.
Varuṇa said: "How can I transgress the command of the gods and carry it out? Ask for something else; you are wise, so let me do what I can for you."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of that high-souled Varuṇa, Gotama, who was intent on helping others, spoke this speech.
Gautama said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then that which I now request must indeed be performed by you."
Since you are the lord of the mass of waters, therefore, O Lord of all gods, water must be given to me—imperishable, divine, and bestowing eternal fruit.
Sūta said: Thus entreated by Gautama, Varuṇa spoke these words to him: "A pit must indeed be dug by you."
When this was said, he dug a pit measuring one cubit in size, and it was filled with that divine water by Varuṇa.
Then the god Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, spoke to the sage Gautama, that tiger among sages who is devoted to the welfare of others.
Varuṇa said: "O great sage, let this water of yours be inexhaustible and become a sacred ford (tīrtha); it shall become famous on earth by your name."

Whatever is given here, offered in sacrifice, performed as austerity, or offered in worship to the gods, and whatever śrāddha is performed for the ancestors—all this shall indeed become inexhaustible.
Sūta said: Having been thus addressed and praised by that great sage, the Lord vanished; and the sage Gautama, having performed this service for another, attained happiness.
For when the self is intoxicated by pride, it becomes the basis for men's greatness; the truly great perceive its true nature, but others who are impure do not.
Whatever kind of person one serves, one reaps a corresponding fruit; by serving the great, one attains greatness, and likewise, by serving the base, one attains baseness.
Service rendered in the temple of a lion is considered to yield the fruit of pearls; service in the temple of a jackal is remembered as resulting only in the acquisition of bones.
This is the nature of the noble: an inability to endure the suffering of others; even when suffering has come upon oneself, one considers it as something to be warded off from another.
The trees, gold, sandalwood, and likewise sugarcane—these alone on earth are capable of serving the highest purpose for others; no others are so.
Compassionate, untouched by intoxication, beneficent, and with senses conquered—the earth is supported by these four pillars of merit.
Then Gautama, having obtained there water that was very difficult to find, duly performed his obligatory and occasional rites at that time.
Then, for the purpose of the oblation, the lord of sages sowed rice, barley, and various kinds of wild grain right there.
Various kinds of grains, as well as various trees, flowers, and fruits indeed existed there in great abundance.
Having heard that, thousands of other sages arrived there; many other animals, birds, and living beings also came.
That forest was indeed most beautiful on the supreme circle of the earth; due to the connection with that inexhaustible maker, drought did not cause suffering.
Many sages as well, devoted to auspicious deeds, took up residence there in the forest, accompanied by their disciples, wives, and sons.
They sowed grains for the purpose of sustaining life; indeed, there was joy in that forest due to the power of Gautama.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Gautama’s Power," in the *Tryambakeśvara-māhātmya* of the fourth section, the *Koṭirudra-saṃhitā*, within the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: Once, Gautama sent his own disciples there for the sake of water; those twice-born ones went there with devotion, carrying water-pots in their hands.
Seeing the disciples who had gone near the water, they stopped them; likewise, many wives of the sages who had not gone there for water also turned them back.
"We are the wives of sages; we shall take [the water] first from afar, and only afterwards may you take the water," they thus threatened him.
Then, having returned, they informed the wife of the sage; she too, taking them with her and consoling them herself, [proceeded].
The ascetic woman brought water and gave it to that Gautama; with that water, the best of sages performed his daily ablutions.
And those wives of the sages, thus enraged, reviled her; turning back, they all departed for their huts with crooked intentions.
Then, all that conduct was reported in its entirety—and in a distorted manner—by those women of wicked intent before their master.
Then, having heard their words, those supreme ṛṣis became enraged with Gautama at that time due to the power of their future karma.
In order to obstruct Gautama himself, those wicked-minded ones, filled with rage, worshipped Gaṇeśa with various offerings and oblations.
Then Gaṇeśvara, being pleased, manifested himself; devoted to his devotees and the bestower of fruits, he spoke these words there.
Gaṇeśa said: "I am pleased; choose a boon—what may I do for you? Having heard those words of his, the sages then spoke.
The sages said: "If a boon is to be granted by you, then act in such a way that Gautama is expelled from his hermitage by us sages after having been severely rebuked."
Sūta said: Having been thus entreated by them, the elephant-faced one, the refuge of the virtuous, laughed and spoke these words again with affection, enlightening them.
Gaṇeśa said: "Listen, all you sages; what has been done now is not proper. To be angry with him without any offense results only in loss."
Suffering is certainly not beneficial for those by whom [suffering] was previously prepared; and when suffering is inflicted, then destruction occurs here in this world.
Having performed such austerity, the supreme fruit is accomplished; having personally abandoned the auspicious fruit, one does not accomplish that which is harmful.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, those best of sages then fell into a state of mental confusion and spoke these very words.
The sages said: "O Lord, this indeed must be done by you and not otherwise. Thus addressed, the god Gaṇeśa then spoke these words.
Gaṇeśa said: "The wicked never attain goodness, nor does the good ever attain wickedness; this is the certain teaching of Brahmā."
And when suffering had arisen for you all previously due to fasting, then indeed happiness was bestowed by the great seer Gautama.
Now you are indeed inflicting suffering upon him; this is not at all appropriate in this world, so let it be thoroughly reconsidered in every respect.
"Deluded by the power of a woman, you will not act upon my words; yet this will undoubtedly be for his greatest benefit."
Furthermore, this best of sages will surely grant you happiness; it would not be right for you to cross over [the ocean], so choose another boon instead.
Sūta said: Although these words were thus spoken by that high-souled Gaṇeśa to the sages, they did not believe them.
Then, being dependent upon his devotees, that son of Śiva spoke with an indifferent mind to those sages of wicked intellect.
Gaṇeśa said: "Whatever is requested by you, I shall certainly do so; let that which is destined to happen in the future come to pass. Having spoken thus, he vanished once again.
Gautama did not know the wicked intent of the sages; with a joyful mind, he constantly performed that service for his wife.
O lords of sages, listen now to that account which occurred in the interval through the power of an excellent yoga, brought about by the influence of a wicked ṛṣi.
In Gautama’s field, there were rice and barley; it is said that Gaṇeśa went there in the form of a weak cow.
O best of sages, trembling as she went there, she consumed rice and barley by virtue of that boon.
In the meantime, by chance, Gautama arrived there; out of compassion, he then warded her off with bundles of grass.
Touched by the clump of grass, she fell upon the surface of the earth and died at that very moment, even as the sage was looking on.
Then all those sages in disguised forms, as well as the beautiful wives of the sages, said there: "What has been done by Gautama?"
Gautama also, having thus summoned Ahalyā, was greatly astonished; O Brahmins, he spoke with a heart tormented by grief.
Gautama said: "O Goddess, what has happened and how has the Supreme Lord become angry? What ought to be done, and where should we go? For the sin of killing has arrived."
Sūta said: In the meantime, the brahmins reviled Gautama, and the wives of the brahmins likewise caused Ahalyā pain with harsh words.
And their disciples of evil intellect, as well as their sons, having reviled Gautama, repeatedly uttered words of "Fie! in response.
The sages said: "Your face is not to be looked upon; go away, go away! Upon seeing the face of a cow-slayer, one should immediately perform a bath with one's clothes on."
"As long as you remain in the midst of the hermitage, the fire-eating gods and the ancestors do not accept anything whatsoever offered by us."
Therefore, go elsewhere, you and your retinue; do not delay at all, O cow-killer, O evildoer!
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, they all struck him with stones; they caused him extreme pain and reviled Ahalyā with harsh words.
Struck and reviled by the wicked ones, Gautama spoke these words: "I am departing from here; O sages, I shall dwell elsewhere."
Having spoken thus, Gautama then departed from that place; having gone a *krośa*, he established a hermitage there with his permission.
As long as there is indeed a curse, so long there is no action whatsoever to be performed; one has no authority over rites for the gods, the ancestors, or those pertaining to the Vedas.
Then, having spent half a month there, Gautama, that best of sages, distressed by that sorrow, made a fervent supplication to the munis.
Gautama said: "You should show me compassion; let it be told what must be done by me so that my sin may depart—please inform me."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, those brahmins did not speak to one another; though questioned with great persistence, they remained gathered together in one place.
Gautama, standing at a distance and bowing to those best of sages, asked with humility, "What indeed should be done by me now?"
When this had been said by that great-souled sage Gautama, all those sages assembled together and spoke these words.
The sages said: "Indeed, purification never occurs without expiation; therefore, for the sake of purifying your body, perform a penance."
Traverse the entire earth three times, proclaiming your sin; then, returning once more to this very place, observe the month-long vow in that manner.
By performing one hundred and one circumambulations of this mountain of Brahmā in this manner, you shall attain purification.
Alternatively, having brought them together, perform the ritual bath in the Gaṅgā; likewise, having assembled ten million kings, serve the Lord.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, it shall happen once again; O Mountain, perform eleven circumambulations as you did before.
"By bathing with a hundred jars [of water], there shall be atonement for the offense against the king. Thus addressed by those sages, he accepted their words, saying, "So be it," and "Om."
O best of sages, by the command of these illustrious ones, I shall here perform the worship of the kings as well as the setting forth of the mountain.
Having spoken thus and having descended from the mountain, that best of sages, the most excellent of munis, fashioned earthen images and worshipped them.
Then the virtuous Ahalyā performed all of that; and her disciples and grand-disciples likewise performed service to the two of them at that time.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Gautama’s Settlement," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: When this had been performed by the sage together with his wife, O twice-born ones, Śiva then appeared, gracious and accompanied by his attendants.
Then Śiva, the ocean of compassion, said to the delighted great sage, "O great sage, choose a boon; I am pleased with your excellent devotion."
Then, beholding that beautiful form of the high-souled Śambhu, he bowed to Śaṅkara with devotion and, filled with joy, offered a hymn of praise.
Having praised and bowed many times to the Lord, Gautama stood with his palms joined in reverence and said, "O God, make me sinless."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the high-souled Gautama, Śiva became exceedingly pleased and spoke these words.
Śiva said: "O Sage, you are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are forever free from sin; indeed, you were deceived by these wicked ones who are hostile in soul."
Indeed, by the sight of you, people become free from sin; how much more so are you, who are always devoted to me, even though you are sinful?
O Sage, those evil-minded ones who have caused affliction to you are indeed sinful, of wicked conduct, and guilty of murder.
From the sight of these, others may become even more wicked and ungrateful; for those so born, there is no atonement anywhere.
Sūta said: O brahmins, having spoken thus to him, the Lord Śaṅkara—who bestows rewards upon the virtuous and inflicts punishment upon the wicked—then related their many misdeeds.
Having heard that it was spoken by Śarva, the sage, his mind filled with great wonder, bowed deeply to Śiva with devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again.
Gautama said: O Maheśāna, a great service was indeed rendered by those sages; for if it had not been done by them in this way, how could there have been a vision of you?
Blessed are those sages by whom a most auspicious deed was performed for me; through that very misdeed of theirs, my own great purpose has been accomplished.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, Maheśvara, being highly pleased, looked upon Gautama with a compassionate glance and replied immediately.
Śiva said: "O sage, you are blessed, O lord of brahmins; you are indeed most excellent among sages. Knowing that I am well-pleased, choose an excellent boon."
Sūta said: Gautama, too, having reflected that what is renowned in the world cannot possibly be otherwise, should therefore act according to what has been said.
Having thus resolved, Gautama, the best of sages and a devotee of Śiva, spoke these words to Śaṅkara with palms joined and head bowed.
Gautama said: "O Lord, you speak the truth; nevertheless, that which has been done by the five shall not be otherwise. Let that which has occurred simply occur."
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, let the Gaṅgā be granted to me; indeed, perform this benefit for the world! Salutations to you, salutations to you!
Sūta said: Having spoken these words and having grasped the lotus-feet of the Lord, Gautama offered salutations to the God of gods out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
Then the god Śaṅkara, having extracted the very essence of both the earth and the heavens—which had indeed been preserved from before—[created it].
Śambhu, who is affectionate toward his devotees, gave to that sage whatever had been given by Brahmā during the marriage ceremony and whatever else remained.
Then the water of the Gaṅgā there assumed a supreme female form; and the best of sages, having offered praise to her, performed a prostration.
Gautama said: "Blessed are you; you have fulfilled your purpose, and the world has been purified by you. O Gaṅgā, purify me as well, for I am certain to fall into hell."
Sūta said: Then Śambhu, the benefactor of all, spoke: "O Gaṅgā, by my command, purify this Gautama."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of both Śambhu and Gautama, Gaṅgā spoke to Śiva; for devotion to Śiva is indeed purifying.
Ganga said: "O Lord, having purified the sage along with his retinue, I shall go to my own abode; I speak the truth."
Sūta said: Thus addressed there by Gaṅgā, Maheśa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke these words again to Gaṅgā for the sake of benefiting the world.
Śiva said: "O Goddess, you must remain right here until the Kali Yuga arrives, when Vaivasvata Manu shall become the twenty-eighth."
Sūta said: Having heard those words of her lord Śaṅkara, Gaṅgā, that purifying and most excellent of rivers, replied once again.
Gaṅgā said: "O Maheśvara, my lord, if my greatness should be superior to that of all others, then, O Destroyer of Tripura, I shall remain upon the earth."
Moreover, listen to this further, O Lord: remain indeed near me with your beautiful body, together with your attendants and Ambikā, O Master.
Sūta said: Having thus heard her words, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, spoke again to Gaṅgā for the sake of benefiting the world.
Śiva said: "O Gaṅgā, you are blessed; listen, for I have indeed not been pierced by you. Nevertheless, I shall remain here, and you too must remain."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of her lord, the Supreme Ruler, Gaṅgā became delighted in heart and offered him worship in return.
In the meantime, the gods and the ancient sages [visited] many various sacred sites as well as numerous places for the sake of their sons.
Having arrived, they all approached Gautama, Gaṅgā, and Giriśa, and while crying out "Victory! Victory!", they honored them with great reverence.
Then all those gods, including Hari, Brahmā, and the others, with joined palms and bowed shoulders, joyfully offered praise to them.
Then the Gaṅgā became gracious, and Giriśa spoke to them: "Choose a boon, O best of gods; out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you, I shall grant it to you."
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if you, O best of rivers, are pleased, then by your grace you must remain here for our sake and likewise for the sake of human beings."
Gangā said: "Why do you all remain here for the sake of pleasing everyone? Having purified Gautama, I shall depart just as I came."
"O gods, how is my distinction among you to be known here? If that proof were established, then I would remain without a doubt."
They all said: "When Jupiter, the greatest friend of all, is indeed in the sign of Leo, then we shall all come to you; of this there is no doubt."
And for eleven years, the sin of the worlds has been washed away here; thus it is that we have become soiled, O best of rivers.
O beloved, O Great Goddess, we shall come to you by all means to wash away that very [sin]; this truth is spoken to you with great reverence.
For the sake of favoring the worlds and out of a desire to do what is pleasing to us, Śaṅkara himself and you as well, O best of rivers, must remain here.
"As long as the Guru remains in Siṃha, we shall indeed remain here; for you, there shall be bathing three times a day and the vision of Śaṅkara."
"Having committed all our sins, we shall be liberated without a doubt; by your command, we shall return to our own lands."
Sūta said: Thus entreated by those [gods] and by the great seer Gautama, Śaṅkara remained there with affection, and that best of rivers also remained.
That Gaṅgā, known by the name Gautamī, and the Liṅga called Tryambaka, became renowned as the destroyers of great sins.
For from that day onwards, while Jupiter is situated in Leo, all sacred fords, holy sites, and deities arrive.
Lakes such as Puṣkara, rivers such as the Gaṅgā, and deities such as Vāsudeva truly reside upon the banks of the Gautamī.
As long as they remain there, so long indeed there is no fruit for them here; only when they have arrived in their own region will there be fruit for them.
This is declared to be the Jyotirliṅga known by the famous name Tryambaka; situated on the bank of the Gautamī, it is the destroyer of great sins.
Whoever beholds with devotion the Jyotirliṅga named Tryambaka, worships it, and bows down after offering praise, is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, the Tryambaka Jyotirlinga was worshipped by Gautama; it bestows all desires in this world and grants supreme liberation in the hereafter.
Thus has that which I was asked been fully declared by me, O lords of sages; what else do you wish to hear? I shall tell it to you without a doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Tryambakeśvara," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Lord, tell us from where Gaṅgā was born in the form of water; O Lord, tell us specifically from where her greatness arose.
O Vyāsa, true preceptor, tell me what befell those evil-minded brahmins who inflicted such suffering upon Gautama, just as [the gods did] unto him?
Sūta said: O Brahmins, having been thus entreated by Gautama himself, as well as by Brahmā and the Mountain, Gaṅgā then descended swiftly from there.
From that branch of the udumbara tree, a stream of water issued forth; there the renowned sage Gautama joyfully performed his ablutions.
The disciples of Gautama and other great sages who had assembled there also performed their ablutions with joyful hearts.
O best of sages, that place then became famous by the name Gaṅgādvāra; it was beautiful and removed all sins merely by being seen.
Those sages, who were rivals of Gautama, also arrived there; seeing them for the purpose of bathing, she quickly vanished from sight.
"Save me! Gautama cried out there in rapid words, repeatedly praising the Gaṅgā with joined palms and his head bowed low.
Gautama said: "Whether these people are blinded by the intoxication of wealth, or whether they are virtuous or even wicked—by the power of this merit, may you grant them your vision."
Sūta said: Then a voice arose from Gaṅgā from the expanse of the sky; listen to that, O best of sages, the excellent speech of Gaṅgā.
These most wicked ones—ungrateful, treacherous toward their masters, cruel, and heretics—should always be avoided even from sight.
Gautama said: O Mother, listen to this and also to the words of the Great One; therefore, you must carry out the truth of the Blessed One’s word.
In this world, whoever indeed renders assistance to those who have done them harm—by that act I am purified here; such is the word of the Blessed One.
Sūta said: Having thus heard the words of the high-souled sage Gautama, a voice again arose from Gaṅgā from the expanse of the sky.
"O Sage Gautama, you have indeed spoken auspicious and truthful words; nevertheless, for the sake of reconciliation, let them perform an act of atonement."
Furthermore, one hundred and one strides of the mountain must be performed here; especially so by these [beings] who are under your authority and specifically subject to your command.
And from that very act, the qualification for those who perform evil deeds arises; this is especially true regarding my vision, O Sage—this is the truth spoken by me.
Sūta said: Having heard her words, all of them did exactly so; being distressed, they entreated Gautama, saying, "Our offense must be forgiven."
When this had been done by Gautama at that time according to his command, he established a place named Kuśāvarta, situated below Gaṅgādvāra.
Then, for his pleasure, she appeared there once again; and that most excellent sacred site (tīrtha), renowned as Kuśāvarta, came into being.
The man who bathes there is destined for liberation; having immediately abandoned all sins and attained rare wisdom, he is prepared for release.
Gautama and the other sages gathered together and conversed with one another; those who had previously been ungrateful were then filled with shame.
The sages said: "O Sūta, we have heard this differently; let it be understood that the enraged Gautama cursed those twice-born ones."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, that is indeed true; however, due to the differences between the various kalpas, I shall describe that story in detail, O you of excellent vows.
Gautama also, seeing the sages then afflicted by famine, performed very great penance for the sake of the high-souled Varuṇa.
He prepared an inexhaustible supply of water by means of that *varuṇadā* [mantra], and then he sowed rice and barley in great abundance.
Thus, that Gautama, the best of sages, being a benefactor to others, prepared food for them by the power of his own asceticism.
Once, those wicked women, having been slighted while seeking water, spoke in anger to their husbands words born of envy toward Gautama.
Then those twice-born ones, their minds divided and their intentions crooked, fashioned a wooden cow and made it appear intent on devouring that grain.
Seeing the cow intent on eating his own grain, Gautama then gently struck her with a blade of grass to restrain her.
O Brahmins, at the mere touch of grass, that cow fell to the ground and died instantly due to the power of her past karma.
Then those sages of crooked intent, having gathered together with the local people, all said: "Gauḥ has been killed by Gautama."
Then Gautama became afraid, thinking "I am being seized by a cow," while Śiva’s follower, the noble Āhalyā, was filled with wonder at her disciples.
Then Gautama, the best of sages, having recognized that cow and being overwhelmed with anger, cursed all those ṛṣis.
Gautama said: "All of you are evil-minded and especially cause me distress; as a constant devotee of Śiva, you are forever averse to the Vedas."
From this day forward, may you no longer have faith in virtuous acts prescribed by the Vedas, especially in the path of Śiva which grants liberation.
From this day forward, may you have faith in that evil path, which is indeed devoid of the path to liberation and always turns its back on the Vedas.
"From this day forward, let your foreheads be smeared with clay; by smearing clay on your foreheads, O twice-born ones, you shall fall into hell!"
Sirs, may you never become those for whom Śiva alone is the supreme deity; rather, may you recognize the non-dual Śiva as being equal to all other deities.
May you never again find delight in rites such as the worship of Śiva, nor ever in devotees devoted to Śiva, nor on the festivals of Śiva.
As many curses as have been uttered by me today that cause suffering, let all of them likewise fall upon your progeny forever.
O twice-born ones, may your sons, grandsons, and descendants never be devotees of Śiva; may you certainly remain in hell together with your sons.
Therefore, let them all become outcasts (caṇḍālas), afflicted by suffering and poverty; let them be deceitful, slanders, and forever marked with heated seals.
Sūta said: Having thus cursed all the sages, Gautama went to his own hermitage; he practiced intense devotion to Śiva and became exceedingly pure.
Then all those sages and twice-born ones, their hearts distressed and excluded from the Śaiva dharma, took up residence in Kāñcī.
All his sons became excluded from the Śaiva dharma; likewise, in the future, many wicked people will come to be so in the Kali age.
Thus, O best of sages, that entire account has been told in its entirety; and the wise have all listened with reverence to this ancient history as well.
Thus has the account of Vaśca and the origin of Gautamī been told, along with its supreme majesty, which is the highest remover of all sins.
The majesty of the three-eyed Jyotirliṅga has been proclaimed; having heard it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the majesty of the Jyotirlinga Vaidyanātheśvara; let it be heard, for it removes all sins.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Tryambakeśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Rāvaṇa, the best of the Rākṣasas, proud and devoted to honor, propitiated Hara with devotion on Kailāsa, the most excellent of mountains.
When Hara was not pleased despite being propitiated for some time, he then performed another austerity for the sake of winning Śiva’s favor.
And this illustrious Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, has descended from the Himavat mountain, that abode of siddhis, and now resides in a grove of trees to the south.
O twice-born ones, having dug a pit in the ground and placed a fire therein, he installed Śiva in its proximity and performed the oblation.
In the summer he stood amidst five fires, during the rains he slept upon the bare ground, and in the cold season he remained within water; thus he performed his penance in three ways.
Thus he performed many austerities, yet even then the Supreme Self, Maheśāna, was not pleased; for He is difficult to propitiate by those of wicked soul.
Then, having cut off his own heads, the high-souled Rāvaṇa, lord of the Daityas, began the worship of Śaṅkara.
And each head was severed according to the ritual for the worship of Śiva; thus, when nine had indeed been severed by him in that proper sequence,
When only one remained, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased and satisfied, then manifested himself right there.
Having rendered his heads free from pain as before, the Lord granted him an incomparable and supreme boon according to his heart's desire.
Having obtained his favor, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, with shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, replied auspiciously to Śambhu.
Rāvaṇa said: "Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; I shall carry you to Laṅkā. Grant my desire its fulfillment, for I have come to you for refuge."
Sūta said: Thus addressed then by Rāvaṇa, Śambhu, having fallen into a supreme dilemma, replied with a troubled mind.
Śiva said: Listen, O best of Rākṣasas, to my words which are full of essence. Indeed, let this most excellent Liṅga of mine be taken to your own home with true devotion.
When you establish a linga there upon the ground, it will certainly remain here; of this there is no doubt. Do as you wish.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by that Śambhu, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, saying "So be it," accepted his words and went to his own abode.
For on the road, by the power of Śiva’s illusion, there was one who desired to void urine; the lord Rāvaṇa, son of Pulastya, was unable to restrain him.
Having seen a certain cowherd there, he requested him and gave him that linga; when a mere moment had passed, the cowherd then became distressed.
Oppressed by its weight, he caused it to rest upon the ground; there that Liṅga remained, produced from the essence of diamond, granting all desires and removing sins through its mere sight.
O Sage, that Linga became known by the name Vaidyanātheśvara; it is famous throughout the three worlds as the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the virtuous.
This supreme Jyotirlinga is divine, removing all sins through mere sight or worship; it is the most excellent means for increasing worldly enjoyment.

While that liṅga remained there for the welfare of all the worlds, the great asura Rāvaṇa, having returned to his own home after obtaining that most excellent boon, related everything happily to his beloved wife.
Having heard that, all the gods led by Śakra, as well as the sages—pure-souled ones whose minds were devoted to Śivā—consulted with one another.
At that time, O Sage, all the gods, including Hari and Brahmā, arrived there with great joy and performed worship in an especially distinguished manner.
Then, having beheld him directly and having installed him, those gods addressed him as "Vaidyanātha," and after bowing and offering praise, they departed for heaven.
The sages said: "O dear one, when that liṅga was established there and Rāvaṇa had gone home, what events took place? Tell us that in detail."
Sūta said: Rāvaṇa, too, having returned home and obtained that most excellent boon, related everything to his beloved; that great asura rejoiced exceedingly.
Having heard all that, Indra and the other gods, as well as the sages—those lords of munis—were greatly distressed and spoke thus to one another.
The gods and others said: "This Rāvaṇa is indeed a wicked-souled, evil-minded villain who offends the gods; having obtained a boon from Śiva, he will cause us suffering as well."
What shall we do, and where shall we go? Or what will happen next? Once the wicked one has attained proficiency, what will he not accomplish against us?
Thus, having fallen into distress, Śakra and the other sages and gods, being distraught, then summoned Nārada and questioned him.
The gods said: "O best of sages, you are capable of accomplishing every task; O celestial rishi, devise a means for the destruction of the gods' suffering."
This Rāvaṇa is a great evildoer; what indeed will he not do? Where shall we go, for we are being tormented here by this wicked one?
Nārada said: "O gods, abandon your grief; having devised a plan, I shall go. By the grace of Śaṅkara, I will indeed accomplish the work of the gods."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that divine sage went to the abode of Rāvaṇa; having received due hospitality, he joyfully related all of that to him.
Nārada said: "O best of Rākṣasas, you are blessed, O foremost of Śiva’s devotees, whose mind is fixed on austerity; O Rāvaṇa, having seen you today, my mind has become serene."
"Tell me your own life-story in its entirety, beginning with your propitiation of Śiva. Thus questioned by him at that time, Rāvaṇa spoke these words.
Rāvaṇa said: "O great sage, having gone to Kailāsa for the sake of penance, I indeed performed most severe austerities there for a very long time."
O Sage, when Śaṅkara was not pleased, I turned away; having returned to that grove of trees, I performed penance once again.
In the summer, he stood amidst five fires; during the rains, he slept on the bare ground; and in the cold season, he remained within water—thus he performed his threefold austerity.
O Lord of Sages, I performed such fierce austerities there; nevertheless, Śaṅkara was not pleased with me in the slightest.
Then, filled with rage, I dug a pit in the ground, kindled a fire therein, and prepared an earthen image.
Then Śambhu was worshipped with perfumes, sandalwood paste, various types of incense, and food offerings, according to the ritual procedure for the waving of lights (ārārtika).
Śaṅkara was propitiated by me with prostrations, meritorious hymns of praise, songs, dances, instrumental music, and the offering of my face and fingers.
O Sage, by these and many other diverse means, the Blessed Lord Hara was worshipped according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
When the Blessed Lord Hara did not appear before me with a pleased countenance, I became sorrowful, having failed to obtain the true fruit of my ascetic penance.
"Fie on this body and its strength! Fie on my performance of asceticism! Having said this, I offered much oblation into the fire established there by me.
Reflecting thus once more, I shall cast my own body into the fire, just as severed heads [were offered] into that blazing, pure flame.
Having thoroughly cleansed each one individually and made them pure in every respect, these nine indeed were offered by me to Śaṅkara.
O best of sages, just as he began to cut off the tenth head, Hara himself appeared there in the form of light.
"Come to me," he said with affection; indeed, he who is kind to his devotees was pleased and said, "Choose a boon, and I shall grant whatever is desired by your heart."
When he had spoken thus, I then beheld Maheśvara; with palms joined in deep devotion, I offered praise to him as he approached.
Then I chose this: "Grant me indeed incomparable strength; O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, what could be difficult for me to obtain?"
By the compassionate Śiva, being fully satisfied, everything desired by my mind was granted; having spoken with his voice, "So be it," he bestowed it upon me.
Indeed, with my unfailing and clear vision, like a physician, I have joined together my heads; having thus restored them, they were beheld by the Supreme Self.
When this was done, my body there then became as it was before by his grace, and I obtained the entire fruit [of my merit].
And at that time, having been entreated by me, that Lord whose banner is the bull remained there; he became renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Vaidyanātheśvara.
Through sight and worship, Maheśvara in the form of the Jyotirliṅga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the world, acting for the welfare of all.
Having specially worshipped that very Jyotirliṅga and prostrated before it, I have come here to conquer the three worlds.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the celestial sage Nārada was filled with agitation; smiling within his mind, he spoke to Rāvaṇa.
Nārada said: Listen, O best of Rākṣasas, for I shall tell you what is for your benefit; you must do exactly as I have spoken, and never otherwise.
"That which was spoken by you—that everything beneficial has now been granted to me by Śiva himself—all that must never be considered true by you."
"Having fallen into such a state of transformation, what indeed will he not say? That cannot possibly be true; how can it be known, for he is dear to me?"
Having gone there, you must indeed act again for his detriment; furthermore, you must make an effort to uproot Kailāsa.
And if indeed this Kailāsa is uplifted, then everything will undoubtedly become fruitful at that very moment.
Having established yourself as before, return indeed in comfort; having reached a firm conclusion, do as you wish.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, Rāvaṇa, deluded by fate, considered that advice beneficial; taking the sage’s words to be true, he then departed for Kailāsa.
Having gone there, he performed the extraction of that mountain; and everything situated there was overturned from its original position.
Then Girīśa, having seen that, said, "What has happened? And Girijā then replied to Śambhu with a smile.
Girijā said: "The fruit of a true disciple has arisen; it has indeed been perfectly realized by the disciple, for incomparable strength was bestowed upon this peaceful-souled and heroic one."
Sūta said: Having heard the meaningful words of Girijā, Maheśvara, considering Rāvaṇa—who was arrogant in his strength—to be ungrateful, cursed him.
Mahādeva said: "O Rāvaṇa, you wicked devotee! O evil-minded one, do not harbor pride; very soon, the destroyer of your arrogance shall manifest here before your very hands."
Sūta said: Nārada then heard all that had occurred there; and Rāvaṇa, his soul serene, departed for his own abode just as he had come.
Having formed a supreme resolve, the powerful Rāvaṇa, who humbled the pride of others, brought the world under his control while himself remaining deluded by his own strength.
And by means of that highly powerful divine weapon obtained through the command of Śiva, no opponent whatsoever was then capable of facing Rāvaṇa.
Thus has been fully described the majesty of Vaidyanātheśvara; for those men who hear it, their sin is reduced to ashes.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Vaidyanātheśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe how the supreme and most excellent Liṅga, known as Nāgeśa, which is the light-form of the Supreme Self, came into being.
A certain Rākṣasī named Dārukā, a daughter of the mountain, was arrogant due to a boon; her husband was Dāruka, who was exceedingly powerful.
There, with many rākṣasas, he wrought havoc among the virtuous; he brought about the destruction of the sacrifices of the worlds and the destruction of dharma.
To the west of that ocean is his forest, endowed with every prosperity, extending sixteen yojanas in width in every direction.
That forest where Dārukā goes for her own pleasure is endowed with the earth, trees, and all necessary provisions.
The queen entrusted the protection of that forest to Dāruka; for she herself was about to go to that forest with her husband according to her own will.
Staying there, that Rākṣasa Dāruka, together with his wife Dārukā, then struck fear into everyone.
All those oppressed worlds went for refuge to Aurva; bowing with great affection and with heads bowed low, they spoke to him.
The people said: "O Great Sage, grant us protection; otherwise, we shall be killed by the wicked. You are capable of doing everything, for you are radiant with splendor."
There is no one else on earth besides you who can be our refuge; let us go into his presence and, remaining there, obtain happiness.
Upon seeing you, all the demons flee to a great distance; in you, the splendor of Śiva always shines forth like a blazing fire.
Sūta said: Thus entreated by the people, the excellent sage Aurva, feeling compassion and being a worthy refuge, spoke these words for their protection.
Aurva said: "If the Rākṣasas were to harm living beings on earth, then those exceedingly powerful Rākṣasas would themselves be deprived of their lives."
When sacrifices are no longer destroyed, then let all the Rākṣasas be deprived of their lives; this which I speak is the truth.
Sūta said: Having spoken these words to them and having comforted the subjects once more, Aurva, who brings happiness to the world, performed various kinds of penance.
Then those gods, having understood that very cause of the curse, made preparations for battle with the enemies of the gods.
With every effort and bearing various weapons, all the gods, headed by Śakra, arrived there for the sake of battle.
Seeing them there, all those wicked Rākṣasas who were stationed together became once again intent on deliberation among themselves.
The Rākṣasas said: "What should be done? Where should we go? We have fallen into great peril. He fights and even dies; he fights and is never struck down."
If one remains exactly as one is, why indeed would they devour one another? Suffering has arisen in every way; who could possibly ward it off?
Sūta said: Having reflected thus, Dāruka and the other Rākṣasas there, not knowing any means [to escape], were indeed constantly overcome by sorrow.
And the Rākṣasī Dārukā, perceiving that suffering had arrived, then related that boon of Bhavānī.
Dārukā said: "In the past, I propitiated the consort of Bhava, and she granted me a boon: 'Go to the forest along with your own people, wherever you desire to go.'"
Since that boon has been obtained by me, how can suffering be endured? Indeed, having taken both water and forest, the rākṣasas should dwell in happiness.
The Bhūta said: Having heard those words of the Rākṣasī, all those Rākṣasas then became filled with joy and spoke among themselves without fear.
"Blessed is she, and fulfilled is her purpose; the Queen herself has indeed been restored to life. Having bowed to her, they related everything to her with great reverence.
If you have the power to go, then let us go; why deliberate further? Having gone there to the water, O Goddess, we shall dwell in happiness forever.
In the meantime, the worlds, having been previously afflicted by various sufferings at the hands of the Rākṣasas, assembled together with the gods for the sake of battle.
Then, oppressed by her, they took recourse in the power of Bhavānī and led the entire city, including its waters and lands, away.
Having uttered the praise of the Goddess, "Victory! Victory!", the Rākṣasī then took flight like the king of mountains with its wings.
Then she stood fearlessly in the midst of the ocean, and Śivā’s follower rejoiced along with all her attendants.
Staying there at the Sindhu and in the city, those playful Rākṣasas attained happiness and sported about free from fear.
And the Rākṣasas on earth never came at any time; indeed, out of fear of the sage’s curse, they wandered restlessly then.
Having then brought those people who were situated on the ships to that city, they threw some into the prison and indeed killed others at that time.
Furthermore, however much those Rākṣasas then inflicted suffering there, the inhabitants remained fearless due to the granting of boons by Bhavānī.
O lords of sages, just as there was constant fear on land in the world as before, so too was there perpetual fear for them in the water.
Once that rākṣasī emerged from the city into the water and stood blocking the path upon the earth for the purpose of afflicting the world.
In the meantime, many more beautiful boats arrived there from all directions, crowded with people from every part of the world.
Then, seeing those ships and attaining great joy, the wicked Rākṣasas went quickly to where they were stationed and, with impetuosity, boarded them.
Those mighty ones returned to the city, and having seized them, they bound them with firm shackles and cast them into the prison.
Bound with fetters, those worlds remained in a prison-house; they experienced extreme suffering, being rebuked again and again.
And among them, the one who was the leader was a Vaiśya named Supriya; he was dear to Śiva, of auspicious conduct, and a perpetual devotee of Śiva.
Indeed, he never remains without the worship of Śiva; for one who is adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads is in every way a follower of the Śiva-dharma.
If the worship was not performed, he would not eat; therefore, even on that occasion, the Vaiśya performed the worship of Śiva.
O best of sages, even while he was in prison, he then taught many others the Śiva-mantra and the worship of the Earth-goddess.
And then all of them performed there the worship of Śiva, which grants one's desires, according to the prescribed rites, exactly as it had been seen and heard.
Some remained there absorbed in meditation, having assumed the unsurpassed posture; others, filled with joy, performed mental worship of Śiva.
O lords of sages, the lord of that very place performed the worship of Śiva there in person, according to the ritual procedure for the earthen linga.
And others, who did not know the supreme rite of recollection, remained meditating upon Śaṅkara with the mantra "Namaḥ śivāya."
He who was the eminent Vaiśya named Supriya, a lover of Śiva, performed the worship of Śiva there while meditating upon him with his mind.
And Śambhu, possessing the form described above, perceives everything directly; yet he himself does not know it, for it is indeed not grasped by Śiva.
O lords of sages, while the Vaiśya was performing the worship of Śiva in this manner, six months passed there without any obstacles.
O best of sages, listen now with attentive minds to the deeds of the moon-crested Lord that occurred after this.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Harassment by the Rākṣasa in Dārukāvana," in the Nāgeśvara Jyotirliṅga Māhātmya of the fourth Koṭirudra Saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Once, the servant of that evil-minded Rākṣasa beheld before him the beautiful form of Śaṅkara.
The king was then informed of the entire conduct of the Rākṣasas exactly as it had occurred—both its curious and its marvelous aspects.
King Dāruka also arrived there, and along with his army, being greatly distressed, he quickly inquired after the welfare of Śiva.
Dāruka said: "O Vaiśya, what are you meditating upon? Speak the truth before me; if this is so, death shall not come to you, for my word cannot be otherwise."
Sūta said: He replied, "I do not know him. Hearing this, the enraged king indeed dispatched the Rākṣasas, saying, "O Rākṣasas, let this man be slain!"
Thus addressed, they then took up various weapons and went swiftly to slay that tiger among Vaiśyas, whose mind was entirely devoted to Śaṅkara.
Seeing them arrived at that time, his eyes trembling with fear, he remembered Śiva with great devotion and repeatedly recited His names.
The Lord of the Vaiśyas said: "Protect me, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods! Protect me, O Śambhu, O Śiva! O Lord of the Three Worlds, slayer of the wicked, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!"
O Lord, today you are indeed my everything; I am yours, dependent on you, and my very life always belongs to you, O Master.
Sūta said: Thus entreated, Śambhu then emerged from the opening, accompanied by an excellent mansion provided with four gates.
Having beheld that wonderful form of Śiva, which is the very nature of the light of the center and is accompanied by his retinue, he indeed worshipped it.
Then Śambhu, being thus honored, became personally pleased; having bestowed the weapon named Pāśupata upon him, he [subdued] the foremost of the Rākṣasas.
He swiftly struck down all of them along with their equipment and their hosts; for Śaṅkara, the slayer of the wicked, indeed protected his own devotee.
Having then slain them all, Śambhu—who assumes a beautiful form through his own divine play—bestowed a boon upon the forest, performing a most marvelous deed.
In this forest, let the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) always prevail—those of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise of the Śūdras.
O best of sages, let them never be of a tamasic nature here; rather, let them be proclaimers of the Śiva-dharma and promoters of the Śiva-dharma.
Sūta said: At that time, that Rākṣasī named Dārukā, with a distressed mind, offered praise to the goddess Pārvatī.
Then the goddess, being pleased, said, "What shall I do? She replied once more, "Let my lineage be protected by you."
"I shall protect your lineage; this is the truth spoken by me. Having said this, Śiva indeed assumed a physical form.
Even Śiva, the Lord who is subject to his boon, seeing the Goddess enraged, replied with great affection: "Do as you wish."
The Sūta said: Having heard these words of her husband Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, being well-pleased, smiled and immediately spoke these words.
Pārvatī said: "Your word shall come true at the end of the age; meanwhile, let there be a creation characterized by darkness—this is my resolve."
Otherwise, O Śiva, there would surely be universal dissolution; my word is true, I declare. Let it be accepted as authoritative, O Lord: I am yours, and you are my refuge.
And this Queen Dārukā, my powerful Rākṣasī Śaktikā, shall rule over the kingdom of the Rākṣasas among all the most mighty female demons.
These wives of the Rākṣasas shall give birth to sons; I consider that they all together shall dwell in the forest with me.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Pārvatī, his own wife, the Lord Śaṅkara became pleased in mind and spoke these words.
Śaṅkara said: "If you speak thus, O beloved, listen to my words: I shall dwell with affection in this forest for the sake of protecting my devotees."
In this matter, whoever shall grant me a vision accompanied by joy while abiding by the duties of his own caste, he indeed shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Otherwise, O Lord of Kings, at the beginning of the Kali age, there will be a son of Mahāsena who is renowned as Vīrasena.
Out of devotion, he will overcome all obstacles and grant me his vision; having obtained my vision, he shall indeed become a universal monarch.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having thus exchanged jests with one another, that couple remained there in person as the very causes of their own greatness.
Indeed, Śiva, in the form of a Jyotirliṅga, became known by the name Nāgeśvara, and the goddess Śivā became Nāgeśvarī; they were beloved by the virtuous.
The sages said: "O high-minded one, tell us how Vīrasena will go there to the Dāruka forest, and how he will worship Śiva."
Sūta said: In the beautiful land of Niṣadha, in a family of Kṣatriyas, was Vīrasena, the son of Mahāsena and a beloved of Śiva.
Having performed the worship of the Lord of the Earth, Vīrasena indeed practiced most difficult penance for a period of twelve years.
Then the Lord of Gods, Śaṅkara, being pleased, spoke directly: "Having fashioned a little fish out of wood and anointed it with tin and minerals..."
"O Vīrasena, having employed my yogamāyā, I shall give her to you; taking her, enter this city now along with men."
Then, having gone there and once the opening has been made by me, you should enter and perform worship to Nāgeśvara.
Then, having obtained the Pāśupata weapon and having slain those headed by the Rākṣasī, nothing will remain lacking for you once I have been seen.
The strength of Pārvatī shall indeed become complete; and others who are of Mleccha form shall also become auspicious in the forest.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to Vīrasena, who was indeed afflicted by grief, the Lord Śaṅkara, having shown great compassion, vanished on that very spot.
Thus, although he had been granted a boon by Śiva, the Supreme Soul, he was indeed unable at that time to carry it out; of this there is no doubt.
Thus was the god Nāgeśvara born, the lord of the luminaries; he exists in the form of a *liṅga*, eternally bestowing all desires upon the three worlds.
The wise person who constantly hears with reverence this account of the origin of Nāgeśa shall attain all desires and achieve the destruction of great sins.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin and Greatness of the Nāgeśvara Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the Liṅga named Rāmeśvara; listen with reverence, O sages, to how it was manifested in the past.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu, the beloved of the virtuous, descended upon the earth.
There, O brahmins, Sītā—the daughter of Janaka—was abducted by the highly deceitful Rāvaṇa and carried to his own home in Laṅkā.
Intent on searching for her, he went to the city named Kiṣkindhā; having become a benefactor to Sugrīva, he slew Vālin.
Having stayed there for some time, intent on searching for him, he indeed held a consultation with Sugrīva and others, as well as with Lakṣmaṇa.
The prince Rāma dispatched monkeys headed by Hanumān to the four quarters for the purpose of searching for her.
Then, having learned from the face of the foremost of monkeys that Sītā had gone to Laṅkā, and having obtained the crest-jewel of Sītā, that descendant of Raghu rejoiced exceedingly.
Then, O twice-born ones, Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and the most powerful, meritorious monkeys headed by Sugrīva, was covered in saffron-colored dust.
Accompanied by the eighteen named Padmas, he went to the shore of the ocean—that very salt-watery expanse which is seen in the southern sea.
Having arrived there, Rāma himself remained upon the shore; served by the monkeys and by Lakṣmaṇa, he was indeed beloved of Śiva.
Alas, Jānakī! Where have you gone? When will she be reunited with us? The ocean is bottomless, and this army of monkeys must be ferried across.
The Rākṣasa named Laṅka, the sustainer of the mountain, possessed great strength and prowess; he was difficult to overcome and difficult to assail, and Indrajit was indeed his son.
Having reflected thus, he stood upon the bank with Lakṣmaṇa, and was comforted by the forest-dwellers led by Aṅgada.
In the meantime, Rāghava, the best of Śiva’s devotees, desiring water, spoke with affection to his brother named Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma said: "O brother Lakṣmaṇa, lord of heroes, I am thirsty and seek water; therefore, bring some water quickly by means of a few monkeys."
Sūta said: Having heard that, the monkeys there ran in the ten directions; and having brought water, they stood before him, prostrated themselves, and spoke.
The monkeys said: "O Master, please accept this water brought here at your command; it is most excellent, delicious, cool, and life-sustaining."
Sūta said: Having become exceedingly gracious and looking upon them with a compassionate gaze, Rāmacandra himself, having heard that, took up the water.
When that devotee of Śiva took that water and began to drink it, then, by the will of Śiva, this recollection arose within him:
How can the sight of Śambhu not be attained, and how can his water not be received—from one's own master, the Supreme Lord, who indeed bestows all bliss?
Having spoken thus, the best of the Raghus then drank the water; thereafter, the joy of the Raghus performed worship to the earthly image.
Having indeed arranged the ritual services beginning with the invocation, he worshipped the god Śaṅkara with devotion according to the prescribed sixteen-fold rite.
Having diligently propitiated Śiva with prostrations and divine hymns, Rāma joyfully entreated Śaṅkara with true devotion.
