Rāma said: O Lord Śambhu, Mahādeva, who are always affectionate toward your devotees, protect me, your devotee who has sought refuge in you with a distressed mind.
This water of the ocean is unfathomable, yet it provides a means of crossing; however, there is a most powerful Rākṣasa hero named Rāvaṇa.
For this army of monkeys is fickle, though it is a means for battle; how then will my task be accomplished for the sake of regaining my beloved?
O Lord of noble vows, you must provide me with assistance in this matter; for without your help, O Protector, my task will indeed be difficult to accomplish.
Even your Rāvaṇa here is invincible in every way by all beings; he is a great hero who has conquered the three worlds and is arrogant due to the boons granted by you.
"I am indeed your servant and entirely dependent upon you; having reflected thus, O Sadāśiva, you should always show me favor."
Sūta said: Having thus made his petition and having bowed down again and again, he then raised loud shouts of "Victory! Victory! and "O Śaṅkara!"
Having thus praised Śiva there, being devoted to mantra and meditation, he performed worship once more and danced before the Lord.
When the lover, his heart melting with emotion, let out a sound from his cheeks, Lord Śaṅkara became truly well-pleased.
Maheśvara, whose form is light, together with his limbs and his retinue, having assumed the stainless form as described, quickly manifested himself.
Then, his heart filled with contentment through devotion to Rāma, Maheśvara said, "May there be auspiciousness; tell me your boon, O Rāma."
Having seen that form at that time, all were themselves purified; then Rāghava, who is devoted to the dharma of Śiva, performed worship.
Having offered various hymns of praise and joyfully prostrated before Śiva, he prayed for his own victory over Rāvaṇa in battle.
Then Maheśvara, his heart gladdened by devotion to Rāma, spoke again out of affection: "Victory be unto you, O great king!"
Having obtained victory granted by Śiva and having received his permission, he again made a request with palms joined in reverence and head bowed low.
Rāma said: "O Lord Śaṅkara, if you are pleased, you must remain here for the purification of the worlds and for the benefit of others."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, Śiva then assumed the form of a Liṅga there, becoming renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Rāmeśvara.
By the power of that [bow], Rāma indeed crossed the ocean with ease; having swiftly slain Rāvaṇa and the other rākṣasas, he recovered his beloved.
The majesty of Rāmeśvara has been wondrous and incomparable upon the earth; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and always grants the desires of his devotees.
He who bathes Śiva and Rāmeśvara with the water of the divine Gaṅgā with true devotion is indeed liberated while living.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, even those difficult for the gods to attain, one shall finally obtain supreme knowledge and certainly reach absolute liberation.
Thus has been fully described the divine Jyotirliṅga of Śiva known as Rāmeśvara, which removes the sins of those who hear of it.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Rāmeśvara," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Beyond this, Ghuśmeśa is proclaimed as a Jyotirliṅga; O best of sages, listen now to its great majesty.
In the southern direction, there is a preeminent mountain known as Devagiri; endowed with great splendor, it shines eternally with a wondrous appearance.
In his very vicinity lived a certain Brahmin named Sudharma, born of the lineage of Bharadvāja and the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman.
His beloved wife was Sudehā, who was devoted to the dharma of Śiva, constantly intent on serving her husband, and skilled in domestic duties.
And Sudharmā, the best of the twice-born, was a worshiper of the gods and guests; he was constantly devoted to the path of the Vedas and dedicated to the service of the sacred fires.
Engaged in the three twilight rituals, possessing a splendor equal to the form of the sun, he was a teacher of his disciples and an expert in the Vedas and Shastras.
He was wealthy, a supreme donor, and a vessel for the quality of benevolence; he was constantly devoted to auspicious deeds, a follower of Śiva, and dear to the devotees of Śiva.
As he practiced righteousness, much of his life passed away; yet no son was born to him, and the fertile season of his wife remained fruitless.
Indeed, suffering is not caused by one who is intent on the knowledge of reality; for the self alone is the savior of the self, and the self alone is its purifier.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he did not then experience sorrow; but Sudehā then felt the grief arising from her son.
She constantly entreated her husband with great effort to procreate a son, for he was an expert in all branches of knowledge.
He too, having then rebuked his wife, said: "What will a son do? Who is a mother? Who is a father? Who is a son? And who is a kinsman or a beloved?"
"O Goddess, everyone in the three worlds is devoted to their own self-interest; there is no doubt about this. Understand this specifically with your intellect, and do not grieve at all."
Therefore, O Goddess, you must certainly abandon your sorrow; you must never speak of it to me, O lady of auspicious vows.
Having thus restrained her, he, devoted to the dharma of the Blessed One, remained supremely contented and completely abandoned the suffering of dualities.
Once, while Sudehā was living with her family in their home, she went for the sake of a pleasant social gathering; there, a dispute arose among those assembled.
Then her wife, out of her feminine nature, was rebuked by her; moreover, Sudehā, who desired a Brāhmaṇa, was addressed with harsh words.
The wife of the twice-born said: "O childless woman, why do you boast? For I am a mother of sons. My son will enjoy my wealth; who will enjoy your wealth?"
"Surely the king will seize your wealth; there is no doubt about this. Fie, fie upon you! Fie on your wealth, and fie indeed on your pride, O barren woman!"
Sūta said: Having been thus rebuked by them, she returned home distressed and related everything they had said to her husband with great care.
Even then, the highly intelligent Brāhmaṇa did not feel sorrow; he said, "Let what has been said simply be told: whatever is destined to happen, O beloved, shall come to pass."
And although she was thus repeatedly consoled by him at that time, she did not then abandon her grief; indeed, she maintained her persistent resolve.
Sudehā said: "In whatever way you must produce a son, for you are dear to me; otherwise, O best of embodied beings, I shall surely cast off my body."
Sūta said: Having heard what was thus spoken by her, Sudharmā, the best of brāhmaṇas, being oppressed by her persistence, then remembered Śiva in his mind.
The Brahmin, unwearied, cast two flowers before the fire; with his mind, he considered the flower on the right as the one that would grant him a son.
Having thus made this wager, he said to his wife and to the brahmin: "O son, one of these two flowers must be taken by you for the attainment of fruit."
And by holding [the flower] with my mind, may a son indeed be mine; and let that flower which was held by my lord come to me.
Having spoken thus, she then paid homage to Śiva there, bowed to the fire, and after praying once more, took up a single flower.
That which was intended by the Lord was indeed not accepted by her of beautiful form, due to her delusion arising from the will of Śiva.
Seeing that, the man let out a sigh; remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he spoke to his beloved wife.
Sudharma said: "Since it was created by the Lord himself, how could it be otherwise? Abandon this hope, my dear, and perform service to the Lord."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin himself abandoned all worldly hope and became devoted to the performance of dharma, intent upon the meditation of Śaṅkara.
Out of desire for her son, Sudehā did not release her grip at all; with palms joined and head bowed, she replied to her husband with affection.
Sudehā said: "Let there be no son for me; by my command, take another wife. Surely a son shall be born of her—of this there is no doubt."
Sūta said: At that very time, that most excellent devotee of Śiva, who was renowned as the son of Brahmā and devoted to righteousness, spoke to his beloved wife, Sudehā.
Sudharma said: "All suffering, both yours and mine, has certainly come to an end. Therefore, my dear one, do not now create an obstacle to dharma."
Sūta said: Having been thus restrained, she then brought her mother’s daughter to the house and spoke this to her husband: "Choose her as your wife."
Sudharmā said: "Now you say, 'I am dear to you,' and then again, 'When she becomes a mother of sons, then you shall compete with me.'"
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having been addressed thus by her husband, Sudehā, his beloved wife, again spoke to her husband Sudharmā with her hands joined in reverence.
"O best of the twice-born, I shall certainly not engage in rivalry with my sister; marry her for the sake of a son, and I command you to do so."
Thus entreated by his beloved, that twice-born Sudharmā married Ghuśmā according to the rites of marriage.
Then, having married her, the twice-born man requested of her: "O sinless, dear one, this younger sister of yours must always be supported by you."
And that righteous-souled Sudharmā, the best among the devotees of Śiva, having been thus addressed, quickly performed the collection of his own religious duties as was appropriate.
And she, too, attended upon her mother’s daughter like a maidservant; for, having abandoned all hostility, she cherished her day and night as a beloved.
And his youngest wife, having obtained her sister's permission, quickly fashioned one hundred and one earthen images of Śrī.
Having performed the rites according to the prescribed rules and accompanied by all the ritual offerings, he cast them into a nearby pond.
In this manner, she constantly performed the worship of Śiva, which grants one's desires, according to the prescribed ritual of dismissal and re-invocation.
As she performed the worship of Śaṅkara in this manner constantly, the number reached one hundred thousand, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
By the grace of Śaṅkara himself, a son was born to her—one who was handsome, fortunate, and possessed of auspicious qualities.
Seeing him, that brahmin, the best among the knowers of Dharma, was supremely delighted; being unattached and devoted to the dharma of knowledge, he enjoyed happiness.
Her beautiful body indeed provoked a fierce rivalry with hers; first her heart was cool, but then it became like a sword.
O lords of sages, listen with an attentive mind to what followed thereafter—that despicable deed which brought suffering.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of Sudeha and Sudharma," in the Ghuśmeśvara-māhātmya of the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, the fourth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having seen the son of the younger wife, the elder wife was overcome with grief; unable to endure his happiness, she immediately created discord.
Everyone praised that birth of a son incessantly; yet she could not endure the child’s beauty and other such qualities.
Seeing her son Supriya, who was a vessel of excellent virtues for his parents, her heart then became inflamed like fire.
In the meantime, O Brahmins, those who had gathered to give their daughters performed his marriage right there according to the prescribed rites.
Sudharmā, together with Ghuśmayā, attained supreme joy; all her kinsmen bestowed honor upon that Ghuśmayā.
Upon seeing him, Sudehā was indeed inflamed in her mind; she fell into extreme distress, crying out, "Alas, I am ruined!"
Having returned home, Sudharmā displayed his enthusiasm to his daughter-in-law and his married son, as if gladdening his two beloveds.
Ghuṣmā, who had been joyful, became distressed; Sudehā, having encountered suffering, could not endure that happiness and, having turned it into pain, fell to the ground.
Ghuśmā said, "The bride and the son are yours, not mine"; yet the bride and the son affectionately regarded her as their mother-in-law and grandmother.
The husband regarded that elder beloved wife as his primary consort and never as the younger one; nevertheless, at that time, the elder wife became indeed possessed of impurity within her heart.
One day, that eldest sister Sudehā, being distressed, reflected in her heart: "How might there be an end to this suffering?"
Sudehā said: "The fire within my heart will certainly be extinguished by the tears from Ghuśmā’s eyes; it cannot be so through anything born of sorrow."
Therefore, I shall kill his son, who speaks so kindly, today; this will surely come to pass in the future—this is my firm resolve.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, those who are miserly have no discernment regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; their disposition is generally harsh, envious, and self-destructive.
One day, Jyeṣṭhā took up a knife at night and cut her sleeping son, who was with his wife, into pieces of his limbs.
That proud and mighty woman, having taken him there at night, mangled all the limbs of Ghuṣmā’s son and cast him into that very lake.
Wherever the *liṅgas* were indeed constantly hurled by Ghuśmā, she went there, threw them down, and having arrived, slept comfortably.
Having risen early in the morning, Ghuṣmā always performed her duties in that manner; and Sudharmā himself, the most excellent, regularly carried out his daily rites.
In the meantime, that eldest sister, her heart's fire perfectly pacified, performed the duties of the household filled with joy.
Having risen at dawn and beholding the bed, drenched in blood and covered with fragments of the body, the bride was overcome with grief.
She informed her mother-in-law: "Where has your son gone? Indeed, the bed is seen wet with blood, as are fragments of the body."
"Alas! I am destroyed! By whom has this wicked deed been committed against me, O lady of pure vows? Having uttered these words, his beloved wife wept most piteously in many ways.
Then Jyeṣṭhā, having fallen into distress, cried out, "Alas! I am ruined! and though her mind was filled with joy, she manifested outward sorrow.
And Ghuṣmā, having heard of the suffering of her daughter-in-law at that time, did not waver from that vow of constant worship of the deity.
Her mind did not become anxious even in the slightest degree, and her husband remained likewise until the conclusion of the vow.
At midday, after the worship was concluded, she saw the terrifying bed; nevertheless, Ghuśmā did not feel even the slightest bit of sorrow at that time.
He to whom this has been entrusted will indeed provide protection; he is renowned as one who loves his devotees, the Death of Death, and the refuge of the virtuous.
If Śambhu, the sole Lord and Master, were not our protector, he would join us with one thing and sever us from it, just like a florist.
Reflecting on the truth of what might happen from her anxiety today, she did not then feel sorrow; having attained fortitude, she remained fixed in Śiva.
Taking up the earthen vessels as before, she, with a composed mind, went to the shore of the lake while uttering the names of Śambhu.
And when she had cast away the kings there and turned back, her son was seen by her on the bank, standing at the edge of the lake.
The son said: "O Mother, come! I shall meet you, for I am now alive though I was dead, solely through the power of your merit and by the grace of Śaṅkara."
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, seeing her son restored to life, his mother Ghuṣmā was so filled with joy that she did not feel sorrow there as she had before.
At that moment, Śiva, the Great Lord, appeared there instantly in the form of light; being well-pleased, he replied.
Śiva said: "I am pleased; choose a boon. Indeed, he has been slain by this wicked woman. O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall slay her with my trident."
Sūta said: Formerly, having bowed deeply to Śiva, she who was prostrate made this request: "O Lord, this sister of mine, Sudehā, must be protected by you."
Śiva said: An injury was done to her; how can you now perform a service for her? Moreover, Sudehā, who has committed evil deeds, ought to be slain.
Ghuśmā said: By the mere sight of you, sin does not remain at all; now that I have seen you, let that evil be reduced to ashes.
Indeed, he who returns a favor for an injury—even by the mere sight of him, one's sin shall go far away.
Thus have I heard, O Lord, these wonderful words of the Blessed One; therefore, that which was done by me has been done, and let it be so always, O Sadāśiva.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by her, Maheśvara, the ocean of compassion and lover of his devotees, became exceedingly pleased once more and spoke.
Śiva said: "Ask for another boon, O Ghuśmā; I shall grant it for your benefit. I am well-pleased by your devotion and by your changeless nature."
Sūta said: Having heard those words, she said: "If a boon is to be granted by you, then for the sake of protecting the worlds, you must remain here under my name."
Then the Great Lord Śiva, being well-pleased, spoke there: "I shall remain here under your name, known as Ghuśmeśa, bestowing happiness."
May the highly renowned and auspicious Liṅga named Ghuśmeśa be born for me; may this lake always become an abode of Liṅgas.
Therefore, this lake is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Śivālaya; for by its mere sight, it shall always grant all desires.
O lady of virtuous vows, in your lineage there shall be one hundred and one such excellent sons, reaching to the end of the generations; of this there is no doubt.
Possessing virtuous wives, abundant wealth, long life, and wisdom; indeed, being learned and noble, they attain the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There will be one hundred and one [descendants] preeminent in virtue; such will be this most auspicious expansion of the lineage.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Śiva then became manifest there in the form of a Liṅga, renowned by the name Ghuśmeśa; and the lake itself became an abode of Śiva.
Sudharmā, Ghuśmā, and Sudehā, having come together, swiftly performed one hundred and one circumambulations of Śiva.
Having performed worship of Maheśa and having gathered together with one another, they cast off their inner impurities there and attained supreme bliss.
O Brahmins, upon seeing her son, Sudehā felt ashamed for having lived; she asked both of them for forgiveness and performed a vow that removes one's own sins.
O lords of sages, this Liṅga known as Ghuśmeśa was thus born; indeed, by seeing and worshipping it, one’s happiness always increases.
Thus, this series of twelve jyotirliṅgas, which bestows all desires and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been fully recounted by me.
Whoever reads or even hears this narrative of the Jyotirliṅga is liberated from all sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Origin of the Dhūśmeśa Jyotirliṅga," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudrasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of the Sūta, O lords of sages, they praised him highly and spoke to him out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The sages said: O Sūta, you know everything; therefore we ask you. O Lord, tell us the greatness of the Liṅga of Harīśvara.
It was heard of old that the Sudarśana discus was obtained by Viṣṇu through its propitiation, O dear one, and especially through his discourse upon it.
Sūta said: O best of sages, listen to the auspicious story of Harīśvara, from which Viṣṇu formerly obtained the Sudarśana [discus] from Śaṅkara.
At a certain time, the Daityas became exceedingly powerful; they oppressed the worlds and brought about the destruction of dharma.
Those gods, oppressed by the Daityas of great strength and prowess, recounted their suffering to Viṣṇu, the protector of the immortals.
The gods said: "O Lord, have mercy! We are being severely oppressed by the Daityas. Where shall we go, and what shall we do, having taken refuge in you, our protector?"
Sūta said: Having heard these words of the gods who were distressed in spirit, Viṣṇu remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, having propitiated Giriśa, I shall accomplish your task; for these enemies are exceedingly powerful and must be conquered with great effort."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, all those gods, considering the wicked Daityas to be slain, went to their respective abodes.
Viṣṇu, too, for the sake of victory over the immortals, sought refuge in Śiva—the lord of all the gods, the witness of all, and the imperishable.
Having gone to the vicinity of Kailāsa, Hari himself performed penance, having prepared a sacrificial pit and established the fire-god Jātavedas before him.
According to the rites prescribed for kings, they joyfully worshipped Giriśa with various mantras and numerous hymns of praise.
O lords of sages, having bound himself there in the lotus-born posture known as Mānasa, Hari himself did not move.
"I must remain here by all means until my mind is purified"—having made this firm resolve, Hari worshipped Śiva.
O twice-born ones, when Hara was not at all pleased with Hari, then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu became intent upon reflection.
Having reflected thus in his own mind, he performed service in many ways; nevertheless, Hara, the Lord who bestows boons, was not pleased.
Then Viṣṇu, filled with supreme devotion, was struck with wonder.
With affection, he praised the Supreme Lord with a thousand names.
Having uttered the name-mantra for each individual lotus, he indeed worshipped Śambhu, who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge.
Then, indeed, for the purpose of testing Viṣṇu’s devotion, Śaṅkara took away one lotus from among the thousand lotuses.
Viṣṇu did not realize that wonderful cause of the illusion; perceiving it to be deficient, he became intent upon searching for it.
Firm in his vow, he wandered over the entire earth for the sake of pleasing him; failing to find him, the pure-souled one uttered this single verse:
Seeing him, Śaṅkara, the destroyer of all suffering, became pleased; he manifested right there and spoke these words to Hari.
Śiva said: "I am pleased with you, O Hari; ask for a boon as you desire. I shall grant whatever your heart longs for; there is nothing that cannot be given to you."
Sūta said: Having heard those words of Śambhu, Keśava, his mind filled with joy and overcome with great delight, spoke to Śiva with palms joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu said: "What indeed should be said by me before you, for you abide as the inner controller? Nevertheless, O Lord, it is spoken out of respect for your command."
The universe is oppressed by the Daityas; O Sadāśiva, we have no happiness. O my Lord, my own weapon does not manifest itself to slay the Daityas.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have no other protector besides you. Therefore, O Supreme Lord, I have come to you for refuge."
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and having offered salutations to Śiva, the Supreme Soul, he himself stood before Śambhu, oppressed by the Puruṣa.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, the God of gods, gave him his own discus, Sudarśana, a mass of splendor.
Having obtained that [discus], the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu swiftly slew all those exceedingly powerful Daityas with that discus, without any exertion.
The world attained supreme well-being, and the gods became happy; having recovered his own weapon, Hari was exceedingly pleased and filled with great joy.
The sages said: "Tell us indeed that thousand names of Śaṅkara by which Maheśvara was pleased and gave the discus to Hari."
Tell me its greatness, preceded by the dialogue with Śiva, as well as the compassionate nature of Śambhu toward Viṣṇu exactly as it is.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, Sūta remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and spoke these words.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu’s Acquisition of the Sudarśana Discus," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sūta said: Listen, O best of sages; I shall relate it just as I have heard it. Today I shall speak of that meritorious thousand names by which the Supreme Lord was entreated by Viṣṇu and became pleased.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: Śiva, Hara, Mṛḍa, Rudra, Puṣkara, Puṣpalocana, Arthigamya, Sadācāra, Śarva, Śambhu, and Maheśvara.
Candrāpīḍa, Candramauli, Viśva, Viśvambhareśvara, Vedāntasārasandoha, Kapālī, and Nīlalohita.

He whose support is meditation, who is indivisible, the husband of Gaurī, the lord of the Gaṇas, who possesses eight forms and is the universal form, and who is the means for attaining the three aims of life and heaven.
He is attainable through knowledge, possessed of firm wisdom, the God of gods, the three-eyed one; he is Vāmadeva, the Great God, the skillful, the sovereign lord, and the steadfast.
Viśvarūpa, Virūpākṣa, Vāgīśa, Śucisattama; he who accords with all means of valid cognition, whose emblem is the bull, and whose vehicle is the bull.

The Lord is the wielder of the Pināka bow, the bearer of the Khaṭvāṅga staff, the one of variegated attire, the ancient one, the dispeller of darkness, the great yogi, the protector, Brahmā, and Dhūrjaṭi.
The death of Death, clad in a hide, the fortunate one whose essence is the *praṇava*, the upward-facing person worthy of enjoyment, Durvāsas, the subduer of cities.
He who possesses divine weapons, the preceptor of Skanda, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest; he who is without beginning, middle, or end, the Lord of the Mountain, the husband of Girijā.

The kinsman of Kubera, the auspicious-throated, the most excellent among the classes of the world, the gentle one, knowable through meditative absorption, the wielder of the bow, the blue-necked, and the supreme knower of the self.
The large-eyed one, the hunter of deer, the lord of the gods, the scorcher with the sun; the abode of dharma, the field of forbearance, the Blessed One who pierced the eyes of Bhaga.
The fierce one, the lord of creatures, Tārkṣya, the lover of his devotees, the scorcher of enemies, the giver, the compassionate one, the skillful, the director of action, and the subduer of desire.
Dwelling in the cremation ground, subtle, Maheśvara residing in the cremation ground; the creator of the world, the lord of beasts, the great creator, the great medicine.

The supreme lord of cattle, the protector, accessible through knowledge, the ancient one; he is right conduct, excellent conduct, the pure-souled one, the moon, the lover of the moon, and the blissful one.

He is the drinker of Soma, the drinker of nectar, the gentle one, possessed of great splendor and great luster; he consists of brilliance, consists of nectar, consists of food, and is the lord of the nectar of immortality.
Ajātaśatru, Āloka, Saṃbhāvya, Havyavāhana, Lokakara, Vedakara, Sūtrakāra, and Sanātana.

The great seer, the teacher Kapila, the light of the universe, the three-eyed one; the wielder of the Pināka bow, the god on earth, the bestower of well-being, the creator of prosperity, and the wise one.

The supporter of the elements, the creator of abodes, all-pervading, the range of all perception; the creator of Brahman, the creator of the universe, the emanation itself, the Karṇikāra tree, the beloved, the wise seer.
Śākha, Viśākha, Gośākha, Śiva, the unsurpassed physician, Gaṅgāplavodaka, Bhavya, Puṣkala, Sthapati, and Sthira.

He who has conquered his self, whose self is disciplined, who is the charioteer of the vehicle of living beings, who is accompanied by his attendants and possesses a body of attendants, who is of fair renown and whose doubts have been severed.
The god of desire, the protector of desires, his body smeared with ashes; fond of ashes, reclining on ashes, full of longing, the beloved, the author of the sacred scriptures.
Samāvarta, Anivṛttātman, Dharmapuñja, Sadāśiva, Akalmaṣa, Puṇyātman, Caturbāhu, and Durāsada.

Difficult to attain, difficult to traverse, and difficult to withstand, he is skilled in all weapons; he is the abode of the yoga of the supreme self, the son of the lineage, and the one who increases the thread of existence.
He of auspicious limbs, the essence of the world, the Lord of the universe, Janārdana; he who purifies with ashes, Meru, the vigorous one, whose form is pure.
Incurable and yet curable by the virtuous, assuming the form of a servant-monkey, the ancient Fire-god is powerful and the taker of the lives of his enemies.

He is the great lake, the great abyss, the perfected one, and the one worshipped by the hosts of gods; he is clad in a tiger-skin garment, the serpent, the great elemental being, and the great treasure.
Amṛta, Amṛtavapu, Śrīmān, Pāñcajanya, Prabhañjana, Pañcaviṃśatitattvastha, Pārijāta, and Parātpara.

Easy to approach, firm in his vows, heroic, a unique treasury of speech, a treasure-house; the preceptor of the castes and stages of life, a celibate student, a conqueror of enemies, and a scorcher of foes.

The hermitage, the destroyer, the emaciated one, the possessor of knowledge, the lord of the immovable, the embodiment of authority, the difficult to comprehend, the well-winged one, and the one whose vehicle is the wind.

He is the wielder of the bow, the science of archery, the quality, and the source of the moon's qualities; he is truth, devoted to truth, and undepressed; he is righteousness and the teacher of the law of cows.
He is infinite vision, bliss, the staff, the subduer, and self-restraint; he is the performer of exorcisms, the master of great illusion, the architect of the universe, and the skilled craftsman.
Free from passion, self-disciplined, an ascetic whose nature is realized, disguised in the garb of a madman, he was hidden, having conquered desire yet remaining dear to those who have not.
Of auspicious nature, the Ordainer, the Lord of all worlds and progeny, the Swift, the Savior, the Wise, the Foremost, the Sovereign, and the Imperishable.
The world-protector, whose nature is hidden, the beginning of the kalpa, lotus-eyed, knowing the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, he is free from fixed rules yet rests in constancy.

He is the moon, the sun, Saturn, and Ketu; his limbs are excellent and his complexion is like coral. He is the Supreme Brahman, subdued by devotion, whose vehicle is the deer and whose weapon is the arrow, and he is free from all sin.

The mountain-dweller whose abode is the mountain, the beloved, the Supreme Self, the teacher of the world; he is the locus of all actions, the gratified one, the auspicious, and surrounded by auspiciousness.
He is the one of great austerity, of long austerity, the most steadfast, the ancient, the eternal; he is the day, the year, the pervader, the measure, and the supreme asceticism.
The mantra is the maker of the year, the means of realization, and the scorcher of all; it is unborn, the Lord of All, perfected, possessed of great splendor and great power.

The yogi is the worthy one, possessed of great virility; he is perfection itself, the beginning of all, and free from grasping. He is the Vasu, the one of noble mind, the truth, the remover of all sins, and Hara.
He of good fame, the beautiful one, the wearer of garlands, the sage who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; the radiant one, the food, the eater, the lord of the world, the invincible.
He is immortal, eternal, peaceful, powerful, with an arrow in hand; he bears a water-pot, is a wielder of the bow, and is indeed beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Beyond the senses, the great illusionist, the abode of all, the crossroads; the yogi of time, the great sound, the one of great energy, and the one of great strength.

He of great intelligence and great heroism, who moves among living beings, the shatterer of cities, the night-walker, the wanderer among the departed spirits, possessed of great power and great splendor.
Possessing an indescribable form, glorious, and the object of the minds of all teachers; one of vast learning, a great illusionist, self-restrained, eternal, yet appearing transient.
He is splendor, the bearer of splendor, the progenitor, the teacher of all; he is fond of dance, eternally engaged in dance, the luminous self, and the illuminator.

The mantra with distinct syllables, the wise one, the equal one, the flood of essential meaning; the creator of the beginning of the ages, the whirlpool of the ages, the profound one, the one whose vehicle is the bull.

He is the desired, the distinguished, the one cherished by the learned, the easily accessible, the seeker of essence, and the wealth itself; he is the embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites, his name is "Pilgrimage," he is invisible even to the holy sites, yet he is the bestower of those sites.
The ocean is his abode; he is victory and the knower of the time of triumph; he is firmly established, the knower of valid means of knowledge, the golden-armored Hari.

The Lord of Liberators, the host of gods, the Lord of Knowledge, resting in the Bindu; he who is of the nature of wind, stainless, free from illusion, the transformer, the impenetrable, and the secret one.
He is the instrument, the cause, and the agent; the liberator from all bonds. He is resolve, the foundation, the bestower of stations, and the primordial source of the world.
The Guru is the delightful non-duality, the essence of being established within the Self; he is Vīreśvara, Vīrabhadra, and the Guru who prescribes the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
The crest-jewel of heroes, the knower, the bliss of consciousness, the upholder of the river, the bearer of the command, the trident-bearer, he who is pervaded by light, and the abode of Śiva.
Bālakhilya, Mahāvīra, Tigmāṃśu, Badhira, Khaga, Abhirāma, Suśaraṇa, Subrahmaṇya, and Sudhāpati.
Maghavān, Kauśika, Gomān, Virāma, Sarvasādhana, Lalāṭākṣa, Viśvadeha, Sāra, and Saṃsāracakrabhṛt.
Amoghadaṇḍin, Madhyastha, Hiraṇya, Brahmavarcasa, Paramārtha, Paramāyin, Śambara, and Vyāghralocana.
Ruci, Bahuruci, Vedyas, Vācaspati, Ahaspati, Ravi, Virocana, Skanda, Śāstṛ, and Vaivasvata Yama.
Yukti, Unnatakīrti, Sānurāga, Purañjaya, Kailāsādhipati, Kānta, Savitṛ, and Ravilocana.
The most excellent in all the universe, free from fear, the sustainer of the universe, unimpeded, eternal, whose auspiciousness is constant, and whose hearing and chanting are meritorious.

He is the one heard from afar, the all-conquering, the one to be meditated upon, the destroyer of evil dreams; he is the deliverer, the remover of misdeeds, the one to be known, the invincible, and the unborn.

Beginningless, the lord of Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ, Lakṣmī, the wearer of a crown, the sovereign of the thirty gods, the protector of the universe, the creator of the universe, the great hero, and the one with radiant armlets.
Janana, Janajanmādi, Prītimat, Nītimat, Dhruva, Vaśiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhānu, Bhīma, and Bhīmaparākrama.
The Praṇava, who follows the path of truth, the great treasury, the possessor of great wealth, the lord of birth, the Great God, who has reached the further shore of all the Āgamas.
The Reality is the one-souled, all-pervading Viṣṇu, the knower of reality, the ornament; he is the seer, the Brāhmaṇa, who transcends sovereignty, birth, death, and old age.
The origin of the five sacrifices, the Lord of the Universe, of pure manifestation, self-born, without beginning or end, compassionate, and the sustainer of the world of devotees.

The beloved of Gāyatrī, the tall one, the abode of the universe, the maker of light; the child, the one who delights in mountains, the sovereign emperor, the one with a beautiful army, and the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
Anemi, Ariṣṭanemi, Mukunda, Vigatajvara, Svayaṃjyotis, Mahājyotis, Tanujyotis, and Acañcala.
Tawny-hued, with tawny beard, with an eye in his forehead, whose body is the triple Veda; he is the trunk of knowledge, great policy, the origin of the universe, and its dissolution.
Bhaga, Vivasvat, Āditya, Gata-pāra, Bṛhaspati, he whose name and qualities are auspicious, the destroyer of sin, and the one of meritorious appearance.
He of noble fame, the industrious one, the true yogi, the shamer of the virtuous and the wicked; he who wears a garland of stars, the lord of heaven, the self-established, and the refuge of the six.
He is the purifier and the remover of sin; he is Maṇipūra, moving through the sky; seated within the lotus of the heart, he is Śakra, the peaceful Vṛṣākapi.

He is the warm one, the householder, the dark one, the capable one, the destroyer of misfortune; he is the enemy of unrighteousness, the unknowable, the one invoked by many, and the one renowned by many.
The womb of Brahman, the vast womb, the cow of dharma, the source of wealth; the one who seeks the welfare of the world, the Sugata, the Youth, the arrival of virtue.
Golden-hued, luminous, delighting in various beings, the sound; health, the presiding lord of bowing, Viśvāmitra, and the Lord of Wealth.
He is the light of Brahman, the abode of the earth, the supreme great light; he is the maternal grandfather, the wind, the possessor of the atmosphere, and the wearer of the serpent-necklace.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Jātūkarṇya, Parāśara, Nirāvaraṇa, Nirvāra, Vairañca, and Viṣṭaraśravas.
Atri was his very self, unceasing, the embodiment of knowledge, and of great renown; he was the foremost hero of the world, a valiant and fierce one of true prowess.
He who resembles a serpent, the great aeon, the wish-fulfilling tree, the bearer of the arts; he who is adorned, the immovable, the radiant, and exalted by his prowess.
Āyuḥ, Śabdapati, Vāgmī, Plavana, Śikhisārathi, Asaṃsṛṣṭa, Atithi, Śatru, Pramāthī, and Pādapāsana.
Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapta, Viśvabhojana, Japya, Jarādiśamana, Lohita, and Tanūnapāt.
He who has dappled horses, whose source is the sky, who is of beautiful countenance, the destroyer of darkness, the summer heat, the burner, the consumer of clouds, and the conqueror of enemy cities.
Sukhānila, Suniṣpanna, Surabhi, Śiśirātmaka, Vasantas, Mādhava, Grīṣma, Nabhasya, and Bījavāhana.
Aṅgiras, Guru, Ātreya, Vimala, Viśvapāvana, Pāvana, Puraji, Śakra, Traividya, and Navavāraṇa.
He is the intellect of the mind, the ego, the knower of the field, and the protector of the field; he is Jamadagni, the treasury of strength, Vigāla, and Viśvagālava.

The sacrifice is non-terrible and unsurpassed, bestowing both worldly prosperity and the supreme good; he is the mountain-like one, white as a jasmine flower in the sky, the enemy of the Dānavas, and the subduer of foes.
Cāmuṇḍa, the progenitor, the beautiful one, free from thorns, the bearer of the world's thorns; the knower of the four Vedas, the fourfold being, the clever one, and the beloved of the clever.

He is the sacred tradition and the collection of scriptures; he is the holy ford, the deity, and the temple of Śiva. He is of manifold forms, of great form, the form of all things, and both the moving and the unmoving.
He is the creator of logic, the one to be led by logic, the one accessible through reason, and the stainless one; he is the thousand-headed Lord of Gods, the destroyer of all weapons.
Shaven-headed, deformed, and disfigured, yet bearing a staff, he is the sound, the highest quality, indeed tawny-eyed, many-formed, blue-necked, and free from ailment.
The thousand-armed Lord of All, the refuge of all, the sustainer of all worlds; seated upon the lotus, the supreme light, the bestower of the fruit of the lineage.
Padmagarbha, Mahāgarbha, Viśvagarbha, Vicakṣaṇa, Parāvarajña, Varada, Vareṇya, and Mahāsvana.
The god who is the preceptor of both gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras alike; the great friend of gods and asuras, the supreme lord of gods and asuras.
The divine lord of gods and asuras, the great refuge of gods and asuras, the god of gods, the peerless, the inconceivable, the soul of the deities, and self-born.
The Sun, the lion among gods, is the immediate slayer of the great asuras; he is the foremost wanderer among the wise, the most excellent among all the highest of gods.
Delighting in the knowledge of Śiva, the illustrious one, the crested one, the lover of Śrīparvata; holding a thunderbolt in his hand, possessing a perfected sword, he is the slayer of Narasiṃha.

He is the observer of celibacy, the wanderer of the world, the practitioner of Dharma, and the lord of wealth; he is Nandin, the Lord of Joy, the infinite one, the bearer of the naked vow, and the pure.

The presiding deity of the *liṅga*, the presiding deity of the gods, the presiding deity of the ages (*yuga*), the destroyer of the ages; he whose abode is his own self, who has attained his own self, who dwells in heaven, the primordial sound (*svara*), consisting of the primordial sound, and the resonance.
The presiding lord of arrows, the sower of seeds, the performer of actions, the source of dharma, deceit, greed, and indeed Śambhu, the great lord of all beings.
Dwelling in the cremation ground, three-eyed, with a form resembling that of a bull, he is a world-transcending manifestation, the three-eyed Lord adorned with serpents.

The dispeller of darkness, the hater of the sacrifice, the one who struck down the neck of Viṣṇu; he who is free from defects, possessed of imperishable qualities, the enemy of Dakṣa, and the breaker of Pūṣan’s teeth.
Pūrṇa, the fulfiller, the meritorious, the delicate, the one with beautiful eyes, the one who delights in the true path, the rogue, the one of virtuous fame, and the healthy one.

He who is as swift as thought, the founder of a religious order, the one with matted hair, the lord of observances, the ender of life, the eternal, he whose seed is wealth, and the bestower of wealth.

He is the auspicious goal, the bestower of perfection, perfection itself, and the noble birth; he is the thorn to the wicked, the possessor of arts, the one who has become Mahākāla, and the one devoted to truth.
The creator of worldly beauty, the abode of supramundane bliss, the life-giver of the moon, the Teacher, the one who captivates the world, the great sovereign.
The kinsman of the world, the lord of the world, grateful, adorned by his deeds, infallible, imperishable, beloved, and the best among all wielders of weapons.
He is composed of splendor, a retainer of the Vedas, the honor of the world, and an ocean of compassion; he possesses a pure smile, a serene soul, and is indeed invincible and difficult to overcome.
The Lord of the World consists of light, yet is formless; he is the Lord of Waters, possessing a gourd-lute and a massive body; he is free from sorrow and the destroyer of grief.

The teacher of the three worlds, the Lord of the three worlds, the purity of all, the one who has transcended the senses; the God whose characteristics are unmanifest, yet manifest and unmanifest, the Lord of the people.
Paraḥ, Śiva, Vasu, Nāsā, Sāra, Mānadhara, Yama, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Prajāpāla, Haṃsa, Haṃsagati, and Vaya.
The creator, the ordainer, the sustainer, the progenitor, and the destroyer; the four-faced one, the dweller on the peak of Kailāsa, the inhabitant of all things, and the eternal movement.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Druhiṇa, Bhūtapāla, and Bhūpati; the one of true yoga, the knower of yoga, the bestower of yoga upon yogins, and the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas.
Beloved by the gods, lord of the gods, the divine one, the thinker of the gods; the odd-eyed one, the deformed-eyed one, the subduer of Vṛṣa, and the increaser of Vṛṣa.
Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from affliction; he is the destroyer of pride, the giver of pride, the proud one, and the transformer of all things.

He who possesses a thousand rays, adorned with ashes, of pleasing form, and who is not easily won; the Lord of the past, the future, and the present; the all-pervading power, and the destroyer of worldly prosperity.
O Mahākośa, you are purpose and yet devoid of purpose; you are uniquely wise regarding the bodies of others; you are free from thorns, a source of joy, guileless, and the crusher of deceit.
He is courageous, virtuous, truthful, affectionate, and learned; he is unshakable, appreciative of merit, versatile in nature, and performs manifold deeds.
He is well-pleased, the bestower of happiness, subtle, easy to perform, the southern breeze, Nandi, Skanda, the supporter, the bearer of the burden, manifest, and the increaser of joy.
Unconquered, all-enduring, Govinda, whose vehicle is living beings; unsupported, self-supported, perfected, pure in form, and whose wealth is glory.
The bearer of the boar’s tusk, the tusked one, the powerful, the sole leader; the illuminator of the Vedas, the possessor of the Vedas, the one who supports the earth, and the sustainer of many.

He who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the auspicious beginning, the one who is peaceful and auspicious, the equanimous, glory itself, he who is the abundance of ornaments, prosperity, the creator of prosperity, and the sustainer of all beings.
Unshakable, his body is devotion; he is the master of the arts who does not waste time; he is devoted to the vow of truth, a great renunciant, and ever dedicated to peace.

He whose conduct is for the sake of others, the giver of boons, the dispassionate one, the wise; the bestower of auspiciousness, the doer of good, he who possesses auspicious names, and auspiciousness itself.
He who is unasked, who accepts virtues, who is a non-doer, whose radiance is like gold; who is naturally auspicious, impartial, the slayer of enemies, and the destroyer of obstacles.
He has a crest-lock, wears armor, carries a trident, has matted hair, is shaven-headed, and wears earrings; he is deathless, all-seeing, a lion, a mass of splendor, and a great jewel.
Incalculable, immeasurable in essence, vigorous, and skilled in vigor; he is indeed to be known as the one whose nature is detachment, the lord of sages who is the seventh in descent.
He is unsurpassed, invincible, sweet, and pleasant to behold; he is the recollection of the Lord of Gods, the all-pervading one, and the best among those who blaze with splendor.

He is the dark fortnight, the death of Death, the performer of good deeds, and the one who has made Vāsuki his girdle; he is the wielder of the great bow, the lord of the earth, the stainless one, and the one free from all fetters.

The radiant jewel, the sun, the fortunate one, the bestower of perfection, the means for attaining perfection; he who is completely encompassed by the universe, the broad-chested one, and the mighty-armed.
The source of all origins, free from fear, beloved by Nara and Nārāyaṇa; untainted, the soul of the ascetic community, devoid of limbs [in form], yet the destroyer of physical defects.

He is the one to be praised, the lover of praise, the praiser, the embodiment of Vyāsa, and the one without lineage; he is the faultless means consisting of truth, the mass of knowledge, and the one who is honored.
He is the one of tranquil intellect, the unbroken, the gathering, the eternally beautiful, the rider of the tiger, the lord of the earth, the resolve, and the lord of the night.

Datta is the spiritual preceptor of the ultimate truth, a teacher compassionate toward those who take refuge in him; Soma is the knower of the aesthetic essence, the bestower of that essence, and the support for all sentient beings.
Thus, with a thousand names, Hari indeed praised Hara; the Lotus-born one entreated Śambhu and worshipped him.
Then, O twice-born ones, that curious Śambhu performed a most wonderful deed that brings happiness; listen to that very account with reverence.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thousand Names of Śiva," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard the divine thousand-name hymn composed by Viṣṇu and adorned with the supreme names, Maheśvara became pleased.
For the sake of testing Hari, Maheśvara, the Lord of the World, concealed one of those lotuses.
Then, among those thousands of lotuses, there was one missing; Viṣṇu became distraught regarding the worship of Śiva.
He reflected in his heart: "From where indeed has the lotus gone? Let it go wherever it wishes with ease; why should my eye not be a lotus?"
Having understood this, he plucked out his eye out of compassion for all sentient beings; he honored it with devotion and praised it with that very [eye].
Then, seeing Hari in such a state as he was being praised, Hara, the teacher of the world, appeared while uttering the words, "Do not! Do not!"
Therefore, Maheśvara quickly descended from the mandala of the king who was established by Hari, and from his own linga.
Having prostrated before Śambhu, who possessed the form described above and had arisen from a mass of splendor, he stood before him and praised him with particular devotion.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, spoke as if laughing, looking with compassion at Viṣṇu who stood there with his palms joined in reverence.
Śaṅkara said: "O Hari, all that is desired in your heart has been understood by me, especially this task for the gods, since your soul is devoted to the service of the gods."
For the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods and for the destruction of the Daityas, I give you this beautiful discus named Sudarśana.
O Lord of Gods, that form which you have seen, which brings happiness to all the world—contemplate it as something firmly maintained for your own benefit.
On the field of battle, that which is remembered indeed destroys the suffering of the gods; this is the discus, this is the form, and this is the thousand names.
O observer of noble vows, those who always listen with devotion shall attain unfailing success through my grace in all their desires.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, he gave to him the Sudarśana discus, which possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, which arose from his own foot, and which destroys all enemies.
Then Viṣṇu also, having performed the purificatory rites, received it while facing north; having paid homage to Mahādeva, Viṣṇu spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said: "Listen, O Lord; tell me, O Creator of the World, what should be meditated upon and what should be recited by me for the sake of destroying all miseries."
Sūta said: Thus questioned by him at that time, Śiva, being well-pleased, spoke with a tranquil mind to Viṣṇu, the helper of the gods.
Śiva said: "O Hari, my form is indeed to be meditated upon for the pacification of all misfortunes; for the sake of destroying manifold sufferings, recite the Thousand Names."
O Viṣṇu, you must always diligently bear this most excellent of all discs for the sake of accomplishing every desired goal of mine.
And others who shall constantly recite it or cause it to be recited—for them, suffering does not arise even in a dream; of this there is no doubt.
And when a king falls into distress, if he performs [the rite] one hundred times according to the rules together with its ancillaries, that man attains auspiciousness.
For this is indeed the destroyer of diseases, the bestower of knowledge and wealth, the supreme; it is meritorious, the granter of all desires, and always the giver of devotion to Śiva.
Whatever supreme fruit men here shall recite for the sake of attaining, they will surely obtain that most excellent fruit; of this there is no doubt, for it is the truth.
And whoever, having risen at dawn and performed worship to me, recites this daily in my presence, for such a person, success is not far off.
One attains all worldly success that fulfills every desire; in the end, one indeed attains liberation through union (sāyujya)—of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: Having thus spoken to Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, with a delighted mind, touched him with both hands and Giriśa spoke to him again.
Śiva said: "I am the granter of boons, O best of gods; choose whatever boons you desire. I, whose vows are firm, have surely been won over by this hymn and by your devotion."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, Viṣṇu bowed down to that God of gods; being exceedingly gratified, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu said: O Lord of Compassion, just as you have now acted, so too must you, O Lord, out of your inherent mercy, especially extend further grace toward others.
O Mahādeva, there is devotion toward you; be gracious and grant this supreme boon: O Lord, I desire nothing else than that the afflictions of your devotees may never exist.
Sūta said: Having heard those words of his, the compassionate Bhava, whose crest is the moon, touched his body and spoke.
Śiva said: "May you always possess unswerving devotion toward me and toward Hari; and may you be ever worthy of salutation and worship in the world, even by the gods."
"O best of gods, by my grace, your name shall be 'Viṣvambharā'—the supreme remover of all sins; of this there is no doubt."
Sūta said: O lords of sages, having spoken thus, the Lord Rudra, the sovereign of all the gods, vanished right there while Viṣṇu was looking on.
The Blessed Janārdana, having obtained that auspicious discus at the word of Śaṅkara, rejoiced exceedingly in his heart.
Having performed meditation upon that Śambhu, he recited this hymn continuously; he taught it and instructed his devotees in it.
Thus, what was asked has been narrated by me; it removes the sins of those who hear it. O excellent ones, what more do you wish to ask further?
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Fruit of the Thousand-Name Hymn of Śiva," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O Sūta, O Sūta, you are highly fortunate, possessed of knowledge, and firm in your vows; tell us once again the life-story of Śiva in great detail."
Ancient kings, sages, and likewise deities indeed performed the propitiation of that very best of gods.
Sūta said: Well asked, O best of sages! Listen, for I shall tell you the delightful life-story of Śaṅkara, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who hear it.
In the past, when questioned by Nārada, the Grandfather (Brahmā), with a serene soul, replied to Nārada, the best of sages.
Brahmā said: Listen with great affection, O Nārada, to the excellent life-story of Śaṅkara; out of love for you, I shall recount it, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Accompanied by Ramā, Viṣṇu performed the worship of Śiva; indeed, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, he attained all his desires.
I and even my grandfather were performers of the worship of Śiva; by his grace alone, O dear one, we have always been the creators of the universe.
My sons, the supreme rishis, constantly perform the worship of Śiva; and so too do the other rishis who are practitioners of the worship of Śiva.
O Nārada, you are especially one who performs the worship of Śiva; the seven ṛṣis, Vasiṣṭha and the others, are also performers of the worship of Śiva.
The virtuous Arundhatī, Lopāmudrā likewise, and Ahalyā, the wife of Gautama—all were performers of the worship of Śiva.
Durvāsas, Kauśika, Śakti, Dadhīca, Gautama, Kaṇāda, Bhārgava, Jīva, and Vaiśaṃpāyana.
All these sages are considered to be performers of Śiva-worship; likewise, Parāśara and Vyāsa are always devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Upamanyu was a great devotee of Śiva, the Supreme Soul; so too were Yājñavalkya, Jaimini, and Garga, who were all great Śaivas.
Śuka, Śaunaka, and others who are worshippers of Śaṅkara, as well as many other sages, O best of sages, exist.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, along with her daughter-in-law, being devoted to love, constantly performed the worship of Śiva on earth with great affection.
Śakra and the other world-protectors, the Vasus, as well as the gods, the Mahārājika deities, and the Sādhyas who worship Śiva.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and other secondary deities (Upasuras) are worshippers of Śiva; likewise, the high-souled Asuras are considered to be performers of Śiva’s worship.
O Sage, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, along with his younger brother and his son, as well as Virocana and Bali, were constant performers of the worship of Śiva.
Bāṇa is remembered as a great Śaiva, as are the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa; O dear one, Vṛṣaparvan and Danu were Dānavas who worshipped Śiva.
And Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others as well—these great nāgas who are devotees of Śiva—and the birds headed by Garuḍa.
O Lord of Sages, both the gods Sūrya and Candra, who perpetuate their lineages upon the earth, are eternally devoted to the service of Śiva along with all their descendants.
And likewise, O Sage, the Manus, headed by Svāyambhuva, wearing the attire of Śiva, performed the worship of Śiva with special devotion.
Priyavrata, his sons, and likewise the son of Uttānapāda—those kings of their lineage were indeed performers of the worship of Śiva.
Dhruva, Ṛṣabha, and Bharata were nine yogins; his other brothers as well were performers of the worship of Śiva.
O Tārkṣya, the sons of Vaivasvata, the kings headed by Ikṣvāku, whose souls were devoted to the worship of Śiva, always enjoyed happiness.
Kakutstha, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, the best of Śiva’s devotees, Mucukunda, Hariścandra, and likewise Kalmāṣapāda.
Many kings, such as Bhagīratha and others, who were the best among rulers, should be known as performers of Śiva’s worship and as those who adopted the attire of Śiva.
And the great king Khaṭvāṅga, who rendered assistance to the gods, always worshipped the earthly form of Śiva according to the prescribed rites.
For his son Dilīpa was always devoted to the worship of Śiva; his son Raghu was a devotee of Śiva who worshipped Śiva with great affection.
Aja was a worshiper of Śiva; his son was Dharmayuddhakṛt, from whom was born the great king Daśaratha, preeminent above all.
For the sake of obtaining a son, that King Daśaratha, who was indeed an embodiment of Śiva on earth, worshipped [the deity] with special devotion at the command of the sage Vasiṣṭha.
And that king, devoted to Lord Śiva, performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice after obtaining the command of the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, O best of kings.
Kausalyā, beloved of him, being instructed by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, joyfully worshipped that earthly image of Śaṅkara for the sake of obtaining a son.
And Sumitrā, as well as Kaikeyī, the king’s beloved, joyfully honored Śiva for the sake of obtaining virtuous sons, O best of sages.
O Sage, by the grace of Śiva, they indeed obtained sons who were bringers of auspiciousness, heroes of great majesty, and devoted to the path of the righteous.
Then, by the command of Śiva, Hari himself appeared from him among those queens as the prince, manifesting in four forms.
Rāma was the son of Kausalyā, Lakṣmaṇa the son of Sumitrā, and Bharata—of firm vows—was the son of Kaikeyī, along with Śatrughna.
Rāma’s younger brother always honored the king; he wore ashes and rudrākṣa beads and was established in the Virajāgama.
O Sage, all those kings who were born in that lineage, along with their followers, worshipped the earthly linga of Śiva.
And Sudyumna, O Sage, the great king and son of the sage Śaivya, became a woman along with his attendants due to the curse of Śiva for the sake of his beloved.
Through the worship of the Lord of the Earth, he became an excellent man once again; for one month he was a woman and for one month a man, and in this way his state as a woman ceased.
Then, having renounced his kingdom and being devoted to the dharma of Śiva, he assumed the garb of a Śiva ascetic and, through devotion, attained liberation which is so difficult to reach.
And his son was the great king Purūravas, a worshiper of Śiva, the God of gods; his son was likewise a worshiper of Śiva.
Bharata, however, always performed great worship of Śiva alone; and Nahuṣa was a great devotee of Śiva, for he was indeed devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Through the worship of Śiva, Yayāti attained all his desires and begot five sons who were devoted to the dharma of Śiva.
His five sons, headed by Yadu, were all worshippers of Śiva; through the power of their worship of Śiva, they obtained all their desires.
O Sage, other illustrious persons as well who have worshipped Śiva—whether they belong to that lineage or to other lineages—attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And Kṛṣṇa himself performed the worship of Śiva daily on the excellent Badarī mountain for a period of seven months.
From that gracious Lord Śaṅkara, he obtained numerous divine boons, and having attained them, he brought the entire world under his control.
O dear one, his son Pradyumna was always a worshiper of Śiva; and other eminent descendants of Kṛṣṇa, such as Sāmba and others, were also worshippers of Śiva.
Jarāsaṃdha was a great devotee of Śiva, as were the kings of his lineage; Nimi was a devotee of Śiva, as were Janaka and his sons, all worshippers of Śiva.
And worship was indeed performed by Nala, the son of Vīrasena—he who in a previous birth was a Bhilla in the forest who protected travelers.
And a certain ascetic was protected by him in the past while near Hara; however, at night, he was devoured by tigers and other beasts and died from his wounds.
By the power of that merit, that Bhilla indeed became Nala; he became a great emperor, a sovereign king, and the beloved of Damayantī.
Thus, O sinless one, I have related to you that divine life-story of Śaṅkara which was asked by you; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotion of Devas, Sages, and Kings to Śiva," in the fourth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, known as the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā.
The sages said: "You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and your life is fruitful, O dear one, since you cause us to hear this auspicious narrative of Maheśvara."
O Sūta, although this matter has been heard by many sages as being true, we still have doubts; therefore, I shall explain it to you.
By what vow is Śiva satisfied so that he bestows true happiness? You are skilled in the rites of Śiva; therefore, we question you.
O disciple of Vyāsa, salutations to you; please explain in detail that vow by which both worldly enjoyment and liberation may be attained through devotion.
Sūta said: O best of sages, you who are compassionate have asked well; remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, I shall relate this according to what I have heard.
Just as you have asked, so indeed was it asked by the Creator, by Hari, and by Śivā regarding Śaṅkara.
At one time, they asked the Supreme Self: "By what vow are you satisfied that you grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation?"
Thus questioned by them at that time, as well as by Hari himself, I shall now relate that which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
Śiva said: I have many vows that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation; among them, ten in number should be known as the principal ones.
Those who have reached the further shore of the Jābāla Śruti declare ten Śaiva vows; these vows must always be performed with diligence by the twice-born.
On every eighth lunar day, one should diligently observe the practice of eating only at night; however, O Hari, on the Kālāṣṭamī in particular, food must be completely renounced.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, O Viṣṇu, food must indeed be renounced; however, on the dark fortnight, one should eat at night after worshipping me, O Hari.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, a meal should be taken at night; however, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, it should be performed there by those observing the Śiva-vow.
O Viṣṇu, on a Monday night, those devoted to Śiva should diligently take their meal at night during both fortnights throughout the entire month.
In all these vows, O best of the twice-born, Śaivas should be fed with great effort according to one's capacity, for the sake of the complete fulfillment of the vow.
These vows must be performed by the twice-born according to the rules; for if they abandon these vows, the twice-born are reborn as thieves.
Those proficient in the path to liberation must practice these according to the rules; indeed, this quartet is declared to be the means for attaining liberation.
Worship of Śiva, the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, fasting in the temple of Śiva, and death in Vārāṇasī—this is eternal liberation.
The eighth day falling on a Monday and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—these bring satisfaction to Śiva; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Hari, among all four [observances], the Śivarātri vow is indeed the most powerful; therefore, it alone should be performed by those who desire the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And there is nothing other than this doctrine that brings benefit to human beings; for this vow is the supreme means for accomplishing the dharma of all.
O Hari, [this applies] to all men alike—whether they are free from desire or possessed of desire—as well as to those of the various castes and stages of life, and likewise to women and children.
This excellent vow is for the benefit of male and female servants, as well as gods and others, and indeed for all embodied beings.
Indeed, that day in the dark fortnight of Māgha is proclaimed as especially distinguished; it should be accepted when it extends through midnight, for it destroys ten million killings.
O Keśava, listen with a focused mind and great affection as I describe to you what must be done on that very day, beginning from the morning.
Having risen in the morning, the wise man, filled with supreme bliss, should perform his daily duties, such as bathing and so forth, without indolence.
Then, having gone to the abode of Śiva and worshipped according to the prescribed rite, and having paid obeisance to Śiva, one should thereafter properly perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Blue-throated One, salutations be unto you! O Lord, I desire to perform your Śivarātri vow.
"O Lord of Gods, by your power may this be accomplished without obstacle; indeed, let enemies such as Kāma and the others never cause me affliction."
Having thus formed this resolve, one should gather the materials for worship, especially that which is a well-known liṅga in a sacred location and is indeed celebrated in the Āgamas.
Having gone there himself at night and performed the supreme rite, [he should do so] on an auspicious spot to the south or west of Śiva.
Having placed that substance near Śiva for the purpose of worship, that best of men should then bathe there again according to the prescribed rite.
Having put on an auspicious outer garment and likewise an auspicious inner garment, and having sipped water (ācamana) three times, one should indeed commence the worship.
One should perform the worship with whatever substance is prescribed for a particular mantra; however, the worship of Hara must never be performed without a mantra.
Endowed with a spirit of devotion, the wise practitioner, having performed worship with songs, instrumental music, and dances during the first watch of the night, should then recite the mantra.
If one who possesses the mantras should perform the excellent rite of the earthen image (pārthiva), he should first complete his daily obligatory duties and afterwards worship the earthen image.
Having first fashioned the earthen image, one should subsequently perform the ritual installation; one should gratify the bull-bannered god with various kinds of hymns.
The greatness arising from the vow should be read by the wise man; it should be heard by the most devoted person with the desire for the successful completion of the vow.
Furthermore, throughout all four watches of the night, one should perform the sequence of the four forms, beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal, in due order.
One should joyfully perform a vigil accompanied by a great festival; then, having bathed in the morning, one should again install and worship Śiva there.
Then, having completed the full vow, he should pray to Śambhu with bowed shoulders and palms joined in reverence, bowing to him again and again.
O Mahādeva, this vow which was undertaken by me at your command is now being released by me, O Lord; the excellent observance has been fulfilled.
O Lord of Gods, being satisfied by this vow performed according to my capacity, be pleased today, O Śarva, and show mercy toward me.
Having offered a handful of flowers to Śiva, one should give gifts according to the prescribed rule; then, having bowed to Śiva alone, one should dismiss that observance.
Having fed, according to one's ability, the twice-born and especially the ascetics of Śiva, and having satisfied them well, one should then partake of food oneself.
O best of devotees, I shall describe to you how worship should be performed by you during each watch of the night, especially on Śivarātri.
And during the first watch of the night, one should worship the image of Hari placed upon the throne with supreme devotion and manifold excellent offerings.
Harass should always be worshipped first with five substances; one should offer each substance separately with its respective mantra.
Having indeed offered that substance, one should pour a stream of water; thereafter, the wise person should cause the substances to be lifted up by means of streams of water.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should worship Śiva there—both as the attribute-less (nirguṇa) and as the embodiment of attributes (guṇarūpin)—with a stream of water.
One should worship the bull-bannered Lord with the mantra given by the guru; otherwise, one should worship Sadāśiva with the name-mantra.
Worship of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, should be performed with variegated sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and black sesame seeds.
Furthermore, one should offer flowers—such as lotuses and oleanders—to Śaṅkara with the eight name-mantras.
Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Mahat, Bhīma, and Īśāna—these indeed are they.
One should worship Śiva with names preceded by "Śrī" and ending in the dative case; thereafter, one should offer incense, a lamp, and then the food offering (naivedya).
In the first watch of the night, the wise devotee should offer cooked food as a sacrificial oblation; having presented the water-offering with a bilva fruit, he should also offer betel leaf.
Then, having performed salutation, meditation, and the recitation of the Guru’s mantra, one should otherwise please Śaṅkara with the five-syllable mantra.
Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with excellent water; and one should arrange for the feeding of five Brahmins according to one's capacity.
A great festival should be celebrated here for as long as a watch (yāma) remains; then, having offered the fruit of the worship to him, one should dismiss [the deity].

Furthermore, one should properly perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) during the second watch of the night; or else, having resolved upon it all at once, one should perform the worship in that same manner.
Having performed worship with the aforementioned substances, one should offer the stream [of water]; having recited the mantra twice as many times as before, one should worship Śiva.
One should worship Śiva with sesame seeds, barley, and lotuses; one should especially worship the Supreme Lord with bilva leaves.

O Janārdana, the *arghya* should be offered with a citron (*bījapūra*), as well as the food offering (*naivedya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*); furthermore, the repetition of the mantra should be double that of the previous [rite].
Then, one should indeed perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for feeding the Brahmins; one should do everything else in that manner until the second [day].
When the third watch has arrived, one should perform worship as before; and in place of barley, one should use wheat, and the flowers should be those produced from the Arka plant.
There, O Viṣṇu, with various kinds of incense and also with various kinds of lamps, with food offerings, cakes, and also with various kinds of vegetables.
Then, having performed the ārārtika rite with camphor, one should offer the arghya water containing pomegranate and perform twice as much recitation of the mantra.

Then, one should perform the formal resolve for the feeding of Brahmins along with the distribution of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and conduct the festival as before until the end of the watch of the night.
When the fourth watch has arrived, one should perform its dismissal; having performed the preliminary rites again, one should carry out the worship according to the rules.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with black gram, millet, mung beans, or likewise with the seven grains, or with conch-flower blossoms and bilva leaves.
One should indeed offer there various kinds of sweet food offerings, or else one should always satisfy Sadāśiva with meals of black gram.
O Hari, one should offer the *arghya* with a plantain fruit, or indeed with various other fruits; one should likewise offer the *arghya* to Śiva with diverse fruits.
The best of men should perform the recitation of mantras twice as much as before; the wise one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the feeding of Brahmins according to his capacity.
One should pass the time with devotion through songs, instrumental music, and dances, along with great festivals and devoted people, until the dawn breaks.
When sunrise has thus occurred, one should bathe again and worship Śiva with various offerings of worship, and then perform one's own consecration.
Various kinds of gifts as well as diverse foods should be offered to the Brahmins and the ascetics according to the number of watches of the night.
Having paid homage to Śaṅkara, one should then offer a handful of flowers; the wise practitioner, having performed a beautiful hymn of praise, should pray with these mantras.
O Mṛḍa, O ocean of compassion, knowing that I am yours, that my life-breaths are centered in you, and that my mind is always fixed on you, act as is appropriate.

Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, whatever recitation, worship, and so forth has been performed by me—O Lord of Beings, out of Your nature as a treasure-house of compassion, knowing this, be gracious unto me.
By the very fruit that has arisen from this fast alone, may the god Śaṅkara, the bestower of happiness, be pleased.
O Mahādeva, may there always be devotion to you in my family; may no one be born in that lineage where you are not the deity.
Having offered a handful of flowers and likewise received the forehead marks and blessings from the Brahmins, one should then bid farewell to Śambhu.
For one by whom such a vow has been made, Hara is indeed not far away; it is impossible to describe the fruit thereof, and there is nothing that I cannot grant.
If indeed this supreme vow has been performed without effort, then the seed of liberation has truly been produced; there is no doubt about this.

Men should perform this vow every month with devotion; thereafter, by performing the rite of formal conclusion (udyāpana), one shall obtain the complete fruit of the practice along with its ancillaries.
"By the performance of this vow, I am surely Śiva, the destroyer of all suffering; I grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation—indeed, every desired fruit."

Sūta said: Having heard these words of Śiva, Viṣṇu returned to his most excellent and wondrous abode; thereafter, he practiced this very same supreme vow among people who were devoted to their own welfare.
Once, Keśava recounted to Nārada this divine Śivarātrivrata, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Śivarātri Vow," within the "Glorification of Vyādheśvara" in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "Tell us the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the Śivarātri vow, by performing which Śaṅkara certainly becomes manifestly pleased."
Sūta said: O sages, listen with devotion and respect to that concluding rite (udyāpana), by the performance of which the vow certainly becomes complete.
The auspicious Śivarātri vow should be observed for fourteen years: eating only one meal on the thirteenth day and fasting on the fourteenth day.
When the day of Śivarātri has arrived, having performed the daily rites according to the rule, one should then go to the temple of Śiva and perform worship according to the prescribed ritual.
And then, one should diligently construct a divine mandala there, which is indeed renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Gaurī-tilaka.
In the center of that, one should cause a divine Bhadramandala to be drawn from the Linga, or otherwise, one should arrange a Sarvatobhadra mandala within the pavilion.
There, water-pots known as *prājāpatya* should be prepared; they should be auspicious, accompanied by cloths, fruits, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
And on the sides of the mandala, they should indeed be placed with great care; and one [vessel] made of gold or another vessel should be established in the center.
There, the observer of the vow, having fashioned an image of Śambhu together with Umā out of gold weighing one pala, half a pala, or according to his capacity;
Having placed the form of Śivā on his left side, unwearied, and having positioned my [form] on his right side, he should worship during the night.
There, one should choose a pure preceptor together with the officiating priests; and being authorized by them, one should perform the worship of Śiva with devotion.
The observer of the vow should keep a vigil at night, performing worship consisting of incense; he should spend the entire night with singing, dancing, and other such activities.

Having thus worshipped according to the rules and satisfied [the deity] early in the morning, one should then perform worship once more and carry out the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the Prājāpatya rite according to one's capacity, feed Brāhmaṇas with affection, and give gifts with devotion.
Having adorned the officiating priests together with their wives according to the prescribed rule with garments, ornaments, and decorations, he should bestow gifts upon each of them individually.
Having spoken thus, one should indeed give a cow along with its calf, together with the necessary implements, to the preceptor according to the prescribed rite, saying: "May Śiva be pleased with me."
One should present that very image, together with its water-pot, clothed and adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a bull, to the preceptor.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, shoulders bowed, and with words faltering out of great devotion, he should pray to the god Maheśāna, the Great Lord.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; O Lord of gods, by means of this vow, show compassion toward me.
O Śivā, this vow has been performed by me according to my devotion; O Śaṅkara, by your grace, may whatever was deficient reach completion.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, whatever recitation, worship, and so forth has been performed by me—may that, O Śaṅkara, become fruitful by your grace.
