Having thus offered a handful of flowers to Śiva, the Supreme Self, one should then perform prostration and offer a prayer once again.
For one who has observed the vow in this manner, no deficiency exists; consequently, he attains the accomplishment desired by his mind—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Śivarātri Vow," in the fourth section, the Koṭirudra Saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, having heard your words, we have attained supreme bliss; please tell us with affection that very same excellent vow in detail.
O Sūta, by whom was this supreme vow performed here in the past? And having performed it even through ignorance, what supreme fruit was obtained?
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages; I shall relate this ancient history of a Niṣāda, which destroys all sins.
In ancient times, there was a certain Bhilla in the forest named Gurudruh; he was a householder, powerful, cruel, and devoted to performing wicked deeds.
Going constantly into the forest, he was always killing deer; and dwelling there in the forest, he committed various kinds of theft.
From childhood onwards, he performed no auspicious deed whatsoever here; a great length of time passed for that evil-minded one in the forest.
Once, the auspicious Śivarātri arrived there; the wicked-souled one, dwelling in that great forest, did not know of it.
At that time, the forest-dweller was entreated by his mother, father, and wife, who were overcome by hunger: "O wanderer of the woods, give us something to eat!"
Thus entreated, he too quickly took up his bow and went forth for the sake of killing deer; he roamed throughout the entire forest.
Due to the turn of fate, he did not obtain anything at all; then, as the sun had set, he fell into great distress.
"What must be done? Where must I go? Nothing has been attained by me today. What will become of those children at home, and what of their parents?"
She shall indeed become my wife, and she will have some [portion] of his; for I must depart having taken something from her, and it cannot be otherwise.
Having reflected thus, that hunter went near the reservoir and, having approached the place where one descends into the water, he stationed himself there.
"Surely some living being will come here; having killed him, I shall go to my own home with joy, my purpose accomplished."
Thinking thus, that Bhilla indeed climbed a certain tree known as Bilva and remained there, taking water with him.
"Will someone ever come? When shall I kill again?"—fixing his mind thus, he remained there, overcome by hunger and thirst.
That night, during the first watch, a single doe arrived; afflicted by thirst and trembling with fear, she then began to leap about.
And having seen her then, O Viṣṇu, he, being greatly delighted, quickly fixed an arrow upon his own bow for the purpose of slaying her.
As he was acting in this manner, the water and the bilva leaves fell down there, and from that, a Śiva-liṅga appeared.
As soon as the worship of Yama and Śiva was performed, by that very power, his sin then dissolved away.
Hearing that very sound from there, the doe, seeing the hunter and becoming agitated with fear, spoke these words.
The doe said: "O hunter, what do you wish to do? Speak the truth before me. Having heard those words of the doe, the hunter spoke these words:
The hunter said: "My family is hungry today; by killing you, I shall satisfy them. Hearing those cruel words and seeing that wicked man who was difficult to restrain, [the deer reflected].
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I must devise a stratagem. Having reflected thus, she spoke these words there.
The doe said: "By my flesh you shall find happiness for this body that causes only misfortune; what greater merit could there be? I am blessed—of this there is no doubt."
The merit that arises here for one who performs an act of assistance cannot indeed be fully described even in hundreds of years.
However, all my children are currently at my own hermitage; therefore, having entrusted them to my sister, I shall then proceed to my husband.
"Know this, O forest-dweller: my word is not false. I shall come here again to your presence; of this there is no doubt."
The earth stands by truth, and the ocean likewise by truth; the streams of water exist by truth—everything is established in truth.
Sūta said: When the hunter did not heed her words even though she had spoken thus, she was then greatly astonished and terrified, and spoke these words once more.
The doe said: "Listen, hunter, I shall speak; indeed, I take an oath: that I may never again come into your presence after having gone to my own home."

A Brāhmaṇa who sells the Vedas, one who neglects the three daily prayers at their appointed times, and women who, having transgressed the commands of their own husbands, engage in ritual acts [independently].
Whatever sin exists in an ungrateful person, that same sin lies in one who turns away from Hari; whatever sin exists in a traitor, that same sin lies in the transgression of dharma.
If I do not return again, may I be smeared with that same sin for betraying trust and likewise for practicing deception.
When the doe had stood there after making many such oaths, the trusting hunter said to her, "Go home."
The doe, having drunk the water with joy, returned to the circle of her own hermitage; meanwhile, the first watch of the night passed for him without sleep.
His sister, who had indeed been transformed into a deer, came seeking water while searching for her path.
Upon seeing her, the Bhilla himself drew his arrow; as before, the water-lily petals fell upon Śiva.
And thus, by that hunter, the worship of the great-souled Śambhu during the second watch of the day was performed incidentally, bringing him happiness.
Seeing him, the doe said to him, "What are you doing, O forest-dweller? Having heard what was said by him as before, the doe spoke again.
The doe said: "O hunter, listen; I am blessed, for my bearing of this body has become fruitful. Through this impermanent body, indeed, a great service will be rendered."
"But my young children and infants remain at home; having entrusted them to my husband, I shall indeed return again."
The hunter said: "I do not believe what you have said; I shall kill you, of this there is no doubt. Hearing that, the doe spoke while taking an oath, O lion:
The doe said: "Listen, hunter, I shall tell you what will happen if I do not come again: he whose word is wavering has lost his merit."
That man who, having abandoned his wedded wife, goes to another woman, or who, transgressing the Vedic dharma, proceeds according to a fabricated [law], [is a sinner].
He who, though endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, utters slander against Śiva, shall encounter emptiness here in this world upon reaching the anniversary of his parents' death.
Having indeed caused distress to others, he speaks words [of regret] again; by that sin I am smeared, should I not come back once more.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by her, the hunter said to the doe, "Go," and she, having drunk the water, went joyfully to her own hermitage.
Thus, his second watch passed indeed without sleep; at that time, when the third watch had arrived there—
Realizing there was a delay, he became anxious and intent on searching for him; then, during that very watch, he saw the deer situated upon the path leading to the water.
Seeing that well-fed deer, the forest-dweller was indeed delighted; fixing an arrow to his bow, he set about to kill it.
At that time, as he was performing his worship in this manner, some bilva leaves fell upon Śiva over Viṣṇu due to the force of his past karma (prārabdha).
By virtue of his good fortune, worship of Śiva alone was performed by him during the third watch of that night, and the Lord’s compassion was thus revealed.
Having heard that sound there, he asked, "What are you doing? and the hunter replied, "I am killing you for the sake of my family."
Having heard those words of the hunter, the deer, with a joyful heart, immediately spoke these words to the hunter.
The deer said: "I am blessed and nourished today; my body shall bring satisfaction to you. For one whose limb does not serve another's benefit, everything has passed in vain."
Indeed, he who possesses capability yet does not perform a beneficial act—that capability becomes useless, and he shall go to hell in the next world.
"But having entrusted my own children and the infants to their mother, and having comforted them all, I shall return again."
Thus addressed by him, that hunter was greatly astonished in his heart; with his mind somewhat purified and his mass of sins diminished, he spoke these words.
The hunter said: "Whosoever have gathered here, they have all departed after speaking with you; even now those deceivers do not return."
And you too have fallen into distress and will meet with misfortune; O deer, how then shall my restoration to life come about today?
The deer said: "Listen, hunter, I shall speak; there is no falsehood in me. By truth alone does the entire universe, with all its moving and unmoving beings, abide."
Indeed, the merit of one whose speech is false perishes in an instant; nevertheless, O Bhilla, listen to my truthful vow.

[One should avoid] sexual intercourse at twilight, eating during the day, and likewise eating on Śivarātri; as well as giving false testimony, misappropriating a deposit, and [associating with] a twice-born man who has neglected his twilight prayers.
He whose mouth is devoid of Śiva is incapable of helping others, even though he be capable; for him, even the breaking of a bilva fruit on a festival day constitutes the eating of what is forbidden.
If I were to fail to worship Śiva, eat food while devoid of sacred ash, or should I not return again—may the sin of these acts be mine.
Śiva said: "Having heard these words of his, 'Go quickly and return,' that deer, being thus addressed by the hunter, drank water and departed."
They all gathered there at their own hermitage and, having offered respectful salutations, thoroughly heard that entire account from one another.
Bound by the noose of truth that they must certainly go, they then consoled the children there and became eager to depart.
And the eldest doe there spoke these words to her husband: "O deer, how indeed will the young ones remain here without you?"
But first, O Lord, a vow was made by me there; therefore, I must go, while you two remain here.
Having heard those words, the youngest spoke this speech: "I am your servant; I shall go today, so please remain here."
Having heard that, the deer said: "I shall indeed go there; you two stay here, for the protection of an infant is the duty of a mother."
Having heard those words of their master, they did not consider them righteous; with affection, they said to their husband, "Fie on life in widowhood!"
Having comforted the children there and entrusted them to their fellow-dwellers, they all went quickly to where the best of hunters was staying.
"All those children have indeed been seen and followed; let whatever be their fate be ours as well."
Seeing them, the hunter was delighted and fixed an arrow upon his bow; yet again, lotus leaves fell upon Śiva.
By that, an auspicious worship of the fourth watch was indeed performed; at that moment, all his sin was reduced to ashes in an instant.
The doe, the doe, and the deer said: "O best of hunters, quickly make our bodies meaningful; indeed, show us mercy."
Śiva said: Having heard these words of theirs, the hunter was filled with wonder; through the power of Śiva’s worship, he attained knowledge that is difficult to obtain.
These deer are indeed blessed and highly esteemed, for though devoid of [human] knowledge, they are devoted to serving others with their very own bodies.
Having attained this human birth, what have I accomplished now? Having oppressed another's body, my own body has been nourished by me.
Having constantly supported my family and committed numerous sins—alas, having thus committed such evils, what will be my destiny?
"To what destination shall I go, having committed a sin since birth? Now I reflect thus: fie, fie upon my life!"
Having attained such knowledge, he then restrained his arrow and said, "O best of deer, you may go; you are blessed."
Śiva said: When he had spoken thus, Śaṅkara was then pleased and revealed his own esteemed form, which had been worshipped.
Having touched him out of compassion, Śambhu spoke with affection to that hunter: "Choose a boon, O Bhilla; I am pleased by this vow of yours."
Even the hunter, upon seeing the form of Śiva, was liberated in an instant; he fell at the feet of Śiva, saying, "Everything has been attained."
Śiva, whose nature is perfectly tranquil, gave him a name and concealed his form; then, beholding him with a compassionate glance, he granted him divine boons.
Śiva said: "Listen, O hunter; today enjoy divine pleasures as you desire, having taken up residence in the supreme capital city of Śṛṅgaverapura."
O hunter, the increase of your lineage shall be free from misfortune and praiseworthy even by the gods; Rāma will certainly come to your house.
He will cultivate friendship with you, acting out of affection for my devotee; with your mind intent on service to me, you shall attain liberation, which is difficult to obtain.
In the meantime, having beheld Śaṅkara and bowed down to him, they all attained the supreme liberation from their birth as deer.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot and assumed divine bodies, they were liberated from the curse merely by the sight of Śiva and went to heaven.
Śiva was born as Vyādheśvara on Mount Arbuda; through seeing and worshipping him, he immediately bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O best of gods, from that day forward, that hunter surely enjoyed divine pleasures and, having attained the grace of Rāma, reached union with Śiva.
Even he, having performed this vow out of ignorance, attained union; how much more so those endowed with devotion, who attain that auspicious state of identity with Him?
Having deliberated upon all the scriptures and manifold duties, this Śivarātri vow is proclaimed as the most excellent of all.
Herein are various vows and various sacred fords, diverse gifts as well as various sacrifices.
Various kinds of austerities and numerous recitations of prayers do not equal the merit of the Śivarātri vow.
Therefore, those who desire their own welfare should perform this most auspicious and divine Śivarātri vow, which always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
All this auspicious Śivarātri vow has been fully described; it is renowned as the "King of Vows. What else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Śivarātri Vow," within the "Greatness of Vyādheśvara" section of the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: Liberation has been described by you; tell us now, what might exist there? What kind of state would prevail in that condition? Please explain this to us.
Sūta said: Liberation is declared to be fourfold; listen as I describe it to you—it is the destroyer of the afflictions of saṃsāra and the bestower of supreme bliss.
It consists of sārūpya, sālokya, sānnidhya, and likewise the fourth, sāyujya; that which is attained through this vow is of these four kinds.
O best of sages, Śiva alone is said to be the giver of liberation; Brahmā and the others are not to be so known, for they grant only the three aims of worldly life.

Brahmā and the others are lords of the three qualities (guṇas), while Śiva is beyond the three qualities; he is the changeless Supreme Brahman, the Fourth State (turya), transcending primordial nature (prakṛti).

He is the embodiment of knowledge, imperishable, the witness, attainable through knowledge, non-dual, and self-existent; he is the bestower of absolute liberation here, and indeed the giver of the three aims of life as well.
The fifth, called Kaivalya, is difficult for men to attain in every respect; O best of sages, listen as I describe its characteristics.
From which everything arises, by which this world is sustained, into which it dissolves, and by which all this is pervaded—that indeed [is Brahman].
O lords of sages, that very form of Śiva is indeed recited as being twofold—both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala)—as described in the Vedas.
That was not known by Viṣṇu, nor was it so known by Brahmā; it was not known by Kumāra and the others, nor indeed was it known by Nārada.
It was not indeed [attained] by Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, nor by Vyāsa, nor by the lords of sages, nor by all the gods of former times, nor by the Vedas, nor likewise by the scriptures.
He is truth, knowledge, and infinite; he is designated as being-existence-bliss (saccidānanda). He is devoid of qualities, free from limiting adjuncts, immutable, pure, and untainted.
Neither red nor yellow, neither white nor blue; neither short nor long, neither gross nor subtle.
That from which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind—that alone is declared the supreme, Brahman itself, known by the name Śiva.
Just as space is all-pervading, so too is this [Self] all-pervading—the Supreme Self which transcends illusion, transcends duality, and is free from envy.
And its attainment shall certainly occur here, O twice-born ones, either from the dawning of the knowledge of Śiva or through the worship of Śiva alone with a subtle intellect by the virtuous.
Knowledge, however, is difficult to attain in this world, while devotion is considered easy; therefore, O best of beings, practice devotion to Śiva even for the sake of liberation.
For Śiva is dependent upon devotion; he is the supreme giver of liberation, whose nature is knowledge. Through devotion alone, many perfected ones have attained supreme liberation with joy.

Devotion to Śambhu is the mother of knowledge, always bestowing both liberation and worldly enjoyment; for by its grace, the sprout of true love, characterized by such qualities, becomes easily attainable.

O twice-born ones, that devotion should be known as manifold—both with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā); that which is ritualistic (vaidhī) and that which is spontaneous (svābhāvikī)—whichever is superior is remembered as the supreme (parā).
It is indeed proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as *naiṣṭhikī* and *anaiṣṭhikī*; the *naiṣṭhikī* is sixfold according to its divisions, while the second is recorded as being of one kind.
The wise know that [the path] to be manifold due to the distinction between the prescribed and the prohibited; and because of the great variety of these two, no further elaboration is described here.

These two, consisting of nine limbs each, are to be known through the distinctions of hearing and so forth; they are extremely difficult to accomplish without his grace, yet easy to accomplish with it.

"O twice-born ones, devotion and knowledge are indeed not different, as described by Śambhu; therefore, one should never make a distinction between them, for the doer of that [non-duality] shall always possess happiness."
O twice-born ones, consciousness does not arise at all for those who oppose devotion; however, for one who practices devotion to Śambhu, the dawn of knowledge occurs swiftly.
Therefore, O lords of sages, devotion to Maheśa must be cultivated; by that alone everything will be accomplished, without a doubt.
Thus, that which was asked by you has been told by me; having heard that, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: Who is Śiva, or who is Hari? Who is Rudra, and who is Vidhi? Among these, which one is indeed devoid of attributes (nirguṇa)? Cut through this doubt of ours.
Sūta said: That which indeed first arose from the attributeless Supreme Self—that very thing they who know the Vedas and Vedānta know by the name Śiva.
Therefore, Prakṛti, having arisen and being united with Puruṣa, performed penance there in the water situated at the root by those two, O wise one.
Kāśī, renowned as the "Five-Casketed," is beloved by all; indeed, this entire world is pervaded by its water which extends everywhere.
Having manifested through his illusory power (māyā), Hari indeed slept there; he is renowned as Nārāyaṇa, and Prakṛti is considered to be Nārāyaṇī.
He who was born from that lotus at the navel is indeed the Grandfather (Brahmā); by that very ascetic power, he beheld him who is called Viṣṇu.
O wise ones, that form which was manifested by the attribute-less Śiva during the subduing of both [the gods and the asuras] is indeed renowned as Mahādeva.
He said: "I shall become Śambhu from the forehead of Ka; he will be renowned by the name Rudra, the one who bestows grace upon the worlds."
For the sake of meditation by all, he who is formless became possessed of form; he alone is Śiva himself, manifest, acting out of affection for his devotees.
In Śiva, who is permeated by the three qualities, and in Rudra, the abode of those qualities, there is in reality no difference at all, just as there is none between gold and its ornaments.
They possess identical forms and activities, grant equal food and destinations, are equally served by all, and engage in various divine pastimes.
For Rudra, of fierce prowess, is in every way the form of Śiva; he has appeared for the sake of his devotees' tasks, acting as an assistant to Hari and Brahmā.
And other things that have arisen likewise go to dissolution in due order; but Rudra does not dissolve in Śiva in such a manner—Rudra dissolves into Śiva [as his very essence].
These beings, having indeed united with Rudra, proceed as they were originally constituted; but Rudra, having united with these, does not depart from the teaching of the Śruti.
Everyone indeed worships Rudra, but Rudra does not worship anyone at all; yet, out of affection for his devotees, he sometimes worships by means of his own self.
Those wise ones who constantly devoted themselves to another have become absorbed in him; through that very [devotion], they have attained Rudra after a long time.
Whosoever are devotees of Rudra attain the state of Śiva at that very moment; they have indeed no need for anything else—this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Indeed, this ignorance is manifold, but knowledge is not manifold; O twice-born ones, listen with respect as I describe its various forms.
Whatever is seen here, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all that is indeed Śiva alone; the conceptualization of manifoldness is false.
Before creation, Śiva is proclaimed; likewise, during creation, Śiva is proclaimed; at the end of creation, Śiva is proclaimed; and when all is void, then too, Śiva is proclaimed.

Therefore, O lords of sages, Śiva alone is declared to possess four qualities; he alone is to be known as possessing attributes (saguṇa), for by virtue of his possession of power (śaktimat), he is twofold.
By him alone were all the eternal Vedas given to Viṣṇu—along with their phonemes, vowels, various accents, meditations, and his own modes of worship.
The Lord of all sciences—this is the eternal Vedic revelation; because he is the creator of the Vedas and the Lord of the Vedas, Śambhu is so proclaimed.
He alone is Śaṅkara manifest, the bestower of grace upon all; he is the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer, yet he is the witness and truly devoid of attributes.
There is no measurement of time for others, nor indeed any reckoning of time; Mahākāla himself is directly dependent upon Mahākālī.
And so the Brahmins proclaim Rudra and likewise Kālī; everything is obtained from those two through their will, by way of true play.
There is no one who produces it, nor indeed any master who can take it away; for you yourself are the cause of all things, while Viṣṇu and the others have become their effects.
And it is never the case that a cause is its own effect; though a single entity may attain multiplicity, even a manifold entity may return to oneness.
A single seed, having become external, is born again as a seed; and when it has become manifold, Maheśvara himself, whose form is Śiva, is everything.
This supreme knowledge of Śiva has been declared according to its true nature; O lords of sages, only one who possesses true knowledge knows it, and no other whatsoever.
The sages said: "Tell us knowledge along with its characteristics, by knowing which one may attain the state of Śiva; how is Śiva all that, and how is everything indeed Śiva?"
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words, Sūta, the best of those who recite the Purāṇas, remembered the lotus feet of Śiva and spoke these words to the sages.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Distinction between Saguna and Nirguna," in the fourth book, the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to the knowledge of Śiva exactly as it was heard by me; I shall relate this great secret, which is the very nature of supreme liberation.
In the assembly of Kanāradakumāra, Vyāsa, Kapila, and others, it was determined and proclaimed by them.
Thus, knowledge should always understand that the entire world is composed of Śiva; and Śiva, who is all-pervading, should be known by the wise one who possesses all-knowing insight.
Whatever is seen in this world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all that is Śiva alone; that deity is called Śiva.
Whenever the desire arises in him, then this is performed; he alone knows everything, while no one knows him.
Having himself fashioned that [body] and entered it, he remains at a distance; yet he has not truly entered therein, for he is untainted and possesses the nature of pure consciousness.
And just as light is reflected in water and other media, yet in reality there is no actual entry [of the light], even so is Śiva himself.
In reality, however, the auspicious sequence itself appears as everything; there is neither ignorance nor difference of the intellect, nor is there anything else besides these two.
In all philosophical systems, a diversity of opinions is demonstrated; however, the Vedāntins maintain that there is eternally only non-duality.

For the individual soul (jīva), which is a portion of His own part, is deluded by ignorance and remains under its control; it perceives "I am another," but when liberated from that [ignorance], it becomes Śiva.
Pervading all, Śiva is directly the omnipresent one within all living beings; he is the lord of both the conscious and the unconscious, and Śaṅkara himself is everywhere.
The wise person who employs a means for the purpose of seeing Him, by resorting to the path of Vedānta, shall obtain the fruit of that vision.
Just as fire is all-pervasive and resides within every piece of wood, so too he who rubs that particular wood undoubtedly beholds it.
The wise person who practices the means such as devotion here will certainly behold that Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Śiva alone, Śiva alone, and Śiva alone—there is nothing else whatsoever; for Śaṅkara, though eternally one, appears through delusion in manifold forms.
Just as the ocean, whether consisting of clay or gold, acquires diversity through limiting adjuncts (upādhi), so too does Śaṅkara.
The distinction between cause and effect does not exist in reality; it arises solely through deluded cognition and perishes when that [delusion] is absent.
Then, from the seed, the sprout emerges and indeed manifests diversity; yet in the end, there remains only the seed, and that sprout perishes.
The knower is indeed the seed, and the sprout is considered to be the transformations; when those cease, one is again a knower—of this there is no need for deliberation.
All is Śiva; all is auspicious; there is no duality whatsoever. How then does one perceive diversity, and how again does one perceive unity?
Just as the single light called the sun is seen by people in various ways, especially in water and other such media, so too is he [the Buddha].
Just as the nature of touch is not obstructed even though it is all-pervasive, so too the Lord, being all-pervasive, is indeed never bound anywhere.

Thus, the individual soul (jīva) is possessed of egoism, whereas Śaṅkara himself is liberated from that; the jīva is insignificant and experiences the fruits of karma, while the great Śaṅkara is untainted.
Just as a single substance such as gold, when mixed with silver and so forth, [is perceived differently].
Just as that which is of little value is produced, so too is the living being possessed of the sense of "I."
For just as gold and other substances, when purified by means of alkaline salts and the like, regain their former value, so too does the living soul through refinement.
Having first obtained a true guru, endowed with a spirit of devotion, one performs worship, remembrance, and other rites with great intensity, regarding him as Śiva himself.
Through that realization, all impurities such as sins depart from the body; at that time, when one becomes possessed of knowledge, ignorance is destroyed.
Then, liberated from that egoism, the soul, possessing stainless intelligence, attains once again the state of Śaṅkara through the grace of Śaṅkara.
Just as one's own form is seen within the very nature of a mirror, so too does one certainly behold Śambhu, who is omnipresent.

This body of the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) shall dissolve into Śiva once it has decayed; yet, as long as the body remains subject to the force of prārabdha-karma, he is considered a man of knowledge distinct from that body.

One should not rejoice upon obtaining the auspicious, nor indeed become angry upon obtaining the inauspicious; he who possesses equanimity amidst the pairs of opposites is said to be a man of knowledge.
Either through the yoga of the self or through the discernment of the principles, one who desires liberation should depart from the body as if departing from a mere physical frame.
Sadāśiva dissolves, as does liberation and even Viraha; likewise, his root is knowledge, as well as spiritual realization and devotion to Śiva.
From devotion, love is said to arise; from love, likewise, listening [to the scriptures]; from listening, association with the virtuous; and from association with the virtuous, the wise guru.
When such knowledge is perfected, one certainly becomes liberated; therefore, whoever possesses that knowledge should always worship Śambhu alone.
Furthermore, one should worship Śambhu with exclusive devotion; at the end, one attains liberation—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, there is no deity superior to Śaṅkara for the attainment of liberation; by taking refuge in him alone, one turns away from the cycle of worldly existence.
Thus, O Brahmins, having deliberated upon these various words of mine and those spoken by the assembled sages, you should retain them with effort through your intellect.
First it was given by Śambhu to Viṣṇu in the presence of the Liṅga; Viṣṇu gave it to Brahmā, and Brahmā gave it to Sanaka and the others.
Then that knowledge was proclaimed to Nārada by Sanaka and the others; it was told to Vyāsa by Nārada, and by him, the compassionate one, it was told to me.
Both by me and by you, for the sake of the world, that which brings about the attainment of Śiva must be established with great effort.
Thus has that which I was asked been fully declared, O lords of sages; it must be guarded with great effort. What else do you wish to hear?
Vyāsa said: Having heard this, the sages attained supreme bliss; bowing down with voices faltering with joy, they praised him repeatedly.

The sages said: O disciple of Vyāsa, salutations to you! You are blessed, the most excellent among the devotees of Śiva. You have caused us to hear the supreme reality, the unsurpassed knowledge of Śiva.
Indeed, the delusion of our minds has vanished through your compassion; we are satisfied, having obtained from you the auspicious knowledge that grants liberation.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, this should not be told to an atheist, nor to one lacking faith, nor to a rogue, nor to one who is not a devotee of Maheśa, nor to one who does not wish to listen.
Having repeatedly examined the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Vedas, and Śāstras, and having extracted their essence, it was spoken to me by Vyāsa.
Upon hearing this even once, sin is indeed reduced to ashes; the non-devotee attains devotion, and for the devotee, it increases their devotion.

Furthermore, true devotion arises from hearing it again, and liberation occurs when it is heard yet again; therefore, those who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation should cause it to be heard repeatedly.
Five repetitions should be performed with the supreme fruit as the objective; one attains that without a doubt—this indeed is the word of Vyāsa.
Indeed, it is not difficult for one by whom this supreme [teaching] has been heard; by repeating it five times, the vision of Śiva is obtained.
Ancient kings, brahmins, and excellent vaiśyas, having heard this five times and reflected upon it with their intellects, attained supreme perfection.
Even today, any human being who, intent on devotion, hears this knowledge known as Śiva, shall indeed obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words, they attained supreme bliss and respectfully honored that being with various offerings.
With prostrations and hymns of praise, preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions, they—being satisfied and with their doubts dispelled—strengthened him with blessings.
Content with one another, O Sūta, those wise ones, regarding Śambhu as the supreme deity, bowed down to him and worshipped him.
This great and divine, excellent knowledge of Śiva is exceedingly dear to Śiva; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and increases devotion to Śiva.
This meritorious and supreme Saṃhitā, called the Koṭirudra, is the fourth of the Śiva Purāṇa; it has been narrated by me as a bringer of joy.
Whoever should hear this with devotion, or cause it to be heard while composed in mind, shall enjoy all pleasures here in this world and, at the end, attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Knowledge," in the Koṭirudra-saṃhitā, the fourth book within the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.

We meditate upon that auspicious, full, and eternal Brahman—the abode of names such as Brahmā and others—which, by its association with *sattva*, is attained; which sustains the seven worlds; which, endowed with qualities, is the creator resting in *rajas*; which, joined with *tamas*, is the destroyer; and which stands transcending the qualified *māyā*, being pure, infinite consciousness, and blissful truth.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, disciple of Vyāsa, salutations be unto you! You have recited the fourth collection of scriptures, known as the Rudra-saṃhitā.
Now, O Śambhu, please recount the life-story of the Supreme Soul, Sāmba, which is contained within the Upaniṣads and accompanied by various narratives.
Sūta said: O great sages, Śaunaka and the others, listen with love to this auspicious, divine account of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.
Having thus asked such a question concerning merit, Vyāsa, the best of sages, indeed recounted to Sanatkumāra the true life-story of Śiva.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, that account of the Great Lord which was told to Vāsudeva by the great sage Upamanyu is now being related by me.
In ancient times, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara, in order to perform penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
Having seen Upamanyu performing austerities there on the highest peak, that [prince], bowing with devotion and joining his palms in reverence, questioned the sage.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Upamanyu, of great wisdom, foremost among the devotees of Śiva and of noble mind, I have come here indeed to perform austerities for the sake of a son before Giriśa.
O Sage, speak of the greatness of Śaṅkara, which ever bestows bliss; having heard it with devotion, I shall perform the supreme austerity dedicated to Īśvara.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the wise Vāsudeva, Upamanyu, his soul serene, replied while remembering Śiva.
Upamanyu said: Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, great devotee of Śiva, to the majesty of the Great Lord, which I have beheld; it is the supreme increaser of devotion to Śambhu.
Established in austerity, I then beheld Śaṅkara, his weapons, and his entire retinue, including Viṣṇu and the other foremost of the immortals.
Shining with three parts, it was eternal bliss and imperishable; it had one foot and great tusks, with mouths full of flaming morsels.
It was exceedingly radiant with the light of two thousand rays, invincible against all excellent weapons, possessing many eyes and a thousand feet.
And he who surely withdraws the universe at the time of the end of the aeon—he would have no one in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, who could not be slain by him.
Released from the arm of Maheśvara, it swiftly consumed the entire three worlds, including all moving and non-moving beings, in less than half a blink of an eye; of this there is no doubt.
While established in austerity, I beheld the Unmanifest One standing by the side of Rudra; he possesses a supreme secret weapon, equal to which there is nothing greater anywhere.
That which is known as the Trident of the Wielder of the Trident throughout all the worlds is exceedingly fierce, named Vijaya, and is the destroyer of all weapons and missiles.
One might split the entire earth, dry up the great ocean, or cast down the whole wheel of the stars; of this there is no doubt.
By him was Yauvanāśva slain in former times—Māndhātṛ, the sovereign emperor of great splendor, the king who had conquered the three worlds along with his army.
The Haihaya king, possessed by pride, and the Asura Lavaṇa, having challenged King Śatrughna from all sides in battle, were cast out.
When that Daitya had been destroyed, that which had come into the hand of Rudra became a great trident with a sharp point, generating intense terror.
With his three-pronged brow furrowed, he stood as if threatening, resembling a smokeless fire like the newly risen morning sun.
With hands like the sun, he was indescribable; like the Destroyer with noose in hand, he held a sharp-edged axe and was adorned with serpents and other ornaments.

It had the appearance of the fire at the end of an eon and likewise the form of a man; it was that [missile] of the best of the Bhṛgus which, in battle, brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
Relying upon that very strength of Rāma, the sage Śivadatta, filled with joy, formerly consumed the constellation twenty-one times.
I beheld the Lord in human form, possessing the Sudarśana discus, a thousand faces, two thousand arms, and all-pervading power.
With two thousand blazing eyes and a thousand feet crowding together, resembling ten million suns, he is capable of consuming the three worlds.
A vajra, greatly blazing, sharp, and unsurpassed by even a hundred joints; a great bow, the Pināka, together with a quiver, possessing great splendor.
He beheld a spear, a sword, and a noose, as well as a great, blazing goad, a massive divine mace, and various other weapons.
And likewise, all those weapons belonging to the world-protectors which I beheld were at the side of the blessed Lord Rudra.
To the left of the god is Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, seated upon a divine celestial chariot drawn by swans that follows the speed of thought.
On his very left side, Nārāyaṇa stands mounted upon Vainateya, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, and the deities beginning with Śakra—all indeed proceeded together.
Skanda, taking up his spear and standing upon his peacock with his bell, stationed himself near the Goddess like a second Fire-god.
Nandī, having taken up his trident, stood at the summit of existence (bhavāgra); likewise, all the hosts of spirits and various Mothers were stationed there.
Having saluted Maheśāna and surrounded him on all sides, the gods then praised Mahādeva with various hymns of praise.
Whatever is seen or heard in this world, all that I beheld in the presence of the Blessed One; I was utterly amazed.
Resorting to great fortitude and with palms joined in reverence, I became immersed in supreme bliss through various hymns of praise, O Kṛṣṇa, during my sacrifice.
Having beheld Śaṅkara face to face, I worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with a voice faltering with tears, endowed with deep faith.
Then the Blessed One, Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, being well-pleased, spoke to me with affection in sweet words, as if smiling.
O Brahmin, you cannot be turned away by me again and again; you have been tested—blessings upon you—you are firm and endowed with devotion.
Therefore, I am well-pleased with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows! There is nothing among all the gods that is difficult to obtain or that cannot be granted to you.
Having heard those words of Śambhu, which were filled with true affection, I joined my palms in reverence and spoke to that Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees.
Upamanyu said: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if my devotion toward you is firm, by that truth may knowledge concerning the three periods of time arise within me."
Grant me abundant and unwavering devotion toward you, and may there always be an abundance of milk-rice for me and my lineage.
O Lord, may Your presence be with me constantly in this hermitage; may there always be mutual friendship between You and Your devotees.
O scion of the Yadu dynasty, having been addressed thus by me, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, laughed and, looking at me quickly with a compassionate glance, spoke to me.
Śrī Śiva said: "O sage Upamanyu, my dear child, you shall be freed from the defects born of old age and death; may you be endowed with all your desires."
Worthy of worship by the sages and endowed with the wealth of fame, he shall possess virtue, beauty, merit, and sovereignty at every step through my grace.
O Sage, the presence of the Ocean of Milk, that reservoir of waters, shall be with you there eternally, wherever you may desire to go.
That milk, being of the nature of nectar, is churned; then, you shall behold this Vaivasvata Kalpa together with your kinsmen.
"By my grace, let your lineage indeed be eternal; O great sage, I shall maintain my presence in your hermitage forever."
"May my devotion, however, remain steadfast; I shall always grant you my vision. And when remembered by you, O child, you are dear to me in every way."
Dwell according to your desire and happiness; you should not feel longing. May everything that has been thought of reach fulfillment; there is no doubt in this.
Upamanyu said: Having spoken thus, that Blessed One, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, granted me boons as my Lord and vanished right there.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, was Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord who bestows devotion and liberation, seen by me together with his retinue.
Whatever was spoken by the wise Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, all that has been attained by me through meditative absorption upon the God of gods.
And they have directly perceived the Gandharvas and Apsarases born there; behold the Ṛṣis, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas stationed there.
Behold these delightful trees, with glossy leaves and fragrant scents, endowed with the blossoms of all seasons and always laden with flowers and fruit.
O mighty-armed one, all this universe, endowed with its various states of being, exists through the grace of the high-souled Śaṅkara, the God of gods.
By the grace of the wielder of the trident, I possess all knowledge; I know everything—past, present, and future—in its true essence.
I have beheld that God whom even the gods and the lords of the immortals do not see without having worshipped him; who else is more blessed than I?
The supreme, eternal reality is known as the Twenty-sixth; thus do the wise meditate upon the Great One, the Supreme, the Imperishable.
He who knows the ordinances of all principles, who perceives the true meaning of all principles—he alone is the Blessed Lord, the God, the Sovereign of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
The Lord created Brahmā, the cause of the world, from his own right side, and he also created Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the world from his left side.
And when the end of the kalpa had arrived, the Lord created Rudra from his heart; thereafter, he withdrew the entire world, both the stationary and the moving.
At the end of the age, Mahādeva, having become Time itself, stands devouring all beings like the fire of universal destruction.
The omniscient Lord, the self of all beings, the source of the existence of all beings, being omnipresent, dwells as one who is visible even to all the deities.
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a son, propitiate Śaṅkara; Śiva, who is affectionate toward his devotees, will soon become pleased with you.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of One's Own Destiny," in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Upamanyu within the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of the high-souled sage Upamanyu, Kṛṣṇa, in whom devotion for Mahādeva had arisen, spoke to that sage.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O sage Upamanyu, my dear father, show me your grace; tell me of those who, having propitiated Śiva, attained their desires.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, that great sage Upamanyu, the foremost of Śiva’s devotees and a treasure-house of compassion, highly praised them and replied.
Upamanyu said: "O scion of the Yadus, listen as I describe those various devotees who have indeed attained the very desires of their hearts through the propitiation of Bhava."
In ancient times, Hiraṇyakaśipu obtained from Śarva, the moon-crested Lord, sovereignty over all the gods for ten hundred thousand years.
Now, his most excellent son was the renowned Nandana; and by virtue of a boon from Śarva, he brought Indra down for ten thousand years.
O Kṛṣṇa, in that great battle in the past, even Viṣṇu’s terrible discus and Indra’s thunderbolt were shattered against his limbs.
Weapons, even those headed by the discus and the thunderbolt, could not pierce the body of that wise one in battle, for he was possessed of such extraordinary power through his righteousness.
And being oppressed by that exceedingly powerful planet, the lords of the asuras—who had received boons from the gods—violently struck at the deities.
Delighted by the pride of being the lord of the three worlds, Vidyutprabha also became the lord of all the worlds for a hundred thousand years.
Likewise, Śiva granted him ten million sons and said, "You shall be my constant attendant."
In Kuśadvīpa, the Blessed Lord Bhava, Śaṅkara, with a delighted mind, affectionately bestowed a beautiful kingdom upon him, O Vāsudeva.
In ancient times, Śatamakhā, the son of Dhātr̥, having performed penance for a thousand years, obtained from Bhava a hundred sons.
The sage renowned as Yājñavalkya, who is indeed celebrated in the Vedas, attained supreme knowledge after propitiating Mahādeva.
Furthermore, he who was named Vedavyāsa and attained incomparable fame, even he, having propitiated Śaṅkara, obtained knowledge of the three periods of time.
Having been humiliated by Indra, those Vālakhilyas obtained from Śaṅkara Garuḍa, the stealer of Soma, who is invincible to all.
All the waters had vanished due to the former wrath of Kapardin; they were brought back into circulation by the gods after they had worshipped Śarva with a skull.
Atri’s wife Anasūyā, having remained without food for three hundred years while sleeping among pestles, then obtained sons from Śarva.
She obtained Dattātreya, the sage, as well as Candra and Durvāsas; that devoted wife caused the Gaṅgā to flow at Citrakūṭa.
And Vikarṇa, O Madhusūdana, having propitiated Mahādeva, who brings happiness to his devotees, attained great perfection.
King Citrasena, possessing firm devotion, propitiated Śambhu and obtained freedom from fear from all kings as well as incomparable happiness.
Śrīkara, the son of a cowherd woman, having developed devotion for Mahādeva upon witnessing the worship offered by kings, attained supreme perfection.
O Hari, King Citrāṅgada, the husband of Sīmantinī, having plunged into the Yamunā through the grace of Śiva, did not die.
And that man of noble vows, having gone to the carpenter’s workshop and obtained his friendship, returned to his own home joyful and endowed with various kinds of wealth.
O Kṛṣṇa, his beloved wife Sīmantinī, who was devoted to the vow of the Moon, attained supreme good fortune through the grace of Śiva.
By the power of that vow, in former times, a certain son of a twice-born man became a woman out of greed, having deceitfully assumed the form of a wife.
In ancient times, the wicked and unchaste Cañcukā, having heard a discourse on dharma from a twice-born man at Gokarṇa, attained the supreme goal through devotion to Śambhu.
By the grace of his sister-in-law, the sinful Bindugu, the husband of Cañcukā, heard the Śiva Purāṇa and attained the auspicious state of Śaṅkara.
The courtesan Piṅgalā and the lowest of brahmins named Mada, having worshipped the bull of Śiva, both attained a state of supreme felicity.
A certain courtesan named Mahānandā, who was devoted to the state of Śiva, propitiated Śiva through her firm resolve and attained the supreme goal.
Kaikeyī, along with the young brahmins, respectfully invoked Śiva; indeed, by observing the vow of Śiva-Īśa, she attained supreme happiness.
And King Vimarṣaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, having indeed performed devotion to Śiva, attained the supreme goal in ancient times through the grace of Śiva.
Though he was a wicked king, sinful, addicted to many women, and base, he attained Śiva through devotion to Śiva, remaining untainted by all his actions.
A Śabara named Śaṅkara, accompanied by his wife and devoted to the vow of Śiva, attained that supreme state through devotion, being intent upon the ashes of the funeral pyre.
O Kṛṣṇa, that Caṇḍālī named Sauminī, having worshipped [the Lord] out of ignorance, attained the state of Śiva through the supreme grace of Śaṅkara.
A hunter named Mahākāla, a Kirāta who used to harm others, worshipped Śiva with devotion and attained the supreme state.
In former times, Durvāsas, the tiger among sages, by the grace of Śiva, spread his own doctrine in the world—a devotion to Śiva that bestows liberation.
And Kauśika, having propitiated Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, became a Brāhmaṇa while remaining a Kṣatriya, like a second Brahmā.
O Kṛṣṇa, having worshipped Śiva with true devotion, Virañci, the best of Śiva’s devotees, became the creator of the universe and the grandfather of all the worlds.
O Hari, the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, a long-lived and great lord, was the foremost devotee of Śiva by virtue of Śiva’s grace.
Indeed, O Kṛṣṇa, Devendra was formerly a great Śaiva who enjoyed the three worlds; by the grace of Śiva, he became the sovereign lord of all the gods.
Bali’s son Bāṇa, a great devotee of Śiva who had attained self-control through Śiva’s grace, became the leader of the universe and the lord of all.
Hari, Śakti, Dadhīca, and Maheśvara became [so] through true devotion; likewise, Rāma was indeed a devotee of Śaṅkara by virtue of Śiva’s grace.
Kaṇāda, Bhārgava, Guru, and Gautama—through devotion to Śiva, they became lords of great power.
O Mādhava, Śākalya, having purified his soul, propitiated Bhava for nine hundred years through a mental sacrifice.
The Blessed One was pleased and said: "Child, you shall become an author of treatises; your fame shall be imperishable and shall prevail throughout the three worlds."
"May your lineage be imperishable and adorned by great seers; thereafter, O best of seers, you shall become the author of Sūtras."
Thus did that best of sages indeed obtain a boon from Śaṅkara, O delighter of the Yadus, by which he became renowned throughout the three worlds and worthy of worship.
In the Kṛta age, there was a sage renowned as Sāvarṇi; he performed austerities here for six thousand years.
To him the Blessed Lord Rudra said: "O sinless one, I am truly pleased with you; you shall become a world-renowned author of this work, free from old age and death."
When Mahādeva, being of such a nature, is worshipped by those whose previous merits are most abundant, he bestows auspicious desires exactly as they are wished for.
Even with but a single mouth, I am unable to speak of all the virtues that belong to the Blessed One, even in the course of hundreds of years.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Instruction of Upamanyu," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of his, he, having reached a state of supreme wonder, spoke to that great sage Upamanyu, whose mind was tranquil.
Vāsudeva said: "O best of brahmins, you are blessed; what accomplished man is capable of praising you, for even the God of gods himself attends upon you with his presence amidst your toil?"
O tiger among sages, may that Blessed Lord Śiva grant me a vision; or at the very least, may he bestow such grace upon me.
Upamanyu said: "O Puruṣottama, by his very grace, you shall indeed behold Mahādeva before long; of this there is no doubt."
"In the sixteenth month, you shall obtain boons from Maheśvara together with his wife; O Hari, how could the Lord not grant us boons?"
"You are worthy of worship by all the deities and are always praiseworthy for your virtues. O Acyuta, I shall declare to you, who are full of faith, the mantra to be recited."
By the power of that recitation, you shall truly behold Śaṅkara; you will obtain from Maheśvara a son whose strength is equal to your own.
O Hari, perform the recitation (*japa*) of this king of mantras, "Namaḥ śivāya," which is divine, bestows all desires, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sanatkumāra said: As he was thus recounting stories centered on Mahādeva, O ascetic, eight days passed by as if they were but a single moment.
When the ninth day arrived, he was initiated by the sage and taught the great Śārva mantra from the Atharvaśiras.
Instantly he became one with matted hair and a shaven head, perfectly composed; with his body raised upon his big toe, he performed penance with his arms held upward.
When the sixteenth month had arrived, the Supreme Lord Śambhu, together with Pārvatī, being well-pleased, granted an audience to Kṛṣṇa.
The God, accompanied by Pārvatī, three-eyed and moon-crested, was being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, and worshipped by tens of millions of Siddhas.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, he was especially bowed down by gods and asuras who were humble with devotion, and he was adorned with various ornaments.
The Lord Maheśa—wonderful in every way, lovely, unborn, and imperishable—is accompanied by various hosts, is well-pleased, and is joined by his two sons.
Seeing Śaṅkara in such a state, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his eyes wide with wonder and his hands joined in reverence, bowed down with great joy and a sense of festive celebration.
Then, with various words of praise and through the medium of speech, he worshipped the Lord of Gods; bowing his head, he offered hymns of praise using the Thousand Names.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas, released a rain of flowers and uttered heart-pleasing cries of "Well done! (sādhu).
Then, having beheld the face of Pārvatī, the Lord Rudra, who is compassionate toward his devotees, being pleased with Viḍaujas, spoke to Keśava.
Śrī Mahādeva said: "I know you, Kṛṣṇa, to be my devotee, eternally firm in your vows toward me. Choose from me auspicious boons that are difficult to obtain even in the three worlds."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, Kṛṣṇa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Śambhu, the Lord of All, after bowing down to him again and again.
Kṛṣṇa said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Lord Maheśvara, I beg from you eight excellent boons, as they have been indicated by you.
May my mind be ever fixed upon your Dharma, may your great fame be unshakable, and may there be constant, steadfast devotion toward you and your proximity for me forever.
May I indeed have ten sons as the first of my progeny; and may all those enemies, arrogant in their strength, be slain by me in battle.
O Lord, may I never suffer any insult from enemies anywhere; may I become exceedingly dear even to all the yogis.
"Thus, O God of gods, grant me eight excellent boons; salutations be unto you! You alone are the Lord of all, and especially my own master."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, the Blessed Lord Bhava said to him, "Everything shall come to pass. Then the wielder of the trident spoke to him once more.
A powerful son named Sāmbo, possessed of great heroism, shall be born to you; he was indeed cursed by the sages as being like the terrible Saṃvartaka sun.
"You shall become a human being; he shall be your son. Whatever else you have requested, may you indeed obtain all of that."
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus obtained all those boons from the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa gratified him with many various kinds of hymns of praise.
Then the auspicious Pārvatī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, being pleased, spoke to the high-souled Vāsudeva, the ascetic and devotee of Śambhu.
Pārvatī said: O Vāsudeva, O Kṛṣṇa of great intelligence, O sinless one, I am pleased with you; accept from me boons that are delightful and difficult to obtain on earth.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of Pārvatī, that scion of the Yadu dynasty, with a highly pleased soul and a mind filled with devotion, spoke.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Goddess, if you are well-pleased and grant me boons, then by this penance and by this truth, may [hostility] never arise toward the Brāhmaṇas.
May I never feel hatred; may I always honor the virtuous and the twice-born; and may my mother and father remain forever satisfied with me.
Wherever I may go, may I maintain a disposition of kindness toward all living beings; and from this family onwards, may I be dear to you through the sight of you.
I would satisfy the gods, headed by the Lord of the Suras, with a hundred sacrifices, and likewise always provide for thousands of ascetics and guests.
May I always feed those purified by faith in my home with food; may there be constant joy and perfect peace together with my kinsmen.
O Goddess, O Śāṅkarī, by your grace may I become the beloved of thousands of wives, and may my desire for them never diminish.
And may their fathers in this world be speakers of truth; O Pārvatī, by your grace, may such excellent boons be granted.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words of his, the Goddess, filled with wonder, said to him: "So be it; may prosperity be yours! I am eternal and the granter of all desires."
Having granted those boons to him and having bestowed their supreme grace upon Kṛṣṇa, Pārvatī and Parameśvara vanished right there.
The lord of sages, Kṛṣṇa, considered himself to have achieved his purpose; he quickly reached the unsurpassed hermitage of the sage Upamanyu.
Then, having bowed his head there to that sage, the slayer of Keśin related to Upamanyu all that had occurred with her.
And he said to him: "O Janārdana, who else in this world besides the god Śarva could be such a great lord of charity, or so utterly unbearable in his wrath?"
O Govinda, O you of great renown, hear now of the divine sovereignty of Śambhu regarding wisdom, austerity, heroism, steadfastness, and even his station.
Having heard that, he became endowed with faith and devoted to Śambhu; he asked about the majesty of Śiva, and the lord of sages spoke to him.
Upamanyu said: Formerly, in the world of Brahmā, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara was praised with a thousand names by the high-souled Daṇḍin, a yogi devoted to Brahman.
The Sāṃkhyas recite that song, which is as extensive as a lexicon; though difficult for humans to understand, that hymn grants all desires.
Constantly remembering Śaṅkara, go home happily, O Kṛṣṇa; you shall always remain, my dear, the foremost among the hosts of Śiva’s devotees.
Having been addressed thus, Keśava Vāsudeva, after bowing to that lord of sages and mentally recollecting Śambhu, departed for Dvārakā.
Sanatkumāra said: O best of sages, having thus propitiated Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, Kṛṣṇa attained his purpose and likewise became invincible to all.
Likewise, O best of sages, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having propitiated Śiva with devotion, attained his purpose and became victorious in every respect.
O sage, in former times, having performed extensive austerities on the mountain, Rāma obtained from Śiva a bow, an arrow, a weapon, and indeed the most supreme knowledge.
Having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts and having built a bridge across the ocean, he recovered Sītā, returned home, and enjoyed the entire earth.
And likewise, Rāma Bhārgava, having propitiated the Lord through austerity and beholding his father slain by Kṣatriyas, was filled with grief.
He obtained a sharp axe and, by means of it, he incinerated those Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Invincible and immortal, that treasury of asceticism is even today constantly seen by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas as being devoted to the worship of the Liṅga.
Rāma remains on Mount Mahendra, established in austerity; at the end of the kalpa, he shall once again attain the station of a ṛṣi.
Formerly, Asita’s younger brother, a practitioner named Devala, performed austerities with the intent of seizing the very root of the universe through his affliction.
But that ascetic, having been cursed by Purandara, worshipped my Liṅga—which is unworthy of the Dharma, yet firm and bestows all desires.
The son of Cākṣuṣa Manu became a deer in the desert due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha; Gṛtsamada was likewise alone in the Daṇḍaka forest.
With devotion, he placed Śiva, who was endowed with humility, within his heart; from that, a deer-faced Gaṇa emerged, appearing like the very mouth of Death.
Having crossed over the curse, he was led to a state free from old age and death; furthermore, out of affection, Śaṅkara made him an eternal follower of Lambodara.
Śarva bestowed upon Gārgya liberation, which is difficult to attain on earth, as well as the power to move at will, the great sacred field, and the highly efficacious knowledge of time.
Śiva bestowed upon Sarasvatī the four-footed [Veda] and eternal mastery over its further shore; he did not grant her even a thousand sons as an equal match for that.
The wielder of the Pināka bow, being pleased, bestowed upon Parāśara his son Vedavyāsa, the lord of yogis, who was exempt from old age and death.
Māṇḍavya was released by Śaṅkara himself after he had granted him his life; having remained upon the tip of the stake for ten hundred thousand years, he was finally taken down.
A certain poor Brāhmaṇa, who had formerly been a householder, deposited his son Gālava in the house of his preceptor.
Or, while he was hidden in the hermitage, a mendicant came to that house; she said to her husband, "It must be someone who is certainly destitute."
"But he must be told by you: 'He is not seen, though he is dear. Even when a guest has arrived, what shall I give him while he dwells in my house?"
Once, a certain guest, emaciated and parched by hunger and thirst, said to her, "Where has your husband gone? And she [replied] to him:
"My husband has indeed spoken, but he is not seen at present. Having perceived this through his divine eye, that sage said this to her:
Remaining there as a householder in disguise, that twice-born one died; and his son, Gālava, was likewise authorized by Viśvāmitra.
Having returned home and heard his mother’s most terrible curse, he propitiated the god Śaṅkara and performed the worship dedicated to Śambhu.
Departing from his home while remembering Śaṅkara in his heart, the father then saw his son and spoke to him with palms joined in reverence.
And by the grace of Mahādeva, I have accomplished my purpose through my duty; possessing wealth and sons, I who was dead have been restored to life once more.
Thus has this been told to you in its entirety; I am not able to speak of the qualities of Śambhu, whether in brief or in detail, for even the mouths of Śeṣa would not suffice.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śiva and the Deliverance of Kṛṣṇa and Other Devotees of Śiva," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O father, O father, O highly fortunate one, you are indeed blessed, O great-minded one! This wonderful tale of Śambhu, which bestows supreme devotion, has been narrated by you."
Speak again, O Vyāsa, of the story of Śambhu in accordance with our questions; for you, disciple of Vyāsa, are omniscient and an expert in the principles of Śiva.
Sūta said: In this very manner, my preceptor Vyāsa questioned Sanatkumāra—the unborn-born, omniscient lord of sages, and devotee of Śiva.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, this auspicious narrative has been narrated concerning Śaṅkara, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who sports in various divine pastimes.
Speak again, O Mahādeva, especially regarding your majesty; my faith to hear it, O Father, increases greatly.
By that majesty of Śambhu, whoever in the world have been deluded—having had their knowledge withdrawn by his illusory power (māyā)—sport in various divine plays.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, to this auspicious and joy-bestowing narrative of Śaṅkara; by the mere hearing of it, devotion to Śiva arises.
Śiva is the Lord of all, the God who is the self of all and the seer of all; indeed, by his majesty, the entire universe is pervaded.
The supreme form of Śiva alone consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara; it is known as the self-nature of all beings, possessing three genders yet embodied in the form of the Liṅga.
There are eight wombs of the gods and the ninth which is human; there are five wombs of animals; thus, there are fourteen.
Whether past, present, or future, all things in every respect proceed from Śiva; having attained growth, they dissolve back into him.
Of Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Candra; of the gods, dānavas, and bhogins; of the gandharvas, humans, and all others whatsoever.
A relative, a friend, a teacher, a protector, one who speaks for one's welfare, a guru, a wish-fulfilling tree, a brother, a father, or a mother—these are considered to be Śiva.
Śiva, who consists of all things, is to be known by men for himself; he is higher than the highest, and that which is both beyond the supreme and yet subsequent to it cannot be described.
O Sage, that Māyā is supreme and divine, pervading everywhere; the entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is dependent upon it.
Indeed, every hero—even powerful ones such as Viṣṇu and others—has been overwhelmed by Kāma, the powerful Mind-born one, who acts as his own companion.
O lord of sages, by the power of Śiva’s māyā, Hari became infatuated with desire and repeatedly committed the violation of another's wife.
Indra, having become the husband of Gautama’s wife and being deluded by her, that evil-minded one committed a sin and then received a curse from the sage.
Even Pāvaka, the best in the world, was deluded by the Māyā of Śiva; made subject to desire through his pride, he was then uplifted by that very same [Śiva].
O Vyāsa, even the life-breath of the universe, deluded by pride and Śiva’s māyā, was formerly conquered by desire and took pleasure with another’s wife.
But the sun-god Caṇḍaraśmi, deluded by the Māyā of Śiva, became instantly overwhelmed by desire upon seeing the mare in the form of a horse.
And Candra, deluded by the māyā of Śambhu and overwhelmed by desire, abducted the preceptor’s wife; then, joined by that very [māyā], he was rescued.
Formerly, however, Mitra and Varuṇa, established in terrible asceticism, were deluded—even those two sages were bewildered by the māyā of Śiva.
Upon seeing the youthful Urvaśī, both became filled with lust; Mitra discharged his semen into a water-jar, and Varuṇa likewise into the water.
Then Vasiṣṭha, born from a water-jar, arose from Mitra; and Agastya, possessing a splendor equal to the submarine fire, was born from Varuṇa.
In ancient times, Dakṣa, the son of Brahmā, deluded by the māyā of Śambhu, desired to enjoy his own sister along with his brothers.
Indeed, Brahmā was deluded many times by the Māyā of Śiva, and he became desirous of enjoying his own daughters and those of others.
The great yogi Cyavana, too, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, sported with Sukanyā and became utterly addicted to desire.
In former times, Kaśyapa, deluded and overwhelmed by passion, approached Śiva and out of infatuation begged for the king Dhanvan’s daughter.
Garuḍa, deeply infatuated, desired to take away the maiden Śāṇḍilī; however, as soon as he was discovered by her, his wings were instantly burnt.
The sage Vibhāṇḍaka, upon seeing a woman, fell under the sway of desire; his son, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, was born of a deer by the command of Śiva.
And the sage Gautama, his mind deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śambhu, became agitated upon seeing Śāradvatī naked and took delight with her.
That ascetic held his own spilled semen in a wooden vessel (droṇī), and from that jar was born Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons.
The great yogi Parāśara, deluded by the māyā of Śiva, sported with Matsyodarī, the daughter of a fisherman and a maiden.
Then Viśvāmitra, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva, fell under the sway of desire and took pleasure with Menakā in the forest, O Vyāsa.
Having lost his senses, he indeed created a conflict with Vasiṣṭha; yet, through the grace of Śiva, he once again became that very same Brāhmaṇa.
Rāvaṇa, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, became lustful through the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva; the evil-minded one abducted Sītā and, being deluded, met his death.
Bṛhaspati, the best of sages, though self-controlled, was deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śiva; he took pleasure with his brother’s wife, and from that union Bharadvāja was born.
Thus, O Vyāsa, I have described to you the power of the illusion of the great-souled Śaṅkara; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of Śiva’s Māyā," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, salutations to you; please describe those living beings who are devoted to sin and are the cause for rebirth in the great hells.
Sanatkumāra said: Those living beings who are devoted to sin and are the causes for great hells are now described in brief; listen with attentiveness.
Mental action is fourfold: intention toward another's wife or property, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and intentness upon what ought not to be done.
Idle chatter, untruthfulness, that which is unpleasant, and backbiting behind one's back—verbal action is fourfold.
Eating what is unfit to be eaten, violence, engaging in false actions, and the appropriation of others' property—this fourfold [list] constitutes physical action.
Thus, this tenfold action, which has three means of accomplishment, has been declared; I shall further describe its divisions, the fruits of which are infinite.
Those who hate Mahādeva, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, commit a most grievous sin and are destined for the ocean of hell.
Those intoxicated ones who revile the speaker of the knowledge of Śiva, the ascetic, the gurus, and the ancestors, go to the ocean of hell.
Censuring Śiva, censuring the Guru, reviling the knowledge of Śiva, misappropriating the property of the deities, and destroying the property of the twice-born.
And those deluded ones who steal a manuscript of Śiva-knowledge—these six are said to be great sins that yield infinite fruit.
Those who, upon seeing the ritual worship of Śiva being performed, do not rejoice; who, seeing the worshipped Śivaliṅga, do not bow down nor offer praise;
Free from hesitation, they remain and take delight before Śiva and in the presence of the Guru, acting as they please and liberated from formal ritual observances.
Those who do not perform the purification and worship of the sacred site on festival days, nor properly serve their gurus while established in the yoga of action;
Those who abandon the conduct of Śiva, who hate the devotees of Śiva, and who study or write the knowledge of Śiva without having worshipped it;
They bestow [gifts] unjustly, listen to them, and recite them; they even dally with them out of greed and through the constraint of false knowledge.
They cause one to sleep at will in the unconditioned realms; and he who, having interrupted the discourse on the knowledge of Śiva, speaks of something else.
He who does not speak the truth, nor bestows gifts, and he who, being impure, speaks or listens in an impure place;
He who desires to hear the scripture without having performed worship of the guru, and who does not offer service or obey commands with a spirit of devotion;
They do not welcome those words and offer no reply; furthermore, they show indifference toward any task that is heavy or impossible to accomplish.
That evildoer who abandons his guru when he is afflicted by illness, incapacitated, about to depart for a foreign land, or oppressed by enemies;
And he who shows contempt for his wife, son, or friends—even toward such a teacher as Suvācaka, who perceives the Dharma—[is likewise reborn in hell].
O best of sages, indeed all these actions are said to be most grievous sins, equal to the reviling of Śiva.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the great sinners (mahāpātakins), and the fifth is he who associates with them.
He who, out of anger, greed, fear, or hatred, utters words that strike at the vital points of a Brahmin—a grave offense—becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā).
He who, having invited a Brahmin, does not give after having promised; and he who defames one who is faultless—that man becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā).
And he who, out of pride in his learning, humiliates a virtuous twice-born man who is merely a neutral spectator in the midst of an assembly, is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who forcibly elevates himself by means of false virtues, having even suppressed his own true qualities, is indeed a slayer of a Brahmin.
O Brahmin, he who behaves toward cows overcome by bulls or toward twice-born men in the manner one treats a preceptor, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
But he who seizes land given to the gods, the twice-born, or cows—even if it has been lost over time—is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
The seizing of the property of gods or twice-born men, or whatever is acquired by unjust means, should be known as a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
If a twice-born man, having studied the Veda, should abandon the knowledge of Brahman which is of the nature of Śiva, that fool is equal to one who drinks liquor.
Indeed, whatever vow one undertakes, whatever restraint, sacrifice, or even the abandonment of the five great sacrifices—[if one fails in these], it is equal to the drinking of liquor.
Abandoning one's father or mother, giving false testimony, lying to the twice-born, eating meat, and consuming what is forbidden to eat—[these are sins].
A virtuous person may kill innocent creatures in the forest for the sake of a twice-born, but he should not employ such killing for the sake of his own religious merit.
Those by whom fire is set upon the paths of cattle, in the forest, or in the village—these are terrible sins, equal even to the murder of a Brahmin.
The seizure of all the property of the destitute, as well as of men, women, elephants, horses, cattle, land, silver, clothing, medicinal herbs, and liquids;
If the sale of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and fine silken garments is performed by twice-born men out of ignorance, except in times of distress;
The theft of a hand-ornament is remembered as equal to the theft of gold; likewise, the failure to give daughters who are marriageable to a suitable suitor [is a grave offense].
Going to one's son, friend, or wife, as well as to one's sisters; the terrible violation of virgins, and consorting with women who drink liquor.

Sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste is recorded as equal to violating the wife of one's guru; these are declared to be great sins (mahāpātakas). Now listen to the minor offenses (upapātakas).
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Major Sins," in the Umā Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said: The misappropriation of a twice-born’s property, the violation of inheritance rights, excessive pride, extreme anger, hypocrisy, ingratitude, excessive attachment to sensual objects, meanness, envy toward the virtuous, adultery with another's wife, and the defilement of a virtuous maiden;

The elder brother who is superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him, the woman by whom he is superseded, the gift of the maiden to those two, and the officiating as priest for them both—[all these are sins].
He who destroys flower gardens belonging to the trees of Śiva’s hermitages, or who inflicts even the slightest injury upon those residing in the hermitages;
The theft of cattle, grain, or wealth, along with one's servants and retinue; likewise, the theft of base metals, grain, or cattle, as well as the defilement of water.
The sale of sacrifices, pleasure gardens, and tanks; of one's wife and children; and of pilgrimages, fasts, vows, and the rite of initiation.
They live off women’s property, utterly conquered by women, fail to protect their wives, and pursue women through deceitful means.
Not giving when the time for payment has arrived, dealing in the increase of grain, taking wealth from those who are censured, and living by fraudulent means regarding merchandise.
One who constantly wears leaves from a poisonous forest, rides a bull, performs rites of eradication and malevolent magic, takes grain, and practices as a physician;

He whose undertaking of virtuous deeds is always for the sake of enjoying the pleasures of the tongue, and who makes known his knowledge of the Vedas and so forth merely for the sake of profit; [he is a false ascetic].
The abandonment of vows such as those pertaining to Brahman, the practice of other ways of conduct, the study of false scriptures, and the reliance on dry logic.
By censuring the gods, the sacred fire, teachers, virtuous persons, and Brahmins—whether in their presence or in their absence—even before kings or provincial rulers.
Those who have abandoned the worship of ancestors and gods, those who have forsaken their own duties, the ill-behaved, the atheists, the sinful, and those who are always speakers of untruth;
