He who engages in sexual intercourse on a sacred festival day, during the daytime, in water, in a non-vaginal opening, in the wombs of animals, or in the womb of a woman during her menses;
Those who shatter one's hopes upon the acquisition of a wife, son, or friend; those who speak unpleasantly to people; those who are cruel and aware of their own transgressions.
One who breaks dikes of tanks and wells, or those of irrigation channels, or of embankments; and one who causes a breach in the cooking of those seated in a single row.
Thus, by these sins, women and men are considered secondary offenders (upapātakin). Listen as I describe to you others who are likewise joined with such [sins].
Those men who destroy the affairs of cows, Brahmins, maidens, their masters, friends, and ascetics are considered to be destined for hell.

Those who lust after the wives of others, those who point out the property of others, those who constantly steal the wealth of others, and those who give false testimony in legal scales—[these suffer].
Those who cause suffering to the twice-born, those who strike them, those who serve Śūdra women, and those who drink liquor out of desire—these are bound.

Those men who are devoted to evil, who are cruel, and even those who delight in violence, as well as those who perform acts such as giving gifts and sacrifices merely for the sake of a livelihood; [all these attain the same state].
Those who void excrement and other waste in cow-pens, near fire, in water, on roadways, in the shade of trees, on mountains, in pleasure groves, or in temples—[they incur sin].
Those who take delight in drinking wine in palaces that are but the labor of shame, who act like playful serpents, and who are intent on seeking out vulnerabilities;
Those who obstruct the path with bamboo, bricks, stones, wood, horns, or even stakes, and those who seize the boundary of another;
Those who forge official decrees, those who delight in fraudulent actions, those who deal in counterfeit cooked food and clothing, and those who engage in dishonest trade.
He who is the maker, buyer, or seller of bows, weapons, and arrows; he who is utterly merciless toward his servants; and he who is a tamer of animals.
He who quietly listens to the words of one speaking falsely is a betrayer of his master, friends, and teachers; he is a deceiver, fickle, and a rogue.
Those who eat while leaving their wives, sons, friends, children, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, their servants, guests, and kinsmen hungry;
He who eats sweet food himself but does not give it to the Brahmins should be known as one whose cooking is in vain; he is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.

Those who, having voluntarily taken up the religious observances, abandon them because their senses are unsubdued; those who have been expelled from the order of mendicancy; and those who have pierced the face of Hara.
Those cruel ones who beat the cow, those who yoke her again and again, those weaklings who do not nourish her, and those who constantly abandon her.
They oppress those who cannot endure excessive burdens and force them to carry loads; they yoke those who have not eaten and do not release those who are exhausted.
Those who do not diligently protect cows and bulls that are afflicted by burdens, thorns, or disease, and those who are distressed by hunger, are considered cow-slayers destined for hell.
Those most wicked men who are destined for the great hells are those who, being themselves like bulls, cause other bulls to be milked, and who drive barren cows.
Likewise, guests who have arrived with hope, emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, as well as those who are helpless or independent persons who have come to his house.
Those fools who do not show compassion toward those who are distressed by hunger, the wretched, children, the elderly, the emaciated, or the sick, go to the ocean of hell.
Wealth turns back at the house, and kinsmen even at the cremation ground; only one's good and evil deeds follow the departing soul.

One who keeps goats and sheep, one who keeps buffalo, one who lives by the sea, a husband of a Śūdra woman, and one who follows the livelihood of a Kṣatriya like a Śūdra—this lowest of the twice-born shall go to hell.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, goldsmiths, royal heralds, and laborers who employ deceit—all these are recorded as destined for hell.
He who, transgressing what is appropriate, collects taxes according to his own will, and even that man who delights in inflicting punishment, is cooked in hell.
That king whose subjects in his kingdom are oppressed by bribe-takers, those bought by favors, and thieves, is himself cooked in the hells.
Those twice-born ones who accept gifts from a king who acts unjustly undoubtedly go to terrible hells.
He who, having acquired wealth through unjust means, bestows it upon the twice-born, is cooked in the hells just like that king.
Sin exists for adulterers, thieves, and the fierce; it likewise exists constantly for a king who is devoted to another's wife.
One should regard a non-thief as a thief, or a thief as one who is not a thief; therefore, a king who executes anyone without investigation shall go to hell.
Clarified butter, oil, food, and drinks; honey, meat, wine, and fermented liquors; molasses, sugarcane, vegetables, milk, curd, roots, and fruits.
Grass, wood, leaves, flowers, medicinal herbs, and his own food; sandals, an umbrella, a cart, a seat, and a water-pot.
Copper, lead, tin, weapons, and water-born items such as conch shells; a physician, bamboo products, and other household utensils.
And those who, out of greed, indeed steal garments made of wool, cotton, silk, or woven thread, whether they be coarse or fine;
And other such various substances as these, even when taken away in small quantities, certainly go to the hells.
Whether it be that or whatever else, even if it is another's property as small as a mustard seed, men who steal it go to hell; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through such sins as these, immediately after the soul's departure from the body, a person shall undergo every form of bodily torment.
These people go to the realm of Yama in their very bodies by the command of Yama, being led by his most terrible messengers and suffering great misery.
For gods, animals, and humans whose minds are devoted to unrighteousness, Dharmarāja is remembered as the teacher who punishes them with various most terrible forms of execution.

For those who are devoted to the practice of restrictive observances but whose selves have stumbled through negligence, the Guru is held by the wise to be the instructor through expiations; Yama is not so regarded.
The king is declared to be the punisher of adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly; he is the King of Dharma for those who act in secret.
Therefore, one should perform expiation for the evil that has been committed; otherwise, there is no destruction of what has not been experienced even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Whoever performs an action themselves, causes it to be performed, or approves of it—whether by body, mind, or speech—the result for them is a state of suffering.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varieties of Sins," in the fifth book, the Umā-Saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Now, by means of four kinds of sins, men go to the world of Yama—all embodied beings, rendered helpless and terrified by that which is dreadful and produces great fear.

It should be understood that among all living beings, [this applies] to those dwelling in the womb, those being born, and those who are infants, youths, or middle-aged, whether female, male, or neuter.
And here, the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of embodied beings are deliberated upon by Citragupta and all others, as well as by Vasiṣṭha and his foremost associates.
There are no living beings who do not go to the abode of Yama; for whatever action has been performed must necessarily be experienced—let this be reflected upon.
Among them, those men who have performed auspicious deeds, whose minds are gentle, and who are endowed with compassion, go first to the abode of Yama by a pleasant path.
Furthermore, those who are evil-doers, sinful, and devoid of charity travel by the terrible southern path to the abode of Yama.
Beyond eighty-six thousand yojanas from here, one should know that the city of Vaivasvata is situated, existing in various forms.
It appears as if close at hand to men of meritorious deeds, yet it remains exceedingly distant for sinners who travel by a terrible path.
It was covered with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel, and constructed of stones as sharp as the edges of razors.
In some places [the path] was covered with great mud and massive heaps of sins; in other places, it was composed of darbha grass resembling iron needles.
Afflicted with suffering, they travel along a path filled with extremely rugged mountains resembling riverbanks, crowded with trees, and strewn with glowing embers.
In some places with uneven pits, in others with extremely difficult lumps of earth, with scorching sands, and likewise with sharp spikes;
In some places it was pervaded by bamboo groves spreading with many branches; in other places, the path was difficult due to darkness and lacked various supports.
In some places it was filled with sharp iron tridents, in others with forest fires; in some places with heated rocks, and in others with snow.
In some places it was filled with sand up to its neck, in some places it was covered by foul water, and in some places by the fire of chaff.
In some places there were lions, wolves, tigers, and most dreadful mosquitoes; in some places there were great leeches, and likewise in others, pythons.
In some places there were fierce flies, in others serpents with virulent poison, and in others herds of rutting elephants, intoxicated by their strength and intent on destruction.
With sharp-toothed boars scratching up the path, with buffaloes possessing sharp horns, and with all manner of predatory beasts;
Indeed, being tormented by fierce ḍākinīs, by terrifying rākṣasas, and by most dreadful diseases, they go [to their end].
Being struck by a fierce wind mixed with great dust and by a rain of massive stones, they were left without any refuge.
In some places they go being burned by the falling of lightning, and in others they are pierced on all sides by a great rain of arrows.
Indeed, they are being scorched by falling thunderbolts, by terrible falls of meteors, and by a rain of blazing coals.
Being filled by a great rain of dust, they weep; and they are terrified again and again by the terrible roars of massive clouds.
Being pierced on all sides by a rain of sharpened weapons, they also pass away as if being drenched by streams of water from a great salt ocean.
Afflicted on all sides by a wind that is exceedingly cold, harsh, and rough, they wither away and shrink.
Thus, by means of a path that was fierce, devoid of provisions for the journey, without support, difficult to traverse, and entirely waterless;
By means that were indeed treacherous and great, devoid of human refuge, of the nature of darkness, painful, and the resort of all the wicked.
All embodied beings who are deluded and performers of sinful deeds are forcibly led away by the most terrible messengers of Yama, who carry out his commands.
Alone, dependent on others, and deprived of friends and kinsmen, they grieve over their own deeds and weep again and again.
Having become hungry ghosts (pretas), they were naked, with parched throats, lips, and palates; they were unlovely, terrified by fear, burning with heat, and possessed by hunger.
Some men, with their feet turned upwards, are bound with chains and dragged by the messengers of Yama, who are exceedingly powerful.
Others, with their faces cast downward, are crushed against their chests in great agony; they are also dragged along by ropes tied to the mass of their hair.
Other embodied beings, pierced in the forehead by a goad, suffer; some lie face upwards on paths of thorns, while others are on a path of glowing embers.
With their arms bound behind them and their bellies crushed, they were filled with chains and their hands were firmly fastened.
Some are dragged by a noose around their necks and proceed in great misery; others are indeed pulled along by ropes through the insertion of a goad into their tongues.
Others are likewise dragged by means of a rope through their nostrils; some, having had their cheeks split, are dragged by a rope through them, and others through their lips.
With their feet and hands severed at the ends, with their ears, lips, and noses cut off, with their penises and testicles cut away, and with their limbs and joints mangled and split asunder.
Being struck by spears and pierced by arrows, they ran hither and thither, crying out in distress, left without refuge.
They are struck again and again with mallets and iron clubs, and with various terrible thorns that possess a radiance equal to blazing fire and the sun.
Terrified by bhindipāla missiles, men are led along helpless, oozing pus and blood, smeared with excrement and infested with worms.
Those seeking water, or being hungry and seeking food; those desiring shade, and again, those afflicted by cold seeking fire.
Thus, men who are devoid of charity go [to the abode of Yama] while merely praying for happiness; however, those who have taken the provisions of charity set out happily toward the realm of Yama.
When they have thus reached the city of the pretas through such painful means, they are then presented by the messengers and stationed before Yama.
There, Yama honors those who have performed virtuous deeds with a welcome, the offering of a seat, water for the feet, the respectful arghya-offering, and pleasant words.
Blessed are you, O great-souled ones, who act in accordance with the scriptures; for by you, for the sake of divine bliss, meritorious deeds have been performed.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot adorned with the enjoyments of divine women, go to the stainless heaven endowed with all objects of desire.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there until the exhaustion of your merit, you shall then experience whatever small amount of evil remains here once again.
Those men who are righteous in nature, who regard their friends as themselves, perceive gentleness and happiness, as well as the very sovereignty of the King of Dharma.
Furthermore, those of cruel deeds behold him as terrifying, with a face formidable with fangs and eyes crooked with a frown.
With hair standing on end, a great beard, and his lower lip quivering upward, he has eighteen arms, is wrathful, and resembles a mass of black collyrium.
With hands raised holding all kinds of weapons, threatening with every staff, mounted upon a great buffalo, and possessing eyes like blazing fire.
Wearing red garlands and garments, as lofty as Mount Meru, with a roar like the clouds at the end of an aeon, he seemed as if drinking up the great ocean.
He appeared like the king of mountains covered in mist, or as if vomiting fire; and Death himself stood nearby, possessing a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
Kāla, resembling collyrium, and the terrifying Kṛtānta; Mārīcī, Ugrā, Mahāmārī, and the dreadful Kālarātri.
Various diseases and leprosy of many forms are terrifying; [the demons] hold spears, tridents, and goads, with nooses, discs, and swords in their hands.
The Rudras, bearing adamantine beaks, carry razors, quivers, and bows; all of them are great heroes, wielding various weapons and inspiring fear.
Innumerable great heroes, with a luster like black collyrium, holding all kinds of weapons aloft in their hands, were the terrifying messengers of Yama.
Surrounded by this retinue, the most wicked sinners behold Yama, who is terrible to behold, as well as the fearsome Citragupta.
Yama severely rebukes those of evil deeds, and the venerable Citragupta awakens them with words of dharma.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Path to the World of Hell and the Nature of Yama’s Messengers," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Citragupta said: "O you performers of evil deeds, stealers of others' property, arrogant because of your beauty and prowess, and violators of the wives of others!
This very action that is performed is what is experienced again; so why have you committed this evil deed for the sake of destroying yourselves?
Now, why do you lament while being tormented by your own actions? Let your own deeds be experienced; for there is no fault attributable to anyone else.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus those protectors of the earth arrived in his presence, arrogant due to the power of their wicked deeds and their own terrible actions.
The great lord Citragupta, who knows the Dharma, being filled with wrath, likewise instructs them according to the instruction of King Yama.
Citragupta said: "O kings, you who are of wicked conduct and destroyers of your subjects! For the sake of a kingdom lasting but a short time, why have you committed such evil deeds?"
O kings, now experience the fruit of that [karma] whereby you punished the subjects through royal indulgence, delusion, force, and injustice.
Where is that kingdom and where is that wife for whose sake evil was committed? Having abandoned all of that, you now stand here alone.
I see that power destroyed by which the subjects were devastated; now, being joined with the messengers of Yama, what will it become?
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Yama with many kinds of words, those kings, reflecting upon their own deeds, remained silent in sorrow.
Having thus pointed out the deeds of kings, Yama, the King of Dharma, spoke these words to his messengers for the sake of purifying the mire of their sins:
King Yama said: "O Caṇḍa and Mahācaṇḍa, having seized these kings by force, purify them through the prescribed rites in the fires of hell in due order."

Sanatkumāra said: Then, quickly seizing the kings by their feet and whirling them with great force, he lifted them up and cast them down upon a vast, exceedingly heated surface of stone; there they were violently dashed, like great trees struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, being shattered by the ear, the embodied soul flows out with blood; deprived of consciousness, he becomes forever motionless.
Then, touched by the wind, he is revived once more; thereafter, for the sake of purifying his sins, they cast him into the ocean of hell.
Twenty-eight crores below the earth, situated at the end of the seventh level in terrible darkness, [is Raurava].
The first level is called Ghorā; below that is Sughorā; then Atighorā, Mahāghorā, and Ghorarūpā as the fifth.
The sixth is called Talātala, and the seventh is Bhayānakā; the eighth is Kālarātri, and the ninth is Bhayotkaṭā.
The tenth is Caṇḍā below that, and Mahācaṇḍā further below; then there is another, Caṇḍakolāhalā, as well as Pracaṇḍā and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Padmā, Padmāvatī, Bhītā, Bhīmā, Bhīṣaṇanāyikā, Karālā, Vikarālā, and Vajrā are remembered as the twenty.

The triangular and the five-cornered [forms] bestow all suffering; the very long one is formidable and fierce; the equal-sided one possesses terrible strength; and the last is known as the blazing flame.
Thus have those twenty-eight terrible hells been described to you by name; they consist of torments for the wicked.
The leaders of these [families] are to be known in sequence as five for each; learn their names individually for all the millions.
Raurava is the first among them, where embodied beings cry out; and due to the torments of Mahāraurava, even the great weep.
Then, Śīta, as well as Uṣṇa, are known as the first five leaders; Sughora, Mahātīkṣṇa, and likewise Saṃjīvana are recorded.
Mahātama, Viloma, Vilopa, Kaṇṭaka, Tīvravega, Karāla, Vikarāla, and Prakaṃpana.
Mahāvakra, Kāla, Kālasūtra, Pragarjana, Sūcīmukha, Suneti, Khādaka, and Suprapīḍana;
Kumbhīpāka and Supāka, the most dreadful Krakaca, the abode of heaps of burning coals, Meru, and then Asṛkprahita.
And there is the bird with a sharp beak, Mahāsaṃvartaka, Kratu, Taptajaṃtu, Paṅkalepa, and Pratimāṃsastrapūdbhava.
Ucchvāsa, Sunirucchvāsa, Sudīrgha, Kūṭaśālmali, Duriṣṭa, Sumahāvāda, Pravāda, and Supratāpana.
Then there were Megha, Vṛṣa, Śālma, and those with the faces of lions, tigers, and elephants; as well as those with the faces of dogs, boars, kings of buffaloes, owls, cuckoos, and wolves.
Those known as Grāha, Kumbhīna, and Nakra; those called Sarpa, Kūrma, and Vāyasa; those named Gṛdhra, Ulūka, and Haloka; and Śārdūla, Kratha, and Karkaṭa.
Maṇḍūka, Pūtivaktra, Raktākṣa, Pūtimṛttika, Kaṇadhūmra, Agni, and Kṛmigandhivapu.
Agnīdhra, Apratiṣṭha, Rudhirābha, Śvabhojana, Lālā, Bhekṣa, Aṃtrabhakṣa, and the most terrible Sarvabhakṣa.
Kaṇṭaka, Suviśāla, Vikaṭa, Kaṭapūtana, Ambarīṣa, Kaṭāha, and the terrible river Vaitaraṇī.
The bed of well-heated iron where one stands on a single leg until it is filled; the terrible forest of black palm trees where bones are shattered and the body is completely filled.
Vilāta, Asuyaṃtra, Kūṭapāśa, Pramardana, Mahācūrṇa, Sucūrṇa, and likewise that which consists of heated iron.
Parvata, Kṣuradhārā, and likewise Yamalaparvata; Mūtra-viṣṭhā-aśru-kūpa, Kṣārakūpa, and Śītala.
The machine of pestle and mortar, the stone, the cart, and the plow; the thicket of palm leaves and swords, and the great pavilion of carts.
Delusion, the breaking of bones, being heated, molten iron, and molasses; great suffering, immense affliction, impurity, and defilement from filth.
Hālāhala, Virūpa, Svarūpa, Yamānuga, Ekapāda, Tripāda, Tīvra, and Acīvaratama.
These twenty-eight [Buddhas] consist of five groups of five in sequence; in their proper order, there are exactly five leaders for each group of ten million.
One hundred hells are recorded, beginning with Raurava; the circle of great hells is said to consist of one thousand four hundred.
Thus, O Vyāsa, I have fully described to you the state of hell; now hear that path of sin and the detachment resulting from such enumeration.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Hell," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: In these [hells], sinners are intensely cooked and withered by the fires of hell, undergoing various tortures until the exhaustion of their own karma.
Just as metals are purified in fire through the removal of their own impurities, so too, upon the destruction of their sins, sinful men are purified there according to their respective karma.
Then, having bound their hands tightly with chains, the servants of Yama hang them from the branches at the tops of great trees.
Then, being swung with all their might by the servants, they sway; and as they swing with extreme velocity, they become unconscious and travel for a yojana.
Furthermore, for those situated in the intermediate space, a hundred loads of iron are bound to their feet by the mighty messengers of Yama.
Severely struck by that great burden, the men reflect upon their own past deeds; they remain silent and motionless.
Then, those evildoers are struck from all sides by the terrible servants with goads the color of fire and with fierce iron clubs.
Then, they are repeatedly smeared all over with a blazing caustic substance, even more intense than fire.
With their limbs cut and shattered by the extremely sharp arrows, their bodies were torn apart again in succession, beginning from the head.
They are cooked like eggplants in heated iron cauldrons, and likewise in a well filled with excrement and a swarm of worms.
Furthermore, they are thrown into a pond filled with fat, blood, and pus; there they are devoured by sharp worms and by crows with iron beaks.
They are devoured by dogs, gadflies, wolves, and tigers with fierce and deformed faces, and they are cooked like fish upon heaps of blazing charcoal.
Men are pierced by sharp spears due to their sinful deeds, and are crushed in oil-presses because of their own terrible actions.
Like sesame seeds, the masses of people are crushed in the place called Cakra; and they are roasted in many ways within iron vessels heated by the scorching sun.
Again and again, their tongues are cooked in many ways within cauldrons filled with oil and heated to a fierce boil; they are then crushed against their chests and feet.
And here, there are great torments for the body in every respect; thus, men pass through all the hells one after another in succession.
And in all the hells, O Vyāsa, various torments of Yama are inflicted by the agents of Yama upon every limb, causing extreme suffering.
Taking glowing embers, he fills his mouth and strikes it; then, again and again, with caustic lye and molten copper.
Then, having squeezed that face here and there and filled it thoroughly with extremely heated ghee or oil, it is struck.
Filled here and there with excrement and worms, they embrace the most fierce and blazing iron śālmalī tree.
Then, at the back of their necks, they are further tormented by blazing, massive clouds, by jagged saws, and by powerful plows.
They are tormented from the head downwards by their own terrible deeds; they devour their own flesh and drink their own blood.
Those who always nourish only themselves and have never given food or drink will be crushed like sugarcane, being pounded to pieces with hammers.
In the terrible Asitāla forest, they are then cut into pieces; their entire limbs pierced by needles, they are impaled upon the points of heated spikes.
Though they are moved about many times and suffer greatly, they do not die; likewise, their bodies are capable of enduring both pleasure and pain.
The flesh is torn from their bodies by the fierce messengers of Yama, who are formidable in strength and have the terrifying forms of fanged beasts, as they strike with their own mallets.
In the Nirucchvāsa hell, men remain for a long time without breathing; likewise, in the Vālukāsadana hell, they are beaten while gasping for breath.
In the Raurava hell, they are tormented by various forms of slaughter while weeping; even the great beings cry out due to the agonies of the Mahāraurava hell.
In their feet, mouth, anus, head, eyes, and crown, they are struck with heavy, sharp, and intensely heated iron spikes.
They are repeatedly cast upon well-heated sand, and when thrown into the intensely heated mire of living beings, they cry out discordantly.
O Sage, likewise, the sinners of cruel deeds are cast into the Kumbhīpāka hells and into boiling oils, which are altogether unbearable.
Those sinners are cast into the Lālābhakṣa hells, which are indeed sources of suffering; they are cooked again and again in various places within the hells.
The sinful man, devoid of merit, is cast into the hell of Great Affliction with Needle-Mouths, where he is beaten by the servants of Yama.
Cast into iron cauldrons, sighing very slowly, human beings are cooked by a great fire on account of their own sins alone.
Bound tightly with ropes and other means, they are crushed against rocks; they are cast into blind wells and bitten violently by bees.
With all their limbs pierced by worms and shattered in a hundred ways, they are thereafter cast into pits of extremely sharp caustic lye.
In this hell of great flames, the sinners, tormented by suffering, cry out; being scorched by its fire, they run hither and thither.
Having brought it onto his back, with its two snouts placed upon his shoulders and joined there, he pulled it firmly between them by means of his forearms and back.
All of them, having been tightly bound together by the ropes of sin, are seen as a single mass within the great flames of torment.
Bound with ropes and smeared with mud, they are cooked in fires of dried cow-dung and chaff, yet they do not die.
For those wicked ones have practiced extremely sharp conduct upon harsh rocks; having been crushed there hundreds of times, they are then cooked like blades of grass.
Men are intensely devoured by numerous worms with sharp mouths residing within their bodies until the destruction of their own physical frames.
Cast into heaps of worms and upon piles of pus, flesh, and bones, they remain with agitated hearts, crushed between two mountains.
Their bodies were smeared with molten vajra-ointment, and with their faces downward and feet upward, they were scorched by fire.
Dependent on others, they are made to eat a fiercely heated iron chain that has been thrust into their mouths; they are beaten by them with hammers.
Thus, O Vyāsa, those of evil deeds indeed cook in the hells; I shall now describe for you the state of those doers of action, according to their true nature.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The General Description of the Path to Hell," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: But he who has set out upon a false path goes to the hell named Dvijihva; there he is tormented by sharp ploughs as wide as half a krośa, drawn by his own tongues.
The cruel one who reviles his mother, father, or teacher is struck down after having his mouth filled with excrement mixed with worms.
Those men who flee from temples of Śiva, groves, ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as from the dwellings of the twice-born, take pleasure in those very places.
Intoxicated by passion, they indulge in anointing with unguents, massage, bathing, drinking water, eating, sporting, sexual union, and gambling.
They are crushed by various tortures, such as being pressed in sugarcane mills and the like; they are cooked in the fires of hell until the dissolution of all beings.
In that very same form, adulterers are beaten; they are made to embrace tightly a woman fashioned of intensely heated iron.
And men with their former forms blaze forth on all sides; they tightly embrace a woman of evil conduct and weep.
For those who listen to the censure of the virtuous, their ears shall be filled with red-hot iron pegs and nails made of copper and other metals, glowing like fire.
One should repeatedly apply water from the sap of the trapuṣī fruit, milk, well-heated sharp oil, or even diamond-paste (vajralepa).
Having filled the ears in succession, these torments in the hells arise in due order throughout all of them on every side.
In this same way, through each of the sense organs and by means of the body that was committed, there arise, in succession, terrible torments on account of evil deeds.
Those fools who, out of the fault of touch, violate another's wife, their hands are completely filled with ashes glowing like fire.
Their bodies are smeared with all [substances] such as caustic lye and the like, and they undergo most agonizing torments in all the hells.
Those men who knit their brows at their parents have their peaceful faces violently pierced by spikes.
By whichever senses men commit adultery with another's wife, those very senses of theirs they likewise cause to become disordered.
Those who, being greedy, look upon the wives of others with a fixed gaze, have their eyes filled with needles glowing like fire.
O tiger among sages, all the torments of Yama occur right here in this world through [the application of] caustics and so forth in succession; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Those who eat without first offering [food] to the gods, the fire, the guru, and the brahmins, have their tongues and mouths filled with hundreds of heated iron spikes.
Those men who, out of greed, pluck the flowers of the divine groves with their hands, smell them repeatedly, and even wear them upon their heads;
Their heads are filled with heated iron spikes, and then their noses are violently pierced with very thick ones, followed by caustic substances and the like.
Those who revile the Great Soul, the reciter, the teacher of Dharma, those devoted to the gods, the fire, and the guru, and the eternal scripture of Dharma—[they go to hell].
Upon their chests and throats, on their tongues and the junctions of their teeth, on their palates, lips, noses, heads, and all the joints of their limbs—
Red-hot iron spikes, glowing like fire and having three prongs, are repeatedly driven into these various spots with mallets.
Then, indeed, it is filled on all sides with blazing caustic; moreover, there are truly great torments for the body everywhere.
Furthermore, those who seize the property of others and touch a Brahmin with their feet wander, one after another, through all the hells without exception.
The implements of Śiva, a cow, and whatever is written concerning knowledge and so forth—their hands, feet, and other limbs are filled on all sides by these.
And in all the hells, there are manifold and grievous bodily torments arising from the hands and feet that occur repeatedly.
Those wicked people who discharge feces and urine anywhere within the precincts of a temple of Śiva or in divine groves [are guilty].
Their penis, along with the testicles, is crushed with iron hammers; then their anus is filled once again with needles glowing like fire.
Then, the anus and the penis of the embodied being are repeatedly and intensely filled with a great, sharp, and flowing caustic alkali.
Since suffering arises for the mind and all the senses because of those who, despite possessing wealth, do not bestow gifts due to craving;
And he who disregards a guest when the proper time has arrived while living the life of a householder—therefore, having incurred that evil deed, they go to an impure hell.
Those who eat after giving food, yet do not first offer it to dogs and crows, their mouths shall be forced open and struck by two stakes.
It is tormented within by worms, fierce creatures, and iron-beaked crows, as well as by many kinds of violent afflictions.
To Śyāma and Śabala, who follow the path of Yama—to those two I offer this; may they accept this bali-offering.
May those crows who belong to Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and Nirṛti—those crows of meritorious deeds—accept this offering from me.
Having worshipped Śiva with effort and offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rites, those who offer the bali-offering with Śaiva mantras do not go to Yama.
They behold the third heaven and go there; therefore, one should offer [this] day after day, having prepared a square mandala scented with perfumes and other substances.
One should offer to Dhanvantari in the northeast, to Indra in the east, to Yama in the south, and to Sudakṣa and Umā in the southwest.
Having first offered to the ancestors, he should then cast [the offerings] toward the east for Aryaman; he should place those for Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the doorway.

One should scatter [the remains] on the ground for dogs, for those who feed on dog-flesh, and for birds; as well as for the gods, the ancestors, human beings, the deceased (pretas), spirits (bhūtas), and the guhyakas.
The householder is sustained by birds, worms, and insects; [he is the vessel for] the utterance of *svāhā*, the utterance of *svadhā*, and thirdly, the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
Likewise, another is the *haṃtakāra*; the cow has four udders: the gods [suckle] from the *svāhākāra* udder, and the ancestors likewise from the *svadhā* udder.
Likewise, other gods and the lords of beings drink the Vaṣaṭ-call, while humans constantly drink the Haṃta-call; thus they praise [the Lord].
That man who, with faith, constantly performs this sequential rite for the cow at the proper time, is prepared for the state of maintaining the sacred fires.
He who, being healthy, abandons that [offering] sinks into the Tāmisra hell; therefore, having offered the bali to them, one standing at the door should reflect for a moment.
One should properly feed with wholesome food, according to one's ability and from one's own meal, a guest afflicted by hunger who resides in the same village.
When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, he transfers his own misdeeds to that person and departs taking away their merit.
Then, eating only food that is dear to him, the man becomes once again bound by chains; pierced here by the force of his own tongue, he remains for a long time.
For they tear out that flesh from me, even in pieces the size of sesame seeds, and having pierced it, they give their blood for them to eat.
Furthermore, he is gradually tormented by whips until nothing remains; indeed, he undergoes extreme suffering from hunger as well as from thirst.
Such are the most terrible torments for those of evil deeds; now hear in brief that which they experience at the end.
Listen to the state of those two: one who commits a great sin but practices dharma even slightly, and one who practices dharma that is very weighty.
The fruit of his good deeds is not mentioned here due to the influence of his teacher's sin; he does not experience happiness there, even though endowed with many enjoyments.
Likewise, being agitated and intensely tormented, he finds no pleasure in foods day after day, as there is a lack of anything else before him in every kalpa.
A man who follows the dharma of his preceptor, even while fasting like a householder, being wealthy and established in his observances, does not experience suffering.
Those terrible sins exist by which a man on earth undergoes a hundredfold shattering, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Experience of the State of Hell," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: "O Lord, men who have committed sins travel along the path of Yama endowed with great suffering; tell me those dharmas by which they may find happiness."

Sanatkumāra said: "Indeed, whatever action has been performed must necessarily be experienced without hesitation; whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. Now, I shall describe those dharmas that bestow happiness."
In this regard, those men who have performed auspicious deeds, whose minds are gentle, and who are endowed with compassion, travel by way of happiness along the terrifying path of Yama.
That man who gives wooden sandals as footwear to the best of the twice-born goes happily to the abode of Yama by means of a great horse.
By the gift of an umbrella, embodied beings proceed as if under an umbrella; by the gift of a palanquin, one shall travel happily in a chariot.

By the gift of beds and seats, one goes with ease and finds perfect rest; those who provide shade for groves or plant trees along the road travel to the realm of Yama with their fatigue entirely dispelled by the cool shade.
Those men who create flower gardens travel by means of a flower-chariot; those who build temples for the gods sport within the interior of a celestial palace.
Furthermore, those who were the builders of the hermitages for ascetics and the pavilions for the destitute now sport within the interiors of houses.
Those men who worship the gods, the sacred fire, their gurus, the brahmins, and their mother and father, proceed at will according to their pleasure, being honored by all.
Those who give lamps go forth illuminating all directions; by the gift of shelter, they go happily, free from ailment.
Men who serve their gurus proceed with ease; those who give musical instruments and food to Brahmins go happily to their own homes.
Just as those who give cows travel with all their desires fulfilled, so too does a man obtain on his journey the food and drink given here.
By providing water for washing the feet, one may travel along a path made of water; and he who performs an oil massage of the feet travels upon the back of a horse.
O Vyāsa, Yama does not approach that person who always provides washing for the feet, as well as oil massage, a lamp, food, and shelter.
By the gift of gold and jewels, he crosses over difficulties; by the gift of silver, an ox, and a garland, he goes to the world of Yama with ease.
By means of such gifts as these, men go happily to the abode of Yama, and in heaven they always obtain various enjoyments.
Among all gifts, the gift of food is remembered as supreme; it provides immediate gratification, is pleasing to the heart, and increases strength and intelligence.
O best of sages, there is no gift equal to the gift of food; from food all beings arise, and in its absence they die.
Blood, flesh, fat, and semen increase in sequence from food; from semen beings are born; therefore, the world consists of food.
Even when all these things—gold, jewels, horses, lordly elephants, women, garlands, sandalwood, and so forth—are obtained, those who are hungry do not find delight in them.
Those dwelling in the womb, those being born, children, the elderly, and those of middle age—even gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas—all long for food.
Hunger is considered the foremost of all diseases; it is destroyed in this world by the medicine of food, without a doubt.
There is no suffering equal to hunger; there is no disease equal to hunger. There is no happiness equal to health; there is no enemy equal to anger.
Therefore, the gift of food is proclaimed to be of great merit; likewise, all embodied beings die when tormented by the fire of hunger.
The giver of food is declared to be the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything; therefore, by the gift of food, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
Of the merit accumulated by one whose limbs are nourished by another's food and drink, half belongs to the giver of the food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever jewels, enjoyments, women, and vehicles exist in the three worlds, the giver of food shall obtain all of them both in this world and the next.
The body is the supreme means for attaining virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; therefore, one should preserve one's own body with food and drink.
They praise food alone, for everything is established upon it; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to that of food.
O Sage, this entire universe is sustained by food; food provides vigor in the world, for the vital breaths are established in food.
Food must be given by a monk, even at the expense of his own household, to a high-souled Brahmin who desires his own prosperity.
He who gives food to a needy person, specifically to a Brāhmaṇa in distress, provides for himself the most excellent treasure pertaining to the world beyond.
Seeking prosperity, a householder should honor at the proper time a twice-born guest who has arrived at his home, weary from the road and seeking sustenance.
O Vyāsa, one who gives food, is well-behaved, and free from envy, having abandoned rising anger, attains great happiness both in heaven and here on earth.
One should not disparage what has been acquired, nor should one ever reject it; even when given to an outcaste or a dog, a gift of food is never lost.
He who gives food, free from affliction, on the road to one who is weary and has never seen such hospitality before, shall attain prosperity.
O great sage, that man who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and guests with food reaps a vast fruit of merit.
Food and drink are distinguished neither by whether one is a Śūdra nor by whether one is a Brāhmaṇa; one should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or even his country.
Whatever man here gives food to one who has been begged by a brahmin goes to the supreme heaven for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
And for the giver of food, trees endowed with the fruits of all desires arise here on earth, just as the brahmins are filled with joy in the third heaven.
O Sage, listen, O great sage, to those most divine worlds fashioned in heaven for the giver of food by virtue of his gift of food.
The palaces of those great-souled ones shine in the heavens, possessing various forms and structures, and endowed with every variety of desired objects.
Furthermore, trees that yield all desired fruits stand within the dwellings; there are auspicious golden ponds, wells, and oblong lakes on every side.
And they proclaimed thousands of auspicious drinks, as well as mountains consisting of various kinds of food, garments, and ornaments.
Rivers flow with milk, and likewise there are mountains of clarified butter; the palaces have a white luster, and the couches shine with gold.
They go to those who give food; therefore, one should become a giver of food if one desires one's own welfare in this world and in the next.
These worlds of great splendor belong to those who perform meritorious deeds and give gifts of food; therefore, food must certainly be given by men with special care.
Food is Prajāpati himself; food is Viṣṇu; food is Hara himself. Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to that of food.
Even after committing a very great sin, he who subsequently becomes a giver of food is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
Food, drink, horses, cattle, clothing, beds, umbrellas, and seats—these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the hungry ghosts (preta).
Since a person goes to the city of the King of Dharma by means of a celestial chariot through such a distinction of giving, one should therefore practice generosity.
Whoever reads this faultless narrative concerning the power of the gift of food, or causes others to read it, shall become prosperous.
O great sage, whoever should listen to or cause others to hear this during a śrāddha ceremony, for that person there shall be an inexhaustible gift of food that reaches the ancestors.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Gift of Food," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: The gift of water is always the supreme among gifts, the most excellent; it is remembered as the satisfaction and the very life of all multitudes of living beings.
Therefore, one should provide water-stations without restriction out of great affection; the construction of reservoirs for water brings about great bliss.
In this world or in the next, truth is indeed truth; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, a person should cause step-wells, wells, and tanks to be constructed.
A well that constantly provides flowing water removes half the sin of a person who has committed a wrongful act.
He whose reservoir is dug always delivers his entire lineage, for cows, Brahmins, and virtuous men always drink from it.
He for whom water remains available without restriction during the heat of summer will never encounter a difficult, treacherous, or arduous situation.
And I shall describe the virtues that are traditionally ascribed to constructed reservoirs: one who possesses a reservoir is honored everywhere throughout the three worlds.
Alternatively, the construction of tanks in the abode of a friend is excellent; it is friendly, free from distress to friends, and generates great renown.
The wise say that the fruit of dharma, artha, and kāma is obtained by one who constructs a reservoir for meritorious deeds; his merit is infinite.
A pond is the supreme refuge for the four kinds of living beings; all such things as ponds bestow the highest prosperity.
Gods, humans, gandharvas, ancestors, nagas, rakshasas, and even immobile beings take refuge in a reservoir of water.
"The Self-born One has declared that for him whose water remains in a pond during the rainy season, there arises the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice."
In the autumn season, for him whose water remains in a pond, there shall be the fruit of a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
He in whose [tank] water remains during both the winter and the cool season indeed obtains the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
The wise say that for one whose water remains during both spring and summer, there is the fruit of the Atirātra and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
O Sage Vyāsa, now hear the merits of planting trees; the fruit of constructing reservoirs has been described as the supreme gratification of living beings.
One who plants trees in a wilderness saves all the ancestors of one’s lineage, both past and future; therefore, one should indeed plant trees.
In that regard, these trees become his sons; of this there is no doubt. Having gone to the higher world, he too attains imperishable realms.
With their flowers they worship all the hosts of gods, with their fruits likewise the ancestors, and with their shade all guests—the trees thus perform worship.
Kinnaras, uragas, rakshasas, gods, gandharvas, and humans, as well as hosts of sages, likewise take refuge in trees.
Those who are like flowering and fruit-bearing trees, satisfying human beings both in this world and in the next, are considered sons according to the Dharma.
The twice-born who constructs a pond, the one who plants trees, and the one who performs sacrifices with devotion—these, as well as others who speak the truth, do not fall from heaven.
Truth alone is the supreme Brahman; truth alone is the supreme austerity; truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme sacred learning.
Truth awakens while others sleep; truth is the supreme state. By truth alone is the earth supported; everything is established in truth.
From that come sacrifice and merit, as well as the worship of gods, sages, and ancestors; water and knowledge—all these, indeed, are established in truth.
Truth is sacrifice, austerity, and charity; the mantras and the goddess Sarasvatī; likewise celibacy, truth, and the syllable Om are indeed truth itself.
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun gives heat; by truth the fire burns; by truth heaven endures.
The preservation of all the Vedas and the bathing in all sacred fords are carried out in this world through truth; one attains everything without a doubt.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale; even hundreds of thousands of sacrifices, truth alone was found to be superior.
By truth the gods, the ancestors, humans, serpents, and rākṣasas are pleased; by truth all the worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, are satisfied.
They say truth is the supreme dharma; they say truth is the supreme state; they say truth is the supreme Brahman; therefore, one should always speak the truth.
The sages, devoted to truth and delighting in the dharma of truth, performed most difficult austerities; having attained perfection, they then went to heaven.
One should always speak the truth, for there is nothing higher than truth; [one should do so] with celestial chariots filled with hosts of Apsarases and accompanied by attendants.
In that unfathomable, vast, perfected, and pure lake whose bathing-place is truth, one should bathe with a disciplined mind; that is remembered as the supreme state.
Those men who do not speak untruth, whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even for the sake of their sons, are destined for heaven.
The Vedas, sacrifices, and likewise the mantras reside eternally within the Brahmins; yet they do not shine even among those who are untruthful. Therefore, one should practice truthfulness.
Vyāsa said: "O you whose wealth is asceticism, tell me once more in detail the fruit of my penance, as well as that of all the social classes and especially of the Brāhmaṇas."
Sanatkumāra said: I shall proclaim the chapter on penance, which accomplishes all desires and purposes, though it is extremely difficult for the twice-born to practice; listen as I speak it.
For austerity is declared to be supreme; through austerity, the fruit is obtained. Those who are constantly devoted to austerity indeed rejoice together with the gods.
Through austerity heaven is attained; through austerity fame is attained; through austerity desire is attained; austerity is the means for accomplishing all goals.
Through austerity one attains liberation; through austerity one finds greatness, as well as the perfection of knowledge and realization, good fortune, and beauty itself.
A person obtains various kinds of objects through austerity; through austerity one obtains everything that one desires in one's mind.
Those who have not performed intense austerities never go to the world of Brahmā; Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord, is not attainable by those who have not practiced penance.
Whatever purpose a person undertakes when performing austerity, a human being attains all of that both in this world and in the next.
The drinker of spirituous liquor, the adulterer, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—all these cross over their sins through austerity and are liberated from everything.
Even Sthāṇu, the Lord of All, Viṣṇu the eternal, Brahmā, Agni, Śakra, and whoever else is endowed with ascetic power.
Eighty-eight thousand sages who have sublimated their vital energy rejoice in heaven through their asceticism, united with the gods.
Through austerity, sovereignty is obtained; and that Śakra, the lord of the gods, the slayer of Vṛtra, protected the entire world day after day by means of austerity.
The two gods, the sun and the moon, who are devoted to the welfare of all the worlds, as well as the stars and the planets, shine forth solely through austerity.
Indeed, there is no such happiness in this world that exists without austerity; those who know the Vedas understand that all happiness comes through austerity alone.
Through austerity, wisdom, discernment, health, as well as physical beauty, good fortune, and constant happiness are always attained.
Through austerity, Brahmā creates the universe; Viṣṇu protects the entire world free from decay; and Hara consumes it, while Śeṣa supports the whole earth.
O great sage, by means of asceticism alone, Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, though a Kṣatriya, became a Brahmin; this is well known throughout the three worlds.
Thus has the supreme majesty of austerity been described to you, O one of great wisdom; now hear the majesty of study, which is even more excellent than that of austerity.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Austerity," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, the fruit obtained by one who performs penance in the forest subsisting on wild roots and fruits is equal to that of one who recites even a single Ṛgvedic verse.
The merit that the best of the twice-born obtains from hearing and studying the Śruti, he attains double that fruit by teaching it as well.
O Sage, just as the world would become devoid of light without the moon and the sun, so indeed should this Purāṇa always be studied by us.
Therefore, he who, according to the scriptures, awakens the world from ignorance while it is being scorched as if in hell, is to be honored above all as one who has gone to the Purāṇas.
Among all vessels, the knower of the Purāṇas is the most excellent; because he protects one from falling, he is therefore called a vessel (pātra).
One should never conceive the thought that a knower of the Purāṇas is a mere mortal; for the knower of the Purāṇas is an omniscient teacher who is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Wealth, grain, gold, and various garments should be given after recognizing one as a knower of the Purāṇas, for the sake of happiness both in this world and the next.
That virtuous person who, with great joy, gives auspicious objects to a worthy recipient who is knowledgeable in the Purāṇas, goes to the supreme destination.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who bestows land, a cow, chariots, or beautiful elephants and horses upon a worthy recipient.
A man obtains inexhaustible fulfillment of all desires both in this life and in the next, as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
He who gives to such a person auspicious, fertile land that has been tilled, truly delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants of his lineage.
Having enjoyed all desires here, he goes at the end to the world of Śiva in a divine body and by means of a celestial chariot.
The gods do not attain such satisfaction through sacrifices, nor even through ritual sprinklings, as they do through offerings, worship with flowers, and the recitation of sacred texts.
Listen now to the fruit obtained by that person who causes a Dharma manuscript to be made in a temple of Śambhu, or of Viṣṇu, or of the Sun, or of anyone else.
A human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices; having swiftly pierced through the world of the Sun, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Having remained here for hundreds of kalpas, one becomes a king upon the earth; he enjoys pleasures free from all obstacles—of this there is no need for doubt.
Whoever performs the recitation (japa) before the gods obtains that same fruit which is proclaimed as the result of a thousand horse-sacrifices (aśvamedha).
In the auspicious temple of Śambhu, through the study of Itihāsas and Purāṇas, there is nothing else so pleasing to Śambhu as well as to the other inhabitants of heaven.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the recitation of this book; likewise, listening to it with love bestows the fruit of all desires.
By listening to the Purāṇas of Śambhu, a man becomes free from sin; having enjoyed vast pleasures, he shall attain the world of Śiva.
Whatever merit is obtained through the Rājasūya sacrifice and a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, one attains that same merit merely by listening to the stories of Śambhu.
O Sage, by listening to the story of Śambhu, one obtains that same fruit which is gained by bathing in all the sacred fords and by the gift of ten million cows.
Those who always listen to the story of Śambhu, which purifies the world, should not be considered mere mortals; they are indeed Rudras, without a doubt.
For those who hear the auspicious renown of Śiva and for the virtuous who proclaim it, the sages know that the very dust of his lotus feet is the true sacred ford.
Those embodied beings who desire to go to the state of supreme beatitude should always listen with devotion to the Puranic stories concerning Śiva.
If one is always unable to hear the ancient narrative (purāṇa), one should, with a self-restrained mind, listen to it every day for even a single moment.
O Sage, if a person should be unable to listen every day, he should listen to the story of Śaṅkara during meritorious months and other such occasions.
O lord of sages, a person who listens to the narrative of Śiva indeed crosses over saṃsāra, having burnt away the great forest of karma.
Those men who listen with devotion to the Śaiva narrative for even a moment, half a moment, or a single instant, shall never fall into an evil state of existence.
O Sage, whatever merit is found in all forms of giving or in all sacrifices, that same fruit shall become steadfast through listening to the Purāṇas of Śambhu.
O Vyāsa, especially in the Kali age, for men there is no higher dharma than listening to the Purāṇas; indeed, that which is devoted to liberation through meditation is not remembered [as such].
Listening to the Purāṇas and likewise chanting the names of Śambhu yield the delightful fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree for human beings; of this there is no doubt.
In the Kali age, for the benefit of men of dull intellect whose souls have abandoned the practice of dharma, Śambhu composed this nectar-like essence known as the Purāṇa.
Truly, while one man alone drinks the nectar of immortality, it is by drinking the nectar of Śambhu’s stories that the entire family becomes free from old age and death.
O dear one, that very destination which belongs to those of virtuous conduct, to sacrificers, and to ascetics, is indeed attained instantaneously through the hearing of the Purāṇas.
As long as the attainment of knowledge does not occur, the Yoga scriptures should be studied with diligence, and the Puranic scriptures must certainly be heard.
Evil is constantly destroyed and dharma indeed increases; through hearing the Purāṇas, the wise man does not enter into saṃsāra again.
Therefore, the Purāṇas should be listened to with great effort for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as for reaching the path to liberation (mokṣa).
Whatever fruit is obtained through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and the visiting of sacred fords, a person attains that same fruit by listening to the Purāṇas.
The ancient moments on the path of Dharma would not exist, nor would there be any discourse here concerning the next world, were it not for one who stands firm in his vows.
Whoever, endowed with devotion, listens to or recites even one among the twenty-six Purāṇas, is liberated; of this there is no doubt.

No other path is seen that grants such happiness; indeed, the ancient path is always the most excellent. Without the scripture, all this does not shine, just as the worlds of living beings do not shine without the sun.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Purāṇas," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Terrible gifts and great gifts are always praised; when bestowed upon worthy recipients, they cause one's own self to cross over [saṃsāra].
O best of the twice-born, those who accept gifts of gold, gifts of cows, and gifts of land—these purifiers indeed deliver him himself.
The gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of land—by making these most excellent gifts, one is liberated from sins.
The gift of scales, cows, land, and Sarasvatī are praised; however, two of these are equal in power, yet Sarasvatī is indeed superior.
Indeed, oxen, cows, umbrellas, clothing, sandals, as well as drink and food, should always be given to those who ask for them.
Whatever object is given to Brahmins according to one's resolve, and even to those who seek it without causing distress, by that a person becomes wise.
Gold, sesame seeds, elephants, a maiden, a female slave, a house, a chariot, jewels, and tawny cows—these indeed are the ten great gifts (mahādāna).
Having always accepted all these, a Brāhmaṇa who possesses knowledge immediately delivers the generous donors as well as himself; of this there is no doubt.
Those men who bestow gold with a pure mind—the deities bestow it back upon them from every side; thus have I heard.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold is the consumer of oblations; therefore, by giving gold, all the deities are given.
The gift of earth is most excellent, bestowing the fruits of all desires; it is especially meritorious when made of gold, as was performed by Pṛthu in ancient times.
Beholding the earth being given away, adorned with gold, they, liberated from all sins, go to the supreme goal.
Furthermore, O Sage, I shall describe another gift that is supreme among all, by which one does not behold the wilderness that brings manifold suffering from Yama.

One whose mind is pure should indeed perform the gift of a forest according to the prescribed rite, using wealth acquired through righteous means and free from any stinginess regarding one's resources.
Having fashioned a cow made of a prastha of sesame seeds, endowed with all auspicious qualities, along with a golden calf that is most divine and possessed of every characteristic;
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with auspicious unbroken rice grains smeared with saffron, one should worship Rudra and all the other deities there with great devotion.
Having thus worshipped her, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa according to one's capacity, adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by gems and gold.
Then one should eat at night and offer lamps in abundance; this should be performed with diligence on the full moon day of Kārttika.
Thus, whoever performs this correctly according to the prescribed rite and to the best of their ability, shall not behold the terrible fear of the path of Yama nor the hells.
O Vyāsa, having committed every kind of sin along with his kinsmen and friends, he sports in heaven for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
According to the sacred injunctions, the gift of a cow is indeed remembered here as the most excellent of all; O Vyāsa, no other supreme gift is proclaimed to be equal to it.
He who bestows a tawny cow along with her calf, possessing horns tipped with gold, a bell-metal vessel, and silver hooves, and endowed with all auspicious marks;
O Vyāsa, having become a cow that milks all desires through those various virtues, she approaches that man who gave her, both in this life and in the next world.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is cherished in the home, that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtue by him who desires that it become inexhaustible.
Indeed, the gift of the person on the scale is the supreme among all gifts; one who desires his own welfare should perform the act of ascending the scale.
By performing which one is liberated from sins arising from killing and imprisonment—the gift of the scales (tulādāna) is a great merit that causes the destruction of all evil.
Whoever performs the gift of a balance after having committed all sins without exception, being liberated from all transgressions, goes to heaven without a doubt.

Whatever evil has been committed during the day, at night, at the two twilights, at midday, or at the end of the night—in all three periods of time—this Tulā-man purifies that [evil] through body, mind, and speech.

Whatever sin has been committed by me—whether as a child, an old man, or a youth—whether knowingly or out of devotion to worldly knowledge, may the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), who is indeed the Man on the Scales, swiftly take all that which belongs to me.

The wealth employed by me today has been placed upon the scale in full measure; may whatever remains of mine—both what has been done and what has not been done, whatever merit there may be—be united with that very [weight].
Sanatkumāra said: Having uttered this, one who seeks the welfare of all should give it to the twice-born; it must not be given to even a single person, for from such a gift no liberation would arise.
O Vyāsa, he who thus gives this supreme Tulāpuruṣa gift shall destroy his sins and remain in heaven for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of General Gifts," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Tell me that one gift by which, when given, the fruit of all gifts is obtained, for the sake of the welfare of human beings.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen; I shall tell you how human beings obtain the fruit from even a single gift among all possible gifts that Kāla has bestowed.
Indeed, among all gifts, the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa is the supreme; it should certainly be given by men desiring liberation for the sake of crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving away the entire universe, he attains that through single-minded devotion and shall become the sovereign of the seven worlds.

As long as the moon and sun remain in the sky, and as long as the earth endures, so long shall that man, together with his kinsmen, sport among all those who follow his heart within the abodes of his own kin throughout the quarters of the universe; thereafter, he goes to the most difficult-to-attain station of Mādhava for the joy of the gods.
Vyāsa said: O Blessed One, tell me of the Brahmāṇḍa—what its measure is, what its nature is, what its support is, and how it truly exists, so that I may have full conviction.
Sanatkumāra said: O Sage, listen; I shall describe its height and its extent. By hearing this account of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in brief, one is liberated from sin.
From that unmanifest cause, which is manifest, auspicious, and free from affliction, Brahmā is born when it has become twofold through the power of time.
Brahmā creates the cosmic egg consisting of fourteen worlds; O dear one, listen attentively as I describe that in brief and in due order.
There are exactly seven netherworlds (pātālas), and likewise as many worlds above; the height of that [mountain] situated in the midst of the waters is double that amount.
The serpent remains as its support, and Viṣṇu is proclaimed as his; by the power of Brahmā’s word, he sustains this entire universe.
Even the gods and dānavas are not able to describe the qualities of this remaining portion, which is recited by the Siddhas and honored by the hosts of celestial rishis as Ananta.
Endowed with a thousand heads, he illumines all directions; with a thousand jewels upon his hoods, he is adorned with beautiful svastikas.
With eyes rolling from intoxication, he shines like a white mountain enveloped in fire; wearing garlands and a crown, he indeed appears resplendent, always adorned with a single earring.
In the evening, adorned by the flow of the Gaṅgā, clad in blue garments and overflowing with pride, he was like another Mount Kailāsa.
With the tips of his hands resting on a plow and wielding an excellent mace, he is reverently worshipped by golden-hued Naga maidens.

Rudra, whose essence is Saṃkarṣaṇa, blazes with flames of poisonous fire; we have heard that at the end of a kalpa, flames of fire repeatedly issue forth from his mouths, and after burning the three worlds, they become extinguished.
Seated at the base of Pātāla, Śeṣa remains supporting the circle of the earth upon his own back; he is the Lord of Beings, Śeṣa, honored for his infinite virtues.
Neither can his power of vigor be described even by the longing gods, nor can his true nature be known.
He upon whose entire earth this rests, red as the jewels on his hoods like a garland of flowers—who shall describe his prowess?
When Ananta yawns, his eyes rolling with intoxication, then this earth, together with its mountains, waters, and forests, trembles.
O best of sages, each of the netherworlds—Atala, Vitala, Sutala, and Rasātala—is ten thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Tala, Talātala, and the foremost Pātāla is considered the seventh; these seven worlds beneath the earth are to be known by the wise.
The height of all these is double [their width], and their grounds consist of jewels; moreover, the palaces are adorned with gems and their floors are made of gold.
In them dwell the Dānavas and Daityas, as well as various species of Nāgas, great serpents, and Rākṣasas born of the Daityas.
Nārada declared in the midst of the assembly of heaven that the netherworlds (pātālas) were more delightful than the celestial realm; it was from those regions that he had come to the heavens.
Wherein the brilliantly radiant jewels among various ornaments provide such white splendor and delight, with what could Pātāla be compared?
In the netherworld (pātāla), who would not feel delight? For one who has been liberated from here and there by the daughters of gods and dānavas, a sense of joy arises.
Where there are no rays of the sun by day nor of the moon by night, where there is neither cold nor heat, but only the radiance of jewels.
O best of sages, where food, edibles, meals, and drinks are consumed with great joy, time does not even seem to pass, even though it has gone by.
Where there are the songs of male cuckoos, lotuses, and lotus-pools; and delightful rivers and lakes that flow and wander among one another.
O twice-born one, there were exceedingly brilliant ornaments, fragrant and richly scented ointments, the sounds of lutes, flutes, and drums, and songs.
In Pātāla, the Daityas and Uragas indeed enjoy various pleasures; one attains these through austerity, as well as the powers achieved by Dānavas and Siddhas.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Netherworlds (Pātālaloka)," in the *Umāsaṃhitā*, the fifth book of the *Śrīśivamahāpurāṇa*, within the narrative of the Cosmic Egg (*Brahmāṇḍakathana*).
Sanatkumāra said: O best among the foremost of sages, hear from me about those hells situated above their heads, wherein sinners are cooked.
Raurava, Śūkara, Rodha, Tāla, as well as Vivāsana, Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, and Vilohita.
The Vaitaraṇī river flowing with pus, the Kṛmiṇa hell, the Kṛmibhojana hell, the terrible Asipatravana forest, and the dreadful Lālābhakṣa hell.
Likewise, there are the Pūyavaha, which mostly flows with pus; the Bahirjvāla; the Adhaḥśiras; the Sandaṃśa; the Kālasūtra; the Tamas; the Avīci; and the Rodhana.
Śvabhojana, Ruṣṭa, Mahāraurava, Śālmalī, and many other such hells that inflict suffering are located there.
Those men who were devoted to evil deeds are cooked within them; O Vyāsa, I shall describe them to you in order, so listen with attentiveness.
He who gives false testimony, excluding [falsehood regarding] Brahmins, gods, or cows, and he who always speaks untruth—that man goes to the Raurava hell.
The killer of an embryo, the stealer of gold, the obstructer of cows, the destroyer of all beings, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the thief of another's property—
O Vyāsa, he who associates with such a person indeed goes to hell upon death for having killed his guru; likewise for killing one’s own sister, mother, cow, or daughter.
The seller of a virtuous woman, the usurer, the seller of hair, and he who abandons food—all these are cooked in heated metals.
That lowest of men who treats his gurus with contempt, who eats after [they have already eaten], who defiles the gods, and who sells the gods;

O twice-born one, he who approaches those who should not be approached, he who at the end goes to the One of Seven Powers (the Buddha), as well as a thief, a cow-killer, an outcast, and likewise one who violates established boundaries—these are all equal.
He who hates the gods, the twice-born, and the ancestors, and he who defiles gems, goes indeed to the Kṛmibhakṣa hell; the performer of improper sacrifices eats worms.
That lowest of men who eats before his ancestors, gods, and deities goes to the world of those who consume saliva; so too does the man who forges weapons.
That twice-born man who serves outcastes, who holds improper views, who performs sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and likewise who eats forbidden food;
These sellers of Soma fall into a flood of blood; the killer of honey and the destroyer of villages go to the cruel Vaitaraṇī river.
Those intoxicated by fresh youth, those who transgress the bounds of propriety, those who are impure, and those who live off the family—these go to their destruction.
He who cuts down trees in vain goes to the Forest of Sword-leaves; those hunters with razor-sharp arrows fall into the Blazing Fire.
O twice-born one, a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, or even a Vaishya who has fallen from right conduct goes to that very place; as does he who gives fire to dog-cookers (outcastes).
Those who violate their vows and those who have fallen away from their own stage of life fall into the midst of the extremely terrible Saṃdaṃśa torment.
Those men who, though practicing celibacy, discharge semen even in dreams, and those by whom sons have not been instructed in sacred knowledge, fall into the world of the dog-eaters.
These and other hells exist by the hundreds and thousands, wherein those who have performed evil deeds are cooked, having undergone their torments.
In the same way, these and thousands of other evils are experienced by men who have come within the range of the various hells.
Those men who perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—whether by deed, thought, or speech—fall into hell.
The denizens of hell are seen by the gods in heaven with their heads downward; conversely, all the denizens of hell see the gods below them with their faces turned downward.
Immovable beings, worms and insects, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, the righteous, the gods, and likewise those destined for liberation, respectively.
As many as are the creatures in heaven, so many are the inhabitants of hell; the evildoer who is averse to expiation goes to hell.
O Kāleya, Svāyambhuva Manu has declared that penances are heavy for heavy sins and light for light sins.
Regarding all those various actions that have been described without exception, the supreme expiation for them all is the constant remembrance of Hara.
As for expiation, it arises for that very man in whom sin has been produced; even when a sin has been committed, remorse and the supreme remembrance of Śiva are required.
By recollecting [the Lord] at midday and other such times, one attains the state of Maheśvara; by recollecting Him in the morning, at night, and during the twilight, a person becomes cleansed of sin.
Merely by remembering Śiva, that Lord of Umā, one attains liberation, heaven, or the total destruction of all afflictions.
O best of Brahmins, O most excellent sage, obstacles to sin, as well as recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and so forth, certainly exist nowhere else in the three worlds.
Whatever merit is performed by one whose mind is fixed on Maheśvara through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth—the fruit of that is the status of Indra over the gods and the like.
O Sage, that man who, remembering Śiva with devotion day and night, has all his sins destroyed, does not go to hell.
O best of the twice-born, regarding the notions of hell and heaven, sin and merit: one of these leads to suffering, while the other leads to happiness and rebirth.

That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, arises again as a source of suffering; therefore, it is essentially suffering by nature, and there is nothing whatsoever that is essentially pleasurable.
This transformation of the mind, characterized by pleasure and pain, is indeed knowledge; knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman, and knowledge leads to the realization of reality.
This entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is of the nature of knowledge; O Sage, there exists nothing whatsoever beyond supreme consciousness.
Thus have I described this entire mandala of the hells; hereafter, I shall now describe the mandala of the earth.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Deliverance from Hell," in the Description of the Cosmic Egg within the Umā Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Parāśara, listen as I speak in brief about the orb of the earth, correctly including its seven continents and other features.
Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣpaka as the seventh—all are surrounded by seven oceans.
The oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, clarified butter, wine, curd, milk, and fresh water—Jambūdvīpa stands in the midst of all of these.
In the midst of that Kāla ocean, Mount Meru, the golden mountain, has entered sixteen yojanas below; its height is equal to that depth.
This mountain, standing upon the surface of the earth, measures eighty-four [yojanas] at its summit; its width is thirty-two [yojanas], and its extent is equal on all sides.
At its base, it stands sixteen thousand [yojanas] wide, situated in the form of a pericarp; Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are on its southern side.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges in the north; each is ten thousand [yojanas] in extent, rich in jewels, and possesses a reddish glow.
They are one thousand yojanas in height and as many in breadth; Bhārata is the first region, and after that, Kiṃpuruṣa is recorded.
O Sage, Harivarṣa is indeed another region to the south of Meru; Ramyaka is on its northern side, and Hiraṇmaya occupies its [southern] portion.
The Uttarakurus are just like Bhārata; each of these regions, O best of sages, measures nine thousand [yojanas].
In the center of that is Ilāvṛta, and in its center Mount Meru rises; there, extending in the four directions from Meru, it is nine thousand [yojanas] high.
