O best of sages, in Ilāvṛta there are four mountains that serve as buttresses for Meru; they are arranged and joined together, rising high once more.
For Mandara is in the east, Gandhamādana in the south; Vipula is on the western side, and Supārśva is situated in the north.
The kadamba, jambu tree, pippala, and vaṭa—these trees, eleven hundred *yojanas* in height, serve as the banners of the mountain.
O great sage, hear now the reason for the name Jambūdvīpa; I shall describe to you the nature of those magnificent trees that shine there.
Fruits of that Jambu tree, as large as great elephants, fall upon the back of the mountain, shattering on all sides.
Due to their juice, it is indeed renowned as the Jambū River; it flows all around there and is drunk by its inhabitants.
Neither perspiration, nor foul odor, nor old age, nor the impairment of the senses occurs for those people who stand upon her banks.
Having reached the riverbank mud, which has been dried by the breath from one's mouth, it becomes the gold known as Jāmbūnada, the ornament of the Siddhas.
To the east of Meru is Bhadrāśva, and to the west is Ketumāla; O best of sages, between those two regions lies Ilāvṛta.
To the east is the Caitraratha forest, to the south is Gandhamādana; likewise, Vibhrāja is in the west, and Nandana is recorded to be in the north.
Aruṇoda, Mahābhadra, Śītoda, and Mānasa—these are remembered as the four lakes that are enjoyed by the gods in every respect.
Śītāñjana, Kuruṅga, Kurara, and Mālyavat—these are the Kesara mountains situated to the east of Meru, each preceded by its own name.
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka, and Niṣadha are the Kesara mountains to the south of Kapilā.
Sinīvāsa, Kusumbha, Kapila, and Nārada, as well as the mountains beginning with Nāga, are the filament-mountains (kesarācala) in the west.
Then there are Śaṅkhacūḍa, the mountain named Ṛṣabha, Haṃsa, Kālañjara, and others, as well as the Kesara mountains to the north.
Indeed, in the center above Mount Meru is the city of Brahmā, made of gold, measuring fourteen thousand yojanas in extent.
Around those eight world-protectors, in their respective order, eight images were prepared in front of them according to their directions and forms.
And in that city of Brahmā, having caused the lunar orb to fall, the river Gaṅgā, which has issued from the foot of Viṣṇu, indeed falls down.
Sītā, Alakanandā, Cakṣus, and Bhadrā—descending there in succession, she became fourfold throughout the quarters.
Sītā indeed flows to the east of the mountain, Nandā to the south; Cakṣus flows to the west, and Bhadrā proceeds to the north.
Having crossed all the mountains in the four directions and reached the great ocean, that daughter Sūti, the Ganges flowing through the three paths, proceeded on her way with great care.
Sunīla and Niṣadha are those two [peaks] which are Mālyavat and Gandhamādana; situated in their midst, Meru stands in the form of a pericarp.
Bhārata, Ketumāla, Bhadrāśva, and likewise the Kurus are the petals of the world-lotus; the boundary mountains of the world are its petals.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa extend from south to north, while Gandhamādana and Kailāsa stretch from east to west.
To the east and west of Mount Meru are the Niṣadha and Nīla mountains; extending from south to north, they are situated within the pericarp.
Jaṭhara and the others are situated on Meru, with two positioned at each [side]; these are the Kesara mountains, beginning with Śveta, which are most beautiful.
To the north of the mountains are valleys frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; likewise, within them are most delightful forests and cities.
And all the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas, as well as the deities and the sons of Diti, sport day and night upon those mountain-like regions.
For these earthly and celestial realms are proclaimed to be the abodes of those who possess virtuous qualities; sinners do not go there, nor can they ever see them anywhere.
O Great Sage, in those eight regions beginning with Kimpuruṣa, there is no sorrow, no calamities, no agitation, nor hunger, fear, and the like.
The subjects will be healthy, free from fear, and devoid of all suffering; they will have a stable lifespan of ten or twelve thousand years.
The ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā, as well as the earthly waters, exist everywhere; yet the god does not rain upon them, for in those places there is no conception of time.
In these seven [mountains], there are hundreds of well-born rivers with golden sands; there are also small streams, and people take delight in sporting within them.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Regions of Jambūdvīpa," in the Brahmāṇḍa-narrative of the Umāsaṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: I shall describe Bhāratavarṣa, which lies to the south of the Himālaya mountains and to the north of the ocean, where the worldly existence of the descendants of Bharata occurs.
O Great Sage, its extent is nine thousand yojanas; this is remembered by the wise as the land of action for both heaven and liberation.
That which is attained by men—both heaven and even hell—is found within this; I shall now describe to you the nine divisions of the land of Bhārata.
Indradyumna, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva, and Vāruṇa.
This, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean; this island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
The Kirātas were in the east, the Yavanas were situated in the south; likewise, those to be known as ascetics were in the west and in the north.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and many Shudras in their midst remained established, subsisting through sacrifice, the profession of arms, trade, and service.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Sudāmā, Ṛkṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these are the seven principal mountain ranges here.
O Sage, the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, are born from the Pāriyātra mountain; they should be known as destroyers of all sins through both sight and touch.
The Narmadā, Surasā, and seven others, numbering in the thousands—all auspicious great rivers originating from the Vindhya mountains that remove all sins.
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tāpī, and other principal rivers, having issued forth from the Ṛkṣa mountain, immediately remove the fear of sin.
Likewise, there are rivers originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountains, such as the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇī; and those arising from the Malaya mountains, headed by the Kṛtamālā and Tāmraparṇī.
The Triyāmā, Ṛṣikulyā, and others are known to originate from Mahendra; the Ṛṣikulyā, Kumārī, and others arise from the foothills of Śuktimat.
Indeed, people from various regions dwell within those circles, and they drink water from these diverse lakes.
O great sage, there were four ages, beginning with Kṛta, in the land of Bhārata; indeed, they do not prevail in other continents.
In this place, gifts are bestowed, and sacrifices are performed here by those skilled in ritual; likewise, ascetics diligently practice austerities with devotion for the sake of the world beyond.
For this Jambūdvīpa, O Great Sage, is the land of action; even within it, Bhārata is the most excellent, while all others are lands of enjoyment.
O best of sages, a mortal sometimes attains human birth here after thousands of births, through the accumulation of merit.

Blessed indeed are those regions of the land of Bhārata, which serve as the path to the abodes of heaven and liberation; for the gods sing songs of praise concerning them, saying that men there become once again like the gods themselves.
Having somehow attained this human state and having sported within the supreme self-form of Śambhu, I shall indeed depart to that very essence of his after reaping all fruits born of my past actions.
Truly fortunate will be those men, endowed with happiness and established in their duties; for those whose birth indeed occurs in Bhārata possess the attainment of both heaven and liberation.
Jambūdvīpa, which is completely circular and has an extent of one hundred thousand yojanas, surrounded by the salt ocean, has been described by me.
Having surrounded the salt ocean, which measures one hundred thousand [yojanas], Plakṣadvīpa is proclaimed, O Brahmin, to be twice that size.
Gomanta, Candra, Nārada, Dardura, Somaka, Sumanas, Śaila, and Vaibhrāja, O best of beings.
In these delightful mountain ranges of Varṣa, the gods and Gandharvas dwell together with the subjects at all times, residing eternally in these regions.
Neither mental afflictions nor physical diseases exist for people anywhere there; humans live there for ten thousand years.
Anutaptā, Śikhī, Pāpaghnī, Tridivā, Kṛpā, Amṛtā, and Sukṛtā—these seven indeed are the rivers here.
Likewise, there are thousands of small rivers and mountains there; the inhabitants of those regions drink from those rivers with great joy.
Even there, O great sage, throughout all time, the duration in those seven locations remains equal to the Tretā Yuga.
O best of sages, among those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, there was a very great tree that was like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
O best of the twice-born, that island named after the Plakṣa tree is indeed Plakṣadvīpa; there the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, is worshipped.
The blessed Lord Hari and Brahmā [bound it] with Vedic machines and mantras; listen further to how they did so both briefly and at length regarding the Śālmali tree.
They remained right there for seven years; hear their names from me: Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, and likewise Rohita.
Vaikala and Mānasa, and Suprabha as the seventh, O Sage; by means of the Śālmali tree, that island is named Śālmali.
It stands constantly surrounded by an ocean twice its size; listen to me as I name the rivers that manifest the rains there.
Śuklā, Raktā, Hiraṇyā, Candrā, Śubhrā, Vimocanā, and Nivṛtti as the seventh—these rivers possess holy waters and are most refreshing.
Those seven regions, consisting of forty thousand four-caste communities, constantly worship the Blessed Śambhu with various sacrifices.
The presence of the gods is exceedingly delightful there; this island is surrounded by the Suroda ocean.
Kuśadvīpa, twice as large, is situated all around it on the outside; there dwell the Daityas and Dānavas together with human beings.
In that very same way, there are gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, kimpuruṣas, and others; and right there are the four castes, devoted to their own respective duties.
And in that very Kuśadvīpa, they worship Brahmā, Janārdana, and likewise Īśāna, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Kuśeśaya, Hari, Dyutimān, Puṣpavān, Maṇidruma, Hemaśaila, and the seventh, Mandarācala.
And there are seven rivers; hear their names according to reality: Dhūtapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, and likewise Saṃmiti.
Vidyā, Daṃbhā, Mahī, and another, these are all removers of every sin; there are thousands of others as well, such as Śubhāpā and Hemavālukā.
In Kuśadvīpa there is a clump of Kuśa grass, surrounded by the Ghṛtoda ocean; O highly fortunate one, now hear of another great island, Krauñcadvīpa.
O one of great intelligence, it is surrounded by the ocean of curd-cream, which is twice its size; hear from me the names of those mountain ranges.
Krauñca, Vāmana, and the third, Andhakāraka; Divāvṛti, Mana, Puṇḍarīka, and Dundubhi.
Free from fear, those subjects dwell upon those mountain ranges, which are entirely golden and delightful, together with their friends and hosts of gods.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are found there in their proper order; furthermore, there are seven great rivers and thousands of others.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojava, Śānti, and Puṇḍarīkā—these are the ones who drink the auspicious milk.
There the Blessed One is worshipped in the form of Yogarudra; and the Sea of Curd-Water is likewise surrounded by Śākadvīpa.
The seven mountains are double [the preceding] in size; hear their names from me: Udayagiri is to the east, and Jaladhāra is to the west.
Behind it are the Sunset Mountain (Astagiri) and Avikeśa-kesarī; there stands the great Śāka tree, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
There, the regions are meritorious and inhabited by the four castes; and there are rivers of great merit that remove all sins and fears.
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nalinī, and likewise Veṇukā; Ikṣu, Reṇukā, and Gabhasti as the seventh.
O great sage, there are thousands of other small rivers there, as well as mountains by the hundreds and thousands.
There is no decline of dharma for those men; having returned from heaven, they roam the earth together with one another during those years.
In Śākadvīpa, however, the Sun is always worshipped with affection by the inhabitants through their prescribed rites, being self-restrained in mind.
Surrounded on all sides by the Ocean of Milk, which is twice its size, that Ocean of Milk in turn, O Vyāsa, is encompassed on every side by the sea named Puṣkara.
Twice that size is the great rain-cloud known there as Mānasa; it rises five thousand yojanas high.
And those very lakṣas are circular in shape on all sides; the circle of Puṣkaradvīpa divides them through the middle.
It is ring-shaped and has the same configuration as the continents and sub-continents; there, human beings live for ten thousand years.
Free from disease, devoid of sorrow, and liberated from passion and hatred—for them, O Sage, neither unrighteousness exists, nor do bondage and slaughter.
Truth and falsehood did not exist for him; his dwelling was always constant. All men were alike in appearance, possessing a single form of golden hue.
Moreover, O Kāleya, this earthly year is considered equal to heaven; it bestows happiness upon everyone at the proper time and is free from old age and disease.
O great sage, in Puṣkara, in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, and in Mahāvīta—there is the Nyagrodha tree on Puṣkaradvīpa, the supreme abode of Brahmā.
Brahmā dwells there, being worshipped by gods and asuras; that Puṣkara is surrounded by an ocean of sweet water.
Thus the continents are surrounded by seven oceans; both the continents and the oceans are equal to one another in their respective dimensions, each being double the size of the preceding one.
Their quantity exceeds what has been stated; indeed, the waters in the oceans remain equal at all times, and never do they become diminished.
O best of sages, just as the water at the bottom of a pot rises upward through contact with fire, so too, during the waxing of the moon, the water certainly ascends.
With the rising and setting of the moon, the waters increase and decrease; consequently, they become deficient or excessive during the bright and dark fortnights.
O best of sages, you have described to me how the increase and decrease of the waters of all the oceans are observed to be ten times greater than the preceding one, up to a hundredfold.
O Brahmin, all the inhabitants of Puṣkaradvīpa always partake of food that appears there of its own accord, O sage.
Before Svāṅgada, there was no stability for the world; there was a golden land twice as vast, devoid of all living beings.
Beyond that is the mountain Lokāloka; for that immovable mountain extends for thousands [of yojanas], being as many thousands high and ten thousand yojanas in width.
And this earth, O great sage, together with its islands and mountains, extends fifty crores [of yojanas] and is enveloped by the shell of the cosmic egg within the darkness.
O Kāleya, she is the foundation of all things, superior to all beings in her qualities; she is this very Earth (Ilā), the nurse of all the worlds.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seven Continents," in the *Umā-saṃhitā*, the fifth book of the *Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*, within the narrative of the Cosmic Egg (*Brahmāṇḍa-kathana*).
Sanatkumāra said: "As far as the rays of the sun and the moon indeed illuminate, to that extent is the earth; it is thus sung of as the world of beings (bhūloka)."
The solar orb is situated at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth, and its circumference is always calculated to be several thousand yojanas.
They declare the moon to be the standard of measure for the world; the moon stands above the sun at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas.
The entire mandala of the planets is situated above the moon; together with the stars, it extends ten thousand yojanas above it.
From that [the sphere of Mercury], then from that [the sphere of] Kāvya (Venus), comes the orb of Bhauma (Mars); above that is Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), and above him is Śanaiścara (Saturn).
The constellation of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala) is situated one hundred thousand [yojanas] from that; and Dhruva is situated a hundred thousand yojanas above the Sages.
Of that wheel of light which is indeed the central pivot, it should be known as Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar; [the region] above Bhuvar and below Dhruva.
The Maharloka, where those inhabitants of the Kalpas reside, is one crore yojanas above Dhruva; these seven are the sons of Brahmā.
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana; as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha.
Above that, Śukra is situated at an interval of two hundred thousand [yojanas]; below that, at a distance of two hundred thousand yojanas, is said to be the son of Soma (Budha).
O Sage, Bhauma is situated two hundred thousand yojanas above that; Jīva and Guru are situated two hundred thousand yojanas above that.
Two hundred thousand yojanas above Jupiter, Saturn is situated. These seven planets are said to be established in their respective zodiac signs.
The sages are situated seven lakhs of yojanas above Rudra; the station of Dhruva is declared to be at one lakh yojanas from Viśva.
Beyond Janaloka, at a distance four times greater, Tapoloka is said to be situated; there dwell the Vairāja deities, who are indeed free from the affliction of burning.
Sixfold in extent from the world of austerity (tapas), the world of truth (satya) is situated; it is to be known as the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), where those of stainless minds dwell.
Indeed, those men who delight in truth and righteousness, who possess knowledge, who observe celibacy, and who go to that [place], dwell in the world of the earth.
In the Bhuvarloka, the perfected sages dwell in divine forms; in the Svargaloka, there are the gods, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Rudras, Sādhyas, Nāgas, birds, and others, the nine planets, and then the sages free from all taint were present there.
O Kāleya, these seven great worlds have been described to you, as well as the seven nether regions; such is the extent of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Just as the fruit of the dadhi-tree has its fibers extending both upward and downward, so too this [egg] is entirely enveloped on all sides by the shell (aṇḍakaṭāha).
It is surrounded on all sides by water ten times its size, and likewise by fire, air, ether, and darkness.

Enveloped by the great element beginning with earth, each successively ten times greater than the preceding and surrounded by the qualities of the directions, the Puruṣa stands enveloping the Pradhāna which itself envelops the Mahat.
There is no number even for that infinite Supreme Self; therefore He is known as Ananta (the Infinite), because indeed there is no measure of Him.
O Sage, that supreme Prakṛti is the cause of everything; she is the source of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of cosmic eggs.
From that Unmanifest Source, many such beings arise, just as fire exists in wood, oil in sesame seeds, and ghee in milk.
Thus, that Supreme Self, the knower of the self, pervading all, brings forth from the primordial seed; from those [beings] arise the subsequent egg-born creatures.
From them, as well as from others, sons and various other seeds arise; from those [seeds] come the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, as well as the gods and other beings.
Just as there is no diminution of the tree through the sprouting of a seed, and just as fire is produced from the sun-stone by means of the sun; so too [is the case with the Self].
In that same way, creation arises; Śiva does not desire it there. Indeed, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the gods and other beings come into existence.
Likewise, they indeed attain growth through their own respective actions alone; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Rudras—he is celebrated as Śiva.
Therefore, he from whom everything arises and into whom everything shall dissolve, who is the agent of all actions—he is celebrated as Śiva.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, sever my great doubt: O sage, do worlds indeed exist above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), or not?
Sanatkumāra said: "O Lord of Sages, there are worlds above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Listen to them; I shall describe them to you in detail, having come before you."
Beyond the world of ritual injunctions lies the world renowned as Vaikuṇṭha; there Viṣṇu is established, shining with great splendor.
Above that is the world of Kumāra, which is indeed most wonderful; there the commander-in-chief, the son of Śambhu, shines with great splendor.
Beyond that, the great divine Umā-loka shines forth, where the one Śakti, the auspicious mother of the three gods, manifests.
For the primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of rajas, sattva, and tamas, is higher than the highest; yet the Goddess herself is beyond qualities (nirguṇā), changeless, and of the essence of Śiva.
Above that, one should know, is the eternal world of Śiva; it is imperishable, supremely divine, and always endowed with great splendor.
There shines the Supreme Brahman, where Śambhu Maheśvara resides—the Lord who is the progenitor of the three gods and who transcends all that consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
Above that are no worlds, but near it is Goloka; there dwell the mothers of the cows named Suśīlā, who are dear to Śiva.
Indeed, its guardian named Kṛṣṇa shines by the command of Śaṅkara; he was established by Śiva himself, who moves according to his own will through his power.
O Vyāsa, the world of Śiva is wonderful, supportless, and captivating; it is beyond description and resplendent with various objects.
Śiva, however, is its presiding deity, the crest-jewel of all gods; he is the stainless Supreme Self, to be served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara.
Thus, my dear son, I have described to you the arrangement of the entire cosmic egg; what else do you wish to hear regarding the structure of the worlds beyond that?
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worlds," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, O most excellent one, tell me of that attainment reaching which men endowed with devotion to Śiva do not return.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, son of Parāśara, listen with affection to this auspicious path—the vow of those with pure devotion as well as that of the pure ascetics.
Those who possess auspiciousness and pure actions, and who are endowed with perfectly purified austerity, constantly worship Him; they are to be revered in every way every day.
Those who have not performed intense austerities do not go to the stainless world of Śiva; O great sage, austerity alone is the true cause for Śiva’s grace.
Through austerity, the hosts of deities, the ṛṣis, and the munis rejoice in heaven; know my words to be true.
That which is very difficult to bear, difficult to accomplish, a heavy burden, and hard to overcome—all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Hara are eternally established in austerity; all the gods and goddesses have attained through austerity that fruit which is difficult to obtain.
For by whatever disposition one remains while performing austerity, that very state is attained by them in this world; of this there is no doubt.
O Vyāsa, austerity is known to be of three kinds—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa—and it should be understood as the means for accomplishing all spiritual goals.

For the gods and for ascetics whose vital energy is drawn upward, it is indeed *sāttvika*; for the *dānavas* and likewise for human beings, it is *rājasa*; and for the *rākṣasas* and for men of cruel deeds, it is indeed *tāmasa*.
That fruit has been declared by the sages who perceive reality to be threefold: recitation, meditation, and the auspicious worship of the gods with devotion.
For that is declared to be sattvic, accomplishing all fruits in this world and in the next, and achieving whatever the mind desires.
Austerity that is performed with a view toward the fruits of desire is said to be rajasic; it involves excessively afflicting one's own body with unbearable practices that wither the physical frame.
Austerity performed with a mind intent on worldly desires is designated as tāmasa.

One should know that the sattvic type is the highest; it possesses an unwavering inclination toward dharma, as well as bathing, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, pure purification, and non-violence.
The practice of vows and fasting, silence, restraint of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, forbearance, self-control, and compassion.

The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and other such edifices, as well as the performance of the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, sacrifices, visits to sacred pilgrimage sites, and the life of the These are the abodes of Dharma that grant happiness to the wise; they are the supreme, righteous Dharma, O Vyāsa, and the cause of devotion to Śiva.
Let the yoga of the transits and equinoxes be applied to the release of sound; let there be meditation on the light of the three times and the concentration on the state beyond mind (unmanībhāva).

Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) are known as the threefold prāṇāyāma; it involves the knowledge of the movement through the channels (nāḍīs) and the restraint of the senses (pratyāhāra).

Below that is the Fourth (Turiya), which is the intellect (buddhi) endowed with the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā); this is declared to be the supreme among the aforementioned [levels], serving as the means for attaining supreme knowledge.
The stages of wood, the stage of death, and the green stage are thus proclaimed; for these various attainments indeed destroy all sins.
A woman, a bed, as well as drink, clothing, incense, and ointment, and the chewing of betel—these five are the manifestations of royal sovereignty.
Loads of gold, as well as copper, houses, jewel-cows, proficiency in the Vedic scriptures, and the adornment of song and dance.
Conchs, lutes, and drums, as well as lordly elephants, parasols, and chowries—these are the forms of enjoyment; by means of these, one who is capable is gratified.
Like a reflection in a mirror, the sage is not affected by attachments; yet, like sesame seeds being pressed, he is crushed, and deluded by knowledge, he thinks, "Go quickly! to this [world].
Even though he knows this, he wanders here in saṃsāra like a water-wheel, afflicted by suffering in all wombs—among both the immobile and the mobile.
Having thus wandered through all the wombs by way of delusion, one eventually attains, through the power of time, the human state which is exceedingly difficult to find.
Even by skipping over [successive stages], human birth is attained through the weight of merit; for the various destinies are said to result from the relative gravity or lightness of karmic actions.
Having attained human birth, which is the means for accomplishing heaven and liberation, he who does not practice what is beneficial for himself grieves for a long time after death.
Human birth is exceedingly difficult to attain for all the gods and asuras; having attained it, one should act in such a way that one does not go to hell.
If there is no exertion for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation, then having obtained this rare human birth, that life is said to be in vain.
Human birth is proclaimed to be the root of all four aims of life; having attained it through righteousness, O Vyāsa, one should protect it with diligent effort.
Having obtained human birth, which is rooted in dharma and capable of accomplishing all goals, one should personally protect that very root if there is to be effort for the sake of further gain.
And even having attained the state of a Brahmin in human form—which is indeed difficult to obtain—he who does not practice what is for his own welfare; who else is more senseless than he?
Of all the continents, this alone is called the land of karma; from here, heaven and liberation are attained through well-accumulated merit.
Having attained this transient human birth in this land of Bhārata-varṣa, if one does not perform what is beneficial for oneself, then indeed one has deceived one’s own self.
O Brahmin, this is known as the land of action, while that is remembered as the land of fruition; whatever action is performed here is experienced in heaven.
One should practice dharma as long as the body is healthy; for when one is unwell, even if urged by others, one lacks the strength to perform anything at all.
He who does not accomplish the permanent by means of this impermanent body has surely lost what was permanent, and his impermanent gains are truly destroyed.
Pieces of one's lifespan fall away before one's very eyes; for what reason is this not understood through the instruction of days and nights?
Since it is not known when or for whom death will occur, who indeed can find composure in the face of such sudden mortality?
Since one will certainly depart alone, having abandoned everything, why does one never give this wealth for the sake of provisions for the journey?
Having taken the provisions of generosity as his travel rations, a being goes happily to the abode of Yama; otherwise, a creature suffers on a path devoid of provisions.
O Kāleya, for those whose merits are entirely fulfilled on all sides, there is indeed gain at every step as they go to the heavenly realm.
Knowing this, a person should perform meritorious deeds and avoid sin; through merit one attains divinity, while the meritless goes to hell.
Those who have sought refuge even slightly with Śiva, the Lord of Gods, do not behold the terrible Yama nor likewise hell.
However, due to their great delusions caused by sins, human beings dwell there for a short time by the command of Śiva, and from there they go to the abode of Śiva.
But those who have practiced with their whole being toward Maheśvara are not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
O best of sages, those by whom the name "Śiva" has been uttered, as well as "Hara, Hara," have no fear of hell or of Yama.
The provisions for the journey to the next world, the healthy means to liberation, and the sole abode of the entire collection of merit—this is the two-syllable word "Śiva."
The name of Śiva alone is the sole healer of the great disease of saṃsāra; I see nothing else that can cure this disease of worldly existence.
In ancient times, a Pulkasa, having committed thousands of Brahman-murders, attained liberation upon hearing the pure name "Śiva."
Therefore, a wise person should constantly increase their devotion to the Lord; O highly intelligent one, through devotion to Śiva, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Specific Account of Manu," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Vyāsa said: Indeed, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain; one becomes a Brāhmaṇa by nature alone. From the mouth of the Lord [Brahmā] came the Kṣatriyas, from his arms the Vaiśyas, and from his thighs the Śūdras.
The Veda declares that the Śūdra was produced from his feet; tell me then, how can those situated below attain a higher standing?
Sanatkumāra said: "O descendant of Kali, by means of evil deeds men fall from their station; therefore, having attained a superior station, a wise man should protect it."
But he who, having abandoned the state of a Brahmin, is born from a Kṣatriya womb, has fallen away from Brahminhood and takes to the status of a Kṣatriya.
Through the practice of unrighteousness, the fool likewise wanders on; for he enters into darkness for thousands of future births.
Therefore, having attained the supreme state, one should not let it perish through negligence; even when facing calamities, a man should always protect his own position.

That man who, having attained the auspicious status of a Brahmin and the state of Brahminhood, disregards it and does not distinguish between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten, shall become a Kṣatriya.
I shall explain to you in its entirety that action by which an intelligent Śūdra or Vaiśya is indeed born, and by which one becomes the highest of the social classes (varṇas).
Having become a Śūdra, he should perform the duties of a Śūdra as they have been prescribed, namely, service toward the three other castes at all times in the proper manner.
If even a Śūdra acts with such desire, he shall indeed attain the status of a Vaiśya; and a Vaiśya who employs wealth and performs oblations according to the prescribed rule [attains the same].
Having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice and having eaten only the remaining food, that Vaiśya is born into a Kṣatriya family; of this there is no doubt.
A Kṣatriya is born purified by sacrifices accompanied by the giving of sacrificial fees; seeking heaven, he should always study and take refuge in the three sacred fires.
With hands and feet always moist, he should protect the earth with righteousness; approaching his own wife only during her season, he should be devoted to the duties of his spouse.
"Let hospitality be extended to all, and let the three goals of life be bestowed upon all beings; for one should enter battle only for the sake of cows, Brahmins, or one's own self."
By that [rite], the Kṣatriya whose soul is purified by the fire-mantra becomes a Brāhmaṇa; having become a Brāhmaṇa according to the rule, he is then born as an officiating priest (yājaka).
One who is constantly devoted to his own duty, truthful in speech, and has conquered his senses, attains a vast heaven and becomes beloved even by the gods.

For the state of being a Brahmin is indeed difficult to attain and is achieved by men only with great hardship; yet from that state of Brahminhood, O Lord of Sages, everything is obtained, including even liberation.
Therefore, with every effort, a Brahmin devoted to dharma should protect his supreme Brahminhood, which is the means for achieving all goals.
Vyāsa said: O best of sages, you have described here the greatness of battle; I wish to hear this, so speak, O foremost of eloquent men.
Sanatkumāra said: One does not obtain that fruit by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees which one would obtain in battle.
Thus have those who know reality and are ever conversant with the rituals of sacrifice declared. Therefore, I shall explain to you that fruit which belongs to those who live by the sword.
There is the attainment of dharma, the attainment of wealth, and likewise the attainment of fame for him who, being brave, desires battle while crushing the enemy host.

For him, virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees, are attained; indeed, he who mounts that vehicle after having given a gift facing toward the Supreme attains them.
He who remains undefeated in battle shall be born in the world of Viṣṇu; if he does not die, he obtains the merit of four horse-sacrifices.
But he who dies at the head of the army without casting aside his weapon, remaining brave and facing the enemy, does not return from heaven.
Whether he be a king, a prince, or even a commander of the army, for that hero who has slain a Kṣatriya, there shall be an imperishable world.
As many hairs as are severed from his body by weapons in the great battle, so many worlds, yielding all desires and imperishable, does he obtain.
The heroic posture, the heroic bed, and the firm abiding in the state of the hero—these, O Vyāsa, exist eternally both in this world and in the next.
Those who die for the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, and for the sake of the master of their land, go to happiness just like those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Whoever, having slain a Brahmin, subsequently gives up his own life, does not return from heaven after that, even if he dies in battle for his master.
For one slain by carnivorous beasts or by tusked animals for the sake of Brahmins, cows, or masters, there shall be the highest destiny, provided there has been abundant and inexhaustible generosity.
One who is capable may be able to perform even a hundred sacrifices here; however, to renounce one's own body in battle is exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
Battle is most meritorious, leading to heaven, a manifestation of form, and facing in all directions; it is for all castes indeed, but especially for the Kṣatriya.
And I shall explain at length the eternal dharma of battle: against whom one should strike and what one should avoid.
Even if a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedanta approaches as an assassin intent on killing, one may kill him; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
Even one who deserves to be killed must not be slain, nor he who begs for water; O Vyāsa, that man who kills those who are distressed in battle becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.

Having killed one who is diseased, weak, a child, one without a protector such as a woman, a miserable person, or one who is certainly broken-bowed or whose string is severed, one indeed becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
Having reflected thus, the wise man, becoming fond of battle through joy, attains the fruit of his birth and rejoices both in this world and the next.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Battle," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Vyāsa said: O dear one, O lord of sages, speak now of the procedure regarding the birth of a living being from its conception, as well as its stay within the womb, for the sake of cultivating detachment.

Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, to the essence of all scriptures in brief; I shall declare that excellent dispassion which brings about liberation for one seeking release from the bonds of worldly existence.
Within the cooking vessel, however, the food and the water should be kept separate; the water should be placed above the fire, and that food should be placed upon the water.
For fire is situated beneath the water; it slowly fans the fire, and the fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water exceedingly hot.
That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water; once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter separately and the nutrient essence separately.
Through the twelve impurities, the waste is separated from the body and passes outside; however, the essence (rasa) circulates within the body, and by that, nourishment is produced.
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, nails, the phlegm that is the seat of impurities, sweat, feces, and urine are known as the twelve [impure substances].
O Sage, all the channels are connected on every side to the heart-lotus; they should be known as carriers of the vital essence (rasa). I shall now describe that manner to you.
One should place that subtle essence (rasa) within their mouths; by means of that essence, the vital breath (prāṇa) fills those channels once again.
Again, they go forth completely, pervading the body on all sides; then that essence, situated within the channels, [unites] with the self through the body.
From that which is being cooked, two types of cooking occur again; first it is enveloped by skin, and then blood is produced.
From blood arise body hair and flesh; from flesh come the hair of the head and the sinews; from the sinews likewise come the bones; and the nails and marrow are produced from the bones.
Due to the deficiency of marrow as a cause, semen is indeed of the nature of procreation; thus, the twelvefold transformation of food is proclaimed.
From food, semen is produced; from semen, the birth of the divine body occurs. When, during the period of conception, faultless semen is situated within the womb, [the embryo is formed].
That [sperm], touched by the wind, attains oneness with the female blood at the time of the emission of the semen; then the *jīva*, conjoined with its causes, enters.
Constrained by its own past actions, it enters the womb; that semen and blood, united in one place, become a *kalala* within a single day.
Within five nights, the *kalila* (the mass of cells) attains the form of a bubble; after seven nights, that bubble becomes a *māṃsapeśī* (fleshy lump).
The neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, as well as the abdomen, the hands and feet, the sides, the hips, and likewise the limbs.
Within just two months, these will gradually come into being here; indeed, within three months, all the joints of the sprouts are produced.
In four months, the fingers are produced in their proper order; and in five months, the mouth, nose, and ears are formed.
Likewise, the rows of teeth, the private parts, and the nails are produced again; moreover, the openings of the ears occur within six months.
The anus, the urinary tract, the generative organ, and the navel are produced; and the joints within the limbs are formed over the course of seven months.
O best of sages, fully developed in all his limbs and members, he remains within his mother’s womb, covered by the placenta.
Through the sixfold essence of the mother’s food, which is conveyed by means of the umbilical cord, he grows day by day.
Then, while still within this very body, the living being regains memory; it perceives pleasure and pain, as well as sleep and dreams resulting from its past actions.
I have died and been born again; having been born, I have died again. While being born, thousands of various wombs were seen by me.
Now that I have just been born and have already received the sacraments, I shall perform that which is most beneficial, by which there will be no further birth in a womb.
While still within the womb, he reflects thus: "Once I have emerged from the womb, I shall seek the knowledge of Śiva, which brings an end to the cycle of worldly existence."
Thus, intensely tormented by the great suffering of the womb, the living being remains there under the power of karma, contemplating the means for liberation.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain remains in suffering, so the embodied soul remains in pain, enveloped by the fetal membrane.
Just as one who has fallen into the ocean remains distressed and agitated, so too does he then remain perpetually troubled, his limbs drenched by the fluids of the womb.
Just as someone placed in an iron cauldron is cooked by fire, so too one cast into the womb-cauldron is cooked by the digestive fire.
The suffering that arises for one who is pierced continuously by needles the color of fire is even greater for one situated there [in that hell].
There is no suffering anywhere more painful or difficult than dwelling in the womb; for embodied beings, it is full of misery, most terrible, and exceedingly constricted.
This is proclaimed as the great suffering of sinners; for those whose intellects are solely devoted to dharma, however, existence [in this world] always lasts but seven months.

O Vyāsa, the suffering arising from the compression of the womb-mechanism, which is extremely difficult to endure within the womb, occurs for those of sinful nature, but certainly not for those whose souls are endowed with dharma.
O sinner, [he suffers] as if sugarcane being crushed on all sides by a press, and his head is struck with a mallet.
Just as sesame seeds, when pressed by a machine, become devoid of essence in an instant, so too does the body become devoid of essence from being compressed by the machine of the womb.
It has bones for its pillars and feet, is bound together by the cords of sinews, is plastered with the clay of blood and flesh, and is a vessel for the substances of feces and urine.
Covered with hair, body-hair, and nails, this sickly abode of disease has the mouth as its single great door and is adorned with eight windows.
With the two lips as its door-panels and the tongue as its bolt, it is a fool afflicted by thirst for enjoyment, following the sway of passion and hatred.
With its major and minor limbs contracted and enveloped by the fetal membrane, it emerged through the narrow and impure birth canal.
In this world, the body should be understood as a well-known skeletal cage, its limbs drenched in feces, urine, and blood, and produced from a seed that has cast off its husk.
There are three hundred and sixty [bones], and five hundred peśīs; it is covered on all sides by thirty-five million hairs.
The body is indeed surrounded on all sides by these tens of millions of channels, which are known to be both gross and subtle, and visible and invisible.
By those [teeth] which, being without sweat or honey, cause what is within to flow out; thirty-two teeth are proclaimed, and twenty nails are recorded.
One *kuḍava* of bile should be known [as the quantity], while one *āḍhaka* is recorded for phlegm; there are twenty *palas* of muscle fat (*vasā*), and half of that for the brown (*kapila*) variety.
The liver is known to weigh five and a half *tulās*, or ten *palas* of fat; the great blood (*mahārakta*) is three *palas*, and the marrow is four times that amount.
The semen of embodied beings should be known as one *kuḍava* in weight; it is their seed and their strength. And the flesh, taken as a single mass, is said to weigh one thousand *palas*.
O best of sages, it should be known that blood is one hundred palas in measure, while feces and urine are each four añjalis.
Thus, this body-house belongs to the eternal Self, which is itself impermanent; it is impure for that which is pure, being constructed from the bondage of karma.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Body," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa of great intelligence, O sage, to the impurity of the body and the greatness of its true nature; I shall describe them to you in brief.
Since this body is born from the union of semen and blood, and is constantly filled with feces and urine, it is therefore remembered as impure.
Just as a jar that is full of impurity within is not pure on the outside, so too this body, even when being cleansed, remains impure because of that internal impurity.
Having obtained the most purifying five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sacrificial oblations, they become impure in an instant; what else, then, could be more impure than that?
Even foods and drinks that are pleasing to the heart and fragrant, upon reaching this [body], quickly turn into impurity; what else could be more impure than that?
O people, do you not see that filth and stench which issues forth from your own bodies day after day; how then can its receptacle be pure?
Even though the body is being purified with the five products of the cow and water infused with kuśa grass, it does not attain purity, just as charcoal does not become clean even when scrubbed.
How can that body be purified, from which streams constantly flow like those from a mountain, consisting of phlegm, urine, feces, and the like?
In this body, which is a storehouse of all impurities, not even a single spot is pure, just as there is no clean place on a leather bag filled with excrement and urine.
Even after creating streams from one's own body, the hand is cleansed with earth and water; nevertheless, does the hand not remain part of that vessel of impurity?
Even if one's body is well-adorned with fragrant perfumes, incense, and the like, it does not abandon its inherent nature, just as a dog's tail cannot be bent [to stay up].
Just as an object that is black by its very nature cannot become white through any means, so too a physical form, even when being thoroughly cleansed, cannot become stainless.
Even while smelling his own foul odor and seeing his own filth, this world does not become dispassionate, even though it causes its own nose to suffer.
Oh, the greatness of delusion, by which this world is obscured! Even while quickly perceiving its own defects, one does not become dispassionate toward the body.
If a man is not repelled by the foul odor of his own body, what cause for detachment can possibly be taught to him?
In the midst of the entire world, the body itself is impure; through contact with its excretions and constituent parts, even that which is pure becomes impure.

Purification of the body is proclaimed for the purpose of removing odors and smears; purity results from the removal of both, and one becomes thoroughly pure through contact with something already pure.
Even if one were to perform purification until death with all the water of the Gaṅgā and with loads of earth as large as mountains, one whose internal disposition is corrupt is not purified.
A person of wicked soul is never purified by bathing at sacred fords or by austerities; does a dog-skin water-bag attain purity even when washed at a sacred ford?
For one whose inner being is corrupted, even if they enter the sacrificial fire, there is neither heaven nor liberation; rather, it results only in the burning of the body.
We declare that a person whose mind is corrupted does not become pure, even if they are devoted to bathing with all the water of the Gaṅgā and even with a mountain of clay from birth until death.

Having kindled a great fire, drenched with ghee and oil, its flames curling to the right, one who enters it and is consumed by the flames—if his heart is corrupt—attains neither dharma nor any other fruit.

Fish dwell constantly in sacred bathing places such as the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds reside eternally in temples; yet, being devoid of pure intention, they do not obtain the fruit of plunging into those holy sites nor likewise from giving gifts.
Purity of intention is the supreme cleanliness in all actions according to the authoritative scriptures; otherwise, a beloved wife is embraced with one kind of feeling, while a daughter with another.
The function of the mind differs even with respect to objects that are not distinct; a woman thinks of her son in one way, and her husband in another.
Behold the complete and great fortune of this state: that even when embraced by a noble woman, one devoid of such feeling does not desire her.
One should not eat various kinds of food, nor fragrant delicacies, if one harbors thoughts within the mind regarding the three beginning with desire.
A person is grasped by that state of being, yet through that very state they are liberated from being; one whose self is pure through such being attains both heaven and liberation.

With his inner self purified through devotion, burning, offering oblations, and praising, he died; yet, through the attainment of knowledge, he quickly reached the worlds of those who perform many sacrifices.
Furthermore, by means of the stainless water of knowledge and the clay of true detachment, there is the purification of the stains and odors of the excrement and urine of ignorance and passion.
Thus, this body is indeed known to be impure by its very nature; it has skin alone as its essence, yet is devoid of substance, resembling the core of a plantain tree.

Having thus understood the body to be full of defects, the wise man becomes detached; through the cessation of the mental states arising from bodily enjoyments, his mind becomes tranquil and his intellect clear.
He transcends saṃsāra and becomes liberated while living; he remains within saṃsāra as one who firmly grasps its core, which is like the pith of a plantain tree.
Thus, this birth is proclaimed to be a great hardship and suffering for men, caused by the fault of ignorance and the power of various karmas.
I shall state in half a verse what has been taught by millions of books: "It is mine" is the supreme suffering; "it is not mine" is the supreme happiness.
Even many kings here, though bound by hundreds of thousands of ties, have gone from this world to the next once they were endowed with the state of selflessness.
The memory that he possessed while remaining in the womb perishes for him due to the intense suffering of being crushed by the mechanism of the birth canal.
Or, by the external wind, through its terrible and deluding contact, as soon as it touches this embodied being, a fever arises.
By that great fever, a profound delusion arises; for one who is deluded, a loss of memory quickly occurs once again.
Then, due to that loss of memory, no memory of his previous karma arises; instead, a longing for that very birth quickly takes hold of the living being.
This world, being both attached and deluded, does not engage in what ought to be done; it knows neither itself, nor another, nor the divine.
O noble sage, even though he possesses ears, he does not hear the highest good; and even though he possesses eyes capable of seeing it, he does not behold the highest good.
Walking slowly on the very same path, as if stumbling at every step, he does not recognize it even when being enlightened by the wise, despite his intellect being present.
Driven by the power of craving for the womb, he is afflicted in saṃsāra; his mind abandoned by the sin of being mindful of the womb, the man [wanders on].
Thus has this great, supreme, and divine scripture been spoken by Śiva for the purpose of explaining austerity, which is the means for achieving heaven and liberation.
That those who do not bring about their own welfare, despite possessing true, auspicious knowledge that accomplishes all desired aims—this, indeed, is a great marvel here.
Furthermore, in childhood there is great suffering because the functions of the senses are unmanifest; even though one desires to do so, one is unable to speak or to take remedial action.
There is great suffering during the emergence of the teeth, as well as from minor ailments, various childhood diseases, and even from the afflictions of infantile spirits.
In some places his body is overcome by hunger and thirst; in others he stands crying out, and out of delusion the fool may even practice such acts as eating excrement and urine.
In childhood, during the pain of ear-piercing, and through the upbringing by mother and father, as well as through the study of the alphabet and so forth, various sufferings arise.
Having already transcended suffering in childhood, even while seeing it clearly, one of deluded intellect does not perform what is for his own welfare; this is a great marvel in this world.
Because the functions of the senses are active and one is constantly tormented by the disease of desire, how can there be happiness in youth when that [object of desire] is not attained?
Through envy there is great suffering, and for one who is deluded and attached to it, it leads only to misery—just like an eye that has become inflamed; therefore, one should abandon it.
Tormented by the fire of desire, he finds no sleep at night; and even by day, how can there be happiness, given the anxiety of acquiring wealth?
Those drops of semen belonging to a man whose mind is fixed upon women do not lead to happiness; they are regarded as such, like things born of sweat.
Those who know the nature of women understand that the pleasure they experience is like that of a leper or a monkey being tormented by worms, which arises from the heat of scratching.
Just as one considers pleasure to arise from the discharge of pus from an abscess, so should it be regarded regarding women; nothing more exists within them.
The pleasure that arises from the voiding of feces and urine is exactly the same as that found with women; it is only by fools that this is otherwise imagined.
Regarding women who are essentially unreal or the abode of all defects, not even an atom of happiness is said to exist in them by Pañcacūḍā.
Through honor and dishonor, through separation and union with the beloved, youth is seized by old age; where, then, is there any happiness free from affliction?
With his body rendered flaccid by wrinkles, gray hair, and baldness, and made infirm in all activities, he was worn out by old age.
In the past, the youth of both man and woman was heart-stealing and dear to one another; yet that very same youth, when seized by old age, is no longer dear even to them.
Who else could be more senseless than he who, even while seeing his own self transformed by old age as if it were something new, still remains attached to it?
A man overcome by old age is humiliated by his sons, grandsons, and other kinsmen, as well as by servants who are difficult to restrain because of their attachment.
One who is afflicted by extreme old age is unable to accomplish either dharma, wealth, pleasure, or liberation; therefore, a young man should practice dharma.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Impurity of the Body and the Sufferings of Infancy and Other States," in the *Umā-Saṃhitā*, the fifth book of the glorious *Śiva-Mahāpurāṇa*, concerning the medical treatment of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-cikitsā*).
Vyāsa said: O Sage, if you are pleased with me, tell me in brief that which was spoken disparagingly regarding women by Pañcacūḍā.
Sanatkumāra said: O Brahmin, listen as I describe the true nature of women exactly as it is; by the mere hearing of which, supreme detachment shall arise.
For women are indeed the root of faults, O Sage, being always fickle-minded; therefore, those who desire liberation and are unwearied should not form an attachment to them.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history: the dialogue between Nārada and the unchaste woman Pañcacūḍā.
In ancient times, while wandering through the worlds, the wise celestial sage Nārada beheld the peerless young Apsaras Pañcacūḍā.
Nārada, the best of sages, questioned the fair-browed Apsaras: "O slender-waisted one, there is a certain doubt in my heart; explain that to me."
Thus addressed, that excellent Apsaras replied to the Brahmin: "If there is an object [of desire], I shall speak; you consider me to be capable."
Nārada said: "O blessed lady, I shall by no means employ you in a matter that is beyond your scope. O slender-waisted one, I wish to hear from you about the nature of women."
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard these words of that celestial sage, the most excellent of Apsarases replied to that lord of sages, the celestial sage and best of munis.
Pañcacūḍā said: "O Sage, listen; it is not possible for one virtuous woman to censure another woman. You already know what women are like and what their nature is by its very character."
"O celestial sage, you ought not to enjoin me with such a question," having said this, Pañcacūḍā, the best of Apsarases, became silent.
Then the eminent celestial sage, having heard those excellent words, replied once more to her out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Nārada said: "There is fault in speaking falsehood; no fault exists in truth. Know this to be the truth, O lady of beautiful waist, and speak accordingly."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, she—resolute, impetuous, and sweetly smiling—began to speak of the eternal and true defects of women.
Pañcacūḍā said: "O Nārada, women who are of noble birth, possessed of protectors, and endowed with beauty do not abide within the bounds of propriety; that is the fault inherent in women."
Indeed, there is nothing else more evil than women; for women are the root of all evils, as you yourself well know.
Having obtained men who are well-known, wealthy, handsome, and as desired, women are not able to wait even for a moment longer.
O Lord, this is indeed an unrighteous thing for us women, that we abandon our modesty and resort to sinful men.
Women desire that very man who seeks them out, approaches them closely, and even performs a slight service for them.
Due to the lack of suitors among men and out of fear of their husbands, women—who are otherwise unrestrained—remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands.
There is no one they do not despise, nor do they have any regard for age; whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy the company of any man.
Neither out of fear, nor from reproach, nor for the sake of wealth in any way, nor due to ties with their paternal kin or family, do women remain faithful to their husbands.
Women of noble family long for those women who, being in the prime of youth, adorned with desirable ornaments and garments, live according to their own will.
For even those beloved women who are constantly cherished and guarded may become attached to hunchbacks, the blind, the mentally dull, or dwarfs.
O divine sage, even among the lame and other men who are despised, there is no one in the worlds whom women may not approach, O great muni.
O Brahmin, if the destiny of men cannot be fulfilled in any way, they even act toward one another and do not remain faithful to their husbands.
Due to the lack of men, fear of their attendants, and the dread of execution or imprisonment, those women indeed have their hopes shattered.
Fickle by nature and characterized by wicked conduct, you are likewise difficult to grasp, just as it is for a wise man in this world when he is possessed by passion.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women with men.
O celestial sage, this and another secret of all women is that as soon as they see a man, a woman’s womb immediately becomes moistened.
Upon seeing a man who is well-bathed, fragrant, and free from impurity, the female organ of women becomes moistened, just as water flows from a leather bag or a vessel.
Women cannot endure even a husband who gives them their bodies, who provides mental comfort, and who protects them, if he is not supreme.
They do not consider the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, nor the accumulation of ornaments and wealth, to be as beneficial as the acquisition of sexual pleasure.
The Ender, the ascetic, death, the underworld, the submarine fire, the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire—all these are on one side, while women are on the other.
Since the five great elements were created, since the world was ordained by the Creator, and since men and women were fashioned, O Nārada, there has always been fault in women.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard her words, Nārada was pleased in his mind; considering them to be true, he then indeed became detached from those [women].
Thus has the nature of women been described by you with care, as spoken by Pañcacūḍā; O Vyāsa, what else, which may cause detachment, do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Women," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: O omniscient Sanatkumāra, O sage, I have heard about the nature of women from you with great affection; now, please tell me the knowledge of time.
Sanatkumāra said: In former times, having heard various divine stories, Pārvatī became delighted; she bowed deeply before the Supreme Lord and asked him this very same thing.
Pārvatī said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, I have understood your entire doctrine—how you are to be worshipped, O God, with which mantras, and according to what ritual procedure."
O Lord, even now there remains one doubt regarding the Wheel of Time: O God, what are the signs of death, and what is the measure of the lifespan?
"O Lord, tell me thus if I am dear to you. Being questioned in this way by the Goddess, Maheśvara replied:
Īśvara said: O beloved, I shall tell you the truth regarding the scripture that is supreme among all, by which scripture, O Goddess of gods, men awaken to the nature of time.
Day, fortnight, month, season, solstice, and year—[all these are known] through signs that are gross or subtle, and likewise external or internal.
I shall explain that to you here; listen to it in its true essence, O beautiful one, for the benefit of the worlds and for the sake of dispassion, O Umā, now.
O beloved, if the body suddenly becomes pale with a reddish tint all over, one should know that death will occur within six months.
When there is stiffness of the mouth, the ears, as well as the eyes and the tongue, then one should know that death will occur within six months, O beloved.
O auspicious one, if one does not quickly hear the sound following the *raurava* [note], those who know the times should understand that death will occur within six months.
When one no longer perceives the radiance resulting from the conjunction of the sun, moon, and fire, and sees everything as entirely black, then one's life remains for only six months.
O Goddess, O beloved, when the left hand throbbs for seven days, then his life span is one month; of this there is no doubt.
When the limbs begin to droop and the palate becomes parched, his life will last for exactly one month; of this there is no doubt.
If one's nose drips due to the three humors (tridoṣa), the life span is but a fortnight; if the mouth and throat become parched, the life of such a person has departed at the end of six months.
O beautiful woman, if one's tongue becomes thick and the teeth become moist, death will occur within six months; one should recognize this by those signs.
O woman of excellent complexion, when one does not see oneself as distorted or even as mere flesh in water, oil, ghee, or in a mirror;
One who understands the *Kālacakra* should know that his lifespan is six months. Listen to something else, O Goddess of Gods, by which death is recognized.
When one perceives one's own shadow to be headless, or when one is deprived of a shadow, one does not live for even a single month.
O Pārvatī, I have described the bodily signs of death; O auspicious lady, listen now as I speak of the external signs.
O Goddess, when the orbs of the moon and the sun appear devoid of rays and take on a pale-red hue, one perishes within half a month.
The Arundhatī star is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) devoid of the mark of the moon; he who does not see that star lives for only one month.
When a planet is seen, a confusion of the directions certainly arises after six months; one would not see either the pole star (Uttarāṣāḍhā) or the solar disc.
If one should see a rainbow at night or the falling of meteors at midday, and if one is surrounded by vultures and crows, there is no doubt that his lifespan is but six months.
Sages and the paths to heaven are no longer visible in the sky; men who understand the signs of time should recognize that their lifespan is now limited to six months.
If one suddenly sees the sun or the moon as if swallowed by Rāhu, and perceives the circle of the quarters as if spinning, he will clearly die within six months.
If a man is suddenly swarmed by blue flies, his lifespan should be known, according to ultimate truth, to be exactly one month.
A vulture, a crow, and a pigeon stand having perched upon his head; there is no doubt that the creature will die within one month.
Thus has the classification of external signs of death been proclaimed; for the benefit of human beings, I shall now describe them in brief.
O Goddess, just as one discerns [the breath] in both hands at the appropriate time—between the left and the right—it is declared to be "perceptible" (pratyakṣa).
Thus, O beautiful goddess, these two sides have been briefly established; having become pure, having bathed well, and having restrained the senses, one should remember the God.
Having washed both hands, one should rub them with milk and lac; then, having applied perfumes and flowers to the hands, one should seek out the auspicious and the inauspicious.
O Dear One, beginning with the little finger and proceeding up to the thumb, one should perform this for both hands in the sequence of three mountain-like stages.
Having placed the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) starting from the first day, one should stand facing the eastern direction with both hands in the *saṃpuṭa* (casket) gesture.
One should recite the nine-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times, and then carefully examine both hands at every joint.
On that lunar day (parvan), that line resembling a bee is seen; on that very date, O beloved, death is to be known, whether in the dark or the bright fortnight.
Now I shall briefly describe the characteristics of time born of *nāda*; having understood the outgoing and incoming [breaths], one should perform the ritual action—listen, O beloved!

O lady of beautiful hips, having diligently understood the movement of self-consciousness—the moment (kṣaṇa), the instant (truṭi), the minute (lava), the blink of an eye (nimeṣa), and the duration of a wood-pile (kāṣṭha)—[one attains liberation].
A moment, a day and night, a fortnight, a month, a season, a year, an age, as well as a kalpa and likewise a mahākalpa.
In this way, that ever-auspicious Time (Sadāśiva) carries [the soul] away in regular succession; this is known as the triple path consisting of the left, the right, and the middle.
Beginning from five days and extending up to twenty-five days, the measure of the sound (nāda) in the practice of the left-hand path (vāmācāra) has been explained to you.
O lady of excellent complexion, the Bhūta, Raṃdhra, and Diś directions, as well as the Dhvaja, are the measures of sound for one who knows time when moving in a counter-clockwise direction.

O beautiful woman, the qualities that arise as modifications of the seasons are likewise present there; those who know the nature of life-force should understand that the right side is declared to be the standard of measure.
When the elements, such as Iḍā and the others, carry the vital breaths in their numerical proportions during the course of a year, his life will indeed continue; of this there is no doubt.
With a flow of ten [breaths] per day, he lives for a full year; with a flow of fifteen [breaths] per day, his life span has reached its end after one year.
Then, by a flow of twenty days, one should mark six months; for twenty-five days, the left channel (vāmanāḍī) flows.
At that time, the life of one whose lifespan has expired lasts for three months; two months are said to consist of a measure of twenty-six days.
Flowing for a duration of twenty-seven days with extreme rest, it is declared that life lasts for one month when in the domain of the left.
This measure is to be understood from the measure of the left wind; on the other side [the right], there are exactly four days in successive order.
O Goddess, these sixteen are proclaimed as being situated in four locations; I shall now describe their measurements according to the truth.
Having begun from the first day and calculated according to the rule for six days, this has been revealed within the left nostril.
When [the sign] has been established for six days, he lives for two years; one should know that those [other signs] last for eight months and eight days.
Know that the life span is seventeen years without a doubt; one should know it to be seven months along with six days, without a doubt.
Indeed, by the division of eight days, he lives for two years; the four months should be understood as having a limit of twenty-four days.
When the vital breaths flow for nine days, that constitutes three months; for two months, it is two months; and for twelve days, it is proclaimed as two months.
The time previously mentioned for those [periods] is the same as before; however, the intermediate days are expressed by means of that month.
He lives for one year by means of the flow; likewise, nine months and eight days are also declared [to remain].
With the twelfth flow, he lives for one year; one should know that with seven months, and also declare it to be six days.
When the channel flows for a period of thirteen days, that constitutes one year; four such months are proclaimed [to equal one year].
There is no doubt that twenty-four days of life remain; for when the flow of the vital breath is in the left [nostril] for fourteen days, [the remainder is as stated].
His lifespan is proclaimed to be one year, consisting of six months and exactly twenty-four days; of this there is no doubt.
With a flow of fifteen [breaths], he lives for nine months and exactly twenty-four days; thus it has been declared by those who know time.
By a flow of sixteen days, he lives for ten months; an excess of twenty-four days has been declared by those who know time.
O Mistress of Sādhanas, it is said here that when the lifespan has been reduced by nine months through seventeen flows, eighteen days remain.
O Goddess, when the movement is to the left for a period of eighteen days, life is said to last eight months and twelve days.
Determine with certainty that here it lasts for twenty-four days; O Goddess, when the flow of the vital breath lasts until the end of twenty-three days.
Four months and six days are declared [as the duration]; furthermore, by means of twenty-four flows, he lives for three months.
In this [cycle], eighteen days are indeed withdrawn through the movement [of the breath]; that which occurs on the intermediate day has thus been described to you in brief.
The practice of the left has been fully explained; now hear concerning the right. It lives by the measure of the lunar days within the twenty-eighth flow.
By a flow lasting ten days, one perishes; by a flow lasting thirty days, one perishes after five days.
O Goddess, when [the breath] flows continuously for thirty-one [instants], then his life lasts for three days; of this there is no doubt.
When the Sun indeed flows for a duration numbering thirty-two breaths, then his life lasts for two days; of this there is no doubt.
The right [channel] has been described as the prāṇa; now I shall describe to you that which is situated in the middle: the flow of the wind located in a single part within the circle of the mouth.
He lives for one day by means of a flowing current; indeed, that is described by those who know the ancient lore as the cycle of the one whose life has passed away.
This Kālacakra of those whose life has expired has been told to you, O Goddess, for the benefit of the worlds. What else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of Time," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, you have indeed explained the knowledge of time according to its true meaning; now tell me, in accordance with reality, how yogis deceive time."
For time indeed draws near for all living beings; and just as death does not bypass one for whom its appointed time has arrived.
O Lord, bestower of all happiness, having shown affection toward me, speak thus for my sake and for the benefit of the yogis.
Śaṅkara said: Listen, O Goddess Śivā, for I shall explain that which I have been asked by you—in brief—for the benefit of all human beings.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—indeed, the combination of these constitutes the body composed of the five elements.
But space is more pervasive than that; it stands as all-pervading for all things. In space they dissolve, and from it they arise again.
But upon separation, O beautiful one, who among them has ever attained their own abode? Such stability belongs only to that [state] which is free from the collision [of the humors].
Likewise, even those who possess knowledge, through the power of austerity and mantra, all of them thoroughly understand all this; of this there is no doubt.

The Goddess said: That terrible and formidable Time (Kāla), the sole lord of the three worlds, who was perishing by means of the void, was burnt by you; yet, being praised with hymns, he became satisfied once more and regained his own original nature.
And he was told by you: "You shall move about among people in an invisible form. There, that being of great power was seen by you, and by the boon of the Lord, he rose up once again.

Therefore, O Lord Kāla, tell me now if there is anything remaining here that must be destroyed; for you are the best of yogis, a self-dependent master, and a Great Lord who assumes a body solely for the sake of helping others.
Śaṅkara said: "They are not slain by the best of gods, nor by Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Uragas, or humans. Those yogins who are devoted to meditation and remain embodied, they easily conquer Time."

Sanatkumāra said: Having heard this from the teacher of the three worlds, Gaurī laughed and said, "Tell me truly, how is it that this Time (Kāla) is slain? Śambhu said to her immediately: "O fish-faced one, those sinless yogins who quickly cast off the serpent of Time—listen to that with a focused mind."
Śaṅkara said: O lady of excellent hips, the body, composed of the five elements, is always joined with their qualities; it is produced, and indeed, the earthly being dissolves back into them.
From space, wind is born; from wind, fire is born; from fire, water is said to arise; and from that, indeed, earth comes into being.
The elements, beginning with earth, gradually merge into the Supreme. Earth is said to possess five qualities, and water possesses four qualities.
Likewise, fire has three qualities, and air has exactly two; space is proclaimed to have the single quality of sound among the elements beginning with earth.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—when each element abandons its own respective quality, then that element perishes.
Then it grasps the quality that has manifested; this is called its appearance. Know thus, O Goddess of Gods, the five elements according to their true nature.
Therefore, O Goddess, a yogi who desires to conquer time must always diligently contemplate the qualities born of their respective parts at their own specific times.
The Goddess said: O Lord, knower of yoga, how is time overcome by yogis? Is it through meditation or through mantra? Tell me all of that.
Śaṅkara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim [this] out of a desire for the welfare of yogins; this exposition of supreme knowledge must not be given to just anyone.
It should be given to one who has faith, who is endowed with devotion, and who is wise; to one who is not an atheist, who is pure, and who is constant in dharma, O beautiful lady.
The knower of yoga should practice yoga on a comfortable bed with easy breathing; he should maintain his concentration even in darkness without a lamp while all beings are asleep.
Having covered his ears with his index fingers and pressed them for a moment, he then heard a sound arising from fire that was piercingly intense.
Indeed, even that which has been eaten at twilight or has become stale for a moment quickly destroys all diseases and many complications of fever.
And whoever perceives the form for two *ghaṭikās* as eternal, having conquered death as well as desire, may wander here according to his own will.
One who is all-knowing and all-seeing shall attain every accomplishment, just as the cloud, well-restrained by the waters of the rainy season, thunders in the sky.
Having heard that, the yogi is immediately liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra; thereafter, he shall become ever more subtle than the subtlest among yogis.
