This sequence of the ritual procedure for the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) has been told to you, O Goddess; like one seeking grain discards the straw, one should abandon bondage entirely.
Those who, having attained this Brahman that is Sound, still desire anything else, strike at empty space with their fists and long for hunger and thirst.
Having known this supreme Brahman—which bestows happiness, is the cause of liberation, is non-external, imperishable, and entirely free from all limiting adjuncts—[one attains the goal].
Deluded by the noose of Time and fallen under the power of the noose of Death, those sinners of wicked intellect do not know the Brahman of Sound.
They remain in saṃsāra as long as they do not find the abode; but when the supreme reality is known, one is released from the bondage of birth.
Having diligently conquered sleep, laziness, and great obstacles as enemies, one should remain constantly in a comfortable posture, practicing the *śabdabrahman*.

A man even a hundred years old, having obtained this, should practice it for as long as he lives; it results in victory over death, the stabilization of the body, health, and the increase of vital energy (vāyu).
A sign is seen even in an old man, how much more so in a young person; yet there is no *oṃ* syllable, nor mantra, nor seed-syllable, nor even a letter.
O Goddess, O beloved, the wise constantly and with effort meditate upon the unstruck, ineffable, supreme Śiva, the Brahman of Sound.

Therefore, nine sounds have been proclaimed and identified by those who know the vital breath (prāṇa); I shall explain them with effort, in due order, for the sake of attaining perfection in sound (nāda).
A bell-metal vessel (ghoṣa), bronze (kāṃsya), a horn (śṛṅga), a bell (ghaṇṭā), a lute (vīṇā), and a flute (divaṃśaja).
The sound of a drum (7), the sound of a conch (8), and the ninth is the roar of clouds (9).
Abandoning the nine sounds, the yogi should practice the syllable *tuṃ*; meditating thus at all times, he is not stained by merits or sins.
O Goddess, when the practitioner of yoga does not hear what he hears through the practice of yoga, the yogi who is thus absorbed shall remain day and night as if dying.

From that, sound arises after seven days; indeed, O Goddess, it is of nine kinds, which I shall describe to you according to the truth. First, it resounds with a sound that brings supreme purification of the self; it is a resonance that removes all diseases and is the most excellent means for subjugation and attraction.
The second [mantra] should not be recited; it would paralyze the movement of living beings and bind all poisons, spirits, and planetary influences—of this there is no doubt.
One should not take the third horn; one should employ it for malevolent rites, for causing enmity and the eradication of an enemy, and for the purpose of killing.
The Supreme Lord declares the ringing of the bell to be the fourth; it attracts all the gods, so what need be said of humans on earth?
Indeed, the daughters of the yakṣas and gandharvas, being drawn by him, bestow upon the yogin the great siddhi as desired, whether according to his wish or even spontaneously.
The fifth sound, however, is always heard by yogis as the lute; from that, O Goddess, arises indeed the vision of the distant.
By meditating on the sound of the flute, all reality is produced; by meditating on the kettledrum, one becomes free from old age and death.
O Goddess of the gods, by the sound of a conch, the yogin attains the form of his desire; by the roar of thunder, he shall not encounter misfortune.
O fair-faced one, for him who constantly recites the syllable *tuṃ* with a single-minded focus as the very form of Brahman, what is there that cannot be accomplished, according to his understanding?
Omniscient and all-seeing, he moves about assuming any form at will; he is not affected by transformations, for he is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Goddess, this nature of the Śabdabrahman has been explained to you in its ninefold entirety. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Deceiving Time," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The Goddess said: "One attains the station of Vāyu, which arises from the ether of yoga; if you are pleased with me, O Lord, explain all of that to me."
Śaṅkara said: In the past, everything was told to me out of a desire for the welfare of yogins—how he completely conquered Time, and what the true nature of the sign of the wind is.
Having understood this, O beautiful one, the yogi remains devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma); he conquers the time that has arrived in just half a month.
The wind residing in the heart is the perpetual illuminator of the fire; it is the non-consumptive fire itself. That great wind is all-pervasive, both external and internal, and is omnipresent.
Knowledge, discernment, and enthusiasm—all these proceed from the wind; he by whom the wind is conquered here has conquered this entire world.
Desiring to destroy old age and death, the yogi, devoted to yoga and intent upon concentration and meditation, should always remain established in dhāraṇā.
Just as a blacksmith, O Sage, fills a bellows from the mouth and accomplishes his work by means of the air, so should the yogi practice.
The deity has a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and a thousand hands; having completely covered all the knots, he stands ten finger-breadths in front.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras, preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, three times while the breath is restrained; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, come and go; yet those devoted to yoga and meditation do not return even to this day.

O Goddess, by performing austerity for a hundred years and drinking water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass, a twice-born man obtains that same fruit through the single act of upholding the Brahmins.
That twice-born man who, having risen at dawn, performs even a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma), swiftly destroys all sin and goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who, unwearied, is constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) in solitude, having conquered old age and death, becomes one who moves through the air like the wind.
One partakes of the form, luster, intelligence, prowess, valor, and speed equal to the wind of a perfected being (siddha), as well as praiseworthy happiness and supreme bliss.
All this has been told in its entirety regarding the perfection which a yogi attains through Vāyu; O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now declare that which he also obtains from Tejas.
Having sat upon his own comfortable seat, he lies down in a place devoid of people, radiating splendor like the sun and moon in the middle region.
The yogi who, unwearied, beholds that which shines within the fire at the center of the eyebrows, undoubtedly sees less darkness in this world than one devoid of a lamp.
Gently pressing the eyes with the fingers of the hands with effort, the yogi, being single-minded, should meditate for half a muhūrta while beholding the *tāra*.
Then, meditating upon that in the darkness, he beholds the divine light—white, red, yellow, black, and possessing the brilliance of a rainbow.
Having known that [Self] situated between the eyebrows on the forehead, possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun, the one whose limbs are desire sports, assuming forms at will.
The entry into the state of the pacification of causes, the penetration into another's body, the attainment of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā), and observation with the mind.
Through the constant practice of yoga, there arises the power of hearing from afar, invisibility, the assumption of many forms, and the state of moving through the sky.
Even those endowed with learning and study, experts in various scriptures, and possessed of knowledge, become deluded when following the influence of their past karma.
Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they are like the deaf; just like blind men in this world, these fools are utterly deluded by sin.
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness. Only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the final journey.
This supreme procedure for attaining perfect splendor has been fully explained to you; by mastering time through this, the yogi attains immortality.
Furthermore, I shall speak of that which is even more supreme, whereby death does not arise; listen with heedfulness, O Goddess, with a one-pointed mind.
O Goddess, for all beings, as well as for yogis and meditators, the fourth [state] is attained when the yogi, with a restrained mind, remains in his proper place upon a comfortable seat.
Though his body was tall, he joined his palms together and, with his mouth shaped like a beak, slowly drank in the air.
From the palate, life-bestowing waters flow forth in an instant; one should inhale that cool nectar-like water by means of the breath.
Drinking this daily, the yogi shall not fall under the power of death; possessing a divine body and great luster, he becomes free from thirst and hunger.

In strength he was like an elephant, in speed like a horse, in vision like Suparṇa, and in hearing like one who hears from afar; his black hair was curled and ringed, and his complexion was equal to that of a Gandharva or a Vidyādhara.

A man of excellent intellect may live for a hundred years among the gods, attaining equality with Vākpati; practicing thus, he attains the power of moving through the sky, wandering at will and always happy.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, listen to another ritual procedure which has been diligently guarded even by the gods.
The yogi should practice by contracting the rasanā toward the palate; after a short period of time, he gradually reaches the lambikā.
Then, being touched, it flows forth as cool nectar; by constantly drinking this, the yogi indeed attains immortality.

The tip of the letter *ra*, the tip of the hanging *laṃ*, and the joining of the palms upon the drop of the white lotus—by this, that nectar which brings joy to the deities is drawn up and falls into the supreme state. He whose limbs are drenched by this essence—which crosses over the cycle of existence, purifies committed sins, and transcends time, along with its stars—becomes immortal, free from hunger and thirst.

O Daughter of the Mountain, this earth belongs to those yogis who possess these four qualities; for what end could she have, since she exists eternally through fortitude only to provide happiness to the entire world? Indeed, a living being always regards everything—even suffering—as pleasure within a dream, and thus one who attains heaven from this earth gains no more than a fraction of those four [qualities].

Therefore, through mantras, austerities, vows, and observances, as well as medicinal herbs and yoga, a nurse who is devoted and endowed with human qualities, discipline, and knowledge of dharma, should gradually [attend to the child]. For the primordial god of all beings does not indeed become unstable when united with these four; therefore, I shall thus explain the prescribed procedure known as the "Shadow" (Chāyika) rite dedicated to Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Deception of Time and the Attainment of Śiva," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you have explained the deception of Time, the nature of the Śabdabrahman, and the supreme characteristics of Yoga.
The supreme knowledge of the shadow has been told to you in brief; explain it in detail out of a desire for the welfare of yogins.
Śaṅkara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the characteristics of the shadow-person (icchāyā-puruṣa); by knowing which, a person is completely liberated from all sins.
Having placed the sun or the moon behind him, O fair-complexioned one, wearing white garments and garlands, and perfumed with scents, incense, and other fragrances;
One should recollect my great mantra, which bestows the fruit of all desires; having become a single compact mass as the ninefold self, one should gaze at one's own reflection.
Having seen her again in the sky in the form of a white color, he, being of single-minded devotion, beholds Śiva, the supreme cause.
It has been declared by those who know the proper time that the attainment of Brahman shall belong to him; he is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—of this there is no doubt.
When one perceives [the body] as headless, decay will occur within six months; for that yogi, however, the entirety of the Veda (vāṅmaya) becomes manifest in whatever way it may be.
One should recognize virtue in white, and designate evil in black; one should recognize bondage in red, and predict enmity in yellow.
In Dvitunda, there will be marriage and the loss of kinsmen, as well as fear of hunger; in Vikaṭa, the wife perishes, while in Vijangha, there is indeed wealth.
"O Maheśvarī, it has been stated by me that in the absence of the feet there would be a foreign land; this must be carefully considered with effort by a person."
Having beheld the person established in rightness and having settled him within himself by means of the self, one should mutter the nine-syllabled mantra, which is my heart, O Maheśvarī.

When a year has passed, there is nothing that the practitioner cannot accomplish; he attains the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and achieves the state of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
Furthermore, I shall speak of another matter to understand that power which is difficult to approach: it is seen directly in the world, standing before the eyes of the wise.

That which is written in the world as "ajñeyā" (unintelligible), formed with the *kuṇḍalī* [anusvāra], is that *mātrā* which, though situated in the vehicle [of the consonant], is neither seen nor recited.
She who reaches the summit of the cosmic egg and is eternally praised by the Vedas is the mother of all sciences and is celebrated as the "Secret Knowledge" (Guptavidyā).
She is designated as Khecarī, residing within all living beings; she is visible and invisible, immovable, eternal, manifest and unmanifest, and everlasting.
Colorless yet endowed with color, she is called Bindumālinī; beholding her at all times, the yogi becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Whatever fruit results from bathing at all sacred fords, and whatever fruit results from all sacrifices—that is obtained simply by the sight of Mālinī.
One attains this result here, there is no doubt; this truth has indeed been spoken by me—[the merit one gains] by bathing in all the sacred fords and giving gifts in every way.
O Goddess, a man shall obtain whatever fruit belongs to all sacrifices; O Maheśānī, what need is there for much speaking? He attains all his desires.
Therefore, the wise person should constantly practice knowledge as appropriate; from practice comes accomplishment, and yoga increases through practice.
Realization is attained through practice; through practice one enjoys liberation. Practice, the cause of liberation, must be performed constantly by the wise.
Thus has this been told, O Goddess, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. What else is asked? Speak the truth; I tell you the reality.
Sūta said: O lords of sages, having heard these words of the son of Brahmā which bestow the supreme truth, Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, became exceedingly pleased.
Vyāsa, being supremely satisfied, bowed down again and again to Sanatkumāra, the omniscient son of Brahmā and a treasure-house of compassion.
Then Vyāsa, that lord of sages, praised Sanatkumāra, the sage who is an ocean of divine knowledge, while the Kāleyas were listening. O sages, he was the master of the gods' wisdom.

Vyāsa said: O best of sages, my purpose is fulfilled; you have bestowed the state of Brahmanhood upon me. Salutations to you, salutations to you; you are blessed, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.
Sūta said: Having thus praised the great sage, the son of Brahmā, that Kāleya became silent, well-pleased and overflowing with supreme bliss.
Having been honored by him, Śaunaka, the son of Brahmā, took his leave and departed for his own abode well-pleased; Vyāsa also went away with a joyful mind.
Thus, O brahmins, has been described to me this discourse between Sanatkumāra and Kāleya, which bestows happiness, is endowed with the ultimate truth, and increases wisdom.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Shadow-Person," in the Umā-Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: I have heard this great narrative which you have related—the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Kāleya, which bestows the supreme truth.
Therefore, I wish to hear how the creation of Brahmā came about; tell me that exactly as it was heard by you from Vyāsa.
Sūta said: O Sage, listen to the divine narrative that destroys all sins—a wondrous tale being told by me, rich in meaning and extensive in its scriptural detail.
Whoever should teach this or listen to it repeatedly, having ensured the continuity of his own lineage, is honored in the heavenly world.
Pradhāna and Puruṣa, which are eternal and consist of both being and non-being—having become Pradhāna-Puruṣa, the creator of the worlds fashioned [the universe].
Know him, O best of sages, to be Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, the creator of all beings, who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
O tiger among sages, salutations to that Self-Existent One, by whom the end of the eons was fashioned and from whom the foremost pure beings arise.
Having paid homage to that Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa, and the Lord, I shall again proclaim the unsurpassed creation.
Brahmā is the creator, Hari is the protector, and Maheśvara is the destroyer; there is no other [agent] for that creation once time has thus passed from age to age.
Then that self-existent Lord, desiring to create various kinds of beings, first created the waters alone and cast his seed into them.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; since they were his first place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That egg, resting upon the water, became golden in color; there, Brahmā himself was born, renowned as the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū).
The blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, having dwelt for a full year, split that egg in two and fashioned heaven and earth.
The fourteen worlds were established below and above; between those two halves, the Lord created space.
Within the waters, he saw the earth floating, as well as the ten directions in the sky; there, in that time, he beheld the mind, speech, desire, anger, and pleasure.
The one of great splendor created the seven mind-born sons: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha.
"These seven are the Brahmas," such is the certainty established in the Purāṇas; thereafter, Brahmā again created the Rudras, who were born from his wrath.
And the sage Sanatkumāra, the eldest of all; these seven are born first, and afterwards the Rudras are born everywhere.
Then Sanatkumāra remains with his splendor withdrawn; these are their seven great lineages, divine and honored by the celestial rishis.
Active beings adorned by great seers are born from them, as well as lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, and red rainbows.
In the beginning, he created the waters and indeed created Parjanya; he fashioned the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses for the accomplishment of sacrifice.

We have heard that he worshipped the venerable gods with them; he generated the gods from his mouth and the ancestors from his chest, while he created humans from his private parts and the asuras from his hips.
High and low beings were born from his limbs as the Prajāpati Āpava was engaged in the creation of progeny.
When the creatures being created did not increase, he then divided his own body into two parts, becoming both female and male.
Then, having pervaded the universe in its entirety by his majesty, Viṣṇu created all beings; that Virāṭ Puruṣa was created as Virāj.
Know that second one to be Manu and the very interval of the Manvantara; that powerful Puruṣa, Vairāja, created all living beings.
From that creation of Nārāyaṇa, his progeny was not born from a womb; consequently, they were long-lived, famous, prosperous, and possessed of offspring.
Thus, O best of sages, this primary creation has been described by me; having understood the primary creation in this way, one shall attain the destination desired.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Primary Creation," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: When the creatures had been created, Āpava, the lord of progeny, indeed obtained Śatarūpā as his own wife. She was a woman who was not born of a womb.
But by the greatness of Āpava, as he stood pervading the heavens, that high-souled one was born through dharma alone as Śatarūpā.
Having performed most difficult austerities for a hundred years, she obtained as her husband a man of radiant ascetic power.
He was indeed born as Svāyaṃbhuva; he is called the Puruṣa Manu. His period of authority here is said to be a Manvantara consisting of seventy-one yugas.
From the Puruṣa Vairāja was born Śatarūpā, the heroic woman; from that heroic woman were born Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
The highly fortunate Kāmyā was the daughter of the progenitor Kardama; Kāmyā had three sons: Samrāṭ, Sākṣi, and Raviṭprabhu.
The lord Uttānapāda begot sons equal in power to Śakra, and a divine son named Dhruva, who was as radiant as his own self.
Dharma’s daughter, renowned by the name Sunīti, was fair-hipped; she was born of Dharma and likewise became the mother of Dhruva.
For three thousand divine years, that boy Dhruva performed austerities in the forest, seeking the imperishable station.
To him, the Lord Brahmā, the Prajāpati, being pleased, granted a station equal to his own, an immovable place situated before the Seven Sages.
From him, Puṣṭi and Dhānya were born as two sons from Dhruva. Thus, Puṣṭi, having risen up, gave birth to five sinless sons.
Ripu, Ripuñjaya, Vipra, Vṛkala, and Vṛṣatejas were the sons of Ripu; and the queen of Ripu likewise gave birth to Cākṣuṣa, who was renowned in every direction.
Cākṣuṣa Manu begot Varuṇa in Puṣkariṇī; ten sons of great prowess were born to Manu by Naḍvalā.
O best of sages, in the Kanyā [nakṣatra] the birth of a Vaiśya occurs; Purumāṃsa, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavit, and Kavi [are its names].
Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, Atimanyu, and Suyaśas—these ten sons Pūru begot upon Āgneyī, who was of great splendor. She gave birth to six sons of immense radiance.
From Aṅga, his wife Sunīthā gave birth to one son, Vena, who was known as Sumanas, Khyāti, Sṛti, Aṅgiras, and Gaya.
Due to the misconduct of Vena, a great anger arose among them; the sages, devoted to dharma, struck him down with a mere "hum" sound.
Then, requested by Sunīthā for the sake of offspring, the Sārasvata sages churned his right hand.
When the hand of Vena was churned, Pṛthu was born from it; he was born equipped with a bow and armor, radiant as the sun through his splendor.
For indeed, the descent of Viṣṇu was for the purpose of protecting the subjects, for the sake of preserving dharma, and for the purpose of punishing the wicked.
Then Pṛthu, the son of Vena and the first of the Kṣatriyas, protected the broad earth; he was the first lord of the world among those consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And from that very [cow] were born the skillful Sūta and Māgadha; by him, O best of sages, was this cow milked for the welfare of all.
The king, who performed a hundred sacrifices, became the provider of sustenance for all—the celestial sages, gods, and rākṣasas—and for human beings especially.
Two sons were born to Pṛthu, both knowers of dharma and kings upon the earth: Vijitāśva and Haryakṣa, great heroes of wide renown.
And Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to a son, Prācīnabarhis; for him, as he wandered upon the surface of the earth, the blades of Kuśa grass grew with their tips pointing eastward.
The daughter of the ocean was wedded by him according to dharma; having taken a wife, the great lord, the king, shone with even greater splendor.
The son of Samudratanayā, Prācīnabarhis, who performed many sacrifices, had ten divine sons.
All those known by the name Prācetasas were masters of the science of archery; practicing their duties without deviation, they performed great austerities.
For ten thousand years they lay within the waters of the ocean, reciting the Rudragīta and remaining devoted to the meditation on Śiva.
While the ascetics were performing penance on the earth, the trees ceased to grow; and as the earth remained unprotected, there occurred a destruction of the population.

Having seen them, O tiger among sages, those who had obtained excellent boons through their asceticism turned back; possessing the power of penance, they became enraged, desiring to consume them with fire.
From their mouths, the sons of Pracetas emitted fire and wind; having uprooted the trees, the wind blew them away, and the carrier of oblations (Agni) consumed them.
Then, seeing the destruction of the trees when only a few branches remained, the powerful King Soma approached them and spoke.
Soma said: "O kings, all you descendants of Prācīnabarhis, restrain your anger; this lady of excellent complexion has been experienced by the trees."
Knowing what was to come, I indeed carried her in my womb; let this highly fortunate woman be your wife, for she shall increase the Lunar dynasty.
In her shall be born the wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa, the creator of beings, possessed of great splendor, the ancient son of Brahmā.
With half of your splendor and with this splendor of mine, the king, composed of the splendor of Brahman, shall cause the subjects to prosper.
Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas affectionately and according to dharma accepted that beautiful woman born of a tree as their wife.
From them was born to her the Prajāpati named Dakṣa; he too, O Sage, was born of a portion of Soma and possessed great splendor.
Having mentally created both the immobile and the mobile, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds, Dakṣa began the creation of sexual reproduction.
He married Vīraṇī, the daughter of Prajāpati Vīraṇa, who was devoted to her husband, according to the proper rites and in accordance with righteous dharma.
In her, he begot ten thousand meritorious sons who had bay horses; they became dispassionate through the instruction of Nārada.
Having heard that, Dakṣa again begot upon her thousand sons by name called Subalāśvas.
Following the path of their brother due to that sage's instruction, they too did not return to their father’s presence; detached and following the way of mendicants, they departed.
Hearing that curse, he became enraged and pronounced an unbearable one upon the sage: "O lover of quarrels, may you find no stable footing anywhere!"
Then, having been consoled by the Creator, that lord of sages subsequently created women, who were of the nature of great flames and possessed of [excessive] qualities.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, two to the son of Brahmā, and likewise two to Aṅgiras.
O best of sages, the lord Dakṣa gave two to the wise sage Kṛśāśva, and he gave the remaining ones called the Nakṣatras to Soma.
From those daughters of Dakṣa were born the gods, asuras, and others; many sons became renowned, and by them all the world was filled.
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, progeny were born from sexual union; whereas for the earlier beings, it is said that creation occurred through mere intention, sight, or touch.
Śaunaka said: You previously stated that Dakṣa was born from the thumb of Brahmā; how then did that great ascetic again obtain the status of being a son of the Pracetas?
O Sūta, you ought to resolve this doubt of mine: how is it that this wonderful being became the father-in-law of Soma?
Sūta said: O Sage, arising and cessation occur constantly among all beings; in every kalpa, all these [beings], beginning with Dakṣa, come into existence.
Whoever should know this creation of Dakṣa, together with all things moving and unmoving, shall be endowed with progeny, filled with long life, and honored in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: O son of a Sūta, tell me quickly this creation of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rakṣasas in detail.
Sūta said: When that daughter of Vīraṇa, the Prajāpati, did not grow, he summoned her, who was endowed with great asceticism, for the purpose of creation.
He created various offspring through the method of sexual union; listen to them, O highly wise one, as I describe them in brief.
Upon that Viriṇī, the powerful Prajāpati Dakṣa himself begot five thousand sons.
Having seen those who had been created, the sage Nārada indeed spoke; for all of them had been produced by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), and Nārada himself was born from him.
"Or rather, through Kaśyapa, there will be a creation of men among the daughters of Dakṣa, just as it was with Dakṣa himself"; therefore, he spoke to them.
"How indeed will you ignorant fools create the world? Since you do not know any direction, therefore, having first ascertained that earth,"
Thus addressed, they all set out with vigor to discover the direction; yet, failing to reach its end, they did not return to their father's home.
Having understood that, he again begot five hundred sons; then Nārada, the all-seeing one, spoke to them once more.
Nārada said: "Not knowing the measurement of the earth, how will you perform the creation? For you are all but children; why indeed have you set out to be creators?"
Sūta said: Having heard those words, they too set out in every direction—the sons of Subala and Aśva, the offspring of Dakṣa—just like the Haryaśvas of old.
Having reached the infinite Puṣkara, they too have met their defeat; even today they do not return, like rivers into the oceans.
From that time forward, O Sage, a brother set out in search of his brother and perished; therefore, a wise man should not do such a thing.
And having learned that his sons were lost, Dakṣa Prajāpati, out of anger, pronounced a curse upon the high-souled Nārada.
O lover of strife, you shall find no stability anywhere; by your very presence, there shall always be quarrel in the world.
Then, having been consoled by the Creator, that Prajāpati Dakṣa subsequently begot sixty daughters upon Vīriṇī; so we have heard.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were given then to Brahmaputra, two to Aṅgiras, and two to the learned Kṛśāśva; hear their names from me.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sandhyā, and Viśvā, O Sage.
O Sage, these are my lawful wives; hear from me regarding their offspring: Viśvā gave birth to the Viśvedevas, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas.
In Marutvatī were born the Marutvats; likewise, from Vasu came the Vasus. All the Bhānus were born of Bhānu, and the Muhūrtas were born of Muhūrtā.
From Lambā was born Ghoṣa, and from Yamī was born Nāgavīthī; from her, Pṛthivī was born, and from Viṣamā was born Arundhatī.
From Saṃkalpā was born Saṃkalpa himself, whose essence is truth. From Vasu were born eight sons beginning with Ayās; hear of them, O Śaunaka.
Aya, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are the eight Vasus by name.
The sons of Ayas were Vaitaṇḍa, Śrama, Śānta, and Muni; and the son of Dhruva was the blessed Kāla, the creator of the worlds.
The venerable Varcas was born from Soma, by whom one becomes radiant; likewise, Draviṇa and Hutahavyavaha were the sons of Dharma.
Manoharā’s sons were Śiśira, Prāṇa, and Ramaṇa; Anila’s wife was Śivā, whose sons were Purojava and the others.
Furthermore, Avijñātagati was one of the two sons of Anila; and Kumāra, the son of Agni, [was born] in a clump of reeds enveloped in splendor.
Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya followed behind him; he was known as Kārttikeya, the offspring of the Kṛttikās.
Pratyūṣa’s son was the sage named Devala; Devala, in turn, had two wise sons who were blessed with offspring.
The sister of Bṛhaspati, an excellent woman observing celibacy, having attained perfection through yoga, then wandered everywhere throughout the entire world.
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus; O highly fortunate one, from him was born Viśvakarman, the Prajāpati.
He is the creator of thousands of crafts, the carpenter of the thirty gods, the maker of all ornaments, and the best among those skilled in the arts.
He who indeed fashioned the celestial mansions for all the deities, and upon whose craftsmanship human beings depend for their livelihood—that high-souled one.
He states another opinion: "Raivata, Aja, Bhava, Bhīma, Vāma, Ugra, Vṛṣākapi, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, and Mahat."
O Sage, listen to the names of those eleven principal ones who were born from a woman of similar form, by the millions of Rudras.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra; Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Aparājita.
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and Raivata—these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
Thus, a hundred Rudras of immeasurable splendor have been described; now hear, O best of sages, the names of Kaśyapa’s wives.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Aditi, Diti, Surasā, Ariṣṭā, Ilā, Danu, Surabhi, Vinatā, Ilā, Tāmrā, and likewise Krodhavaśā.
And Kadūrmuni, O best of Brahmins—listen to me regarding their offspring. In the excellent previous Manvantara, there were twelve supreme gods.
In the interval of Vaivasvata Manu, when the period of the highly illustrious Cākṣuṣa Manu was approaching, those known as the Tuṣitas said to one another:
For the welfare of all the worlds, they gathered together and spoke to those who were approaching, having indeed entered into Aditi.
"We shall be born in the Manvantara; it will be for the welfare of the virtuous. Thus addressed, they all [remained] during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
Born from Kaśyapa Mārīca by Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa, Viṣṇu and Śakra were indeed born there once again.
Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan; Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and also Mitra and Varuṇa.
Aṃśa, Bhaga, and Atitejas—these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas; formerly, they were the Tuṣita gods.
"O Śaunaka, it is said that twelve Ādityas were formerly born within her; thus have the offspring of Aditi been described to you in order."
The twenty-seven wives of Soma who were proclaimed to be of virtuous vows had offspring known as the Dīptis, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
The offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi here were sixteen; and the four daughters who are recorded as belonging to the learned Bahuputra—
O divine sage, it is remembered that the celestial weapons were born of Kṛśāśva; likewise, O sage, Dhūmrakeśa was born of Arciṣ, the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Svadhā and Satī were his two wives; Svadhā was the elder and Satī the other. Svadhā gave birth to the Pitṛs, while Satī gave birth to the Atharvāṅgirasa Veda.
Indeed, at the end of a thousand yugas, all these hosts of gods, numbering thirty-three and born of desire, are born once again.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun occur here eternally, so too do those classes of gods come into being age after age.
We have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa: Hiraṇyakaśipu and the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa.
Siṃhikā was indeed the daughter who became the wife of Vipracitti; and Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of renowned power.
Anuhrāda, Hrāda, the powerful Saṃhrāda, and his younger brother Prahrāda, whose mind was intent on devotion to Viṣṇu and spiritual inquiry, were there.
Anuhrāda’s [sons] by Sūryā were Pulomā and Mahiṣa; Hrāda’s wife Dhamani gave birth to Vātāpi and Ilvala.
The son born of the wife of Saṃhrāda was Pañcajana; Virocana was the son of Prahrādi, and Bali was his son by Devī.
O Lord of Sages, Bali had a hundred sons born of Aśanā; Bali was a great devotee of Śiva, solely intent upon devotion to Śiva.

He is known as one who is generous, virtuous, noble, meritorious, famous, and ascetic. His son was named Bāṇa, who was a wise and eminent devotee of Śiva; having fully propitiated Śiva, he indeed attained the status of a Gaṇapati.
Indeed, you have heard before that story of the high-souled Bāṇa, who, as a hero in battle, rendered Kṛṣṇa well-pleased.
Hiraṇyākṣa had five sons who were wise and possessed great strength: Kukura, Śakuni, and Bhūtasaṃtāpana, as well as [the others].
Mahānāda, Vikrānta, and likewise Kālanābha—these, O Sage, are the sons of Diti; now hear of the sons of Danu.
And there were one hundred sons of Abhava, possessed of fierce prowess: Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapola, and Vamana.
Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Vidrāvaṇa, Mahāśiras, Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the valiant Vipracitti.
All these sons of Danu were born from Kaśyapa; O sinless sage, listen now to their sons as well, for I shall speak of them to you in this context.
Prabhā was the daughter of Svabhānu, while Śacī was the daughter of Puloman; Upadānavī was the mother of Hayaśiras, and Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Pulomā and Pulomikā were both daughters of Vaiśvānara; they were highly virtuous and prolific, and became the wives of Mārīci.
Marīci, endowed with great ascetic power, begot sixty thousand sons who were the delight of the Dānavas.
The Paulomas and Kālakhañjas were Dānavas of great strength, inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura who were incapable of being slain by the gods.
Those who were slain by Savyasācin through the grace of his grandfather, as well as those born of Siṃhikā and the sons of Vipracitti;
Born from the union of Daityas and Dānavas, there were thirteen of great strength and fierce prowess, known as the Saiṃhikeyas.
Rāhu, Śalya, Subalin, and Bala of great strength; Vātāpi, Namuci, as well as Ilvala and Svasṛpa.
Ajika, Naraka, and likewise Kālanābha, Śaramāṇa, and Śarakalpa—these were the increasers of the lineage.
Their sons and grandsons, who increased the lineage of Danu, were born in great numbers; however, they have not been described here due to their vast extent.
In the lineage of Saṃhrāda, the Daityas known as the Nivātakavacas were born; among them arose the Maruts, whose souls were purified by ascetic penance.
The great beings beginning with Ṣaṇmukha are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā; likewise Kākī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, and Śukī.
Gṛddhrikā, Aśvī, Ulūkī, and Tāmrā are proclaimed to be the daughters [of Kaśyapa]. Kākī gave birth to crows, and Ulūkī to owls.
Śyenī gave birth to hawks, Bhāsī to Bhāsas, Gṛdhī to vultures, Śukī to parrots, and Sugrīvī to auspicious birds.
Tāmrā, the beloved of Kaśyapa, gave birth to horses, camels, and donkeys; thus are the lineages of Tāmrā proclaimed.
And Vinatā had two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa; Suparṇa was the best of those who fly, while Aruṇa was not so by virtue of his own deeds.
There were a thousand Surasās, serpents of immeasurable power, many-headed, high-souled beings who traverse the sky.
Of whom Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Airāvata, Mahāpadma, and both Kambala and Aśvatara are the principal kings.
Ailāputra, as well as Padma, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Mahākarṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Balāhaka.
Kuhara, Puṣpadanta, Durmukha, Sumukha, Bahuśa, Khararoman, Pāṇi, and others such as these.
The hosts of Krodhavaśā and all those with fangs, as well as egg-born birds, water-born creatures, boars, and beasts, are considered her progeny.
Anāyuṣā had fifty sons of great strength; they were Balavṛkṣa, Vikṣara, and Bṛhan.
Surabhi gave birth to the deer and likewise to the buffaloes; Ilā produced trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all varieties of grasses.
Khaśā gave birth to Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, while Muni gave birth to Apsarases; Ariṣṭā gave birth to serpents and, through her powers, to the best of men.
O Lord of Sages, these descendants of Kaśyapa have been enumerated to you; their sons and grandsons are numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Kaśyapa," in the fifth section, the Umā-Saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: O dear one, this creation in the Svārociṣa Manvantara is thus recorded; but now, during the great Vaivasvata Manvantara, at the extensive sacrifice of Varuṇa.
The creation of progeny by Brahmā while performing sacrifice is now described here; first, those seven mind-born Brahmarṣis who were produced previously.
The Grandfather himself indeed fashioned sons; O great sage, there was a great conflict between those gods and the Dānavas.
Diti, her sons having been destroyed, approached Kaśyapa; that Kaśyapa, his mind being pleased, was honored by her with the utmost devotion.
He invited her to choose a boon, and she then chose this boon: a son of immeasurable splendor, capable of slaying Indra.
That great ascetic granted her the boon she requested and prescribed a vow of celibacy and other observances for a hundred years.
That pure and beautiful woman bore the fetus; likewise, Diti maintained her vows of celibacy and other religious observances.
Then, having placed that embryo within Aditi, Kaśyapa, whose vows were well-praised and whose mind was joyful, departed to perform austerities.
Seeking an opportunity against her, that subduer of Pāka (Indra) waited; when she was less than a hundred years old, he indeed perceived an opening.
Then, without having performed the purification of her feet, Diti fell asleep with her head turned downward, due to the weight of what was destined to happen.
In the meantime, Śakra, Vajrapāṇi, having entered her womb, cut that embryo into seven pieces.

As that embryo was being split apart by the thunderbolt, it cried out. As each of the seven parts cried, the wielder of the thunderbolt cut them again, saying, "Do not cry," yet they did not die even so.
O Sage, as they were being struck down, they all spoke to him with palms joined in reverence: "O Śakra, why do you wish to kill us? We are your brothers, the Maruts."
For they were all indeed accepted by Indra as his brothers; O brahmin-sage, by the will of Śaṅkara, they abandoned their state as Daityas.
Those gods named Maruts were indeed possessed of great strength; they were forty-nine birds who became the companions of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
When they had grown powerful, Hari, the Lord of Creatures, bestowed those kingdoms upon them in succession, beginning with Pṛthu; hear that from me.
Kṛṣṇa is the unassailable hero, the victorious Lord of Creatures; he is Parjanya, the presiding deity of wealth, and this entire world belongs to him.
O great sage, I have correctly described this creation of beings to you; now listen to the division of kingdoms, which I shall now declare in due order.
Having consecrated Pṛthu, the son of Vena, in the supreme sovereignty, the Grandfather then proceeded to assign the kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over the twice-born, the plants, the constellations and planets, as well as sacrifices and ascetic penances.
He appointed Varuṇa to the sovereignty over the waters, Vaiśravaṇa as the lord of kings, Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, and Pāvaka among the Vasus.
Among the Prajāpatis, he chose Dakṣa; among the Maruts, Vāsava; and among the Daityas and Dānavas, Prahlāda of immeasurable splendor.
He consecrated Vaivasvata Yama in the sovereignty over the ancestors, as well as over the mothers, the vows, the mantras, and likewise the cows.
[They praised] Giriśa, the wielder of the trident, [the lord] of the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and likewise of kings, as well as of all bhūtas and piśācas.
Of mountains, [he saw] the Himavat; of rivers, the ocean; of wild beasts, the tiger; and of cattle, the bull.

He consecrated the banyan tree (*vaṭa*) among the lords of the forest and the trees as king in the kingdom; thus was the sovereignty bestowed by Prajāpati, and it has indeed descended in succession everywhere.
In the eastern direction, the all-pervading Lord of the Universe, the soul of all beings, installed the son of the Prajāpati Vairāja upon the throne.
In that very same manner, O tiger among sages, he likewise created Sudhanvan as a son for the patriarch Kardama in the southern direction.
In the western direction, the Lord assigned the high-souled King Ketumān, the son of Rajas, who is steadfast and unshakable.
Likewise, he consecrated Hiraṇyaroman as the invincible king of Parjanya Prajāpati in the northern quarter.
O Śaunaka, the extent of that realm of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, has been declared; its foundation of great power is celebrated in the Purāṇa.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: Narrate all the Manvantaras in detail; I wish to hear about as many Manus as there are.
Sūta said: Svāyambhuva Manu, and then Ārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and likewise Cākṣuṣa.
O bull among sages, these six Manus have been fully described to you; O best of sages, Vaivasvata is said to be the current Manu.
Sāvarṇi and Manu, then Raucya as the next, and likewise Brahmasāvarṇi—these are the four Manus.
Likewise, Dharmasāvarṇi, Rudrasāvarṇi, Devasāvarṇi, and Indrasāvarṇi have been described.
Those who have passed, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come—these Manus also have been proclaimed by me exactly as they were heard.
O Sage, these fourteen [ages] follow you throughout the three periods of time; they declare that a *kalpa* created by you consists of a cycle of a thousand *yugas*.
I shall proclaim to you their sages, as well as their sons and the hosts of gods; listen with great pleasure, O Śaunaka, to those illustrious ones in due order.
Marīci, the venerable Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, and Vasiṣṭha—these seven are the sons of Brahmā.
Likewise, O Sage, in the northern direction were the Seven Sages, and there were the gods named Yāmas during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vasu, Jyotiṣmat, Dhṛtimat, Havya, Savana, and Śubhra.
O tiger among sages, those ten sons of the high-souled Svāyambhuva Manu have been proclaimed; among them, Yajña is said to be the Indra.
The first divine Manvantara has thus been described to you, dear one; I shall now declare the second to you—learn it exactly as it is.
Ūrjastaṃbha, Parastaṃbha, Ṛṣabha, Vasumān, as well as Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, and Rociṣmat as the seventh.
These are to be known as the great ṛṣis there; likewise, Indra was Rocana, and the gods are remembered by the name Tuṣitas during the Svārociṣa interval.
Harighna, Sukṛti, Jyotis, Ayomūrti, Ayasmaya, Prathita, Manasyu, Nabhah, and likewise Sūrya.
O tiger among sages, those ten sons of the high-souled Svārociṣa Manu have been proclaimed, possessing great heroism and prowess.
O Sage, this second Manvantara has been described by me; I shall now speak of the third to you—learn it exactly as it is.
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were renowned as the Vāsiṣṭhas; they were the highly powerful sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, known by the name Ūrjā.
The sages who are celebrated here—learn from me as I recount them: O best of sages, ten sons of Manu are remembered as the descendants of Uttama.
Iṣa, Ūrjita, Ūrja, Madhu, Mādhava, Śuci, Śukravaha, Nabhasa, and Nabha.
O Sage, there was Ṛṣabha, as well as the gods Satyaveda, Śruta, and others; and there, O Sage, was Indra, named Satyajit, the sovereign of the three worlds.
This third supreme Manvantara has been described; O Sage, listen as I tell you of the fourth Manvantara.
Gārgya, Pṛthu, Vāgmī, Jaya, Dhātṛ, Kapīnaka, and Kapīvān are the seven Ṛṣis; likewise, the Satyas and the hosts of gods.
In that regard, O Sage, Indra is to be known as Triśikha; hear now of the sons of Manu: Dyutipota, Sautapasya, Tama, Śūla, and Tāpana.
Taporatirakalmāṣa, Dhanvī, Khaḍgī, and Mahānṛṣi—these are remembered as the ten sons of Tāmasa, all of whom were observers of great vows.
I have described to you the Tāmasa Manvantara; O dear one, now hear of the fourth and fifth, the subsequent Manvantaras.
Devabāhu, Jaya, the sage Vedaśiras, Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ūrdhvabāhu, and Somapa;
Others, devoted to Truth as their leader, are these other Seven Sages; and there are also the gods known as Bhūtarajasas, whose nature is austerity.
There, Indra was named Vibhu and likewise the lord of the three worlds; the Manu there should be known as Raivata, the uterine brother of Tāmasa.
O Sage, Arjuna, Paṅktivindhya, and Dayāyāsya’s son dwell indeed upon the summit of Mount Meru, endowed with great ascetic power.
The son of Ruci was Prajāpati, who is remembered as the Manu named Raucya; and the son begotten by the goddess Bhūti was the one named Bhautya.
These seven Manus are recorded as yet to come in this kalpa; and these seven great ṛṣis are likewise recorded as yet to come in heaven.
Rāma, Vyāsa, and likewise Ātreya, who is radiant and highly learned; Bharadvāja, and likewise Drauṇi Aśvatthāman of great splendor.
The son of Gautama was Śaradvān Gautama Kṛpa; also Kauśika Gālava, Ruru, and Kaśyapa.
These seven high-souled ones shall be the best of sages in the future; and three gods of the future have been proclaimed there by the Self-born One.
And those sons of the high-souled Kaśyapa were indeed the sons of Marīci; among them, Bali, the son of Virocana, shall become Indra.
Viṣāṅga, Avanīvat, Sumanta, Dhṛtimān, Vasu, Sūri, the one named Surā, Viṣṇu, and King Sumati.
O Śaunaka, the ten sons of Manu Sāvarṇi will be the future [kings]; here the eighth period has been described, so now hear the ninth interval.
First, I shall proclaim Dakṣasāvarṇi; listen to the Manu. Medhātithi will be of the lineage of Pulastya, and Vasu and Kaśyapa likewise.
Jyotiṣmat Bhārgava, Dhṛtimat Āṅgirasa, Savana Vāsiṣṭha, and Havya Ātreya.
"Pulaha, [Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Marīci]—these seven sages were present during the Rauhita interval; and there, O great sage, were exactly three groups of deities."
These were the sons of Rohita Prajāpati, who was himself the son of Dīkṣā: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Dīptaketu, Pañcahasta, and Nirākṛti.
Pṛthuśravas, Bhūridyumna, Ṛcīka, Bṛhat, and Gaya—these nine were the sons of great power belonging to the first Sāvarṇi.
Now, in the tenth period, during the interval of the second Manu, there were Haviṣmat, Pulaha, and Prakṛti, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Āya, Muktis, Tathātreyas, and Vasiṣṭha are remembered as the imperishable; likewise Paulastya, Prayati, Bhāmāras, and Kaśyapa.
Aṅgiras, Anenas, and Satya—these seven are the supreme ṛṣis; they are also remembered as the hosts of deities and as those possessed of enmity.
Among them, Śambhu, this very Maheśvara, is remembered as Indra; he is Akṣa, Anuttamaujas, Bhūriṣeṇa, and the heroic Vīryavān.
Śatānīka, Nirāmitra, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha, Bhūridyumna, Suvarcas, and Arci—these ten were the sons of Manu.
In the eleventh period, during the interval of the third Manu, listen to me as I proclaim his seven sages as well.
Haviṣmān Kaśyapa, Vapuṣmān Vāruṇa, Atreya, Vasiṣṭha, Anaya, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Cārudhṛṣya, Paulastya, Niḥsvara, and Agni—the fiery one; these seven are declared to be the sages (ṛṣis), and three are remembered as the hosts of gods (devagaṇas).
For they were indeed the sons of Brahmā; these are remembered as the Vaidhṛtas: Sarvaga, Suśarman, Devānīka, and Kṣemaka.
Dṛḍheṣu, Khaṇḍaka, Darśa, Kuhu, and Bāhu are remembered as the sons of the third Manu, Sāvarṇa; indeed, nine are recorded as his grandsons.
Now learn from me the seven sages of the fourth Sāvarṇi: Dyuti, the son of Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Sutapas, the son of Atri.
Aṅgiras is the embodiment of austerity, as is the ascetic Kaśyapa; Paulastya is rich in austerity, and Pulaha delights in austerity.
The seventh among them is to be known as Bhārgava, a treasure-house of asceticism; five groups of gods are declared to be the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
O Sage, in the twelfth cycle within the future Raucya Manvantara, Indra will indeed be named Ṛtadhāmā; he will be the happy ruler of the three worlds.
Aṅgiras, the steadfast Paulastya Havyavān, the truth-seer Paulaha, and Bhārgava Nirutsava.
Niṣprapañca, Tathātreyī, Nirdeha, Kaśyapa, and Sutapas, as well as Vāsiṣṭha—these seven alone are the great ṛṣis.
The Self-Existent One himself declared that there are exactly three classes of deities: Divaspati, Indra, Vicitra, and Citra.
Naya, Dharma, Dhṛtīndhra, Sunetra, Kṣatravṛddhaka, Nirbhaya, Sutapas, Droṇa, and Manu—these were the sons of Raucya.
In the fourteenth interval of Manu Satya, there were Āgnīdhra Kāśyapa and Paulastya Māgadha.
Bhārgava is also to be honored, as well as the pure Āṅgirasa; likewise Atri, and the grandson of Vasiṣṭha.
Ajita and Pulaha, as well as those who are the final seven sages, the Pavitras, and the Cākṣuṣas shall be the gods; Śuci will be the Indra.
By constantly reciting the names of these great sages of the past and the future upon rising at dawn, men indeed increase in happiness.
O great sage, hear the five groups of deities that have been proclaimed: Turaṅgabhīru, Budhna, Tanugra, and Anūgra.
Atimānin, Pravīṇa, Viṣṇu, Saṃkrandana, Tejasvin, Sabala, and Satya—these were the sons of Manu.
Indeed, within the jurisdiction of Bhauma alone, the previous kalpa is completed. Thus have these past and future Manus been proclaimed by me.
Thus it was told by Sanatkumāra of immeasurable splendor to Vyāsa: "At the end of a full thousand yugas, [the earth] must be protected according to one's own dharma."
Endowed with austerity, those people go to the world of Brahmā; one period of four yugas, including its full duration, is called an Antara.
These fourteen Manus have been proclaimed as the increasers of fame; at the end of every Manvantara, following the period of dissolution, there is a new creation.
It is not possible to state the interval between them even in hundreds of years; when a full hundred thousand [years] have passed, it is called a complete kalpa.
There, O sage, all beings were scorched by the rays of the sun, with Brahmā placed at their head along with the hosts of the eternal suns.
O best of gods, they enter again and again at the ends of the kalpas into Hari Nārāyaṇa, the supreme creator of all beings.
Furthermore, the Blessed One Rudra is indeed the destroyer, Time itself; I shall explain that at the end of the Kalpa of Vaivasvata Manu.
Thus, everything concerning the origin of the Manvantaras has been told to you—this meritorious and auspicious narrative which increases one’s lineage.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of All the Manvantaras," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Vivasvat was born to the great ṛṣi Kaśyapa from Dākṣāyaṇī; his wife was the goddess Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, also known as Sureṇukā.
O Sage, she, endowed with beauty and youth, was not satisfied with him who, though her husband, possessed a splendor that was intolerable and difficult to endure.
For that was the form of the Sun; unable to endure its brilliance, the fair-complexioned lady felt a burning sensation and was filled with agitation.
O Sage, the Sun begot three offspring upon this Saṃjñā: first, Manu, the lord of creatures (Prajāpati) known as Śrāddhadeva.
Yama and Yamunā were born as twins; thus, three offspring were born to her from the Sun.
Seeing that form of Vivasvat to be perfectly round, Saṃjñā, unable to endure it, then created an auspicious shadow of herself.
But she, who was composed of illusion, spoke with devotion to Saṃjñā: "O auspicious one, O lady of pure smiles, tell me what task I should perform for you here."
Saṃjñā said: "I shall go—blessings be upon you—to my father's own abode; you must dwell truthfully in this house without any change of heart."
"These two sons of mine are virtuous, and this daughter is slender-waisted; they must be protected with ease if you wish to do what is pleasing to me."
Chāyā said: "O Goddess, I shall endure this great wrong even unto the seizing of my hair; I will not disclose your secret intention to you. Go, O Goddess, as you please."
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, the goddess, feeling ashamed, went into the presence of her father; there she was reproached by her father and repeatedly urged [to go].
Then, having become a mare and concealed her form within her skin, she went to the northern Kurus and wandered among men.
Thinking that she was indeed Saṃjñā, the Sun-god Savitṛ then begot a virtuous son, Sāvarṇi Manu, in Chāyā.
That shadow-like reflection, which Saṃjñā had constantly longed for, showed even greater affection for her own son than she did for her firstborn child.

His younger brother Yama was unable to tolerate that, yet he did not show him any resentment; for though he was filled with wrath due to his youth, he was restrained by the weight of what was destined to happen.
When Yama, the son of Vivasvat, threatened Chāyā, she, becoming agitated with anger, cursed him in return.
"Your foot is for those who fall," [said Yama]. Then, greatly incensed, Yama reported everything regarding his father with palms joined in reverence.
Greatly agitated by the fear of the curse, he was moved by the words of Saṃjñā; indeed, a mother must behave with affection toward all her sons.
Having cast aside her affection for us, she supports only her younger son; therefore, I have raised my foot against him, and you ought to forgive me for that.
"O Lord of Gods, O best of those who radiate heat, I have been cursed by my mother; yet, by your grace, O Lord of Rays, may my foot not fall [to the ground]."
Savitṛ said: "Without doubt, my son, there must be a great cause for this, by which anger has taken possession of you, who are a knower of dharma and a speaker of truth."
It is not possible to make those words of your mother false; the worms, having taken up the flesh, will depart into the earth.
Those words shall come true, and you shall be our protector; O Father, O Lord, reassure your own mind and do not entertain any doubt.
Sūta said: O lord of sages, having thus spoken to his son named Yama, the Sun, the Āditya, addressed Chāyā while filled with anger.
Sūrya said: O dear one, O evil-minded and wrathful woman, what indeed have you done? You ought to explain this to me, for my affection for you is exceedingly great.
Sūta said: Having heard the words of the Sun, she reported exactly what had happened; then, though scorched by the fire of desire, she consoled him.
Chāyā said: "Burned by your excessive brilliance, this form of mine does not shine; unable to endure it, that consciousness dwells in the forest upon the grassy meadow."

O Lord of the Cowherds, having attained yoga and being endowed with the power of yoga, you are praiseworthy; O Lord of Gods, being well-disposed, you have declared your own intent to be identical with the Self.
"I shall now transform my form; I will make myself dear to you. Sūta said: Having heard that, the anger of Mārtaṇḍa Vivasvat subsided.
Having placed that splendor upon a lathe, the sage indeed whetted it; then its form was brilliantly illuminated by the energy with which it was enveloped.
Tvaṣṭṛ then fashioned a most beautiful form, which shone brilliantly; thereafter, applying himself with effort, he beheld his own wife.
Invincible to all beings by virtue of his splendor and self-restraint, he assumed the form of a horse and went to her with a desire for sexual union.
O Sage, seeing her struggling for sexual union out of suspicion that it was another man, he deposited his semen into her nose instead of her mouth.
From that, two gods were born, the Aśvins, the best of physicians; they are known as both the Nāsatyas and the Dasras—these two being the Aśvins.
Then Bhāskara revealed himself in his most beautiful form; seeing him, she was delighted and respectfully regarded her husband.
Accompanied by that husband, Satī returned to her own home with a joyful countenance; then the couple rejoiced with affection even more than before.
But Yama, his mind deeply distressed by that deed, as the King of Dharma, gladdened these subjects through righteousness.
By that deed, the highly effulgent Dharmarāja obtained sovereignty over the ancestors as well as the status of a world-guardian (lokapāla).
Manu Sāvarṇi, rich in asceticism, was indeed Prajāpati; by that deed, he was destined to become the Manu in the Sāvarṇika interval.
The Lord still practices severe austerity on the summit of Mount Meru; as for their younger sister, the illustrious maiden Yamī—
She became the Yamunā, the best of rivers, the purifier of the world; she is called Manu in the world and is also called Sāvarṇi.
Whoever hears or retains this account of the birth of the gods shall be liberated from calamity upon encountering it and shall attain great renown.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Vaivasvata," in the *Manvantara-kīrtana* section of the *Umā-saṃhitā*, the fifth book of the glorious *Śiva-mahāpurāṇa*.
Sūta said: To Vaivasvata Manu there were indeed nine sons equal to him; later they became highly exalted, wise, and devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas.
Ikṣvāku, Śibi, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Karūṣa, and Priyavrata.
Desiring sons, the Prajāpati Manu performed a sacrifice; O bull among sages, while his sons were yet unborn, he performed that sacrifice.
Wearing celestial garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and possessing a celestial physique, she was indeed born as the renowned Ilā.
"O Tamiḍa," said Manu, the wielder of the staff; "follow me," he said. To him, Tamiḍā replied.
Iḍā said: "O best among speakers, these words of yours are consistent with dharma; I was born from portions of Mitra and Varuṇa for the sake of one desiring offspring, O Prajāpati."
"I shall go into their presence, for I have no taste for dharma. Having spoken thus to Mitra and Varuṇa, that virtuous woman then departed.
Approaching them, the woman of beautiful limbs spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: "O great sages, you were born from portions of yourselves in the sacrifice of Manu."
"We have come to you for refuge; tell us, what shall we do for you? O Lord, create other sons, for by them your lineage shall continue."
Sūta said: To that virtuous lady Iḍā, born from the sacrifice of Manu, who was speaking in such a manner, the two sages named Mitrāvaruṇa spoke with respect.
Mitra and Varuṇa said: "O knower of dharma, O lady of beautiful hips and excellent complexion, we both are pleased with this humility, self-restraint, and truthfulness of yours."
O highly fortunate one, you shall indeed attain fame for both of us, and you alone shall become the son who brings about the fulfillment of Manu’s lineage.
Renowned as Sudyumna, he was famous throughout the three worlds; beloved by the world, virtuous in character, and the increaser of Manu’s lineage.
Sūta said: Having heard that, she turned back; while going toward her father’s presence, she was approached by Budha and invited for sexual union.
From that son of Soma, King Purūravas was born of her—a most handsome, wise, and exalted son who became the husband of Urvaśī.
And having there, through the grace of Śiva, respectfully begotten a son named Purūravas, she returned once more to her state as Sudyumna.
Sudyumna had three heirs who were supremely righteous: Utkala, Gaya, and the heroic Vinatāśva.
O tiger among sages, the eastern region is known as Utkalā belonging to Utkala, the western regions belong to Vinatāśva, and Gayā is remembered as belonging to Gaya.
O dear one, when Manu had entered the body of the Sun, Manu then divided that field into ten parts.
Ikṣvāku, the preeminent heir, obtained the Middle Country; by the word of Vasiṣṭha, Pratiṣṭhāna became the capital of that high-souled one.
Then Sudyumna established the foundation of the kingdom of Dharma; having attained that sovereignty, the highly illustrious one bestowed the kingdom upon Purūravas.
O best of sages, Mānava was the lord who possessed the characteristics of both male and female; from Nariṣyanta were born the Śakas as sons, and Nabhaga had a son.
Ambarīṣa, the son of Bāhlīka, obtained the land of Bāhlīka; Śaryāti, however, had a pair of children, and Ānarta became renowned by name.
His son was Sukanyā, who became the daughter and wife of Cyavana; and the heir of Ānarta was named Raibhya, also known as Raivata.
In the region of Ānarta, his city named Kuśasthalī is a great divine place, which is considered the seventh among the seven cities.
He had a hundred sons, of whom Kakudmin was the eldest and most excellent; they were radiant, very powerful, capable, most righteous, and protectors of the Veda.
To Kakudmin was born a daughter named Revatī, endowed with great beauty, like another divine Lakṣmī.
To inquire about a bridegroom for his daughter, King Kakudmin, the sovereign of all, went together with his daughter to the world of Brahmā in accordance with the prescribed rites.
While the Gandharva music was proceeding, he, having found a moment’s opportunity, stood for a brief instant and listened to that Gandharva performance in the presence of Brahmā during the dance.
At that time, although it was but a moment, many yugas had passed; yet King Kakudmin and the sages perceived nothing at all.
Then, having bowed to Brahmā with joined palms, he, being humble in spirit, announced his own intention to that Supreme Soul.
Having heard his intention, that Lord of Creatures smiled and, addressing the great king Kakudmin, spoke to him.
Brahmā said: Listen, O King Kakudmin, son of Raibhya and father of the earth; out of affection for you, I shall specifically speak these truthful words of mine.
Indeed, those boons which were cherished in your heart have been withdrawn by Time; for there is no lineage that exists there [in safety], as Time is the devourer of all.
O King, your city too was destroyed by the Puṇyajanas, those Rākṣasas; yet today, in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, it has been rebuilt by Kṛṣṇa.
The city named Dvāravatī, possessing many gates and enchanting to the mind, was established and protected by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, led by Vāsudeva.
Therefore, O King, go there with a joyful heart and give this daughter of yours to Vāsudeva and Baladeva.
Sūta said: Having been thus instructed, the king bowed to him and went to that city; realizing that many Yugas had passed, he was filled with wonder, accompanied by his daughter.
Then, according to the prescribed rites, he quickly gave his own young daughter, Revatī, there to Bala, the brother of Kṛṣṇa.
Then that great lord, the king, went to the divine peak of Meru and, established in austerity, propitiated Śiva.
The sages said: "Having remained there in the world of Brahmā for many yugas, that Revata returned to the mortal world while still a youth; this is a great doubt of ours."
Sūta said: O sages, in the presence of Brahmā, there is indeed neither old age, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor any such afflictions; nor is there untimely death for anyone.
Therefore, neither the king nor that daughter attained old age or death; he returned there while still young, having consulted with his son regarding the latter's choice.
Having gone to the divine city of Dvārāvatī, which was built by Kṛṣṇa, he indeed had the marriage of his daughter performed with Bala.
That righteous and great lord had a hundred sons; thereafter, Kṛṣṇa also begot immeasurable sons from his many wives.
The lineage there of both those great-souled ones was vast; the Kṣatriyas, exceedingly righteous and joyful, spread in all directions.
Thus has the lineage of Śaryāti been described; now I shall speak of the other descendants of Manu. Listen with respect, O twice-born ones, for I shall describe them in brief.
Nābhāga was the son of Diṣṭa, but he attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa; having established his own Kṣatriya lineage, he became devoted to the duties of a Brāhmaṇa.
From Dhṛṣṭa was born the Dhārṣṭa kṣatriya lineage, which attained the status of Brahman on earth; from Karūṣa came the Kārūṣas, kṣatriyas who were fierce in battle.
Nṛga, the son of Manu, was a great donor, especially of various riches and likewise of cows to the Brahmins with great affection.
But he who, through his own evil intellect and his own sin, committed a transgression regarding the gift of a cow, attained the state of a lizard and was delivered by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He had an excellent son named Prayāti, who likewise knew the Dharma; thus have I heard from Vyāsa, and so it has been told by me in brief.
Vṛṣaghnas, the son of Manu, was appointed as a cowherd by his preceptor; observing the vow of the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), he diligently protected the cows during the night.
Once, having heard that a powerful tiger had come to the cow-pen to harm the cows, the wise one, perceiving the slaughter of the cattle, went forth wielding his sword to slay it.
Not knowing it was Babhru, he struck off his head, mistaking him for a tiger; but the tiger, seeing that the Lord was a rhinoceros, emerged in fear.
Thinking the tiger slain, he went to his own place; during that night, however, he became bewildered, his mind ruined by the rain and wind.
When the night had dawned, he rose at daybreak and went there; he saw that Babhru had been killed, but not by a tiger, and he became sorrowful.
Having heard that account and recognized him as the offender, he cursed him, saying: "Since you acted without reflection out of desire, become a Śūdra, not a Kṣatriya."
Thus cursed by his preceptor, the family teacher, out of anger, Pṛṣadhra departed and went into the great forest.
Filled with world-weariness through his suffering, that practitioner of yoga became dispassionate; and with his body consumed by the forest fire, he attained the supreme goal.
The wise Kavi became the son of Manu through the grace of Śiva; having enjoyed divine happiness, he attained liberation, which is very difficult to obtain.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineages of Manu’s Nine Sons," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: From the nostril of Manu was born his son Ikṣvāku; that Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons who were givers of abundant sacrificial fees.
Before them were the kings and twice-born ones of Āryāvarta; among them, Vikukṣi was the eldest, and he became the king of Ayodhyā.
Listen with affection to that deed which occurred in the lineage of Brahmā; for he was designated for the śrāddha rite, yet the śrāddha rite had not been performed.
Having quickly devoured a hare, he therefore acquired the name Śaśāda (Hare-eater). Abandoned by Ikṣvāku, Śaśāda entered the forest.
When Ikṣvāku had passed away, Vasiṣṭha’s word established him as king; fifteen sons are recorded for him, with Śakuni at their head.
The kings were the protectors of the region of the Northern Path; the heir of Ayodha, however, was the valiant one named Kakutstha.
Ariṇābha was the son of Kakutstha, and Pṛthu was indeed his son; Viṣṭarāśva was the son of Pṛthu, and from him came Indra Prajāpati.

Yuvanāśva was the son of Indra; from him was born Śrāvasta, the lord of progeny. From him was born the wise Śrāvastaka, by whom the city of Śrāvastī was founded. The heir of Śrāvasta was the highly illustrious Bṛhadaśva.
Yuvanāśva was his son, and Kuvalāśva was his son; for that best of kings became known as Dhundhumāra because of the slaying of Dhundhu.
Kuvalāśva had one hundred sons who were excellent archers; there, his father installed Kuvalāśva in the kingdom.
Having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king entered the forest; then Uttaṅka restrained that royal sage as he was departing.
Uttaṅka said: "Listen, O King; you must protect the earth according to dharma. For when the earth is protected by you, O high-souled monarch,"
You will be free from anxiety; you ought not to go to the forest, but rather [stay] near my hermitage in the snowy desert wastes.
The Dānava was filled with the sands of the ocean; arrogant in his strength, he possessed a massive body and great power, and was indeed incapable of being slain by the gods.
There, situated beneath the earth and hidden within the sands, dwelt the exceedingly fierce son of the Rākṣasa Madhu, named Dhundhu.
Having undertaken a severe penance for the destruction of the world, he lies there; at the end of each year, he releases a single breath.
Whenever that occurs, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles; and the water-bearing [element] becomes accompanied by sparks, embers, and even smoke.
Therefore, O Rāghava, I am unable to remain in my own hermitage; for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, O mighty-armed one, restrain him.
"May the worlds be at peace today now that he has been slain by you; for you alone, O lord of the earth, are capable of his destruction."
And a great boon was granted by Viṣṇu in a former age, O sinless one: "Viṣṇu shall augment your splendor with his own splendor."
For the great dharma of protecting subjects is seen here in this world; it is not seen in the forest in such a way. Let not your mind be inclined toward such a thought.
O Indra among kings, such dharma as was practiced of old by the royal sages in the protection of their subjects is not found anywhere else.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Uttanka, the royal sage Kuvalāśva gave his son to him for the purpose of subduing Dhundhu.
"O Blessed One, having laid down my weapons, this son of mine shall become Dhundhumāra, O best of the twice-born; of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus and instructed his son, that king departed for ascetic penance; and Kuvalāśva, accompanied by Uttaṅka, set out to subdue Dhundhu.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, the powerful Master, entered him with his splendor at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
As that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in the sky: "This illustrious son of a king shall become Dhundhumāra."
The gods surrounded him on all sides with divine garlands and offered praise, crying out, "Victory! Live long!"
Having gone there with his sons, that king, the best among victors, caused the ocean to be dug out from the midst of the sea of sand.
Sustained by the splendor of the brahmin-sage Nārāyaṇa, he became possessed of exceedingly great luster and was further endowed with strength.
O Brahmin, while his sons were digging for sand, Dhundhu was discovered by them as he took refuge in the western direction.
As if destroying the worlds with the fire born from his mouth out of anger, he violently discharged water like the blood of the moon at its rising.
Then, struck by those fires, that hundred of sons was indeed consumed; O Lord of Sages, only three remained among them.
Then, O best of Brahmins, that king of great splendor encountered the mighty Rākṣasa Dhundhu, the destroyer of brahmins.
Having swallowed his watery torrent, that lord of men extinguished the fire with water by means of his fiery arrow.
Having slain that water-demon of massive body by force, the lord of men showed Uttanka what had been accomplished.
O great sage, Uttanka granted a boon to that king: he gave him inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against his enemies.
They shall have constant devotion to the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven; and for those who were slain by the Rākṣasa, their sons shall attain an eternal world.
Of his three remaining sons, Dṛḍhāśva is said to be the eldest; Haṃsāśva and Kapilāśva were the two younger princes.
Dhundhumāri’s son was Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son; Haryaśva’s son was Nikumbha, who was always devoted to righteousness.
Saṃhatāśva, the son of Nikuṃbha, was skilled in battle; Akṣāśva and Kṛtāśva were the sons of Saṃhatāśva.
His daughter was Vṛṣadvatī, born of Haimavatī and honored by the virtuous; she was renowned throughout the three worlds, and her son was Prasenajit.
Prasenajit obtained as his wife a devoted wife named Gaurī; however, cursed by her husband, she was turned into the river Bāhudā.
He had a great son, Yuvanāśva, the lord of the earth; Māndhātṛ was the son of Yuvanāśva, renowned throughout the three worlds.
His wife was Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu; she was devoted to her husband and was the eldest among ten thousand brothers.
Then Māndhātā begot two sons upon her: Purukutsa, who was knower of dharma, and the righteous Mucukunda.
The son of Purukutsa was the learned and wise Trayyāruṇi; he had a son, a prince named Satyavrata, who was possessed of great strength.
The high-souled ones created obstacles for the marriage mantras of him who had previously abducted the wife of another after the wedding had already been performed.
Out of force, lust, delusion, and intense excitement, he carried off the daughter of a certain city-dweller out of desire.
But King Trayyāruṇi, filled with anger, repeatedly said to that man who was attached to unrighteousness, "Begone! as he cast him out.
Once released, he said to his father, "Where indeed shall I go? Then the king spoke to him: "Dwell near the outcastes."
For that hero Satyavrata, having been abandoned by his father, King Dharmapāla, lived near the dwellings of the outcaste dog-cookers.
Thereupon, King Trayyāruṇi, becoming dispassionate through his son's actions, abandoned everything and went to the forest to perform penance to Śaṅkara.
Then, O brahmin sage, because of that unrighteousness, Indra did not send rain upon his own realm for twelve years.
But in his kingdom, the great ascetic Viśvāmitra abandoned his wife and practiced intense penance on the shore of the ocean.
His wife, having tied her own middle son by the neck, sold him for a hundred cows in order to provide for the maintenance of the remaining children.
Seeing her selling her own son—the son of a great seer—with a rope tied around his neck, that righteous-souled man then set him free.
The mighty-armed Satyavrata undertook the maintenance of him [Viśvāmitra], both for the sake of pleasing Viśvāmitra and out of compassion.
From that time on, that son of the sage Viśvāmitra became known by the name Gālava, a great ascetic so called because of his being bound to his mother's neck (galabandha).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Manu," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Out of devotion to him, out of compassion, and by virtue of his vow, Satyavrata then indeed sustained Viśvāmitra’s wife.
O Sage, having killed deer, boars, and wild buffaloes, they threw that meat near the hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
The sage Vasiṣṭha protected the sacred ford, the cow, the night, and likewise the inner apartments, due to his connection with his patron and his teacher.
Either because of Satyavrata’s words or by the power of the destiny that was to come to pass, Vasiṣṭha constantly maintained an even greater degree of wrath.
But the sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain his son when he was being abandoned from the kingdom by his father, for a specific reason.
"The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step; yet Satyavrata, remaining steadfast in his vow, did not perceive that [act] as being in secret."
O Brahmin, he acted so that he might bring satisfaction to his high-souled father and provide atonement for his lineage.
