The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him when he was abandoned by his father; nor did the muni say, "I shall consecrate my son upon this throne."
That powerful one maintained that initiation for twelve years, during which time meat was unavailable to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The prince beheld that cow who milks all desires; yet, overcome by anger, greed, fatigue, and hunger, he [tried to milk her].
O Sage, the king, having attained ten qualities, indeed killed her; he himself ate that meat and gave some to the son of Viśvāmitra.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha indeed became enraged; and the best of sages, filled with anger, then spoke to him.
Vasiṣṭha said: I would strike down this cruel iron stake of yours, if only those two stakes previously fashioned by you were to perish.

"Due to the dissatisfaction of your father, the killing of the cow that provides milk for your guru, and the consumption of meat not consecrated by sprinkling, you have committed a threefold transgression."
"He shall be known as Triśaṅku," he said; thus he was remembered as Triśaṅku. Viśvāmitra, however, returned when the maintenance of his wives had been secured.
The sage, being pleased, granted a boon to Triśaṅku; then, being invited to choose a boon, the prince chose a boon.
When this twelve-year drought and its attendant fears had arisen, the sage consecrated him in the kingdom of the ancestors and performed a sacrifice for him.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha were looking on, the powerful Kauśika then ascended to heaven with his very body.
His wife, named Satyarathā, born of the Kekaya lineage, gave birth to a sinless prince, Hariścandra.
That King Hariścandra is indeed remembered as Traiśaṅkava; he was renowned as a sovereign emperor who performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
For Hariścandra had a son renowned by the name Rohita; Rohita’s son was Vṛka, and from Vṛka, Bāhu was born.
The Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas were casting that king aside, for he was a righteous brahmin who was devoted solely to dharma and did not act for his own sake.
Bāhu indeed gave birth to Sagara along with his sons, who were born with poison; having reached the hermitage of Aurva, he was protected by the descendant of Bhṛgu.
And having obtained the Āgneya weapon from Bhārgava, King Sagara conquered the earth after slaying the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas.
He established the Śakas, Bahūdakas, Pāradas, Antagaṇas, and Khaśas in the true dharma; he ruled the earth according to righteousness.
Śaunaka said: "O son of Sūta, tell me in detail how he was indeed born from a Kṣatriya while possessing poison, and how he conquered [the world]."
Sūta said: O sage, listen with a one-pointed mind as I relate that which Vaiśampāyana, when questioned by the son of Parīkṣit, proclaimed.
Pārīkṣita said: O Sage, how was that King Sagara born together with poison, and how did he subsequently slay it? You should explain this to me.
Vaiśampāyana said: O dear one, lord of the people, it is said that the kingdom of Bāhu was seized by the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the Śakas.
The Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, the Pahlavas, and the Bahūdakas—these five groups are said to be among the Rākṣasas.
O King, these five hosts of Rākṣasas, having displayed their prowess for the sake of the Haihayas, forcibly took the kingdom from them.
O brahmins, having been deprived of his kingdom, that Bāhu went to the forest; followed by his wife and filled with sorrow, he indeed gave up his life.
His Yādava wife, who was pregnant, followed behind him; previously, out of jealousy toward her son, a co-wife had given her poison.
Having prepared her husband's funeral pyre and being about to descend into the flames, O King, Aurva of the Bhṛgu lineage restrained her out of compassion.
The queen, staying in his hermitage for the sake of protecting the fetus, attended upon that best of sages while remembering Śaṅkara in her heart.
Once, indeed, that fetus was expelled along with the poison itself, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, endowed with five planets in exaltation.
And at that auspicious moment, O best of sages, when the planetary positions were entirely powerful, the mighty-armed king named Sagara was born.
Aurva, having performed for that high-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies, and having instructed him in the Vedas and Shastras, then imparted to him the divine weapon.
That illustrious Sagara, the best of kings, received with joy that Agneya weapon—which was indeed unbearable even for the immortals—according to the prescribed rites.
Endowed with that very power of weapons and physical strength, he, being enraged, swiftly struck down the Haihayas by means of his weapon-power.
And that Sagara, the best among the famous, brought forth renown throughout the worlds and established righteousness upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Śakas, along with the Yavanas, Kāmbojas, and Pahlavas, being slaughtered, sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha.
Having made a deceptive agreement, the immensely radiant Vasiṣṭha restrained King Sagara by granting them an assurance of safety.
Having heard his own vow and the words of his preceptor, Sagara indeed struck down their dharma and changed the state of their hair.
Having shaved half the heads of the Śakas, he let them go; and he did the same for all the heads of the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas.
The Pāradās have shaven hair, while the Pahlavas wear beards; deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call, they were made so by that high-souled one.
The entire earth was conquered by that king through righteousness; yet all those Kṣatriyas, O dear one, were formerly rendered devoid of dharma.
Having conquered this earth, that king, a victor through righteousness, prepared his horse for the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), O monarch.
O Sage, as he was discharging that horse, it went to the southeastern ocean accompanied by his sixty thousand sons.
Indeed, that horse was carried off by Śakra, the king of the gods, who was intent on accomplishing his own purpose; he was taken to the vicinity of the shore and made to enter the earth.
Then, in order to search for that horse, the great king Sagara had that region excavated on all sides by his sons.
Then, as that great ocean was being dug there, they beheld that primordial Being, the divine Kapila, who possesses a universal form.
As he was awakening, sixty thousand [beings] were consumed by the fire arising from his eyes, while four remained as survivors.
Harṣaketu, Suketu, and likewise Dharmaratha, as well as the heroic Pañcajana—these were the kings who perpetuated his lineage.
And the Blessed Lord Hari himself granted him five boons: a lineage, intelligence, fame, an ocean as a son, and wealth.
By that very deed, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean; and he recovered from the sea that horse belonging to the horse sacrifice.
That highly illustrious one performed a hundred horse-sacrifices; there he worshipped Śambhu, the lords of prosperity, and the deities of excellent vows.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Genealogy from Satyavrata to Sagara," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: How were the heroic sons of Sagara born, so mighty and valiant, sixty thousand in number? And by whom were they deprived of their wealth? Tell me.
Sūta said: Sagara had two wives whose sins were burnt away by ascetic penance; the best of sages, Aurva, being gratified, granted them a boon.
One woman chose sixty thousand swift sons, while another, endowed with the power of choice as she desired, chose but one son to continue the lineage.
Having returned to that very place and obtained it, she then gave birth to many heroic sons from a gourd-like fruit that had been separated from its seeds.
Indeed, all those boys, who increased the joy [of their parents], grew up in due order under their own nurses in jars filled with clarified butter.
Among those great-souled ones who were consumed by the Kapila fire, there was one son named Pañcajana who became king.
From Pañcajana was born the powerful Aṃśumat; his son was Dilīpa, whose son was Bhagīratha.
But he who is the Lord that brought down Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, led her to the ocean and ordained her as his daughter.
The son of Bhagīratha was the king known as Śrutasena; his son was Nābhāga, who was supremely righteous.
Ambarīṣa was the son of Nābhāga, and from him Sindhudvīpa was born; the valiant Ayutājit was the heir of Sindhudvīpa.
The son of Āyutājit was the highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa; knowing the secret of divine dice, that king became a friend of Nala.
The son of Ṛtuparṇa was the highly effulgent Anuparṇa; his son was indeed Kalmāṣapāda, who was also known by the name Mitrasaha.
The son of Kalmāṣapāda was renowned as Sarvakarman; and the son of Viśvaśarman was the famous Anaraṇya.
The learned King Anaraṇya was the son of Muṇḍidruha; his sons were Niṣadha, Rati, and Khaṭvāṅga.
O sinless one, by means of wisdom and truth, all three worlds have been accumulated by him who, having come here from heaven, obtained life for but a moment.
Dīrghabāhu was his son, and Raghunātha was born as his son; Aja was his son, and from him Daśaratha was born.
Rāma, the righteous and highly illustrious one, was born from Daśaratha; he was a portion of Viṣṇu, a great devotee of Śiva, by whom the descendant of Pulastya was slain.
And that conduct has been described in many ways in the Purāṇas; for it is well known in the Rāmāyaṇa, and thus it has not been recounted here in detail.
A son was born to Rāma, renowned as Kuśa; from Kuśa was born Atithi, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nabhā was the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabhā, and Kṣemadhanvan is recorded as his [Puṇḍarīka’s] son.
The son of Kṣemadhanvan was the powerful Devānīka; the lordly son of Devānīka was named Ahīnagu.
The heir of Ahīnagu was the powerful one named Sahasvān; he was the son of Vīrasena and was born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The heir of Vīrasena was Pāriyātra; from him was born a son named Bala, and from him Sthala was born as a son.
From him was born a powerful Yakṣa son named Arkāṃśasaṃbhava; his son was Aguru, and from him was born a son named Vidhṛti.
His son was Hiraṇyanābha, who became a master of yoga; he was a disciple of the sage Jaimini and was highly proficient in the science of the self.
Then Kauśilya Yājñavalkya learned from that best of kings the yoga known as adhyātma, which severs the knots of the heart.
His son was indeed named Puṣpa, and his son was known as Dhruva; Agnivarṇa was his son, and from him came the son named Śīghra.
His son, named Maru, became accomplished in yoga; even today, that lord resides in the village known as Kalāpa.
And by the sages dwelling there, at the end of the Kali age, he alone shall indeed restore the lost solar dynasty once more, especially.
Pṛthuśruta was his son, and Saṃdhi is recorded as his son; Amarṣaṇa was his son, and Marutvān became his son.
Viśvasāhva was his son, and his son was Prasenajit; Takṣaka was his son, and Bṛhadbala was indeed his son.
These past kings of the Ikṣvāku lineage have been fully proclaimed; now hear of those who are yet to come, the future ones of that same lineage, who will be the most eminent knowers of dharma.
For Bṛhadbala’s son will be Bṛhadraṇa; and Bṛhadraṇa’s son will indeed be Urukriya.
Vatsavṛddha was his son; from him came Prativyomasuta; Bhānu will be his son, as will be Divāka, the lord of the army.
His son will be Sahadeva’s son, a great hero; his son will indeed be Bṛhadaśva, and his son will be the powerful Bhānumat.
The son of Bhānumat will be the heroic Pratīkāśva; his son will be Supratīka, an excellent king.
O twice-born ones, Sunakṣatra will be the son of that Marudeva; Puṣkara will be his son, and Antarikṣa will be his son.
Sutapāt was his son, a hero; and he was the son of Mitracitta. Bṛhadbhāja was his son, and Barhi was his son.
Kṛtañjaya was his son, and his son was indeed Raṇañjaya; Sañjaya was the son of Maya, and Śākya was indeed his offspring.
Śuddhodana was his son, and Lāṅgala was his offspring; Prasenajit was his son, and his son was named Śūdraka.
Ruṇaka will be his [son], and Suratha is known as his son; Sumitra will be his son, for he indeed marks the very end of the lineage.
This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall indeed end with Sumitrā; it belongs to those kings who are descendants of Vicitravīrya, most righteous and performers of virtuous deeds.
Having obtained King Sumitra, that auspicious lineage shall reach its conclusion in the Kali age; then, in the Brāhma period, it will flourish once again during the Kṛta age.
These kings of the lineage of Vaivasvata, who gave profuse sacrificial fees, have been proclaimed primarily as those born from the Ikṣvāku dynasty.
This is the supreme creation of the meritorious Vivasvat Āditya, the god who bestows the Śrāddha and who grants nourishment to all creatures.
A person who recites or hears this account of the creation and of the Sun attains union [with the deity], having enjoyed supreme happiness here in this world and being blessed with progeny.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kings Born in the Lineage of Vaivasvata," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Having heard this unsurpassed account of the solar lineage, Śaunaka, the best of sages, questioned Sūta, the god of the śrāddha rites, with great respect.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O Sūta, may you live long! O disciple of Vyāsa, salutations to you. You have caused us to hear this supreme, divine, and most purifying narrative.
You have spoken of Śrāddhadeva, the Sun, the increaser of the noble lineage; a doubt has arisen in me regarding that, which I shall state before you.
Whence indeed does the Sun-god Vivasvat derive his status as the deity of the Śrāddha? Out of affection for me, I wish to hear this; please sever this doubt of mine.
O Lord, tell me also of the majesty of the śrāddha and its fruit—that by which the ancestors, being pleased, unite one with the highest good.
And I wish to hear this supreme creation of the ancestors; tell it to me in detail, O high-minded one, and show me your compassion.
Sūta said: O Śaunaka, out of affection I shall relate to you in its entirety that creation of the ancestors (pitṛsarga), which was told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Bhīṣma when he questioned him.
O wise Mārkaṇḍeya, I shall fully declare to you that song sung by Sanatkumāra, which is the source of the fruit of all desires.
Questioned by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma, spoke while lying upon his bed of arrows; listen as I relate what he said to you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "How indeed is nourishment obtained by men who desire prosperity? I wish to hear this: by doing what does one not come to grief?"
Sūta said: Having heard the question asked by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, the knower of dharma, spoke these words with great affection while everyone was listening.
Bhīṣma said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who perform śrāddha rites even with affection, all that they satisfy through those śrāddhas is indeed by the grace of the ancestors.
And men who desire rewards always perform ancestral rites (śrāddha), aiming for their father, as well as for their father’s father.
The father and the grandfather are always present within the three rice-balls (piṇḍas) for one who desires dharma and for one who desires progeny, they grant offspring.
And they bestow nourishment upon one who desires nourishment, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "The ancestors of some dwell in heaven, while those of others are in hell; yet it is taught that for all living beings, the fruit of action is inevitable."
How indeed do those offerings of faith reach the ancestors? And how are they able to bring back that fruit for one who resides in hell?
I have heard that even the gods worship the ancestors in heaven; I wish to hear this—please explain it to me in detail.
Bhīṣma said: O subduer of enemies, I shall relate to you here that which I heard in the past as it was sung by my father when he had departed to another world.
At the time of the ancestral rite for my father, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) was prepared by me; my father, piercing the earth with his hand, begged for it from me.
Having decided that this was not seen as the prescribed ritual procedure, I nevertheless offered the funeral cake upon the kusha grass itself, without further deliberation.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, my father, being pleased with me and delighted, spoke these sweet words, O sinless one.
Through you, a wise knower of dharma, I have become possessed of an heir; yet I have been tested by you, O Puruṣottama.
For whatever standard a king establishes through righteous conduct, the subjects always follow that standard as it is practiced.
Listen, O best of the Bharatas, to the eternal duties of the Vedas; O son, you have established the authority of the Vedic dharma.
Therefore, being well-pleased with you, I grant you an unsurpassed boon out of affection; wait for it, for it is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds.
Death shall have no power over you as long as you wish to live; only after obtaining your permission will death once again prevail.
Or what further supreme boon do you desire that I may grant you? Speak that, O best of the Bharatas, whatever dwells in your mind.

When he had spoken thus, I saluted him with joined palms and said: "O giver of honor, now that you are pleased, I have achieved my purpose; I shall ask a certain question, which must indeed be answered by you yourself."
He said to me, "Tell that which you desire; I shall give it to you. Having been addressed thus, O King, the monarch then spoke when questioned by me.
Śantanu said: Listen, my dear son, I shall explain your question to you according to the truth; I have heard from Mārkaṇḍeya the entire account concerning the Pitṛs.
O dear one, regarding that which you ask me, I indeed asked the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya; for he, the knower of dharma, spoke to me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, O King, to what I once saw while observing the heavens; at that time, a celestial chariot was approaching from afar between the mountains.
In that celestial chariot sat one who resembled glowing embers, possessing great splendor, blazing with light, and incomparably beautiful.
And there I beheld a person of blazing splendor lying down, the size of a thumb, like fire placed within fire.
Having thus paid homage to that Lord and bowed my head to him, I asked him: "O All-pervading One, how may we know you?"
The righteous-souled one said to me: "O sage, by that very [merit] you possess such ascetic power (tapas) that you indeed recognize me as the son of Brahmā."
"Know me as Sanatkumāra; what may I do for you? Those other sons of Brahmā are indeed my younger brothers."
There were seven invincible brothers whose lineages remain established; we, however, have adopted the dharma of ascetics, restraining the self within the Self.
"O Sage, because I am known as 'Kumāra' (the Youth) precisely as I was when I first arose, this name Sanatkumāra has been told to me."
Since you have performed penance with devotion out of a desire for a vision of me, here I am seen by you; may it be well with you—what desire of yours shall I fulfill?
To him who had spoken thus, I said: "Listen, O Lord; tell us truly of the primordial creation of the ancestors."
Thus addressed, he said to me: "Listen, my dear, as it truly is; I shall tell you in accordance with reality the auspicious creation of the ancestors."
Sanatkumāra said: In ancient times, Brahmā created the gods and said to them, "Worship me. Desiring rewards, they abandoned him and worshipped that Self instead.
Cursed by Brahmā, those fools were told, "You shall lose your senses. Consequently, being ignorant of anything and deprived of their senses, they [approached] the Grandfather.
"Bowing down to Procusta, they all said, 'Please show us favor. Being thus addressed, he spoke this to them for the very purpose of their atonement."
"Ask your own sons; from them you shall obtain knowledge. Having been told this, they, having lost their composure, questioned their sons with vigor.
"O sinless one, having regained their consciousness for the sake of penance, those dwellers of heaven were addressed by their sons as follows: 'Go, O dear sons!'"
Cursed by their sons, those gods went to the Creator and asked him, saying, "We have been told by our sons that we are no longer their fathers."
Then the god Brahmā spoke to those gods who were filled with doubt: "Listen, all you immortals; you are not speakers of Brahman."
Therefore, what has been spoken by those sons of yours, the best among the wise, should be accepted as such after abandoning all doubt; it is not otherwise.
"O gods and ancestors, you who dwell in the third heaven, perform sacrifice with great mutual affection; you are the bestowers of the fruits of all desires."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O tiger among sages, their doubts severed by the words of Brahmā, they became joyful toward one another, bestowing happiness upon each other.
Then the gods indeed said to them, "O sons, since we have been addressed [by you] as 'putrakas,' therefore you shall undoubtedly become the Pitṛs (Fathers)."
Someone will undoubtedly perform the ritual at the ancestral Śrāddha; Soma, nourished by the Śrāddhas, will in turn nourish the worlds.
Those men who, desiring prosperity, shall perform Śrāddha rites at the ocean, the mountains, and the forests, which are filled with all things moving and unmoving;
The ancestors, being always gratified, bestow nourishment upon those who offer three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at a śrāddha ceremony according to name and lineage.
Existing everywhere, those ancestors and great-grandfathers will always be sustained when they are gratified by the offering of the śrāddha.
"O dwellers of heaven, let these words of his be true: that we all—both sons and fathers—are indeed one with respect to each other."
Thus those gods became fathers through the power of dharma; indeed, they became celebrated as fathers to one another upon the circle of the earth.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Power of the Ancestors," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Umā-saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: O best of those who practice austerity, seven groups of ancestors are remembered in heaven; four of them indeed possess form, while three are formless.
The primordial hosts of gods and likewise the Brahmins and others sacrifice those [oblations]; they first cause Soma to swell by means of the power of yoga.
Therefore, offerings of faith should be given, especially to yogins; for all of them, the vessel should be made of silver or at least adorned with silver.
Having placed the *svadhā* offering at the forefront, one indeed gratifies the ancestors during the *śrāddha* rite; for it effects the nourishment of Agni, Soma, and Yama.
Whether at the northern solstice, or even in the absence of fire, by offering into the water with devotion, one who pleases the ancestors is himself pleased by the ancestors.
The ancestors bestow nourishment as well as abundant progeny, heaven, the increase of health, and whatever else is desired.
O Sage, the rite for the ancestors is superior even to the rite for the gods; since you are devoted to the ancestors, O brahmin-sage, you shall therefore be free from old age and death.
O Sage, the state attained by one devoted to his ancestors cannot be reached even through yoga; therefore, O great sage, devotion to the ancestors must be practiced with special care.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods quickly bestowed upon him the eye—difficult even for the gods to obtain—along with spiritual discernment, and departed by his yogic power.
Listen again, Bhīṣma, to how in former times the twice-born sons of Bharadvāja, having attained the dharma of yoga, fell away indeed through their evil conduct.
One who is foul-mouthed, wrathful, violent, slanderous, or even a poet; one who is devoted to his sister or obedient to his father—these are [designated] by names as well as by their actions.
O dear one, the sons of Kauśika became the disciples of Garga; when their father had passed away, they all lived abroad at that time.
Then, at the command of their guru, all those who had acquired wealth through unjust means gathered together a milch cow that was tawny and had a calf of the same color.
O Bhārata, as they were afflicted by hunger on the road, a cruel thought arose in them due to their youth and delusion—that they should then kill that cow.
Then both Kavi and Śvasṛpa entreated her, but she did not comply; nor indeed could her own people be restrained by them at that time.
But that twice-born man among them who was devoted to his father, always performing the daily ancestral rites (śrāddha), being endowed with devotion to his father, spoke to them all in anger.
If it is impossible to perform [the rites] oneself, let them be accomplished on behalf of the ancestors; for all who perform the śrāddha with a concentrated mind [attain merit].
In this way, this cow will attain dharma; there is no doubt about this. By honoring the ancestors according to dharma, no unrighteousness shall befall us.
Having been addressed thus, O Bhārata, they all then sprinkled the cow with water, offered it to the ancestors, and consumed it.
Having consumed the cow's milk, they all reported it to their teacher, saying, "The cow has been killed by a tiger; please accept this calf."
The twice-born man indeed accepted that calf as if it were his own suffering offspring; however, through that improper conduct, sin accrued to those who had killed the cow.
Then, after some time had passed, O dear one, those seven brothers met their end when their lifespans were exhausted.
Indeed, due to their cruelty, lustfulness, ignobility, and likewise toward their guru, those seven brothers were born as those who take delight in fierce violence.
The sons of the hunter were born powerful and wise; seven hunters, experts in dharma, arose among the Daśārṇas.
All the deer on the beautiful Kālañjara mountain were devoted to their own nature, free from delusion, yet they remained agitated and distressed.
Reflecting upon that very same purpose—the knowledge arising at the time of death—the forest-dwellers remained patient, free from dualities, and without possessions.

All of them were performers of auspicious deeds, followers of the true Dharma, and dwellers of the forest; they were devoid of unrighteous conduct and possessed the siddhi of recollecting their past births.
Whatever dharma was indeed heard by him in former births within the households of his gurus remained fixed in his intellect, even as he did not turn back from cyclic existence.
Having obtained food, those ascetics gave up their lives in the midst of the mountain; O Bhārata, such were the places where they fell.
Even today, O King, they are seen on Mount Kālañjara; by that deed, they have become those who avoid both auspicious and inauspicious [rebirth].
Having attained a more auspicious birth as ruddy geese, those seven water-dwellers came to exist in the auspicious region of Śaradvīpa.
Having abandoned the duty of companionship, the sages who uphold dharma are free from attachment, devoid of the sense of "mine," peaceful, beyond dualities, and without possessions.
The birds known by the name Nivṛtti and Nirvṛti are all remembered as celibate students (brahmacārins), for these birds are upholders of dharma.
Remembering their past births, well-grown, and practicing celibacy, these seven remained together in one place, devoted to the true Dharma and forever free from transformation.

Yet, because they had behaved falsely toward their guru out of delusion while in the womb of a demoness, they took birth in the animal realm; nevertheless, through the śrāddha rite, they obtained knowledge.

Thus, when the Śrāddha was performed for the sake of the ancestral rites by those established [in their duties], they then gradually attained knowledge and birth, each superior in quality to the last.
Whatever Brahman was heard from one's ancestors and others in the houses of one's gurus, that very knowledge remains established; therefore, one should thoroughly practice that knowledge.
Sumanas, Suvākchuddha, Pañcamachidradarśaka, Svatantra, and Suyajña are remembered as the names of the Kulīnas.
O great sage, listen to that virtuous conduct which prevailed there among those birds as they lived their lives according to dharma.
The lord of the Nīpas, a king endowed with great power and majesty, entered that forest surrounded by his inner apartments.
The independent cakravāka bird, seeing him traveling endowed with happiness and possessed of the splendor of sovereignty, yearned for that king.
If there is any merit whatsoever from my austerity or my observance of vows, then let me be exhausted by fasting and by unwavering ascetic practice.
Indeed, even by performing all of this with its fruit fully realized, may I become such a vessel of all good fortune.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then two ruddy geese became his companions, saying, "We two shall indeed be your ministers, desiring your pleasure and welfare."
Having said "So be it," the movement of that one whose self was absorbed in yoga then ceased; in this manner, those two cakravāka birds responded to their own words.
Since you, while proclaiming your own karma, have attained this dharma of yoga and thus pray for such a boon, therefore listen to my words.
"My dear son, you shall become king in Kāmpilya, the most excellent of cities; these two, who have been overcome by misconduct, shall be your ministers."
The three brothers, traveling together with their fourth, did not speak of the kingdom; however, Sumanas, being well-disposed toward them, spoke again in their midst.
"The curse shall be internal, yet you two shall attain union once more; Sarvasattva and Suyajña shall become independent."
Through the grace of the ancestors, you have attained this merit; having sprinkled the cow according to the law, she has been prepared for the ancestors.
The union with our knowledge is the means of yoga for all; this task has been undertaken, and a single verse has been cited.
"Having heard this from another person, you will then attain yoga. Having spoken thus, that wise bird Sumanas became silent.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O dear one, son of the eminent Śantanu, for the welfare of the worlds, I have thus related that history to you. What more do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Ancestors and the Description of the Fate of the Seven Hunters," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Bhīṣma said: O Mārkaṇḍeya, O highly wise one, best among those who bear devotion to the ancestors, tell me out of compassion, O best of sages, what happened after that?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Those seven, devoted to the yoga of dharma, wandering in Lake Mānasa, constantly withered their bodies, subsisting only on air and water.
Surrounded by his harem like Maghavan in the Nandana grove, that king sported there for a very long time with his wife and then returned to his own city.
He had a son named Anūha, who was supremely righteous; having established that son Vaibhrāja upon the throne, he departed for the forest.
He began to perform austerities at that place where his companions were; there, that great ascetic remained without food, subsisting only on air.
Thereupon, that forest, illuminated by him, became well-known by the name Vibhrāja; indeed, it was a bestower of yogic perfections.
For among those very birds, four were practitioners of yoga, while three, having fallen from yoga, brought about the abandonment of their bodies.
In the city of Kāmpilya, those seven great-souled ones, led by Brahmadatta, were all born free from all taints.
Among them, four were possessed of mindfulness while three were utterly deluded; from the one named Svatantra was born the highly energetic Brahmadatta.

Chidradarśin and Sunetra were both masters who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; they were born as heirs to Vedic scholars, possessing the impressions of their previous births.
Pañcāla was a master of the Ṛgveda and indeed acted as a teacher; Puṇḍarīka, who knew two Vedas, was likewise a master of the Sāmaveda and the Yajurveda.
Then the king, having seen his son Brahmadatta free from blemish and having consecrated him in his own kingdom, attained the supreme goal.
Having established their sons Pañcāla and Puṇḍarīka in the palace, the two entered the forest there and attained the supreme goal.
O descendant of Bharata, the wife of Brahmadatta was named Sannati; she, being endowed with single-minded devotion, took delight solely with her husband.
But the remaining cakravāka birds, O King, were born as heirs of Vedic scholars in the family of a poor man at Kāmpilya, where they lived together as companions.
He was steadfast, high-souled, a seer of reality, and free from worldly desire; there were four others, accomplished in the study of the Vedas, who were observers of his vulnerabilities.
All those perfected ones, devoted to yoga, set forth after taking leave of one another and bowing down to the lotus feet of Śambhu.
May those heroes who have set out, desiring non-rebirth, destroy their evil today—that which is the supreme state of Śambhu.
O great sage, when physical, mental, or verbal sin has been committed, one should recite this properly with devotion and endowed with faith.
One is liberated from all sins by the chanting of the names of Śiva; indeed, while these names of that God of gods are being uttered, [liberation occurs].
Indeed, evil goes to dissolution like an unbaked clay vessel in water; therefore, as soon as that evil has been accumulated, [one must act immediately].
O Great Sage, this should be recited by men of faith in abundance for the pacification of sin and for the attainment of the fruits of all desires.
One who reads this chapter for the sake of nourishment, or hears it, is liberated from all sins and attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the State of the Ancestors," in the Pitṛ-kalpa of the Umā-saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, tell me now about the worship of the preceptor; indeed, what also ought to be done at the conclusion of hearing this work? Ah, tell me that as well!

Sūta said: Having heard the supreme narrative, one should worship the preceptor with devotion according to the prescribed rules; at the conclusion of the book, being of serene mind, one should duly bestow gifts upon the preceptor.

Then, having bowed to the speaker and honored him according to the prescribed rite with ornaments for the hands and ears, as well as gentle garments and other such gifts, the wise man [should proceed].
Upon the completion of the Śiva-pūjā, one should give a cow with its calf, having fashioned a seat of gold weighing one pala and covered with a cloth.
Having placed a beautiful manuscript written in elegant characters there, the wise person should give it to the preceptor; thus he shall be liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
O Sage, a village, an elephant, a horse, and all other things according to one's capacity should be given to the high-souled reciter.
O Sage Śaunaka, it is traditionally held that a Purāṇa, when properly recited along with its ritual prescriptions, is indeed fruitful; this which I have spoken is the truth.

Therefore, O Sage, one should listen with devotion to that Purāṇa which is declared according to the injunctions, which is rich in the meaning of the Vedas, and which bestows merit and is the very heart of the Śruti.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Method for Worshipping Vyāsa," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta of great intelligence, O ocean of compassion, tell us of the birth of Vyāsa. O Lord, out of supreme grace, O Master, make us fulfilled.
The auspicious mother of Vyāsa is said to be Satyavatī by name; that goddess was indeed married to King Śantanu.
How was the great yogi Vyāsa born from Parāśara upon her? A great doubt has arisen here; you ought to sever it.
Sūta said: Once, while traveling on a pilgrimage, the yogi Parāśara went by chance to the beautiful and auspicious bank of the Yamunā.
Then the righteous-souled one said to the Niṣāda who was eating at that time: "Take me across to the other side of the Yamunā by means of a water-vehicle."
Thus addressed by that sage, the Niṣāda said to his daughter, "O girl, take this man across to the other shore quickly by boat."
O illustrious lady, this ascetic, born from the womb of Dṛśyantī, has mastered the four Vedas and desires to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus informed by her father, Matsyagandhā ferried the great sage, who was seated in the boat and radiant as the sun, across the water.
Due to the conjunction of time, the great yogi became overcome by passion for her—he who, having seen the beauty of the apsarases, was never before deluded.
Desiring to take the beautiful maiden Dāśakanyā, that sage touched her right hand with his own right hand.
He spoke these words with a smile to the large-eyed lady: "O silent one, why do you perform this despicable act?"
"O high-minded one, you were born into the beautiful lineage of Vasiṣṭha; I, however, O Brahmin, am born of a Niṣāda woman—how can a union between us be possible?"
Human birth is difficult to obtain, and the status of a Brahmin is especially so; even therein, O best of sages, the state of an ascetic is difficult to attain.
Endowed with learning, physical beauty, speech, noble lineage, and virtuous conduct, he has nonetheless fallen under the power of the arrows of desire; indeed, this is a great marvel!
No one on earth was able to prevent him from performing even an improper act, for they were all afraid of the curse of this yogin.
Having reflected thus in his heart, he spoke to the great sage: "O Mistress, maintain your composure for as long as it takes me to rescue you."
Sūta said: Having heard these words of hers, Parāśara, the king of yogins, swiftly released her hand and went once more to the further shore of the ocean.
Afflicted by desire, he seized the young woman again; trembling, however, that young woman spoke to him, the ocean of compassion.
"O best of sages, I am foul-smelling, dark-complexioned, and born of a Niṣāda; you, however, are most noble in thought and the foremost among yogis."
A union between us two is not possible, like that between glass and gold; a union between those of equal birth and form would be a source of happiness.
When she had spoken thus, in that very instant, the lovely woman was transformed by him into Yojanagandhā, possessing a beautiful form and enchanting to the mind.
Afflicted by desire, that sage seized the young woman again; seeing him wishing to take her, the daughter of Vasava spoke once more.
The Śruti declares that sexual intercourse should be performed at night and not by day; for in daytime union there is great fault and even irreproachable censure.
Therefore, wait for as long as it takes for night to fall; for here men will see me, and my father stands upon the bank.
Having heard these words spoken by her, that bull among sages immediately created a mist through the power of his merit.
When a mist arose, resembling the darkness of night, the young woman, fearing intimacy, spoke again to that sage.
"O Yogi of unfailing valor, if you depart after having enjoyed me, O Lord, I shall then become pregnant; what will my fate be?"
"O one of great intelligence, my vow as a maiden will be ruined; then the people will laugh at me. What shall I say to my father?"
Parāśara said: "O young girl, sport with me at your will according to the flavors born of passion; tell me your own desire, O beloved, and I shall fulfill it now."
By making my command true, become Satyavatī by name; you shall be worthy of salutation by all yogis as well as by the gods.
Satyavatī said: "Neither my father, nor my mother, nor any other men on earth know [of this]. My maidenhood would not be destroyed; therefore, accept me."
O Lord, may there be a son equal to you, possessed of wonderful power; and may my body always possess fragrance and ever-new youth.
Parāśara said: Listen, my dear; everything you desire shall be fulfilled. A son of great renown, born from a portion of Viṣṇu, shall be yours.
Know that there is indeed a certain cause for which I am afflicted by desire; having seen the form of an apsaras, my mind was not deluded anywhere.
Perceiving you to have the fragrance of a fish, I fell under the sway of delusion; yet, O young girl, the decree of Brahma inscribed upon the tablet of my forehead cannot be otherwise.
O lady of beautiful hips, your son shall be the author of the Purāṇas and the divider of the Vedic branches; his fame shall be renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having spoken thus and having enjoyed that woman of most beautiful limbs, the expert in yoga, O great sage, bathed in the waters of the Yamunā and departed swiftly.
She too quickly conceived a fetus possessing a radiance equal to that of the twelve suns, and gave birth on the island of Sūryaja to a son who was like the god Kāmadeva.
Bearing a water-pot in his left hand and an excellent staff in his right, he is a mass of splendor, resplendent with tawny matted locks.
But as soon as he was born, the radiant one addressed his mother: "Go, mother, wherever you desire; from this point forward, I shall go."
O Mother, whenever there is any task desired by you in your heart, I shall come upon being remembered for the sake of fulfilling your wish.
Having spoken thus and having prostrated at his mother's feet, that treasury of asceticism departed to perform penance at a sacred ford that purifies all sins.
She too, overcome with affection for her son, went to her father's presence, remembering her son’s conduct and describing her own good fortune.
Because he was born on an island (dvīpa) as a child, he became known as Dvaipāyana; because of his division of the branches of the Vedas, he is celebrated as Vedavyāsa.
First, one should visit the king of holy places (tīrtharāja), which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa; as well as Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, and Avantikā.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Dvārakā, and Amarāvatī; the Sarasvatī, the confluence of the Sindhu, and the junction of the Gaṅgā with the ocean.
Kāñcī and Tryambaka, the banks of the Saptagodāvarī, Kālañjara and Prabhāsa, as well as Badarikāśrama.
Likewise, Mahālaya, the sacred field of Oṃkāra, Puruṣottama, Gokarṇa, Bhṛgukaccha, Bhṛgutuṅga, and Puṣkara.
Having gone to sacred pilgrimage sites such as Śrīparvata and likewise to Dhārātīrtha, he bathed according to the prescribed rites and performed supreme austerity.
Thus wandering through many sacred fords situated in various lands, the son of Kālikā reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Where Viśveśvara himself and the Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, both treasuries of compassion, reside to bestow the nectar of immortality upon their devotees.
Having reached the sacred site of Vārāṇasī and beheld Maṇikarṇikā, that lord of sages cast off the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes.
Having visited all the lingas, headed by Viśveśa, and having bathed in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), tanks, wells, and lakes;
Having bowed to all the Vināyakas and prostrated before all the Gaurīs, and having fully worshipped Kālarāja Bhairava, the devourer of sins;
Having diligently praised the chief leaders of the staff and the Gaṇas, and having gratified the Keśavas, foremost among whom is Ādikeśava;
Having bowed down again and again to the suns headed by Lolārka, he tirelessly performed the offering of funeral cakes at all the sacred fords.
The meritorious soul installed the Liṅga named Vyāseśvara, by the sight of which, O Brāhmaṇa, a man becomes a master of speech in all branches of knowledge.
Having worshipped the Lingas, headed by Viśveśa, with great devotion, he reflected repeatedly: "Which Linga bestows swift success?"
Having propitiated Mahādeva, may we obtain all the sciences; and by his grace, may the power to compose Purāṇas be mine.
Is it Śrīdamoṃkāranātha, or perhaps Kṛttivāseśvara; or Kedāreśa, Kāmeśa, or Trilocana Candreśa?
One may worship Kāleśa, Vṛddhakāleśa, or indeed Kālaśeśvara; or Jyeṣṭheśa, Jambukeśa, or Jaigīṣavyeśvara.
One should visit Daśāśvamedheśāna, or Drumicaṇḍeśa, or Dṛkkeśa, or Garuḍeśa, or Gokarṇeśa, or Gaṇeśvara.
[One should worship] Prasannavadaneśa, or Dharmeśa, Tārakeśvara, Nandikeśa, Nivāseśa, Patrīśa, and Prītikeśvara.
Parvateśa, Paśupati, or indeed Hāṭakeśvara; or else Bṛhaspatīśvara, or Tilabhāṇḍeśa.
Is it Bhārabhūteśvara, or perhaps Mahālakṣmīśvara; or Maruteśa, Mokṣeśa, Gaṅgeśa, or Narmadeśvara?
Kṛṣṇeśa, Parameśāna, or likewise Ratneśvara; Yāmuneśa, Lāṅgalīśa, and the all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara.
Or else [one should worship] Avimukteśvara, or Viśālākṣīśa, or Vyāghreśvara, Varāheśa, or even Vidyeśvara.
One may worship Varuṇeśa, Vidhīśa, or Harikeśeśvara; or Bhavānīśa, Kapardīśa, Kandukeśa, and Majeśvara.
Or Viśvakarmeśvara, or Vīreśvara, or Nādeśa, Kapileśa, or indeed Bhuvaneśvara.
Bāṣkulīśa Mahādeva, or likewise Siddhīśvara, Viśvedeveśvara, Vīrabhadreśa, and Bhairaveśvara.
Either Amṛteśa or Satīśa, or indeed Pārvatīśvara; or Siddheśvara, Mataṅgeśa, or even Bhūtīśvara.
Āṣāḍhīśa, Prakāmeśa, Koṭirudreśvara, as well as Madālaseśvara and Tilaparṇeśvara—what more need be said?
"Or should I resort to Hiraṇyagarbheśa, or Śrīmadhyameśvara? Amidst these millions of liṅgas, which one shall I take refuge in?"
Thus Vyāsa, whose soul was devoted to the worship of Śiva, being troubled by these thoughts, reflected for a moment with a mind made steady through meditation.
It was understood; it had been forgotten for a while, but now my heart's desire has been fulfilled—the Linga, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa, has been worshipped by the Siddhas.
By the sight and touch of which the mind attains purity—that indeed is where the gate of heaven stands perpetually open.
Indeed, that supreme Siddhakṣetra is within the great field of Avimukta, where the supreme Liṅga known as Madhyameśvara resides.
Indeed, no other liṅga exists in Kāśī besides Madhyameśvara, for the sake of beholding which the gods arrive on every auspicious occasion.
Therefore, Mahādeva, known by the name Madhyameśvara, should be served; through his propitiation, O Brahmins, many have attained perfection.
Since Śaṅkara resides in the center of Kāśī as the primary deity for the sake of the welfare of the people of his own city, he is therefore called Madhyameśvara.
The gandharva named Tumburu and the celestial sage Nārada likewise attained mastery as experts in the science of song by propitiating him.
By propitiating this very [deity], Viṣṇu became the bestower of liberation; likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer.
Even Kubera, the lord of wealth, was indeed Vāmadeva, the sovereign of the Śaivas; and the king named Khaṭvāṅga, though previously childless, became possessed of offspring.
An Apsarā named Candrabhāmā, dancing with her own natural emotion, possessing a voice like the song of a cuckoo, attained dissolution within the center of the Liṅga while still in her physical body.
Śrīkara, the son of a cowherd woman, having served Madhyameśvara, attained the status of a Gaṇapati through the compassion of Śiva, whose nature is mercy.
Both Bhārgava and Gīṣpati, the two gods worshipped by Daityas and Suras, attained mastery over all knowledge through the grace of the Lord of Madhyama.
I too, having fully worshipped the Lord Maheśvara here at Madhyameśvara, shall surely and swiftly attain the power of being the author of the Purāṇas.
Having thus formed this resolve, the wise Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, being a practitioner of vows, bathed in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī and undertook his religious observances.
In some places he subsisted on leaves, in others on fruits and vegetables; at times he fed on air or water, and at other times he observed the vow of total fasting.
In accordance with such rules, the righteous yogi worshipped Madhyameśvara three times a day with fruits produced from various trees.
When a great deal of time had passed in this manner, the son of Kālikā, having bathed in the waters of the triple-pathed river, arrived there at dawn.
The meritorious soul beheld the Lord Maheśvara, the Īśāna of Madhyameśvara, who grants the desired boons to his devotees, as the Liṅga situated in the center.
His left side was adorned by Umā, he wore a tiger skin as an upper garment, and his beautiful form was graced by the waves of the Gaṅgā flowing through his mass of matted hair.
His locks of hair were illuminated by the moonlight of the young autumnal crescent moon; his entire body was smeared with ashes, and his form was as white as camphor.
With eyes reaching to the ends of his ears and lips as red as coral, he was a child appearing five years of age, adorned with ornaments befitting a boy.
Possessing a bodily luster that destroys the pride of ten million Cupids, naked, with a smiling lotus-face, he was playfully singing the Sāman hymns.
To Hara, who is the ocean of the waters of compassion, whose name is "Affectionate toward Devotees," who is easily pleased, the beloved of Umā, and whose face is gracious with favor.
Having beheld him, he offered praise with a voice faltering with love—to that friend of the wretched, whose nature is consciousness, and who is inaccessible even to yogis.

Vedavyāsa said: O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, you who are difficult to attain through speech, mind, or action, and who are beyond the reach even of yogis!
O Lord of Umā, even the Vedas do not know your greatness; you alone are the creator, the sustainer, and likewise the destroyer of the universe.
You are the primordial Lord of all the gods, the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss; you have neither name nor lineage, for you are the omniscient Sadāśiva.
You alone are the Supreme Brahman, the remover of the bonds of Māyā; you are unstained by the three qualities (guṇas), just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
Neither your birth, nor your conduct, nor your country, nor your lineage is known; yet, being such as you are, you bring about at will the lordship over the three worlds.
Neither Brahmā, nor Lakṣmī’s lord, nor the gods including Indra, nor the lords of yogis know Your true nature; we worship You, who are such.

From you everything comes, for you are all; you are the Lord of Gaurī, you are the Destroyer of the Cities. You are the child, you are the youth, and you are the old man; I unite that very you within my heart.
Salutations to that Great Lord, Śambhu, the object of meditation for his devotees, the Ancient Person, truly Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self.
Having praised him thus, just as he fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, that boy, with a joyful heart, addressed Vedavyāsa.
"Choose a boon, O Yoginī, whatever dwells in your mind; for there is nothing that should not be given, since I am subject to the will of my devotees."
Then, rising up with a joyful heart, the sage Vyāsa of great asceticism replied: "O Lord, what is unknown to you, who are omniscient?"
The Lord Śarva is the inner self of all and you are the bestower of everything; why does the Master direct me toward a request that causes such wretchedness?
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, whose mind was stainless, Mahādeva, who had assumed the form of a child, smiled with a pure smile and spoke.
The boy said: "O best among the knowers of Brahman, whatever desire you have formed in your heart will, without doubt, be fulfilled in a very short time."
O Brahmin, abiding within your throat as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) and Lord, I shall perfectly cause the Itihāsas and Purāṇas to issue forth.
This meritorious hymn, the *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka*, which you have uttered, grants all desires when recited three times a day for a year in the abode of Śambhu.
The recitation of this hymn is said to increase knowledge and intellect; it bestows all prosperity upon men, and grants both dharma and liberation.
Rising early in the morning, having bathed well, and having worshipped the Liṅga of Śaṅkara, even a fool would become Bṛhaspati himself by reciting this hymn for a year.
Whether by a woman or even by a man, this hymn, when recited for a year according to the prescribed rule in the presence of a linga, shall increase one's intellect and knowledge.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, appearing as a child, merged into the *liṅga*; Vyāsa too, shedding tears, became overwhelmed with love for Śiva.
Having thus obtained this boon from Maheśa at Madhyameśvara, Vyāsa composed the eighteen Purāṇas by his own effortless play.
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata; the Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya.
The Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Liṅga, and the Vārāha; then the one called Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, and the Gāruḍa.
Likewise, the Skānda Purāṇa and that known as the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa have been proclaimed; they bestow fame and merit upon men, and the Śāṅkara Purāṇa brings glory to those who hear it.
Sūta said: O best among the knowers of the Vedas, you have previously mentioned the names of the eighteen Purāṇas; now provide their etymological explanations.
Vyāsa said: This very same question was asked by Taṇḍi, who was born from Brahmā; regarding that which he spoke concerning Nandikeśvara, I shall now relate it.
Nandikeśvara said: O Sage, because Brahmā himself, the four-faced one, was the speaker therein, that Purāṇa is therefore called the first, the Brāhma.
Because the greatness of the Padma Kalpa is proclaimed therein, this second Purāṇa is therefore known as the Pādma.
That Purāṇa which was composed by Parāśara and makes Viṣṇu known is indeed the same as that spoken by Vyāsa, due to the non-difference between father and son.
In which the former and latter sections contain many accounts of Śiva’s deeds—this is indeed the Śaiva Purāṇa, as those who know the Purāṇas declare.
That in which the life-story of the Blessed Durgā is found is indeed called the Bhāgavata; it is, in fact, the Devīpurāṇa.
The Purāṇa spoken by Nārada is called the Nāradīya, wherein the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya was the speaker to Tāṇḍi.
The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is indeed declared as the seventh; it is called Āgneya because of its connection with Agni, and Bhaviṣyaka because of its narration of future events.
Because it describes the manifestation (vivarta) of Brahmā, it is called the Brahmavaivarta; because it recounts the deeds of the Liṅga, the Purāṇa is called the Liṅga.
And the twelfth Purāṇa, O Sage, is the Vārāha, belonging to Varāha; in it, Skanda himself is the listener and Maheśvara is the speaker in person.
That which is proclaimed as the Skānda is the Vāmana of Vāmana; the Kaurma is the life-story of the Tortoise, and the Mātsya was narrated by the Fish.
That which was spoken by Garuḍa himself is designated as the Gāruḍa; it is celebrated as the Brahmāṇḍa because it describes the history of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Sūta said: This very same question was posed by me to the wise Vyāsa; from him, I heard the definitive exposition of all the Purāṇas.
Thus, born of Parāśara upon Satyavatī, Vyāsa composed the Purāṇa-saṃhitās and the supreme Mahābhārata.
O Brahmana, you ought not to entertain doubt regarding this, just as there was no doubt concerning Satyavati’s union with Parashara and again with Shantanu.
This wondrous arising has been described along with its cause; indeed, the wise should extract only the virtues from the conduct of the great.
Whoever hears or even reads this supreme secret shall be liberated from all sins and be honored in the world of the ṛṣis.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vyāsa," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The sages said: Having heard the delightful stories of Śambhu, which are endowed with various narratives and joined with accounts of his various incarnations, and which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Now we wish to hear from you, O best among the knowers of Brahman, the captivating life-story of the Blessed Mother, the Mother of the World.
The primordial, eternal power of Maheśa, the Supreme Brahman, who is celebrated as Umā, the supreme mother of the three worlds.
Satī is Hemavatī; two of her incarnations have been heard by us. O high-minded Sūta, tell us of her other incarnations.
What wise person would become dispassionate toward the practice of hearing of virtues—those which the glorious and wise never abandon?
Sūta said: Blessed are you, O great-souled ones; you have always accomplished your purpose, since you inquire about the great life-story of Umā, the Supreme Mother.
The sages know that for those who hear, inquire about, and likewise recite it, the very dust of the lotus feet [of the Lord] is the sacred bathing place.
Blessed and fulfilled shall they be; blessed is their mother and their lineage—those whose minds are absorbed in the Śrī Devī, the supreme consciousness.
Those who do not praise the Goddess of the gods, the cause of all causes, are deluded by the qualities of *māyā* and are surely of ruined fortune; of this there is no doubt.
They do not resort to the Great Goddess, who is an ocean of the essence of compassion; they fall into the terrible blind well that is the nature of saṃsāra.
Just as one might abandon the Gaṅgā to seek satisfaction from the water of a desert, so too does one abandon the Goddess to go to another deity who is different from her.
What superior man would abandon her, by the mere remembrance of whom one obtains the four aims of human existence without effort?
Formerly, when Medhā was questioned by the high-souled Suratha, he spoke; listen as I relate to you what was said by Medhā in the past.
Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Viratha; his son was Suratha, who possessed great strength and prowess.
He was generous in giving, truthful in speech, skilled in his own duty, and accomplished; devoted to the Goddess, an ocean of compassion, and the protector of his subjects.
While he, whose splendor was like that of Indra, ruled the earth, there were nine kings who became intent on seizing the land.
They besieged that king’s capital, named Kolā; a fierce and tumultuous battle ensued with them.
In battle, that king was utterly defeated by those powerful hosts of enemies; having been driven from Kolā and stripped of his entire kingdom, he was cast out.
That king returned to his own city and ruled the kingdom with his ministers; yet even there, he was defeated by his adversaries who possessed great power.
By fate, the groups headed by the ministers attained enmity with him, and all the wealth that was situated in the treasury was appropriated for themselves.
Then the king, having departed from the city under the pretext of hunting, mounted his horse and went alone into the dense forest.
Wandering here and there from that place, the king beheld the hermitage of the eminent sage, which shone in every direction, adorned with groves of flowers.
It was filled with the sound of the Vedas, inhabited by peaceful beings, and surrounded on all sides by disciples, grand-disciples, and their own disciples.
O Mahāmati, tigers and other beasts of great prowess do not harass those of little strength in that hermitage, due to the power of the most excellent of the twice-born.
There the wise king, possessed of great compassion, dwelt, having been honored by the lord of sages with kind words, food, and seats.
Once, that great king fell into an insurmountable anxiety: "Alas! For me, who am of wretched fortune, evil intellect, and diminished luster..."
The kingdom, which was protected by my ancestors, has been seized in its entirety by hosts of enemies arrogant with pride; now it is being enjoyed by those foes.
"There has never been any king like me in this lineage of Caitra; what shall I do, where shall I go, and how may I regain the kingdom?"
As for my own ministers and counselors who have served me since ancient times, I do not know which king they have now approached and are dwelling with.
Having now destroyed the kingdom, I know not what state they have gone to—those who were great in their enthusiasm for the field of battle and the slaughter of enemy hosts.
Those great heroes of mine who have taken refuge with another king—those elephants resembling mountains and horses swift as the wind—[are now lost].
The treasury accumulated by their predecessors is now being protected by them as if it were new; thus has this most righteous king fallen under the sway of delusion.
In the meantime, a certain Vaiśya arrived there; the king asked him, "Who are you, sir, and for what purpose have you come here?"
"Why do you appear dejected? Tell me this now. Having heard these pleasing words spoken by the protector of men, [he replied].
Shedding tears from his eyes, the eminent Vaiśya, Samādhi, bowed low with affection and addressed these words to the protector of the earth.
The Vaiśya said: "O Lord of the Earth, I am a Vaiśya named Samādhi, born of a wealthy lineage; yet, out of greed for wealth, I have been abandoned by my sons, wife, and others."
Afflicted by his own karma, that king has come to the forest; such as I am, along with my sons, grandsons, and likewise my wives.
O Lord, ocean of compassion, I do not truly know the welfare of my brothers, my nephews, nor of my other friends.
The king said: Why do you show affection toward those sons and others who have cast you out—those ill-behaved ones greedy for wealth—as if you were a foolish creature?
The Vaiśya said: "O King, you have spoken well; your words are enriched with essential meaning. Nevertheless, my mind is exceedingly deluded by the bond of affection."
Thus, O best of sages, the Vaiśya and the king, both agitated by delusion, then went into the presence of Medhas, the most excellent of munis.
Accompanied by the Vaiśya king, that powerful lord of men, a great hero, bowed his head in salutation to the best of yogis.
Joining his palms in reverence, the king spoke these words to the sage: "O Blessed One, you ought now to sever the delusion of us both."
Abandoned by royal fortune, I have taken refuge in the dense forest; nevertheless, no contentment arises for me, whose kingdom has been seized.
And this Vaiśya has been expelled from his home by his kinsmen, wives, and others; nevertheless, his sense of "mine-ness" does not attain cessation.
Tell us, what is the cause here that even the minds of these two wise men have become agitated by delusion? Indeed, their ignorance is great.
The sage said: Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, is eternal and exists in the form of power; she indeed deludes everyone by completely drawing away their minds.
O Lord, since even all the gods beginning with Brahmā are deluded by Your māyā and do not know the supreme reality, what need is there to speak of human beings?
She creates the entire universe, she alone protects it, and she alone withdraws it at the time of dissolution; thus the Supreme Goddess is composed of the three qualities.
O best of kings, he upon whom she—who is gracious, the giver of boons, and able to assume any form at will—bestows her favor, alone transcends delusion; it cannot be otherwise.
The king said: Who is that goddess Mahāmāyā who deludes all beings? And how was that goddess born? O sage, please tell me out of compassion.
The sage said: When the world had become a single ocean, Keśava, the sovereign of yoga, having spread out Śeṣa and resorted to yogic sleep, fell asleep.
Then two asuras were born from the ear-wax of Viṣṇu, renowned on the surface of the earth by the names Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Terrible as the suns at the time of universal dissolution, with massive bodies and great jaws, their faces formidable with fangs, they seemed to devour the worlds.
Seeing the Lord in the lotus at his navel, those two, who were intent on killing him, cried out, "Who are you, sir? as they stood there.
Having beheld those two Daityas and Janārdana lying in the ocean of milk, the eldest of the gods praised the Supreme Goddess.
Brahmā said: Protect, protect me, O Mahāmāyā, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge! From these two Daityas of terrible form, O Mother of the Universe!
I bow to Mahāmāyā, Yoganidrā, Umā, Satī, Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Moharātri, and the one higher than the highest.
The eternal mother of the three gods, who bestows the fruits of the desires of her devotees, the protectress of all the deities, and the ocean of compassion.
By Your power, I am Brahmā, Mādhava is the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, and he creates, protects, and at the proper time, destroys the world.
You are Svāhā, you are Svadhā, you are Hrī; you are considered the pure intellect (Buddhi). O Mother, you alone are Contentment, Nourishment, Peace, Forbearance, Hunger, and Compassion.

O Mother, you alone are the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu; you alone are considered consciousness (cetanā). You are declared to be the supreme energy (śakti), and you alone are modesty (lajjā) and thirst (tṛṣṇā).
You are delusion, you are of the nature of memory, and you abide in the form of the Mother; you are the Lakṣmī in the homes of those men who set their minds upon meritorious syllables.
You are birth, you are considered to be existence, and you alone are indeed pervasion in its essential form; you alone, having pervaded everything by way of consciousness, are firmly established.
Therefore, O Ambikā, you must delude these two invincible Asuras; O Source of the World, awaken the unborn and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa.
The sage said: She was requested by Brahmā for the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; she is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the sustainer of the world, and the presiding deity of all sciences.
O King, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the Śakti known as Mahākālī, who deludes the three worlds, came into being.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "Do not fear, O Lotus-seated One! Today I shall destroy the thorn by slaying Madhu and Kaiṭabha in battle."
Having spoken thus, that Mahāmāyā emerged from the eyes, face, and other parts of Hari, and stood within the sight of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
And Hṛṣīkeśa, the god of gods, Janārdana, arose; he saw before him the two Daityas known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
A battle ensued between those two and Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor; at that time, there was a wrestling match for five thousand years.
Deluded by the power of Mahāmāyā, the two foremost Dānavas spoke to the beloved of Ramā: "Accept the boon you desire."
Nārāyaṇa said: "If you two are pleased with me, let this boon be granted to me: that both of you are to be slain by me; I ask for no other boon from you."
Ṛthi said: Having seen the earth as a single ocean, they spoke these words to Keśava: "Slay us both where this earth is not submerged by water."
Having said, "So be it," the Blessed One raised his brilliantly blazing discus and, placing it upon their own hips, severed their heads.
Thus, O King, the origin of Kālikā has been narrated to you; now, O high-minded one, listen to the birth of Mahālakṣmī.
The Goddess Umā, who is both with form and without form, and who is changeless and so forth, has appeared age after age for the sake of destroying the suffering of the gods.
The assumption of a body by her is said to be the manifestation of her entire will; she does so through her divine play (līlā) for the purpose of describing the virtues of her devotees.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Mahākālī during the Slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sage said: There was a Daitya named Rambhāsura, the crest-jewel of the demon lineage; from him was born a Dānava of great splendor named Mahiṣa.
Having utterly defeated all the gods in battle, that lord of the Danujas established his rule in the heavenly world, seated upon the throne of Mahendra.
Then the defeated gods went to Brahmā for refuge; Brahmā also, taking them with him, went to where Vṛṣākapi was.
Having gone there, all the gods bowed to Śaṅkara and Keśava and related their own account exactly as it had happened, in proper sequence.
O Blessed Ones, we have all been driven out from the heavenly realm by the evil-minded Mahisha, having been defeated upon the field of battle.
We wander in this world of mortals and find no peace anywhere; what misfortune have the gods, led by Indra, not been subjected to?
The sun and the moon, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Yama; Indra, Agni, Vāyu, and the Gandharvas, along with the Vidyādharas and the excellent Cāraṇas.
That sinful-souled son of Asura, who brings terror to the side of the Daityas, himself performs the duties of these and others.
Therefore, you ought to protect us gods who have sought refuge in you; O Lords, quickly devise a means for his destruction.
Having heard these words of the god, Dāmodara and Satīśvara became extremely enraged, their eyes rolling with fury.
Then, from the mouths of Viṣṇu and Śambhu, who were filled with extreme wrath, as well as from the bodies of the other gods, a great radiance issued forth.
Beholding a mass of exceeding brilliance blazing in the ten directions, all the gods became intent on meditation upon Durgā.
The extremely terrifying splendor arising from the bodies of all the gods coalesced and became a woman, Mahiṣamardinī herself.
Her face, exceedingly radiant, was produced from the splendor of Śambhu; her thighs were born from that of Yama, and her arms from that of Viṣṇu.
By the splendor of Candra, her pair of breasts was produced; by Indra, the waist; and by Varuṇa, the shanks and thighs came into being.
The hips were formed from the splendor of the Earth, the two feet from that of Brahmā, the toes of the feet from that of the Sun, and the fingers of the hands from that of Indra.
The nose and teeth were formed by the splendor of Kubera; the three eyes by that of Pāvaka; and the two eyebrows by that of Sandhyā.
By her breath she created the pair of ears for the other celestial beings; that supreme goddess Padmālayā is the source of all splendors.
Then, beholding her who had arisen from the mass of splendor of all the gods, all the deities attained supreme joy.
Seeing her weaponless, Brahmā and the other lords of the heavens resolved in their minds to provide Śivā with weapons.
Then Maheśāna presented the trident to Maheśānī; and the Blessed Kṛṣṇa [gave] the discus, and Pāśabhṛt [gave] the conch and the noose.
Agni bestowed upon him a spear, and Vāyu a bow; the Lord of Śacī gave him two quivers filled with arrows and a thunderbolt and a bell.
Yama gave him the staff of Time (kāladaṇḍa), Prajāpati gave him a rosary of beads, Brahmā presented him with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and the Sun-god gave him rays of hair.
Time (Kāla) gave her a sword and a brilliantly shining shield; the Ocean of Milk gave a beautiful necklace and likewise two imperishable garments.
The crest-jewel, the earrings, and likewise the bracelets, the crescent-shaped ornament, the armlets, and the charming anklets.
Viśvakarman gave her a beautiful neck-ornament, rings for all her fingers, and a charming axe.
The ocean gave many missiles, as well as impenetrable armor, and a garland of most beautiful lotuses from its lakes.
Himavat gave her a lion and various jewels, and Kubera presented her with a vessel filled with wine.
And Śeṣa, the leader of the serpents, gave her a serpent-necklace, beautifully fashioned with various designs and inlaid with many gems that possess diverse powers.
Honored by these and other gods with ornaments and weapons, the goddess let out a loud roar again and again with a boisterous laugh.
The vault of the sky was filled by her terrifying roar; there was a great echo, and the three worlds were shaken.
The four oceans trembled and the earth shook; then a cry of "Victory! was raised by the gods who had been oppressed by Mahiṣa.
Then all the gods praised Ambikā, the supreme Śakti, who is the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī, with voices faltering with devotion.
Beholding the world in turmoil, those adversaries of the gods rose up with their troops arrayed and weapons uplifted.
And Mahiṣa, filled with rage, rushed toward that sound; he then beheld the Goddess pervading the three worlds with her radiance.
In the meantime, millions of great heroes protected by Mahiṣāsura arrived there, bearing their weapons.
Cikṣura, Cāmarodagra, Karāla, Uddhata, Bāṣkala, Tāmrogrāsya, Ugravīrya, Biḍāla, and Andhaka.
Durdhara, Durmukha, Trinetra, and Mahāhanu—these and many other heroes were experts in the art of war.
Those who had mastered all weapons and missiles fought with the Goddess in battle; thus did the terrifying time pass as those two continued their combat.
The heaps of various weapons and missiles hurled by the hosts of enemies became fruitless in an instant through the power of Mahāmāyā.
Then that goddess struck her enemies, headed by Cikshura, along with their hosts, using her mace, arrows, spears, javelins, and axes.
Thus, when his own armies had been slain, Mahiṣāsura perceived those Gaṇas to have been produced from the breath of the Goddess.
He struck some with his hooves and others with his two horns; he repeatedly pierced them with his tail and his snout.
When the host of goddesses had bathed in this manner and rushed toward him, that lord of the asuras attacked the lion; thereupon, the Goddess became enraged.
Out of anger, that one of great prowess, striking the earth with his hooves, uprooted a mountain with his two horns, hurled it, and let out a roar.
O best of kings, heavy mountains hurled by him as he whirled about in every direction with great speed fell from the sky into the midst of the earth.
The clouds, split by his horns, fell apart in fragments; and the ocean, struck by his tail, surged and overflowed in all directions.
Beholding Mahishasura thus enraged, Ambika, who grants fearlessness to the gods, devised the means for his destruction.
Then the Sovereign Goddess, having raised her noose and cast it over him, bound Mahiṣa; he too abandoned his buffalo form.
Then the illusory being quickly became a lion; as Ambikā was about to split its head, it suddenly appeared with a sword in hand.
The goddess struck him with arrows as he was making his body small; then, assuming the form of an elephant, he tore the lion apart with his trunk.
Then the goddess cut off his hand with her own great sword, and that Rākṣasa assumed his own form once again.
At that very moment, she agitated the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile; thereupon, the Great Illusion, Caṇḍikā, who possesses the prowess of Manu, became enraged.
She drank the beverage again and again and laughed with her eyes rolling in excitement; and that asura too roared, arrogant with the pride of his own strength and heroism.
That asura, having uprooted mountains, hurled them upon her; and she, with the blows of her volleys of arrows, quickly reduced them to powder.
Her voice intoxicated by the essence of wine, her facial complexion flushed, and her senses agitated, the Supreme Goddess spoke in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Goddess said: "O fool! O you of ruined intellect! Why do you persist in this futile obstinacy? No demons whatsoever can stand before me in the three worlds."
The sage said: Having addressed him with a single word and leaped forward, the Goddess, who embodies all arts, stepped upon the Asura by the neck and pierced him with her fierce trident.
Then, as he was being trampled by her foot, he emerged only halfway from his own mouth, enveloped by the seed-vigor of the Goddess.
While that great sinner was still fighting with only half his body emerged, [the other] severed his head with a great sword, and it fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then, uttering cries of "Hā! Hā!", his followers, with their faces cast downward, fled from the battle in fear, crying out, "Save us! Save us!"
Then all the gods, headed by Indra, praised the Goddess; the Gandharvas sang aloud, and the dancers danced.
Thus, O King, has the origin of Mahālakṣmī been recounted to you; now listen with a steady mind to the birth of Sarasvatī as well.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Mahālakṣmī," within the Narrative of the Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa, in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sage said: There was a Daitya named Śumbhāsura and the powerful Niśumbha; by the prowess of these two brothers, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were pervaded.
Afflicted by those two, the gods went to the Himavat mountains and paid homage to the mother of all beings, the granter of desires.
The gods said: Victory to you, O Durgā, O Great Sovereign! Victory to you, who are dear to your own people! Salutations again and again to you, Śivā, the protector of the three worlds!
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Mother, the bestower of liberation; salutations to her who effects the origin, maintenance, and end of the entire cycle of worldly existence.
Salutations to you who are endowed with the form of Kālī; salutations to you in the form of Namaskārā; salutations to you, Śrīvidyā, whose very nature is Chinnamastā.
O Mistress of the World, salutations to you; salutations to you who have the form of Bhairava. Salutations be to Bagalāmukhī; repeated salutations to Dhūmāvatī.
Salutations to Tripurasundarī; salutations again and again to you, Mātaṅgī. Salutations to you, Ajitā; salutations again and again to Vijayā.
Salutations again and again to you, Jayā, Maṅgalā, and Vilāsinī; salutations to you in the form of Dogdhrī, and salutations be to you of terrible form.
Salutations again and again to you who possess the form of the unconquerable mind and the eternal form; salutations again and again to you, Rudrāṇī, the protector of those who have come for refuge.
Salutations to her who is known through the Vedanta; salutations to you, the Supreme Self; repeated salutations to the Mistress of infinite millions of cosmic eggs.
Thus praised by the gods, Gaurī—the gracious, boon-granting, and auspicious one—spoke to all the deities: "Who is it that is being praised here by you?"
Then, from the body of Gaurī, a single young maiden appeared; while they looked on, she spoke with great reverence to Śiva’s Śakti.
O Mother, a hymn of praise is being offered to me by all the inhabitants of heaven, who have been tormented by the two powerful Daityas, Niśumbha and Śumbha.
Because she emerged from the sheath of her body, she is celebrated by the name Kauśikī; she is the manifest destroyer of the demon Śumbha.
She is declared to be Ugratārikā and Mahogratārikā as well; because she has manifested from that source, she is indeed called Mātaṅgī on earth.
He spoke to all the gods: "Remain fearless; I shall accomplish your task, for I am independent and require no support."
Having spoken thus, the goddess then suddenly vanished; meanwhile, Cāṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the two servants of those [demons], beheld the goddess.
