Having seen her enchanting form, which brought delight to the eyes, they both fell to the ground, deprived of consciousness and utterly bewildered.
Having gone there, they related the entire account to the king from the beginning: "O King, a certain beautiful woman was seen by me previously."
Seated upon a beautiful peak of the Himalayas, she who rides a lion is attended on all sides by celestial maidens with their hands joined in reverence.
One woman massaged her feet, another adorned her hair; one massaged her hands, while another applied collyrium to her eyes.
One woman, taking a mirror in her hand, shows her face; another offers betel leaf together with cloves, cardamom, and other spices.
One female companion stood before her holding an alms-bowl in her hand, while another adorned all her limbs with ornaments, garments, and the like.

Her shanks and thighs were like plantain trunks; her nose was like that of a parrot; she was like a slender vine entwined with serpents; her feet resounded with tinkling anklets, and she was adorned with a beautiful girdle.
Her breasts were adorned with a pearl necklace emitting the fragrance of shimmering musk; her neck was graced by a tinkling necklace, and she was beautified by dangling garlands.
The Goddess wears a crescent moon, adorns her ears with jeweled earrings, possesses beautiful braided hair, has large eyes, and is graced by three eyes.
She was adorned with garlands of beads, her hands graced by rings and bracelets, her fingers set with golden signets, and her wrists radiant with glittering armlets.
Gaurī is clothed in auspicious garments, resplendent upon the lotus seat, adorned with a tilaka of Kashmiri saffron, and her head graced by the moon.
Possessing the brilliance of lightning, her breasts were uplifted by garments of great value; with eight lofty arms, she bore excellent weapons.
Neither among the asuras, nor the nāgas, nor the gandharvas, nor the dānavas, does there exist in the three worlds anyone as enchanting as that woman.
Therefore, her fitness for enjoyment shines forth only in you; for she is indeed a jewel among women, O Lord, and you are a jewel among men.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, that great asura dispatched a messenger named Sugrīva to her.
Go, messenger, to the Snowy Mountain; there dwells a certain beautiful woman. She must be brought here with great effort after you have delivered my words.
Having been thus informed by him, Sugrīva, the best of dānavas, went to the Himālaya mountains and spoke to the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World.
The messenger said: "O Goddess, there is the Daitya Śumbhāsura and his younger brother Niśumbha, who are renowned throughout the three worlds for their great strength and prowess."
O Queen of the Gods, listen now to that which Cāroha, having been dispatched by him, sang upon his arrival in your presence.
Having conquered Indra and the others in battle, I seized their jewels; I myself enjoy the portion of the gods given by the deities and others during sacrifices.
I consider you a jewel among women, standing above all other jewels; as such, do you favor me or my younger brother with the delights born of passion.
Having heard these words spoken by the messenger, which were uttered by Śumbha, that Mahāmāyā, the beloved of the Lord of Beings, replied.
The Goddess said: "O messenger, you speak the truth; nothing false is being said. However, listen to me regarding a single vow that was made by me previously."
"He who shakes off my pride and conquers me in combat—him alone I am determined to make my husband, and certainly no other."
Therefore, you speak my words to Śumbha and Niśumbha, so that he may act in this matter exactly as is appropriate.
Having heard these words of the queen, the Dānava named Sugrīva went there and reported the matter in detail to the king.
Then, having heard what was said by the messenger, Śumbha, whose command is terrible, spoke with anger to Dhūmrākṣa, the commander of the army and the best among the strong.
"O Dhūmrākṣa, a certain beautiful woman resides on the snowy mountain; go quickly and bring her here, so that she may indeed come to this place."
O best of asuras, you should not feel fear regarding her capture; however, if she desires to fight, you must engage in battle with great effort.
Thus informed, the Daitya named Dhūmralocana went to the Himālaya mountain and spoke to Umā, the daughter of the Lord of the World.
"Go to my husband; otherwise, O lady of shapely hips, I shall have you killed along with thousands of Asuras, well-nourished and accompanied by them."
The Goddess said: "O hero, if you are sent by the king of the Daityas and you slay him, what can I do for you? However, I consider it impossible to go there without a battle."
Thus addressed, the Dānava Dhūmralocana pursued her; but Maheśvarī burned him up with the mere utterance of the syllable "Hum."
From that time forth, that goddess is called Dhūmāvatī on earth; when propitiated, she is the destroyer of the hosts of enemies for her own devotees.
When Dhūmrākṣa was slain by the goddess’s mount, which became exceedingly enraged, all of his hosts were devoured; those who remained fled away.
Having thus heard that the Daitya had been slain by the Goddess, the powerful Śumbha was overcome with intense rage, his two lips biting each other.
He dispatched Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Raktabīja against the Asuras in succession; and those Daityas, thus commanded, went to where Ambikā was stationed.
Having seen the Blessed Lady mounted upon a lion, endowed with the [eight] siddhis such as maṇi and others, and illuminating the quarters with her radiance, the foremost of the Dānavas spoke.
"O Goddess, go swiftly to the abode of Śumbha and Niśumbha; otherwise, we shall slay you along with your attendants and your mount."
Choose him as your husband, O beautiful one, who is praised by the world-protectors and others; you shall attain a great bliss that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having considered what was thus said, the Supreme Goddess, the Mother, smiled and that Devi uttered words that were both true and full of aesthetic flavor.
The Goddess said: "Maheśāna Sadāśiva is the non-dual Supreme Brahman; even the Vedas do not know His true nature—what then can be said of Viṣṇu and the others?"
I am her subtle nature; how could I choose another as my husband? A lioness, even when afflicted by desire, never chooses a jackal.
An elephant never [desires] a donkey, nor does a tigress a hare; O Daityas, you who are bound by the serpent of death, speak falsely!
"Go to the netherworld and fight, if you have the power! Hearing these words, which incited their anger, they spoke thus to one another.
Knowing you to be weak in mind, we do not strike you; however, if there is a desire for battle in your heart, then stand firm against the five-faced one.
As they were thus disputing, their quarrel grew ever greater; sharp arrows rained down in battle from both sides.
Having thus waged battle with them as if in sport, the Supreme Goddess slew the great asura Raktabīja along with Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Even though they harbored thoughts of hatred, these inhabitants of the celestial realms ultimately did not attain that supreme world which ordinary people reach.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Raktabīja," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The king said: "O Blessed One, having heard that Dhūmrākṣa, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and likewise the asura Raktabīja have been slain by the Goddess, Śumbha, the oppressor of the gods,"
O Brahman, tell me now what he did thereafter; for I, desiring to hear it, wish to hear the sin-destroying life-story of the Source of the World.

The sage said: O King, having heard that these foremost Daityas had been slain, the great Asura of exalted prowess informed his own hosts—hosts who were difficult to approach and filled with joy at the mere mention of the word "battle."
Let those born of the Kālakas, as well as the Asuras, Mauryas, and Daurhṛdas, and others endowed with strength, assemble at my command with the hope of victory, and let them set out quickly.

Having commanded those sons of Diti, Niśumbha and Śumbha mounted their chariots and set forth; the armies of those two powerful ones followed from the earth like swarms of locusts risen for destruction.
They delighted in the mṛdaṅga, mardala, bherī, ḍiṇḍima, jharjhara, and ānaka drums; those who love battle rejoiced on the field of war, while those who love their lives fled from the combat.

Then those warriors, clad in battle-dress and possessing bodies free from sin, reached the field of combat; having taken up a multitude of weapons and missiles, they fiercely contended with one another out of a desire for victory.

Mounted on elephants, mounted on horses, and others likewise mounted on chariots, those asuras, unable to distinguish between their own people and the enemy, shouted with joy in the battle upon encountering the lord of the asuras.
The sound produced by the *śataghnī* weapon resounded repeatedly, and by it the gods were utterly overwhelmed; a great darkness arose in the sky, so that the orb of the sun could no longer be seen.

Foot soldiers marched forth by the tens of millions, filled with great pride and desiring victory; others, mounted on chariots, horses, and elephants—those asuras went out by the many millions with joy.
In the battle, the white mountain-like elephants let out trumpeting cries like those of rutting tuskers; and even the camels, resembling small hills, produced a lowing sound from their throats.

And horses born in the northern lands, with wide neck-ornaments and skilled in their gait, neighed as they bore their feet upon the heads of elephants; they pranced like birds along the path of the sky.
Having thus observed the enemy's strength, Ambikā then drew her strung bow and attacked; she rang her bell, which brings about the destruction of foes, while the lion too roared, shaking his mane.

Then Niśumbha, skilled in the expression of amorous gestures, beholding Śivā standing upon the snowy mountain adorned with beautiful ornaments and weapons, spoke these supreme words, overflowing with passion, just as one expert in the arts of love would speak.

O Great Goddess, it is indeed painful that a scattered petal of *mālatī* should fall upon the lovely body of one such as you; how then will you wage a terrible battle with that very same enchanting form?

Having spoken these words, the great asura became silent; then Caṇḍikā said to him: "O foolish asura, why do you speak in vain? Enter into combat, or else go elsewhere, not to the abode of the serpents."

Then, exceedingly enraged in battle, that great car-warrior unleashed a wondrous shower of volleys of arrows; it was as if the rain-clouds had arrived during the monsoon and were pouring down water upon the field of combat.

He fought with those arrogant with pride, using sharp arrows, spears, axes, and other weapons, along with slings, iron clubs, bows, *bhuśuṇḍika* missiles, darts, razor-headed shafts, and great swords.

In that battle, great elephants resembling dark mountains, with their frontal globes split open, wandered about; they were as white as moving cranes, their banners and standards shattered, bearing the emblems of Śumbha and Niśumbha.

The sons of Diti, their bodies mangled like fish, and the terrifying hosts of horses with severed necks, were deprived of life by Kālikā in battle; other asuras likewise were devoured by her, who was like a lion among deer.

Blood flowed through the channels between them like rivers, and there, amidst the slain, the hair of the warriors—resembling water-weeds—floated about, while their white upper garments appeared like foam.

The horseman attacked the rider of a horse, those mounted on elephants were assailed by elephant-riders, the chariot-warrior indeed struck the lord of chariots, and the foot-soldier fell upon those on foot; thus, a great battle took place with no opposing side left unengaged.

Then Niśumbha thought in his heart: "This terrible time has now arrived; through the reversal of fortune, even a pauper may become immensely wealthy, and an immensely wealthy man may become a pauper."

The dull-witted may become one of expanded intellect, and the great-minded may become dull; the cruel man may be highly honored by many, while the mighty suffer defeat in battle, and the weak prevail at the front of the fray.
Victory or defeat occurs for embodied beings effortlessly, according to the will of the Supreme Lord. Neither the Lotus-born Brahmā nor the Lord of Ramā was able to live by transgressing Time.
Having approached the front of the battle, noble heroes do not approve of flight in their hearts; however, how was victory lost in this battle, such that my entire army has been destroyed?

This is surely the Supreme Śivā, the primordial form and primal nature, who has come to accomplish the work of the gods and to subdue the host of the Daityas; she is never an ordinary woman of the world.

Even killing performed by women is proclaimed to bring dishonor by those desiring to savor the essence of war; nevertheless, how can we show our faces in the presence of the king of the asuras without having fought in battle?

Having reflected thus, the great chariot-warrior mounted his massive chariot urged on by the driver and proceeded swiftly to where the wife of Maheśvara dwelt—she whose burgeoning youth was coveted even by the celestial nymphs.

The Great Lord said to her: "What would be gained by killing these soldiers who live for their wages? If you have the desire to fight between us two, then let there be a battle with those who possess the true skill of combat."

Then Kauśikī said to Kālī: "Let this stubborn persistence of these two be observed; Time, the instigator of both the good and the evil, brings about a divided disposition of mind when calamity approaches."
Then Niśumbha struck Caṇḍikā with thousands of arrows, and likewise Kālikā; but Śivā, with her own volleys of shafts, shattered those arrows sent by the Asura into a thousand fragments.
Then, rising up, he struck the lion’s head with his sword and shield; but Ambikā split that [shield] as well with her great sword, just as a woodcutter cleaves a tree with an axe.

With his sword shattered, he struck an arrow into the chest of the Supreme Mother; she, however, cut that too. He then hurled a trident at her heart, but she pulverized that as well with a blow from her fist.

Taking up his mace once more, the great chariot-warrior Asura, intent on death, rushed toward Ambā; he shattered that mace with the edge of his trident, and then he tore the trident apart with another weapon.

Then Ambikā, having slain Niśumbha with her own sharp arrows—which resembled fearsome serpents, were accustomed to sucking the blood of the enemies of the gods, and were drenched in the gore of their foes—cast him to the earth.
When his younger brother Amānabala had been struck down, the lord of the asuras, filled with rage, mounted his chariot and, surrounded by eight arms, went to where the consort of Maheśvara was.
Then he blew his enemy-subduing conch and produced an unbearable sound from his bow; the lion too roared, shaking its mane, and the sky was made to resound by those three sounds.

Then the Mother of the World let out a loud laugh, by which all the enemies of the gods were utterly terrified; at that moment, when Ambikā said, "Be firm in battle," the gods cried out the word, "Victory! (Jaya).

The king of the Daityas released a great spear with blazing crests, but it was struck down by the fire-missile; Śivā shattered the arrows sent by Śumbha, and he too split the arrows discharged by Śiva into a thousand pieces.
Raising her trident, Caṇḍikā struck that great asura; he fell down unconscious, shaking the heavens, the earth, and the ocean, like a mountain whose wings have been torn off by a hawk.

Then, having endured the pain arising from the trident and having extended his ten thousand arms, the one of great strength struck the Great Goddess Kālikā, who was mounted upon a lion, with discuses that bring destruction even to the immortals.
Having effortlessly shattered their weapons, she raised her trident and struck down the asuras; having attained death from the world-purifying lotus-hand of Śiva, they reached the supreme state.
When that Niśumbha of great heroism and terrible prowess was slain, as well as Śumbha, all the Daityas entered the abode of Bali.
Other enemies of the gods were devoured by Kālī, Siṃha, and the others; likewise, still others fled in the ten directions, overwhelmed by fear.
The rivers flowed along their courses with clear waters; the winds blew with pleasant touch, and the sky attained a state of stainless purity.
The sacrifice was commenced once again by the gods and the brahminical sages; and all the inhabitants of heaven, headed by Mahendra, became happy.
O Lord, whoever should recite with faith this supreme, purifying, and meritorious account of Umā’s life, including the slaying of the king of the Daityas, [attains the highest goal].
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, which are difficult even for the gods to attain, he shall go to the abode of Umā in the hereafter through the grace of Mahāmāyā.
The sage said: "O King, thus was the Goddess born as the slayer of the demon Śumbha; she is Sarasvatī herself, manifested from a portion of Umā."

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Sarasvatī," in the account of the slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha within the Umā-Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, most excellent knower of all things, tell us of the incarnation of Umā, the sovereign of the world, from which Sarasvatī was born.
She who is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman, the Root Nature (Mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign Goddess; though formless, she possesses form, and is eternal, blissful, and the Reality.
Sūta said: O ascetics, listen with devotion to this supreme and great narrative, by the mere knowledge of which a person attains the highest goal.
Once, there was a mutual battle between the gods and the dānavas; by the power of Mahāmāyā, victory belonged to the immortals.
Then the arrogant immortals spread their own praises: "We are blessed! We are blessed! What can the asuras do to us?"
Those who, beholding our exceedingly unbearable power, became terrified and fled to the abode of the Nāgas, crying out, "Go away! Go away!"
"Oh, what strength! Oh, what splendor, which brings about the destruction of the Daitya lineage! Oh, what fortune for the gods!"—thus did they all describe it.
Then, at that very moment, a mass of splendor appeared in the form of a peak; having seen that which had never been seen before, the gods were struck with wonder.
"What is this? What is this? they cried out with choked throats, not understanding the supreme disposition of Śyāmā, which shatters all pride.
Then the leader of the gods commanded the gods: "Go, and examine thoroughly what this truly is."
Urged by Surendra, Vāyu approached that great light; addressing it as "O, who are you?", that light spoke to him.
Thus questioned then by Mahas with great reverence, Vayu, the life-breath of the world, spoke these words with a sense of self-importance: "I am Vayu."
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, is woven warp and woof within me alone; as the support of all, I set the whole universe in motion.
Then the one of great splendor said: "O Vāyu, if you are capable of moving it, move this blade of grass held here according to your own will."
Then Sadāgati exerted himself with every effort; when he could not move from his place, he became ashamed.
Then Vāyu, having become silent, went to Indra’s assembly hall and related that event, including his own defeat.
"We all falsely imagine ourselves to be the lords of all; yet we are unable to accomplish even the slightest of trivial tasks."
Then Indra dispatched all the gods; when they were unable to find out [who he was], Indra himself went there.
Then, seeing Maghavan approaching with his exceedingly unbearable splendor, [the demon] instantly vanished, and Vāsava was filled with wonder.
"I take refuge in him alone whose conduct is such as this"—thus the thousand-eyed Indra reflected again and again.
In the meantime, there, the consort of Śiva, whose body is composed of unfeigned compassion, arrived to bestow grace upon them and to remove their pride.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, when the sun was at its meridian, the goddess Umā, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, manifested herself.
Shining resplendent in the midst of Mahā, illuminating the quarters with her luster, she clearly awakens all the gods to the realization: "I am indeed Brahman."
Holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness with her four hands, she is served by the Vedas, beautiful, and proud of her fresh youth.
Clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, she resembles ten million gods of love and possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Mahāmāyā, who is the form of the inner ruler of all, the witness of all beings, and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, spoke.
Uma said: "Neither Brahmā, nor the enemy of the gods (Viṣṇu), nor the Lord who is the destroyer of cities (Śiva) can boast anything in my presence; what then to say of other deities?"
I alone am the supreme Brahman, the supreme light, whose form is the pair of Praṇavas; I am everything, and there is nothing whatsoever other than me.
Though formless, she possesses form; she is the essential nature of all reality. Her qualities are beyond conceptualization; she is eternal, embodying both cause and effect.
Sometimes I have the form of a beloved woman, sometimes the appearance of a man, and sometimes the form of both; I am the Sovereign, possessing every possible form.
I am Virañci, the creator; I am Acyuta, the protector of the world; I am Rudra, the agent of dissolution; and I am she who deludes the entire universe.
Indeed, all the Śaktis, beginning with Kālikā, Kamalā, and Vāṇī, as well as all these various arts (kalās), have arisen solely from my own portion.
All these sons of Diti have been conquered by you through my power; yet, failing to recognize me, you all vainly consider yourselves the lords of all.
Just as a magician makes a wooden puppet dance, even so do I, the Sovereign, cause all beings to dance.
Out of fear of me, the wind blows; the consumer of oblations (fire) burns everything; and the guardians of the world perform their respective duties without ceasing.
Sometimes I bring about the complete victory of the hosts of gods, and sometimes that of the sons of Diti; independent, I do so through my own divine play.
That which the Vedas describe as the imperishable supreme abode, beyond illusion and higher than the highest—that very form is indeed mine.
My form is considered to be twofold: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa). One is variegated by māyā, and the second is independent of it.
Knowing me thus, O gods, and casting aside each of your respective pride, worship me, the eternal Prakṛti, with affection.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, which were filled with compassion, the gods, their necks bowed in devotion, praised the Supreme Sovereign Lady.
Forgive us, O Mistress of the World; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess. May such pride never arise in us again; O Mother, show us mercy.
From that time forward, having abandoned their pride through divine grace, they became composed and worshipped Umā as before, according to the prescribed rites.
Thus, O brahmins, the manifestation of Umā has been recounted to you by me; by the mere hearing of which one attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Umā," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: "O one of great wisdom, we all desire to hear the daily deeds of Durgā; furthermore, describe to us that other wonderful truth."
O Sūta, best among those who know all things, our minds are not satiated as we hear various stories like nectar from your lotus-like mouth.
Sūta said: The son of Ruru, renowned by the name Durgama, was possessed of great strength; by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he obtained four Vedas.
Having also obtained invincible power upon the surface of the earth, he wrought many portents, and the gods trembled in heaven.
When all the Vedas were lost, ritual action indeed perished; and at that time, the Brahmins became ill-behaved and addicted to liquor.
There was no charity, no most intense austerity, no sacrifice, and no oblation; consequently, a hundred-year drought arose upon the earth.
A great cry of lamentation arose throughout the three worlds, and all people became deeply afflicted by hunger and thirst.
The rivers and the oceans, as well as the ponds, wells, and lakes, all became waterless; the trees and the creepers were completely withered.
Then, seeing the suffering of the people caused by pride—their minds being dejected—the gods went for refuge to the Great Goddess Yogamāyā.
The gods said: "Protect, protect all your own subjects, O Mahāmāyā! Withdraw your anger; otherwise, the worlds will surely perish."
The story of how the Daitya Śumbha was slain, as well as the mighty Niśumbha, Dhūmrākṣa, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and the exceedingly powerful Raktabīja.
O ocean of compassion, O friend of the distressed, quickly slay that Daitya Madhu, Kaiṭabha, and Mahiṣāsura as well.
Children indeed commit offenses at every step; who in this world, other than a mother alone, can endure them?
Whenever suffering arose for the gods as well as for Brahmā, you would swiftly descend at those very times and make the people happy.
Having heard their lamentations thus, she, who is composed of compassion, now manifested her form consisting of infinite eyes.
Holding a bow and arrow, as well as a lotus and various roots and fruits in her four hands, she possesses a serene lotus-like face.
Then, seeing the people tormented, her eyes filled with compassion, she wept for nine days and nine nights in great agitation.
He released thousands of streams of water from his eyes; by them, all the worlds and all medicinal herbs were thoroughly satiated.
The rivers became unfathomable in their waters, as did the oceans; and vegetables, roots, and fruits grew upon the surface of the earth.
He offered fruits held in his hand to the *sumanas* flowers, pleasant grasses to the cows, and likewise other things to others, each according to their merit.
All the twice-born men and humans became forever content; then that goddess said, "What else shall I do for you?"
Then the gods, having assembled, said: "O Lady, the people have been satisfied by you; out of compassion, grant us the Vedas that were recovered with great difficulty."
Having said, "So be it," he spoke: "Go, go to your own abodes; I shall bestow the Vedas upon you in no long time."
Then the gods, filled with joy, returned to their respective abodes after bowing deeply to the Source of the Universe, whose eyes were like blossoming blue lotuses.
Then a great clamor arose in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space; hearing that, Raurava immediately besieged the city on all sides.
Then, having fashioned a wheel of radiant energy all around for the protection of the deities, Śivā herself went outside of it.
Then a battle took place between both the goddess and the demon; in that conflict, they rained down sharpened arrows capable of piercing armor.
In the meantime, from her body emerged Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Śrīvidyā, and Bhuvaneśvarī, each possessing a beautiful form.
Bhairavī, Bagalā, Dhūmrā, Śrīmat Tripurasundarī, and Mātaṅgī—these ten great vidyās emerged, each accompanied by her weapon.
From that, innumerable mothers were born, possessing divine forms; all of them bore crescent moons and all possessed a radiance equal to lightning.
Then a terrifying battle commenced with the hosts of Mothers; the army of Raurava was destroyed by them, along with a hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
Then she struck the Daitya Durgama with the point of her trident; he fell upon the surface of the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Having thus slain the Daitya named Durgamāsura, the Sovereign Goddess took the four Vedas and restored them to the gods.
The gods said: "O Ambikā, you have assumed for our sake a form consisting of infinite eyes; therefore, the sages shall celebrate you as Śatākṣī (the Hundred-eyed One)."
"Since people shall be nourished by the vegetables produced from your own body, your name shall become renowned as Śākaṃbharī."
O Śivā, because the great Daitya named Durgama has been slain, human beings shall henceforth address the Blessed Goddess as Durgā and Bhadrā.
O Yoganidrā, salutations to you; salutations be to you, O one of great power! Salutations to you, the bestower of knowledge; salutations again and again to you, the Mother of the Universe.
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Goddess who is revealed by such statements as "That thou art," the Mistress of infinite millions of universes.
O Mother, we are ignorant; we are unable to praise you, whose power is difficult for speech, mind, and body to attain, and who has the sun, moon, and fire as your eyes.
Seeing immortals such as myself, who would show such compassion, except for the Mother Śatākṣī, the Queen of the Gods?
The three worlds must not be overwhelmed by constant afflictions; thus, you must exert effort for the destruction of our enemies.
The Goddess said: Just as cows, upon seeing their calves, run forward in haste and agitation, even so do I run toward you, overcome with distress.
For me, who beholds you as if you were children, even while offering my very life, a single moment stretches out like an eon.
No anxiety whatsoever should be felt by you who are possessed of devotion, while I remain present, destroying your own calamities.
Just as the Daityas were slain in the past, so shall I slay the Asuras; no doubt should be entertained in this matter, for I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
When Śumbha and Niśumbha become two other Daityas, then I, consisting of glory, shall be born from Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda.
"Assuming a form born of a womb, I shall be born in the cowherd settlement; there I shall slay the two asuras, and therefore they shall call me 'Nandajā' (Born of Nanda)."
"Assuming the form of a bee, I shall slay Aruṇa; therefore, men in the world shall proclaim me as 'Bhrāmarī'."
"When I assume my terrible form again and devour the Rākṣasas, my name shall become renowned as the goddess Bhīmā."
Whenever and wherever affliction arising from asuras shall occur upon the earth, at that very time I will descend and bring about peace, without a doubt.
The goddess who is remembered as Śatākṣī is considered to be the very same as Śākaṃbharī; she alone is celebrated as Durgā—for there is but one manifestation among all three.
There is no deity on earth as compassionate as Śatākṣī; seeing her, the tormented subjects wept, for she is the Great Goddess herself appearing in a new form.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnations of Śatākṣī and Others," in the Umā Saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O fortunate disciple of Vyāsa, O Sūta, best among the knowers of the Purāṇas! We wish to hear another narrative concerning the Lord.
The unsurpassed Kriyāyoga of Umā, the Mother of the World, was proclaimed by Sanatkumāra to the high-souled Vyāsa.
Sūta said: Blessed are you, O great-souled ones, firm in your vows of devotion to the Goddess; listen with reverence to the supreme, secret mystery of Parāśakti.
Vyāsa said: O Sanatkumāra, omniscient son of Brahmā, of great intellect, I wish to hear about the most wonderful Kriyāyoga of Umā.
What are its characteristics, for what purpose does it yield fruit, and what is pleasing to the Supreme Mother? Tell me all of that in its entirety.
Sanatkumāra said: O Dvaipāyana, O one of great intelligence, listen as I describe everything regarding that secret which you ask about.
The yoga of knowledge, the yoga of action, and likewise the yoga of devotion—these three paths have been proclaimed as bestowing liberation upon the venerable Mother.
The yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga), however, is the union of the mind with the Self alone; whereas that which is the union with external objects is called the yoga of action (kriyāyoga).

The path of devotion (bhaktiyoga) is considered by the Goddess to be the contemplation of the identity of oneself with the Self; it is said to be the yoga of action (kriyāyoga) among all three types of yoga.
Devotion is born from action; from devotion, knowledge arises; from knowledge, liberation is born—this is the certainty established in the scriptures.
O best of sages, yoga is the primary cause of liberation; however, the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga) is the supreme means for accomplishing the object of meditation.

One should know that Māyā is Prakṛti and that the eternal Brahman is the master of Māyā; by realizing that his own body is non-different from that [Brahman], one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.

O Kāleya, listen now to the fruit of the merit of one who builds a temple for the Goddess, whether of stone, wood, or even of clay; it is equal to the great fruit obtained by one who conquers through disciplined practice day after day.

The virtuous soul who causes a temple to be built for the Goddess obtains that fruit; by constructing the abode of the Illustrious Mother, he delivers a thousand future generations and a thousand past generations of his lineage.
Sin committed over ten million lifetimes, whether it be small or great, perishes at the very moment the foundation for the temple of the Glorious Mother is laid.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers and the Śoṇa among all streams; just as the Earth is in forbearance and the Ocean in profundity.
Just as the sun excels among all the planets, so too does the venerable Parāmbā excel among all the gods.
She is the foremost among all goddesses; he who causes a house to be built for her attains stability in birth after birth.
At Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and likewise at Puṣkara; on the banks of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and at Naimiṣa and Amarakaṇṭaka.
On the highly meritorious Śrīparvata, at Gokarṇa on the Mountain of Knowledge, as well as in Mathurā, Ayodhyā, and likewise in Dvāravatī;
By having a residence for his mother constructed in such meritorious places or at any location whatsoever, one becomes liberated from bondage.
For as many years as the arrangement of bricks remains intact, for that many thousands of years one is honored in Maṇidvīpa.
He who causes images to be made, endowed with all the auspicious marks, will certainly go fearlessly to the supreme world of Umā.
Having installed the image of the Goddess during an auspicious season, under favorable planets and stars, a mortal shall have fulfilled his purpose through the grace of Yogamāyā.
By installing a beautiful image of the Goddess, one causes all those men who have been born in the family throughout the past and up until the end of the eon to cross over [to liberation].
O best of sages, whatever merit may arise from establishing the three worlds, ten million times that merit shall arise from the installation of the Śrī Devī.
Having established the Goddess in the center, he who establishes the deities of the fivefold abode in the four directions—his merit cannot be calculated.
The fruit that is obtained from reciting the names of Viṣṇu ten million times during an eclipse of the moon or sun is surpassed by a hundred-fold increase [through this practice].
Therefore, from the mere chanting of Śiva’s name alone, [the merit] is ten million times greater; and from the chanting of the name of the Śrī-devī, it is ten million times greater than that.
Merit is fully attained from the construction of a temple for the Goddess; by whomsoever that Goddess, the Mother of the World, who consists of the three Vedas, is installed.
Nothing whatsoever is difficult for him to obtain by the power of Śrīmātā’s compassion; his sons, grandsons, and others increase, and all his impurities perish.
Those who desire in their minds to perform the supreme installation of the image of Umā go to her supreme world, which is difficult even for sages to attain.
But when one sees [a work] being performed and reflects upon it with the mind, thinking: "I shall have this done once my wealth has become sufficient."
By the power of Mahāmāyā, his family immediately goes to heaven without a doubt; for what is difficult to attain in the three worlds?
Those who have taken refuge solely in the venerable Parāmbā, the source of the universe, should not be considered mere humans; they are indeed the very hosts of goddesses themselves.
Those who, whether walking, sleeping, or standing, utter the two-syllable name "Umā" day and night, they are the attendants of Śiva.
Those who worship the supreme goddess Śivā with regular and occasional rites, using flowers, incense, and likewise lamps, shall go to the abode of Umā.
Those who daily smear the pavilion of the Goddess with cow dung or clay, and sweep it clean, shall go to the abode of Umā.
To those people of noble lineage who cause a beautiful and unsurpassed temple to be built for the Goddess, the Mother indeed bestows her blessings.
"May my devotees live for a hundred years, free from the affliction of calamities"—thus does the venerable Mother speak day and night.
By him who had a beautiful image of the Great Goddess Umā fashioned, ten thousand men born of his lineage are honored on Maṇidvīpa.
Having established the form of Mahāmāyā and having worshipped it perfectly, the practitioner obtains whatever desire he may pray for.
Who could possibly calculate the fruit of that person who bathes the supreme installed image of the Illustrious Mother with ghee mixed with honey?
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with water mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, spikenard, nut-grass, and other such ingredients, along with the milk of cows of a single color.
One should offer the supreme oblation with incense consisting of eighteen ingredients, and one should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana) for the Goddess with wicks made of ghee and camphor.
On the eighth or ninth day of the dark fortnight, or on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī), one should especially worship the Mother of the Worlds with perfumes and flowers.
Reciting the Jananī-sūkta, or else reciting the Śrī-sūkta, or even the Devī-sūkta, or likewise the Mūka-mantra.
Excluding *viṣṇukrāntā* and *tulasī*, all flowers are to be known as pleasing to the Goddess, especially the lotus.
He who offers a golden flower, or even one made of silver, to the Goddess goes to the supreme abode accompanied by ten million Siddhas.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should always perform the expiation for faults with servants, saying: "Be gracious, O Supreme Goddess, O Bestower of Joy to the World!"
Praising with these words, the mantra-practitioner, devoted to the Goddess, should meditate upon her as mounted on a lion, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Sovereign Goddess, who bestows the fruits of the devotee's desires, one should offer various kinds of ripe fruits as a food offering (naivedya).
That man who consumes the food offering (naivedya) of Śambhu, the Supreme Soul and Power, shall be cleansed of all impurity and become stainless.
He who observes the Bhavānī-vow on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra shall be liberated from the bonds of existence and attain the supreme state.
On this very third lunar day, the wise man should perform the festival of the swing; he should worship Umā, the mother of the worlds, together with Śaṅkara.
With flowers, saffron, garments, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood; with incense, lamps, food offerings, garlands, perfumes, and other such things.
One should then cause the goddess Mahāmāyā, the Great Sovereign, the auspicious Gaurī joined with Śiva, who brings about all welfare, to sway.
To him who performs the vow of swinging on this [day] every year according to the prescribed rule, Śivā grants everything he desires.
On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, known as Akṣayā, he who performs the vow of the Mother of the Universe with vigilance [attains great merit].
One should worship Gaurī, accompanied by Śaṅkara, with flowers such as mallikā, mālatī, campā, japā, bandhūka, and lotuses.
Having shaken off the sins committed over ten million births through mind, speech, and body, he enjoys here in this world the four inexhaustible goals.
Whoever, having observed the vow on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, worships Maheśvarī with supreme devotion, for him there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the chariot festival, which is most dear to the Goddess, according to one's means.
One should know the earth to be the chariot, and the moon and sun to be its two wheels; one should know the Vedas to be the horses, and the lotus-born Brahmā to be the charioteer.
Having thus fashioned a chariot strewn with various clusters of jewels and adorned with garlands of flowers, one should install Śivā upon it.
A wise man should contemplate that the Supreme Mother is stationed in the middle of the chariot in order to protect the world and to behold it.
When the chariot has moved forward slowly, one should utter the cry of victory: "Protect us, O Goddess, who have sought refuge in you, O you who are compassionate toward the distressed!"
Thus one should gratify [the deity] with these words and with the sounds of various musical instruments; having led the chariot to the boundary, one should worship [the deity] there in the chariot.
Then, having praised her with various hymns, he should bring her to his own home; having performed hundreds of prostrations, he should pray to the Mother of the World.
Thus, the wise person who performs this festival of worship, vows, and chariot processions shall enjoy all pleasures in this world and, at the end, attain the state of the Goddess.
He who performs the vow and the worship of the Mother according to the prescribed rites on the third day of the bright fortnight in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada—
He rejoices here perpetually with sons, grandsons, wealth, and other blessings; at the end, he shall go to the world of Umā, which stands above all worlds.
One should observe the Navarātra vow during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina; by performing it, all desires are indeed accomplished, without a doubt.
Neither the four-faced one, nor the five-faced one, nor the six-faced one, nor anyone else is capable of describing the power of this Navarātra vow.
O best of sages, having performed the Navarātra vow, King Suratha, whose son had been deprived of his chariot, regained his own kingdom which had been seized.
The wise King Sudarśana, son of Dhruvasandhi and lord of Ayodhyā, regained his seized kingdom through his power.
Having performed this king of vows and having propitiated Maheśvarī, he was liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra; through meditative absorption, he became a partaker of liberation.
And on the third, fifth, seventh, eighth lunar day, or on the ninth or fourteenth, the man who worships the Goddess—
Having performed the vow according to the prescribed rules during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, Śivā constantly fulfills all that one desires in the mind.
Whoever shall observe the vow on the third day of the bright fortnight of the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Tapas, and likewise Tapasya;
One should worship the auspicious goddess with red flowers such as karavīra and fragrant incenses; he shall obtain all that is auspicious.
This great vow should always be performed by women for the sake of good fortune; it should also be undertaken by men for the purpose of attaining knowledge, wealth, and sons.
Likewise, those seeking liberation should perform other vows such as Umāmaheśvara and others that are dear to the Goddess, solely through their own devotion.
This compendium is of great merit, increasing devotion to Śiva; endowed with various narratives, it is auspicious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever hears this with devotion, or causes it to be heard with a concentrated mind, or reads it, or causes it to be read, attains the supreme goal.
He in whose house this [mantra] remains written in graceful letters and is worshipped according to the prescribed rites shall obtain all his desires.
There shall be no fear anywhere from malevolent beings such as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas; one will certainly obtain the prosperity of sons, grandsons, and so forth—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, this highly meritorious and beautiful Umā-saṃhitā should always be heard and recited by those who desire devotion to Śiva.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Kriyā-yoga," in the Umā-saṃhitā, the fifth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Salutation to Śiva, who is with Ambā, with his attendants, and with his son; the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

The sages said: We have heard the delightful Śrīmadbhāgavata-saṃhitā, which is endowed with various narratives; now please speak the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, which increases the realization of the true nature of Śiva.
Vyāsa said: Listen with affection, my children, to the supreme and divine Saṃhitā known as Kailāsa, which is devoted to the principles of Śiva; out of love for you, I shall relate it to you.
Formerly, on a peak of the Himavat, sages of great luster, having made a mutual agreement, were performing austerities with the desire to go to Vārāṇasī.
Having departed from that mountain and reached Kāśī with composed minds, they thought, "We must certainly bathe," and then they beheld Maṇikarṇikā.
Having bathed there and properly gratified the gods and others, those lords of sages beheld the Ganges, and having bathed again, they saw Viśveśa, the lord of the thirty deities.
Then, having bowed down and worshipped with supreme devotion, those who had mastered the Vedas praised him with hymns such as the Śatarudriya.
They all considered themselves to have achieved their purpose, being fully satisfied through the grace of Śiva and always devoted to the worship of Śiva.

At that moment, seeing the charioteer arrive after having gone out with the desire to behold the Pañcakrośa, they greeted him with joy and paid him homage. He too, having prostrated before Viśveśvara himself—the God of gods and Lord of Umā—then entered the Muktimaṇḍapa together with them.
Then all the sages honored the high-souled Sūta, the best among those who know the Purāṇas, as he sat there with offerings such as the arghya water.
Then the charioteer, with a serene mind, looked upon the sages of excellent vows and inquired after their welfare; they, in turn, spoke of their own well-being.
Perceiving that his heart was indeed filled with joy, those lords of sages spoke these introductory words for the sake of attaining an understanding of the meaning of the Praṇava.
The sages said: O disciple of Vyāsa, illustrious Sūta, best among the knowers of the Purāṇas! You are blessed, for you are a devotee of Śiva and an ocean of all knowledge.
The Blessed Vyāsa, the preceptor of the entire world, having consecrated you yourself, appointed you to the position of the teacher of the Purāṇas.
Therefore, the ancient wisdom resides within your heart; for all the Purāṇas indeed proclaim the meaning of the Vedas.
The Vedas are born from the Praṇava, and the meaning of the Praṇava is Maheśvara; therefore, the abode of Maheśvara is established within you as your own domain.
Having drunk the nectar of the meaning of the Praṇava, so enchanting that it flows from the makaranda of your lotus-face, we shall become free from all feverish distress.
O Great-minded One, you alone are our preceptor in particular; none other. Out of supreme compassion, please speak of the ultimate nature of Maheśvara.
Having heard these words of theirs, the wise charioteer, the beloved disciple of Vyāsa, [beheld] Gaṇeśa, the six-faced Kārttikeya, Maheśāna himself, and Maheśvarī.
Having prostrated before the god who is the son of Śilāda, Nandīśa, the husband of Suyaśas, as well as Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa, he spoke this.
Sūta said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate sages whose impurities have been destroyed! A most firm resolve has arisen [in you], which is difficult even for evildoers to attain."
O best of sages, that which was taught by my preceptor, the son of Parāśara, to the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, that I shall now declare.
By the mere hearing of which, devotion to Śiva arises in men; therefore, being attentive today, listen with supreme joy.
Formerly, during the Svārociṣa Manvantara, sages of firm vows were performing austerities in the Naimiṣa forest, which is frequented by all the Siddhas.
Performing a long-duration sacrifice, they propitiated Rudra, the leader of the ritual, desiring to know his supreme nature and sovereign power.
They all dwelt there, longing for a vision of Vyāsa, constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, and wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Having observed their state of being, the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa, the soul of all, manifested as the fruit of Parāśara’s ascetic penance.
Seeing him, all the sages, their faces and eyes beaming with joy, honored him with every form of respectful service, beginning with rising from their seats.
Having honored him, they presented him with an auspicious golden seat. Then, as he was comfortably seated upon that golden seat, the great sage Pārāśarya spoke in a profound voice.
Vyāsa said: "Is all well with you? Tell me this at this great sacrifice: has the Lord of the Sacrifice been properly honored by you?"
For what purpose have you here, at this sacrifice, worshipped with a spirit of devotion the Supreme Lord, accompanied by Ambā, the liberator from saṃsāra?
Indeed, your activity appears to me as a desire for instruction from the very beginning, concerning the supreme state of Maheśvara and Śiva, who is the cause of liberation.
Thus addressed by Vyāsa, the lord of sages and possessor of immeasurable splendor, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest were filled with supreme energy.
Having prostrated before that high-souled great sage, the son of Parāśara, whose mind was gladdened by his devotion to Śiva, they spoke to him.
The sages said: O Blessed One, tiger among sages, born directly from a portion of Nārāyaṇa; O ocean of mercy, O one of great wisdom, O Lord, sovereign of all branches of knowledge!
For you are yourself the treasury of the graces of this Great God, the Creator, the sustainer of the entire world, who is accompanied by Ambā and his retinue.
With our minds made to drink the honey of the nectar from your lotus feet, we have attained our life's purpose this very day by the sight of your lotus feet.
Indeed, the sight of your lotus-like feet is difficult for sinners to obtain; yet we have obtained it, and therefore we are virtuous ones.
O highly fortunate one, in this region known as the Naimiṣa forest, all [the sages] were engaged in long sacrificial sessions and were illuminators of the meaning of the Praṇava.
Having resolved that "the Supreme Lord must be heard," they deliberated among themselves regarding the supreme nature of the Great Lord.
Since we have remained ignorant of this, O Lord, you ought to sever all those doubts of ours who are of limited intellect.
Indeed, there is no one other than you in the three worlds who can sever this doubt; therefore, [you alone can save] me as I am sinking into the ocean of profound and boundless delusion.
O ocean of compassion, ferry us across by means of the boat of the knowledge of Śiva; we are full of faith, desiring to know the true meaning of the reality of devotion to Śiva.

Thus entreated by those sages who had mastered the Vedas, the great sage Śukatāta—the foremost among those who know the meaning of all the Vedas—[expounded] the Praṇava, the Supreme Lord, which is the very essence of the entirety of Vedānta.
Having meditated upon the Lord accompanied by Ambā, the liberator from the cycle of existence, in the center of the lotus of his heart, the great sage, with a joyful mind, spoke.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Vyāsa, Śaunaka, and Others," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Well asked is this by you, O most fortunate Brahmins! For the knowledge of Śiva, which illuminates the meaning of the Praṇava, is indeed difficult to attain.
Only for those with whom the Blessed One, who personally bears the trident as his supreme weapon, is pleased, does the knowledge of Śiva arise that illuminates the meaning of the Praṇava.
"There is no doubt that it does not arise for others"—such is the Vedic revelation; "for those devoid of devotion to Śiva"—this is the certain conclusion regarding the true meaning of reality.
"By you, through this long sacrificial session, the Blessed Lord Ambikāpati has been worshipped; this I have seen today and am certain of."
Therefore, O believers, I shall relate to you an ancient history in the form of a wonderful dialogue between Umā and Maheśa.
In ancient times, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and mother of the entire universe, cast off her body at her father’s sacrifice on account of the censure of Śiva.
Then, by the power of that goddess, she became the daughter of Mount Himavat; indeed, at the instruction of Nārada, she performed austerities for the sake of Śiva.
When the Lord of Gods had been wedded according to the rites of a svayaṃvara on that best of mountains, Pārvatī attained great happiness.
Likewise, at one time, while seated comfortably with her husband on a great mountain, Gaurī, the Great Goddess, addressed the God.
The Great Goddess said: O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, performer of the fivefold acts; O Omniscient One, easily accessible through devotion, whose form is the supreme nectar!

"O Maheśāna, having cast off my body as Dākṣāyaṇī due to the occasion of your censure, I have today become the daughter of the mountain Himavat. O Supreme Lord, by your grace and through the ritual of mantra-initiation, O Maheśvara, make me eternally established in the reality of the pure Self."
Thus entreated by the goddess, the god who is adorned with the cool-rayed moon then replied to the goddess with a joyful heart.
Mahādeva said: "O Goddess of the gods, you are blessed since such an intellect has arisen in you; having gone to the peak of Kailāsa, I shall make you just like that."
Then, having gone from the Himavat to Kailāsa, the lord of mountains, he recited the mantras beginning with the Praṇava in their proper order according to the ritual of initiation.
Having spoken those mantras and established the Goddess within his pure self, Mahādeva went to the celestial garden together with the Goddess.
Then, with those blossoming flowers produced from the *kalpa* trees, which had been gathered by the dear female companions of the goddess, headed by Sumālinī;
Having adorned the Great Goddess and placed her upon his own lap, Śaṅkara stood with a joyful countenance, gazing upon her face.
Then, for the benefit of all the worlds, there arose pleasant conversations between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, which were in direct accord with the meaning of the Vedas.
Then, O ascetics, the Mother of the entire world, having taken refuge on her husband’s lap and gazing upon his face, spoke these words.
The Śrī Devī said: O Lord, you have taught me the mantras together with the Praṇava; among them, I first desire to hear the definitive meaning of the Praṇava.
How was the Praṇava produced? How is it called "Praṇava"? How many mātrās are declared for it? And how is it called the beginning of the Vedas?

How many deities are proclaimed, and how is the contemplation of the Vedas and so forth performed? How many kinds of ritual actions are taught, and what is the nature of the pervaded and the pervader?
How do the five Brahmans reside in this mantra in their proper sequence? How many Kalās are declared to be there, and how does the nature of the phenomenal world (prapañca) arise?

O Śiva, how do the relationships between the signified and the signifier, as well as their locations, function? Who is to be known as the qualified authority here, and what is declared to be the subject matter?
What connection is to be understood here, and what is said to be its purpose? What is the nature of the worshipper, and what is the locus of the worship?
O Lord, what is the nature of the object to be worshipped, or what is the fruit for the worshipper? What is the rule for its performance, and what is the place of worship?
O Hara, what is the maṇḍala for worship, or what are the ṛṣis and other elements? What is the procedure for the various types of nyāsa, or what is the sequence of the ritual for worship?
O Great Lord, explain all of this in detail; I wish to hear it according to its true nature, if you have compassion for me.
Thus questioned by the Goddess, the Blessed One, adorned with the moon, praised Maheśānī and began to speak.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Questions Put by the Goddess," in the *Kailāsa-saṃhitā*, the sixth section of the glorious *Śiva-mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between the Goddess and the God.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, for I shall declare that which you ask of me; by the mere hearing of it, the living being shall become Śiva himself.
The thorough knowledge of the meaning of the Praṇava alone is the wisdom that constitutes my own self; it is the seed of all sciences and the mantra named Praṇava.
It should be known as exceedingly subtle and of great significance, like the seed of a banyan tree; it is the beginning of the Vedas, the essence of the Vedas, and especially my own form.
The God who transcends the three qualities, the omniscient, the all-creating Lord—Śiva, who is omnipresent, abides within me as the single-syllable mantra "Om."

Whatever entity exists, all of it—whether taken as a whole or in its individual parts—is declared to be the meaning of the Praṇava, through its connection with the predominance of its constituent qualities.
Therefore, this single imperishable Brahman is the accomplisher of all goals; by means of it, Śiva first creates the entire universe with the syllable "Om."
Śiva is indeed this Praṇava, and the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva; for there is no absolute difference between the expressed and the expresser.
Therefore, the wise Brahman-sages know me as the God of the single syllable, considering the identity of the signified and the signifier.
Therefore, the seeker of liberation, being free from modification, should know that very Praṇava as the cause of all—that which is me, the attributeless Supreme Lord.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall indeed bestow this very crest-jewel of all mantras in Kāśī for the sake of the liberation of living beings.
In this regard, O Mother, I shall first explain the extraction of the *praṇava*, by the mere knowledge of which supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall be attained.
One should first extract Nivṛtti, and after that, Indhana; then one should extract Kāla, Daṇḍa, and Īśvara.
Thus has this Praṇava, consisting of five phonemes and composed of three measures (mātrās), the bindu, and the nāda, been extracted; it always bestows liberation upon those who recite it.
Indeed, for all living beings from Brahmā down to the stationary entities, this very *praṇava* is their life-force; therefore it is called *praṇava*.
The first letter is the syllable *a*, then the syllable *u* follows; the syllable *m* is in the middle, and its end is the *nāda*, which is the *om*.

O best of sages, the first syllable has a color like water; likewise, there is [the letter *da*] in the south and the north, while the letter *ma*, which is pure, is in the center within the syllable *oṃ*.
The letter 'A', the letter 'U', and the letter 'M'—these three are declared to be the three measures (mātrās) in succession; beyond that is the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
O Maheśānī, the half-mātrā is the very nature of the Bindu and Nāda; it cannot truly be described, for it is to be known only by those possessed of wisdom.
O beloved, the Vedas truly declare that the scriptural passages beginning with "The Lord of all sciences" originate from me alone.
Therefore, I am indeed the beginning of the Vedas; the *praṇava* is my designator (*vācaka*). Because it is my designator, this [praṇava] is also called "the beginning of the Vedas."
The letter *a* is the great seed, Rajas, and the four-faced Creator; the letter *u* is Prakṛti, the womb, Sattva, and the protector Hari.
The letter *ma* is the Puruṣa, the seed-sower, Hara, the destroyer of darkness; the nasal drop (*bindu*) is the god Maheśvara, declared to be the state of disappearance.
Nāda is declared to be Āśiva, the performer of grace toward all; having meditated upon Śiva, who is higher than the highest, at the summit of Nāda.
He is omniscient, the creator of all, the Lord of all, stainless and immutable; he is indefinable, the Supreme Brahman, manifest, and beyond both being and non-being.
One should contemplate that among the letters beginning with 'a', each subsequent one is all-pervasive, while each preceding letter is pervaded; thus one should meditate in this manner everywhere.
The five Brahmans, beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna, reside respectively within the five vowels starting with 'a'; they are my own forms in due order.
Eight digits (kalās) born of Sadyojāta are declared to reside in the letter 'A' within Śiva; thirteen belonging to Vāmadeva are proclaimed to reside in the letter 'U'.
The eight digits of the non-terrible form are established in the letter *ma*; four digits, which fall within the domain of the Puruṣa, are produced in the *bindu*.
Five kalās originating from Īśāna are declared to reside in the Nāda; through the contemplation of their sixfold unity, the nature of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is described.
Mantra, yantra, deity, the phenomenal world, the guru, and the disciple—these are the six categories; hear their meaning, O beloved.
The mantra previously mentioned is the synthesis of the five colors; that very same [mantra] has attained the state of a yantra, and I shall now describe the sequence of its maṇḍala.
The yantra is the form of the deity, and the deity is the universal form; the guru is said to be the universal form, and therefore the disciple possesses the body of the guru.
Based on the Vedic revelation that "All this is Om" and "The All is Brahman," this very meaning is declared to be the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
The foundation is Maṇipūra, and after that the heart; then Viśuddhi and Ājñā, followed by Śakti and Śānti in sequence.
O Goddess of the Gods, these are the stages beyond Śānti, the supreme beyond the supreme; he for whom firm dispassion arises shall become an authority over them.

"O Goddess, may I become the object [of Your grace] through the contemplation of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (jīvabrahmaikya). O Sovereign of the Gods, hear the relationship; the object has been correctly described."
In this context, the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman), as well as that of the Praṇava, is declared to be one of denoted and denoter (vācyavācakabhāva).
Devoted to vows and other observances, peaceful, an ascetic with senses conquered, endowed with purity and right conduct, such a Brahmin is firmly established in the Vedas.
Being detached from sense objects pertaining to both this world and the next, even a Brāhmaṇa here who observes the vow of Śiva among those born in the world of the gods [attains liberation].
Having approached the teacher—a renunciant, the best among the wise, who knew the reality of the meaning of all scriptures and had reached the further shore of the knowledge of Vedānta—

A wise disciple, endowed with qualities such as tranquility and possessing excellent character, should strive to please [the teacher] through prostrations with long staffs and other such acts. He is the most excellent [disciple].
"He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru. Having thus resolved in one's mind, one should communicate one's own inquiry.
Having received permission from his guru, he should subsist on milk for twelve days on the shore of the ocean, by a river, on a mountain, or in a temple of Śiva.
On the fifth or likewise on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, having bathed in the morning, the wise one, with a purified soul, should perform his daily obligatory rites.
Having summoned the preceptor and performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to the prescribed rite, he then had his hair shaved, excluding the armpits and the pubic region.

Having bathed with a restrained mind, one should indeed consume barley meal after the removal of hair, beard, and nails; then, having bathed again in the evening and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
Having performed the evening *aupāsana* rite, the twice-born, accompanied by his preceptor, should offer the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to Śiva in the form of the Guru.

Having prepared the materials for the fire sacrifice according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra, one should duly establish the fire, distinguishing between the types such as the worldly (laukika) and others.
But he who has established the sacred fires should perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice in the consecrated Śrauta Vaiśvānara fire, duly giving away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee.

Then, having internalized the sacred fire within himself, the Brāhmaṇa should depart from his home as a wandering mendicant; having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru) therein, according to the distinctions of fuel-wood, food, and clarified butter.
Having offered oblations verse by verse with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the self-possessed man, having also offered the Sauviṣṭakṛta oblation according to the procedure prescribed in his own Sūtra;

Having performed the subsequent ritual procedure, the wise man, standing to the north of that fire upon a seat covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass, should remain silent and, with a firm mind, recite the Gāyatrī until the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Then, having bathed as before and having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru), the wise one should offer oblations beginning with the Puruṣasūkta and ending with the Virajā mantra.
Whether according to the opinion of Vāmadeva or that of Śaunaka and others, the Vāmadevya hymn is primary therein, since the sage was possessed by a fetus at that time.
Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should then offer oblations; thereafter, having internalized the fire within oneself and performed the morning twilight devotions (*prātaḥsandhyā*).
After the sun has risen, one should enter the Sāvitrī mantra in due order; having abandoned the three types of seeking (eṣaṇās), one should then recite the *preṣa* formula in sequence.
Then, having abandoned the topknot, the sacred thread, the waist-string, and so forth, he should depart facing either the east or the north.

One who is detached should adopt the staff, the loincloth, and other such items appropriate for living in the world; however, if one is not detached, one should not adopt them while considering the conduct of the world.
Then, having approached the presence of the guru, one should prostrate like a staff three times; rising thereafter, one should remain standing near the feet of the guru.
Then the Guru, having taken the cool ashes produced from the fire of Virajā, should raise that disciple up with those very ashes according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should apply the Tripuṇḍra with the mantras beginning with "Agni" and so forth; thereafter, one should meditate upon me, seated within the lotus of the heart together with you.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple with a joyful mind, he should recite [the mantra], together with its seer (ṛṣi) and other components, into the disciple's right ear.
Then the best of teachers should explain the meaning of the Praṇava in its three forms, together with a thorough understanding of its sixfold meaning.
Having prostrated on the ground like a staff before his teacher—who possesses twelve qualities—he should remain perpetually dependent upon him and practice the Vedānta thoroughly.
One should constantly contemplate Me alone—the Supreme Self within the self, the pure, changeless, and imperishable witness of Brahman.
One who is devoted to qualities such as tranquility, who has reached the further shore of the knowledge of Vedānta, and who is free from envy—that ascetic is declared to be qualified for this.
The heart-lotus is stainless, free from sorrow, pure, supreme, eight-petaled, rich with filaments, and radiant upon its pericarp.
Having meditated upon the state consisting of the three principles (tattvas) beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should contemplate the small void (dahara-vyoma) in its center.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om," one should constantly contemplate Me together with you in the midst of it, with a mind ever-diligent.
O beloved, such a devotee, having obtained knowledge from me, attains both rebirth in my own world and the fruit of union with me.
Īśvara said: Hereafter, O Great Goddess, out of affection for you and in accordance with the tradition, I shall proclaim the daily duties of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the ascetic should meditate upon the Guru seated within a white lotus on his head, in the thousand-petaled [cakra].
Resembling pure crystal, with two eyes, bestowing boons and fearlessness, he holds within himself the very essence of Śiva, enchanting to the mind.
Having worshipped in due order with perfumes and other offerings brought forth through meditative cultivation, one should then pay homage to the Guru with palms joined in reverence.
O Mahādeva, whatever I do from morning until the end of evening, and from evening until the next morning, let that be an offering unto you.
Having informed his guru and received permission from him, he then sat with his vital breath restrained, having conquered his self and mastered his senses.

One should contemplate the six chakras, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), as being like ten million flashes of lightning, consisting of all splendor, and supreme.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon me as the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss—the supreme Brahman, devoid of attributes, the eternal Śiva, free from all ailment.
Having realized the identity of "I am He," the wise one, having experienced oneness with Me, should go forth from there and travel far away as he pleases.
Having covered his head along with his nose with a cloth, the wise man, having purified his body according to the rules, should place a blade of grass upon the ground.
Having held his penis, he should rise from there and go to a body of water; having drawn up water in the prescribed manner, he should perform purification without sloth.
Having thoroughly cleansed his hands and feet and sipped water twice while recollecting the syllable "Om," he should perform the cleaning of the teeth facing north in silence.
One should always subsist on grass and leaves, except on the Amāvāsya and Ekādaśī days; thereafter, one should cleanse the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
Having sipped water twice and performed the purification of the waist with earth and water, one should perform the bath with earth at the time of dawn.

Having recollected the Guru and me as well, one should perform the bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and other rites; these have not been described here for fear of prolixity, and should be sought elsewhere.
Having formed the conch mudrā, one should perform the consecration with the *praṇava* (Om) over the head twelve times, or half of that, or half of that again.
Having reached the bank, washed his loincloth, and sipped water twice, he should sprinkle his garment and wipe his limbs with the *praṇava* alone.
Having first wiped the face, one should wipe the entire body starting from the head, while remaining in the presence of the Guru.
Having tied on a pure loincloth along with its cord on the left side, he should then wear the sacred ash; O Daughter of the Mountain, that procedure is now being declared.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water twice and having taken up the sacred ash with the *Sadyojāta* and other mantras, one should touch one's body after consecrating it with the mantras beginning with "Agniriti."
Then, having consecrated the water with the mantra "āpo vaḥ," one should sprinkle it with that very water; having recited "oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" and the mantra "mā nas toke."
O Supreme Goddess, having today joined the pair of lotuses, one should divide each into five parts [and assign them] to the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet.
Beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta, one should successively apply the five [mantras] in order; then, having smeared the mouth, one should consecrate it with the Praṇava.
Then, having washed both hands and all the limbs, one should take up another [substance]; having honored it as before, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* marks with it.
With the *triyāyuṣa* mantras, the *tryambaka* mantras, the *praṇava*, and the *śiva* mantra, [he should apply the ashes] upon the head, the forehead, the chest, and the shoulders.

Having washed [the hands] at the navel, the joints of the arms, and the back in due order, and having then washed the hands again, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rules.
Having recited the Pañcīkaraṇa mantra, the wise one should meditate upon his own guru and perform six rounds of prāṇāyāma according to the method that will be described.
Holding water with the right hand and covering it with the left hand, one should consecrate it over the syllable *praṇava* twelve times.
Having sprinkled [the water] thus three times, one should then drink it three times from the head, meditating with a concentrated mind upon the Lord as the syllable Om.
Situated in the center of the solar mandala, consisting entirely of supreme splendor, possessing eight arms and four faces, he is the wonderful half-male, half-female form.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] as endowed with all wonderful qualities and adorned with every ornament, one should then duly offer three *arghya* libations.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform libations (tarpaṇa) twelve times; then, having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rules, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should approach the hall of worship while mentally recollecting Śiva; having reached the door and washed one's feet, one should silently perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
The wise one should enter there according to the prescribed rite, placing his right foot forward; then, within the pavilion, he should gradually construct the mandala.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Conduct of Renunciation," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

The Lord said: Having duly examined the ground according to its fragrance, color, taste, and other qualities, one should perform [the rite] there, where the mind desires, beneath a canopy spread across the sky.
On the surface of the earth, well-smeared and resembling the interior of a mirror, one should fashion a square measuring two *aratnis*.
Taking a palm leaf of equal length and breadth, one should divide it into thirteen equal parts.
Having placed that leaf there, he stood facing the west; then, taking a very firm, dyed thread from its eastern side, [he proceeded].
O Goddess of the gods, one should cast threads in the four directions—east, west, south, and north—resulting in one hundred and sixty-nine [squares].
From that, there should be compartments for it; the central compartment is the pericarp (karṇikā), and the eight compartments outside of it are here called the eight petals.

The petals here are said to be eight in number and white in color; one should fashion all the petals as white in color. Having made the pericarp yellow in form, the circle [of the lotus] should be red.
O Goddess of the Suras, beginning from the tip of the leaf of the Vanabhit tree, one should decorate the junctions of the petals in sequence with red and black colors.
One should draw the yantra that illuminates the meaning of the Praṇava within the pericarp; having drawn the pedestal below, one should draw Śrīkaṇṭha above it.
Above that, one should draw Amareśa and Mahākāla in the center; then, one should draw the staff situated upon their heads, and beyond that, Īśvara.
One should decorate the pedestal with dark blue and Śrīkaṇṭha with yellow; likewise, Amareśa and Mahākāla should be colored red and black respectively.
The wise one should make the staff dark-smoky and the Lord white; having thus drawn the yantra, he should envelop it with red [saffron] while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra.
O Īśvarī, by means of that very resonance arising from it, one should grasp the lords of the Vidyās and their rows of dwellings, indeed in the sequence beginning with the southeast (Āgneya).
O beautiful one, these four corners of the chambers should be filled with white [pigment], and the group of four letters beginning with *ca* should be filled with red minerals.
Having filled those four doors, one should arrange them; then, on both sides of them, one should fill the two pairs with yellow alone.
In the center of the southeastern square, which is yellowish in appearance, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus that is reddish in color with a yellow pericarp.
Being composed, one should write the letter *ha* joined with a bindu in the center; then, in the southwestern square of the lotus, one should draw a square.
A red eight-petaled lotus with a yellow filaments and pericarp; [the seed-syllable] is the third letter of the *śa*-group joined with the sixth vowel.
Endowed with the fourteen vowels and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, O auspicious lady, one should inscribe this excellent seed-syllable in the center of the lotus.
In the northeast quadrant of the lotus, one should likewise draw a lotus; it consists of the third letter of the *ka*-group conjoined with the fifth vowel.
One should draw a well-adorned *bindu* in its center at the throat; then, in the three outer rows, one should proceed in order from the east and around.
O Śivā, daughter of the King of Mountains, one should take five squares; in the center, one should make a yellow pericarp and a red circle.
The one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion the petals as red in color; outside the petals, he should fill the apertures with black.
One should fill the four [squares] beginning with the southeast (āgneya) with white alone; in the east, one should draw a black hexagon accompanied by six dots.
