To the south is a red-colored triangle, and to the north from there is a white-colored half-moon; to the west is a yellow-colored [triangle].
One should draw a square and, in sequence, write the four seed-syllables within it; having drawn a white dot in the east, one should draw a black one in the south.
Then, having thus established the four colors—the syllable U in the north, red; the syllable Ma in the west; and the syllable A, yellow.
O beautiful one, beginning from the row below the topmost row, there are four [colors]: yellow, white, red, and black.
Below that, there is a group of four: white, dark blue, yellow, and red; and at the bottom of the triangle, O fair-faced one, there are red, white, and yellow.
O Īśvarī, one should proceed in this manner starting from the south and ending at the Soma [quarter]; then, on the outer row, one should decorate it starting from the east and ending at the center.
Yellow, red, black, dark blue, white, and yellow; beginning from the southeast (āgneyī) and so forth, O beloved, [the colors are] red, dark blue, and white.
Red, black, and red—this group of six is proclaimed, O Maheśānī, beginning from the south and extending as far as the east.
O Īśvarī, it should be understood that [the sequence] begins from Nairṛta and extends up to Āgneya; however, beginning from Vāruṇa, it is said to extend up to Dakṣiṇa.

O Great Goddess, it is proclaimed as extending from the northwest (Vāyavya) up to the southwest (Nairṛta); O Supreme Sovereign, for the sake of Soma, it is proclaimed as extending up to the west (Vāruṇa).
O Ambikā, it should be understood that [the sequence] begins with Īśāna and extends as far as Vāyu; thus, O Pārvatī, has the procedure for the maṇḍala been described by me to you.
Having thus drawn the mandala, the self-controlled ascetic himself should perform the solar worship, for he is truly intent upon that reality.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Circle of Renunciation," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Ishvara said: Then, having spread a beautiful tiger skin to the south of the mandala, one should sprinkle it with pure water while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should thereafter extract Ādhāra; after that, Śaktikamala, ending in the dative case and followed by Namaḥ.
Having thus recited the *manu* and remained there facing north, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the rules, preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava*.
Then, one should apply the sacred ash with the mantras beginning with "Agniriti"; thereafter, having bowed to the venerable Guru at the head, one should again prepare the mandala.
Having worshipped in sequence a triangle, a circle, and externally a square, one should place the conch upon its stand with the syllable "Om" and worship it.
Having filled it with pure, fragrant water while reciting the *praṇava*, and having worshipped it seven times with the *praṇava* using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Having consecrated it with mantras, one should then display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā) and the conch-mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā) upon it, and sprinkle it with water while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra).

Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) over oneself and the ritual implements such as perfumes and flowers, one should then perform the assignment of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other components.
Of this Śrī Saura mantra, Devabhāga is the seer (ṛṣi); its meter (chandas) is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Great Lord Sūrya.
One should assign the six limbs of the deity, beginning with *hrāṃ* and so forth; then, one should sprinkle the lotus with the *astra-mantra*, out of the range of sight of the fire.
In that [mandala], the wise one should worship Prabhūtā and Vimalā; then, having propitiated Sārā, he should worship them in sequence starting from the east and proceeding to the west.
Then [he meditated upon] Kālāgnirudra, Śakti known as Ādhāra, Ananta, the Earth, and likewise Ratnadvīpa.
Then, having worshipped the garden of the wish-fulfilling tree (saṃkalpavṛkṣodyāna), the palace made of jewels, and the red pedestal (raktapīṭha) at the feet, beginning from the east;
One should worship the fourfold group consisting of Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) corner.
Afterwards, one should worship Māyā as the lower covering and Vidyā as the upper covering, having duly honored Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas in their proper sequence.
In the directions beginning with the east and in the center, [one should worship] Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Amoghā, and Vaidyutā as well.
Then the consciousness of all directions, as well as the bulb and the stalk; thereafter the hollow, and immediately after that the thorns.
[One should meditate on] the entire self, shining like the filaments that cover the root; then the pericarp with its five knots, and after that, the petals.

Within the filaments [of the lotus], one should meditate upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Self (Ātman), as well as the Inner Self (Antarātman) within the Knowledge-Self (Jñānātman) and the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Having performed worship, one should thereafter honor the Yoga-pīṭha known as Saura; the knower of the root-mantra, having projected the form upon the pīṭha with the root-mantra, [should proceed].
Seated with the vital breath restrained, having raised the Śakti from her own root by means of the Root-mantra through the power of that radiance, [he proceeds] via the path of Piṅgalā.

Having offered the handful of flowers, [he should offer them] to the radiant one situated within the mandala, whose body is crimson with vermilion and who has his beloved as the left half of his own body.
With his four faces, he holds a rosary, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a skull-cup, a goad, a lotus, a conch, and a discus, [all] being gazed upon by his eyes.
In the center of the heart-lotus of that [deity] adorned with twelve [ornaments], one should first extract the Praṇava (Oṃ), and immediately after that, Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ.
Then, after that, one should perform the invocation with the words "I invoke Mārtaṇḍa, together with the power of light; obeisance," using the rite known as invocation.
Then, one should display the mudrās for the installation and other rites; thereafter, one should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with the mantra ending in *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūm*.
Having mentally prepared the five offerings, one should worship them thrice with the root mantra; O Maheśvarī, the six limbs [should be worshipped] upon the filaments of the lotus.
In the second enclosure, the wise practitioner should worship the four forms in order, situated respectively around the southeast, south, southwest, and northwest.
O Pārvatī, from the east to the north at the bases of the petals, [the deities] are Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi, in successive order.
Furthermore, O beloved, Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are to be worshipped again in the third enclosure, starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
One should worship these—Soma, Kuja, Budha, Jīva, Kavi, and Mandam—the darkness within darkness, equally on all sides, from the center of the petals starting with the eastern one.
Alternatively, one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure, and likewise worship the twelve zodiac signs in the third enclosure.
Outside of this, on all sides, are the seven oceans and the Gaṅgās; there dwell the ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, pannagas, and hosts of apsarases.
One should likewise worship the village chiefs, the yakṣas, the yātudhānas, the horses, the vālakhilyas who consist of the seven meters, and so forth.
Having thus worshipped the three-fold-enclosed deity Divākara, one who is composed should then construct a square mandala.
Having placed a common copper vessel, one *prastha* in width, and having filled it with pure water scented with flowers and other fragrances;
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having knelt upon the ground, one should take up the vessel of *arghya* and lift it up as far as the center of the earth.
Then one should recite this Sāvitra mantra, which bestows all accomplishments; listen to it, O Great Goddess, for it always grants devotion and liberation.

Salutations to you who are the color of vermilion, who possess a beautiful mandala, and who are adorned with vajras; salutations to you whose eyes have the luster of lotuses, who are like a magnificent lotus, and who are the cause of Brahmā, Indra, and Nārāyaṇa.
O Blessed One, please be gracious; accept this excellent *arghya*, offered together with red powder, golden water, garlands, saffron, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and a golden vessel.
Having spoken thus and then having offered that for the sake of the form of the Sun, one should perform obeisance while reciting this mantra with a well-composed mind.
Salutations to Śiva, who is with Ambā, accompanied by his attendants, and the primordial cause; salutations to you, the threefold form consisting of Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Having spoken thus and offered salutations, he sat down upon his own seat; then, having again performed the rites beginning with the *ṛṣi*-assignment, he purified his hands with water.

Furthermore, having applied the sacred ash again by the very same path previously described, one should perform the entire series of ritual placements (nyāsa) for the sake of increasing the state of being Śiva.

Having worshipped the venerable Guru with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra), the wise one should then prostrate with his head, uttering the Praṇava followed by the Guru’s name in the dative case ending and the word "namaḥ."
The fivefold [syllable] joined with the *bindu* and conjoined with the fifth vowel; that same [syllable] accompanied by the *bindu* but devoid of the fifth vowel.
Having extracted Maṃtrīśa joined with the fifth vowel and accompanied by the bindu, one should then extract Saṃvartaka together with the bindu.
With these very seed-syllables extracted in sequence, the wise one should prostrate to the Guru and Gaṇapati on the two arms and the pair of thighs respectively.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, he should worship Durgā and Kṣetrapāla; having uttered "Oṃ Astra-āya Phaṭ," he should purify his two hands in the sequence of the six [limbs].
Having uttered "apasarppantu" (let them depart), followed by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and then saying "astrāya phaṭ," one should [drive away obstacles] with three strikes of the heel.
Having dispelled the numerous obstacles by clapping the hands three times, and having observed those situated in the sky and those established in the heavens.
Seated with the vital breath restrained and recollecting the Haṃsa-mantra, one should unite the living consciousness residing in the heart with [the Supreme] through the Brahma-nāḍī.
Within the pure twelve-petaled great thousand-spoked lotus, situated inside the lunar orb of consciousness, is the Supreme Lord whose form is consciousness.
One should perform the practices of drying, burning, and floating through the sequence of exhalation (recaka) and so forth, using counts of sixteen, sixty-four, and thirty-two respectively.

Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) through those [elements] beginning with air, fire, and water, and by means of the [mantras] beginning with *svāhā* in their proper order, one should cause Kuṇḍalinī, who resides at the base, to go to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Having brought [it] into the interior of the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the dvādaśānta, by means of the stream of supreme nectar arising from the lunar orb of consciousness (cic-candramas),...
Once the body has been sprinkled, becoming a pure vessel through excellent contemplation, he then descends into his own self within the lotus of the heart, thinking "I am He."

Having absorbed the self into the Self by means of the immortal stream of existence, one should, being composed, perform the ritual installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) here according to the rules.
With a one-pointed mind, the yogi should contemplate that Mātṛkā, encased within the Praṇava, and then install the Mātṛkā on the exterior.

Furthermore, with his vital breaths restrained, the wise man should perform the visualization and other rites; remembering Śaṅkara in his mind, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) free from envy.
The seer of the Praṇava is Brahmā; O Goddess, the metre is said to be Gāyatrī; and its deity is indeed I, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva.
The letter A is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), the letter U is called the power (śakti), and the letter M is proclaimed as the peg (kīlaka); it is employed for the sake of liberation.

Beginning from the two thumbs and extending to the palms, one should wipe them clean; then, O Goddess of the Gods, having uttered "Oṃ," one should commence the ritual placement upon the hands (karanyāsa).
Beginning with the thumb situated on the right hand, one should place [the fingers] in sequence, ending with the little finger of the left hand, according to the previous order.

Having uttered the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* joined with the *bindu*, ending each with *namaḥ*, one should then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) everywhere, beginning with the heart and so forth.

Having first extracted the syllable *a*, one should then practice [the meditation] upon Brahmā as the Self; likewise, one should again apply it to the heart, ending with the dative case (*ṅe*) and the word *namaḥ*.
One should place the syllable *U*, accompanied by Viṣṇu, on the region of the head; one should place the syllable *Ma*, accompanied by Rudra, upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Having spoken thus, O Goddess of the gods, the sage-mantrin should, with a mind full of vigilance, perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the armor, the eyes, and the head.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five Brahmans according to the divisions of limbs, faces, and digits; one should place these upon the head, face, heart, genitals, and feet.
The five kalās of Īśāna are placed in these five [faces] respectively; thereafter, the kalās of Puruṣa are also placed in the four faces.
Four aspirations should be made according to the sequence starting from the east, [placing them] in the heart, the throat, the shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest.
The eight digits (kalās) of Aghora should be worshipped in their proper order; thereafter, the thirteen digits are to be worshipped in the anus, the genitals, the thighs, and the knees.
One should contemplate the eight digits of Vāmadeva in the calves, buttocks, hips, and flanks, and likewise the eight digits of Sadyojāta in the eyes, in due order.
Those very digits (kalās) have been proclaimed for the feet and the hands; the knower of ritual procedures should likewise assign them to the vital breath, the head, and the two arms.

Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās in every respect, the wise one, skilled in the Praṇava, should thereafter perform the placement of the Praṇava: on the two arms, the two elbows, as well as the two wrists, on the sides, the belly, the shanks, the two feet, and likewise on the back.
Having thus performed the placement of the *praṇava*, one skilled in ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should perform the *haṃsa*-placement, O awakener of the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of Renunciation," in the Saṃnyāsa-paddhati of the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Īśvara said: One should fashion a square mandala to one's left; having worshipped it with "Oṃ," one should place there a conch adorned with weapons.
Having established that common vessel, one should then worship it with the syllable Om (praṇava), filling it with pure water scented with sandalwood and other fragrant substances.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having consecrated it seven times with the *praṇava*, one should then display the *dhenumudrā* over it.
One should fashion a conch-seal (śaṅkhamudrā) in front, a square within that, a half-moon within that, and a triangle within that.
One should fashion this mandala as a circle containing a hexagon; then, having worshipped it in the center with the syllable Om (praṇava) and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having placed the common arghya vessel, one should worship it with scents and other offerings; then, having filled it with pure water, one should cast [the substances] into that vessel.
Kuśa grass tips, unbroken grains, barley, rice, and sesame seeds, as well as clarified butter, white mustard seeds, flowers, and sacred ash, O fair-faced one.

Having worshipped with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, along with the six limbs and the Praṇava, and having consecrated [the object] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the Varman mantra;

Having veiled [the area] with the Astra-mantra, one should display it for the sake of protection; then, by that same mantra, one should sprinkle [it] with the Dhenu-mudrā while reciting the Astra-mantra.

One should [offer] one's own self as well as the ritual implements for worship, such as perfumes and flowers, beginning with the utterance of the *praṇava* (oṃ), to the lotus in the northeast direction of the [central] lotus.
One should prepare the seat with the mantra "Salutation to the Seat of the Guru," and there, according to the oral instruction, one should likewise fashion the form of the Guru.
Having uttered the Praṇava, the syllable *guṃ*, and "Obeisance to the Gurus," and having likewise invoked the Preceptor, one should then meditate upon him as standing facing the south.
With a most serene face, gentle, and as pure as clear crystal, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, two-eyed, he is the very embodiment of Śiva.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order; [one should place the deity] upon the seat of Gaṇapati on the southwestern lotus of the [central] lotus.
Having fashioned a form right there with the mantra "Gaṇānāṃ tvā," one should then invoke the deity and meditate upon him with a one-pointed mind.
Red in color and possessing a massive body, he is adorned with all ornaments and holds a noose, a goad, and his wish-granting fangs in his lotus-like hands.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord Gajānana, the destroyer of the multitude of all obstacles for the worshiper, one should worship him with offerings such as perfumes, flowers, and other services.
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) consisting of plantains, coconuts, mangoes, and sweetmeats (laḍḍukas), one should then pay homage to Gajānana.
Having mentally conceived the seat of Skanda upon the lotus in the northwest direction of the lotus, and having then fashioned the form of Skanda, the wise one should invoke Skanda.
Having recited the Gāyatrī of Skanda, one should then meditate upon Kumāra, who resembles the rising sun and has the excellent peacock as his vehicle.
Four-armed and of noble form, adorned with a crown and other ornaments, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a spear and a cock.
Having meditated thus, one should then worship, in due order, with offerings such as fragrances and so forth, the deity stationed at the right branch of the eastern door.
One should properly worship Nandin himself as the lord of the inner apartments—resembling a mountain of gold and adorned with all ornaments.
The Lord is gentle, adorned with a crescent moon as a crown, possessing three eyes and four arms, and holding a blazing trident, a deer, a water-pot, and a golden staff.
He had a face like the orb of the moon or else the face of a monkey; likewise, his wife was the daughter of the Maruts from the northern quarter.
Having duly honored Suyaśā, who was observant of her vows and devoted to adorning the feet of her mother, with offerings such as perfumes and flowers according to the prescribed rites.

Then one should sprinkle that lotus with drops of water consecrated by the Astra-mantra; thereafter, one should fashion the seat, beginning with the support (ādhāra) and so forth, in the proper sequence.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Ādhāraśakti, dark-complexioned, beneath the earth; and before her, Ananta, coiled in the shape of a serpent, with his neck uplifted.
Above that is a white throne with five hoods, as if licking the sky, and upon it is an auspicious seat supported by four lions.
Dharma, knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty are indeed the steps; they are white, yellow, red, and dark blue in color, beginning with the southeast (āgneya) direction.
One should meditate upon his limbs as being like the rājāvarta gem, starting from the southeast (adharma) and proceeding clockwise through the directions beginning with the east, ending in the north.
Having visualized the lower and upper coverings, the bulbous root, the stalk, the thorns, the petals and so forth, and the pericarp, one should worship them in due order.
On the petals are the eight Siddhis, and on the filaments are the Śaktis; the eight Rudras, beginning with Vāma, are situated in order around the directions starting from the east.
In the pericarp is detachment (vairāgya), and in the seed-syllables are the nine powers, beginning with Vāmā in the east and so forth, ending within that [pericarp] with Manonmanī.
In the bulb (kanda) resides Dharma whose essence is Śiva; in the stalk (nāla) is Jñāna, which has Śiva as its refuge. Above the pericarp (karṇikā) are the mandalas of Agni, Sūrya, and Candra.
Beyond this is the triad of principles known as Ātmavidyā and Śiva; it rests happily upon all the seats, radiant with various flowers.
Having first arranged flowers, one should conceptually construct for the Form a seat known as the expanse of the supreme void, which is exceedingly radiant through Vidyā.

Beginning from the Power of the Foundation (Ādhāraśakti) up to the Throne of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyāsana), one should recite the name-mantra beginning with "Oṃ," ending in the dative case, and concluding with "Namaḥ."

Having uttered [the mantras], the wise one should perform worship; this is the sequence of ritual everywhere. Due to the divisions of limbs, faces, and digits, the five Brahmans are worshipped as before.

One who is skilled in the respective mudrās should place [the deities] in order within the form; then, with hands joined in a hollowed gesture holding a handful of flowers, one should invoke the deity.

Reciting the mantra beginning with "I take refuge in Sadyojāta" and ending with "Om," one should [experience] the resonance (nāda) arising from the foundation through the piercing of the twelve knots.
Having recited [the mantra] up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should meditate upon the Lord who is the object of the syllable Om—partless, imperishable, and resembling pure crystal.
The supreme cause of all worlds, consisting of all worlds, it stands pervading both within and without; though subtler than an atom, it is the greatest of the great.
The immutable Lord is visible to his devotees without effort, yet he remains beyond the reach even of the gods such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
It is heard by the learned that this essence of the Vedas is beyond their reach; it is manifest, devoid of middle or end, and is the medicine for those diseased by worldly existence.

Having meditated thus upon the Supreme Lord with a concentrated mind, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the confinement (sannirodha), and the inspection (nirīkṣaṇa).
One should offer salutation while forming the various mudrās individually, and should meditate upon Sadāśiva, the Lord who is both with parts and without parts.
Resembling pure crystal, serene, with a cool radiance, resembling a circle of lightning, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a slightly smiling lotus-face, his palms, soles, and lips resemble the petals of a red lotus.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament, holding divine weapons in his hands, and anointed with celestial perfumes.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with a crescent moon as his crest-jewel; his eastern face is gentle, with a radiance like that of the rising sun.
Abounding with lotus-like eyes in three places, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, and possessing the beautiful luster of a dark blue cloud on his right side.
His face was terrible, distorted by a frown, with three round red eyes; it was formidable with protruding fangs, difficult to behold, and its sprout-like lower lip was quivering.
The upper [face] resembles coral, adorned with dark locks of hair; it possesses three eyes full of grace and has the crescent moon as its crest-ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon, radiant with three eyes, bearing a crescent moon, gentle, and enchanting with a mild smile.
The fifth [face] resembles crystal, radiant with a crescent moon; it is exceedingly gentle and brilliant with three wide-open eyes.
In the right [hands], he holds a trident, an axe, a vajra, and a sword blazing with fire.

In the east, [one should worship] the Pināka bow, the iron arrow (nārāca), the bell, the noose, and the goad, radiant with light; from the knees up to the navel, one should worship with the Nivṛtti-kalā, and up to the navel with the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā.
Likewise, [the body] up to the throat is filled with Vidyā, and up to the forehead with Śāntā; above that, it is similarly filled with the supreme Kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
Therefore, [one should worship] the ancient God known as Puruṣa, who pervades the five paths, whose form consists of the five kalās, and who has Īśāna as his crown.
Likewise, the Aghora-heart, the Vāma-secret, Maheśvara, and Sadyojāta—this form consists of thirty-eight kalās.
[He meditated upon] Īśāna as consisting of the Mātṛkās, likewise as consisting of the five Brahmans, as consisting of that which is called Oṃkāra, and likewise as consisting of the Haṃsa-nyāsa.
The deity consists of five syllables, and likewise consists of six syllables; he consists of the six limbs and is endowed with the six classes of beings.
Having meditated thus, he then, with devotion, addressed you, Manonmanī Gaurī, on my left side, using the mantra beginning with the Praṇava.
O Goddess, having invoked [the deity] as before, one should perform the rites ending with the salutation; then, O Queen of Devas, the sage, with a concentrated mind, should meditate upon you.
Her complexion was like the petals of a full-blown blue lotus; her eyes were wide and long; her face possessed the splendor of the full moon; and her hair was dark and curled.
She resembles the petals of a blue lotus, has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, and possesses breasts that are exceedingly round, firm, lofty, smooth, and full.
She had a slender waist and broad hips, was dressed in very fine yellow garments, was adorned with all types of ornaments, and was radiant with a tilaka mark upon her forehead.
Adorned with a mass of hair strewn with various flowers, her form was graceful in every respect, and her face was slightly downcast with bashfulness.
Holding a radiant golden lotus in her right hand, she sits upon a comfortable throne with her left hand resting on a fly-whisk like that of Caṇḍa.
O Goddess of the gods, having thus meditated upon you with a restrained mind, one should bathe [the deity] with water from a conch shell according to the procedure of sprinkling with the *praṇava*.
One should offer water for the feet, saying, "In every existence, may there be no further becoming"; then, having said, "Salutation to Vāmā," one should give the water for sipping.
Having said, "Salutation to the Eldest," one should offer a white garment; having said, "Salutation to the Most Excellent," one should give a sacred thread.
Having said, "Obeisance to Rudra," one should offer water for sipping again; having said, "Obeisance to Kāla," one should offer well-prepared fragrant paste.
One should offer unbroken rice grains with the mantra "Salutation to Kalāvikaraṇa," and one should cause flowers to be offered with the mantra "Salutation to Balavikaraṇa."
Having said "Salutation to Bala," one should diligently offer incense; and with "Salutation to Balapramathana," one should likewise cause a well-kindled lamp to be offered.
Then, [one should worship] with the Brahma-mantras, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and together with the Mātṛkā, followed by the Praṇava and Śiva conjoined with Śakti, in due order.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should display the mudrās to me and to you; first, one should perform the ritual services toward me, and thereafter toward you.
But when one should perform [the rite] for you, then one should employ the feminine gender; for this alone is the difference, O Pārvatī, and no other whatsoever.
Having thus performed meditation and worship according to the correct procedure, the wise practitioner should begin the worship of my retinue.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Meditation and Worship of Śiva," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Īśvara said: O Great Goddess, here indeed is the fivefold enclosure; one should commence the worship of the five enclosures in due order.
The wise one should first worship the two deities Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings, in that very place where they were previously worshipped, following the proper sequence.
One should worship the five Brahmans in order around the perimeter: in the northeast, the east, the south, and likewise the north.
And then, in that western [direction], one should worship the six limbs; likewise in the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest.
In the center is the Eye, and its twelve weapons are placed in order around the east and the other directions; this is declared to be the first enclosure. Now hear about the second enclosure.
Ananta is on the eastern petal, Sūkṣma likewise on the south; Śivottama is on the west, and Ekanetra on the north.
One should worship Ekarudra in the northeast, Trimūrti on the petal in the southeast direction, Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest, and Śikhaṇḍīśa in the northwest.
On the second enclosure, those universal monarchs (cakravartins) are to be worshipped; in the middle of the eastern gate, one should worship Vṛṣeśāna.
To the south of that, one should worship Nandin; to the north of that, Mahākāla; and to the west of the southern gate, Bhṛṅgīśa.
Having worshipped Vināyaka with perfumes and other offerings in the eastern cell, one should worship Vṛṣabha in the northwestern cell and Guha in the southern [cell].
To the east of the northern gate, according to the rule of circumambulation, one should worship by means of the eightfold name-ritual; indeed, that is now being declared.
Bhava, Śarva, likewise Īśāna, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva—this indeed is the third enclosure.
Having invoked Maheśvara with the mantra "The vowel at the beginning of the Veda," one should worship him upon the pericarp of the lotus in the eastern quarter.
One should worship Īśvara on the eastern petal, Viśveśa to the south, Parameśāna in the north, and Sarveśa in the west.
To the south, one should worship Rudra with the verse "ā vo rājānam" (RV 5.43.12), having invoked him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings upon the pericarp and the petals.
Śiva is in the east, Hara in the south, Mṛḍa in the north, and Bhava on the western petal; these are to be worshipped in this sequence.
Having invoked Viṣṇu in the north, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, reciting the mantra "pra tad viṣṇuḥ" upon the pericarp and the petals.
One should worship Vāsudeva in the eastern quarter, Aniruddha in the south, Saṃkarṣaṇa in the north, and Pradyumna in the west.
Having invoked Brahmā into the western lotus, the knower of mantras should worship him with the mantra: "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata."
One should worship Hiraṇyagarbha in the east, Virāja to the south, Puṣkara in the north, and Kāla in the west.
In the uppermost row, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective places in sequence according to the rule of clockwise circumambulation starting from the east;
*Rānta*, *pānta*, likewise *jñānta*, *lānta*, *lānta* (again), *apūrvaka*, *ṣānta*, *sānta*, the beginning of the Vedas (*vedādya*), and the *śrībīja*—these ten in sequence.
One should worship these seeds of the world-protectors with these [mantras]: likewise in the southwest, the north, and the south of the northeast.
One should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rites with ritual offerings; one should worship the Lord of Gods on the outer lines in the fifth enclosure.
One should worship the glorious trident in the northeast, the vajra in the direction of Indra (the east), the axe in the region of the fire (southeast), and the arrow in the south.
One should worship Khaḍga in the southwest, the noose in the domain of Varuṇa (the west), the goad in the northwest, and the Pināka bow in the north.
One who knows the ritual procedures should worship the fierce Kṣetrapāla facing west, according to the rules, solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva.
With palms joined in reverence, all those worthy of thought, their lotus-like faces smiling, were constantly gazing with devotion upon the God and the Goddess.
Having thus performed the worship of the enclosure for the sake of pacifying distractions, one should worship the Lord of Gods once more and utter the Praṇava and the word "Śiva."

Having thus worshipped according to the rules with offerings such as perfumes and the like, and having performed the service, one should then present the food offering (naivedya) prepared according to the prescribed ritual.
Again, one should offer water for sipping and the respectful offering (arghya) as before; then, according to the instructions, one should present drinking water and betel leaf.

Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites, one should complete the remainder of the worship; then, having meditated upon the God and the Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having risen and standing with his hands joined in a hollowed cup of flowers, he should meditate upon Mahādeva and recite the hymn beginning with "yo devānām" in the proper sequence.
O Supreme Goddess, having recited from "The sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda" up to the end, one should then offer a handful of flowers and perform three circumambulations.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he should prostrate before him with the eight limbs; then, having performed a circumambulation, he should prostrate once again.
Having sat upon his seat and worshipped the Lord with the eight names, [he said]: "Whatever action has been performed by me, whether good or bad—"
"O Blessed One, O Śambhu, may all of this be the supreme worship of you. Thus he should offer it with water from a conch shell, together with flowers.
Having worshipped the venerable one once again, one should mutter the eightfold name along with its meaning; listen to that very thing, O Goddess of gods, for I shall speak it to you out of devotion.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Enclosures," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Īśvara said: Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha are primarily known as the Physician of Saṃsāra, the Omniscient One, and the Supreme Self.
This eightfold name eternally establishes Śiva; therein, the first five [names] follow the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā.
The designation of Śiva and the others arises from the appropriation of the five limiting adjuncts; however, upon the cessation of those adjuncts, it ceases accordingly.
The state alone is eternal; those who possess states are known to be impermanent. For it is through the transformation of states that those who possess them are liberated.

But in another cycle of transformation, through yet another limiting adjunct (upādhi), there occurs a further designation of that very self by another name; this constitutes the first pentad of names, beginning with "Pāda."
However, the other triad of names, due to the distinction of appropriation and so forth, exists as Śiva alone through the arrangement of three kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Because it is by its very nature devoid of the prior non-existence of the attachment to beginningless impurity, this Self is called Śiva, being absolutely pure.
Alternatively, the Lord who is the singular mass of all auspicious qualities is called Śiva by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva).
Beyond the twenty-three principles (tattvas), primordial nature (prakṛti) is said to be supreme; they declare the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, to be beyond even that nature.

That which they call the first syllable at the beginning of the Veda, by virtue of the relationship between the signifier and the signified; which is to be known solely through the Veda according to its true nature, and which is established in the Vedānta.

He alone is the enjoyer who is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti), because he is the source of that nature; and he who is beyond him, being dissolved in primordial nature, is the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Because both Prakṛti and Puruṣa function in dependence upon that [consciousness], this undecaying reality consisting of the three guṇas is Māyā.
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara; the infinite one is the liberator from Māyā through his union with Maheśvara.
He who, as the Lord, causes that which is suffering or the cause of suffering to flow away (dru) is called Rudra; therefore, Śiva is the supreme cause.
Pervading everything from the principle of Śiva down to the earth, including the body and objects such as a jar, Śiva presides over them; therefore, he is declared to be Viṣṇu.
Śiva is the father even of those who are the fathers of the world in their embodied forms; by virtue of being the father of all, he is proclaimed as the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
Just as a physician who knows the cause of a disease brings it to an end through skillful means and medicines, so too does he who possesses mastery over the dissolution and enjoyment [of existence].
He is the eternal Lord of saṃsāra, the one who brings about the cessation of the gross; he is called the Physician of saṃsāra by those who know the meaning of all principles.

For the sake of attaining the fivefold knowledge, even though the sense faculties are present, [he perceives] all things existing in the three periods of time, whether gross or subtle, without exception.
The individual souls (aṇus), obscured by the impurity of the ocean of illusion, do not know at all, even though there exist those who have realized all objects and possess complete knowledge.
Sadāśiva knows each and every object exactly as it exists, without any effort; therefore, he is called "the Omniscient One."
Because he is eternally endowed with these supreme qualities as the self of all, and because he is devoid of any other self than his own, Śiva himself is the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Having thus praised Mahādeva, the imperishable essence of the Praṇava, and having offered the *parāṅmukha* oblation, he then placed it upon the head of Īśāna.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods again with the Praṇava while remaining composed, and having taken the flower for worship in his hands with palms joined in reverence;
Having led Śiva to the end of *unmanā*, one should then dismiss the Goddess by way of the left nostril, and subsequently [dismiss Him] by way of the right nostril.
Having experienced that oneness through the realization "I am indeed Śiva," one should again dissolve all the presiding deities of the coverings into the heart.
Having performed the worship of the Vidyā and the worship of the Guru, one should thereafter, in due order, sequentially place the mantras of the conch and the arghya-vessel within the heart.

Then, having offered the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) to Caṇḍeśa in the direction of Īśāna, one should again restrain the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and recite the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs of the mantra].
The mandala named Kailāsaprastara has been described; one should worship this constantly, or at least once every fortnight, or month by month.
Whether it be every six months, or once a year, or on festival days such as Cāturmāsya, a believer must certainly and constantly worship my liṅga.
In that sequence, O Great Goddess, a certain special instruction is told: on the day of the oral instruction, the Linga is worshipped together with the Guru.
"I shall accept [this] and worship Śiva until the dissolution of my life"—having thus uttered this oath three times in the presence of the Guru.
Thereafter, O beloved, one should worship daily according to the previously mentioned procedure; and one should offer the *arghya* upon the top of the *liṅga* with the *arghya* water.
Having worshipped with the Praṇava, one should offer incense and a lamp; and having propitiated Caṇḍa in the northeast, one should present the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
Then, having washed the linga and the pedestal with water filtered through a cloth, one should place a flower upon the head of the linga while reciting the Praṇava.
Having mentally visualized everything from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the seat of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), one should establish the Supreme Lord there.
With substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) collected according to one's means, or with pure water alone scented with fragrant substances.
With the Pāvamāna, the Rudra, the Nīla, and the Tvarita [mantras], and also with the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, or indeed the five Brahma-mantras.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the Praṇava and with the Śiva-mantra; one should also consecrate him with the water of the special arghya while reciting the Praṇava.
Having purified the flower with a cloth, one should place it upon the top of the liṅga; then, having installed the liṅga upon its pedestal, one should perform the worship beginning with the Sun.
One should worship the two, Ādhāraśakti and Ananta, beneath the seat (pīṭha); then, having worshipped the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) above that, one should proceed according to the sequence.
Then, one should worship Skanda on the foot of the pedestal beneath the upper covering; having conceived the form within the *liṅga*, one should worship it together with Mā and You.
A yogi who is intent on meditation upon Me, practicing with right devotion according to the prescribed rule—O beloved, this which I have told you is an exceedingly secret matter.
This must be guarded with great effort and not given to just anyone; it should be given to my devotee, to an ascetic who is free from passion.
To one who is devoted to the guru, peaceful, and a participant in yoga for my sake—he who, being of deluded intellect, bestows this while transgressing my command.

That hell-dweller will become my enemy, of this there is no doubt; yet, O Goddess of Gods, by giving to my devotee, he shall certainly become dear to me. Having enjoyed all pleasures here, he shall attain proximity to me.
Vyāsa said: Having heard this spoken by Mahādeva, the Great Goddess praised the God with various hymns exalting the meaning of the Vedas.
O best of sages, with her heart overflowing with joy, the Supreme Goddess rejoiced upon pronouncing the *praṇava* over the lotus feet of her Lord.
O Brahmins, this is an extreme secret that illuminates the meaning of the *praṇava*; for it is the supreme knowledge of Śiva and the destroyer of your suffering.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Parāśarya, that tiger among sages and possessor of great ascetic power, was honored with supreme devotion by the sages who were exponents of the Vedas.
Having departed from that penance grove, he went toward Mount Kailāsa; they too, with joyful hearts, [approached] the Supreme Lord at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Having worshipped Soma, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, with supreme devotion, they became intent on the yoga of Yama and other practices, devoted to the meditation upon Śiva.
This was indeed told by the Goddess to Guha, and he in turn to Nandin; that Blessed One then spoke it to the sage Sanatkumāra.
Therefore, this was obtained by my guru Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor; from him, O best of sages, this merit has been obtained by me as well.
Indeed, this which has been proclaimed by me is the supreme secret among secrets; having known it with devotion, you shall become dear to Giriśa, as are those beloved of Śiva.
You too must give this secret, which is dear to Śiva, to ascetics of tranquil mind who are devotees at the feet of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, the highly fortunate Sūta, the best of those who recite the Purāṇas, wandered over this earth in the course of his pilgrimage.
Having obtained this supreme secret from Sūta, the lords of sages remained in Kāśī itself and, being liberated, went to the abode of Śiva.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Method for the Meaning of the Praṇava," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Vyāsa said: When the charioteer had departed, the sages were greatly amazed; reflecting among themselves, they said, "O Lord of Sages, that which was the opinion of Vāmadeva has been forgotten by us, and indeed it has now perished."

When indeed shall we experience the sight of the best of sages, for that is the supreme remover of the flood of suffering from the ocean of worldly existence? By virtue of the merit gained from worshipping Maheśvara, may the Lord of Sages appear before us immediately.
Thus absorbed in thought, the sages, having worshipped Vyāsa, the bull among sages, remained within the lotus of their hearts, eager for his vision.
At the end of the year, that great sage—who was devoted to the worship of Śiva, possessed of wisdom, and an illuminator of the meaning of the Purāṇas—returned once more to Kāśī.
Seeing the charioteer approaching, the sages, with joyful hearts, honored him by rising from their seats and offering worship with water for the feet, a seat, and other traditional offerings.
He too, having greeted those tigers among sages with a gentle smile, bathed with joy in the supremely purifying waters of the Jāhnavī.
Having gratified the sages, gods, and ancestors with sesame seeds and rice, he returned to the bank, sprinkled himself with water, and put on two garments.
Having sipped water twice and taken up the sacred ash with the Sadyojāta and other mantras, the lord of sages should then apply it according to the sequence beginning with *uddhūlana*.
Adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and having performed his daily rites, the wise man applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) upon his limbs according to the prescribed injunctions.
He worshipped Viśveśvara, the beloved of Umā, together with his sons and the lords of his hosts, with true devotion; having bowed down again and again, he praised him.
Having worshipped Lord Kālabhairava according to the prescribed rite, one should then circumambulate him and prostrate three times and five times.
Having circumambulated him once more and prostrated on the ground like a staff, he praised him with a supreme hymn while remembering his lotus feet.
Having recited the glorious five-syllabled mantra one thousand and eight times, and having stood before Maheśvara and asked for his forgiveness;
Then, having fully worshipped Caṇḍeśa, he took the seat assigned to him in the center of the Muktimaṇḍapa by the sages who had mastered the Vedas.
When all were thus seated, he paid homage with the accompanying mantra and then spoke words that increased the spiritual fervor of the lords of sages.
Sūta said: Blessed are you, O highly wise sages of praised vows; I have come here for your sake, so hear this account.
When, after I had instructed you in the meaning of the *praṇava*, I departed for the purpose of wandering among sacred sites (*tīrthas*), I shall relate that account to you.

Having departed from here and reached the shore of the southern ocean, and having bathed and duly worshipped the Goddess Śivā in her maiden form according to the prescribed rites, O best of Brahmins, they returned once more to the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī.
In the most wonderful city known as Śrī Kālahastiśaila, having bathed in the waters of the Suvarṇamukharī river, [he worshipped] the gods and the sages as well.
Having gratified [the deity] according to the rules with devotion and joyfully remembering Giriśa, he worshipped Kālahastīśa, who possesses a luster like that of a moonstone.
Facing westward, with five heads, most wonderful; by the mere sight of it once, it is the cause for the destruction of all sins.

[He worshipped] the Lord of the Three Qualities, the bestower of all perfections and the giver of enjoyment and liberation; and then, with supreme devotion, [he worshipped] his Śivā situated to the right.
Having indeed worshipped the five-syllabled, illustrious Vidyā—the mother of the universe and the bud of the flower of knowledge—one thousand and eight times.
Having recited [the mantra], having circumambulated, and having praised and bowed down again and again;
Then, having circumambulated the mountain every day with devotion, he rejoiced in his mind as he daily maintained his religious observances.
In this manner, the lords of sages remained there for four months, [cultivating] the buds of the flowers of knowledge through the grace of the Great Goddess.
Once, having spread out a seat consisting of cloth, antelope skin, and kusha grass in that order, the sage sat upon it, having restrained his senses.
Abiding in samādhi, with my heart free from agitation, I became one whose essence is the wealth of supreme bliss, realizing, "I am the perfectly full Śiva."
At that very moment, the true guru, a treasury of compassion, appeared resembling a dark blue cloud, wearing matted locks as tawny as lightning.
He was tall in stature, personally bearing a water-pot, a staff, and a black antelope skin; his entire body was purified by white ashes, and he was endowed with all the auspicious marks.
His forehead was radiant with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), his form was adorned with rudrākṣa beads, and his two eyes were long and wide, as red as lotus petals.
O believers, having suddenly appeared within the lotus of my heart at that very moment, he quickly deluded me; this is indeed a marvel!
Then, opening my eyes, I uttered a lament; my shedding of tears was like the roar of a mountain torrent.
At that very moment, O brahmins, a most wonderful disembodied voice was heard from the sky; listen to it with reverence.
O illustrious son of a Sūta, go to the city of Vārāṇasī; there were formerly sages who have now been instructed by you.
"Helpless and intensely longing for the auspiciousness of your arrival, they remain without food," she said, and then she fell silent.
Then, rising up with haste, he circumambulated the God and the Goddess with devotion, and again prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
Then, having received the command of the Guru regarding Śiva and Śivā twelve times, he departed swiftly from the sacred site within forty days.
I have come, O best of sages; may you show me favor here. What should I say now? May you tell me that.
Having heard these words of the Sūta, the sages, their minds filled with joy, bowed repeatedly to Vyāsa, that tiger among munis, and spoke.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Sūta," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said: O Sūta, O Sūta, you are highly fortunate and our supreme teacher; therefore, we question you, if you will grant us your favor.
"Among faithful disciples, teachers such as yourself are always affectionate; this has now been demonstrated by you."
O Sage, at the time of the Viraja oblation, the doctrine of Vāmadeva was previously indicated by you; it was not heard by us in detail.
O Ocean of Compassion, we are all now desirous of hearing this with supreme faith and great reverence; you should kindly speak of it out of affection for us.
Having heard these words of theirs, the charioteer, his hair standing on end with joy, paid homage to Mahādeva, the teacher of teachers.
Vyāsa, out of devotion, spoke these words in a profound voice to the Great Goddess, the Mother of the Three Worlds, and to his Guru, gladdening the sages.
Sūta said: May there be well-being for all you sages; may you be happy at all times—you who are devotees of Śiva, steadfast in soul, and promoters of devotion to Śiva.
Indeed, this most wonderful thing has been heard from the lotus-mouth of the Guru; previously, I had not spoken of it, out of fear of revealing what is secret.
"You are indeed highly fortunate devotees of Śiva, firm in your vows. Having thus ascertained this, I shall speak to you; listen with joy.
In former times, during the Rathantara Kalpa, the great sage Vāmadeva was himself liberated from the womb and became the supreme teacher among those who possess the knowledge of Śiva.
He was a knower of the meaningfulness of all scriptures, such as the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas; he was a knower of the births and deeds of living beings, including gods, asuras, and humans.
With his entire body white with ashes, adorned with a circle of matted locks, he was without support, free from desire, beyond the pairs of opposites, and devoid of egoism.
Naked and possessed of great wisdom, he was like a second Maheśvara, surrounded by such lords of sages who had become his disciples.
Wandering over this earth, purifying it daily through the merit of the touch of his feet, his heart was immersed in the supreme abode.
With joy, they entered the southern side of Mount Kumāraśikhara, where the Lord Śiva, whose vehicle is the peacock, resides.
The hero who wields the power of knowledge, the crusher of all asuras, joined with Gajāvallī, and saluted by all the gods.
There is a lake named Skandasaras, resembling the ocean, with cool and sweet water, clear, deep, and abundant in its waters.
Endowed with all wonderful qualities, it exists in the presence of the Lord; having bathed there, the great sage Vāmadeva, together with his disciples, [performed his rites].
The youth seated upon the mountain peak, attended by hosts of sages, resembling the rising sun, and having a magnificent peacock as his vehicle.
Four-armed and of noble form, adorned with a crown and other ornaments, he is worshipped by Śakti and Ratnadvaya, and he holds a spear and a cock.
Seeing Skanda with his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the lord of sages worshipped him with supreme devotion and began to offer praise.

Vāmadeva said: Oṃ! Salutations to the one who is the meaning of the Praṇava, to the one who ordains the meaning of the Praṇava; salutations again and again to the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the letters of the Praṇava.
Salutations again and again to the one whose very nature is the meaning of Vedānta, who ordains the meaning of Vedānta, who eternally knows the meaning of Vedānta, and who is himself known.
Homage to Guha, who is established in the secret places of all beings; homage to the Secret One, whose form is secret, and who knows the secret scriptures.
Salutations to you, who are subtler than the subtle and greater than the great; salutations to the knower of the high and the low, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self.
Salutations always to Skanda, who possesses the form of Skanda, whose splendor is like that of the sun and the dawn, and who eternally wears a crown from which a garland of Mandāra flowers emerges.
Salutations to the disciple of Śiva, to the son of Śiva, to the bestower of auspiciousness, to the beloved of Śiva, and to the treasure-trove of bliss for the two Śivas.
Salutations to you, O son of Gaṅgā; salutations to the wise Kārttikeya, the great son of Umā who lies within the forest of reeds.
Salutations again and again to the six-faced one, whose body consists of the six syllables, who ordains the sixfold purpose, and whose form transcends the six paths.
Salutations to you, the twelve-fold self, whose eyes are the twelve sense-bases, whose twelve arms are uplifted, and who wields twelve weapons.
Salutations to the four-armed, peaceful one who holds a spear and a cock, the granter of boons with hands raised in blessing, the destroyer of the asuras.
Salutations to the one whose chest is marked with saffron smeared from the breasts of Gajāvallī, and whose self is delighted by the great honor of the joy of Gajānana.

Salutations to you, whose abode of fame is purified by the recitation of specific verses sung by Brahmā, the primordial gods, sages, and kinnaras; O Lord, whose beautiful lotus feet are worshipped by the garlands adorning the crest-jewels of the gods and demigods!
Thus ends the divine hymn to Skanda spoken by Vāmadeva; whoever recites it or even hears it attains the supreme goal.
For this indeed produces great wisdom, increases devotion to Śiva, bestows long life, health, and wealth, and always grants all desires.
Having thus praised the Lord, the commander-in-chief, Vāmadeva performed three circumambulations and prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
O brahmins, having again performed the eight-limbed prostration and circumambulation with reverence, he stood at his side, bowed down in humility.
Having heard the hymn composed by Vāmadeva, which unfolds the ultimate reality, the Lord, the son of Maheśvara, indeed became pleased.
Mahāsena said to him, "I am pleased with your worship, your devotion, and your hymn of praise; may it be well with you—what shall I do for you now?"
O Sage, you are the foremost of yogis, perfectly fulfilled and free from desire; for those such as yourself, there is nothing in this world to be sought after.
Nevertheless, for the protection of the Dharma and out of a desire to favor the world, virtuous and holy men like you wander upon the surface of the earth.
O Brahmin, if there is something to be heard, you should speak it now; I shall therefore speak it now for the sake of favoring the world.
Having heard these words of Skanda, the great sage Vāmadeva, bowing with humility, spoke in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Vāmadeva said: O Blessed One, you are the Supreme Lord, the bestower of both the transcendent and the immanent; you are the omniscient creator of all, the sovereign who wields all powers.
We are indeed living beings, yet we speak in the presence of the Supreme Lord; nevertheless, it is your grace toward me that you speak thus to me.
O one of great wisdom, my purpose is fulfilled by this mere spark of realization; impelled by that, I ask you these questions—my transgression should be forgiven.
The Praṇava is indeed the supreme, direct designator of the Supreme Lord; its designated referent is the divine Paśupati, the liberator of bound souls from their fetters.
Summoned by the designator, one releases the bound souls (paśus) in an instant; therefore, the accomplishment of the status of a designator occurs through the *praṇava* with respect to Śiva.
The eternal Śruti declares: "Om, this all is Mitra"; and it has likewise stated: "Om is Brahman, for all is indeed Brahman."
O Lord of the celestial army, salutations to you, the Lord of the gods; salutations to the Lord of the ascetics, salutations to you who are perfectly complete.
This being the case, in this world nothing exists other than Śiva; the Lord Śiva, the Great Sovereign, is all-pervading and assumes every form.
The meaning of the Praṇava has been heard by me in its aspects as both the collective whole and the individual parts; O Mahāsena, never before have I obtained a teacher such as you.
Therefore, having shown compassion, you ought to explain that matter according to the method of instruction and the sequence of right conduct.
The Master alone is the lord of all living beings and the Guru who severs the bonds; therefore, O Guru, by your grace, that truth must indeed be heard by me.

Thus questioned by the sage, Skanda bowed to Sadāśiva—the embodiment of the Praṇava, characterized by the thirty-six excellent kalās, eternally accompanied by Umā at his side and joined by the foremost of sages—and began to speak of that supreme good which is hidden even in the Vedas.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Vāmadeva and Brahmā," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Brahmaṇya said: "Excellent, excellent, O illustrious Vāmadeva, lord of sages! You are an exceedingly devoted worshipper of Śiva and the foremost among those possessed of spiritual knowledge."
There is nothing whatsoever in all the worlds that is unknown to you; nevertheless, I shall speak to you, who act for the benefit of the world.
In this world, all beings are like cattle, deluded by various scriptures and deceived by the most wonderful Māyā of the Supreme Lord.
He does not know the Supreme Maheśvara, the manifest meaning of the Praṇava, the Brahman with attributes and without attributes, the supreme progenitor of the three gods.
Raising my right arm, I pronounce this oath to you: truth, truth, again truth; truth, truth, again and again.
Śiva is proclaimed as the manifest meaning of the syllable Om (praṇava) in its primary sense within the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas.
From whom words turn back along with the mind, unable to reach him—him who knows that bliss, from nothing whatsoever does he fear.
Because this entire world, headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, along with the collection of elements and sense organs, is first brought forth [by him].
That from which nothing whatsoever is ever produced, in which lightning does not shine, nor the sun, nor the moon;
He whose light shines forth upon this entire universe on all sides, endowed with all sovereignty, is himself by name Sarveśvara (the Lord of All).

He who is indeed to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation—Śambhu, dwelling in the midst of space, all-pervading, whose nature is light, whose form is radiance, and who consists of consciousness.

That Supreme Power of the Puruṣa, which is accessible through meditative states, enchanting, devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), yet concealed by her own qualities, partless (niṣkalā), and auspicious (śivā).
O Sage, His threefold form—gross, subtle, and supreme—is to be meditated upon constantly and in successive order by yogis seeking liberation.
He who is partless, the primordial god of all gods, eternal, whose nature consists of knowledge and action, is celebrated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
The form of that God of gods is Sadāśiva himself; the Lord has the five mantras as his body and the five kalās as his physical manifestation.
Resembling pure crystal, serene, and possessing cool radiance, the Lord has five faces, ten arms, and fifteen eyes.
He is endowed with Īśāna as his crown, has Puruṣa as his face, is the primordial one; he has Aghora as his heart and Vāmadeva as the region of his private parts.
Sadyojāta is his form, manifest as both the differentiated and the undifferentiated; his body is constituted by the six limbs consisting of the six powers, such as omniscience and the rest.
He is resplendent with the heart-lotus blossoming through the power of sound and the other [tattvas], and is adorned on his left side by his own power, Manonmanī.

In this chapter, which presents the meaning of the sixfold objects beginning with mantra, I shall explain that which consists of the *praṇava* for the purpose of understanding its collective and individual states.
First, the sequence of instruction must be stated; listen to this, O Sage: for the system of the four castes is well-established among human beings in this world.

In this context, the harmony between the Vedic revelation and established practice pertains only to the three higher castes; for Śūdras, whose essence consists solely in service, are excluded from the Veda.
For all members of the three varṇas who are devoted to their respective stages of life (āśramas), the dharma proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti is to be practiced; never another.
"By performing the actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, one shall attain perfection"—thus was it said by the Supreme Lord, the revealer of the path of the Vedas.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord through the merits of the conduct prescribed for their respective castes and stages of life, many of the best of sages attained union with Him.
"By the practice of celibacy the sages are satisfied, by the path of sacrificial rites the gods, and by progeny the ancestors; thus indeed the Śruti has declared."
Thus, liberated from the three debts and having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he endures cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and the like, with his senses fully conquered.
An ascetic who has conquered his appetite should practice yoga for the sake of self-restraint, so that his intellect may become exceedingly firm and unshakable.
In this manner, having gradually purified the self, one should consign all actions [to the deity]; having consigned all actions, one should become intent upon the worship of knowledge.

For that [state], by virtue of its direct identity with Śiva, bestows the fruit of liberation while living; it should indeed be known as the most excellent among those of self-restraint, being free from all modifications.
Out of a desire to benefit the world, O highly wise one, I shall describe that method out of affection for you; listen with full attention.
That ascetic, the best among the wise, should approach a teacher who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures and has reached the further shore of the knowledge of Vedānta.
Having approached him in accordance with the prescribed rules, the wise and discerning person should diligently seek to please him through prostrations with long-stretched arms and other such acts.
"He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva, and he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru"; having thus resolved with the mind, one should offer one's own reflection.

Having received permission from his guru, he shall observe a vow of subsisting on milk for twelve days, according to the prescribed rule, on either the fourth or the tenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having bathed in the morning, the wise one, with a purified soul and having performed his daily rites, should invite the Guru and duly commence the Nāndī-śrāddha.
The Viśvedevas are proclaimed to be those possessing the names Satya and Vasu; in the Śrāddha for the gods, the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa is prescribed.
In the Śrāddha for the sages (ṛṣi-śrāddha), those born of gods, fields, and humans are prescribed; however, in the Śrāddha for the gods (deva-śrāddha), the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are proclaimed.
In the śrāddha for humans, there are the four lords of sages beginning with Sanaka; in the śrāddha for spirits, there are the five great elements (mahābhūtas), and after that—
The collection of sense organs, beginning with the eye, and the fourfold collection of elements; at the ancestral śrāddha rite, there are three: the father, his father, and his father.

In the śrāddha for the mother, one offers to the mother, the paternal grandmother, and the paternal great-grandmother; but in the śrāddha for oneself, there are four: oneself, the father, and the grandfather.

And those named after the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) are declared to be accompanied by their wives; in the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather (mātāmaha), there are three, beginning with the maternal grandfather.
Having arranged pairs of Brāhmaṇas for each Śrāddha ceremony and invited them, he himself should diligently wash their feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

May the dust from the feet of the Brahmins purify me—they who are the cause for attaining all prosperity, who have arisen as comets to destroy the masses of calamities, and who are the bridges across the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.

May the dust from the feet of Brahmins protect me—dust that is a thousand suns for the darkness of calamity, a wish-fulfilling cow for the attainment of desired goals, and a form as pure as the waters of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having thus recited the mantra and prostrated with eight limbs like a staff upon the ground, he stood facing east, meditating on the pair of lotus feet of Śambhu.

With hands holding the purifier (pavitra), pure, wearing the sacred thread (upavītī), and seated firmly, he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) after again hearing the guest-offering (ātithya) and other rites.

Likewise, that which consists of the Viśvedevas and others as ancillaries to my renunciation, as well as the eightfold Śrāddha pertaining to the maternal grandfathers, should indeed be performed according to the Pārvaṇa rite.
"I shall perform [the rite] according to the injunction, preceded by your command. Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he should discard the darbha grasses toward the north.
Having sipped water and risen, he should begin the procedure for choosing the officiants; with the *pavitra* in his hand, having touched the hands of the two Brahmins, he should speak.
"Regarding the Viśvedevas," and so forth, as well as "the moment has come for you both."
The ritual procedure is the same everywhere up to the point "worthy of being propitiated. Having thus completed the selection, one should arrange the mandalas.
Having risen and performed worship ten times with unbroken grains (akṣata), he should again place the Brahmins in order at his feet.

One should utter the names of the Viśvedevas and others, along with the word "saṃvibodhana" (awakening), saying: "This is the water for washing the feet (pādya) for you," using water mixed with kuśa grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
Having offered water for the feet and having himself washed his feet while facing north, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and seat them in pairs upon the seats.
"This is the seat for the Brāhmaṇa, who is the embodiment of the Viśvedevas. Having thus offered the seat of Darbha grass, he himself stood with Darbha grass in his hand.
Regarding this Āndīmukha śrāddha, for the sake of the Viśvedevas, one should say, "May you two grant your consent," and they should respond, "Let it be done."
Having said, "May you two attain [it]," he should address them; and those two bulls among Brahmins should say, "May we both attain it."
"May it be complete; may there be the fulfillment of my resolve"—thus he should entreat those eminent brahmins, saying, "May you show me your favor."

Then, having placed the various edible foods, such as rice and other grains, into separate vessels made of pure plantain leaves and the like that have been washed, he should cover each portion individually with *darbha* grass.
Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] there himself and sprinkled it with water, he should then hold each vessel with both hands with great reverence.

Having performed the rite beginning with "The earth is your vessel," one should address the deities and others established therein, reciting their names in the dative case along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having taken it up, one should offer food for the sake of the gods, saying "Svāhā"; at the end, one should say "Not mine"—this is the sequence of the ritual in all cases.
I bow to that Lord Īśvara accompanied by Ambā, by the remembrance of whose lotus feet or even by the chanting of whose name deficient action becomes complete.
Having recited this, he should then say: "This Nāndīmukha-śrāddha has been performed by me," and thereafter he should speak as previously prescribed.
Having propitiated those eminent brahmins by saying, "So be it; say 'so be it'," and having dismissed them, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, with the water remaining in his own hand.
Having risen from there, he should say to the twice-born, "May it become nectar," and with palms joined in reverence, the noble-minded one should pray with supreme affection.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva in his heart, one should recite the Śrī Rudra, the Camaka, the Sūkta, and the Pauruṣa hymn according to the rules, as well as the five Brahma-mantras.
At the end of the meal, having recited the Rudra-sūkta and asked the twice-born sages for forgiveness, he should then offer the *uttarāpośana* water in front of them with that same mantra.

Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then proceed to the place for the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). Seated there facing east and observing silence, he should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍadāna) as an ancillary part of the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha," one should proceed from Dakṣa onwards until the end of the water libation.
Having drawn nine lines and twelve lines pointing eastward in sequence, and having spread darbha grass, one should prepare the five locations beginning with the south and beginning with the gods.
One should silently offer water with unbroken grains (akṣata) in three places in succession; thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling for the other mothers in their respective places.
Here, having first honored the Pitṛs with water mixed with unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should then offer [the oblation] in due order into the five locations beginning with the Devas.
Having uttered the names of the respective deities and others ending in the dative case, one should then offer three *piṇḍas* at each of the five locations.

One should offer the piṇḍas individually according to the path prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra; one should offer this along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) for the sake of attaining excellence for the ancestors.
One should meditate on the Lord Sadāśiva in the center of the lotus of the heart, while repeatedly reciting the verse beginning with "By the remembrance of His lotus feet."

Having paid homage to the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees according to his capacity, and having asked them for forgiveness and dismissed them, he should then proceed with the subsequent rites in due order.

Having set aside the rice-balls, one should give a morsel to a cow; if not, one should cast it into water. Then, after the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), one should eat together with one's own kinsmen.

On the following day, having risen at dawn and performed his daily obligatory rites, the wise man, having observed a fast, should undergo the rite of shaving and so forth, excluding the armpits and the private parts.
Having first shaved off the hair of the head, beard, and nails as the limit of the ritual action, he should have his hair trimmed according to the rules and the prescribed injunctions.

Having bathed, wearing a clean washed garment, purified, and having sipped water twice while remaining silent, he should apply the sacred ash according to the prescribed rite and perform the Puṇyāhavācana ceremony.
Having sprinkled [him] with that and attained the state of a pure body by nature, [the disciple], setting aside the materials for the fire-oblation and the fee for the preceptor, [should proceed].
Having bestowed the collection of substances upon Maheśa, especially upon the twice-born, and upon his devotees, he then offered them to Śiva in the form of the Guru.

Having given garments and other items as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and prostrating on the ground like a staff, he should wash his staff, the waist-belt, the loincloth, and the garment upon the earth.

Having taken the materials for the oblation, such as sacrificial fuel (samidh) and so forth, in their proper order, [he should go] to the shore of the ocean, or to a river, or to a mountain, or to a temple of Śiva.
Having deliberated upon an excellent location, whether in a forest or a cow-pen, one should stand there, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and first form the mental maṃjarī.
Having recited the Brahma-mantra together with the syllable *oṃ* and also "namo brahmaṇe," he should then recite three times the verse beginning, "I praise Agni, the domestic priest."

Now, regarding the "Great Vow" (*mahāvrata*): Agni is indeed the deity by name. Thus, its traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*) begins with "For food, for strength, thee! (*iṣe tvorje tvā*). This is it.
"O Agni, come for the feast; may the goddesses be for our protection"—this is said after [the first line], together with the ganas *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *sa*, *ta*, *ja*, *bha*, *na*, and *la*.

Then follows the *Sammita*, consisting of five chapters; after that, the *Samāmnāya* is recited. Then one should speak the *Śikṣā* again, having first uttered "I shall explain," and then recite "Vṛddhir ādaic."

Then, having uttered "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma," one should again recite "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (Athāto Brahmajijñāsā) and likewise the opening verses of the Vedas.
Brahmā, Indra, Sūrya, Soma, and Prajāpati; the Self, the Inner Self, and the Self of Knowledge beyond that.

Having recited the mantra of the Supreme Self, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, in the dative case, and then taking a handful of barley meal (*saktu*), he should proceed.

Then, having consumed [the remainder] with the *praṇava* alone and having sipped water twice, he should touch his navel while reciting the mantras to be described hereafter, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with the word "namaḥ."
Having recited "Ātmānam," "Antarātmānam," "Jñānātmānam," and again "Puram," one should then recite "Ātmānam" following the opinion of Prajāpati.

Thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] ending with "svāhā"; then, having consumed milk, curd, and ghee separately three times while uttering only the *praṇava*, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice again.
Then, sitting facing east with a firm mind and a steady posture, one should properly perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Renunciation," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.

Subrahmaṇya said: Then, at the time of midday, having bathed with a restrained mind, one should bring forth the materials for worship, such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). One should worship the Lord Vighneśa, who is adored by the gods, in the southwest (nairṛtya) direction; one should invoke him according to the proper rite with the mantra beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
Red in color and of great body, adorned with all ornaments, holding a noose, a goad, a rosary, and his desired object in his lotus-like hands.
Having thus invoked and meditated upon the elephant-faced son of Śambhu, one should worship him with milk-rice, cakes, coconut, jaggery, and other offerings.

One should offer the supreme food offering (naivedya), followed by betel leaves and other items; having satisfied [the deity] and offered salutations, one should then pray for the removal of obstacles.
