It should be performed in the *aupāsana* fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*; thereafter follows the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Āgneya sacrifice, ending with the portioning of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
Having offered the full oblation with the three-verse mantra "Bhūḥ Svāhā" and having completed it, one should recite the Gāyatrī without weariness until the afternoon.
Then, having performed the evening twilight devotion preceded by a bath, and having offered the evening *aupāsana* oblation, he should inform his guru while observing silence.

Having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) in this [fire], one should offer oblations with the *Raudra-sūkta* and with the five [mantras] beginning with *Sadyojāta*, according to the distinction of fuel-sticks, food, and clarified butter.
One should meditate upon Mahādeva together with Ambā in the fire while reciting the Brahma-mantras; having offered oblations with the mantra "Gaurīrmimāya," one should keep Gaurī in mind.

Then, one should offer a single oblation with the mantra, "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having offered it, the wise man should then perform the subsequent ritual procedure (tantra) to the north of the fire.
Seated upon a seat of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass, one should recite the Gāyatrī with a firm mind and in silence during the Brāhma-muhūrta.

Then, having bathed—or if unable to do so, having performed the rite with ashes according to the rules—he should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) on that fire or on another, and have it sprinkled with clarified butter.

Having taken it out with the *udag* [ladle] and placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should then pour clarified butter over the *caru*, recite the *vyāhṛtis*, the *raudra-sūkta*, and the five [verses].
Having fixed the mind upon the lotus feet of Śiva, one should mutter the Brahma-mantras; then Prajāpati, Indra, and thereafter the Viśvedevas.
Having recited the mantra for Brahmā ending with the dative case and followed by "svāhā," preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and having had it recited, one should thereafter perform the Puṇyāha ceremony.
Having first performed the *tantra* for Agni with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni" at the mouth of the fire, he should afterwards offer oblations with the five [mantras] beginning with "Svāhā to Prāṇa."
Thereafter, he should offer the *caru* oblation mixed with clarified butter into the fire as an offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; then he should again recite the Raudra hymn and the five Brahma-mantras.

One should again recite the mantras of the fourfold emanation (caturvyūha) beginning with Maheśa; having performed the oblation thereafter according to the method prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (tantra), one should proceed.
The wise one should perform [the rite] for each respective deity along with its ancillaries; thus is the ritual procedure, beginning with the "mouth of fire" (agnimukha), set in motion.
From this point forward, one should perform the Virajā-homa for the purification of oneself who has become dissolved within this body consisting of the twenty-six principles (tattvas).
Meditating thus: "May these principles within my body be purified," he [proceeds] there for the sake of purifying the *ātmatattva* with the *āruṇaketuka* mantras.

O Sage, while reciting [the names] in order from Earth up to Puruṣa, remaining silent and remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he should offer oblations with sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter.
Furthermore, there are the pentads beginning with earth and sound, as well as speech and the rest; and the fourfold group consisting of the head, the two sides, the back, and the belly.

Then one should join the calves, followed by the seven bodily constituents beginning with the skin; then the five vital breaths beginning with *prāṇa*, and finally the five sheaths beginning with food (*anna*).
Mind, consciousness, intellect, ego-sense, and indeed discernment, as well as volition—these are the qualities; thereafter come primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa).
However, for the Puruṣa who has attained the state of being an enjoyer, the pentad of principles is proclaimed as being internal with respect to that enjoyment.
Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, and Vidyā immediately following that, and Kalā—O Lord of Sages, this pentad was produced by me.
"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti"—thus Māyā is declared in the Śruti; there is no doubt that these principles (tattvas) born from it are also spoken of in the Śruti.
The Veda declares that Time, Nature, and Destiny [are its causes]; this very pentad is called its fivefold wheel.
Whether ignorant of the five principles or learned yet of deluded intellect, this person falls below primordial nature and remains above it.
Relying on the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), this principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) exists perpetually on both sides; it is said to consist of Śuddhavidyā and Maheśvara.
Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva—this is the pentad; this, O Brahman, is the Śiva-tattva, for Brahman is consciousness and restrained speech.
O Lord of Sages, let the purification of this entire collection of principles, beginning with earth and ending with Śiva, be performed by means of their dissolution into their respective causes.
For the eleven mantras, preceded by the *parasmaipada* [terminations], one should then utter this word "Śivajyotis" in the dative case.
One should say "not mine" afterwards; this is declared to be the renunciation of the dedication. Beyond this, there are the two mantras: "May he know it" and "To the pigeon."
At the end of the word *vyāpaka*, one should also add *paramātmane*; then the word *śivajyotis* in the dative case, followed again by the word *viśvabhūta*.
Then one should utter the word *ghasanotsuka* in the dative case (ending in *-e*), pronounce the term *parasmaipada*, and then utter the word *devāya*.
One should utter the word "Puruṣāya" for the mantra "uttiṣṭhasva" according to the Viśvarūpa [tradition], and one should recite "svāhā" for the mantra "osvāhā."
After the words "to the one pervading the three worlds," he should say, "to the Supreme Self, to Śiva—this [is for Him], not for me"; thereafter, he should utter the word "pada."

Having performed the ritual procedures prescribed in his own Vedic branch, and having first completed the tantric rites, he should consume the sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter and give a portion to the officiating priest.
One should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) augmented with gold and other items; then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should perform the morning aupāsana oblation.
A person should mutter the mantra "saṃ māṃ siñcantu marutaḥ" and then heat [the object] over the fire with the mantra "yāte agne".
Having placed his hand upon the fire within his own self, which is the abode of non-duality, he should then perform the morning twilight ritual and likewise worship the sun.
Having approached and entered the water, causing it to reach the level of his navel, he should recite those mantras with devotion, his mind steady and full of eagerness.

But he who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should duly perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice in the Śrauta Vaiśvānara fire, accompanied by the gift of all his possessions as the sacrificial fee.
Then, having internalized the sacred fire within himself, the Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home; reciting "Sāvitrī" first, he should pronounce the first quarter of the Sāvitrī verse.
I cause [the disciple] to enter at the end of the sound, and he should respond "Bhūḥ, Om. Having uttered the second foot, he should recite "Sāvitrī" as before.
I cause [the disciple] to enter at the end of the word; he should respond, "Bhuvar om. Then, having uttered the third foot, [he should recite] "Sāvitrīm" thereafter.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter at the end of the sound, uttering "Suvarom"; first one should recite the three-footed [Gāyatrī], and after that, the Sāvitrī.
"O Lord of Sages, with a steady mind and supreme affection, one should utter: 'I enter into the end of sound—bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ'."
This Blessed Lady is the manifest embodiment of half the body of Śaṅkara; she has five faces, ten arms, and is radiant with fifteen eyes.
Adorned with a crest-jewel of a crescent moon rising from her crown of nine gems, resembling pure crystal, she is auspicious and bears compassion as her weapon.
Her limbs were adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, tinkling bells, anklets, and the like; she was clothed in divine garments and decorated with jewel ornaments.
Śivā, who pervades the soul of all, is always to be served by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the leaders of the gods, sages, and gandharvas, as well as by human beings.

The beautiful Dharmapatnī of Lord Sadāśiva is the Mother of the World, the mother of the three worlds; she consists of the three qualities (triguṇā) yet is also beyond qualities (nirguṇā), unborn (ajā).
Having reflected thus, the wise man should then recite the Gāyatrī—the primordial goddess consisting of three feet, which bestows the status of Brahminhood and other virtues.
For that sinner who recites the Gāyatrī, which is the very form of Śiva, in any other manner, he is cooked in a most terrible hell for the duration of a kalpa.
She was born from the Vyāhṛtis and has gone to dissolution within them; they, in turn, were produced from the Praṇava and have gone to dissolution within the Praṇava.
The Praṇava is the beginning of all the Vedas; the Praṇava is the designator of Śiva; it is the king of kings among the sovereign mantras, the great seed-syllable, and the supreme mantra.
Śiva is indeed this Praṇava, and the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva; for there is no absolute difference between the signified and the signifier.
Having caused this very great mantra to be heard by living beings who cast off their bodies at Kāśī at the time of death, Śiva grants them supreme liberation.
Therefore, the best of ascetics worship that single-syllabled deity Śiva, the supreme cause, who resides in the center of the lotus of the heart.
Others, wise men of the world seeking liberation and free from passion, having understood sense objects through the mind, worship the supreme Śiva.
Having thus dissolved the Gāyatrī into the Praṇava, which denotes Śiva, one should again recite the Anuvāka beginning with "Ahaṃ vṛkṣasya rerivā."
Having recited the section beginning with "He who is the bull among the meters" and ending with "protect me," one should then say, "I have arisen."

O Sage, one should utter [the mantra] threefold according to the sequence of slow, medium, and fast elevations; first extracting the *praṇava* (Om) according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

Then, for them, [the earth] became increasingly vast in sequence; likewise, having said "The earth is renounced," he uttered the word "renounced" over the ground, saying "The good earth is renounced."
One should utter the word "by me" at the beginning of all mantras; having first extracted the *praṇava*, one should then recite the *vyāhṛtis* as a collective whole.
"Therefore, one should say 'all this,' and he replied, 'by me. Then, O Sage, having meditated upon Sadāśiva in his heart, he said, 'by me and others.'"
Having thus recited the Praiṣa mantras with a vigilant mind, while muttering "Fearlessness to all beings; from me, Svāhā!"—
Then, having drawn up water in the eastern direction, he should cast it as an añjali; likewise, wherever his topknot or sacred thread might be caught, he should pull them free with his hand.
Having taken hold of the *praṇava* (Om) and the word *bhūḥ*, one should say, "Go to the ocean," and then, having uttered the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), [one should offer] with a handful of water.

One should offer oblations into the waters, then consecrate them with the *preṣa* formulas; having sipped the water three times, one should come to the bank and discard one's clothes and other belongings upon the ground.
Facing either north or east, he should walk more than seven steps; then, after going a short distance, the teacher should say, "Stop! Stop!"
"For the sake of worldly convention, O Blessed One, please accept a loincloth and a staff"; saying this, one should give them with one's own hand.

Having given him a very fine loincloth and then a saffron-colored garment, and having clothed him and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should address the disciple in two ways as follows.
One should recite the mantra, "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra, O Father," and after making a formal request, one should take hold of the staff while muttering the verse, "O friend."
Then, having gone to the presence of the Guru while remembering the lotus feet of Śiva, he, with his self restrained, should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground three times.
Rising again slowly and gazing upon his own guru with affection, he should stand near the guru’s feet with his palms joined in reverence.
Having first taken auspicious cow dung before the commencement of the ritual, one should form balls the size of large myrobalan fruits and allow them to dry.

Having cast those [offerings] situated within the fire at the start of the oblation by means of the solar rays themselves, one should collect the ashes upon the completion of the oblation and preserve them.
Then, having taken white ash produced from stainless fire, the Guru [should apply] that very ash to the disciple in due order with the mantras beginning with "Agnis" (Agni).
Having touched the limbs with the [five] limb-mantras from the head down to the feet, and with the five mantras beginning with Īśāna, one should touch everywhere starting from the head.

Then, having extracted it according to the prescribed rite, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with the *triyāyuṣa* and *tryambaka* mantras, starting from the crown of the head and proceeding in due order.
Then, with a mind endowed with true devotion, that best of disciples should meditate upon Śiva, the consort of Umā, seated within the lotus of his heart.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, that guru should recite the Praṇava three times into the right ear, accompanied by the names of the Ṛṣis and other details.
Then, having cultivated compassion, the best of teachers should instruct the meaning of the *praṇava*, accompanied by a thorough understanding of its sixfold meaning.
Twelve times he should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground before his guru; he should remain perpetually dependent on him and perform no other action.

Then, by his command, the disciple, in accordance with the meaning of the Vedānta, should become intent upon the knowledge of Śiva through the distinction between the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa).

Then, the Guru should have that very disciple perform the morning rituals and other observances, preceded by the ancillaries such as listening (śravaṇa), up until the conclusion of the recitation (japa).
And the disciple should perform worship right there in that mandala called Kailāsaprastara, according to the path taught by Śiva.
If one is unable to worship the auspicious Lord daily through the preceptor, one should take up the Ishvara-linga made of crystal, provided with a pedestal.
Better for me the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of my head, than that I should eat without having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord.
Having thus uttered this oath three times in the presence of the Guru, the disciple, possessing a firm mind and bearing devotion to Śiva, should perform it.
Therefore, with a mind constantly disciplined, one should worship Mahādeva with supreme devotion according to the path of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vāmadeva said: O Blessed One, ocean of the nectar of all-encompassing knowledge, son of the Lord of all the immortals, destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before you!
What is described as the thorough knowledge of the sixfold meaning that bestows what is desired? O Lord, what are those sixfold meanings therein, and what is this thorough knowledge?
Who is the one to be instructed, and what is the fruit of that thorough knowledge? O Guha, explain all of this to me, whatever I have asked.
O Mahāsena, not understanding this truth and deluded by the scriptures of the beasts, I remain even now wandering in the illusion of Śiva.
Just as I shall become free from delusion by drinking the elixir of the nectar of knowledge of the pair of Śiva’s feet, so shall it be.
Having gazed upon me for a long time with a glance moistened by the nectar of compassion, please bestow Your grace upon me, who have come for refuge at Your glorious lotus feet.
Having heard these words spoken by the Lord of Sages, the omnipresent Jñānaśaktidhara spoke words that produce great terror in those who hold other views.

Subrahmaṇya said: O tiger among sages, listen with respect to that which you have asked: the thorough knowledge of the Great Lord in His aspects as both the collective whole and the individual manifestations.

O observer of noble vows, I shall explain in detail that which consists of the thorough knowledge of the meaning of the *praṇava*, through the complete understanding of the unity of its sixfold meanings.
The first is the form of the mantra; the second is that which is permeated by the mantra; the third is the meaning of the deity; and beyond that is the meaning of the phenomenal expansion.
The fourth is the meaning of the fifth [letter], which reveals the form of the Guru; the sixth is the meaning of the disciple’s own self-nature. Thus, the sixfold meanings have been proclaimed.
In this regard, O best of sages, I shall declare the true nature of mantra, by the mere knowledge of which a person becomes a possessor of great wisdom.
The first vowel, the fifth [vowel], that which follows the end of the fifth [vowel], and both the Bindu and the Nāda—these five syllables have been proclaimed by the Vedas and not otherwise.

Indeed, the Veda and so forth are declared to be the collective totality (samashṭi) of this; the Sound (nāda) would be the universal totality of all, which consists of the four [states] enriched by the Bindu.
O wise one, listen to the form of the yantra which is perfectly established within the *praṇava* that denotes Śiva as the individual aspect; for that indeed is the Śivaliṅga itself.
One should draw the pedestal at the very bottom; above that, the first vowel (a); above that, the letter u; and above that, the final letter of the pa-group (ma).
One should draw the bindu situated upon its head and the nāda above it; when this is complete within the yantra, all desires are fulfilled.

Having drawn this yantra, one should encircle it nine times with the *praṇava*; by means of the very resonance (*nāda*) arising from that, one should know [the mantra] ending with the resonance (*nāda*).
O Sage Vāmadeva, out of affection for you, I shall proclaim that which is everywhere hidden regarding the purpose of the deities, just as it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
Beginning with "I take refuge in Sadyojāta," the Śruti declares "Sadāśiva" as the loud mantra that denotes the fivefold Brahman.
These five subtle deities, whose nature is Brahman, should be known; they alone are augmented as the very forms of Śiva.
The mantra is the designator of Śiva and the designator of Śiva’s form; for there is no absolute difference between the form and that which possesses the form.
Beginning with "endowed with the crown of Īśāna," the form of Śiva has been previously described; now hear of his five faces.
Beginning from the fifth [face] and following the sequence starting with Sadyojāta, the five faces are described as extending from the top to the end of Īśāna.
Established in the state of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) of the Lord Īśāna itself is the tetrad of forms of Brahman, beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Sadyojāta.
O Sage, the collective totality (samāṣṭi) of the five Brahmans is known as Īśāna-Brahman; however, that which begins with Puruṣa and ends with Sadyojāta is their individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi).
This wheel, consisting of grace, is the cause of the five purposes; it is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, subtle, changeless, and free from affliction.
Grace is also twofold, having as its object concealment and so forth; and there is another Lord who bestows liberation from the higher and the lower upon living beings.
This is declared to be the twofold activity of Sadāśiva alone; even within the act of grace, there is the pentad of activities beginning with emanation belonging to the All-pervasive Lord.
O Sage, even there, the deities beginning with Sadyojāta have been proclaimed; they are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and always bestow the five auspicious blessings.
The wheel consisting of grace, composed of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta), and presided over by Sadāśiva, is called the supreme state.
This very state is to be attained by ascetics of purified soul, who are worshippers of Sadāśiva and whose minds are fixed on the Praṇava.
Having attained this very state together with him, O lords of sages, he enjoyed vast pleasures along with that god who possesses the form of Brahmā.
Indeed, at the occurrence of the great dissolution, those people attain equality with Śiva and do not fall again anywhere into the ocean of saṃsāra.
The eternal Śruti declares, "They [dwell] in the world of Brahmā"; for this indeed is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of even Śiva’s sovereignty.
The *Atharva-śikhā* declares that he is endowed with all sovereignty; indeed, they proclaim that he alone is the bestower of all sovereignty.
There exists no state superior to the state of *camaka*; indeed, the entire expansion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is seen as the unfolding of the fivefold Brahman.
Thus, the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti are considered to have arisen from the Brahmas; they consist of the nature of the subtle elements and are renowned as their causes.
O observer of noble vows, that which exists in fivefold states within this phenomenal world of gross form and essential nature is held to be the fivefold Brahman.
O best of sages, the pentad consisting of the person (puruṣa), the ear, speech, sound, and space is pervaded by Brahman in the form of Īśāna.
O Lord of Sages, the fivefold group consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti), skin, the hand, touch, and air is pervaded by Brahman alone in the form of the Puruṣa.
Ego-consciousness, as well as the eye, the foot, form, and fire—this pentad is pervaded by the Aghora-Brahman and is thus consecrated.
Intellect, the tongue, the anus, taste, and water—this pentad is eternally pervaded by Brahmā in the form of Vāmadeva.
The mind, the nose, the generative organ, smell, and the earth—this pentad is pervaded by Sadyojāta Brahmā; the universe consists of the five Brahmas.
The Praṇava, which denotes Śiva, is taught in the form of a yantra; it is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of the five syllables, consisting of the four [parts] beginning with the Bindu.
One should contemplate the form of the Yantra according to the path taught by Śiva, as the supreme Praṇava, the sovereign king of mantras, whose very nature is Śiva.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praṇava as the Form of Śiva," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Īśvara said: Thereafter, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the supreme method of creation for the fourfold group beginning with Maheśa and Sadāśiva.

Sadāśiva is the collective totality (samaṣṭi), the Lord who is the sovereign of space; from him alone, having attained the state of individuality (vyaṣṭi), arise the four [deities] beginning with Maheśa.
The emergence of Maheśa is from a thousandth part of Sadāśiva; because his face has the form of a person, he is also the lord of the wind.

Endowed with the power of *māyā* on the left, he is *sakala* (possessing all parts) and preeminent in action; the fourfold group beginning with Īśvara constitutes his very form of individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*).
Īśa, Viśveśvara, Paścāt, Parameśa, and thereafter Sarveśvara—this indeed is the supreme wheel of concealment (tirodhānacakra).

Concealment is divided into two kinds: one pertains to the sphere of Rudra and others, and the other pertains to the continuous stream of the class of bound souls (paśus) by way of embodied existence.
Intent on delighting in enjoyments until the moment of the equilibrium of karma, when that equilibrium occurs, he alone becomes the all-pervading Lord consisting of grace.
In that regard, all those deities who have been proclaimed as sovereign lords are in essence the Supreme Brahman; they are directly non-conceptual and free from all affliction.
The wheel consisting of concealment (tirobhāva) is composed of the power of tranquility (śāntikalā); this unsurpassed state is presided over by Maheśvara.
This very state is to be attained by those who serve the station of Maheśa; for the devotees of Maheśvara, it bestows liberation through the sequence of *sālokya*.
From a thousandth part of Maheśvara, the form of Rudra was born; he has the aspect of a non-terrible face and is the lord of the principle of fire (tejas).
The Lord, joined with Gaurī-Śakti on his left, is the agent of universal dissolution; from him arises the fourfold group beginning with Śiva, which constitutes his individualized form (vyaṣṭi-rūpa).
O Lord of Sages, Śiva, Hara, Mṛḍa, and Bhava have indeed known this wondrous, great, divine, and supreme wheel called Saṃhāra.

That withdrawal is declared by the wise to be threefold, according to the distinctions of the eternal and so forth: the eternal is known as the deep sleep of the individual soul (jīva), while that of the Creator is remembered as the occasional (naimittika).
But its dissolution is great, as shown by the Veda, for living beings whose births, sufferings, and so forth have been stilled, and whose selves are at rest.
O best of sages, for the sake of providing rest and as the cause for the ripening of karmas, withdrawal has been ordained in three ways by Rudra of immeasurable splendor.
This triad has been declared as the very functions of Rudra; however, for the All-pervasive Lord, there is a pentad of functions beginning with creation, even including withdrawal.
O Sage, the deities beginning with Bhava who reside there have been fully described; they are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and are the performers of grace for the worlds.
This wheel, known as Saṃhāra, consists of the aspects of Vidyā and Rūpa; it is presided over by Rudra, and this state is free from all affliction.
O Sage, this very state is to be attained by those who desire to worship Rudra; for that [attainment] grants the Rudras sālokya and, through the sequence [of stages], sāyujya.
The birth of Viṣṇu arose from a thousandth part of Rudra’s form; he is the soul of Vāmadeva and the Discus, and the sole leader of the water-element.
Joined with the power of Ramā on his left, the great one who provides all protection has four arms, lotus-like eyes, a dark complexion, and bears the conch and other emblems.
This very [reality] has become the fourfold group beginning with Vāsudeva in its individualized form; it indeed bestows liberation upon Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to its worship.
Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, then the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Pradyumna—this is known as the unsurpassed wheel of maintenance (sthiticakra).
The maintenance of the created world together with its creator, and the protection of living beings who experience the fruits [of their actions] until the exhaustion of their commenced karma.

This task has been described as belonging solely to Viṣṇu, the protector; yet for the All-pervading Lord, the fivefold set of tasks beginning with creation also exists during the state of maintenance.
There, those deities headed by Pradyumna are celebrated; they are free from conceptual construction, devoid of fear, and always bestowing the bliss of liberation.
O Brahman, this wheel of sustenance (sthiti-cakra) is the supreme form of establishment; presided over by Janārdana, it is called the highest state.
This wheel of the Vaiṣṇavas, which bestows the states of sālokya and the others, is the very state to be attained by those who serve the lotus feet of Viṣṇu.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) was born from a thousandth part of Viṣṇu himself; he is the essence of whose face is Sadyojāta and who is the leader of the earth-element.
Accompanied by Vāgdevī on his left, the Lord of the World is the creator of emanation; he has four faces, is red in color, and possesses the very nature of the quality of passion (rajas).
The fourfold individualized form (vyaṣṭi-rūpa) of this very [unmanifest] consists of Hiraṇyagarbha, Virāṭ, Puruṣa, and Kāla.
O Brahmin, this wheel of creation is served by the sons of Brahmā and other sages; it bestows all desired objects and grants the happiness of one’s retinue.

Creation, however, consists in bringing this soul—which had been withdrawn into its primordial nature (prakṛti)—outward again, together with the means, the limbs, and the fruits, for the sake of experiencing the results of its karma.
Those who understand the process of world-creation know that this act of "conjunction" (saṃyojana) is the duty of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which brings happiness to the entire cosmic manifestation.
O Sage, even in the creation of the world, the fivefold functions of the Lord exist; therein, the emergence of Time is proclaimed as the presiding deities.
This wheel of emanation is declared by the wise to be of the nature of cessation; and this beautiful station is presided over by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
This very state is to be attained by those men whose intellects are offered to Brahman; for this [state] of the descendants of Pitāmaha bestows liberation, such as Sālokya and the rest.
In this tetrad as well, the Praṇava (Oṃ) shall be the [seed-syllable] of the wheels; by virtue of the sequence beginning with Maheśa, it is their designator through figurative usage.
O Sage, the Veda indeed praises this wheel of the world, whose majesty is renowned in the scriptures, as the "five-spoked wheel."
The single wheel of the universe, which is the manifestation of Śambhu’s power and possesses the five components beginning with creation, is called the five-spoked wheel (pañcāra).
Because it revolves all around with uninterrupted dissolution and emergence, like the whirling of a firebrand, it is therefore called a "wheel" (cakra).
Because it is the vast creation of the primordial creator, it is perceived as something vast—the creation of the golden god Śambhu, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
This wheel, which is the effect of Śakti, rests upon the golden light; this is enveloped by water, and the water is enveloped by fire.

Fire is enveloped by air; the Great Principle (mahat) is enveloped by space (ākāśa); likewise, space is enveloped by the origin of the elements (bhūtādi), and the origin of the elements is enveloped by the Great Principle.
O best of sages, the teachers who follow the path of the faithful have declared that the Mahat is likewise enveloped by the Unmanifest; this is what is called the "Cosmic Egg" (Brahmāṇḍa).
The seven enclosures have been described for the protection of this universe; it is ordained that the water [enclosure] possesses a power ten times greater than the wheel.
O leader of sages, it should be understood by the twice-born that the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) increases tenfold at each successive level above one another.
Accepting this meaning, the Śruti itself declares that [the soul] "dwells near the wheel" and "in the midst of the water."
The one Śiva, endowed with power, incessantly performs his divine play through grace, concealment, withdrawal, maintenance, and creation.
O Sage, what is the use of much speaking here? I shall tell you the essence: it is certain that this entire universe is Śiva alone, endowed with power.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Forms for Worship," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said: Having heard the meaning of the Vedas as instructed by his teacher, that bull among sages respectfully inquired about what remained doubtful regarding the Supreme Self.
Vāmadeva said: O Lord, wielder of the power of knowledge, embodiment of supreme bliss! The nectar of the meaning of the Praṇava has been drunk, flowing forth from the lotus of Your glorious mouth.
I have become firm in wisdom and my doubt has vanished. O Mahāsena, I ask you one further thing; listen, O Lord.
The persistence of the universe, which ranges from Sadāśiva down to an insect, is seen everywhere in the form of male and female; of this there is no doubt.
Is that eternal cause of the world of such form female, or is it male, or perhaps neuter?
Whether it be mixed or something else entirely, no certainty has arisen in that regard; for here, learned men, deluded by the scriptures, dispute in many ways.

Indeed, even the Vedic scriptures that ordain the creation of the world, along with Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and other gods, as well as the Siddhas, do not know [the ultimate reality] together with the world itself.
Make known this and other matters so that they may attain a state of unity; for the worldly convention, "I know" and "I act," is clearly observed.
For that dispute, which arises from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and ego, is established as the self of all; thus, there is no dispute here for anyone.
Or is it the form of the Self? Here too there is great doubt; for both of these are wonderful subjects of dispute for everyone.
Having uprooted the poisonous tree known as doubt, which arises from ignorance, may it become the ground for the great kalpa-tree of the non-duality of Śiva.
O Lord, according to my mind, may I be awakened by your compassion; through your grace, O Lord of Gods, may I become one possessed of firm knowledge.
Sūta said: Having heard these words thus questioned by the sage, which were grounded in Vedānta, the Lord, with a slightly smiling face, spoke this secret.
Subrahmaṇya said: O Vāmadeva, this very secret was indeed expounded by Śiva to me as well, while the Goddess Ambā was listening.
Having drunk her milk then, I was repeatedly satisfied; having heard that which is indeed immovable, it has been firmly resolved by me through reflection.
Out of compassion for you, O Vāmadeva, great sage, I shall tell you that which is a supreme and profound secret; my son, listen now.

O Sage, there exists a very extensive scriptural discourse concerning karma from the perspective of ultimate reality; it should be heard by the wise seeker of knowledge according to their discernment, for it bestows wisdom.
Among those disciples instructed by you, who indeed is equal to you? Even today, those base ones continue to wander in delusion regarding the scriptures of Kapila and others.
In former times, those six who were intent on reviling Śiva were cursed by the sages: "Indeed, their news must not be heard, for they speak otherwise than the truth."
There is no scope even for the application of inference consisting of five members; rather, that [inference] arises from the perception of smoke.
O observer of noble vows, they say that even here there is the presence of fire in the mountain; therefore, it serves as the objective basis for the perception of this manifest world.
The Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, is to be known without a doubt; the universe, consisting of the forms of male and female, is perceived directly through perception itself.
For the physical body consists of six sheaths; among these, three arise from the maternal portion, while another three arise from the paternal portion—so says the sacred tradition.
O Sage, just as people perceive the states of female and male in all bodies, so too do the wise perceive the states of female and male even in the Supreme Self.
The Śruti declares that Brahman has the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss; the word "Being" (sat) is spoken of as the Self in order to exclude non-existence.
The cessation of the state of being the world is enjoined by the word "cit"; let the word "sat," which exists in three genders, be understood here as referring to the Puruṣa.
It is clear that the word *sat* denotes light; the word *cit*, which is a synonym for the word *jñāna*, has acquired a feminine gender.

Light and consciousness, as a couple, have attained the state of being the cause of the universe; likewise, within the *saccidātman* (the Being-Consciousness-Self), they have attained the state of being the cause of the universe.
In one and the same place, the state of Śiva and Śakti is established; even for light, there exists [a dependence] due to the impurity of the oil, the wick, and so forth.
Impurity and inauspiciousness are observed in funeral pyres and the like; likewise, auspiciousness is enjoined by the Śruti through the principle of illusory manifestation (vivarta).

The power of consciousness residing in the individual soul (jīva) is always subject to weakness; it is precisely for the sake of its removal that its nature as power (śaktitva) is eternal in this context.
O great sage Vāmadeva, the conventional usage "one who is strong" and "one who is powerful" is constantly observed in both the world and the Veda.
Thus, the nature of Śiva and the nature of Śakti have been shown within the Supreme Self; from the union of Śiva and Śakti, bliss is eternally arisen.
Therefore, O Sage, having fixed their minds on Śiva with reference to Him, the sages whose impurities were exhausted attained the auspicious state that is free from all ailment.

Thus, the state of being the self of all belongs to those two alone; and in the Upaniṣads, it is celebrated by the word "Brahman," which falls within the semantic range of the verbal root *bṛh* (to expand).

The quality of nourishment and the state of vastness reside in the form known as Śambhu, which consists of the five Brahmans; the perception of the universe therein is designated by the word "Brahman."
O Vāmadeva, out of affection for you, I shall explain the origin of the Praṇava within the Haṃsa that consists of the reverse order; listen with attentiveness.
By the removal of the consonants *sa* and *ha*, the gross designator of the Supreme Self becomes simply "Oṃ."
The Great Mantra is to be understood by the sages who perceive reality; therein lies the subtle Great Mantra, and I shall describe its extraction to you.
When the first [syllable] consists of the three and five forms, and when the sixteenth vowel occurs in the three [positions], the Great Mantra comes first; that is when it becomes the syllable *sa*.
The reverse of *haṃsa* would be *sakāra*; its meaning is traditionally held to be Śiva. It is the essence of power (*śakti*), expressible by the Great Mantra; such is the definitive conclusion.

But at the time of the Guru’s instruction, when [the disciple realizes], "I am Śiva, consisting of the power of 'so'ham'," then the Great Mantra becomes both the individual soul and the Supreme, and the bound soul (paśu) is liberated.

Being of the nature of power (śakti) and a portion of Śiva, he partakes in equality with Śiva due to his oneness with Śiva; for in the statement "Brahman is consciousness" (prajñānaṃ brahma), the meaning of "consciousness" (prajñāna) is clearly perceived.
The word *prajñāna* is undoubtedly a synonym for consciousness (*caitanya*). O Sage, the *Śivasūtra* has been established thus: "Consciousness is the Self."
Consciousness is that sovereignty which consists of all knowledge and action throughout the universe; that which is its essential nature is proclaimed to be the Self (Ātman).
Thus has the commentary (*vārtika*) on the *Śivasūtras* and so forth been told by me; "Knowledge is bondage"—this is the second sūtra of the Lord.

"Knowledge is that which belongs to the Self and consists of some degree of the activity of knowing"—thus the Lord, by means of the first term, has stated the defining characteristic of the class of bound souls (paśu).
This dyad has first attained the state of vibration from the Supreme Power (parā-śakti). It is precisely this Supreme Power that the followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch [revere].
And they joyfully praised the innate power of knowledge and action; for the wise know that Śambhu’s threefold vision consists of knowledge, action, and will.
Having entered into this [Self] which resides within the mind and is the constant object of the senses and their cognitions, the bound soul (paśu) always knows and acts.

Therefore, having firmly ascertained that this [universe] is indeed the form of the Self alone, I shall explain the demonstration of the oneness with the Praṇava for the sake of the expansion [of understanding].
"Oṃ, this all is Brahman"—thus says the eternal Śruti; and beginning with "From that [Brahman]," the creation of the world is proclaimed.
O Vāmadeva, out of affection for you, I shall state the purport of that Śruti, which is manifested for the sake of discernment; listen to this.
It is certain that the union of Śiva and Śakti is the Supreme Self; from the Supreme Śakti, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is born, and she arises from Him.

O Sage, from that [Ātman] arises the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti); from that, the power of will (icchā-śakti) is born; from that, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is produced; and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is the fifth. From these very [powers], O Sage, the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti are born.

Nāda and Bindu are proclaimed to have arisen from the bliss of consciousness (cidānanda); the letter 'M' belongs to the power of will (icchā-śakti), while the fifth [letter] belongs to the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
O Lord of Sages, the vowel 'a' is indeed born from the power of action (kriyā-śakti); thus has been described the origin of the Praṇava. Now hear the emergence of the five Brahmans.
From Śiva, Īśāna was born; from him, Tatpuruṣa arose; from him, Aghora; from him, Vāma; and from him, Sadyojāta was born.
From this Mātṛkā arises the origin of the thirty-eight Mothers. From Īśāna is born the Kalā called Śāntyatītā; then from Puruṣa the Śānti-kalā is produced, and Vidyā originates from Aghora.
In the Sadyodbhava system, Vāmā is considered Pratiṣṭhā and Sadyojāta is Nivṛtti; from the pervasive Lord (Īśa) through the mouth of Cit-śakti, there arises this pentad of couples.
The group of five is held by wise sages who know it and who reveal the supreme reality to be the cause of activities such as bestowing grace.

In this pentad, whose nature consists of the digits (kalās) and phonemes (varṇas), which has attained the state of a couple through the relationship of the signified and the signifier, lies the pentad of the elements (bhūtas).
O bull among sages, space and the other elements arose in succession; they know that which consists of the fifth [element], beginning from the primordial pair.
Space has sound as its sole quality; wind possesses the qualities of sound and touch; fire is said to have sound, touch, and form as its primary qualities.
Water is traditionally held to possess the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; earth is traditionally held to be enriched with sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
This alone is proclaimed as the pervasiveness of the elements; their state of being pervaded occurs in the reverse order, starting from smell and so forth.
This phenomenal world is proclaimed to consist of the five elements; it is clearly known as Virāṭ, the universal aggregate-self, and as the Brahmāṇḍa (the cosmic egg).
Beginning from the earth-principle (pṛthivītattva) up to the Śiva-principle (śivatattva), the individual soul (jīva) indeed dissolves by merging sequentially into the aggregate of principles.
Furthermore, at the time of re-creation, he who possesses power emerges through the gateway of Śakti and remains happily in the form of the gross phenomenal world until the dissolution.
The first vibration of the Great Lord, who is intent on creating the universe by His own will, is called the Śiva-tattva.

This very [power] is the principle of the power of will (*icchā-śakti-tattva*), because it follows after all actions; when the pair of the powers of knowledge and action is present, Sadāśiva exists when there is a predominance of knowledge.
O Lord of Sages, know that Maheśvara is the principle (tattva) in the predominance of action; the equilibrium of the powers of knowledge and action is considered to be the nature of Śuddhavidyā.
When Śiva perceives the distinction of the principle of Māyā within the entities that constitute his own body, he [manifests] his own form preceded by supreme sovereignty.
Having restrained [the intellect] through Māyā, one becomes the grasper of all objects; then the Śruti declares, "Having created that, he became known as Puruṣa."
For this very transmigrating being is a beast deluded by illusion; indeed, being devoid of the knowledge of Śiva, his intellect is utterly bewildered by various karmas.
For this bound soul (paśu) who perceives the world as non-different from Śiva, yet also as different from his own self, delusion persists; it does not exist for the Lord (prabhu).
Just as even a master of illusion would have no delusion, so too one who has been granted sovereign power by the Guru becomes Śiva, a mass of consciousness.
She is the embodiment of universal agency and the very nature of omniscience; she is the form of perfection and the essence of eternity and omnipresence.
The five powers of Śiva are suns whose form is contracted.

They shine eternally even in the form of contraction; for the bound soul (paśu), there are those called *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*. Here, that which is called *kalā* exists in the form of this pentad of principles (*tattva*).
That which is the cause of limited agency is the means for achieving a specific reality; that indeed is knowledge (vidyā), while passion (rāga) is that which causes attachment to sense objects.
For time, which consists of the manifestation of manifestations and entities, is called "the past" and so forth by becoming that which delimits succession.
This regulating power of the Lord, which determines "this must be done by me" and "this must not be done," is Niyati; through its impulsion, the bound soul (paśu) falls [into bondage].
This very pentad, because it conceals His true nature, is called the "fivefold sheath" (pañcakañcuka), and it is the internal means [of obscuration].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śiva-Tattva," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vāmadeva said: "Previously you stated that the Puruṣa stands above Prakṛti and below Niyati; how is it now otherwise?"
"O Lord, that [universe] exists beneath that [foundation] as a form contracted by māyā; O Protector, you ought to sever this doubt of mine according to the truth."
Śrī Subrahmaṇya said: This doctrine of Advaita Śaivism does not tolerate duality anywhere; duality is perishable, whereas the non-dual Brahman is supreme and imperishable.
Śiva is omniscient and the creator of all, the Lord of all, devoid of [material] qualities; he is Brahmā, the progenitor of the three gods, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That very Lord Śaṅkara, by his own will and through his own māyā, became a Puruṣa, as if assuming a contracted form.
Determined as an enjoyer by means of the pentad beginning with *kalā*, this person, abiding in *prakṛti*, experiences the qualities born of *prakṛti*.
Thus, the Person situated within these two states is not contradictory; he is the aggregate of his own contracted forms, such as knowledge and the rest.

And that principle of the mind, which consists of the triad beginning with intellect (buddhi) and is to be accomplished through the qualities such as sattva, existed as the primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva) due to its causes being sattva and the other qualities.

The qualities (guṇas) arising from primordial nature (prakṛti) are distinguished as sāttvika and so forth; from these qualities, the intellect (buddhi) is produced, which effects the determination of objects.
From that arises the great ego (mahān-ahaṅkāra), and from that the sense organs; the form of the mind (manas) is born as conceptualization and discrimination (saṃkalpa-vikalpaka).
The organs of cognition are the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose; and their respective objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Then, from the *vaikārika* ego, the sense organs were said to arise in the order beginning with the ear; subsequently, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) arose in sequence from that same ego.
These subtle organs of action have been declared by the seers who perceive reality; they are to be known together with their respective functions.
O brahmin-sage, the organs of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, along with their respective functions, are designated as speaking, grasping, locomotion, excretion, and sexual pleasure.

From the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) consisting of the *bhūta-ādi* (the origin of elements), the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) arose in succession; it is established that these are the subtle forms of sound and the other [sensory objects].
From these, O tiger among sages, the birth of space, air, fire, water, and earth occurs in succession; this is recognized as the five elements.
Providing space, carrying [the water], and purifying; their agitation and their flow—these are proclaimed as their functions.
Vāmadeva said: "The creation of beings from the *kalās* and other principles was previously described; how is it now described otherwise, O Skanda? I have a great doubt in this matter."

The letter *A* shall be the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), and beyond that, the letter *U* shall be the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*). The letter *M* shall be the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*); let it be contemplated as Vāmadeva.
The Bindu and the Nāda should both be understood as containing the meaning of all the Tattvas; O Sage, now hear from me concerning the deities residing therein.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva—these are indeed the manifest forms of Śiva himself, as renowned in the Vedas.
Thus was it stated by you previously, yet now it is said otherwise; that [the elements] arise from the tanmātras—this is the source of my great doubt.
"O Skanda, having shown compassion for that, you ought to sever his doubt. Having heard these words of the sage, Kumāra replied:
Śrī Subrahmaṇya said: O Sage, O one of great wisdom, listen attentively and with care from the beginning of the verse starting with "tasmād vā" regarding the sequence of the creation of beings.
It is certain that the five elements were born from the *kalās*; these elements, which constitute the form of the gross phenomenal world, are the body of the Lord of Beings (*Bhūtapati*).

O Sage, in the sequence of the emergence of the principles (tattvas) from Śivatattva down to Earth, it must be stated that [the gross elements] arise from the subtle elements (tanmātras) in due order.

O best among the knowers of Brahman, understand that here there is no contradiction: the unification of the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the creative powers (kalās) constitutes the cause of the gross elements.
Within this universe, consisting of both the gross and the subtle, the planets such as the moon and the sun, along with the constellations and other hosts of luminaries, have come into being.
The deities beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; the various classes of elemental beings; even Indra and the other guardians of the quarters; the gods, the ancestors, and the asuras.
Rākṣasas, humans, and others belonging to the category of the mobile—beasts, birds, insects, and the various kinds of serpents and the like.
The trees, shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs; the eight renowned mountains; the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā; and the oceans of great prosperity.
Whatever collection of things exists, all that is established herein; it should be investigated with a discerning intellect, not by looking outward, O best of sages.
This universe, appearing in the forms of male and female, consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti; it should be worshipped by the wise like you, who are proficient in the knowledge of Śiva.
"One should meditate upon everything as Brahman, and likewise, 'Everything is indeed Rudra'—thus says the Śruti, O Sage; therefore, Sadāśiva is the self of the phenomenal world."
Through the power of the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās, the non-dual realization arises: "I am indeed Sadāśiva. Thus, the Guru, whose nature is realized, is Śiva.
A true disciple who reflects in this manner shall himself become Śiva; he is undoubtedly the very essence of the phenomenal world, the deities, the yantras, and the mantras.
O Brahmin, with all his bonds severed by means of the form of the Teacher, the disciple, devoted to the state of Śiva, certainly becomes one whose self is the Guru.
Whatever entity exists, all of that—whether taken collectively or individually—is declared to be the meaning of the Praṇava, by virtue of its connection with the predominance of [its] qualities.
Śiva, the essence of the Vedas, who is free from defects such as passion, has out of affection taught you this non-dual knowledge dear to Śiva.
For whoever, intoxicated by pride in me, thinks otherwise of these words of mine—be it a god, a human, a siddha, a gandharva, or even a mortal.
I shall certainly sever the head of that evil-souled one with my true power, which is like the fire of time at the end of an aeon for his enemies; of this there is no doubt.
O Sage, you alone are the manifest preeminent among those who know the non-duality of Śiva; for you are the instructor of the knowledge of Śiva and the demonstrator of the conduct of Śiva.
Through contact with the ashes of your body, that impure great piśāca, whose multitude of sins was severed, attained the goal of the virtuous by your grace.
You are the one known as Śivayogin, whose glory pervades the three worlds; through contact with the glance of your eye, even a bound soul (paśu) becomes the Lord of Beings (Paśupati).
Out of respect for you, he has directed his gaze toward me for the sake of instructing the world; for virtuous ones wander here in this world performing deeds that benefit all beings.
This supreme secret is firmly established in you; therefore, you too, with faith and devotion, should respectfully apply yourself to the *praṇavas* alone.
Having seated them all and united them with the Supreme Lord, cause them to adopt the conduct of Śiva, which is characterized by the application of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
For you are indeed Śiva, acting with auspicious conduct, having attained the state of non-duality; wander for the protection of the world and attain imperishable happiness.

Sūta said: Having heard this wonderful doctrine spoken by the Six-faced One, which is firmly established in Vedānta, the sage, with a bowed body, prostrated himself many times on the ground like a staff; thus, by sporting within the lotus-feet of that Lord, he attained the state of a bee.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of Creation Beginning with the Exposition of the Knowledge of Śiva’s Non-duality," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Śaunaka said: Having heard that essence of Vedānta, its most wonderful secret, what did Vāmadeva then ask the son of Maheśvara?
Blessed is the yogi Vāmadeva, who is ever devoted to the knowledge of Śiva; through his connection, this divine and supremely purifying narrative has arisen.
Having heard those words of the sages, which were imbued with affection, the wise Sūta, his mind devoted to Śiva, spoke to them with a serene heart.
Sūta said: Blessed are you, devotees of Mahādeva who benefit the world; O all you sages, listen once more to the dialogue between those two.
Having heard the words of the son of Maheśa, which destroy duality and generate the knowledge of non-duality, the great sage became satisfied.
Having bowed to and praised Kārttikeya, the son of Śiva, in various ways, the great sage again questioned him about the truth with humility.
Vāmadeva said: O Blessed One, knower of all principles, ocean of nectar for the six-faced one, how is it that these ascetics of purified souls possess the status of gurus?
By virtue of which the attainment of enjoyment, liberation, and so forth for living beings is accomplished—without this lineage, there is no eligibility for instruction.
"And how is it that the bath, which is a part of the rite of shaving, is of such a nature? O Lord, please explain this so that you may dispel our doubt."
Having heard these words of Vāmadeva and recollecting them, Kārttikeya began to describe Śiva and Śivā in his mind.
Śrī Subrahmaṇya said: O Vāmadeva, out of affection for you, I shall explain the yoga-band by which the status of a Guru is attained; it is a great secret that bestows liberation.
In the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, as well as Āśvayuja, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, or Māgha, on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight.
On the fifth lunar day or the full moon, having performed the morning rites, and having received permission from the Guru, he should bathe with a restrained mind.
Having performed the purification of the bed and wiped his limbs with those same cloths, he should fasten a double-stranded cord around his arm and put on two garments.

Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice, he should take up the sacred ash with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras and apply it according to the method of *samuddhūlana*.
O Sage, with his hand taken by a favorable guru, that good disciple, with palms joined together, should stand facing the east.
Thus wrapped, he should remain in the well-decorated pavilion upon an excellent, pure seat for the Guru, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kuśa grass.
Then the preceptor, having taken the conch along with its stand and purified it with the Astra-mantra, should place it before him in a favorable position.
Having worshipped the conch along with its base with flowers and other offerings, one should pour into it pure water that has been purified by the *astra* and *varma* mantras.

Having filled [the vessel] and worshipped it as before, and according to the sequence prescribed for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should then consecrate that very [vessel] seven times with the Praṇava.
Having worshipped [the conch] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having presented incense and lamps, one should protect that conch with the Astra-mantra and then veil it with the Varma-mantra.
Then the preceptor should display the mudrās known as the Dhenu and the Śaṅkha; again, he should place the conch in front of himself in the excellent southern location.

One should fashion a beautiful and auspicious maṇḍala according to the prescribed rules for worship and the offering of arghya, and one should worship it with fragrant flowers and other such offerings.
The vessel, which has a common base, is cleansed, pure, adorned with a cloth and thread, fumigated, consecrated, and filled with pure, scented water.
O Lord of Sages, one should smear that [image] with the five barks, the five leaves, the five types of earth, and combined with fragrant substances.
Then, one should thoroughly decorate that jar with cloths, mango leaves, tips of dūrvā grass, coconuts, flowers, and other such articles.
O Lord of Sages, one should place five jewels in that jar, or else, in their absence, one should devoutly place gold there.
The gem called nīla, as well as ruby, gold, coral, and gomedaka—these are known as the five gems.
Having uttered "nṛmlaskam" and then "glūm" at the end, the preceptor, being well-disposed and acting with affection according to the proper ritual procedure, should perform the worship.
Beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) according to the prescribed rules for worship, one should invoke and worship the deity by way of the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa).
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), betel leaves, and other items as before, and having performed the worship up to the end of the eight-name rite, one should consecrate him with mantras.
One should recite the Praṇava one hundred and eight times with the five Brahma-mantras in sequence, from Sadyojāta to Īśāna; furthermore, the weapon (astra) is protected by the armor (varman).
Having veiled [the deity] and then presented incense and lamps with devotion, one should properly display there the mudrās known as the Cow and the Yoni.
Then the preceptor, having covered his head with *darbha* grass, should fashion a square in the northeastern portion of the mandala.
Having prepared a beautiful seat above that according to the prescribed rite, he should establish the disciple there, treating him like a child with great kindness.

Then, having lifted up the pitcher and preceded by the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), the preceptor should consecrate the disciple by pouring water over his head while moving clockwise.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* seven times with the [seven] Brahma-mantras, one should then surround [the deity] with conch-water at the conclusion of the fivefold consecration (*pañcābhiṣeka*).
Then, having shown him the beautiful island and wiped him with a cloth, one should cause him to put on a new waistband, loincloth, and two garments.
Having washed his feet and sipped water twice, the preceptor, smeared with sacred ashes, took the child by both hands and led him into the center of the pavilion.
Then, having smeared that ash upon his limbs according to the prescribed rite, the Guru, having led him onto the prepared seat, should settle him there comfortably.
To the disciple who faces the east and desires knowledge of his own true nature, the Guru, seated upon his own seat, should say to him: "Become one whose self is stainless."
And the Guru, with a mind hidden from the world, should properly practice meditative absorption (samādhi) for a muhūrta, remaining firm in the conviction, "I am Śiva, perfectly complete."
Afterwards, opening his eyes with a favorable mind, he should look upon the pure disciple who stands with palms joined in reverence, remaining unperturbed.
Having placed his hand—smeared with white ash—upon the head of the child, he should clearly instruct him into the mantra "Haṃsaḥ so 'ham" at the right ear.
Therein, the meaning of the first word "I" (aham) is Śiva himself, whose nature is power; contemplate your own self as "I am that very Śiva."
He who, having thus taught the true meaning of the subtle [self], should then respectfully explain the intended meaning of the intermediate statements.
O Brahmin, I shall speak these words to you; listen with an attentive mind. Indeed, retain them in your heart, for he will speak them clearly.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiating a Disciple," in the *Sannyāsapaddhati* (Manual on Renunciation) within the *Kailāsasaṃhitā*, the sixth book of the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
The meaning of the Vedic statement "Brahman is consciousness" has already been explained: it is the Supreme Lord, whose nature is power, who constitutes the referent of the word "I."
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, and the ultimate Śiva; the letter Ha is of the nature of space and is proclaimed to be the essence of Śakti.
From the union of Śiva and Śakti, bliss is eternally manifest; it is clear that Brahman is the universal selfhood of both Śiva and Śakti.
One should contemplate that very thing previously taught as "I am That. In the phrase "That Thou Art," the meaning of the word "That" has been explained.

Otherwise, in the expression "he is I," there would be a cultivation of a contrary meaning; for the word "I" refers to the person (puruṣa), whereas "that" (tad) would be neuter. Thus, due to their mutual contradiction, no syntactic connection between the two could exist.
Otherwise, the world consisting of the forms of female and male would have no cause; thus, "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is the contemplation of the meaning of the instruction.
In the statement "This is the Self," the two words [denoting] the male form [are used]; because it must be protected by the Lord, this world is certainly under the Lord's control.

One should reflect that "whatever is here as the self consisting of wisdom, that is indeed there"; this is what is stated here by the learned proponents of established doctrine: "He who is here is that very same one."
And regarding the statement "he who was there above is now situated here," the meaning is exactly as before: that the Puruṣa is so understood by the wise.
"That is indeed other than the known, and also other than the unknown"—in this statement, there is also the discernment of the reversal of the fruit.
O Sage, listen as I shall explain here exactly how this is so: the word "from the unknown" (aviditāt) is used here just as "from the known" (viditāt) was used previously.
Activity may proceed from that which is known, and likewise from that which is unknown; however, it is certain that something entirely other than these is required for the attainment of perfection.
This is your inner controller (antaryāmī), who is himself the immortal and auspicious Śiva; he who is Śambhu residing within the person and he who is established in the sun.

That which is both "he" and "she" is distinct; he is not one, for he is said to be everything. The meaning of this is that there are two with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), which are spoken of in that way through metaphorical designation (upacāra).
The Vedas indeed describe that Śambhunātha as golden; the phrase "golden-armed" is an indicative mark for his entire body.
Otherwise, his status as that Lord would not be possible; thus, this Śambhu, who is heard of in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as "He who is within," is Śiva.
Likewise, he has a golden beard and golden hair; from the tips of his nails to the ends of his hair, he is golden throughout.
"I am the Supreme Brahman, higher than the high and the high beyond the highest"—hear this, for I shall state the intended meaning of this statement.
Śiva, whose nature is power (śakti), is said to be the referent of the word "I"; the application of the meaning of the sentence "I am indeed He" is thus certain.
He is declared to be the Supreme Brahman, the most excellent of all and the soul of all; he is threefold: as the Higher (para), the Lower (apara), and the Higher-than-the-Higher (parātpara).
Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu have been declared by the Śruti itself and not otherwise; and the Supreme Lord who is higher than them is indicated by the word "para" (the Supreme).
Through the words of the Vedas, the scriptures, and the gurus, and by the power of self-restraint, Śambhu, who consists of perfect bliss, shall manifest within the heart of the disciple.
Śambhu abides within all beings, and he is indeed I; of this there is no doubt. Of the entire collection of principles, I am the vital breath; I am Śiva.

Having spoken thus, Śiva spoke again concerning the three principles: "O Sage, because in the statement 'I am the vital breath' (prāṇo'smi), there is the inclusion of everything from earth up to the qualities."
Meditate that all the principles of the self (ātmatattva) have been grasped; furthermore, there is a further grasping of the principles of knowledge (vidyātattva) and Śiva.

I am the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of these two principles (*tattva*), for I am everything and the Self of all; and because I am the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), I am always the soul of that [soul].
Whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—all that is indeed myself; because everything consists of me, I am all, and indeed, all is Rudra.
O Sage, Śruti declares that she is indeed the direct emergence from the mouth of Śiva; for she is the Self of all, by virtue of her eternal conjunction with these supreme qualities.
Indeed, because there is no other self apart from my own, I alone am non-dual; the meaning of the statement "All this is indeed Brahman" was explained previously.
I am full because of my nature as pure being; indeed, I alone am eternally liberated. By my grace, the bound souls (paśus) become liberated, having taken refuge in my own state of being.
"He who is Śambhu, the soul of all, he am I; I am that Śiva"—this indeed is the meaning of all statements uttered by Śiva to Vāmadeva.
Thus, with reverence, the Guru should instruct the disciple in the meaning taught by both the *Īśa-śruti* and the *Vākya*, which grants men direct identity with Śiva.
Having taken up the conch along with its stand, having purified it with ashes using the weapon-mantra, and having placed it before one in a consecrated square mandala;
Having worshipped with "Oṃ" using perfumes and other offerings, and having adorned it with cloth, one should fill it with scented water and worship it with the mantra "Oṃ."
Then, having consecrated it seven times with the Praṇava, he who perceives even the slightest difference therein becomes a partaker of great fear.
"Thus has the true essence of the Śruti been declared; become firm in soul and free from fear. Having thus addressed his disciple, he should himself meditate upon the Lord and perform worship.
Having fully worshipped the seat of the disciple according to the path of the sixfold arousal, and having conceived the seat of Śiva, one should fashion the form of Śiva.

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of the five Brahmans, beginning from the head and ending with the feet, one should likewise perform the placement of the parts of the Praṇava according to the divisions of the Muṇḍa and Krakala.
Then, having invoked Śiva in the form of the thirty-eight mantras into the body and the head of the disciple, one should display the mudrās and perform the ritual installation.

Then, having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-vinyāsa*) in sequence with the mantra "O Omniscient One," one should arrange the sixteen ritual offerings (*upacāra*), preceded by the preparation of the seat.

Having offered milk-rice as the food offering (naivedya) with the wife of Agni (svāhā), one should then offer water for rinsing the mouth, water for sipping, water for honor (arghya), and so forth, followed by incense, lamps, and the rest, in due order.
Having performed worship with the eight names by means of Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, one should recite: "The knower of Brahman attains [it]; Bhṛgu, indeed, was the son of Varuṇa."
"He who is the one to be approached by the gods, he who is supreme—he is Maheśvara. Having said this much, [she offered] lotuses and other flowers before him.
Having taken up the garland and risen, one should slowly recite the "Siddhi-skandha" from the *Pañcāśikā*, the work composed by the venerable Virūpākṣa.
With a favorable mind, the teacher should impart the realization "I am the Fullness" into the throat region of that disciple.
Then, one should apply the *tilaka* with salutation and subsequently anoint all the limbs, performing these according to the rules and in accordance with one's own tradition.
Then the preceptor, with affection, should give the umbrella and sandals known as Nāmaśrīpāda, along with an offering of *dūrvā* grass and the ritual arrangement of the *kalpa-vṛkṣa*.

And having explained the matter and having favored that disciple who is of the nature of Śiva by bestowing upon him the acceptance of the guru’s seat regarding ritual actions and so forth, the guru [proceeds].
Having addressed him, "Be always established in samādhi with the thought, 'I am Śiva,'" he should then himself perform a salutation to him.

Others should likewise offer salutations in accordance with their own tradition. Then the disciple, having risen, should likewise salute his own guru, as well as the guru of his guru and the disciples of his own guru.
To the disciple who has thus performed his salutation—well-behaved, restrained in speech, and standing bowed in humility—the Guru himself should grant [the initiation].
From this day forward, be intent upon bestowing grace upon the worlds; after examining a disciple for a year, accept him according to the prescribed rites.
Having completely abandoned defects such as passion and the like, become intent on the meditation of Śiva; cultivate association with those perfected in the true tradition, and not with others.
Without having worshipped Śiva, do not eat for as long as life lasts; remaining steadfast in devotion to the Guru, be happy, be happy!
Thus, the excellent and compassionate guru, an ocean of knowledge, should conduct himself toward the disciple with a favorable mind in due order.
Out of affection for you, O Vāmadeva, lord of sages, I have indeed explained this method of the yoga-band to you, even though it is most secret.
Having spoken thus, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), out of affection and compassion for the ascetics, began to explain to him the auspicious sequence of the rules for shaving and bathing.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for the Yoga-Band," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Subrahmaṇya said: O great sage Vāmadeva, I shall describe the procedure for shaving and bathing, by the immediate performance of which an ascetic attains supreme purity.
O Lord of Sages, having obtained the procedure for the type of yogapaṭṭa, that disciple, being fully observant of his vows, should prepare himself for the act of shaving.

Having bowed especially to the Guru and received his permission, he should then wash his head, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and undergo the shaving of hair while wearing his lower garment.
Afterwards, one should wash the garment, the razor and other tools, and the hands with clay and water; having smeared them with clay, one should give the clay for washing.
Having consecrated it with water-sprinklings while uttering "Śiva, Śiva," he should cover his own eyes with the ring finger and thumb, which have been consecrated with mantras.

Having opened [the eyes] with the Astra-mantra and beheld the razor and other implements for the sake of the ritual, one should then consecrate them twelve times and sprinkle them with water while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Taking a razor with the *tāra* mantra, one should shave on the right side; having first shaved some hairs at the front, one should then shave the entire head.
Having taken a leaf from the ground, one should scatter it, but not upon the bare earth; one should also trim the beard and the nails of the hands and feet.
Having collected earth from the vicinity of the bilva, aśvattha, tulasī, and other such trees, and having immersed himself in the water twelve times, he should go to the bank and sit down.
Having established it in a pure place and divided the earth into three parts, and having likewise done so a second time into three, one should sprinkle it and consecrate it with the Astra-mantra.

There, having taken a single portion of clay and having caused it to be applied with the other hand, one should smear both hands twelve times and wash each [hand] separately with [the remaining clay].
Furthermore, having anointed one foot and another on the face and hand in succession, and having washed them with water, he should enter the water again.
Having divided other clay into twelve portions, one should apply them to the head in sequence, and having submerged the face in the clay again and again.

Having gone to the bank, one should perform sixteen mouthfuls of water and the sipping rite (ācamana) twice; then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should again recite the Praṇava eighteen times.

Then, having divided another portion of clay into three parts, one should perform the purification of the hips and the purification of the feet with one of them, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
Then, having restrained the breath sixteen times with the *praṇava* while remaining silent, one should again place another [mantra] three times upon the region of one's own thighs, saying "Oṃ."

Having sprinkled [the water] and consecrated it seven times, one should place it once upon the palms of one's own hands; then, having smeared it three times, one should gaze upon the purifying form of the Sun.
Then the disciple, being of good intellect and firm mind, having smeared clay upon his two armpits, should rub it with his two hands joined in reverse order.
Then, having taken another pure clay, that disciple, devoted to his guru, should smear himself from head to foot while keeping his gaze fixed upon the sun.
Then, having risen from there and taking up his staff upon the ground, he should remember his own guru with devotion toward the mantra and steadfastness in knowledge.
Then, O disciple, one should remember with devotion Śiva—the Great Lord, Śaṅkara, the moon-crested one, the Lord of all sovereignty, and the Auspicious One.

One should prostrate with devotion three times to the Guru, who is Śiva, performing the *sāṣṭāṅga* (eight-limbed) salutation; and rising up, one should salute him once with the *pañcāṅga* (five-limbed) gesture.
Having entered the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and immersed himself therein, he should emerge, place that clay upon his shoulder, and smear it according to the previously described method.
Having gathered what remained there and entered into the midst of the water, he thoroughly stirred it and smeared it over all his limbs.
Having uttered "Om" three times while recollecting the lotus feet of Śiva—the means by which one is always delivered from the ocean of saṃsāra according to his ordinance—indeed, he [is so].
Having consecrated himself with the water mixed with viraja-ash while reciting "Om," and having performed the wiping of his limbs, he should then bathe thoroughly with the ash.
And then, O Sage, having applied the auspicious triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rite upon all the aforementioned limbs with great attentiveness;
Then, having become pure in mind, one should perform the midday rites after paying homage to Maheśvara, the gurus, and the sacred fords and other such objects.
O Sage, one should worship Maheśāna together with Ambikā, the bestower of knowledge and the protector of the three worlds, with supreme devotion.
Then that ascetic, firm-minded and established in his own duty, should go forth for alms, pure, among groups of virtuous Brahmins.
Then, there, the pure-souled one should collect alms in five ways as appropriate, and he should avoid defiled food.
Purity, bathing, begging for alms, and constant resorting to solitude—these are the four duties of a mendicant; a fifth does not exist.
A gourd, a bamboo vessel, one made of wood, and likewise one made of clay—these are the four bowls permitted for a monk; a fifth does not exist.
Betel, a vessel made of metal, the emission of semen, white clothing, sleeping during the day, and eating at night—these six things are to be avoided by ascetics.
Those who possess letters [of the Veda] yet act contrary to them are known as Rākṣasas; therefore, an ascetic should never perform any action that is contrary to the scriptures.
