An ascetic should diligently perform a ritual bath after shaving for the sake of purification, while mentally recollecting the pure Supreme Brahman, Sadāśiva.
Thus, O tiger among sages, out of affection for you, I have explained the entire procedure for shaving and bathing; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Shaving and Bathing," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vāmadeva said: For those ascetics who are liberated, no rite of cremation exists; I have heard that when their bodies die, they are to be buried.
O preceptor Kārttikeya, please explain that rite to me with great kindness; for indeed, there is no other speaker to be found in the three worlds besides you.
Those who, relying on the state of "I am the Fullness," are liberated from the cage of the body, and those who, by way of the path of worship, have abandoned the body and reached the Supreme;
O Blessed One, son of Śaṅkara, having considered me as your disciple, you ought to speak with great kindness regarding the specific destinies of those beings.
Sūta said: Having heard the request of the sage, the son of Śakti, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, spoke that supreme secret which had been heard by Bhṛgu from the Lord.
Subrahmaṇya said: O Sage, this very secret was spoken by the Lord himself, the omniscient wielder of the Pināka bow, to Bhṛgu, the yogi of Śiva.
O Brahman, I shall speak of that to you today; it must not be given to just anyone. It should indeed be given to a disciple who is peaceful and endowed with devotion to Śiva.
If there is some ascetic established in samādhi who experiences the body with the nature of Śiva, he is a great sage and becomes the perfectly complete Śiva.
I shall explain the means for anyone whose mind lacks steadiness and who does not attain samādhi; listen with careful attention.

Having gained a thorough understanding of the three categories arising from the statements of the Vedānta scriptures by hearing them from the mouth of a guru, one should practice yoga, beginning with the restraints (yamas) and so forth.
Performing that correctly, O Sage, the ascetic should constantly be intent on meditation upon Śiva, his mind perpetually absorbed in the *praṇava* according to the prescribed rule.
If, due to the weakness of his body, the ascetic loses his fortitude and, being free from desire, remembers Śiva, he may cast off his worn-out body.
O Sage, impelled by Nandin through the grace of Sadāśiva, five renowned deities appeared in their subtle, transportive forms (ātivāhika-rūpa).
One has the form of the slayer of the self, possessing a body like a mass of light; another is the presiding deity of the day, and another is the presiding deity of the bright fortnight.
And she is the form of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), intent upon the fivefold grace; she is the smoky, dark night, the presiding deity of the dark fortnight.
O great sage Vāmadeva, listen now to the function of those five deities renowned as the forms of the southern solstice.
O Sage, those five deities take the souls of those intent on the performance of ritual acts and, by the power of that merit, lead them to the third heaven.
Having enjoyed the pleasures as described, upon the exhaustion of that merit, they reach the world of humans again and undergo birth as before.
Furthermore, having divided the path into five parts starting from the surface of the earth and taking up the sequence beginning with fire, the ascetic reaches the state of Sadāśiva.
Having led the venerable feet of the God of gods behind him, they stand there, appearing as if seeking grace, yet truly impelled toward their respective duties.
Beholding him arrived, Sadāśiva, the God of gods, if he is dispassionate, instructs him in the essential meaning of the Great Mantra.
Having consecrated him among the Gaṇapatyas, Śaṅkara, the Lord of All and the Leader of All, bestows upon him a body equal to his own and grants him his grace.
Adorned with a deer, an axe, a trident, and the gesture of granting boons; possessing three eyes and a crescent moon, he bears matted locks in which the Gaṅgā flows.

This supreme, presided-over celestial chariot grants everything and fulfills all desires; thus, if one is detached from the branches [of worldly existence], it is surrounded by the daughters of Rudra.
It was enchanting with the sounds of dancing, singing, and musical instruments such as the mṛdaṅga drum, and it was adorned with divine garments, garlands, ointments, and ornaments.
Filled with jars of divine nectar and overflowing with celestial water, it was as radiant as ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.

And having taken possession of a celestial chariot that possesses the speed of thought and is all-pervading, even for him who has enjoyed his pleasures, when the curiosity for further enjoyment has ceased;
Having hurled a spear that was exceedingly fierce by nature and extremely difficult to withstand, it shone like the fire of Malaya, as if desiring to consume the forest to its very end.

Having bestowed the essential meaning of the Great Mantra, the Supreme Lord [instructed him]: "I am the Full One, whose nature is pure contemplation; I am Śambhu—this must be held with unwavering firmness."

Having bestowed grace, [the Lord grants] concentration (*samādhi*) and unimpeded supernatural powers (*siddhis*), which consist of the vibration of one's own servitude and take the form of the capacity for actions such as becoming like the sun.
Upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, the Teacher of the World grants him supreme liberation, from which there is no return to the lotus-born Brahmā.
Therefore, this very state possesses all sovereignty and is the collective totality; it is the highway to liberation—such is the definitive conclusion of the Vedāntas.
Then, out of kindness, other ascetics belonging to the true tradition should remain surrounding that dull-witted ascetic who was about to die.
Then all of them there, being composed in mind, taught the Praṇava and other mantras in their proper sequence, as well as the sentences and their underlying purport.
They should describe [Śiva] clearly and with affection, always causing him to be remembered; having prostrated before the attributeless supreme light until their own dissolution.
The sequence of consecration for these is stated here to be the same; for those whose bodies have been consecrated, misfortune never arises.
Since they have renounced all actions and are solely devoted to taking refuge in Śiva, the kingdom of that king perishes along with his body being defiled by them.
The inhabitants of that village would also become exceedingly distressed; therefore, the following procedure is prescribed for the removal of that defect.
At that time, with a humble mind, he should recite the mantra beginning with "namaḥ hariṇyāya" and ending with "namo amīvatkebhyaḥ."
Then, reciting "Oṃ" at the end, one should fill the sacrificial ground for the deity; O Lord of Sages, by this, there shall indeed be peace from that fault.
O Brahmin, out of compassion I shall describe how sons and others should perform the supreme sacramental rites according to the rules; listen with careful attention.

Having worshipped and bathed [the deity] with pure waters, and having worshipped again with flowers and other offerings, one should proceed in order with the Śrī Rudra, the Camaka, and the Rudrasūkta.
Having placed a conch shell in front and sprinkled [the disciple] with its water, one should place a flower upon the head and wipe it with the syllable *praṇava*.
Having discarded his loincloth and other such items, he should put on others; then, he should smear all his limbs with ashes according to the prescribed rite.
Having fashioned the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rule and a forehead mark (tilaka) with sandalwood paste, one should adorn the body with flowers and garlands.
One should adorn the chest, neck, head, arms, wrists, and ears in sequence with ornaments of rudrākṣa rosaries, accompanied by the recitation of mantras.
Having thoroughly fumigated it and raised it up, and having placed it upon a swing, one should install that body upon a beautiful chariot composed of the five Brahmans.
One should adorn that chariot with fragrant flowers and garlands, using the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta* and others, in their proper sequence.
Accompanied by dancing, instrumental music, and the Vedic chants of Brahmins on all sides, one should circumambulate the village and proceed while carrying that deceased spirit.
Then all those ascetics, likewise in the eastern or even the northern direction, in a meritorious region near a sacred tree, [performed their rites].

Having dug a sacrificial pit for the gods to the measure of a staff, and having sprinkled it with water while reciting the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then strew [sacrificial grass] upon it in the proper sequence.
Having spread śamī leaves with flowers above that, with their tips pointing north, he should then spread darbha grass upon that seat, arranged in layers of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
Having sprinkled that body with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) accompanied by the syllable Om and Vedic mantras, and having consecrated it with the Raudra Sūkta and the syllable Om;
Having consecrated [the disciple] with water from a conch shell, one should cast a flower upon his head; he to whom it falls is favorable, being intent on the remembrance of Śiva.

Then, having extracted [the seed-syllable] with the utterance "Oṃ," preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), one should place it in the pit upon a yogic seat (yogāsana) so that it faces the east.
Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes and flowers, and then with incense of guggulu, he should say, "O Viṣṇu, this is the oblation," and while saying, "Protect it," he should offer it.
One should hold a staff in the right hand and a water-pot in the left; with the mantra "O Prajāpati, none other than you [knows] these," one should offer it along with water.
Touching his head while reciting the mantra "brahmajajñānaṃ prathamam," and then touching the space between his eyebrows while reciting the Rudrasūkta.
Then, with the four [verses] beginning with "māno mahāntam," one should pierce the head with a coconut; thereafter, one should fill the cavity.
Having touched the ground with the five brahman-mantras, one should recite [the following] with undistracted mind: "He who is the beginning of the gods, he who is supreme, he is Maheśvara."
Having thus recited [the mantra] to Mahādeva—who is accompanied by Ambā, the medicine for the world, the omniscient, the independent, and the bestower of grace upon all—
Having fashioned a pedestal out of clay, one cubit in height and two cubits in width, one should then protect it by smearing it with cow dung.
And in its center, one should worship a square [mandala] provided with fragrant unbroken rice grains (akṣata), fragrant flowers, bilva fruits, and tulasī.

Then, with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should offer incense, a lamp, milk, and an oblation of clarified butter; having offered these and performed circumambulation, one should prostrate five times.

Having recited the Praṇava twelve times, one should then prostrate; and one should offer [oblations] to Brahmā and the others, starting from the cardinal and intermediate directions, with the Praṇava.
Thus, O best of sages, the procedure for up to ten days has been declared to you; now hear the procedure for the eleventh day for ascetics.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Rites to be Performed for Ascetics from Death until the End of Ten Days," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Subrahmaṇya said: O tiger among sages, out of affection for you, I shall describe that rite which was proclaimed for the eleventh day when it has arrived, specifically for ascetics.
Having swept the altar, smeared it with cow-dung, and performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, he should sprinkle water starting from the west and proceeding in order to the east five times.
Facing the northern direction, one should personally prepare the mandalas; having conceived a square measuring one span in size in the center.
Having placed, in sequence, the forms of a dot, a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle, as well as a conch shell in front, according to the path of the ritual procedure for worship.

Having restrained the vital breaths, formed the ritual intention, and worshipped the Queen of the Gods, one should worship the five deities previously mentioned, who possess the form of the subtle vehicle (ativāhika).
Having cast away the darbha grasses from the north, he who then touches [the seat] starting from the west, following the path of the six-fold rising posture (ṣaḍutthāsana).
Having placed flowers within those mandalas like a seat, and having uttered "Oṃ Hrīṃ," [one should invoke] the transportive deity (ativāhikadevatā) ending with the form of fire.
One should contemplate [the mantra] ending with "āvāhayāmi namaḥ" in all instances; one should respectfully display each of the mudrās, beginning with the sthāpanā, one by one.

One should perform their limbs in sequence with *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and so forth; they possess the splendor of moonstones, with hands holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
The faces of all the directions were colored by the glow of their red finger-rings; they wore red garments and were adorned with the lotuses that were their feet.
Charming with full-moon faces radiant with three eyes, they are adorned with crescent moons shining from their ruby crowns.
Their cheeks were rubbed by earrings, their breasts were full and elevated, and they were enchanting with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and girdles.

With slender waists and broad hips, they were draped in divine red garments; their lotus-feet tinkled with anklets made of rubies, and their toes and hips were adorned with beautiful and most enchanting rings.
What indeed cannot be accomplished by means of a manifest form through grace, just like Śiva? Therefore, everything can be accomplished by means of a form consisting of power, just like Maheśvara.
The five divine forms were assumed solely for the purpose of bestowing grace upon all; they accomplish every task and are intent upon the supreme favor of others.
Having meditated thus upon all those auspicious goddesses who are intent on bestowing grace, one should offer water for the feet at their feet with drops of water from a conch shell.
One should cause water for sipping to be offered into their hands and the arghya offering onto their crowns; one should then visualize the rite of bathing them with drops from the conch water.
One should cause divine red garments, together with upper cloths, to be given; and one should present priceless ornaments, such as crowns and the like.
One should cause to be offered well-perfumed sandalwood, most beautiful unbroken grains of rice, and fragrant, pleasing flowers.
"I offer all—incense of supreme fragrance and a lamp with a wick soaked in ghee"—beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Then, ending with the word "namas," one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in honey, along with cakes filled with ghee, sugar, plantains, and jaggery.
Having placed [the offerings], each filled with fragrant substances upon a plantain leaf, one should perform the rites of sprinkling and so forth while reciting "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ."
Having uttered "oṃ hrīṃ," one should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the wife of fire (svāhā); having said "pānīyaṃ namaḥ" for the drinking water, one should present it with supreme love.

Then, O best of sages, one should joyfully remove [the previous offerings] from the east; having purified the ground, one should cause the rinsing of the mouth, the sipping of water, and the respectful offering (arghya) to be presented.
Having offered betel-leaf, incense, lamps, circumambulations, and prostrations, he should offer prayers while placing his joined palms upon his head.
May the glorious Mothers, being well-pleased, declare that this ascetic, who seeks the state of Śiva, is to be protected by the two lotus-feet of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus prayed and dismissed them all to their respective places, and having extracted their grace, one should cause it to be bestowed upon the maidens.

One should cast [the remains] either into the mouths of cows or into the midst of water, and never otherwise; in this very case, one should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for the ascetic, and never the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
In this regard, I shall declare the rule for the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha; listen to it, O best of sages, so that through it there may be spiritual welfare.

The performer, having bathed, restrained his breath, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, composed in mind, and holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand, should say: "On this auspicious lunar day."
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha," he should offer excellent Darbha grass for the purpose of a seat on the northern side and touch water.
There, having invited four Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva and firm in their vows, he should with devotion seat them after they have performed their ablutions including an oil massage.
"May you grant favor for the sake of the Viśvedevas; and afterwards, may you grant favor for yourself and for the inner self as well."
Having thus addressed them as the Supreme Self and having made his request, the ascetic should respectfully perform service at their feet with faith according to the true purpose.
Having washed their feet and seated them facing the east, one should adorn them with perfumes and other offerings and feed them in the presence of Śiva.
Having smeared this place with cow-dung and having spread darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward, one should, with breath controlled, perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Having formed the resolve, "I shall do [this]," and having worshipped the three mandalas—namely, the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—thereafter...
Speaking the name ending in the dative case, and subsequently uttering "this pinda," and pronouncing "I give," one should offer the pindas with one's own devotion.
Then one should offer water with kuśa grass according to the prescribed ritual rules; thereafter, having raised [the image], one should indeed perform circumambulation and prostrations.
Then, having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali on that very spot on that same day.
The ritual procedure for the worship of Viṣṇu is prescribed everywhere solely for the purpose of protection; one should perform the great worship of Viṣṇu and offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation.
Then, having summoned twelve Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, he honored Keśava and the others with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
Having given them sandals, umbrellas, garments, and so forth according to the prescribed rite, one should satisfy them with great devotion through various auspicious words.

Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, and having uttered "Bhūḥ svāhā," "Bhuvaḥ svāhā," and "Svaḥ" preceded by the Praṇava, one should offer a bali-oblation of milk-rice upon the ground.
O Lord of Sages, I have declared the procedure for the eleventh day; O twice-born one, listen with respect as I shall now describe the procedure for the twelfth day.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Eleventh Day for Ascetics," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Subrahmaṇya said: Having risen on the twelfth day, bathed in the morning, and performed his daily rites, he [should approach] Śiva-devotees, ascetics, or Brāhmaṇas who are dear to Śiva.

Having addressed them and invited them, he should devoutly feed those who have bathed at midday and are purified, according to the prescribed rites, with various kinds of delicious and auspicious foods.

Having established [the deity] in the presence of the Supreme Lord, one should worship according to the path of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa), having restrained the vital breaths and controlled one's speech.
Having made a formal resolve by way of the Great Resolve (mahāsaṃkalpa), saying, "I shall perform the worship of our Guru here," one should then touch the darbha grass.
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the performer himself, remaining silent and adorned with sacred ash, should seat them upon the seats facing the east.

One should meditate there upon those eight [deities] in the sequence beginning with Sadāśiva; and, O Sage, one should also honor the other twice-born ones with supreme devotion. One should meditate upon the Preceptor of the Supreme (Parameṣṭhiguru) by his own name, conceiving him as being together with Ambā. Beyond that Guru is the Supreme Guru, and beyond that is the Parāparaguru.
Having said, "This is the seat," one should offer the seats while pronouncing one's own name preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending in the dative case.

Having invoked [the deity] with "I invoke, obeisance," one should offer water for the arghya, as well as water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, clothing, fragrance, and unbroken grains.

Having offered [the oblation] and adorned [the deity] with flowers, one should then [worship] with fragrant flowers while reciting the eight names preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, accompanied by the dative case.
Having offered incense and lamps, one has indeed performed the entire worship; saying "May it be complete," one should stand up and pay obeisance.
Having spread out plantain leaves as plates and purified them with water, [he should serve] pure rice preceded by milk-rice, cakes, soup, and side dishes.
Having offered articles consisting of plantains, coconuts, and jaggery, one should then offer separate vessels and seats, consecrating them in due order.
Having sprinkled and consecrated with water while reciting "viṣṇor havyam," and having caused the touch of the hand [of the deity] while saying "rakṣasva," he stands up.
Having offered the *āpośana* water, he should then pray to them as follows: "May Sadāśiva and the others be pleased with me and grant me boons."
Then, having recited "ye devāḥ" and so forth, he should cast this [water] along with unbroken grains (akṣata); having bowed and stood up, he should say everywhere, "May there be nectar (amṛta)."

Having spoken thus and having propitiated [the deity], one should recite the *Gaṇānāṃ tvā* mantra at the beginning, followed by the beginnings of the Vedas, the two *Rudra-camaka* mantras, the *Rudra-sūkta*, and the five [mantras].

At the conclusion of the meal, having offered the Brahma-mantras along with the remaining mantras together with grains of rice, and having provided the *uttarāpośana* water as well as the means for cleansing the hands, feet, and mouth;
Having made them contented and established them comfortably upon their seats, one should then offer pure water and camphor and other items as prescribed.
Having given them mouth-perfume, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), sandals, a seat, leaves, a fan, wooden planks, and a bamboo staff;
Having satisfied [the deity] with circumambulations and prostrations, one should invoke a blessing; then, having bowed again and prayed for unwavering devotion to the Guru.
"May Sadāśiva and the others depart happily as they please. Having thus performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana), he follows them properly as far as the entrance.
Having been dismissed from there by the gatekeepers, the brahmins, and his kinsmen, he should remain at ease after eating together with the wretched and the helpless.

It shall never be otherwise; this is the truth, the truth again and again. Performing the supreme propitiation of the Guru every single year, one shall enjoy great pleasures in this world and attain the realm of Śiva.

Sūta said: Having thus spoken to the eminent sage Śrī Vāmadeva, his own disciple who had been granted grace, the great-souled Lord—the best among the wise, whose intellect was serene—quickly bestowed supreme favor upon him.

That which was proclaimed of old by the lord of sages Vyāsa to the lords of sages at the Naimiṣa forest—therefore, he is the primordial teacher, while you are the second noble one, renowned throughout the world.
Having heard from your lotus-like mouth that Sanatkumāra, who is filled with devotion to Śiva, will speak it to Vyāsa, and that excellent devotee of Śiva, Vyāsa, will in turn speak it fully to Śuka;
To each of those tigers among sages, he assigned a group of four disciples who were accomplished in the study of the Vedas and dedicated to the establishment of the Dharma.
Vaiśampāyana, Paila, Jaimini, and Sumantu—these four were the disciples of Vyāsa, possessed of great luster.
Agastya, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu—these high-souled ones, O great sage Vāmadeva, are your disciples.
Sanaka, Sananda, the sage Sanātana, and Sanatsujāta—these were the foremost among yogis, beloved of Śiva.

They were the disciples of Sanatkumāra, the most excellent among all knowers of the meaning of the Vedas; and Śuka-yogin’s gurus—namely Guru, Parama-guru, Parātpara-guru, and Parameṣṭhi-guru—were likewise worthy of worship.
This knowledge of the Praṇava resides within the four classes; it is the most excellent cause and the means for true liberation in Kāśī.

May this wondrous mandala, the form of the abode of Supreme Śiva, which is always to be worshipped by the lords of ascetics whose minds are filled with the investigation of the meaning of the Vedānta, and which is encompassed even by the great ether conceived through the divisions of the Vedas and other scriptures—may it thus bring satisfaction to You, and likewise bestow welfare and auspicious fortune upon the worlds.
This supreme secret spoken by Śiva, which is firmly established in the tenets of Vedānta, has been heard by you from me; therefore, O Sage, those most wise declare your opinion to be the correct one.

Therefore, having traveled by this very path, the ascetic should become Śiva, realizing "I am Śiva," for the sake of liberation from the distinctions of being the Grandfather (Brahmā) and so forth, just as these rivers flow into the ocean.
The venerable Sūta said: Having thus instructed the lord of sages, the Lord of the Gods called to mind the lotus feet of his parents, which are worshipped by all the deities.
The Guru, who bestows supreme and wondrous divine knowledge, reached the peak of Kailāsa, which was covered with summits and resplendent. Kumāra also arrived at that mountain peak.
Vāmadeva also, surrounded by his excellent disciples, bowed down to Śikhivāhana and quickly departed for the most wonderful Kailāsa.
Having gone to the peak of Kailāsa and approached the presence of Īśa, the sage beheld the feet of the two Lords, which bestow liberation and destroy illusion.
With all his limbs offered through devotion and having forgotten his own body, he fell down again and again in the presence [of the Lord], and rising up, he bowed repeatedly.
Then, with various hymns steeped in the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, the sage praised the Supreme Lord, who is accompanied by Ambikā and his son.
Placing the lotus-feet of the God and the Goddess upon his own head, and having obtained their full grace, he dwelt there in happiness.
O sirs, having thus understood Maheśvara as the meaning of the Praṇava, the secret of the Vedas, the essence of all, the supreme Brahman that bestows liberation;
Seated here itself in happiness at the feet of the illustrious Viśveśvara, may you attain the peerless and supreme liberation in the form of union (sāyujya).
I shall go to Badarāśrama to serve the lotus feet of my guru; may I have further opportunity for virtuous conversation with you.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties for the Twelve Days Preceded by the Account of the Group of Disciples Beginning with Vyāsa," in the Kailāsa-saṃhitā, the sixth book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vyāsa said: Salutations to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, by his attendants, and by his son; the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
His power is indeed incomparable, and his sovereignty is all-pervading; they declare his lordship and omnipresence to be his very nature.
I go for refuge to that unborn Viśvakarman, the eternal, auspicious, and imperishable Mahādeva, the Great Soul, the Auspicious One.
At the great sacred ford of Dharmakṣetra, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Kālindī, at Prayāga, in the Naimiṣa forest, on the path to the world of Brahmā.
Sages who had purified their souls, devoted to the vow of truth, possessed of great luster and great fortune, performed a great sacrificial session.
There, having heard of that sacrificial session of those performers of unblemished deeds, [he went] to the presence of the wise Vedavyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
The disciple was a high-souled and intelligent man, renowned throughout the three worlds, and an expert in discerning the merits and defects of a five-membered syllogism.
And he was a speaker of ever-increasing excellence, even compared to Bṛhaspati as he spoke; his words were sweet to the ears and consisted of charming phrases and syllables.
An expert speaker of narratives, a poet who knew the proper time and understood policy, that Sūta, the best of those versed in the Purāṇas, arrived at that place.
Seeing the charioteer approaching, the sages, with joyful hearts, offered him the traditional rites of welcome and honored him according to the prescribed rules.
Having accepted the worship offered by the sages, he, being duly appointed, attended to his own appropriate task with a focused mind.
Then, from that very meeting, the minds of the sages of purified souls became filled with longing to hear the ancient narrative.
Then, having honored him with favorable words and having made him very well-disposed, the great seers spoke these words:
The sages said: O Romaharṣaṇa, O omniscient one, O highly fortunate and great-minded king of the Śaivas, you have arrived here today for us through the weight of our good fortune.
You have directly received the entire science of the Purāṇas from Vyāsa; therefore, you are indeed the vessel for these wondrous stories.
Like the ocean, the mine of jewels, for great and precious gems; whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever other thing exists.
There is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you; you have come here for the sake of seeing us by the power of destiny.
Since you have accomplished no meritorious deed, you ought not to depart in vain; therefore, listen to this most excellent merit, which is comprised of noble stories and knowledge.
"Quickly recite for us the Purāṇa, which is the very essence of all the Vedāntas. Thus was Sūta requested by the sages who were exponents of the Vedas.
And he replied with gentle, auspicious words that were consistent with reason. Sūta said: "I have been honored and favored by you, as you have thus exhorted me."
Why should I not correctly proclaim this ancient [teaching] honored by the sages, after having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Goddess, Skanda, and Vināyaka?
And likewise, O Vyāsa, I shall declare to you Nandī, the son of Satyavatī himself, [this] supreme and meritorious Purāṇa which is equal to the Vedas.
The Śivajñānārṇava directly bestows the fruits of devotion and liberation; it is adorned with the meanings of the Āgamas, joined with words, meanings, and logic.
In connection with the Śvetakalpa, Vāyu formerly recounted all the branches of knowledge as well as the sequence of the Purāṇas.
Listen as I describe the origin of that Purāṇa: the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya; these are its limbs.
The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and these fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās), followed by Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda in sequence.
The science of polity (arthaśāstra) is supreme; indeed, eighteen branches of knowledge are traditionally recorded. Of these eighteen sciences, which follow diverse paths—
The scripture declares that the trident-bearing Lord Śiva is the manifest primordial creator and poet; for he, the Lord of the entire universe, desired to bring forth the whole world.
He directly appointed the eternal Brahmā as his first son; to that Brahmā, the first-born son and source of the universe.
In the past, the Lord gave these sciences for the purpose of universal creation; thereafter, he gave the power of protection to the divine Hari for the sake of preservation.
Indeed, the middle son Viṣṇu was the protector even of Brahmā, by whom—having acquired knowledge and being engaged in the expansion of the creation of progeny—the rites were performed.
First, the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the source of all scriptures; immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths.
From his mouth, the activity of all the scriptures then originated; for when the people on earth were no longer able to comprehend its full extent, [he divided it].
Then, at the command of Viśveśvara, for the purpose of condensing the knowledge, the Lord Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe and sustainer of the world, [appeared] at the ends of the Dvāpara ages.
Having descended to this earth under the name of Vyāsa, he acts therein; and thus, O twice-born ones, the Vedas are divided in every Dvāpara age.
Thereafter, he composed other ancient and new works; and again, in this Dvāpara age, under the name Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Like a consumer of oblations born in the forest, he was born of Satyavatī; that sage, having condensed the Vedas, divided them into four parts once again.
Because he divided the Vedas in the world, he is known as Vedavyāsa; and he [compiled] the Purāṇas in an abridged form measuring four hundred thousand [verses].
Even today in the world of the gods, that twice-born man who knows the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and Upanishads would find them to extend for a hundred crore verses.
If the Purāṇas were not to exist, one would certainly not be truly wise; therefore, one should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me. [Likewise, it fears] the primary creation, the secondary creation, the genealogies, and the periods of the Manus.
The lineage history and the Purāṇa with its five characteristics—this Purāṇa is taught as being tenfold and eightfold.

According to the distinction between extensive and subtle [versions], by the sages who are the best among the knowers of reality, there are the Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
The Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya; the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga, and the Vārāha as well.
The Skānda, the Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and the Brahmāṇḍa—this is the meritorious sequence of the Purāṇas.
Therein lies the Śaiva Turīya, which is the Śārva [scripture] that accomplishes all aims; that text, measuring one hundred thousand [verses], is divided into twelve Saṃhitās.
That [system] was indeed created by Śiva himself; therein Dharma is established. By the very Dharma taught therein, men of the three castes are Śaivas.
Therefore, one seeking liberation should take refuge in Śiva alone; by taking refuge in him alone, even the gods attain liberation, and not otherwise.
Listen as I describe in brief the various divisions of that Purāṇa known as Śaiva, which is proclaimed to be equal to the Vedas.
Likewise, the Vidyeśvara, the Raudra, the unsurpassed Vaināyaka, the Auma, the Mātṛpurāṇa, and the Rudraikādaśaka.
Kailāsa, Śatarudra, and that which is called Śatarudrākhya; then the one called Sahasrakoṭirudra, and after that, Vāyavīya.
The *Dharmasaṃjñā* and the *Purāṇa*—these are the twelve *saṃhitās*. The *Vidyeśa* is said to consist of ten thousand verses by way of its total count.
The Raudra, Vaināyaka, Cauma, and that which is called Mātṛka; each of these consists of eight thousand verses, while the latter [the Mātṛka] consists of thirteen thousand.
That which is called Raudrakādaśaka consists of six thousand [verses], Kailāsa consists of three thousand, Śatarudra consists of three thousand, and beyond that is Koṭirudra.
Endowed with nine thousand [verses] and joined with the knowledge of all purposes, it is known as the eleven-thousand-verse Rudrādhyāya, consisting of ten thousand and one thousand verses.
The supreme Vāyavīya Purāṇa consists of four thousand verses; that which is known as the Dharmapurāṇa consists of twelve thousand verses.

Thus, one hundred thousand verses have been indicated as the Śaiva [scripture], distinguished by its various branches; it is the Purāṇa that is the essence of the Vedas, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That was then condensed by Vyāsa into twenty-four thousand verses; therein, the fourth Purāṇa is indeed the Śaiva, consisting of seven Saṃhitās.
The first there is named Vidyeśvara; the second is the Rudra-saṃhitā; the third is named Śatarudra; and the fourth is Koṭirudra.
The fifth is said to be the Comā, the sixth is the Kailāsasaṃhitā, and the seventh is named the Vāyavīyā; thus, there are exactly seven Saṃhitās here.
The Vidyeśvara [tattva] is said to consist of two thousand; the Raudra [tattva], five hundred and ten; and the [Śiva-tattva] is declared to be thirty-two thousand one hundred and fifty.
Likewise, the Śatarudra, the Koṭirudra, the Vyomayugādhika, the Dvisāhasra, the Dviśata, the Ugra, and the Bhūsahasraka.
One hundred and forty-eight thousand [yojanas] is Kailāsa, and one thousand [yojanas] is the earth; beyond that, two hundred and forty thousand [yojanas] is the realm of Vāyu.
Thus, according to its numerical divisions, the Purāṇa known as Śiva consists of exactly four thousand verses; it is a supreme merit-bestowing scripture.
That which is proclaimed as the Vāyavīya consisting of four thousand [verses], that very work I shall now set forth, complete in its two parts.
This unsurpassed scripture must not be spoken to one who does not know the Vedas, nor to one who lacks faith, nor likewise to one who is ignorant of the Purāṇas.
It should be given to a disciple who has been tested, who is righteous, free from malice, a devotee of Śiva, and a follower of the Śiva-dharma.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, by whose grace this Purāṇa-saṃhitā exists within me.
Sūta said: Long ago, after many great cycles of time (kalpas) had passed again and again, this present kalpa arrived and the work of creation began.
When the means of livelihood were firmly established and the subjects were awakened, the sages belonging to the six clans spoke with one another.
A very great dispute arose as to "this is supreme" and "this is not"; because the nature of the other was difficult to determine, no certainty was reached therein.
They went to see the creator, the imperishable Brahmā, where the blessed Brahmā sat being praised by gods and asuras.
On the auspicious and beautiful peak of Meru, crowded with gods and dānavas, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas, and served by yakṣas and gandharvas.
Resounding with the calls of flocks of birds, adorned with jewels and coral, and beautified by bowers, caves, mountain clefts, dwellings, and waterfalls.
There, a forest named Brahmavana, crowded with various wild animals, extends ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.
A delightful lake filled with the water of the *surasā* fruit, its blossoming trees beautiful and covered by intoxicated bees.
There was a great and beautiful city, resembling the rising sun, belonging to the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas who were arrogant due to their invincible strength.
It was made of refined gold, with lofty walls and gateways, adorned with hundreds of turrets, balconies, domes, and main streets.
Adorned with many millions of great palaces, variegated with highly precious jewels, it seemed as if it were licking the very sky.
While Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, was dwelling there together with his courtiers, [the sage] went there to the high-souled Grandfather of the worlds in person.
The sages and gods beheld him, who was served by hosts of celestial rishis, resembling pure gold, and adorned with every ornament.
With a serene countenance and gentle mien, his eyes were as broad as lotus petals; he was endowed with divine splendor and anointed with celestial perfumes.
Wearing divine white garments and adorned with celestial garlands, his lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of gods and asuras and by the masters of yogis.
He was resplendent with Sarasvatī, whose limbs were endowed with all auspicious marks and who held a chowrie in her hand, like the sun with its radiance.
Seeing him, all the sages, their faces and eyes radiant with joy, placed their joined palms upon their heads and praised that bull among the gods.
The sages said: Salutations to you, the triple-formed one, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction; to the ancient Puruṣa, to Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to the one whose body is primordial matter (pradhāna), who causes the agitation of primordial matter, who is transformed through twenty-three divisions, yet remains unchanging.
Salutations to Him whose body is the cosmic egg, who dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg, whose purpose is fully accomplished therein, and who is the perfect instrument of accomplishment.
Homage be to the one who belongs to all worlds, the ordainer of all worlds, and the cause of the laws of union and separation for the bodies of all souls.
By you alone has the entire world been created, withdrawn, and protected; yet even so, O Lord, O Grandfather, we do not know you because of your illusory power.
Sūta said: Thus praised by the highly fortunate great ṛṣis, Brahmā spoke with a deep voice, as if gladdening the sages.
Brahmā said: O highly fortunate sages, endowed with great being and great splendor, for what purpose have you all assembled here together?
To the god Brahmā who was speaking thus, all those most proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, with palms joined in reverence, addressed him with words imbued with humility.
The sages said: "O Blessed One, we are enveloped by a great darkness; distressed and disputing among ourselves, we do not perceive that which is supreme here."
For you are the sustainer of the entire world, the cause of all causes; O Protector, there is indeed nothing here that remains unknown to you.
Who is that person who is more ancient than all beings, the Supreme Person, pure, perfect, eternal, and the Supreme Lord?
By what creative act is the world first created? Tell me that truth, O one of great wisdom, for the removal of my own doubt.
Thus questioned then, Brahmā, his gaze smiling with wonder, [spoke] in the presence of the gods, the dānavas, and even the sages.
Having risen and meditated for a long time, lifting up the mountain while uttering "Rudra," his entire body drenched with tears of joy, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Brahmā said: From whom words, together with the mind, turn back without reaching Him—Him whose bliss the knower indeed does not fear from anything whatsoever.
Because all this—beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, together with all the elements and the senses—is first brought forth by him.
And he who is the sustainer of causes, the meditator, the supreme cause—he is never produced from anything else at any time.
Endowed with all sovereignty, he is himself Sarveśvara by name; Śambhu, dwelling in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all seekers of liberation.
He who first made me his son and bestowed knowledge upon me—it is through his grace that I have attained this station of Prajāpati.
The Lord stands firm like a tree, the one who dwells alone in heaven; by that Great-Souled Puruṣa, this entire universe is filled.
He who alone is active among many inactive beings, and who, being one, makes the seed manifold—he is Maheśvara.
The Lord, who rules over all these worlds by means of these living beings.
He who is the one Bhagavān Rudra—there is no second whatsoever.
Although he is ever seated within the hearts of all people, he remains unperceived by others; yet perceiving the entire universe, he presides over it at all times.
But the Lord alone, who possesses infinite power, presides over all causes whatsoever that are liberated from time.
For whom there is no day nor night, no equality nor excess; for him, supreme power is innate, as are eternal knowledge and action.
That which is the perishable unmanifest and that which is the immortal imperishable—both these imperishable natures are the one God, Hara himself.
Through meditating upon that, through union, and through cultivating the state of being, [the Lord] rules; for at the end of this bound soul, the universal illusion (viśvamāyā) indeed ceases.
"In which lightning does not shine, nor the sun, nor the moon; by whose light all this is illumined"—such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
The one God, Mahādeva, is to be known as Maheśvara; no state whatsoever superior to him is found.
This [reality] is beginningless and endless, pure by its very nature, independent, complete, and the cause of all that moves and is immobile, subject only to its own will.
Possessing a non-material body, glorious, and devoid of both the defined and the definition; he is the liberated one and the liberator, beyond time yet the impeller of time.
Dwelling above all, yet dwelling in all, he is the omniscient Lord of this entire universe composed of the sixfold path.
He is the highest among all successively higher beings, and he is unsurpassed; he is the bee that drinks the nectar from the blossoms of an infinite multitude of infinities.
He is the master in condensing all the unbroken cosmic eggs; he is the ocean of magnanimity, heroism, profundity, and sweetness.
There is no object whatsoever equal to him, nor indeed anything superior; incomparable among all beings, he stands as the king of kings.
By this act of painting, the universe is first created; at the time of the end, it shall again undergo dissolution into that very same [source].
All beings are subject to him; he is the director of all. He is perceived only through supreme devotion, and never otherwise.
Vows, all forms of giving, austerities, and likewise restraints were taught of old by the virtuous for the sake of inner disposition; of this there is no doubt.
Hari, I, Rudra, and likewise other gods and asuras, even today, long for a vision of him through our fierce austerities.
Invisible to the fallen, the deluded, the wicked, and even the contemptible, he is to be worshipped and indeed addressed by his devotees, both internally and externally.
This form is threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond that. The gross is visible to us and the immortals, while the subtle is perceived by yogis.
But beyond that is the eternal, imperishable knowledge and bliss; it is perceived by devotees who are established in it, devoted to it, and who have taken recourse to its vow.
What is the use of saying more here? Devotion to Śiva is supreme, more secret than the secret; there is no doubt that one endowed with it is liberated.
That devotion arises solely from grace, and grace is born from devotion; just as a seed comes from a sprout, or a sprout from a seed.
All accomplishments for the seeker are preceded by serene faith; that very faith is ultimately realized through all the various means of practice.

The means for accomplishing serenity is dharma, and that has been shown by the Veda; through the power of its practice, there occurs the neutralization of the two previously mentioned [states], merit and demerit.

From that equanimity arises contact with serenity, and from that comes the excellence of dharma; having attained this excellence of dharma, there is the complete destruction of the fettered being's sins.
Thus, for one whose sins have been gradually exhausted over many births, devotion preceded by knowledge arises toward Sāmba Sarveśvara.

The grace of the Lord is bestowed in accordance with one's disposition; through that grace comes the renunciation of karma, which occurs in terms of its fruit and not in terms of its essential nature.
Therefore, from the renunciation of the fruits of action, there arises the auspicious lineage of Śiva-dharma; and that is twofold: independent of a guru and dependent upon a guru.

In this regard, the state of being endowed with dependence is a hundred times superior to the state of independence; for one who follows the Śiva-dharma, the possession of Śiva-knowledge is the highest attainment.

Through the power of the succession of knowledge, a person perceives the defects within cyclic existence; from that arises detachment from sense objects, and from detachment comes the means for the realization of the ultimate state.
For one who has attained the realization of the true nature of existence, the culmination lies in meditation, not in ritual action; for the person devoted to knowledge and meditation, yoga proceeds.
Through yoga, however, supreme devotion arises; immediately thereafter comes grace. By grace, a living being is liberated, and once liberated, he becomes equal to Śiva.
This sequence of the modes of grace is not intended [to be fixed]; rather, the grace accorded to a person is of such a kind as corresponds to his own capacity.
One is liberated while still in the womb, another likewise while being born; yet another is liberated as a child, or as a youth, or even as an old man.
One who has gone to the animal realm is liberated; another, a denizen of hell, is liberated; yet another, having attained his station, is liberated upon the exhaustion of that station.
Someone, having reached the end of the path, is liberated after returning; someone else, having gone partway on that path, is liberated by stopping again and again.
Therefore, liberation for human beings is not held to be achieved by a single means; rather, nirvāṇa comes only through grace that corresponds to the nature of one's knowledge.
Therefore, for the sake of his grace, they—along with their wives, sons, and sacred fires—meditated solely upon Śiva, free from the defects of speech and mind.
All of them were devoted to Him, intent on Him, united with Him, and taking refuge in Him; performing every action, they had reached Him alone with their minds.
Having begun a sacrificial session lasting for a thousand divine years, at the conclusion of that session, Vāyu will go there by means of the application of mantras.
He alone will tell you the means for your ultimate welfare; from there, one reaches the holy city of Vārāṇasī, which is supremely beautiful.
One should go to where the Lord of the Universe, the illustrious wielder of the Pināka bow, always sports together with the Goddess for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
Having seen a great marvel there, you shall come into my presence; then, O best of the twice-born, I will tell you the means to liberation.
By means of which liberation in a single birth rests in the palm of your hand—that which effects release from the bondage of the cycle of existence spanning many births.
This mind-made wheel, created by me, is now being cast forth; that place where its rim shatters shall be a land auspicious for asceticism.
Having spoken thus and beholding the mind-born discus, which resembled the sun, the Grandfather prostrated before Mahādeva and dismissed him.
Those brahmins, even more delighted, bowed down to the Lord of the worlds and proceeded to the place where the rim of that wheel had shattered.
That wheel, too, was gathered together on a smooth and beautiful stone surface somewhere in his own forest, which possessed pure, sweet water.
That forest, honored by sages and crowded with many yakṣas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas, became renowned as Naimiṣa because of him.
Purūravas, having devoured the eighteen islands of the ocean, fell under the power of Urvaśī’s charms, impelled by fate.

While he was carrying off the golden sacrificial ground of Yajña by means of delusion and other stratagems in a disorderly manner, he was struck down there by the enraged sages with *kuśa*-grass as their thunderbolts.

In ancient times, when the creators of the universe (Viśvasṛjas), who were knowers of Brahman, desired to bring forth the entire world, they commenced a celestial sacrificial session (satra) while remaining within the household fire (gārhapatya).
There, the ritual was performed by learned sages who were experts in grammar, semantics, and logic, through the application of their power, wisdom, and action.

There, those who know the Vedas, being constant exponents of Vedic doctrine, destroy with their words—by the power of debate and discourse—those excluded from the Vedic teachings who are excessive talkers.

Naimiṣa was a place suited for the austerities of those sages: its rocky slopes were formed from the foothills of mountains made of crystal; it was delightful with clear water flowing like nectar; it abounded in trees yielding fruits of exceeding sweetness; and it was free from predatory beasts and venomous creatures.
Sūta said: In that region, illustrious sages of celebrated vows then commenced a sacrificial session (sattra), worshipping Mahādeva.
And that sacrificial session of the great seers proceeded, filled with every marvel.
Like those who created the universe in the past, they were desirous of bringing forth the world.
Then, when time had passed and the sacrifice—characterized by abundant sacrificial fees—had been completed, Vāyu himself arrived there at the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The divine disciple of the Self-Existent One, who perceives everything directly and is self-controlled, under whose command the Maruts are stationed in seven groups of seven.
And constantly impelling the limbs by means of its own functions, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and others, it performs the sustenance of the bodies of all living beings.
Endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*, he who sustains the worlds through the pure [means] such as the horizontal directions and time.
Having space as its source and possessing double the qualities due to the association with touch and sound, it is called the primal nature of the fires by those who contemplate reality.
Seeing him arrived at the hermitage, the sages performing long sacrificial sessions remembered the words of the Grandfather and experienced incomparable joy.
Then they all rose up, bowed to the one born from the sky, and prepared for him a seat made of gold.
Seated there and duly honored by the sages, he in turn greeted them all and then inquired after their welfare.

Vāyu said: "O Brahmins, is all well with you now that this great sacrifice has been performed? I hope that the Daityas, those enemies of the gods who destroy sacrifices, do not cause you any further harassment."
Did no expiation for a poorly performed rite ever arise? [And did they worship] the gods with hymns and recitations, and the ancestors with ancestral rites?
I trust that you have properly performed the ritual after honoring [the officiating priests]; and now that the great sacrifice has concluded, what do you intend to do next?
Thus addressed by Vāyu, who is devoted to Śiva, all the sages, purified and with delighted minds, replied with humility.
The sages said: Today all is well with us; today our ascetic merit shall become truly auspicious, since you have come here for the sake of increasing our spiritual welfare.
Listen to this ancient account: in former times, we, whose minds were overcome by darkness, worshipped Prajāpati for the sake of higher knowledge.
He too, the protector of those who seek refuge, having shown us favor, said: "O brahmins, Rudra is superior to all; he is the supreme cause."
Only one possessed of devotion perceives that inconceivable true nature; devotion arises through His grace, and from grace alone comes liberation.
Therefore, for the sake of his grace, perform a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) at Naimiṣa through the practice of a Sattra sacrifice, offering worship to Rudra, the supreme cause.
By his grace, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, Vāyu will arrive there; from his mouth you shall obtain knowledge, and through that, your ultimate welfare will be secured.
Having thus instructed us, O illustrious one, we have all been sent by the Supreme Lord, longing for your arrival in this region.
Having sat for a long sacrificial session for a thousand divine years, there is nothing whatsoever remaining for us to pray for other than your arrival.
Having heard this account of the past from the sages who were performing long sacrificial sessions, Vāyu became delighted in mind and remained there surrounded by the munis.
Then, questioned by those sages for the sake of increasing their spiritual realization, the omnipresent Lord spoke in brief of the sovereignty of Śiva, beginning with the creation of the universe.
Sūta said: Thereupon, the highly fortunate residents of the Naimiṣa forest first prostrated themselves according to the prescribed rule and questioned the lord Pavana.
The residents of Naimiṣa said: How did you attain this knowledge concerning the Lord? And how did you come to possess the nature of Śiva, who is Brahman born from the unmanifest?
Vāyu said: The nineteenth kalpa is to be known as Śvetalohita; in that kalpa, the four-faced one, desiring to create, performed penance.
Pleased by that intense austerity, his father himself, the best among the beautiful, assumed a divine youthful form.
Having become a sage named Śveta and uttering divine speech, Maheśvara, the God of gods, granted him a vision of Himself.
Having seen his father, Brahmā, the sovereign lord of Brahmā, he prostrated himself and received supreme knowledge together with the Gāyatrī.
Then, having attained consciousness, the four-faced Viśvakarman created all beings, both stationary and moving.
Since the nectar was obtained by Brahmā from the Supreme Lord after hearing it, I too have obtained it from that very mouth through the power of austerity.
The sages said: What is that auspicious knowledge obtained by you, which is more truthful than truth itself, and by attaining supreme steadfastness in which a person reaches happiness?

Vayu said: "The knowledge of the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), the fettered soul (Paśu), and the fetter (Pāśa) which was obtained by me in the past—therein a person seeking happiness should establish supreme steadfastness."
Suffering arises from ignorance and is ceased by knowledge alone. Knowledge is the discernment of reality, and reality is traditionally held to be of two kinds.
The non-inert, the inert, and the controller of both—these three are called, respectively, the bound soul (paśu), the bond (pāśa), and the Lord (pati).
The imperishable (akṣara), the perishable (kṣara), and likewise that which is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable—this triad is extensively described by those who know the reality.

The imperishable (akṣara) is said to be the individual soul (paśu), while the perishable (kṣara) is declared to be the bond (pāśa). That which is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable is designated as the Lord (pati).
The sages said: What is that which is called the Imperishable (akṣara), and what is cited as the Perishable (kṣara)? And what indeed is the Supreme beyond those two? Tell us this, O Māruta.
Vāyu said: Nature is called the perishable, while the Puruṣa is called the imperishable. Another, the supreme Parameśvara, impels these two.

The sages said: What is this that is called *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and who is considered this *puruṣa* (spirit)? By what means is there a connection between these two, and who is this impelling Lord?
Vāyu said: Māyā is designated as Prakṛti; Puruṣa is enveloped by Māyā. His connection arises from primordial karma; Śiva is the impelling Lord.

The sages said: What is this that is called Māyā? Of what form is he who is enveloped by Māyā? What is its root, and from where does it arise? What is the nature of Śivatva, and from where does Śiva come?
Vāyu said: The power of Māheśvarī is Māyā; the one whose form is consciousness is enveloped by Māyā. Impurity is innate and obscures consciousness, whereas purity and the state of Śiva are inherent.
The sages said: How does Māyā veil [the Self], and for what reason? For what purpose is there this veiling of the Person, and by what means is it removed?

Vāyu said: "Though all-pervasive, there must be a covering, because even that which is pervasive, such as the *kalā* and other principles, exists. Action alone is the cause for the sake of experience; it ceases upon the destruction of impurity (*mala*)."
The sages said: What is this that is called "kalā" and so forth? Or what is described as "karma"? What is its beginning, what is its end, what is its fruit, and what is its support?

Whose is the enjoyment, what is the object of enjoyment, or what is the means for that enjoyment? What is the cause of the destruction of impurity, and what is the nature of the person whose impurity has been destroyed?
Vāyu said: "Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati—these are declared to be Kalā and the others; he who is the enjoyer of them is the Puruṣa."

Action, consisting of merit and demerit, which has happiness and suffering as its fruit, begins in the beginningless past, ends with the experience [of its results], and has its locus in the self through ignorance.
Experience leads to the destruction of karma; experience is said to be unmanifest. The body, with its external and internal organs as its gateways, is the instrument of experience.
Through the clarity attained by the excellence of one's disposition, there is the destruction of impurity; and when that personal impurity is destroyed, the person becomes equal to Śiva.
The sages said: What are the distinct functions of the five principles beginning with *kalā*, by which the Self is designated as both "the enjoyer" and "the person"?
What is the nature of that unmanifest, and in what form is it experienced? What is its refuge during experience, and what is called the body?
Vāyu said: Space, action, manifesting knowledge, time, and passion are the motivators; therein, time is the delimiting factor and necessity is the regulator.
That which is the unmanifest cause, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), and the source of origin and dissolution—what the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti.
Manifested through *kalā*, yet characterized by non-manifestation, it is experienced in three ways as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, being thus endowed with the *guṇas*.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities born of Prakṛti; they reside within Prakṛti in a subtle form, like oil in a sesame seed.
Happiness and the cause of happiness are briefly remembered as being of the nature of sattva; that which is the opposite is rājasa; while rigidity and delusion are tāmasa.
The upward movement is said to be sāttvika; the downward movement would be tāmasa; but that movement which is intermediate is recited as rājasa.
The five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (bhūtas), the fivefold unity of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas), and the five organs of action (karmendriyas).

The fourfold group consisting of primordial matter (pradhāna), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas) is thus briefly described as the unmanifest (avyakta) together with its modifications (savikāra).
That which has reached the state of being a cause is called the unmanifest (avyakta); that which has reached the state of being an effect is the manifest (vyakta), such as the body or a jar.
Just as an effect such as a jar does not differ significantly from its cause, such as clay, so too the manifest, such as the body, does not differ significantly from the unmanifest.
Therefore, the Unmanifest alone is the cause of unity, as are the instruments; the body is their substratum, and it is also that which is to be experienced, and nothing else.
The sages said: From what basis does there exist, even in reality, any entity denoted by the word "self" that is distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body?
Vāyu said: "The existence of some eternal Self, distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body, is indeed certain; yet the proof for that is very difficult to find."

The wise do not accept that the intellect, the sense organs, or the body are the self, because memory is not invariably known [simultaneously with them] and because they persist only as long as the body exists.
Therefore, He who is the object of all that is to be known—both what has been experienced and what is remembered—is celebrated in the Vedas and the Upanishads as the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī).
He, the eternal one, remains there pervading everything everywhere; nevertheless, he is not clearly perceived by anyone anywhere.
This Great Self is not to be grasped by the eye, nor even by the other sense organs; it is perceived only by the mind when it is fully illumined.
This is neither female, nor male, nor even neuter; it is not above, nor across, nor below, nor from anywhere at all.
The wise man always perceives that which is bodiless within bodies, immovable within the moving, and imperishable—by means of reflective discernment.
What is the use of saying more in this matter? The person is distinct from the body; those who see them as non-distinct indeed possess an incorrect vision.
That which is called this body of the Puruṣa, beyond that, exists as impure, powerless, suffering, and unstable; it does not truly exist.
Endowed with that which is the seed of calamities, a person becomes happy, miserable, or deluded through his own karma.
Just as a field saturated with water produces a sprout, so too does karma, saturated by ignorance, produce a body.
His thousands of bodies, both past and future, are known to be abodes of extreme suffering and destined for certain death.
Embodied beings come again and again, yet when their bodies have decayed, no one attains an ultimate dwelling anywhere.
Covered and yet separated from bodies, he is perceived within these [bodies] like the lunar orb in the sky by shifting masses of clouds.
The activity of the self here appears divided according to the distinction of various bodies, just as the impression of a die is perceived when it rolls across a checkered board.
No one shall belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone; this association with wives, sons, and kinsmen is merely a meeting on the road.
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart again—such is the meeting of living beings.
He sees that body, yet he does not see that [other] body; some other person sees both of them, yet they both do not see him.
All beings from Brahmā down to the immovable are proclaimed to be bound souls (paśus); this illustration has been declared for all such bound souls.
This very one, who feeds upon pleasure and pain, is bound by fetters as a beast; he is the instrument for the sport of the Lord—so say the wise.
This ignorant creature is not its own master over its pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Anila, the sages, with delighted minds, bowed down to that Vāyu, who was an expert in the Śaiva Āgamas, and spoke.
The sages said: "Regarding this one who is called 'the bound soul' (paśu) and that which is designated as 'the bond' (pāśa)—what is this Lord who exists distinct from these two?"
Vāyu said: There is a certain Lord, the creator of the universe and the liberator from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), who is the abode of boundless and most beautiful qualities.
In the absence of that [Lord], how could this creation of the universe come to be, given the insentience and ignorance of these two—the bound soul (paśu) and the bond (pāśa)?
Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth, has been observed to be produced by an agent without an intelligent cause.

The world is dependent upon a creator because it is an effect and possesses constituent parts; therefore, the status of being the creator of the effect belongs to the Lord (pati), and not to the bound soul (paśu) or the fetter (pāśa).
Even the agency of the animal is preceded by the impulse of the Lord; it is like the movement of a blind man who knows how to act otherwise [than stumbling].
Having considered the self as distinct and the Impeller as distinct from it, he, being thus favored by Him, becomes fit for immortality.
In reality, there exists a supreme state belonging to the bound soul, the fetter, and the Lord; having known that through the knowledge of Brahman, one will be liberated from the womb.
The Lord, the liberator of the universe, sustains this entire world—the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as these two joined together: the perishable and the imperishable.
The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—these three are declared to be the objects of thought. For those who know, there is indeed nothing further to be known beyond this.
Just as oil is contained within sesame seeds, or clarified butter within curd, as water pervades a stream, and as fire exists within the fire-sticks;
In this very way, one who is constantly disciplined by truth and austerity perceives the Great Self within oneself as distinct from the individual self.
He who alone, possessing a net, is the Lord through his sovereign powers, having created all these worlds, rules as the one Lord alone.
At that time, Rudra was indeed alone; there was no second being whatsoever. Having created the entire universe, he who is its protector withdrew it back into himself.
He indeed has eyes on all sides, and likewise he has faces on all sides; similarly, he has arms on all sides and is endowed with feet on all sides.
The one God Maheśvara, generating heaven and earth, is himself the source and the origin of all the gods.
"He generated Hiraṇyagarbha as the first among the gods; Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe"—so indeed says the Śruti.
I know this great Puruṣa, immortal and eternal, resplendent like the sun, the Lord established beyond darkness.
There is nothing whatsoever beyond this Supreme Self; there is nothing smaller and nothing greater than it, for by it this entire world is filled.
The Blessed One has all faces, heads, and necks; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings; and the Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, he exists pervading everything.
He is the manifestation of the qualities of all the senses, yet he is devoid of all senses; he is the Lord and Sovereign of all, the refuge and the well-wishing friend of all.
He who sees though he has no eyes, who hears though he has no ears, who knows all yet is not known by anyone—him they call the Supreme Person.
Subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, this immutable Maheśvara is hidden within the cave of the heart of every living being.
Through the grace of the Creator, one whose sorrow has departed beholds that Lord, who is the embodiment of will, filled with supreme greatness, and endowed with an abundance of creative power.
I know this undecaying, ancient, all-pervading, and sovereign Lord, whose cessation of birth the exponents of Brahman proclaim.

Though he is one, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) first creates the universe in manifold ways through the application of his power; he ordains these three worlds, and yet he is perceived as distinct from them.

The supreme, variegated form of Śiva is called the "All-Sustainer" (Viśvadhātrī) and the "Unborn" (Ajā). That single Unborn One is red, white, and black; from her, the Unborn One, all creatures are born.

One unborn soul lies within the womb of the Mother who possesses his own form, while enjoying her; yet another unborn soul abandons that very same Unborn One after having experienced the enjoyments of her devotees.
Two birds, inseparable companions, dwell upon the same tree; one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
A person submerged in this tree, remaining hidden, grieves; but when he beholds another, the beloved Lord who is the supreme cause, [he is liberated].
Then, free from sorrow, one becomes happy through its majesty; for the Vedas, the sacrifices, the seasons, and all that has been and all that is to be, are contained therein.

The Supreme One, having entered this world through Māyā, creates the universe by means of Māyā; one should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and the Great Lord as the possessor of Māyā (Māyin).
By her very limbs, this entire world is pervaded—even the extremely subtle Īśāna within the midst of the embryo.
Having known Śiva alone as the Lord, the creator of the universe and its enveloper, one attains ultimate peace.
He alone is Time, the protector, the sovereign lord, and the master of the universe; by knowing Him as the Lord of the Universe, one is liberated from the noose of death.
Having known the Lord who abides subtle like the cream upon clarified butter, hidden within all beings, one is liberated from all sins.
This indeed is the supreme deity, Viśvakarman, the Great Lord; by knowing him as dwelling within the heart, one attains immortality.
When everything is neither day nor night, neither existent nor non-existent, and only Śiva alone remains, from that arises primordial wisdom.
Neither above, nor across, nor in between can one grasp him; there is no likeness of him whose name is Great Renown.
Some wise ones, fearing birth, take refuge in this very unborn [state], the auspicious right side of this Rudra, for the sake of protection.
Two syllables, supreme to Brahman and infinite, have been proclaimed; they are designated as knowledge and ignorance, hidden therein as if concealed.
The perishable is indeed ignorance, while the immortal is proclaimed as knowledge; he who rules over both of these is truly the other, the Great Lord.
He who, manifesting each single web in many ways and yet remaining as one, exercises supreme sovereignty after having created all things, is the majestic one.
Illuminating the directions—above, below, and across—he shines by himself; he who, though devoid of intrinsic nature, alone presides as the most excellent.
Transforming all denoters of intrinsic nature as well as their denoted objects, and the qualities into the states of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, he presides over that entire universe.
In the secret Upanishad, the gods and great seers know that hidden Brahman, which is higher than the highest, the source of Brahman, and the primordial world.

Those who know the God—who is graspable through contemplation, known as "effortless," the auspicious one who brings about both existence and non-existence, and the creator of the emission of the *kalās*—they have abandoned the body.

Some, being deluded, consider [the world] to be of the nature of inherent essence (svabhāva), while others consider it to be Time (kāla); for this is the majesty of the Divine by which this universe is made to revolve.
Since this [universe] is eternally enveloped by that which has the nature of the Time of times, it is impelled by Him and revolves together with the elements.
Having repeatedly performed that action and having repeatedly withdrawn from it, one indeed attains union with reality through reality itself.
Thus, by means of eight, three, two, or even one [of these qualities], and also through time and his own personal attributes, he himself [pervades] the entire world.

One should apply actions, such as those arising from inherent nature and so forth, by means of the qualities (guṇas); in the absence of these [qualities], there would be the destruction even of an action already performed.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, he truly proceeds from that state to another; he himself is the beginningless cause of yoga for both the enjoyer and the enjoyment.
The Supreme Lord is indeed beyond time, beyond the kalās, omniscient, the master of the three guṇas, the direct Brahman, higher than the highest.
We worship Him who is the multiform, the non-existent and the existent, the adorable Prajāpati, the God of gods, the one honored by the world, who dwells within one's own mind.
Because the phenomenal world revolves through time and other factors, [He is] the bringer of dharma, the dispeller of evil, the Lord of enjoyments, and the abode of the universe.
Let us know Him as the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities, the supreme lord among lords, the God who is the Lord of the lords of the worlds.
For him, no effect exists, nor does a cause exist; neither his equal nor his superior is seen anywhere in the world.
His manifold power is heard in the Veda as innate; it consists of knowledge, strength, and action, by which this entire universe is created.
He has no master whatsoever, neither a mark nor a ruler; he is the cause of causes and the sovereign lord over them all.
He has no progenitor whatsoever, nor is there any birth for him from anywhere; likewise, the causes of birth known as impurity, māyā, and so forth, do not exist for him.
He alone is hidden within all beings and pervades them on every side; he is the inner self of all beings and is called the presiding lord of dharma.
He is the abode of all beings, the witness, the perceiver, and devoid of qualities; he is the one controller of the many inactive ones who are themselves powerless.
He is the eternal among the eternal, the conscious among the conscious; though one, he is the desireless Lord who bestows desires upon the many.
Having known that Lord, the cause who is attainable through Sāṃkhya and Yoga and the master of the worlds, the bound soul (paśu) is liberated from all fetters (pāśas).

The creator of the universe, the knower of the universe, the one who knows his own self as the source, the maker of time, the possessor of qualities, the primary principle, the lord of the individual soul, the master of the qualities, and the liberator from bonds.
I have realized that God who, in the beginning, created Brahmā and himself taught him the Vedas, by means of the clarity of my own self-knowledge.
Desiring liberation from this saṃsāra, I take refuge in Śiva—He who is fruitless, actionless, peaceful, blameless, and untainted.
When men shall roll up space like a hide, as one rolls up a piece of leather, then they shall see the supreme bridge to immortality, which is like the wind that has consumed its fuel.
Then, through the power of their asceticism and by the grace of the Lord, the great seers will come to know Śiva, and there will be an end to suffering.
This knowledge, appropriate for those beyond the stages of life, is pure and destructive of sin; it is the supreme secret in the Vedānta, proclaimed in a former age.
This has been obtained by me from the mouth of Brahmā through the weight of my good fortune; this unsurpassed knowledge must not be given to one who is not tranquil.
