It should not be given to a son who does not behave properly, nor to one who is not a disciple in every respect; [it is for] him whose supreme devotion is to the Divine, and as it is to the Divine, so it is to the Guru.
For these truths have indeed been declared to that high-souled one; therefore, listen to this summary: Śiva is beyond both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
At the time of creation, he brings forth everything; at the time of dissolution, he takes it all back again.
The sages said: Everything arises from Time; indeed, everything perishes by Time alone. For nothing whatsoever exists anywhere that is independent of Time.
When the entire universe, the eternal circle of saṃsāra, revolves like a wheel within this [consciousness] by means of the two seals of emanation and reabsorption;
Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, and likewise the other gods and asuras, having encountered the destiny ordained by him, are not able to transcend it.
Dividing living beings into the past, future, and present, and causing them to decay, this most terrifying one acts according to his own will as the supreme lord.
Who is this Blessed One Time, and whose is he under the sway? Who indeed would not be under his control? Tell me this, O wise one.
Vāyu said: "The supreme Māheśvara splendor, whose form is composed of the divisions of time such as *kāla*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *nimeṣa*, is known as Kālātman."
That which is insurmountable for all that is stationary and moving, the form of the Lord’s command, is the power that governs the universe.
Liberation consists of the subtlest portions of that [nature] within the Great Self who is Time; having emerged from that, it has entered [into him], like iron cast into fire.

Therefore, the universe is under the control of time, but time does not abide under the control of the universe; rather, time is under the control of Śiva, but Śiva is never under the control of time.
Since the unimpeded splendor of Śarva is established in Time, the great boundary of Time is indeed difficult to transcend.
Who is able to transcend Time by means of any particular excellence of wisdom? For no one can escape the action performed by Time.
Even those who, through their prowess, rule the entire earth under a single umbrella do not transcend the appointed time, just as the oceans do not overstep their shores.
Those who, having restrained the collection of their senses, conquer the entire world—even they do not conquer Time; rather, Time conquers even them.
Even physicians who know the science of Ayurveda and have practiced the elixirs of rejuvenation do not transcend death; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Through wealth, beauty, character, strength, and lineage—whatever a living being thinks of, Time forcibly makes something else.
The Lord indeed unites living beings with both the unpleasant and the pleasant, whose arrivals and departures are beyond thought, and likewise separates them from them.
At the very moment that someone is suffering, another is happy; oh, how wonderful is the diversity of Time, whose nature is so difficult to comprehend!
O twice-born ones, he who is young becomes old; he who is powerful becomes weak; and even he who is prosperous becomes destitute—for Time has a manifold course.
Neither noble birth, nor conduct, nor strength, nor skill would be sufficient for success, even if time itself were unimpeded.

Time acts with equal impartiality toward those who have protectors and are generous, attended by songs and instrumental music, as well as toward those who are protectorless and subsist on the food of others.
Elixirs do not bear fruit at the wrong time, nor do medicines, even when properly administered; yet those very same things, gathered at the right time, quickly attain success and bestow happiness.
This one does not die nor is born out of season; one does not attain supreme growth out of season; one is not happy or miserable out of season; there exists no thing whatsoever that is untimely.
In due season the cool wind blows; in due season the rain-clouds bring their showers; in due season the heat subsides; and in due season everything attains fruition.
Time is the cause of all existence; by time the crops always come to fruition; by time the crops go to their destruction; and by time the world of living beings is brought back to life.
He who thus understands the reality of the self of time according to its true nature, having transcended the self of time, beholds that which is beyond time.

Salutation to that Supreme Lord Śiva, the ultimate reality, who is neither time nor bondage and liberation; who is neither the individual soul nor primordial nature nor the universe; yet who possesses manifold forms.
The sages said: By what measure is the calculation of lifespan determined in this time? Furthermore, what is the ultimate limit of time, which consists of numerical units?
Vāyu said: Here, they declare that the first measure of time, known as a *nimeṣa*, is the beginning of time in its numerical form, extending up to the limit of the *kalā* of Śāntvatīta.
The closing of the eyelashes is designated as a *nimeṣa*; fifteen such *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are called a *kalā*; thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* are declared to be one day and night (*ahorātra*).

A month, consisting of two fortnights, is known to consist of thirty days and nights; this is to be understood as a day and night of the ancestors (pitrya), wherein the month consists of the dark and bright fortnights.
Six months constitute an *ayana*, and two *ayanās* are considered a year; this is the human year as reckoned by worldly measurement.
This is the divine day and night; such is the certainty of the scripture: the southern solstice is the night, and the northern solstice is the day.
A month of the gods is known to consist of thirty days and nights, just like that of humans; likewise, a year of the gods consists of twelve such months.
Three hundred years, plus sixty years, are to be known as one divine year, as proclaimed according to human reckoning.
The calculation of the ages proceeds by divine measure alone; the sages know that there are four ages in the land of Bhārata.
First is that which is called the Kṛta Yuga, and after that the Tretā is ordained; then the Dvāpara and the Kali—these are all the Yugas in their entirety.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years; its morning twilight (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its evening twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three [ages], along with their twilights and twilight-portions, the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This period of twelve thousand years, increased by a little more, constitutes a cycle of four yugas; a thousand such cycles of four yugas is what is called a *saṃkalpa*.
The interval between Manus is said to consist of seventy-one cycles of the four yugas; within a single kalpa, there are fourteen such successions of Manus.
By this sequential process, hundreds and thousands of kalpas and manvantaras, along with their inhabitants, have passed away.
Furthermore, because all things are unknowable and incalculable, it is simply impossible to describe them in detail according to their sequential order.
A *kalpa* is said to be a day of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest; a thousand such *kalpas* are here called a year of Brahmā.
Eight thousand years constitute one *yuga* of Brahmā; a thousand such *yugas* form a single day (*savana*) of Brahmā, who is born from the lotus.
A thousand times three hundred and thirty-six such sacrificial sessions constitute the entire lifespan of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Indeed, on that day fourteen Purandaras pass away; in a month, four hundred and twenty [Purandaras] pass away.
In years, [the lifespan] is five hundred and forty thousand; in tens of thousands, it is forty-five lakhs.
One day of Viṣṇu consists of one day of Brahmā; likewise, one day of Rudra consists of one day of Viṣṇu; in the day of Īśvara, there is Rudra, and similarly, Īśvara [constitutes] the day of Sadākhya.
That Sadāśiva is also equal in number to Śiva himself; his lifespan consists of five hundred and forty thousand years.

In that [state], this very soul of time proceeds directly from Śiva. O twice-born ones, that interval of time which has been described here as belonging to creation is to be known as the day of the Supreme Lord; his night is to be known as being of equal duration in its entirety. His day is remembered as creation, and his night as dissolution.
One should hold the conviction that for him there is neither day nor night; this conventional practice is performed out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
The progeny, the lords of progeny, and the embodied forms of gods and asuras; the sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the five great elements.
Then the subtle elements, the source of the gross elements, and the intellect, together with the presiding deities—all these abide within the wise Supreme Lord.

At the end of the day, all things dissolve; at the end of the night, the source of the universe arises. He is the soul of the universe, whose power regarding the objects of karma, time, and inherent nature cannot be transgressed.
Salutations to that great Śaṅkara, under whose command alone all this depends.
The sages said: How does the Supreme Lord, having created and then withdrawn this entire universe, perform his supreme sport by his own command?
What was that which first came into being? By whom was this entire universe pervaded? And by whom, moreover, is this world swallowed up by one of vast belly?
Vāyu said: Śakti was first produced, following the state beyond peace (śāntyatīta); from that [came] Māyā, and from that, the Unmanifest (avyakta) from the Lord Śiva, who possesses Śakti.

From that [state] comes the state of Śakti, which transcends peace (śānti), by way of the sequence of the states of peace; from that comes the state of Vidyā, and from that arises the state of Pratiṣṭhā.
The state of cessation arises sequentially from the state of establishment; thus has the creation impelled by the Lord been described in brief.
Just as their manifestation occurs in direct order, so too is their withdrawal in reverse order; from this fivefold sequence thus taught, the Supreme Creator is intended.
This entire world is pervaded by the five kalās; that which is the unmanifest cause is established through the Self.

It is also accepted that [Prakṛti] creates everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa); however, even in that regard, agency belongs neither to the Unmanifest (avyakta) nor to the Self (ātman).
Because primordial matter (prakṛti) is insentient and the person (puruṣa) is ignorant, whatever is insentient—such as primary matter, atoms, and so forth—is [unfit for the role of creator].
The world is seen by [the opponent] himself to have that [mountain, etc. as its agent; however, it is dependent upon an intelligent cause because it is an effect possessing constituent parts.
Therefore, he who is capable, independent, possessed of all powers, and all-knowing—this one is without beginning or end and endowed with great sovereignty.
He alone is the creator of the world, Mahādeva, the Great Lord; he is the protector and the destroyer of all, and therefore he is distinct and unrelated to anything else.
The transformation of Pradhāna and the activity of Puruṣa—all this proceeds solely by the command of Satyavrata.
Thus, this eternal conclusion dwells in the minds of the virtuous; one of feeble intellect does not abide by resorting to such a position.
From the initial commencement until the great dissolution, all this remains for a hundred autumns of Brahmā.
The name *para* belongs to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest; that which is called *para* has half of it designated as a *parārdha*.
At the end of two parārdhas, when the dissolution has arrived, he remains within himself, taking his unmanifested effect into his own self.
When the unmanifest self is established and all transformation has been withdrawn, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide together in a state of similarity.
These two qualities, tamas and sattva, exist in a state of equilibrium; neither being predominant, they are infinite and mutually interwoven.
Then, when the qualities were in equilibrium, while that undifferentiated state prevailed and the darkness had arisen—like water alone, calm and windless—not a single thing could be discerned.
While this world remains unawakened, Maheśvara alone is the one to be worshipped throughout the entire night of supreme Māheśvarī.
When the night had turned to dawn, the Great Lord, through the application of his illusory power (māyā), entered and agitated both of those two principal beings.
Then, once again, from the Unmanifest, through the command of the Supreme Lord, there arose the creation of all beings without exception, according to their origin and dissolution.

Salutations to Him who is distinct from all worlds, whose single fragment of power completes the entire manifold of ever-surpassing and diverse desires; whom those who know the path call the Self and the Lord of the path.

Vāyu said: Previously, by the command of the Lord, from the unmanifest (avyakta) presided over by the Puruṣa, the modifications beginning with the intellect (buddhi) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) came into being in succession.
Then, from those transformations, the three gods—Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha—were born as the causes of all things.
The power to pervade all worlds unimpeded anywhere, incomparable knowledge, and eternal sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Maheśvara, together with his sovereignty, is pleased to act as the cause for these three activities known as creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
In another Kalpa, however, to those who were non-contentious yet deluded in intellect, he assigned individually the duty of creation, protection, dissolution, and conduct.
These, produced from one another, support one another; they increase through one another, being devoted to one another.
In some places Brahmā is praised, in some Viṣṇu, and in some Rudra; yet by this, their superiority or their sovereignty is not exceeded.
Fools, possessed by agitation and dogmatic attachment, revile them with their words; they undoubtedly become Yātudhānas and Piśācas.

The God Maheśvara, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas) and consists of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), is the possessor of all parts and the cause of the origin of the power that supports all.
This Self, established in its state as Lord, effects the creation of the world through its play, [presiding over] these three: primordial nature, the individual soul, and the Lord.
That Supreme Lord, who is eternal, partless, and superior to everything, is Himself the support of that [universe], its very self, and its presiding controller.
Therefore, Maheśvara, as well as Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Sadāśiva, Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—all are of the nature of Śiva.
From Pradhāna, first were born Vṛddhi, Khyāti, Mati, and Mahat. From the agitation of the Mahat-tattva, Ahaṃkāra became threefold.

The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the elements, the subtle essences (tanmātras), and the sense organs arise from the ego-sense; specifically, the sattvic [ego] arises from the ego-sense when sattva is predominant.
That creation, however, which is of the nature of transformation (vaikārika), proceeds simultaneously: namely, the five organs of perception and the five organs of action.

The eleventh therein is the mind, which by its own quality partakes of both natures; from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) conjoined with tamas arises the origin of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the gross elements (bhūta).
Because he is the primordial source of the elements (bhūtas), he is called Bhūtādi; from Bhūtādi arises the subtle element of sound (śabdamātra), and from that, the origination of space (ākāśa).
From space, touch was produced; from touch, wind arose; from wind, form; from that, fire; and from fire, the production of taste.
From taste water was produced; from them, fragrance arose. From fragrance earth was born, and from the elements came everything else, both moving and unmoving.
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest, they produce the cosmic egg, beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements.
When the effect and the instrument were fully established from Brahman, then the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), designated as Brahman, became fully developed within the cosmic egg.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa. He is the original creator of all beings, and as Brahmā, he existed at the beginning.
The image of that Lord is the intellect (buddhi) belonging to Brahmā, characterized by knowledge and dispassion; it bestows righteousness and sovereignty upon the one who presides over the sacrifice.
From the unmanifest, whatever is desired by him arises through the mind; this is due to his mastery, his transformation, the three qualities, his dependence, and his inherent nature.
Having divided himself threefold, he proceeds throughout the three worlds; by means of these three, he himself creates, devours, and beholds.
As Brahmā, he is four-faced; as Time, he is known as the Ender (Antaka); and as the Self-born (Svayambhū), he is the thousand-headed Puruṣa—these are the three states of the Self-existent One.

In his state as Brahmā, the pervasive Lord possesses both *sattva* and *rajas*; in his state as Time (*kāla*), he possesses *tamas* and *rajas*; and in his state as Viṣṇu, he possesses *sattva* alone—the increase of the qualities (*guṇa*) thus occurs in three ways within the All-pervading One.

In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the state of Time, he even withdraws them; and in the state of the Puruṣa, he is utterly indifferent—such is the threefold activity of the All-pervading Lord.
Thus, because he is divided threefold, Brahmā is called "possessing the three qualities" (triguṇa); and because he is divided fourfold, he is celebrated as the "fourfold manifestation" (cāturvyūha).
Because he is the beginning, he is the Primordial God; because he is unborn, he is remembered as the Unborn (Aja); and because he protects all creatures, he is remembered as Prajāpati.
The golden Mount Meru is the amnion of that Great-Souled One; the Garbhodaka ocean is his amniotic fluid, and the mountains are his placenta.
Within that egg were these worlds, this entire universe, including the moon and the sun with the stars and planets, together with the wind.
The egg is surrounded on the outside by water ten times its size; the water, in turn, is surrounded on the outside by fire ten times its size.
Fire is surrounded on the outside by air ten times its size; air is surrounded by space, and space is surrounded by the source of the elements (bhūtādi).

Likewise, the source of the elements (bhūtādi) is enveloped by the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta). By these seven coverings, the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) is surrounded on the outside.
O best of the twice-born, these eight primordial natures (prakṛtis) remain encompassing one another, performing the functions of creation, preservation, and destruction.
In this way, the modifications, having arisen from one another, support one another through the relationship of the container and the contained within the modified entities.
Just as a tortoise first extends its limbs and then withdraws them, so too does the Unmanifest, having emitted the modifications, again withdraws them.
Everything arises from the Unmanifest in a forward order; but when the time of dissolution arrives, it merges back in a reverse order.

The qualities (guṇas) become unbalanced or balanced solely by the power of time; when there is equilibrium of the qualities, it should be known as dissolution (laya), and in their imbalance, it is called creation (sṛṣṭi).
This very thing is the womb of Brahmā; this is the great, solid egg. It is designated as the field (kṣetra) of Brahmā, and Brahmā is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Thus, millions upon thousands of such eggs are to be known; because the *pradhāna* is all-pervasive, they are situated horizontally, above, and below.
In various places, four-faced Brahmās, Haras, and Bhavas were created by Pradhāna; likewise, having obtained the presence of Śambhu, they [acted].
Maheśvara is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arose the cosmic egg, and from the egg was born the pervasive Brahmā, by whom these worlds were created.
This first primary creation has been described by me as proceeding without prior conscious intent; and at the time of the final dissolution, it is withdrawn solely as a sport of the Lord.
That which is known as the immeasurable cause—Brahmā, the Pradhāna, the source of Prakṛti; without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power, white and deep red, joined with the Puruṣa.

Because it is the generator and due to the predominance of the quality of rajas, it creates at the time of the beginning even the eight transformations that cause the expansion of the world's continuity, and likewise consumes them at the time of its end.

Whatever stability and whatever further activity belong to causes established by their own nature—all that is due solely to the mere volition of the Great Lord, whose majesty is beyond the natural order.
The sages said: "Tell us of all the Manvantaras and all the various divisions of the Kalpas, as well as the intermediate creation and the secondary creation within them."
Vāyu said: A *parārdha* is recorded as the duration of Brahmā’s life-cycle; another period of equal length follows him, at the end of which he is re-created.
Day after day, fourteen fortunate cycles of Manus pass for that Brahmā of his previous birth.
Because they are beginningless, endless, and entirely unknowable, the Manvantaras and Kalpas cannot be described individually in their entirety.
Even though all these have been stated, what fruit is there for you who hear my words? Therefore, I do not venture to speak further.
Indeed, among all the aeons, it is this very aeon that is currently proceeding; within it, the processes of creation and re-creation occur in an abbreviated manner.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, in this present aeon known by the name Vārāha, there are likewise fourteen Manus.
There are seven Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, and seven others beginning with Sāvarṇika; among them, the seventh Manu, named Vaivasvata, is currently presiding.
A wise person should employ reasoning [to understand] that in all Manvantaras, the processes of creation and dissolution generally occur in the same manner.
When the previous aeon had passed away and the wind of time had begun to blow, the trees and the forests were uprooted from their very foundations.
When the god Agni burns, even those with mouths like blades of grass survive; yet when rain is poured upon the earth and the waters overflow the oceans, they perish.
When all the quarters were submerged in a vast flood of water, by means of the circles of wave-arms with their playful tossings of spray, [the world was overwhelmed].
Then, while the waters of the dissolution were engaged in fierce dancing, Brahmā, having become Nārāyaṇa, slept happily upon the water.
And reciting this mantra and verse concerning Nārāyaṇa, listen, O best of sages, to it and to its meaning based on the syllables.
The waters are called "nārāḥ," for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; since they were his place of movement (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The Siddhas dwelling in Janaloka, with their palms joined in reverence, [beheld] the Lord of the Thirty Gods as he was performing a sleep consisting of Śiva-yoga.
At the time of dawn, the gods awakened Him with hymns of praise, just as the Vedas formerly awakened the Lord at the time of the initial creation.
Then, having awakened and risen from his bed, he emerged into the midst of the water; with eyes languid from yogic sleep, he gazed at all the directions.
At that time, he did not perceive anything whatsoever distinct from his own self; sitting as if filled with wonder, he fell into deep reflection.
Where is that blessed, delightful, and vast earth, with its various great mountains, rivers, cities, and forests?
Reflecting thus, Brahmā did not perceive the state of the earth at all; then he remembered his father, the three-eyed Lord.
By remembering Bhava, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor, the lord of the earth realized that the earth was submerged in water.
Then, desiring to lift up the earth, Prajāpati meditated upon his divine form as a boar, which was suited for sporting in the waters.
With a stature like a great mountain, a voice like a massive thundercloud, resembling a dark blue cloud, he was terrifying with his blazing roar.
With thick, round, and dense shoulders, and full, elevated hips; with short, rounded thighs and shanks, and a very sharp, circular tip.
Resembling a ruby gem, with round and terrifying eyes, possessing a large body that was both rounded and long, and radiant with stiff ears and temples.
With its heaving inhalations and exhalations tossing it like the ocean at the end of an aeon, it was beautiful with its cheeks and shoulders covered by quivering, fine manes.
Adorned with various jewels, ornaments, and great gems, it shone like a towering mass of clouds illuminated by flashes of lightning.
Assuming a vast and immeasurable boar-form, the Ordainer entered the netherworld for the purpose of uplifting the earth.
Then that boar shone exceedingly, resembling a mountain, as if he had gone to the foot of the Great Lord (Maheśa) who is in the form of a *liṅga*.
Then the upholder of the earth, having lifted the earth submerged in the waters and embraced it with his tusks, emerged from the netherworld (rasātala).
Seeing him, the sages and perfected beings dwelling in Janaloka rejoiced, danced, and showered flowers upon his head.
The body of the Great Boar, covered with flowers, shone like Mount Añjana when it is strewn with falling fireflies.
Then, having brought the great earth to its proper configuration, the omnipresent Lord Varāha resumed his own form and established it.
Having leveled the earth and established the mountains upon it, he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before.

Thus, having placed the vast earth together with its mountains from within the depths of the great ocean of dissolution, both below and above, Viśvakarman once again created the world of moving and non-moving beings.

Vāyu said: As he was then contemplating creation with deliberate intent, at the time of deep reflection, a delusion consisting of *tamas* appeared. This fivefold ignorance—namely *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and that known as *andha-tāmisra*—manifested from the Great Soul.

As he meditated, the fivefold creation of the conceited one was completely enveloped by darkness, like a seed within a jar; it was without light inside or out, motionless, and utterly devoid of consciousness. Consequently, their intellects, as well as their faces and organs, were shrouded.

Therefore, those self-restrained beings are proclaimed as the foremost of mountains. Seeing that such a first creation was unsuccessful, Brahmā became displeased in mind and resolved upon a second. As he was intending to create, the "animal-stream" (tiryaksrotas) turned toward him.

The animals were luminous within but again obscured without; they were born as beings of the nature of cattle and were followers of the wrong path. Knowing that creation also to be unsuccessful, he reflected upon another creation; then the upward-streaming creation occurred, which was the divine creation characterized by goodness (sattva).

They were abundant in happiness and joy, unobstructed both internally and externally; they were designated as being luminous by their very nature, both within and without. Then, from that unmanifest state, as he was brooding, there arose the creation known as the "downward-flowing" (arvāk-srotas), consisting of those called humans—a creation characterized by the intensity of suffering.

The fifth creation is the Anugraha-sarga (the benevolent creation), which is established in four ways: through error (viparyaya), power (śakti), contentment (tuṣṭi), and attainment (siddhi). These beings are all without possessions and instead delight in sharing.

Those who eat and lack moral conduct are proclaimed to be the *bhūtādi* [creation]. The first is the creation of Mahat from Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; the second is the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is called the elemental creation (*bhūtasarga*). The third is known as the *vaikārika* creation, which pertains to the senses (*aindriyaka*).

Thus this creation from Prakṛti has been described as occurring without prior intelligence. The fourth is the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), and the immobile beings are indeed known as the primary ones. That which is called the horizontal-streamed (tiryak-srota) is the fifth, the animal creation (tiryag-yoni). The sixth is the upward-streamed (ūrdhva-srota), which is known as the divine creation (deva-sarga).

Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which is the human creation. The eighth is the Anugraha (grace) creation, and the ninth is recorded as the Kaumāra (youthful) creation. The first three creations are primordial (prākṛta) and proceed without conscious intent; the five subsequent modified (vaikṛta) creations, beginning with the primary one, proceed with conscious intent.

In the beginning, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, indeed created from his own mind seven beings equal to himself: Sananda, Sanaka, the wise Sanātana, Ṛbhu, and Sanatkumāra—these he created first. All of them are to be known as yogis, free from passion and devoid of envy.

With their minds attached to the Lord, they did not set their thoughts upon creation. When Sanaka and the others had departed, having no desire for creation, Brahmā, wishing to create once more, performed supreme austerity. While he was thus performing penance, nothing at all manifested before him.

Then, after a long time, anger was born from sorrow. From the eyes of him who was possessed by anger, drops of tears fell. From those drops of tears, spirits and *pretas* then came into being. Seeing all those born of tears, Brahmā censured himself.

A violent fainting fit, born of anger and resentment, came upon him; and the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), overcome by that fainting and possessed by wrath, gave up his life. Then the Lord Rudra, the Master of Life, the divine Nīlalohita, appeared from the mouth of the Lord in order to grant incomparable grace.

The Lord, the Sovereign, divided himself tenfold and onefold. Those high-souled ones were addressed by him: "O children, you have been created by me in ten ways and one way for the sake of showing grace to the worlds; therefore, act for the establishment and the welfare of the entire world."

"And for the sake of the continuity of progeny, strive without sloth! Thus addressed, they wept and fled in all directions; because of their weeping (*rodana*) and fleeing (*drāvaṇa*), they are known by the name Rudras. Those who are Rudras are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); those who are the vital breaths are the Great-Souled Ones (*mahātman*).

Then, when the god Brahmā Parameṣṭhin had died, Maheśvara, the compassionate son of Brahmā, restored his life-breaths once more. With a joyful countenance due to the return of the Lord’s vital breaths, Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, addressed these supreme words to Brahmā:

"Do not fear, do not fear, O illustrious one, O Viriñca, teacher of the worlds! Your life-breaths have been restored by me; arise happily, O observer of noble vows. Hearing those enchanting words, which were like an experience in a dream, he slowly opened his eyes, which possessed the luster of blooming lotuses, and gazed upon Hara.

Then, having regained his life-breaths, Brahmā addressed him with palms joined in reverence, speaking these words in a gentle and profound voice: "Indeed, by the mere sight of you, you delight my mind; who are you, standing here in an elevenfold form as the embodiment of the universe?"

Having heard those words of his, Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods, spoke while touching Brahmā with his two very pleasant hands: "Know me to be the Supreme Self who has come to you as your son; and these eleven Rudras have also come to protect you well."

"Therefore, having shaken off this intense fainting spell through my grace, awaken as before; you ought indeed to create progeny. Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Brahmā became joyful in mind and, as the soul of the universe, praised the Supreme Lord with eight verses beginning with "Nāma."

Brahmā said: Salutations to you, O Blessed Rudra, whose splendor is immeasurable like that of the sun; salutations to the god Bhava, whose essence is the sap and whose nature is water; salutations to Śarva, who is the form of the earth, and to Nandin, who is the source of abundance.

Salutations to you, Īśa, the Vasu, whose self consists of touch; salutations to the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) and to Pāvaka of exceeding brilliance. Salutations to you, Bhīma, whose form is space (vyoman), consisting of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra). Salutations to the Fierce One (Ugra), whose nature is fierce, the self of the sacrificer (yajamāna). Salutations to Mahādeva, to Soma, to you whose form is nectar (amṛta).

Having thus praised Mahādeva, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, entreated Viśveśa with words preceded by prostration: "O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, my son Maheśvara! You, the destroyer of Ananga, were born from my body for the sake of creation."

"Therefore, O Lord of the World, as you are engaged in this great task, grant me assistance in every respect; you ought to create those subjects. By him, the god Rudra, the destroyer of Tripura, was thus entreated. "So be it," Śaṅkara replied, accepting her words.

Then the Blessed Brahmā, having greeted him with joy, was authorized by him to create; thus he created other progeny. He created Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha by means of his mind alone.
In the beginning, Brahmā created Dharma and Saṃkalpa. Thus, these twelve are proclaimed as the sons of Brahmā; together with Rudra, they were born in ancient times as householders.

Their twelve lineages shall be divine, accompanied by hosts of gods; they will be prolific, observant of sacred rites, and adorned by great sages. Then, desiring to create the fourfold world—gods, asuras, pitṛs, and humans—together with Rudra, the Creator indeed [placed] these into the waters.

Having entered into meditative absorption for the sake of creation, Brahmā joined his own self [to that purpose]. From his mouth he generated the gods, and from his sides the ancestors; from his thighs all the asuras, and from his organ of generation the human beings. From his excrement were born the rākṣasas, who were possessed by hunger.

His sons were night-stalkers (niśācarāḥ) who were powerful and abounding in the qualities of darkness and passion (tamas-rajaḥ-prāyāḥ); likewise, serpents, yakṣas, spirits (bhūtas), and gandharvas were born from him. Birds were created from his wings, and he produced winged creatures from his chest; he created goats from his mouth and fashioned serpents from his sides.
And with his feet, [he struck] horses, elephants, śarabhas, gavayas, deer, camels, mules, nyaṅkus, and other species of animals.
From his body hairs were born medicinal herbs, fruits, and roots; as well as the Gāyatrī, the Ṛc, the Trivṛt Sāman, and the Rathantara.

From his eastern mouth, he fashioned the Agniṣṭoma as the first of sacrifices, as well as the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh meter, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and the Uktha. From his southern mouth, he brought forth the Sāmans, the Jagatī meter, and the seventeen-fold Stoma.

From his western mouth, he created the Vairūpa, the Atirātra, the twenty-first [Sāman], the Atharvan, and the Āptoryāma; from his northern mouth, he created the Anuṣṭubh, the Vairāja, and all beings, both high and low, were born from his limbs.

Yakṣas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, as well as hosts of Apsarases; Nāgas, Kinnaras, Rākṣasas, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents; and whatever is imperishable here—whether stationary or moving—they indeed assumed those very actions which were assigned to them at the time of the original creation.

Those very same things they resort to again and again as they are created: the violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood. Impregnated by those [past tendencies], they resort to them; therefore, that which is pleasing to one becomes dear to him. [This applies] to the diversity among the great elements, the objects of the senses, and the states of liberation.

The Creator himself ordained the specific functions of all beings, as well as the names and forms of created entities and their manifold expansion. At the beginning, that Grandfather fashioned these from the very words of the Veda, including the names of the seers and the modes of expression found within the Vedas.

At the end of the night, the Unborn One gave those very same things back to them; just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle according to the season, so too do those same states of being reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas. Thus is the creation of the world by the Self-born, brought forth from his instruments.

The transformation of Prakṛti itself begins with Mahat and ends with the specific elements (viśeṣa). It is graced by the radiance of the moon and sun, adorned with the circles of planets and stars, and embellished by rivers, oceans, and mountains, as well as by various other delightful and prosperous inhabited lands.

In that forest of Brahman, the unmanifest, all-knowing Brahmā moves about; he is born from the seed of the unmanifest and abides in the grace of the Lord. He has the intellect as his trunk and great branches, the sense organs as the hollows within him, the great elements as his dimensions, and the specific qualities as his pure sprouts.

Rich with the excellent flowers of dharma and adharma, yielding the fruits of happiness and suffering, the eternal Brahma-tree is the livelihood of all beings. The wise declare heaven to be its head, space its navel, and the moon and sun its two eyes; the quarters are its ears and the earth its feet—it is that inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings.

From his mouth the Brahmins were produced; from the front part of his chest the Kṣatriyas; from his thighs the Vaiśyas; and from his feet the Śūdras—all the social orders were produced from his limbs.
The sages said: "The creation of Bhava, the Supreme Self, has been described by you as proceeding from the mouth of the Four-faced One; yet a doubt arises within us regarding that."
The best of gods, Virūpākṣa, the radiant Hara who wields the trident; the Lord Rudra, the soul of Time, with matted hair, blue and red.
He who, when the end of the age has arrived, becomes enraged and withdraws this world—including its Brahmā, its Viṣṇu, and even its Fire—is [the Supreme Being].
To him before whom both Brahmā and Viṣṇu bow out of fear, he who causes the contraction of the worlds, and under whose control those two remain.
That very God who formerly created Brahmā and Viṣṇu from his own body is indeed their eternal Lord, the provider of their acquisition and preservation.
How did that Blessed One Rudra, the primordial god and ancient one, Śambhu, come to be the son of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest?
We have heard even before that Prajāpati and Viṣṇu are both mutually related to Rudra in the act of creation, having arisen from each other’s limbs.
But how, moreover, does the manifestation of all beings from one another occur through the relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities within their causal natures?
Nothing has been left unasked by you, nor has anything remained unheard; as a disciple of the Blessed One, everything has been remembered by you.
"Tell us the truth, just as the all-pervading Brahmā told it to the sages; for we are full of faith, O father, to hear the true glory of the Lord."
Vāyu said: "O Brahmins, you who are skilled in questioning have asked this appropriately. In former times, when I was questioned in this very same way, my Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke thus."
I shall now fully declare how Rudra came into being, and how, furthermore, the mutual origination of Brahmā and Viṣṇu occurred.

These three, whose nature is that of the causal agents, were born directly from Maheśvara; they are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile.
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, permeated by the Supreme Lord, and perpetually presided over by His power, they are capable of performing His work.
In the past, all three were appointed by their father to three tasks: Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and likewise Rudra for destruction.
Nevertheless, out of mutual envy and vying with one another for superiority, they gratified their own father, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance.
Having obtained [this power] through the grace of the Supreme Lord with his whole being, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were first created by Rudra in a previous kalpa.
In another kalpa, however, Brahmā—the one who consists of the universe—became Rudra and Viṣṇu; and the Lord Viṣṇu again created Rudra and Brahmā.
Furthermore, Brahmā created Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa in turn created Brahmā; thus, in every single kalpa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [arise].
Desiring each other's welfare, they are born from one another; this has been established by the great seers with reference to the various occurrences at the end of the kalpas.
Their power is described as arising from their mutual interaction; listen to their wondrous, meritorious story, which grants liberation from sin.
Formerly, during the Meghavāhana kalpa, in the Tatpuruṣa kalpa, there occurred [this event] concerning Brahmā Parameṣṭhin; indeed, it was in the kalpa named Nārāyaṇa.
Having become a cloud, he carried Dharā for a thousand divine years; perceiving his state, Viṣṇu, the teacher of the entire universe, [acted].
He bestowed his entire, imperishable power with his whole being; having then received that power from Śiva, the Lord of All, he became the soul of all.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, together with the Creator of the Universe, emitted the entire world; having witnessed that majesty of Viṣṇu, the Grandfather was created by him.
Seized by supreme envy, he laughed and said this: "Go, Viṣṇu! I have understood the purpose of your creation."
Rudra is superior to us both; of this there is no doubt. This is by the grace of that supreme Lord, the God of gods.
You are the primordial Lord, the creator and the protector in the ultimate sense; and I, having propitiated Rudra, the leader of the gods, through ascetic penance.
"Along with you, I shall create the entire world; of this there is no doubt. Having thus reproached Viṣṇu, the Lord born from the lotus [spoke].
Having attained Śaṅkara through ascetic penance, he made this request: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the universe, Great Lord!"
Viṣṇu was born from your left side, and I am indeed born from your right side; nevertheless, Acyuta created the entire universe along with me.
Though he was censured by me out of envy, it was through the power of taking refuge in you that he said, "He is not superior to my state of being"—such is the sentiment toward you, O Maheśvara.
Since our origin is from you alone and is thus identical for both of us, you have bestowed your grace upon him through his devotion just as you did before.
"O Śaṅkara, you ought to grant all of that to me as well. Thus was the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, entreated by him.
That ocean of compassion bestowed everything upon him according to the proper method; having thus obtained it from the Lord himself, Brahmā attained the state of being the self of all in an instant.
Then, hastening forward, he approached and beheld Puruṣottama in a radiant celestial chariot, brilliant as the sun, situated within the abode of the Ocean of Milk.
Upon a divine bed of infinite enjoyments, fashioned by his own mind and adorned with gold and jewels, he beheld the lotus-eyed Lord reclining.
Four-armed and of noble form, adorned with all ornaments, holding a conch and a discus, gentle, with a face like the orb of the moon.
The Lord, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, possesses a serene and sweet smile; his lotus-like feet were reddened by the touch of the soft lotus-hands of the Earth.

He who lies in yogic sleep like the nectar of the milk-ocean, who is called Kālarudra through the quality of darkness (tamas), and the one born from the golden egg through the quality of passion (rajas).
Seeing that Viṣṇu is all-pervading through his being (sattva) and Maheśvara is devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), Brahmā beheld that Puruṣa and spoke these bold words.
"I shall swallow you, O Viṣṇu, just as you formerly swallowed yourself. Having heard those words of his, he woke up and recognized the Grandfather.
The mighty-armed one looked up and smiled slightly; at that moment, Viṣṇu was swallowed by that high-souled being.
And he was created instantly and effortlessly by Brahmā from the middle of his eyebrows; at that very moment, the Lord adorned with the moon appeared in person.
In order to behold their power as well, he who is formless assumed a form; for in former times, he had granted them a boon so that he might bestow upon them incomparable grace.
He came to the place where Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were staying; then, both pleased and yet fearful out of curiosity, they praised the God.
And they both bowed many times from afar with great reverence; even the Blessed Lord Bhava, the wielder of the Pināka bow, having thus shown them favor.
Even as the two of them were looking on with reverence, he vanished from their sight.
Vāyu said: I shall declare the cause for the manifestation of Rudra in every kalpa, by which the creation of Brahmā proceeds even when its continuity has been interrupted.
In age after age, Brahmā, born from the cosmic egg, having created living beings, became deeply distressed and deluded by the lack of increase among those creatures.
For the sake of pacifying his suffering and for the increase of all creatures, Rudra—the soul of time and lord of the hosts of Rudras—manifests in various kalpas.
The Great Lord Nīlalohita, having been designated as the son of Pañcameśa, shows favor to Brahmā as the younger brother of Brahmā.
He alone is the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, a mass of splendor, free from affliction; he is the creator without beginning or end, the restrainer of beings, and the all-pervading one.
Endowed with supreme sovereignty, permeated by the state of the Supreme Lord, he is perpetually presided over by His power and marked by His very symbols.
He bears that name, possesses that form, is capable of performing those functions, engages in conduct similar to his, and is the observer of his commands.
Resplendent like a thousand suns, adorned with the moon as his ornament, wearing serpents as necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, and a girdle of muñja grass.
He was radiant with the fragments of the skulls of Jalandhara, Viriñci, and Indra; his face and hair were tawny from being half-splashed by the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā.
The beautiful lower lip was pressed by the tips of his broken fang-sprouts, and his earring was drawn into a circle against the region of his left ear.
He whose departure is like that of a great bull, whose voice is like the roar of a great rain-cloud, who is as radiant as a great fire, and who possesses great strength and prowess.
Thus, Maheśvara, assuming a most terrible and great form, having bestowed consciousness upon Brahmā, assists him in the work of creation.
Therefore, by the grace of Rudra, the creation of beings proceeds eternally in every kalpa through the form of a continuous flow for Prajāpati.
Once, requested by Brahmā to create, the omnipresent Nīlalohita, by his own mind, brought forth all beings who were similar to himself.
With matted hair, free from fear, blue-throated, and three-eyed; liberated from old age and death, and bearing blazing tridents as their supreme weapons.
By them, the entire fourteenfold world was completely covered; seeing those various Rudras, the Grandfather spoke to Rudra.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods! Do not create such offspring; create others instead, may you be blessed, who are endowed with death.
Thus addressed, the Supreme Lord laughed and said to Brahmā: "I have no such creation; you yourself create inauspicious beings."
But those high-souled and mighty ones who have been created by my mind—all of them shall indeed wander with me as officiating priests at sacrifices.
Having spoken thus to Viśvakarman, Hara, the Lord of all beings, together with the Rudras, withdrew from the creation of progeny and remained composed.
From that time forward, that god did not procreate auspicious offspring; remaining as Sthāṇu with his vital energy drawn upward, he stayed thus until the dissolution of all beings.
Vāyu said: When the creatures created by the Creator did not multiply, Brahmā then resolved to bring about creation through sexual union.
Because the race of women had not previously emerged from the Lord, the Grandfather was unable to create beings born of sexual union.
Then he formed the resolve that leads to the determination of his purpose: "The Supreme Lord must be questioned for the very sake of increasing my progeny."
"Without his grace, these subjects will not prosper. Having reflected thus, the Soul of the Universe began to perform austerities.
Then there is the primordial, supreme, infinite Power (Śakti) who brings forth the worlds; she is the first, most subtle, pure, accessible through contemplation, and captivating to the mind.
She is devoid of qualities, free from conceptual proliferation, partless, and undisturbed; she is most exceedingly continuous, eternal, and eternally situated by the side of the Lord.
Having meditated upon the Blessed Lord Tryambaka with that supreme power within his heart, Brahmā performed the highest austerity.
As that supreme lord was engaged in intense austerity, his father became truly gratified within a very short time.
Then, having entered a certain form with a portion of himself and becoming Ardhanārīśvara, the god Hara himself departed.
Having seen that supreme deity, who is beyond darkness, immutable, non-dual, indefinable, and invisible to those of unrefined self;
The creator of all worlds, the Lord of the lords of all worlds, endowed with the supreme power that brings about all worlds.
Beyond ratiocination, without appearance, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal; immovable, devoid of qualities, tranquil, and the abode of infinite majesty.
All-pervading, bestowing all, devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence, liberated from all points of comparison, the refuge, eternal, and auspicious.
Having prostrated like a staff, Brahmā rose up with palms joined in reverence and spoke words endowed with faith and humility, which were worthy of being heard and refined by their composition.
With hymns whose scope was subtle meaning, which were endowed with all truths according to reality and augmented by the purport of the Vedas, he praised the God and the Goddess.
Brahmā said: Victory, O God, Mahādeva! Victory, O Īśvara, Maheśvara! Victory, O most excellent of all qualities! Victory, O sovereign of all the gods!
Victory to you, O naturally auspicious one! Victory to you, O mistress of nature! Victory to you who are beyond nature! Victory to you, O beautiful one by nature!
Victory to you, O Amoghamahāmāyā! Victory to you, O Amoghamaṇorathā! Victory to you, O Amoghamahalīlā! Victory to you, O Amoghamahābalā!
Victory to you, O Mother of the entire world! Victory to you, O you who consist of the entire world! Victory to you, O Sustainer of the entire world! Victory to you, O Friend of the entire world!
Victory to you, whose sovereignty is eternal; victory to you, whose abode is eternal! Victory to you, whose form is eternal; victory to you, who are the follower of the eternal!

Victory to you, the creator of the threefold self; victory to you, the protector of the threefold self; victory to you, the destroyer of the threefold self; victory to you, the leader of the threefold self!

Victory to You, the expansion that is the cause of the world, dependent upon Your glance of grace! Victory to You, who have consumed the material elements with the fire arising from Your indifferent sidelong glance!

Victory to you, O Goddess, who are unknowable even to the gods and others, and who blaze with the subtle vision of your own self! Victory to you, O Mistress of the power of the gross self! Victory to you, who pervade all that is moving and unmoving!

Victory to You, O Goddess, in whom the collection of all principles of reality is unified within a single name! Victory to You, who possess a multitude of supreme followers seated upon the heads of the asuras!
To you, who are most skillful in providing the protection that relies upon victory, and in uprooting the sprouts of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra;
Victory to you, who manifest the sovereignty, power, and heroism of the primordial expanse! Victory to you, who transcend the universe and have cast aside the splendor of all others!
Victory to you, O supreme nectar of the application of the fivefold meaning! Victory to you, whose very nature is the hymn of the nectar of the wisdom of the fivefold meaning!
Victory to the supreme physician for the terrible disease of saṃsāra! Victory to the moonlight that dispels the thick veil of darkness consisting of beginningless impurities and ignorance!
Victory to you, O Fire of the Triple City! Victory to you, O Bhairavī of the Triple City! Victory to you, O One liberated from the three qualities! Victory to you, O Subduer of the three qualities!
Victory to you, the first omniscient one! Victory to you, the awakener of all! Victory to you, whose limbs are abundantly divine! Victory to you, the bestower of what is prayed for!
Where is Your supreme abode, O Lord, and where are our insignificant words? Nevertheless, O Blessed One, please forgive me as I prattle on out of devotion.
Having thus addressed him with such eloquent words, Viśvakarman, the four-faced one, repeatedly offered salutations to Rudra and Rudrāṇī.
This supreme hymn of praise, meritorious and proclaimed by Brahmā, is named Ardhanārīśvara; it increases the joy of Śiva and Śivā.
Whoever recites this with devotion, even at the request of anyone whatsoever, obtains that fruit by virtue of causing pleasure to Śiva and Śivā.

I perpetually bow down to the two Śaṅkaras, who bring about the existence of all beings in the entire world, whose forms are devoid of birth and destruction, and who assume the bodies of an excellent man and a young woman.
Vāyu said: Then the god Mahādeva, with a voice like the roar of a great rain-cloud, spoke in words that were sweet, deep, auspicious, and composed of gentle syllables.
With words endowed with meaningful substance and possessing the characteristics of royalty, she was pure and skillful in protecting the undertakings of all her domains.
Filled with great joy, the Lord addressed Viśvakarman with words preceded by a most captivating, noble, and sweet smile.
Īśvara said: "O child, O child, O highly fortunate one, my son, O Grandfather! I am already fully aware of the entire weight of your words."
"Now you have performed penance solely for the sake of the prosperity of all creatures; I am pleased by this penance and I grant you your desire."
Having spoken these most noble words, sweet by their very nature, Hara, the best of gods, produced a goddess from a portion of his own body.
Those who know Brahman call her the Goddess endowed with divine qualities, the supreme power of Bhava, the Supreme Self.
In her, indeed, birth, death, old age, and the like do not exist; she is Bhavānī, who truly manifested from the body of Bhava.
She, from whom words turn back along with the mind and the senses, appeared as if born from a portion of her husband’s own body.
That goddess, who stands pervading this entire world with her majesty, appeared as if she were embodied within that wondrous form.
She deludes this entire world with her illusory power; though born from the Lord, she is in fact unborn from the perspective of ultimate reality.
She whose supreme nature is not within the range of even the gods, and who is the sovereign of all immortals, has manifested herself from the body of her husband.
Having beheld her, the Supreme Sovereign, the Great Mistress of all the worlds—omniscient, omnipresent, subtle, and devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence.
Having prostrated before the Great Goddess, who illuminates this entire world with her supreme radiance, the Virāj indeed made this request.
Brahmā said: O Goddess, who embodies the entire universe, I was created by the Lord in the beginning; appointed to the creation of progeny, I create the whole world.
O Goddess, all the gods and others were created by me through the mind; though they are created again and again, they do not undergo increase.
Having established creation as originating from sexual union, I thereafter desire to cause all my offspring to flourish.
"The imperishable race of women did not previously emerge from you; therefore, I possess no power to create the race of women."
Indeed, the origin of all powers is from you alone; therefore, you are the bestower of all powers upon everyone in every circumstance.

I pray to you alone, O bestower of boons, the illusory power (māyā), the sovereign of the gods; for the sake of the increase of all that is moving and unmoving, O omnipresent one, [act] with one portion of yourself.
"O destroyer of worldly existence, become the daughter of my son Dakṣa. Thus was the Goddess entreated by Brahmā, whose source is Brahman.
From the middle of his eyebrows, Hara, the best of the gods of gods, emitted a single Śakti whose radiance was equal to his own; looking at her, he spoke to her with a smile.
"Having propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance, fulfill his desire as he wishes. Having received that command of the Supreme Lord upon her head, she [did so].
By the word of Brahmā, the Goddess became the daughter of Dakṣa; thus, having bestowed upon Brahmā this incomparable power in the form of Brahman.
The god entered the body of the deity and vanished; from that time forward, sensual enjoyment became established in women in this world.
O best of Brahmins, O eminent sages, the creation of progeny proceeds through sexual union; even Brahmā attained bliss and satisfaction, O bulls among ascetics.
All this has been narrated to you, concerning the origin of the Goddess’s power; it increases merit and is worthy of being heard as an account following upon the creation of beings.
Whoever constantly recites this account of the origin of the Goddess’s power attains all merit and obtains auspicious sons.
Chapter.

Vāyu said: Having thus obtained from the Lord himself that supreme, eternal power, the Prajāpati, desiring to perform creation originating from sexual union, became himself wonderful; he became half female and half male. That which was the female half was born from him as Śatarūpā.

Brahmā created Virāj; he became a Puruṣa by means of his half. He was indeed the first Svāyaṃbhuva Puruṣa, known as Manu. That goddess Śatarūpā, having performed most difficult austerities, approached Manu himself as her husband, he who was of radiant fame.

From him, Śatarūpā gave birth to two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, the best among those who possess sons, and two highly fortunate daughters, from whom these progenies were born; one is to be known as Ākūti, and the other is remembered as Prasūti.

The Lord Svāyambhuva gave Prasūti to Dakṣa; and the Prajāpati Ruci likewise begot Ākūti. From Ākūti, the auspicious pair of twins was born to the mind-born Ruci: Yajña and Dakṣiṇā, by whom the world was set in motion.
In Prasūti, the daughter of Svāyaṃbhuva, were born the mothers of the worlds.
The lord Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters: Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Medhā, Kriyā, as well as Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth.

The Lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives. From among them, eleven younger sisters with beautiful eyes remained: Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā.

Bhṛgu, Śarva, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pāvaka, and the Pitṛs—these best of sages took as wives the daughters beginning with Khyāti. Furthermore, those thirteen sons beginning with Kāma and ending with Yaśas [were born].

From Dharma were born those [qualities] beginning with Faith (Śraddhā), which culminate in supreme happiness; and from the progeny of Adharma and Hiṃsā were born those beginning with Deceit (Nikṛti), which culminate in suffering. These sons are characterized by the nature of Dharma; they are recorded as having neither wives nor sons, and all of them are considered to be without fixed constraints.

This very creation, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), was born as the regulator of dharma. She who was the daughter of Dakṣa and the beloved wife of Rudra, Satī, having abandoned her body born of Dakṣa on account of the censure of her husband, and having reviled Dakṣa, his wife, and their kinsmen;

She appeared as the daughter of Menā, the wife of Himavat, the mountain. As for Rudra, having seen that Satī, he created the Rudras of equal splendor to himself; how he created them in numberless quantities has already been told. Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, was born to Bhṛgu by Khyāti.

The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, who sustain the Manvantaras, had sons, grandsons, and others by the hundreds and thousands; all of them in the Svāyambhuva interval are considered to be Bhārgavas. From Marīci also, Sambhūti gave birth to Paurṇamāsa.

There were four daughters, and their descendants were very great; in their lineage was born Kaśyapa, the father of many sons. Smṛti, the wife of Aṅgiras, gave birth to two sons, Āgnīdhra and Śarabha, as well as four daughters.

His sons and grandsons who have passed away are by the thousands. Through Pulastya’s wife Prīti, Dantaka was born as a son; he is remembered as Yogi in his previous birth during the Svāyambhuva interval. Many belonging to that lineage are renowned as the Paulastyas. Kṣamā, however, gave birth to the sons of the patriarch Pulaha.

Kardama, Suri, and Sahiṣṇu—these three were all as radiant as the three sacred fires, and their lineage remains well-established. From Kratu, his wife Sannati gave birth to sons equal to sacrifices themselves; they had no wives nor sons, for they were all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).

These sixty thousand are known as the Vālakhilyas; they travel ahead of Anūru, surrounding the sun. And Atri’s wife, Anasūyā, gave birth to five Ātreyas and a daughter named Śruti, who was the mother of Śaṅkhapada.

Satyanetra, Havya, Āpomūrti, Śanaiścara, and Soma as the fifth—these are proclaimed as the five Ātreyas. The sons and grandsons of those high-souled Ātreyas passed away by the hundreds and thousands during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.

In Ūrjā, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha; their elder sister was Puṇḍarīkā, who was slender-waisted. Rāja, Gātra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana, Anaya, Sutapas, and Śukra—these seven are remembered as the Saptarṣis.

The lineages by name of those high-souled Vāsiṣṭhas during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara have passed away in hundreds and billions. Thus, this creation of the sages has been proclaimed along with its branches; O twice-born ones, it is impossible to describe this in detail, though it has been told in brief.

He who is that fire of the nature of Rudra, the mind-born son of Brahmā—Svāhā obtained from him three sons of immeasurable luster: Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci. Of these three, Pavamāna is produced by friction, while Pāvaka is known as that which is lightning-born.

While the sun was shining, he who was pure was proclaimed as Saura; Havyavāha, Kavyavāha, and Saharakṣas were the three [others]. The gods, the ancestors, and the *asuras* were respectively the sons of these three. Their sons and grandsons numbered exactly forty-nine.

Those established in the three types of rites—those performed for specific desires, those for occasional occasions, and those performed continuously—all such ascetics are to be known as observers of vows; they are all of the nature of Rudra and all are devoted to Rudra. Therefore, whatever is offered by anyone into the mouth of the fire is indeed [offered to them].

"All that shall be given with Rudra as the intended recipient; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus has the determination regarding the fires been set forth exactly as it is. O Brahmins, I shall not speak of them at great length; hereafter I shall describe the Pitṛs, for the six seasons are their abode, being the presiding deities of those abodes.

"The seasons are the ancestors; therefore, this is the Vedic revelation: for from you, the seasons, all things—both stationary and moving—are born. Therefore, it is heard that these are the ancestors known as the Ārtavas (season-born). Thus [is the nature] of these ancestors who preside over the seasons.

The high-souled ones, possessing mastery over themselves, remain here as long as the clouds gather. The ancestors (Pitṛs) are remembered as being of two kinds: the Āgniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣadas. These householders are, respectively, those who have not performed sacrifices and those who have performed sacrifices. From Svadhā were born two daughters to the Pitṛs, world-renowned.

And there were Menā and Dharaṇī, by whom this entire universe is supported; Menā was the daughter of the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, and Dharaṇī was the daughter of the Barhiṣad Pitṛs. Menā became the wife of Himavat and gave birth to Maināka and Krauñca, as well as Gaurī and Gaṅgā, who is purified by the embrace of Śiva’s body.

Dharaṇī, the wife of Meru, gave birth to a son, Mandara, who was endowed with divine medicinal herbs and possessed shoulders as beautiful as a painting. That glorious Mandara, the son of Meru, by the power of his asceticism, became the actual abode of the Lord Śiva, known as Śrīkaṇṭha.

She gave birth again to thirty daughters who were renowned; Velā, Niyati, and the third, Āyati. Āyati and Niyati were the two wives of the two sons of Bhṛgu. Their lineage has been previously described by you during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.

From the ocean, the shoreline gave birth to one irreproachable daughter named Savarṇā, the daughter of the sea, who became the wife of Prācīnabarhis. Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis; all were known as the Prācetasas and were masters of the science of archery.

O Brahmins, these [descendants] of the high-souled sons of Brahmā, beginning with Dharma, have been recounted in due order, neither too briefly nor too extensively, regarding how in former times Dakṣa attained the status of a son to Svāyaṃbhuva Manu and to Tryambaka during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.

I have indeed described these divine lineages, accompanied by hosts of gods, endowed with ritual acts and progeny, and adorned with great supernatural powers. This arrangement of subjects originates from Prajāpati; it is impossible to enumerate it even in hundreds of millions of years.

The lineage of kings also proceeds in two ways: the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa) and the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa), which are most meritorious on earth. Ikṣvāku, Ambarīṣa, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, and others—those of virtuous fame who are heard of here—were also born from those two lineages.

And there were other royal sages endowed with various powers; what fruit is there in recounting those ancient ones who have passed away? Furthermore, when a discourse on the Lord occurs, the praising of others therein is not approved by the virtuous; considering this, I do not venture to speak much.
Furthermore, even the accounts of creation and so forth were related here as incidental elaborations, in order to illuminate the power of the Lord alone.
The sages said: How did the goddess, the daughter of Dakṣa, having abandoned her body as a Dākṣāyaṇī, formerly become the daughter of Himavat through Menā?
And how was Rudra censured by the high-souled Dakṣa? What was the occasion there, by which Bhava came to be censured?
O Māruti, tell me how Dakṣa was born from the curse of Bhava during the previous interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
Vāyu said: "Listen, for I shall relate the conduct of the light-minded Dakṣa, which, through sin and negligence, brought reproach upon all the immortals."
In ancient times, all the gods, asuras, perfected beings, and supreme rishis once went to the peak of the Himalayas to behold Īśāna.
Then, O best of the twice-born, both the god and the goddess, seated upon their divine throne, granted their vision to those gods and others.
At that very moment, Dakṣa also went there together with the immortals, to see his son-in-law Hara and to see his own daughter Satī.
Then, due to his self-importance, when the Goddess arrived at Dakṣa’s side, the Lord never once remembered her with any special regard, even more so than he did for the gods and others.
Because he did not know her true nature and was utterly deluded, thinking only that she was his daughter, enmity toward her arose within him.
Then, impelled by that very enmity and by fate, Dakṣa, having been initiated for the sacrifice, did not invite Bhava, hating him as well.
Having summoned all the other mothers in due order, he performed extensive and separate worship for each of them by the hundreds.
Then, having heard from the mouth of Nārada that they had gathered together in such a manner, Rudrāṇī informed her father and went to his abode.
Then there appeared a celestial chariot, present before him, facing every direction, rich in auspicious marks, easy to ascend, and exceedingly enchanting.
Resembling molten gold, adorned with various jewels, featuring a canopy of pearls, and beautifully decorated with garlands of flowers.
It had turrets of refined gold, was surrounded by hundreds of jeweled pillars, possessed stairs fashioned from diamond, and featured coral pillars and archways.
A great throne spread with flowered cloths, variegated with precious gems, its jeweled floor made seamless by a lattice of vajras that left no gaps.
With a banner as white as a cloud, adorned at its front with a beautiful jeweled shaft and the emblem of a great bull;
Its great gates were guarded by invincible lords of virtue, whose limbs were protected by jeweled armor and who held variegated cane-staves in their hands.
It was surrounded by many women skilled in playing the mṛdaṅga drum, keeping time, singing, and playing the flute and lute, who were dressed and spoke with clever grace.
The great queen ascended together with her dear female companions; for her, there were fly-whisks and fans with handles as beautiful as diamonds.
Having taken up two auspicious *rudrākṣa* maidens, both of them fanned [her]; then, between those two whisks, the face of the Goddess shone forth.
Between those two who were fighting each other like two swans over a lotus, Sumālinī held her moon-like parasol above her crest.
Filled with overflowing love, the Queen held that radiant parasol, encircled by pearls, which shone above her face.
Above the vessel of nectar was a circle like that of the moon; and before it sat Śubhāvatī, her face graced with a gentle smile.
Suyaśas amused the virtuous Satī with the diversion of a game of dice, while she herself occupied the auspicious sandals of the Goddess, which were adorned with jewels.
Then, placing the goddess between their breasts, they served her; another woman, with beautiful limbs of gold, took up a radiant mirror.
One beautiful woman held a palm-leaf fan, another a betel-box, and yet another placed a lovely pet parrot in her hand.
One lotus-eyed woman bore very pleasing and fragrant flowers, while another bore an ornament-case.
Some brought ointments, well-prepared auspicious collyrium, and others brought various similar articles, each performing their appropriate duties as was fitting for them.
They attended upon that Great Goddess from all sides; in their midst, the Supreme Goddess shone with exceeding splendor.
In the midst of Tārā’s assembly, she was like an autumnal crescent moon; then, immediately following the sound arising from the conch shell—
The great drum for departure was struck, followed by sweet musical instruments accompanied by the sounds of rising cymbals.
Hundreds of kettledrums resounded spontaneously, along with the hosts of Gaṇeśas who were armed and possessed splendor equal to that of Maheśa.
At that time, eight hundred thousand [attendants] went before him; in their midst he was mounted upon a bull, like Bṛhaspati mounted upon an elephant.
The glorious leader of the Gaṇas, honored by Somanandīśvara, departed; in the heavens, divine drums resounded and clouds of celestial bliss rumbled.
All the sages danced, the perfected yogis rejoiced, and the clouds released a rain of flowers over the canopy.
Then, accompanied everywhere along the way by hosts of gods and others, the Great Goddess entered her father’s house as if in a mere moment.
Seeing her, Dakṣa became enraged because she was the cause of his own ruin; he accorded a formal honor to her that was even greater than that given to his younger sisters.
Then the moon-faced goddess Ambika, composed and noble-minded, spoke these words to her father as he sat in the assembly.
The Goddess said: "O Father, that God, under whose command everything from Brahmā down to the Piśācas must abide, has apparently not been worshipped according to the prescribed rites at this time."
Let that be; why have you committed such a despicable act, disregarding the improper treatment and insult shown to my eldest daughter?
Thus addressed, Dakṣa, provoked by anger, spoke to her: "My young daughters are superior, more distinguished, and worthy of worship than you."
But those who are their husbands are highly esteemed by me with joy; they are superior in all virtues even to your husband, Tryambaka himself.
"O Śarva, you are of a tamasic nature and stubborn-souled; having resorted to such as this, I hold you in contempt, for Bhava is indeed adverse to me."
Having been addressed in this manner, the goddess, filled with wrath, spoke to her father Dakṣa while all those present in the sacrificial assembly were listening.
O Dakṣa, you have groundlessly defamed my husband with your speech—him who is free from every blemish and the Great Lord of the World himself.
The thief of knowledge, the betrayer of the guru, and the reviler of the Vedas and the Lord—these are all great sinners and must be punished; such is the Vedic revelation.
Therefore, by fate, a sudden and terrible punishment, strictly commensurate with this exceedingly heinous sin, shall befall you.
"Since you have not worshipped Tryambaka, the God of gods, therefore consider it certain that your wicked lineage is destroyed."
Having spoken thus to her father, Satī, filled with wrath and casting aside all fear, abandoned her body and departed for the Himavat mountain.
That glorious one, devoted to the mountain and having attained the arising of the fruits of merit, performed difficult austerities for a very long time for that very purpose.
Therefore, the Sovereign Lady favored that Lord of Mountains; by her own will and through her power of yoga-māyā, she made him her father.
When she had departed, having censured Dakṣa while overwhelmed by fear, the mantras then vanished and the sacrifice was destroyed.
Having overheard that the Goddess was departing, the destroyer of Tripura became enraged at Dakṣa and the sages, and he cursed them.
For although she was treated with contempt by Dakṣa, she was innocent; whereas all her other daughters were honored by their husbands along with themselves.
Therefore, in the Vaivasvata interval, all these sons-in-law of yours shall be born together, not from a womb, during the sacrifices to Brahman.
"You shall become a human king in the lineage of Cākṣuṣa, the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas."
O evil-minded one, I shall create obstacles for you even there, repeatedly, even in those actions connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
Thus addressed by Rudra of immeasurable splendor, Dakṣa, having cast off his body born of Svayambhū, fell to the earth in deep distress.
Then, during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, Dakṣa Prācetasa was born as the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetas.
Bhṛgu and the others were indeed born during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu at the sacrifice of Brahmā, while he was assuming the form of Varuṇa.
Then, while Dakṣa’s sacrifice for the sake of dharma was proceeding, Maheśa created an obstacle for that evil-minded one when Satī had passed away.
The sages said: "How did Maheśa create an obstacle for the evil-minded Dakṣa, who was engaged in the pursuit of dharma? We wish to know this."
Vāyu said: Through the power of the asceticism of the Goddess, the mother of the entire world, the Himavat mountain became joyful as he attained the state of a father.
When that marriage had been performed by the gods, he sported with her in their dwelling upon a peak of the Himalayas; and after a very long time had passed, [the following occurred].
When the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, Dakṣa Prācetasa himself, intending to perform the horse sacrifice, set about his preparations.
Then Dakṣa indeed performed a sacrifice on the slopes of the Himavat, in the auspicious region of Gaṅgādvāra, frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Then, all the gods, led by Śakra, having assembled at that sacrifice of his, resolved upon going there.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts; likewise the drinkers of steam, the drinkers of soma, the drinkers of clarified butter, and the drinkers of smoke.
The Aśvins, the Pitṛs, and likewise other great Ṛṣis—all together with Viṣṇu—were welcomed as sharers of the sacrifice.
Seeing the entire assembly hall devoid of Īśvara, Dadhīca, overcome with indignation, addressed Dakṣa in this manner.
Dadhīca said: "By worshipping those who are unworthy of worship, and by failing to worship those who are worthy of worship, a man incurs great sin; of this there is no doubt."
Where there is the approval of the wicked and likewise the contempt of the virtuous, there a terrible punishment ordained by the gods falls instantly.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin-sage addressed Dakṣa once more: "Why do you not worship the Lord, the Master of Creatures, who is worthy of honor?"
Dakṣa said: "I have many Rudras with tridents in their hands and matted hair, who abide as the eleven; I know no other Maheśvara."
