Dadhīca said: "What fruit is there in honoring these other immortals at the sacrifice, if Rudra is not honored by you as the king of this sacrifice?"
He who is the imperishable Lord, the creator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; he to whom all beings, from Brahmā down to the Piśācas, offer their service.
He who is beyond the primal natures (prakṛtis) and even beyond the Puruṣa is meditated upon by the seers who are learned in yoga and perceivers of reality.
The syllable is indeed the supreme Brahman, which is both non-being and being; it is without beginning, middle, or end, inconceivable, and eternal.
I see no one other than Śaṅkara himself at this sacrifice—he who is the creator, the destroyer, and the sustainer, the Great Lord.

Dakṣa said: "I now take this entire oblation, purified by ritual and mantras, from the golden vessel of the Lord of Sacrifice; having divided it, I shall today present the portion of the incomparable Lord Viṣṇu, who is to be carried forth."
Dadhīca said: "O Dakṣa, because Rudra, the Lord of the lords of all gods, was not propitiated by you, therefore this entire sacrifice of yours shall not take place."
Having spoken these words in anger, Dadhīca, the best of sages, departed from that region and went to his own hermitage.
Even though that Sage had departed, the gods did not abandon Dakṣa, because of the inevitability of the calamity that was about to occur.
At that very time, O brahmins, having learned all this from the Lord, the Goddess urged the God to consume Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Urged by the Goddess with the intent to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the Lord suddenly created the heroic Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas.
The god with a thousand faces, with eyes like a thousand lotuses, bearing a thousand mallets and holding a thousand arrows in his hands.
Holding a trident, an axe, and a mace in his hands, bearing a blazing bow, wielding a discus and a thunderbolt, he is formidable, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Holding a vajra that illuminates his hand, with hair blazing like lightning, possessing fangs and a terrifying face, he has a massive mouth and a great belly.
With a tongue like lightning and protruding lips, possessing a voice like the roar of clouds and the ocean, he wore a tiger skin dripping with profuse blood.
His earrings were formed into circles, joined together at both temples; his crest was adorned with a garland of the heads of the foremost gods.
Adorned with great golden ornaments, including tinkling anklets and armlets, it was radiant with heaps of jewels and its chest encircled by a necklace of bright pearls.
Possessing prowess equal to that of the great śarabha, the tiger, and the lion, and possessing a gait as majestic and languid as that of a noble, rutting elephant.

His radiance was like that of a conch shell, a chowrie, a kunda flower, the moon, or a lotus stalk; he was like the king of mountains covered in snow, yet had attained the state of being truly mobile.
Surrounded by garlands of flames and adorned with blazing pearls, he was shining with splendor like the fire at the end of an eon.
Then, having knelt upon the earth and bowed with palms joined in reverence, the Lord of the Gaṇas stood by the side of the God of gods.
And out of anger, he created Bhadrā, the Great Goddess Bhadrakālī, so that she might go along with him to serve as the witness to his own deeds.
Seeing Vīrabhadra standing there, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction and accompanied by Bhadrā, Śaṅkara said, "May it be well."
And he, together with the Goddess, made this request to Maheśvara: "Command me, O Mahādeva; what task shall I perform?"
Then the destroyer of Tripura, desiring to please Haimavatī, spoke to the mighty-armed Vīrabhadra with a voice of great resonance.
The God of gods said: "O Lord of the Gaṇas, together with Bhadrakālī, you must immediately destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas; this is your task."
I too, staying together with her near the hermitage of Raibhya, shall observe your unbearable prowess, O Lord of the Gaṇas.
The trees that stand at Kanakhala in the vicinity of Gaṅgādvāra are like the golden-peaked mountain Meru and Mandara.
In that region, Dakṣa’s sacrifice is currently taking place; cause its destruction suddenly and without delay.
When the Lord had spoken thus, the Goddess, daughter of the King of the Snowy Mountains, gazed upon her son with auspiciousness and joy, as a cow looks upon her own calf.
Having embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, as she would for the Six-faced One, she herself spoke these exceedingly sweet words with a smile.
The Goddess said: "O child, O auspicious one, O highly fortunate one of great strength and prowess! You have been born for my sake; you shall wipe away my grief."
Without having invited the Lord of Sacrifice, he became intent on the performance of the sacrifice; therefore, O Lord of the Gaṇas, destroy that Dakṣa and his sacrifice out of enmity.
"O Bhadra, having rendered the auspicious fortune of the sacrifice into misfortune by my command, and having slain that sacrificer, O child, destroy it with your auspicious weapon."
Placing that entire command of Śiva and Śivā—who were engaged in their artistic creation—upon his head and bowing down, Bhadra proceeded to depart.
Then this Blessed One, Vīrabhadra, the Great God who dwells in the abode of the pretas and who wipes away the wrath of the Goddess, became enraged.
From the pores of his skin, he created the hosts of Gaṇeśvaras known as Romajas; and from the region of his right arm, he created hundreds of millions of Gaviśvaras.

From the feet, from the region of the thighs, from the back, from the sides, from the face, from the throat, from the private parts, from the ankles, from the middle of the head, from the neck, from the mouth, and likewise from the belly.
Then the entire world, including the very gaps of the sky, was completely covered by the auspicious lords of the Gaṇas, whose prowess equaled that of Bhadra himself.
All of them had a thousand hands, all held a thousand weapons in their palms; they were all attendants of Rudra, and all possessed a splendor equal to that of Rudra.
Holding tridents, spears, and maces in their hands, and bearing iron clubs and stones; resembling the Rudra of the fire of time (Kālāgnirudra), they have three eyes and wear matted locks.
Hundreds of noble steeds, borne by riders on lion-backs, fell violently from the sky; and like clouds, they let out great roars.
Surrounded by those auspicious Madras, the Blessed One shone like Kālabhairava at the end of time accompanied by hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction.
Having ascended the lordly bull in their midst, the Blessed Lord Bhava, whose banner bears the bull, proceeded auspiciously like a favorable cloud.
When Bhadra had mounted that bull, Bhasitaprabha held a pearl umbrella and grasped white chowries.
Then he shone at the side of Bhadra with the luster of ashes, like the Blessed Lord Śiva, the king of mountains, at the side of the Teacher of the entire world.
That noble one also shone with him who held a white chowrie in his hand, like the wielder of the excellent trident accompanied by the gentle young moon.
The highly effulgent Bhānukampa, adorned with gold and jewels, blew his auspicious white conch, the Bhadra, in front of Bhadra.
The divine drums resounded with a tumultuous celestial sound, and clouds rained down showers of flowers by the hundreds upon his head.
On the road, winds blew that were kinsmen to the fragrance of blossoming flowers filled with honey, and they moved favorably along the path.
Then all the lords of the Gaṇas, intoxicated and arrogant with the power of battle, danced, rejoiced, roared, laughed, spoke, and sang.
Then, standing amidst the host of Bhadras, that Bhadra shone with Bhadrā, just as Tryambaka shines amidst the host of Rudras together with Ambikā.
At that very moment, the mighty-armed Vīrabhadra, followed by a great retinue, entered Dakṣa’s golden sacrificial enclosure.

Then, the preeminent leader of the hosts entered the sacrificial ground of that foremost rite established by Dakṣa, like the auspicious Rudra at the end of time desiring to consume the world with fire.
Vāyu said: Then he beheld a great sacrificial session belonging to the gods of immeasurable luster, headed by Viṣṇu, and adorned with variegated banners and equipment.
It was strewn with excellent sacrificial grass, possessed a well-kindled sacrificial fire, and was adorned with radiant golden sacrificial vessels.
It was performed with many ritual steps well-executed according to the procedure seen in the Vedas by sages who were experts in sacrifice and performers of rites in the prescribed manner.
Abounding with thousands of celestial nymphs and served by hosts of apsarases, it was graced by the sounds of flutes and lutes and amplified by the chanting of the Vedas.
Having seen this at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the powerful hero Vīrabhadra then let out a lion’s roar, deep as a thundercloud.
Then a great sound of "kila-kila" arose from the lords of the Gaṇas, as if filling the sky and surpassing the roar of the ocean.
Overwhelmed by that great sound, all the inhabitants of heaven fled in fear in every direction, their garments and ornaments falling away.
"Has Mount Mahāmeru been shattered? Is the earth being rent asunder? What is this? What is this? the gods cried out repeatedly.
Just as lordly elephants in the dense forest, upon hearing the roar of the lions, some abandoned their very lives out of fear.
The mountains shattered, the earth trembled, the winds whirled about, and the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, was agitated.
The sacrificial fires do not blaze, nor does the sun shine; the planets do not gleam, nor do the lunar mansions or the stars.
At that very time, the blessed Lord Bhadra, together with his auspicious attendants and Bhadrā, arrived at that radiant sacrificial enclosure.
Seeing him, though terrified, Dakṣa stood as firm as if unshaken; speaking words like one enraged, he said: "Who are you, and what do you desire here?"
Having heard those words of the evil-minded Dakṣa, the immensely radiant Vīrabhadra, whose voice was as deep and formidable as a thundercloud, [acted].
Looking at Dakṣa as if with a smile, the gods and the officiating priests spoke these appropriate words, which were composed and pregnant with meaning.
Vīrabhadra said: "We are all indeed the attendants of Śarva, who possesses immeasurable splendor; we have arrived here with the desire for a share, so let a share be granted to us."
If, however, no share has been assigned to us in this sacrifice, let the reason for that be told, or else let me fight with the immortals.
Thus addressed by the lord of the Gaṇas, the gods, led by Dakṣa, said: "The mantras are our authority; we ourselves have no power."
The mantras said to the gods: "You are those whose minds are struck by delusion, since you do not worship Maheśvara, who is worthy of the first portion."
Even though those gods were addressed with mantras, they were all bewildered in mind; desiring his destruction, they did not grant a share for Bhadra.
When their own words, though true and beneficial, proved to be in vain, they then departed slowly from there to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Then the leader of the hosts spoke to the gods, headed by Viṣṇu: "The mantras have not been made authoritative by you who are arrogant in your strength."
"Since we have been thus insulted by the gods in this sacrifice, I shall therefore remove your pride along with your lives."
Having spoken thus, the enraged Blessed One consumed the great peak of Yakṣavāṭa with the fire from his eyes, just as Hara destroyed the three cities.
Then all the lords of the Gaṇas, their bodies as lofty as mountains, uprooted the sacrificial posts and bound them around the necks of the Hotṛ priests with ropes.
Having broken and pulverized the various sacrificial vessels into the water, they took the components of the sacrifice and cast them into the current of the Gaṅgā.
There were mountain-like heaps of divine food and drink, rivers of milk flowing with nectar, and marshes of very smooth curd.
There were various kinds of meats, both high and low, as well as fragrant foods; there were flavorful drinks, and indeed things to be licked and sucked.
The heroes devour it with their mouths, snatch it away, and hurl it back with thunderbolts, discuses, great spears, javelins, nooses, and sharp-edged axes.
With pestles, swords, ṭaṅkas, bhidhipālas, and axes, he struck down all the arrogant gods led by the world-protectors.
The powerful heroes born from the body of Vīrabhadra split [them] apart, crying out: "Cut! Pierce! Strike quickly! Let him be slain! Let him be torn asunder!"
"Seize! Strike! Tear asunder! Uproot!"—such cruel words, born of fury, were like spikes to the ears.
In various places, leaders of the hosts were born, prepared for battle; some had rolling eyes, while others bared their fangs and bit their lips and palates.
They will drag away those dwelling in hermitages and kill the ascetics; they will seize the sacrificial ladles and cast the sacred fire into the waters.
Breaking the water-jars and shattering the jeweled altars, they sang, shouted, and laughed again and again.
And drinking blood-liquor, the leaders of the Gaṇas danced; having crushed the gods including Indra, those lords of the Gaṇas were as powerful as the best of bulls, serpents, and lions.
Those of incomparable nature performed many gestures with their hair standing on end in joy: some rejoiced, some struck out, some ran, and some prattled.
Some of the Pramathas dance, some laugh, and others leap about with might; some desire to seize the water-laden clouds, while others spring up to catch the sun.
Some of those terrifying Pramathas, stationed in the sky, desired to rush forth along with the wind; others, having seized their excellent weapons, were like Garuḍas snatching up great serpents.
Resembling mountain peaks, some even caused the gods to flee as they rushed through the circle of the sky; others repeatedly uprooted houses along with their latticed windows and balconies.
Repeatedly tossing them into the midst of the water, the Pramathas, resembling dark clouds, roared; they overturned the doors, panels, and walls, and destroyed the halls, eaves, and windows.
Alas! The sacrificial ground has been shattered like one who is helpless, like a word that has lost its meaning—crying out, "O protector! O father! O son! O brother! O my mother! O maternal uncle!"
As the houses were being torn down, the women indeed raised many cries of "we are helpless!"
Vāyu said: Then those leaders of the thirty gods, headed by Viṣṇu and Śakra, all fled, terrified with fear and overwhelmed by panic.
Seeing the gods afflicted by their own limbs which had not been corrupted, and perceiving those who deserved punishment as unpunished, the leader of the Gaṇas became enraged.
Then, taking up his trident—which destroys even the power of Śarva—the mighty-armed one, casting flames from his mouth, gazed upward.
He rushed even at the immortals as a lion charges elephants; his movement as he pursued them was exceedingly beautiful.
Like Vārāṇasī when intoxicated, it became a sight to behold; then the powerful one agitated that great army of the gods.
Just as a rutting leader of an elephant herd agitates a great lake, manifesting many colors—blue, pale-white, and red.
Wearing a tiger-skin garment with excellent golden stars, he was cutting, piercing, tearing, rending, and even crushing [his enemies].
He moved among the hosts of gods like a noble fire in dry grass; wherever he went, the wielder of the trident moved with great speed.
All the gods perceived that single being as if it were a thousand; and Bhadrakālī, enraged and arrogant with the pride increased by battle, [assumed her form].
With a spear emitting blazing flames, he pierced the gods in battle; with it, that auspicious one, born from the wrath of Rudra, shone resplendently.
Then, with her flickering radiance darkened by smoke like the fire at the end of an eon, Bhadrakālī shone in battle as the gods fled.
Just as at the end of the eon the entire world is consumed by the flames of the remaining fire, so then [did he consume] the Sun with his horse and the Rudras, leading the hosts of Rudra.
Bhadra quickly struck Mūrdhan playfully with his left foot; Bhadra struck Pāvaka with swords, while Yamī struck Yama with *paṭṭiśa* spears.
With a firm trident he struck Rudra, with firm mallets Varuṇa, with iron clubs Nirṛti, and with axes Vāyu himself, who was bearing an axe.
In battle, the heroic Lord of the Gaṇas effortlessly and instantly pierced all the hosts of gods and the sages who were opposed to Śambhu.
Then the God, with the tip of his fingernail, cut off the beautiful tip of Sarasvatī’s nose, and likewise that of the Mother of the Gods.
And with an axe, he cut off the arm-staff of Vibhāvasu; and in front of his mother, the goddess, he lopped off her tongue to the extent of two finger-breadths.
Likewise, the god tore out the right nostril of the goddess Svāhā with the tip of his fingernail, as well as her left nipple.
The exceedingly swift Bhadra forcibly tore out the two large eyes of Bhaga, which were as radiant as a hundred-petaled lotus.
And with the tip of his bow, he struck Pūṣan’s row of teeth, which was as radiant as a string of pearls; by that act, Pūṣan’s speech became indistinct.
Then the Lord, having playfully stepped upon the moon with his big toe for a moment as if it were a mere insect, ground it against the surface of the earth.
In a state of supreme rage, Bhadra severed the head of Dakṣa; even as Vairiṇī was still crying out, he gave it to Bhadrakālī.
Greatly delighted, that goddess took up his head, which resembled a palm fruit, and played with it like a ball upon the field of battle.
Then, just as unchaste women are beaten by their husbands with hands and feet, Dakṣa’s sacrificial wife was likewise struck with hands and feet by the lords of the Gaṇas.
To Ariṣṭanemi, Soma, Dharma, Prajāpati, Bahuputra, Aṅgiras, Kṛśāśva, and likewise Kaśyapa;
Seizing him by the throat, the powerful leaders of the hosts, possessing the prowess of lions, rebuked him severely with their words and struck him on the head with their fists.
Wives, children, and possessions were violated by spirits and vetālas, just as noble women are forcibly violated by paramours in the Kali age.
And that [city] had its water-jars shattered and its sacrificial posts broken; its festivals had ceased, its great palaces were set ablaze, and its gates and archways were shattered.
The army of the gods had been torn asunder, the ascetics were being slaughtered, the sound of Vedic chanting had been silenced, and the multitudes of people had perished.
With women wailing in distress and all the attendants slain, the sacrificial ground, thus afflicted, then became like a desolate wilderness.
Afflicted by the force of the tridents, with their arms, thighs, and chests shattered, and their heads severed, the foremost of the gods fell upon the earth.
When those gods had fallen by the thousands in their hatred, Gaṇeśāna entered the Āhavanīya fire in an instant.
Then, seeing that auspicious one who resembled the fire of cosmic destruction as he entered, Yajña, assuming the form of a deer, fled in fear of death.
Stretching his great bow, which was terrifying with the sound of its firm string, Bhadra rushed toward him while scattering arrows.
Drawing his cloud-like bow back as far as his ear, he made the bowstring resound, filling the heavens, the sky, and the earth in every direction.
Taking refuge in that roar, the hero, overwhelmed with the thought "I am slain," [sought] the Lord of Sacrifice with his face turned half toward him for protection.
With feet faltering from great fear, trembling and deprived of luster, he who was running in the form of a deer he then rendered headless.
Seeing that son of the Sun thus treated with contempt, Viṣṇu became exceedingly enraged and prepared for battle.
Garuḍa, the king of all birds and devourer of serpents, carried him on his shoulder with great speed, its joints being bent.
And the gods who remained after the slaughter, led by the king of the gods, rendered him assistance as if prepared to sacrifice their very lives.
Seeing the gods together with Viṣṇu like jackals before a lion, the Lord of Beings laughed, while the King of Beings trembled like a frightened lion.
At that moment, a chariot appeared in the sky, resembling a thousand suns and bearing the beautiful banner of the bull.
Exalted by two precious horses, with four wheels, it was adorned with a collection of many divine missiles, weapons, and jewels.
He indeed shall be the charioteer of that excellent chariot as well, just as he formerly stood at the head of Śarva’s chariot in the battle against the three cities.
At the mere command of the wielder of the trident, Brahmā brought that excellent chariot into the presence of Hara and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O Bhagavan-bhadra, O you of auspicious limbs, the Lord Indubhūṣaṇa, the immutable Hero, commands you to mount the chariot."
O mighty-armed one, Tryambaka, staying near the hermitage of Rebha together with Ambikā, beholds this unbearable prowess of yours.
Having heard those words of his, that heroic leader of the Gaṇas ascended the divine chariot, honoring the Grandfather.
Likewise, while that excellent chariot stood with Brahmā as its charioteer, Bhadra’s splendor increased like that of Rudra, the enemy of the cities.
Then the mighty Bhānukaṃpa, placing that excellent, blazing conch—whose luster was like the full moon—to his mouth, blew it.
Hearing that sound of the conch, which resembled the cry of a distressed crane, the digestive fire within the bellies of the gods flared up with fear.
In an instant, the quarters of the sky, including their intermediate spaces, became completely filled with Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, lords of serpents, and Siddhas, all eager to witness the battle.
Then, from the corner of his bow, that cloud-like Nārāyaṇa tormented the bull of the Gaṇas with a great rain of arrows using the Śārṅga bow.
Seeing Viṣṇu approaching, showering arrows by the hundreds, Bhadra took up his victorious bow and released thousands of shafts.
And having taken up that divine bow, which was terrifying in battle, he slowly drew it back, just as Lord Śiva draws the bow Meru.
As that bow was being drawn, there arose a great sound; by that immense noise, he caused the earth to tremble.
Then the illustrious leader of the hosts, himself of fierce prowess, seized a terrible, excellent arrow that was blazing like a venomous serpent.
As he drew out the arrow, his arm, joined to the mouth of the quiver, appeared like a serpent wishing to enter an anthill.
Seized by his hand at that very moment, the arrow shone like a young serpent bitten by a great serpent.
Enraged, the noble Bhadra, possessing the prowess of Rudra, deeply pierced the imperishable Viṣṇu in the forehead with an arrow that was thick and fierce.
Struck upon the forehead by him, Viṣṇu, who had already been insulted, became enraged at the lord of the Gaṇas like a bull at a lion.
Then, with that great arrow, cruel-mouthed and like a thunderbolt, he pierced the arm of the Lord of the Gaṇas, which resembled a serpent.
Then the mighty Vīrabhadra again swiftly discharged an arrow, possessing a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns, at his arm.
And that Viṣṇu again struck Bhadra, and Bhadra likewise struck Viṣṇu; O brahmins, they both pursued and struck each other with arrows in that manner.
As the two of them swiftly discharged arrows at one another with great force, a tumultuous and hair-raising battle ensued between the two.
Seeing that tumultuous battle between those two themselves, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! was raised in the sky by the sky-dwellers.
Then Bhadra pierced Viṣṇu’s broad chest very deeply with a fire-mouthed arrow, radiant as the sun.
Struck firmly by that arrow with its sharp descent, he suffered great pain and fell down, deprived of his senses.
Then Hari, having regained consciousness as if awakening from a momentary trance, hurled back all his divine weapons at him.
And that general of Śiva’s army, Viṣṇu, suddenly warded off all those arrows released from the bow with his own terrible counter-arrows.
Then Viṣṇu, his eyes red with anger, discharged toward that Lord of the Gaṇas an unimpeded arrow marked with his own name.
But the Blessed One, with an excellent arrow called Bhadra, cut that shaft into a hundred pieces on its path before it had even reached him.
Then, with a single arrow he severed Śārṅga, and with two more he cut off the wings of Garuḍa; all this occurred in the mere blink of an eye, and it was like a marvel.
Then, by the power of yoga, Viṣṇu emitted from his body thousands of most formidable deities, holding conchs, discs, and maces in their hands.
In a mere instant, the mighty-armed one utterly consumed them all with the fire emitted from his eye, just as Śaṅkara did to the inhabitants of Tripura.
Then Viṣṇu, becoming even more enraged, swiftly raised his discus and was then prepared to hurl it at that hero.
Seeing that discus raised and standing before him, Gaṇeśāna, as if smiling, paralyzed it effortlessly.
With his limbs paralyzed, Viṣṇu was not even able to release that terrible and peerless discus, even though he desired to do so.
As if gasping for breath, he raised one arm equipped with the discus and stood there, becoming listless and motionless like a stone.
Just as a living being without a body, or a bull without horns, or a lion without fangs, so does Viṣṇu abide.
Seeing Viṣṇu fallen into such a wretched state, Indra and the other gods were emboldened by the Lord of the Gaṇas, like bulls by a lion.
With weapons raised to fight, they stood there enraged; seeing them in battle, Bhadra looked upon them as a lion looks at small deer.
The hero, whose body is Rudra himself, surrounded by hosts of excellent heroes, laughed a terrible, loud laugh; thus the blameless one caused fear to be dispelled.
Likewise, even the right hand of Indra, though holding his thunderbolt, seemed as if it were rendered motionless, as if paralyzed with wonder, at the very moment he desired to hurl it.
Even the arms of all others, though full of passion, turn back in such a manner, like the undertakings of the indolent.
Thus, because all his power had been thwarted by the Blessed One, the immortals were unable to stand before him in battle.
With their limbs rendered rigid, they fled, overwhelmed by fear; agitated by both heroic splendor and terror, they could find no footing in the battle.
The mighty-armed Vīrabhadra pierced the fleeing heroic gods with sharp arrows, just as Maghavat strikes mountains with showers of rain.
The many arms of that hero, resembling iron clubs, shone with their blazing weapons like serpents with tongues of fire.
Discharging numerous missiles and weapons, that hero shone like the Source of the Universe discharging all beings at the beginning of time.
Just as the sun covers the earth with its rays, so did the hero in an instant cover the quarters of the sky with his arrows.
In the circle of the Lord of the Gaṇas, arrows adorned with gold, as they flew upward, became the very standard for comparison with flashes of lightning.
Those great ones deprived the hosts of gods of their lives, like large water-snakes devouring frogs, and drank the wine of their blood.

And having thus seized him by his faults, they bound him with strong iron shackles upon his hands, feet, necks, and bellies.
At that moment, Brahmā, having received affection for his role as charioteer, bowed down and spoke while entreating Bhadra, the son of the Mountain King.
"Enough with this anger, O Blessed One; these gods have been destroyed. Be gracious, O you of noble vows, and let all be forgiven along with the hair-born ones."
Thus addressed by that supreme Brahmā, the Lord of the Gaṇas became pacified and filled with joy out of respect for him.
And the gods, having obtained the opportunity, their ministers to the God of Gods, held their joined palms to their heads and praised him with various hymns.
The gods said: "Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the destroyer of the sacrifice, the bearer of the trident; to Rudra-Bhadra, the lord of the Rudras, the source of all Rudra-beings."
Salutations to the one whose form is Kālāgnirudra, who took away the limbs of Kāla and Kāma, and who struck off the heads of the gods and of the evil-minded Dakṣa.
O hero, through our association with this sinful Dakṣa of unwearied deeds, we, though blameless, have been chastised by you in battle.
O Lord, we have all been scorched and are terrified of you; you alone are our refuge—protect us who have come to you for shelter.
Vāyu said: Thus praised, the Lord, being pleased, dismissed the gods from their fetters and brought the immortals here into the presence of the God of Gods.
There the Lord, the Blessed One, the omnipresent Śarva, the Great Lord of all worlds, stood in the sky together with his retinue.
Having seen that Supreme Lord, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, though both pleased and afraid, paid homage to Maheśvara.
Seeing those gods terrified, Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, Mahādeva, looked toward Pārvatī and spoke this while smiling.
Mahādeva said: "Do not fear, O all you gods; you are indeed my own offspring. This staff has been wielded here by the compassionate one solely for the sake of bestowing grace."
O liberated ones, we have indeed forgiven your transgression; yet if we were enraged, neither your stability nor your lives would remain.
Vāyu said: Having been addressed thus by Śarva of immeasurable splendor, all the thirty gods, their doubts instantly dispelled, danced with joy, O Vibudhas.
Having become serene in mind and their hearts overwhelmed with joy, the denizens of heaven began to offer praise to Śaṅkara.

The gods said: You alone are the creator, protector, and destroyer of all the worlds; you are the Supreme Lord, whose embodied forms uphold the qualities of passion, darkness, and goodness through the distinct manifestations known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

O you who possess all forms, salutations be unto you, O creator of the universe, O purifier! O formless one, you have indeed assumed a physical form for the sake of your devotees, bestowing happiness upon them.
O Śaṅkara, Lord of the Gods, it was indeed through your compassion that Candra, who had died from drowning, attained happiness along with Sūrya and Agastya.
O Lord, by worshipping you through the Monday vow, this woman whose husband had passed away attained incomparable good fortune and sons.
The Lord granted his own unsurpassed station to Śrīkara; you, however, did not protect Sudarśana out of fear of the circle of kings.
The ocean of compassion rescued Medura along with his wife; by your action, you turned the widow Śāradā into one who possesses a husband.
O Bhadrāyus, you have severed misfortune and bestowed happiness; indeed, through your service, Sauminī has been liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.

Viṣṇu said: O Śambhu, you and Brahmā and Iśa, through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, are the creator, the protector, and likewise the destroyer, out of a desire to bestow grace upon living beings.
He is the remover of all pride, the one who causes the splendor of all brilliance to shine; he is hidden within all sciences and directions, and the performer of grace toward all.
Everything comes from you, you are everything, and everything is within you, O Lord of the Mountain! Save me, save me, save me again; have mercy upon me.
Then, in the meantime, Brahmā, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence and having thus found the opportunity, made this request to the wielder of the trident:
Brahmā said: Victory to you, O God, Great God, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before you! Among such offenses, who else but you would be gracious?
Those who were previously slain in battle shall come back to life; for when the Supreme Lord is pleased, who would not experience restoration?
That which is considered a fault among the gods of gods, one should regard that very thing as an ornament because of the dignity of acceptance.
Thus being addressed by Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin, the God of gods, as if smiling, gazed upon the face of the Goddess.
Out of affection for him who had become his son, the Lord Brahmā, born from the lotus, bestowed upon the gods and others their respective limbs as before.
And to those goddesses, the mothers of the gods, who had been punished by the first [deity] and the others, Giriśa likewise restored their limbs as they were before.
The Blessed One himself, the Grandfather Brahmā, made the face of Dakṣa into that of an old goat, in accordance with his sin.
Having regained consciousness from that state and seeing that he was alive, the wise man, filled with fear, joined his palms in reverence and praised Śambhu while uttering many words of praise.
Dakṣa said: Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World, who bestows grace upon the worlds! Have mercy, O Great Lord; forgive my transgression.
O Lord of the worlds, you alone are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer; I have come to know specifically that you are the sovereign of Viṣṇu and all others.
Everything has been spread out, pervaded, created, and not destroyed by you alone; for there are no lords superior to you, such as Acyuta and the others.
Vāyu said: Beholding him thus agitated, terrified, lamenting, and having committed an offense, the ocean—a treasure-house of compassion—spoke as if smiling, saying, "Do not fear."
Having spoken thus, the Lord, desiring to do what was pleasing to his father Brahmā, granted that Dakṣa the imperishable status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, having saluted him with palms joined in reverence, praised Śaṅkara, the lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, with humble words.
Brahmā and the others said: Victory to you, O Śaṅkara, Lord of gods, protector of the distressed, Great Lord! Show us mercy, O Maheśāna, and indeed forgive our offense.
O protector of sacrifice, sovereign of sacrifice, you who cause the destruction of sacrifice! Show us mercy; forgive our transgression regarding the cremation ground.
O God of gods, Supreme Lord, nourisher of the life-breath of your devotees, giver of punishment to the wicked, O Master, show mercy; salutations be unto you!
O Lord, you are indeed the remover of the pride of the wicked who do not know you; for you are especially the protector of the virtuous whose minds are attached to you.
Truly, your conduct is wonderful, for it is certain that it arises from your compassion; you, who are affectionate toward the wretched, must forgive all offenses.
Vāyu said: Thus praised by Brahmā and the other immortals, the Lord Mahādeva—the Master who is compassionate toward his devotees and an ocean of mercy—was gratified.
Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward the distressed, bestowed his grace upon those gods beginning with Brahmā and, out of great affection, granted them human beings as well.
Then the Supreme Lord, who is supremely compassionate, having pacified all their fears with words characterized by a gentle smile, addressed the thirty gods who had come to him for refuge.

Śiva said: "Whatever offense has been committed here by the gods, who were as if constrained by the force of destiny's decree—having seen that you have come for refuge, all of that is indeed forgotten by us."

Therefore, you too, O shameless ones, disregarding the crushing conflict that has arisen here in your minds, proceed now at ease toward the city of the gods, led by Hari, Viriñci, and the lords of the immortals.

Having thus addressed the gods, Hara—the Lord of the Suras, who had rendered Dakṣa’s sacrifice fruitless and was himself without a sacrifice—vanished from the sky along with Girijā, his attendants, and his retinue, as if he had been standing there.

Then those gods also, their afflictions dispelled and having recounted the auspicious and excellent valor [of the Buddha], immediately departed as they pleased through the sky by their own ease, led by Indra and possessing many faces.
The sages said: Having vanished along with the Goddess and his attendants, where did Hara go? Where does he dwell, and what did he do before he ceased?
Vāyu said: The glorious Mandara, the best of mountains, with its wonderful caves, was the beloved abode of the God of gods and became the site for his ascetic penance.
Great penance was performed by him so that the two Śivas might bear [him] upon their own heads; after a long time, he obtained the bliss born from the touch of their lotus feet.
The beauty of that mountain cannot be described in detail even by one with a thousand mouths, even in hundreds of millions of years.
Even though its beauty could be described, I do not venture to do so; for the beauty of another mountain would be rendered common through such a description.
However, this can be said regarding this mountain-beauty: by some supernatural power, its beauty possesses the fitness to be the abode of the Lord.
For this very reason, out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the Queen, the King has made this exceedingly beautiful mountain his inner palace.
The grounds of his girdle, with their trees of spotless stones, eclipse the entire world due to the eternal presence there of Śiva and Śivā.
Having acquired the purificatory merit of sacred rites through the constant use of bathing and drinking water from his parents for the sake of the world, [he] spreads forth in every direction.
With the clear waters of mountain torrents, cool and light to the touch, this king of mountains is consecrated with the sovereignty over all hills.
At night, that mountain shines with the moon resting upon its peak, as if with the imperial parasol of a sovereign of mountains.
And that mountain was fanned by the swaying tails of the yak-mares, as if by fly-whisks belonging to the entire empire of all mountains.
At dawn, when the sun has risen, the mountain adorned with jewels stands as if desiring to behold the beauty of its own form in a mirror.
It was filled with the warbling of birds, with creeper-arms tossed by the wind, with flowers constantly falling, and with soft sprouts hanging down everywhere.
The king of mountains was honored with blessings of victory by the trees, which were matted together with spreading creepers as if they were ascetics, and seemed to be attended upon by them.
With peaks facing downward, upward, and sideways, it seemed as if it were falling into the netherworld or leaping up from the surface of the earth.
Surrounded on all sides in every direction, as if wandering in the sky, as if beholding the entire world, and as if dancing incessantly.
With its cavernous mouths wide open day after day and its vast bellies, the mountain seemed to be yawning, as it were, due to the indigestion of its own beauty.
As if swallowing the entire world, as if drinking the ocean, as if vomiting the darkness within, and as if intoxicating the sky with clouds;
Those various dwelling places, with interiors like the surface of a mirror, were shaded by the dense foliage of trees that provided refuge from the heat.
The breezes, cooled by contact with rivers, lakes, ponds, and the like, were rendered fruitful by the two Śivas as they sat here and there.
Having remembered this [mantra], which is the most excellent of all, Sāmba Triyambaka, staying near Raibhya’s hermitage, vanished and departed.
Having reached the garden there with the Goddess, Maheśvara took his pleasure in the delightful grounds of the Goddess’s inner apartments.
As time passed in this manner and the progeny had multiplied, two Daitya brothers named Śumbha and Niśumbha were born.
By the power of their asceticism, Brahmā Parameṣṭhin granted them invincibility in this world against all men whatsoever.
But that maiden who was not born from a womb, having arisen from a portion of Ambikā, had never experienced the pleasure of a man's touch and possessed invincible prowess.
Requested by them both, who were overcome by desire, saying, "By her alone shall our death in battle come to pass," Brahmā replied, "So be it."
From that time forward, having defeated the gods beginning with Śakra in battle, they caused the world to be devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call through their tyranny.
For the sake of slaying those two, Brahmā again entreated the Lord of Gods, saying, "By whatever means possible, even by censuring you or by provoking your anger through some secret matter."
"You ought to grant to the gods that power born from the treasury of their own colors, who is in the form of a maiden, free from desire, and the slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha."
Thus entreated by the Creator, the Lord Nīlalohita, as if censuring your secret name "Kālī," spoke with a smile.
Then the goddess Suvarṇā, enraged by the cause of her complexion, smilingly addressed her husband with words that could not be gainsaid.
The Goddess said: "If you have no pleasure in such a complexion as mine in this world, how was it that she was restrained by you for so long a time?"
Even though you dwell in discontent, how is it that you take delight with me? For there is nothing impossible in this world for the Lord, the Master of the universe.
For you, who delight in your own self, sensual pleasure is not a means to happiness; for this reason, Smara was forcibly reduced to ashes by you.
Even if she is beautiful in all her limbs, if she is not desired by her husband, she is born in vain despite all her other virtues.
For this very creation of women has as its sole purpose the enjoyment of a husband; if it were otherwise, for what use would a woman be?
Therefore, having abandoned this caste which you have censured in private, I shall either resort to another caste or not resort to one at all on my own accord.
Having spoken thus, the queen rose from her bed and, with a faltering voice, spoke; having resolved upon asceticism, she begged for her husband's permission.
Thus, fearing a breach of affection, the Lord of Beings himself, while bowing at her feet, addressed Bhavānī.
Īśvara said: O beloved, not understanding my playful words, why are you angry with me? How could delight arise from you, if you are displeasure to me?
"You are the mother of this world, and I am its father and sovereign; how could it be that my lack of delight arises from you?"
Is even our mutual desire caused by passion? For the origin of the world occurred long before the arising of desire.
I fashioned this sensualist for the delight of ordinary worldlings; how then can I be reproached by you for the burning of desire?
Thinking me to be equal to the gods of the thirty-three, the Mind-born One (Kāma) committed a slight act of insolence toward me; indeed, he was reduced to ashes by me.
"Furthermore, our dwelling here is for the sake of protecting this world; therefore, for that purpose, I have today addressed you with playful words."
And this very matter shall soon be revealed to you; having taken to heart these words that provoke anger, he spoke as follows.
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, I have indeed heard your flattering words before, by which even I, though exceedingly steadfast, was formerly deceived."
A virtuous woman of noble family who does not even abandon her life when it is displeasing to her husband is indeed regarded with contempt by the wise.
Moreover, you have a great aversion to my body because it is not fair; otherwise, how could even a playful remark such as "Kālī" (the Black One) be appropriate?
Therefore, this blackness of yours is censured by the virtuous and is not approved; unable to abandon it, I do not venture to remain here through the power of my ascetic yoga.
Śiva said: "If you are performing such penance as this, what is the purpose of your austerity? By my will or by your own will, become possessed of another caste."
The Goddess said: "I do not wish to change my complexion by myself; rather, having propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance, I shall quickly become fair-complexioned."
Īśvara said: "In former times, O Great Goddess, Brahmā attained the status of Brahmā through my grace; having summoned him, what will you achieve by means of penance?"
The Goddess said: "All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, have indeed obtained their positions from you; nevertheless, at your command, they propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance."
Long ago, it is said, I was the daughter of Dakṣa by the name Satī; in that manner, I obtained you, the Lord of the worlds, as my husband.
Thus, even now, having gratified the twice-born Brahmā through ascetic penance, I wish to become Gaurī; tell me, what fault is there in this?
Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, Vāmadeva, as if smiling, did not press her further, desiring to accomplish the purpose of the gods.
Vāyu said: Then the devoted mother, having circumambulated her husband and restrained the pain of separation, went to the Himavat mountain.
Out of affection, she chose once again for the sake of penance that very same region where she had previously performed austerities with her circle of friends.
Then, having seen her father and mother in their house, she bowed to them, informed them of what had occurred, and received their permission.
Having gone again to the forest of asceticism and cast off her ornaments, she bathed and assumed the supremely purifying garb of an ascetic.
Having resolved upon a most intense penance that was exceedingly difficult to perform, she constantly held the lotus-feet of her husband in her mind.

Having meditated upon that very [deity] in the momentary *liṅga* according to the external ritual procedure, she worshipped it at the three junctions of the day with wild flowers, fruits, and other offerings.
Thinking, "He alone, assuming a physical form, will grant me the fruit of my asceticism," he performed penance constantly, having made this resolve.
While she was thus practicing austerities, after a long period of time had passed, a certain great tiger was seen and approached her with a wicked intent.
Even as that exceedingly wicked-souled one approached her, his body became as motionless as if it were a painting before her presence.
Even upon seeing that tiger approaching with such a malevolent intent, the queen did not waver from her innate nature like an ordinary person.
With all his limbs paralyzed and tormented by hunger, he thought incessantly, "There is no food for me other than my own flesh."
Constantly gazing at the goddess alone day and night, he remained before her as if performing her worship.
And in the heart of the Goddess there arose constant compassion, thinking: "This man is my very own devotee, and he is a protector against wicked beings."
By the power of her very compassion, his three impurities were instantly destroyed; he suddenly became a tiger and then recognized the Goddess.
His hunger ceased as well as the stiffness of his limbs; his innate wickedness vanished, and satisfaction arose within him.
Then, having realized through supreme devotion that his own purpose was fulfilled, he, though still a neophyte, immediately served the Supreme Goddess.
Becoming the very one who puts to flight even wicked beings as well as other evil-minded ones, he wandered through the forest of asceticism.
The goddess’s asceticism increased, becoming more intense and even fiercer; and the gods, due to the oppression by the Daityas, went to Brahmā for refuge.
The gods reported their own suffering caused by the oppression of their enemies, as well as how Śumbha and Niśumbha had acted out of the intoxication of the boons they had received.
Having heard of the suffering of the gods, Brahmā was filled with compassion; he resolved upon the destruction of the Daityas, recalling the narrative concerning the underlying cause.
Requested by the gods, Brahmā went to the goddess’s penance grove, mentally reflecting on how to liberate the gods from their suffering through his own effort.
And the best of gods beheld Bhavānī, the supreme goddess, established in the highest asceticism, like the very foundation of the universe.
And he bowed down to the mother of this world, the noble wife of his father Hari and of Rudra, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Seeing that Brahmā had arrived along with the hosts of gods, the Goddess offered him the appropriate arghya and attended to him with words of welcome and other honors.
Having honored and welcomed her with words of polite reception, the Lotus-born One, as if ignorant of the reason for her asceticism, questioned her about it.
Brahmā said: "What is to be accomplished here by this intense austerity of the Goddess? For the success of all fruits of austerity is indeed dependent upon you."
Having obtained as her own husband that very Supreme Lord who is the sustainer of the worlds, she has attained the fruit of her ascetic penance.
Or rather, all this is merely the playful sport of you, the Lord; yet this is a wonder: how is it that you endure separation?
The Goddess said: When it is heard that at the beginning of creation your birth occurred from the God, then you were the first of all creatures and my first-born son.
Furthermore, when Bhava was born from your forehead for the sake of increasing progeny, at that time you became my elder through your status as my father-in-law.
When your son, the lord of mountains, was my very own father, then you became my grandfather, O Grandfather of the World.
How then shall I speak of your conduct within the inner apartments, you who are such a person as this, engaged in the affairs of worldly life?
What need is there for much here? This darkness that exists in my body, having abandoned it through the application of *sattva*, I strive to become fair-complexioned.
Brahmā said: O Goddess, for what purpose was such intense austerity performed? Was your own will not sufficient? For such is your sport.
O Mother of the World, even this play of yours is indeed for the welfare of the world; therefore, let some desired fruit be accomplished for me by means of this.
The two Daityas named Niśumbha and Śumbha, having been granted boons by me, are arrogant and oppress the gods; their death shall come from you.
Enough with delay here; remain steady for a moment. As their power is being discharged today, it will become their death.
And when entreated by the brahmins, the goddess, daughter of the mountain king, suddenly cast off her bark garment and became Gaurī.
Casting off her own skin, she became a maiden known by the name Kauśikī; dark as a black rain cloud, she was called Kālī.
That power, consisting of Māyā, is indeed the Yoganidrā of Viṣṇu; she possesses eight great arms equipped with weapons such as the conch, the discus, and the trident.
Gentle, terrible, and mixed; three-eyed and moon-crested; she who has never experienced the pleasure of a man's touch, invincible, and exceedingly beautiful.
And this eternal Śakti was bestowed upon Brahmā by the Goddess; she is the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, those two lions among the Daityas.
Brahmā, being greatly delighted, gave that supreme Śakti a powerful lion as her vehicle, which then approached her.
Having performed her worship in the Vindhya mountains with offerings beginning with wine, along with meat, fish, and cakes, he gave her this instruction:
And that very power, esteemed as belonging to Brahmā Viśvakarman, having prostrated before his mother Gaurī and before Brahmā in due order, [proceeded].
Surrounded by many of her own daughters who were equal to her in power, she set out for the Vindhya mountains, intent on slaying the two lords of the Daityas.
And there in that battle, those two foremost of Daityas were slain by her, their limbs and minds pierced and shattered by her arrows and the arrows of Kama.

The details of that battle have not been recounted here, as they have already been described elsewhere; they are to be inferred from those other sources, and I shall describe to you what is relevant to the present context.
Vāyu said: Having created Kauśikī and presented her to Brahmā, Gaurī then spoke to the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) for the sake of repaying his kindness.
The goddess said: "Have you seen this tiger who takes refuge with me? By him, my penance grove has been protected from wicked creatures."
With his mind offered unto me, he worships me with undivided intellect; there exists nothing dearer to me than the protection of him.
Therefore, he must become an attendant in my inner apartments; and Śaṅkara will affectionately grant him the rank of Gaṇeśvara.
Making him my leader, I am eager to go with my friends; let permission be granted to me by you, the Lord of Creatures.
Thus addressed, Brahmā laughed and, smiling as if at a charming maiden, described her wickedness through her intense past deeds.
Brahmā said: O Goddess, since cruel beasts dwell in this animal, where is your auspicious grace? Is nectar being poured directly into the mouth of a venomous serpent?
This is some wicked night-stalker who has merely assumed the form of a tiger; by him, cows and Brahmins rich in asceticism have been devoured.
Assuming any form at will, he wanders about gratifying them according to his desire; indeed, the fruit of an evil deed must necessarily be experienced.
Therefore, what is the use of compassion toward such evil-minded beings? What business has the Goddess with this one, who is by nature foul-souled?

The Goddess said: "Everything that has been spoken by you is true; he is indeed such as this. Nevertheless, since he has sought refuge with me, one who has come to me for protection must not be abandoned."
Brahmā said: "Without knowing his devotion, I previously related your past history to you. If he possesses such devotion, what can his sins do? Your devotee shall not perish."
What could even one of meritorious deeds accomplish without regard for your command? You alone are the Supreme Goddess, the unborn, primordial wisdom.
For the entire arrangement of bondage and liberation for all beings depends upon you; apart from you, O Supreme Power, by whose action could perfection be attained?
You alone are the manifold power, or perhaps you are yourself the Lord; for one who is incapable of performing action, what can a creator do?
For Viṣṇu, for me, and for others—whether gods, dānavas, or rākṣasas—the cause for attaining their respective sovereignties is indeed your command alone.
Indeed, countless Brahmās, Haras, and Bhavas have passed away; and countless [beings] yet to come shall likewise follow your command.
O Goddess of the gods, without propitiating you, the fourfold aims of human life cannot be attained even by us, the best of all the gods.
There would also be an immediate reversal of the states of being Brahman and being stationary, because merit and demerit have been established by you alone.
For you are the primordial, eternal power of Śiva, the Supreme Self and sustainer of the entire world, who is without beginning, middle, or end.
For the sake of the entire course of worldly existence, you assume some form and sport with various states of being; who knows you in reality?
Therefore, even though he is a tiger who has committed evil deeds, may he attain supreme perfection here through your grace; what obstacle could there be to this?
Having thus reminded him of his own supreme nature in a fitting manner, Gaurī, entreated by Brahmā, desisted even from her ascetic penance.
Then, having taken leave of the Goddess, when Brahmā had vanished, he beheld the Goddess, his mother Menā, together with Himavat.
Having prostrated and consoled in many ways his parents, who were unable to endure their separation, the Goddess [Sītā] paid homage to the trees of the ascetic grove that were devoted to penance.
As if out of grief at their impending separation, the trees shed tears in the form of flowers; meanwhile, the birds perched upon their branches uttered plaintive cries.
Agitated, distressed, and lamenting in many ways, she spoke thus to her friends, eager for a sight of her husband.
Placing that tiger in front of her, out of affection as if toward her own biological son, she illuminated the ten directions with the radiance of her body.
Gaurī went to Mandara, where her husband Maheśvara resides—the creator, sustainer, protector, and destroyer of all the worlds.
The sages said: Having assumed a divine fair-complexioned form, how did the goddess Satī, the daughter of the mountain king, enter and behold her husband adorned?
O Lord, what was done by the Gaṇeśas stationed at the gateway of her palace at the time of her entrance, and what did You do upon seeing them then?
Vāyu said: Such a supreme rasa cannot be accurately described—that which, pregnant with affection, has captivated the hearts of those possessed of feeling.
The attendants at the gate, filled with agitation, announced that the Lord was eager for the Goddess's arrival; suspecting something, she entered within and beheld him.
Honored by those lords of the Gaṇas dwelling within the palace with various expressions of affection, she bowed her voice in salutation to the Three-eyed Lord.
Before she could rise from her prostration, the Supreme Lord took her in his arms, embraced her, and surrounded her with supreme joy.
Although he proceeded to take her onto his own lap, she sat down upon the couch; then, forcibly lifting the smiling goddess from the couch, he placed her on his lap.
Smiling and as if drinking in her face with his wide-open eyes, the Lord spoke these words first, in order to address her.
The God of gods said: "That state has passed; what is it to you, O beautiful in every limb, in which no means of conciliation whatsoever can be found because of your anger?"
"O fair-browed one, even by my own will, I cannot think of you as Kālī nor as having any other complexion; my mind, captivated by your very nature, brings me only anxiety."
How can the supreme state be forgotten through the union with one's own will, wherein the causes of mental turbidity do not arise?
If there were even the slightest cause for mutual displeasure between us, as there is among ordinary people, then this entire world of moving and non-moving beings would surely not exist.
I am established at the head of Agni, and you reside at the head of Soma; the universe, consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma, is presided over by us both.
For if there were a separation between us—who move for the welfare of the world and have assumed these bodies by our own will—the world would indeed be left without support.
There is another reason for this, determined by both scripture and logic: this entire world, both stationary and moving, appears to me like a word and its meaning.
For you are the nectar of speech itself, and I am the supreme nectar of the self; how could these two nectars possibly exist separated from one another?

You are the knower who makes knowledge manifest to me, and I am the object of knowledge through your cognition; how then can there be a separation between us, whose very natures are that of knowledge and the object of knowledge?
I do not create this world through karma, nor do I dissolve it; for since everything is obtainable solely through my command, the state of being the Command is indeed the most exalted.
Since sovereignty has command as its sole essence and is characterized by autonomy, what kind of sovereignty can belong to me when I am deprived of command?
"There has never been a time when we two were separated; it was only for the sake of the gods' business that I employed these playful words."
"There is nothing unknown to you; why then have you become angry? Therefore, for the sake of protecting the three worlds, you have directed your anger even toward me."
"O Priyamvadā, nothing exists in you, the manifest Supreme Lord, that could be for the harm of living beings."
The natural birthplace of the essence of the erotic sentiment, she regarded what was said by her own husband as charming and true, and responded with a smile.
Out of modesty, Kauśikī said nothing further after her description; I shall now describe that very same thing—listen to the description of the Goddess.
The Goddess said: "Has she not been seen by the Lord, she whom I created as Kauśikī? A maiden such as she has never existed in the world, nor will she ever exist."
Her valor, strength, and victory over those two—Śumbha and Niśumbha—were displayed in the battle for their slaying.
He will always bestow visible fruits upon the world, and Brahmā will constantly proclaim his protection of the worlds.
While the queen was speaking thus, by her very command, a tiger was then brought by her friend and stationed before her.
Seeing him, the queen spoke again to the one brought by the gods: "Look at this tiger; there is no devotee of mine equal to him."
By him, my penance grove has been protected from wicked assemblies; he is exceedingly devoted to me and trusts me because of his own protection.
Having abandoned my own country, I have come here for the sake of your favor; if you have found pleasure in me, then grant me the highest pleasure.
By the command of Nandin himself, let this lord always remain at the gate of the inner apartments together with guards bearing his insignia.
Vāyu said: Having heard the auspicious words of the goddess, which were sweet and concluded with affection, the god said to him, "I am pleased," and at that very moment he became visible.
Carrying a golden cane-staff and a tunic variegated with jewels, and bearing a dagger resembling a serpent, Gaṇeśa assumes the guise of a protector.
Since Soma is Mahādeva and Nandin was gladdened by him, he is therefore renowned by the name Somanandi.
Having thus done what was pleasing to the Goddess, the God adorned with the crescent moon decorated her with divine ornaments set with jewels.
Then Hara, the moon-crested Lord of the Mountains, respectfully placed Gaurī—the daughter of the Mountain King who enchants all—with her excellent limbs adorned with ornaments, upon his lap.
The sages said: What was this spoken by the Lord while he was absorbed in meditation upon the Goddess—that the universe consists of fire and moon, and likewise consists of word and meaning?
Sovereignty has command as its sole essence, and you have been declared to be that command; we desire to hear this, exactly as it is and in due order.
Vāyu said: That which is called Agni is the fierce and terrible fiery body of Rudra; Soma is the nectar-like body of Śakti, the bringer of peace.

That which is the nectar (amṛta) is her foundation; she herself is splendor, knowledge, and the creative power (kalā). Within all the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), she alone is both essence (rasa) and splendor (tejas).
The function of fire is twofold: that which consists of the sun and that which consists of fire; likewise, the function of taste consists of the moon and that which consists of water.

Light consists of lightning and other such forms, while taste consists of sweetness and other such qualities; by means of these various distinctions of light and taste, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained.
The production of nectar occurs from fire; by means of that nectar, fire prospers. For this very reason, the powerful Agni and Soma are beneficial to the world.
The abundance of grain is for the sake of the oblation; rain is for the growth of the grain; the oblation consists of rain alone; therefore, the world is sustained by Agni and Soma.
This fire blazes upwards as far as the gentle supreme nectar; as long as the gentle nectar flows downwards to the seat of the fire.
For this very reason, Kālāgni is below and Śakti is above; until the upper limit of burning and the lower limit of immersion are reached.
Supported by the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) alone, this fire of time (kālāgni) moves upward; likewise, the moon (soma), which is the locus of the state of Śiva’s power, moves downward.
Śiva is above and Śakti is below; Śakti is above and Śiva is below. Thus, there is nothing here whatsoever that is not pervaded by Śiva and Śakti.
The world has been repeatedly burnt by fire and reduced to ashes; they say this is the power of fire, and therefore that which is ash is its power.
Whoever, having thus understood the true nature of the ash, bathes with the ash while reciting the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," is released from the bonds by which he was bound.
The ash, which is the virility of fire, when drenched again with Soma, becomes fit for the governance of Prakṛti through the application of yoga.
But by means of yogic method, that ash, being drenched on all sides by the rain of nectar from the Śakti, shall cause one to turn back from [further] worldly authority.
Therefore, one should always perform this immersion in nectar for the sake of conquering death; for one by whom the touch of the nectar of Śiva and Śakti has been attained, whence can there be death?
He who knows the secret burning and the flooding as they have been described, having abandoned the state of Agni and Soma, is not born again.
Having burned the body with the fire of Śiva, he who drenches it with the nectar of Śakti through the path of yoga is fit for immortality.
Having taken this meaning to heart, which was indeed proclaimed by the Lord—that the entire universe consists of the nature of Agni and Soma—in accordance with its true form.

Vāyu said: I shall explain the nature of speech and meaning as it has been established for the world; I shall provide a correct understanding of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) in summary, but not in detail.
There is no object that is not denoted by a word, nor is there any word that is devoid of meaning; therefore, in conventional usage, every word is capable of conveying every object.

This transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) is twofold, consisting of the manifestation of sound and meaning; they call this the natural form (prākṛtī mūrti) of the two supreme souls, Śiva and Śivā.
That manifestation whose nature is sound is said by the wise to be threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme; of these, the gross is that which falls within the range of hearing.
The subtle power is said to consist of reflection, while the supreme is devoid of reflection; that which is power is the supreme power, resting upon the principle of Śiva.

Thus, through union with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of will (icchā-śakti) is likewise strengthened; consisting of the aggregate of all powers, it is designated by the name of the principle of Power (śakti-tattva).
She who has become the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) of the entire multitude of effects—that very Māyā is Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme reality of the pure path.
She herself, whose very nature is differentiation, unfolds as the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan); therein, three paths are declared to be words and three to be meanings.
Indeed, for all persons, according to their own respective purity, there arise dissolution, enjoyment, and authority, through the differentiation of all the principles (tattvas).
Those principles are pervaded by the *kalās* exactly as they are, through the fivefold transformation at the outset of the supreme *prakṛti*.

And it is certain that those levels, beginning with Nivṛtti, are fully sufficient; and from the perspective of sound, there is the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).

The path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of principles (tattvādhvan), and the path of limited powers (kalādhvan) are, in fact, presented in sequence; herein, the mutual relationship of pervaded and pervader among all of them is described.
Mantras are pervaded by all words because they constitute sentences, and words are composed of phonemes; for the wise say that a word is indeed a collection of phonemes.

The castes (varṇas), however, are pervaded by the worlds, because they are perceived within them; and the worlds, too, are pervaded by the multitudes of principles (tattvas) through their emergence in both internal and external sequences.
Some worlds here have arisen from within, being commenced manifoldly by the pervasive causal principles (tattvas).
Other ancient accounts are to be understood from the Śiva-āgamas, as well as certain principles (tattvas) well-known from Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Furthermore, all other principles well-known from the Śiva scriptures are likewise pervaded by these kalās exactly as they are.

At the beginning of the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), through its fivefold transformation, there arise the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti; these five pervade [the subsequent levels] in successive order.

Therefore, the supreme power (parā śakti) is all-pervasive and undivided from the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), because of its existence as the state of the supreme primordial nature (paraprakṛti) within the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
The principles beginning with Śakti and ending with Earth arise from the Śiva-tattva; they are pervaded by that very same [Śiva-tattva], just as a pot and other such objects are pervaded by clay.
That is the supreme abode of Śiva, which is to be attained through the six paths; it is the pervasive and non-pervasive Power [of Śiva] resulting from the purification of the five principles.

Through Nivṛtti, the stability of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) is purified up to the level of Rudra; through Pratiṣṭhā, however, it is purified from there upwards as far as the sphere of the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Above that, up to the middle [of the body] as far as Viśveśvara, purification is effected by Vidyā; above that, at the end of Madhu, purification is effected by Śānti and by Śāntyatītā.

That which they call the supreme ether (*parama-vyoman*) due to its union with the supreme nature (*parā-prakṛti*); these are the five principles (*pañca-tattva*) by which the entire world is pervaded.
In that very place, indeed, all this must be perceived by the practitioners; for he who desires to perform purification without understanding the pervasion of the paths [of existence].
That deceiver is not capable of attaining the fruit of purity; his exertion is in vain and leads only to hell.
Without the conjunction of the descent of power (śaktipāta), it is impossible to know the principles (tattvas) according to their true nature, nor their pervasion, nor their progressive development.
Power (śakti) is the supreme command, the Śiva-natured Mistress of the Maras, whose form is consciousness; by her, who has become the cause, Śiva presides over everything.
Upon investigation, this is neither the self nor an illusion, nor is it a transformation; there is neither bondage nor liberation, for it is that which brings about both bondage and liberation.
The supreme limit of all sovereignty belongs to Śiva; she shares his common attributes and is distinguished by those various specific states of being.
He is always the householder by means of her, and she too is the housewife by means of him; their offspring is that which is to be done, the world born of the primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is the agent and she is the instrument; thus their distinction is established. Śiva alone is directly present, yet he exists in a twofold manner.
Some maintain that the distinction between them consists in their being female and male; others, however, hold that Śiva’s supreme power (parā śakti) is inherent (samavāyinī) within him.
The nature of consciousness, like the radiance of the sun, is established as if it were distinct [from its source]; therefore, Śiva is the supreme cause, and his command is the Supreme Goddess.
Impelled by that very [power], the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) of Śiva—indestructible, known as Mahāmāyā, Māyā, and Prakṛti consisting of the three qualities—is set in motion.
Through the piercing of its effects, that [power] gives birth to the six paths; and that path, consisting of both word and meaning, is sixfold—the entire universe.
They declare that the entire collection of scriptures is but an expansion of this very [work].
The sages said: Your deeds are diverse, domestic, and profound; they are difficult even for the gods to comprehend and they bewilder our minds.
In the relationship between the two principles of Śiva and Śakti, no fault is perceived; yet, through their activities, even a natural (prākṛta) disposition is manifested in them as well.
Even Brahmā and the others, who are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds, remain subject to Śiva’s will when they exercise their powers of restraint and grace.
Furthermore, Śiva is not the object of anyone's restraint or favor; therefore, it is certain that his sovereignty is entirely independent.
If such sovereignty as this exists, it is characterized by absolute freedom; and since it is established by its very nature, it must have a corporeal basis.
A form for that which is independent cannot be established by means of a fundamental cause; furthermore, since even a form is an effect, its establishment would be causeless.
In all cases, the supreme state is said to be one thing, and the non-supreme another; how could the supreme and the non-supreme states be conjoined in one place?

For the supreme intrinsic nature of this Supreme Self is indeed fruitless; why then is that very same nature described as being "entire" (sakala), since an intrinsic nature is by definition non-erroneous?
If intrinsic nature were subject to reversal, and if the Lord acted independently according to his own will, why would he not bring about the reversal of the eternal into the non-eternal?
One is the embodied Self, the Sakala (the differentiated), and the other is the fruitless Śiva; it is briefly stated everywhere that [the former] is presided over by Śiva.
Then the very self of the form would become the form of this Śiva; for in the case of a form and its possessor, dependence is indeed certain.
Otherwise, how could a form be accepted by one who is independent? Therefore, the acceptance of a form is due to the desire for the fruit to be accomplished through that form.
For the state of having a body at will does not result in true independence; for such "will" in men is itself governed by their past karma.
From Brahmā down to the Piśācas, all are capable of assuming a body or abandoning it at their own will; how then could they ever transcend karma?
They know the creation of a body by will to be like a magical illusion (indrajāla), because it does not transcend the mastery over the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Assuming his universal form, Viṣṇu was encountered by the great seer Dadhīca while the latter was fighting, having himself assumed that very same form.
Even for Śiva, the Supreme Self who is superior to all, his similarity to other selves appears to us because he possesses a body.
They declare Śiva, the supreme cause, to be the benefactor of all; yet how can he, who is the benefactor of all, exclude the gods?
The Lord repeatedly severed the fifth head of Brahmā, who, out of the obstinacy of his evil intellect, was reviling Śiva while calling him "son."
Even Viṣṇu, in his form as Nṛsiṃha, was suddenly attacked by one in the shape of a Śarabha; having stepped upon him with its two feet, it pierced his heart with its sharp claws.
Among the celestial women and the gods, on account of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, there was indeed no one who was not punished by the heroic Vīrabhadra.
And in a single moment, the three cities, along with the women, the Daityas, and the children, were turned into fuel for the fire of his eye by the Lord.
Kāma himself, the cause of delight for all creatures and the lord of pleasure, was offered as a sacrifice into the fire of their eyes even as the gods cried out in protest.
Seeing some cows in the sky streaming a flood of milk over his head, the Lord looked upon them with wrath and reduced them to ashes at that very moment.
The Asura Jalandhara was pierced by him when he turned the waters into a discus with his foot; he who, bound by Ananta, hurled Viṣṇu a hundred yojanas away.
Aiming at him alone, he struck him with his very spear; having obtained that discus through ascetic penance, Hari, ever possessed of valor, [prevailed].
The chest of Andhaka, whose heart was merciless and who sought to slay the host of the gods' enemies, was scorched by the trident as if by fire.
Having created Kālāṅganā from his throat, he also brought about the downfall of Dāraka; and having produced Kauśikī from the sheath of Gaurī’s skin, he [acted].
Śumbha, along with Niśumbha, was brought to death in battle; and I have heard this great narrative concerning Skanda from the Skanda Purāṇa.
Requested by Brahmā for the sake of slaying the lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, the enemy of Indra, the God went to his inner apartments on Mount Mandara.
Having dwelt for a very long time with the Goddess due to excessive indulgence in pleasure, he then made her name "Rasā," as if she had been led down to the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
And deceiving the Goddess, he did not discharge his own seed—which was exceedingly difficult to bear—into her, but instead discharged it into the fire like purified oblation or nectar.
Having cast it even into the Gaṅgā and other waters by means of fire, he should slowly collect those portions from here and there bit by bit.
By Svāhā, who had assumed the form of the Kṛttikās and was sporting with her own husband, [the seed] was deposited somewhere in the Śara forest on Mount Meru as she turned into gold.
Having illuminated the ten directions with its radiance at the proper time, it gladdened all the mountains and rendered them golden like Mount Meru.
Then, after a long time, when that splendor had arisen in the prince—whose limbs were delicate and who was the very model for all princes—
And having seen that enchanting childhood form of his, the worlds, together with the gods and asuras, were both struck with wonder and utterly bewildered.
The god himself also arrived, longing to see his son; having placed him on his lap together with the goddess, he then gazed upon his smiling face.
With his inner self overwhelmed by affection, as if drinking yellow nectar, he did so even while the dispassionate ascetics looked on among the gods.
Having freely caused the young boy to dance upon his own chest, and having experienced his play, they honored one another.
Commanding the queen to give her breast-milk, which was like nectar, and instructing her, saying, "Your incarnation is for the welfare of the worlds," he caused her to drink it.
Neither the god himself nor the goddess attained satisfaction; then, out of fear of the demon Tāraka, Śakra entered into an alliance with him.
Having performed the consecration for the generalship of the gods, the Lord, the enemy of Tripura, placed his son in the center.

Then Skanda himself, having vanished from sight, [confronted] him who was protected by Indra and the other gods, using that spear capable of piercing Krauñca and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction in battle.
Even the head of Tāraka was severed out of fear of Śakra; then the gods, headed by Hari and Dhātṛ, offered special praise.
Likewise, Rāvaṇa himself, the lord of the Rākṣasas, proud of his strength, lifted Mount Kailāsa with his own long arms as if it were his own.
Then, unable to endure that offense, the trident-bearing God of gods, having crushed him, caused him to sink into the earth by the movement of his big toe.
On account of a certain matter concerning his dependent, the young boy, whose life had reached its end, the Lord arrived in haste and sent Death away to the edge of his feet.
