Failing to recognize his own vehicle, the king of bulls, the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala) was brought with his throat seized; consequently, the world became a single expanse of water.
By means of those various modes of conduct, beautiful with bliss and renowned throughout the world, this universe has been repeatedly set in motion through the spontaneous movement of its limbs.
If Śiva, being eternally peaceful, were to bestow grace upon all, he would surely fulfill all [their desires]; how then could one who is so capable grant liberation?
Even the diversity of beginningless karma is not the determining factor here; for even karma must indeed be brought about by the Lord.
What is the use of speaking much more on this matter? O Māruta, explain how atheism, which is the cause of [this state], may be swiftly dispelled.
Vāyu said: "O Brahmins, it is appropriate that you have entertained doubt when urged by reasons; for the desire to know does not establish atheism in those of virtuous intellect."
I shall here state the authoritative means that dispels the delusion of the virtuous; for the wicked, however, there is only the opposite state, except through the grace of the Lord.
It has been rightly determined that for Śiva, who is perfectly complete, there is nothing whatsoever to be done except for the supreme grace [bestowed upon others].
Intrinsic nature alone is sufficient for the act of benefiting others; otherwise, that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot benefit anything at all.

Furthermore, the entire world, consisting of bound souls (paśu) and their fetters (pāśa), is to be graced; however, the application of the Lord’s (pati) command is for the sake of bestowing grace upon that supreme [world].
A master who issues commands always favors everything; how then could Śiva, who accepts wealth for that purpose, be dependent on others?
There is indeed no favor that is independent of one who is to be favored; therefore, the meaning of the word "sovereignty" (svātantrya) is characterized by independence.

Furthermore, this dependent nature (paratantra) is held to be that which is to be favored; for without such favoring, it cannot be associated with either worldly enjoyment (bhukti) or liberation (mukti).
Even those who possess embodied forms are to be graced by [Śiva] through the removal of ignorance; for there is nothing here that exists apart from Śambhu’s presiding over ignorance.
That Śiva, whose nature is form, who is partless even though perceived by us as having parts, is metaphorically designated as the "Śaiva-mūrti" (the Form of Śiva).
For he is not the partless Śiva, the supreme cause, directly perceived; he is not characterized by any manifest form or experience whatsoever.

The mere fact of being accessible through valid cognition establishes its nature; it does not, however, constitute the cognition of indifference (*upekṣābuddhi*) here without a further defining characteristic.
Indeed, she is a certain manifest form whose essence is the comparison with the Self; she is the very form of Śiva, while the supreme [Śiva] is characterized by that form as his self.
Just as fire is not perceived when it has not yet ascended into wood, so too is the established principle that Śiva is not perceived when he has not yet ascended into the form of the embodied image.
Just as when it is said, "Bring fire," fire cannot be brought by itself apart from a burning piece of wood, so too Śiva is to be worshipped through his embodied form.
For this very reason, in worship and other rites, one should conceive of the image as the Self; for what is performed toward the image-as-Self is performed directly toward Śiva himself.

That same function [of worship] applies even to the *liṅga* and other forms, and especially to the image (*arcā*); for Śiva is worshipped by us through identification with the essence of each respective form.
Just as that very self of form is favored by the Supreme Lord, so too are we, the bound souls (paśus), favored by Śiva who is established within the self of form.
For the very sake of favoring the worlds, all [deities] beginning with Sadāśiva, though they are the very self of the [five] forms, have been presided over by Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
For the enjoyment and especially for the liberation of the selves themselves, there is the lineage of Śiva within the embodied selves whose natures consist of both reality and unreality.
Experience is considered to consist of the ripening of karma and to be of the nature of pleasure and pain; since Śiva possesses no karma, of what nature could his experience be?
Śiva bestows grace upon all; he does not withhold anything from anyone, for those defects which belong to those who withhold grace cannot possibly exist in Śiva.
Furthermore, whatever punishments have been demonstrated for Brahmā and the others, those too were enacted by the form of Śrīkaṇṭha solely for the benefit of the world.
The sovereignty over the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) belongs to Śrīkaṇṭha; of this there is no doubt. Śiva presides over the form known as Śrīkaṇṭha, which sports [in the world].
The gods and others, who were indeed possessed of faults, were subdued as previously described; consequently, they too became free from sin, and the subjects likewise became free from affliction.
Even punishment is not loathsome to the wise in its true nature; for this very reason, the infliction of punishment upon those deserving of it is praised by kings.
If he who has achieved mastery over the entire range of effects as their Lord were not to exercise lordship, how could he be the Lord of the world?

The will of the Lord constitutes His authorship; the supreme function of the Ordainer is the issuing of commands. This command is authoritative: "One must do this," and "One must not do that. Such is the teaching.
Following that teaching is the characteristic of saintliness; for one whose concentration is perverted, all of that is not seen.

That which is good should be well protected, while that which is evil must be turned back; for even through conciliation and other means, it may turn back, since punishment is indeed the final instrument of success.
This instruction, ending with the administration of punishment, is characterized by its aim for welfare; therefore, that which is contrary to it is declared to be harmful.
For those who are always established in what is beneficial, he is the very manifestation of the Lord; how could he be censured by the virtuous, since he is the restrainer of the wicked?
In this world, those who act improperly are censured for their lack of discernment; that which causes distress to the world is declared to be improper.
Every form of restraint in the world is not preceded by hatred; for a father does not hate his son when he restrains him in order to instruct him.
Even one who restrains those who ought to be restrained out of a sense of neutrality does so by means of the path; for even in him, some degree of cruelty necessarily persists.
Otherwise, he does not harm others even when they are at fault; yet this person also harms others while practicing neutrality out of ignorance.
Therefore, some insist that "one who is merciless while committing violence, which is essentially suffering [for the victim]," while others say there is no such restriction.
For a physician who knows the cause of the disease, there is not even the slightest cruelty when he inflicts harm upon the patient; rather, it is compassion alone that motivates him in this matter.

Even compassion is not for the sake of virtue when directed toward violent adversaries; for one who feels compassion for such as these is, through delusion, merely a compassionate person whose cruelty is concealed by that very compassion.

In this world, even equanimity toward those who are hostile yet capable of causing harm is a fault; for if one remains indifferent when capable of acting, that which is to be protected will immediately perish.
He who, seeing one already within the mouth of a serpent, neglects that which must be protected, is likewise merciless, for he imagines faults where there are only mere appearances.
Therefore, it is not accepted that compassion is in every way a virtue; rather, it is accepted that one should desire only what has been attained, while everything else is considered undesirable.
In reality, defects such as passion and the like certainly exist even within the individual selves; nevertheless, these belong only to them and not to Śiva in any way whatsoever.
Indeed, copper that has been cast into fire becomes black; yet, because of its contact with copper, that fire does not become defiled.
Fire does not depend upon contact with impurity to become impure; likewise, from contact with fire, even impurity becomes pure.
Thus, through contact with the object of purification, Śiva would not become impure; rather, it is precisely this object of purification that becomes pure through contact with Śiva.
When fire has entered iron, the burning belongs to the fire alone and not to the iron; likewise, sovereignty over embodied beings belongs to the Lord alone and not to individual souls.
For it is not the wood that burns upward; it is fire alone that burns. The state of being charcoal belongs to the wood, not to the fire; let this same principle be applied here as well.
For this very reason, even in wood, stone, and clay within this world, the state of being Śiva is metaphorically attributed solely by virtue of the descent of Śiva's power.
Virtues such as loving-kindness and the rest are secondary; therefore, they function differently. For those who are colored by these virtues, they lead both to defects and to qualities.
For Śiva, who encompasses all that is both figurative and non-figurative, the functions of his qualities lead neither to merit nor to defect.
The wise do not say that the meaning of the word "favor" (anugraha) is secondary; rather, it is the liberation from saṃsāra, consisting of the command of Śiva, which is beneficial.
To carry out his command is beneficial; that which is beneficial is a favor. We shall employ everyone in what is beneficial, acting as the benefactor of all.
Furthermore, they call that which is the meaning of the word "assistance" (upakāra) "favor" (anugraha); because it also consists of benefit, Śiva is the benefactor of all.

But when everything consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious is always engaged in what is beneficial, it does not obtain that benefit which is equivalent to [the benefit derived from] an essential connection with its own nature.
Just as the sun causes the lotuses to bloom with its rays, yet they do not all bloom at once, owing to their respective natures.
For even the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things is the cause of a future object; indeed, an intrinsic nature cannot bring about an object that is perishing among its agents.
Just as contact with fire melts gold and not charcoal, so too does one release only those whose impurities have been ripened, and not those who are already devoted to Śiva.
If a thing were not to exist in the manner that it is fit to exist by its own nature, then the agent would be independent and eternal even without cultivation.
Just as the Auspicious One (Śiva) is naturally pure and the benefactor of all, so too are the selves designated as individual souls (jīvas) naturally impure.
Otherwise, how could these beings transmigrate according to fixed rules, while Śiva does not? For the wise declare that transmigration consists of his connection with karma and māyā.
This consequence belongs to this very [individual soul] alone, and not to Śiva; it possesses a cause. That cause is the innate impurity (mala) of the selves themselves, not adventitious.
If anything were adventitious, it would have to be produced by some cause; yet that very cause is one, owing to its non-variegated nature.
Although the state of selfhood is equal [for all], some are bound while others are liberated; furthermore, among those who are bound, only some possess the authority for dissolution and enjoyment.

They partake in inequalities of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, being ranked as superior or inferior; some attain the nature of the [divine] forms, while others remain within the sphere of proximity.
Some Śivas reside at the summits of the paths within the embodied selves; the Maheśvaras are in the middle, while the Rudras reside in the lower station.
And even when Māyā is near, due to another cause, there is a triad; therein, the Self (Ātman) is situated below and the Inner Self (Antarātman) is in the middle.
Beyond that are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, known as the Supreme Self; some of the Vasus also abide in the state of the Supreme Self.

Some [Śaivas] are in the state of the inner self (antarātman), some likewise in the state of the self (ātman); then there are the Śaivas in the state beyond peace (śāntyatīta), and in the peaceful state of Maheśvara.

Just as those who are fierce belong to the Vidyā-tattva, and the Vaiṣṇavas to the Pratiṣṭhā-tattva, so too do the Ātman-s belong to the Nivṛtti-tattva; Brahmā and those born from the limbs of Brahmā likewise [belong there].
The eight classes of divine beings are the foremost; the human class is middling; and the five classes beginning with birds are the lowest—these constitute the fourteen types of birth.

The state of being higher or lower is also to be known as a stain of the transmigrating soul; just as there is no such state for one who is liberated, there is first [the state of] rawness and afterwards [the state of] ripeness.
Even a small [taint], whether raw or matured, becomes a cause for saṃsāra; among men, however, it leads progressively to inferiority when raw, but to superiority when matured.

The animal-selves (paśvātman) are divided into three types according to their impurities (mala), being respectively one, two, or three-fold impure. Among these, those with a single impurity are considered the highest, while those with two impurities are considered intermediate.
The three impurities (mala) are to be known as the lowest, established in ascending order; those with two impurities and those with one impurity preside over the three impurities respectively.
Thus, this conditioned differentiation of the universe is purely imagined; Śiva alone presides over all things, whether they possess one, two, or three impurities.
Just as this world, though its nature is inauspicious, is presided over by Śiva, so too the universe, though not of the nature of Rudras, is presided over by the Rudras.

For the great earth extends as far as the Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), presided over by the hundred Rudras and others; while the intermediate space (antarikṣa) extends up to Māyā, presided over in succession by Amareśa and the rest.
The sky, extending down to the size of a thumb, is completely covered on all sides by the lords of the worlds, beginning with Vāyu and ending with Mahāmāyā.

They are presided over by those who dwell within the intermediate paths and are not dependent on extremes; for they are truly the inhabitants of heaven as well as the dwellers of the intermediate space.
Thus the gods were praised by those devoted to the divine with the word "Earth" (Pṛthivī); likewise, they were praised separately with each of these three types of impurities—whether raw or cooked.
The disease of saṃsāra arises for men because it serves as its primary cause; the medicine for this disease is knowledge alone, and nothing else.
Śambhu, Śiva, the supreme cause, is the commander of physicians; this Śiva is capable of liberating the bound souls even without [inflicting] suffering.
There is no need for deliberation here as to how it produces suffering; for it is certain that the entire cycle of existence is nothing but suffering.
How could suffering become non-suffering? For intrinsic nature is non-erroneous; indeed, a sick person does not become healthy merely through a physician or medicine.

Just as a physician should relieve one afflicted by disease from that illness through medicines and bring them to comfort, so too [should one deliver] these animals, who are impure by nature and suffering by nature.
Through the application of the medicine of his own ignorance, Śiva liberates one from suffering; yet Śiva is not the cause of the disease, for he is the cause of transmigratory existence itself.
Even this disparity does not constitute a fault for him; for if suffering were established by its own inherent nature, how could Śiva be its cause?
The innate impurity of persons indeed causes them to transmigrate; that which is the cause of transmigration is the insentient impurity consisting of Māyā and the rest.
That [activity] would not proceed by itself without the proximity of Śiva, just as a magnet is effective only through its proximity [to iron].
Just as that [shadow] follows moving iron, so too does Śiva follow him; O wise ones, his presence cannot be turned away, for it is eternal and without cause.
Therefore, Śiva is eternally the unperceived presiding controller of the world; nothing whatsoever exists here that functions without Śiva.
All this is impelled by Him, yet He is not deluded; His power, consisting of His sovereign command, is the controller facing every direction.
By her this [universe] is perpetually pervaded, yet he is not defiled; all that is not first-born is subject to his rule, for he is the Lord.
Because he is the Lord, his command is authoritative; nevertheless, he does not incur fault. But that evil-minded one who, out of delusion, thinks otherwise shall perish.
Nevertheless, he is not at fault because of the very majesty of his power; meanwhile, an unembodied voice was heard from the sky.
"Truth, Om, the Immortal, the Gentle"—thus it was clearly manifested. Thereupon, all were exceedingly joyful, with every doubt completely destroyed.
The sages, filled with wonder, paid homage to the Lord Pavana; for Pavana had likewise rendered the sages free from all doubt.
Thinking, "These do not possess established knowledge," he spoke thus. Vāyu said: Knowledge is held to be of two kinds: indirect and direct.
They say that which is indirect is unstable, whereas that which is direct is very stable; that which is to be understood through the instruction of logical reasons is declared to be indirect.
Furthermore, direct realization will arise from the most excellent performance [of practice]; having reached the firm conviction that there is no liberation apart from direct realization.
Exert yourselves with vigilance for the sake of accomplishing the highest practice.
The sages said: O Māruta, you ought to tell us today what that supreme practice is by which liberation is perceived, as well as its means of accomplishment.

Vāyu said: "The supreme dharma is indeed that of Śiva, which is designated as the most excellent practice; for therein Śiva, who directly bestows liberation, is perceived through immediate realization."
That [discipline] should be known as fivefold, according to its five successive stages, consisting of the unsurpassed acts, austerities, recitations, meditations, and knowledge.
By those very means, including the higher ones, the supreme Dharma is established; it is that wherein both indirect and direct knowledge bestow liberation.
For both the supreme and the non-supreme dharmas are indeed enjoined by the Śruti; regarding the meaning denoted by the word "dharma," for us the Śruti alone is the authoritative means of knowledge.
The supreme Dharma, which is the ultimate limit of Yoga, resides at the crest of the Vedas; likewise, the subordinate Dharma arises from the mouth of the lower scriptures.
That dharma which is considered supreme belongs to one whose self is not that of a beast; other than that, however, is the common dharma, which pertains to the authority of all.
And this supreme Dharma is the means for accomplishing the highest goal; it has been fully augmented by the treatises on Dharma and other sciences, along with all its constituent parts.
That which is the supreme Śaiva Dharma, designated as the most excellent practice, has been somewhat augmented by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
It is fully endowed with the Śaiva Āgamas, including their limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas) in detail, and is perfectly augmented by the qualifications for those purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Indeed, the Śaiva Āgama is of two kinds: the Śrauta and the Aśrauta. The Śrauta is refined and consists of the essence of the Vedas (Śruti), while the other is considered independent.
The independent [scripture] was previously tenfold, and then eighteenfold; established under the names beginning with *Kāmika*, it is designated as the Siddhānta.
That which consists of the essence of the Vedas, with an extent of one hundred crores [of verses], wherein the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are expounded.
In the revolutions of the ages, it is set in motion by Śiva himself, who has descended in various places in the form of a master of yoga (yogācārya).
To summarize, its expounders were four supreme sages: Ruru, Dadhīca, Agastya, and the highly illustrious Upamanyu.
And those Pāśupatas should be known as the originators of the Saṃhitās; their lineages of teachers number in the hundreds and thousands.
Therein, the supreme Dharma has been described as being fourfold, consisting of conduct and so forth; among these, the Pāśupata Yoga will firmly bring Śiva into direct perception.
Therefore, the Pāśupata yoga is considered the most excellent practice; even therein, that which is joined with the means is declared by Brahmā.
The eightfold yoga consisting of names was devised by Śiva; through that yoga, the wisdom of Śiva arises instantaneously.
Through wisdom, one swiftly attains supreme and stable knowledge; Śiva is pleased with him whose knowledge is firmly established.
The supreme yoga arises from grace, which brings about the direct perception of Śiva; through the direct perception of Śiva, one is liberated from the cause of saṃsāra.
From that, one becomes liberated from saṃsāra; being liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva. This is the means proclaimed by Brahmā, and it is described separately as follows.
Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, the Physician of Saṃsāra, the Omniscient One, and the Supreme Self—these are his primary names.
This primary octad of names expresses Śiva; the first five should be known as following the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā.
The designations of Sadāśiva and the others arise from the assumption of five limiting adjuncts; however, upon the cessation of those adjuncts, they cease accordingly.

For that [reality] alone is eternal, while those who possess the words (the individual souls) are known to be impermanent; since those who possess the words are liberated upon the dissolution of the words.
It is said that through another transformation, there is again the attainment of that state; this would be the designation of another self, namely the first pentad of names.
But as for the other triad of names, because of their connection with appropriation and so forth, and because they express three kinds of limiting adjuncts, Śiva alone persists [through them].
Because it is by its very nature free from the prior non-existence of the attachment to beginningless impurities, this Self is called Śiva, as it is absolutely pure.
Alternatively, the Lord, who is the sole treasure of all auspicious qualities, is called Śiva by the virtuous who speak according to the true meaning of the principle of Śiva.
Indeed, among the twenty-three principles, Prakṛti is considered supreme; they say that the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, is higher than Prakṛti.

That which they call the first sound at the beginning of the Veda, by virtue of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, and which is established in the Vedānta because its true nature is to be known solely through the Veda; [that is Brahman].
For that [Prakṛti] which is dissolved in its own nature, he who is beyond it is Maheśvara; for both Prakṛti and Puruṣa have their activity dependent upon him.

Alternatively, this imperishable reality consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) is that which is to be attained; one should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā.
The agitator of Māyā, Ananta, through his connection with Maheśvara, is proclaimed as the Self of Time (Kālātman), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and so forth, both gross and subtle.
The Lord causes us to flee from that which is suffering or the cause of suffering; thus Śiva, the supreme cause, is called Rudra by the wise.
Pervading everything from the principles (tattvas) down to the gross elements (bhūtas) within bodies and so forth, Śiva dwells there unwearied; therefore, he is Rudra here and there.
Śiva is the father even of those who are the fathers of the world, existing in the form of the [eight] Mūrtis; by virtue of being the father of all, he is proclaimed as the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).

Just as a physician who knows the cause of a disease brings it to an end through skillful means and medicines, so too [the Buddha] does so by means of the stages, enjoyments, and authoritative powers.
He is the eternal Lord of cyclic existence who brings about its cessation along with its very root; he is called the Physician of Saṃsāra by those who know the meaning of all principles.

For the sake of accomplishing the knowledge of the ten objects, even though these sense organs exist, [one perceives] all entities—whether gross or subtle—that occur in the three periods of time, without exception.
The individual souls (aṇus), being veiled by impurity, do not know at all through mere illusion, even though all the causes for the knowledge of all objects exist, albeit in an unreal manner.
Sadāśiva knows each and every object exactly as it exists, without any effort; therefore, he is called the Omniscient One.
Because he is eternally endowed with these supreme qualities as the self of all, and because he is devoid of any other self distinct from himself, Śiva is himself the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Having obtained these eight names through the grace of the teacher, one [severs] the knot of the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, by means of the five names beginning with Śiva.
Having cut and purified each according to its own sequence and quality, [the result is obtained] by means of those very multipliers, whether with subtractions or even without obstructions.

Having severed [the path] through the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā—[a path] shaped like a wheel of eight spokes—one leads one's own self through the *suṣumṇā*.

Having led the moon situated at the end of the twelve [fingers] upward into the energy of Śiva, one should subsequently withdraw the mouth [of the breath] through dissolution according to the prescribed refinement.
When the body has been sprinkled again with the rain of nectar from the Śakti, one should descend one's own self into the heart, assuming a form consisting of nectar.
Beyond the moon situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], he beheld Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who is seated upon a white lotus and is affectionate toward his devotees.
The Lord Ardhanārīśvara, stainless and sweet in form, resembling pure crystal, gracious and cool in radiance.
Having meditated upon the Lord in his mind, a person with a composed heart should then worship Him with the flowers of devotion using the eight names of Śiva.
At the conclusion of the worship, however, the person, having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and having properly composed the mind, should mutter the eight names of Śiva.
Having offered eight oblations at the navel, followed by the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the salutation, one should perform the final worship by offering eight flowers.
One should offer oneself by means of a handful of water; having done this, after a long time, one attains the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge.
He obtains its foundation as well as supreme conduct; and having attained the highest yoga, he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
The sages said: "O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the supreme Pāśupata vow, by performing which even Brahmā and the others are all remembered as Pāśupatas."
Vāyu said: I shall declare to you a secret that cuts away all sins—the Pāśupata vow, which is revealed in the Atharvaśiras as Śrauta.
The time is the full moon day of Caitra; the place is a sanctuary of Śiva, or a field, grove, and so forth, or a forest that is praiseworthy and possesses auspicious characteristics.
There, on the thirteenth day, having bathed well and performed his daily rites, he should request permission from his own preceptor, worship him, and prostrate before him.
Having performed a special worship, he himself should wear white garments, a white sacred thread, and white garlands and unguents.
Seated upon a seat of darbha grass and holding a handful of darbha grass, he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), facing either the east or the north.
Having meditated upon the God and the Goddess, and having formed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) along the path of their petition—"I shall perform this vow"—one becomes initiated.
Either until the fall of the body, or for twelve years, or half of that, or half of that again, or for twelve months.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or even for one month; or for twelve days, or even for six days.
For half of that time, or for one day, beginning from the moment of the vow's formal resolve, one should duly establish the sacred fire for the purpose of performing the Virajā oblation.

Having offered oblations with clarified butter, fuel-sticks, and sacrificial porridge in due order, he should again fill that vessel to the brim while aiming for the purification of the constituent principles (tattvas).
One should offer oblations with those very materials, such as fuel-sticks and so forth, using the root mantra while recollecting: "May these principles within my body be purified."
The five elements, the five subtle essences, and the five organs of action are distinguished according to knowledge and action, through the fivefold division of action.

The seven constituents beginning with skin, the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa, mind, intellect, ego-consciousness, and the manifesting principle (ahaṃkhyāti), the gunas, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa).
Rāga, Vidyā, and Kala, as well as Niyati and Kāla; Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva.

They know the principles (tattvas) in their proper order as Śakti and Śivatattva; by offering oblations with mantras that are free from passion (virajas), this sacrificer shall become free from passion.
Having obtained the grace of Śiva, he indeed becomes possessed of knowledge; then, having taken cow dung, formed it into a ball, and consecrated it with mantras.

Having performed the ritual placement in the fire and sprinkled [the materials], one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) on that day; then, at dawn on the fourteenth day, having performed everything previously described.
On that day, one should spend the remainder of the time without food; likewise, having performed the rites at dawn on the festival day, one should conclude with the fire-oblations.
Having extinguished the Rudra-fire, one should carefully collect the ashes; thereafter, one may wear matted hair, be shaven-headed, or have a single tuft of hair.
Having bathed after becoming [so], if he should then be free from shame, he may be naked (digambara), or even clothed in saffron robes, or else dressed in garments of skin or bark.
He should wear a single garment or a bark dress, carry a staff, and wear a girdle; then, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water twice, he should [purify] his own body.
Having thoroughly mixed that ash produced from the Viraja fire with the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning with "Agniriti," in due order.
Having divided the limbs from the head down to the feet, one should touch them with those [ashes]; then, having likewise gathered them up in that same sequence with the ashes.
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with ashes using either the Praṇava or the Śiva-mantra; thereafter, one should fashion the Tripuṇḍra known as the Triyāyuṣa.
Having attained the state of Śiva, one should then practice the yoga of Śiva; one should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow at the three junctions of the day.

This bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśu). Having abandoned that state of being a bound soul and having performed the Pāśupata vow, [one attains the goal].
The eternal Mahādeva, whose form is the Liṅga, is worthy of worship; there is a golden eight-petaled lotus adorned with nine gems.
One should prepare a seat provided with a pericarp and filaments; according to one's means, or in their absence, it may be red or even white.
In its absence, however, there should be a lotus consisting solely of meditative visualization; having placed a small *liṅga* in the center of the pericarp of that lotus.
Having installed that liṅga according to the prescribed rite after it has been purified, one should worship the crystal [liṅga], complete with its pedestal, in due order and according to the rules.
One should mentally construct a seat and a form according to the five-faced mode, using vessels filled with the five products of the cow and other substances, prepared according to one's means.
One should bathe [the deity] with full jars produced from the eight auspicious substances (aṣṭāpada), using fragrant materials such as sandalwood and saffron, along with camphor.
Having smeared the liṅga with sacred ash (śivadhūlika) and adorned it with ornaments, [one should worship] with bilva leaves, lotuses, and red and white water-lilies.
With blue lotuses and other various fragrant flowers, with meritorious and praiseworthy leaves, and with variegated dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and so forth.
Having worshipped according to one's means through the procedure for the great worship (mahāpūjā), one should likewise offer incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya).
Having offered his wealth, he should perform auspicious deeds, as well as desirable and distinguished acts acquired through righteous means.
All substances should be given as gifts during that vow, especially those consisting of a thousand units each of *śrīpatra*, blue lotus, and red lotus.
O twice-born ones, there is another specific number for each, namely one hundred and eight; and even therein, one should especially not omit the bilva leaf.
They say that a single golden lotus is superior to a thousand ordinary lotuses; this same principle applies equally to blue lotuses and the like, as well as to bilva leaves.
Regarding flowers, there is no fixed rule; one should offer whatever is available. The eightfold *arghya* is excellent, especially when accompanied by incense and unguents.
Sandalwood is used in the Vāmadeva [quarter], yellow orpiment in the Puruṣa [quarter], and some say that ashes are the ointment in the Īśāna [quarter]. Such are the [prescriptions].

They do not consider [ordinary] incense [sufficient], because of the prescription for other types of incense: white agallochum (sitāguru) is used in the mouth called Aghora, while black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is used in the [other] mouths.
One should specifically offer incense in the Pauruṣa direction with guggulu, in the Savya and Saumya directions with saugaṃdhika, and in the Īśāna direction with uśīra and other substances.
Sugar, honey, camphor, and the ghee of a tawny cow, combined with sandalwood, agallochum wood, and other such substances, are declared to be the general [ingredients].
Then, a series of lamps enriched with camphor wicks and ghee should be offered; thereafter, water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for sipping (ācamana) should be given for each face.
In the first enclosure, Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha are to be worshipped in succession, followed by the limbs of Brahmā; thus they are honored in the first enclosure.

In the second enclosure, the Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas) who are universal monarchs (cakravartins) are to be worshipped; in the third enclosure, the eight forms beginning with Bhava (Bhavādyā aṣṭamūrtayaḥ) are to be worshipped.
Mahādeva and the others, as well as the eleven forms (mūrtis), are all the lords of the Gaṇas who are to be worshipped there in the fourth enclosure.
Outside the lotus, however, in the fifth enclosure, the lords of the ten directions should be worshipped in sequence, together with their weapons and their attendants.
All the hosts of luminaries are the mind-born sons of Brahmā; so too are all the goddesses, all the gods, and all the sky-dwellers.
Others dwelling in the netherworld, all the hosts of sages, indeed all the yogis, as well as the birds and the mothers.

The guardians of the fields along with their retinues, and all this world of moving and unmoving beings, should be worshipped out of love for Śiva, considering them to be the manifestations of Śambhu.

Then, having worshipped the Supreme Lord at the conclusion of the offering to the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should devotedly present the oblation (havis)—which consists of clarified butter, rice, and pulses—along with what is pleasing to the heart.
Having given mouth-fresheners and the like, along with betel-leaf and snacks, and having adorned her once more with various flowers and ornaments;

At the conclusion of the lustration (nīrājanā), one should complete the worship by distributing the remaining offerings; then, one should offer the drinking vessel along with its accessories and the bed.
One should offer a necklace resembling the moon and a bed worthy of a king—pleasing and excellent—in its entirety, according to what is appropriate.

Having performed [the rites], having caused them to be performed, and having offered worship, and having recited the hymn of praise and the dispelling [mantra], one should recite the five-syllabled vidyā.
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, one should offer oneself; thereafter, one should worship the Guru and the Brahmins in front of the Deity.
Having offered the *arghya* and eight flowers, he should dismiss the deity from the *liṅga*; likewise, having carefully restrained the fire of the hearth, he should also dismiss that fire.
And every day, a person should perform the aforementioned service; then, that lotus-liṅga, together with all its appurtenances, [should be worshipped].
One should offer it to one's own guru, or place it in a temple of Śiva, after having especially honored the gurus, the Brahmins, and those observing the vow.
If he is able, he should satisfy his devotees, the twice-born, and the poor and helpless; and he himself should be capable of fasting or subsisting on fruits and roots.
Or he may observe a vow of milk, subsist on alms, or likewise eat only once a day; he should always eat only at night, sleep upon the ground, and remain pure.
Sleeping on ashes or sleeping on grass, wearing rags or deerskins, he should constantly observe this vow of celibacy.
On Sunday, as well as on the day of Ārdrā, on the fifteenth day of both fortnights, and on the eighth and fourteenth days, one who is capable should even observe a fast.

One should avoid with every effort—through thought, deed, and speech—those who follow heretical paths, those who have fallen from their caste, women in their courses, those in a state of birth-impurity, and outcasts.

One should always be characterized by forgiveness, generosity, compassion, truthfulness, and non-violence; likewise, one should be contented, tranquil, and devoted to the recitation of mantras and meditation.
One should perform the ritual bath three times a day, or alternatively, the ash-bath; and one should perform the special worship with mind, speech, and voice.

What need is there for much speaking here? One who observes the vow must not perform anything inauspicious; however, if such an act is performed through negligence, one must then weigh its gravity or lightness.
One should perform the appropriate expiation through worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth; one should act in this manner until the completion of the vow, without negligence.
Free from all desires, a devotee should perform the gift of a cow, the rite of releasing a bull, and worship with abundant offerings for the sake of pleasing Śiva.
This general outline of this vow has been told in brief; now I shall proclaim the specific details for each month as they have been heard from tradition.
In Vaiśākha, one should know the vajra-liṅga; in Jyeṣṭha, the auspicious emerald; in Āṣāḍha, the pearl; and in Śrāvaṇa, that which is fashioned from sapphire.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should know that the supreme [liṅga] is made of ruby; in the month of Āśvina, one should indeed know the excellent liṅga to be of gomedaka stone.
On the full moon of Kārttika, one should worship a coral liṅga; in Mārgaśīrṣa, a lapis lazuli one; in Pauṣa, one made of topaz; and likewise in Māgha, one made of sapphire.
In the month of Phālguna, it should be made from moonstone; in Caitra, the reverse; or, if gems are unavailable in any month, it may be made of gold alone.
In the absence of gold, it may be made of silver, copper, stone, or clay; or, according to availability, even of lac or some other material.
Or else, at the conclusion of the vow, having performed his daily rites, he should fashion a linga composed of all kinds of fragrances according to his preference.
Having performed the special worship and offered the oblations as before, he should likewise honor the preceptor and especially those observing the vow.
Permitted by the preceptor as well, facing either east or north, seated on a mat of *darbha* grass with *darbha* grass in hand, and having restrained the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths;

Having recited the root mantra according to one's ability and meditated upon the three-eyed Lord accompanied by Ambā, he should seek permission as before and, with palms joined in reverence, offer salutations.
"O Blessed One, by your command I renounce this vow. Having said this, he should discard the darbha grass situated at the base of the liṅga toward the north.
Then one should discard the staff, matted hair, bark garment, and girdle; having again performed the ritual sipping of water according to rule, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra.
He who, having undertaken the ultimate initiation, performs this vow without distraction until the end of his body is indeed remembered as a *naiṣṭhika*.

He is to be known as one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī) and likewise as a Mahāpāśupata; he alone is the best among those who practice austerity, and he alone is the observer of the Great Vow (mahāvratī).

Among those seeking liberation, there is no one equal to him who has accomplished his task; that ascetic who has become a lifelong renunciant (naiṣṭhika) is called the supreme among the lifelong renunciants.
Whoever should perform this vow every day or for twelve days, he too would be equal to a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) due to his adherence to this intense vow.
Whoever, anointed with ghee, should observe this vow while being devoted to its practice—even for two, three, or even a single day—that person is truly a steadfast ascetic (naiṣṭhika).
He who, free from desire, performs this supreme vow thinking "this is my duty," and is constantly dedicated to Śiva with his whole being—there is no one anywhere equal to him.
A learned twice-born man covered in ashes is instantly liberated from the most terrible sins arising from great transgressions; of this there is no doubt.
That which is the supreme virility of Rudra-Agni is proclaimed to be ashes; therefore, at all times, one who is endowed with ashes is possessed of virility.
The defects of one devoted to ash are destroyed through contact with the fire of ash; one whose self is purified by the bath of ash is known as "devoted to ash."
A person whose entire body is smeared with ashes, who wears the radiant triple-tilaka of ashes, who bathes in ashes, is known as one who is established in ashes (bhasmaniṣṭha).
Spirits, ghosts, and demons, as well as diseases that are exceedingly difficult to endure, flee without a doubt from the mere presence of one who stands upon ashes.

It is called *bhāsita* because it shines; it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities; it is *bhūti* because it brings about prosperity, and it is *rakṣā* because it is the supreme protector.
What more need be said here regarding the cause of the greatness of the sacred ash? One who observes the vow and bathes with the ash is Maheśvara himself.
This ash of the Supreme Lord is the supreme weapon of the devotees of Śiva, by which the calamities that befell the elder brother of Dhaumya during his ascetic penance were warded off.
Therefore, having performed the Pāśupata vow with every effort and having acquired sacred ash like wealth, one should be devoted to the ritual bath of ashes.
The sages said: "Indeed, penance was performed by the child, the elder brother of Dhaumya, for the sake of milk; therefore, the ocean of milk was granted to him by the trident-bearing God."
How did that child obtain the status of an expounder of the Śiva scriptures? Or how, having realized the true nature of Śiva, did he become established in ascetic practice?
And how did I, having attained wisdom during the stage of practicing austerities, obtain the supreme potency of the fire of Rudra—the sacred ash that protects one's own self?
Vāyu said: "This is no ordinary child who has performed such penance; he is the son of the wise Vyāghrapāda, the best of sages."
Having attained perfection in another birth through some unknown cause, he has fortunately reached the state of a young sage, though fallen from his own station.
For him who was destined to attain the grace of Mahādeva through his good fortune, his asceticism became the gateway arising from his longing for milk.
Therefore, Śaṅkara himself bestowed upon him the eternal lordship over all the Gaṇas and the state of being Kumāra, along with the Ocean of Milk.
His acquisition of knowledge also comes solely through the grace of Śaṅkara; for they know that the supreme knowledge of Kaumāra is directly composed of power (śakti).
Indeed, his status as a proponent of the Śiva-śāstra was brought about by him; he was like Kumāra, the son of Nandin, who obtained the ocean of knowledge from the Sage.
The visible cause for his attainment of the knowledge of Śiva was the direct words of his own mother, born of grief because of the [lack of] milk.
Once, in his maternal uncle’s hermitage, he drank very little milk out of envy for his maternal cousin, who had been fully satiated with excellent milk.
Having seen his maternal uncle’s son standing there after drinking as much as he desired, Upamanyu, the son of Vyāghrapād, spoke with affection to his mother.
Upamanyu said: "O Mother, O Mother, O highly fortunate one, O ascetic woman! Give me some very sweet cow's milk; I shall drink it warm, not a little."
Vāyu said: Having heard those words of her son, his ascetic mother, the queen of Vyāghrapāda, was then overcome with grief.
Then, having fondled her son with great affection and embraced him respectfully, she lamented in sorrow, remembering her own destitution.
Remembering again and again, that boy Upamanyu, weeping, spoke to her once more: "Give me milk! Give me milk! O one of great splendor.
Having fully understood that obstinacy, the ascetic wife of the twice-born then devised an auspicious means for its pacification.
Then, having herself seen the seeds gathered by the practice of gleaning, she who spoke with the sweet voice of a young elephant stirred the ground meal of those seeds with water.
Then, with gentle words, she said to her son, "Come, come, my son! and embracing him, she, afflicted by grief, gave him artificial milk to drink.
Having drunk the artificial milk given by his mother, that boy, becoming extremely distressed, said to her, "This is not milk."
Then, filled with grief, she spoke after gazing at him and smelling his head; having wiped her son’s lotus-like eyes with both hands.
The Mother said: "Those rivers filled with jewels, which range through heaven and the netherworld, those devoid of fortune do not behold, nor do those who lack devotion to Śivā."
When Śiva is not pleased, they do not obtain kingdom, heaven, liberation, or food produced from milk—none of these dear things are theirs.
Everything arises from grace toward Bhava, and nothing else arises from grace toward other gods; those devoted to other gods wander about, afflicted by suffering.
"How can there be milk for us who dwell perpetually in the forest? Where is the means for obtaining milk, O child, and where are we, the forest-dwellers?"
"Due to my total lack of wealth and my misfortune, I, being devoid of luck, have given you this false milk, having merely stirred flour with water."
Having drunk a small amount of sweet boiled milk at your maternal uncle’s house, you drank it knowing it to be sweet, recollecting that which belongs to its same class.
"Having said, 'The milk has been given,' you make me weep in sorrow; O Śambhu, without your grace, your milk does not exist."
That which is offered with devotion at the lotus feet of Sāmba and his attendants is the cause of all prosperity.
Now we have not worshipped Mahādeva, the bestower of wealth, who grants the desired fruits according to the wishes of those who possess desires.
"Previously, we did not worship Śiva for the sake of wealth; therefore, we have become poor, and for that reason, there is no milk for you."
O son, whatever was given in a previous birth dedicated to Śiva, that alone is obtained, and not anything else, even if dedicated to the Lord Viṣṇu.
Vāyu said: Having heard these truthful words of his mother, which indicated her grief and other emotions, the boy, though young, felt remorse within and spoke this bold reply.
Upamanyu said: "Enough of this grief, O Mother; if Śaṅkara exists along with Ambā, abandon your sorrow, O illustrious lady, and all will turn out well."
Listen to my words now, O Mother: if Mahādeva exists anywhere, whether it takes a long time or not, I shall surely conquer the Ocean of Milk.
Vāyu said: Having heard these words of that high-minded boy, his mother, wise and well-pleased in mind, then replied.
The mother said: "O dear one, you have thought auspiciously, which increases my joy. Do not delay; you must indeed worship Sadāśiva along with Ambā."
Śiva alone exists as superior to all, the supreme cause; for the entire world is created by him, and Brahmā and the others are his servants.
Having attained sovereignty through his grace, we are the servants of that Lord; apart from him, we know no other, even Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
Abandoning all other gods, with action, mind, and speech, worship Him alone—Sāmba, together with His attendants—with a heart full of devotion.
This mantra, "Namaḥ Śivāya," is traditionally held to be the direct designator of that Śiva, the God of gods, the bestower of boons.
All the seven crores of great mantras, together with the Praṇava, are supreme; they dissolve back into that very [source] and emerge from it once again.
And those mantras are accompanied by specific permissions according to their respective jurisdictions; however, by the command of the Lord, this one mantra alone possesses universal jurisdiction.
Just as Śiva is always able to protect all beings, whether lowly or exalted, so too is this mantra always capable of protecting them.
Moreover, this mantra is more powerful than any other mantra; it is capable of providing all forms of protection, and no other is desired for this purpose.
Therefore, abandoning other mantras, become devoted to the five-syllabled mantra; when that has entered the interior of the tongue, nothing in this world is difficult to attain.
The Aghora-weapon is the unsurpassed means of protection for the followers of Śiva; considering that [the world] originates from it, be devoted to it and not otherwise.
This supreme sacred ash, perfected by the fire of Virajā and capable of warding off great calamities, has been obtained by me from your father himself.
And I have given you this mantra; receive it with my permission. By reciting it quickly, protection will be yours.
Vāyu said: Having been thus instructed by his mother and having uttered, "May it be auspicious," the sage then departed, placing her words upon his head.
Having bowed to her and spoken thus, he set about performing penance; and then his mother said to him, "May the gods grant you prosperity."
Permitted by her, he went to the Himavat mountain and, being composed, practiced difficult austerities there while subsisting on air alone.
Having constructed a temple with eight bricks and a linga made of clay, he invoked there the imperishable Mahādeva, together with Ambā and his attendants.
Having worshipped for a long time with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra alone, as well as with his sons and forest-grown flowers, he performed supreme austerity.
Then, [he saw] that boy Upamanyu, the best of the twice-born, performing penance alone, emaciated, with his mind entirely devoted to Śiva.
In former times, certain sage-ghouls (munipiśācaka) were cursed by Marīci; having harassed [the sages] with demonic dispositions, they created obstacles to their asceticism.
And although he was being tormented by them, he continued to perform his ascetic penance; somehow or other, he constantly cried out "Namas Śivāya" with a voice as resonant as that of a drum.
Upon merely hearing that sound, those sages who were obstructing his asceticism abandoned the boy and approached him.
O sages, by the ascetic power of that high-souled brahmin Upamanyu, the entire world, with its mobile and immobile beings, was set ablaze.
Vāyu said: Then, with their limbs ablaze, all those best of gods quickly went to Vaikuṇṭha; having prostrated before Hari, they told him everything.
Having heard their words at that time, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, reflected, "What is this? and understood its cause.
He went quickly to Mount Mandara out of a desire to see Maheśvara; having seen the God and bowed down, he spoke thus with his hands joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu said: "O Blessed One, there is a certain Brāhmaṇa known as Upamanyu; he has scorched everything for the sake of milk through his ascetic power—please restrain him."
Vāyu said: Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the god Maheśvara said, "I shall ward off the child; you, go to your own hermitage."
Having heard those words of Śambhu, Viṣṇu, the beloved of the gods, took leave of all those led by the immortals and departed for his own world.
In the meantime, the god Pinākin, the Supreme Lord, then set his mind upon going there, having assumed the form of Śakra.

Then Sadāśiva, having personally assumed the body of the king of the gods, went to the sage’s penance grove on his excellent white elephant, accompanied by the gods, asuras, siddhas, and great serpents.
Then that elephant, having fanned the Lord with a divine chowrie, held a white parasol over the Lord of the Gods together with Śacī with his left trunk.
The blessed Lord Sadāśiva, in the form of Śakra, shone resplendent with that parasol, like Mount Mandara with the orb of the moon.
Having thus assumed the very form of Śakra, the Supreme Lord went to Upamanyu’s hermitage in order to bestow his grace.
Having seen that Supreme Lord Śiva assuming the form of Śakra, the great and eminent sage himself bowed his head and spoke.
Upamanyu said: "O Lord of Gods, this hermitage of mine has been purified by you yourself, O Blessed One, O Best of Devas, since you, the Lord of the World, have arrived here."
Vāyu said: Having spoken thus, Hara, assuming the form of Śakra, beheld the twice-born one standing with his palms joined in reverence and spoke with a profound voice.
Śakra said: "I am pleased with you; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows, by virtue of this asceticism. O great sage, elder brother of Dhaumya, I shall grant you all that you desire."
Vāyu said: Thus addressed then by Śakra, that bull among sages, with palms joined in reverence, replied: "I shall ward off devotion to Śiva."
Having heard that, Hari said: "You do not know me, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, the scribe of the gods, who is saluted by all the deities."
"O brahmin-sage, become my devotee; worship me alone at all times. I shall grant you everything—may it be well with you—so abandon Rudra, who is devoid of qualities."
What business will you have even with Rudra, though he be devoid of qualities—he who was excluded from the ranks of the gods and has fallen into the state of a piśāca?
Vāyu said: Having heard that, the sage, reciting the five-syllabled mantra, perceiving it to be an obstacle to his dharma, spoke to him who had come to perform that [deed].
Upamanyu said: "All this has indeed been told by you, who were intent on censuring Bhava; yet, in the course of conversation, you have also described the quality-less nature of the Great-Souled God."
Indeed, you do not know Rudra, the Lord of the lords of all gods, the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
That which the exponents of Brahman call both existent and non-existent, manifest and unmanifest, eternal, one and many—that supreme boon I choose from him.
I choose that supreme boon from which those who know reality worship Him—Him who is free from the doctrine of causality and who bestows the goal of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
There is no reality higher than Śambhu, the cause of all causes, the pervasive Lord who is beyond the qualities and the creator of the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
What need is there for much speaking here? I have now inferred a great evil committed by me in a previous existence, since I have heard this censure of Bhava.
Having heard this censure of worldly existence, one should abandon it at that very moment; by swiftly slaying that [attachment], one goes to the world of Śiva.
"Let this desire of mine for milk be set aside for now, O lowest of gods; having slain you with the Śiva-weapon, I shall cast off this body."
Vāyu said: Having spoken thus, Upamanyu himself resolved to die; having abandoned even his desire for milk, he prepared to kill Śakra.
Then, taking up that terrible ash consecrated with the Aghora weapon-mantra and casting it toward Śakra, the sage let out a roar.
Remembering the pair of Śambhu’s feet, Upamanyu stood firm, maintaining the fire-element concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā) and intent on burning his own body.
When the brahmin had thus resolved, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, gently restrained that yogi from his concentration.
At the command of Nandīśvara, Nandi, the beloved of Śaṅkara, caught that Aghora weapon released by him as it was hurled into the midst [of the fray].
Assuming his own true form, the Supreme Lord revealed himself to Śibi, with the crescent moon serving as his crest-ornament.
A thousand oceans of milk, or even an ocean of nectar, as well as oceans of curd and so forth, and an ocean of clarified butter;
And that Lord showed the child an ocean of fruits, likewise an ocean of various kinds of food, and even a mountain of cakes.
Thus the god was seen together with the goddess upon the bull, surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas and divine weapons such as the trident.
In the heavens, kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell; the ten directions were covered by gods led by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra.
Then Upamanyu, overwhelmed by the waves of an ocean of bliss, fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, his mind bowed with devotion.
At that time, the Lord Bhava, smiling there, called out to him, "Come, come! and having smelled his head, granted him boons.
Śiva said: "Always eat all kinds of foods and delicacies as you desire with your kinsmen; be forever happy, liberated from suffering, and remain devoted to me."
O illustrious Upamanyu, this Pārvatī is indeed your mother; for today the Ocean of Milk has been given by me as my adopted son.
And there was an ocean of honey, as well as an ocean of curd-rice; an ocean of ghee-rice, and indeed an ocean of fruits and other offerings.
"Mountains of cakes and oceans of various foods and delicacies—these have indeed been given by me to you; accept them, O great sage."
Mahādeva is your father and Jagadambikā is indeed your mother; immortality and the eternal status of a leader of the Gaṇas have been granted to you by me.
Choose with great joy whatever supreme boons your heart desires; I am well-pleased and shall grant them—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Vāyu said: Having spoken thus, Mahādeva took him up with both hands, smelled him on the head, and presented him to the Goddess, saying, "This is your son."
And the Goddess, out of affection like that of Guha, placed her lotus-hand upon his head and bestowed upon him the imperishable rank of Kumāra.
The Ocean of Milk itself, assuming a form and holding sweet milk in its hand, approached and presented him with that milk in a solid, imperishable mass.
With a satisfied mind, he granted him mastery over yoga, eternal contentment, the imperishable knowledge of Brahman, and supreme prosperity.
Then Śambhu, his soul being pleased upon seeing the greatness of that sage's austerity, granted another divine boon to the muni Upamanyu.
He bestowed upon him the Pāśupata vow, knowledge, and the yoga of the vow according to their true essence, as well as supreme eloquence for teaching for a very long time.
Having obtained divine boons and perpetual youth from that Śiva and from that Śivā, he too became filled with joy.
Then, with a serene mind and having bowed deeply with palms joined in reverence, that brahmin requested a boon from Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Upamanyu said: Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! Grant me your supreme, divine, and unfailing devotion.
O Mahādeva, grant me faith always toward those connected to You; grant me Your supreme servitude, Your affection, and Your constant presence.
Having spoken thus, Upamanyu, the best of the twice-born, his soul serene, praised Mahādeva with a voice faltering with joy.
Upamanyu said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge; be gracious, O ocean of compassion, O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, forever!
Vāyu said: Thus addressed, Mahādeva, the bestower of boons upon all, with a gracious soul, replied to Upamanyu, the best of sages.
Śiva said: "O child Upamanyu, I am pleased; indeed, everything has been granted to you by me. You are firm in devotion, O brahmin-sage, for you have been tested by me."
May you become free from old age and death, devoid of suffering, illustrious, endowed with splendor, and possessed of divine knowledge.
O best of the twice-born, your kinsmen, family, and lineage shall always be inexhaustible, and your devotion to me shall be eternal.
O best of the twice-born, I shall always maintain my presence in this hermitage; you indeed shall dwell joyfully in my vicinity.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Hara, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, granted boons to Īśāna and vanished right there.
Upamanyu, with a tranquil soul, having obtained excellent boons from him, went to his mother’s abode and attained supreme happiness.
Oṃ! Homage to him who is the cause of the wandering of the entire wheel of saṃsāra, whose chest is marked with the saffron from the pair of slopes of Gaurī’s breasts.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Vāyu, who had obtained grace from the Blessed One through Upamanyu, rose from his observance when the sun reached the meridian.
And all those sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, having reached the firm conclusion that "this matter must be asked," [approached him].
Having performed their respective duties daily as before, they sat down upon seeing the Blessed One approaching.
Then, at the conclusion of his vow, the Blessed One, born from the sky, took his place upon a prepared, excellent seat in the midst of the assembly of sages.
Seated upon a comfortable throne and saluted by the world, Vāyu, having placed the glorious majesty of the Lord in his heart, spoke as follows.
I take refuge in that Mahādeva, the omniscient and unconquered, whose manifestation is this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Having heard these auspicious words, the sages, whose impurities were exhausted, spoke these supreme words, desiring to hear the detailed expansion of the divine manifestations.
The sages said: "The life-story of the high-souled Upamanyu has been told by your holiness—how, even through penance performed for the sake of milk, he obtained [his goal] from the Supreme Lord."
He was seen by Vāsudeva Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless; then, having performed the Pāśupata vow, he became the elder brother of Dhaumya.
We have already heard before that he attained supreme knowledge; how did Kṛṣṇa obtain that supreme Pāśupata knowledge?
Vāyu said: Although the eternal Vāsudeva had descended by his own will, he performed the purification of his body as if censuring the human condition.
For the sake of obtaining a son, that great sage had gone to perform austerities; his hermitage was seen by the sages, and there they indeed beheld the sage.
His entire body was white with ashes, his forehead was marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra), he was adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, and he was graced by a mass of matted locks (jaṭā).
He saw the tranquil Upamanyu of great luster, devoted to meditation on Śiva, surrounded by his disciples—the sages—just as the Veda is encompassed by its auxiliary sciences (śāstras).
Upon seeing him, Kṛṣṇa, his hair standing on end with joy, paid homage with great reverence, circumambulating him three times.
With his shoulders bowed and palms joined in reverence, he offered praise with great affection; indeed, by the mere glance of that wise sage Kṛṣṇa, [he was transformed].
All impurity born of illusion and that which is born of karma was destroyed; Kṛṣṇa’s impurity was consumed by penance, just as Upamanyu performed according to the prescribed rite.
Having smeared him with ashes in sequence with the mantras beginning with "Agnir ityādi," [he performs] the Pāśupata vow itself for twelve months.
Having performed this, the Sage bestowed upon him supreme knowledge; from that time forth, the sages of celebrated vows [regarded] that Kṛṣṇa.
All the divine Pāśupatas stood surrounding him; then, by the command of his preceptor, Kṛṣṇa, possessed of supreme power, [prepared to act].
For the sake of a son, she performed penance directed toward Śaṅkara along with Ambā; at the end of a year of that penance, the Supreme Lord was seen by her.
Endowed with supreme splendor, Śiva, together with Ambā and his attendants, appeared before Hara of auspicious form, who had manifested for the sake of granting a boon.
Having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, Kṛṣṇa offered a hymn of praise; he who was intent on the company of the divine hosts obtained Sāmba as his own son.
Indeed, Śiva, with a mind satisfied by ascetic penance, granted this to Viṣṇu; for it was from him that Mahādeva, along with Ambā, gave his own son.
Therefore, he gave the son of Jāmbavatī the name Sāmba by name. Thus has been related all this concerning Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable deeds.

The great seer obtained both the attainment of knowledge and the birth of a son from Śaṅkara; whoever should constantly recite this, hear it, or cause others to hear it likewise [shall obtain the same].
Having attained the knowledge of Viṣṇu, he rejoices together with Him alone.
The sages said: What is that Pāśupata knowledge? How is Śiva Paśupati? And why was Dhaumya’s elder brother questioned by Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless?
O Vāyu, whose form is Śaṅkara, explain all of this; for there is no other lord equal to you as a speaker within the three worlds.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of those great ṛṣis, Prabhajana, calling to mind Śiva, the Lord, began to speak.
Vāyu said: Formerly, on Mount Mandara, the supreme Pāśupata knowledge was directly spoken by the Great Lord, known as Śrīkaṇṭha, to the Goddess.
That very matter was asked by Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu, the source of the universe: namely, the state of being a beast for the gods and others, and the lordship of Śiva.
Just as it was taught to Kṛṣṇa by the sage Upamanyu, so shall I speak of it in brief; listen to that with an alert mind.
Then Viṣṇu, assuming a dark-complexioned form, approached Upanamyu as he sat, and having prostrated according to the prescribed rule, spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear the divine Pāśupata knowledge spoken by the Lord to the Goddess, as well as His entire manifestation of power in its totality.
How is the god Paśupati [defined], and what are those proclaimed as the paśus? By what fetters are they bound, and how are they liberated?
Thus urged by the high-souled one, the illustrious Upamanyu, having bowed to the God and the Goddess, spoke as if he were fully restored.
Upamanyu said: "From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, all who are subject to the power of saṃsāra are proclaimed as 'paśus' (bound souls) of the trident-bearing God of gods."

Because he protects them from falling [into bondage], Śiva, the Lord of Devas, is known as Paśupati; as their Lord (pati), he binds the bound souls (paśus) with the fetters (pāśas) such as impurity (mala) and māyā.
He alone, when properly worshipped with devotion, is the liberator of those [beings]. These are the twenty-four principles: Māyā, Karma, and the Guṇas.
Objects of the senses are called "nooses" that bind the individual soul; having bound the fettered beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, Maheśvara [exercises his sovereignty].
By these nooses, the divine Lord causes his own purpose to be accomplished; by the command of that Maheśvara, Prakṛti [effects] what is appropriate for Puruṣa.
That [unmanifest] produces the intellect; that intellect produces the ego; and the ego [produces] the eleven organs as well as the five subtle elements.
By the command of Śiva, the God of gods, the bestower of auspiciousness, even those subtle elements [were established] by his most exalted decree.
They cause all the great elements, without exception, to manifest in successive order, forming the connection with bodies for all embodied beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
By the command of Śiva, all the great elements (mahābhūtas) without exception are produced; the intellect (buddhi) indeed determines, and the ego (ahaṃkāra) conceives the sense of "I."
The mind (citta) wills, and the intellect (manas) also forms intentions; the ears and other senses likewise perceive their respective objects, such as sound and the rest.
By the divine power of his command, he indeed created only his own [sons] and no others; these were the organs of action, beginning with speech and the rest.
Just as they perform their respective functions by the command of Śiva and not anything else, so too are sound and the other objects perceived, and speech and the other faculties are set in motion.
For the most venerable command of Śambhu is indeed inviolable by all; it grants space for all beings without exception.
Space is all-pervasive solely by the command of the Supreme Lord; likewise, through the vital breaths and other such distinctions of names, it constitutes the world both internally and externally.
By the command of Śarva, the wind sustains everything; he carries the oblation for the gods and the ancestral offering for those who consume the offerings to the ancestors.
By the command of the Supreme Lord, fire performs the digestion of food and so forth; by His command, water performs the animation of all things and so forth.
By the command of the Lord of the Universe, Viśvambharā constantly supports the world; she protects the gods, slays the asuras, and guards the three worlds.
By his command, which cannot be transgressed by any of the gods, Varuṇa, the lord of the gods, eternally exercises sovereignty over the waters.
And just as he binds those deserving of punishment with nooses by his own command, so too does the lord of Yakṣas, the master of wealth, constantly bestow riches.
In accordance with merit, through the instruction of a person, it constantly brings about prosperity for all beings as well as knowledge for those of great intelligence.
And by the command of Śiva, Īśāna effects the suppression of the wicked; and by the injunction of Śiva, Śeṣa supports the earth upon his head.
That which they call the dark and fierce form of Hari, the bringer of the end—by the command of the Lord, the four-faced Brahmā creates everything from it.
Through his own various forms, he protects and, at the end, destroys; Viṣṇu sustains the universe by the command of the Destroyer of Time.
He creates and also trembles by means of his own three bodies; at the end, he withdraws the entire universe by the very command of that same Hara.
The Soul of the Universe, though divided threefold, creates and protects; Time performs everything, and Time withdraws all creatures.
Time protects the universe by the command of the Time of Time; sustaining the world with its three parts, it ordains heat and rain through its splendors.
By the command of the God of gods, that sun rains down from the sky; it nourishes the various kinds of medicinal herbs and also gladdens all living beings.
And by the command of the Moon-ornamented One (Śiva), the moon is drunk by the gods—the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts.
Sky-dwellers, sages, perfected beings, enjoyers, humans, wild animals, domestic beasts, birds, insects and the like, and even immobile things.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes; the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the scriptures, and the collections of mantras, sacrifices, and so forth.
The worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva, along with their presiding deities, as well as the innumerable cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and their surrounding enclosures.
The present, the past, and the future in their entirety; the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions; and the divisions of time, such as the *kalās* and so forth.
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world, all that is presided over by the power of Śaṅkara’s command.

By his power of command, the earth, the mountains, the clouds, and the oceans remain here; so too do the hosts of luminaries and the gods headed by Śakra; indeed, whatever exists, whether conscious or unconscious, remains stable for a long time through his will.
Upamanyu said: "O Kṛṣṇa, this is most wonderful regarding Śambhu, whose deeds are immeasurable. Listen to this account of how he was made to obey commands, which I heard from the mouth of Śruti."
It is said that in ancient times, the gods, including Indra, were disputing among themselves after defeating the asuras in battle, each exclaiming, "I am the victor! I am the victor!"
Then Maheśvara, assuming an excellent disguise among them, himself became like a Yakṣa, his limbs devoid of his own characteristic marks.
He said to those gods: "Taking a single blade of grass upon the ground, whoever is able to transform it—such a person shall be the conqueror of the Daityas."
Having heard the words of the yakṣa, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of Śacī, somewhat incensed, laughed and prepared to seize him as if he were a blade of grass.
It was not even possible to pick up that blade of grass with the mind; nevertheless, the Wielder of the Vajra fashioned the vajra so as to cut it.
That vajra, as if struck on all sides by his own vajra, was hit by him with a blade of grass and fell down with its point turned sideways.
Then other world-protectors of great strength, highly incensed, discharged their weapons by the thousands, aiming them at a blade of grass.
The great fire blazed forth and a fierce wind blew, like the swollen ocean when the time of universal dissolution has arrived.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, the effort undertaken by the gods with great exertion directed toward that blade of grass proved futile, indeed, due to the Yakṣa’s own power.
Then the Lord of the Gods, provoked to indignation, asked the Yakṣa, "Who are you? Thereupon, he vanished even as they were looking on.
In the meantime, the goddess Haimavatī, adorned with divine ornaments, appeared in the expanse of the sky, radiant and smiling with a pure smile.
Seeing her, the gods, led by Śakra, were overcome with wonder; bowing down to the yakṣa, they asked: "Who is this extraordinary yakṣa?"
The goddess said with a smile: "He is beyond your perception; by him this wheel called saṃsāra, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is caused to revolve."
By that the universe is first created, and by that it is withdrawn again; there can be no other controller of it, for everything is governed by that.
Having spoken thus, that Great Goddess vanished right there; and all the gods, filled with wonder, bowed to her and departed for heaven.

Upamanyu said: Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, to [the nature] of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self. This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded by His forms and essential selves. That Śiva, the immeasurable soul, presides over all this through His own manifestations; indeed, all this is remembered as such.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśāna, and Sadāśiva are to be known as his forms by which this entire universe is pervaded. Furthermore, there are five other bodies called by the name Brahma; there is nothing here that is not permeated by those bodies.

Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and likewise Sadyojāta—these are the five celebrated forms (mūrtis) of the God, which are the Brahmans. Among them, that first and most venerable form called Īśāna presides over the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is the direct enjoyer of primordial matter (prakṛti).

The form of the Lord known as Sthāṇu-Tatpuruṣa, which consists of the substratum of the qualities (guṇas) and is the unmanifest object of experience, presides over it. The form of the wielder of the Pināka bow known as Aghora, which is exceedingly worshipful, presides over the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), which is endowed with the eightfold limbs beginning with dharma.

Those who know the scriptures declare that the form of the great god, the Creator, called Vāmadeva, is the presiding deity of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra). The wise proclaim that the form of Śambhu of immeasurable splendor, called Sadyojāta, is the presiding deity of the mind (mānasa).

The wise know this sovereign power of the Lord—named Īśā—to be the mistress of the ear, speech, sound, and likewise of all-pervading space. All those expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas know this embodied form of the Lord, named Puruṣa, to be the mistress of the skin, the hand, touch, and the wind.

The wise declare that the presiding form called Aghora governs the eye, the feet, visible form, and likewise fire. They know that the form called Vāmadeva, devoted to those [elements], governs the tongue, the anus, taste, and likewise water.

The form of the Lord known as Sadyojāta is said to consist of the sense of smell, the organ of generation, fragrance, and the earth element. These five forms of the God should be diligently worshipped by men seeking spiritual welfare, for they are the sole cause of all auspicious things.
