The universe consists of the eightfold forms of that God of gods; the entire world remains pervading him, like clusters of gems upon a thread. [These forms are] Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Paśupati.
And Īśāna is Mahādeva, as well as the eight renowned forms.

Earth, water, fire, wind, space, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the sun, and the moon—these are presided over by Maheśa through his eight forms beginning with Śarva. The form of Śiva known as Śārvī, which is of the nature of the Earth, sustains the entire universe consisting of the moving and the non-moving; such is the certainty of the scripture.

The supreme self, whose nature is existence, is celebrated as having a form consisting of water, which brings life to the entire world. That auspicious, radiant form, both internal and external, pervading the universe, is established as the terrible Raudrī—the immutable form of Rudra that assumes a fearsome aspect.

That which causes vibration, bestows the nature of wind, sustains itself, and vibrates by its own power—this is called the form of the fierce Creator (Ugra) by the wise; it is known as Aumgrī. The form of Bhīma, known as Bhīmā, is of the nature of space, providing room for all, pervading everything, and the shatterer of the multitude of beings.

The presiding deity of all souls, dwelling in all fields, she is to be known as the form of Paśupati, the severer of the bonds of bound souls (paśu). Illuminating the entire world, she is called by the name of the Sun; this form of the Great Lord known as Īśāna spreads through the heavens.

The moon, the portion of nectar that nourishes the entire universe, is a form of Mahādeva known by the name Mahādeva. The Self (Ātman) is the eighth form of Śiva, the Supreme Soul; it pervades all other forms, and therefore the universe has Śiva as its essence.

Just as the branches of a tree flourish by watering its root, so too does the world flourish as the body of Śiva through his worship. They know that the propitiation of Śiva consists of granting fearlessness to all, bestowing favor upon all, and performing service for all.

Just as a father becomes delighted by the affection of his sons, grandsons, and others in this world, so too does Śaṅkara become delighted by the universal affection of all beings. If any embodied being whatsoever is subjected to oppression, it is undoubtedly inflicted upon the Eight-formed Lord himself; there is no doubt of this.
Worship Śiva with your whole being—he who stands presiding over the universe through his eightfold form, Rudra, the supreme cause.
Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, I have heard how this entire universe is pervaded by the forms of Śarva, the Supreme Lord of immeasurable splendor.
Now I desire to know the true nature of these two, the Supreme Lord and his Śakti, and how this world, consisting of the states of female and male, is presided over by them.
Upamanyu said: I shall describe in brief the glorious majesty and the true nature of Śiva and Śivā; to explain it in detail would be impossible even for Bhava himself.
Śakti is the Great Goddess herself, and Mahādeva is the possessor of Śakti; indeed, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is but a mere fragment of their divine manifestation.
Some entity is of the nature of the insentient, while some entity consists of consciousness; both are pure and impure, as well as supreme and non-supreme.
That wheel of consciousness which revolves, accompanied by the wheel of the insentient, is impure and inferior; the other, however, is supreme and auspicious.
Furthermore, both the transcendent and the immanent—this duality consisting of the conscious and the unconscious—is by its very nature the domain of sovereignty belonging to Śiva and Śivā.

The entire universe is indeed under the control of Śiva and Śivā, but Śiva and Śivā are not under the control of the universe; because this world is subject to their sovereignty, Śiva and Śivā are the Lords of the Universe (Viśveśvarau).
As is Śiva, so is the Goddess; as is the Goddess, so is Śiva. One should perceive no difference between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.
Just as this moon indeed does not shine without its moonlight, so too Śiva does not shine without his Śakti, even though he exists.
For this sun does not exist without its radiance, and that radiance, being entirely dependent upon him, exists all the more through the sun.
Thus, the relationship between power and the possessor of power exists through mutual dependence; there is no Śiva without Śakti, and no Śakti without Śiva.

That primordial, singular, supreme Śakti, consisting of consciousness and resting in Śiva, is that by which Śiva is eternally capable of bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon embodied beings.
She whom they call the one who shares the same essential nature as Śiva, the Supreme Self and Lord of all, by virtue of His various corresponding qualities.
The supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, possesses the quality of procreation; by the will of Śiva, she divides the universe in many ways and brings it forth.
That primordial nature is Māyā, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) and remembered as being threefold; it is by Śivayā that this entire world is pervaded and rendered subject to transformation.
In one way, in two ways, and likewise in a hundred thousand ways, the powers (śaktis) are indeed divided manifoldly according to conventional usage.
By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva); thereafter, at the beginning of creation, she vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed.
Then, by means of the power called Kriyā (Action), which arises from the Possessor of Power within that Power, as that [Power] was being stirred, Nāda first emerged.
From the Nāda emerged the Bindu; from the Bindu came the god Sadāśiva; from him Maheśvara was born, and from Maheśvara arose Śuddhavidyā.
She is indeed the sovereign power of speech, known as Vāgīśā, belonging to the Wielder of the Trident; she who manifests even as the Mātṛkā in the form of the phonemes.

Then, through infinite immersion, Māyā brought forth Time (kāla), Necessity (niyati), and Limited Agency (kalā); from Limited Agency, she brought forth Knowledge (vidyā), Attachment (rāga), and the Individual Soul (puruṣa).

From Māyā, moreover, the unmanifest (avyakta) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) came into being; and from that manifest [state] consisting of the three qualities, the three qualities became differentiated.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—by these the entire world is pervaded; from these qualities being agitated, the three forms known as the Lords of the Qualities (Guṇeśa) arise.
The principles beginning with Mahat arose in their proper sequence; from them, by the command of Śiva, innumerable cosmic eggs and individual bodies came into being.

Presided over by the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) such as Ananta and others who rule the wheel, the various manifestations of power (śakti) are proclaimed through the differentiation of internal bodies.
These forms, however, should be understood as manifold through the distinction between gross and subtle; that power of Rudra is Raudrī, while that of Viṣṇu is indeed considered Vaiṣṇavī.
The consort of Brahmā is called Brāhmāṇī, and that of Indra is called Aindrī; what is the use of saying more here, for she is celebrated as the entire universe itself?
Just as the body is pervaded by the inner self through its very power, so too this entire world of the moving and the stationary consists of power.
That which is called the supreme power (kalā) of the Supreme Self is thus this transcendent power (parā śakti), which follows the will of the Lord.
It is certain that [the Lord] creates the entire universe, both the stable and the moving, by means of his three inherent powers: knowledge, action, and the desire to act.
The omnipotent Lord, pervading the universe eternally, presides over it with a nature such as this: "Let this be thus; let this not be otherwise."
The power of will (icchā-śakti) of the Great Lord is eternal and the regulator of effects; the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), however, is its effect, as well as its instrument and its cause.

The causal purpose determines the object in its true nature through the form of the intellect; the power of action [realizes] the world according to what is desired and according to what has been determined.
Taking the form of volition (*saṃkalpa*), she brings about every effect in an instant, just as the emergence of the three powers occurs through her nature of generating power.
Impelled by the supreme power (śakti), she brings forth the entire universe; thus, through union with power, Śiva is called "the Possessor of Power" (śaktimān).
This world arises from Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti; it is Śākta and Śaiva. Just as a son is not born without a father and a mother, [so this world does not exist without them].

Likewise, without Bhava and Bhavānī, this world of moving and non-moving beings would not exist; for the universe originates from the female and the male, and its very essence consists of the female and the male.
The manifestation of both woman and man, presided over by woman and man, is declared to be Śiva as the Supreme Self, and she is celebrated as Śivā.
Śiva is declared to be Sadāśiva, and Śivā is Manonmanī; Śiva is to be known as Maheśvara, and Śivā is called Māyā.
The Supreme Lord is Puruṣa; the Supreme Goddess is Prakṛti. Rudra is Maheśvara himself, and Rudrāṇī is the beloved of Rudra.
Viṣṇu is the Lord of the Universe, and Lakṣmī is the beloved of the Lord of the Universe; when Brahmā is the Creator, Śiva is likewise, and Brahmāṇī is the beloved of Brahmā.
The Lord Bhāskara is Śambhu, and the goddess Prabhā is Śivā; Maheśvara is the enemy of Manmatha, and Śacī is the daughter of the King of Mountains.
Jātavedas is Mahādeva; Svāhā is she who shares half the body with Śarva. Yama is the three-eyed god; his beloved is Girikanyakā.
The lord Nirṛti is Īśa; Nairṛtī is the daughter of the mountain. Varuṇa is the lord Rudra; Vāruṇī is the daughter of the mountain-bearer.

The wind has the crescent moon as its crest; Śivā is the one who captivates the heart of Śiva; the Yakṣa is the one who took the head of Yajña; and Ṛddhi is the daughter of the lord of the snowy mountains.
The moon is the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; Rohiṇī is the beloved of Rudra. Īśāna is the supreme lord, and his Āryā is the supreme sovereign lady.
He who possesses infinite armlets is indeed infinite, with infinite and boundless beloveds; he is Kālāgnirudra, the enemy of Time, Kālī, and the beloved of the Ender of Time.
The one called Puruṣa was Manu Śambhu, and Śatarūpā was the beloved of Śiva; Dakṣa was Mahādeva himself, and Prasūti was the Supreme Goddess.
Ruci, Bhava, and Bhavānī are called Ākūti by the wise; Bhṛgu is the god who destroyed the eye of Bhaga, and Khyāti is the beloved of the Three-eyed One.
The Lord Rudra is Marīci, and Saṃbhūti is the beloved of Śarva; Gaṅgādhara is to be known as Aṅgiras, and Smṛti is said to be Umā herself.
Pulastya has the moon as his crest-jewel; Prīti is the beloved of the wielder of the Pināka bow. Pulaha is the destroyer of Tripura; his beloved is the beloved of Śiva.
Kratu is said to be the destroyer of sacrifices, and Saṃnati is the beloved of the Lord. Atri is the three-eyed god, and Anasūyā is remembered by the wise as Umā herself.
Kaśyapa is the god Kālahā; Maheśvarī is Devamātā; Vasiṣṭha is Manmathārāti; and Arundhatī is the goddess herself.
All men are Śaṅkara, and all women are Maheśvarī; therefore, all men and women are indeed the manifestations of those two alone.
The Lord Īśa is the subject, and the Supreme Goddess Parameśvarī is the object; everything audible is the form of Umā, and the hearer is the one whose excellent weapon is the trident.
The beloved of Śaṅkara holds within her all the categories of objects to be inquired about, while he who is the soul of the universe, adorned with the crescent moon, is the inquirer himself.
The beloved of the Speaker bears the form of the object to be seen; the Seer is the Lord of the Universe, the God whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon.
The Great Goddess is the source of all flavors, and Lord Śiva is the taster; Girijā is the source of all beloved things, and the poison-consumer is indeed the beloved.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī always assumes the state of the object of thought; He alone is the thinker, the Soul of the Universe, Mahādeva Maheśvara.
The beloved of worldly existence bears the form of the object to be known; the Blessed Lord himself, whose crest is the charming moon, is the knower.
The Lord Prāṇa, the sovereign master, is the Pinākin of all living beings; while Ambikā, in the form of water, is the sustenance of the vital breath of all.
The Goddess, beloved of the Destroyer of Tripura, assumes the state of the field (kṣetra), while the Blessed Lord, the slayer of Death, then assumes the state of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The day is the god who wields the trident as his weapon, and the night is the beloved of the trident-bearer; the sky is the god Śaṅkara, and the earth is the beloved of Śaṅkara.
The Blessed One is the ocean, the Lord is the shore, the Daughter of the Mountain King is the tree, and the beloved of the Lord of the Universe is the creeper.
The Lord, the Subduer of Tripura, assumes every masculine form, and the Goddess, who delights the gods, assumes every feminine form.
The beloved of all bears the entire web of words without exception, while the one whose crest is the charming moon bears the complete nature of their meanings.
Whatever power is proclaimed to belong to whatever object, that is the Goddess Viśveśvarī; whoever that [object] may be, he is Maheśvara.
Whatever is supreme, whatever is purifying, whatever is meritorious, and whatever is auspicious—all that, O highly fortunate ones, is the manifestation of the splendor of those two.
Just as the flame of a burning lamp illuminates a house, so does this radiance of those two, pervading it, illuminate the world.
The progressive gradation of universal renown extends from blades of grass up to the form of Śiva; this sequence of proximity between those two is the supreme Vedic revelation.
These two, who possess all aspects and bestow every excellence, are to be worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon at all times.
O Kṛṣṇa, this true nature of the two Supreme Lords has indeed been told by me to you today according to my wisdom, but not in its entirety.
How, then, can the true nature of the two Supreme Lords be described, which transcends the minds of even all the great ones?
It is internal to those who are single-minded and whose hearts are offered to the Lord; it is not ascended upon the intellect of others, yet for them it is ascended exactly as it is.

This manifestation that has been described as pertaining to Prakṛti is considered the lower; those who know the secret know another, higher manifestation, which is beyond Prakṛti and is the supreme secret.
From which speech, along with the mind and the senses, turns back—this is the supreme, non-material majesty of the Supreme Lord.
That alone is the supreme abode here; that alone is the supreme goal here; that alone is the supreme limit and the sovereign power of the Parameṣṭhin.
To attain that state, those who have conquered their breath and subdued their senses strive here, just as one would attempt to bolt the door of a prison cell so that it is free of any gaps.
Knowing that the divine power (vibhūti) of Śiva and Śivā is the life-restoring medicine for one bitten by the venomous serpent of saṃsāra, the wise man fears nothing whatsoever.
He who knows the higher and the lower manifestation truly, transcending the lower manifestation, attains the higher manifestation.
O Kṛṣṇa, this true nature of the two Supreme Souls has been told to you; even though it is a secret, I have revealed it because you are a worthy devotee of Bharga.
"One should never disclose the nature of the two Lords to those who are not disciples, nor to those who are not Śaivas, nor to those who lack devotion; such is the instruction of the Vedas."
Therefore, you should not speak this to those who are devoted to what is exceedingly evil; rather, speak it to those like you who are worthy, and not otherwise.
Whoever causes this manifestation of Śiva and Śivā to be bestowed upon those who are worthy shall be liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra and attain union with Śiva.
By chanting this, millions of great sins are destroyed; by practicing it three or four times, even more than that are annihilated.
Unwanted enemies perish and friends likewise flourish; Śiva’s knowledge increases, and the mind is directed toward truth.
If one has supreme devotion toward Śiva, who is accompanied by Ambā, his attendants, and his retinue, then whatever else is most desired, that too one obtains without a doubt.
If one who is pure within, devoted to Śiva, and full of confidence should recite [this], yet the fruit is obstructed by powerful past karmas;
One should practice this again and again; for such a person, nothing in this world is difficult to attain.

Upamanyu said: "This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is the body of the God of gods; yet, due to the weight of their bonds, the bound souls (paśus) do not recognize it as such."
O descendant of Yadu, those great sages who do not understand the supreme, non-conceptual state speak of that which is truly one as being manifold.
Some say that Mahādeva is the supreme reality, without beginning or end, who is both the form of the lower Brahman and the essence of the higher Brahman.
The lower Brahman is designated as consisting of the elements, the senses, the internal organ, primordial matter (pradhāna), and objects; the higher Brahman consists of pure consciousness.
It is called Brahman because of its vastness or because it causes growth; both of these are forms of Brahman, the sovereign Lord and Master.
Some declare that the Lord has both knowledge and ignorance as his essential nature; they say that knowledge is consciousness, while ignorance is unconsciousness.
The entire universe, consisting of both knowledge and ignorance, is indeed the very form of the all-pervading Guru of the universe; of this there is no doubt, since the universe is under his control.
They know the supreme form of Śiva to be both delusion (bhrānti) and supreme knowledge (vidyā). Delusion is said to be the incorrect cognition of objects in various ways.
The direct perception of the form of reality as it is is proclaimed as *vidyā* (knowledge); the reality free from conceptual construction is designated as the supreme (*parama*).

By their opposite nature, the word "non-existent" (asat) is spoken by the exponents of the Vedas; however, because he is the Lord of both, Śiva is called the Lord of the Existent and the Non-existent (sadasatpati).

They say that [the manifest world] consists of the perishable and the imperishable, while the Supreme is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are called the perishable; the immutable is called the imperishable.
Both of these are forms of the Supreme Lord, for they are under His control; beyond them is Śiva, the peaceful one, remembered as the supreme being who is both perishable and imperishable.

Some sages declare Śiva to be the supreme cause, who exists in the form of both the collective whole and its individual manifestations, and who is the cause of both the collective whole and its individual manifestations.
They say that the unmanifest is the totality (samaṣṭi) and the manifest is likewise the individuality (vyaṣṭi); these two are the forms of the Supreme Lord, brought forth by His will.

Those who understand the meaning of causality declare that Śiva is the supreme cause, existing as the causal state of those two [Śakti and Māyā], being the cause both as a collective whole and as individual manifestations.
Some describe the Lord as having the nature of both genus and individual; that which persists even in the individual body is called the genus.

Individuality is that which has the nature of exclusion; it rests upon the collection of physical forms and the universal classes. Both the universal classes and the individuals are governed by His command.
Therefore, Mahādeva is remembered as having the form of both genus and individual; Śiva is said to be the self consisting of primordial matter, the individual soul, the manifest, and time.

The wise call primordial matter (pradhāna) "nature" (prakṛti), and likewise, they call the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) the "person" (puruṣa); they say that the twenty-three principles (tattvas) are the manifest (vyakta).
Time is the sole cause of the transformation of the manifold of effects; it is their lord, sovereign, creator, and that which sets them in motion and brings them to rest.

He is the sole cause of manifestation and concealment, self-ruling and unborn; therefore, He possesses the nature of primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), the manifest (vyakta), and time (kāla).
He is said to be their cause, leader, and sovereign lord, as well as the Sustainer and Maheśvara; by some, he is called the Lord who is the self of Virāj and Hiraṇyagarbha.
Śiva is described by the wise as Hiraṇyagarbha, the cause of the worlds; as Virāṭ, the soul of the universe; and as Antaryāmī, the supreme inner controller.
Others declare that the wise one is the self of the Taijasa and Viśva; others speak of the Turiya, while still others know it as the Saumya alone.
Others say that it is the measurer, the object to be measured, and the act of measuring; while still others say it is the agent, the action, the effect, the instrument, and the cause.
Some declare it to consist of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; others speak of the fourth (turiya); and still others [speak] of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Some call him devoid of qualities, while others know him as possessing qualities; some say he is subject to transmigratory existence, while others say he is beyond transmigratory existence.
Some declare it to be independent, while others know it to be dependent; some call it terrible, while others know it to be indeed gentle.
Some call him one possessed of passion, while others call him free from passion; some call him inactive, and other people call him active.
Some say it is without sense-faculties, while others say it possesses sense-faculties; some call it eternal, and others declare it to be non-eternal.
Some indeed say it is formless, while others know it as possessing form; others declare it to be invisible, and still others know it as visible.
Some say it is expressible, while others say it is inexpressible; some say its nature is sound, and others say it transcends sound.
Some say it consists of thought; others say it is devoid of thought. Others say its nature is knowledge, while still others call it consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Some say it is knowable, while others say it is unknowable; some call it supreme, and others likewise call it non-supreme.
But when the true nature of the Supreme Lord is thus conceptualized, sages do not arrive at a definitive conclusion, due to the cause of their various differing perspectives.
But those who have surrendered to the Supreme Lord with their whole being, they indeed know Śiva, the supreme cause, without effort.

As long as one does not behold the Ancient One, the Lord of the world, who is beyond the power of the senses, so long does one remain bound by the noose in this cycle of existence, wandering through suffering like the rim of a wheel.

When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, becomes stainless and attains the supreme state of equanimity.

Upamanyu said: "Śiva has no bondage consisting of atoms (āṇava), nor one consisting of māyā, nor one consisting of primordial matter (prākṛta), nor one consisting of the intellect (buddhi), nor likewise one consisting of the ego (ahaṃkāra)."

He has no bondage consisting of the mind, nor that of the intellect, nor that of the senses; he has no bondage even to the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor any bondage whatsoever to the gross elements (bhūtas).
Neither time nor its divisions, nor knowledge, nor destiny, nor passion, nor hatred exists for Śambhu of immeasurable splendor.
He has no attachment even to wholesome or unwholesome actions, nor to their maturation, nor to pleasure and pain, which are their fruits.

There is no connection with latent dispositions (*āśaya*), nor with the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) of actions, nor with enjoyments, nor with the impressions of enjoyment, throughout the three periods of time.
It has no cause, no agent, no beginning, no end, and no interval; it has neither action nor instrument, nor anything that is not an effect, nor even the effect itself.
For him there is no kinsman or stranger, no restrainer nor even an instigator; he has no husband, no teacher, no protector, and none who is superior or equal to him.
For him there is neither birth nor death, neither desire nor lack of desire; there is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither liberation nor bondage.
Whatever is not auspicious never exists in him at any time, for he is Śiva, the Supreme Self, who possesses every form of auspiciousness.
That Śiva, presiding over all this by means of his own powers, remains as one whose nature never deviates from itself; therefore, he is remembered as Sthāṇu (the Immovable).
Since the world, both stationary and moving, is presided over by Śiva, Śarva is remembered as being of all forms; knowing this, one is not deluded.
Śarva, Rudra—salutations to him! He is the Supreme Puruṣa, the Great One; the Lord with golden arms, the Blessed One, the Master of gold, the Sovereign.
The Lord of Ambikā, Īśāna, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull—Rudra is the one, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny.
One the size of a young grain of rice should be meditated upon within the heart, inside the small cavity (dahara), as one with golden hair, lotus eyes, and who is both reddish and copper-colored.
He who advances is that god with a blue throat and golden form; he is gentle, terrible, and likewise mixed, as well as imperishable, immortal, and undecaying.
He is that supreme Person, the Blessed One, the ender of the ender; he is free from both the conscious and the unconscious, and is higher than the highest beyond all phenomenal manifestation.
When knowledge and sovereignty are perceived as being surpassed by Śiva, the wise declare that he stands as the supreme among the lords of the world.
He alone was, in the beginning, the instructor of the expansion of the scriptures for those Brahmins born at the commencement of each secondary creation, who exist within the constraints of time.
He is the teacher even of those teachers who are bound by the limitations of time; he is the Lord of all, himself devoid of the limitations of time.
His power is pure, innate, and surpasses all; his knowledge is eternal and incomparable, and his body is perfectly fashioned.
Sovereignty without rival, absolute happiness, strength, splendor, majesty, valor, as well as forgiveness and compassion.
For the Self, which is already complete, there is no purpose for creation and the like; the sole fruit of all its activity is the favoring of others.
The syllable *praṇava* is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self; indeed, among words such as "Śiva" and "Rudra," the *praṇava* is traditionally held to be the highest.
O Śambhu, that supreme perfection which is attained by meditating upon Him who is denoted by the Praṇava, as well as by the recitation of it, will certainly be achieved; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures and are wise, considering the identity of the signified and the signifier, declare the God to be the single syllable.
Its measures are declared to be four at the summit of the Vedas: the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and also the resonance (*nāda*).

They say that the syllable *a* is the Ṛgveda, the syllable *u* is called the Yajurveda, and the syllable *m* is the Sāmaveda; the Atharvaveda is remembered as the hearing (*śruti*) of this [syllable *oṃ*].

The letter *a* is the great seed-syllable, the quality of passion (*rajas*), the creator, and the four-faced one; the letter *u* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb, the quality of goodness (*sattva*), and the protector Hari.
The letter *ma* is the Puruṣa, the seed, Tamas, the destroyer, and Hara; it is Nāda, the Supreme Person, the Lord, devoid of qualities, actionless, and Śiva.
Having expressed this entire universe in its threefold form through these very three measures, it awakens the one whose nature is Śiva by means of the half-measure.
Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom there is nothing smaller or greater; like an immovable tree, He stands alone in heaven, and by that Puruṣa all this is pervaded.
Upamanyu said: His power is innate, and his knowledge is distinct from all else; he shines in both singular and manifold forms, like the radiance of the sun.
Her infinite powers—such as will, knowledge, and action, as well as Māyā and the rest—arose from her just as sparks arise from a fire.
For Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and others, as well as Vidyā, Avidyeśvara, and so forth, were born from her; and her primordial nature (prakṛti) is higher than the highest.

The principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣas), as well as the forms such as the Unmanifest (aja) and others—whatever else exists—all that is her effect; of this there is no doubt.
That power is all-pervading, subtle, and consists of the nature of awakening and bliss; the Lord Śiva, adorned with the cool-rayed moon, is said to be the possessor of that power.
Śiva is the object of knowledge; Śivā is knowledge, as well as wisdom, revelation, and tradition; she is fortitude, stability, and steadfastness, as well as the powers of knowledge, will, and action.
Ājñā is indeed the supreme Brahman, as are the two knowledges, the higher and the lower; it is pure knowledge and the pure aspect, since everything is produced by Śakti.
Māyā, primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (jīva), modification (vikāra), and transformation (vikṛti)—whatever is non-existent and whatever is existent, all this is pervaded by her.
That Goddess, by her illusory power, effortlessly deludes the entire universe, including all things moving and unmoving, and she liberates it as well, through her mere play.
The Lord of All, having pervaded the universe, abides together with this twenty-seventh form; therefore, liberation proceeds from this.
In ancient times, certain sages who were seekers of liberation and exponents of Brahman, their minds possessed by doubt, reflected upon the matter as it truly is.
What is the cause? From where are we born? By what do we live? Where is our foundation? And by whom are we presided over?
By what means do we constantly abide in various pleasures and comforts? And by whom was this inviolable order of the universe established?
The state of time, necessity, or chance is not applicable here; rather, the elements, the womb, the person, or the yogin is the supreme among these.
Because time and the like are insentient, and even if the self were sentient, pleasure and pain would arise from its being a [mere] product and its lack of mastery; thus it is investigated.
Beholding that sovereign power (aiśvarī śakti) which follows from the yoga of meditation—that which directly severs the bonds, yet remains deeply hidden by its own qualities—[he attains liberation].
With their bonds severed by her, they beheld Mahādeva, the possessor of power and the cause of all causes, with divine vision.
He who, being immeasurable, presides over all things through this power—along with all causes without exception, including Time and the Self.
Then, through the yoga of grace and through the supreme yoga, as well as by the perceived yoga of devotion, they shall attain the divine goal.
Therefore, those who perceive Śiva in their hearts according to their capacity attain eternal peace; for others, it is not so—thus says the Śruti.
For there is never a separation between the possessor of power and its power; therefore, because of the identity of the power and the possessor of power, the cessation of both occurs simultaneously.
The sequence of knowledge and action regarding liberation is certainly intended [in this way], because when there is clarity, that very form stands within the palm of one's hand.
Whether a god or a dānava, an animal or even a bird, a parrot or even a worm—one is liberated by his grace.
Whether staying in the womb, being born, or as a child, a youth, or even an old man; whether dying, residing in heaven, or dwelling in hell.
Whether he be fallen, righteous, wise, or even foolish, by that very moment of grace he is liberated; there is no doubt in this.
And out of compassion for unworthy devotees, the Supreme Lord becomes gracious toward them, having seized and removed their various impurities; of this there is no doubt.
Devotion arises from grace alone, and grace is born of devotion; having discerned this distinction between their states, the wise man is not deluded therein.
This [path], preceded by serene faith, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, cannot be attained by men in a single lifetime alone.
Maheśvara is pleased with those who have attained perfection over many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, who are dispassionate, and who are awakened.
O Lord of Gods, when that sacrificial victim has become serene, there arises in him a modest devotion preceded by the realization: "I have a Master."
Through various forms of austerity and by being united with the Śaiva dharmas, a person becomes fit for yoga; through the practice of that yoga, supreme devotion shall arise.
And through that supreme devotion, the highest grace is obtained; from grace comes liberation from all fetters, and for the liberated one, there is bliss.
Even a mortal who possesses only a small portion [of this merit] shall, after three births, no longer be subject to the pain of the womb; of this there is no doubt.
Service that is both with and without limbs is called devotion; it is further divided into three kinds according to the means of mind, speech, and body.

Mental service is defined as the contemplation of the form and other attributes of Śiva; vocal service consists of recitation and the like; and physical service consists of ritual worship and other such acts.
This service, which possesses three means of accomplishment, is called the Śivadharma; it has been declared by Śiva, the Supreme Self, to be fivefold.

In brief, [the means] are austerity (tapas), ritual action (karman), recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), and knowledge (jñāna); as well as the worship of the ritual emblems (karmaliṅga) and so forth, and austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Japa is the threefold practice of Śiva; meditation is contemplation of Śiva; and that knowledge which is declared in the Śiva-āgamas is here called jñāna.
The Śiva-āgama was spoken by Śrīkaṇṭha Śiva to Śivā out of compassion for those who take refuge in Śiva; it is the sole means for attaining the highest good.
Therefore, a wise man seeking his own welfare should increase his devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, and abandon attachment to sense objects.
Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, I desire to hear the knowledge of Śiva as expounded by Śiva himself in the Vedasāra, for the liberation of those who have taken refuge in him.
It is beyond the reach of those who lack devotion, those devoid of intelligence, and those who do not practice yoga; it is endowed with the ten and five objects, profound, and censured by the unwise.

Having extracted [the essence] entirely from the Vedas with their six limbs and from Sāṃkhya and Yoga, [this work is] in some places contrary to, and in others equal to, the duties performed according to the castes and stages of life.
It was taught by the Supreme Lord as being extensive, measuring one hundred crores in the number of its verses; therein, O Lord, how is the worship of the Master performed?
Who is entitled to the worship and other rites? How do the yoga of knowledge and the rest proceed? O you of noble vows, you should explain all of that in detail.

Upamanyu said: [I shall describe] that which is Śaiva, summarized from what is declared in the Vedas, expounded by Śiva himself, free from praise, censure, and the like, and the cause of immediate conviction.
I shall describe in brief that which is born of the Guru’s grace—divine and bestowing liberation without effort—for its detailed exposition cannot be accomplished.
In the past, out of a desire to create, the Lord Śiva, Sthāṇu, Maheśvara, endowed with both cause and effect, manifested himself from the unmanifest.
And then the Lord, the Rishi who transcends all, brought forth Brahmā, the first god of the gods, the Lord of Veda.
Brahmā also beheld his father, the god, as he was being born; and Janaka, the god, beheld him as he was being born by his command.
Beheld by Rudra, that Lord, the Sovereign, emitted the universe; he established the distinct systems of the social classes and stages of life.
He emitted Soma for the sake of sacrifice; from Soma, heaven was born, as well as the earth, fire, the sun, sacrifice, Viṣṇu, and the lord of Śacī.
They and the other gods praised Rudra with the Rudrādhyāya; the Lord stood before the gods with a gracious countenance.
Having stolen away their knowledge for the sake of his own sport, the Great Lord [remained there]; then the gods, being deluded, asked him, "Who are you?"
The Blessed Lord Rudra said: "I alone am the ancient one; O best of gods, I existed first, and I exist now."
And there shall be no one other than myself or distinct from me; I alone satisfy the entire world by my own splendor.
"There is none superior to me, nor is there anyone equal to me; he who knows me is liberated. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished right there.
Not seeing that Lord, they praised him with Sāman hymns, having undertaken the Pāśupata vow established in the Atharvaśiras.
Then the immortals had all their limbs covered in ashes; thereafter, for the sake of granting them grace, the Lord, the Master of Creatures (Paśupati), [appeared].
The Lord, together with his attendants and accompanied by Umā, made his presence known there—he whom sleepless yogis, having conquered their breath and burnt away their sins, behold.
Beholding that God within their hearts, those foremost of deities saw him whom they call the Supreme Power, who acts in accordance with the will of the Lord.
Those who have shaken off saṃsāra and attained the supreme state of Śiva do not behold that beautiful-eyed consort of Maheśa on his left side.
And those other lords of the Gaṇas who are eternally perfected were also seen; then the gods, together with the Goddess, praised Maheśvara.
Even the Lord whose banner is the bull, having looked upon the gods with compassion, [was moved] by divine hymns to Maheśvara and also by the ancient Puranic verses.
"I am pleased," he said, speaking with words naturally sweet and full of joy; then, having prostrated before the bull-bannered god whose mind was well-pleased.
The gods asked this matter of the greatest significance with great respect. The gods said: "O Blessed One, by what path are you to be worshipped upon the surface of the earth?"
"Whose authority regarding worship do you wish to speak of? Please tell me according to the truth. Then, the best of gods, Hara, looked at the Goddess with a smile.
He revealed his supreme, terrible form, which is of the nature of the sun, endowed with all sovereign powers and qualities, and consisting entirely of supreme splendor.
He was surrounded by Śaktis, Mūrtis, Aṅgas, Grahas, and deities; he had eight arms, four faces, and was wonderfully half-female.
Having seen this wondrous form, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, recognized the god Divākara and the goddess Niśākara.
"The five elements remain, as do all things moving and unmoving composed of them. Having spoken thus, they indeed paid homage to him and offered the arghya water.

Salutations to you, who are the color of vermilion, who possess a beautiful mandala, and who wear ornaments of golden hue; to you whose eyes resemble lotuses, who hold a lotus, and who are the cause of Brahmā, Indra, and Nārāyaṇa.

O Blessed One, be gracious; accept this excellent *arghya*, offered with a golden vessel, filled with precious gems, containing water mixed with gold, saffron, and other ingredients, along with *kuśa* grass and flowers.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, who is accompanied by his attendants and is the primordial cause; salutations to you, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, who are the embodiment of the Sun.
He who, being composed, having worshipped Śiva in the solar maṇḍala, should offer the excellent arghya in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
One should bow down or recite these verses, which have the Vedas as their source; for such a person, nothing is difficult to attain, and if he is a devotee, he is certainly liberated.
Therefore, one should constantly worship Śiva, who is in the form of the Sun, with mind, action, and speech, for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Then Maheśvara, stationed within the mandala, having beheld the gods and bestowed the scripture that is the culmination of all Āgamas, Hari vanished.
"Regarding this matter, the right to perform worship belongs to the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. Having understood this and bowed to the Lord of Gods, the deities departed as they had come.
Then, after a long time, when that scripture had disappeared, Maheśvarī, seated upon her husband’s lap, questioned him regarding it.
Urged by that goddess, the Moon-adorned Lord raised his hand and spoke this scripture, which is the supreme among all sacred traditions.
And that [teaching] was set in motion in the world by command of the Supreme Lord, by me, by Agastya, by my preceptor, and by the great seer Dadhīci.
Descending himself upon the earth during the cycles of the ages, the wielder of the trident establishes a lineage of knowledge for the sake of the liberation of those who take refuge in him.
O twice-born ones, Rbhu, Satya, Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, Savitṛ, Mṛtyu, the wise Śatakratu, and Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages;
Sārasvata, Tridhāman, Trivṛta, the bull among sages, Śatatejas, Dharma himself, and he who is known as Nārāyaṇa.
Svarakṣa, the wise Āruṇi, as well as Kṛtañjaya; Kṛtañjaya, Bharadvāja, and Gautama, the supreme sage.
Vācaḥsravas, the sage Sākṣāt, as well as the pure Sūkṣmāyaṇi; the sage Tṛṇabindu, Kṛṣṇa, Śakti, and the later Śākteya.
Let them hear in due order the incarnations of Vyāsa—the Lord of Yoga—beginning with Jātūkarṇya, Hari himself, and the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.

Indeed, O those of excellent vows, in the Dvāpara ages there are incarnations of Vyāsa from the lineage of Śiva; likewise, the wielder of the trident has incarnations as masters of yoga among his disciples.
In each of those places, there shall be four disciples of great power belonging to the Lord; their disciples and grand-disciples, moreover, shall be by the hundreds and thousands.
Through the esteem accorded to them in the world, by carrying out the commands of Śiva and other such acts, those fortunate ones who are intensely permeated by devotion are liberated.
Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, tell me indeed of all the incarnations of Śarva during the cycles of the ages, appearing under the guise of masters of yoga, as well as his disciples.
Upamanyu said: Śveta, Sutāra, Madana, Suhotra, and Kaṅka; as well as Laugākṣi, Mahāmāya, and likewise Jaigīṣavya.
Dadhivāha, Ṛṣabha, the sage Ugra, Atri, Supālaka, Gautama, and likewise the sage Vedaśiras;
Gokarṇa, Guhāvāsī, and another known as Śikhaṇḍī; likewise Jaṭāmālī, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, and Lāṅgulī.
Mahākāla, Śūlin, Daṇḍin, Muṇḍīśa, Viṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Lakulīśvara.
In this Vārāha Kalpa, during the seventh interval of Manu, these twenty-eight Yogācāryas appear in succession through the ages.
Each of these has four disciples with tranquil minds, beginning with Śveta and ending with Ruṣya; I shall describe them to you in their proper order.
Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāśva, Śvetalohita, Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka, and likewise Ketumān.
Vikośa, Vikeśa, Vipāśa, Pāśanāśana, Sumukha, Durmukha, Durgama, and Duratikrama.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana; Sudhāmā, Virajas, Śaṅkha, and Aṇḍaja.
Sārasvata, Megha, Meghavāha, Suvāhaka, Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and Bāṣkala.
Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, and likewise Aṅgiras; Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga, and Tapodhana.
Lambodara, Lamba, Lambātman, Lambakeśaka, Sarvajña, Samabuddhi, as well as Sādhyasiddhi.
Sudhāmā, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viraja; Atri, Ugra, the best of preceptors, Śravaṇa, and Śraviṣṭhaka.
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, Kunetraka, Kāśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, and Bṛhaspati.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahākāla, Mahānila, Vācaḥśravas, Suvīra, Śyāvaka, and Yatīśvara;
Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala, Lokākṣi, Kuthumi, Sumantu, Jaimini, Kubandha, and Kuśakandhara;
Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, Ketumān Gautama, Bhallavī, Madhupiṅga, and likewise Śvetaketu.
Uśija, Bṛhadaśva, Devala, and Kavī himself; Śālihotra, Suveṣa, Yuvanāśva, and Śaradvasu.
Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Ulūka, Vatsa, Kulika, Garga, Mitraka, and Ruṣya.
These are the disciples of Maheśa, who exists in the form of a master of yoga; their number is one hundred and twelve.
All the Pāśupata Siddhas had their bodies smeared with ashes; they were knowers of the true meaning of all scriptures and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
All were devoted to the stage of life dedicated to Śiva, intent upon the knowledge of Śiva; all were liberated from attachment and had their minds solely absorbed in Śiva.
The wise endure all dualities; they delight in the welfare of all beings; they are upright, gentle, self-composed, and have conquered anger and mastered their senses.

Adorned with rosaries of rudrākṣa beads, their foreheads marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra), some wore tufts of hair, others had matted locks, some were entirely shaven, and others had bald heads.
Subsisting primarily on fruits and roots, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), endowed with the sense of identity with Śiva, and solely intent upon meditation on Śiva.
Having utterly uprooted the sprouting shoots of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, they are fully prepared to proceed toward the supreme city of Śiva.
He who constantly worships Śiva, regarding these [deities] as having a guide, attains union with Śiva; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.

Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, sovereign of all yogīs, lord of the Gaṇas, chief of sages, you who possess a splendor equal to that of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), O Guru, treasure-house of all knowledge! Having descended for the most part upon the earth to sever the bonds of men, you remain here, O Supreme Lord, assuming the form of a great ṛṣi.

Otherwise, in this world, who else—whether a god or even a dānava—besides you could know the supreme state whose essence is Śiva? Therefore, having drunk the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva issued from your mouth as if directly from the wielder of the Pināka bow, my mind has not yet reached satiety.

"O Blessed One, what indeed did the Supreme Goddess ask her husband, who has directly taken refuge on the lap of the Lord, the creator of the entire world? Upamanyu said: "O Kṛṣṇa, you have asked a fitting question; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is, for you are devoted to Bhava, disciplined, and of virtuous mind."

On the divine Mandara, the best of mountains, which possesses beautiful caves, Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, became absorbed in divine meditation. Then the auspicious Susmitāsyā, the dear friend of the Goddess, gathered flowers that were most enchanting and in full bloom.

Then the best of gods placed the goddess upon his own lap, adorned her with those flowers, and remained there himself, exceedingly joyful. Thereafter, the ladies of the inner apartments, adorned with divine ornaments, and the intimate lords of the Gaṇas [honored] the Great Sovereign of all the worlds.

With chowries held in their hands, they served the Goddess and the God—their Lord, who is complete and the Great Lord of all the worlds. Then, pleasant conversations took place for the amusement of the two Great Lords, as well as for the protection of those men in the world who have gone to Śiva for refuge.

Perceiving that opportunity, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds questioned her husband, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds. The Goddess said: "By what means can Mahādeva be brought under control by mortals of dull intellect, who are incapable of realizing the truth of the Self and whose minds are undisciplined?"

Īśvara said: Neither by ritual action, nor by austerity, nor by recitations, nor by yogic postures and the like, nor by knowledge, nor by any other means am I brought under control except through faith. If men possess faith in me, for whatever reason it may be, I become subject to them, touchable, visible, worthy of worship, and indeed fit for conversation.

Therefore, faith in me must be cultivated by one who desires to bring me under his control. Faith is the cause of the preservation of one's own duty for those belonging to the social orders (varṇas) here. Only that man who conducts himself according to the dharma of his own class and stage of life possesses faith in me, and no one else.

All the dharma of those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas) established here by tradition was previously proclaimed by Brahmā at my very command. That dharma of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), however, involves many material riches and ritual acts; it does not yield an abundance of ultimate fruit and is accompanied by great hardship.

Having gained through that great Dharma the rare faith which is so difficult to obtain, those belonging to the castes who take refuge in me with no other resort, for them there shall be the attainment of virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation by an easy path.

The conduct of the castes and stages of life has been further ordained by me; however, the authority for this belongs only to my own followers among those belonging to the castes who possess devotion, and not to others—this is my final command.

Then, by the path commanded by me, those ascetics who took refuge in me were liberated from the bonds of impurity, illusion, and the like through my grace. Having attained my supreme state, from which return is difficult, and having reached the highest similarity with me, they attained final liberation.

Therefore, whether one has received it or not, if my devotee relies upon the dharma of the castes as proclaimed by me, he shall uplift himself by means of his own self. This is indeed the attainment of what was previously unattained, exceeding [all other gains] by millions upon millions of times. Therefore, one should practice the dharma of the castes as received from my own mouth.

O auspicious one, my incarnations indeed exist within all the inner scriptures in the guise of Yoga teachers, O Noble Lady, and my lineage exists there by the thousands. O Sovereign of the Gods, for those who are undisciplined, lacking in intellect, and devoid of devotion, the knowledge of this lineage is difficult to attain; therefore, one should take refuge in it with diligent effort.

That is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is blinding muteness—to exert effort elsewhere while being excluded from the path to liberation. O Goddess of the Suras, my eternal dharma is declared to have four feet: knowledge, action, conduct, and yoga.

The knowledge of Paśu, Pāśa, and Pati is designated as *jñāna* (knowledge). The purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*) according to the prescribed rule under the guidance of the Guru is called *kriyā* (action). And the practice of my own ordained dharma, consisting of my worship and so forth, as performed by one belonging to a specific caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), is termed *caryā* (conduct).

For one whose mind is established in me by the very path I have described, the cessation of other mental modifications is designated as Yoga. O Goddess, the purification of the mind is superior to a multitude of horse-sacrifices; it bestows liberation and is indeed difficult for those who crave sense-objects to attain.

Yoga, which destroys former sins, is said to belong only to one who is detached and has subdued the group of senses through self-restraint (yama) and observance (niyama). From detachment arises knowledge, and from knowledge yoga proceeds.

Even one who has fallen from his status, if he knows yoga, is liberated; of this there is no doubt. One should always practice compassion, non-violence, and the accumulation of knowledge; as well as truthfulness, non-stealing, faith, devotion, and restraint of the senses.

Teaching and studying, sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices, as well as meditation, the state of being the Lord, and constant adherence to the nature of knowledge—whosoever, being a Brahmin, conducts himself thus for the sake of attaining the yoga of knowledge, shall soon acquire higher realization and find yoga. O Beloved, having burnt this body in an instant with the fire of knowledge, the man of wisdom [attains liberation].

Through my grace, the knower of yoga shall cast off the bondage of karma—both meritorious and demeritorious karma, which acts as an obstacle to liberation. Therefore, by necessity, the yogi should abandon both merit and demerit.

Action is obstructed by performing it with a desire for its fruit; it is not so by the mere performance of action. Therefore, one should renounce the fruit of action. O Dear One, having first worshipped Me externally through the sacrifice of action, one should then become devoted to the yoga of knowledge and subsequently practice yoga.

When my true nature is known, embodied beings who are disciplined and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal do not worship me through the sacrifice of ritual action alone. The best of sages, ever-disciplined, devoted to me, and composed, being a yogi intent on the yoga of knowledge, shall attain union with me.

Furthermore, those of the various castes who have taken refuge in me but whose minds are not yet dispassionate should be authorized only in the practices of knowledge, conduct, and ritual action, for they are fit for those alone. My worship is to be known as twofold: external and internal. And the wise know my devotion to be threefold, according to the distinctions of speech, mind, and body.

Penance, ritual action, recitation, meditation, and knowledge—these are said by the wise to be the fivefold worship in their proper sequence. Furthermore, that which is known through another is external, such as our own acts of adoration and the like; however, that very same worship when experienced by oneself is declared to be internal.

A mind that is inclined toward me is called "mind," but not merely that which consists of thought alone; speech that delights in my name is truly considered "speech," and no other; a body marked with the signs prescribed by my teaching, such as the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra) and others, and devoted to my service, is a "body," and no other.

The ritual of worshiping me is to be understood as that which is described externally as sacrifice (yāga) and so forth; the emaciation of the body for my sake is not considered by me to be penance such as the *kṛcchra* and other such fasts. Recitation (*japa*) is the practice of the five-syllable mantra and indeed the practice of the *praṇava*; it is the practice of the *Rudrādhyāya* and similar texts, not the study of the Vedas and the like.

Meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of the contemplation of my form and so forth, not concentrations on objects such as the self (*ātman*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the realization of the meaning of my scriptures, not the cognition of other matters. Whether externally or internally, O Goddess, wherever the mind finds delight, one should practice steadfastness in reality (*tattvaniṣṭhā*) there, according to the influence of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Internal purity is superior to external purity by a factor of a hundred; for it is free from the intermixture of defects and because even those defects that are perceived cannot possibly exist there. One should know that internal purity is true purity, whereas external purity is not called purity at all; for one whose self is devoid of internal purity is impure, even if he is outwardly clean.

Worship, whether external or internal, must be preceded by devotion; O Goddess, that which is devoid of devotion is solely a cause for deception. For me, who am purified and have accomplished all that was to be done, what can be done by men? Indeed, it is devotion—whether external or internal—that is accepted by me.

O Goddess, my eternal dharma consists solely of the internal disposition toward action; for in thought, deed, or word, I never look for any fruit whatsoever. O Queen of the Gods, my refuge is considered inferior when it is undertaken with a view toward a result, because one who seeks a reward is capable of abandoning me in its absence.

O blameless one, even for those who seek a fruit, if their mind is established in me alone, I grant them a fruit corresponding to their disposition. Those whose minds are inclined toward me without regard for a fruit, yet might later pray for one—such devotees are dear to me.

Those who, by the power of their past impressions alone, having reflected upon what is beneficial and what is not, helplessly take refuge in me, are considered my most beloved. For them, there is truly no gain greater than the attainment of me; and for me too, O Supreme Goddess, there is no gain other than the attainment of them.

Through my grace, their devotion is offered unto me; it bestows the supreme fruit of final liberation as if by force. For those great-souled ones who are non-dual toward me, whose minds are surrendered to me, and who are entitled to my dharma, they declare the eightfold characteristic.

Affection for my devotees, rejoicing in their worship, worshipping me myself, and bodily exertion for my sake; devotion to hearing my stories, with resulting transformations of voice, eyes, and limbs; constant remembrance of me, and whoever subsists upon me.

Thus, even if these eightfold marks exist in a barbarian (mleccha), he is a lord of Brahmins, a sage, a glorious one, an ascetic, and a scholar. One who is my devotee, even if he be a dog-eater (śvapaca), is dear to me, not one who knows the four Vedas. To him gifts should be given, from him [gifts] should be accepted, and he is to be honored just as I am.
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—to him I am never lost, and he is never lost to Me.
Īśvara said: Now, O Goddess of the gods, I shall speak in brief regarding the duties of the castes for those who are qualified devotees and for the learned, foremost among the twice-born.
Bathing three times a day, performing the fire-ritual, the sequential worship of the Liṅga, generosity, devotion to the Lord, and compassion toward all at all times.
Truthfulness, contentment, faith, non-violence toward all living beings, modesty, faith, study, yoga, and constant teaching;
Exegesis, celibacy, listening [to the scriptures], austerity, forbearance, purity, the topknot, the sacred thread, the turban, and the upper garment.
Abstaining from forbidden things, wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and performing worship on festival days, O Goddess—especially on the fourteenth day.
And month after month, O beloved, one should drink the *brahmakūrca* according to the prescribed rite, and especially perform my worship by bathing me with that very substance.
There is no abandonment of any ritual action, nor the avoidance of food offered with faith, nor likewise of stale food, especially of barley gruel (yāvaka).
The avoidance of liquor, the smell of liquor, and food offerings is common to all castes, and especially so for Brāhmaṇas.
Forgiveness, peace, contentment, truthfulness, and non-stealing; celibacy, my knowledge, dispassion, and the application of sacred ash.
The cessation of all attachments—these ten, in particular, are the further marks of yogis, as is likewise eating alms during the day.
This same rule is prescribed for those in the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life: no one among all these celibates (brahmacārins) should eat at night.
Teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and not accepting gifts—these are specifically not ordained by me for the Kṣatriya and especially not for the Vaiśya.
The protection of all social classes, the slaying of enemies in battle, and the destruction of wicked men as well as predatory birds and beasts.
I have distrust toward everyone everywhere, yet trust in my yogis; I avoid contact with women at all times, and I guard my army.
Constantly obtaining knowledge of the world's affairs through wandering spies, always carrying weapons, and wearing a mantle of ashes.
This is the summary of the dharma for kings dwelling in my hermitage; the protection of cattle, trade, and agriculture are said to be the duty of the Vaiśya.
Service to the other castes is declared to be the duty of the Śūdra; likewise, the cultivation of gardens and reliance upon my fields [are his duties].
Sexual union with a lawful wife is prescribed for the householder; celibacy is prescribed for forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students.
For women, however, service to the husband is the eternal dharma and no other; and for me, O auspicious lady, worship of you is my duty if there is a command from my husband.
That woman who, abandoning service to her husband, is intent upon religious vows, goes to hell; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Now I shall declare the eternal dharma for a woman deprived of her husband: [the practice of] vows, charity, austerity, purity, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
Celibacy, constant bathing with either ashes or water, tranquility, silence, perpetual forbearance, and the distribution of food according to the rules.
On the eighth and fourteenth days, especially on the full moon day, and on the eleventh day, one should perform fasting and worship according to the prescribed rules.
Thus, O Goddess, I have briefly declared [the duties] for those who dwell in the stages of life—the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, as well as for ascetics and religious students.
In the same way, O beautiful one, this is the eternal dharma for forest-dwellers, householders, Śūdras, and women.

O Goddess of gods, I am to be meditated upon by you, and the six-syllabled mantra is to be constantly recited; this entire dharma declared in the Vedas is the summary of the goals of dharma and artha.
Now, those men in the world who by their own will have assumed physical forms, who are endowed with an excellence of disposition and possessed of the impressions from previous births;
Whether detached or attached, they are not smeared by sins regarding objects such as women and the like, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
For them—those who possess self-knowledge, who are pure and discerning, and who have become purified through my grace—their suffering arises from the protection of their hermitages.
For them, there is neither duty nor non-duty, nor meditative absorption as a final resort; for them, there is neither injunction nor prohibition, just as it is for me.
Likewise, here there is no goal remaining for me who am fully accomplished; and in the same way, there is no doubt that for them as well, their duty has been fulfilled.
Having descended to the human state for the benefit of my devotees, those Rudras have fallen from the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Just as my instruction is the impeller for Brahmā and the others, so too is his command the impeller for other men.
By virtue of being the support for my command and through the excellence of its true existence, the destruction of all sins occurs merely by beholding it.
And for those men who possess devotion toward me, auspicious omens arise, indicating excellent fruits and pertaining to objects not previously perceived.
Trembling, perspiration, the shedding of tears, a change in the voice within the throat, and the experience of bliss and other such states may occur repeatedly and quite unexpectedly.
Those best of men are to be recognized by those unfailing signs, whether taken individually or collectively, according to their weak, middling, or superior dispositions.
Just as iron does not become fire merely through contact with it, so too, by my presence, they do not become mere mortals.
A wise person should not despise those who bear mortal bodies, such as Rudra, because they possess common characteristics like hands and feet, thinking them to be merely ordinary beings.
Contempt has been shown toward them by men of deluded intellect; having abandoned longevity, prosperity, lineage, and virtue, it leads to hell.
The state of even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods is like a mere tuft of cotton compared to those great souls who have been uplifted by me, who are independent of anything else.

Therefore, those who seek the state beyond the qualities (guṇātīta) must renounce impure sovereignty—whether pertaining to the Buddha, Prakṛti, or Puruṣa—as well as that of the lords of the qualities.
Now, what is the use of saying more? The sole means for attaining the highest good is the fixing of the mind upon me by whatever cause whatsoever.
Upamanyu said: Thus was this compendium of the essential meaning of knowledge spoken by Śiva, the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the Supreme Self, for the welfare of the worlds.
For this compendium of consciousness, the Vedas and Shastras in their entirety, along with the Itihasas and Puranas, constitute the sciences and the detailed expositions thereof.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, that which is to be practiced, the qualification, the means, and the goal—this is the compendium of the six topics.

The knowledge received from the Guru is what is to be known; the fetter, the bound soul, and the Lord are also to be known. The worship of the *liṅga* and so forth is to be performed by the devotee who is likewise authorized.
The means is the mantra of Śiva and so forth; the goal is equality with Śiva. Through the knowledge of this compendium of the six meanings, omniscience is said to be attained.
First, one should perform the ritual of sacrifice and so forth with devotion according to one's means; having worshipped Śiva externally, one should thereafter become intent upon internal sacrifice.
He whose delight is within and not without due to the weight of his merit—for such a great soul, no further ritual action need be performed externally.
O Kṛṣṇa, for one who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge, whose self is Śiva through devotion to Śiva, there is never any duty to be performed, neither internally nor externally.
Therefore, having gradually abandoned both the external and the internal, and having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should also relinquish ignorance itself.
If the mind is not one-pointed toward Śiva, what is the use of performing ritual action? And if the mind is indeed one-pointed, what is the use of performing ritual action?
Therefore, whether by not performing actions or by performing them, internally or externally, one should fix the mind upon Śiva by whatever means possible.
For the virtuous whose minds are fixed on Śiva and whose intellects are firmly established, there shall be supreme bliss everywhere, both in this world and in the hereafter.
Success is attained through this mantra, "I bow here to Śiva"; therefore, it should be mastered for the sake of attaining both the higher and lower manifestations of power.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of great sages, omniscient one, great ocean of all knowledge! I desire to hear the majesty of the five-syllabled mantra according to its true essence.
Upamanyu said: "The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years; therefore, hear it in brief."
In both the Veda and the Śiva-āgama, this [mantra] consisting of six syllables is the accomplisher of all goals for all devotees of Śiva.
This statement consists of few syllables yet is rich in meaning; it is the essence of the Vedas, bestowing liberation, established by command, free from doubt, and identical with Śiva.
That speech of the Supreme Lord is endowed with various supernatural powers, divine, pleasing to the minds of the world, profound, and its meaning is perfectly certain.
For the sake of accomplishing all goals, the Omniscient One, the Lord of all embodied beings, proclaimed the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," which is to be uttered with ease and clarity.
That six-syllabled mantra, the first of all vidyās, should be known as its seed—extremely subtle yet of great significance, like the seed of a banyan tree.
The God Śiva, who transcends the three qualities (guṇas), is omniscient, the Lord who creates all, omnipresent, and established in the single-syllable mantra "Om."
The subtle Brahman-mantras beginning with Īśāna, each consisting of a single syllable, are established in their proper order within the mantra "Namaḥ śivāya."
In the subtle six-syllabled mantra, Śiva, whose body is the five Brahmans, exists directly by his very nature through the relationship of the signified and the signifier.

Śiva is the denoted because he is the object of cognition, and the mantra is traditionally held to be its denoter; this relationship of denoted and denoter between the two has existed since beginningless time.
Just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has been flowing without beginning, so too Śiva stands as the liberator from that beginningless saṃsāra.
Just as a medicine is by its very nature the antidote to diseases, so too is Śiva remembered as the antidote to the defects of saṃsāra.
If this Lord of the World did not exist, this world would become shrouded in darkness, because primordial matter (prakṛti) is insentient and the person (puruṣa) is ignorant.
Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth, has never been observed to be an agent by itself without an intelligent cause.
The instruction on dharma and adharma, as well as bondage and liberation through investigation, cannot be established for men without an omniscient being at the beginning of creation.
Just as patients suffer without joy in the absence of a physician, so too [without Him] would all be afflicted; therefore, Sadāśiva is beginningless, omniscient, and perfectly complete.
There is a Lord, a protector of men from the ocean of saṃsāra; a Master who is free from beginning, middle, and end, and whose nature is intrinsically pure.
In the Śiva-āgama, Śiva is to be known as omniscient and perfect; this mantra is His designation, and He is remembered as that which is designated.
Because it consists of the signifier and the signified, the mantra is the perfected Supreme Śiva. This much indeed is the knowledge of Śiva; this much is the supreme state.
"Om, obeisance to Śiva"—this six-syllabled statement of Śiva is a scriptural injunction belonging to Śiva; it is not a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), for its essence is Śiva himself.
How could he who is omniscient, perfectly complete, pure by nature, auspicious, and the benefactor of the world speak words of falsehood?
Whatever object exists as it truly is, with its inherent qualities and defects, and to whatever extent its result extends—that is complete; and the Omniscient One speaks of it exactly as it is.
One might speak untruth because of being seized by defects such as passion and ignorance; since those do not exist in the Lord, how could he speak otherwise?
That stainless word which was composed by Śiva—the omniscient one who has no remaining defects—is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the words of the Lord should be trusted by the wise; one who lacks faith in them regarding merit and demerit as they truly are goes to a lower state.
That beautiful speech which has been uttered by the peaceful, eminent sages for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation should be known as *subhāṣita*.
Speech that follows after passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, desire, and craving is called "ill-spoken," because it is a cause for rebirth in hell.
Of what use is that refined speech, whether soft or elegant, which consists of words born of ignorance and passion, and which is the cause of the afflictions of saṃsāra?
That speech which, upon being heard, gives rise to spiritual welfare and the subsiding of passion and other defilements, should be understood as beautiful, even if its form is unseemly.
For even though there are many mantras, there is nowhere a pure mantra equal to that which was composed by the omniscient Śiva.
The Vedic scriptures along with their auxiliary limbs are established within the six syllables; therefore, there is no other mantra anywhere equal to it.
The six-syllable mantra is differentiated in many ways by means of seventy million great mantras and secondary mantras, just as a sutra is expanded through the nature of its commentary.
Whatever Śiva-knowledges there are, and whatever branches of learning there may be, they are, in brief, the commentary upon the six-syllable Sūtra.
What need has he for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent, if this mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" is established in his heart?
By him everything has been studied, heard, performed, and accomplished, by whom the practice of the mantra "Unnamah Śivāya" has been made firm.
The life of that person is fruitful whose tongue-tip bears the three syllables "Śivāya," preceded by salutations and the like.
Whether one is an outcaste, a low-born person, a fool, or even a scholar, by being devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, one is liberated from the cage of sin.
Thus was it spoken by the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the trident, when questioned by the Goddess, for the benefit of all mortals and especially for the twice-born.
The Goddess said: In the Kali age, a turbid time difficult to conquer and hard to transcend, when the world is shrouded by the deepest lack of merit and turned away from dharma.
When the conduct of the castes and stages of life has declined, when a crisis has arisen, and when all authority is either in doubt or has reached its inevitable end;
When that instruction has been destroyed and the lineage of teacher and disciple has passed away, O Great Lord, by what means are Your devotees liberated?
The Lord said: By taking refuge in my supreme, heart-pleasing five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī), men born in the Kali age whose souls are purified by devotion are liberated.
[This applies] to those corrupted by faults born of mind, speech, and body that are beyond the scope of expression or recollection—to the ungrateful, the slanderers, and the deceitful.
Even for those who are greedy and crooked-minded, if their hearts are inclined toward me, my five-syllabled mantra is the savior from the fear of saṃsāra.
O Goddess, I have thus repeatedly vowed upon this earth that even one who has fallen may be liberated by my devotee through this vidyā.
The Goddess said: "If a mortal is fallen, he would be entirely unfit for ritual action; for indeed, any action performed through the absence of yoga leads to hell."
"Then how could one who has fallen [into sin] be liberated by this knowledge? The Lord said: "What you have spoken is true; therefore, listen, O beautiful one."
Thinking this to be a secret, I previously concealed it; yet, if one who has fallen [into sin] should worship me along with the mantra, even though he is deluded.
Without my five-syllable mantra, there is no doubt that one will become a denizen of hell—even those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others emaciated by vows.
For those who perform these vows, there is no meeting with my world; for he who worships me even once with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra alone [attains it].
He too shall go to my abode through the very power of this mantra; therefore, penances, sacrifices, vows, and likewise religious observances [are surpassed by it].
Neither one bound nor one liberated by the five-syllable mantra is equal to even a ten-millionth part of this worship of the five syllables.
He who worships me—whether he be without Śiva or with Śiva—shall be liberated by means of the five-syllabled mantra even once; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Whether fallen or even deluded, a man who worships with either the six-syllabled or the five-syllabled mantra, O Goddess, is liberated.
If he should worship me with devotion through this limb of Brahman, he is liberated—whether he be fallen or not fallen; one should worship with this mantra.
My devotee who has conquered anger—whether he has attained his goal or not, whether he has failed to attain it or not—is here superior by millions upon millions of times.

Therefore, O Goddess, having indeed obtained me, one should worship me with this mantra; for he who, endowed with qualities such as friendliness and the like, worships me after having obtained me, [attains success].
One who delights in the celibate life of Brahmacharya with devotion shall attain similarity to me; what need is there for much speaking on this matter? All devotees are entitled [to this].
Therefore, he is indeed superior even to my five-syllabled mantra; by the power of the five-syllabled mantra, the great seers of the worlds and the Vedas [attained their status].
The eternal dharmas, the gods, and this entire world remain; yet when the dissolution arrives, all that is stationary and moving perishes.
Everything has returned to its primordial nature and will there attain dissolution; I alone remain established, O Goddess, for there is no second anywhere.
At that time, the Vedas and all the scriptures remained established within the five-syllabled mantra; they did not meet with destruction at all, for they were protected by my power.
Then, from me, creation arose through the differentiation of Prakṛti and the Self; likewise, there was the intermediate dissolution of the Guṇas, the Mūrtis, and the Ātman-s.
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa lies upon his serpent-couch in the midst of the waters, having assumed a body composed of māyā.
From that lotus at his navel was born the five-faced Grandfather (Brahmā); desiring to create the three worlds, he was indeed unable to do so as he lacked assistance.
In the beginning, the Lord of Sages created from his mind seven sons of immeasurable splendor; for the sake of increasing their spiritual perfection, the Grandfather spoke to me.
"O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant power to my sons. Thus was I, the five-faced one, entreated by him.
He spoke five syllables in succession to the Lotus-born; the Grandfather of the World received them with his five faces.
