Having known me, Maheśvara, through the relationship of the signified and the signifier, and having understood various applications, Prajāpati became one whose mantras were perfected.

He bestowed the mantra and the true meaning of the mantra upon his sons exactly as it is; and they, having received that jewel of a mantra directly from the Grandfather of the Worlds himself, [attained their goal].
Then, by the path commanded by him, desiring to propitiate me, [he went] to the beautiful peak of Meru, where there is a mountain named Muñjavat.
He is my constant beloved, glorious, and always protected by my devotees; eager to create the world, we shall perform intense penance in his presence.
For a thousand divine years they practiced subsisting only on air; seeing their devotion, I immediately manifested myself before them.

The seer, the meter, the ritual pin (kīla), the seed-syllable, the power, the deity, the ritual placement (nyāsa), the six-limbed rite, the binding of the directions, and the application—all these in their entirety.
I have proclaimed this for the noble ones so that the creation of the world may increase; consequently, by the power of the mantra, those sages were restrained from their ascetic penance.
They properly extend the creation consisting of gods, asuras, and humans; now the true nature of this supreme vidyā is being described.
First, the word "namaḥ" should be employed, and after that, "Śivāya. This is that five-syllabled lore (vidyā) which resides at the head of all the Vedas.
The eternal, primordial speech, which has become the seed of everything that is born, was first uttered from my own mouth; it belongs to me alone.
Resembling molten gold, with full and elevated breasts, four-armed and three-eyed, she has the young moon as her crest-ornament.
Holding a lotus and a blue lotus in her hands, she is serene, with her two hands granting boons and fearlessness; she is endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, with dark, curly hair, her fivefold colors radiate circles of shimmering rays.
Yellow, black, smoke-colored, golden-hued, and red—these should be applied individually, adorned with the bindu and nāda.
O fair-faced one, the bindu of this mantra resembles a half-moon, the nāda has the form of a lamp-flame, and it is the second seed among seeds.
One should indicate the fifth [syllable] of the fourth [quarter], preceded by a long vowel, as the Śakti. Vāmadeva is named the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is declared to be the meter (chandas).
"O fair-faced one, I am Śiva himself the deity of this mantra; O lady of excellent hips, Gautama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras [are its seers]."
And Bharadvāja is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the social classes (varṇas) in their respective order; the meters (chaṃdas) are Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Virāj.
Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda—O fair-faced one, they say these are the deities corresponding to my five faces in their respective places.
From the first [letter] up to the end of the upward series, beginning with *na*, the first letter is unaccented (*anudātta*), as are the fourth and the second.
The fifth is indeed the svarita (circumflex) accent, while the third is known as the depressed (anudātta). Likewise, there is the root-vidyā, Śiva, the Śaiva-sūtra, and the five-syllabled mantra.
One should know its names; this great heart-mantra of Śiva is as follows: the letter *na* is said to be the head, while the letter *ma* is called the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
The letter Śa is the bow, and likewise the letter Va is said to be the armor; the letter Ya is the weapon, as are *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ*.

And when the syllable *phaṭ* is also at the end of the letters [of the mantra], it constitutes a limb (*aṅga*); even in that case, this is the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) due to its slight connection with variation.
Therein, the fifth letter is adorned with the twelfth vowel; therefore, by means of this mantra, one [should worship] through the divisions of mind, speech, and body.
One should perform our worship, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, according to one's wisdom, at the proper time, in accordance with the scriptures, and with due intelligence.

According to one's ability, according to what is available, according to what is appropriate, and according to one's inclination—whether at any time whatsoever, or with devotion, wherever it may be performed.
O Goddess, by whatever means worship may lead to liberation; O beautiful one, that which is performed with a mind attached to me is for my sake.
Whether by gradual means or all at once, they attain my beloved Śiva; nevertheless, those who are my devotees are not utterly helpless again.
I myself have established the rules for all of those scriptures; therein, I shall first explain the auspicious collection of mantras.
Without which the recitation is fruitless, or by means of which it becomes fruitful.

Īśvara said: O fair-faced one, that which is devoid of the command (ājñā), devoid of ritual action (kriyā), and devoid of faith (śraddhā)—even if muttered constantly—is fruitless. That which is perfected through the command, perfected through ritual action, and perfected through faith, being of my own nature—if it is thus joined with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), there is the great fruit of mantra-perfection.

Having approached the Guru—the Brahmin preceptor who knows reality, who has performed the recitation of mantras, who is endowed with excellent qualities, and who is devoted to the yoga of meditation—one should strive to please him, being possessed of purity of intention, through speech, mind, body, and material wealth.

A Brahmin should always honor his teacher with the utmost diligence. He should give to his guru—provided he has the means—the gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, jewels, fields, houses, ornaments, garments, grain, and wealth, all with devotion.

One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires one's own success. Having subsequently offered oneself along with one's belongings to the guru, and having thus worshipped him according to the rules and to the best of one's ability without deception, one should receive the mantra and the knowledge from the guru in due order.

Thus satisfied, the Guru [should initiate] the disciple—who has resided for a year, who is a worshiper, who is obedient, free from egoism, bathed, pure, and has fasted—having first bathed him with water from a full jar containing ghee, consecrated by mantras, and mixed with auspicious substances, for the sake of purification.

Having adorned [the image] with fine attire and ornaments of perfumes, garlands, and garments; having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having honored the Brahmins; on the shore of the ocean, by a river, in a cow-pen, in a temple, or in a pure place within the house, at a time when the lunar day (*tithi*) brings success;

When the lunar mansion and the astrological conjunction are auspicious and free from all defects, one should then bestow my knowledge according to the prescribed rite. With a very serene mind, one should correctly pronounce it with the proper tone in a secluded place; having thus pronounced that supreme mantra of ours again and again—

"May it be auspicious, may it be propitious, may it be beautiful, may it be dear"—in this manner the Guru should give the mantra and the command thereafter. Having thus received the mantra and the command from the Guru, being composed in mind, one should perform the daily recitation after forming the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), preceded by the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).

One should recite [the mantra] eight hundred and more times daily throughout one's life; becoming single-minded and devoted to that alone, he attains the supreme goal. He who eats only at night, remains self-controlled, and recites four hundred thousand syllables with devotion is known as one who has performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite.

He who, having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), becomes a constant reciter (*nityajāpī*)—to him there is no equal in the world; he is a perfected one (*siddha*) and becomes a bestower of perfection (*siddhada*). Having bathed in a pure place and fixed a joyful mind, you should meditate upon me in your heart, and then meditate upon your own guru.

Facing either north or east, observing silence and with a one-pointed mind, having purified the five elements through burning, flooding, and other rites; having performed the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, his body thus rendered fruitful; meditating upon the forms of us two and restraining the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.

Having recollected one's own field of knowledge, form, sage, meter, presiding deity, seed-syllable, power, and likewise the mantra-phrase, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra. Those expert in the meaning of the scriptures declare that mental recitation is the best, whispered recitation is middling, and vocal recitation is the lowest.

They say that, in descending order, [recitation] having Rudra as its deity is the best, that having Viṣṇu as its deity is middling, and that having Brahmā as its deity is the lowest. When one recites the mantra with speech—using high, low, or circumflex tones, and with words and syllables that are either clear or indistinct—this is known as *vācika* (verbal) *japa*.

That which is uttered slightly through the mere movement of the tongue, not heard by others, or heard only faintly, is called *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation. Furthermore, the mental contemplation of the meaning of words, proceeding syllable by syllable and word by word through the sequence of phonemes by means of the intellect, is declared to be *mānasa* (mental) recitation.

The whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold [of the audible], while the mental is declared to be a thousandfold; however, when accompanied by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), it is called "with seed" (*sagarbha*) and is more than a hundredfold. Recitation joined with breath control is termed "with seed," whereas breath control at the beginning and end is praised even if it is "without seed."

Having restrained the breaths forty times, the wise one who knows the meaning of the mantra should recollect it; if unable, he should recite it according to his capacity. He should perform five, three, or even one breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma), whether it be "without seed" (agarbha) or "with seed" (sagarbha); among these, the "with seed" is praised.

Recitation performed with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is said to be a thousand times more effective than even that which is done with a rosary (*sagarbha*). Among these five types, one should perform recitation according to one's capacity. Counting the recitation with a finger is declared to be a single unit; one should know that counting with a line (*rekhā*) is eightfold, and with *putrajīva* seeds it is tenfold more.

A rosary made of conch shells is said to be worth a hundred; one made of coral, a thousand; one of crystal, ten thousand; one of pearls, a hundred thousand; one of lotus seeds, a million; and one of gold, ten million. However, a rosary made of *kuśa* grass knots or *rudrākṣa* beads possesses infinite merit.

A rosary made of thirty beads grants wealth for the practice of recitation; one consisting of twenty-seven beads bestows nourishment; one made of twenty-five beads grants liberation; and one made of fifteen beads yields the fruit of malevolent magic.

One should know that the thumb bestows liberation, the index finger destroys enemies, the middle finger grants wealth, and this ring finger indeed brings about peace. A rosary of one hundred and eight beads therein is the most excellent of the excellent; a rosary of one hundred beads is excellent, while one of fifty is mediocre.

The heart-mantra is indeed proclaimed as the best when performed with fifty-four beads; thus one should perform the recitation with this rosary and not show it to anyone. The little finger is said to be the "flowing" (kṣariṇī) finger, auspicious for the act of recitation; one should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers.

Since a recitation performed without the thumb is fruitless, one should know that recitation in the home is equal [in merit]; they say it is a hundredfold in a cow-pen; likewise, it is said to be a thousandfold in a sacred forest or a grove; ten thousandfold on a holy mountain; and a hundred thousandfold by a river is declared.

They say that ten million recitations performed in a temple yield infinite merit when done in my presence. Recitation is praised when performed in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, Brahmins, and cows. Facing east therein brings subjugation (*vaśya*), while facing south is for malevolent rites (*abhicārika*).

One should know that the western direction bestows wealth, while the northern direction brings peace. In the presence of the Sun, fire, Brahmins, deities, and teachers, as well as in the presence of others who are engaged in spiritual practice, one should not recite the mantra with one's face turned away. One should not recite it while wearing a turban, a bodice, or while bowing down; nor while having loose hair or the neck covered.

With hands unwashed and impure, one should not mutter prayers anywhere while lamenting. One should avoid anger, intoxication, and sneezing—these three—as well as spitting and yawning during the rite of recitation. Furthermore, one should avoid the sight of dogs and low-born people while performing the act of recitation. If these occur, one should sip water for purification or otherwise remember me along with you.

One may either observe the celestial lights or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). One should not recite [the mantra] while lying down without a seat, nor while walking, nor while standing; nor in a street, nor in an inauspicious place, nor in the midst of darkness. One should not recite with the feet extended, nor while in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana).

Whether mounted on a vehicle or lying down, or perhaps distracted by anxious thoughts—if one is capable, one should perform all of this; if incapable, one should recite according to one's ability. What is the use of speaking much here? Listen to my words in brief: one who possesses good conduct, while reciting and meditating with purity, attains auspiciousness.

Conduct is the supreme dharma; conduct is the supreme wealth; conduct is the supreme knowledge; conduct is the supreme goal. A person devoid of conduct is censured in this world and shall not be happy in the next; therefore, one should be possessed of good conduct.

Whatever action is prescribed for a person by the Veda and the Vedic scriptures, his performance of that is right conduct (*sadācāra*), and nothing else. It is called right conduct because it is practiced by the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*). They say that the root cause of such right conduct is faith in the hereafter (*āstikyam*).

If a person is a believer (*āstika*) and does not fall away from right conduct due to negligence or other such causes, that man is never defiled; therefore, one should embrace the state of being a believer. The conviction that just as there is happiness and suffering here in this world through good and evil deeds, so too it exists in the next world—that is called *āstikya* (theism).

O beloved, I shall speak another secret that must be kept hidden: it should not be told to anyone who is an atheist, a beast, devoid of good conduct, fallen, or an outcaste. In the Kali age, there is no protection superior to the five-syllabled mantra.

Whether one is walking or standing, performing actions according to one’s own will, or whether one is impure or pure, this mantra is never fruitless. Even for men who lack proper conduct and whose six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan) are unpurified, this mantra is not fruitless even if it has not been formally bestowed by a Guru.

Even for one who is an outcaste, a fool, a deluded person, or fallen, even for one who is lawless or base, this mantra is not fruitless. For one who possesses supreme devotion toward me, even if they have reached every possible state of degradation, it certainly succeeds—of this there is no doubt—but for no one else whatsoever.

O Dear One, for this [mantra], the consideration of the ascendant, lunar day, asterism, weekday, yoga, and so forth, is not at all necessary; for this is ever-risen and never sets. This great mantra is never an enemy to anyone; it will be either well-accomplished, accomplished, or even yet to be accomplished.

One who has been instructed by an accomplished (siddha) guru is called "well-accomplished" (susiddha). Or, one to whom it has been given even by one who is unaccomplished (asiddha) is simply "to be accomplished through accomplishment" (siddhasādhya). Whether it was previously unaccomplished or already accomplished, there is no doubt that it will be realized for one who possesses an excess of faith in me, in the mantra, and likewise in the guru.

Therefore, having abandoned other mantras that are fraught with obstacles due to their specific qualifications, the wise person should directly take refuge in the supreme knowledge, the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī). Even when other mantras have been mastered, this mantra may not be mastered; yet, when this great mantra is mastered, those others become mastered as well.

O Maheśvarī, just as I am not obtained among the gods even when they are obtained, so too, when I am obtained, you are obtained; the rule regarding these mantras is the same. Whatever defects exist in all other mantras, they do not occur in this one either, because this mantra functions without regard for caste and the like.

Nevertheless, one should not hastily employ this [mantra] against insignificant fruits or [ordinary] practitioners; therefore, it is of great power. Upamanyu said: Thus was the five-syllable procedure, which is beneficial for the worlds, spoken directly by Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, to Mahādevī.
Whoever recites this with devotion or listens to it with a concentrated mind, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord, O Master, you have described the greatness of the mantra, as well as its method of application, exactly as it is found in the direct Vedic revelation.
Now I wish to hear about the supreme rite of purification for Śiva; although something was indicated during the collection of mantras, it has not been forgotten.
Upamanyu said: "Come, I shall tell you of that supreme and meritorious consecration which purifies all sins and was spoken by Śiva himself."
Since a person should perform their duties correctly in acts such as worship, the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva) is therefore called a *saṃskāra* (consecration).
Because by means of this, consciousness is bestowed and the bond of the fetters is destroyed, it is for that reason called "saṃskāra" and is also termed "dīkṣā."
In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: the Śāmbhavī, the Śākta, and the Māntrī.
By the mere sight of the Guru, or even by his touch or conversation, consciousness immediately arises in the living being, bringing about the destruction of its bonds.

That initiation is declared to be Śāmbhavī; it is further divided into two types: intense (tīvrā) and more intense (tīvratarā), according to the distinction between the weakening and the destruction of the bonds (pāśa).
That very [intense] state which brings immediate relief is considered the most intense; however, for a person who is still living, that which is merely intense is what thoroughly purifies their sins.
The empowerment that possesses knowledge, having entered the body of the disciple by means of yoga through the path of the Guru, is performed with the eye of wisdom.

The initiation consisting of mantras and ritual action, preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit and mandala, should be performed by the Guru outside [the inner circle] for those who are dull or very dull in their faculties.
A disciple deserves grace according to the descent of power (śaktipāta), because, in brief, conformity with the Śaiva dharma has that as its root.
Where power has not descended, there purity does not arise; there is neither knowledge, nor the conduct of Śiva, nor liberation, nor the supernatural attainments.
Therefore, having observed the signs of an abundant descent of power (śaktipāta), the Guru should purify the disciple through either knowledge or ritual action.
The evil-minded one who, out of delusion, acts otherwise perishes; therefore, the teacher should examine the disciple in every possible way.
The characteristic sign of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is the arising of awakening and bliss; for that [descent] is the Supreme Power, whose very nature is awakening and bliss.
The marks of bliss and awakening are the modifications of the internal organ, such as trembling, horripilation, changes in voice, and transformations of the eyes and limbs.
The disciple, too, should examine the guru by these characteristics, or through his associations with him, or through those connected to or devoted to the worship of Śiva and other such practices.
But because a disciple is one who must be trained and because he is a cause for the teacher’s respect, he should therefore practice respect toward the teacher with every effort.
He who is declared to be Śiva for the Guru is remembered as the Guru; or else, the Guru is indeed Śiva himself, abiding in the form of knowledge.
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. The fruit of the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Gurus is identical.
This Guru is the embodiment of all deities and consists of all mantras; therefore, with every effort, one should bear his command upon one's head.
If one who seeks the highest good should not transgress the teacher’s command even in thought, for by observing the teacher’s command, one attains the perfection of knowledge.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, he should not perform any other action; if he must act in their presence, he should do so entirely with the permission of his guru.
One should not sit as one pleases in the presence of the guru or in his house; for the guru is the manifest God himself, and his house is a temple of the Divine.
Just as gold sheds its impurity through contact with fire in this world, so too one falls from virtue by association with sinners and through their sin.
In the same way, through contact with a guru, a human being abandons sin, just as a pot of ghee melts when placed near a fire.
In the presence of the teacher, evil is indeed dissolved, just as a blazing fire consumes both the dry and the moist.
Likewise, this preceptor, when satisfied, may burn away one’s sin in an instant; therefore, one should not provoke the anger of the preceptor through thought, deed, or word.
By his anger, indeed, one's lifespan, prosperity, knowledge, and virtuous deeds are consumed; and for those who provoke his anger, even their sacrifices become fruitless.
Yama and the observances (niyamas) are indeed present here; there is no need for deliberation on this point. A person should never speak words that are contrary to the teacher.
If one should speak [falsely] out of great delusion, one would go to the Raurava hell; therefore, one should strive with effort in thought, deed, and speech for the sake of the Guru.
If a wise man desires his own welfare, he should not practice false conduct; he should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to his guru, whether commanded by him or not.
Whether in his presence or in his absence, one should carry out his work; thus, being devoted and possessing such conduct, one should always have a mind intent on exertion.
A disciple who acts to please the guru is therefore worthy of the Śaiva teachings, provided that the guru is virtuous, wise, and a radiance of supreme bliss.
One who is devoted to Śiva as the knower of reality bestows liberation, and no other; the reality that generates consciousness is born of supreme bliss.
He alone by whom that reality has been known is the seer of bliss; not, however, he who is devoid of true consciousness and possesses it merely in name.
A boat may carry one from another; can a stone ever carry a stone? By the mere mention of this [name], liberation is indeed merely nominal.
But those by whom reality has been known are liberated and liberate others as well; for how can there be awakening in one devoid of reality, and how indeed can there be grasping at a self?
One who is devoid of [right] appropriation is called a "bound soul" (paśu); even when impelled by other bound souls, one does not transcend the state of being a bound soul.

Therefore, in this world, one who knows reality is considered both liberated and a liberator; such a person, though endowed with all auspicious marks and learned in all the scriptures, is [the true teacher].
Even one who knows all methods and rituals is fruitless if devoid of reality; however, he whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it culminates in direct experience is successful.
From beholding her and so forth, supreme bliss arises; therefore, from contact with her alone, the emergence of the bliss of awakening occurs.
A wise man should choose that very teacher and no other; such a teacher is worthy of being served by disciples who are adept in disciplined conduct.
As long as he is being understood, he should be served by those seeking liberation; once he is known, one should maintain firm devotion until one takes refuge in the ultimate reality.
One should never abandon reality, nor should one ever be indifferent toward it, where even the slightest bliss or awakening is not to be found.
Even after a year, a disciple may resort to another teacher; yet even when he has approached another teacher, he should not disregard his former one.
Having first approached there the teacher’s brothers, as well as his sons, his instructors, and even those who urge him on, he should then approach a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
A wise person should propitiate a guru who is auspicious, pleasing to behold, the bestower of fearlessness in all things, and whose mind is permeated with compassion.
The disciple should please him with effort through mind, action, and speech; he should serve him until the teacher becomes well-pleased.
When he is pleased, the disciple’s sins are immediately destroyed; therefore, [one should offer] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses.
Ornaments, garments, vehicles, beds, and seats—one should give these to the teacher with devotion, according to one's means.
One should not practice stinginess with wealth if one desires the supreme goal; he alone is father, mother, husband, kinsman, wealth, and happiness.
Since he is a friend and a companion, one should disclose everything to him; having disclosed it, one should thereafter reveal oneself along with one's lineage and one's possessions.
Having offered himself along with water to him, he should remain perpetually subject to his will, once he has surrendered his own self to Śiva, who is embodied as the Guru.
Then that embodied being becomes a Śaiva, and from that there is no further rebirth; moreover, the Guru should examine the disciple who has taken refuge in him for one year.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya—whether two years or three years old—[should be honored] by the offering of life-saving goods and by various commands, both high and low.
Those who, having relegated superiors to a lowly position and placed inferiors in high tasks, do not fall into despondency even when reviled or beaten;
They are fit for the rite of Śiva-consecration—self-controlled, pure, non-violent, compassionate, and always possessed of an alert mind.
Free from pride, possessed of intelligence, having abandoned rivalry, speaking kindly, upright, gentle, pure, humble, and steady-minded.
The twice-born who are devoted to Śiva, endowed with purity and right conduct, and possessed of such behavior through their actions of speech, mind, and body;
"They are to be purified and awakened according to the rule; such is the certainty in the scriptures. A woman has no inherent entitlement to the rite of Śiva-initiation."
If she is endowed with devotion to the Lord by the command of her husband, then likewise for one deprived of a husband, it is so by the permission of her sons and others.
The authority indeed belongs to the father by his command in the case of a maiden, especially for Śūdras, those of mortal birth, and those who have fallen from their status.

Likewise, the purification of the path is not prescribed for those of mixed castes; however, if their disposition toward Śiva, the supreme cause, is genuine and unartificial, [then they are eligible].
They should perform the purification of sins through such acts as offering water for the feet; those born here in the natural order (anuloma) are indeed considered fit among the twice-born.

For them, one should perform the purification of the path and other rites appropriate to their mother’s lineage; however, as for a maiden who has been initiated by her father and others into the Śiva-dharma.
She should be given to a devoted man, and not to another who is antagonistic; if she is given to one who is hostile, she should, out of negligence, cause her husband to realize [the error].
Being unable [to maintain her vows], she should abandon him and practice dharma with her mind, just as the devoted wife abandoned her husband Atri, the best of sages.
She had previously accomplished her purpose by propitiating Śaṅkara through austerity, just as the Pāṇḍavas did by propitiating the god Nārāyaṇa through austerity.
Having obtained a husband in accordance with the Dharma, she was not constrained by her elders; in the ultimate sense, there is no fault here arising from a lack of independence.
For one who is devoted to the Śivadharmas out of reverence for the teaching of Śiva—what need is there to say more here? Even whoever else may be a refuge in Śiva [attains the same].

If one who is to be consecrated is dependent upon a guru, then the consecration is not differentiated [from the ordinary]; it occurs simply through the guru’s gaze, or even through touch or conversation.
For one in whom wisdom is born, there is no defeat; for that which is cultivated by the mind through the path of yoga, [is never lost].

This secret [teaching] has not been described here; it is accessible solely through the mouth of the Guru. As for the ritual procedure involving the preparation of the sacrificial pit and the pavilion, it is for one who is already engaged in ritual action.
It shall be explained in brief; its detailed exposition cannot be accomplished.
Upamanyu said: On an auspicious day, in a pure place free from many defects, the preceptor should first perform the consecration known as the *samaya*.

Having examined the ground according to the prescribed rules by means of its smell, color, taste, and other qualities, one should construct a pavilion there according to the methods taught in the treatises on architecture.
Having prepared the altar, one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in its center, as well as in the eight directions, and then again in the northeast in due order.
One should construct the principal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) from the western side; or else, having made only one principal pit, one should arrange for its beauty.
Then, with various and numerous canopies, banners, and garlands, one should construct a mandala of auspicious characteristics in the center of the altar.
One should prepare a powder suitable for the invocation of Īśvara using red gold and other such powders; or, if one is poor, with vermilion and the powder of śālinīva rice.
It may be one cubit or two cubits in size, and either white or red; for a lotus of one cubit, the pericarp is considered to be eight finger-breadths wide.
The filaments are half of that [measure], and the remainder is for the eight petals and so forth; for a two-cubit lotus, the pericarp and other parts are doubled.
Having made it rich with primary and secondary ornaments, one should prepare a mandala for it in the northeast, measuring one cubit or half of that, as the sacrificial altar.

Upon a surface strewn with rice grains, husked rice, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, flowers, and kuśa grass, one should there prepare the auspicious Śiva-pitcher endowed with all its characteristic marks.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; it should be strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and adorned with blades of kuśa grass and dūrvā shoots.

It is encircled at the neck with a white thread, covered with a pair of new cloths, filled with pure water, provided with a tuft of kusha grass, containing the ritual substances, and equipped with a lid.
One may also use a water-pot (bhṛṅgāra), a ritual pitcher (vardhanī), a conch, or even a discus; or, omitting the cord and other such items, one may use a lotus leaf instead.
On the northern petal of that lotus-seat, and in front of it, one should prepare the *vardhanī* vessel for the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) with sandalwood water.
Then, having performed the ritual in the eastern part of the mandala and at the mantra-vessel as before, one should perform the great worship of the Lord according to the rules.
Now, [this may be done] on the shore of the ocean, or by a river, or even in a cow-pen, or on a mountain, or in a temple, or in a house, or in any other pleasing place.

Having performed everything previously mentioned—either with or without the pavilion and so forth—and having prepared the mandala as before, as well as the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the Fire-god;
Having entered the hall of worship with a joyful countenance, the Guru, endowed with all auspiciousness, performed his daily obligatory rites.
Having performed the great worship of Maheśa in the center of the maṇḍala, one should likewise invoke Śiva into the Śiva-vessel and worship him again.
Having meditated upon the Lord who protects the sacrifice while facing westward, one should worship the weapon of the Lord with the *astravardhanī* mantra to the south of the Lord.
Having placed the mantra into the mantra-vessel, the one skilled in mantras, having performed all the mudrās and so forth, should carry out the mantra-sacrifice.
Then the best of preceptors should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the Śivāgni; other twice-born ones should offer oblations around the principal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

For them, the fire offering (homa) is prescribed as either one-quarter or one-half of that performed for the preceptor; furthermore, the most excellent teacher should perform the oblation in the primary sacrificial pit (pradhānakuṇḍa) alone.

Others should perform the private recitation of sacred texts, hymns of praise, and auspicious readings; and others, devoted to the worship of Śiva, should perform the ritual recitation of mantras according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed dancing, singing, instrumental music, and other auspicious rites, as well as the worship of the members of the assembly according to the proper ritual procedure.
Then, having performed the *puṇyāha* rite and having worshipped Śaṅkara once more, the preceptor should pray to the God with the desire to bestow grace upon his disciples.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods; entering my body, O Lord of the universe, release him out of compassion, O treasury of mercy!
Then, having received permission with the thought, "I shall do thus," the preceptor brings the disciple, who has fasted or is at least eating sacrificial food (haviṣya).

[One should approach] him who eats but one meal a day, who has abstained [from food], who has bathed, who has performed his morning rites, who is reciting the *praṇava*, who is meditating on the Lord, and who has performed auspicious ceremonies.
Having seated the child facing north upon a seat of darbha grass at the front mandala of the western door, or the southern one;

Standing himself facing east, he should sprinkle the disciple—who stands with the upper body erect and palms joined in *añjali*—on the head with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, using the *astra-mantra* and the appropriate mudrā.
Having struck [the disciple] with a scattering of flowers, the Guru should bind his eyes with a fresh garment, half of which is silk, that has been consecrated with mantras.
Then the Guru should lead the disciple into the mandala through the door; impelled by him, the disciple should perform three circumambulations of Śambhu.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers mixed with gold to the Lord, facing either east or north, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
Then, having sprinkled [the disciple] with the root mantra and struck him on the head with the weapon mantra as before, the preceptor should release his eye-bandage.
Having beheld the mandala, he should again bow to the Lord with palms joined in reverence; then the Śivācārya sits to the south of the mandala.
Having seated the disciple upon a seat of darbha grass to his own left, the preceptor, having propitiated Mahādeva, should apply the Śiva-hand (śivahasta).
Uttering the Śiva-mantra, he should place his hand, which consists of the splendor of Śiva, upon the head of the disciple, being fully endowed with the sense of identity with Śiva.
The preceptor should likewise perform the visualization of all the limbs; the disciple, too, should prostrate on the ground before the Lord who has been manifested by the preceptor.
Then, having worshipped the Lord in the Śivāgni fire according to the prescribed rite, and having offered three oblations, he seated the disciple as before.
Touching him with the tips of *darbha* grass, one should enter the self through the *vidyā*; having paid homage to Mahādeva, one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*).

Having caused the departure of the vital breath according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures, and having performed the entry into the disciple’s body, one should satisfy the mantras while remaining mindful of them.

For the satisfaction of the root mantra, ten oblations should be offered with that very same mantra; likewise, three oblations for each of the limbs should be given with the limb-mantras themselves in their proper order.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, the preceptor who knows the mantras should again offer ten oblations with the root mantra for the sake of expiation.

Having again worshipped the Lord of Gods and properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the preceptor, having offered oblations according to the rule, shall indeed uplift the Vaiśya by means of his own caste.
The preceptor should thus generate for him the status of a Kṣatriya and then again perform an extraction; having likewise established his Brahminhood, he should generate it for him once more.
Having likewise extracted the Kṣatriya and made him a Brāhmaṇa again, one should generate the state of Rudra within the Brāhmaṇa; thus, one should accomplish the very name of Rudra in the Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the sprinkling and striking of the child, one should contemplate oneself within the Self as being of the nature of Śiva, vibrating like a spark.
The Guru should expel the breath through the aforementioned channel with the mantra; having emerged, it likewise enters the heart of the disciple through that same channel.
Having entered it, one should remember its consciousness as resembling a blue drop, and contemplate it as blazing, with all impurities dispelled by its own splendor.
Having taken that [deity] through that channel with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, the practitioner, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), should cause it to enter for the sake of its becoming one with himself.
Just as before, by means of kumbhaka and likewise through the nāḍī and recaka, one should take that [power] from there and place it within the heart of the disciple.
Having touched that [thread] obtained from Śiva and having offered it to him, one should offer three oblations and then give the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having seated the disciple on an excellent seat strewn with kuśa grass and flowers to the right of the deity, he should face northward with palms joined in reverence.

Having caused [the deity] to assume the svastika posture, he himself, facing eastward and seated upon an excellent seat, [should perform the rite] with mantras accompanied by the sounds of great auspiciousness.
Taking up a full jar, filled and perfectly purified, the preceptor, meditating upon Śiva, should consecrate the disciple.
Then, having removed the bath-water and put on white garments, the disciple—having sipped water and adorned himself—should proceed to the pavilion with palms joined in reverence.
Having seated him as before upon a seat of darbha grass, the Guru, having worshipped the deity in the mandala, should perform the ritual placement of mantras on the hands (karanyāsa).
Then, meditating upon the Lord within his mind, the preceptor should touch the child with both hands using sacred ash and utter the name of Śiva.
Then the Śivācārya, having performed the rites of cremation, immersion, and so forth, as well as the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa by means of the method of mātṛkā-nyāsa;
Then, having meditated upon the Śivāsana above the head of the disciple, the preceptor, having invoked Śiva there according to the rule, should worship Him mentally.
With palms joined in reverence, one should pray to the God: "Be ever present here. Having thus made this request, one should meditate upon Him, radiant with the splendor of Śambhu.
Then, having worshipped Śiva and received the Śaiva command which is identical with Śiva himself, he should softly utter the Śiva-mantra into the ear of the disciple.
Having heard the mantra with palms joined in reverence, the disciple, with his mind fixed upon it, should recite it slowly at the command of the Śiva-ācārya.
Then, having instructed him in the Śākta mantra, the expert in mantras, having caused it to be recited, should joyfully bestow upon him the auspicious blessing.
Then, having briefly explained the meaning of the mantra through the connection between the signified and the signifier, one should indicate the form of the Lord and prescribe the yoga-posture.
Then, by the command of the guru, the disciple, in the presence of Śiva, the fire, and the guru, should utter the words of initiation while intending thus with devotion:
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head, than that I should eat without having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord.
He alone should give with constancy until the reversal of delusion occurs; until then, one should propitiate the Lord, being established in Him and devoted solely to Him.
Then, in the hermitage of Śiva, there shall be one named Samaya; having obtained authority and being a follower of the guru’s command, he shall remain under his control.
After this, having performed the ritual placement of the hands (nyāsa) and taken ashes from his own hand, he should give the consecrated rudrākṣa to the disciple while reciting the root mantra.
Or else, there may be an image of the deity, or even one with a concealed body; and when possible, the means of worship, fire-oblation, recitation, and meditation should be employed.
That disciple, having received [the teachings] from the Śivācārya with great respect, should accept them by the command of that preceptor and not otherwise.
Having received everything from the teacher and placed it upon one's head with devotion, one should protect and worship Śambhu, whether in a monastery or in one's own home.
Thereafter, the preceptor should instruct him in the conduct of Śiva, according to his devotion and faith, and in accordance with his wisdom.
Whatever has been spoken, whatever has been authorized, and whatever else has been proclaimed by the Śivācārya regarding the covenant—that all one should bear upon one’s head.
One should undertake the acquisition, recitation, and hearing of the Śivāgama from the instruction of a preceptor, neither according to one's own whim nor from anyone else.
Thus has been briefly explained the consecration known as the *samaya*, the supreme means for men to attain the city of Śiva directly.
Upamanyu said: Thereafter, having duly examined the disciple’s fitness, the Guru should perform the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva-śuddhi) for the sake of liberation from all bonds.
The Kalā, the Tattva, the Bhuvana, the Varṇa, the Pada, and beyond that the Mantra—this, in brief, is recited as the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan).
The five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti are called the *kalādhvan* by the wise; however, the other five paths are pervaded by these five kalās, each one by five.
The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is proclaimed to extend from the principle of Śiva down to the earth, consisting of twenty-six principles and being of a nature that is pure, impure, or both.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is proclaimed to extend from Ādhāra up to Unmanā, consisting of sixty divisions when excluding both the primary and secondary subdivisions.
The phonemes, numbering fifty and having the form of the Rudras, are designated as the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan). The path of words (padādhvan) is declared to be endowed with manifold divisions.
The path of mantra is pervaded by all mantras through supreme vidyā; just as Śiva, the leader of the principles (tattvas), is not counted among the principles themselves.
In the path of mantra, that leader of mantras is not to be counted [as a mere part]; he is the pervasiveness of the path of kalā and the pervaded nature of the other paths.
He who does not know [the sixfold path] in its true essence is not entitled to the purification of the paths; for by him the nature of the sixfold path has not been understood.

Therefore, it is impossible even to know the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader; hence, one must likewise understand the nature of the time-periods (adhvan) as well as that relationship of the pervaded and the pervader.
Having understood this exactly as it is, one should perform the purification of the paths, having established everything from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the mandala there, just as before.

One should construct a mandala for the water-pots (kalaśas) measuring two cubits in the eastern direction; then the Śivācārya, having bathed and performed his daily rites, together with his disciples, [should proceed].
Having entered the mandala of Śambhu, one should perform the worship as before; there, for the Lord, one should prepare milk-rice (pāyasa) with rice grains measured by at least one āḍhaka.
Having offered half for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), one should set aside the remainder; or else, [one may offer it] before a mandala that has been prepared and adorned with colors.
The preceptor should place five water-pots in the cardinal directions and in the center; in them [he should place] the Brahma-mantras with the root-syllables accompanied by the bindu and nāda.

The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should arrange [the deities] with the names beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Ya'; he should place Īśāna in the central jar and Puruṣa in the one situated in front.

Having performed protection by assigning Aghora to the south, Vāma to the north, and Sadyojāta to the west, and having formed the mudrās, one should perform the consecration of the water-jar (kumbha).
Having performed the fire-oblation with the Śiva-mantras as before, one should then begin [the rite] using half of that milk-rice which was previously prepared for the purpose of the oblation.
Having performed the oblation, he should prepare the remainder for the disciple to eat; and having performed the rites for the mantras up to the libation (tarpaṇa) as before.
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for them, one should then perform the kindling: following the syllable Oṃ, the syllable Huṃ, and then the root mantra ending with Phaṭ.
They say that the limbs [of the mantra] for the rite of kindling (dīpana) end with "svāhā" in their proper sequence; three oblations of these should be offered in the act of kindling.
Each of these should be visualized with their respective mantras as having radiant forms; having multiplied them three times by three, one should employ a white [thread] made by a brahmin girl.
Having recited the Sūtra over another Sūtra, one should bind it to the crest-lock of the child while the child stands with the body erect, reaching down to the big toe of the foot.
Having suspended that thread, the knower of mantras should join it there with the Suṣumṇā, taking hold of it with the Śāntā mudrā while reciting the root mantra.
Having offered three oblations into her, one should effect her presence; then, having struck the heart of the disciple, as before, by the casting of a flower.
Having taken up consciousness and offered it at the end of the twelve [fingers], one should join the thread with the thread, protecting it with the Astra and Varma mantras.

Then, having wrapped that thread around [the disciple], one should contemplate the disciple's body as a bond consisting of the three roots, characterized by the state of being an enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment.

One should contemplate its producer as the source of the objects, senses, body, and so forth; these are the kalās, such as Śāntyatītā and the others, which possess the nature of the elements beginning with space.

One should join [the deities] with their own names in the sūtra and worship them with [mantras] accompanied by "namaḥ"; or else, having performed that using their seed-syllables (bīja) in the sequence previously described.

Then, one should observe the pervasion of the Tattvas and so forth by Impurity (mala) and the rest; and having offered oblations into Impurity and the rest for the sake of the pervasion of the Kalās, one should inflame the Kalās.
Having struck the disciple on the head, one should mark the thread upon the body in due order; reciting the mantra, one should mark the thread at the stage beyond tranquility (śāntyatīta).
Having performed this up to the end of the Nivṛtti-kalā, and having offered three oblations in sequence for Śāntyatītā, one should thereafter worship Śiva in the maṇḍala.
Having seated the disciple facing north on the right side of the deity upon a mandala strewn with darbha grass, the Guru should give him the sacrificial caru-remnant.
The disciple, having respectfully received what was given by his guru, beginning with "Śiva," should eat; thereafter, having sipped water twice, he should recite the Śiva-mantra.

The Guru should likewise offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) within another mandala; he too, having drunk it according to his capacity and performed the ritual sipping of water twice (dvirācamya), should meditate upon Śiva.
Having seated the disciple in the third mandala as before, he should provide him with a tooth-stick possessing the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures.
Facing either the east or the north, with his speech restrained and sitting down, the disciple should clean his teeth using the tip of that [twig], which should be soft.

Having rinsed his mouth, discarded the tooth-stick, and sipped water for purification, he should meditate on Śiva; then, permitted by the Preceptor, he should enter the Śiva-maṇḍala with palms joined in reverence.
If that discarded tooth-stick is seen by the teacher with its tip pointing east, north, west, or behind him, it is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious.
When that face of an inauspicious quarter occurs, the preceptor, for the sake of pacifying that defect, should perform one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations with the root mantra.
Then, having touched the disciple and murmured the name of Śiva into his ears, he should cause that disciple to dwell in the southern part of the deity's [sanctuary].
Having spread out a new, unwashed covering and a bed of *darbha* grass, being pure, he should lie down at night with his head toward the east, reciting mantras and meditating on Śiva within himself.
The Guru, having tied the disciple's topknot with a thread already bound to his own topknot, and having covered him with an unwashed cloth while reciting the Armour-mantra (varma), [proceeds].
Having drawn three lines all around with ashes mixed with sesame and mustard seeds consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should offer oblations to the lords of the directions outside of that.
The disciple also, having performed this consecration while fasting from others, should wake up, rise, and report the dream he has seen to the guru.

Upamanyu said: Then, having completed all the rites such as bathing and being urged by the preceptor, one should go to the side of the Śiva-maṇḍala with palms joined in reverence, meditating upon Śiva.
Then, having performed everything except the worship on the previous day as prescribed, the Guru should reveal the maṇḍala, ending with the binding of the eyes.
When the disciple, with eyes blindfolded, has performed the scattering of flowers, the teacher should assign him a name according to where the flowers fall.
And having brought that [offering], one should worship the Lord Īśāna in this mandala of floral remains as before, and one should also offer oblations into the fire of Śiva.
If a disciple sees a bad dream, for the pacification of its defects, he should perform one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations with the root-vidyā.

Then, having suspended the thread tied at the topknot as before, [one performs] everything from the worship of the support (ādhāra-pūjā) onwards, which rests upon the power of cessation (nivṛtti-kalā).
One should perform the worship of Vāgīśvarī preceded by the fire-oblation (homa); then, having prostrated before Vāgīśa, one should worship the virtuous goddess who pervades the Nivṛtti-kalā.
Having worshipped the deity in the maṇḍala and offered three oblations, one should cause the disciple to attain simultaneously the experience of all wombs.
Then, having performed the striking, sprinkling, and other rites upon the disciple’s thread-body, and having taken up the self and offered it at the end of the twelve [fingers], [one should proceed].
Then, having taken [the substance] with the root mantra and the seal (mudrā) prescribed in the scriptures, the preceptor should mentally unite it simultaneously within all wombs.
There are eight classes of gods and five classes of animals; with the single class of humans, there are fourteen modes of birth.
In order for the disciple’s intellect to enter all of them simultaneously, he should, according to the prescribed rule, cause the disciple’s self to enter Vāgīśānī.

Having fully worshipped and prostrated before the deity for the sake of the completion of the womb, and having offered oblations according to the rule, one should meditate upon that which has been accomplished.

For one who has thus attained perfection, [the practice] of the arising and persistence of action through ritual duty brings about straightforwardness, the accomplishment of enjoyment, and likewise supreme joy.
For the sake of expiation and for the perfection of caste, lifespan, enjoyment, and latent impressions, the supreme preceptor, having offered three oblations, should pray to the Lord.
Having thus purified the disciple’s body—which is stained by attachment to the objects of enjoyment and the state of being an enjoyer—he should then sever the three bonds.
By completely severing the bond of the snare that was bound through deceit, one should consider the consciousness of the disciple to be rendered purely translucent.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation into the fire, one should then worship Brahmā; having offered three oblations to him, one should communicate the command of Śiva.
O Grandfather, you must not place any obstacle in the way of this traveler toward the supreme state of Śiva; for this is the most weighty command of Śiva.
Having thus instructed him, having honored him, and having dismissed him according to the rules, one should worship Mahādeva and offer three oblations.
Having purified and extracted the disciple’s self by means of withdrawal, and having established it within his own self and in the thread as before, he should then worship Vāgīśa.
Having offered three oblations to him, bowed down, and dismissed her, one who has withdrawn from that [state] should perform the reconnection along with the *kalā* for the sake of *pratiṣṭhā*.
Having performed worship simultaneously during the conjunction and having offered three oblations, one should then contemplate the entry into the consecration of the disciple’s self.
Then, having invoked the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and performed everything previously mentioned, one should meditate upon Vāgīśānī as its pervasive power that pervades it.
Having visualized [the disciple] as resembling the orb of the full moon and having performed the remainder as before, he should communicate the command of Śiva, the Supreme Self, to Viṣṇu.
Having performed the dismissal (visarjana) of Viṣṇu and the remaining rites with the Vidyā, and having contemplated the installation (pratiṣṭhā), one should proceed within it just as before.

Having performed [the rites] and reflected upon their pervasion, as well as that of Vāgīśā in due order, one should complete the ritual up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the blazing fire, and perform the remainder as before.
Having invoked Nīlarudra and performed worship and other rites for him, one should grant the command of Śiva according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having caused even that [element] of austerity (tapas) to depart and having performed its pacification, one should then establish the digit of knowledge (vidyā-kalā) and contemplate its pervasion.
Likewise, one should visualize Vāgīśī pervading one's own self, as before, illuminating the ten directions with a form resembling the rising sun.
Then, having performed the remaining rites as before, one should invoke and worship the god Maheśvara, offer oblations to him, and mentally impart the command of Śiva.
Likewise, having abandoned Maheśvara and performed this other digit (kalā), one should lead it to the digit beyond peace (śāntyatītā) and contemplate its pervasion.
In the same manner, one should contemplate Vāgīśā pervading one’s own self, resembling the expanse of the sky, and full until the end, as previously described.
Having performed the remaining rites and worshipped Sadāśiva, he should impart to him the command of Śambhu, whose actions are immeasurable.
And there too, as before, having worshipped Śiva on the head as previously described, and having paid homage to Vāgīśa, one should dismiss him.
Then, having sprinkled the disciple on the head as before with the Śiva-mantra, he should contemplate the dissolution of the Śāntyatītā level into the Śakti-tattva.
One should meditate upon the supreme Śiva-śakti, who is beyond the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), situated on the further shore, pervading all paths, and resembling ten million suns in brilliance.
Having brought the disciple before him—pure like clear crystal—and having washed the scissors according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures;
The preceptor should cut off his topknot together with the thread; then, having placed it upon cow-dung, he should offer that topknot as an oblation into the Śiva-fire.
Having washed the scissors again with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should withdraw the consciousness from the disciple's body into one's own hand.

Then, having caused the child—who had bathed, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and had the rites for auspiciousness (svastyayana) performed—to enter the vicinity of the mandala, he prostrated himself like a staff.
Having performed the worship according to the rule for the purification of any deficiency in the ritual, the officiant should offer three oblations with the very mantra used for recitation.
One should offer three oblations by means of whispering recitation; then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, for the purification of any deficiency in the mantra.
One should offer three oblations through the practice of mental recitation; there, one should worship Śambhu, who resides within the mandala together with the Mother.
Having offered three oblations, the preceptor, with palms joined in reverence, should thereafter pray: "O Blessed One, by Your grace, let there be purification of this sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan)."
"Therefore, lead him to your supreme, imperishable abode. Having thus informed the God, [he performed] the joining of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna).

Having performed the ritual up to the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as before, one should then purify the elements (*bhūtas*). Then, for the sake of purification, [one should purify] the stable and unstable, and then the two states of cold and heat.

In the rite of purifying the elements, one should meditate upon the form of oneness through pervasion; having severed the knots of the elements, one should abandon them along with their presiding deities.
Having purified his body through the yoga of stability, one should recite [the mantra] for the supreme Śiva; then, having burnt it, one should drench it with drops of nectar.

Then, having established oneself, one should fashion a body composed of the pure path; therein, first of all, [one should contemplate] the pervasive *kalā* of one's own path, which is beyond peace (*śāntyatītā*).

One should place the Śuddhā [kalā] upon the head of the child, and likewise the Śānti [kalā] on the face; the Vidyā [kalā] from the throat down to the navel, and the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā] below that in due order.

One should place that [mantra] ending at the knees below it and contemplate Nivṛtti; then, having performed the placement of the thread-mantra with one's own seed-syllables, one should contemplate that [thread] as being of the nature of Śiva.

Having realized that [reality] within the lotus of the heart, the Guru should invoke and worship the Lord; then, having prayed for the disciple’s perpetual presence [of the deity] and his identity with Śiva, [he should proceed].
One should cause this child, who consists of the splendor of Śiva, to attain the qualities beginning with *aṇiman*; saying "Be gracious," one should offer three oblations.
In that very same way, one should further bestow upon him only the qualities: omniscience, as well as contentment and awakening devoid of beginning and end.
[He perceives] that very power which is infinite sovereignty with unimpaired potency; then, having obtained permission from the deity, [he consecrates] him with the kalaśas beginning with Sadyojāta.

One should consecrate the Lord of Gods while meditating upon Him in the heart according to the prescribed sequence; then, having seated that disciple and worshipped Śiva as before, [one should proceed].
Having received permission from Śiva, one should impart the Śaiva Vidyā to him—preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, enclosed within [the two parts], and ending with *namaḥ*.

And likewise, [he taught] Śiva joined with Śakti, as well as the Śakti-vidyā of that same nature; the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity, as well as the state of Śiva belonging to both Śiva and Śakti.

One should instruct [the disciple] regarding the worship of Śambhu along with his retinue and the seats; then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, [one should say]: "Whatever has been performed by me..."
"Perform all that which is well-done"—thus should he inform Śiva; then the Guru, together with his disciples, should prostrate like a staff upon the surface of the earth before the Lord.

Having prostrated, one should dismiss [the deities] from that maṇḍala and also from the fire; thereafter, all those worthy of worship who are present in the assembly hall should be honored in due order.
The members of the assembly and the officiating priests should be served according to one's wealth; one who desires his own welfare must not practice stinginess regarding the sacrificial gifts.

Upamanyu said: Hereafter, I shall explain the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) according to its designation, as well as the greatness of the purificatory mantra (saṃskāra-mantra), which has been indicated by me in this discourse.

Having worshipped the deity in the mandala and established him in the water-pot as before, and having performed the fire-oblation, he should lead the disciple, who is without a turban, onto the ground within the mandala.
Having performed the preliminary rites as before and likewise offered a hundred oblations, the most excellent preceptor should satisfy [the deity] with the root mantra using the ritual jars.
Having kindled [the fire] as before and performed the sequence previously described, and having consecrated [the disciple] as before, one should bestow the supreme mantra.
There, having performed the instruction of the mantra in detail and in due order, one should impart the Śaiva mantra into the hand of the disciple using water and flowers.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, this great mantra indeed becomes the bestower of the fruit of all accomplishments in both this world and the next.
Having spoken thus and worshipped the God, the Guru, having received permission from Śiva, should instruct the practitioner in the means of accomplishment and in Śiva-yoga.
Having heard that command of the preceptor, the practitioner of the mantra should perform the mantra-sādhana in due order prior to the viniyoga.
The practice of the root mantra is called *puraścaraṇa*, because it must be performed prior to the ritual action known as *viniyoga*.

For one desiring liberation, the practice of mantra-sādhana is not to be performed to an extreme degree; yet, if it has been performed here or elsewhere, it will still bring auspicious results even for such a person.
On an auspicious day, in an auspicious place, or at a time free from defects, one whose teeth and nails are clean, having bathed and performed the morning rituals;
Having adorned himself with whatever perfumes, garlands, and ornaments were available, wearing a turban and an upper garment, and being fully composed in all-white attire;
In a temple, in one's own home, or in another very beautiful place, having taken one's seat with a posture that has been previously practiced with ease.
Having assumed his own Śaiva form according to the path taught in the scriptures of Śiva, he worshipped the Lord of the gods, the Sovereign Nakulīśvara.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) to him and completed the sequence of worship, he prostrated before that god and received permission from his mouth.
One should recite the name of Śiva ten million times, or half of that, or half of that again; or twenty lakhs, or even ten lakhs.
Thereafter, he should always subsist on a single meal of milk-rice, free from pungent and salty flavors; he should be non-violent, patient, tranquil, and self-controlled.
In the absence of milk-rice, one may eat fruits, roots, and so forth; these have been ordained by Śiva himself as progressively superior options.
Rice-porridge, edible food, as well as barley-meal, broken grains, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water.
Having consecrated with the mantra the various kinds of food, both solid and soft, one should always eat them while maintaining silence, especially during this spiritual practice.

The observer of the vow, being pure, should bathe in water originating from a river or stream that has been purified by one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra, or else he should sprinkle himself according to his ability.
And likewise, one should daily perform libations and offer oblations into the fire of Śiva with seven, five, or three substances, or else with clarified butter alone.
In this way, for that Śaiva practitioner who accomplishes Śiva through devotion, there is nothing whatsoever that remains difficult to attain, both in this world and the next.
Alternatively, with a one-pointed mind, one may recite the mantra a thousand times every day without eating, even without the formal practice (sādhana) of the mantra.
For him, nothing is difficult to obtain, and nowhere does anything inauspicious exist; having attained knowledge, prosperity, and happiness in this world, he finds liberation.

In the performance of rites, in ritual application, and likewise in daily or occasional ceremonies, one should recite the mantra after bathing with water, ash, and [performing] the [prescribed] sequence of mantras.

Pure, with his topknot tied, wearing the sacred thread, likewise with pavitra-grass in his hand, and bearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and rudrākṣa beads, he should mutter the five-syllabled mantra.
Upamanyu said: Then, one should consecrate the disciple who has been thus purified and has performed the Pāśupata vow for the office of teacher, or otherwise according to his fitness for that yoga.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before and having worshipped the Supreme Lord, one should place five water-pots (kalaśas) in the cardinal directions and in the center, as previously described.
Having placed Nivṛtti in the eastern jar, Pratiṣṭhā in the western, Vidyā in the southern, Śānti in the northern, and Parā in the center;

Having performed the protection rites and other rituals there, and having bound the *dhainavī* mudrā, one should consecrate the jars and perform the fire oblation (*homa*) up to the final *pūrṇāhuti*, just as before.

Having caused the disciple to enter the maṇḍala and removed his turban, the preceptor should perform the libation and other rites for the mantras, beginning with the preliminary and ending with the concluding acts.
Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission as before, he should cause that disciple to ascend the seat for the sake of consecration.

Having subsequently performed the sakalīkaraṇa upon him, who consists of the five kalās and whose body has been invested with the installed mantras, one should bind him and present the disciple to Śiva.
Then, having sequentially removed the jars for cessation and the others starting from the middle one, he should consecrate that disciple with the Śiva-jar alone.
Then, having placed the hand of Śiva upon the head of the child, the preceptor, having attained the state of Śiva, should designate him as a Śivācārya.
Then, having adorned that deity and propitiated him within the Śiva-maṇḍala, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more and prostrated on the ground like a staff, the Guru, placing his joined palms upon his head, should address a petition to Śiva.
O Blessed One, by your grace, this man has been made my guide; having shown him favor, O Lord, please grant him a divine command.
Having made this request and having bowed once more together with the disciple, the Guru should worship Śiva and the divine Śivāgama just as he would Śiva himself.
Then, having again obtained the permission of Śiva, the preceptor should give the book of Śiva-knowledge to the disciple with both hands.
Having placed that [image] upon his head and having mounted it upon the seat of knowledge (vidyāsana) according to rule, he should salute it and worship it.
Then the guru should also give him the royal regalia, for one who has attained the status of an *ācārya* is worthy even of a kingdom.
Then he should provide instruction as it was practiced by the ancients, as it is declared in the teachings of Śiva, and as it is honored in the worlds.
Having carefully examined the disciples according to the characteristics described in the Śiva scriptures, and having purified them, the preceptor should impart the knowledge of Śiva to them.
In this way, one should diligently cultivate all these qualities—effortlessness, purity, patience, compassion, as well as lack of desire and freedom from envy.
Having thus instructed that disciple and having dismissed Śiva from the mandala, one should worship the Śiva-pitcher, the fire, and so forth, as well as the members of the assembly.
Or else, the Guru, together with his retinue, should perform the consecrations simultaneously; for in that case, both [methods] are taught as the ritual application.

Therefore, at the very outset, one should prepare the ritual jars according to the procedure for the purification of the paths, having performed the entire consecration of the pledges (samaya-saṃskāra) even without the formal initiation (abhiṣeka).
Having worshipped Śiva once more and performed the purification of the paths (adhva-viśodhana), one should worship the Lord again once that [purification] is completed.

Having offered oblations, having gratified the mantra, having kindled it and invoked blessings upon the Lord, and having placed the mantra into the hand of the disciple, he should complete the remainder of the rite.

Alternatively, having reflected upon the entire sequence of mantra-consecration in its proper order, the Guru should perform the purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi), concluding with the consecration (abhiṣeka).
In that regard, whatever procedure has been prescribed for the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā, all of that must be performed during the purification of the three principles (tattvas).
The triad of principles known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman has been proclaimed. Śiva resides within Śakti; from Him arises Vidyā, and from her, Ātman emerged.

The path beyond Śānti is pervaded by Śiva; the one following that is pervaded by the Supreme (Para); the remaining path is pervaded by Vidyā; and indeed, the entire path is pervaded by the Self (Ātman) in due order.
Considering the Śāmbhava [initiation] to be difficult to attain, the wise who have mastered the meaning of the Śiva scriptures should praise the Śākta purification, which is rooted in mantra.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, I have explained to you all this fourfold nature of the action known as formative predisposition (saṃskāra). What more do you wish to hear?
Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the obligatory and occasional rites prescribed in the Śiva scriptures for those who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva.

Upamanyu said: Having risen from bed at dawn, having meditated upon the God together with his Mother, and having reflected upon his duties, he should depart from the house when the sun has just begun to rise.
Then, in an unobstructed and solitary place, he should perform his necessary duties; having performed purification according to the rule, he should practice the cleansing of the teeth.
In the absence of tooth-sticks, or on days such as the eighth day of the lunar fortnight and others, one should perform the cleansing of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, one should thereafter perform the Varuṇa-bath in a river, a sacred pool, a lake, or even at home.
Having placed the bathing materials on its bank and having removed external impurities, one should smear oneself with clay, bathe, and then smear oneself with cow-dung.
Having bathed again and again, having discarded the garment and purified himself once more, he, being well-bathed like a king, should put on a clean cloth.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), an ascetic, and likewise a widow should not perform a bath for removing dirt, a bath with perfumes and the like, or the cleansing of the teeth.
Having put on the sacred thread, tied his topknot, and entered the water, he should immerse himself, perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana), and then draw a triple mandala within the water.

Immersed in the northern direction, he should again recite the mantra according to his capacity and meditate on Śiva; then, having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should consecrate himself with that very [mantra].
With a cow-horn together with darbha grass, or with a leaf of the palāśa tree, or with a lotus leaf, or else with the two hands, [one should perform the rite] five times or indeed three times.
In a garden, at home, or elsewhere, one should perform an ablution with consecrated water using either a vardhanī vessel or a water-pot at the time of immersion.
If, however, one is unable to perform the Vāruṇa rite, one should purify the body from the soles of the feet to the head with a clean, wet cloth.
One should perform the bath either with fire, or with mantras, or with Śiva; for one who is disciplined, the bath consisting of supreme contemplation upon Śiva is said to be one's own.

Having performed the libations for the gods and others, one should perform the rites up to the Brahma-yajña according to the procedure prescribed in one's own scripture, preceded by the sipping of water (mantra-ācamana).
Having meditated upon Mahādeva situated within the maṇḍala and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, one should then offer the arghya water to that Śiva who has the form of the Sun.

Alternatively, having performed this as prescribed in one's own sūtra, one should purify the hands; then, having performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one's body becomes fully empowered (sakalīkṛtavigraha).
Having sprinkled [the area] with water held in the left hand, combined with scents and white mustard seeds, or with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, while reciting the root mantra.
Having smelled the remaining water with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should contemplate the white deity through the left nostril alone.

Taking the *argha* water, one should visualize it as residing within the body; then, through the left nostril and by means of a black-colored [wind], one should contemplate it as being outside, located upon the stone.
Then he should gratify the gods and especially the sages; he should offer the arghya according to the prescribed rule to the spirits and the ancestors.
One should fashion a perfectly circular mandala on the ground, one cubit in size, using red sandalwood water and adorned with red powder and other such materials.
There, one should worship the Sun together with his own retinues, using the mantra "svakholkāya" along with its ancillaries for the sake of easy accomplishment.
Furthermore, having prepared a mandala and worshipped it with its constituent parts, one should place there a golden vessel measuring one prastha of the Magadha measure.
One should fill [the vessel] with scented water mixed with red sandalwood, along with red flowers, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having gone to the ground on one's knees with *dūrvā* grass, *apāmārga*, products of the cow, or even with water alone, one should bow to the deity within the mandala.

Having placed that vessel upon his head, he should offer that *arghya* to Śiva; or else, with water and *darbha* grass held in his joined palms (*añjali*), he should offer it with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Having performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) preceded by the purification of the hands, one should offer [the oblation] to Śiva, who is stationed in the sky in the form of the Sun.
Having understood Śiva as consisting of the five Brahmans, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta, one should take the sacred ash with the mantras, smear it, and touch the limbs.
