Having touched the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet in sequence with the [five] concluding mantras, one should then touch all the limbs with the root mantra and put on another garment.

Having put on [the garment] and sipped water twice, having sprinkled himself with water consecrated eleven times, and having covered himself with another cloth, he should sip water twice again and meditate upon Śiva.

Having again placed his hands [in the prescribed mudrās], the practitioner of mantra should clearly mark the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes on his forehead using fragrant water, ensuring it is applied straight.
Furthermore, whatever mark (puṇḍra) is drawn with ashes on the forehead—whether circular, square, a dot, or even a half-moon—
One should draw such [marks] on the two arms, on the head, and between the breasts; indeed, the smearing of all the limbs is not equal to the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍraka).
Therefore, one should apply only the single triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) without using sacred ash; and one should wear Rudrākṣa beads on the head, the neck, the ears, and likewise on the hands.
It is golden-colored, unbroken, auspicious, and not worn by others; it is auspicious and excellent for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively—yellow, red, and black.

If that is unavailable, one should wear whatever is available provided it is unblemished; even in that case, a superior garment must not be worn by those of lower status, nor should an inferior one be worn by those of higher status.
One who is impure should not wear the rosary; one should always wear it at the proper times—thus either at the three junctions of the day, or at two junctions, or even just once.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites according to his ability, he should worship the Supreme Lord; then, having reached the place of sacrifice, he should assume a beautiful seat.
Facing either the east or the north, one should meditate upon the God and the Goddess; one should bow to the Guru and to his disciples, beginning with Śveta and ending with Nakulīśa.
Having again bowed to the god Śiva, one should then recite the eight names: Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
Or else, one may recite the eight verses beginning with "The physician of saṃsāra, the omniscient, the supreme self," or simply recite the name of Śiva alone eleven times plus one more.
For the pacification of diseases and other ailments, one should meditate on a mass of fire at the tip of the tongue; then, having washed both feet and anointed the hands with sandalwood paste.
One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), preceded by the purification of the hands.
Chapter.

Upamanyu said: Renunciation (nyāsa) is declared to be threefold, according to the sequence of maintenance, origination, and dissolution. Maintenance-renunciation belongs to householders; origination-renunciation belongs to students; dissolution-renunciation belongs to ascetics and likewise to forest-dwellers. That same [dissolution-renunciation] would be the maintenance-renunciation for a housewife who is bereft of her husband.

I shall now describe the re-origination of the maiden and the characteristics of the ritual placement (nyāsa). The placement beginning from the thumb and ending with the little finger is declared to be the "placement of persistence" (sthitinyāsa). Starting from the right thumb and ending with the left thumb is called the "placement of origination" (utpattinyāsa); the reverse order, however, is the "dissolution" (saṃhṛti).

One should assign the letters beginning with *na* along with their nasal dots (*bindu*) in successive order upon the fingers; one should assign *Śiva* upon the palms and also upon the two ring fingers. Then, having performed the assignment of the *astra* (weapon) mantra in the ten directions, one should assign the five kalās, beginning with *Nivṛtti*, which have the nature of the five elements.

Together with the lords of the five elements, each endowed with their respective insignia, they reside in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). One should contemplate these knots within their respective seed-syllables using those same seed-syllables; for the purpose of purifying them, one should recite the five-syllabled Vidyā.

Having restrained the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) according to the number of the qualities (guṇas), one should then sever the knot of the elements with the Astra-mantra and the Astra-mudrā. Then, having impelled the self through the Suṣumṇā channel by means of the vital breath, one should unite it with the splendor of Śiva as it emerges through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

After drying the body with the wind, one should subsequently burn it with the fire of time (kālāgni). Then, having withdrawn the constituent parts (kalās) by means of the wind in an upward direction, and having indeed consumed the body, one should touch the kalās along with the ocean and, having flooded the body with nectars, settle it back into its proper places.

Then, having indeed withdrawn [the breath], one should burn away the creation of the constituent parts (kalāsarga) even without residue; thereafter, one should perform the immersion in nectar for that which has been reduced to ashes. Then, within that body consisting of wisdom (vidyāmaya), one should join the Self—which has emerged from Śiva in the form of a lamp-flame—through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).

Having meditated upon that [deity] entered within the heart-lotus of the body, one should again sprinkle the body composed of vidyā with a shower of nectar. Then, preceded by the purification of the hands, one should perform the placement of the hands (karanyāsa); thereafter, one should perform the placement on the body (dehanyāsa) with the great mudrā.

Then, having performed the *aṅganyāsa* according to the path taught by Śiva, one should next perform the *varṇanyāsa* upon the joints of the hands, feet, and other limbs. Thereafter, having assigned the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) together with the six seed-syllables (*jāti*), one should subsequently carry out the *digbandha* (binding of the directions) starting from the southeast (*āgneya*) in due order.

Alternatively, one may simply perform the five-limbed placement (nyāsa) beginning with the crown of the head, as well as the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), even without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other such rites. Having thus performed the purification of the body and self in this abbreviated form, and having attained the state of Śiva, one should worship the Supreme Lord.

Now, he who has the opportunity or who is free from confusion of mind should perform the rite of Nyāsa according to the extensive ritual procedure. Therein, first is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, after that the Brahma-nyāsa; the third is the Praṇava-nyāsa, and following that is the Haṃsa-nyāsa.

The fifth is described by the virtuous as the *nyāsa* consisting of five syllables. Among these, one may employ either one or all of them in rites such as worship. Having placed the syllable *a* on the crown of the head and the syllable *ā* on the forehead, one should likewise place *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, and *u* and *ū* on the two ears.

One should assign *ṛṃ* and *ḥṃ* to the two cheeks, *ḷaṃ* and *ḹṃ* to the two nostrils, *eṃ* and *emoṃ* to the two lips, and *oṃ* and *auṃ* to the two rows of teeth respectively. Then, one should apply *aṃ* to the tongue and *aḥ* to the palate in due order. One should place the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) upon the five joints of the right hand.

Likewise, one should place the *ca*-group upon the joints of the left hand; the *ṭa*-group and *ta*-group upon both feet; *pa* and *pha* on the two sides and the back; then *ba* and *bha* on the navel; and one should place the letter *ma* in the heart, [and the remaining letters] upon the skin and other elements in their proper order.

One should assign the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa* to the seven constituent elements (*dhātus*). One should place the syllable *haṃ* within the heart and the syllable *kṣa* between the two eyebrows. Having thus assigned the fifty letters according to the path of Rudra, one should then assign the five Brahmans through the distinctions of limbs, faces, and digits.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and so forth by them, either in sequence or not, one should assign these [mantras] to the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet. Then, one should assign the faces, beginning from the top and ending with the western one. And one should assign the five kalās of Īśāna to these five [locations] in sequence.

Then, four digits (kalās) of the Puruṣa should be assigned to his four faces according to the sequence starting from the east. Furthermore, the eight digits of Aghora should be assigned to the heart, throat, shoulders, navel, belly, back, chest, feet, and hands.

Thereafter, one should contemplate the thirteen digits (*kalā*) of Vāmadeva in the anus, the genitals, the thighs, and the knees; in the calves, the hips, the waist, and the sides. The best of those who know the ritual procedure should likewise assign [the remaining] thirty-eight digits to the nose, the head, and the two arms. Having thus performed the assignment of the digits in due order, [one proceeds].

Thereafter, the wise one, skilled in ritual placement (*nyāsa*), should perform the placement of the *praṇava*. Having performed the placement of the *praṇava* in this manner—on both arms, at the two elbows, as well as at the two wrists, on the sides, the belly, the thighs, the calves, the feet, and likewise on the back—the expert in ritual placement should proceed.

One should perform the Haṃsanyāsa as it is declared in the Śivaśāstra: having divided the seed-syllable of the Haṃsa, one should place it on the two eyes and the two nostrils; having divided it again, one should place it on the two arms, the two eyes, the mouth, the forehead, the two nostrils, the two armpits, the two shoulders, the two sides, and likewise the two breasts.

Having performed this *haṃsa-nyāsa* on the two hips, the two hands, and the two ankles—or alternatively, by way of the five limbs—one should then install the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) according to the previously mentioned method, by which the state of Śiva is attained. One who is not Śiva himself should not practice Śiva; one who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva.

One should not meditate on Śiva as something inauspicious, nor should one obtain auspiciousness from what is inauspicious. Therefore, having assumed the body of Śiva and abandoned the state of being a bound soul (paśu), and reflecting "I am Śiva," one should perform the rites of Śiva. Among these, the sacrifice of action (karmayajña), the sacrifice of austerity (tapoyajña), and the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña)—each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.

The sacrifice of meditation and the sacrifice of knowledge—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices. Some are devoted to the sacrifice of ritual action, others to the sacrifice of austerity; some are devoted to the sacrifice of recitation, and likewise others to the sacrifice of meditation.

Others are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*), and they are increasingly distinguished one after another. The sequential sacrifice (*kramayajña*) is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by desire (*kāma*) and lack of desire (*akāma*). One who possesses desire, having enjoyed desires from that [sacrifice], becomes attached to desire once again. One who is without desire, having enjoyed enjoyments in the abode of Rudra, falls from there.

Having become devoted to the sacrifice of austerity (tapo-yajña), one is born [therein]; of this there is no doubt. And the ascetic, having enjoyed pleasures therein and subsequently descended from that state, becomes a human being on earth, devoted to recitation and meditation (japa-dhyāna). By virtue of that excellence, the mortal who is devoted to recitation and meditation [attains this state] here.

Having attained knowledge, one will very soon reach union with Śiva. Therefore, for embodied beings, even the sacrifice of action (karmayajña) becomes liberation when performed according to the command of Śiva; however, when devoid of desire or bound by desire, it leads only to bondage. Consequently, among the five sacrifices, one should be devoted to meditation and knowledge.

He who possesses both meditation (*dhyāna*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) has crossed the ocean of existence. Free from defects such as violence and the like, he is pure and accomplished through the mind. The sacrifice of meditation is superior to that, bestowing the fruit of liberation; for those who perform external rituals do not share in the fruit to such an extent.

Just as one sees [images] in the palace of a king, so too here among those who perform rituals; for the subtle body of those absorbed in meditation becomes directly perceptible as divine. Just as here the gross [forms] of ritual acts are fashioned from clay, wood, and so forth, therefore those devoted to the sacrifice of meditation [should regard] the gods as made of stone or clay.

They do not proceed to the extreme [of worldly existence] because of their knowledge of the true nature of Śiva. That man who, having abandoned Śiva who resides within himself, worships him externally, is like one who discards the fruit held in his hand and licks his own elbow. From knowledge comes meditation, and from meditation, knowledge proceeds further.

Liberation arises from both of these; therefore, one should be devoted to meditation. With a mind pierced by faith, one should [meditate] at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], or likewise on the crown of the head, the forehead, between the two eyebrows, on the tip of the nose, or on the mouth, the throat, the heart, or the navel—that is, in the eternal locus.

One should worship the God and the Goddess with the ritual offerings of external sacrifice; or else, one should worship daily in a linga, whether it be an artificial one or otherwise; or in the fire, or on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), with devotion according to one’s means. Or else, one should worship the Supreme Lord both internally and externally. One who is devoted to internal sacrifice may perform external worship or not at all.
Upamanyu said: I shall explain, in brief, the procedure for worship as it was taught by Śiva himself to Śivā within the Śiva-śāstra.
Having performed the internal sacrifice (aṅgayāga), which concludes with the fire-rite (agnikārya), one may or may not subsequently perform the external sacrifice (bahiryāga).
There, having mentally conceived the substances and purified them, and having meditated upon the god Vināyaka and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite;
Having properly propitiated Nandīśa in the south and Suyaśas in the north with his mind, the wise practitioner should prepare the seat.
Engaged in propitiation and other rites, he should assume the lion posture (siṃhayoga), the seated posture (āsana), or the pure lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with the three principles (tattva).
Above that, one should meditate upon Śiva together with Ambā, who is enchanting to all, endowed with every auspicious mark, and beautiful in every limb.
Endowed with every excellence and adorned with all ornaments, his face, hands, and feet are red, and his countenance bears a smile like the kunda flower or the moon.
Resembling pure crystal, with three eyes like blossoming lotuses, four-armed, with noble limbs, and bearing the beautiful crescent moon.
Hara has hands granting boons and fearlessness, and he holds a deer and an axe; he wears serpents as necklaces and bracelets, and his throat is beautifully dark blue.
Then, one should contemplate Maheśvarī on his left side, together with her attendants and retinue, and beyond all comparison.
Her complexion was like the petals of a full-blown blue lotus; her eyes were wide and long; her face possessed the splendor of the full moon; and her hair was dark and curled.
Resembling the petals of a blue lotus, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, and possessing breasts that are exceedingly round, firm, lofty, smooth, and full.
She had a slender waist and broad hips, was dressed in fine yellow garments, was adorned with all ornaments, and was radiant with a tilaka mark upon her forehead.
Adorned with a mass of hair strewn with various flowers, her form was pleasing in every respect, and her face was slightly downcast with modesty.
Holding a shining golden lotus in her right hand, and placing another like a staff in her other hand, she was seated upon a great throne.
Having thus meditated upon the God and the Goddess—who are the direct embodiments of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who sever the bonds—upon an auspicious and excellent seat;
One should worship with devotion using all ritual offerings and the flowers of one's inner disposition; or else, having thus mentally conceived any one of the forms of the All-pervading Lord.
Either the Śaivī known as Sadāśiva, or likewise the supreme Māheśvarī, or that which is designated as the twenty-sixth principle, or else that called Śrīkaṇṭha.

And having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and other rites upon one's own body as prescribed, one should likewise perform them upon this image of Śiva, who is embodied and transcends both the existent and the non-existent.

Having meditated, one should indeed perform the worship mentally according to the external sequence; afterwards, one should visualize the fire-oblation (homa) in the navel with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and other offerings.
And one should meditate on Śiva between the eyebrows, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp; thus, in this auspicious yoga consisting of meditation, whether within the body or independently.
The ritual procedure ending with the fire-rite (agnikārya) is the same everywhere; then, having completed the entire sequence of worship consisting of mental contemplation, [one should proceed].
One should worship the God in a linga, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even in the fire.
Upamanyu said: One should sprinkle the place of worship with the root mantra for the sake of purification; one should then cast a flower there with water scented by sandalwood.
Having dispelled the obstacles with the Astra-mantra and veiled [the site] with the Varma-mantra, and having assigned the Astra-mantra to the directions, one should prepare the ground for worship.
There, having spread darbha grass around and washed [the vessels] with sprinkling and other rites, one should purify all the vessels and perform the purification of the ritual substances.
The sprinkling vessel (prokṣaṇī), the arghya vessel, and after that the pādya vessel, as well as the vessel for the ācamanīya—this is the quartet.
Having washed, sprinkled, and inspected them, one should then pour auspicious water into them; one should also cast all meritorious substances therein according to their availability.
Jewels, silver, gold, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth; fruits, sprouts, and darbha grass—these are the various kinds of meritorious substances.
One should place cool and pleasing flowers and other offerings into the bath water, and especially into the fragrant water used for drinking.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with *uśīra* and sandalwood, as well as *jātī*, *kōlaka*, camphor, *bahumūla*, and *tamālaka*.
One should especially cast camphor, sandalwood, and cardamom—having ground them—into all the vessels for the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Blades of kusha grass, unbroken grains, barley, rice, sesame seeds, clarified butter, white mustard, flowers, and sacred ash [should be placed] in the arghya vessel.
One should sequentially cast kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, tamālaka, and sacred ash into the prokṣaṇī vessel.

Having placed the mantra everywhere and having enveloped it on the outside with the armor-mantra (varman), one should thereafter protect it with the weapon-mantra (astra) and display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Having sprinkled all the articles of worship with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using the root mantra, one should then purify them according to the prescribed rule.
In the absence of a single *prokṣaṇī* vessel for all rites, the best of practitioners should prepare the *arghya* with water; that is the general rule.
Then, having worshipped the deity Vināyaka with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, according to the prescribed ritual in due order, one should proceed to the right side of the door.
One should properly worship Nandin himself as the lord of the inner apartments—resembling a mountain of gold and adorned with all ornaments.
The Lord is gentle, crowned with the crescent moon, possessing three eyes and four arms, holding a blazing trident, a deer-skin, and a sharp cane-staff.
One with a face like the lunar orb or else with the face of a lion, and the wife of the Maruts, the daughter of the wind, at the northern side of the gateway.
Having worshipped his mother Suyashā, who was devoted to virtuous vows and intent upon adorning his feet, he entered the inner apartment of the Supreme Lord.
Having worshipped the liṅga with those materials, one should remove the floral remains (nirmālya); having washed it, one should place a flower upon one's head for the sake of its purification.

Holding flowers in his hand, he should recite the mantra according to his ability for the purification of the mantra; having propitiated Caṇḍa in the northeast, he should offer him the remains of the flowers (nirmālya).

Afterwards, one should fashion the seat and the supporting base (ādhāra) and so forth in due order; one should meditate upon the auspicious Ādhāra-śakti, who is dark-complexioned, situated below on the ground.
In front of her was Ananta, white, with five hoods in the form of a coil, his neck uplifted, as if licking the sky.
Above that is an auspicious seat consisting of four lions; its feet are indeed Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.

In terms of color, those beginning with the southeast (Āgneya) are white, red, yellow, and dark; and the factors beginning with non-virtue (Adharma), starting from the east and ending in the north, follow in sequence.
One should meditate upon his limbs as resembling lapis lazuli gems; his upper covering is a pure, white lotus seat.
They say its eight petals are the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*, and its filaments are the Rudras beginning with Vāma, together with the powers beginning with Vāmā.
The seeds are those very powers, internal and transcendent (manonmanī); the pericarp is supreme detachment, and the stalk is knowledge whose essence is Śiva.

And the bulb (kanda), whose nature is the dharma of Śiva, is at the end of the pericarp within the three circles; above the three circles is the seat consisting of the triad of principles beginning with the Self (ātman).
Upon all the seats, one should fashion a divine seat, spread with various beautiful coverings, which is radiant with pure knowledge.
One should perform the invocation, the installation, the confinement, the inspection, and the prostration, forming each respective mudrā individually.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, and thereafter incense, a lamp, and betel leaf, one should then cause the two Śivas to be bathed.

Alternatively, having thus mentally constructed the seat and the form itself, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and likewise with the other mantras.
Then one should invoke Śiva, the supreme cause of the Goddess—the Lord who resembles pure crystal, who is immovable and imperishable.
The supreme cause of all worlds, consisting of all worlds, abiding both within and without, pervading everything—smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest.
The immutable Lord is visible to His devotees without effort, yet He remains beyond the reach even of the gods such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.

The wise have heard that the essence of the gods is beyond the reach [of ordinary perception]; it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and is the medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
Known as the Śiva-tattva, which exists eternally in the world for the sake of Śiva, one should worship that supreme liṅga with devotion, offering the five-fold services.
At the time of bathing, one should perform auspicious rites such as the utterance of "Jaya" for the Liṅga-form of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
With the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), ghee, milk, curd, honey, and so forth; with roots, fruits, and essences; and with sesame, mustard seeds, and parched grain flour.
Having bathed [the image] with auspicious seeds such as barley and having anointed it with pastes made from mung beans and other ingredients, one should bathe it with warm water.

One should rub [the image] with bilva leaves and other substances to remove the odor of the ointment; then, having bathed it again with waters according to the ritual procedures for a universal monarch (cakravartin).
One should offer fragrant *āmalaka* fruit and turmeric in the proper sequence; thereafter, having cleansed the *liṅga* or the image (*bera*) with water.
One should bathe [the deity] with fragrant water, with water containing *kuśa* grass and flowers, and with water containing gold and gems, using mantras perfected according to the proper sequence.
But in the absence of these materials, one should bathe Śiva with faith using whatever substances are available, or even with water consecrated by mantras alone.
Then, one should perform the ritual bath preceded by mantras, using a water-pot, a conch shell, a vardhanī vessel, or even the hand, provided it is accompanied by kuśa grass and flowers.
With the Pavamāna, Rudra, Nīla, and Tvarita hymns, as well as the Liṅgasūkta and other sūktas, and with the Śiras-atharvaṇa.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the Ṛg verses, the Sāman chants, the Śaiva mantras, the five Brahma-mantras, and with the Śiva-mantra and the Praṇava.
Just as one should perform the bathing and other rites for the god, so should one do for the goddess; there is no distinction whatsoever between them, since they are equal.
Having first performed the rites such as bathing and so forth dedicated to the Deity, one should subsequently perform them for the Goddesses, according to the command of the God of Gods.
When Ardhanārīśvara is worshipped, no distinction of priority or posteriority exists, whether the ritual services are performed at the Linga or elsewhere.
Having performed the consecration of the linga with pure and fragrant substances, and having wiped it with a cloth, one should offer garments and a sacred thread.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, ornaments, incense, a lamp, food offerings, drinking water, and water for cleansing the mouth.
Furthermore, [he offered] water for sipping and mouth-perfume thereafter; then a beautiful and auspicious crown, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Adornments, purifying substances, and various kinds of garlands; fans, chowries, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan, and a mirror.

Having offered the *nīrājana* lamp, one should perform the rite accompanied by the sounds of all auspicious instruments, as well as songs, dances, and the like, together with shouts of "Victory! (*jaya*).
In a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or an auspicious earthenware one, [one should offer] lotuses, beautiful flowers, seeds, curd, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
With a trident, a pair of conchs, a lotus, and a nandyāvarta—all made from dried cow dung—and marked with the signs of Śrīvatsa, svastika, mirror, and thunderbolt, starting from the southeast (Agni).
Having arranged eight lamps all around and one in the center, one should contemplate and worship those nine Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, within them.

Having covered it with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and protected it on all sides with the weapon-mantra (astra), and having displayed the cow-seal (dhenumudrā), one should lift up the vessel with both hands.
Alternatively, one should place five lamps in the vessel in due order—either in the intermediate directions and in the center, or else just a single lamp.
Then, having lifted that vessel, one should rotate it three times clockwise over the *liṅga* and other objects in succession, reciting the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon the head and fragrant ashes; after making a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should subsequently present the offerings (*upahāra*).
Then one should offer water for drinking, and having offered water for sipping (ācamana) once more, one should present betel-leaf accompanied by the five fragrant substances (pañcasaugaṃdhika).

One should sprinkle the items to be sprinkled and cause songs and dances to be performed; having meditated upon Śiva and Śivā in the linga and other icons, one should recite the mantra of Śiva with the power [of concentration].
One should perform circumambulation, prostration, praise, self-surrender, and the presentation of one's tasks with humility.

Having offered the *arghya* and a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and having bound the mudrās according to the rule, one should thereafter ask the deity for forgiveness, dismiss the deity, and contemplate it within oneself.

In times of extreme distress, one may perform the rites from the water for the feet (pādya) up to the mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), or even from the water of honor (arghya) onwards, or simply offer a scattering of flowers, provided it is done with sincere devotion.
By that alone, the supreme dharma would be well-performed in meditation; one should not eat without having worshipped Śiva until the movement of the vital breaths has ceased.
If a wicked person should eat [forbidden food] at will, there is no atonement for him; but if he eats it through negligence, he should diligently vomit it up.
Having bathed, worshipped the God and the Goddess twice as much, and observed a fast, one should practice the ten-thousand-fold recitation of Śiva while observing celibacy.
On the following day, having offered gold and other gifts to Śiva according to one's ability, or to a devotee of Śiva after performing a great worship, one shall become pure.
Upamanyu said: "I shall now declare briefly, and not in detail, that which was left unsaid here regarding worship, as if out of fear of exceeding the lotuses [of my intellect]."

One should perform the worship of the retinue (āvaraṇābhyarcā) either before the offering of the oblation (havirnivedana), after the offering of the lamp (dīpadāna), or when the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) has arrived.
There, from Īśāna to Sadyojāta and from Rudra to the Weapon (astra), one should recite [the mantras] for Śiva or Śivā in the first enclosure.
In the northeast, in the eastern part, and likewise in the south and north; and in the west, in the southeast, in the northeast, and likewise in the southwest.
Then, from the northwest to the northeast, and subsequently in the four cardinal directions, the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) is described, which consists of a collection of mantras.
Alternatively, one may worship [the deities] beginning with the Heart-mantra and ending with the Weapon-mantra; outside of that, one should worship Śakra in the east and Yama in the south.
A wise man should worship Varuṇa in the western quarter, Dhanada in the northern, Īśa in the northeast, Anala in his own [southeastern] quarter, and Nirṛti in the southwest.

In the northwest, one should place Māruta; in the southwest, Viṣṇu; in the southeast, Vidhi (Brahmā); and in the northeast, Īśvara. Outside the lotus, one should also place the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt and ending with the lotus.

One should worship the world-protectors in their well-known forms in their respective directions in due order, having gazed upon the god and the goddess, as well as all the deities of the surrounding enclosures.

They should be meditated upon as seated at ease with their palms joined in the añjali gesture; [one should worship] all the deities of the enclosures by reciting their respective names preceded by "namaḥ."
One should perform worship with flowers, bowing to all in due order; one may also worship the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) by means of its own specific enclosure.
In yoga, meditation, recitation, or fire-sacrifice—whether external or internal—the sixfold oblation should be offered, consisting of pure food and indeed mung-bean rice.
Rice-milk mixed with curd, or molasses-based food soaked in honey—either one of these or several combined, accompanied by various side dishes.
One should offer excellent churned curd mixed with pieces of jaggery, as well as various foods, primarily cakes, and delicious fruits.
Water exceedingly cool, enriched with red sandalwood and flowers, along with soft betel nut smeared with the juice of cardamom and sugar.
The leaves of the *nāgavallī* (betel vine) are joined with *khadira* and other woods; they are made white or golden-colored, auspicious, and well-prepared.
One should take white powdered stone that is neither too dry nor spoiled, as well as camphor, *kaṅkola*, and fresh, auspicious *jāti* and other spices.
The ointment should consist of sandalwood, root-wood dust, musk, saffron, and the essence of deer-musk.
Flowers that are fragrant, pure, and auspicious are acceptable; those that are odorless, foul-smelling, defiled, or stale are not.
Garments that have already worn out by themselves should not be offered in the worship of Śiva; rather, only soft garments made of gold should be given.
These ornaments, especially those resembling circles of lightning, are all [perfumed] with camphor, resin, agallochum, and sandalwood.
They were fanned with masses of flowers and perfumed on all sides with powders of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, wood-fragrance, and guggulu resin.
Incense prepared with ghee and honey is highly praised, especially with the very fragrant ghee produced from a tawny cow (kapilā).
Lamps constantly lit and combined with camphor are recommended; likewise, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sweet milk, curd, and ghee [are prescribed].
The origin of Kapila is desired by Śambhu for bathing and drinking; likewise, auspicious seats made of ivory are favored.
And there were variegated coverlets adorned with gold and jewels, provided with soft pillows and made of fine cotton.
There were high and low, beautiful and comfortable beds; and there was water brought from rivers flowing to the ocean or drawn from the Nandī lake.
And that water, cooled and filtered through cloth, is superior for bathing and drinking; likewise, a beautiful parasol, moon-like in appearance and adorned with strings of pearls.
A divine fly-whisk, set with nine gems, beautiful with its golden handle, and two white whisks, fine and adorned with gold.
Adorned with two royal swans in form and embellished with jeweled handles, there was also a mirror that was exceedingly smooth and anointed with divine perfumes.
Covered all over with jewels and adorned with garlands and pearls, the conch shell, sounding with a deep resonance, resembled a swan, a jasmine flower, and the moon.
Upon the backs of these elephants and other parts, they were adorned with jewels and gold; there were also delightful trumpets that produced various sounds.
There were kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, timiṅgila-drums, paṭaha-drums, and others, fashioned entirely of gold and adorned with pearls.
Those who possess voices resonant like the ocean should be employed with great effort; likewise, beautiful vessels and all types of leaf-plates should be prepared.
One should construct all the bases for that [temple] out of gold alone, as well as the abode of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
It should be constructed like a royal residence, possessing the characteristics described in the treatises on architecture, with high walls surrounding it and gate-towers shaped like mountains.
It was covered with many jewels, with golden doors and panels, made of refined gold, and surrounded by hundreds of jeweled pillars.
It was enriched with canopies of pearl necklaces, featuring coral door-arches, and adorned with divine golden crowns marked by the sign of the water-pot.
Its upper portion was adorned and marked with the sign of a goat, and it was graced by royal roads and the like, which were suitable dwellings for kṣatriyas.
It was surrounded on all sides by palaces with lofty and towering peaks, and by excellent assembly halls situated in every direction and intermediate quarter.
The outskirts were exquisitely adorned, as if by inner veils, with thousands of excellent women skilled in dance and song.
It was filled with many men skilled in the flute and the lute, and guarded by heroic protectors accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots.
It was resplendent in all directions and intermediate points, adorned with numerous flower gardens, many lakes, and numerous oblong ponds.

By those who know the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, who are devoted to the Śiva-śāstra, who delight in the Śiva-āśrama, who are bhaktas, and who possess the characteristics prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra;
It was inhabited by Śaivas and Māheśvaras who were serene, with smiling faces, expansive in spirit, devoted to virtuous conduct, and honored as illustrious twice-born brahmins.
Thus, whether internally or externally, according to one's capacity, [the deity should be installed] in a place made of stone, ivory, wood, or brick.
Whether it be made merely of clay, in a sacred forest, or on a mountain; by a river, in a temple, or in another place, or even in an auspicious house.
Whether wealthy or poor, one should worship the God with devotion using only wealth acquired through righteous means, without deceiving one's own capacity.
Moreover, even if one worships Śiva with devotion using wealth acquired through improper means, there is no transgression for him, because the Lord is subject to the devotee's inner disposition.
Even if one worships with wealth acquired through righteous means, if it is done without devotion, one does not obtain the fruit thereof; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Whatever is performed with devotion according to one's means, dedicated to Śiva—whether it be small or great—the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor.
Impelled by devotion, even a man of meager means may perform [the rite]; yet one who is devoid of devotion would not perform it, even if he possessed the essence of great wealth.
Even if one should give away all one's possessions to Śiva while devoid of devotion, one would not partake of the fruit thereof; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Neither by extremely fierce austerities nor by all the great sacrifices does one go to the divine city of Śiva, except through devotion whose essence is Śiva.
O Kṛṣṇa, devotion to Śiva, the Supreme Lord who is present everywhere, is more secret than the most secret; of this there is no doubt, and by it the devotee is liberated.
The recitation of Śiva-mantras, meditation, fire-offerings, sacrifice, austerity, sacred learning, charity, and study—all these are for the sake of inner disposition; of this there is no doubt.

A man devoid of meditative cultivation is not liberated even after performing everything; conversely, one endowed with meditative cultivation is liberated even without having performed anything at all.

What need is there to speak of one who is a devotee of Śiva, for whom even thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa penances, hundreds of Prājāpatya penances, month-long fasts, and other such observances are of little consequence?
In this world, men who are not devotees perform austerities in mountain caves for the sake of meager enjoyments; however, a devotee is liberated through his devotion.

Yogis established in *sattva* perform *sāttvika* action, which indeed grants liberation; those engaged in ritual action (*karmis*), enveloped by *rajas*, perform *rājasa* action, which bestows supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
The Asuras and Rākṣasas, endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas), worship the Lord for the sake of worldly ends, as do other men of a similar nature.
Whether resorting to a tamasic, rajasic, or even a sattvic disposition, one who performs worship and other rites with devotion attains auspiciousness.
Since devotion has been fashioned like a boat to save one from the ocean of evil, what use have those endowed with devotion for passion (rajas) or darkness (tamas)?
O Kṛṣṇa, whether one is an outcaste, a low-born person, a fool, or even a fallen man—if he has taken refuge in Śiva, he is worthy of worship by all gods and demons.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śiva through devotion alone; for there is no fruit anywhere for those who have not worshipped him.
I shall tell you a supreme secret; listen, O Kṛṣṇa, to my words, which have been well-determined after deliberation by the Vedas, the scriptures, and those who know the Vedas.

Upamanyu said: Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed; whether a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a slayer of a hero, or even a destroyer of an embryo.
Having worshipped with devotion the supreme cause, Śiva, even without mantras, one shall be gradually liberated from those various sins over the course of twelve years.
Therefore, with every effort, even if one has fallen, one should worship Śiva; provided one is a devotee, possessing no other [attachment], subsisting on alms, and having conquered the senses.
Even after committing a very great sin, if one worships the Lord of Gods with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra, one is liberated from that sin.
Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by vows—even with these observances, there is no attainment of the world of Śiva for them.
Whoever worships Śiva even once with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra alone shall also go to the abode of Śiva, by virtue of the majesty of the Śiva-mantra.
Therefore, all austerities and sacrifices in which one's entire possessions are given as the sacrificial fee are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of Śiva’s form.
Whether bound or even liberated, if a devotee subsequently worships with the five-syllable mantra, he is released; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether he be without Rudra or with Rudra, a man who worships Śiva with this hymn—even if he has fallen once or is deluded—is liberated.
One should worship the Lord with the six-syllabled mantra or with the hymn-mantra; for a devotee of Śiva who has conquered anger is indeed one who has attained all that is unattained.

In this matter, that which is obtained from one who has not yet attained it is indeed superior; of this there is no doubt. By means of that limb of Brahman, or together with the *haṃsa*, he is liberated.
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva with devotion using the Sūkta-mantra, either once, twice, thrice, or indeed at all times.
Those who worship Mahādeva are to be known as Maheśvaras; yet the Blessed Lord Śiva is not truly worshipped by means of knowledge alone, even when that knowledge is aided by the self.
Having attained the rare human state, the fool does not worship Śiva; consequently, he wanders for a long time in this saṃsāra, an ocean of suffering.
Their birth is fruitless because it does not lead to liberation; for those who, having obtained the rare human state, worship the wielder of the Pināka bow.
For their birth is indeed fruitful; those best of men have achieved their life's purpose who are devoted to Bhava and whose minds are bowed in prostration to Bhava.
Those who are intent on recollecting their past lives do not partake in suffering; they possess delightful palaces and women adorned with playful ornaments.
Those who desire wealth to the point of insatiability as the fruit of the rite of Śiva’s worship, or great enjoyments and sovereignty in the abode of the gods;
They always long for the lotus feet of Hara: good fortune, radiant beauty, strength, and a disposition tender with generosity.
Indeed, for one who worships Śiva, valor and renown shall arise in the world; therefore, abandoning everything else, let the mind be fixed solely upon Śiva.
One who desires their own welfare should perform the ritual for the worship of Śiva; for life passes swiftly, and youth passes swiftly.
Disease approaches swiftly; therefore, the wielder of the Pināka bow should be worshipped, as long as death has not arrived and as long as old age has not overtaken one.
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long worship Śaṅkara; there is no other dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in the three worlds.
Having understood this, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped with effort, including the door-sacrifice, the curtain, and the offering of oblations to the retinue.
If one should perform worship in the temple, one should maintain a perpetual festival; this may be done either by oneself or by an attendant after the offering of the oblation.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the attendants of Prasāda in due order; then, having gone outside with musical instruments, one should stand facing that direction.
One should offer flowers, incense, a lamp, and food along with water; then, standing upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) facing north, one should present the bali offering.
Then, whatever food and other offerings were previously presented to the deity, one should present all of that—whether with some remaining or not—to Caṇḍa.

Having performed the oblation according to the rules, one should afterwards complete the remainder of the worship; having performed the ritual application according to the rules, one should then recite the mantra.
One should perform the perpetual festival as prescribed in the teaching of Śiva, using a large vessel made of radiant metal, adorned with a red lotus.
Having invoked the divine Pāśupata weapon there, one should worship it; that vessel should then be placed upon Śiva and upon a decorated twice-born man.
And as he, having laid down his weapons, stood with his body visible, auspicious sounds issued from the palace attendants outside toward him who held a blazing staff.
Accompanied by dancing, singing, and the like, as well as lamps, banners, and so forth, one should perform three circumambulations, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
Having circumambulated the great seat three times by way of circumambulation from left to right, the patron enters again and stands at the door with palms joined in reverence.
Having taken it and led it inside, one should then discharge the weapon (astra), performing the circumambulation and other rites in the sequence previously described.
Having taken eight flowers, one should then conclude the worship.

Upamanyu said: Now I shall describe the fire-rite (agnikārya), whether performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), or indeed upon an altar (vedi), or in a vessel made of iron, or in a new, auspicious earthen vessel.
Having established the fire according to the prescribed rules and performed its consecration thereafter, one should worship Mahādeva there and carry out the rite of oblation.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring either two cubits or one cubit, and likewise prepare an altar (vedi) and a mandala, which may be circular or square.
The pit should be as wide as it is deep; in its center is an eight-petaled lotus, with a height of either four finger-breadths or two finger-breadths.
They declare that the interior of the navel has a height of two *vitastis*, and the middle [of the navel] is measured by the middle joint of the middle finger.
The hand is said by the wise to consist of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas). There may be three, two, or even one girdle (mekhalā).
One should fashion it as is aesthetically pleasing, smooth, desirable, firm, and made of clay; the womb (yoni) should be like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree or like the frontal globe of an elephant.
One should fashion a beautiful opening, slightly depressed and gradually widening, at the center of the girdle, either toward the west or the south from the fire.
Having moved forward a little toward the pit, leaving aside the girdle, there is no rule regarding the height of the altar; it may be made of clay or of sand.

The mandala should be made with cow-dung and water; the measurement of the vessel has not been specified. The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made of clay, and one should smear the altar (vedi) with cow-dung and water.

Having washed the vessel, one should heat it and sprinkle another with water; then, one should draw [the lines] upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth, according to the method prescribed in one's own Sūtra.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water, one should prepare a seat for the fire using darbha grass or flowers; then, one should prepare all the ritual substances for the purpose of worship and for the fire sacrifice (homa).

Having washed those things that require washing and having sprinkled them with the *prokṣaṇī* water, one should purify them—whether they be made of gemstone, wood, or produced from the house of a *śrotriya*.
Or else, one should bring another fire that is worthy of honor, together with its receptacle, having circumambulated it three times clockwise above the sacrificial pit and so forth in due order.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ), one should place the fire upon the seat, either through the path of the yoni or likewise facing oneself.

The wise practitioner should fashion the entire sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the specific injunctions; he should visualize the fire situated within his own navel as sparks emerging from that cavity.

Having emerged from the external fire, one should meditate on [the deity] merged within it in the form of a *bimba*; this should be preceded by the *anvādhāna* rite and continued up until the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

The knower of mantras should perform [the rite] according to the sequence stated in his own sūtra with the root mantra; having worshipped the form of Śiva, he should then [proceed] from the right side.

Having placed the mantra upon the clarified butter, one should display the mudrā known as the "Cow" (dhenu). The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of precious metal; they must not be made of bell-metal, iron, or lead.

They may be made of sacrificial wood, or according to the Smṛtis, or approved by artisans; or they may be made of the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other such trees, provided they are without holes and grow upright from the center.

Having joined those two with *darbha* grass and heated them over the fire, he should sprinkle them again, following the sequence prescribed in his own *sūtra*, beginning with Śiva, along with the *ṛṣis*, the *ṛcs*, and the *yajus*.
One should perform oblations with eight seed-syllables for the sake of accomplishing the consecration of the fire: *bhruṃ*, *stuṃ*, *bruśruṃ* in sequence, followed by *puṃḍraṃdram*.
There are seven seed-syllables for the seven tongues in successive order; the middle tongue is named Triśikhā, also called Bahurūpā.
The southeast direction is red, the southwest is black, and another is considered to be of beautiful luster; the northwest is known as Marujihvā, possessing a radiance corresponding to its own name.

Following each respective seed-syllable, the word *svāhā* should be uttered in due order; having offered clarified butter with those tongue-mantras, one should offer to each of the tongues individually and in sequence.
Having offered three oblations into the center with the mantra "Raṃ Vahnyai Svāhā," one should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) using either clarified butter or sacrificial fuel-sticks.
When this has been done, the fire shall become the Śiva-fire; there one should remember the seat of Śiva (Śivāsana). Having invoked the Lord there, one should worship Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara.

Then, having sprinkled water around the edge of the lamp, one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks (*samidh*); these should be made of *palāśa* wood or other sacrificial woods, twelve finger-breadths in length.

The sacrificial ladles (avakras) should not be hollowed out by themselves, nor should they be dry, nor possessed of bark, nor scarred; they should be even, ten finger-breadths long, or measured according to the little finger.

If [proper fuel] is unavailable, even all [the remaining materials] may be offered when they are the size of a span (prādeśa). [The fuel should be] shaped like a blade of dūrvā grass and four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) in length.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations of clarified butter, and likewise fried grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds, in the measure of an akṣa.
If available, foodstuffs smeared with clarified butter—whether solid foods, lickables, or suckables—should be offered there as ten oblations, or five, or three.

One should offer oblations according to one's ability; or else, one may offer even a single oblation. Ghee should be offered with the *śruva* ladle, fuel-sticks and other items with the *sruk* ladle, or the remainder may be offered by hand.

In that regard, one should offer oblations using the divine or the ṛṣi-designated sacred portion (tīrtha); likewise, if other materials are unavailable, one should offer with even a single substance, provided it is done with faith.

For the sake of atonement, one should offer three oblations after consecrating them with mantras; then, having indeed filled the sacrificial ladle (sruk) with clarified butter distinguished by the preceding oblation.

Having placed a flower before it, he should cover it with the downward-pointing *śruva* ladle together with *darbha* grass, and then, standing up, he should cover it with his joined palms (*añjali*) using the root-end of the grass.
One should offer a continuous stream of oblations, measured by a barley grain, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*. Having thus performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sprinkle water around as before.
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Devas, one should conceal the sacrificial fire; or, having dismissed that as well, one should worship it daily by joining it within the navel.

Alternatively, having brought forth the fire according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures, one should worship it after consecrating it, born from the womb of Vāgīśī, in accordance with the prescribed rite.
Having performed the *anvādhāna* again and having laid the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) around the fire, one should place the ritual vessels in pairs and then worship Śiva.
Having purified the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle those [articles] with its water; then, having placed the *praṇītā* vessel filled with water in the northeast, one should set it down.

Having performed the rites up to the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya-saṃskāra) and having purified the sacrificial ladle (sruc) and spoon (sruva), he then performs the impregnation (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Having performed the oblations separately for each and offered the fire, one should contemplate the arisen fire as having three feet, seven hands, four horns, and two heads.
Honey-tawny, with three eyes, adorned with matted hair and the moon as a crest, red in complexion, clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents, and decorated with garlands and ornaments.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, wearing the sacred thread and three girdles, he holds a spear and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in his right hands.
Having meditated upon the newborn as having taken the form of a chowrie, a palm-leaf fan, a vessel of ghee, and so forth with the other [implements], one should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman).
Having removed the stalk and then purified the *sūtaka* (the inner core), one should give it the name "Śivāgniruci" after first performing an oblation (*āhuti*).
Having performed the dismissal of his parents, and having completed for him the sacraments beginning with the tonsure and initiation up to the conclusion of the Aptoryāma sacrifice;
Having performed the oblation of the stream of clarified butter (ājyadhārā) and so forth, and then the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, one should thereafter sprinkle [the site] with the seed-syllable "Raṃ."
Having likewise performed worship in due order all around [the central deity] for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Īśāna, and the world-protectors (lokeśas), as well as their weapons.

Having extracted the fire for the purpose of accomplishing the offerings of incense, lamps, and so forth, the one who knows the ritual procedures should once again prepare the substances, beginning with clarified butter.
Having prepared a seat within the fire and invoked [the deity] there as before, one should worship the God and the Goddess and then perform the rites up to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Alternatively, having understood that the fire-ritual prescribed for one's own stage of life is to be offered to Śiva, one who belongs to the Śiva-order should perform it; there is no other rule in that regard.
The ash of the Śiva-fire should be collected, or that produced from the Agnihotra fire, or even that arising from the nuptial fire; it should be thoroughly cooked, pure, and fragrant.
The dung of a tawny cow is recommended when it is caught falling from the sky—neither moist, nor too hard, neither foul-smelling, nor dried up.

If it falls, one should pick it up after discarding what is above and below; having rolled it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire or other [consecrated fire] while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the unripe and the over-ripe [substances], one should take white ash, either after stirring it well, and cast it into a receptacle for ashes.
One should prepare a vessel for the sacred ash made of metal, wood, clay, or stone; or any other beautiful and pure material.
In a similar place that is auspicious and pure, one should deposit wealth-like ashes; one should not give them to an unworthy person, nor should one cast them upon an impure surface.
One should not touch it with the lower parts of the body, nor neglect it, nor step over it; therefore, having taken the ashes, one should employ them according to the mantra.
One should cause it to be given at the times specified and not otherwise, nor to those who are unworthy; one should collect the ashes while the deity has not yet been dismissed.
O Prajāpati, because the fierce ashes [remain] after the ritual dismissal has been performed, and after the fire-ritual has been completed according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures.
Or one should perform the bali-rite according to the method taught in one's own sūtra; then, having performed the placement of the seat of the Vidyā upon a well-smeared mandala.
Having established the treasury of knowledge, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings in due order; having prepared a mandala for the Vidyā and also for the Guru in front of the Vidyā.
Having prepared an excellent seat there, one should worship the Guru with flowers and other offerings; thereafter, one should honor those worthy of worship and feed those who are hungry.
Then one should personally eat pure food at ease, either that which has been offered to the deity or the remainder thereof for the sake of one's own purification.
One who has faith should not offer [flowers] out of greed, nor those presented by a Caṇḍāla; this same rule applies to perfumes, garlands, and whatever else.
But the wise person should not form the notion "I am Śiva" therein; rather, having eaten and sipped water, one should meditate on Śiva in the heart and recite the root mantra.

One should pass the remainder of the time with suitable persons through discourses on the Śiva scriptures and other such activities; then, when the first watch of the night has passed, one should perform a captivating worship.
One should prepare a single, most beautiful bed for the two Śivas, as well as food, edibles, garments, ointments, flower garlands, and so forth.
Having performed everything that is pleasing with both mind and action, one, being pure, should sleep at the feet of the God and the Goddess.
The householder, together with his wife, and others as well alone, having recognized the time of dawn, should recite the first portion of the Veda.

Having mentally prostrated before the imperishable Lord Sāmba together with his attendants, and having performed purification and other rites as far as possible, in accordance with the requirements of place and time.
One should awaken the God and the Goddess with divine sounds of conchs and other instruments; then, with flowers that are exceedingly fragrant and blossomed at that very time.
Having completed the worship of Śiva and Śivā, one should commence that which was previously described.
Upamanyu said: Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of occasional rites (naimittika-vidhi) for those who dwell in the hermitage of Śiva, according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures.
And in all months, during both fortnights, on the eighth and fourteenth days, as well as on the festival days (parvan) in due order.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and especially during eclipses, a great worship—or even one exceeding that—should be performed according to one's capacity.
Having prepared the Brahmakūrca according to the rule every month, and having bathed Śiva with it, one should drink the remainder while fasting.
For even the most grievous faults, such as the killing of a Brahmin, there is no atonement that excels the drinking of the Brahmakūrca.

In the month of Pauṣa, under the Puṣya constellation, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord; in the month of Māgha, under the constellation named Maghā, one should offer a blanket of ghee.

In the month of Phālguna, at the end of the Uttarā-phalgunī constellation, one should indeed commence the great festival; in Caitra, on the full moon day of Citrā, one should perform the swing ceremony according to the prescribed rite.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, under the Viśākhā asterism, one should perform the Puṣpamahālaya rite; in the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the asterism called Mūla, one should cause a cold water-pot to be offered.

Likewise, the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha or Uttarāṣāḍha; furthermore, one should arrange the ordinary mandalas in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Then, under the lunar mansion named Śraviṣṭhā on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, one should perform the water-sport consecration on the day when the moon is situated in Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Then, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should offer milk-rice and fresh grain; and on the day of Śatabhiṣaj, one should perform the fire-ritual with that very same offering.

On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation, one should offer a thousand lamps; likewise, on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the conjunction with Ārdrā, one should bathe Śiva with clarified butter.
If one is unable to perform those [rites] at those times, one should instead hold a festival, or a formal assembly, or a great worship, or an especially extensive ritual adoration.
Even when auspicious [omens] have turned back, or during praiseworthy deeds, in cases of dejection, misconduct, bad dreams, or the sight of the wicked;

In the event of a portentous calamity, or any other inauspicious occurrence, or when a disease is severe, one should perform such rites as ritual bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and charity.

The rites should be performed in accordance with the specific deity created, preceded by the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa); and if the fire of Śiva is extinguished, one should perform the re-consecration.
To him who thus abides in the supreme dharma, remaining ever diligent, Maheśvara grants liberation in a single lifetime.
He who performs these rites in successive order during the daily and occasional ceremonies goes to the divine, primordial abode of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for hundreds of millions of kalpas, that person, passing away from that state after some time, attains the states of Auma and Kaumāra.
Having attained the realms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and especially that of Rudra, and having dwelt there for a long time, he enjoys the pleasures as described.
Furthermore, having ascended from there and passed beyond the five abodes, one attains knowledge from Śrīkaṇṭha and thence proceeds to the city of Śiva.
And even one who delights in half-observance, having likewise performed it twice over, shall afterwards attain knowledge and reach union with Śiva.

But that embodied soul who has practiced half of the half [of the path], after the destruction of the body, transcends the two worlds up to the end of the cosmic egg, or even beyond to the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Having reached that fierce abode of the Lord of the Mountain-Daughter, he enjoyed manifold pleasures for many thousands of yugas.
When his merit is exhausted, having reached the earth, he is born into a great family; even there, by the power of his former impressions, he possesses great splendor.
Having abandoned the ways of the beasts, one should be devoted to the way of Śiva; by virtue of the very gravity of that dharma, and having meditated upon it, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
Having enjoyed various pleasures, one shall go to the station of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara). There, together with the Lords of Knowledge, one shall enjoy many pleasures in succession.
Whether within or outside the cosmic egg, he then returns once more; thereafter, having obtained the knowledge of Śiva and attained supreme devotion, he [proceeds].
Having attained similarity with Śiva, one does not return again, even though he is intensely devoted to Śiva like one whose mind is attached to sense objects.
Whether performing or not performing the Śiva-dharmas, one is liberated; whether practicing them once, twice, or thrice, one becomes a turner-away from saṃsāra.
Furthermore, one who possesses authority over the dharma of Śiva shall not become a universal monarch; therefore, for whatever reason, one should take refuge in Śiva.
If one has exerted oneself for the sake of the highest good, one should direct the mind toward the Śivadharmas; we shall not impose any restrictions here regarding anything by anyone.
By its very nature, this does not please those who are prone to obstinacy and excessive disputation; yet it may please others due to the weight of their virtuous mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, having reflected upon this in its entirety, one should act in accordance with one's own nature, so that the cause of saṃsāra may not be able to take root within them.
One should apply oneself to the Śivadharmas if one desires welfare for oneself.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, from your own lips I have heard that which is equal to the Vedas—the teachings on the obligatory and occasional rites for those who have taken refuge in you, as proclaimed by Śiva.
Now I wish to hear concerning those entitled to the Śiva-dharma; if there is also any action for specific desires (kāmya-karma), you should speak of it now.

Upamanyu said: There is that which has fruit in this world, and likewise that which has fruit in the next world; and there is also that which has fruit in both this world and the next, and that is further of five kinds.
Some action consists of physical activity; some action consists of austerity; some consists of recitation and meditation; and likewise, some consists of all of these combined.
Likewise, that which consists of ritual action is divided according to the sequence of fire-offerings, gifts, and worship; it bears fruit only for those who possess all powers, and not for others.
The power and the command belong to Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self; therefore, the twice-born who upholds the command should perform rites for the fulfillment of desires.

Now I shall describe the rites for specific desires, which bestow fruits both in this world and the next; these should be performed by the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, both internally and externally, in due order.
Śiva and Maheśvara do not differ here at all; in the same way, the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras also do not differ.
For those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are known as Śaivas; those on earth who are devoted to the sacrifice of ritual action are called Māheśvaras.
Therefore, the Śaivas should perform [the rites] internally, while the Māheśvaras should do so externally; however, the application of the ritual action to be described hereafter must not differ.

Having examined the ground according to the rules by its fragrance, color, taste, and other qualities, one should perform the rite there—wherever the mind desires—in a place covered by a spread canopy.
On the surface of the earth, well-smeared and resembling the interior of a mirror, one should first establish the eastern direction according to the method prescribed in the scriptures.
One should prepare a mandala measuring one cubit or two cubits; there, one should draw a stainless eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
With powders of jewels, gold, and other materials gathered as available, it was endowed with five enclosures and possessed great splendor.
The Siddhis are to be assigned to the petals, and the Rudras, beginning with Vāma and accompanied by their Śaktis, are to be placed on the filaments in order, starting from the eastern petal.
In the pericarp is dispassion; in the seed-syllables are the nine powers; in the stalk is dharma whose nature is Śiva; and in the fiber is knowledge which has its refuge in Śiva.
Above the pericarp are the mandalas of Fire, the Sun, and the Moon; beyond these is the triad of principles known as Śiva-tattva, Vidyā-tattva, and Ātman-tattva.
Upon all the seats, comfortably provided with various flowers and joined by the fivefold enclosure, one should worship together with the Mother.
Resembling pure crystal, serene, and possessing a cool radiance, he was adorned with a crown of matted locks resembling a circle of lightning.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a slightly smiling lotus-face, his feet, palms, and lips resemble the petals of a red lotus.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament, equipped with the finest divine weapons, and anointed with celestial perfumes.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with a crescent moon as his crest-jewel: his eastern face is gentle, with a radiance like that of the rising sun.
The right [face] was enriched with lotus-like eyes, adorned with the crescent moon as its crest, and possessed a beautiful luster like that of a dark blue cloud.
His three eyes were red and round, his brow was furrowed into a terrible frown, his fangs were formidable, he was invincible, and his sprout-like lower lip quivered.
The northern face resembles coral, adorned with dark locks of hair; it is playful, possesses three eyes, and has the moon as its crest-ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon, radiant with three eyes, bearing the crescent moon, gentle, and enchanting with a mild smile.
The fifth [face] resembles crystal, radiant with the crescent moon; it is exceedingly gentle and brilliant with three wide-open eyes.
In the right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a vajra, a sword, and a blazing fire; and in the left, he holds a serpent, an iron arrow, a bell, a noose, and a goad, all radiant.
It is connected up to the knees by Nivṛtti, up to the navel by Pratiṣṭhā, up to the throat by Vidya, and likewise up to the forehead by Śānti.
Beyond that, by means of the supreme kalā known as Śāntyatītā, he directly perceives [the Lord] who pervades the five paths and whose form consists of the five kalās.
The god whose crown is Īśāna is called Puruṣa, the ancient one; likewise, Maheśvara has Aghora as his heart and Vāma as his secret organ.
And that form of his has feet that are immediate; it consists of thirty-eight kalās, is composed of the Mātṛkās, is Īśāna, and likewise consists of the five Brahmans.
It consists of that which is called the syllable Oṃ, endowed with the power of Haṃsa, and likewise has its maṇḍala ascended by the power whose nature is Will (icchā).

One should [worship] Sadāśiva, who is the embodiment of Vidyā and consists directly of the three principles (tattvas), with the aspect called Jñāna on the right and the aspect called Kriyā on the left.
Having conceived the form through the root-mantra and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order, one should worship according to the rule with the root-vidyā up to the offering of arghya.
Having invoked there the Great God, Śiva himself in embodied form together with his supreme Śakti, who is devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence;
Having prepared the five offerings, one should worship the Supreme Lord with the Brahma-mantras, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and then together with the Mātṛkā.
By means of the Praṇava, by Śiva himself joined with Śakti in due order, or likewise by the peaceful [mantras] and other Vedic mantras in their entirety.
One should worship the supreme deity with Śiva alone, performing the rites from the water for the feet (pādya) up to the mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), excluding the ritual dismissal (prasthāpana).
One should indeed commence the fivefold offering in its proper sequence.
There, first, one should worship the two deities Heraṃba and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings on the right and left sides of Śiva and Śivā respectively.
Then, in the first enclosure, one should worship the Brahmās, starting from Īśāna and proceeding in order, together with their Śaktis, ending with Sadyojāta.
Therein, one should likewise worship the six limbs, beginning with the heart and following the sequence, as well as those of Śiva and Śivā, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth.

There, one should worship the eight Rudras beginning with Vāma together with their powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā, either subsequently or not, in order, surrounding [the central deity] starting from the east.
O descendant of Yadu, the first enclosure has been described by me to you; now, out of affection, the second enclosure is being told—listen with faith.
One should worship Ananta on the petal in the eastern direction and his Śakti to his left; one should worship Sūkṣma on the petal in the southern direction together with his Śakti.
Then, one should worship Śivottama together with his Śakti on the petal of the western direction, and likewise worship Ekanetra on the petal of the northern direction.
One should worship Ekarudra and his Śakti on the petal in the northwest (Īśāna), and one should worship Trimūrti and his Śakti on the petal in the southeast (Agni).
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha on the southwestern petal and his Śakti to his left; likewise, one should worship Śikhaṇḍīśa on the northwestern petal.
In the second enclosure, all the universal monarchs (cakravartins) are to be worshipped; in the third enclosure, the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis) together with their Śaktis are to be honored.
In the eight directions, starting from the east and proceeding in order around them, [the lords] are Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Rudra, and then Paśupati.
Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva—these are the eight forms in sequence; immediately following those, Mahādeva and the others likewise in order.
There, the eleven forms should be worshipped together with their Śaktis: Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita;
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava, and Kapardīśa are proclaimed, as well as the eleven Śaktis.
There, eight [deities] are to be worshipped first, starting from the southeast (vāhneya) in due order: the God of gods on the eastern petal, and Īśāna in the direction of fire (the southeast).
Between those two is Bhavodbhava, and after that is Kapālīśa; in that enclosure, one should further worship Vṛṣendra in front.
One should place Nandin to his right and Mahākāla likewise to his left; the Teacher on the petal in the southeast direction, and the Mothers on the petal in the southern direction.
One should worship Gajāsya on the petal in the southwest, Ṣaṇmukha in the west, Jyeṣṭhā on the northwest petal, Gaurī in the north, and Caṇḍa in the northeast.
One should worship the Lord of Sages (the Buddha) between Śāstṛ and Nandīśa; one should worship Piṅgala to the north of Mahākāla.
Then, one should worship Bhṛṅgīśvara in the midst of the assembly of the Teacher and the Mothers, and Vīrabhadra in the midst of the Mothers and Vighneśa.
One should worship the goddess Sarasvatī between Skanda and Vighneśa, and Śrī, who is honored at the feet of Śiva, between Jyeṣṭhā and Kumāra.
One should worship Mahāmoṭī between Jyeṣṭhā and Gaṇāmbā; one should worship the goddess Durgā between Gaṇāmbā and Caṇḍa.
In this very section, there is further a diverse assembly of Śiva’s attendants, known as the Rudras and the Bhūtas, together with their Śaktis.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra for the group of Śivā’s female companions; thus, when the third enclosure has been expanded and worshipped.
Having meditated upon the fourth enclosure, one should worship outside of it: Bhānu is to be worshipped on the eastern petal, and the four-faced one (Brahmā) on the southern.
Rudra is on the petal in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), and Viṣṇu is on the petal in the northern direction; next are the individual enclosures for each of these four deities.
Its six limbs are first [consecrated] by the powers (śaktis) beginning with Dīptā: Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and Vimalā, in sequence.
Amoghā and Vidyutā are likewise situated around the east and the other directions; these four forms are to be worshipped in sequence in the second enclosure.
Beyond that are the Śaktis, beginning with the East and ending with the North; then, in successive order, Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi.
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—these sons of Vivasvat are situated extensively in the eastern quarter and especially in the south.
Bodhanī is in the western part, and Āpyāyinī is again in the north; then Uṣā, Prabhā, and likewise Prājñā, and after that Sandhyā.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the directions beginning with Īśāna, one should worship in the second enclosure Soma, Aṅgāraka, and Budha, the best among the wise.
Bṛhaspati of vast intellect, Bhārgava the treasury of splendors, Śanaiścara, as well as Rāhu, Ketu, and the smoke-colored, terrifying Dhūmra.
One should worship these [deities] all around in the third enclosure in sequence; or else, one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure, one should worship the twelve zodiac signs, and outside of that, all around, the seven groups of seven.
The sages, gods, gandharvas, serpents, hosts of apsaras, as well as the village chiefs, yakṣas, yātudhānas, and horses.
