One should worship those who consist of the seven Vedic meters as well as the Vālakhilyas; thus, having worshipped the Sun-god in the third enclosure.
One should then worship Brahmā along with his three enclosures: Hiraṇyagarbha in the east, and Virāj in the south.
One should worship Kāla in the western quarter and Puruṣa in the north; Hiraṇyagarbha is the first Brahmā, resembling a lotus in appearance.
Time is like a collyrium-stick; the Puruṣa is like a crystal. He consists of the three qualities: indeed, he is rājasa, tāmasa, and likewise sāttvika.
These four are situated respectively in the first enclosure; they are to be worshipped in the second enclosure, proceeding in order around the east and the other directions.
One should then worship Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana—the Prajāpatis—in the third enclosure.
In the east and the other directions, there were eight [sages], three in each direction in sequence: Dakṣa, Ruci, Bhṛgu, Marīci, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Kaśyapa, and Vasiṣṭha—these are renowned as the lords of progeny (Prajāpatis).
Their wives, Prasūti, Ākūti, Khyāti, and Sambhūti, should also be worshipped together with them in due order.
Dhṛti, Smṛti, Kṣamā, Sannati, Anasūyā, Devamātā, and Arundhatī—all of them were indeed devoted to their husbands.
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva should worship the four Vedas—splendid and of pleasing appearance—in the first enclosure.
Furthermore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are in the second enclosure; thereafter, in the third enclosure, are those preceded by the Dharmaśāstras.
All Vedic sciences are indeed to be honored on all sides; the Vedas are foremost in the east and other directions, while the others are according to one's preference.
Having performed worship on all sides, either eightfold or fourfold, one should thus honor Brahmā together with his three enclosures.
One should subsequently worship Rudra along with his enclosures in the south, west, and behind; his six Brahma-aṅgas are known as the first enclosure.
In the second enclosure, it likewise consists of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras); in the third enclosure there is a division, which is now described.
His four forms are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east; the three qualities are the manifest god, known as Śiva, who stands in the front.

In the south, Brahmā, the creator who is characterized by passion (rājasa), is worshipped as Bhava; and in the west, Agni, the destroyer who is characterized by darkness (tāmasa), is worshipped as Hara.

In the gentle [quarter], Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, the compassionate one who brings about happiness through the quality of sattva—thus is the twenty-sixth Śiva of Śambhu in the western direction.

Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly, one should then worship Vaikuṇṭha on the northern side; placing Vāsudeva at the forefront, one should perform sacrifice in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
One should worship Aniruddha in the south, Pradyumna in the west, and Saṃkarṣaṇa in the north; or alternatively, one may worship these two in reverse order.
The first enclosure has been described; now the auspicious second enclosure: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana.
Rāma, another Kṛṣṇa, and you, Aśvamukha—these three one should worship in the eastern part of the third enclosure.
One should worship the weapon of Yama known as Nārāyaṇa, which is unimpeded in any direction; then Pāñcajanya in the west, and the Śārṅga bow in the north.
Thus, having manifested the supreme Hari known as Viśva—the Great Viṣṇu, the Ever-Viṣṇu—along with the three enclosures, one should worship Him in embodied form.
Having thus worshipped the fourfold form of Viṣṇu according to the sequence of the four manifestations (caturvyūha), one should then worship his four powers (śaktis) in due order.
One should worship Prabhā in the south-eastern direction, Sarasvatī in the south-west, Gaṇāmbikā in the north-west, and Lakṣmī in the north-east.

Having thus performed the worship of the forms of Bhānu and the others, as well as their respective powers (śaktis), one should then worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) in that very same enclosure (āvaraṇa).
One should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and thereafter Īśāna.
Having thus worshipped the fourth enclosure according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter worship the weapons of Maheśa and the outer [enclosure].
One should worship the glorious Trident in the northeast, the Vajra in the direction of Indra (the east), the Axe in the region of Agni (the southeast), and the Arrow in the south.
One should worship the sword in the southwest, the noose in the domain of Varuṇa (the west), the goad in the northwest region, and the Pināka bow in the north.
One should worship the fierce Kṣetrapāla facing west; immediately thereafter, one should worship the fifth enclosure on the outside.
One should worship all the Āvaraṇa deities either outside or in the fifth [circle]; in the fifth [circle], one should sacrifice a great bull before them together with the Mothers.
Then all those of divine origin were to be worshipped from every side: the sky-dwellers, the sages, the Siddhas, the Daityas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas.
And the lords of the nāgas, beginning with Ananta, together with the nāgas born of their respective lineages; as well as the ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, and the leaders of the bhairavas.
Others dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), born from various wombs; there are rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes.
Beasts, birds, trees, insects and other such low-born creatures; humans of various forms, and wild animals of low birth.
Within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) are the worlds; from that [egg] arise millions of cosmic eggs, and outside those are innumerable other cosmic eggs along with their presiding deities and worlds.
The Rudras who support the cosmic egg are stationed in the ten directions; whatever is Gauda, whatever is Māmeya, and whatever is Śākta beyond that—[all these arise from them].

Whatever exists that can be expressed by words, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious—having understood all that to be at the side of Śiva and Śivā, one should worship it in its general aspect.
With palms joined in reverence, all of them possessed inconceivable splendor and smiling faces; they gazed with constant affection upon the God and the Goddess.
Having thus performed the worship of the enclosures to pacify distractions, and having worshipped the Lord of Gods once again, one should cook [the offering] and utter the syllable.
Thereafter, one should offer to Śiva and Śivā a pure and beautiful great oblation (mahācaru), which is like nectar, well-prepared with various side-dishes, and excellent.
Having prepared thirty-two āḍhakas for the best [offering], and at least one āḍhaka for the lowest, one should offer it with faith according to one's means.

Then, having offered water for drinking along with betel leaf and side-dishes, and having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
One should procure only those excellent materials suitable for enjoyment; when wealth is available, one who possesses devotion should not practice stinginess regarding funds.
It is the teaching of the virtuous that the ritual acts performed for specific desires do not bear fruit at all for one who is deceitful, indifferent, or even one who merely pretends to perform them.

Therefore, having abandoned all improper equanimity and through the application of all its constituent parts, one should perform rites for specific desires if one wishes for the attainment of their fruits.
Having thus completed the worship and bowed to the God and the Goddess, one should then recite the hymn with devotion, having composed the mind in meditative concentration.

Then, at the conclusion of the worship with hymns of praise, one who is eager should recite the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) at least one hundred and eight times, or even more than a thousand times.

Having performed the worship of the Vidyā and the worship of the Guru, one should thereafter worship the members of the assembly according to the sequence, according to one's means, and according to one's faith.
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Gods along with all the surrounding deities, one should present the mandala to the Guru together with the implements of the sacrifice.
Or he may give everything in due order to those who have taken refuge in Śiva; or else, he should offer it all to Śiva himself in a sacred field of Śiva.
Or one should worship the God in the Śiva-fire with the seven oblation substances, having duly worshipped all the deities of the surrounding enclosures according to the rule.
He is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Yogeśvara; there is no sacrifice anywhere in the universe superior to him.
There is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by this [practice], whether it be some fruit pertaining to this life or a fruit pertaining to the next.
It is not restricted by the rule that "this is its fruit" and "this is not"; rather, this is the supreme means for the entirety of that which constitutes the form of the highest good.
It cannot be said what it is that is worshipped by the person; from this [deity], like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), that very fruit is obtained by him.
Nevertheless, one should not employ this for the sake of a trivial result; for he who seeks a small gain becomes himself even more insignificant than that small thing.
Whether the fruit be great or small, if an action has been performed, it succeeds; let the action be undertaken dedicated to Mahādeva.
Therefore, a wise person should perform this [rite] for the sake of fruits—both seen and unseen—that cannot be obtained by other means, such as victory over enemies or conquest of death.

Even during great calamities, such as intense passion, fear, and the like, or during famines and other such misfortunes, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) with this [mantra] for the sake of peace.
"What is the use of much talk? Maheśvara has declared this to be his own weapon for the Śaivas, which wards off great calamities."
"Therefore, realizing that there is no protection for oneself here beyond this, one who applies himself [to practice] attains auspiciousness through this action."
Whoever, having become pure and being well-concentrated, should recite even this mere hymn, shall obtain an eighth part of the fruit from his most desired object.
Having reflected upon its meaning, one should recite it while fasting on a festival day; or by reciting it on the eighth or the fourteenth day, one shall obtain half the fruit.
But he who, intent on the goal, observes the vow on the festival days and so forth, and recites this hymn for one month, shall obtain the full fruit.

Upamanyu said: "O Kṛṣṇa, I shall recite to you this meritorious hymn of praise according to the path of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa), by which this yoga of the Lord of Yoga is brought to completion."

Victory, victory to you, O Śambhu, sole Lord of the world, naturally enchanting, whose essential nature is eternal consciousness! You are the reality that transcends even the path of the mind and of words, which have passed beyond the realm of the impure phenomenal world.
Victory to you, O one of beautiful conduct, whose effortless exertion is pure by nature! Victory to you, O ocean of pure qualities, who possesses a great power equal to your own self!
Victory to you, endowed with infinite splendor, whose form is peerless; victory to you, the support of inconceivable majesty, the source of undisturbed auspiciousness!
Victory to You, the stainless and supportless, who arise without cause! Victory to You, the eternal supreme bliss, the cause of liberation!
Victory to you, O supreme sovereign! Victory to you, O abode of exceeding compassion! Victory to you, the independent essence of all! Victory to you, whose majesty is peerless!
O you who pervade the great universe with victory, you who are not pervaded by anything; O you who are superior to all, victory to you who are utterly unsurpassed!

Victory to you, O Wondrous One! Victory to you, O Non-minuscule! Victory to you, O Unwounded! Victory to you, O Immutable! Victory to you, O Immeasurable! Victory to you, O Free from Illusion! Victory to you, O Non-existent! Victory to you, O Stainless!
O mighty-armed one, O great essence, O possessor of great virtues, O you of great renown! O you of great strength, O master of great illusion, O you of great flavor, O great chariot-warrior!
Salutations to the supreme deity; salutations to the supreme cause; salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one; salutations to you, the most auspicious one.
For this entire world, including the gods and asuras, is dependent upon you; therefore, who would dare to transgress the command ordained by you?
Furthermore, these people always rely solely upon you; therefore, please favor them by granting what they have requested.
Victory to you, O Mother Ambikā! Victory, O Mother of the World! Victory, O you who pervade the entire universe! Victory, O you of infinite sovereignty! Victory, O you of incomparable form!

Victory to you who transcend speech and mind! Victory to you, the shatterer of the darkness of insentience! Victory to you who are devoid of birth and old age! Victory to you who are higher than the highest!
Victory to you who abide in manifold forms; victory to you, beloved of Viśveśvara! Victory to you, worshipped by all the gods; victory to you, who cause the universe to expand!
Victory to you, O lady of divine and auspicious limbs! Victory to you, O lamp of auspiciousness! Victory to you, O one of auspicious conduct! Victory to you, O bestower of auspiciousness!
Salutations to the embodiment of the accumulation of supremely auspicious qualities! Indeed, the world arises from you alone and dissolves back into you alone.
Even Īśvara himself would not be able to grant the fruit from this [act] without you; O Queen of Gods, from birth onwards, this person has relied upon you.
Therefore, fulfill the desire of you, your devotee: [may he become] five-faced, ten-armed, and resembling pure crystal.
The Lord, whose body consists of the kalās of Varṇa and Brahmā, is both sakala and niṣkala; established in devotion to Śiva, he is Sadāśiva, who transcends even Śānti.
May the Power named Śivā, who is mounted upon the lap of Sadāśiva, grant me the welfare I have prayed for, as she has been worshipped by me with devotion.
May the Mother of all worlds grant our heart's desire; she who is beloved by Śiva and Śivā has two divine sons, Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha.

Possessing the power of Śiva, they are both omniscient and consumers of the nectar of Śiva-knowledge; satisfied with one another and affectionate toward each other, they are eternally honored by the two Śivas.
The two gods are always honored even by the thirty deities headed by Brahmā; they are ever intent upon effecting the protection of all the worlds.
Manifesting their own incarnations in manifold ways through various portions of themselves, these two are thus constantly worshipped by me at the side of Śiva and Śivā.
Honoring their command, let them grant my request: [the vision of] Sadāśiva, known as Īśāna, who resembles pure crystal.

This is the form of Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is designated as Mūrdhābhimānin; he is devoted to the worship of Śiva, tranquil, beyond the state of tranquility (śāntyatīta), and established in sacrifice.
The seed-syllable at the end of the five syllables, joined with the five digits (kalās), was previously worshipped together with Śakti in the first enclosure.
May the supreme Brahman, the sacred purifier, who is ancient, known as Puruṣa, and resembling the rising sun, grant my prayer.
And there is the conceit of the eastern face of Śiva, the Supreme Lord; it consists of peace, resides in the wind, and is devoted to the worship of the feet of Śambhu.
First, in the seed-syllables of Śiva and among the Kalās, that which possesses four Kalās was worshipped by me with devotion and according to my capacity in the eastern quarter, together with Śakti.
May the supreme Brahman, the purifier, grant me that which I have requested—the non-terrible one who possesses a terrible form, resembling collyrium and other such substances.
The right face of the God, which worships the feet of the God of gods, is mounted upon the Vidyāpāda and resides in the center of the circle of fire.
The second [seat] is among the seed-syllables of Śiva, endowed with eight kalās; it is worshipped together with Śakti on the southern side of Śambhu.
May the middle *pavitra*, the supreme Brahman which I have prayed for, grant it to me—[the one] resembling powdered saffron, known as Vāma, and wearing the attire of an excellent bridegroom.
The face of the Lord is situated in the north, established upon the foundation; it stands in the midst of the circle of water, devoted to the worship of Mahādeva.
The fourth [seed-syllable] among the Śiva-bījas, endowed with thirteen kalās, is worshipped together with Śakti in the northern direction of the Lord.

May the supreme Brahman, the sacred purifier, which is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, and which possesses the gentle characteristics known as the Twilight (Sandhyā), grant my prayer.
The western face of Śiva is devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet; it is established upon the earth and is intent on the state of cessation (nivṛtti).
The third [seat] among the Śiva-bījas is endowed with eight kalās; it is worshipped together with Śakti on the western side of the Lord.
May the supreme Brahman, the purifier, grant what I have prayed for—O you who are the heart-form of Śiva and Śivā, and are permeated by the nature of Śiva.
Honoring their command, may they both grant my desire to Śiva and Śivā, who are established in the form of the crest-jewel.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire; through the armor of Śiva and Śivā, which is purified by the auspicious state.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire to me—Śiva and Śivā, whose form is the Eye and who are established in Śiva.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire; and may you two, who are the embodiments of their weapons and eternally devoted to their worship, do the same.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant my desire: Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, and likewise Kāla and Vikaraṇa.
Bala, Vikaraṇa, Balapramathana, Para, Sarvabhūtadamanas, and others—such are the eight Śaktis.
"By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, let them grant what I have requested. Then Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and Ekanetraka [spoke].
Ekarudra, Mṛti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍaka, as well as their eight Śaktis, are worshipped in the second enclosure.
May they grant my desire by the very command of Śiva and Śivā; [so too may] the eight forms beginning with Bhava, and their respective Śaktis.
Mahādeva and the others, as well as the other eleven forms (mūrtis), all together with their Śaktis, are stationed in the third enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant the desired fruit; he is the king of trees, possessed of great splendor, with a voice like that of a great cloud.
Resembling the peaks of Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and the Himālaya, he has the form of a white cloud-peak and is graced by a hump.
He was resplendent with a tail like that of the lord of great serpents (Śeṣa), with red face, horns, and hooves, and eyes that were predominantly red.
With all his limbs full and elevated, he was radiant with a most graceful gait; endowed with auspicious marks, glorious, and resplendent with ornaments of blazing jewels.
He is dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and has the banner and vehicle of the two; likewise, his other body is purified by the placement of their feet.
The illustrious cow-king, whose excellent weapon is the glorious trident, honoring their command, may he grant my desire.
Nandīśvara, of great splendor and son of the daughter of the mountain king, is eternally worshipped and saluted by the gods together with Nārāyaṇa.
He stood at the gate of Śarva’s inner apartments together with his attendants, possessing a splendor equal to that of the Lord of All, and the crusher of all the Asuras.
He was consecrated as the presiding authority over all the Śiva-dharmas; he is beloved by Śiva, devoted to Śiva, and possesses the glorious, supreme trident as his weapon.
Devotedly attached to those who have taken refuge in Śiva and likewise beloved by them, may he, having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire.
May Mahākāla, the mighty-armed one who is like another Mahādeva, eternally protect those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and always a worshiper of the two, may he—who honors the command of Śiva and Śivā—grant my desire.
He who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, the teacher, the supreme body of Viṣṇu—[how could he be] the son of Mahāmoha, fond of honey, meat, and liquor?
Placing their command before him, may he grant my desire; likewise Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā of fierce prowess—these indeed are the seven Mothers, the mothers of all the worlds.
May he whose face is like a rutting elephant, the son of Gaṇeśa and Śaṅkara, grant my request by the command of the Supreme Lord.
With space for his body and the directions for his arms, with the moon, sun, and fire for his eyes, he is eternally worshipped by the divine elephants of the quarters, such as Airāvata and the rest.

Pervaded by the nature of Śiva, Vighneśa causes no obstacles for the gods whose pride has been shattered by the intoxication of the knowledge of Śiva, yet he creates obstacles for the asuras and others.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant my desire—he who is the six-faced one, born of Śiva, the lord who wields the spear and the thunderbolt.
He is indeed the son of Agni, and again the son of Aparṇā; likewise, he is the son of Gaṅgā, of Gaṇāmbā, and of the Kṛttikās.
He was surrounded by Viśākha, Śākha, and Naigameya; likewise by Indrajit, the commander of Candra’s army, and the conqueror of the Asura Tāraka.
He was the piercer of the mountains, chief among which is Meru, by means of his own splendor; he resembled molten gold and had eyes like the petals of a hundred-petaled lotus.
The example of the prince’s exquisite beauty was great; he was beloved by Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and always a worshiper of Śiva’s feet.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may she grant my desire; she is the eldest, the most excellent, the bestower of boons, and devoted to the worship of Śiva and Śivā.
Placing their command before me, may she—the Mother of the Gaṇas, who is directly like a meteor and is worshipped by the three worlds—grant my desire.
Requested by Brahmā for the sake of the creation and expansion of the world, they emerged from between the eyebrows of Śivā, who had been divided [from Śiva].
She was Dakṣāyaṇī, Satī, Menā, as well as Haimavatī and Umā; she was also the mother of Kauśikī and likewise of Bhadrakālī.
The mother of Aparṇā and likewise of Pāṭalā was Rudrāṇī, the beloved of Rudra, who was constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may she grant my desire; Caṇḍa is the lord of all the Gaṇas, born from the mouth of Śambhu.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may that illustrious Piṅgala, the leader of the Gaṇas, who is devoted to Śivā and beloved by Śiva, grant my desire.
"By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, let that leader of the Gaṇas named Bhṛṅgīśa—who is devoted to the worship of Śiva—grant my desire."

The genitive case is used here for the object (*karman*) because of the intended expression of a general relationship. May Vīrabhadra, who possesses great splendor and resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, grant my desire, preceded by his husband’s command.
He is eternally dear to Bhadrakālī and the constant protector of the Mothers; he is also the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and of the evil-minded Dakṣa.
Aṅga-takṣaka is among the gods headed by Upendra, Indra, and Yama; he is the glorious attendant of Śiva and the protector of Śiva’s command.
By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may she grant my desire; Sarasvatī, who has arisen from the lotus-mouth of Maheśa.
May Lakṣmī, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu and delights in the worship of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire. She is devoted to the worship of the two Śivas.
By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may she—who is devoted to the worship of the feet of the Great Goddess Mahāmoṭī—grant my desire.
By her very command, may she—who is Kauśikī, mounted upon a lion, and the supreme daughter of Pārvatī—grant my desire.
She is the sleep of Viṣṇu, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the slayer of the great Mahiṣa, the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and she who is fond of honey, meat, and wine.
Having honored the teaching of my mother, may she grant my desire; [and may] the Rudras, equal in splendor to Rudra, foremost and renowned for their power, [grant it].
Known as the Bhūtas, they possess great heroism and a splendor equal to that of Mahādeva; they are eternally liberated, incomparable, free from dualities, and undisturbed.
Accompanied by their powers and attendants, they are honored by all the worlds; they are capable of the creation and destruction of all the worlds.
Mutually affectionate and devoted to one another, they were exceedingly tender toward each other and offered salutations to one another.
They are eternally most dear to Śiva, characterized by the attributes of Śiva; they consist of the gentle, the supporting, the mixed, and those composed of two intermediate states.
Whether they be deformed, beautiful, or likewise bearers of various forms, having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they indeed grant my desire.
The group of the Goddess’s dear friends, endowed with the marks of a goddess, was accompanied by many Rudra-maidens and Śaktis.
May he who is constantly worshipped with devotion in the third enclosure of Śambhu, having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant me auspiciousness.
Divākara is a form of Maheśa, a circle of radiant light; he is without qualities, yet permeated by qualities, and likewise consists solely of qualities.
And this primordial One is of an unchanging nature, yet possesses a common transformation; He is also the possessor of unique actions through the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Thus divided threefold and fourfold, and again fivefold, he was worshipped by his attendants in the fourth enclosure of Śambhu.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent upon the worship of Śiva’s feet—having honored the command of the two, may he grant me auspiciousness.
The six limbs of Divākara and the eight powers beginning with Dīptā; Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi, in their proper order.
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu are the forms of Āditya; furthermore, there are others known as Vistarā, Sutarā, Bodhinī, and Āpyāyinī.
Uṣā, Prabhā, Prājñā, and Sandhyā are likewise the Śaktis; and the planets, from Soma up to Ketu, are permeated by Śiva.
Impelled by the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they bestow auspiciousness upon me; or likewise, may the twelve Ādityas and the twelve Śaktis do so.
The sages, gods, gandharvas, hosts of pannagas and apsaras, as well as the grāmaṇīs, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and asuras.
These seven groups of seven horses consist of the seven Vedic meters; likewise, the Vālakhilyas and all others are worshippers of Śiva’s feet.
May the two honored ones, Śiva and Śivā, bestow auspiciousness upon me; and may Brahmā, the lord of the earth and the very embodiment of the God of gods, likewise grant it.

Possessing the sovereignty of sixty-four qualities, he is established in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva); he is both devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and yet mingled with qualities (guṇasaṃkīrṇa), as well as being solely composed of qualities (guṇakevala).

The Lord is of an unchanging nature; from Him, the common [world] arises before [creation], as well as that which possesses uncommon karma, through the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Śambhu, you were worshipped along with your attendants in the fourth enclosure, having divided the earth into three parts, four parts, and again into five.
Dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent on worshipping the feet of Śiva—having duly honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the World, Virāṭ, Kāla, and Puruṣa; Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana.
And the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), Dakṣa and the others, the sons of Brahmā—eleven of them together with their wives—as well as Dharma and Saṃkalpa.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to devotion toward Śiva, may all these who are subject to the command of Śiva grant me auspiciousness.
And likewise, the four Vedas together with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, along with the Dharmaśāstras endowed with Vedic sciences;
May those [scriptures] whose meanings appear mutually contradictory, yet which establish Śiva as the primordial nature, bestow auspiciousness upon me by honoring the command of Śiva and Śivā.
Then Rudra, the Great God, the most venerable form of Śambhu, the sovereign of the fiery mandala, the Lord endowed with manly sovereignty, [appeared].
Endowed with the conceit of being Śiva, he is both devoid of qualities and yet consists of the three qualities; he is purely sattvic, as well as rājasic and tāmasa.
Formerly delighting in changelessness, he then became subject to equal modification; and his action is unique, being distinct from the performance of creation and other such acts.
Janaka was the one who severed even the head of Brahmā; his son was likewise Janaka, and he too was the controller of even Viṣṇu.
And Rudra, the Lord who abides both within and outside the cosmic egg, is the eternal awakener of those two and the one who bestows grace upon them; he is the sovereign of the two worlds.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent upon the worship of Śiva’s feet—he who places Śiva’s command foremost—may he grant me auspiciousness.
His Brahman consists of the six limbs, as well as the group of eight ending with Vidyeśa; and there are the four distinct forms beginning with Śiva, who are the worshippers of Śiva.
May Śiva, Bhava, Hara, and likewise Mṛḍa, placing the command of Śiva before them, grant me auspiciousness.
Now, Viṣṇu is indeed the supreme body of Maheśa Śiva; he is the direct lord of the water-element, established in the state of the unmanifest (avyakta).

Though devoid of qualities, he is yet abundant in sattva; likewise, though consisting solely of qualities, he is free from the conceit of modification, yet undergoes the threefold common transformations.
And his karma was extraordinary, for he performed acts such as creation independently; even though born from the right limb of the Self-born, he vied with him.
Directly created by the primordial Brahmā, Viṣṇu is his creator as well; he dwells both within and outside the cosmic egg, presiding over the two worlds.
The wielder of the discus, the destroyer of the Asuras, who is likewise the younger brother of Śakra, has manifested here in ten forms under the pretext of Bhṛgu’s curse.
For the sake of suppressing the burden of the earth, he descended by his own will as Kṛṣṇa; possessing immeasurable power and master of illusion, he deluded the world with his māyā.
Having fashioned an image of Mahāviṣṇu or even Sadāśiva, he was constantly worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas upon a seat consisting of the three forms.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet—placing Śiva’s command foremost, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and thereafter Saṃkarṣaṇa—these are declared to be the four forms of Hari.
The Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar; Narasiṃha and Vāmana; the three Rāmas, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu with the horse’s face.
May the discus, the weapon of Nārāyaṇa, the conch Pāñcajanya, and the bow Śārṅga—having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā—bestow auspiciousness upon me.
May Prabhā, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, and Lakṣmī, who are meditated upon by Śiva, bestow auspiciousness upon me at the command of the two Śivas.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and likewise Īśāna, the wielder of the trident.
May all those who are devoted to the worship of Śiva and imbued with the true nature of Śiva, honoring the command of Śiva and Śivā, bestow auspiciousness upon me.
Then the trident and the thunderbolt, as well as the axe and the arrow, the sword, the noose, the goad, and the Pināka, the supreme weapon.
These divine weapons of the God and the Goddess, having always honored them, shall perpetually provide protection for me in accordance with the command of Śiva and Śivā.
The god who assumes the form of a bull, the son of Surabhi, possessed of great strength, surrounded by the five mother-cows and rivalling the submarine fire known as Vaḍavānala.
Having attained the status of a vehicle for the two Supreme Lords through his ascetic power, may he, honoring their command, grant my desire.
Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā—these five mothers of the cows are established in the world of Śiva.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to the adoration of Śiva, may they grant my desire solely by the command of the two Śivas.
The protector of the field possesses great splendor and resembles a dark blue cloud; his face is formidable with fangs, and it is radiant with throbbing, red lips.
The glorious one has red hair standing upright, with eyes curved by a frown; he has three round red eyes and is adorned with the moon and serpents.
Naked, with a trident, noose, sword, and skull-bowl raised in his hands, Bhairava is surrounded by Bhairavas, Siddhas, and Yoginīs.
He who dwells in every field as the protector of the virtuous, who is devoted to prostrating before Śiva and whose being is permeated by the true nature of Śiva.
May he who especially protects those who have taken refuge in Śiva like his own biological sons, and who honors the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant me auspiciousness.
May Tālajaṅgha and the others, who are worshipped in his first enclosure, having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, protect me in four ways.
May Bhairava and the others, as well as all those who surround him on every side, likewise show me favor out of reverence for the teaching of Śiva.
The divine sages such as Nārada and others, who are honored by the gods; the Sādhyas and those gods who dwell in Janaloka.
And those residing in Maharloka whose offices have ceased, as well as the Seven Sages and others, together with the qualities of the celestial chariots (vaimānika).
May all those devoted to the worship of Śiva, who abide by the command of Śiva, grant my desire to me by the command of the two Śivas. 1.
The four divine classes of beings, beginning with the Gandharvas and ending with the Piśācas; as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others who roam the sky.
The Asuras and Rākṣasas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, the lords of the Nāgas beginning with Ananta, and the birds beginning with Vainateya, O twice-born ones.
The kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, vetālas, grahas, and other hosts of bhūtas; likewise the ḍākinīs, yoginīs, and śākinīs of that kind.
Fields, groves, houses, and the like; sacred fords and shrines; islands, oceans, rivers, streams, and other lakes.
The mountains, beginning with Sumeru, and the forests on all sides; the beasts, birds, trees, worms, insects, and other animals; and the deer.
All the worlds as well, the Lord of the worlds, the cosmic eggs along with their coverings, ten months, and the elephants of the quarters.
The phonemes, words, and mantras, as well as the principles (tattvas) together with their presiding deities; the Rudras who sustain the cosmic egg, and other Rudras accompanied by their Śaktis.
And whatever is seen, inferred, or heard in this world—may all of that, by the command of Śiva and Śivā alone, grant every desire.
Now, the supreme Śaiva knowledge is that which liberates from the bonds of the bound (paśu); it is known as the "Fivefold Object" (pañcārtha), divine, and excluded from the knowledge of the bound.
The scripture known as the Śivadharmas, and that which follows it called simply Dharma, the Purāṇa known as the Śaiva and the Śivadharmas, are equal in authority to the Vedas.
The Śaiva Āgamas and those others, such as the Kāmika and so forth, which are of four kinds, have been honored here with due respect, without distinction, by the two Śivas.
Recognized by those two alone for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal, may they approve this rite, well-performed and now bearing fruit.
The teachers beginning with Śveta and ending with Nakulīśa, along with their disciples, and the gurus belonging to their lineage, are especially my own gurus.
May the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, who are devoted to knowledge and action, approve of this rite as successful and well-performed.
All the worldly brahmins, as well as the kṣatriyas and vaiśyas in their respective order, were knowers of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and were experts in all the śāstras.
The Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, the Yogins, the Naiyāyikas, the Sauras, the Brahmās, as well as the Raudras and other men who are Vaiṣṇavas.
May all the learned and the distinguished, restrained by the teaching of Śiva, approve of this rite which accomplishes my intended purpose.
The Śaivas who abide by the path of the Siddhānta, the Pāśupata Śaivas, the Śaivas who observe the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), and others, the Kāpālika Śaivas.
Those who uphold the command of Śiva are worthy of worship by me as well, according to the teaching of Śiva; may they all favor me and declare my ritual action to be fruitful.
May those established in the knowledge of the South and those traveling on the Southern and Northern paths abide without conflict for the sake of my spiritual welfare through mantra.
May the nihilists, the deceitful, the ungrateful, those of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), the heretics, and the exceedingly sinful remain far away from me.
What is the use of many praises here? Whatever virtuous people there may be who possess faith, may they all favor me and proclaim auspiciousness.
Salutations to Śiva, accompanied by Ambā and his sons, the primordial cause, who is enveloped by the phenomenal world in the form of the five enclosures.
Having spoken thus and prostrating like a staff upon the ground before Śiva and Śivā, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra at least one hundred and eight times.
In the same manner, having recited the Śakti-vidyā and performed its offering, and having asked the Lord for forgiveness, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
This most meritorious hymn is dear to the hearts of Śiva and Śivā; it directly bestows all desired objects and is the sole means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever should constantly recite this or listen to it with a concentrated mind, shall quickly shake off all sins and attain union with Śiva.
A cow-killer, an ungrateful person, a slayer of heroes, or even a destroyer of an embryo; one who kills those who have sought refuge, and one who betrays the trust of a friend.
One who has engaged in wicked and sinful conduct, even if he is a matricide or a patricide, is liberated from those respective sins by the recitation of this hymn.
If one should recite this when faced with fears indicated by bad dreams and other such great misfortunes, then one shall not suffer from those evils.
Through the recitation of this hymn, a person obtains longevity, health, sovereignty, and whatever else is desired; all that remains present for him.
The fruit that is proclaimed for reciting the Śiva-stotra without first performing worship is one thing; but when one recites it after having performed worship, its fruit cannot be described.
"Let this attainment of fruit remain aside; when this is recited, the Lord dwells in heaven together with Ambikā, as soon as it is heard."
Therefore, having worshipped the God together with Umā in the sky, one should stand with palms joined in reverence and recite this hymn of praise.

Upamanyu said: "O Kṛṣṇa, this supreme deed, which bestows success both in this world and the next, consisting of the combination of ritual action, austerity, recitation, and meditation, has been told to you."

Now I shall describe here the great [practice] consisting of worship, fire-offerings, recitation, meditation, austerity, and charity, which bestows fruit upon men even in this very life for the followers of Śiva.
In that regard, one who is most skilled in knowing the meaning of mantras should first accomplish the mantra; for a rite that produces visible results does not grant its fruit otherwise.
Even if a mantra has been mastered, a wise person should not hastily perform an action whose fruit is obstructed by some powerful unseen force.
However, a remedy for that obstacle can be performed here; having examined it through omens and other means, one should first perform the expiation.
If a man, out of delusion, performs an action intended for results in this life in a different manner, he shall not partake of its fruit and will instead incur ridicule.
One should never perform an action with visible results without full confidence; for such a person would indeed be lacking in faith, and one who lacks faith does not attain the fruit.
There is no fault on the part of the Lord, even when actions are fruitless, because we observe the attainment of results in this very life for those men who act according to what has been taught.
The practitioner who possesses a perfected mantra, has dispelled all obstacles, is confident, and full of faith, attains that fruit by performing [the rite].
Alternatively, for the attainment of that fruit, one should be devoted to celibacy; at night, one should eat sacrificial food (havisya), or milk-rice (pāyasa), or fruits.
Whatever is prohibited, such as violence and the like, one should not perform even in thought; always smeared with ashes, well-attired, and pure, one should remain.

Having thus become possessed of proper conduct, on an auspicious day favorable to himself, in a location endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and adorned with garlands of flowers and other ornaments;
Having smeared the ground with cow dung to a size of at least one cubit, one should draw a lotus in the auspicious [mandala], shining with its own brilliance.
It was made of refined gold, eight-petaled with filaments, possessed a pericarp in the center, and was adorned with all kinds of jewels.
It was provided with a stalk resembling its own form, properly fashioned according to the rules within a bulb made of gold of that same kind.
There, having again mentally conceived all [the qualities] beginning with *aṇimā*, [one should fashion the seat] made of jewels, or gold, or crystal, endowed with the proper characteristics.
Having installed the Liṅga together with its pedestal according to the prescribed rite, one should invoke there and worship the immutable God, accompanied by Ambā and His attendants.
Therein, the form of the embodied Lord Maheśvara is to be conceived as four-armed, four-faced, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a slightly smiling face, her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she likewise holds a deer and a water-jar.

Alternatively, for the meditator who desires it according to their preference, she may be visualized as having eight arms; in that case, she holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a vajra in her right hands.
In her left hands she likewise holds a noose and a goad, as well as a shield and a serpent; she has the brilliance of the rising sun and possesses three eyes in each face.
Her eastern face was gentle, with a radiance corresponding to its form; her southern face resembled a dark blue cloud and was terrible to behold.
The northern face resembles coral and is adorned with dark locks of hair; the western face has the luster of the full moon and is gentle, bearing a crescent moon.
Then, seated upon the circle of his lap was the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara, renowned as Mahālakṣmī—dark-hued and enchanting to all.
Having thus fashioned the form and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order, one should then invoke the Embodied One and worship the Supreme Cause.
For the purpose of bathing, one should prepare there the five products of the Kapila cow (pañcagavya), as well as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the various seeds in their entirety.
Having first prepared a mandala adorned with jewel-dust and other ornaments, one should then place the Īśāna-pitcher upon the pericarp.
Thereafter, one should arrange the jars of Sadyojāta and the others around it; then, the eight jars of the Vidyeśvaras in order, starting from the east.

Having filled them with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and wound them with thread as before, one should deposit the auspicious substances while reciting the mantras according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
Having completely covered [the object] with a cloth such as dukūla on all sides, one should assign the mantra everywhere, preceded by its respective mantra.
When the time for bathing has arrived, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with the sounds of all auspicious instruments and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances.
Then, water with kuśa grass and other materials, as well as water with gold and jewels, consecrated with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and empowered by mantras, [should be offered] in due order.
Having repeatedly lifted [the deity] with various mantras and bathed Maheśvara, one should perform the ritual of worship with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and so forth.
The ointment should consist of eleven *palas* and more; there should also be auspicious and fragrant flowers made of gold and gems.
Blue lotuses and other varieties of water-lilies, numerous bilva leaves, and both red and white lotuses [should be offered] to Śambhu.
Incense produced from black agallochum, along with camphor, clarified butter, and guggulu; lamps prepared with the ghee of a tawny cow and featuring wicks made of camphor.

The five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas) are to be worshipped; the food offering consists of a great sacrificial porridge (mahācaru) prepared with milk, jaggery, and clarified butter.
The water shall be made fragrant with pāṭala, utpala, padma, and other such flowers; likewise, there should be well-prepared betel-leaf (tāmbūla) endowed with the five aromatic ingredients.
Ornaments especially perfected with gold and jewels, as well as various garments that are fine and new.

Beautiful objects should be given as gifts along with songs, instrumental music, and so forth; and the recitation of the root mantra should be performed one hundred thousand times according to the highest count.
In this world, worship may consist of at least one or three offerings according to the power of the fruit; the fire-oblation for each substance should number at least ten, or exceed one hundred.
Śiva, who possesses a formidable form, is to be meditated upon in rites such as killing and expulsion; [he is present] in the Śivaliṅga, in the Śivāgni fire, and indeed in other images.
Śambhu, whose body is peaceful, should be meditated upon in rites for pacification and nourishment; however, in rites such as killing, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of iron.

But in all other cases, such as in rites for peace (śāntika) and the like, [the ladles] should be made entirely of gold; likewise, [the oblation] should consist of dūrvā grass mixed with ghee, cow’s milk, and honey.
One should offer oblations with ghee mixed with *caru*, or with milk alone; for victory over death, one should offer sesame seeds, and for the pacification of disease, [the same].
One desiring prosperity should offer oblations with ghee and milk, or even with lotuses alone, for the pacification of great poverty.
One seeking subjugation should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers together with clarified butter; and a twice-born man should effect attraction by offering *karavīra* flowers with clarified butter.

One should perform eradication (uccāṭana) with oil, and again, immobilization (stambhana) with honey; immobilization may also be performed with mustard seed, while causing a downfall (pātana) is done with garlic.
Beating with blood [is used] for both the donkey and the camel; for killing and expulsion, one should perform [the rite] with *rohi* seeds mixed with sesame.
One should perform the rite of causing enmity with the oil of the lāṅgalaka plant; likewise, one may effect binding with the seed of the rohiṇī and the immobilization of an army.
In rites of malevolent magic (ābhicārika), one should offer as oblations, without exception, substances mixed with red mustard seeds and oils produced from hand-presses.
In rites of malevolent magic (ābhicārika), one should perform oblations with cotton seeds mixed with *kaṭukī*, chaff, and mustard seeds, combined with oil.
Milk brings about the pacification of fever and likewise bestows good fortune; a fire-oblation (homa) performed with honey, clarified butter, and curd brings about all spiritual accomplishments.

With milk, rice, or even plain *caru* oblation, as well as with the seven types of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, one performs either the rite for peace (*śāntika*) or the rite for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*).

Through specific substances in the fire sacrifice (homa), there is subjugation (vaśya) as well as attraction (ākarṣaṇa); indeed, through these specifically, one attains subjugation, attraction, and the state of prosperity (śrīpada).
Offerings made with bilva leaves likewise grant victory over enemies; for rites of pacification, the sacrificial fuel (samidh) should consist of palāśa, khadira, and other such woods.

For acts of cruelty, one should use Karavīra and Arka; for conflict, thorny plants; and for pacification, one who is tranquil should perform rites of peace (śāntika), especially those of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
One who is merciless and possesses a wrathful mind may perform malevolent rites (ābhicārika) in an extremely dire situation, provided there is no other means of remedy.
One may perform malevolent magic (ābhicārika) directed against an assassin; however, one must not perform malevolent magic directed against the ruler of one's own kingdom.
Even if he be a believer, most virtuous, or honorable—whosoever he may be—one should not act [offensively] toward him, even if he is an assassin.
Whoever, by thought, deed, or word, has taken refuge in Śiva—whether directed toward the ruler of his own kingdom or toward one who has taken refuge in Śiva—[is protected].

Having performed a rite of malevolent magic (*abhicārika-karma*), a man would fall into ruin immediately; therefore, one should appoint someone who is a devotee of Śiva as the protector of one's own kingdom.
One should not cause harm through malevolent rites and the like if one desires happiness for oneself, nor should one perform acts such as killing directed toward anyone else.
Filled with remorse, one should perform an expiatory rite; whether poor or wealthy, one should do so even at a Bāṇaliṅga.
Whether it be a self-manifested linga, one fashioned by a seer, or even one according to the Vedic tradition; or in the absence of gold and jewels, or when there is an inability to acquire them.
One should perform this practice with the mind alone, or with substitute materials; for one may be capable in some respects, yet incapable in others.
If even he, acting according to his capacity, attains the fruit, then why is it that when this very action has been performed, the fruit is not seen?
One should repeat it two or three times there; in every way, the fruit is seen, consisting of the unsurpassed materials used for worship, such as gold, gems, and the like.
One should give all of that, as well as a separate sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to the guru; if he does not desire it, one should offer all of it to Śiva.
Alternatively, it is given to the devotees of Śiva and not to others; specifically to one who would accomplish it himself through his own power, independent of the guru and others.

He too should act in this manner here and should not take anything for himself; yet, he who out of greed takes for himself the most excellent materials that are components of the worship, [commits a fault].
The fool shall not obtain what he desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point. As for that Linga which has been worshipped, he may take it himself or not.

If one should adopt that [practice] as a constant duty, whether one performs it oneself or causes another to perform it, one should carry out this very rite exactly as described, so that no error occurs.
Since the fruit would not otherwise deviate, what need is there for further inducement? Nevertheless, I shall describe the supreme accomplishment of the rite by way of brief indication.
Even one who is assailed by enemies or by numerous diseases, or even one who has entered the jaws of death, is liberated from harm.
The extremely miserly man is honored; though empty, he acts like Vaiśravaṇa. Though ugly, he acts like a god of desire; though old, he acts like a youth.
An enemy immediately becomes a friend, and an adversary becomes a servant; even nectar acts like poison, while even poison acts like nectar.
Even the ocean becomes dry land, and dry land becomes like the ocean; a chasm becomes a mountain, and that mountain becomes a chasm.
Fire acts like a lotus pond, and the lake acts like the fire Vaiśvānara; the garden acts like a forest, and that forest acts like a garden.
A lowly deer acts like a lion, while a lion acts like a pet deer; women act like women going to meet their lovers, and Fortune acts like one of virtuous conduct.
Speech acts like a servant-girl acting on her own will, fame acts like a courtesan, intelligence acts with unrestrained conduct, and the mind acts like a diamond needle.
Power acts like a great wind, strength like an elephant in rut; yet every action directed toward the enemy's side becomes paralyzed despite all efforts.
To enemies, every friend indeed acts as an adversary; even their living kinsmen become like corpses to them.
Even when afflicted by disease, he whose life-span is not exhausted truly behaves as if he were immortal; even unwholesome food, when consumed, constantly acts as a tonic for him.
Even though it is being practiced incessantly, delight becomes ever-new; everything yet to come and so forth appears as if it were an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
Even the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest yield results only by chance; what need is there to say more regarding the attainment of all desired objects?
When this task is accomplished, there remains nothing unattainable.
Upamanyu said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the rite that bears fruit solely in the hereafter; there is no ritual action in the three worlds equal to this.
Endowed with a preeminent merit, it is practiced by all the gods, especially by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
And by the world-protectors such as Indra, by the nine planets beginning with the Sun, and by great seers who know Brahman, such as Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha;
By Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīci, and others like them, as well as by us who have taken refuge in Śiva, and by the lords of the Gaṇas such as Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, and the rest;
By the Daityas dwelling in the netherworld, by the great serpents beginning with Śeṣa, and by the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas;
Having each attained their respective station, all of them have practiced this; by means of this method, all the gods attained godhood.
Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā; Viṣṇu came to the state of Viṣṇu; Rudra attained the state of Rudra; and Indra came to the state of Indra.
And Gaṇeśa attained the status of Gaṇeśa by this very rite, having bathed the Linga of Śiva and Śivā with water mixed with white sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped with white, blooming lotuses and having prostrated, he established there a beautiful lotus-seat endowed with all the proper characteristics.
When there is wealth, one should install a small *liṅga* in the center of a mass of filaments, using gold or other precious gems according to one's own capacity.
Having placed a beautiful and auspicious image the size of a thumb, composed of all fragrances, on the right side, one should worship it with bilva leaves.
One should place agallochum on the southern side, realgar on the western, sandalwood on the northern, and yellow orpiment on the eastern.
One should worship with fragrant, beautiful, and variegated flowers; one should offer incense made of black agallochum along with guggulu everywhere.
One should present extremely fine and radiant garments, and cause milk-rice mixed with ghee and ghee-lamps to be offered.
Having offered everything with the mantra, one should then perform circumambulation; having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods and praised him, one should finally ask for forgiveness.
Then, relying upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should offer the Liṅga mixed with all the sacrificial offerings to Śiva, using the Śiva-mantra.
Thus, whoever constantly worships this auspicious object made of the five fragrances, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
This supreme, secret vow, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga, has been fully declared to you because of your devotion; it must not be given to just anyone.
And it was declared by Śiva in the past that this should be given to the devotees of Śiva.

Upamanyu said: Whatever accomplishment is proclaimed here as arising from obligatory, occasional, or optional rites—all that may be attained immediately by the consecration of a *liṅga* or an image (*bera*).
The entire world consists of the Liṅga; everything is established in the Liṅga. Therefore, when the Liṅga is installed, everything becomes established.
Neither by Brahmā, nor by Viṣṇu, nor by Rudra, nor by anyone else, can one’s own station be maintained while neglecting the consecration of a Liṅga.
What else need be said here regarding the cause for consecration, since even the Vaiśveśvara Liṅga has been consecrated by Śiva himself?
Therefore, with every effort, for the sake of well-being both in this world and the next, one should install a *liṅga* or a *bera* (image) of the Supreme Lord.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: What is this called "liṅga," and how is Maheśvara the "possessor of the liṅga" (liṅgin)? How does he possess the state of being a liṅga, and for what reason is Śiva worshipped in this [liṅga]?

Upamanyu said: The unmanifest (avyakta) is declared to be the mark (liṅga), the source and dissolution of the three qualities (guṇas); it is without beginning or end, the material cause of the universe.
That very [reality] is the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) and Māyā, whose essence is like space; from that alone has this entire world of moving and non-moving beings arisen.
That which is impure, that which is pure, and that which is both pure and impure—thus it is threefold. From these arise Śiva, Maheśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
And the elements, having arisen through the senses, dissolve here by the command of Śiva; for this very reason, Śiva is the *liṅgin*, since he commands the *liṅga*.
Since that [Supreme Reality] is not unknown by itself, it cannot independently bring about any effect; for the dissolution of the entire world that has arisen occurs within that very [Reality].
By this alone, and not by anything else, its status as a *liṅga* is established; for the body of Śiva and Śivā is called a *liṅga* because it is presided over by them both.
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva along with Ambā there; the pedestal of the Liṅga is the Great Goddess, and the Liṅga itself is Maheśvara manifest.
By the mere worship of those two, both he and she are fully honored; for in the ultimate sense, they possess no nature of having a body in the form of a *liṅga*.
Since these two are pure, the body is designated as such only through figurative usage; that very [purity] is the supreme power of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
When Śakti receives the command and brings forth this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, her greatness cannot be fully described even in hundreds of years.
By whom even Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were first deluded in the past, when the dissolution of these three worlds had arrived.
Viṣṇu, having gone to his bed upon the waters, slept peacefully and undisturbed; meanwhile, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there by chance.
Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śambhu, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) beheld the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu sleeping there undisturbed and spoke to him.
"Who are you? Speak!"—saying this, he struck Mādhava with indignation and raised him up; yet, being struck by that violent blow of the hand, [Mādhava] was instantly [overcome].
Having awakened and risen from his bed, Hari saw the Supreme Lord; though inwardly enraged, he spoke to him as if he were not angry.
"From where have you come, my child? Tell me, why are you so distressed? Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, which indicated his quality of lordship, [the boy replied].
Bound by enmity because of the dust, Brahmā spoke to him again: "Why do you address me as 'child,' as a teacher would his own disciple?"
Do you not know me as the Lord, whose creative activity is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which, having divided itself threefold, creates this world and then sustains it?
"I withdraw [the world]; there is no creator whatsoever found in the universe. When this was said, the imperishable Viṣṇu spoke thus to Brahmā.
I alone am the original creator, the destroyer, and the protector of this world; even you have descended from my own imperishable body in ancient times.
By your own volition, having divided yourself threefold, you create the three worlds, you sustain them, and at the end, you dissolve them once again.
You have forgotten Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who is free from all affliction; you thus disregard even me, his very own progenitor.
There is no fault of yours in this matter; you have been deluded by my māyā. By my grace, this delusion shall depart from you before long.
Listen to the truth, O four-faced one: I am indeed the Lord of all gods; I am the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer; there is no omnipresent being equal to me.
In this very way, a dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and there occurred a great battle, terrifying and hair-raising.
As those two gods struck each other fiercely with their fists, bound by enmity through the dust, it was for the purpose of removing their pride and awakening them.
In the center, there appeared the wondrous, divine Liṅga, enriched by thousands of garlands of flames, immeasurable and incomparable.
Free from decay and growth, devoid of beginning, middle, and end—by its thousand flames, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were utterly deluded.
Having desisted from the battle, they then wondered, "What is this? For as long as the true nature of that [illusion] had not been awakened in them, it remained so.
Then the two would strive to examine its beginning and end; there, Brahmā was in the form of a swan, possessed of wings on all sides.
Having become as swift as the mind, he ascended upwards with great effort; Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe, [saw him] resembling a mass of collyrium used for play.
Assuming the immeasurable form of a boar, Viṣṇu went downwards; thus, for a thousand years, he proceeded downward with haste.
The boar did not see even the slightest root of this linga; he continued upward for that length of time, desiring to find its end.
Having failed to see its end, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became utterly exhausted and fell downward; likewise, the Lord Viṣṇu also grew weary, his eyes filled with agitation.
Rising swiftly from below with great effort, they then met one another, their eyes smiling with wonder.
Deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śambhu, they did not perceive what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; both stood behind him, at his side, and before him.
Having prostrated, they then reflected: "What is this? and "Who is he?"
Upamanyu said: Then there appeared there, accompanied by sound, the syllable characterized by sound—the single-syllabled *oṃ*, which is Brahman and the means of attaining Brahman.
Even that was not known by Brahmā or likewise by Viṣṇu, because their minds were obscured by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
Then that one imperishable syllable became divided into four parts: *a*, *u*, and *m* with three morae (*mātrās*), and beyond them, the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*).
In that regard, the letter *A* is situated on the southern part of the blazing liṅga; likewise, the letter *U* is on the northern part, and the letter *M* is in its center.
The sound consisting of half a mora is heard at the top of the *liṅga*, even when that supreme syllable, the *praṇava*, has been divided.
And for the sake of manifestation, those two gods did not go anywhere; then the unmanifest *praṇava*, whose nature is the Veda, underwent transformation.
Therein, the letter *a* became the *Ṛgveda*, the imperishable letter *u* became the *Yajurveda*, the letter *m* became the *Sāmaveda*, and the resonance (*nāda*) became the *Atharva-śruti*.
He established Ṛgaya for his own purpose in brief; he established Brahmā among the qualities of rajas, as the first among the forms and also among ritual actions.
[He perceives] creation among the worlds, the earth among the principles (tattvas), the imperishable Self, cessation on the path of the Kalās, and Sadyojāta among the five Brahmans.

Among the parts of the *liṅga*, the lower part is called the "seed" (*bīja*) within the three causes; it is the intellectual sovereignty consisting of the sixty-four qualities, such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Thus, the entire world was pervaded by these ten meanings through the Ṛgveda; then he presented his own purpose, the tenfold Yajurveda.

One should know him as *sattva* among the qualities (*guṇas*), Viṣṇu among the forms, the Primordial One among actions, stability among the worlds, the intermediate space, and knowledge among the three principles (*tattvas*).
One should establish Vāma in the five Brahmans at the junctions of the Kalās, Madhyama in the parts of the Liṅga, and Yoni in the three Hetus.
And from that primordial sovereignty, the universe consisting of the Yajus was produced; thereafter, he established his own self as the Sāman in ten ways.

Furthermore, he is Rudra among the qualities of tamas, the primordial one among the forms, and the act of withdrawal among activities; he is the supreme Śiva among the principles within the three worlds.
One should worship Aghora in the branches of knowledge (vidyā-kalā), as well as in the five Brahmans; the Bijin in the portions of the Liṅga above the seat (pīṭha) and in the three causes.
Thus, through conciliation, the world was pervaded by manly effort and likewise by sovereignty; then Atharvan spoke first of his own purpose: the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya).
Then [he saw] Maheśvara himself, as Sadāśiva even within his physical forms, manifesting through the activities of Śiva, the Supreme Self, though he is himself actionless.
And it is for the sake of favoring all beings that living creatures are liberated by it; for even speech, together with the mind, has desisted from [describing] it in the worlds.
Above that world is the extraordinary world of Soma, where the Lord Soma dwells eternally together with Umā.
Beyond that, having reached the Unmanā state, which is the beginning of the worlds, one does not return; [one attains] Śānti, Śāntyatītā, and the pervasive [state] even within the kalās.
Likewise, among the five Brahmās, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna are the head and the supreme [face] within the portions of the Nāda of the Liṅga.
In those [levels] as well, Śiva—unqualified and partless—is to be invoked and worshipped; that [worship] proceeds then from the Bindu, from the Nāda, from the Śakti, and from that which is beyond.
Even beyond reality is a reality that is, in the ultimate sense, non-reality; for it transcends the triad within the causal principles due to its being the cause of the agitation of *māyā*.
Beyond the infinite Śuddhavidyā, and beyond Maheśvara, the sovereign lord of all lords of knowledge, and beyond Sadāśiva;
From the God who is the embodiment of all mantras, endowed with the three powers, possessing five faces and ten arms, manifest as both the differentiated and the undifferentiated.
Therefore, it is superior even to the supreme *bindu*, and from that, to the supreme *nāda*; from that, to the supreme Lord of Night (*niśādhīśa*), and from that, to the one called *nāda*.
Then from Suṣumneśa, who is beyond that; also from Brahma-raṃdhreśvara, who is beyond that; then from Śakti, who is beyond that; and from Śiva-tattva, which is further beyond.
The supreme cause, directly manifest, himself without cause, the auspicious one; the sustainer of all causes, the meditator, the object of meditation, and the imperishable.
Situated in the midst of the supreme ether, abiding above the supreme self, endowed with all sovereignty, he is the Lord of all, yet himself has no lord.

Furthermore, [the world] arises from the power of illusion (*māyā*) due to sovereignty; it is impure, consisting of humans and so forth, and is inferior. It must be abandoned because it is other than the supreme, which is the domain of the path of ultimate purity.
Beyond that, from the supreme beyond the supreme—beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Unmanā—lies the ultimate sovereignty, which is both beginningless and transcending the state of Unmanā.
Thus, by means of these ten kinds of attributes—being shoreless, independent, devoid of anything superior, and stable—this Atharva-śruti [describes Brahman].
Because it is more venerable than that, the universe is pervaded by the Atharvaveda; furthermore, the Ṛgveda declares: "That which is spoken of by me is the waking state."
That which the Yajurveda declared as the eternal designator of the reality of the Self—that very state is now described by me as the dream state.

Since that which is to be known through knowledge has been transformed into the nature of the object of enjoyment within me, it is called "Sāman" by me; thus, everything is designated as "Suṣupti" (deep sleep) by me.
This is proclaimed by me, Śiva, through my tamasic aspect; it is called the Atharva, the Turīya, and indeed that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta).
Therefore, I declare that I am beyond the state of the paths; for the triad consisting of the paths is designated as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman.
The seeker of the state must purify that triad of qualities (triguṇya) which is accomplished by the three Vedas; the supreme state is Nirvāṇa, known as the Fourth (turīya), which transcends the path.

That which has passed beyond is the purifier of this path due to its freedom from qualities (nairguṇya). Nāda is the means of valid cognition for the two [states], and the end of sound (nadānta) consists of the state of intoxication (mada).
Therefore, because of his independence regarding all objects, the Supreme Lord is primary; for whatever entity exists, it is so through the conjunction of subordinate and primary qualities.
They declare that the meaning of the *praṇava* is both collective and distributive; therefore, this single imperishable syllable is Brahman, the denoter of all meanings.
First, Śiva makes this entire universe with the syllable "Om"; for Śiva is indeed this Praṇava, and the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva.
Since there is no absolute difference between the signified and the signifier, Rudra is devoid of thought, along with speech and mind.
Failing to reach it, they turn back; yet he is to be expressed by the single syllable. From that single syllable called "A," the Self is designated as Brahman.
From the single syllable known as *u*, Viṣṇu is proclaimed in two ways; from the single syllable known as *ma*, Śiva is declared to be Rudra.
From the right side of Maheśa was born the one known as Brahmātman; from the left side arose Viṣṇu, who is designated as Vidya.
From the heart of Śiva arose Nīlarudra, who is known as Śiva; Brahmā is the initiator of creation, Viṣṇu is the sustainer, and he [Śiva] is the deluder.
Likewise, Rudra is the eternal regulator of dissolution; therefore, those three are declared to be the causes of the world.
And Śiva is the supreme cause, the cause of the three causes; yet, failing to understand this truth, the two of them became bound by enmity through the quality of passion (rajas).
"A Linga has appeared between you two for your enlightenment; thus they say 'Om' to me, as was declared here by the Atharvan."
"Even as he himself spoke clearly with his own voice within the Vedas—'The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and thousands of other branches [exist] within the Vedas alone.'"
Like an experience in a dream, that [object] is not determined by those two; rather, it serves for their awakening therein and for the removal of darkness.
Everything was likewise sealed upon the Liṅga, just as it had been proclaimed by the Vedas; having seen that it was sealed upon the Liṅga, the possessor of the Liṅga (Śiva) then showed his grace.
The two gods, their minds perfectly tranquil, became awakened; they realized the origin, the dissolution, and the true nature of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Beyond that is the supreme abode and the Puruṣa who possesses all abodes; the unsurpassed Brahman, the partless, auspicious Lord.

[He is] the eternal Lord of this phenomenal world consisting of both individual souls (paśu) and bonds (pāśa), who is fearless from all sides, absolutely free from increase or decrease, and immutable.
Pervading both the external and the internal, yet devoid of externality and internality; eternally free from all excess, it is distinct from the entire world.
It is without characteristics, indefinable, beyond the reach of speech and mind; its sole essence is luminosity, tranquil, serene, and eternally manifest.
Then, having recognized the three-eyed Lord as the abode of all auspiciousness and endowed with such power, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa [worshipped him].
Placing their joined palms upon their heads in fear, the two spoke these words. Brahmā said: "Whether ignorant or wise, O Lord, I was created by you at the very beginning."
Who is at fault here that you have fallen into such a delusion? Let this ignorance of mine rest, O Lord, while you are present.
Who would speak fearlessly regarding his own or another's duty? Indeed, even a dispute between us and the God of gods is auspicious.
"Since you, O Lord, grant the fruit of prostrating at your feet," Viṣṇu said: "O God, there is no speech capable of praising your greatness."
For those who are obedient in the presence of their lord, silence is a transgression; "What task might be accomplished here?"—this alone is appropriate for the occasion.
Though I was ignorant and prattled whatever came to mind, I have now bowed to you; that the status of being the cause was granted by you has been forgotten through your *māyā*.
Deluded and filled with egoism, I have been instructed once again; what is the use of many explanations? O Lord, I am utterly afraid.
Since I am endeavoring to define you, who are indefinable, they call you Mahādeva, the destroyer of the suffering of those who are afraid.
"Therefore, O Śaṅkara, you ought to forgive my transgression today. Thus was Maheśvara entreated by those two lords.
Pleased, the Lord favored those two gods and spoke with a smile. The Lord said: "O child, child Vidhi and Viṣṇu! You have been deluded by my Māyā."
It is said that you two, out of pride in your power, became enemies of one another; having engaged in a dispute that culminated in war, you did not desist.
Consequently, the creation of progeny has been severed for you two, who are the causes of the world, due to a disagreement arising from ignorance and pride.
To turn back that pride and delusion of yours, I have indeed now restrained them through this playful manifestation of my own form.
Therefore, completely casting aside further dispute and shame, may you both perform your respective duties, free from envy.
Formerly, by my command, all the compendia of knowledge were indeed given by me to you two for the sake of establishing the state of being the cause.
The supreme jewel of mantras known as the Sūtra, consisting of five syllables, was entirely taught by me; yet today, all of that has been forgotten by you both.
Furthermore, by my command, I restore everything to its former state; for without you two, he is not capable of protecting creation.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva bestowed the King of Mantras upon Nārāyaṇa and Pitāmaha, together with the Jñānasaṃhitā.
Having obtained that great, supreme, divine command of Maheśvara, as well as the jewel of mantras of great significance and all the arts (kalās), they [departed].
Having prostrated like a staff at the feet of the God of gods, they then stood there, free from fear, motionless with joy.
In the meantime, that wonderful and divine linga, like a magical illusion, vanished somewhere and was no longer perceived by the two of them.
Then, lamenting "Alas! Alas! due to the sudden shattering of their affection, they said to one another, "Is this event not true?"
Having reflected upon the inconceivable majesty of Śambhu, they were freed from all distress; approaching one another with supreme friendship, they embraced each other.
The two preeminent gods departed for the sake of the world's affairs; from that time forward, all the gods and asuras, beginning with Śakra, [acted accordingly].
Sages, men, nāgas, and women also perform the installation of the liṅga according to the prescribed rites, and they worship it within that liṅga.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme procedure for installation, as it was ordained by Śiva for both the Liṅga and the Bera.

Upamanyu said: On a day that is not unfavorable to oneself, during the bright fortnight, one should fashion a linga according to the prescribed measurements, following the path taught in the scriptures of Śiva.

Then, having accepted an auspicious site and performed the examination of the ground (bhūparīkṣā), one should perform the ten ritual services (daśopacāra) preceded by the removal of defects (lakṣaṇoddhāra).
Having first worshipped Vināyaka with those ten services (upacāras) and having performed the purification of the site and other rites, one should lead the liṅga to the bathing pavilion.
Then, one should mark the characteristics according to the treatises on iconography (śilpaśāstra) using a golden stylus smeared with saffron and other pigments.
Alternatively, one should purify the linga together with its pedestal using the waters of eight types of earth or five types of earth, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
