Having worshipped the *savedikam* [the pedestal with its altar] and having led it to a divine water reservoir or similar site, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) there for the *liṅga* together with its base (*piṇḍikā*).
In a pure dwelling for the ritual residence, endowed with all splendor, provided with archways and enclosures, and surrounded by garlands of *darbha* grass.

Endowed with the eight elephants of the quarters, accompanied by the jars of the eight guardians of the directions, joined with the eight auspicious symbols, and honored with worship to the guardians of the directions.
Having fashioned [the seat] from metal or even wood, marked with a lotus posture, one should place therein a spacious and well-constructed pedestal in the center.
Having worshipped the four gatekeepers in sequence, beginning with Bhadra—namely Samudra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, and Vinandaka.
Having bathed and duly worshipped the Liṅga along with its pedestal, one should wrap it completely on all sides with two cloths together with two bunches of Kuśa grass.
Having gradually brought it to the water, one should lay it upon the pedestal with its head toward the east and its base-thread toward the west, and likewise the piṇḍikā.
One should consecrate the Liṅga there, endowed with all auspicious rites, for five nights, or three nights, or even for a single night.
Having dismissed the worshipped deity there and purified the area as before, one should worship [the deity] again and lead him to the bedchamber by way of the festival procession.
There too, one should prepare a place for the bed in the center of the maṇḍala; having bathed the liṅga with pure waters, one should worship it in due order.
Having drawn a lotus in the northeast on a ground surface that has been cleanly smeared, and having purified the Śiva-vessel, one should worship Śiva after invoking him therein.
Having fashioned a white lotus in the center of the altar according to the prescribed rite, one should also draw the lotus of Caṇḍikā to its west.
Having prepared a bed there with unwashed linen garments or other cloths, or even with flowers and darbha grass, one should place a golden flower upon it.
There, having brought the *liṅga* amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments, [one should wrap it] on all sides with a pair of red cloths together with a tuft of *kūrca* grass.
Having wrapped it together with the *piṇḍikā*, one should lay it down as before; having first drawn a lotus, [one should place the items] upon its petals in due order.

One should place the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa) in the center, and the *vardhanī* jar of Śiva; then, having circumambulated the triad of lotuses, the best of the twice-born should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).

And those eight forms are to be visualized as situated all around, starting from the east; or alternatively, there should be four students of the Vedas, accompanied by reciters, stationed in the cardinal directions.
Virañci and the others, known as the four forms (mūrtis), should perform the oblation; the preceptor [should do so] first in their northeast or in the west.

One should perform the principal oblation with seven substances in the proper sequence; other twice-born ones should offer oblations as well, either one-quarter or one-half of the amount offered by the preceptor.

In this case, the preceptor should offer either the primary oblation alone, or first having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should then offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter.
One should place the Hand of Śiva upon the top of the liṅga with the root mantra, using the seven substances in sequence for one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five [repetitions].

Having offered oblation after oblation, he should repeatedly touch the liṅga and the pedestal; then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in due order.
One should give to the preceptor one quarter or one half [of the fee], as well as to the Hotṛ priests and the Sthapati; half of that should be given to the other Sadasyas according to one's ability.
Then, having placed a golden bull or even a tuft of grass in a pit, one should [purify it] with earth and water, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and again with pure water.
One should cast the purified Brahma-stone, smeared with sandalwood paste, into the pit; then, having performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the nine names of the Śaktis.
One should place minerals such as yellow orpiment, as well as seeds, perfumes, and medicinal herbs, upon the Brahma-stone according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva scriptures.
Having installed the linga according to its specific characteristics and having ascertained that the milk produced from the tree has settled, one should place that linga upon the Brahma-shila.
One should place the pedestal slightly inclined toward the northeast while reciting the root mantra; then, having joined it [to the base], one should contemplate the Śakti-mantra.
Having performed the binding with binding substances and having purified the location, and having offered the water of honor (arghya) and flowers, they should again set up a curtain.

Then, having brought the ritual vessels (kalaśas) from the place of rest in their proper order, he should arrange them before the Liṅga according to the appropriate rites beginning with the sprinkling (niṣeka).
Then, having commenced the great worship and fully worshipped the ten jars, one should recollect the Śiva-mantra within the water of the Śiva-jar.
Joining the thumb and the ring finger, the knower of mantras should take it up and utter [the mantra]; he should then place it in the center of the northeast portion of the liṅga.
One should likewise install Śakti, Vidyā, and the Vidyeśvaras in their proper order; then, at the base of the liṅga, one should consecrate the liṅga with the waters of Śiva.
Having consecrated the pedestal-liṅga (piṇḍikāliṅga) in the Vardhanī vessel with the jars of the Vidyeśvaras, one should thereafter prepare the seat, beginning with the support (ādhāra).
Having performed the placement of the five kalās, one should meditate upon the blazing Liṅga; facing east or north with palms joined in reverence, one should invoke Śiva and Śivā directly.
Recalling the god accompanied by the goddess, he should remember him as mounted upon the king of bulls or a celestial chariot, adorned and approaching through the expanse of the sky.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by the sounds of every auspicious instrument, [the assembly was attended] by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Arka, Śakra, and other gods and dānavas.
It was surrounded on all sides by those whose every limb was drenched with joy, who stood with their heads bowed in joined palms, praising, dancing, and weeping.
Then, having performed the fivefold offerings, one should conclude the worship; there is no ritual superior to this fivefold offering.

One should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) for images in every respect just as for the liṅga; at the time of extracting the defining marks (lakṣaṇoddhāra), the opening of the eyes (nayanamocana) must be performed.
During the preliminary consecration in water, one should have her lie upon the bed face downwards; having placed her upon the water of the pitcher, one should unite her with the mantras in the heart.

They say that consecration performed with a permanent residence is superior to that which is without a residence; one who is capable and has established a residence should subsequently perform the rite of consecration.
If one is unable [to build a temple], having installed either a *liṅga* or an image (*bera*) according to one's capacity, one should subsequently construct a temple for Śiva.
I shall now further describe the supreme ritual for the installation of a domestic image (gṛhārcā), having fashioned a small Śiva-liṅga or a Śakti-image endowed with the proper characteristics.
When the northern solstice has arrived, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day, having established the Goddess in a pure location, one should draw a lotus there as before.
Having scattered leaves, flowers, and other offerings, and having placed the central jar in the middle, one should arrange four jars around it in the cardinal directions.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the five Brahmans with their respective seed-syllables upon those five [limbs] using the five [mantras], and having worshipped them, displayed the mudrās and so forth, and provided protection;
Having purified the *liṅga* or the image (*bera*) with clay, water, and other substances as before, one should place it covered with flowers upon an excellent seat situated toward the north.

Having placed a flower upon his head, one should sprinkle him with the waters from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel; then, having worshipped him again with flowers preceded by shouts of "Victory! (*jaya*) and other such cries.

One should bathe [the deity] with the root mantra using pitchers ending with the Īśāna-vidyā; then, having performed the placement of the five kalās (pañcakalānyāsa), one should perform the worship as before.
There, one should constantly worship the three-eyed God together with the Goddess; or else, one may worship a single water-pot accompanied by the deity’s form-mantra.
Having deposited everything within the lotus, one should perform the remaining rites as before; a linga that is extremely defiled should be purified and then reinstalled.
One should sprinkle with water that which is slightly defiled, and sacrifice to that which is not defiled at all. Liṅgas known as Bāṇa-liṅgas may or may not be installed.
Since those [five] were previously consecrated by Śiva himself, the remaining ones that appear like arrows should be installed.

In the case of a self-manifested (svayambhū) linga, as well as in divine (divya) and sage-made (ārṣa) lingas—even when there is no pedestal—one should install a pedestal and perform the rite of consecration (saṃprokṣaṇa).
One should worship Śiva there; for them, no formal re-installation (pratiṣṭhā) is prescribed. A liṅga that is burnt, loose, or has damaged parts should be cast into a body of water.

Having performed the ritual of joining (saṃdhāna) for that which is fit to be joined, one should carry out the procedure for installation (pratiṣṭhā), preceded by the worship of the deity, either from a sculpted image (bera) or from an incomplete linga.

Having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*), one should practice either the internal reintegration (*saṃdhāna*) into the heart or renunciation (*tyāga*). If the worship for a single day is omitted, one should perform double the worship.
On the second night, one should perform a great worship, and after that, a consecration; if the worship is interrupted for many days beyond a month, [the following rites are required].

Some describe it as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), while others describe it as the procedure of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*). In the case of sprinkling, however, one should first dismiss the deity from the *liṅga* and other objects as before.
Having bathed [the image] with clay and water according to the sequence of eight five-fold [mantras], and having bathed it with the products of the cow and purified it with water from *darbha* grass;

One should sprinkle [the linga] one hundred and eight times with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra, placing the hand—adorned with flowers and *kuśa* grass—upon the top of the linga.
Then one should recite the root mantra five times and subsequently one hundred and eight times; thereafter, one should touch [the body] with the root mantra from the head down to the seat.
And one should perform a great worship after invoking the deity as before, whether in an installed linga that was not previously obtained, or in a place sacred to Śiva, or in water.
One should worship the Blessed Lord Śiva in the fire, in the sun, and likewise in the sky.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having extracted the essence from knowledge, ritual action, and conduct, everything has been spoken by the Blessed One; it has been heard by me as being equal to the Vedas.
Now I wish to hear about the yoga that is most difficult to attain, along with its authority, its limbs, its ritual procedure, and its purpose.
If death were to occur before the destruction of yoga and the like, it could be accomplished immediately by that means, whereby a man would not be a self-destroyer.
You should explain in accordance with reality that which is the object, its cause, the instruments for its realization at that time, and the gradations of its various types.
Upamanyu said: "O Kṛṣṇa, you who know the meaning of all questions have asked what is appropriate. Therefore, I shall explain all of that in due order; listen with a concentrated mind."
That steady state of the mind within Śiva, once all other fluctuations have ceased, is briefly defined as Yoga; it is indeed fivefold.
Mantra-yoga, Sparśa-yoga, Bhāva-yoga, and another, Abhāva-yoga; among all these, Mahā-yoga is considered supreme.
The mental state that, through the power of mantra practice alone, has as its object the meaning expressed by the mantra and is free from distraction, is declared to be mantra-yoga.

That very [practice], beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), is designated as the yoga of touch; when it is free from the touch of mantras, it is proclaimed as the yoga of contemplation (bhāvayoga).
Since the universe is perceived as a form whose constituent parts have dissolved, that is declared to be the yoga of non-existence, arising from the non-appearance of the existing reality.
Only the one nature of Śiva is contemplated as being free from limiting adjuncts; this mental state of the Śaiva practitioner is here called Mahāyoga.
He whose mind is detached from objects, both those perceived in this world and those heard of in sacred tradition, is qualified for yoga; no one else is so qualified.
By the constant perception of the defects of the two types of objects, as well as their virtues and those of the Lord, the mind becomes perpetually dispassionate.
In brief, every yoga consists of eight limbs or six limbs: namely, restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and likewise the postures (āsana) such as the svastika and others.
Prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi—these are declared by the wise to be the eight limbs of yoga.
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption: these, in brief, are the six limbs of yoga.
The distinct characteristics of these [deities] have been proclaimed in the Śiva-śāstra, and especially in other Śiva-āgamas such as the Kāmika and others.
In the Yoga treatises as well, and in certain Purāṇas, [the five yamas are] non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness.
It is called *yama* by the virtuous because of its fivefold composition: purity, contentment, austerity, recitation, and indeed meditative concentration.
Thus, there are five varieties of the *niyama* according to the divisions of its own parts: the *svastika*, the *padma*, the *madhya-indu*, the *vīra*, and the *yoga* as established.
The seat (āsana) is said to be of eight kinds, including the paryanka and others as desired. Prāṇa is the wind born within one's own body; its āyāma is its restraint.
That is said to be threefold: recaka (exhalation), pūraka (inhalation), and kumbhaka (retention). One should press one nostril with a finger, while the other remains open.
One should expel the abdominal air; this is known as recaka. One should fill the body with external air, like a leather bag.
Filling through the other nostril is considered *pūraka*; one neither releases nor takes in the air situated inside or outside.
When it remains completely full like a water-pot, that indeed is *kumbhaka*. These three—*recaka* and the others—should be performed neither too quickly nor too slowly.

Therefore, the practitioner of yoga should practice by means of gradual application; that practice consisting of exhalation (recaka) and the rest is preceded by the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana).
The restraint of the breath through the sequence beginning with the maiden and so forth is said in the *Yogānuśāsana* to culminate in voluntary departure [from the body].
That [vowel] is taught as being fourfold according to the division of its measure (mātrā) and qualities; the short vowel (kanyaka), however, is fourfold, and it consists of twelve measures.
The middling [breath] consists of twenty-four measures and involves two obstructions; the superior, however, consists of twenty-six measures and involves three obstructions.
Prāṇāyāma that follows [the previous stage] produces perspiration, trembling, and so forth; it brings about the arising of bliss, horripilation, and the shedding of tears from the eyes.
For the yogin, there may arise extreme talkativeness, dizziness, fainting, and so forth; [therefore] one should circumambulate the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly.

One should perform the snapping of the fingers; that is proclaimed as a *mātrā*. They are to be understood according to the sequence of *mātrās* and through the application of the process of *udvātaka*.

One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) preceded by the purification of the channels (nāḍīviśuddhi). Breath control is traditionally taught to be of two kinds: that with seed (sagarbha) and that without seed (agarbha).

Recitation and meditation without [the breath] are "without the womb" (agarbha), while those accompanied by it are "with the womb" (sagarbha). Prāṇāyāma conjoined with the womb is a hundred times superior to that which is without the womb.
Therefore, yogis perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) along with its internal retention (garbha); for it is only through the conquest of the vital breath that the diseases of the body are overcome.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Because it initiates departure (prayāṇa), it is therefore called prāṇa; that which is known as apāna leads downward the food and other substances that are consumed.
Vyāna pervades all the limbs without exception; Udāna is said to be the wind that agitates the vital points (marmas).
Because it leads all the limbs equally, it is called *samāna*; *nāga* is said to be in the act of belching, while *kūrma* resides in the opening of the eyes.
Kṛkala is to be known as [the wind] in sneezing, Devadatta in yawning; and Dhanañjaya, the all-pervading, does not leave even the dead.
Practiced gradually and according to its proper measure, this breath control burns away every defect and protects the body of the practitioner.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) has been fully conquered, one should observe its signs: first, there arises a diminution of feces, urine, and phlegm.
The capacity for eating much, exhalation after a long duration, as well as lightness of body, swift movement, enthusiasm, and excellence of voice;
The destruction of all diseases, as well as strength, splendor, beauty of form, fortitude, intelligence, youthfulness, stability, and clarity of mind.
Austerities such as sacrifices, gifts, and vows, which serve to destroy evil, do not equal even a sixteenth part of that practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
When one forcibly restrains the senses here, which are attached to their respective objects, that is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
The senses, preceded by the name [of the Lord], lead either to heaven or to hell; when restrained, they lead to heaven, and when released, to hell.
Therefore, one who desires happiness, being wise and established in knowledge and dispassion, should quickly restrain the horses of the senses and rescue the self by means of the self.
In brief, *dhāraṇā* is the binding of the mind to its locus; and that locus is Śiva alone, and nothing else, because [in Him] the three defects do not exist.
When the mind is fixed upon a specific object for a certain period of time and does not deviate from that focal point, that is *dhāraṇā* (concentration); it is not otherwise.
The first steadiness of the mind arises from concentration (dhāraṇā); therefore, one should make the mind firm through the practice of concentration.
The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally understood to mean "reflection"; it is the repeated reflection upon Śiva with an undistracted mind that is called *dhyāna*.
For one whose mind is established upon the object of meditation, that continuous flow of similar cognition, free from any other intervening cognitions, is called dhyāna (meditative absorption).
Having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone, the bringer of auspiciousness, the supreme Lord of the gods, is to be meditated upon; thus ends the Atharvaṇa Śruti.
Likewise, the supreme Śivā is to be meditated upon; both Śiva and Śivā reside within all beings. They are heard of in the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures as being omnipresent and eternally manifest.

The two omniscient ones should be constantly meditated upon through their various distinct forms: liberation is the primary causal state, while the powers such as *aṇimā* are the subsequent causal states.
Thus, this twofold purpose of this meditation is to be known: the meditator, the meditation, as well as the object of meditation and that which is the purpose of meditation.
Having understood this fourfold [set], the knower of yoga should practice yoga, being endowed with knowledge and dispassion, full of faith, and possessed of forbearance.

Free from the sense of "mine" and always full of enthusiasm—such a person is known as a meditator (dhyātṛ). When weary from recitation (japa), one should meditate again; when weary from meditation, one should recite again.

For one who is devoted to recitation and meditation, yoga is quickly perfected. Twelve breath-retentions (dhāraṇās) constitute one breath-extension (āyāma), and twelve such breath-extensions constitute one meditation (dhyāna).
Up to the twelvefold meditations (dhyāna), it is designated as "concentration" (samādhi); concentration is proclaimed as the final limb of yoga.
And through meditative concentration, the light of wisdom arises everywhere; it manifests only the object itself, remaining as motionless as curdled milk.
The appearance of [the mind] as if devoid of its own nature is called samādhi; having fully absorbed the mind in the object of meditation, one should behold it with perfect steadiness.
The yogi established in meditative absorption is praised as being like the fire of nirvāṇa; he neither hears, nor smells, nor speaks, nor sees.
He does not perceive touch, nor does the mind form conceptual constructions; he does not conceive anything at all, and like a piece of wood, he is not bound.
Thus, one whose self is dissolved in Śiva is said here to be established in samādhi; like a lamp in a windless place, he never flickers.
Therefore, the wise person, though established in meditative concentration, should not waver from it; thus does the yogi practice the supreme yoga with steady effort.
All obstacles and hindrances to that will gradually perish.
Upamanyu said: "Laziness, intense diseases, negligence, doubt regarding one's station, instability of mind, lack of faith, and deluded vision."
Suffering, mental distress, and longing for sense objects—these ten are proclaimed as the obstacles for men who are striving [for liberation].

Laziness and impurity of being belong to the body and consciousness of yogis; defects born from an imbalance of the bodily constituents are diseases, while those born from the defects of karma are afflictions.
Heedlessness is the failure to practice yoga; cultivation is the practice. "This is it"—consciousness pervaded by both of these is the doubt regarding the state.
For the non-abiding of the mind is called instability; indeed, on the path of yoga, it is a state devoid of faith and lacking in being.
That cognition which is inverted is designated as "delusion"; they know that the suffering born of ignorance within the minds of men is internal.
The suffering arising from the body is caused by past actions; that which is declared to be caused by divine forces includes lightning, weapons, poison, and so forth.
They declare that dejection born from the frustration of desires is *daurmanasya*; it is a wandering among various objects of sense and a restless longing for them.
When these obstacles have been stilled, for the yogi intent on yoga, divine portents arise as omens of spiritual accomplishment.
Inspiration, hearing, news, seeing, tasting, and feeling—these six are obstacles; they are the perfections of yoga when it is in a state of decline.
Intuition (*pratibhā*) is said to be the appearance of an object exactly as it is, even when that object is subtle, concealed, past, remote, or yet to come.
The hearing of all sounds without effort upon hearing, and the knowledge of all news regarding all embodied beings—this is the nature of *vārttā*.
"Vision" means the effortless perception of divine things; likewise, "taste" refers to the tasting of divine flavors.

In the same way, that which is known as sensation (*vedanā*) is the attainment of touch; and [the attainment] of divine odors and so forth extends to the lords of the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.
Jewels remain present and bestow many gifts; a voice, sweet and spontaneous, issues forth from his mouth in various ways.
All elixirs of longevity and likewise divine medicinal herbs attain success by bowing down to him; the celestial damsels bestow their favors upon him.
Even when only a single portion of the perfection of yoga has been perceived, the thought may arise regarding liberation: "Just as this has been seen by me, so too shall liberation come to be."
Leanness, stoutness, childhood, old age, and youth, as well as various other forms and the maintenance of the body by the four [elements].
The collection of fragrant scents is eternally devoid of any earthly portion; thus they describe the earthly state of the Piśācas as possessing eight qualities.
Dwelling in water and likewise emerging from the earth—being capable, he would wish to drink even the ocean himself without distress.
Wherever one desires it in this world, there indeed is the sight of water; even without jars and such, there is the holding of a mass of water in the hand.
Whatever object is even tasteless, at that very moment he desires to eat; it becomes flavorful and so forth, for the sustenance of the bodies of the three.
The flawlessness of his body, endowed with the qualities of the earth element—this is the wonderful, sixteen-fold sovereignty belonging to the water element.
The emanation of fire from the body and the avoidance of the fear of its heat; such is the power [of this yoga] that it could, if one so desired, burn this entire world without effort.
Or the establishing of fire in water, the holding of fire in the hand, and, when the world has been consumed by fire, the cooking of food and other things in the mouth just as before.
Through two [powers], there is the manifestation of bodies endowed with sovereign power; this twenty-fourfold [power] is designated as the Taijasa.
The swiftness of beings equal to that of the mind, entering within [the body] in an instant, and the effortless bearing of great burdens such as mountains.
He perceives heaviness and lightness, the holding of air in the hand, and even the shaking of the earth by the mere touch of his fingertips.
The wise know that the Māruta [element] is endowed with the formation of a body and with luminous enjoyments, possessing a sovereignty of thirty-two qualities.
The manifestation of a form devoid of shadow, the invisibility of the sense faculties, the power of moving through the sky at will, and the complete mastery over the objects of the senses.
Leaping into space, the entry of that [space] into one's own body, the solidification of space, and indeed the state of bodilessness.
Endowed with the sovereignty of the wind and possessing forty great qualities, it is called the sovereignty of Indra; that is declared to be the celestial garment (āmbara).
Obtaining whatever one desires, departing at will, the mastery over all things, and the vision of the meaning of all secrets.
He possesses mastery over emanations in accordance with his karma, a pleasing appearance, the vision of cyclic existence itself, and is endowed with enjoyments equal to those of Indra.
And this sovereignty over the lunar realm is mental and superior in quality; it includes the power to cut, strike, bind, and likewise to release.
It is the grasping of all beings who are subject to the power of saṃsāra, as well as the grace of all and likewise the victory over the time of death.
They declare that the sovereign power of Prajāpati is characterized by conceit; this great [power] is fifty-six times greater than the enjoyments of the lunar realm.
Creation by mere volition, as well as protection and withdrawal, the exercise of authority over all, and the impelling of the minds of living beings.
And there is the dissimilarity of everything, the distinct emanation of the world, the performance of good and evil deeds, and that which is joined with the states of Prajāpati.

They declare that the Brahma-sovereignty possesses sixty-four qualities; they know that the sovereignty pertaining to primordial matter (prākṛta), which is secondary, is superior even to this Buddhahood.
That is declared to be Vaiṣṇava; the stability of its world belongs to Him alone. That entire state cannot be described by others, even by Brahmā.
That state of Viṣṇu—which is both characterized by personal effort and subordinate, yet is the supreme status of Gaṇeśa—cannot be known even slightly by others.
All the accomplishments of consciousness, as well as all adventitious obstacles, must be suppressed with effort through supreme detachment.
For one whose mind is attached to impure appearances and qualities, the supreme sovereignty—free from fear and fulfilling all desires—will not be attained.
Therefore, for one who would renounce like a blade of grass the virtues and enjoyments of gods, asuras, and kings, there shall be the supreme perfection of yoga.
Alternatively, if he desires to show favor to the world, the sage may wander about; having enjoyed qualities and pleasures according to his wish, he shall attain liberation.
Now I shall describe the practice of yoga; listen with a concentrated mind. At an auspicious time and in an auspicious place, such as a sacred site of Śiva and the like, [one should practice].
In a secluded place, free from living beings, silent, devoid of disturbances, well-smeared with plaster, pleasant, and perfumed with incense, fragrance, and the like.
It was strewn with scattered flowers, variegated with canopies and the like, and provided with kusha grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, water, fruits, and roots.
Not near fire, nor near water, nor even upon a heap of dry leaves; nor in a place infested with gadflies and mosquitoes, nor crowded with snakes and wild beasts.

Nor [should one practice] in a place infested with wicked beasts, nor where there is danger, nor where it is crowded with evil people; nor in a cremation ground, at a shrine, on an anthill, in a dilapidated house, or at a crossroads.
Neither on the banks of rivers, streams, or oceans, nor even in the middle of a street; nor in a dilapidated garden, a cow-pen, or the like; nor in an undesirable place, nor in one that is censured.

Not during indigestion, nor when there is an eructation of sour fluid, nor when defiled by feces or urine, nor during vomiting or diarrhea, nor after eating too much, nor when one is overcome by fatigue.
One should not practice yoga while agitated by excessive anxiety, nor while excessively afflicted by hunger or thirst, nor when preoccupied with one's own heavy duties and the like.
Moderate in diet and recreation, moderate in his exertion in all activities, moderate in sleep and wakefulness, he is free from all weariness.
One should practice on seats that are soft, pleasant, spacious, level, and pure, such as the lotus posture (padmaka), the cross-legged posture (svastika), and others.
Having paid homage to his own gurus and having saluted those worthy of respect in due order, he should stand with neck, head, and chest erect, looking slightly downward.
With the head slightly raised, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth; and having placed the tongue motionless against the edge of the upper teeth.
Protecting the testicles with the two heels, and likewise the generative organ, he should effortlessly place his arms across the thighs.
Placing the back of the right hand upon the palm of the left, slowly raising the back, and bracing the chest forward.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the directions, he restrained the movement of his vital breaths and remained as motionless as a stone.
Having meditated upon Śiva together with Ambā within the abode of one's own body, one should worship him in the center of the pedestal of the heart-lotus through the sacrifice of meditation.

One should meditate [on the deity] at the base, at the tip of the nose, at the navel, at the throat, or at the two openings of the palate; or between the eyebrows, at the region of the gateway, on the forehead, or on the crown of the head.
Having fashioned, according to the rule, the supreme seat for Śiva and Śivā—therein, whether it be with its enclosures or indeed without them—
One should meditate on Śiva within a two-petalled, sixteen-spoked, or twelve-spoked lotus according to the rules, or within a ten-spoked, six-cornered, or square [mandala].
Between the two eyebrows is a two-petalled lotus, brilliant as lightning; situated at the midpoint of the brows, it extends sequentially to the right and left.
On the petals at the end of the colors, which are the color of lightning, are the sixteen vowels; these indeed constitute the petals of the sixteen-spoked [wheel].
Starting from the east and proceeding in order, these petals of the lotus extend from the root of the bulb; the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭa* are, in sequence, the petals.

That [syllable] should be meditated upon within the heart as a lotus with the color of the sun; for that which is white as cow's milk, the letters from *ḍa* to *pha* are said to be arranged in their proper sequence.
Of this lotus, there are six petals on its lower surface; their colors are like smokeless embers, and they are to be sounded with the letters ending in *la*.
In the golden-hued lotus of the mūlādhāra, the letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa* are situated upon its petals in their proper order.
Now, among these lotuses, wherever the mind finds delight, there one should contemplate the God and the Goddess with a steady intellect.
The size of a thumb, stainless, and blazing on all sides, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp, it is fully adorned by its own power.
It has the appearance of a line of lightning, or else the form of a star; it resembles the awn of a grain of wild rice, or indeed has the luster of a lotus fiber.
Even if the meditator desires the conquest of the principles beginning with earth—which is shaped like a kadamba bud and resembles a drop of frost—
One should meditate upon the gross form of each respective presiding deity of those principles (tattvas), beginning with Brahmā and Bhava and ending with Sadāśiva; these are the eight forms.
The gross forms of Śiva are determined in the Śiva-śāstra; those forms are declared by the lords of sages to be the Terrible (ghorā), the Mixed (miśrā), and the Tranquil (praśāntā).

Those skilled in contemplation should contemplate [these mantras] while free from desire for fruits; if even terrible things are contemplated in this way, they will bring about the destruction of evil diseases.

In a mixed [period] characterized by gentleness, [liberation occurs] neither immediately nor after a long time; in a particularly gentle [period], liberation is attained, and peace, wisdom, and success are achieved.
And here the supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished in due order; there is no doubt about this.
Upamanyu said: "Thinking that the accomplishments of all goals are instantly attained for those who remember the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, some yogins indeed meditate upon him."
Some perform gross meditation for the sake of stabilizing the mind; however, when the mind becomes steady through the gross, it becomes stable in the subtle.

When Śiva himself is meditated upon, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are directly accomplished; even when other forms are meditated upon, one should contemplate them as having the very form of Śiva.
One should observe the steadiness of the mind and meditate upon that object again and again; they say that meditation is first with an object and subsequently without an object.
In this regard, it is the opinion of the wise that there is no such thing as meditation without an object; for meditation is defined as a certain continuity of the intellect.
Therefore, the intellect functions here in its pure state, free from objects; hence, meditation with an object takes recourse in the rays of the rising sun.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no other meditation that has a subtle basis and is without an object; or rather, whatever meditation possesses an object, it necessarily relies upon a mental image (*sākāra*).
Meditation is considered to be the self-awareness of the formless Self, free from all objects; that very meditation is said to be both "seedless" (nirbīja) and "with seed" (sabīja).

Because it has as its basis that which is formless, and likewise because it has as its basis that which possesses form, therefore, having first established meditation with an object—that is, with seed—one should practice.
In the end, one should render it objectless and seedless for the sake of all accomplishments; through breath control (prāṇāyāma), the goddesses beginning with Śānti are attained in succession.
Peace, tranquility, radiance, and thereafter serenity; as well as the pacification of all calamities—this is designated as "Śānti."
The destruction of darkness, both internal and external, is celebrated as tranquility; that which is the illumination within and without is designated as radiance.
That state of well-being which is the Buddha is proclaimed as serene confidence; so too are all causes, both external and internal.
Through the clarity of the intellect, indeed, the meditator, the meditation, the object of meditation, and whatever the purpose of meditation may be, quickly become clear.
Having understood this fourfold [set], the meditator, endowed with knowledge and dispassion and always possessing an undistracted mind, should practice meditation.

One who is full of faith and possesses a serene mind is described by the virtuous as a meditator (*dhyātā*). The verbal root *dhyai* is remembered to mean "reflection," and thus it refers to the repeated contemplation of Śiva.
In the same way, even a brief practice of yoga may destroy evil, such as meditating with faith upon the Supreme Lord for even a single moment.
Meditation is defined as a state of mind that is undistracted; its support is this meditation, which consists of a continuous flow of cognition.
That which is called the object of meditation by the wise is Śiva himself along with Ambā; it is the conviction of liberation and the full sovereignty consisting of the powers such as aṇimā.
The direct purpose of the complete meditation on Śiva has been stated: because from such meditation one obtains happiness, liberation, and fearlessness.
Therefore, having renounced everything, a person should become devoted to meditation; for there is no knowledge without meditation, and there is no meditation for one who lacks yoga.
He who possesses both meditative absorption and knowledge has crossed the ocean of existence; that knowledge is serene, one-pointed, and free from all limiting adjuncts.
Success indeed comes to the yogi who is disciplined through the practice of yoga; for those whose sins have been entirely destroyed, the mind becomes intent upon knowledge and meditation.
For those whose intellects are struck down by evil, even the mere mention of that [truth] is very difficult to obtain; just as a great, blazing fire consumes both the dry and the moist.
In the same way, the fire of meditation burns away both auspicious and inauspicious karma in an instant; just as even a very small lamp can dispel a vast darkness.
Likewise, even a slight practice of yoga may destroy great sin, or even meditating upon the Supreme Lord with faith for a mere moment.
Whatever supreme good there may be, its end is not found; there is no sacred ford equal to meditation, and there is no austerity equal to meditation.
There is no sacrifice equal to meditation; therefore, one should practice meditation. Sacred fords are merely full of water, and deities are made of stone and clay.
Yogis do not attain [the supreme state] because they rely on the conviction of their own self; yet the subtle body of yogis becomes the perceptible divine form.

Just as for those who are unrefined, [the self] is imagined through gross means such as clay and wood; and just as in this world, those who move within the king's inner circle are his favorites, not those who move outside.

Likewise, those dear to Śambhu who are devoted to internal meditation are not ritualists; for as long as they remain externalized in this world, they do not enjoy the fruits [of their practice] to any great extent.
Just as it was seen in the palace of the king, so too here, those engaged in action who exert themselves for the sake of the yoga of knowledge may perish along the way.
By the mere effort of yoga, he shall go to the world of Rudra; having experienced happiness there, he will be born into a family of yogins.
Furthermore, having regained the yoga of knowledge, he transcends worldly existence; indeed, such is the goal attained by a man who even merely desires to know yoga.
One does not attain that state even through all the great sacrifices which is the fruit obtained by honoring ten million Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
The fruit that results from giving alms alone to a Śiva-yogin is equal to the fruit obtained through sacrifices, the agnihotra fire-ritual, gifts, pilgrimages, and burnt offerings.
By giving food to yogins, one obtains all that fruit; whereas those fools who utter slander against the Śiva-yogins [reap the opposite].
They fall into hells until the destruction of the earth, along with those who hear them; for if there were a listener, there would be a speaker of this slander against the yogins.

Therefore, according to the opinion of the great ones, the listener who is more wicked than the speaker should be punished; whereas those who constantly worship the Śava-yogins with devotion [are not].
They know infinite great enjoyments and the Yoga of Śaṅkara; therefore, Śiva-yogins should be worshipped by men who desire enjoyments.
Through shelter, food, drink, and the like, as well as beds and clothing, the dharma of yoga—possessing such essential substance—is indestructible by the hammers of evil.
The yogi should be known to be like a diamond grain; likewise, he is not smeared by the floods of affliction, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
In whatever land a sage constantly dwells, devoted to the yoga of Śiva, that land itself becomes purified; how much more so, then, is he himself purified?
Therefore, having abandoned all other duties, the wise person should practice Śiva-yoga for the sake of abandoning all suffering.

The yogi who has attained the fruit of perfected yoga, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, may either enjoy pleasures according to his wish and wander about, or remain here [in this state].
Alternatively, considering sensual pleasure to be trivial, one may abandon it through the yoga of dispassion and be liberated from karma by one's own will.
But that mortal who perceives his death to be near and observes many signs of impending death should devote himself to the practice of yoga and take refuge in a sacred field of Śiva.
If that man, while dwelling there, being firm-minded, should himself relinquish his life even without diseases or other such causes;
Having even performed a fast unto death, or offered one's limbs as oblation in the fire of Śiva, or by casting one's own body into the sacred waters (tīrthas) of Śiva through immersion;
Whoever should renounce their life according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva scriptures shall be liberated immediately; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Or if one, rendered helpless by disease and other afflictions, takes refuge in a sacred field of Śiva and dies there, he too is likewise liberated; of this there is no doubt.
For just as they desire death through fasting and other such means as the most excellent, since it is performed with a mind made firm by confidence in the scriptures.
Having killed one who delights in reviling Śiva, or having been afflicted by him himself, he who renounces his life-breaths—which are so difficult to give up—is not born again.
He who, being unable to kill one devoted to reviling Śiva, dies of his own accord, shall be instantly liberated along with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
There is no man standing on the path to liberation who is equal to him who would give up his life for the sake of Śiva, or even for the sake of a devotee of Śiva.
Therefore, his liberation from the cycle of existence will be even swifter, provided he relies on one or another of these means by some way or other.
If one who has duly attained the purification of the six paths should die, one should not perform funeral rites for him here on earth, as one would for ordinary fettered beings (paśus).
One should not undergo impurity on account of that [death], especially regarding sons and others; whether for the sake of the conduct of Śiva or indeed for the sake of the knowledge of Śiva.
One should either bury that body in the earth, or cremate it with pure fire, or cast it into auspicious waters, or else discard it like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Furthermore, if one desires to perform a rite intended for him as well, one should perform only an auspicious rite according to one's ability and satisfy the devotees.
A follower of Śiva shall inherit his wealth if his progeny is also Śaiva; if not, he should offer it to Śiva, for the offspring of a paśu (non-initiate) does not inherit.

Śrī Sūta said: Having thus explained to the sages—who had bowed before him—the yoga of knowledge obtained from Upamanyu by the Yādava who had conquered his pride, the self-exalted Vāyu suddenly vanished into the sky at evening.
Then, at the time of dawn, all the ascetics of Naimiṣa set out together to perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the conclusion of the sacrificial session (*satra*).
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the goddess Sarasvatī herself appeared; gracious and with sweet waters, that auspicious river began to flow.
Seeing the river Sarasvatī, the sages were delighted in their hearts; having completed the sacrificial session they had begun, they performed their ritual ablutions there.
Then, having satiated the gods and others with those auspicious waters and recollecting their former history, they departed toward Vārāṇasī.
Then, having seen the Bhāgīrathī falling from the foot of the Himavat toward the south, they bathed there and proceeded along its bank.
Then, having reached Vārāṇasī, they were all filled with joy; and having bathed in the north-flowing Gaṅgā, they remained there.
Having beheld and worshipped the Avimukteśvara Liṅga according to the prescribed rites, they prepared to depart and saw a radiant light in the sky.
Resembling ten million suns, it was divine light, most wonderful; by the manifestation of his own radiance, he pervaded the entire expanse of all directions.
Then hundreds of Pāśupata siddhas, sages whose bodies were covered in ashes, approached and became absorbed there in that splendor.
As those high-souled ascetics were thus dissolving away, that splendor suddenly vanished, which was like a marvel.
Having seen that great marvel, the great sages of Naimiṣa, not knowing what it was, went toward the forest of Brahmā.
Long before their departure, the Wind, the purifier of the world, granted the inhabitants of Naimiṣa his vision and engaged in conversation with those great-souled ones.

Then, for them, Śiva, together with Ambā and his attendants, restored their faith and understanding, as well as the completion of the long-standing sacrificial session of those performers of the rite.
Having informed Brahmā, the creator of the worlds and source of the Vedas, he was granted permission for his task and departed toward his own city.
Then Brahmā, having gone to his abode, [heard] Tumburu and Nārada disputing with one another over their singing out of mutual rivalry.
Maintaining equanimity amidst the aesthetic sentiments arising from the songs produced by them, he dwells in happiness, attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Then, being barred at the door by the gatekeepers precisely because there was no opportunity, the sages sat down on the side outside the Brahma-abode.
Then, having attained equality with Tumburu in singing, Nārada was authorized by the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin to share in his companionship.
Having abandoned mutual rivalry and attained supreme friendship, he was accompanied by him and surrounded by Apsarases and Gandharvas.
To play the lute for the god Nakulīśvara, the Lord, he emerged from his dwelling like the sun emerging from a cloud.
Seeing him, those members of the six clans bowed down to Nārada, the bull among sages, and with great reverence asked him about the opportunity for an audience with Śambhu.
"This is precisely the right moment; enter within," he said, as another person, intent on some other business, was possessed by the utmost haste.
Then those who were standing at the gate informed Brahmā; by his command, they entered the abode of the egg-born one, having formed themselves into a single mass.
Having entered from afar and prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff before the Lord, they were permitted by him to approach and stood around him.
Having inquired after their welfare while they were situated there, the Lotus-Seated One said: "I have learned your story from Vāyu himself, for he told it to us."
"What have you done afterwards now that the Wind-god has vanished?"—when the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, the sages [replied] after the ritual bath (avabhṛtha).
The journey to the banks of the Gaṅgā, the pilgrimage toward Vārāṇasī, and the beholding there of the Liṅgas installed by the lords of the gods.
The worship of the Liṅga of Avimukteśvara even once, and the vision of that great mass of splendor in the sky.
Therein lies the dissolution of the sages and the cessation of their splendor; even that which was contemplated by the self-realized ones is known in its true nature.
Having bowed down to him again and again, they told him everything in full detail; and having heard what was related by the sages, Viśvakarman, who has four faces, [spoke].
Shaking his head slightly, he spoke with a profound voice: "Your supreme success in the world beyond is drawing near."
"The Lord has been propitiated by you for a long time through this long sacrificial session; he has become inclined toward showing grace"—thus was the actual fact indicated.
That radiant object which was seen by you in the sky over Vārāṇasī is the supreme, manifest splendor of Maheśvara, known as the Liṅga.

There, the sages who were absorbed in meditation and devoted to the Śrauta Pāśupata vows became liberated; established in their own true nature, these lifelong practitioners had their sins burnt away.
May liberation be attained by you all through this [teaching] without delay; and may this very purpose be indicated by the splendor seen by you.
In this matter, this very time has come to you of its own accord through destiny; set forth for the southern peak of Meru, which is frequented by the gods.
There dwells my son Sanatkumāra, the supreme sage, awaiting the arrival of Nandin, the manifest Lord of Beings.
In ancient times, even Sanatkumāra, though he had beheld the Supreme Lord, was corrupted by a lack of humility because of his ignorance, considering himself the foremost of all masters of yoga.
Because he failed to perform such duties as rising to greet him and was utterly fearless, Nandin, provoked by that offense, turned him into a great camel.
Then, after a long time, while grieving for his sake, I worshipped the God and the Goddess, and indeed entreated Nandin.
By some effort, his state of being a camel was somehow averted; for he was restored to his former childhood as Sanatkumāra.
Then Mahādeva, as if smiling, said to the Lord of the Gaṇas: "Indeed, having shown contempt for me alone, that sage acted with such arrogance."
Therefore, O sinless one, you yourself must explain my true nature to him; for he, though the first-born son of Brahmā, regards me as if I were a fool.
I myself shall instruct Datta, who is the promoter of my knowledge; he will also perform for you the consecration as the overseer of the Dharma.
Thus addressed, he—the leader of the hosts of all beings—received with his head at dawn that command of his superior.
Likewise, Sanatkumāra also, by my command, performs difficult penance on Mount Meru for the sake of gaining the favor of this Gaṇa.
"You must see him before your meeting with Gaṇeśa; for the sake of his grace, Nandin will arrive there shortly."
Having thus swiftly commanded them, the sages were sent by Viśvayogin and went to Kumāraśikhara on the southern side of Meru.
Sūta said: There is a lake named Skandasaras, resembling the ocean, with water that is as sweet as nectar, cool, clear, deep, and light.
It was joined together on all sides by heaps of crystal stones, and its entire expanse of directions was covered with blossoming flowers of every season.
With moss, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white water-lilies resembling stars, and with waves like clouds, it was like the sky descended to the earth.
With landing places made of blue stone that were easy to descend from and ascend to, and with beautiful flight-of-stairs paths, it shone forth toward the faces of the eight directions.
There, those who had descended and those who had ascended once again were for the most part bathed, wearing white sacred threads and white loincloths or bark garments.
[He was surrounded] by young ascetics with matted locks, shaven heads, and those adorned with the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra), their faces smiling with an expression of dispassionate detachment.
With jars, lotus-leaf cups, auspicious water-pots, ascetic's bowls, and other such vessels like *karaka*s.
For his own sake, for the sake of others, and especially for the sake of the deities, he constantly brought water and gathered flowers.
By sages who were observant of proper conduct, who stood upon rocks within the water out of fear of touching those of low birth, and whose limbs were grey with applied ashes;

With offerings submerged here and there in the water, with remaining oblations resting upon stones, along with sesame seeds mixed with unbroken rice, flowers, and discarded *darbha* blades and purifiers;
Having performed the libation for the ancestors, which begins with the gods and ends with the sages, one should inform the learned twice-born who have come for the daily bath.

In various places, they performed worship and other rites upon sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), preceded by the offering of water for the sun (*saurārghya*), accompanied by the scents of numerous offerings of oblations and flowers.
In some places, herds of elephants were sinking and emerging as they wandered; and in others, deer, wild beasts, and horses had arrived, driven by thirst.
In some places, excellent peacocks and elephants had emerged from the yellow mud; in other places, it was illuminated by bulls and rival bulls that had struck against the banks.
In some places with the excellent cries of water-fowls, in some with the warbling of cranes, in some with the calls of ruddy geese, and in some with the songs of bees;
It seemed as if it were repeatedly speaking out of affection to those various living beings who subsisted on the trees of its own abundance by means of bathing, drinking, and other activities.
With the warbling of flocks of cuckoos perched upon the treetops along the banks, it seemed as if the forest were calling out day and night to all those afflicted by the heat.
On the northern shore of that lake, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), upon an altar made of diamond-stone and a soft deerskin;
Sanatkumāra was seated there, eternally maintaining the form of a child, having recently emerged from a state of unwavering self-absorption in samādhi.
The residents of Naimiṣa beheld him being worshipped by sages and honored even by the lords of yogis; they bowed down and stood before him in attendance.
Just as they explained the reason for the welcome to him who had questioned them, a tumultuous sound of celestial drums was heard in the sky.
At that very moment, he beheld a celestial chariot radiant as the sun, surrounded on all sides by innumerable lords of the Gaṇas.
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases, surrounded by the daughters of Rudra, resounded with the sounds of mṛdaṅga and muraja drums, and filled with the melodies of flutes and lutes.
It was enriched with canopies of variegated jewels, adorned with strings of pearls, and frequented by sages, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, cāraṇas, and kinnaras.
It was surrounded by those dancing, singing, and playing instruments, with a staff made of coral wood bearing the emblem of a heroic bull.
Having performed the honor of decorating the gateway with a banner for reasons of respect, [he placed it] in the middle of that celestial chariot, between a pair of chowries.
Beneath a pure parasol with a jeweled handle like the moon, he was seated upon a divine lion-throne together with the goddess Suyashā.
By its splendor, by its form, and by its three eyes, it was a sign that made the Lord recognizable as the abode of the Abhikṛtis.
It was as if the inviolable command of the Creator of the world had arrived, and like the very grace of Śambhu standing manifest before one’s eyes.
To Śilāda’s son himself, who bears the illustrious and excellent trident as his weapon, the presiding lord of Viśveśvara’s attendants, like another Viśveśvara;
Capable of both restraint and grace even toward the creators of the universe, he has four arms, noble limbs, and is adorned with the crescent moon.
Adorned with a serpent around his neck and the moon upon his crown, he was like sovereignty incarnate and like power endowed with action.
Seeing him as if he were the very perfection of Nirvana, as if he were the Omniscient One himself, the son of Brahmā, with a joyful countenance, was filled with delight along with the sages.
Rising up with palms joined in reverence, he stood there as if offering himself to him; then, in that interval, that celestial chariot descended to the earth.
Having prostrated like a staff before the god and praised the sage, they addressed him: "These members of the six families have been engaged in a long sacrificial session at Naimiṣa."
Commanded by Brahmā and having come previously out of longing, they heard the words of the son of Brahmā; then Nandin, by a mere glance, instantly severed their bonds.

Having bestowed the Śaiva dharma and the yoga of knowledge pertaining to Īśvara, he returned once more to the presence of the God; and all of that was told by Sanatkumāra to my own direct guru, Vyāsa.

This was spoken by the honored Vyāsa to me, and it has been related by me to you in brief. This jewel of a Purāṇa concerning the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) must not be told to those who do not know the Vedas.

Indeed, that which is given out of delusion to a disciple who is not devoted or to atheists leads to hell; yet by those who have followed the path through service, it has been given, received, recited, or heard.

To them, it grants happiness, the gateway to the Dharma, the threefold aims of life, and ultimately, Nirvana with certainty; through the application of the ancient path, you have rendered mutual assistance to one another and to me.

"Therefore, having attained my desire, I shall depart; may all prosperity ever attend us. When the Sūta had thus pronounced his blessing and departed, the sages of virtuous conduct, as the great ritual performance was concluded, [proceeded with their duties].

In this Kali age, when the world is being defiled by sense-objects, they took up residence in the vicinity of Vārāṇasī; and furthermore, with the desire for total liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), they performed the Pāśupata vow in its entirety.

Having mastered all forms of knowledge and meditative absorption, those blameless ones attained supreme liberation. Vyāsa said: Thus indeed this Śiva Purāṇa, which is beneficial, has been completed with reverence.
It should indeed be recited with diligence and likewise listened to; it must not be spoken to an atheist, nor to one lacking faith, nor to a rogue.
For one who is not a devotee of Maheśa, as well as for one who merely displays the banner of dharma—upon hearing this even once, their sin shall indeed be reduced to ashes.

The non-devotee attains devotion, and the devotee becomes endowed with the abundance of devotion; furthermore, through hearing [the teaching], there arises true devotion, and from that hearing, liberation shall follow.
Therefore, those seeking liberation must indeed listen to this again and again; with a virtuous mind, one should perform a fivefold recitation of this Purāṇa.
Aiming for the supreme fruit, one attains it without a doubt; so too did the kings of old, as well as the most excellent Brahmins and Vaiśyas.
By repeating this seven times, they obtained the vision of Śiva; moreover, any human being who, devoted to faith, shall hear this [will likewise attain it].
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, he shall attain liberation at the end; for this Śiva Purāṇa is indeed supremely dear to Śiva.
This [work], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is equal to Brahman and increases devotion; it is always [beneficial] for both the speaker and the listener of this Śiva Purāṇa.
May that Śaṅkara bring about the welfare of the son of Ambā, together with his attendants.
